subject: surgery
title: Q1.1: Malignant Melanoma (Classification, Clinical Features, Prognostic Factors, Staging & Management)
text:
(Covers KU 24, 21, 18; Short Essay & Short Answers)

Definition: A malignant tumour of melanocytes (cells of neural crest origin located in the basal epidermis). It can arise in skin, mucosa, retina, and leptomeninges.

Epidemiology & Risk Factors:

Accounts for <5% of skin malignancies but causes >75% of skin cancer-related deaths. Commonest cancer in young adults (20–39 years).

Risk Factors: Ultraviolet radiation (UVR – especially intense intermittent “flash-fry” exposure), fair skin/red hair, >30 sun-acquired naevi, ≥5 severe sunburns before age 16, family history, genetic syndromes (Xeroderma pigmentosum, FAMMM syndrome), Giant Congenital Pigmented Naevus (GCPN), and immunosuppression (increases risk 20–30-fold).

Macroscopic Features Suggestive of Malignant Change in Naevi (ABCDE / Summary Box 45.5):

Asymmetry / Change in shape.

Border irregularity.

Colour variation.

Diameter (>6 mm) / Change in size.

Elevation/Thickness (nodularity or ulceration), Satellite lesions, Tingling/itching/serosanguineous discharge (late signs).

Macroscopic Classification (Clinical Variants):

Superficial Spreading Melanoma (SSM - 70%): Most common; usually arises in a pre-existing naevus after years of slow radial change followed by rapid vertical growth (nodularity).

Nodular Melanoma (NM - 15%): Aggressive; arises de novo (more common in middle-aged men on trunk/head/neck). Blue/black papules; lacks a radial growth phase (vertical growth from the outset); up to 5% are amelanotic.

Lentigo Maligna Melanoma (LMM - 5–10%): Arises from Hutchinson’s melanotic freckle (melanoma in situ) on sun-damaged face/neck/hands of elderly patients (women > men). Slowest to enter vertical growth phase.

Acral Lentiginous Melanoma (ALM - 2–8% in whites, 35–60% in Asian/African/Hispanic populations): Affects glabrous skin of palms, soles, and nail beds (subungual).

Hutchinson’s Sign: Pigmentation of the proximal/lateral nail fold widening into a triangular macule with nail dystrophy (diagnostic of subungual melanoma).

Miscellaneous: Amelanotic melanoma (flesh-coloured, poor prognosis due to late diagnosis) and Desmoplastic melanoma (head/neck, propensity for perineural infiltration and local recurrence).

Microscopic Growth Phases:

Horizontal (Radial) Growth Phase: Atypical melanocytes spread laterally along the dermoepidermal junction.

Vertical Growth Phase: Invasion deep into the dermis; confers metastatic potential.

Staging & Prognostic Determinants:

1. Breslow Thickness (Most important prognostic indicator in Stage I/Node-negative disease): Measured vertically with an ocular micrometer to the nearest 0.1 mm from the top of the stratum granulosum to the deepest point of tumour invasion.

2. Clark’s Levels of Invasion (Historical/Anatomical):

Level I: Confined to epidermis (in situ).

Level II: Invasion into papillary dermis.

Level III: Filling papillary dermis up to the papillary–reticular dermal interface.

Level IV: Invasion into reticular dermis.

Level V: Invasion into subcutaneous fat.

3. Other Prognostic Factors: Regional lymph node metastasis (single most important overall prognostic index; once clinically involved, 70–85% have occult distant metastases), high mitotic index, ulceration, extranodal extension, and elevated serum LDH.

AJCC 8th Edition T-Staging: Tis (in situ), T1 (≤ 1.0 mm; T1a <0.8 mm without ulceration), T2 (1.01–2.0 mm), T3 (2.01–4.0 mm), T4 (>4.0 mm).

Management:

1. Diagnosis (Biopsy): Full-thickness excision biopsy with a 2–3 mm clinical margin of skin and a cuff of subdermal fat. (Incision biopsy is only done for very large facial/acral lesions where complete excision is disfiguring).

2. Wide Local Excision (WLE) Margins (Definitive Local Control):

In situ (Tis): 5 mm margin.

Breslow <1 mm (T1): 1 cm margin.

Breslow >1 mm (T2–T4): 2 cm margin.

3. Management of Regional Lymph Nodes:

Clinically Node-Negative (cN0): Offer Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) for tumours T2a (>1.0 mm) and above (or >0.8 mm with ulceration).

Clinically Node-Positive or Positive SLNB: Therapeutic/Completion regional lymphadenectomy.

4. Adjuvant & Systemic Therapy (Stage III/IV):

Targeted Therapy: BRAF V600 inhibitors (Dabrafenib, Vemurafenib) combined with MEK inhibitor (Trametinib) for the 50% of melanomas harbouring BRAF mutations.

Immunotherapy (Checkpoint Inhibitors): Anti-CTLA-4 (Ipilimumab) and Anti-PD-1 (Nivolumab, Pembrolizumab).

subject: surgery
title: Q1.2: Basal Cell Carcinoma (Rodent Ulcer) & Mohs Micrographic Surgery
text:
(Covers KU 24, 20, 18, 17, 15)

Definition: A slow-growing, locally invasive malignant tumour of pluripotential epithelial cells arising from the basal layer of the epidermis and outer root sheath of hair follicles (affects pilosebaceous skin; never occurs on palms/soles).

Epidemiology & Risk Factors:

Commonest skin malignancy in white-skinned populations (outnumbers SCC by 4:1); 95% occur between ages 40 and 80 years; males > females.

Predisposing Factors: UVR (proportional to initial carcinogen dose), arsenic exposure, coal tar, aromatic hydrocarbons, ionising radiation, immunosuppression, and genetic syndromes (Gorlin’s syndrome [PTCH1 gene mutation on Chr 9q], Xeroderma pigmentosum).

Macroscopic Types:

Localised (90% are nodular/nodulocystic):

Nodular / Nodulocystic: Translucent, pearly nodule with surface telangiectasia; central necrosis produces a classic “Rodent Ulcer” with a rolled, beaded edge. 

Cystic: Large cystic spaces.

Pigmented: Contains melanin; mimics malignant melanoma.

Naevoid.

Generalised:

Superficial (Multifocal / Superficial spreading): Erythematous scaly plaques, often on the trunk.

Infiltrative (Morphoeic, Ice-pick, Cicatrising): Synthesises type IV collagenase, leading to rapid, ill-defined subclinical spread with scar-like plaques.

Microscopic Features: Nests of ovoid basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm and a characteristic peripheral “palisading” single layer of columnar nuclei. Only the outer layer actively divides.

Prognostic Stratification:

High-Risk BCC: Size >2 cm, high-risk embryonic fusion planes (“H-zone” of face: periorbital, nose, ear – risk of cranial invasion), recurrent tumours, immunosuppression, or morphoeic/infiltrative/micronodular histology.

Metastasis is exceedingly rare (<0.1%).

Management:

1. Surgical Excision: Excision under loupe magnification with a 4 mm peripheral margin for well-defined low-risk lesions (2–15 mm depending on macroscopic variant) and reconstruction via primary closure, skin graft, or local flaps.

2. Mohs Micrographic Surgery (MMS):

Principle: Serial horizontal/tangential excision of skin cancer with immediate 100% microscopic mapping of frozen-section margins by a dermatological surgeon before defect reconstruction.

Indications: Morphoeic/ill-defined BCCs, recurrent tumours, and lesions in tissue-sparing sites (eyelids, nasal tip, periauricular).

3. Non-Surgical Modalities:

Radiotherapy: Reserved for elderly/infirm patients (similar recurrence rates to surgery, but risks radiation-induced malignancy 10–20 years later).

Topical Therapy: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) or Imiquimod (immune response modifier) for biopsy-proven superficial BCCs.

Cryotherapy / Curettage & Cautery: For small, low-risk superficial lesions.

subject: surgery
title: Q1.3: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) & Marjolin’s Ulcer
text:
(Covers KU 23, 22, 16, RGU, TU)

Definition: A malignant tumour of keratinising cells of the epidermis (stratum spinosum/basalis) or its appendages; expresses cytokeratins 1 and 10.

Etiology & Premalignant Precursors:

Risk Factors: Cumulative chronic UVR exposure, ionising radiation, chemical carcinogens (arsenic, tar, soot), HPV subtypes 5 and 16, smoking (doubles risk), immunosuppression (renal transplant recipients), and chronic inflammation.

Premalignant / Precursor Lesions:

Actinic (Solar) Keratosis: Sun-damaged dyskeratotic scaly plaques; up to 20% progress to SCC.

Cutaneous Horn: Hyperkeratotic projection where height > base diameter (10% harbour underlying SCC at the base).

Keratoacanthoma: Rapidly growing dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin plug; now classified as a well-differentiated, self-healing variant of SCC (excision recommended).

Bowen’s Disease (SCC in situ): Slowly enlarging erythematous, crusted plaque (full-thickness epidermal atypia). On the glans penis, it is termed Erythroplasia of Queyrat. Treated with topical 5-FU, Imiquimod, or 4 mm surgical excision.

Pathology:

Macroscopic: Verrucous, papillomatous, or ulcerated lesion with a characteristic heaped-up, everted edge and indurated base.

Microscopic: Irregular masses of atypical squamous cells invading the dermis with keratin pearls (epithelial nests). Graded by Broders’ Histological Grading based on the proportion of undifferentiated cells (Grade I: <25%, Grade II: 25–50%, Grade III: 50–75%, Grade IV: >75% undifferentiated).

Prognostic Factors (High-Risk SCC): Depth >2 mm (>6 mm has 15% metastasis rate), surface diameter >2 cm, high Broders’ grade, perineural or lymphovascular invasion, anatomical site (lips, ears, extremities), immunosuppression, and Marjolin’s ulcers. Overall metastasis rate is 2% (low-risk) to 30% (high-risk).

Management:

Primary Tumour: Surgical excision under loupe magnification:

Tumour <2 cm: 4 mm clearance margin.

Tumour >2 cm (or high-risk): 1 cm clearance margin (or Mohs micrographic surgery).

Regional Nodes: Ultrasound/FNAC of palpable nodes; therapeutic lymph node dissection (with adjuvant radiotherapy if multiple nodes or extracapsular spread).

Marjolin’s Ulcer (Short Note):

Definition: A well-differentiated but locally aggressive squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic unstable scar, burn wound, chronic venous ulcer, or osteomyelitis sinus tract.

Unique Features:

Painless: Devoid of nerve fibrils due to surrounding dense scar fibrosis.

Slow-growing & Initially Lymph-node negative: Scar fibrosis obliterates local lymphatic channels; however, once it breaches the scar bed into normal tissue, it metastasises rapidly with a poor prognosis.

Clinical Suspicion: Foul-smelling discharge, raised everted edge, or fungating growth appearing in a longstanding scar/ulcer.

Management: Wedge biopsy from the edge to confirm diagnosis → Wide local excision with a 1–2 cm margin + skin grafting/flap cover (or amputation if underlying bone is invaded).

subject: surgery
title: Q1.4: Classification of Ulcers
text:
(Covers KU 19)

Definition: A discontinuity of an epithelial surface characterised by progressive destruction of surface epithelium and a granulating base.

1. Clinical Classification (Based on Progression):

Spreading Ulcer: Surrounding skin is inflamed and oedematous; floor is covered with profuse offensive slough without healthy granulation tissue; draining lymph nodes are enlarged and tender.

Healing Ulcer: Surrounding inflammation has subsided; floor has healthy pink/red granular tissue with serous discharge; edge shows three classic zones (inner red zone of vascular granulation, middle bluish zone of growing epithelium, outer white zone of hyperkeratosis).

Callous (Chronic/Stationary) Ulcer: Floor contains pale, avascular granulation tissue; base and edge are heavily indurated and fibrosed; shows no tendency towards healing (e.g., chronic venous ulcer).

2. Etiological Classification (Bailey & Love):

Non-Specific Ulcers:

Traumatic: Mechanical (dental ulcer of tongue), physical (electrical/radiation), or chemical.

Venous: Gravitational ulcer in the gaiter area.

Arterial (Ischaemic): Atherosclerosis, Buerger’s disease.

Neuropathic (Trophic/Perforating): Diabetic neuropathy, tabes dorsalis, leprosy, spina bifida.

Metabolic & Tropical: Diabetes mellitus, tropical phagedenic ulcer, pyoderma gangrenosum, cryoglobulinaemia.

Specific Infective Ulcers: Tuberculosis, syphilis (hard chancre, gummatous ulcer), actinomycosis, Meleney’s ulcer.

Malignant Ulcers: Squamous cell carcinoma, Basal cell carcinoma (Rodent ulcer), Malignant melanoma, Marjolin’s ulcer.

3. Morphological Classification Based on Edges: 

Sloping (Shelving) Edge: Healing non-specific or venous ulcers.

Punched-Out Edge: Deep vertical edge seen in tertiary syphilitic gumma, trophic/neuropathic ulcers, and ischaemic ulcers.

Undermined Edge: Tuberculous ulcer (infection spreads faster in subcutaneous fat than in overlying skin) and Pyoderma gangrenosum (purple undermined edge).

Rolled (Beaded) Edge: Basal cell carcinoma (Rodent ulcer).

Everted (Heaped-Up) Edge: Squamous cell carcinoma / adenocarcinoma (rapidly proliferating malignant cells spill over normal skin).

4. Wagner’s Classification (Diabetic Foot Ulcers):

Grade 0: Pre-ulcerative lesion / high-risk foot with bony deformity.

Grade 1: Superficial ulcer involving full skin thickness only.

Grade 2: Deep ulcer penetrating to ligaments, tendons, or joint capsule (no abscess/osteomyelitis).

Grade 3: Deep ulcer with abscess, osteomyelitis, or joint sepsis.

Grade 4: Localised gangrene of forefoot or heel.

Grade 5: Extensive gangrene of the entire foot.

subject: surgery
title: Q1.5: High-Yield Short Answers in Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue
text:
1. Epidermal Cyst (Sebaceous Cyst) [KU 22, 21, 20, 18, 15]:

Pathology: Retention cyst lined by true stratified squamous epithelium derived from the hair follicle infundibulum (or traumatic implantation) containing cheesy, foul-smelling keratinaceous material (not sebum). Trichilemmal (pilar) cysts (90% on scalp, 70% multiple) lack a punctum and derive from the external root sheath.

Clinical Features: Smooth, firm, spherical swelling fixed to the skin with a characteristic central bluish/black punctum (blocked duct opening); freely mobile over deeper planes; occurs anywhere except palms and soles (common on scalp, face, scrotum).

Complications: Infection/abscess formation, ulceration (Cock’s peculiar tumour –granulating infected scalp cyst mimicking SCC), Sebaceous horn, Calcification. Associated with Gardner’s syndrome (FAP).

Treatment: Complete surgical excision of the cyst along with its entire capsule/wall and an elliptical wedge of skin containing the punctum. If infected/abscessed: Initial incision and drainage (or avulsion) followed by formal excision once inflammation subsides.

2. Carbuncle [KU 24, 18]:

Definition: An infective gangrene of the skin and subcutaneous tissue caused by Staphylococcus aureus, consisting of multiple communicating furuncles (boils) draining through multiple sieve-like openings on the skin.

Clinical Features: Predominantly affects middle-aged/elderly diabetics or immunocompromised patients. Commonest site is the nape of the neck and back (hairy, thick skin with poor vascularity). Starts as a painful, indurated, dusky-red swelling; softens centrally into a honeycombed slough (“cribriform appearance”) discharging pus; heals leaving a deep crateriform ulcer.

Treatment: Control diabetes mellitus; parenteral anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (Flucloxacillin/Co-amoxiclav); surgical cruciate incision and debridement of all necrotic slough and loculi, followed by daily packing and secondary healing or split-skin grafting.

3. Keloid vs Hypertrophic Scar [KU 24, 21, RGU]:

[[TABLE:surgery-tbl-001]]

4. Types of Haemangioma & Vascular Malformations [KU 17]:

Classified biologically (Mulliken & Glowacki) into Vascular Tumours (Haemangiomas) (endothelial hyperplasia) and Vascular Malformations (normal endothelial turnover; structural errors).

Haemangiomas: Present at or shortly after birth (female:male = 3:1); rapid proliferation in the first year followed by slow involution (“70% resolve by age 7”).

Capillary Haemangioma (Strawberry Naevus): Bright red, raised, compressible lesion on head/neck.

Cavernous / Compound Haemangioma: Deeper bluish-red spongy swelling. Large lesions can trap platelets causing consumptive thrombocytopenia (Kasabach–Merritt Syndrome).

Vascular Malformations: Present at birth; grow proportionately with the child; never involute.

Capillary Malformation: Salmon patch (nape of neck; fades by 1 year) and Port-Wine Stain (purple macule in V1/V2 trigeminal dermatomes; associated with Sturge–Weber syndrome; treated with Pulsed-Dye Laser).

Venous / Arteriovenous (High-flow vs Low-flow) / Lymphatic Malformations (Cystic hygroma).

subject: surgery
title: Q2.1: Pathophysiology, Assessment, Classification & Management of Major Thermal Burns
text:
(Covers KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 20, 17, 16, 15 — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. Pathophysiology of Burn Injury:

Local Response (Jackson’s Three Concentric Zones):

Zone of Coagulation: Central area of irreversible coagulative necrosis at the point of maximum heat transfer.

Zone of Stasis: Surrounding area of decreased tissue perfusion; potentially salvageable with prompt cooling and fluid resuscitation, otherwise progresses to necrosis.

Zone of Hyperaemia: Outer zone of vasodilation due to inflammatory mediators; recovers fully.

Systemic Inflammatory & Circulatory Shock Response (Summary Box 46.6):

Thermal protein alteration and pain fibres trigger complement activation, neuropeptide release, and Hageman factor (Factor XII) activation (driving arachidonic acid, thrombin, and kallikrein cascades).

Massive systemic capillary permeability occurs in burns >15% TBSA in adults (>10% in children), causing shift of water, electrolytes, and plasma proteins into the interstitial space → hypovolaemic burn shock and generalized oedema.

Respiratory / Inhalational Injury (Summary Box 46.4 & 46.5):

Warning Signs: History of fire in an enclosed space, burns to face/neck, singed nasal vibrissae, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness of voice, stridor.

Three Components:

Supraglottic Upper Airway Thermal Injury: Inhaled hot gases cause progressive laryngeal oedema within 4–24 hours → life-threatening airway obstruction.

Subglottic Lower Airway Injury (Chemical Pneumonitis): Inhaled smoke particles and steam cause sloughing of respiratory epithelium, fibrin casts, and ARDS (peaks at 24 hours to 5 days).

Metabolic Poisoning: Carbon monoxide (CO) binds haemoglobin with 250 times the affinity of oxygen (forming carboxyhaemoglobin) and inhibits cytochrome oxidase; Hydrogen cyanide (from burning plastics/polymers) binds ferric iron (Fe³⁺) in mitochondrial cytochrome a_3.

Gastrointestinal, Immune & Metabolic Effects:

Splanchnic vasoconstriction → mucosal ischaemia (Curling’s ulcer), ileus, bacterial translocation, and abdominal compartment syndrome.

Suppression of cell-mediated immunity and hypermetabolic catabolic drive.

2. Assessment of Area (TBSA) & Classification of Burn Depth:

Assessment of Percentage Total Body Surface Area (% TBSA): (Note: Simple erythema is excluded).

Palmar Surface Method: Patient’s palm and fingers (distal wrist crease to fingertips) = ~1% TBSA (useful for small/patchy burns <10%).

Wallace’s Rule of Nines (Adults):

Head & Neck: 9%.

Each Upper Limb: 9% (× 2 = 18%).

Anterior Torso (Chest 9% + Abdomen 9%): 18%.

Posterior Torso & Buttocks: 18%.

Each Lower Limb: 18% (× 2 = 36%).

Perineum / Genitalia: 1%.

(Clinical Scenario Calculation [KU 24 / TU]: Head & neck [9%] + Both upper limbs [18%] + Front & back of chest [9% + 9% = 18%] = 45% TBSA; if abdomen [9%] is also included = 54% TBSA).

Modified Lund and Browder Chart: Most accurate method, mandatory in children (at birth: head is 18% and each lower limb is 13.5%; for each year up to age 10, subtract 1% from the head and add 0.5% to each leg). 

Classification by Depth of Burn: 

[[TABLE:surgery-tbl-002]]

3. Management of a Major Burn Patient (e.g., 60% TBSA Burn):

A. Prehospital Care: Ensure rescuer safety → Stop the burning process (“Stop, Drop, and Roll”) → Cool the burn with running tepid tap water (15°C for 20 minutes, effective up to 1 hour post-burn; avoid ice/hypothermia) → Administer high-flow oxygen → Cover with clean cling-film → Elevate limbs.

B. Primary Survey (ATLS ABCDEF Protocol):

A – Airway with Cervical Spine Control: Inspect for signs of inhalational injury. Early elective endotracheal intubation is mandatory for suspected airway burns before laryngeal oedema obliterates the airway (within 4–24 hours).

B – Breathing & Ventilation:

100% high-flow humidified oxygen (reduces half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin from 4 hours to 40 minutes). If cyanide toxicity is suspected, give intravenous Hydroxocobalamin (Vitamin B12).

Nebulised heparin, N-acetylcysteine (mucolytic), and salbutamol (albuterol) for smoke inhalation.

Chest Escharotomy if circumferential full-thickness torso eschar restricts chest excursion.

C – Circulation: Insert two wide-bore (14G/16G) IV cannulae (through unburned skin if possible), send baseline bloods (FBC, U&E, clotting, lactate, ABG, COHb, group & crossmatch), and insert a Foley urinary catheter to monitor hourly urine output.

D – Disability: Assess GCS (rule out hypoxia, CO poisoning, or head trauma).

E – Exposure & Environmental Control: Remove all jewellery/clothing, assess TBSA, and prevent hypothermia (warmed IV fluids, Bair Hugger, warm room >28°C).

F – Fluid Resuscitation (Indicated for >15% TBSA in adults; >10% TBSA in children):

Modified Parkland Formula (Crystalloid): Total Fluid in first 24 hours = 4 mL × Body Weight (kg) × % TBSA Burned (Using Ringer’s Lactate / Hartmann’s solution).

Rate of Administration: Give 50% in the first 8 hours (calculated from the time of the burn injury, not arrival) and the remaining 50% over the next 16 hours.

Example Calculation (60% burn in a 60 kg patient): 4 × 60 × 60 = 14,400 mL (7,200 mL in first 8 hours; 7,200 mL over next 16 hours).

Children: Add maintenance dextrose-saline (100 mL/kg for first 10 kg + 50 mL/kg for next 10 kg + 20 mL/kg for each kg >20 kg).

Muir and Barclay Formula (Colloid alternative after 12h): (0.5 × Weight (kg) × % TBSA/1) = 1 ration of Human Albumin Solution given in 6 rations over 36 hours (three 4-hourly, two 6-hourly, one 12-hourly).

Monitoring Resuscitation: Formulae are only a starting guide; titrate fluids dynamically to maintain Urine Output of 0.5–1.0 mL/kg/hour in adults (1–2 mL/kg/hour in children).

C. Supportive Systemic Care:

Analgesia: Titrated intravenous morphine (avoid IM route due to unpredictable absorption in shock).

Nutrition: For burns ≥ 20% TBSA, insert a nasogastric or nasojejunal tube and start enteral feeding within 6 hours to prevent gut mucosal atrophy and bacterial translocation.

Ulcer & DVT Prophylaxis: Proton pump inhibitors (for Curling’s ulcer), LMWH, and tetanus prophylaxis.

D. Wound & Surgical Management:

1. Emergency Escharotomy: 

Indication: Circumferential full-thickness burns of the limbs (causing tourniquet-like ischaemia) or chest wall (causing mechanical respiratory restriction).

Technique: Incise full thickness of burned eschar into subcutaneous fat using cutting diathermy:

Chest: Longitudinal incisions along anterior axillary lines joined by transverse incisions below the clavicles and across the costal margin/xiphisternum.

Upper Limb: Mid-axial incisions (passing anterior to the medial epicondyle at the elbow to protect the ulnar nerve).

Lower Limb: Mid-axial incisions (passing posterior to the medial malleolus to spare the long saphenous vein, and anterior to the fibular head to spare the common peroneal nerve).

2. Group A (Superficial Partial-Thickness) Wound Care: Cleanse, debride ruptured blisters, and apply biological/biosynthetic dressings (Biobrane), hydrocolloids (Duoderm), silicone sheets (Mepitel), or nanocrystalline silver dressings (Acticoat).

3. Group B (Deep Partial-Thickness & Full-Thickness) Excision & Grafting:

Early Tangential Excision (Watson’s knife / Humby knife): Shave necrotic burn layers sequentially until brisk punctate dermal/fat bleeding is reached (exploiting the anaesthetic, haemodynamic, and bacterial windows within 48–72 hours). Blood loss is minimised using tourniquets and subcutaneous tumescence with 1:500,000 adrenaline.

Topical Antimicrobials (whilst awaiting staged surgery): 1% Silver sulphadiazine (Flamazine), Silver sulphadiazine + Cerium nitrate (forms a sterile leathery eschar and boosts cell-mediated immunity), 5% Mafenide acetate (penetrates eschar/cartilage well; side effect: carbonic anhydrase inhibition causing metabolic acidosis), or Acticoat.

Wound Closure: Autologous Split-Thickness Skin Grafts (STSG) (sheet grafts for face/hands/neck; meshed 1:1.5 to 1:6 or Meek micrografting for extensive burns). If TBSA >50% and donor sites are insufficient, use temporary cadaveric allografts or dermal matrices (Integra or Biodegradable Temporising Matrix [BTM]).

E. Rehabilitation & Post-Burn Sequelae:

Physiotherapy & Splinting: Start from Day 1; splint hands in the position of safe immobilisation (intrinsic-plus), neck in extension, and axillae in 90° abduction.

Hypertrophic Scar Management: Custom-fitted pressure garments (worn 23 hours/day for 6–18 months), topical silicone gel sheets, intralesional steroid injections, and antipruritics.

Surgical Release of Contractures: Z-plasty or multiple Y-to-V advancement flaps for linear scar bands; incision + full-thickness skin graft (FTSG), dermal substitutes, tissue expansion (especially for post-burn scalp alopecia), or free flaps for broad contractures. Urgent eyelid release + grafting if ectropion threatens exposure keratitis.

subject: surgery
title: Q2.2: Electrical and Chemical Burns
text:
(Covers KU 23, 21, 18, RGU)

1. Electrical Burns:

Classified into Low-Voltage (<1000 V) and High-Voltage (>1000 V) injuries.

Low-Tension (Domestic) Injuries:

Alternating current causes muscle tetany (“let-go phenomenon”), locking the victim’s hand onto the source and causing deep local contact burns in the fingers with underlying nerve/tendon damage.

Systemic Danger: Disrupts normal cardiac pacing → ventricular fibrillation / cardiac arrest without direct myocardial necrosis.

High-Tension Injuries (>1000 V):

Three Mechanisms of Injury: Flash (arcing superheated air), Flame (ignition of clothing), and Direct Current Conduction (victim acts as a conductor to earth).

Pathophysiology (“Iceberg Effect”): Small, charred entry and exit wounds mask massive deep myonecrosis along neurovascular bundles and bone (bone has the highest electrical resistance and generates intense heat, cooking surrounding deep muscle bellies).

Complications:

Acute Compartment Syndrome: Rapid muscle swelling within intact fascia.

Rhabdomyolysis & Myoglobinuria: Massive release of myoglobin causes dark “port-wine” urine and acute tubular necrosis / renal failure.

Direct Myocardial Damage & Arrhythmias.

Severe Metabolic Acidosis and associated fractures/spinal injuries from blast propulsion.

Management of High-Voltage Burns:

Aggressive Fluid Resuscitation: Maintain a higher target urine output of 1.5–2.0 mL/kg/hour (using Hartmann’s solution + sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine and mannitol to flush myoglobin casts).

Continuous ECG Monitoring for 24–48 hours.

Urgent Decompressive Fasciotomy (not just escharotomy) of affected limb compartments, serial surgical debridement of necrotic muscle, or primary amputation if the limb is unsalvageable.

2. Chemical (Acid & Alkali) Burns:

Pathophysiology: Damage occurs via local tissue corrosion/protein denaturation and systemic toxicity from absorption.

Acids: Cause coagulative necrosis, forming a coagulum/eschar that limits deeper penetration.

Alkalis (Cement, Lime, Bleach, Drain cleaners): Cause liquefactive necrosis and saponification of fats, allowing deeper, progressive tissue destruction (far more dangerous, especially in ocular injuries).

Management:

Brush off any dry solid chemical powders first (e.g., elemental sodium, white phosphorus).

Immediate, Copious Water Lavage for 30–60 minutes (dilutes and washes away the agent; do not attempt to neutralise with an opposite chemical as the exothermic reaction worsens thermal injury).

Hydrofluoric (HF) Acid Burns (Special Case): HF chelates tissue calcium and magnesium, causing excruciating pain, deep necrosis, and potentially fatal systemic hypocalcaemia and cardiac arrhythmias. Treated with topical 10% Calcium Gluconate gel, local infiltration, or intra-arterial / intravenous Bier’s block with Calcium Gluconate (and urgent excision if concentration >50%).

subject: surgery
title: Q3.1: Skin Grafts (Types, Split-Skin Graft / Thiersch Graft, Full-Thickness / Wolfe Graft)
text:
(Covers KU 24, 23, 19, 15, RGU, TU)

Definition: A Graft is a piece of tissue completely detached from its blood supply at the donor site and transferred to a recipient bed, from which it must acquire a new blood supply to survive. 

Mechanism of Skin Graft “Take” (Three Phases):

Plasmatic Imbibition (0–48 hours): The graft absorbs nutrients and oxygen via passive diffusion from the plasma exudate of the recipient bed, held by a fibrin layer.

Inosculation (48–72 hours): Capillary buds from the recipient bed align and connect with existing cut vessels on the undersurface of the graft.

Neovascularisation / Revascularisation (Day 4–7): New blood vessels actively grow into the graft, establishing definitive circulation.

Causes of Graft Failure:

Haematoma or Seroma collection beneath the graft (prevents capillary contact during inosculation).

Shearing forces (disrupts fragile new capillary buds).

Infection: Specifically Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes (produces fibrinolysins/streptokinase that dissolve the fibrin attachment and destroy the entire graft).

Avacular Recipient Bed: Bare cortical bone (devoid of periosteum), bare tendon (devoid of paratenon), bare cartilage (devoid of perichondrium), or irradiated tissue cannot support a skin graft and require a vascularised Flap.

Comparison of Split-Thickness vs Full-Thickness Skin Grafts:

[[TABLE:surgery-tbl-003]]

Operative Technique of Split-Skin Grafting: 

Harvested under local or general anaesthesia using a manual skin-grafting knife (Humby’s knife, Watson’s knife, or Silver’s knife) or a powered Dermatome after lubricating the skin and blade with liquid paraffin.

The graft is fenestrated/meshed, laid shiny-side (dermis) down on the debrided recipient bed, secured with absorbable sutures/staples or fibrin glue, and immobilised with a bolster (tie-over dressing) or Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy (VAC) for 5 days. The donor site is dressed with calcium alginate (Kaltostat) and left undisturbed for 10–14 days.

subject: surgery
title: Q3.2: Flaps & Vascular Grafts
text:
(Covers TU, RGU)

1. Flaps:

Definition: A block of tissue transferred from a donor site to a recipient defect while maintaining its own innate blood supply via a vascular pedicle (or re-established via microvascular anastomosis).

Indications: Covering avascular beds (exposed bone, tendon, cartilage, orthopaedic metalwork, major vessels), reconstructing composite 3D defects, providing padding over pressure points (pressure sores), and transferring functional muscle/sensate skin.

The “Five Cs” Classification of Flaps (Bailey & Love):

Circulation (Blood Supply):

Random Pattern Flaps: Supplied by the subdermal vascular plexus without a named vessel (limited by length-to-breadth ratio, typically 1:1 to 2:1, up to 3:1 on the face).

Axial Pattern Flaps: Contain a specific anatomically named artery and vein running along the long axis of the flap (e.g., Forehead flap based on supratrochlear artery; Groin flap based on superficial circumflex iliac artery).

Composition: Cutaneous, Fasciocutaneous (Cormack & Lamberty Types A–D, e.g., Radial forearm flap), Myocutaneous/Muscle (Mathes & Nahai Types I–V, e.g., Latissimus dorsi [Type V], Gracilis [Type II], TRAM [Type III]), Osseocutaneous (Free fibula flap).

Contiguity (Proximity to Defect): Local (adjacent to defect), Regional (nearby, e.g., Pectoralis major flap to neck), and Distant (Pedicled groin flap or Microvascular Free Flap such as Anterolateral Thigh [ALT] or DIEP flap).

Contour (Method of Movement for Local Flaps): 

Advancement Flaps: Rectangular, V-Y advancement (e.g., fingertip amputation), Y-V plasty.

Pivot Flaps: Rotation flap (semicircular arc), Transposition flap (Rhomboid/Limberg flap, Bilobed flap, Z-plasty), and Interpolation flap (Indian forehead flap).

Conditioning: Flap “delay” (surgical division of part of the blood supply 2 weeks prior to transfer to open choke vessels and augment axial survival).

2. Vascular Grafts:

Autologous Vein Grafts: Gold standard for small/medium-calibre infrainguinal arterial bypasses (femoropopliteal, femorodistal, coronary, and traumatic vascular repair).

Great Saphenous Vein (GSV): Used either reversed (so venous valves do not obstruct arterial flow) or in situ (after disrupting valves with a valvulotome). Alternatives: Small saphenous vein, cephalic/basilic arm veins.

Synthetic Prosthetic Grafts: Used for large-calibre high-flow vessels (aortoiliac bypass, AAA repair) or when autologous vein is unavailable.

Dacron (woven or knitted polyethylene terephthalate): Used for aortic/iliac replacement.

ePTFE (expanded polytetrafluoroethylene): Used for femoropopliteal bypass (with a distal autologous vein collar — Miller cuff or St Mary’s boot — to reduce intimal hyperplasia) and arteriovenous grafts for haemodialysis.

subject: surgery
title: Q4.1: Premalignant Conditions of the Oral Cavity & Leukoplakia
text:
(Covers KU 18, 16, RGU, TU)

Potentially Malignant (Premalignant) Oral Lesions:

High Risk:

Erythroplakia: Bright red velvety plaque that cannot be characterised clinically or pathologically as any other condition; carries the highest risk of malignant transformation (>50% harbour severe dysplasia or carcinoma in situ at biopsy).

Speckled Leukoplakia (Erythroleukoplakia): Mixed white nodular patches on an erythematous base; carries a much higher malignant risk than homogeneous leukoplakia.

Proliferative Verrucous Leukoplakia (PVL): Multifocal, exophytic, progressive white lesions in elderly women (often non-smokers) with a near 100% eventual malignant transformation rate.

Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSMF): Chronic, insidious progressive juxta-epithelial fibrosis of the oral mucosa caused by areca nut (betel quid/gutka) chewing; causes burning sensation, blanching of mucosa, palpable fibrous bands, and progressive trismus.

Chronic Hyperplastic Candidiasis.

Intermediate / Low Risk:

Homogeneous Leukoplakia (see below).

Oral Lichen Planus (especially the erosive/atrophic type; 1% risk).

Syphilitic Glossitis, Sideropenic dysphagia (Plummer–Vinson syndrome), Discoid lupus erythematosus, and inherited Dyskeratosis congenita.

Oral Leukoplakia (Detailed Note):

WHO Definition: A predominantly white patch or plaque of the oral mucosa that cannot be scraped off and cannot be characterised clinically or pathologically as any other definable disease.

Etiology (The “6 S’s”): Smoking (tobacco/bidi/reverse smoking), Spirits (alcohol), Sharp tooth/ill-fitting dentures, Spices/betel quid (areca nut + slaked lime), Syphilis, and Sepsis.

Clinical Types: Homogeneous (flat, thin, uniform white plaque with low malignant potential) vs Non-homogeneous (nodular, verrucous, or speckled/erythroleukoplakia).

Factors Increasing Malignant Transformation Risk (Summary Box 53.2):

Female sex, lesion size >200 mm², non-homogeneous/speckled appearance, high-risk anatomical subsite (floor of mouth and ventral/lateral border of tongue), presence of multiple lesions, and leukoplakia in a non-smoker. Overall transformation rate is 0.13% to 34%.

Management:

Cessation of Risk Factors: Stop tobacco, betel quid, and alcohol; smooth sharp teeth.

Incisional Biopsy: Mandatory from the most indurated or red/speckled area to grade dysplasia (mild, moderate, severe) or rule out invasive SCC.

Treatment: Mild dysplasia may be observed with serial photography and medical antioxidants (retinoids/lycopene). Moderate-to-severe dysplasia requires surgical excision (scalpel or CO_2 laser ablation) with lifelong surveillance.

subject: surgery
title: Q4.2: Oral Cavity Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Carcinoma Tongue & Buccal Mucosa)
text:
(Covers KU 20, RGU, TU)

Epidemiology & Etiology:

>95% of oral cavity cancers are Squamous Cell Carcinomas (OCSCC).

Geographical Variation: In Western countries, the lateral border of the tongue and floor of the mouth are the commonest sites; in India and South Asia, the buccogingival sulcus and retromolar trigone account for >40% of cases (“alveolobuccal complex” cancer due to keeping smokeless tobacco/gutka/khaini quid in the gingivobuccal sulcus).

Risk Factors (Summary Box 53.1): Tobacco (smoking and smokeless), alcohol (synergistic with tobacco), betel quid (areca nut, catechu, slaked lime), HPV-16/18 (accounts for ~5% of oral cavity SCC vs 50–70% of oropharyngeal SCC), chronic dental trauma, immunosuppression, and Fanconi anaemia.

Pathology:

Site Distribution in Tongue: Lateral border of middle third (45–50%), anterior/ventral aspect (20%), posterior third/base (20%), dorsum/tip (5–10%).

Macroscopic Types: Ulcerative (commonest — hard indurated base with raised everted edges), Exophytic/Papillary, Infiltrative/Endophytic, or Verrucous carcinoma (Ackerman’s tumour — slow-growing, locally invasive, pushing margins, rarely metastasises). 

Mode of Spread:

Local: Infiltrates intrinsic/extrinsic tongue muscles (causing ankyloglossia), floor of mouth, lingual/inferior alveolar nerves, and mandible (via direct erosive or infiltrative contact). Buccal mucosa cancer invades buccinator, skin of cheek (resulting in an orocutaneous fistula), and pterygoid muscles (causing trismus).

Lymphatic: Drains primarily to Levels I, II, and III (submental, submandibular, and upper/middle jugular nodes). Tongue tip drains to Level IA; lateral tongue drains to Levels IB and II, with a known propensity for “skip metastases” directly to Level III or IV and bilateral drainage if the lesion approaches/crosses the midline.

Clinical Features:

Early: Painless non-healing ulcer (>2 weeks), indurated nodule, or persistent red/white patch.

Late (Advanced Disease):

Severe local pain and referred ipsilateral otalgia (mediated via the lingual nerve → chorda tympani / mandibular nerve (V_3) → auriculotemporal nerve).

Excessive salivation, foetor oris, bleeding, and dysarthria (“hot potato speech”).

Ankyloglossia: Fixation of the tongue to the floor of the mouth; tongue deviates to the ipsilateral side on protrusion.

Trismus: Indicates invasion of the medial pterygoid muscle / masticator space.

Unexplained tooth mobility or palpable hard cervical lymphadenopathy.

AJCC 8th Edition TNM Staging (Key Updates):

Incorporates Depth of Invasion (DOI) (measured from the basement membrane of adjacent normal mucosa) into T-staging, and Extranodal Extension (ENE) into N-staging:

T1: Size ≤ 2 cm and DOI ≤ 5 mm.

T2: Size ≤ 2 cm with DOI 5–10 mm; OR Size 2–4 cm with DOI ≤ 10 mm.

T3: Size >4 cm OR any tumour with DOI >10 mm.

T4a (Moderately advanced): Invades through cortical bone of mandible/maxilla, maxillary sinus, inferior alveolar nerve, deep/extrinsic muscles of tongue (genioglossus, hyoglossus, palatoglossus, styloglossus), or skin of face.

T4b (Very advanced / Unresectable): Invades masticator space, pterygoid plates, skull base, or encases the internal carotid artery.

Investigations & Work-Up:

Incisional / Wedge Biopsy from the growing edge of the ulcer (avoid central necrosis) for histopathological confirmation.

Imaging:

MRI with contrast: Gold standard for defining soft-tissue extent, tongue muscle invasion, perineural spread, and marrow invasion.

Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT): Superior for assessing cortical bone invasion of the mandible/maxilla and staging the neck and thorax.

Orthopantomogram (OPG): Evaluates dental status prior to radiotherapy and gross mandibular erosion.

USG Neck + FNAC of suspicious cervical lymph nodes.

Examination Under Anaesthesia (EUA) / Panendoscopy: For posterior tumours and to rule out synchronous upper aerodigestive tract primaries (present in 2.5–4.5%).

Management (Primary Surgery ± Adjuvant Therapy):

1. Surgical Excision of Primary Tumour:

Excision with a 1 cm circumferential clinical margin of normal tissue.

Access: Transoral approach for anterior T1/T2 lesions; Lip-split mandibulotomy for posterior oral cavity/tongue base lesions. 

Tongue Resection: Partial glossectomy / hemiglossectomy / total glossectomy.

Management of the Mandible:

If tumour abuts periosteum without bone invasion → Rim (Marginal) Mandibulectomy (preserving continuity of the lower border).

If gross medullary/cortical bone invasion is present → Segmental Mandibulectomy (or hemimandibulectomy).

2. Management of the Neck:

Clinically Node-Negative (cN0) in T1/T2 tumours (especially DOI >3–4 mm): Prophylactic Elective Selective Neck Dissection (Supraomohyoid Neck Dissection: Levels I–III) (or I–IV for oral tongue) significantly improves overall and disease-free survival compared with “watch and wait” (Tata Memorial Hospital / D’Cruz et al. NEJM Trial). Sentinel lymph node biopsy is an alternative in select early T1 lesions.

Clinically Node-Positive (cN+): Therapeutic Modified Radical Neck Dissection (Levels I–V).

3. Reconstruction (Following the Reconstructive Ladder):

Small Defects: Primary closure or local flaps (Facial Artery Myomucosal [FAMM] flap, nasolabial flap, buccal fat pad).

Moderate Soft-Tissue Defects (Partial Glossectomy / Buccal Mucosa): Radial Forearm Free Flap (RFFF) (thin, pliable, long pedicle).

Large / Subtotal Glossectomy Defects: Anterolateral Thigh (ALT) Free Flap or pedicled Pectoralis Major Myocutaneous (PMMC) Flap (provides bulk to contact the palate for speech and swallowing).

Segmental Mandibular Defects: Free Fibula Osseocutaneous Flap (gold standard; provides up to 25 cm of bone suitable for dental implants), Deep Circumflex Iliac Artery (DCIA), or Scapula free flap.

4. Adjuvant Radiotherapy / Chemoradiotherapy:

Adjuvant Radiotherapy (60–66 Gy): Indicated for T3/T4 primary, close margins (1–4.9 mm), multiple positive nodes, N2/N3 disease, Perineural Invasion (PNI), or Lymphovascular Invasion (LVI).

Concurrent Cisplatin-based Chemoradiotherapy: Mandatory for Major High-Risk Features: Positive surgical margins (<1 mm) and/or Extranodal Extension (ENE).

subject: surgery
title: Q4.3: Dentigerous Cyst & Differential Diagnosis of Tongue Ulcers
text:
(Covers KU 24, 20, 18, TU)

1. Dentigerous Cyst (Follicular Odontogenic Cyst) [KU 24, 20, 18]:

Definition: A benign odontogenic cyst that surrounds the crown of an unerupted (impacted) permanent tooth, attached at the cementoenamel junction, arising from fluid accumulation between the reduced enamel epithelium and the tooth crown.

Clinical Features:

Second most common odontogenic cyst (after radicular/dental cyst); occurs in young adults (10–30 years).

Most commonly involves the mandibular third molar or maxillary permanent canine.

Presents as a painless, slow-growing bony swelling expanding the outer cortical plate of the jaw (resulting in egg-shell crackling on palpation) with a missing permanent tooth in the dental arch.

Radiology (OPG): Well-defined unilocular radiolucency with a sclerotic margin enveloping the crown of an unerupted tooth, displacing the tooth towards the lower border of the mandible.

Complications: Pathological fracture, secondary infection, root resorption of adjacent teeth, and potential transformation of the lining into an ameloblastoma or mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

Treatment:

Small cysts: Complete surgical enucleation along with extraction of the unerupted tooth.

Large cysts (in children or where enucleation risks jaw fracture/nerve injury): Initial marsupialisation (decompression) to allow bone regeneration and tooth eruption, followed by delayed enucleation if necessary.

2. Differential Diagnosis of Tongue Ulcers [TU]:

Traumatic: Dental ulcer (caused by a sharp jagged tooth or denture along the lateral border; heals within 2 weeks of removing the cause).

Inflammatory / Immunological: Aphthous ulcers (small, painful, recurrent, yellowish floor with erythematous halo), Behçet’s syndrome, Lichen planus.

Specific Infective:

Tuberculous Ulcer: Painful, shallow, multiple ulcers at the tip/anterior margin with undermined edges.

Syphilitic Ulcer: Primary chancre (painless indurated ulcer at the tip), Secondary (“snail-track” mucous patches), Tertiary gummatous ulcer (deep punched-out painless ulcer on the midline dorsum).

Neoplastic: Squamous cell carcinoma (painless non-healing ulcer >2 weeks with everted edges and indurated base).

subject: surgery
title: Q5.1: Classification of Salivary Gland Tumours, Pleomorphic Adenoma & Parotidectomy
text:
(Covers KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 17, RGU, TU — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. General Principles (“Rule of 80s”):

80% of salivary gland neoplasms arise in the major glands, and ~80% of these occur in the Parotid gland.

80% of parotid tumours are benign, and 80% of benign parotid tumours are Pleomorphic Adenomas.

Conversely, the smaller the salivary gland, the higher the likelihood of malignancy (Parotid: 20% malignant; Submandibular: 50% malignant; Sublingual & Minor salivary glands: 50–85% malignant).

2. WHO Classification of Salivary Gland Neoplasms (Table 54.3):

Benign Epithelial Tumours:

Pleomorphic adenoma (Mixed tumour — commonest overall).

Warthin’s tumour (Adenolymphoma / Papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum — second commonest benign tumour).

Basal cell adenoma, Myoepithelioma, Oncocytoma, Canalicular adenoma, Ductal papillomas.

Malignant Epithelial Tumours:

Low-to-Intermediate Grade: Low-grade Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (commonest salivary malignancy overall and in children), Acinic cell carcinoma, Polymorphous low-grade adenocarcinoma, Epithelial–myoepithelial carcinoma.

High Grade: High-grade Mucoepidermoid carcinoma, Adenoid cystic carcinoma (propensity for perineural invasion and “Swiss-cheese” cribriform histology), Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, Salivary duct carcinoma, Squamous cell carcinoma.

Non-Epithelial / Lymphoid: Haemangioma, Non-Hodgkin’s MALT lymphoma (associated with Sjögren’s syndrome).

3. Pleomorphic Adenoma (Mixed Parotid Tumour):

Epidemiology: Commonest salivary gland neoplasm; peaks in the 3rd to 5th decades (average age 45 years); slight female preponderance. >80% occur in the parotid (mostly in the superficial lobe / tail of parotid).

Pathology:

Macroscopic: Well-circumscribed, firm, lobulated/bosselated mass with a whitish-tan, cartilaginous cut surface. Crucially, the fibrous capsule is incomplete and has microscopic pseudopods (finger-like extensions) projecting into the surrounding normal gland parenchyma. Therefore, simple enucleation is contraindicated as it leaves behind pseudopods, leading to multifocal recurrence.

Microscopic (“Mixed Tumour”): Biphasic admixture of epithelial and myoepithelial cells (ducts, sheets, strands) embedded in a mesenchymal-like stroma (myxoid, mucoid, chondroid/cartilaginous, and hyalinised matrix). Luminal cells express CK7; myoepithelial cells express p63, S-100, and SMA.

Clinical Presentation (Substantiation of Case [KU 23]):

Slow-growing, painless, firm-to-cartilaginous swelling in the parotid region (in front of and below the ear lobule, obliterating the retromandibular groove and lifting the ear lobule).

Freely mobile over deeper structures (becomes less mobile when the masseter is contracted), overlying skin is pinchable, and the facial nerve is completely intact (0% palsy in benign lesions).

Deep Lobe Tumours (10%): May pass through the stylomandibular tunnel (“dumbbell tumour”) to present as a medial paratonsillar / soft palate bulge pushing the tonsil medially.

Clinical Features Suggestive of Malignant Transformation (Carcinoma ex Pleomorphic Adenoma):

Sudden rapid increase in size of a longstanding swelling, onset of pain, facial nerve weakness/palsy (House–Brackmann grading), skin infiltration/ulceration, fixity to underlying masseter/mandible, trismus, and cervical lymphadenopathy.

Investigations:

High-Resolution Ultrasonography (USG): First-line imaging; shows a well-defined, lobulated hypoechoic mass with posterior acoustic enhancement.

Ultrasound-Guided Fine-Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC): Reported using the Milan System (Categories I–VI; Pleomorphic adenoma = Category IVA); 96–98% specificity (Core biopsy is reserved for inconclusive cases or suspected lymphoma; open incisional biopsy is contraindicated due to tumour seeding).

MRI / Contrast CT Scan: Indicated for large tumours (>4 cm), suspected deep lobe involvement, recurrent tumours, or suspected malignancy.

Surgical Management (Parotidectomy):

Excision of the tumour with a cuff of normal surrounding parotid tissue while preserving the facial nerve:

Superficial Parotidectomy (or Adequate Parotidectomy / Extracapsular Dissection in select mobile tail lesions) for tumours lateral to the facial nerve plane (Patey’s faciovenous plane).

Total Conservative Parotidectomy (excising both superficial and deep lobes while preserving the facial nerve) for deep lobe tumours.

Radical Parotidectomy (sacrificing the facial nerve with immediate cable nerve grafting using the great auricular nerve or sural nerve, plus neck dissection and adjuvant radiotherapy) for invasive malignancies.

Operative Steps of Superficial Parotidectomy: 

Incision: Lazy-S (Modified Blair) incision (preauricular crease, curving around the ear lobule over the mastoid, and running forward in a neck crease two finger-breadths below the angle of the mandible).

Flap Elevation: Raise an anterior skin flap in the subplatysmal / sub-SMAS plane; divide the anterior branch of the great auricular nerve while preserving its posterior branch if possible.

Anatomical Landmarks to Identify the Facial Nerve Trunk (Antegrade Technique):

Conley’s Tragal Pointer: Facial nerve trunk lies 1 cm deep and 1 cm inferior to the cartilaginous tip of the tragus.

Posterior Belly of Digastric Muscle: Nerve lies just superior to the upper border of the posterior digastric near its mastoid insertion.

Tympanomastoid Suture Line: Nerve lies 6–8 mm deep/inferior to the drop-off of this bony suture line (most constant landmark).

Styloid Process: Nerve lies superficial to its base.

(Retrograde technique: Tracing peripheral branches — e.g., buccal branch parallel to Stensen’s duct or marginal mandibular branch crossing facial vessels — proximally to the trunk).

Dissection: Dissect in Patey’s faciovenous plane immediately superficial to the facial nerve branches using fine mosquito forceps and bipolar cautery up to Stensen’s duct, which is ligated; place a suction drain and close in layers.

Complications of Parotidectomy (Summary Box 54.8):

Early: Haematoma, wound infection, temporary facial nerve paresis (neuropraxia; commonest in the marginal mandibular branch), permanent facial nerve palsy (requires eye care to prevent exposure keratitis), sialocele, and salivary fistula.

Late: Numbness of the ear lobule (due to division of the great auricular nerve — C2, C3), retromandibular hollowing/cosmetic deformity, tumour recurrence, and Frey’s Syndrome.

subject: surgery
title: Q5.2: Warthin’s Tumour & Frey’s Syndrome
text:
(Covers KU 24, 21, 19, RGU, TU)

1. Warthin’s Tumour (Papillary Cystadenoma Lymphomatosum / Adenolymphoma):

Epidemiology: Second most common benign salivary gland tumour (5–15% of parotid neoplasms).

Key Clinical Characteristics:

Occurs almost exclusively in the Parotid gland (typically in the lower pole / tail).

Strongly associated with cigarette smoking (8-fold higher risk).

Affects older men in their 6th to 7th decades (male:female historically predominance, now equalising with smoking trends).

10% are bilateral and 10% are multifocal (synchronous or metachronous).

Pathogenesis & Pathology:

Thought to arise from heterotopic salivary ductal inclusions trapped within intraparotid lymph nodes during late embryological encapsulation of the parotid.

Macroscopic: Soft-to-cystic encapsulated mass; cut surface shows cystic spaces filled with murky, chocolate-brown mucoid fluid (“motor-oil fluid”).

Microscopic: Papillary and cystic structures lined by a characteristic double layer of eosinophilic oncocytic epithelial cells (rich in mitochondria) resting on a dense reactive lymphoid stroma with germinal centres.

Investigations: USG + FNAC (Milan Category IVA). On Technetium-99m ((99m)Tc) pertechnetate scintigraphy, Warthin’s tumour is uniquely “Hot” (concentrates radioisotope due to high mitochondrial content in oncocytic cells) and is also FDG-avid on PET-CT.

Treatment: Conservative superficial parotidectomy / extracapsular dissection. Malignant transformation is exceedingly rare (<1%).

2. Frey’s Syndrome (Auriculotemporal Syndrome / Gustatory Sweating):

Pathophysiology: Following parotidectomy or parotid trauma, severed postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres (derived from the inferior salivatory nucleus → Glossopharyngeal nerve [CN IX] → Jacobson’s nerve → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve) undergo aberrant regeneration and cross-innervate the sympathetic-innervated dermal sweat glands and cutaneous blood vessels of the overlying skin flap (both use acetylcholine as their neurotransmitter).

Clinical Features: Eating or thinking of food (salivary stimulus) triggers inappropriate sweating, flushing, erythema, and warmth over the preauricular/cheek skin in the distribution of the auriculotemporal nerve.

Diagnosis (Minor’s Starch–Iodine Test): Paint the affected preauricular skin with iodine solution, allow it to dry, dust with dry white starch powder, and give the patient a sialogogue (lemon slice). Sweating dissolves the iodine to react with starch, turning the affected skin dark blue-black.

Prevention (Intraoperative): Raise a thick skin flap (preserving SMAS) or interpose a physical barrier between the parotid bed and skin (e.g., sternocleidomastoid muscle flap, temporalis fascia flap, acellular dermal matrix [Alloderm], or autologous fat graft).

Management of Established Frey’s Syndrome (Summary Box 54.9):

Reassurance (most cases are mild).

Topical antiperspirants (20% Aluminium chlorohydrate roll-on).

Intradermal Botulinum Toxin A injections into the affected skin (gold standard; blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuroglandular junction; effective for 9–12 months).

Tympanic Neurectomy (division of Jacobson’s nerve on the promontory of the middle ear) for refractory cases.

subject: surgery
title: Q5.3: Ranula, Submandibular Sialolithiasis & Stafne Bone Cyst
text:
(Covers KU 24, 21, 20, 18, 15, RGU, TU)

1. Ranula & Plunging Ranula:

Definition: A mucous extravasation retention cyst of the floor of the mouth arising from rupture or obstruction of the ducts (ducts of Rivinus / Bartholin’s duct) or acini of the sublingual salivary gland.

Clinical Types & Features:

Simple (Oral) Ranula: Presents in children/young adults as a unilateral, painless, soft, fluctuant, translucent bluish swelling in the anterior floor of the mouth lateral to the frenulum, resembling a frog’s belly (Latin: rana = frog). Brilliant transillumination is positive.

Plunging (Deep/Cervical) Ranula: The mucus collection herniates/insinuates through a dehiscence in the mylohyoid muscle (or around its posterior free border) into the submandibular/submental space, presenting as a painless neck swelling with or without an intraoral component (bidigitally palpable). 

Investigations: Clinical diagnosis; MRI or USG confirms a cystic lesion with a “tail sign” extending into the sublingual space; aspiration yields thick, viscid, mucinous saliva with high amylase (distinguishing it from a lymphatic malformation/cystic hygroma or dermoid cyst).

Treatment:

Excision of the ipsilateral Sublingual Gland along with decompression/evacuation of the cyst via a transoral approach (definitive cure; simple incision/drainage or marsupialisation has a high recurrence rate because the sublingual gland has multiple autonomous ducts).

Non-surgical alternatives: Intralesional injection of sclerosant OK-432 (Picibanil) or Botulinum toxin.

2. Submandibular Sialolithiasis (Salivary Calculus):

Epidemiology & Etiology: 85% of all salivary calculi occur in the submandibular gland/Wharton’s duct (vs 15% in the parotid) because:

Submandibular secretion is rich in mucin, calcium, and phosphate, making it more viscous and alkaline.

Wharton’s duct is long, tortuous, and has an antigravity ascending course with a narrow orifice (punctum), predisposing to salivary stasis.

Clinical Features:

Classical mealtime syndrome: Acute, colicky pain and rapid tense swelling of the submandibular gland just before or during meals (especially sour foods), which slowly subsides over 1–2 hours after eating.

Examination: Enlarged, firm, tender submandibular gland; reduced saliva from the inflamed sublingual papilla; stone is palpable on bidigital palpation of the floor of the mouth (palpating from posterior to anterior).

Investigations:

Intraoral Lower Occlusal Radiograph: 80% of submandibular stones are radio-opaque (composed of calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate). 

High-Resolution Ultrasonography or non-contrast CT (detects radiolucent and small stones with acoustic shadowing).

MR Sialography / Diagnostic Sialendoscopy.

Treatment:

Conservative: Hydration, sialogogues, gland massage, and antibiotics if infected.

Stones in Anterior/Distal Wharton’s Duct:

Small (<5 mm) mobile stones: Sialendoscopic basket extraction.

Larger (>5 mm) impacted stones in the floor of the mouth: Transoral Choanal Duct Slitting (Sialolithotomy): Place a stay suture behind the stone to prevent it from slipping back into the hilum → incise the longitudinal axis of Wharton’s duct directly over the stone → extract stone → leave the duct open or marsupialise (never suture the duct closed as it causes stricture).

Intraparenchymal / Hilar Stones: Sialendoscopy, Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL for stones <7 mm), or Submandibular Gland Excision (preserving the marginal mandibular nerve, lingual nerve, and hypoglossal nerve).

3. Stafne Bone Cyst (Static Bone Cavity of Mandible) [KU 18]:

A developmental pseudocystic depression on the lingual cortex of the mandible containing ectopic/entrapped submandibular salivary gland tissue and branches of the facial artery.

Presents as an asymptomatic, incidental finding on OPG: a well-corticated, round, unilocular radiolucency (0.5–2 cm) located in the posterior mandible below the inferior alveolar nerve canal between the first molar and the angle of the mandible. Requires reassurance and no surgical intervention.

subject: surgery
title: Q6.1: Thyroglossal Cyst & Thyroglossal Fistula
text:
(Covers KU 25, 21, 17, 16, 15, RGU, TU)

Embryology: The thyroid gland develops from the median endodermal bud at the foramen caecum of the tongue and descends caudally in front of the pharynx as the hollow thyroglossal duct, passing in intimate continuity with (anterior, through, or posterior to) the body of the developing hyoid bone before reaching its final position in the lower neck. The duct normally obliterates by the 6th–8th week; persistence of an unobliterated segment forms a Thyroglossal Cyst. 

Anatomical Sites of Thyroglossal Cyst:

Subhyoid / Infrahyoid (60–75% — Commonest): Between the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage.

Suprahyoid (20%).

Over the thyroid cartilage (often slightly to the left of the midline).

Floor of the mouth / Intralingual (Foramen caecum).

Clinical Diagnosis:

Presents most commonly in children and young adults as a painless, smooth, cystic midline neck swelling.

Two Pathognomonic Clinical Signs:

Moves upwards with deglutition (attached to the pretracheal fascia/larynx).

Moves upwards on protrusion of the tongue (Tugging Sign): Because the cyst remains tethered to the base of the tongue (foramen caecum) via the patent thyroglossal tract passing through the hyoid bone. (Holding the cyst between thumb and index finger while asking the patient to protrude the tongue elicits a distinct upward tug).

Complications:

Recurrent Infection & Abscess Formation (due to lymphoid tissue in its wall).

Thyroglossal Fistula: Never congenital; always acquired following spontaneous rupture or inadequate surgical incision/drainage of an infected thyroglossal cyst. Presents as a midline pinpoint opening below the hyoid, discharging mucus/pus, covered by a characteristic crescentic hood of skin (“hood sign”) superiorly that is pulled inwards on tongue protrusion.

Malignancy (<1%): Almost always Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma arising in ectopic thyroid tissue within the cyst wall.

Investigations:

Neck Ultrasonography: Confirms the cystic nature of the swelling and verifies the presence of a normal orthotopic thyroid gland in the lower neck (mandatory before excision, lest the cyst contains the patient’s only functioning thyroid tissue).

Thyroid Function Tests (TSH, Free T_4) and FNAC (if a solid mural nodule is seen).

Treatment (Sistrunk’s Operation):

Principle: Excision of the cyst alone has a >40% recurrence rate because microscopic epithelial ductules pass through the hyoid bone up to the foramen caecum.

Components of Sistrunk’s Operation: Complete en bloc excision of:

The thyroglossal cyst (and fistulous tract with an ellipse of skin, if a fistula is present).

The central segment (body) of the hyoid bone (1–1.5 cm between the lesser cornua).

A core of suprahyoid muscle tissue (mylohyoid, geniohyoid, genioglossus) along the entire embryonic tract up to the foramen caecum.

subject: surgery
title: Q6.2: Solitary Thyroid Nodule (Discrete Thyroid Swelling) & Preoperative Evaluation
text:
(Covers KU 24, 23, 20, 15, RGU, TU — Long Essay & Short Answers)

Definitions:

Isolated (Solitary) Swelling (70%): A discrete palpable nodule in one lobe with an otherwise impalpable thyroid gland.

Dominant Swelling (30%): A prominent discrete nodule in a gland with clinical evidence of generalised abnormality/multinodularity elsewhere.

Differential Diagnosis (Causes) of a Solitary Thyroid Nodule:

Dominant nodule of a Multinodular Goitre (~50% of clinically “solitary” nodules reveal impalpable nodules on USG).

Follicular Adenoma (30–40%).

Thyroid Cyst (simple colloid cyst or haemorrhage into a necrotic nodule/adenoma).

Thyroid Malignancy (15% in isolated nodules; 7.5% in dominant nodules): Papillary, Follicular, Medullary, or Anaplastic carcinoma.

Focal Thyroiditis (Hashimoto’s or subacute de Quervain’s thyroiditis).

Autonomous Toxic Adenoma (Plummer’s disease).

Risk of Malignancy in Discrete Swellings (“Rule of 12” — Fig 55.13): 

Malignancy risk is twice as high in isolated nodules (24% solid / 12% cystic) compared with dominant nodules (12% solid / 6% cystic), twice as high in solid nodules compared with cystic nodules, and four times higher in males (48% in a solid isolated nodule in a man vs 12% in a woman).

Clinical Red Flags for Malignancy: Extremes of age (<20 or >60 years), male sex, history of childhood neck irradiation, family history (MEN 2 / MTC), rapid painless growth, hard/irregular consistency, fixity (failure to move on swallowing), hoarseness of voice / vocal cord palsy (RLN invasion), and cervical lymphadenopathy.

Stepwise Preoperative Investigations (Summary Box 55.1):

1. Thyroid Function Tests (Serum TSH, Free T_3, Free T_4):

Most patients are euthyroid. If TSH is suppressed (hyperthyroid), perform a Radioisotope Uptake Scan ((99m)Tc or ¹²³I) to differentiate a hyperfunctioning “Hot” Autonomous Toxic Adenoma (with suppression of the contralateral lobe; malignancy risk <1–5%) from a cold nodule in Graves’ disease. 

2. High-Resolution Ultrasonography of Neck:

Gold standard imaging; evaluates nodule size, composition (solid vs cystic), margins, and lymph nodes (Levels II–VI).

Sonographic Features of Malignancy: Hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications (psammoma bodies in PTC), irregular/infiltrative margins, “taller-than-wide” shape, intranodular hypervascularity, and extrathyroidal extension. Graded via U-Classification (U1–U5) or ACR TI-RADS (TR1–TR5).

3. Ultrasound-Guided Fine-Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC):

Investigation of choice for all indeterminate/suspicious nodules. Reported via the UK RCPath Thy Classification (Table 55.2) (or Bethesda System):

Thy1 / Thy1c: Non-diagnostic / Non-diagnostic cystic → Repeat USG-guided FNAC.

Thy2: Non-neoplastic (Benign colloid nodule / thyroiditis) → Reassure & observe (unless compressive).

Thy3 (Thy3a / Thy3f): Follicular neoplasm / atypia → Diagnostic Hemithyroidectomy (Total lobectomy + isthmusectomy), because FNAC cannot distinguish benign Follicular Adenoma from Follicular Carcinoma (requires histological proof of capsular and/or vascular invasion).

Thy4: Suspicious of malignancy → Diagnostic Hemithyroidectomy or Total Thyroidectomy.

Thy5: Diagnostic of malignancy (e.g., Papillary/Medullary carcinoma) → Definitive thyroid cancer surgery.

4. Optional / Ancillary Investigations:

Flexible Nasolaryngoscopy: Mandatory preoperatively to document vocal cord mobility.

Serum Thyroid Autoantibodies (Anti-TPO, Anti-Tg) and Serum Calcitonin / CEA (if Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma is suspected).

Indications for Surgery in a Solitary Thyroid Nodule (Table 55.4):

Neoplasia on FNAC (Thy3, Thy4, Thy5).

Strong Clinical Suspicion (male sex, extremes of age, hard/fixed mass, RLN palsy, cervical lymphadenopathy, recurrent cyst after aspiration).

Toxic Adenoma (Hemithyroidectomy is curative).

Compressive Symptoms (dysphagia, dyspnoea, stridor).

Cosmesis / Patient Preference.

subject: surgery
title: Q6.3: Multinodular Goitre (MNG) & Retrosternal Goitre
text:
(Covers KU 24, 22, 19, 18, RGU, TU — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. Etiopathogenesis & Natural History of Simple Multinodular Goitre:

Etiology: Driven by chronic or fluctuating TSH stimulation (and local growth factors/immunoglobulins) in response to subnormal circulating thyroid hormone synthesis:

Iodine Deficiency (Endemic Goitre): Daily iodine requirement is 0.1–0.15 mg. Common in mountainous regions (Himalayas, Alps, Andes).

Dyshormonogenesis (Sporadic Goitre): Genetic enzyme defects in iodine trapping, organification, or coupling (e.g., Pendred syndrome).

Dietary & Drug Goitrogens: Brassica vegetables (cabbage, kale, turnips contain thiocyanates that inhibit iodide trapping), Cassava, Lithium, Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), Carbimazole, and excessive iodides (Wolff–Chaikoff effect).

Physiological Increased Demand: Puberty and pregnancy (Female:Male preponderance due to oestrogen receptors on thyrocytes).

5-Stage Natural History of Simple Goitre (Bailey & Love):

Stage 1 (Diffuse Hyperplasia): Persistent TSH stimulation causes uniform, diffuse follicular hyperplasia (Diffuse Hyperplastic Goitre — soft, smooth, reversible if TSH stimulus ceases).

Stage 2 (Fluctuating Stimulation): Alternating periods of stimulation and involution produce mixed areas of active hyperplastic lobules and inactive colloid-filled lobules (Colloid Goitre).

Stage 3 (Focal Haemorrhage & Necrosis): Active hyperplastic lobules outgrow their blood supply → central haemorrhage and necrosis, leaving a surrounding rim of active follicles.

Stage 4 (Nodule Formation): Necrotic lobules coalesce to form discrete nodules filled with iodine-free colloid or inactive follicles, surrounded by fibrous tissue, cystic degeneration, and calcification.

Stage 5 (Multinodular Goitre - MNG): Continual repetition of this cycle produces an asymmetric, bosselated Multinodular Goitre, where most nodules are inactive and hormone synthesis occurs only in the internodular tissue. 

2. Complications of Multinodular Goitre:

Tracheal Compression & Displacement: Lateral deviation or “scabbard trachea” from retrosternal extension → dyspnoea and stridor (Kocher’s test: slight lateral compression of the thyroid lobes elicits stridor).

Acute Airway Obstruction: Sudden haemorrhage into a cyst/nodule impacted in the rigid thoracic inlet.

Secondary Thyrotoxicosis (Plummer’s Disease): Develops in up to 30% of longstanding MNGs in middle-aged/elderly patients; hyperfunction occurs in internodular tissue or autonomous nodules; predominantly manifests with cardiovascular symptoms (atrial fibrillation, tachycardia, heart failure) without eye signs.

Malignant Transformation (<3–5%): Usually Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (or Papillary carcinoma) in endemic goitres.

3. Retrosternal Goitre (Short Note & Long Essay [KU 24, 18]):

Definition & Pathogenesis: A goitre in which >50% of the thyroid mass lies below the plane of the thoracic inlet. Arises from the lower pole of a multinodular goitre being drawn downwards into the superior mediastinum by negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration, gravity, and swallowing. Blood supply remains strictly cervical (from the inferior thyroid arteries).

Clinical Features:

Often asymptomatic; when symptomatic, causes dyspnoea (worse at night or on lying flat), stridor, dysphagia, and a persistent cough.

Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Obstruction Syndrome: Dilated non-pulsatile neck and chest wall veins, facial plethora, and Pemberton’s Sign (raising both arms straight above the head for 1 minute corks the goitre into the narrow thoracic inlet, causing facial congestion, cyanosis, distended neck veins, and inspiratory stridor).

Examination: Lower border of the thyroid swelling cannot be palpated (“cannot get below the swelling”), dullness to percussion over the manubrium, and tracheal deviation.

Investigations:

TFTS (TSH, Free T_3, T_4).

CT Scan of Neck & Thorax (Gold Standard): Defines the exact lower limit of extension (anterior vs posterior mediastinum), relationship to the aortic arch, and severity of tracheal compression. 

Surgical Management of MNG & Retrosternal Goitre:

Indications for Surgery: Compressive symptoms, retrosternal extension with tracheal narrowing, secondary toxicity, suspicion of malignancy, or cosmetic deformity.

Choice of Operation: Total Thyroidectomy (followed by lifelong levothyroxine replacement at 1.6 μg/kg/day) is the procedure of choice for bilateral MNG to eliminate recurrence and avoid hazardous reoperative surgery. For asymmetric MNG confined to one lobe, Total Hemithyroidectomy is appropriate. (Subtotal thyroidectomy and Dunhill’s procedure [total lobectomy + contralateral subtotal lobectomy] are largely obsolete due to high recurrence rates).

Approach for Retrosternal Goitre: >95% can be delivered and excised via a standard cervical collar incision (because the arterial supply is in the neck; ligate superior pole vessels and middle thyroid vein first, then use gentle digital mobilisation on the capsule to deliver the retrosternal component upwards). Median Sternotomy (with cardiothoracic backup) is required in <5% (malignancy, recurrent goitre, posterior mediastinal extension below the aortic arch, or “iceberg” goitres wider than the thoracic inlet).

subject: surgery
title: Q6.4: Thyrotoxicosis & Graves’ Disease
text:
(Covers KU 23, 22, 19, RGU, TU — Long Essay, Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. Classification / Clinical Types of Thyrotoxicosis:

Diffuse Toxic Goitre (Graves’ Disease — Primary Thyrotoxicosis): Autoimmune disorder in young women (20–40 years); diffuse vascular goitre appearing simultaneously with hyperthyroidism; CNS overactivity + extrathyroidal manifestations (ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema, thyroid acropachy).

Toxic Multinodular Goitre (Secondary Thyrotoxicosis / Plummer’s Disease): Superimposition of hyperthyroidism on a pre-existing simple nodular goitre in patients >50 years; cardiovascular symptoms predominate (atrial fibrillation, high-output cardiac failure); eye signs are absent.

Solitary Toxic Adenoma (Autonomous Nodule): Single hyperfunctioning follicular adenoma producing T_3/T_4 autonomously, suppressing pituitary TSH and the rest of the thyroid gland.

Rare Causes: Jod-Basedow phenomenon (iodine/amiodarone-induced), Hashitoxicosis, early de Quervain’s thyroiditis, Struma ovarii, Hydatidiform mole/Choriocarcinoma (hCG cross-reacts with TSH receptor), and TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma.

2. Pathogenesis & Pathology of Graves’ Disease:

IgG autoantibodies (TSH Receptor Antibodies [TRAb / TSH-RAb / LATS]) bind to and stimulate TSH receptors on follicular cell membranes with a protracted action (16–24 hours vs 1.5–3 hours for normal TSH).

Histology: Diffuse acinar hyperplasia and hypertrophy lined by tall columnar epithelium with papillary infoldings and pale, vacuolated colloid showing a characteristic peripheral “scalloped” appearance. 

3. Clinical Features:

Symptoms: Weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, excessive sweating, palpitations, dyspnoea on exertion, fine tremors, irritability/insomnia, proximal muscle weakness, diarrhoea, and oligomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea.

Signs:

Sinus tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, wide pulse pressure (water-hammer pulse), warm moist palms, fine resting tremor of outstretched hands and protruding tongue.

Thyroid Gland: Diffuse, smooth, symmetrically enlarged, soft-to-firm vascular goitre with a palpable thrill and audible systolic/continuous bruit (best heard at the upper pole, where the superior thyroid artery enters).

Graves’ Ophthalmopathy: Driven by autoimmune inflammation and glycosaminoglycan deposition in retro-orbital fat and extraocular muscles:

Sympathetic Spasm Signs (Lid retraction): Dalrymple’s sign (visible upper scleral rim above the cornea), Von Graefe’s sign (lid lag on downward gaze), Stellwag’s sign (infrequent blinking/staring look), Joffroy’s sign (absence of forehead wrinkling on looking up).

Infiltrative Signs: True Exophthalmos/Proptosis, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia (Moebius’ sign — failure of convergence; earliest muscle affected is the inferior rectus limiting upward gaze), and optic nerve compression.

Pretibial Myxoedema (Thyroid Dermopathy): Bilateral, symmetrical, non-pitting, violaceous/reddish plaque-like thickening of the skin over the shins and dorsum of the feet due to dermal mucopolysaccharide (hyaluronic acid) deposition; occurs only in Graves’ disease.

4. Investigations:

Thyroid Function Tests (Table 55.1): Undetectable/Suppressed TSH (<0.01 mU/L) with elevated Free T_4 and Free T_3 (in T3-toxicosis, Free T_4 is normal while Free T_3 is high).

Autoantibodies: Elevated TRAb (diagnostic of Graves’ disease, >95% sensitive) and Anti-TPO antibodies.

Isotope Scan ((99m)Tc or ¹²³I): Shows diffuse homogeneous high uptake in Graves’ disease, patchy hot/cold areas in Toxic MNG, and a single “hot” nodule with complete suppression of the remaining gland in Toxic Adenoma.

5. Management of Thyrotoxicosis (Three Modalities):

A. Antithyroid Drugs (ATDs):

Carbimazole (30–40 mg/day initially for 8–12 weeks until euthyroid, then titrated down to maintenance 5–15 mg/day or a “Block and Replace” regimen adding Levothyroxine 100–150 μg/day for 12–18 months) or Propylthiouracil (PTU) (preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm as it also inhibits peripheral conversion of T_4 → T_3).

Mechanism: Inhibits thyroid peroxidase (TPO), blocking iodide oxidation and organification.

Disadvantages: High relapse rate (>50%) upon stopping; cannot cure autonomous toxic nodules; 0.2% risk of Agranulocytosis (warn patient to stop drug immediately and check FBC if sore throat or fever develops).

β-Blockers (Propranolol 40 mg TDS): Rapidly controls adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor, anxiety) and inhibits peripheral conversion of T_4 → T_3.

B. Radioactive Iodine Therapy (¹³¹I):

Destroys hyperfunctioning thyroid cells via β-particle emission over 6–12 weeks.

Indications: Relapsed Graves’ disease after ATDs, Toxic Adenoma, and elderly/frail patients.

Contraindications: Pregnancy, lactation (absolute), young children, and active moderate-to-severe Graves’ ophthalmopathy (can worsen eye disease unless covered with oral prednisolone). Leads to eventual hypothyroidism in 80% of Graves’ patients.

C. Surgery (Total Thyroidectomy; or Hemithyroidectomy for Solitary Toxic Adenoma):

Indications: Large goitre with compressive symptoms, Toxic MNG, severe Graves’ ophthalmopathy, relapsed Graves’ disease in young women planning pregnancy, suspicion of coexisting malignancy, or drug intolerance/non-compliance.

Preoperative Preparation (Mandatory to prevent Thyrotoxic Crisis/Storm):

Render biochemically euthyroid with Carbimazole (until the evening before surgery).

β-Blockade (Propranolol 40 mg TDS) continued for 7 days postoperatively (as half-life of circulating T_4 is 7 days).

Lugol’s Iodine (5% iodine + 10% potassium iodide; 10 drops TDS orally for 10 days prior to surgery): Reduces gland vascularity and friability (Plummer’s effect) and transiently blocks hormone release (Wolff–Chaikoff effect).

Choice of Operation in Graves’ Disease (Table 55.5): Total Thyroidectomy is preferred over subtotal thyroidectomy as it provides immediate cure with 0% risk of recurrent toxicity (trading for predictable lifelong thyroxine replacement).

subject: surgery
title: Q6.5: Thyroid Malignancies (Papillary, Follicular, Medullary) & Complications of Thyroidectomy
text:
(Covers KU 25, 21, 20, 18, 17, 16, RGU, TU — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. Classification & Relative Incidence of Primary Thyroid Malignancies (Table 55.6 & 55.7):

Derived from Follicular Epithelium (Differentiated Thyroid Cancer - DTC):

Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC): 80%.

Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (FTC) & Hürthle Cell Carcinoma: 10%.

Derived from Follicular Epithelium (Poorly Differentiated / Undifferentiated):

Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma: 5%.

Derived from Parafollicular C-Cells (Neuroectodermal / Ultimobranchial body):

Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC): 2.5%.

Derived from Lymphoid Tissue:

Primary Thyroid Lymphoma (B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma arising in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis): 2.5%.

2. Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC) & Management of DTC with Nodal Metastasis (Long Essays KU 17, 18):

Etiology & Genetics: Childhood neck irradiation (e.g., Chernobyl disaster), RET/PTC1 and RET/PTC3 rearrangements, and BRAF V600E mutations.

Pathology:

Often multifocal and non-encapsulated; cystic change is common.

Diagnostic Microscopic Hallmarks: Papillary fronds with fibrovascular cores; “Orphan Annie eye” nuclei (optically clear, ground-glass chromatin with nuclear grooves and intranuclear cytoplasmic pseudoinclusions); and Psammoma bodies (concentric laminated calcified spherules).

Lymphatic Spread: Strong propensity for cervical lymph node metastasis (central compartment Level VI [Delphian/pretracheal/paratracheal] and lateral jugular chain Levels II, III, IV, V). (Note: An isolated cystic lateral neck node metastasis from an occult <1 cm papillary microcarcinoma was historically misnamed “Lateral Aberrant Thyroid”).

Risk Stratification (AMES / AGES / MACIS Criteria):

Age (<55 years vs ≥ 55 years in AJCC 8th Ed.), Metastases (distant), Extent (extrathyroidal invasion), Size (>4 cm), Grade, and Completeness of resection.

Management of Differentiated Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC & FTC):

1. Surgery for Primary Tumour:

Low-Risk Unifocal Tumour (1–4 cm, cN0, no extrathyroidal extension): Thyroid Lobectomy + Isthmusectomy. (Tumours <1 cm [Papillary microcarcinoma] can be managed by lobectomy or active surveillance).

High-Risk Tumour (>4 cm, extrathyroidal extension, multifocal/bilateral, or Node-Positive [as in Long Essays KU 17/18]): Total Thyroidectomy (removes all thyroid tissue to enable subsequent Radioiodine ablation and serum Thyroglobulin monitoring).

2. Management of Cervical Lymph Nodes:
