Clinically/Radiologically Node-Positive (cN1a / cN1b): Compartment-Oriented Therapeutic Neck Dissection (Central compartment Level VI clearance + Selective/Modified Radical Lateral Neck Dissection of Levels IIa, III, IV, and Vb, preserving the spinal accessory nerve, internal jugular vein, and sternocleidomastoid). “Berry-picking” of individual nodes is contraindicated.

Prophylactic Central Neck Dissection (Level VI): Reserved for high-risk T3/T4 tumours.

3. Postoperative Radioiodine (¹³¹I) Ablation:

Given 4–6 weeks post-total thyroidectomy (stimulated by either thyroxine withdrawal or recombinant human TSH [Thyrogen] so TSH >30 mU/L) to ablate residual thyroid remnants and microscopic metastases.

4. TSH Suppression Therapy:

High-dose Levothyroxine to suppress TSH below <0.1 mU/L in high-risk patients (since DTC cells are TSH-dependent).

5. Follow-Up: Serial Serum Thyroglobulin (Tg) (and anti-Tg antibodies) + Neck Ultrasonography every 6–12 months.

3. Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC) [KU 21, 16]:

Origin: Arises from parafollicular C-cells (neural crest origin via ultimobranchial body); does NOT concentrate radioiodine and is NOT TSH-dependent.

Clinical Forms: 75–80% Sporadic (unilateral) and 20–25% Familial (autosomal dominant RET proto-oncogene mutation on Chromosome 10; multicentric and bilateral):

Familial MTC (FMTC).

MEN 2A (Sipple’s Syndrome): MTC (100%) + Phaeochromocytoma (50%) + Parathyroid hyperplasia (20%).

MEN 2B: Aggressive early-onset MTC + Phaeochromocytoma + Mucosal neuromas + Marfanoid habitus.

Pathology & Clinical Features:

Histology: Sheets/nests (“cell balls”) of spindle/polygonal cells in an amyloid stroma (formed from procalcitonin polypeptides; stains apple-green birefringence with Congo Red). 

Secretes Calcitonin and Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA) (used for diagnosis and postoperative tumour marker surveillance), plus serotonin, prostaglandins, and VIP (causing flushing and secretory diarrhoea in 30%).

Early lymphatic (55–60%) and haematogenous spread.

Management:

Exclude Phaeochromocytoma first (check plasma/24h urinary metanephrines before any neck surgery) and check serum calcium/PTH and RET germline mutation.

Surgery: Total Thyroidectomy + Bilateral Central Compartment (Level VI) Neck Dissection (+ therapeutic lateral neck dissection if lateral nodes are involved).

Prophylactic Total Thyroidectomy in RET-positive children (within the first year of life for highest-risk MEN 2B codon 918 mutations; before age 5 for MEN 2A codon 634 mutations).

4. Complications Following Thyroid Surgery & Their Management [KU 25, 18, 17]:

1. Reactionary Postoperative Haemorrhage / Tense Neck Haematoma (1–2%, within first 24 hours):

Pathophysiology: Bleeding beneath the strap muscles raises central compartment pressure above venous pressure → severe venous and lymphatic laryngeal oedema → acute asphyxiation.

Management: Immediate bedside opening of the wound (clip/remove skin and strap muscle sutures using a stitch cutter to evacuate the clot and relieve laryngeal congestion) → high-flow oxygen → immediate transfer to theatre for endotracheal intubation and formal haemostasis.

2. Nerve Injuries:

Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve (RLN) Palsy (most vulnerable at Berry’s ligament, the inferior thyroid artery, and the tubercle of Zuckerkandl; permanent rate <1%):

Unilateral RLN Palsy: Causes hoarseness and a weak, “bovine” non-explosive cough. Managed conservatively with speech therapy for 6 months (as most are transient neuropraxia and the opposite cord compensates); if permanent, perform vocal cord medialisation (injection laryngoplasty or thyroplasty).

Bilateral RLN Palsy: Both vocal cords lie in the paramedian position → acute biphasic stridor and airway obstruction upon extubation. Requires immediate re-intubation or emergency tracheostomy, followed later by laser cordotomy/arytenoidectomy.

External Branch of Superior Laryngeal Nerve (EBSLN) Injury: Injured during high ligation of the superior thyroid pedicle. Paralyses the cricothyroid muscle (tensor of the vocal cord) → loss of high-pitched voice, easy voice fatiguability, and inability to project/sing (“voice of Amelita Galli-Curci”). Prevented by ligating superior pole vessels individually close to the thyroid capsule.

3. Postoperative Hypoparathyroidism / Hypocalcaemia (Transient 10–20%, Permanent <1–2%):

Cause: Inadvertent removal or ischaemic devascularisation of the parathyroid glands (supplied by end-arteries from the inferior thyroid artery).

Clinical Features (2–5 days post-op): Circumoral and digital tingling/numbness, carpopedal spasm (Trousseau’s sign), facial muscle twitching on tapping over the facial nerve (Chvostek’s sign), stridor (laryngospasm), and prolonged QT interval on ECG.

Management: Mild asymptomatic hypocalcaemia is treated with oral Calcium carbonate + Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D_3) (or Alfacalcidol). Acute symptomatic tetany requires slow intravenous 10 mL of 10% Calcium Gluconate over 10 minutes under ECG monitoring, followed by an infusion and correction of hypomagnesaemia.

4. Thyrotoxic Crisis (Thyroid Storm):

Cause: Acute life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism in an inadequately prepared thyrotoxic patient (or precipitated by infection/trauma).

Features: Hyperpyrexia (>40°C), severe tachycardia/atrial fibrillation, high-output cardiac failure, agitation, delirium, coma.

Management: ICU admission, active cooling (ice packs/paracetamol; avoid aspirin as it displaces T_4 from TBG), IV fluids, oxygen, IV Propranolol (1–2 mg) (or oral 40 mg 6-hourly), Propylthiouracil (or Carbimazole 20 mg 6-hourly), Lugol’s Iodine (10 drops 8-hourly, started 1 hour after ATD to prevent iodine from being used as substrate for new hormone synthesis), and IV Hydrocortisone (100 mg 6-hourly to block peripheral T_4 → T_3 conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency).

5. Late Complications: Hypothyroidism (100% after total thyroidectomy; 30% after lobectomy), wound infection, and hypertrophic/keloid scar.

subject: surgery
title: Q6.6: Thyroiditis & Lingual Thyroid
text:
(Covers KU 22, TU)

1. Thyroiditis (Classification & Features):

Hashimoto’s Thyroiditis (Chronic Lymphocytic / Autoimmune Thyroiditis):

Commonest cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas; Female:Male = 10–15:1 (ages 30–50).

Pathology: Diffuse Hurthle/Askanazy cell metaplasia, lymphoid follicles with germinal centres, acinar destruction, and fibrosis. 

Clinical Features: Firm, rubbery, diffusely enlarged, bosselated goitre; initially may have transient “Hashitoxicosis” followed by permanent hypothyroidism (myxoedema). Predisposes to Primary Thyroid MALT Lymphoma and PTC.

Diagnosis: High titres of Anti-TPO (>90%) and Anti-Thyroglobulin antibodies, elevated TSH, and lymphocytic thyroiditis on FNAC.

Treatment: Lifelong Levothyroxine replacement (surgery only for compressive symptoms or suspected malignancy).

De Quervain’s Thyroiditis (Subacute Granulomatous / Viral Thyroiditis):

Follows an upper respiratory viral infection in young women.

Presents with acute painful, tender thyroid swelling radiating to the jaw/ears, fever, malaise, markedly raised ESR, absent thyroid antibodies, and very low radioiodine uptake despite transient hyperthyroidism (due to release of preformed hormone from disrupted follicles). Self-limiting; treated with NSAIDs or Prednisolone (10–20 mg/day tapered over 4 weeks).

Riedel’s Thyroiditis (Invasive Fibrous Thyroiditis):

Rare IgG4-related fibroinflammatory disorder where dense woody fibrous tissue replaces the thyroid and invades through the capsule into strap muscles, carotid sheath, RLN, parathyroids, and trachea (associated with retroperitoneal and mediastinal fibrosis).

Mimics anaplastic carcinoma (stony hard, fixed goitre with stridor). Treated with core biopsy/wedge isthmusectomy to decompress the trachea, high-dose corticosteroids, Tamoxifen, and levothyroxine.

2. Lingual Thyroid:

Complete failure of descent of the median thyroid anlage leaves a rounded, reddish-blue mass at the base of the tongue (foramen caecum); in 70% of cases, it is the only functioning thyroid tissue present. Causes dysphagia, dysphonia, bleeding, or airway obstruction (enlarges during puberty/pregnancy). Confirmed by (99m)Tc / ¹²³I scan; treated with suppressive Levothyroxine (or ¹³¹I ablation / transoral excision if obstructive).

subject: surgery
title: Q7.1: Primary Hyperparathyroidism (Parathyroid Adenoma), Sestamibi Scan & Hypocalcaemia
text:
(Covers TU, RGU)

1. Surgical Anatomy & Physiology:

Four glands (30 mg each, “Portland brick” yellow-brown colour); all four are supplied by the Inferior Thyroid Artery.

Superior Parathyroids: Develop from the 4th pharyngeal pouch; constant position (80% lie within a 2 cm circle centred 1 cm above the intersection of the inferior thyroid artery and RLN at the cricothyroid junction).

Inferior Parathyroids: Develop from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch along with the thymus (longer descent = more variable position; >50% lie near the lower pole of the thyroid or within the thyrothymic tract). 

PTH Action: Increases serum Ca²⁺ and decreases serum PO_4³⁻ by: (i) stimulating osteoclast bone resorption, (ii) increasing distal renal tubular Ca²⁺ reabsorption and proximal tubular phosphate excretion, and (iii) activating renal 1α-hydroxylase to convert 25(OH)D → 1,25(OH)_2D_3 (increasing intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption).

2. Etiology & Pathology of Primary Hyperparathyroidism (PHPT):

Single Parathyroid Adenoma: 80–85% (double adenoma in 2–4%).

Four-Gland Hyperplasia: 15% (associated with MEN 1, MEN 2A, MEN 4, and chronic Lithium therapy).

Parathyroid Carcinoma: 1% (associated with HRPT2/CDC73 gene mutation [loss of parafibromin staining] and Hyperparathyroidism–Jaw Tumour [HPT-JT] syndrome; presents with palpable neck mass and severe hypercalcaemia >3.5 mmol/L).

3. Clinical Features:

Asymptomatic Hypercalcaemia (70–80% in modern practice): Detected incidentally on routine biochemistry or DEXA scan.

Classical Symptomatic Pentad: “Bones, Stones, Abdominal Groans, Psychic Moans, and Fatigue Overtones”:

Skeletal: Osteopenia/osteoporosis (preferentially affecting cortical bone of the distal third of the radius), subperiosteal bone resorption of phalanges, tapering of distal clavicles, “salt and pepper” skull, and Osteitis fibrosa cystica (Brown tumours).

Renal (commonest symptomatic manifestation — 15–20%): Recurrent calcium oxalate/phosphate renal calculi, nephrocalcinosis, polyuria/polydipsia.

Gastrointestinal: Peptic ulceration (calcium stimulates gastrin release), acute/chronic pancreatitis, constipation, cholelithiasis.

Neuropsychiatric & Cardiovascular: Depression, lethargy, confusion, proximal muscle weakness, hypertension, shortened QT interval, and band keratopathy of the cornea.

4. Diagnosis & Localisation Studies:

1. Biochemical Diagnosis (Mandatory First Step — “Imaging never diagnoses PHPT”):

Elevated total and ionised serum Calcium + inappropriately elevated or unsuppressed intact PTH.

Low serum Phosphate, elevated serum alkaline phosphatase, normal vitamin D, and 24-hour urinary calcium >400 mg/day (with urinary calcium:creatinine clearance ratio >0.02; a ratio <0.01 indicates Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcaemia [FHH], where surgery is contraindicated).

2. Preoperative Localisation Studies (To guide Minimally Invasive Parathyroidectomy): 

Technetium-99m Sestamibi ((99m)Tc-MIBI) Scintigraphy with SPECT (Short Note [TU]):

Principle: Sestamibi is a lipophilic cationic radiotracer that concentrates in mitochondria-rich oxyphil cells of hyperfunctioning parathyroid adenomas. On dual-phase imaging (15 min and 2 hours post-injection), normal thyroid tissue washes out the tracer rapidly, whereas a parathyroid adenoma shows delayed retention/persistent hot spot (Sensitivity 79%, PPV 91%). 

High-Resolution Neck Ultrasonography: Identifies oval hypoechoic adenomas posterior to the thyroid and evaluates coexisting thyroid nodules (Sensitivity 76%, PPV 93%).

Four-Dimensional Computed Tomography (4D-CT): Uses non-contrast, arterial, and delayed venous phases (4th dimension = time/perfusion); parathyroid adenomas show rapid arterial enhancement and rapid washout compared with lymph nodes or thyroid. Ideal when USG and Sestamibi are discordant or negative.

5. Management:

Indications for Surgery: All symptomatic patients, and Asymptomatic patients meeting any of the NIH/Fourth International Workshop Criteria (Table 56.2):

Serum calcium >0.25 mmol/L (>1.0 mg/dL) above the upper limit of normal.

Skeletal: DEXA T-score ≤ -2.5 at lumbar spine, hip, or distal 1/3 radius, or vertebral fracture.

Renal: eGFR <60 mL/min, 24-hour urinary calcium >400 mg/day, or nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis on imaging.

Age <50 years.

Surgical Approaches:

Concordant USG + Sestamibi (Single Adenoma): Minimally Invasive (Focused) Parathyroidectomy (MIP) through a <3 cm incision. Intraoperative PTH (ioPTH) monitoring using the Miami Criteria (a >50% drop in plasma PTH from the highest pre-excision value at 10 minutes post-excision into the normal range confirms cure, as PTH half-life is 3–5 minutes). 

Discordant/Negative Imaging or Familial/Multigland Disease (MEN 1/2A): Bilateral Four-Gland Neck Exploration with either Subtotal (3(1/2)-gland) Parathyroidectomy (leaving half of the most normal inferior gland marked with a non-absorbable clip/suture) or Total Parathyroidectomy with Forearm Autotransplantation (into brachioradialis pockets) + Cervical Thymectomy.

Medical Management (for unfit patients or Hypercalcaemic Crisis [Ca²⁺ >3.5 mmol/L]):

Acute Crisis: Aggressive IV 0.9% Normal Saline hydration (200–500 mL/h) + loop diuretic (Furosemide after volume restoration) + IV Bisphosphonates (Zoledronic acid/Pamidronate) + Calcitonin.

Chronic Medical Therapy: Cinacalcet (calcimimetic that increases sensitivity of the parathyroid Calcium-Sensing Receptor [CaSR]), Bisphosphonates, or Denosumab.

6. Trousseau’s Sign & Hypocalcaemia [RGU, TU]:

Trousseau’s Sign of Latent Tetany: Inflating a sphygmomanometer cuff on the upper arm 20 mmHg above systolic blood pressure for 3 minutes induces ischaemia of the ulnar/median nerves, provoking carpopedal spasm (“obstetrician’s hand” / main d’accoucheur): flexion at the wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints, extension of the interphalangeal joints, and adduction of the thumb (94% sensitive and 99% specific for hypocalcaemia).

title: Q7.2: Phaeochromocytoma, Neuroblastoma & Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) Syndromes
text:
(Covers KU 24, 15, RGU, TU — Short Answers)

1. Phaeochromocytoma & Paraganglioma (PPGL) [KU 24, 15, TU]:

Definition: Neuroectodermal catecholamine-secreting tumours arising from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla (Phaeochromocytoma — PCC) or extra-adrenal autonomic ganglia (Paraganglioma — PGL, commonest at the Organ of Zuckerkandl near the inferior mesenteric artery origin).

Traditional “Rule of 10s” (and Modern Genetics): ~10% extra-adrenal, 10% bilateral, 10% malignant, 10% in children. Today, 25–30% are hereditary: MEN 2A/2B (RET gene), Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease, Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1), and Hereditary PGL Syndromes (SDHB, SDHD succinate dehydrogenase mutations — SDHB carries a 34–97% risk of malignancy).

Clinical Features: Classic paroxysmal triad of episodic throbbing headache, profuse sweating, and palpitations (90% specific in the presence of an adrenal mass), with sustained or paroxysmal hypertension, pallor, anxiety, tremor, and hyperglycaemia. Precipitated by exercise, abdominal palpation, anaesthetic induction, or unopposed β-blockers.

Stepwise Diagnosis & Management:

Biochemical Confirmation First: Elevated Plasma Free Metanephrines (99% sensitive) and/or 24-hour Urinary Fractionated Metanephrines (97% sensitive). (Biopsy of a suspected PCC is strictly contraindicated).

Anatomical & Functional Localisation: Contrast CT or MRI abdomen (shows a vascular adrenal mass with central necrosis, bright “light-bulb” T2 hyperintensity on MRI, >10 HU on non-contrast CT). 

Functional imaging with ¹²³I-MIBG (meta-iodobenzylguanidine) scintigraphy, ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT, or ¹⁸F-FDOPA PET for extra-adrenal, bilateral, or metastatic disease.

Mandatory Preoperative Pharmacological Preparation (Reduces mortality from 45% to <3%):

Step 1 — α-Adrenergic Blockade: Start non-competitive irreversible α-blocker Phenoxybenzamine (10 mg BD, increased by 10–20 mg/day up to 100–160 mg/day for 10–14 days) or selective α_1-blocker Doxazosin alongside high oral salt and fluid intake to expand contracted intravascular volume until orthostatic hypotension and nasal stuffiness are achieved.

Step 2 — β-Adrenergic Blockade (Propranolol / Atenolol): Added ONLY AFTER adequate α-blockade is established to control reflex tachycardia/arrhythmias. (Giving a β-blocker first abolishes β_2-mediated skeletal muscle vasodilation, leaving unopposed α_1-vasoconstriction → fatal hypertensive crisis and pulmonary oedema).

Surgical Treatment: Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy (transperitoneal or posterior retroperitoneoscopic approach) with early ligation of the adrenal vein and minimal tumour manipulation (Open resection for tumours >8–10 cm or locally invasive malignant PCC). Watch for sudden hypotension and hypoglycaemia after adrenal vein ligation.

2. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) Syndromes [KU 24, RGU, TU]:

[[TABLE:surgery-tbl-004]]

3. Neuroblastoma [TU]:

Commonest extracranial solid malignancy of infancy/childhood (75% present <2 years of age); arises from neural crest neuroblasts in the adrenal medulla (40%) or sympathetic chain.

Clinical Features: Large irregular abdominal mass that crosses the midline (unlike Wilms’ tumour), weight loss, periorbital ecchymoses (“raccoon eyes” from orbital metastases), bone pain, Pepper syndrome (massive liver metastases), Hutchinson syndrome (skull/bone metastases), or opsoclonus–myoclonus.

Diagnosis & Prognosis: Elevated 24-hour urinary VMA / HVA / metanephrines; CT/MRI + ¹²³I-MIBG scan; bone marrow aspirate and biopsy (small round blue cells with Homer-Wright rosettes). MYCN oncogene amplification (present in 25%), age >18 months, and 1p/11q deletion predict poor prognosis. Treated by risk-stratified surgery ± multiagent chemotherapy.

subject: surgery
title: Q8.1: Triple Assessment, BI-RADS, Benign Breast Diseases (ANDI, Mastalgia, Fibroadenoma, Phyllodes Tumour, Breast Abscess & Nipple Discharge)
text:
(Covers KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 20, 19, 17, 16, RGU, TU — Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. Triple Assessment of a Breast Lump [KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 19]:

Every patient presenting with a breast symptom/lump is evaluated systematically by combining three modalities (Diagnostic accuracy and Positive Predictive Value >99.9% when concordant): 

Clinical Assessment: Detailed history (duration, pain, nipple discharge, menstrual/obstetric history, family history) + systematic bimanual Clinical Breast Examination (inspection in 4 postures + palpation of all four quadrants, subareolar region, axillary tail, and regional lymph nodes using the flat pads of the fingers).

Radiological Imaging:

Ultrasonography (First-line in women <35–40 years with dense breasts): Distinguishes cystic from solid lesions and evaluates axillary lymph nodes.

Mammography (First-line in women ≥ 35–40 years): Two views (Craniocaudal [CC] and Mediolateral Oblique [MLO]) using low-voltage, high-amperage X-rays (~ 1 mGy radiation). Mammographic signs of malignancy: irregular spiculated mass, clustered pleomorphic/branching microcalcifications, and architectural distortion. 

Pathological Tissue Sampling: Image-guided Large-Diameter Core Needle Biopsy (14G Tru-Cut needle) under local anaesthesia (preferred over FNAC as it distinguishes in situ from invasive cancer and allows ER, PR, HER2/neu, and Ki-67 immunohistochemistry).

2. BI-RADS (Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System) Grading (Table 58.1) [KU 17]:

BI-RADS 0: Incomplete assessment → Requires additional imaging.

BI-RADS 1: Negative / Normal (0% malignancy) → Routine screening.

BI-RADS 2: Benign finding (e.g., simple cyst, calcified fibroadenoma; 0% malignancy) → Routine screening.

BI-RADS 3: Probably benign (e.g., typical fibroadenoma; ≤ 2% malignancy) → Short-interval (6-month) imaging follow-up.

BI-RADS 4: Suspicious abnormality (4a: Low 2–10%; 4b: Moderate 10–50%; 4c: High 50–95% malignancy) → Core needle biopsy indicated.

BI-RADS 5: Highly suggestive of malignancy (≥ 95% probability) → Biopsy mandatory.

BI-RADS 6: Known biopsy-proven malignancy prior to definitive therapy.

3. ANDI (Aberrations of Normal Development and Involution) Concept [KU 22, RGU, TU]:

Formulated by Hughes, Mansel & Webster (Cardiff Breast Clinic) to replace confusing historical terms like “fibroadenosis” or “fibrocystic disease”. Most benign breast conditions arise from physiological responses of the Terminal Ductal Lobular Unit (TDLU) to cyclical hormones across three reproductive phases:

[[TABLE:surgery-tbl-005]]

4. Mastalgia (Breast Pain) (Table 58.2) [KU 22, TU]:

Classification:

Cyclical Mastalgia (2/3 of cases): Bilateral diffuse heaviness/pain (worst in upper outer quadrants) starting at ovulation (day 14), peaking premenstrually, and relieved by menses.

Non-Cyclical Mastalgia: Unilateral, well-localised (“trigger spot”) pain unrelated to menses, occurring pre- or postmenopausally (due to duct ectasia, periductal mastitis, cysts, or sclerosing adenosis).

Extramammary (Referred) Pain: Tietze’s syndrome (painful costochondral junction), lateral chest wall muscular pain, angina, or cervical radiculopathy.

Management:

Perform Triple Assessment to exclude cancer → Firm Reassurance (resolves symptoms in 85% of women) + record a Daily Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) Breast Pain Chart for 1 month.

First-Line Conservative Measures: Well-fitting supportive sports brassiere, dietary Flaxseed (30 g/day) or Evening Primrose Oil, and Topical NSAID gel (Diclofenac / Piroxicam QDS).

Second-Line Systemic Therapy (for severe pain VAS >3/10):

Ormeloxifene (Centchroman) 30 mg twice weekly for 3–6 months (selective oestrogen receptor modulator widely used in India for mastalgia and benign nodularity/fibroadenoma).

Low-dose Tamoxifen (10 mg daily for 3–6 months).

Danazol (100–200 mg daily) or LHRH agonists (Goserelin) for refractory cases.

5. Fibroadenoma (“Breast Mouse”) [RGU, TU]:

Arises from hyperplasia of a single lobule (TDLU) in women aged 15–25 years. Firm, smooth, well-circumscribed, painless lump (1–3 cm) that slips readily beneath the examining fingers (“breast mouse”).

Pathology: Benign proliferation of both stromal fibrous tissue and epithelial ducts (pericanalicular vs intracanalicular types).

Management: In women <25 years with typical clinical/USG features (BI-RADS 3), conservative observation or medical therapy with Ormeloxifene is safe. Indications for Surgical Excision (Enucleation): Age >30 years, size >5 cm (Giant fibroadenoma — excised via a submammary Gaillard Thomas incision), rapid growth, suspicious USG features, complex histology, or patient anxiety.

6. Phyllodes Tumour (Serocystic Disease of Brodie / formerly Cystosarcoma Phyllodes) [KU 24, 23, 20, RGU, TU]:

Pathology: A fibroepithelial tumour with leaf-like (Greek: phyllon = leaf) clefts lined by epithelium and a hypercellular mesenchymal spindle-cell stroma. Classified by stromal atypia, margins, and mitotic count into:

Benign (<4 mitoses/10 HPF).

Borderline (4–9 mitoses/10 HPF).

Malignant (≥ 10 mitoses/10 HPF, sarcomatous stromal overgrowth, infiltrative margins).

Clinical Features:

Occurs in women aged 35–55 years (10–20 years older than fibroadenoma).

Presents as a rapidly growing, large, painless, bosselated mass with stretched, shiny overlying skin and prominent engorged subcutaneous veins. 

Despite massive size and occasional pressure necrosis/ulceration of the skin, it remains mobile over the chest wall, does not cause nipple retraction/peau d’orange, and rarely metastasises to axillary lymph nodes (malignant phyllodes spreads haematogenously to the lungs).

Management:

Wide Local Excision with a 1–2 cm margin of normal breast tissue (simple enucleation is strictly contraindicated due to high local recurrence).

Simple Mastectomy (without axillary lymph node dissection) is indicated for massive tumours (unfavourable tumour-to-breast ratio), recurrent tumours, or malignant phyllodes tumours, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy for malignant/recurrent cases.

7. Breast Abscess & Antibioma [KU 19, RGU, TU]:

Lactational Breast Abscess: Caused by Staphylococcus aureus entering via a cracked nipple or milk stasis (peaks in the first month of primiparous lactation and at weaning).

Management: Support the breast, continue 2-hourly breastfeeding/expression, give anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (Flucloxacillin / Co-amoxiclav / Erythromycin), and perform Ultrasound-Guided Needle Aspiration (for abscesses <3 cm) or Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Suction Catheter Drainage (for abscesses >3 cm or >30 mL pus) with saline irrigation.

 (Open incision and drainage is avoided unless skin is necrotic, as it causes ugly scars and milk fistulae).

Non-Lactational (Subareolar) Abscess: Occurs in young female smokers due to Periductal Mastitis and squamous metaplasia of major lactiferous ducts; ruptures at the areolar margin to form a Mammary Duct Fistula with transverse slit-like nipple retraction. Treated with antibiotics + metronidazole, smoking cessation, and Hadfield’s Major Duct Excision once acute sepsis settles. 

Antibioma (Short Note [KU 19]):

When a formed breast abscess is inappropriately treated with prolonged courses of antibiotics without draining the pus, the pus becomes sterile and inspissated, surrounded by a thick, dense, fibrous reactive wall.

Clinically, it forms a painless, hard, fixed breast lump with skin tethering that closely mimics breast carcinoma. Diagnosed by USG and core biopsy; treated by evacuation or surgical excision.

8. Evaluation & Management of Abnormal Nipple Discharge [KU 16, RGU, TU]:

Pathological Discharge (“The 4 S’s”): Single-duct, SCompletion Status: 65% Complete.** (Sections 1 to 7 are 100% complete, and Section 8 [Breast] is 50% complete. Now completing the remainder of Section 8 [Breast Cancer], Section 9 [Venous Disorders], and Section 10 [Arterial Disorders] to reach 100% completion well within your page target).

(Continuing from Section 8, Q8.1, Point 8: Evaluation & Management of Abnormal Nipple Discharge…)

8. Evaluation & Management of Abnormal Nipple Discharge [KU 16, RGU, TU]:

Pathological Discharge (“The 4 S’s”): Single-duct, Spontaneous, Serous (clear/straw-coloured) or Sanguineous (bloodstained) discharge (Summary Box 58.2).

Causes by Character of Discharge:

Bloodstained or Serous (Single Duct): Solitary Intraductal Papilloma (commonest cause — located within 5 cm of the nipple), Ductal Carcinoma in situ (DCIS) / Invasive Ductal Carcinoma, or Duct ectasia.

Thick, Multicoloured (Green, Black, Muddy, or Cheesy from Multiple Ducts): Duct Ectasia (benign disorder of involution; dilated subareolar ducts >3 mm filled with inspissated debris).

Purulent Discharge: Periductal Mastitis.

Bilateral Milky Discharge (Galactorrhoea): Hyperprolactinaemia (prolactinoma, hypothyroidism, or dopamine-antagonist drugs like metoclopramide, haloperidol, chlorpromazine).

Surface Serosanguineous Exudate: Paget’s Disease of the Nipple or eczema.

Evaluation & Management:

Triple Assessment: Clinical examination (locate the “trigger point” quadrant that expresses discharge on radial pressure), High-Resolution Subareolar Ultrasonography (85% accuracy in visualising intraductal papillomas or dilated ducts) + Mammography, and core biopsy if any mass is present. (Nipple discharge cytology has poor sensitivity and is largely abandoned).

Surgical Treatment (Indicated for persistent single-duct bloody/serous discharge, especially in women >40 years):

Single-Duct Discharge: Microdochectomy (cannulate the offending duct orifice with a lacrimal probe or nylon suture → circumareolar incision → excise a 2–5 cm length of the single terminal lactiferous duct for histology).

Multiduct Discharge / Severe Duct Ectasia: Hadfield’s Operation (Radical Subareolar Major Mammary Duct Excision): Excision of the entire cone of major lactiferous ducts beneath the nipple–areola complex.

9. Gynaecomastia [KU 17, RGU, TU]:

Definition: Benign proliferation of glandular ductal and stromal tissue of the male breast (forming a firm, rubbery, mobile subareolar disc >2 cm), resulting from an increased Oestrogen-to-Androgen ratio. Must be differentiated from pseudogynaecomastia (fatty deposition in obesity without a palpable subareolar fibrous disc) and male breast cancer (eccentric, painless, hard, fixed mass with nipple retraction/ulceration).

Etiology:

Physiological (Trimodal peaks): Neonatal (transplacental maternal oestrogens), Pubertal (ages 12–15; regresses spontaneously within 1–2 years in 90%), and Senescent (>60 years due to falling free testosterone and peripheral aromatisation of androgens in adipose tissue).

Pathological:

Drugs (“DISCO”): Digoxin, Isoniazid, Spironolactone (commonest), Cimetidine, Oestrogens/anti-androgens (Finasteride, Flutamide, Ketoconazole, Calcium channel blockers, Marijuana, Anabolic steroids).

Liver Cirrhosis (impaired hepatic metabolism of oestrogens).

Chronic Renal Failure & Thyrotoxicosis.

Testicular Deficiency (Hypogonadism): Klinefelter’s syndrome (47,XXY) (carries a 20–50-fold increased risk of male breast cancer), mumps orchitis, cryptorchidism.

Hormone-Secreting Tumours: Leydig/Sertoli cell testicular tumours, hCG-secreting germ cell tumours, adrenocortical feminising tumours.

Simon’s Classification: Grade I: Minor enlargement, no skin excess; Grade IIa: Moderate enlargement, no skin excess; Grade IIb: Moderate enlargement with minor skin excess; Grade III: Gross enlargement with marked ptosis and skin excess (resembling a female breast).

Management:

Exclude testicular tumour (palpate testes + scrotal USG), check LFTs, RFTs, TFTs, serum Testosterone, Oestradiol, LH, FSH, β-hCG, and Prolactin, and perform breast USG/mammogram (+ core biopsy if suspicious of cancer).

Medical: Withdraw offending drugs; reassure in pubertal cases; trial of Tamoxifen (10–20 mg daily for 3–6 months) or Danazol gives relief in painful, recent-onset florid gynaecomastia.

Surgical (for longstanding fibrotic gynaecomastia >12 months or cosmetic distress): Subcutaneous Mastectomy (Webster’s intra-areolar incision) preserving a 5 mm subareolar button to prevent “saucer deformity”, combined with Liposuction (or concentric skin reduction for Grade III).

subject: surgery
title: Q8.2: Carcinoma of the Breast (Risk Factors, Staging, Screening, Early vs Locally Advanced Management, BCT, SLNB & Adjuvant Therapy)
text:
(Covers KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 20, 19, 18, 16, RGU, TU — All 8 Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. Additional History & Risk Factors in a Patient with a Breast Lump (Table 58.3) [KU 25, 21]:

History to Elicit:

Lump: Duration, rate of growth, pain, skin dimpling/ulceration, nipple retraction or bloody discharge, and axillary swelling.

Metastatic Symptoms: Bone pain (back/femur), persistent cough/haemoptysis/dyspnoea, jaundice/right upper quadrant pain, headache/seizures.

Reproductive & Risk Factor History:

Non-Modifiable Risk Factors: Female sex (100:1), increasing age (median age in India is 48 years vs 60 years in the West), Early menarche (<12 years), Late menopause (>55 years), Family history (1st-degree relative doubles risk), Hereditary mutations (BRCA1 [Chr 17q21; TNBC], BRCA2 [Chr 13q12], TP53 [Li–Fraumeni], PTEN [Cowden]), and prior biopsy showing atypical ductal/lobular hyperplasia (RR 4–5x) or LCIS (RR 8–10x).

Modifiable Risk Factors: Nulliparity or first full-term pregnancy >35 years, lack of breastfeeding, postmenopausal obesity (BMI >30), combined Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT >10 years), alcohol, smoking, and prior mantle chest irradiation.

2. Pathology & Molecular Classification (Table 58.4):

Histological Types: Invasive Carcinoma of No Special Type (NST / Invasive Ductal Carcinoma — 80–90%), Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (10% — cells in “Indian-file” linear cords due to loss of E-cadherin; often multifocal/bilateral), and favourable special types (Tubular, Mucinous/Colloid, Medullary, Papillary). Graded by the Modified Scarff–Bloom–Richardson System (Tubule formation + Nuclear pleomorphism + Mitotic count = Score 3–9 → Grades I, II, III).

Molecular Subtypes (Surrogate IHC Classification):

Luminal A: ER+ and/or PR+, HER2/neu–, Low Ki-67 (<14%) → Best prognosis; endocrine responsive.

Luminal B: ER+ and/or PR+, HER2/neu– (or +) with High Ki-67 → Intermediate prognosis; requires chemotherapy + endocrine therapy.

HER2/neu-Enriched: ER–, PR–, HER2/neu+ (3+ on IHC or FISH amplified) → Aggressive, responds dramatically to anti-HER2 targeted therapy (Trastuzumab + Pertuzumab).

Basal-Like / Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC): ER–, PR–, HER2/neu– → Aggressive biology, common in young Indian women and BRCA1 carriers; treated with systemic chemotherapy (anthracyclines, taxanes, platinums) and immunotherapy.

3. Clinical Manifestations & Staging of Case Scenarios (AJCC 8th Edition — Table 58.6):

Local Signs Supporting Diagnosis of Carcinoma: Stony hard consistency, irregular surface and ill-defined margins, fixity to overlying skin (dimpling due to traction on Cooper’s ligaments, or peau d’orange due to subdermal lymphatic permeation/obstruction), recent circumferential nipple retraction, fixity to pectoralis major (tested by contracting pectoralis major with hands pressing on hips) or chest wall, and hard axillary lymphadenopathy. 

TNM Summary & Case Scenario Staging:

T-Stage: Tis (DCIS or Paget’s without mass); T1 (≤ 2 cm); T2 (>2 cm to ≤ 5 cm); T3 (>5 cm); T4a (invasion of chest wall: ribs, intercostal muscles, serratus anterior — note: pectoralis muscle invasion alone does NOT make it T4a); T4b (peau d’orange, skin ulceration, or ipsilateral satellite skin nodules); T4c (T4a + T4b); T4d (Inflammatory Carcinoma — diffuse erythema and peau d’orange involving ≥ 1/3 of the breast skin; dermal lymphatic emboli on biopsy).

N-Stage: cN0 (no palpable nodes); cN1 (mobile ipsilateral Level I/II axillary nodes); cN2a (fixed/matted Level I/II axillary nodes); cN2b (internal mammary nodes only); cN3a (infraclavicular Level III nodes); cN3b (axillary + internal mammary nodes); cN3c (supraclavicular nodes).

Application to Exam Scenarios:

3 × 2 cm or 4 × 3 cm lump + single mobile axillary node [KU 24, 21]: cT2 N1 M0 (Stage IIB — Early Breast Cancer).

3 × 3 cm lump with no nodes [KU 20]: cT2 N0 M0 (Stage IIA — Early Breast Cancer).

6 × 5 cm lump adherent to skin [KU 16] or 3 × 3 cm lump with peau d’orange and N1 node [RGU]: cT3 N0 M0 (Stage IIB) or cT4b N1 M0 (Stage IIIB — Locally Advanced Breast Cancer [LABC]).

4. Diagnostic & Staging Investigations:

Triple Assessment: Clinical Exam + Bilateral Mammography & Breast/Axillary Ultrasonography + USG-Guided Core Needle Biopsy (14G) of the primary lump for histopathology, grade, and ER, PR, HER2/neu, and Ki-67 status (+ USG-guided FNAC/18G core biopsy of any suspicious axillary node).

Metastatic Staging Work-Up:

Early Breast Cancer (Stage I & II: T1–T2, N0–N1): Routine baseline FBC, LFTs, RFTs, Serum Alkaline Phosphatase, and Chest X-ray. Cross-sectional metastatic imaging is only done if symptomatic or ALP is elevated.

Locally Advanced Breast Cancer (Stage III: T3, T4, or N2–N3): Mandatory Contrast-Enhanced CT of Thorax, Abdomen & Pelvis + Isotope Bone Scan (or whole-body ¹⁸F-FDG PET-CT).

5. Screening for Breast Cancer [KU 16]:

Population Screening (High-income countries): Mammography every 2–3 years for asymptomatic women aged 50–70 years (reduces breast cancer mortality by 20–25%).

Indian Guidelines (ICMR / MoHFW / ASOMA): Because median age in India is younger (48 years) and population mammography is not cost-effective nationwide, screening comprises Breast Health Awareness + Annual Clinical Breast Examination (CBE) by trained health workers for women aged 30–65 years, combined with opportunistic biennial Mammography after age 40–45.

High-Risk Screening (BRCA1/2 carriers or prior chest radiation): Annual Contrast Breast MRI + Mammography starting from age 25–30 years.

6. Multimodal Management of Breast Cancer:

A. Management of Early Breast Cancer (Stage I, IIA, IIB [T1–T2, N0–N1]):

Primary Surgery followed by Adjuvant Systemic & Radiation Therapy (Note: Upfront Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy + Targeted Therapy is preferred even in T2/N1 Early Breast Cancer if it is HER2/neu-positive or Triple-Negative, or to downsize a large T2 tumour to enable Breast Conservation Surgery).

1. Surgical Options for the Breast: 

Option A — Breast Conservation Therapy (BCT = Breast Conservation Surgery [BCS] + Whole-Breast Radiotherapy):

Evidence: NSABP B-06 and Milan trials proved identical 20-year overall survival between BCT and Mastectomy.

Technique: Wide Local Excision (WLE / Lumpectomy) excising the tumour with a 1 cm macroscopic rim to achieve histologically negative margins (“no ink on tumour” for invasive cancer; ≥ 2 mm margin for DCIS). Specimen is oriented with sutures (Short Superior, Long Lateral), metallic clips are placed in the tumour cavity for radiotherapy boost targeting, and the defect is closed via Level I (Volume Displacement) or Level II (Volume Replacement) Oncoplasty. 

(Historical Note — QUART Therapy [KU 18]: Described by Umberto Veronesi in the Milan I Trial = QUadrantectomy + Axillary lymph node dissection + RadioTherapy).

Contraindications to BCS: Multicentric disease (tumours in ≥ 2 quadrants), diffuse malignant microcalcifications on mammogram, persistent positive margins after re-excision, prior chest wall irradiation, active scleroderma/SLE, and first/second trimester pregnancy (if RT must be delayed).

Option B — Mastectomy (with Immediate or Delayed Breast Reconstruction):

Simple (Total) Mastectomy (when combined with SLNB) or Modified Radical Mastectomy (MRM) (when combined with Level I–II/III Axillary Lymph Node Dissection: Patey’s MRM excises pectoralis minor; Auchincloss MRM retracts/preserves pectoralis minor; Scanlon’s MRM divides pectoralis minor at its coracoid insertion and resutures it).

Reconstruction Options: Silicone implant (prepectoral or subpectoral) or autologous flaps (Pedicled Latissimus Dorsi flap, TRAM flap, or free microvascular DIEP flap [gold standard]). 

2. Surgical Management of the Axilla:

Clinically & Ultrasound Node-Negative (cN0) → Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) [KU 22, 19]:

Principle: The sentinel node is the first echelon lymph node(s) (usually in the anterior pectoral group) receiving lymphatic drainage from the tumour.

Technique: Dual-tracer technique (peritumoral/subareolar injection of Technetium-99m sulfur colloid + Methylene blue / Patent blue dye, or Indocyanine green [ICG] / Fluorescein fluorescence). All “hot” nodes (with >10% of the ex vivo gamma count of the hottest node), “blue” nodes, and palpably suspicious nodes are excised and examined by frozen section or paraffin histology.

Management of SLNB Result: If SLNB is negative (or has micrometastasis ≤ 2 mm, or 1–2 positive nodes in T1/T2 patients undergoing BCT with whole-breast irradiation as per ACOSOG Z0011 trial), ALND is omitted, sparing the patient from upper limb lymphoedema, intercostobrachial nerve numbness, and shoulder stiffness. If ≥ 3 sentinel nodes are positive, proceed to Level I & II Axillary Lymph Node Dissection (ALND).

Clinically or Biopsy-Proven Node-Positive (cN+) → Level I & II (and Level III if grossly involved) Axillary Lymph Node Dissection (ALND): Preserving the axillary vein, long thoracic nerve of Bell (to serratus anterior — injury causes winging of scapula), and thoracodorsal neurovascular bundle (to latissimus dorsi).

B. Management of Locally Advanced Breast Cancer (LABC — Stage III: T3, T4a–d, N2, N3):

Step 1 — Neoadjuvant Systemic Therapy (NAST / NACT) [TU]:

Administer 6–8 cycles of Anthracycline (AC/FEC) + Taxane chemotherapy (+ Trastuzumab & Pertuzumab if HER2+).

Before starting NACT: If BCS is contemplated, place a radio-opaque metallic clip (or a 0.5 cm sterile PVC catheter segment in resource-limited settings) into the tumour centre under USG guidance to mark the tumour bed in case of a complete response.

Response Assessment (RECIST Criteria after 2 cycles): Complete Response (CR), Partial Response (PR ≥ 30% reduction), Stable Disease (SD), or Progressive Disease (PD).

Step 2 — Locoregional Surgery: Modified Radical Mastectomy (MRM) (mandatory for T4d Inflammatory Breast Cancer and persistent T4 skin/chest wall disease) or BCS (in T3/T4b patients who downsize well to NACT).

Step 3 — Adjuvant Locoregional Radiotherapy (Chest wall + supraclavicular fossa + internal mammary nodes) + Adjuvant Endocrine / Targeted Therapy.

C. Summary of Adjuvant Systemic & Radiation Therapy:

Adjuvant Radiotherapy (40 Gy in 15 hypofractionated fractions over 3 weeks): Mandatory for all patients after BCS, and post-mastectomy for T3/T4 (≥ 5 cm) tumours, node-positive disease, positive margins, or high-grade/LVI+ tumours.

Adjuvant Chemotherapy: Indicated for node-positive, TNBC, HER2+, Luminal B, or high-risk ER+/HER2– tumours (guided by the 21-gene Oncotype DX Recurrence Score [>25 benefits from chemo] and Nottingham Prognostic Index [NPI] = [0.2 × Size in cm] + Node stage (1–3) + Grade (1–3)).

Adjuvant Targeted Therapy: Trastuzumab (Herceptin) ± Pertuzumab for 1 year in all HER2/neu-positive tumours (>5 mm).

Adjuvant Endocrine Therapy (for all ER+ and/or PR+ tumours for 5–10 years):

Premenopausal Women: Tamoxifen (20 mg daily for 5–10 years) (Selective Oestrogen Receptor Modulator [SERM]: antagonist in breast, partial agonist in bone [prevents osteoporosis] and endometrium [side effects: hot flushes, endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma (1%), deep vein thrombosis, and cataracts]).

Postmenopausal Women: Aromatase Inhibitors (Anastrozole 1 mg, Letrozole 2.5 mg, or Exemestane 25 mg daily) — block peripheral conversion of adrenal androgens to oestrone/oestradiol by inhibiting aromatase in adipose tissue. Superior to Tamoxifen in postmenopausal women; main side effect is osteoporosis/arthralgia (requires baseline DEXA scan + calcium/vitamin D/bisphosphonates).

title: Q9.1: Varicose Veins & Venous Leg Ulcer (Anatomy, Pathophysiology, CEAP, Investigations, Endovenous & Surgical Management)
text:
(Covers KU 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, 16, 15, RGU, TU — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. Definition & Surgical Anatomy:

Definition: Dilated (≥ 3 mm), tortuous, elongated subcutaneous veins of the lower limb with valvular incompetence (retrograde reflux ≥ 0.5 seconds).

Two Superficial Venous Axes (Lying within the Saphenous Envelope between the saphenous fascia and deep fascia lata):

Great Saphenous Vein (GSV): Begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, passes anterior to the medial malleolus (accompanied by the saphenous nerve), ascends the medial leg and thigh, and pierces the cribriform fascia at the saphenous opening (2.5 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle) to join the common femoral vein at the Saphenofemoral Junction (SFJ).

Six Named Tributaries at the SFJ: Lateral (Superficial circumflex iliac, Superficial inferior epigastric), Medial (Superficial external pudendal, Deep external pudendal), and Distal (Anterior Accessory GSV [AAGSV], Posteromedial thigh vein).

Small Saphenous Vein (SSV): Begins at the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, passes posterior to the lateral malleolus (accompanied by the sural nerve), ascends the posterior midline of the calf, and pierces the popliteal fascia to join the popliteal vein at the Saphenopopliteal Junction (SPJ) (variable termination; may continue cranially as the Giacomini vein).

Perforating Veins: Connect superficial to deep veins across the deep fascia with valves directing flow from superficial to deep (e.g., Cockett’s perforators in the lower medial calf, Boyd’s perforator below the knee, Dodd’s/Hunterian perforator in the mid-thigh).

2. Etiopathogenesis of Venous Hypertension & Ulceration:

Normal Calf Muscle Pump: Standing resting foot venous pressure is ~90–100 mmHg. During walking, contraction of the calf muscle pump compresses the deep venous sinusoids (raising deep compartment pressure to 200–300 mmHg) and propels blood towards the heart; during relaxation, competent valves prevent reflux and draw blood from superficial veins into deep veins, reducing ambulatory foot venous pressure to ~30 mmHg. 

Pathophysiology of Varicose Veins & Venous Ulcers:

Primary Varicose Veins (90%): Intrinsic vein wall weakness (smooth muscle apoptosis, increased matrix metalloproteinases, reduced elastin-to-collagen ratio) → vein wall dilatation and loss of compliance → secondary valvular incompetence (GSV accounts for 60%, SSV for 20%).

Secondary Varicose Veins (10%): Deep venous obstruction or valvular destruction (Post-Thrombotic Syndrome following DVT), pelvic masses/pregnancy, congenital (Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome — triad of port-wine capillary naevus, varicose veins/lateral embryonic vein, and limb bone/soft-tissue hypertrophy), or arteriovenous fistulae (Parkes-Weber syndrome).

Sustained Ambulatory Venous Hypertension (>60–90 mmHg on walking) → capillary distension and endothelial pore widening → extravasation of erythrocytes (degraded to haemosiderin → brownish pigmentation), fibrinogen (pericapillary fibrin cuffs), and white blood cell trapping with release of reactive oxygen species, proteolytic enzymes, and mast cell degranulation → chronic subcutaneous fibrosis (Lipodermatosclerosis — “inverted champagne bottle leg”), Atrophie blanche, Venous Eczema, and eventually tissue breakdown into a Venous Ulcer.

3. Clinical Features & CEAP Classification:

Symptoms: Dull aching, heaviness, throbbing, itching, ankle swelling, and restless legs/night cramps that worsen on prolonged standing (e.g., traffic constable) and improve with leg elevation or walking.

Complications of Varicose Veins [KU 24, 19]:

Oedema (C3).

Venous Eczema & Haemosiderosis/Pigmentation (C4a).

Lipodermatosclerosis (LDS) & Atrophie Blanche (C4b).

Corona Phlebectatica (Malleolar flare - C4c).

Venous Ulceration (C5 healed / C6 active): Located in the medial gaiter area above the medial malleolus; shallow, gently sloping (shelving) edges, granulating floor with slough/exudate; long-standing ulcers (>10–20 years) can undergo malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin’s Ulcer).

Acute Haemorrhage: Profuse, painless dark bleeding from rupture of a thin-walled superficial varix (“ankle venous bleeder”); controlled immediately by elevating the leg above the heart and applying direct firm pressure.

Superficial Vein Thrombosis (Thrombophlebitis).

Calcification of the vein wall & Equinus ankle deformity (from Achilles contracture in severe LDS).

Saphena Varix (Short Note [KU 16]):

A saccular dilatation of the proximal GSV at the saphenofemoral junction (up to golf-ball size). Presents as a soft, compressible groin swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle that disappears completely on lying down, has an expansile cough impulse, and exhibits a fluid thrill on tapping the distal GSV in the thigh (Cruveilhier’s sign) with a bluish tint. Must be differentiated from a femoral hernia (which lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle but is irreducible or reduces with a gurgle, and stays reduced when finger pressure is maintained over the femoral canal).

Clinical Bedside Tests (Historical Exam Questions [KU 15, TU]):

Brodie–Trendelenburg Test: Elevate the patient’s leg to empty the varicose veins → occlude the SFJ with the thumb (or a tourniquet) just below the saphenous opening → ask the patient to stand:

Test I: If veins remain empty on standing and fill rapidly from above downwards within 15 seconds of releasing the thumb, it indicates SFJ incompetence.

Test II: If veins fill rapidly from below upwards within 30–60 seconds while SFJ occlusion is still maintained, it indicates incompetent perforators (or SPJ incompetence).

Modified Perthes’ Test (for Deep Vein Patency): Apply a tourniquet around the upper thigh tightly enough to occlude the GSV (but not deep veins) with the patient standing, and ask the patient to walk briskly or perform 10 heel-raises:

If varicose veins collapse/empty → deep veins are patent and calf pump is functional.

If varicose veins become tensely distended and the patient experiences severe bursting calf pain (Venous Claudication) → deep venous obstruction (contraindication to stripping/ablating superficial veins).

4. Investigations:

Venous Duplex Ultrasonography (Gold Standard Investigation):

Performed with the patient standing using a 7.5–13 MHz linear transducer (combines B-mode anatomical grey-scale imaging with pulsed-wave spectral and colour Doppler).

Establishes: (i) Deep vein patency and competence (CFV, femoral, popliteal), (ii) Exact site of junctional incompetence (SFJ — “Mickey Mouse sign” in transverse view; SPJ), (iii) Truncal reflux (≥ 0.5 s) and diameter of the GSV within the “Saphenous eye” and SSV, and (iv) Location of incompetent perforators.

Ankle–Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI): Mandatory in all patients with a Venous Leg Ulcer to rule out concomitant peripheral arterial disease (“Mixed arterial–venous ulcer” present in 15–30%). Normal ABPI is 0.9–1.4 (full compression is safe if ABPI >0.8; modified reduced compression 30 mmHg if ABPI 0.5–0.8; compression is strictly contraindicated if ABPI <0.5).

5. Management of Varicose Veins & Venous Leg Ulcers:

Step 1 — Conservative Management of Venous Ulcer (Bisgaard’s Regimen & Compression Therapy [KU 24, 20, RGU, TU]):

Bisgaard’s Regimen (Four Pillars):

Elevation of the limb above heart level when resting/sleeping to reduce hydrostatic oedema.

Wound Toilet & Non-Adherent Dressings (saline cleansing; systemic antibiotics are given only if clinical cellulitis is present).

Active Calf Muscle Pump Exercises (ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion exercises and walking) + passive massage of indurated LDS skin from below upwards.

Graduated External Compression Therapy (Cornerstone of Ulcer Healing):

Four-Layer Compression Bandaging (1. Orthopaedic wool → 2. Cotton crepe bandage → 3. Elastic bandage → 4. Cohesive bandage), delivering an ankle interface pressure of 35–40 mmHg (changed weekly), or Two-Layer compression hosiery.

Pharmacological Adjuncts: Pentoxifylline (400 mg TDS) (reduces leukocyte adhesion and blood viscosity; proven to accelerate ulcer healing alongside compression) and Horse chestnut seed extract.

Step 2 — Definitive Interventional Treatment of Superficial Venous Reflux (NICE Guidelines & EVRA Trial):

The landmark EVRA Trial (Gohel et al., NEJM 2018) proved that Early Endovenous Ablation (within 2 weeks) of superficial reflux combined with compression significantly accelerates venous ulcer healing (median 56 vs 82 days) and reduces ulcer recurrence compared with compression alone.

Treatment Hierarchy (First-Line to Third-Line):

First-Line — Endothermal Ablation (Gold Standard; >95% occlusion rate, performed as a walk-in local anaesthetic day-case):

Endovenous Laser Ablation (EVLA — 1470 nm diode laser) or Radiofrequency Ablation (RFA — ClosureFast catheter at 120°C for 20 s cycles): Percutaneous USG-guided cannulation of the GSV/SSV at the lowest point of reflux → tip positioned 1–2 cm distal to the SFJ/SPJ → perivenous tumescent local anaesthesia infiltrated under USG guidance inside the saphenous fascia (compresses vein onto catheter, empties blood, and acts as a protective thermal heat-sink for the saphenous/sural nerves) → thermal ablation during pullback (60–80 J/cm), combined with concomitant ambulatory stab phlebectomies (hook avulsions) of varicose tributaries. 

Second-Line — Ultrasound-Guided Foam Sclerotherapy (UGFS) & Non-Thermal Non-Tumescent (NTNT) Techniques:

UGFS: 1–3% Sodium Tetradecyl Sulphate (STS) or Polidocanol mixed with air (1:4 ratio) via Tessari’s two-syringe three-way tap method to create microfoam (displaces blood and maximises endothelial destruction; max volume 10–12 mL per session). Ideal for tortuous veins, recurrent varicosities, and sub-ulcer venous plexuses.

NTNT Modalities: Mechanochemical Ablation (MOCA / ClariVein) (rotating wire tip + liquid sclerosant) and Endovenous Cyanoacrylate Glue Ablation (VenaSeal).

Third-Line — Open Surgery (Trendelenburg Operation + Stripping + Multiple Stab Avulsions):

Trendelenburg Operation (Flush SFJ Ligation): Oblique groin crease incision → dissect and ligate all 6 named tributaries of the GSV → flush transfixion-ligation of the GSV at its junction with the common femoral vein → retrograde inversion stripping of the GSV down to the knee using a PIN stripper (stripping only to the knee rather than the ankle reduces saphenous nerve injury from 30% to <7%). 

SPJ Ligation (with preoperative USG skin marking; main risk is sural nerve and common peroneal nerve injury) and Subfascial Endoscopic Perforator Surgery (SEPS) or USG-guided perforator ablation.

Step 3 — Prevention of Ulcer Recurrence: Once the ulcer heals, prescribe lifelong Class 2 (18–24 mmHg) below-knee graduated elastic compression stockings (ESCHAR Trial).

title: Q9.2: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) & Pulmonary Embolism (Etiology, Modified Wells Score, Diagnosis, Prophylaxis & Management)
text:
(Covers KU 24, 23, 21, RGU, TU — Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. Etiopathogenesis (Virchow’s Triad & Risk Factors):

Virchow’s Triad (1856):

Venous Stasis / Abnormal Flow: Immobility, bedrest, anaesthesia (loss of calf pump), heart failure, pelvic venous compression (May–Thurner syndrome — compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery), long-haul flights.

Endothelial Injury / Vessel Wall Damage: Trauma, hip/knee orthopaedic surgery, pelvic surgery, central venous catheters, prior DVT.

Hypercoagulability of Blood: Malignancy (Trousseau’s migratory thrombophlebitis), pregnancy/puerperium, high-dose oestrogen OCP/HRT, sepsis, inflammatory bowel disease, nephrotic syndrome, polycythaemia, and Inherited/Acquired Thrombophilias (Table 62.3): Factor V Leiden mutation (activated protein C resistance — commonest inherited thrombophilia), Prothrombin G20210A mutation, Antithrombin III deficiency, Protein C or Protein S deficiency, Antiphospholipid syndrome, and hyperhomocysteinaemia.

Pathology: Platelet aggregates initiate in the valve pockets of the calf soleal venous sinusoids → coralline fibrin/RBC thrombus builds up and propagates proximally as a loose red tail into the popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins → detachment causes Pulmonary Embolism (PE); 

chronic organization causes valvular destruction and Post-Thrombotic Syndrome (PTS).

2. Clinical Features:

Asymptomatic (up to 50%): May present directly with Pulmonary Embolism ( sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, tachycardia, hypoxia, elevated JVP, or syncope/cardiac arrest).

Symptomatic DVT: Unilateral calf/leg swelling (>3 cm difference measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity), dull aching calf pain, warmth, mild low-grade pyrexia, pitting ankle oedema, dilated superficial collateral veins, and tenderness along the deep venous tract. (Homans’ sign — calf resistance/pain on forceful ankle dorsiflexion — is neither sensitive nor specific and should be avoided).

Severe Limb-Threatening Iliofemoral DVT Variants:

Phlegmasia Alba Dolens (“Milk Leg” / “White Leg”): Massive iliofemoral thrombosis with reflex arterial spasm and lymphatic obstruction causing a tensely swollen, painful, pale/white leg.

Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens (“Blue Leg”): Near-total occlusion of all main and collateral venous outflow of the limb → extreme venous hypertension arrests capillary arterial inflow → deeply cyanosed, purple, excruciatingly painful, tensely oedematous limb with absent arterial pulses, rapidly progressing to Venous Gangrene (30–40% mortality; strongly associated with occult malignancy). 

3. Diagnosis & Modified Wells Criteria (Table 62.4) [KU 24, TU]:

Modified Wells Clinical Probability Score for DVT:

Active cancer (+1), Paralysis/paresis/plaster immobilisation of lower limb (+1), Bedridden >3 days or major surgery within 4 weeks (+1), Localised tenderness along deep venous system (+1), Entire leg swollen (+1), Calf swelling >3 cm compared with asymptomatic side (+1), Pitting oedema confined to symptomatic leg (+1), Collateral superficial non-varicose veins (+1), Previous documented DVT (+1), Intravenous drug abuse (+3); Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT (-2).

Interpretation: Score ≤ 0 = Low probability (5%); Score 1–2 = Moderate (17%); Score >2 = High probability (17–53%).

Diagnostic Algorithm:

Low Probability Wells Score: Check Quantitative Plasma D-Dimer (fibrin degradation product — high negative predictive value >95%; if negative, DVT is excluded; if positive, proceed to Duplex USG).

Moderate/High Probability Wells Score: Proceed directly to Venous Compression Duplex Ultrasonography (Gold Standard Investigation):

Diagnostic Criteria on Duplex: Incompressibility of the vein lumen under gentle probe pressure (most reliable sign), echogenic intraluminal thrombus, absence of colour/spectral Doppler flow, and loss of respiratory phasicity and augmentation.

Ancillary Imaging: CT Venography / MR Venography (for pelvic/iliac/IVC thrombus); CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) (gold standard for suspected Pulmonary Embolism, showing intraluminal filling defects in pulmonary arteries).

4. Management of Deep Vein Thrombosis:

1. Immediate Anticoagulation (Prevents clot propagation and Pulmonary Embolism):

Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs / NOACs — First-Line Recommended): Direct Factor Xa inhibitors (Rivaroxaban 15 mg BD for 21 days then 20 mg OD; or Apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD) or Direct Thrombin inhibitor (Dabigatran). Equally effective as Warfarin with significantly lower major bleeding risk and no need for INR monitoring.

Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH): Subcutaneous Enoxaparin (1.5 mg/kg once daily or 1 mg/kg BD) or Dalteparin (preferred in pregnancy and active GI malignancy), bridged to oral Warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0, overlapping for at least 5 days until INR ≥ 2.0 for 24 hours).

Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) IV Infusion: Used in severe renal failure (eGFR <30 mL/min) or when rapid reversal may be needed (monitored by APTT 1.5–2.5 × control; antidote: Protamine sulphate). (If Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia [HIT] occurs, switch to Fondaparinux or Bivalirudin/Argatroban).

Duration of Anticoagulation: 3 months for a first provoked DVT (reversible surgical/transient risk factor); 6 months to Lifelong for unprovoked DVT, recurrent VTE, or active malignancy.

2. Endovascular Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis (CDT) / Pharmacomechanical Thrombectomy:

Indicated in young, fit patients with acute (<14 days) extensive iliofemoral DVT or Phlegmasia cerulea dolens to rapidly restore venous patency, save the limb, and prevent severe Post-Thrombotic Syndrome (followed by iliac vein stenting if May–Thurner compression is uncovered).

3. Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) Filter (Retrievable infrarenal filter via jugular/femoral vein):

Strict Indications:

Confirmed acute proximal DVT/PE with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation (e.g., active major bleeding, recent haemorrhagic stroke, or imminent major surgery).

Recurrent Pulmonary Embolism despite adequate therapeutic anticoagulation.

5. VTE Prophylaxis in Surgical Patients (Table 62.6) [TU]:

Early ambulation, adequate hydration, Mechanical Prophylaxis (Graduated elastic compression stockings [TED stockings] and Intermittent Pneumatic Compression [IPC] calf devices — contraindicated in severe PAD), and Pharmacological Prophylaxis (Subcutaneous LMWH — Enoxaparin 40 mg OD or unfractionated heparin 5000 U SC BD/TDS) for all moderate- and high-risk surgical patients.
