title: Q10.1: Chronic Lower Limb Ischaemia, Atherosclerotic Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD) & Thromboangiitis Obliterans (Buerger’s Disease)
text:
(Covers KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, RGU, TU — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. History Taking & Clinical Features of Chronic Lower Limb Ischaemia [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 19, 15]:

Further History to Elicit in a Claudicant/Gangrene Patient [KU 25]:

Pain Characteristics: Site of cramping muscle pain (calf, thigh, or buttock), exact claudication distance, relief on standing still within 5 minutes, progression to rest pain (burning pain in the forefoot/toes at night relieved by hanging the foot out of bed), and any history of trauma/ill-fitting footwear preceding toe discoloration.

Vascular Risk Factors: Smoking history (pack-years, bidi/cigarettes, cannabis), Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, Hyperlipidaemia.

Systemic Atherosclerosis: History of angina/myocardial infarction (present in 50%), TIAs/stroke (25%), and erectile dysfunction (Leriche’s syndrome = Aortoiliac occlusion triad of bilateral buttock/thigh claudication + absent femoral pulses + impotence). 

Clinical Stages of Chronic Limb Ischaemia (Fontaine & Rutherford Classifications) [KU 15]:

[[TABLE:surgery-tbl-006]]

(Note: Fontaine Stages III and IV together constitute Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischaemia [CLTI], defined objectively as ischaemic rest pain or ulceration/gangrene for >2 weeks with Ankle systolic pressure <50 mmHg or Toe pressure <30 mmHg).

Differentiation of Intermittent Claudication Types [TU]:

Arterial Claudication: Cramp-like calf/thigh pain; never present on taking the first step; brought on by a reproducible walking distance (shortened by walking uphill); relieved within 5 minutes of standing still (does not require sitting or spinal flexion); distal pulses absent/diminished.

Neurogenic Claudication (Lumbar Canal Stenosis / Cauda Equina Compression): Pain, numbness, and tingling radiating down the posterior thighs/calves; worsened by lumbar extension (standing upright or walking downhill) and relieved only by sitting down or leaning forward (lumbar flexion — “shopping-cart sign”) for 15–30 minutes; pedal pulses are normal.

Venous Claudication: Severe bursting pain in the entire calf during walking due to deep venous outflow obstruction (iliofemoral post-thrombotic occlusion); relieved slowly only by sitting down and elevating the leg.

Physical Examination Signs of Chronic Ischaemia:

Thin, shiny, hairless skin; brittle ridged nails; wasting of calf muscles; painful punched-out ulcers over pressure points/malleoli/between toes; or dry black mummified digital gangrene.

Buerger’s Postural Test: With the patient supine, elevate both legs to 45° for 1–2 minutes → the ischaemic foot develops marked cadaveric pallor and venous guttering (collapsed superficial veins look like pale trenches; the angle at which pallor appears is Buerger’s vascular angle, <20–30° indicates severe ischaemia). Then ask the patient to sit up and hang the legs over the side of the bed → delayed capillary refill (>5–10 s) followed by a deep purple-red flushing of the foot due to reactive hyperaemia in maximally dilated capillaries (Dependent Rubor / Sunset Foot Sign). 

Palpation of Pulses & Auscultation for Bruits: Femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses (see Table 61.1 for localising the level of occlusion; Superficial Femoral Artery [SFA] in the adductor canal of Hunter is the commonest site [70%], causing calf claudication with a palpable femoral pulse and absent popliteal/pedal pulses).

2. Thromboangiitis Obliterans (TAO / Buerger’s Disease) vs Atherosclerosis [KU 25, 24, 21, 20, 18, RGU, TU]:

Definition of Buerger’s Disease: A non-atherosclerotic, segmental, pan-inflammatory occlusive vasculitis affecting small- and medium-sized arteries, veins, and nerves of the upper and lower extremities in young male heavy smokers.

Etiopathogenesis & Pathology of TAO:

Exclusively linked to tobacco use (bidi, cigarettes, chewed tobacco — carbon monoxide, nicotine, and autoimmune hypersensitivity to Type I and III collagen in the vessel wall); common in India, South Asia, and the Middle East; associated with HLA-A9 and HLA-B5.

Histopathology:

Acute Phase: Occlusive, highly cellular inflammatory thrombus containing polymorphonuclear microabscesses and multinucleated giant cells, with pan-arteritis of all three coats (intima, media, and adventitia), WHILE THE INTERNAL ELASTIC LAMINA REMAINS INTACT.

Chronic Phase: Organised recanalising thrombus and dense perivascular fibrosis that binds the artery, accompanying venae comitantes, and nerve into a single adherent fibrous cord.

Clinical Features of TAO (Shionoya’s 5 Diagnostic Criteria):

History of heavy smoking.

Onset before the age of 50 years (typically men aged 20–40 years).

Infrapopliteal (distal crural/pedal) arterial occlusions.

Either upper limb involvement (positive Allen’s test, digital ulcers) OR Superficial Migratory Thrombophlebitis (present in 30–40%).

Absence of atherosclerotic risk factors other than smoking (no diabetes, no hyperlipidaemia, no hypertension, no proximal embolic source).

Clinical Progression: Begins with foot arch (instep) claudication → progresses to calf claudication, Raynaud’s phenomenon, excruciating rest pain, and distal digital ulceration/dry gangrene.

Differentiation Between TAO (Buerger’s Disease) and Atherosclerotic PAD:

[[TABLE:surgery-tbl-007]]

3. Investigations for Chronic Limb Ischaemia (PAD & TAO):

General Blood Tests & Cardiac Work-up: FBC (exclude polycythaemia/thrombocythaemia), Fasting blood glucose & HbA_1c, Fasting lipid profile, Renal function (serum creatinine/eGFR), ESR/CRP & autoimmune screen (in young patients to rule out vasculitis), and ECG/Echocardiogram.

Bedside Hand-Held Doppler & Pressure Indices [TU]: 

Ankle–Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI): Ratio of highest ankle systolic pressure (Dorsalis pedis or Posterior tibial) to highest brachial systolic pressure:

0.9–1.4: Normal (triphasic waveform).

0.5–0.89: Mild-to-moderate PAD (Intermittent claudication; biphasic/monophasic waveform).

<0.4–0.5 (or absolute ankle pressure <50 mmHg): Severe / Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischaemia (CLTI).

>1.4: Falsely elevated due to incompressible calcified arteries (Mönckeberg’s medial calcific sclerosis) in Diabetes Mellitus and chronic kidney disease.

Toe–Brachial Pressure Index (TBI): Digital arteries are spared from calcification; TBI <0.6 confirms significant PAD, and absolute hallux toe pressure <30 mmHg indicates CLTI / failure of ulcer healing. 

Vascular Imaging (To Map Inflow, Lesion Length, and Distal Run-Off):

Duplex Doppler Ultrasonography [KU 17]: First-line non-invasive test; combines B-mode anatomy with colour/pulsed-wave Doppler (a Peak Systolic Velocity [PSV] ratio >2.0 across a lesion indicates >50% stenosis).

CT Angiography (CTA) or MR Angiography (MRA): Provides complete 3D roadmap from the abdominal aorta to the pedal arch.

Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): Performed via percutaneous retrograde femoral Seldinger puncture when concurrent endovascular angioplasty/stenting is planned.

4. Management of Chronic Lower Limb Ischaemia:

A. Best Medical Therapy & Risk Factor Modification (Mandatory for ALL Patients):

Complete, Permanent Cessation of Smoking (In Buerger’s disease, total abstinence from all forms of tobacco is the only measure that halts disease progression and prevents major amputation).

Supervised Exercise Programme (for claudicants: walking to near-maximal pain for 30–60 minutes, 3 × /week for 3 months — stimulates collateral vessel development and muscle oxidative enzymes).

Antiplatelet Therapy: Clopidogrel 75 mg daily (preferred by guidelines) or Aspirin 75–150 mg daily (or low-dose Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BD + Aspirin).

High-Intensity Statin Therapy (Atorvastatin 40–80 mg daily): Stabilises plaques and reduces cardiovascular mortality regardless of baseline cholesterol.

Strict Glycaemic (HbA_1c <7%) and Blood Pressure Control, foot care education, and Cilostazol (100 mg BD — phosphodiesterase-III inhibitor; improves walking distance in claudicants; contraindicated in heart failure).

B. Revascularisation (Indicated for CLTI [Rest Pain, Ulceration, Gangrene] or Disabling Lifestyle-Limiting Claudication):

(Note: In Buerger’s disease, direct surgical bypass is rarely feasible due to lack of distal target run-off vessels; medical prostacyclin analogue Iloprost IV infusion, pain control, Chemical/Surgical Lumbar Sympathectomy, or omental transposition may aid ulcer healing).

1. Endovascular Revascularisation:

Percutaneous Transluminal Balloon Angioplasty (PTA) ± Stenting (using drug-coated balloons or bare-metal/drug-eluting stents via intraluminal or subintimal angioplasty): Ideal for short focal stenoses/occlusions (<10 cm) and high-risk/frail patients. 

2. Open Surgical Revascularisation: 

Aortoiliac Occlusive Disease: Aortobifemoral Bypass using a bifurcated knitted Dacron graft (90% 5-year patency). In unilateral iliac occlusion or unfit patients, perform an extra-anatomical Femorofemoral Crossover Bypass or Axillobifemoral Bypass.

Common Femoral Artery Disease: Femoral Endarterectomy with Vein/Bovine Pericardial Patch Angioplasty (+ profundaplasty).

Superficial Femoral / Popliteal / Crural Disease: Femoropopliteal or Femorodistal (Femorotibial) Bypass using autologous Great Saphenous Vein (GSV) (either reversed or in situ after disrupting valves with a valvulotome; 60–70% 5-year patency). If vein is unavailable, use an ePTFE graft with an autologous distal vein cuff (Miller cuff or St Mary’s boot).

C. Management of Gangrene & Amputation (when unreconstructable or after revascularisation improves proximal blood supply):

Wait for a clear line of demarcation in dry gangrene (or perform urgent debridement/amputation after revascularisation in wet/infected gangrene) → local ray/transmetatarsal amputation or major below-knee/above-knee amputation.

subject: surgery
title: Q10.2: Gangrene (Types, Diabetic Foot & Gas Gangrene), Acute Limb Ischaemia, Amputation & Lumbar Sympathectomy
text:
(Covers KU 24, 22, 18, 16, RGU, TU — Long Essays, Short Essays & Short Answers)

1. Definition & Clinical Types of Gangrene [KU 24, 18, TU]:

Definition: Macroscopic death (necrosis) of tissue with superadded putrefaction, turning black due to the breakdown of haemoglobin into iron sulphide by hydrogen sulphide from bacteria/tissues.

Comparison of Dry vs Wet Gangrene:

[[TABLE:surgery-tbl-008]]

2. Diabetic Foot Ulcer & Diabetic Gangrene [KU 22, 16, TU]:

Triad of Pathogenesis:

Diabetic Peripheral Sensorimotor & Autonomic Neuropathy: Loss of protective pain/pressure sensation (“glove and stocking”), intrinsic foot muscle atrophy (claw toes, prominent metatarsal heads, high-arch cavus foot), and anhidrosis (dry fissured skin) + Charcot’s neuropathic joint arthropathy (“rocker-bottom foot”).

Ischaemia (Macrovascular & Microvascular): Atherosclerosis characteristically affecting the infrapopliteal crural arteries (tibial and peroneal) with relative sparing of the pedal arteries (dorsalis pedis and plantar arch — allowing distal pedal bypass), plus Mönckeberg’s medial calcification and capillary basement membrane thickening.

Impaired Immunity & Polymicrobial Infection: Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis; polymicrobial aerobic (S. aureus, Streptococci, E. coli, Pseudomonas) and anaerobic (Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus) infection spreads rapidly along plantar fascial compartments, causing wet gangrene and osteomyelitis.

Investigations:

Blood glucose, HbA_1c, FBC, CRP, RFTs, wound pus culture (deep tissue biopsy), X-ray of the foot (for osteomyelitis and subcutaneous gas), and Doppler ABPI, TBI, and Duplex USG / CT or MR Angiography.

Management:

Resuscitation & Glycaemic Control: IV fluids and soluble insulin infusion (sliding scale).

Broad-Spectrum Parenteral Antibiotics: Covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms (e.g., Piperacillin–Tazobactam or Meropenem + Metronidazole + Linezolid/Vancomycin).

Urgent Surgical Drainage & Debridement (“Puss and Slough Must Go”): Radical excision of all necrotic slough, laying open infected plantar fascial spaces, and local digital (ray) or transmetatarsal amputation (leaving the wound open to granulate). If spreading life-threatening wet gangrene/sepsis is present, perform an emergency guillotine or definitive Below-Knee Amputation.

Revascularisation: Endovascular tibial angioplasty or Femorodistal (Femoropedal) vein bypass once acute sepsis is controlled.

Wound Care & Rehabilitation: Negative-pressure wound therapy (VAC), split-skin grafting, off-loading footwear (total contact cast / bespoke diabetic microcellular rubber [MCR] footwear), and lifelong foot care education.

3. Gas Gangrene (Clostridial Myonecrosis) [KU 18]:

Etiopathogenesis: Rapidly progressive, life-threatening myonecrosis caused by anaerobic, Gram-positive, spore-forming bacilli of the genus Clostridium — most commonly Clostridium perfringens (C. welchii — 80%), C. septicum, C. novyi, and C. histolyticum.

Occurs in deep, devitalised, hypoxic wounds contaminated with soil or faeces (compound fractures, war wounds, crushed muscle, or high above-knee amputations in ischaemic limbs).

Organisms produce potent exotoxins (Alpha-toxin [Lecithinase-C], which hydrolyses cell membrane phospholipids causing massive myonecrosis and intravascular haemolysis, plus collagenase, hyaluronidase, and leukocidin) and ferment muscle carbohydrates to produce gas (H_2, CO_2, N_2).

Clinical Features (Incubation period: 12–48 hours):

Local: Sudden severe, lancinating pain and tense swelling of the wound; thin, foul-smelling, brownish “dishwater” serosanguineous exudate with gas bubbles; overlying skin becomes bronze/tawny then greenish-black with haemorrhagic bullae; palpable surgical emphysema (crepitus) over the muscle bellies. Exposed muscle looks pale/brick-red (like boiled meat), does not bleed on cutting, and does not contract on pinching.

Systemic: Profound toxaemia, disproportionately severe tachycardia, hypotension, haemolytic jaundice, haemoglobinuria, acute renal failure, and septic shock (mental alertness is often eerily preserved until late).

Investigations:

Gram Stain of Wound Exudate: Large Gram-positive rods with no polymorphonuclear leukocytes (destroyed by toxins); anaerobic culture on Robertson’s cooked meat medium (Nagler’s reaction positive for lecithinase).

Plain Radiograph: Feathery linear streaks of gas dissecting within muscle bundles.

Management (Surgical Emergency):

Resuscitation & High-Dose IV Antibiotics: Crystalline Benzylpenicillin (Penicillin G — 2 to 4 million units IV 4-hourly) + Clindamycin (600–900 mg IV 8-hourly) (Clindamycin directly inhibits clostridial toxin synthesis) + Metronidazole.

Emergency Radical Surgical Debridement: Excision of all dead, non-contractile, non-bleeding muscle across all involved compartments, or Emergency Guillotine Amputation (leaving the stump wide open).

Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT): 100% O_2 at 2.5–3.0 atmospheres halts alpha-toxin production and kills obligate anaerobes.

4. Acute Limb Ischaemia (ALI) & Arterial Emboli [TU]:

Etiology: Arterial Embolism (80% cardiac in origin: left atrial thrombus in atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus post-myocardial infarction, prosthetic valves, infective endocarditis; or proximal aneurysm — lodges at arterial bifurcations, commonest being the Common Femoral Artery bifurcation, followed by the trifurcation of the popliteal artery and aortic saddle embolus) vs Acute-on-Chronic In-situ Thrombosis.

Clinical Features (“The 6 P’s”): Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Poikilothermia (perishingly cold), Paraesthesia, and Paralysis (onset of sensory loss and muscle paralysis indicates impending irreversible muscle/nerve death within 6 hours — Rutherford Class IIb [Immediately Threatened] vs Class III [Irreversible: profound anaesthesia, rigor/paralysis, and inaudible arterial and venous Doppler signals] — Table 61.2).

Management:

Immediate IV Unfractionated Heparin bolus (5000 U IV) to prevent proximal and distal thrombus propagation + IV opiate analgesia + oxygen.

Rutherford Class IIa (Marginally Threatened — no motor loss): Urgent CTA/DSA + Catheter-Directed Intra-Arterial Thrombolysis (with recombinant Tissue Plasminogen Activator [rt-PA / Alteplase]).

Rutherford Class IIb (Immediately Threatened — sensory/motor deficit): Emergency Surgical Fogarty Balloon Catheter Embolectomy via a transverse femoral arteriotomy (or emergency bypass if underlying chronic thrombosis) + Four-Compartment Calf Fasciotomy (to prevent Reperfusion Compartment Syndrome [KU 24]).

Rutherford Class III (Irreversible / Dead Limb): Primary Major Amputation (revascularising a dead, paralysed limb causes fatal hyperkalaemia, acidosis, and myoglobinuric renal failure — Haimovici’s myonephropathic metabolic syndrome).

5. Amputation (Indications, Guillotine & Below-Knee Amputation) [TU]:

Indications (“The 3 D’s” — Summary Box 61.3):

Dead Limb: Irreversible gangrene (atherosclerosis, diabetes, embolism, frostbite).

Deadly Limb: Life-threatening wet gangrene, gas gangrene, spreading necrotising fasciitis, osteosarcoma, or massive crush injury.

Dead Loss (Nuisance) Limb: Intractable rest pain with unreconstructable CLTI, severe unrecoverable trauma, or flail/paralysed/contracted limb.

Guillotine Amputation: An emergency, rapid, circular open amputation where skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscles, and bone are divided at the exact same level and left completely unsutured to allow free drainage of pus and gas (indicated in fulminant gas gangrene or overwhelming wet diabetic foot sepsis; followed later by formal revision/higher definitive closure once sepsis resolves).

Below-Knee Amputation (Burgess Long Posterior Flap or Skew Flap): Preserves the knee joint (drastically reducing the energy expenditure of walking with a prosthesis); ideal tibial stump length is 10–12 cm below the tibial tuberosity (never <8 cm), with the fibula divided 2 cm shorter than the tibia and the anterior tibial crest bevelled at 45°. 

6. Lumbar Sympathectomy [KU 22, RGU]:

Principle: Ablation of the L2, L3, and L4 lumbar sympathetic ganglia abolishes sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone specifically to the cutaneous arterioles of the foot and lower leg (opening cutaneous arteriovenous shunts and increasing skin blood flow to aid healing of superficial ischaemic ulcers and relieve rest pain; it does NOT improve intermittent claudication because skeletal muscle vessels are regulated by local metabolites, not sympathetic nerves).

Indications: Non-reconstructable distal small-vessel occlusive disease (Buerger’s disease, severe Raynaud’s phenomenon) with rest pain or minor superficial digital ulceration (where ABPI >0.3), plantar hyperhidrosis, and Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (causalgia).

Techniques:

Chemical Lumbar Sympathectomy (Preferred today): Percutaneous CT- or fluoroscopy-guided injection of 5 mL of 6–10% Phenol in water (or absolute alcohol) anterolateral to the L2–L4 vertebral bodies.

Surgical Lumbar Sympathectomy: Extraperitoneal approach via a transverse flank incision (pushing the peritoneum and ureter medially to expose the sympathetic chain lying in the groove between the psoas major muscle and vertebral bodies; on the right it lies behind the IVC, on the left beside the aorta). Excision of L2, L3, and L4 ganglia (preserving the L1 ganglion bilaterally in young men to prevent retrograde ejaculation).

subject: surgery
title: Q10.3: Aortic Aneurysm, False/Cirsoid Aneurysm, Arteriovenous Fistula & Raynaud’s Syndrome
text:
(Covers KU 24, 18, RGU, TU — Short Answers)

1. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) [KU 24]:

Definition: A permanent localised dilatation of the abdominal aorta to ≥ 1.5 times its normal diameter (≥ 3.0 cm) involving all three layers of the arterial wall (True aneurysm). 95% are infrarenal and degenerative/atherosclerotic (associated with smoking, male sex [4:1], age >65 years, hypertension, and matrix metalloproteinase degradation of medial elastin).

Clinical Presentations:

Asymptomatic (75%): Discovered incidentally on imaging or as a painless expansile epigastric/umbilical pulsation (pulsates both anteriorly and laterally on bimanual palpation).

Symptomatic Non-Ruptured: Back, flank, or abdominal pain (due to rapid sac expansion or an Inflammatory AAA with dense white retroperitoneal fibrosis), or trash foot (distal microembolisation of mural thrombus).

Ruptured AAA (Surgical Emergency; 80% overall mortality): Classic triad of sudden severe abdominal/lumbar back pain + hypotension/shock + pulsatile abdominal mass (80% rupture posterolaterally into the retroperitoneum, allowing a brief window of tamponade; 20% rupture anteriorly into the free peritoneal cavity).

Investigations: Abdominal Ultrasonography (for screening men at age 65 and surveillance of small AAAs) and CT Angiography (CTA) (gold standard for planning open vs endovascular repair; defines neck length/angulation and iliac access). 

Management:

Asymptomatic AAA <5.5 cm: Best medical therapy (smoking cessation, statin, antiplatelet, BP control) + serial USG surveillance (annual if 3.0–4.4 cm; 3-monthly if 4.5–5.4 cm).

Indications for Elective Repair: Diameter ≥ 5.5 cm in men (≥ 5.0 cm in women), rapid growth >1 cm/year, or any symptomatic aneurysm:

Open Surgical Inlay Repair: Midline laparotomy → infrarenal aortic and iliac cross-clamping → longitudinal opening of the aneurysm sac → oversewing lumbar and IMA back-bleeding → suturing a tube or bifurcated Dacron graft end-to-end inside the sac → closing the native sac over the graft (to prevent aortoduodenal fistula). 

Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR): Deployment of a modular stent-graft (Dacron/ePTFE supported by nitinol stents) via the femoral arteries to exclude the aneurysm sac (lower 30-day mortality than open repair, but requires lifelong surveillance for Endoleaks Types I–V — Table 61.3).

Management of Ruptured AAA (Summary Box 61.5): Permissive hypotension (restrict IV fluids to keep systolic BP 70–100 mmHg so as not to blow off the retroperitoneal clot), crossmatch blood, urgent CTA if stable, and immediate transfer to theatre for emergency EVAR or Open clamping & repair.

2. False Aneurysm (Pseudoaneurysm) & Cirsoid Aneurysm [TU]:

False Aneurysm (Pseudoaneurysm): A pulsating haematoma communicating with the arterial lumen through a breach in the arterial wall; its sac wall does not contain the three arterial layers (intima, media, adventitia) but is lined only by compressed perivascular fibrous tissue and organised laminated clot. Caused by penetrating trauma, arterial catheterisation (femoral artery puncture), or anastomotic disruption. Treated by USG-guided percutaneous thrombin injection (if <3 cm with a narrow neck) or open surgical evacuation and suture repair.

Cirsoid Aneurysm: A congenital high-flow arteriovenous malformation (AVM) occurring most commonly in the subcutaneous tissue of the scalp (superficial temporal and occipital vessels). Presents as a warm, compressible, tortuous “bag of pulsating worms” beneath the scalp with a palpable thrill, continuous machinery bruit, headache, and risk of torrential haemorrhage on ulceration. Treated by preoperative superselective transcatheter arterial embolisation followed by complete surgical excision.

3. Arteriovenous Fistula (AVF) [KU 18, RGU]:

Definition & Causes: An abnormal direct communication between a high-pressure artery and a low-pressure vein bypassing the capillary bed:

Congenital: Cirsoid aneurysm, Parkes-Weber syndrome.

Traumatic: Penetrating stab/gunshot injury or iatrogenic catheterisation.

Surgically Created (Therapeutic): Brescia–Cimino radiocephalic or brachiocephalic AV fistula for haemodialysis access in end-stage renal disease.

Structural & Physiological Effects:

Local: Veins become dilated, tortuous, and thick-walled (“arterialisation”); pulsatile mass with a palpable systolic–diastolic thrill and a continuous “machinery murmur” (Gibson’s murmur); distal limb ischaemia (“steal syndrome”) and venous hypertension/ulceration.

Systemic: Decreased total peripheral resistance → increased venous return, tachycardia, wide pulse pressure, cardiomegaly, and high-output left ventricular failure.

Nicoladoni–Branham’s Sign: Digital compression of the feeding artery proximal to a large AVF causes an immediate reflex bradycardia and normalization of pulse pressure (as sudden elimination of the low-resistance shunt raises systemic arterial pressure, stimulating carotid sinus baroreceptors).

Management: Duplex USG + DSA/CTA. Traumatic/congenital AVFs are treated by endovascular coil/glue embolisation, covered stent-graft placement across the arterial defect, or open surgical quadruple ligation/excision with arterial reconstruction (simple proximal arterial ligation alone is contraindicated as collateral steal causes distal gangrene).

4. Raynaud’s Disease vs Raynaud’s Syndrome (Raynaud’s Phenomenon) [KU 24, RGU, TU]:

Definition: Episodic vasospasm of the digital arteries and cutaneous arterioles of the hands (and feet) triggered by exposure to cold or emotional stress, producing a classic triphasic colour sequence:

Local Syncope (White / Blanching): Intense digital arteriolar spasm empties the capillary bed → digits turn dead-white, cold, and numb.

Local Asphyxia (Blue / Dusky Cyanosis): Sluggish accumulation of deoxygenated blood in paralysed dilated capillaries and venules → digits become swollen and bluish-purple.

Reactive Hyperaemia (Red / Engorgement): Relaxation of arteriolar spasm floods the dilated capillary bed with oxygenated blood → digits become bright red with throbbing pain and paraesthesia.

Distinction:

Raynaud’s Disease (Primary / Idiopathic): Occurs in young women (15–30 years), bilateral and symmetrical, normal peripheral pulses, no underlying systemic disease, and almost never causes digital gangrene (only rare micronodular pulp scars).

Raynaud’s Syndrome (Secondary): Secondary to connective tissue/autoimmune diseases (Systemic Sclerosis / CREST syndrome [90%], SLE, Rheumatoid arthritis), occupational vibrating tools (“Vibration White Finger”), Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (cervical rib), Buerger’s disease, β-blockers/ergot, or cryoglobulinaemia. Often unilateral/asymmetric and frequently progresses to severe digital ischaemic ulceration, pulp necrosis, and gangrene.

Management:

Conservative: Strict avoidance of cold (electrically heated mittens/gloves), absolute cessation of smoking, and stopping vibrating tools or β-blockers; treat underlying autoimmune disease.

Medical: Oral Calcium Channel Blockers (Nifedipine 10–20 mg TDS or Amlodipine) (first-line vasodilator), topical nitrates, Sildenafil (PDE-5 inhibitor), or Intravenous Iloprost (prostacyclin analogue) infusion for severe digital ulceration/critical ischaemia.

Surgical: Digital sympathectomy (periarterial adventitial stripping) or conservative amputation of demarcated necrotic fingertips (cervicodorsal sympathectomy provides only transient relief in Raynaud’s and has largely been abandoned).

***********************************************************************************

subject: surgery
title: 1. Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue PYQs
text:
Pyogenic Granuloma (Lobular Capillary Haemangioma) [TU]:

Pathology: Acquired benign vascular lesion sharing histological characteristics with capillary haemangiomas (not truly pyogenic or granulomatous).

Clinical Features: Rapidly growing, small (0.5–1.5 cm), raised, pedunculated, soft bright-red nodular lesion following trivial trauma; shows superficial ulceration and bleeds profusely on slightest touch. Common on fingers, lips, face, and gingiva.

Treatment: Excision with a minimal margin (or curettage with cauterisation of the feeding base to prevent recurrence).

Kaposi’s Sarcoma [RGU, TU]:

Etiology: Malignant proliferative tumour of vascular endothelial cells causally linked to Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8 / KSHV).

Clinical Variants: (i) Classic (elderly Ashkenazi Jewish/Mediterranean men), (ii) Endemic (African), (iii) Iatrogenic (post-transplant immunosuppression), and (iv) Epidemic / AIDS-defining (HIV infection).

Clinical Features & Treatment: Starts as multifocal red-brown/violaceous indurated skin plaques on extremities or oral mucosa that become nodular and ulcerate. Treated with Antiretroviral therapy (HAART), local radiotherapy, intralesional vinblastine, or systemic liposomal doxorubicin.

Hidradenitis Suppurativa [TU]:

Pathophysiology: Chronic, relapsing inflammatory disease of apocrine sweat gland-bearing skin (axillae, groins, perineum, inframammary folds). Characterised by follicular occlusion, folliculitis, and secondary bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus, Propionibacterium acnes), culminating in painful deep abscesses, interconnected epithelialised sinus tracts, and bridged “rope-like” scarring.

Risk Factors: Female:Male = 4:1; begins after puberty and improves at menopause; strongly associated with obesity, smoking, and androgen excess (Hurley Stages I, II, and III).

Management:

General: Weight loss, smoking cessation, loose aerated clothing, antiseptic washes/tea-tree oil.

Medical: Long-term oral tetracyclines (Doxycycline) or Clindamycin + Rifampicin, antiandrogens, retinoids, or biologics (Adalimumab).

Surgical (for severe/refractory disease): Radical wide excision of all affected apocrine-bearing skin and subcutaneous tissue followed by split-skin grafting or flap reconstruction to prevent contractures.

Erysipelas [TU]:

Definition: An acute, sharply demarcated superficial bacterial infection of the upper dermis and superficial cutaneous lymphatics caused by Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes.

Clinical Features: Usually follows a minor skin breach on the face (butterfly distribution) or lower limb. Presents with a fiery-red, hot, oedematous, indurated plaque with a raised, palpable, sharply advancing margin (Milian’s ear sign: involves the pinna, which lacks deeper subcutaneous tissue, unlike cellulitis), accompanied by high fever, rigors, and leukocytosis.

Treatment: Swab any portal of entry; prompt oral or IV Penicillin (Benzylpenicillin / Amoxicillin) or macrolide.

Xeroderma Pigmentosum [RGU]:

Genetics & Pathophysiology: Rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective nucleotide excision repair (NER) of UV-induced DNA pyrimidine dimers.

Clinical Features: Extreme photosensitivity from infancy, severe freckling, xerosis, poikiloderma, ocular photophobia/keratitis, premature skin ageing, and a >2000-fold increased risk of multiple cutaneous malignancies (BCC, SCC, and Malignant Melanoma) appearing before age 10.

Prognosis & Management: 60% mortality by age 20 from metastatic skin cancer. Managed by total UV avoidance, protective clothing/sunscreens, oral retinoids, and early excision of skin tumours.

Desmoid Tumour (Aggressive Fibromatosis) [RGU, TU]:

Pathology: Locally invasive, non-metastasising fibroblastic proliferation arising from musculoaponeurotic structures. Histologically benign (spindle cells in abundant collagen without atypia) but locally malignant due to infiltrative margins and high local recurrence.

Etiology: Associated with pregnancy, prior surgical scars/trauma, oestrogen exposure, and Gardner’s Syndrome / Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (APC gene mutation on Chr 5q22).

Sites: Abdominal wall (especially infraumbilical rectus sheath in multiparous women), intra-abdominal (mesenteric fibromatosis in FAP), and extra-abdominal (shoulder girdle/pelvis).

Management: Active surveillance first, medical therapy (NSAIDs [Sulindac], Tamoxifen, Sorafenib/Imatinib, or low-dose chemotherapy), or wide local excision with mesh reconstruction if symptomatic/progressive.

Collar-Stud Abscess [TU]:

Pathology: A bilocular cold abscess arising from caseating tuberculous lymphadenitis (typically in the jugulodigastric or posterior triangle nodes of the neck).

Mechanism: Caseous pus is initially confined beneath the investing layer of deep cervical fascia (forming the deep loculus). Over time, it erodes through a small pinpoint perforation in the deep fascia to form a second fluctuating collection in the superficial subcutaneous space just beneath the skin (the superficial loculus), connected by a narrow track resembling a collar-stud.

Management: 6–9 months of Anti-Tuberculous Therapy (ATT) + non-dependent zygomatic/oblique aspiration (or incision, curettage of both superficial and deep cavities, enlarging the fascial defect, and primary watertight closure without a drain to prevent a chronic tuberculous sinus).

subject: surgery
title: 2. Oral Cavity PYQs
text:
Cleft Lip & Palate (Types & Timing of Repair) [RGU, TU]:

Embryology: Cleft lip results from failure of fusion of the frontonasal (median nasal) process with the maxillary processes during the 5th–6th week of gestation. Cleft palate results from failure of fusion of the palatal shelves of the maxillary processes during the 7th–10th week.

Classification:

Cleft Lip: Unilateral (Left > Right; Incomplete vs Complete extending into the nostril floor and alveolus up to the incisive foramen [primary palate]) or Bilateral (with a protruding premaxilla/prolabium).

Cleft Palate: Complete or Incomplete (bifid uvula, submucous cleft palate, soft palate only, or hard + soft palate [secondary palate]).

Timing & Technique of Surgical Repair:

Cleft Lip Repair: Performed at 3 to 6 months of age following Millard’s “Rule of 10s” (Weight >10 lbs [4.5 kg], Age >10 weeks, Haemoglobin >10 g/dL, and WBC <10,000/mm³). Technique: Millard’s Rotation–Advancement Repair (or Tennison–Randall triangular flap).

Cleft Palate Repair (Palatoplasty): Performed at 9 to 12 months of age (before speech development begins, while allowing early maxillary growth). Technique: Von Langenbeck bipedicled mucoperiosteal flap, Wardill–Kilner–Veau V-Y pushback, or Furlow’s double-opposing Z-plasty.

Secondary Alveolar Bone Grafting (using cancellous iliac crest bone) at 8–10 years (prior to permanent canine eruption).

Cancrum Oris (Noma) [RGU]:

An acute, fulminating, gangrenous infective stomatitis affecting severely malnourished, debilitated children (often following measles, malaria, or gastroenteritis) in low-income regions.

Caused by a synergistic polymicrobial infection of Fusobacterium necrophorum, Borrelia vincentii, and anaerobes. Begins as a gingival ulcer that rapidly necroses through the full thickness of the cheek and jaws, sloughing off soft tissue and bone to leave grotesque facial defects and severe trismus. Treated with urgent fluid/nutritional resuscitation, IV Penicillin + Metronidazole, wound debridement, and delayed free/pedicled flap reconstruction.

Tongue-Tie (Ankyloglossia) [RGU]:

Congenital anomaly characterised by an abnormally short, thick, fibrotic lingual frenulum tethering the ventral tip of the tongue to the floor of the mouth.

Clinical Features: Infant cannot protrude the tongue tip beyond the lower incisors; on attempted protrusion, the tip is pulled down, creating a heart-shaped (notched) tongue; causes maternal nipple pain/difficulty latching during breastfeeding and later impairs pronunciation of lingual consonants (d, l, n, r, t, th).

Treatment: Simple division (Frenotomy) in infants with breastfeeding difficulty, or formal Frenuloplasty (horizontal division under general anaesthesia with vertical closure or Z-plasty) after age 1–2 years if speech is impaired.

Epulis [RGU]:

Definition: Any benign localised swelling arising from the gingiva (gums) or periodontal membrane (Greek: epi = upon, oulon = gum).

Classification (4 Types):

Fibrous Epulis (Commonest): Firm, pink, pedunculated fibroma arising from the interdental papilla due to chronic irritation/calculus.

Granulomatous (Pyogenic / Pregnancy) Epulis: Soft, bright-red, vascular gingival mass that bleeds easily; Pregnancy epulis appears in the 1st/2nd trimester due to hormonal gingivitis and regresses postpartum.

Giant Cell (Myeloid) Epulis (Peripheral Giant Cell Granuloma): Dark-red/plum-coloured vascular sessile swelling arising from the periosteum/periodontal ligament containing multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells (always check serum calcium/PTH to exclude a brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism).

Carcinomatous Epulis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the gingiva/alveolus.

Treatment: Excision of the epulis along with curettage of its periosteal base and extraction of any involved/irritating tooth root.

Dental Cyst (Radicular / Periapical Cyst) vs Dental Abscess [TU]:

Dental (Radicular) Cyst: Commonest odontogenic cyst. Arises from epithelial cell rests of Malassez in the periodontal ligament stimulated by chronic periapical inflammation beneath a non-vital, carious, dead permanent tooth. Forms a slow-growing, painless jaw swelling lined by stratified squamous epithelium; OPG shows a round radiolucency with a sclerotic rim at the root apex of a carious tooth. Treated by endodontic root canal/tooth extraction + enucleation of the cyst.

Acute Dental (Alveolar) Abscess: Suppurative infection of the dental pulp and periapical tissues tracking through cortical bone; presents with severe throbbing toothache (exacerbated by hot/cold and percussion), fever, trismus, and brawny swelling of the cheek/floor of mouth (Ludwig’s angina if bilateral submandibular/sublingual spaces are involved). Treated with antibiotics (Amoxicillin + Metronidazole), drainage (via root canal, tooth extraction, or intraoral incision), and airway protection.

subject: surgery
title: 3. Vascular PYQs
text:
Palomo’s Operation (Varicocelectomy) [KU 23]:

A retroperitoneal high ligation of the testicular (internal spermatic) vessels performed for symptomatic varicocele or male infertility.

Technique: A 3–4 cm transverse muscle-splitting incision is made slightly above and medial to the anterior superior iliac spine (at the level of the deep inguinal ring). The peritoneum is swept medially to expose the testicular veins (and testicular artery) on the psoas major muscle proximal to the internal ring (where the pampiniform plexus has coalesced into only 1 or 2 trunks), which are ligated and divided en masse (testicular viability is maintained via the artery to the vas deferens and cremasteric artery). Today, it is commonly performed laparoscopically, though subinguinal microsurgical varicocelectomy has lower hydrocele and recurrence rates.

Reverse 3 Sign (Frostberg’s Inverted 3 Sign) [TU]:

A classic radiological sign seen on Plain Chest X-ray (and Barium Swallow) in Coarctation of the Aorta.

On a frontal chest radiograph, the left border of the aorta shows a figure-of-“3” contour (formed by pre-stenotic dilatation of the aortic arch and left subclavian artery above, the inward indentation of the coarctation waist in the middle, and post-stenotic dilatation of the descending aorta below). On a Barium-filled oesophagus, this aortic contour indents the oesophagus in the opposite direction, producing a mirror-image “Reverse 3” (or “E”) sign (associated with inferior rib notching of ribs 3 to 9 — Roesler’s sign — caused by dilated tortuous posterior intercostal collaterals).

subject: surgery
title: PART B: MASTER COMPENDIUM OF ALL TEXTBOOK CLASSIFICATIONS
text:
(Memorise these verbatim for any “Classify…” question)

Classification of Skin Layers & Keratinocytes (Ch. 45):

Epidermis (5% of skin thickness): Stratified squamous keratinised epithelium divided into 5 strata from deep to superficial: (1) Stratum basalis (contains basal keratinocytes, melanocytes, and Merkel cells), (2) Stratum spinosum (contains Langerhans cells), (3) Stratum granulosum (site of active mitosis/differentiation), (4) Stratum lucidum (thick in glabrous skin of palms/soles; absent in eyelids), and (5) Stratum corneum (anucleate keratin).

Dermis (95% of skin thickness): (1) Superficial Papillary Dermis (delicate collagen/elastin, dermal papillae, capillary/lymphatic plexuses, Meissner’s corpuscles), and (2) Deep Reticular Dermis (coarse parallel branching collagen, Pacinian corpuscles, and skin adnexa).

Classification of Cutaneous & Soft-Tissue Infections (Ch. 45):

Classified along two axes: Localised vs Spreading and Non-necrotising vs Necrotising:

Non-necrotising: Impetigo, Folliculitis/Furuncle, Erysipelas, Cellulitis/Lymphangitis (respond to antibiotics alone).

Localised Necrotising: Carbuncle, Hidradenitis suppurativa, Infected sebaceous cyst/abscess (require surgical drainage + antibiotics).

Spreading Necrotising Soft-Tissue Infections (Surgical Emergencies): Necrotising Fasciitis, Meleney’s synergistic gangrene, Fournier’s gangrene, and Purpura fulminans (require immediate resuscitation, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, and radical surgical debridement).

Classification of Benign & Premalignant Skin Tumours (Ch. 45):

Epidermal: Basal cell papilloma (Seborrhoeic keratosis / Verruca senilis), Papillary wart (Verruca vulgaris — HPV), Freckle (Ephelis), Solar Lentigo.

Melanocytic (Naevi): Junctional naevus, Compound naevus, Intradermal naevus, Spitz naevus (“juvenile melanoma”), Spindle cell naevus, Halo naevus, Café-au-lait spot, Naevus spilus, Mongolian spot (sacral), Blue naevus, Naevus of Ota (trigeminal V1/V2) & Naevus of Ito (shoulder).

Hair Follicle (Pilosebaceous) Tumours: Trichoepithelioma, Pilomatrixoma (Calcifying epithelioma of Malherbe), Trichilemmoma (Naevus sebaceous of Jadassohn — 10% lifetime risk of BCC), Adenoma sebaceum (Tuberous sclerosis / Bourneville disease), Rhinophyma (end-stage acne rosacea; 3% harbour occult BCC).

Sweat Gland Tumours: Cystadenoma (Hidradenoma), Eccrine poroma, Cylindroma (“Turban tumour” of scalp).

Premalignant Lesions: Extramammary Paget’s disease, Giant Congenital Pigmented Naevus (GCPN — 3–5% lifetime melanoma risk), Atypical/Dysplastic naevus (FAMMM syndrome), Actinic keratosis, Cutaneous horn, Bowen’s disease / Erythroplasia of Queyrat.

Classification of Congenital & Acquired Vascular Skin Lesions (Ch. 45):

Congenital: (1) Vascular Tumours (Haemangiomas): Capillary haemangioma (Strawberry naevus), Cavernous haemangioma; (2) Vascular Malformations: Salmon patch, Capillary vascular malformation (Port-wine stain), Venous, Lymphatic, and Arteriovenous malformations (high-flow vs low-flow).

Acquired: Campbell de Morgan spots (Cherry angiomas), Spider naevi (pregnancy, chronic liver disease), Pyogenic granuloma, Glomus tumour (Sucquet–Hoyer canal arteriovenous shunt in nail bed), Angiosarcoma / Lymphangiosarcoma (Stewart–Treves syndrome in chronic lymphoedema), and Kaposi’s sarcoma.

Classification of Flaps (Ch. 47):

1. The “Five Cs” Classification: Circulation (Random vs Axial), Composition (Cutaneous, Fasciocutaneous, Myocutaneous, Muscle, Osseocutaneous, Omentum/Jejunum), Contiguity (Local, Regional, Distant [Pedicled vs Free]), Contour (Advancement, Rotation, Transposition, Interpolation), and Conditioning (Delayed vs Non-delayed).

2. Cormack and Lamberty Classification of Fasciocutaneous Flaps (1984): 

Type A: Multiple direct or indirect fascial perforators entering at the base (e.g., Pontén superflap of calf).

Type B: Single consistent direct septocutaneous perforator running along the axis of the flap (e.g., Scapular, Parascapular, Medial plantar flaps).

Type C: Multiple small segmental perforators arising along the course of a deep source artery running in an intermuscular septum (e.g., Radial forearm [“Chinese”] flap, Lateral arm flap).

Type D: Osteomyofasciocutaneous flap supplied by segmental perforators to bone, muscle, fascia, and skin (e.g., Free fibula flap).

3. Mathes and Nahai Classification of Muscle & Myocutaneous Flaps (1981): 

Type I: One single vascular pedicle (e.g., Gastrocnemius, Tensor fascia lata).

Type II: One dominant pedicle + one or more minor pedicles (cannot survive on minor pedicles alone; e.g., Gracilis, Sternocleidomastoid, Soleus, Trapezius, Biceps femoris).

Type III: Two dominant pedicles from separate regional arteries (can survive on either pedicle; e.g., Rectus abdominis [superior & deep inferior epigastric arteries — TRAM/DIEP], Gluteus maximus, Temporalis, Pectoralis minor, Serratus anterior).

Type IV: Segmental vascular pedicles along the muscle belly (least reliable for wide mobilisation; e.g., Sartorius, Tibialis anterior, Flexor hallucis longus).

Type V: One dominant pedicle + multiple secondary segmental pedicles (can survive on either the dominant pedicle or the segmental perforators; e.g., Latissimus dorsi, Pectoralis major).

Brown and Shaw Classification of Maxillectomy Defects (Ch. 53): 

Vertical Component (Classes I–VI): Class I: Maxillectomy without oroantral fistula (alveolar resection); Class II: Low maxillectomy (not involving orbital floor); Class III: High maxillectomy involving orbital floor/periorbita with retention of the globe; Class IV: Radical maxillectomy with orbital exenteration; Class V: Orbitomaxillary defect; Class VI: Nasomaxillary defect.

Horizontal Palatal Component (a–d): a: Unilateral palatal defect ≤ 1/2; b: Bilateral or transverse anterior defect; c: Total palatectomy defect.

Milan System for Reporting Salivary Gland Cytopathology (Table 54.4):

Category I: Non-diagnostic (25% risk of malignancy [ROM] → Repeat USG-FNAC).

Category II: Non-neoplastic (10% ROM → Clinical follow-up).

Category III: Atypia of Undetermined Significance (AUS; 20% ROM → Repeat FNAC or surgery).

Category IVA: Benign Neoplasm (<5% ROM → Conservative parotidectomy).

Category IVB: Salivary Gland Neoplasm of Uncertain Malignant Potential (SUMP; 35% ROM → Surgery with frozen section).

Category V: Suspicious for Malignancy (60% ROM → Surgery).

Category VI: Malignant (>90% ROM → Radical/definitive surgery depending on grade).

Classification of Thyroid Swellings (Table 55.3):

1. Simple Goitre (Euthyroid): Diffuse hyperplastic (Physiological, Pubertal, Pregnancy) and Multinodular goitre.

2. Toxic Goitre: Diffuse toxic goitre (Graves’ disease), Toxic multinodular goitre, Toxic adenoma.

3. Neoplastic: Benign (Follicular adenoma) and Malignant (Primary: Follicular-derived differentiated [Papillary, Follicular, Hürthle cell], Poorly differentiated/Anaplastic, Parafollicular [Medullary], Lymphoma; Secondary: Metastatic [renal cell] or local infiltration).

4. Inflammatory (Thyroiditis): Autoimmune (Chronic lymphocytic / Hashimoto’s), Granulomatous (Subacute de Quervain’s), Fibrosing (Riedel’s), Infective (Acute bacterial/viral, Chronic tuberculous/syphilitic).

5. Other: Amyloid goitre.

Classification of Hyperparathyroidism & Hypercalcaemia (Ch. 56):

Hyperparathyroidism: (1) Primary (85% Single adenoma, 15% Hyperplasia, 1% Carcinoma), (2) Secondary (Compensatory parathyroid hyperplasia due to hypocalcaemia/hyperphosphataemia in chronic kidney disease, malabsorption, or vitamin D deficiency), and (3) Tertiary (Autonomous hypercalcaemic hyperparathyroidism persisting >1 year after successful renal transplantation).

Causes of Hypercalcaemia (Table 56.1): Endocrine (PHPT, Thyrotoxicosis, Phaeochromocytoma, Addisonian crisis), Malignant (Skeletal metastases [breast/lung/prostate], Multiple myeloma, PTHrP-mediated humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy [squamous cell lung/head & neck, renal]), Renal (Tertiary HPT), Nutritional/Drugs (Vitamin D/A intoxication, Milk-alkali syndrome, Thiazide diuretics, Lithium), Granulomatous (Sarcoidosis, Tuberculosis), Genetic (Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcaemia [FHH]), and Skeletal (Paget’s disease, prolonged immobilisation).

Classification of Adrenal Insufficiency & Neuroendocrine Tumours (Ch. 57):

Adrenal Insufficiency (Table 57.1): Primary (Addison’s disease — high ACTH, low cortisol & aldosterone): Autoimmune adrenalitis (70–90%), Tuberculosis, Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage/infarction (Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome), Metastases, CAH; Secondary (low ACTH, low cortisol, normal aldosterone): Pituitary tumour/infarction (Sheehan’s syndrome); Tertiary: Abrupt cessation of exogenous steroids or post-Cushing’s surgery (CRH suppression).

WHO Classification of Neuroendocrine Neoplasms (Table 57.5):

Well-Differentiated NET Grade 1: <2 mitoses/10 HPF AND Ki-67 index <3%.

Well-Differentiated NET Grade 2: 2–20 mitoses/10 HPF OR Ki-67 index 3–20%.

Well-Differentiated NET Grade 3: >20 mitoses/10 HPF OR Ki-67 index >20%.

Poorly Differentiated Neuroendocrine Carcinoma (NEC - Small or Large cell): >20 mitoses/10 HPF and Ki-67 >20%.

Classification of Endoleaks Following EVAR (Table 61.3):

Type I (High-pressure — requires urgent re-intervention): Inadequate seal at the proximal aortic attachment site (Type Ia) or distal iliac attachment site (Type Ib).

Type II (Commonest): Retrograde collateral blood flow into the aneurysm sac from aortic branches (Inferior mesenteric artery or lumbar arteries).

Type III (High-pressure — requires urgent re-intervention): Structural failure of the stent-graft due to modular component disconnection (Type IIIa) or fabric tear/defect (Type IIIb).

Type IV: Blood flow through porous graft fabric (self-limiting).

Type V (Endotension): Continued expansion of the aneurysm sac without any demonstrable radiographic endoleak.

title: 1. Chapter 45: Skin and Subcutaneous Tissue (Remaining Topics)
text:
Skin Dimensions, Blood Supply & Angiosomes:

Surface area is 1–2 m², weight 15–20 kg. Epidermis is thickest on the sole of the foot (0.5–1 mm) and thinnest on the eyelid (0.05–0.09 mm).

Angiosomes (Taylor & Palmer): 3D composite blocks of skin, subcutaneous tissue, and underlying muscle/bone supplied by a specific named source artery and vein. Neighbouring angiosomes are linked within muscle bellies by reduced-calibre “choke vessels” (which dilate during surgical flap delay or myocutaneous flap harvest, e.g., Latissimus dorsi and Rectus abdominis flaps).

Genetic Syndromes with Cutaneous Manifestations:

Neurofibromatosis: 70% autosomal dominant, 30% sporadic. NF-1 (Von Recklinghausen’s disease — Chr 17, 1:4000 births): ≥ 6 smooth-bordered (“Coast of California”) café-au-lait spots, cutaneous/subcutaneous neurofibromas, axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe’s sign), iris Lisch nodules, and optic gliomas. NF-2 (Chr 22): Bilateral acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas) and CNS tumours.

Gorlin’s Syndrome (Naevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome): Autosomal dominant mutation in the PTCH1 (“patched”) tumour suppressor gene on Chromosome 9q22–31. 90% develop multiple BCCs at an early age, palmar/plantar pits, odontogenic keratocysts of the jaw, calcified falx cerebri, bifid ribs, macrocephaly, hypertelorism, and medulloblastoma.

Ferguson-Smith Syndrome: Rare autosomal dominant mutation on Chromosome 9q causing multiple self-healing squamous cell carcinomas unrelated to sun exposure.

Inflammatory, Metabolic & Infective Conditions:

Hyperhidrosis: Excessive eccrine sweating of palms, soles, axillae, and groins. Treated stepwise with topical 20% aluminium chloride antiperspirants, iontophoresis, intradermal Botulinum toxin A injections, or Endoscopic Transthoracic Sympathectomy (ETS) (T2–T3 ganglia for palmar/axillary hyperhidrosis).

Lipodystrophy: Localised or generalised loss of subcutaneous fat (complicating insulin injection sites, HIV protease inhibitors, or transplant drugs); treated with autologous fat grafting (lipotransfer) or poly-L-lactic acid fillers.

Pyoderma Gangrenosum: Rapidly enlarging, very painful necrotic cutaneous ulcer with a characteristic violaceous/purple undermined edge and cribriform scar. Mediated by neutrophil dysfunction (pathergy phenomenon); 50% are associated with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Ulcerative colitis/Crohn’s), Rheumatoid arthritis, Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, or Granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Treatment is medical (high-dose systemic corticosteroids / cyclosporine / infliximab); surgical debridement is contraindicated as pathergy worsens ulceration.

Necrotising Fasciitis (Summary Box 45.1): Polymicrobial synergistic infection (Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus + S. aureus, E. coli, Pseudomonas, Bacteroides, Clostridium) spreading rapidly along the deep fascial planes while initially sparing overlying skin; 80% follow minor trauma/skin breach; 60% occur in lower limbs (perineal variant = Fournier’s gangrene; abdominal wall postoperative variant = Meleney’s synergistic gangrene).

Classic Signs: Severe pain out of proportion to clinical signs, oedema extending beyond visible erythema, woody-hard induration of subcutaneous tissues, haemorrhagic bullae, skin anaesthesia (thrombosis of perforating nutrient vessels and nerves), soft-tissue crepitus, and rapid septic shock (30–50% mortality).

Management: Immediate fluid resuscitation + high-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (Beta-lactam + Clindamycin + Metronidazole) + emergency radical surgical debridement back to healthy bleeding tissue, followed by relook debridement at 24 hours, VAC dressings, and split-skin grafting.

Purpura Fulminans: Acute infectious (Neisseria meningitidis meningococcaemia or varicella in children <7 years or asplenia), neonatal, or idiopathic intravascular thrombosis mediated by endotoxin-induced Protein C deficiency. Causes a petechial rash that coalesces into ecchymoses, haemorrhagic bullae, and sharply demarcated black gangrenous eschars, DIC, and multiorgan failure (40–50% mortality; often requires limb amputations).

Cutaneous Cysts & Rare Tumours:

Milia: Tiny 1–2 mm hard white subepidermal keratin retention cysts seen in neonates and on chronic sun-damaged/smoker’s facial skin in the elderly (Favre–Racouchot syndrome).

Glomus Tumour: Benign hamartoma arising from the neuromyoarterial glomus body (Sucquet–Hoyer arteriovenous shunt canal) responsible for thermoregulation, located most commonly in the subungual corium of the nail bed. Presents with the classic Love’s triad: (1) Paroxysmal lancinating digital pain, (2) Exquisite pinpoint tenderness (elicited with a pinhead — Love’s sign, abolished by inflating a tourniquet — Hildreth’s sign), and (3) Hypersensitivity to cold. Treated by subungual surgical excision.

Merkel Cell Carcinoma: Rare, highly aggressive primary neuroendocrine (mechanoreceptor) carcinoma of the skin in elderly white patients (women > men, 4:1; associated with Merkel cell polyomavirus and UVR). Presents as a rapidly growing, painless, firm, red-purple dome-shaped nodule on sun-exposed head/neck. Treated with wide local excision (2.5–3.0 cm margin), SLNB, and adjuvant radiotherapy.

Congenital Wounds, Pressure Sores, Sinus & Fistula:

Cutis Aplasia Congenita: Congenital absence of epidermis, dermis (and underlying skull bone in 20%) at the vertex of the scalp.

Parry–Romberg Syndrome (Progressive Hemifacial Atrophy): Unilateral self-limiting atrophy of facial skin, subcutaneous fat, muscle, and bone (linear scleroderma variant; cranial forehead cleft variant is called en coup de sabre); reconstructed after burnout (5–10 years) using Coleman autologous lipotransfer or free flaps.

Pressure Sores: Cone-shaped ischaemic necrosis over bony prominences (sacrum, ischial tuberosity, greater trochanter, heel) when external tissue pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure (>32 mmHg); muscle and fat are more susceptible to ischaemia than skin (“iceberg” cone shape). Managed by pressure-relieving mattresses, 2-hourly turning, nutrition, VAC therapy, and surgical debridement + musculocutaneous flap reconstruction (e.g., Gluteus maximus or Tensor fascia lata flap).

Sinus vs Fistula: A Sinus is a blind-ending granulation-lined tract connecting a deep cavity to an epithelial surface; a Fistula is an abnormal communication connecting two epithelialised surfaces.

Causes of Persistence of a Sinus/Fistula: (1) Presence of a foreign body or necrotic tissue (suture, hair, bone sequestrum), (2) Unrelieved distal obstruction, (3) Insufficient/non-dependent drainage, (4) Specific chronic infection (Tuberculosis, Actinomycosis), (5) Crohn’s disease, (6) Epithelialisation of the tract, (7) Malignant change (Marjolin’s ulcer), and (8) Irradiation.

title: 2. Chapter 46: Burns (Remaining Topics)
text:
Admission Referral Criteria to a Specialist Burns Unit (Table 46.1):

Suspected airway or inhalational injury.

Any burn likely to require fluid resuscitation (>15% TBSA in adults, >10% TBSA in children).

Any deep burn likely to require surgical excision and grafting.

Burns of any significance to special anatomical areas: Face, Hands, Feet, Perineum/Genitalia, or across major joints.

Circumferential burns of limbs or chest.

Burns at the extremes of age or with significant medical/psychiatric comorbidities.

Any suspicion of Non-Accidental Injury (NAI) (delayed presentation, inconsistent history, symmetrical “glove and stocking” forced-immersion scalds with sharp water-line sparing flexion creases, or doughnut-shaped buttock sparing).

High-tension electrical burns, chemical burns (especially hydrofluoric acid), or ionising radiation burns.

Cold Injuries & Radiation Burns:

Acute Industrial Cold Injury (liquid nitrogen / LPG contact) vs Frostbite (freezing of extremities with intracellular ice crystal formation and microvascular stasis/thrombosis).

Management of Frostbite: Rapid rewarming in a circulating water bath at 40–42°C for 15–30 minutes (never use dry heat or rub the tissue), analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, and strictly conservative wound care for 1–3 months until complete dry mummification and absolute demarcation occur (“Frostbite in January, amputate in July”), unless wet gangrene/sepsis supervenes.

Ionising Radiation Burns: Localised high-dose radiation causes endarteritis obliterans and chronic painful radionecrotic ulcers that cannot support a skin graft and require wide excision + vascularised free flap cover. Whole-body radiation causing acute skin desquamation indicates a lethal dose.

title: 3. Chapter 47: Plastic & Reconstructive Surgery (Remaining Topics)
text:
Tissue Expansion:

Principle: A deflated silicone balloon expander is placed subcutaneously adjacent to a defect and serially inflated weekly with normal saline via a filling port. Overlying skin expands via mechanical creep (collagen fibre realignment and expulsion of interstitial water) and biological creep / stress relaxation (mitotic epidermal proliferation and dermal angiogenesis), surrounded by a vascular fibrous capsule.

Advantages & Indications: Provides sensate skin of identical colour, texture, and hair-bearing quality without a distant donor defect. Ideal for scalp reconstruction (only way to create new hair-bearing scalp), giant congenital melanocytic naevi, burn scar contractures, and two-stage breast reconstruction.

Autologous Lipotransfer (Coleman Fat Grafting):

Three steps: (1) Low-pressure tumescent liposuction harvest (from abdomen/thigh), (2) Centrifugation (3000 rpm for 3 minutes) to separate oil and blood from viable adipocytes and adipose-derived stromal stem cells, and (3) Micro-droplet reinjection via blunt cannulae into multiple tissue planes (e.g., breast reconstruction contour defects, irradiated scars, Parry–Romberg syndrome). ~20–50% of grafted fat resorbs; rare risk of intravascular fat embolism.

Microsurgery, Free Flap Monitoring & Medicinal Leech Therapy:

Free Flap Monitoring: Keep the patient “Warm, Wet (hyperdynamic normovolaemia), and Comfortable (pain-free to prevent catecholamine-induced vasospasm)”. Monitor hourly in the first 48 hours for colour, temperature, turgor, capillary refill, handheld/implantable Doppler signal, and pinprick bleeding:

Arterial Thrombosis (1/3 of failures): Flap is pale/white, cool, flaccid/empty, absent capillary refill, and no bleeding on pinprick.

Venous Thrombosis/Congestion (2/3 of failures): Flap is dark purple/dusky blue, tense/swollen, very brisk capillary refill (<1 s), and rapid dark venous oozing on pinprick.

Action: Release tight dressings/sutures at bedside and return immediately to theatre for microvascular exploration and revision anastomosis (>60% salvage rate if explored early).

Medicinal Leech Therapy (Hirudo medicinalis):

Indication: Salvage of venously congested flaps or distal digital/ear replants where venous outflow is insufficient or no suitable vein exists for microvascular anastomosis (never used for arterial insufficiency or main-pedicle venous thrombosis that can be surgically revised).

Mechanism: Leech saliva contains hirudin (potent direct thrombin inhibitor), hyaluronidase, and histamine-like vasodilators; each leech ingests 5 mL of blood and the bite oozes up to 50–150 mL over several hours while neovascular venous channels grow in (takes 7–14 days).

Mandatory Prophylaxis: The leech gut harbours the symbiotic Gram-negative bacterium Aeromonas hydrophila, which causes severe flap infection/necrosis; all patients must receive prophylactic Ciprofloxacin (quinolone) or Co-trimoxazole during leech therapy and regular haemoglobin monitoring.

title: 4. Chapter 53: Oral Cavity Cancer (Remaining Topics)
text:
Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) in Early Oral Cancer:

Used in cT1–T2 N0 oral cavity SCC as an alternative to upfront elective neck dissection. Peritumoral injection of (99m)Tc-nanocolloid + ICG/blue dye identifies the first draining node(s) (including unexpected contralateral drainage); if positive on step-serial sectioning and immunohistochemistry, completion neck dissection is performed.

Access Procedures for Oral Cancer Resection:

Transoral Resection: For anterior T1/T2 lesions.

Lip-Split Mandibulotomy: Paramedian stepped osteotomy in front of the mental foramen (preserving the inferior alveolar nerve) to swing the hemimandible laterally for posterior tongue/oropharyngeal tumours.

Visor Flap / Mandibular Lingual Release (“Drop-down” approach): Subplatysmal apron incision releasing floor-of-mouth muscles from the inner mandible to drop the tongue into the neck without splitting the lip or bone.

Weber–Fergusson Incision: Divides upper lip philtrum, curves around the ala and lateral nasal wall, and extends infraorbitally to expose the maxilla for Maxillectomy.

Virtual Surgical Planning (VSP), Zygomatic Implants & Immunotherapy:

VSP: Preoperative 3D CT CAD/CAM stereolithographic models and custom 3D-printed cutting guides for precise mandibular resection and fibula/scapula osteotomies.

ZIP (Zygomatic Implant Perforator) Flap: Immediate placement of long zygomatic dental implants perforating through a radial forearm/ALT soft-tissue free flap to provide immediate fixed dental rehabilitation after maxillectomy without needing a bony free flap.

Immunotherapy in Recurrent/Metastatic HNSCC: Anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors (Pembrolizumab, Nivolumab) prolong overall survival in platinum-refractory or PD-L1-positive recurrent/metastatic oral SCC.

title: 5. Chapter 54: Disorders of the Salivary Glands (Remaining Topics)
text:
Mucoceles, Necrotising Sialometaplasia & Immunological Salivary Disorders:

Extravasation Mucocele: Traumatic rupture of a minor salivary gland duct on the lower lip in children/young adults, spilling mucin into connective tissue (lacks an epithelial lining); presents as a painless, translucent bluish submucosal nodule; treated by surgical excision with the underlying minor salivary gland.

Acute Necrotising Sialometaplasia: Self-limiting ischaemic infarction of minor salivary glands on the hard palate (triggered by local anaesthetic injection, trauma, or bulimia). Presents as a deep crateriform palatal ulcer with rolled margins that clinically and histologically mimics squamous cell carcinoma or mucoepidermoid carcinoma (squamous metaplasia of ducts, but lobular architecture is preserved). Heals spontaneously within 6–10 weeks without surgery.

Sjögren’s Syndrome (SjS) (Table 54.1):

Chronic autoimmune lymphocytic destruction of exocrine glands (Female:Male = 10:1, age 40–60).

Primary SjS (Sicca Syndrome): Xerostomia (dry mouth) + Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) with bilateral parotid enlargement, without an associated connective tissue disease.

Secondary SjS: Sicca symptoms + Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, or Scleroderma.

Diagnosis: Anti-SSA (Ro) and Anti-SSB (La) antibodies, Rheumatoid factor, Schirmer’s test, and Labial Minor Salivary Gland Biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (Focus score ≥ 1 [≥ 50 lymphocytes per 4 mm²]).

Complication: 40-fold increased risk of parotid MALT B-cell Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma (suspect if a parotid gland enlarges rapidly or becomes hard).

Sarcoidosis & Heerfordt’s Syndrome: Non-caseating granulomatous infiltration of the parotid gland; Heerfordt’s Syndrome (Uveoparotid Fever) is the classic triad of bilateral parotid enlargement + anterior uveitis + facial nerve (CN VII) palsy accompanied by low-grade fever.

HIV-Associated Salivary Gland Disease (Summary Box 54.4): Occurs in 5–10% of HIV patients; presents with painless bilateral multicystic parotid enlargement due to Benign Lymphoepithelial Cysts (BLEC) and Diffuse Infiltrative Lymphocytosis Syndrome (DILS — CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration), mimicking Sjögren’s syndrome but with negative anti-Ro/La autoantibodies.

Recurrent Parotitis of Childhood: Rapid recurrent unilateral/bilateral parotid swelling in children aged 3–6 years; sialogram shows characteristic “snowstorm” punctate sialectasis; managed with antibiotics and sialendoscopic washouts (usually resolves spontaneously at puberty).

Sialadenosis (Sialosis): Non-inflammatory, non-neoplastic, painless bilateral symmetrical parotid enlargement caused by autonomic neuropathy and acinar hypertrophy in chronic alcoholism/cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition/bulimia, and drugs (guanethidine, thioridazine).

Salivary Gland & Duct Trauma:

Facial Nerve Injury: If transected posterior to a vertical line dropped from the lateral canthus of the eye, perform immediate primary epineurial microsurgical repair (or cable nerve graft). Branches injured anterior to this line have rich cross-anastomoses and do not require repair.

Stensen’s Duct Injury: Repair within 72 hours by primary end-to-end microsurgical anastomosis over a fine Silastic/epidural catheter stent cannulated via the buccal papilla.

Submandibular Gland Excision (Operative Steps & Nerve Relations — Summary Box 54.6): 

Incision: Horizontal skin-crease incision two finger-breadths (3–4 cm) below the lower border of the mandible (to avoid the marginal mandibular nerve).

Three Crucial Nerves Related to the Submandibular Gland:

Marginal Mandibular Branch of Facial Nerve: Runs in the deep fascia superficial to the facial vein and artery; protected via the Hayes Martin manoeuvre (ligating the facial vein low on the inferior border of the gland and reflecting the tied upper stump superiorly along with the investing fascia). Injury paralyses depressor anguli oris/depressor labii inferioris → drooping/asymmetry of the corner of the mouth on smiling.

Lingual Nerve: Lies on the hyoglossus muscle deep to the mylohyoid; loops beneath Wharton’s duct (“double-crossing” it) and is attached to the deep lobe of the gland via the submandibular ganglion (which must be carefully divided to free the gland). Injury causes ipsilateral loss of general sensation and taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

Hypoglossal Nerve (CN XII): Runs deep to the gland on the hyoglossus muscle below Wharton’s duct, accompanied by the thin-walled ranine veins. Injury causes ipsilateral tongue hemi-atrophy and deviation of the protruding tongue towards the injured side.

title: 6. Chapter 55 & 56: Thyroid & Parathyroid Glands (Remaining Topics)
text:
Surgical Anatomy of the Thyroid & Parathyroids:

Beahrs’ Triangle (for locating the Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve): Bounded by the Common carotid artery (base/laterally), Inferior thyroid artery (superiorly), and Recurrent laryngeal nerve (inferomedially) in the tracheo-oesophageal groove.

Tubercle of Zuckerkandl: Posterolateral pyramidal projection of the thyroid lobe; the RLN almost constantly runs immediately medial/posterior to this tubercle in a fissure between it and the trachea before entering the larynx beneath Berry’s ligament.

Non-Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve (~1–2% on the Right side): Associated with an anomalous retro-oesophageal right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria); arises directly from the cervical vagus and runs transversely into the larynx.

Secondary Hyperparathyroidism & Calciphylaxis (Ch. 56):

Pathogenesis in Chronic Kidney Disease: Impaired renal phosphate excretion → hyperphosphataemia stimulates osteocytes to secrete Fibroblast Growth Factor-23 (FGF-23), which inhibits renal 1α-hydroxylase → **low 1,25(OH)_2D_3 (calcitriol)** → reduced gut calcium absorption and hypocalcaemia → continuous chief-cell stimulation and four-gland parathyroid hyperplasia (initially diffuse polyclonal, later nodular monoclonal hyperplasia with downregulation of Vitamin D receptors and Calcium-Sensing Receptors, rendering it medically refractory).

Medical Management: Low-phosphate diet, Phosphate binders (Sevelamer, Calcium acetate), Calcitriol/Alfacalcidol, and Cinacalcet (calcimimetic). Renal transplantation is the only definitive cure.

Indications for Parathyroidectomy in Secondary HPT (Tables 56.3 & 56.4): Intact PTH >500–800 pg/mL with refractory hypercalcaemia/hyperphosphataemia, largest gland volume >500 mm³ (>1 cm), severe renal osteodystrophy/bone pain, intractable pruritus, erythropoietin-resistant anaemia, or Calciphylaxis. Performed via Subtotal (3(1/2)-gland) Parathyroidectomy or Total Parathyroidectomy with Forearm Autotransplantation + Bilateral Cervical Thymectomy.

Casanova Test: Used in recurrent hyperparathyroidism after forearm autotransplantation; inflating a tourniquet on the grafted arm or selective brachial venous sampling demonstrating a >20:1 PTH gradient confirms graft-dependent recurrence.

Calciphylaxis (Calcific Uraemic Arteriolopathy): Life-threatening syndrome (up to 87% mortality from sepsis) in ~4% of dialysis patients with an elevated Calcium × Phosphate product and deficiency of calcification-inhibitor α_2-Heremans–Schmid glycoprotein (Fetuin-A). Causes medial calcification and thrombosis of dermal/subcutaneous arterioles, presenting with excruciatingly painful violaceous retiform purpuric plaques and black necrotic skin eschars on the thighs, legs, and abdomen. Requires urgent parathyroidectomy, sodium thiosulphate, and meticulous wound care.
