title: 7. Chapter 57: Adrenal Glands & Abdominal Endocrine Disorders (Remaining Topics)
text:
Adrenal Incidentaloma (Algorithm Fig 57.2 & Summary Box 57.1): 

Defined as an asymptomatic adrenal mass (≥ 1 cm) discovered incidentally on cross-sectional imaging performed for non-adrenal reasons.

Two Questions Must Be Answered in Parallel:

Is it Functionally Active? All patients undergo: (i) Overnight 1 mg Dexamethasone Suppression Test (cortisol >50 nmol/L indicates autonomous cortisol secretion / Cushing’s), (ii) Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines (to exclude Phaeochromocytoma), (iii) Plasma Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR) (if hypertensive or hypokalaemic, to exclude Conn’s syndrome), and (iv) Sex hormones / steroid precursors (DHEAS, testosterone, 17-OH-progesterone if virilisation or adrenocortical carcinoma is suspected).

Is it Malignant? (Summary Box 57.1):

Benign Adenoma (Lipid-rich): Size <4 cm, homogeneous, Unenhanced CT attenuation ≤ 10 Hounsfield Units (HU), rapid contrast washout (Absolute washout >60%, Relative washout >40% at 15 minutes), and signal drop on out-of-phase chemical-shift MRI.

Suspicious for Malignancy: Size >4 cm (especially >6 cm), >10 HU density, delayed contrast washout (<60% absolute / <40% relative), no signal loss on chemical-shift MRI, or FDG-PET avidity.

Indications for Adrenalectomy in Incidentaloma: (i) Any hormonally functioning tumour, and (ii) Any non-functioning tumour ≥ 4 cm or with imaging features suspicious for malignancy (Laparoscopic if <6 cm without local invasion; Open radical adrenalectomy if >6 cm or locally invasive).

Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s Syndrome):

Pathology: 30–40% unilateral Aldosterone-Producing Adenoma (APA) (small 1–2 cm golden-yellow “canary tumour” arising in the zona glomerulosa; 40% harbour somatic KCNJ5 potassium-channel mutations) vs 60% Bilateral Idiopathic Adrenal Hyperplasia (and rare Familial Hyperaldosteronism Types I–IV; Type I is Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism treated with low-dose dexamethasone).

Clinical Features: Commonest cause of secondary/endocrine hypertension; causes drug-resistant hypertension, sodium retention, and hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (muscle weakness, cramps, polyuria/polydipsia from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; note that >50% are normokalaemic at presentation).

Stepwise Diagnosis:

Screening: Elevated Plasma Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR >850 suggestive, >1700 diagnostic) after stopping spironolactone/eplerenone and ACE inhibitors for 2–4 weeks and correcting hypokalaemia.

Confirmatory Test: Saline infusion test, oral salt-loading test, or fludrocortisone suppression test.

Subtype Lateralisation (Unilateral APA vs Bilateral Hyperplasia): High-resolution adrenal CT followed by Adrenal Vein Sampling (AVS — Gold Standard in patients >35 years) or ¹¹C-Metomidate PET-CT. 

Treatment:

Unilateral APA: Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy (after preoperative blood pressure and potassium normalization with Spironolactone).

Bilateral Adrenal Hyperplasia: Lifelong medical therapy with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (Spironolactone or Eplerenone — avoids gynaecomastia).

Cushing’s Syndrome:

Etiology: ACTH-Dependent (80–85%): Pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing’s Disease — 70–80%) or Ectopic ACTH Syndrome (10%) (small-cell lung cancer, bronchial/thymic/pancreatic NETs); ACTH-Independent (15–20%): Unilateral Adrenocortical Adenoma, Adrenocortical Carcinoma, or Primary Bilateral Macronodular Adrenal Hyperplasia (BMAH).

Clinical Features (Summary Box 57.2): Central truncal obesity, moon-like plethoric face, interscapular “buffalo hump”, supraclavicular fat pads, proximal myopathy (“lemon on sticks”), wide purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, hirsutism, acne, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, and psychosis/depression.

Stepwise Diagnosis:

Confirm Hypercortisolism (Requires ≥ 2 abnormal first-line tests): (i) Overnight 1 mg Dexamethasone Suppression Test (8 am cortisol >50 nmol/L), (ii) Late-night salivary cortisol (loss of circadian nadir), and (iii) 24-hour Urinary Free Cortisol (UFC) (>3 × upper limit).

Determine ACTH Dependency (Plasma ACTH):

Suppressed ACTH (<5 pg/mL): Adrenal Cushing’s → perform Adrenal CT/MRI.

Normal/Elevated ACTH: Pituitary vs Ectopic → perform Pituitary MRI, High-dose (8 mg) DST, and Bilateral Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling (BIPSS) (or CT Thorax + ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT for ectopic ACTH).

Treatment:

Preoperative Medical Control: Steroidogenesis inhibitors (Metyrapone, Ketoconazole, or IV Etomidate in life-threatening hypercortisolaemic crisis) + DVT and antibiotic prophylaxis.

Surgery: Trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy for Cushing’s disease; Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy for unilateral adrenal adenoma.

Mandatory Postoperative Corticosteroid Replacement: Because chronic hypercortisolism suppresses hypothalamic CRH/pituitary ACTH and causes atrophy of the contralateral adrenal cortex, all patients undergoing unilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing’s require intraoperative and postoperative Hydrocortisone replacement (weaned slowly over 6–12 months once a Short Synacthen Test confirms recovery of the contralateral gland).

Nelson’s Syndrome: Occurs in 10% of patients with Cushing’s disease who undergo bilateral adrenalectomy; loss of cortisol negative feedback causes rapid enlargement of the pituitary corticotroph tumour with massive ACTH and POMC/MSH secretion, causing intense cutaneous hyperpigmentation and visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopia).

Adrenocortical Carcinoma (ACC):

Rare (1–2 per million), highly aggressive malignancy; 60% are functional (rapidly progressive Cushing’s syndrome + Virilisation in women due to co-secretion of cortisol and DHEAS/androgens).

Pathology: Large (>6–10 cm), invasive tumours; histological malignancy is assessed by the Modified Weiss Score (≥ 3 indicates malignancy) and Ki-67 index (>10% high risk).

Treatment: Open En Bloc Radical Adrenalectomy (resecting adjacent kidney, spleen, distal pancreas, or liver wall if invaded to achieve R0 margins) + Adjuvant Mitotane (adrenolytic drug; requires concurrent hydrocortisone replacement) ± EDP (Etoposide, Doxorubicin, Cisplatin) chemotherapy.

Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumours (P-NETs) (Table 57.4):

1. Insulinoma (Commonest Functioning P-NET — 70–80%):

Rule of 90s: 90% are benign, 90% are solitary, 90% are <2 cm, and equally distributed across the head, body, and tail of the pancreas; 10% are associated with MEN 1 (often multiple).

Clinical Diagnosis — Whipple’s Triad:

Symptoms and signs of neuroglycopenia/hypoglycaemia precipitated by fasting or exercise (confusion, visual disturbances, bizarre behaviour, seizures, coma, sweating, palpitations; patients gain weight because they eat frequently to prevent attacks).

Documented plasma glucose <3.0 mmol/L (<50 mg/dL) at the time of symptoms.

Immediate relief of symptoms upon oral or IV administration of glucose.

Biochemical Confirmation (Supervised 72-Hour Fast Test — Gold Standard): Concomitant blood glucose <2.5–3.0 mmol/L + inappropriately elevated serum Insulin (>6 μU/mL) + elevated C-Peptide (>0.2 nmol/L) and Proinsulin, with negative sulfonylurea screen (elevated C-peptide rules out factitious exogenous insulin administration, where C-peptide is suppressed).

Localisation: Pancreatic protocol CT/MRI + Endoscopic Ultrasonography (EUS — >90% sensitive) + Intra-arterial Calcium Stimulation with Hepatic Venous Sampling (for occult/MEN 1 lesions) or GLP-1 receptor PET-CT.

Treatment: Preoperative Diazoxide (inhibits insulin release from β-cells) and frequent carbohydrate meals → Laparoscopic or Open Surgical Enucleation (with intraoperative ultrasound to confirm the tumour is >2–3 mm away from the main pancreatic duct; distal pancreatectomy if in the tail or MEN 1).

2. Gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison Syndrome — ZES):

Pathology: Gastrin-secreting NET causing massive gastric acid hypersecretion; 60–90% are malignant; 20–25% occur as part of MEN 1. 70–80% are actually located in the submucosa of the first/second part of the Duodenum (small <1 cm and multiple in MEN 1) rather than the pancreas.

Passaro’s Gastrinoma Triangle (Houses 90% of Gastrinomas): Bounded superiorly by the junction of the cystic and common bile ducts, inferiorly by the junction of the second and third parts of the duodenum, and medially by the junction of the neck and body of the pancreas. 

Clinical Features: Severe, refractory, multiple peptic ulcers in atypical sites (distal duodenum/jejunum) + chronic secretory diarrhoea and steatorrhoea (high gastric acid inactivates pancreatic lipase and precipitates bile salts; diarrhoea resolves with nasogastric aspiration).

Diagnosis: Fasting Serum Gastrin (FSG) >10 × normal (>1000 pg/mL) in the presence of basal gastric pH <2.0. If FSG is borderline (100–1000 pg/mL), perform a Secretin Stimulation Test (provokes a paradoxical rise in serum gastrin >200 pg/mL in gastrinoma). Localised by ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT (SSTR-PET) and EUS. Always screen for MEN 1 (serum calcium/PTH).

Treatment: High-dose Proton Pump Inhibitors (Omeprazole/Pantoprazole) + Surgical resection/duodenotomy with peripancreatic lymph node dissection for sporadic gastrinomas (in MEN 1, parathyroidectomy is performed first, and surgery is reserved for pancreatic tumours >2 cm).

3. Rare Functioning & Non-Functioning P-NETs:

VIPoma (Verner–Morrison / WDHA Syndrome): Secretes Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide → Watery Diarrhoea (profuse tea-coloured secretory diarrhoea >3–5 L/day), Hypokalaemia, and Achlorhydria (“Pancreatic Cholera”); treated with Octreotide, fluid/electrolyte resuscitation, and distal pancreatectomy.

Glucagonoma (α-cell tumour): Causes the “4 D’s”: Dermatitis (pathognomonic Necrolytic Migratory Erythema around perineum/perioral/extremities), Diabetes mellitus, Deep vein thrombosis, and Depression/Weight loss + painful glossitis/stomatitis and normocytic anaemia.

Somatostatinoma (δ-cell tumour): Classic triad of Diabetes mellitus + Cholelithiasis (gallstones) + Steatorrhoea/Diarrhoea; duodenal periampullary somatostatinomas contain psammoma bodies and are associated with NF-1.

Non-Functioning P-NETs (NF-P-NETs — 60–90% of all P-NETs; Fig 57.16): Express Chromogranin A, Synaptophysin, and Pancreatic Polypeptide (PP) without a hormonal syndrome. Asymptomatic Grade 1 tumours <2 cm can be safely observed with serial EUS/MRI; tumours >2 cm or symptomatic/Grade 2 require surgical resection.

Gastrointestinal Neuroendocrine Tumours (GI-NETs / Carcinoid Tumours):

1. Gastric NETs (3 Types arising from Enterochromaffin-like [ECL] cells):

Type I (70–80%): Multiple small (<1 cm), benign polyps associated with chronic autoimmune atrophic gastritis / pernicious anaemia (achlorhydria → high gastric pH → hypergastrinaemia drives ECL hyperplasia); treated conservatively with endoscopic surveillance/polypectomy.

Type II (5%): Multiple small polyps secondary to Zollinger–Ellison Syndrome / MEN 1 (low gastric pH + high gastrin).

Type III (15–20%): Sporadic, solitary, large (>2 cm) infiltrative tumour with normal gastrin levels; behaves aggressively like gastric adenocarcinoma → requires radical gastrectomy + lymphadenectomy.

2. Small Bowel (Midgut) NETs & Carcinoid Syndrome:

Arise from Kulchitsky (enterochromaffin) cells in the terminal ileum (30% are multifocal). Secrete 5-Hydroxytryptamine (Serotonin), Substance P, Kallikrein, and Histamine.

Desmoplastic Mesenteric Reaction: Nodal metastases at the root of the mesentery release serotonin and growth factors that induce intense retroperitoneal fibrosis, drawing in and kinking bowel loops and constricting the superior mesenteric vessels (“spoke-wheel / sunburst” appearance on CT — Fig 57.18), causing chronic postprandial mesenteric ischaemia and small bowel obstruction.

Carcinoid Syndrome (Occurs in 20–30%, ONLY when liver metastases or retroperitoneal/bronchial primaries bypass hepatic first-pass monoamine oxidase degradation of serotonin):

Episodic Cutaneous Flushing (90%) of face/neck, Secretory Watery Diarrhoea (70%), abdominal cramps, Bronchospasm/Wheezing, telangiectasia, pellagra (niacin/tryptophan depletion), and Carcinoid Heart Disease (Hedinger’s Syndrome): Endocardial fibrosis producing Tricuspid Regurgitation and Pulmonary Stenosis (right-sided heart valves; left heart valves are spared because pulmonary endothelial monoamine oxidase inactivates serotonin).

Diagnosis: Elevated serum Chromogranin A + elevated 24-hour Urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid) + Contrast CT/MRI + ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATOC / DOTATATE PET-CT + Echocardiography.

Management (Summary Box 57.3):

Medical / Perioperative Cover: Long-acting Somatostatin Analogues (Octreotide LAR or Lanreotide) control flushing/diarrhoea and exert an antiproliferative effect (mandatory IV Octreotide infusion during anaesthesia/surgery to prevent a fatal Carcinoid Crisis — profound hypotension, bronchospasm, and arrhythmias). Second-line systemic therapy for metastatic disease is Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT) using ¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTATATE or Everolimus.

Surgical: Radical resection of the small bowel primary, mesenteric nodal mass (preserving SMA branches), synchronous liver metastasectomy/RFA, and prophylactic cholecystectomy (because long-term Octreotide causes gallstones).

3. Appendiceal NETs (Commonest tumour of the appendix):

Found incidentally at the tip of the appendix in 0.3–0.5% of appendicectomies.

Size-Based Surgical Rule:

<1 cm: Simple Appendicectomy alone is 100% curative (no follow-up needed).

1–2 cm: Appendicectomy is sufficient unless high-risk features are present (positive base margin, deep mesoappendiceal invasion >3 mm, Grade 2/3, or lymphovascular invasion), which warrant a right hemicolectomy.

>2 cm: Perform a formal Oncological Right Hemicolectomy.

title: 8. Chapter 58, 61 & 62: Breast, Arterial & Venous Disorders (Remaining Topics)
text:
Breast — Additional Entities (Ch. 58):

Poland’s Syndrome: Congenital unilateral absence of the sternocostal head of Pectoralis Major, hypoplasia/absence of the breast and nipple (amazia/athelia), deficiency of subcutaneous fat, costal cartilage defects (ribs 2–4), and ipsilateral symbrachydactyly (short, webbed fingers). 

Mondor’s Disease [TU]: Superficial thrombophlebitis of the thoracoepigastric or lateral thoracic vein of the breast and anterior chest wall (idiopathic or post-biopsy/trauma). Presents with acute linear pain and a palpable, tender, subcutaneous cord-like structure that forms a characteristic vertical skin groove/furrow (“bowstring sign”) when the arm is raised. Self-limiting within 4–6 weeks; treated with reassurance and NSAIDs (after mammogram excludes occult cancer). 

Paget’s Disease of the Nipple: Eczematous, crusted, weeping erosion of the nipple that destroys the nipple and spreads onto the areola (unlike benign eczema, it is unilateral, destroys the nipple apex first, does not itch severely, and fails to respond to topical steroids). Histologically characterised by large, pale, vacuolated intraepidermal adenocarcinoma cells (Paget cells) derived from underlying DCIS or invasive ductal carcinoma (present in >95%). Diagnosed by wedge/punch biopsy of the nipple + mammography/MRI; treated by central cone excision + radiotherapy (if confined to retroareolar DCIS) or Mastectomy + SLNB.

Breast Cancer in Pregnancy: Often presents late with aggressive TNBC biology. USG and core biopsy are safe (mammogram with fetal shielding is safe; avoid gadolinium MRI, CT, and bone scans). Surgery (MRM) is safe in all trimesters (BCS is only feasible in the 3rd trimester when radiotherapy can be given postpartum). Chemotherapy (Anthracyclines/Taxanes) is contraindicated in the 1st trimester (teratogenic during organogenesis) but safe in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters (stopped at 34 weeks). Radiotherapy, Tamoxifen, and Trastuzumab are strictly contraindicated throughout pregnancy.

Male Breast Cancer: Accounts for <0.5–1% of breast cancers; associated with BRCA2 mutations and Klinefelter’s syndrome (47,XXY). Presents in elderly men as a painless, hard subareolar lump with early invasion of the nipple–areola complex, skin ulceration, and pectoralis major fixation (due to scant breast parenchyma). >90% are ER-positive; treated with Modified Radical Mastectomy (or Simple mastectomy + SLNB), adjuvant radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and Tamoxifen for 5–10 years.

Breast Angiosarcoma: Highly lethal mesenchymal malignancy arising either de novo in young women or secondary to breast-conserving radiotherapy / chronic post-mastectomy lymphoedema (Stewart–Treves syndrome) 5–10 years after treatment; presents as a bruised-looking purple skin plaque/nodule; treated by wide mastectomy.

Arterial Disorders — Additional Entities (Ch. 61):

Carotid Artery Stenosis & Endarterectomy (Summary Box 61.2):

Atheromatous plaque at the carotid bifurcation / origin of the Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) embolises platelet-fibrin thrombi (Hollenhorst cholesterol crystals in retinal arteries), causing ipsilateral Amaurosis Fugax (transient monocular blindness — “curtain coming down over one eye”), contralateral hemiparesis/hemisensory TIA or stroke, or dysphasia.

Indication for Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA) (NASCET / ECST Trials): Symptomatic patients with 50–99% ICA stenosis on Duplex USG/CTA, ideally performed within 2 weeks of the index TIA/minor stroke (preserving the hypoglossal, vagus, glossopharyngeal, and marginal mandibular nerves and closing the arteriotomy with a patch angioplasty using a temporary intraluminal shunt).

Subclavian Steal Syndrome: Proximal occlusion/stenosis of the first part of the subclavian artery proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery. Exercising the ipsilateral arm lowers arm vascular resistance, causing retrograde blood flow down the ipsilateral vertebral artery (“stealing” blood from the basilar/vertebrobasilar cerebral circulation) → arm claudication + vertebrobasilar syncope, vertigo, ataxia, and visual disturbances on arm exercise, accompanied by a >20 mmHg blood pressure discrepancy between the two arms. Treated by subclavian angioplasty and stenting or carotid–subclavian bypass.

Popliteal Artery Aneurysm:

Commonest peripheral arterial aneurysm (70%); 50% are bilateral and 30–40% have a coexisting Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm.

Rarely ruptures; instead, it presents with limb-threatening acute thrombosis or chronic distal thromboembolism (“trash foot”) that progressively occludes the crural run-off vessels (carrying a 50% amputation rate once acute thrombosis occurs).

Indications for Elective Repair: Any symptomatic popliteal aneurysm, or any asymptomatic popliteal aneurysm ≥ 2.0 cm in diameter (especially if lined with mural thrombus). Repaired via Medial approach proximal-and-distal ligation + reversed GSV Exclusion Bypass or Posterior approach inlay graft repair.

Other Arteritides & Cystic Adventitial Disease:

Temporal (Giant Cell) Arteritis: Granulomatous arteritis of medium/large cranial branches in patients >50 years causing unilateral throbbing headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, tender pulseless cord-like superficial temporal artery, and ESR >50 mm/h. Immediate high-dose oral/IV Prednisolone must be started before temporal artery biopsy to prevent irreversible blindness from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (ophthalmic artery occlusion).

Takayasu’s Arteritis (“Pulseless Disease”): Pan-arteritis of the aortic arch and its major branches in young Asian women (<40 years), leading to absent upper limb pulses, hypertension (renal artery stenosis), and ocular/cerebral ischaemia.

Cystic Myxomatous Adventitial Degeneration: Accumulation of mucinous synovial-like jelly within the adventitia of the popliteal artery in young non-smoking men, compressing the lumen to cause intermittent claudication (Ishikawa’s sign: pedal pulses disappear on sharp knee flexion); treated by evacuation or interposition vein graft.

Venous Disorders — Additional Entities (Ch. 62):

Pelvic Congestion Syndrome (PCS): Chronic non-cyclical dull pelvic ache, dyspareunia, and vulval/perineal/posterior thigh varicosities in multiparous premenopausal women caused by incompetence of the ovarian (gonadal) and internal iliac veins; diagnosed by transvaginal duplex/MR venography and treated by percutaneous transcatheter ovarian vein coil embolisation. 

Effort Axillary–Subclavian Vein Thrombosis (Paget–Schrötter Syndrome): Primary thrombosis of the axillary/subclavian vein in young athletes/weightlifters following repetitive overhead arm exertion due to venous thoracic outlet compression at the costoclavicular space (between the first rib, subclavius muscle/costoclavicular ligament, and clavicle, or a cervical rib). Presents with an acutely swollen, aching, cyanosed arm and dilated shoulder collaterals. Treated by urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis followed by surgical thoracic outlet decompression (First Rib Resection) and anticoagulation. 

Venous Trauma & Venous Tumours: Major axial venous injuries (especially the popliteal vein and IVC) should be repaired (via lateral venorrhaphy, vein patch, Carrel triangulation end-to-end anastomosis, or autologous panel/spiral saphenous vein graft) rather than ligated to prevent severe venous hypertension and limb loss, accompanied by calf fasciotomy if combined with arterial injury. Leiomyosarcoma of the Inferior Vena Cava is the commonest primary malignant venous tumour (presents with Budd–Chiari syndrome or lower limb oedema; treated by radical resection and prosthetic graft reconstruction).

HONEST VERDICT: IS THIS ENOUGH IF YOU HAVEN’T READ THE TEXTBOOK?

1. Why it looks "short" on screen, but is actually massive in content:

Word & Page Count: The file you pasted contains ~16,500 words. When pasted into Microsoft Word (Times New Roman, 12 pt, 1.25 spacing, single column) along with the 12 tables and 30 textbook figures, it comes out to 48 to 55 pages.

Why is it 50 pages instead of 210 pages (the length of the 11 textbook chapters)? 

Bailey & Love is written in narrative paragraphs with historical anecdotes, case stories, and conversational filler. 

Your notes strip out 100% of the conversational fluff and convert every paragraph into direct marking-scheme bullet points and side-headings (Definition, Etiopathogenesis, Pathology, Clinical Features, Investigations, Management, Complications).

The Physics of a 3-Hour Surgery Exam:

In a 3-hour theory exam, a student can physically handwrite at most 3,500 to 4,000 words total (~400–500 words for a Long Essay, ~150–200 words for a Short Essay, and ~75–100 words for a Short Answer).

Every Long Essay and Short Essay in your notes already contains 400 to 900 words of pure, high-yield points—which is more than you can physically write in the exam hall.

If you haven't read the textbook yet and have limited time: Trying to read 210 pages of dense 2-column Bailey & Love text for the first time will cause severe information overload, and you will struggle to recall structured headings during the exam. Studying structured, side-headed notes is the fastest and safest way to score distinction marks on a first read.

2. What was slightly too brief in your file? (The 8 Gaps We Need to Expand)

When I audited your pasted file line-by-line from the perspective of a first-time reader facing potential 5-mark surprise Short Essays, I found 8 specific areas where the notes were either condensed into 3–4 lines in Part C or needed a fuller explanation so you can understand them on your first read and fill 1.5 pages in the exam:

Triangles of the Neck (Asked in Question Bank 8.1 Short Essay #4: "Draw and illustrate the triangles of neck...", which was not included in the thyroid section).

Operative Steps of Thyroidectomy & Intraoperative Nerve Monitoring (Explicitly a core Learning Objective of Chapter 55).

Tuberculous Mastitis & Idiopathic Granulomatous Mastitis (IGM) (Very high-yield Indian exam Short Essays in Chapter 58 that were only 4 lines in Part C).

Operative Steps of Modified Radical Mastectomy (MRM) & Breast Reconstruction (Core surgical steps from Chapter 58).

Adrenal Insufficiency (Addisonian Crisis), Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) & Operative Steps of Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy (Chapter 57 topics that were condensed in Part C).

Acute & Chronic Mesenteric Ischaemia (Intestinal Angina) (Chapter 61 topic condensed in Part C).

Cervical Rib & Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (Covered across Chapters 61 & 62).

Post-Amputation Complications & Amputee Rehabilitation (Explicitly asked in Long Essay 10.1 Q1: "How is the patient rehabilitated?").

Below is the 10-Page Zero-Gap Expansion Pack covering these 8 topics in full, easy-to-understand detail. Append this section to the end of your file, and you will not need to open the textbook at all.

1. Triangles of the Neck (Anatomy & Surgical Importance)

(Covers Question Bank 8.1 Short Essay #4 [RGU])

Overview: The side of the neck is a quadrilateral region divided obliquely by the Sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle into a Large Anterior Triangle (in front of SCM) and a Posterior Triangle (behind SCM).

A. Anterior Triangle of the Neck

Boundaries:

Anteriorly: Anterior median line of the neck (from chin/symphysis menti to suprasternal notch).

Posteriorly: Anterior border of the Sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Superiorly (Base): Lower border of the body of the mandible and a line extending from the angle of the mandible to the mastoid process.

Inferiorly (Apex): Suprasternal notch on the manubrium sterni.

Roof: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia, platysma, and skin.

Subdivisions (Divided by the Digastric muscle and Superior belly of Omohyoid into 4 triangles):

[[TABLE:surgery-tbl-009]]

B. Posterior Triangle of the Neck

Boundaries:

Anteriorly: Posterior border of the Sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Posteriorly: Anterior border of the Trapezius muscle.

Inferiorly (Base): Middle third of the clavicle.

Superiorly (Apex): Meeting point of SCM and Trapezius on the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone.

Roof: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia (pierced by the 4 cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus at Erb’s point: Lesser occipital, Great auricular, Transverse cervical, and Supraclavicular nerves, plus the External jugular vein).

Floor: Prevertebral fascia covering Splenius capitis, Levator scapulae, and Scalenus posterior, medius, and anterior.

Subdivisions (Divided by the Inferior belly of Omohyoid into 2 triangles):

Occipital Triangle (Upper, larger part):

Key Contents: Spinal Accessory Nerve (CN XI) (runs obliquely across the roof/levator scapulae from the junction of the upper and middle thirds of SCM to the junction of the middle and lower thirds of Trapezius — highly vulnerable during Level V lymph node biopsy; injury causes drooping of the shoulder and inability to abduct the arm above $90^\circ$), Trunks of the brachial plexus, Transverse cervical vessels, and Level VA posterior triangle lymph nodes.

Supraclavicular (Subclavian / Omoclavicular) Triangle (Lower, smaller part):

Key Contents: Third part of the Subclavian artery, Subclavian vein, Trunks of the brachial plexus, Suprascapular vessels, and Supraclavicular lymph nodes (Level VB) (including Virchow’s node on the left side at the thoracic duct termination).

2. Operative Steps of Thyroidectomy & Intraoperative Nerve Monitoring

(Covers Chapter 55 Learning Objective: "To describe thyroidectomy")

Definitions of Thyroid Operations (Summary Box 55.2):

Total Lobectomy (Hemithyroidectomy): Complete removal of one thyroid lobe + isthmusectomy.

Total Thyroidectomy: $2 \times \text{Total Lobectomy} + \text{Isthmusectomy}$ (and pyramidal lobe if present).

Near-Total Thyroidectomy (Dunhill Procedure): Total lobectomy on one side + isthmusectomy + subtotal lobectomy on the contralateral side.

Subtotal Thyroidectomy: Bilateral subtotal lobectomy + isthmusectomy (leaving up to $4–8\text{ g}$ remnant on each side; rarely performed today due to high recurrence rates).

Step-by-Step Operative Technique of Thyroidectomy: [REFER FIGURE- Fig 55.19, Page 864]

Positioning & Draping:

Supine under general anaesthesia using an electromyographic (EMG) nerve-monitoring endotracheal tube positioned between the vocal cords.

Head is placed on a head ring with a sandbag/roll between the scapulae to extend the neck, and the table is tilted $15^\circ$ head-up (Reverse Trendelenburg to reduce venous engorgement).

Incision & Subplatysmal Flaps:

A curvilinear transverse collar incision (Kocher’s incision) is placed in a natural skin crease $1–2\text{ cm}$ above the suprasternal notch (at the level of the cricoid/upper border of the thyroid isthmus) between the anterior borders of the SCM muscles.

Incise skin and platysma; raise subplatysmal flaps superiorly up to the thyroid cartilage notch and inferiorly down to the suprasternal notch (staying superficial to the anterior jugular veins).

Opening the Midline & Mobilising Strap Muscles:

Incise the investing layer of deep cervical fascia vertically in the avascular midline raphe between the sternohyoid muscles, and then dissect the deeper sternothyroid muscle off the thyroid capsule laterally until the internal jugular vein, common carotid artery, and vagus nerve (stimulated to confirm nerve monitor function — $V_1$ signal) are identified.

Ligation of the Middle Thyroid Vein & Mobilisation of the Upper Pole:

Ligate and divide the middle thyroid vein (the first vascular structure encountered laterally) to allow medial rotation of the thyroid lobe.

Retract the sternothyroid muscle superolaterally to expose the superior thyroid vascular pedicle. Ligate and divide the superior thyroid artery and vein branches individually right on the thyroid capsule (low ligation) to protect:

The External Branch of the Superior Laryngeal Nerve (EBSLN) (which runs medially towards the cricothyroid muscle in Joll’s sternothyrolaryngeal triangle).

The blood supply to the superior parathyroid gland.

Identification of the Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve (RLN) & Parathyroid Preservation:

Rotate the thyroid lobe medially and anteriorly. Identify the Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve in Beahrs’ triangle (bounded by the common carotid artery, inferior thyroid artery, and RLN) or just posterior/medial to the tubercle of Zuckerkandl, and trace it up to its entry point into the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint.

Identify both the superior and inferior parathyroid glands within their surrounding halo of fat and gently sweep them posteriorly off the thyroid capsule on their vascular pedicles. Do not ligate the main trunk of the inferior thyroid artery; instead, ligate its terminal capsular branches on the surface of the thyroid gland to preserve the end-artery blood supply to the parathyroids.

Division of Berry’s Ligament & Delivery of the Gland:

Keeping the RLN under direct vision at all times (where it is at greatest risk of traction or thermal injury), carefully divide the condensation of pretracheal fascia (Berry’s ligament) layer-by-layer using fine ties or bipolar cautery.

Dissect the thyroid lobe and isthmus (along with any pyramidal lobe) off the anterior surface of the trachea. For a total thyroidectomy, repeat the exact same dissection on the contralateral side.

Haemostasis & Closure:

Irrigate with warm saline, perform a Valsalva manoeuvre (raising intrathoracic venous pressure to $40\text{ cmH}_2\text{O}$) to identify any occult venous bleeding points, and confirm recurrent laryngeal and vagus nerve integrity ($R_2$ and $V_2$ signals).

Approximate the sternohyoid strap muscles loosely in the midline with interrupted absorbable sutures (leave a gap inferiorly so any postoperative haematoma can decompress into the subcutaneous space rather than compressing the trachea). Close platysma and skin (subcuticular absorbable suture).

New Technology in Thyroid Surgery:

Intraoperative Neuromonitoring (IONM): Uses surface electrodes on the endotracheal tube to detect vocal cord electromyography when the RLN or vagus nerve is stimulated:

Intermittent IONM: Hand-held stimulator probe aids nerve identification in reoperative/malignant cases and prevents bilateral vocal cord palsy (if loss of signal occurs on the first side, staging the contralateral lobectomy prevents bilateral RLN paralysis and tracheostomy).

Continuous IONM: An electrode clip placed around the vagus nerve provides real-time alerts of amplitude drop/latency increase caused by excessive traction before irreversible nerve injury occurs.

3. Tuberculosis of the Breast & Idiopathic Granulomatous Mastitis (IGM)

(Covers Chapter 58 High-Yield Inflammatory Breast Diseases)

A. Tuberculosis of the Breast (Tubercular Mastitis)

Epidemiology: Rare in Western countries ($<0.1%$), but accounts for up to 3–4% of breast lesions in endemic countries like India, typically affecting multiparous, lactating women aged 20–40 years.

Modes of Spread to the Breast (5 Routes):

Retrograde lymphatic spread (Commonest): From caseating axillary, internal mammary, or cervical lymph nodes.

Direct contiguous extension: From tuberculous osteitis/chondritis of an underlying rib or costochondral junction, or empyema necessitans from the pleura.

Haematogenous spread: In miliary tuberculosis.

Ductal infection: Direct entry through a cracked/abraded nipple during lactation (rare).

Clinical Forms (Tewari & Shukla / McKeown & Wilkinson Classification):

Nodular (Caseous) Tubercular Mastitis (Commonest): Slow-growing, painless or mildly painful, poorly defined, firm-to-hard lump that closely mimics breast carcinoma; later softens centrally to form a cold abscess that ruptures through the skin into multiple chronic discharging sinuses with undermined edges and bluish surrounding skin. [REFER FIGURE- Fig 58.26, Page 930]

Disseminated (Confluent) Tubercular Mastitis: Multiple coalescing caseating tubercles throughout the breast producing numerous sinuses ("watering-can breast").

Sclerosing Tubercular Mastitis: Dense fibrosis dominates over caseation (more common in older women); causes a stony-hard, shrunken breast with nipple retraction and skin dimpling, indistinguishable clinically from scirrhous carcinoma.

Diagnosis:

Imaging: USG/Mammography + Chest X-ray/CT Thorax (to look for pulmonary/nodal/rib foci).

Pathology & Microbiology: Core needle biopsy or wedge biopsy from the sinus wall demonstrates epithelioid cell granulomas with Langhans giant cells and caseous necrosis. Pus/tissue is sent for Ziehl–Neelsen (ZN) staining for Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB), GeneXpert MTB/RIF (CBNAAT — rapid PCR detecting M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance), and Lowenstein–Jensen / MGIT mycobacterial culture (gold standard).

Treatment:

Standard 6–9 Months Anti-Tuberculous Therapy (ATT): 2 months Intensive Phase (HRZE: Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) followed by 4–7 months Continuation Phase (HRE).

Surgical Intervention: Limited to ultrasound-guided aspiration of cold abscesses, curettage/excision of persistent non-healing sinus tracts, or excision of residual fibrotic masses.

B. Idiopathic Granulomatous Mastitis (IGM)

Definition & Etiology: A rare, benign, chronic inflammatory breast disease of unknown etiology occurring in young parous women within 2–5 years of pregnancy/lactation. Postulated triggers include an autoimmune reaction to extravasated fat/protein-rich luminal milk secretions, hyperprolactinaemia, and infection by lipophilic Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii.

Clinical Features: Presents as a firm, tender, unilateral peripheral or retroareolar breast mass that frequently develops multiple sterile microabscesses, skin erythema, ulceration, sinus tracts, peau d’orange, nipple retraction, and reactive axillary lymphadenopathy — clinically and radiologically mimicking locally advanced / inflammatory breast carcinoma and tuberculous mastitis.

Diagnosis (Diagnosis of Exclusion):

Core Needle Biopsy: Shows lobulocentric non-caseating granulomatous inflammation (epithelioid histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells, neutrophils, and lymphocytes centred strictly around breast lobules).

Mandatory Exclusion of Infective Granulomas: Negative ZN stain, negative GeneXpert MTB/RIF, negative mycobacterial culture, and negative fungal (PAS/GMS) stains. (In India, empirical ATT must NOT be given unless TB is proven, as it delays treatment and worsens IGM).

Management:

Conservative / Expectant + NSAIDs & Antibiotics (Doxycycline or Clarithromycin if Corynebacterium is suspected) + USG-guided aspiration of collections (many mild cases burn out spontaneously over 6–12 months).

Immunosuppressive Therapy (for progressive, painful, or ulcerating disease): Oral Prednisolone ($0.5–1\text{ mg/kg/day}$ tapered over 2–3 months) or topical steroid cream $\pm$ weekly low-dose Methotrexate (steroid-sparing agent).

Surgical: Wide excision of persistent chronic abscess complexes or Hadfield’s major duct excision if associated with a mammary duct fistula.

4. Operative Steps of Modified Radical Mastectomy (MRM)

(Covers Chapter 58 Core Surgical Procedure)

Definition: Complete en bloc removal of the entire breast parenchyma (including the nipple–areola complex, skin overlying the tumour, and the axillary tail of Spence), the pectoralis fascia, and Level I and II (with or without Level III) axillary lymph nodes, while preserving the pectoralis major muscle.

Anatomical Boundaries of Dissection:

Superior: Second rib / Subclavius muscle.

Inferior: Inframammary fold (6th rib / upper rectus sheath).

Medial: Lateral border of the sternum.

Lateral: Anterior border of the Latissimus dorsi muscle.

Step-by-Step Operative Technique:

Positioning & Incision: Supine with the ipsilateral arm abducted to $90^\circ$ on an arm-board. Make a transverse/oblique elliptical Stewart incision encompassing the nipple–areola complex, the skin overlying the tumour, and any previous core-biopsy scar.

Elevation of Skin Flaps: Raise superior and inferior skin flaps ($5–7\text{ mm}$ uniform thickness) in the relatively avascular bloodless plane between the subcutaneous fat and the superficial layer of the premammary fascia (just superficial to the attachments of Cooper’s ligaments) up to the anatomical boundaries of the breast.

Excision of the Breast from Medial to Lateral: Dissect the breast and pectoralis major fascia cleanly off the underlying pectoralis major muscle fibres from medial to lateral (ligating or cauterising the perforating branches of the internal mammary artery), leaving the breast attached laterally by the axillary tail.

Axillary Lymph Node Dissection (Levels I & II $\pm$ III):

Incise the clavipectoral fascia at the lateral border of pectoralis major; retract pectoralis major and pectoralis minor superomedially (Auchincloss modification; or divide/excise pectoralis minor in Scanlon/Patey modification).

Identify the Axillary Vein superiorly and clear all fibrofatty lymph-node-bearing tissue inferior to the axillary vein from Level II (behind pectoralis minor) and Level I (lateral to pectoralis minor) down to the floor of the axilla (subscapularis and serratus anterior).

Three Vital Nerves to Identify and Preserve in the Axilla:

Long Thoracic Nerve of Bell ($C_5, C_6, C_7$): Lies closely applied to the medial chest wall on the serratus anterior muscle (investment fascia must be kept intact; injury causes winging of the scapula).

Thoracodorsal Nerve ($C_6, C_7, C_8$) & Thoracodorsal Vessels: Runs vertically on the posterior axillary wall to innervate latissimus dorsi (preserve for shoulder adduction and potential future LD flap reconstruction).

Medial and Lateral Pectoral Nerves: Innervate pectoralis major and minor (injury causes pectoral muscle atrophy). (The intercostobrachial nerve [$T_2$] runs transversely across the central axilla; preserved if possible, or divided if encased by nodes, causing numbness of the upper inner arm).

Haemostasis, Drains & Closure: Irrigate the wound, place two closed-suction Romovac drains (one in the axilla and one under the pectoral skin flaps), and close the skin in two layers without tension.

5. Adrenal Insufficiency, Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH), Adrenal Haemorrhage & Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy

(Covers Chapter 57 Remaining Core Topics)

1. Adrenal Insufficiency & Acute Addisonian Crisis (Table 57.1):

Clinical Features of Chronic Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison’s Disease): Insidious fatigue, weakness, anorexia, weight loss, postural hypotension, salt craving, and buccal/palmar crease/scar hyperpigmentation (high pituitary POMC/ACTH/MSH due to loss of cortisol negative feedback). Biochemistry shows hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, low 8 am serum cortisol, high plasma ACTH, and failure of cortisol to rise 30–60 minutes after $250\text{ }\mu\text{g}$ IV/IM Tetracosactide (Short Synacthen Test).

Acute Adrenal (Addisonian) Crisis (Life-Threatening Emergency):

Precipitants: Sepsis, surgery, trauma, bilateral adrenal haemorrhage/infarction (Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome in meningococcal septicaemia), or abrupt withdrawal of long-term exogenous steroid therapy.

Clinical Presentation: Refractory hypotensive shock, fever, severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting (mimics an acute surgical abdomen), accompanied by hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and hypoglycaemia.

Immediate Management (Do NOT wait for hormone assay results):

Draw blood for random cortisol, ACTH, electrolytes, and glucose.

Immediate IV Hydrocortisone $100\text{ mg}$ stat bolus, followed by $50–100\text{ mg}$ IV 6-hourly ($200–400\text{ mg}/24\text{ h}$; at this high dose, hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity, so fludrocortisone is not needed acutely).

Aggressive IV Fluid Resuscitation: $2–3\text{ L}$ of 0.9% Normal Saline with 5% Dextrose in the first 6 hours to correct hypovolaemia, hyponatraemia, and hypoglycaemia.

Treat the precipitating infection with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

Maintenance (once stable): Lifelong oral Hydrocortisone ($15–25\text{ mg/day}$ in 2–3 divided doses: e.g., $10\text{ mg}$ morning, $5\text{ mg}$ midday, $5\text{ mg}$ early evening) + Fludrocortisone ($0.05–0.2\text{ mg}$ OD in primary AI), medical alert bracelet, and "Sick-Day Rules" (double the oral hydrocortisone dose during intercurrent febrile illness or stress).

2. Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH / Adrenogenital Syndrome):

Pathophysiology: Autosomal recessive deficiency of enzymes required for cortisol synthesis from cholesterol (21-Hydroxylase deficiency accounts for 95% of cases; incidence 1 in 5,000 births).

Cortisol deficiency causes uninhibited pituitary ACTH hypersecretion, which drives bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia and shunts steroid precursors into the androgen pathway, while mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) synthesis is also impaired in 75% ("salt-wasting" form).

Clinical Presentation:

Females at birth: Ambiguous genitalia (Female pseudohermaphroditism) — clitoromegaly and fused labia resembling a scrotum, with normal internal uterus/ovaries.

Males & Females in infancy (2–3 weeks): Salt-wasting Addisonian crisis (vomiting, severe dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, shock) or precocious puberty, virilisation, hypertension (in $11\beta$-hydroxylase deficiency), and short adult stature (due to premature androgen-induced epiphyseal closure).

Diagnosis & Treatment: Markedly elevated serum 17-Hydroxyprogesterone ($17\text{-OHP}$) and adrenal androgens. Treated by lifelong Hydrocortisone + Fludrocortisone replacement (to replace deficient hormones and suppress ACTH-driven androgen excess) and reconstructive feminising genitoplasty in girls.

3. Adrenal Haemorrhage:

Caused by severe sepsis, anticoagulation, trauma, antiphospholipid syndrome, or obstetric delivery. Presents with flank/abdominal pain and shock (if bilateral, causes acute adrenal insufficiency). Diagnosed on Contrast CT [REFER FIGURE- Fig 57.9, Page 899]. Managed conservatively with resuscitation, reversal of anticoagulants, steroid cover, and superselective angiographic coil/gelfoam embolisation of the bleeding adrenal artery if active extravasation persists.

4. Approaches to Adrenalectomy (Chapter 57):

Gold Standard for Benign & Small ($<6\text{ cm}$) Tumours: Minimally Invasive Adrenalectomy via either:

Lateral Transperitoneal Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy (Gagner): Patient in lateral decubitus position ($60–90^\circ$) with table break.

Right Side (4 ports): Retract right lobe of liver cranially, divide triangular ligament and posterior peritoneum along the lateral border of the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC), identify and clip the short right adrenal vein draining directly into the posterolateral IVC, and mobilise the gland off the upper pole of the kidney and psoas.

Left Side (3–4 ports): Mobilise the splenic flexure of the colon and divide the lienorenal ligament so the spleen and tail of the pancreas fall medially, open Gerota’s fascia, identify and clip the longer left adrenal vein draining inferiorly into the left renal vein (along with the inferior phrenic vein tributary), and excise the gland.

Posterior Retroperitoneoscopic Adrenalectomy (Walz): Patient placed prone jack-knife; 3 ports inserted below the 12th rib directly into the retroperitoneal space inflated with $\text{CO}_2$ at $20–25\text{ mmHg}$. Ideal for bilateral adrenalectomy, small tumours ($<5\text{ cm}$), and patients with previous extensive upper abdominal surgery/adhesions. [REFER FIGURE- Fig 57.13, Page 904]

Open Adrenalectomy (via subcostal rooftop or thoracoabdominal incision): Mandatory for Adrenocortical Carcinoma, locally invasive tumours, or large phaeochromocytomas ($>8–10\text{ cm}$).

6. Acute & Chronic Mesenteric Ischaemia

(Covers Chapter 61 Visceral Arterial Occlusive Disorders)

A. Acute Mesenteric Ischaemia (Surgical Emergency; 50–70% Mortality)

Etiology (4 Mechanisms):

Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) Embolism (50%): Arises from left atrium in atrial fibrillation or left ventricular mural thrombus post-MI; lodges $3–8\text{ cm}$ distal to the SMA origin (just beyond the middle colic artery origin, sparing the proximal jejunum).

Acute-on-Chronic SMA Thrombosis (25%): Occurs at the ostium of a pre-existing atherosclerotic SMA plaque (causes pan-intestinal infarction from the duodenojejunal flexure to the splenic flexure).

Non-Occlusive Mesenteric Ischaemia (NOMI — 15%): Severe splanchnic vasoconstriction in critically ill ICU patients on high-dose vasopressors/inotropes or cardiogenic shock.

Mesenteric Venous Thrombosis (10%): Superior mesenteric vein thrombosis in thrombophilia, portal hypertension, pancreatitis, or intra-abdominal sepsis.

Clinical Features:

Classic hallmark early triad: (1) Sudden, severe central abdominal pain "out of proportion to physical signs" (abdomen is initially soft and non-tender until transmural infarction causes peritonitis), (2) Rapid forceful gut emptying (vomiting and diarrhoea, later blood-stained "redcurrant jelly" stool), and (3) Presence of a cardiac embolic source (atrial fibrillation).

Investigations: Marked leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis with elevated serum lactate, and ** Biphasic CT Angiography (CTA) of the Abdomen (Gold Standard):** Shows filling defect/cut-off in the SMA, lack of bowel wall enhancement, bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall), and portal venous gas.

Management:

Immediate fluid resuscitation, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, nasogastric decompression, and IV Unfractionated Heparin infusion.

Emergency Laparotomy:

Assess bowel viability from DJ flexure to rectum; resect all frankly gangrenous, perforated bowel (avoid primary anastomosis in shock/oedematous bowel).

Revascularise the SMA: Perform SMA Fogarty Balloon Embolectomy (for embolus) or Retrograde Iliac-to-SMA / Aorto-SMA Bypass (or endovascular stenting for ostial thrombosis).

Plan a mandatory "Second-Look Laparotomy" at 24–48 hours to reassess borderline bowel segments and restore continuity.

B. Chronic Mesenteric Ischaemia (Intestinal Angina)

Pathophysiology: Because of rich collateral anastomoses between the three visceral trunks (Coeliac axis, Superior Mesenteric Artery, and Inferior Mesenteric Artery via the pancreaticoduodenal arcades, marginal artery of Drummond, and arc of Riolan), at least two of the three major mesenteric arteries must have severe stenosis/occlusion to produce symptoms. [REFER FIGURE- Fig 61.1, Page 997]

Clinical Triad: (1) Postprandial central abdominal pain ("intestinal angina") occurring 15–30 minutes after eating and lasting 1–3 hours, (2) "Food Fear" (sitophobia) leading to profound weight loss/cachexia, and (3) Altered bowel habit (diarrhoea/steatorrhoea), often with an epigastric bruit in a heavy smoker with generalised atherosclerosis.

Diagnosis & Treatment: Confirmed by Duplex USG and CT Angiography. First-line treatment is Endovascular Angioplasty and Balloon-Expandable Stenting of the SMA [REFER FIGURE- Fig 61.25, Page 1009] (or open surgical bypass / transaortic endarterectomy if endovascular stenting fails).

7. Cervical Rib, Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS) & Subclavian Steal

(Covers Chapters 61 & 62 Neurovascular Compression Syndromes)

Anatomy & Pathophysiology: A Cervical Rib is a congenital anomaly arising from the 7th cervical vertebra ($C_7$) in 0.5–1% of the population (50% bilateral; more common in females). It may be complete (articulating anteriorly with the scalene tubercle of the first rib) or incomplete with a fibrous band. It narrows the interscalene triangle (bounded by Scalenus anterior anteriorly, Scalenus medius posteriorly, and the first rib inferiorly), compressing the Subclavian artery and the Lower Trunk ($C_8, T_1$) of the Brachial Plexus (Note: the Subclavian vein passes in front of scalenus anterior in the costoclavicular space).

Three Clinical Types of Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS):

Neurogenic TOS (90–95% — Commonest): Compression of the $C_8, T_1$ nerve roots / lower trunk causes pain, paraesthesia, and numbness along the ulnar (medial) border of the forearm and hand, with wasting and weakness of the small intrinsic muscles of the hand (thenar, hypothenar, and interossei).

Arterial TOS (1–2%): Bony compression of the subclavian artery over the cervical/first rib causes intimal damage and post-stenotic fusiform dilatation (aneurysm) lined with mural thrombus [REFER FIGURE- Fig 61.24, Page 1009]. Showers of platelet/fibrin microemboli travel into the hand, presenting with unilateral Raynaud’s phenomenon, forearm claudication, splinter haemorrhages, digital ischaemic ulcers, or trash hand/gangrene.

Venous TOS (3–5%): Compression of the axillary/subclavian vein in the costoclavicular space between the first rib, subclavius tendon, and clavicle, causing Effort Thrombosis (Paget–Schrötter Syndrome) (swollen, cyanosed, aching arm after overhead exertion). [REFER FIGURE- Fig 62.37, Page 1048]

Investigations: Chest & Cervical Spine X-ray (identifies bony cervical rib or elongated $C_7$ transverse process), Nerve Conduction Studies, and Dynamic Duplex USG / CT or MR Angiography with the arms both at rest and in hyperabduction.

Management:

Neurogenic TOS without muscle wasting: Physiotherapy and postural shoulder-girdle strengthening exercises.

Arterial TOS (and Neurogenic TOS with muscle wasting): Surgical Thoracic Outlet Decompression (transaxillary or supraclavicular Excision of the Cervical Rib AND First Rib + Scalenectomy), combined with subclavian artery interposition graft repair and distal brachial Fogarty thromboembolectomy if an arterial aneurysm/embolus is present.

8. Post-Amputation Complications & Amputee Rehabilitation

(Covers Chapter 61 & Long Essay 10.1 Q1 [KU 22])

Complications of Major Limb Amputation:

Early Complications:

Reactionary or Secondary Haemorrhage (requires return to theatre for ligation).

Wound Haematoma (predisposes to deep infection; prevented by meticulous haemostasis and suction drain).

Stump Infection / Abscess & Gas Gangrene: Gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) is a specific hazard of high above-knee amputations due to contamination of ischaemic thigh muscle by spores from the patient’s own perineum/faeces (prevented by povidone-iodine skin prep and prophylactic benzylpenicillin/metronidazole).

Flap Ischaemia, Necrosis & Wound Dehiscence: Due to performing amputation at too distal a level without adequate blood supply (often requires revision to a higher level, e.g., BKA to AKA).

Deep Vein Thrombosis & Pulmonary Embolism (mandatory LMWH prophylaxis).

Late Complications:

Flexion Contracture of the Proximal Joint: Fixed flexion deformity of the knee (in BKA) or hip (in AKA) due to sitting for prolonged periods or muscle imbalance, preventing prosthetic fitting.

Stump Pain & Amputation Neuroma: A painful, tender bulbous proliferation of regenerating axons at the cut end of a major nerve (e.g., tibial or sciatic nerve; prevented by traction-transection of the nerve high up so it retracts into well-padded muscle).

Phantom Limb Sensation & Phantom Limb Pain: Awareness of the missing limb (universal and benign) vs burning/cramping pain felt in the absent foot (treated with firm reassurance, mirror-box therapy, Gabapentin/Pregabalin, or Amitriptyline).

Bony Spur / Osteitis / Sinus & Stump Ulceration (from ill-fitting prosthetic socket or progressive ischaemia).

Stepwise Rehabilitation of the Lower Limb Amputee [KU 22]:

Preoperative & Immediate Postoperative Phase:

Multidisciplinary team input (surgeon, physiotherapist, prosthetist, occupational therapist, psychologist), adequate analgesia (epidural or perineural stump catheter + opioids), and meticulous protection of the contralateral "good" foot (heel offloading to prevent pressure sores).

Stump Conditioning & Prevention of Contractures:

Apply a rigid dressing or elastic stump shrinker sock once healed to mould a cylindrical/conical stump and reduce oedema.

Strict Physiotherapy from Day 1: Avoid placing pillows under the thigh/knee; encourage prone lying (to extend the hip) and active knee extension exercises to prevent flexion contractures, alongside upper-body and core strengthening (for crutches/parallel bars).

Early Ambulation & Prosthetic Fitting:

Start standing and balance training between parallel bars using a pneumatic Early Walking Aid / Inflatable Artificial Limb (PPAM aid) [REFER FIGURE- Fig 61.38, Page 1017] as soon as wound healing allows, followed at 6–8 weeks by fitting of a definitive custom-moulded suction-socket or PTB (Patellar Tendon-Bearing) prosthesis.

Occupational Therapy & Home Modification:

Assess the patient’s home environment (install grab-rails, ramps, stair-lifts, and widen doorways for wheelchair clearance) and provide vocational retraining.

title: 19. ANATOMY OF NOSE
text:
(Based on PL Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery, 7th Edition)

1. Lateral Wall of Nose

A. Bony and Cartilaginous Framework

The lateral nasal wall is formed by the following bones and cartilages:

1. Bones: Nasal bone, frontal process of maxilla, lacrimal bone, labyrinth of ethmoid (with superior and middle turbinates), inferior turbinate (a separate bone), perpendicular plate of palatine bone, and medial pterygoid plate of sphenoid.

2. Cartilages: Upper lateral cartilage, lower lateral (alar) cartilage, and 2–3 lesser alar (sesamoid) cartilages.

B. Divisions of the Lateral Wall

1. Vestibule: Anterior and inferior skin-lined part containing sebaceous glands, hair follicles, and stiff hairs (vibrissae). Its upper limit is marked by the limen nasi (nasal valve), formed by the caudal margin of the upper lateral cartilage.

2. Atrium of the Middle Meatus: Shallow depression in front of the middle turbinate and above the vestibule. Agger nasi is an elevated ridge just anterior to the attachment of the middle turbinate (contains agger nasi air cells when pneumatized).

3. Turbinates (Conchae) and Meatuses: Scroll-like bony projections covered by mucous membrane. The spaces below them are called meatuses.

C. Turbinates and Meatuses

1. Inferior Turbinate and Inferior Meatus:

• Inferior Turbinate: Largest turbinate; a separate bone. Covered by thick vascular mucosa rich in venous sinusoids (erectile tissue).

• Inferior Meatus: Space below the inferior turbinate. The nasolacrimal duct opens into its anterior part, guarded by a mucosal fold called Hasner’s valve.

2. Middle Turbinate and Middle Meatus:

• Middle Turbinate: An ethmoturbinal (part of the ethmoid bone). Attached to the lateral wall by an S-shaped bony lamella called the ground (basal) lamella:

• Anterior 1/3: Lies in the sagittal plane; attached to the lateral edge of the cribriform plate.

• Middle 1/3: Lies in the frontal (coronal) plane; attached to the lamina papyracea (separates anterior from posterior ethmoidal cells).

• Posterior 1/3: Runs horizontally; attaches to the lamina papyracea and medial wall of the maxillary sinus, forming the roof of the middle meatus.

• Middle Meatus:

Contains key structures of the Ostiomeatal Complex (OMC):

• Uncinate Process: Hook-like bony ridge running anterosuperior to posteroinferior. Its superior attachment varies (lamina papyracea, skull base, or middle turbinate), determining frontal sinus drainage.

• Bulla Ethmoidalis: Prominent anterior ethmoidal air cell located behind the uncinate process. Spaces above and behind it (when present) are the suprabullar and retrobullar recesses (together forming the sinus lateralis of Grunwald).

• Hiatus Semilunaris (Inferior): A two-dimensional crescentic cleft (1–2 mm wide) between the sharp posterosuperior border of the uncinate process and the anterior surface of the bulla ethmoidalis.

• Ethmoidal Infundibulum: Three-dimensional funnel-shaped space bounded medially by the uncinate process, laterally by the lamina papyracea, and posteriorly by the bulla ethmoidalis. The natural ostium of the maxillary sinus opens into its floor.

• Fontanelles: Membranous areas in the lower middle meatus (anterior and posterior to the uncinate attachment to the inferior turbinate) devoid of bone; site of accessory maxillary ostia.

• Drainage in Middle Meatus: Frontal sinus, anterior ethmoidal sinuses, and maxillary sinus (Anterior group of paranasal sinuses).

3. Superior Turbinate and Superior Meatus:

• Superior Turbinate: Part of the ethmoid bone, situated posterosuperior to the middle turbinate. Landmark for the sphenoid ostium.

• Superior Meatus: Space below the superior turbinate; receives openings of the posterior ethmoidal cells (1–5 in number).

4. Sphenoethmoidal Recess:

• Triangular fossa above the superior (or supreme) turbinate; receives the ostium of the sphenoid sinus.

D. Haller Cell & Onodi Cell (Anatomical Variants)

• Haller Cell (Infraorbital ethmoid cell): Air cell situated in the roof of the maxillary sinus (floor of the orbit), pneumatized from anterior or posterior ethmoids. Enlargement narrows the ethmoidal infundibulum and maxillary ostium, predisposing to maxillary sinusitis.

• Onodi Cell (Sphenoethmoidal cell): Most posterior ethmoidal cell that extends laterally and superiorly to the sphenoid sinus. The optic nerve and internal carotid artery are closely related to its lateral wall (risk of blindness/haemorrhage during FESS).

subject: ent
title: 20. PHYSIOLOGY OF NOSE
text:
1. Functions of the Nose and Turbinates

1. Respiration:

• Natural pathway for breathing (newborns are obligate nasal breathers).

• Inspiratory airflow: Passes parabolically through the middle part of the nasal cavity between the turbinates and septum.

• Expiratory airflow: Follows the same path, but friction at the limen nasi (nasal valve) creates eddies under the middle and inferior turbinates, ventilating the sinus ostia.

• Nasal Cycle: Rhythmic, alternating congestion and decongestion of the erectile tissue of the turbinates every 2.5–4 hours, regulated by the autonomic nervous system, while total nasal resistance remains constant.

2. Air-Conditioning of Inspired Air (Function of Turbinates):

• Filtration and Purification: Nasal vibrissae filter particles >3 µm; the mucus blanket traps fine particles (0.5–3.0 µm), pollen, and bacteria.

• Temperature Control ("Radiator" Mechanism): The rich vascularity and cavernous venous sinusoids of the inferior and middle turbinates warm inspired air (from 0°C or subzero) to near body temperature (37°C) within 0.25 seconds.

• Humidification: Seromucinous glands secrete ~1000 mL of water in 24 hours, adjusting the relative humidity of inspired air to >75–80% (essential for ciliary beating and alveolar gas exchange).

3. Protection of Lower Airway:

• Mucociliary Mechanism (Mucociliary Blanket):

• Consists of two layers: an outer viscous mucus (gel) layer and an inner watery serous (sol) layer floating on the tips of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.

• Cilia beat 10–20 times/second (rapid "effective stroke" reaching the gel layer and slow "recovery stroke" in the sol layer), moving the blanket like a conveyor belt towards the nasopharynx at 5–10 mm/min (cleared every 10–20 mins).

• Factors impairing cilia: Drying (<50% humidity stops cilia in 8–10 mins), smoking, extreme temperatures, hypoxia, and decongestants.

• Enzymes and Immunoglobulins: Nasal secretions contain muramidase (lysozyme), secretory IgA, IgE, and interferons (optimal at nasal pH 7.0).

• Sneezing: Protective reflex expelling irritants.

4. Vocal Resonance: Adds resonance to nasal consonants (M, N, NG). Obstruction causes rhinolalia clausa (denasal speech: M/N/NG become B/D/G).

5. Nasal Reflexes: Nasobronchial, nasopulmonary (nasal packing reduces pO_2), and olfactory-salivary/gastric reflexes.

6. Olfaction: Perception of smell and flavour of food.

2. Anatomy of Olfactory Pathway and Anosmia

• Olfactory Region (Area): Situated in the upper one-third of the nasal cavity (roof, cribriform plate, superior turbinate, and upper 1/3 of the nasal septum). Lined by pale yellow neuroepithelium containing bipolar olfactory receptor cells and Bowman’s glands.

• Olfactory Pathway:

Odorous volatile substance → Cilia on olfactory vesicles (Peripheral process of bipolar receptor cells)

↓

Central axons group into 12–20 Olfactory Nerves (Filia olfactoria) → Pass through Cribriform Plate

↓

Synapse with Mitral and Tufted cells in the Olfactory Bulb (Glomeruli)

↓

Axons form Olfactory Tract → Prepyriform cortex, Amygdaloid nucleus, and Hypothalamus

• Anosmia (Total loss of smell):

• Conductive (Obstruction to airflow): Nasal polyposis, DNS, allergic/vasomotor rhinitis, common cold.

• Sensorineural (Neuroepithelial/Central damage): Atrophic rhinitis, post-viral (influenza/COVID-19) neuritis, head trauma (shearing of olfactory filaments at cribriform plate), anterior cranial fossa tumours (olfactory groove meningioma), Kallmann syndrome (congenital anosmia + hypogonadism).

3. Rhinomanometry

Objective test that measures nasal airflow and transnasal pressure simultaneously to calculate nasal airway resistance. Types: Active anterior (most common), active posterior, and passive rhinomanometry. Used to evaluate nasal valve collapse, DNS, and surgical outcomes.

title: 21. NASAL SEPTUM AND ITS DISORDERS
text:
1. Anatomy of Nasal Septum and Little’s Area

A. Parts of Nasal Septum

1. Columellar Septum: Formed by the medial crura of alar cartilages united by fibrous tissue and covered by skin.

2. Membranous Septum: Double layer of skin between the columella and caudal border of the septal cartilage; devoid of cartilage/bone.

3. Septum Proper: Osteocartilaginous framework covered by mucoperichondrium/mucoperiosteum:

• Principal constituents: Perpendicular plate of ethmoid (posterosuperior), Vomer (posteroinferior), and Quadrilateral (septal) cartilage (anteriorly).

• Minor contributions: Crest of nasal bones, nasal spine of frontal bone, rostrum of sphenoid, crest of palatine bones, maxillary crest, and anterior nasal spine of maxilla.

B. Blood Supply of Nasal Septum and Little’s Area (Kiesselbach’s Plexus)

• Little’s Area: Vascular area in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum just above the vestibule. It is the most common site of anterior epistaxis (90%) and bleeding polypus of the septum.

• Kiesselbach’s Plexus: Anastomosis of four arteries in Little’s area:

1. Anterior ethmoidal artery (branch of ophthalmic artery ← Internal Carotid Artery).

2. Sphenopalatine artery (nasopalatine/posterior medial nasal branch ← Maxillary artery ← External Carotid Artery).

3. Greater palatine artery (septal branch ← Maxillary artery ← External Carotid Artery).

4. Superior labial artery (septal branch ← Facial artery ← External Carotid Artery).

(Note: Posterior ethmoidal artery supplies the posterosuperior septum but does not participate in Kiesselbach's plexus).

2. Causes of Unilateral Nasal Obstruction

• Vestibular: Furuncle,nasal vestibulitis, nasoalveolar cyst, squamous papilloma, congenital/traumatic stenosis or atresia.

• Nasal Cavity: Foreign body, Rhinolith, Deviated Nasal Septum (DNS), Antrochoanal polyp, Bleeding polypus of septum, Hypertrophied inferior turbinate / Concha bullosa, Nasal synechiae, Unilateral sinusitis, Inverted papilloma, Sinonasal malignancy.

• Nasopharyngeal: Unilateral congenital choanal atresia, Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, Nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

3. Deviated Nasal Septum (DNS)

A. Aetiopathology

1. Trauma: Most common cause.

• Birth trauma: Compression of nose during passage through the birth canal or forceps delivery.

• Childhood/Adult trauma: Lateral blow displaces septal cartilage from the vomerine groove/maxillary crest; frontal crushing blow causes buckling, twisting, or fractures (Jarjavay fracture—horizontal fracture above vomerine junction from frontal blow; Chevallet fracture—vertical fracture from anterior nasal spine upwards from inferior blow).

2. Developmental Error: Unequal growth between the skull base and palate causes buckling of the septum (e.g., high-arched palate in chronic mouth breathers/adenoid hypertrophy, cleft lip/palate).

3. Racial & Hereditary Factors: More common in Caucasians; familial predisposition.

B. Types of DNS

1. Anterior Dislocation: Caudal border of quadrilateral cartilage dislocates into one nasal vestibule.

2. C-shaped Deformity: Septum curves to one side; the concave (roomy) side shows compensatory hypertrophy of turbinates.

3. S-shaped Deformity: Double curve in vertical or anteroposterior plane causing bilateral nasal obstruction.

4. Septal Spur: Shelf-like projection at the chondrovomerine junction impinging on the lateral wall.

5. Thickening: Due to organized septal haematoma or overriding fractured fragments.

C. Clinical Features

1. Nasal Obstruction: Unilateral or bilateral; high deviations obstruct respiratory currents more than low deviations.

2. Headache: Due to a septal spur pressing on the lateral nasal wall or middle turbinate (Sluder’s / anterior ethmoidal neuralgia—contact point headache).

3. Recurrent Sinusitis: Obstruction of the middle meatus/ostiomeatal complex.

4. Epistaxis: Drying air currents cause crusting over the convex side/spur; picking causes bleeding.

5. Anosmia / Hyposmia: Failure of inspired air to reach the olfactory cleft.

6. External Nasal Deformity: Deviation of cartilaginous/bony dorsum or columella.

7. Middle Ear Infection: Predisposes to Eustachian tube dysfunction and otitis media.

• Cottle’s Test: Used to detect nasal valve abnormality. The cheek on the side of obstruction is drawn laterally and upwards while the patient breathes quietly. If the nasal airway improves on the test side, the test is positive (indicating abnormality of the nasal valve/anterior septal deviation).

• Cottle’s Line: An imaginary vertical line drawn from the nasal process of the frontal bone to the anterior nasal spine. Deviations anterior to this line can only be corrected by Septoplasty (not SMR).

D. Management of DNS (Septoplasty vs. SMR)

Asymptomatic DNS requires no treatment. Symptomatic DNS is treated surgically by Septoplasty or Submucous Resection (SMR) (Full operative steps, differences, and complications are detailed in Section 50: Operative Surgery).

4. Septal Haematoma and Septal Abscess

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-001]]

5. Septal Perforation

• Aetiology:

1. Traumatic (Most common): Septal surgery (SMR with opposing mucosal tears), nasal cautery, habitual nose-picking, septal ornaments.

2. Pathological: Septal abscess, rhinolith/neglected foreign body, nasal myiasis, chronic granulomatous diseases (Tuberculosis, Lupus, Leprosy → perforate cartilaginous septum; Tertiary Syphilis → perforates bony septum), Wegener’s granulomatosis (total septal destruction).

3. Drugs & Chemicals: Cocaine abuse, prolonged intranasal steroid/decongestant sprays, occupational exposure (chromium, arsenic, soda ash).

4. Idiopathic.

• Clinical Features: Small anterior perforations cause a whistling sound on respiration; large perforations cause crusting, nasal obstruction, and recurrent epistaxis when crusts detach.

• Management:

• Investigate cause: Biopsy of perforation edge, VDRL, c-ANCA, chest X-ray.

• Conservative: Alkaline nasal douches, bland antibiotic/petroleum ointment, Silastic septal button obturator.

• Surgical: Closure of small perforations (<2 cm) using local mucoperichondrial rotation flaps with interposition of temporalis fascia or tragal perichondrium/cartilage graft.

subject: ent
title: 22. ACUTE AND CHRONIC RHINITIS
text:
1. Atrophic Rhinitis (Ozaena)

• Clinical Vignette Diagnosis: 30-year-old female with bilateral nasal obstruction, anosmia, roomy nasal cavities, and foul-smelling crusts → Primary Atrophic Rhinitis (Ozaena).

• Definition: Chronic inflammation of the nose characterized by progressive atrophy of the nasal mucosa, seromucinous glands, and turbinate bones, resulting in abnormally roomy nasal cavities filled with foul-smelling crusts.

A. Aetiopathogenesis

1. Primary Atrophic Rhinitis (Mnemonic: HERNIA):

• H – Hereditary: Runs in families.

• E – Endocrinal: Starts at puberty, predominantly affects females, and symptoms/crusting spontaneously subside after menopause (oestrogen deficiency).

• R – Racial: More common in White and Yellow races.

• N – Nutritional Deficiency: Deficiency of Vitamin A, Vitamin D, or Iron (common in lower socioeconomic strata).

• I – Infective: Klebsiella ozaenae (Perez bacillus), Coccobacillus foetidus ozaenae, Proteus vulgaris, E. coli, and diphtheroids (secondary invaders responsible for putrefaction and foul smell).

• A – Autoimmune: Destructive autoimmune response against nasal mucosal antigens.

2. Secondary Atrophic Rhinitis: Due to specific granulomatous infections (syphilis, lupus, leprosy, rhinoscleroma), excessive surgical turbinectomy ("Empty Nose Syndrome"), radiotherapy, or long-standing purulent sinusitis. (Extreme DNS causes unilateral atrophic rhinitis on the roomy side).

B. Pathology

• Replacement of normal pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium by stratified squamous metaplasia with loss of cilia.

• Atrophy of seromucinous glands, venous blood sinusoids, and olfactory nerve elements.

• Obliterative endarteritis and periarteritis of blood vessels in the mucosa and periosteum.

• Osteoclastic resorption of turbinate bones and arrest of paranasal sinus development.

C. Clinical Features

• Symptoms:

1. Foetor (Foul Smell): Repulsive stench making the patient a social outcast, though the patient is unaware of it.

2. Merciful Anosmia: Marked anosmia due to atrophy of olfactory neuroepithelium and crusting blocking airflow; "merciful" because the patient cannot smell their own foul odour.

3. Nasal Obstruction: Paradoxical obstruction despite wide/roomy nasal cavities, caused by large impacted crusts and loss of sensory airflow perception.

4. Epistaxis: Occurs when dry crusts are detached.

• Signs:

1. Greenish or greyish-black dry crusts filling both nasal cavities.

2. Roomy nasal cavities with severe atrophy of turbinates (reduced to mere ridges) allowing direct visualization of the posterior nasopharyngeal wall on anterior rhinoscopy.

3. Pale, dry, atrophic nasal mucosa; occasional septal perforation and saddle nose.

4. Associated atrophic pharyngitis (dry, glazed pharyngeal mucosa) and atrophic laryngitis.

D. Management

1. Medical / Conservative Management (Aim: Nasal hygiene and crust removal):

• Alkaline Nasal Douche: Warm irrigation 2–3 times daily using a solution of Sodium bicarbonate (1 part, loosens mucus) + Sodium biborate (1 part, antiseptic) + Sodium chloride (2 parts, tonicity) dissolved in 280 mL of warm water.

• 25% Anhydrous Glucose in Glycerine Paint: Applied after crust removal. Glycerine is hygroscopic (lubricates and draws fluid), while glucose ferments to lactic acid, lowering pH and inhibiting proteolytic organisms.

• Local Antibiotics: Kemicetine™ antiozaena solution (Chloramphenicol + Oestradiol + Vitamin D2).

• Systemic Antibiotics: Oral Rifampicin (600 mg OD for 6 months) or parenteral Streptomycin (1 g/day for 10 days) against Klebsiella.

• Oestradiol Nasal Spray, Oral Potassium Iodide (promotes/liquefies secretion), Iron, and Vitamin A & D supplementation.

2. Surgical Management:

• Young’s Operation: Complete surgical closure of both nostrils just inside the nasal vestibule by raising circumferential mucocutaneous flaps. Kept closed for 6–12 months; lack of drying air currents allows the mucosa to revert to normal respiratory epithelium.

• Modified Young’s Operation (Kalmeyer’s): Partial closure of the nostrils leaving a 3 mm pinhole opening bilaterally; avoids the distress of total mouth breathing while achieving mucosal recovery.

• Narrowing the Nasal Cavities:

• Submucosal injection of Teflon paste.

• Submucoperiosteal insertion of autogenous bone, cartilage, fat, or Teflon/Silastic strips along the floor, lateral wall, and septum.

• Lautenschlager’s Operation: Section and medial displacement of the lateral nasal wall.

• Wittmaack’s Operation: Transposition of the parotid (Stensen’s) duct into the maxillary sinus to lubricate the nose (rarely done due to gustatory rhinorrhoea).

2. Rhinitis Sicca and Rhinitis Caseosa

• Rhinitis Sicca: Crust-forming occupational disease seen in workers exposed to hot, dry, dusty environments (bakers, goldsmiths, ironsmiths). Confined to the anterior one-third of the nasal septum. Squamous metaplasia and gland atrophy cause adherent crusts; picking leads to ulceration, epistaxis, and anterior septal perforation. Treated with alkaline douches and bland/antibiotic ointments.

• Rhinitis Caseosa (Nasal Cholesteatoma): Uncommon, unilateral condition (mostly males) where the nasal cavity and sinus are filled with offensive purulent discharge and whitish inspissated cheesy debris resembling cholesteatoma, caused by chronic sinusitis with ostial obstruction. Can erode bony walls mimicking malignancy. Treated by surgical debridement and sinus drainage.

subject: ent
title: 23. DISORDERS OF EXTERNAL NOSE AND GRANULOMATOUS DISEASES
text:
(Note on Clinical Vignette in Prompt Section 23: The 30-year-old patient with bilateral pale, glistening, grape-like masses filling both nasal cavities with hyposmia and postnasal drip is a classic case of Bilateral Ethmoidal Polyposis / Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps, which is fully covered in Section 27. Rhinosporidiosis, which presents as a pinkish-purple leafy "strawberry" mass studded with white dots, is detailed below).

Rhinosporidiosis

• Aetiopathogenesis:

• Chronic granulomatous disease caused by *Rhinosporidium seeberi (traditionally classified as a fungus, now grouped as an aquatic protist/protozoan in the DRIP clade—Dermocystidium, Rosette agent, Ichthyophonus, Psorospermum*).

• Endemic in Southern India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala), Sri Lanka, and Chhattisgarh.

• Mode of transmission: Acquired through bathing in stagnant ponds contaminated by the dung of infected cattle/horses; spores enter through traumatized nasal mucosa.

• Life Cycle (Three Stages):

1. Trophic Stage: Oval endospore (6–8 µm) with a chitinous wall enlarges and undergoes nuclear division to form a trophocyte.

2. Development of Sporangium: Mature trophocyte enlarges into a sporangium (200–250 µm) with a thick double wall (outer chitinous, inner cellulose) containing 12,000–16,000 endospores (immature sporoblasts at the periphery, mature ones in the centre).

3. Production of Endospores: High internal pressure ruptures the sporangium through a germinal pore, releasing endospores into surrounding tissues to restart the cycle.

• Clinical Features:

• Affects nose and nasopharynx (most common >70%), conjunctiva, lip, palate, larynx, and skin.

• Symptoms: Epistaxis (often the sole presenting complaint), blood-tinged viscid nasal discharge, and progressive unilateral nasal obstruction.

• Signs: A leafy, friable, polypoidal mass, pink to purple in colour, attached to the nasal septum or floor/inferior turbinate. It is extremely vascular, bleeds on touch, and its surface is studded with tiny white dots representing mature sporangia ("Strawberry appearance").

• Diagnosis / Histopathology:

• Biopsy (H&E stain): Diagnostic. Shows vascular fibromyxomatous stroma infiltrated with chronic inflammatory cells and numerous globular cysts (sporangia) in various stages of maturation filled with thousands of endospores.

• Note: The organism cannot be cultured in vitro and cannot be transmitted to experimental animals.

• Management:

• Surgical (Treatment of Choice): Complete wide excision of the mass using an electrocautery / diathermy knife or Coblation with cauterization of its base to prevent recurrence and seeding.

• Medical: Oral Dapsone (100 mg/day for 6–12 months) arrests the maturation of sporangia and promotes fibrosis, used as an adjunct to prevent recurrence.

2. Rhinoscleroma

• Aetiology: Chronic granulomatous disease caused by the Gram-negative encapsulated coccobacillus *Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis* (Frisch bacillus).

• Clinical Features (Four Stages):

1. Catarrhal / Atrophic Stage: Resembles atrophic rhinitis with foul-smelling purulent nasal discharge and crusting.

2. Granulomatous (Nodular) Stage: Painless, non-ulcerative bluish-red submucosal nodules in the nose with subdermal woody infiltration of the lower external nose and upper lip (Tapir nose / Hebra nose).

3. Cicatricial (Fibrotic) Stage: Extensive fibrosis and adhesions causing stenosis of the nares, nasopharynx, and subglottic larynx (causing stridor).

• Diagnosis / Histopathology:

• Biopsy: Diagnostic. Submucosa shows dense infiltration of plasma cells, lymphocytes, and two pathognomonic features:

1. Mikulicz Cells: Large foamy histiocytes with a central nucleus and vacuolated cytoplasm containing the causative bacilli.

2. Russell Bodies: Homogeneous, eosinophilic, round inclusion bodies inside plasma cells (accumulated immunoglobulins).

• Treatment:

• Medical: Prolonged antibiotic therapy until two consecutive biopsy cultures are negative: Rifampicin (450–600 mg/day), Ciprofloxacin (500 mg BD), or Streptomycin (1 g/day) + Tetracycline (2 g/day) for 4–6 weeks.

• Surgical: Recanalization of nasal/subglottic stenosis and rhinoplasty after the disease is inactive.

3. Saddle Nose Deformity, Rhinophyma, Nasal Vestibulitis, and Wegener’s Granulomatosis

• Saddle Nose Deformity: Depressed nasal dorsum involving the cartilaginous, bony, or both components.

• Causes: Nasal trauma (depressed fractures), Septal abscess/haematoma, Excessive cartilage removal in SMR, Granulomatous diseases (Syphilis destroys bony dorsum; Tuberculosis, Leprosy, Wegener’s granulomatosis, Relapsing polychondritis destroy cartilaginous dorsum).
