• Treatment: Augmentation Rhinoplasty using autogenous cartilage (septal/conchal/costal) for cartilaginous defects or iliac crest cancellous bone graft for osteocartilaginous defects.

• Rhinophyma (Potato Tumour): Slow-growing benign hypertrophy of the sebaceous glands of the nasal tip, associated with long-standing acne rosacea in men past middle age. Presents as a large, pink, lobulated, unsightly mass over the nasal tip causing alar collapse and obstruction. Treatment: Paring down the bulk of the tumour with a sharp cold knife, CO_2 laser, or radiofrequency down to the perichondrium, allowing spontaneous re-epithelialization from deep sebaceous gland remnants.

• Nasal Vestibulitis: Diffuse dermatitis of the nasal vestibule caused by Staphylococcus aureus secondary to rhinorrhoea and nose-picking. Acute: Red, swollen, tender vestibule with crusts/excoriation. Chronic: Induration and painful fissures at the mucocutaneous junction. Treatment: Cleaning crusts with hydrogen peroxide, topical antibiotic-steroid ointment (Mupirocin/Fusidic acid + Betamethasone), and silver nitrate cautery of chronic fissures.

• Wegener’s Granulomatosis (Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis): Multisystem autoimmune disorder characterized by a classic triad of: (1) Necrotizing granulomas of the upper and lower respiratory tracts (nasal crusting, blood-stained discharge, septal perforation, saddle nose, pulmonary cavities), (2) Necrotizing vasculitis, and (3) Focal necrotizing glomerulonephritis. Diagnosis: Positive c-ANCA (anti-PR3), raised ESR, and nasal biopsy. Treatment: Systemic corticosteroids (Prednisolone) + Cyclophosphamide or Rituximab.

subject: ent
title: 24. MISCELLANEOUS DISORDERS OF NOSE
text:
1. Foreign Body in the Nose & Choanal Atresia

• Clinical Vignette Diagnosis: 2-year-old child with unilateral foul-smelling nasal discharge → Neglected Foreign Body in the Nose (Clinical Dictum: "Unilateral, foul-smelling, blood-stained nasal discharge in a child is a foreign body unless proved otherwise").

• Foreign Body Nose:

• Aetiology: Organic (seeds, peas, paper, sponge) or inorganic (chalk, beads, button batteries—cause rapid liquefaction necrosis and septal perforation).

• Clinical Features: Unilateral foul-smelling purulent/blood-stained nasal discharge, unilateral nasal obstruction, excoriation of the vestibule.

• Management:

• Paper/swabs: Removed with crocodile/Tilley’s forceps.

• Rounded smooth objects: Removed by passing a blunt hook (or Eustachian catheter) behind and above the foreign body and dragging it forwards along the nasal floor (never grasp spherical objects with forceps as they slip posteriorly).

• Uncooperative child / impacted FB: Removed under General Anaesthesia with a cuffed endotracheal tube and throat pack using a nasal endoscope.

• Complications: Sinusitis, Rhinolith formation, septal necrosis (button battery), aspiration into the tracheobronchial tree.

• Choanal Atresia:

• Aetiology: Persistence of the embryonic bucconasal membrane. Bony (90%) or membranous (10%); Unilateral (more common, right-sided, presents later in childhood) or Bilateral (neonatal emergency). Associated with CHARGE syndrome (Coloboma, Heart defects, Atresia of choanae, Retarded growth, Genital hypoplasia, Ear anomalies).

• Clinical Features: Bilateral atresia presents at birth with cyclical cyanosis (asphyxia and cyanosis during quiet state/feeding, which is relieved when the baby cries and breathes through the mouth). Unilateral atresia presents with unilateral mucoid discharge and absence of air bubbles.

• Diagnosis: (1) Failure to pass a 6–8 Fr red rubber catheter from nose to pharynx, (2) Absence of mist on cold spatula test, (3) Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy, (4) CT Scan of PNS (Axial view)—gold standard to confirm bony vs. membranous plate and thickness.

• Treatment:

• Immediate Emergency (Bilateral): McGovern’s nipple (feeding nipple with a large hole strapped in the mouth) or oropharyngeal airway.

• Definitive: Transnasal endoscopic recanalization (perforating and drilling out the atretic plate + removing part of posterior vomer) or transpalatal repair.

2. CSF Rhinorrhoea

• Definition: Leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the subarachnoid space into the nasal cavity due to a dural and bony defect at the skull base.

• Aetiology:

1. Traumatic (Most common, >80%): Accidental head injury (frontobasal skull fractures) or Iatrogenic surgical trauma (FESS, trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy, nasal polypectomy).

2. Non-Traumatic: Inflammatory (erosive mucoceles, fungal sinusitis), Neoplastic (skull base tumours, pituitary tumours), Congenital (meningoencephalocele), or Idiopathic/Spontaneous (benign intracranial hypertension).

• Common Sites of Leakage:

1. Anterior Cranial Fossa (Most common): Cribriform plate (lateral lamella—thinnest bone where anterior ethmoidal artery pierces), Fovea ethmoidalis (roof of ethmoid), and posterior wall of frontal sinus.

2. Middle Cranial Fossa: Roof/lateral wall of the sphenoid sinus.

3. Posterior Cranial Fossa / Temporal Bone: Fractures of the petrous temporal bone → CSF enters middle ear → drains via Eustachian tube into nasopharynx (CSF otorhinorrhoea).

• Diagnosis:

• Clinical Features: Unilateral, clear, watery, sweet-tasting fluid dripping from the nose on bending forwards or straining ("Tea-pot sign" / "Reservoir sign"—fluid collected in sphenoid sinus gushes out on bending). It cannot be sniffed back and does not stiffen the handkerchief (no mucin).

• Halo Sign (Target / Double-Ring Sign): In post-traumatic blood-stained discharge, a drop on filter paper shows a central red spot (blood) surrounded by a peripheral clear lighter halo (CSF).

• Laboratory Confirmation:

1. Beta-2 Transferrin Assay: Gold standard confirmatory test. A protein found only in CSF, perilymph, and vitreous humour (100% specific, requires only a few drops).

2. Beta-Trace Protein: Secretory protein of meninges/choroid plexus; highly sensitive.

3. Glucose Estimation: CSF glucose is >30 mg/dL (or >2/3rd of blood sugar), whereas nasal secretions have <10 mg/dL. (Oxidase-peroxidase strips are unreliable).

• Localization of Site:

1. High-Resolution CT (HRCT) of Skull Base (1–2 mm coronal & axial cuts): Identifies the exact bony defect.

2. MR Cisternography (Heavy T2-weighted MRI): Non-invasive; shows hyperintense CSF column herniating through the defect and rules out meningoencephalocele.

3. Intrathecal Fluorescein Study + Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy: 0.25 mL of 5% fluorescein diluted in 10 mL CSF is injected intrathecally; bright yellow-green fluorescence is seen endoscopically at the exact leak site.

• Treatment:

• Conservative (For early post-traumatic leaks <7–10 days): Strict bed rest with head elevated 30°, avoidance of nose blowing/sneezing/coughing, stool softeners (laxatives), Acetazolamide (250 mg TDS—reduces CSF production), lumbar subarachnoid drain, and prophylactic antibiotics (to prevent meningitis).

• Surgical (For persistent, delayed, or iatrogenic leaks): Transnasal Endoscopic Repair (>90% success rate). The bony defect is defined, surrounding mucosa is stripped, and a multilayered "Bath-plug" / Underlay-Overlay repair is done using fat, fascia lata/temporalis fascia, septal cartilage (if defect >2 cm), vascularized Hadad nasoseptal flap, and fibrin glue.

3. Rhinolith, Nasal Myiasis, and Dangerous Area of the Face

• Rhinolith (Nasal Stone): Calcareous concrements formed in the nasal cavity by slow deposition of calcium and magnesium phosphates/carbonates around an exogenous nucleus (forgotten foreign body) or endogenous nucleus (inspissated pus/blood clot). Clinical Features: Adult presenting with unilateral foul-smelling, blood-stained discharge, nasal obstruction, and epistaxis. Probing reveals a greyish-black, irregular, stony-hard mass giving a gritty sensation. Treatment: Endoscopic removal under GA (large ones are crushed into fragments before removal).

• Nasal Myiasis (Maggots in Nose): Infestation of the nose/sinuses by larvae (maggots) of the fly *Chrysomyia, which lays ~200 eggs in foul-smelling noses (atrophic rhinitis, leprosy, syphilis). Clinical Features: Intense nasal irritation, throbbing headache, puffy eyelids/lips, foul serosanguinous discharge, maggots crawling out of the nose, and extensive tissue necrosis (palatal/septal perforation, orbital invasion, fatal meningitis). Treatment: Instillation of chloroform water or turpentine oil* (suffocates/kills larvae), endoscopic forceps removal, warm saline douches, systemic antibiotics, and isolation under a mosquito net.

• Dangerous Area of the Face: Triangular area extending from the angles of the mouth to the bridge of the nose, including the upper lip and nasal vestibule. Veins of this area (facial vein and angular vein) are valveless and communicate directly with the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein and with the pterygoid venous plexus via the deep facial vein. Squeezing a furuncle here causes retrograde thrombophlebitis leading to fatal Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis.

subject: ent
title: 25. ALLERGIC RHINITIS
text:
• Definition: An IgE-mediated (Type I hypersensitivity) immunologic inflammation of the nasal mucosa to airborne allergens, characterized by watery rhinorrhoea, paroxysmal sneezing, nasal obstruction, and nasal/ocular itching.

• Aetiopathogenesis:

• Genetic Predisposition (Atopy): 20% risk if one parent is atopic; 47% if both parents are atopic.

• Inhalant Allergens: Seasonal (pollens from grasses, trees, weeds) or Perennial (house dust mites—Dermatophagoides, fungal moulds, cockroach allergens, animal dander).

• Mechanism (Two Phases):

1. Sensitization: Inhaled allergens stimulate B-cells to produce allergen-specific IgE antibodies, which bind via their Fc end to tissue mast cells and basophils.

2. Early (Acute) Phase (within 5–30 mins): On re-exposure, allergen cross-links two adjacent IgE molecules (Fab end), causing mast cell degranulation and release of preformed mediators (Histamine, tryptase) and newly synthesized mediators (Leukotrienes LTC_4, LTD_4, Prostaglandin PGD_2, PAF). This causes vasodilation, mucosal oedema (blockage), glandular stimulation (rhinorrhoea), and nerve ending stimulation (sneezing/itching).

3. Late (Delayed) Phase (2–8 hours later): Infiltration of eosinophils, basophils, and CD4^+  Th2 cells causing sustained nasal congestion and priming effect (non-specific hyper-reactivity).

• ARIA Classification (Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma):

• By Duration:

• Intermittent: Symptoms <4 days/week OR <4 consecutive weeks.

• Persistent: Symptoms >4 days/week AND >4 consecutive weeks.

• By Severity:

• Mild: Normal sleep; no impairment of daily activities, sport, leisure, school, or work; no troublesome symptoms.

• Moderate-to-Severe: One or more of the above items are affected (sleep disturbance, impaired daily activities/work/school, or troublesome symptoms).

• Clinical Features:

• Symptoms: Paroxysmal sneezing (10–20 sneezes at a time), profuse watery rhinorrhoea, bilateral alternating nasal obstruction, itching of nose/palate/eyes, anosmia, and postnasal drip.

• Signs:

1. Nasal: Pale, bluish, boggy/oedematous nasal mucosa and swollen turbinates; clear watery/mucoid discharge; Allergic salute (upward rubbing of nasal tip with palm) producing a transverse black nasal crease across the dorsum.

2. Ocular: Lid oedema, conjunctival congestion with cobblestone papillae, and Allergic shiners (dark periorbital circles due to venous stasis).

3. Otologic: Retracted tympanic membrane or Otitis Media with Effusion (OME).

4. Pharyngeal: Granular pharyngitis and high-arched palate (Dennie-Morgan lines under lower eyelids).

• Investigations:

1. Nasal Smear Cytology: Shows abundant eosinophils (>10% of cells).

2. Absolute Eosinophil Count (AEC) and Total Serum IgE: Elevated.

3. Skin Prick Test (SPT) (In-vivo test): Gold standard clinical allergy test. Concentrated allergen drops are pricked into the volar forearm alongside a positive control (Histamine) and negative control (Saline diluent); read at 15 minutes for a central wheal (>3 mm) and surrounding erythema (flare).

4. RAST (Radioallergosorbent Test) / ImmunoCAP (In-vitro test): Measures allergen-specific IgE in serum (useful in dermatographism or patients unable to stop antihistamines).

5. Nasal Provocation Test.

• Management (ARIA Step-Care Approach):

1. Avoidance of Allergen: Encasing mattresses/pillows in impermeable covers, washing bedding in hot water (>55°C), removing carpets/pets, using HEPA filters.

2. Pharmacotherapy:

• Intranasal Corticosteroids (INCS): First-line monotherapy for moderate-to-severe or persistent allergic rhinitis (most potent anti-inflammatory; suppresses both early and late phases). Examples: Fluticasone furoate (27.5 mcg/spray, 2 sprays OD), Mometasone furoate (50 mcg/spray, 2 sprays OD), Budesonide, Beclomethasone.

• Antihistamines (Second-generation oral H_1 blockers): Control sneezing, itching, and rhinorrhoea (minimal sedation).

• Generic Name, Dosage & Route: Tab. Cetirizine 10 mg orally once daily at bedtime OR Tab. Fexofenadine 120–180 mg orally once daily OR Tab. Levocetirizine 5 mg orally once daily. (Topical intranasal antihistamine: Azelastine nasal spray).

• Leukotriene Receptor Antagonists (LTRAs): Tab. Montelukast 10 mg orally OD (especially useful with co-existing asthma).

• Mast Cell Stabilizers: Sodium Cromoglycate (2% nasal spray) (prophylactic; safe in children/pregnancy).

• Anticholinergics: Ipratropium bromide (0.03% nasal spray) (specifically controls profuse watery rhinorrhoea).

• Decongestants: Oral (Pseudoephedrine, Phenylephrine) or short-course topical (Xylometazoline <5 days to avoid rhinitis medicamentosa).

3. Allergen-Specific Immunotherapy (Hyposensitization): Subcutaneous (SCIT) or Sublingual (SLIT) administration of gradually increasing doses of specific allergen extract for 3 years. Only disease-modifying therapy; shifts immune response from Th2 to Th1, induces blocking IgG4 antibodies, and prevents progression to asthma.

subject: ent
title: 26. VASOMOTOR AND NON-ALLERGIC RHINITIS
text:
1. Vasomotor Rhinitis (Idiopathic Non-Allergic Rhinitis)

• Pathogenesis: Non-allergic, non-infectious rhinitis caused by autonomic nervous system imbalance (parasympathetic overactivity / sympathetic underactivity) regulated by the hypothalamus. Parasympathetic stimulation causes vasodilation and engorgement of turbinal venous sinusoids (obstruction) and hypersecretion of nasal glands (rhinorrhoea). The hyper-reactive nasal mucosa responds to non-specific triggers: sudden changes in temperature or humidity, cold air blasts, dust, smoke, strong odours, alcohol, and emotional stress.

• Clinical Features:

• Symptoms: Paroxysmal morning sneezing (on stepping out of bed onto a cold floor), profuse watery rhinorrhoea ("runners"), and alternating nasal obstruction (worse on the dependent side at night—"blockers").

• Signs: Turbinates are congested (red) and hypertrophied (unlike pale/bluish mucosa in allergy). All allergy tests (SPT, serum IgE, nasal eosinophils) are negative.

• Treatment:

• Medical: Avoidance of physical triggers; Intranasal corticosteroid sprays (Fluticasone/Budesonide); Topical anticholinergic spray (Ipratropium bromide) for profuse rhinorrhoea; oral antihistamines + decongestants.

• Surgical:

1. For persistent nasal obstruction: Reduction of hypertrophied inferior turbinates via Submucosal diathermy (SMD), Coblation/Radiofrequency turbinoplasty, cryosurgery, or partial inferior turbinectomy.

2. For intractable rhinorrhoea: Vidian Neurectomy (endoscopic sectioning of the nerve of the pterygoid canal to interrupt parasympathetic secretomotor fibres).

2. Rhinitis Medicamentosa

• Definition & Pathogenesis: Drug-induced non-allergic rhinitis caused by prolonged, excessive use (>5–7 days) of topical vasoconstrictor (sympathomimetic) nasal drops/sprays (e.g., Xylometazoline, Oxymetazoline, Naphazoline). Prolonged α-adrenergic stimulation causes rebound vasodilation (reactive hyperaemia), tachyphylaxis (down-regulation of α-receptors), ischaemic mucosal damage, and loss of cilia, forcing the patient into a vicious cycle of increasing drug use.

• Clinical Features: Severe, unremitting bilateral nasal obstruction; nasal mucosa appears fiery red (beefy red), boggy, and granular, showing poor shrinkage on vasoconstrictor challenge.

• Treatment:

1. Immediate and complete withdrawal of the offending topical decongestant drops.

2. Intranasal Corticosteroid Sprays (Fluticasone/Mometasone) and a short tapering course of oral corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisolone for 5–7 days) to relieve severe rebound oedema during the withdrawal period.

3. Surgical turbinoplasty if irreversible fibrous hypertrophy of the inferior turbinates has occurred.

subject: ent
title: 27. NASAL POLYPS
text:
1. Bilateral Ethmoidal Polyposis vs. Antrochoanal Polyp

A. Clinical Vignette Diagnoses

• Case 1 & 2 (30–50 yr old patient with bronchial asthma, bilateral nasal block, anosmia, and multiple pale, glistening, grape-like masses in both nasal cavities insensitive to touch): Bilateral Ethmoidal Polyposis (Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps).

• Samter’s Triad (Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease - AERD): Triad of (1) Nasal Polyposis, (2) Bronchial Asthma, and (3) Aspirin / NSAID Intolerance (due to shunting of arachidonic acid metabolism from cyclooxygenase to the lipoxygenase pathway, overproducing leukotrienes).

• Kartagener’s Syndrome: Autosomal recessive primary ciliary dyskinesia (absence of dynein arms on cilia) characterized by a triad of: (1) Chronic Rhinosinusitis / Nasal Polyposis, (2) Bronchiectasis, and (3) Situs Inversus (Dextrocardia).

B. Etiopathogenesis of Ethmoidal Polyposis

1. Bernoulli’s Phenomenon: High-velocity airflow through a narrow constriction (ostiomeatal complex) creates a local drop in pressure, sucking oedematous mucosa into the lumen to form polyps.

2. Vasomotor Imbalance & Inflammation: Chronic eosinophilic inflammation (Th2 cytokines IL-5, IgE, histamine) increases vascular permeability → extracellular fluid accumulates in the loose lamina propria of the middle meatus/uncinate/bulla → denervated oedematous stroma prolapses under gravity and sneezing.

3. Associated Conditions: Chronic rhinosinusitis, Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS), Asthma, Samter’s triad, Cystic fibrosis (always rule out in a child with bilateral polyps), Kartagener’s syndrome, Churg-Strauss syndrome, and NARES (Non-allergic rhinitis with eosinophilia syndrome).

C. Differences Between Antrochoanal Polyp and Bilateral Ethmoidal Polypi

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-002]]

D. Investigations and Management of Nasal Polyposis

• Investigations:

1. Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy (DNE): Confirms pale, glistening, pedunculated masses arising from the middle meatus that are insensitive to probing and do not bleed on touch (differentiating them from hypertrophied turbinates and neoplasms).

2. NCCT of Paranasal Sinuses (Coronal & Axial cuts): Mandatory road-map before surgery. Evaluates extent of disease, bony erosion/expansion, anatomical variants (Haller/Onodi cells, concha bullosa), and double-density sign (seen in Allergic Fungal Sinusitis).

3. Allergy Work-up: In-vivo (Skin Prick Test) and In-vitro (Total IgE, RAST, AEC, nasal smear for eosinophils and fungal hyphae).

4. Sweat Chloride Test: In children to rule out cystic fibrosis.

• Management:

1. Medical Management ("Medical Polypectomy"):

• Short course of Systemic Corticosteroids: Tab. Prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day tapering over 2–3 weeks (shrinks polyps, restores olfaction, and reduces intraoperative bleeding). (Use with caution/glycaemic monitoring in diabetics).

• Long-term Intranasal Corticosteroid Sprays: Fluticasone or Mometasone (prevents recurrence).

• Antihistamines + Leukotriene Receptor Antagonists (Montelukast): Essential in Samter’s triad and asthma.

• Alkaline/Saline Nasal Douches and antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection.

2. Surgical Management:

• Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS): Treatment of choice. Uses microdebriders (powered shavers) and endoscopes to remove polyps, open the ethmoid cells, and restore ventilation and mucociliary clearance of the maxillary, frontal, and sphenoid sinuses.

• Histopathology: All removed polyps must be sent for histopathology to rule out underlying Inverted Papilloma or Squamous Cell Carcinoma (especially in unilateral polyps in patients >40 years).

2. Causes of Bilateral Nasal Obstruction (Adults & Children)

• In Children: Bilateral congenital choanal atresia, Adenoid hypertrophy (most common), Foreign bodies, Acute viral/bacterial rhinitis, Allergic rhinitis, Septal haematoma/abscess, Ethmoidal polyposis (cystic fibrosis).

• In Adults: S-shaped Deviated Nasal Septum, Bilateral Ethmoidal Polyposis, Allergic / Vasomotor rhinitis, Rhinitis medicamentosa, Hypertrophic rhinitis, Atrophic rhinitis (crusts), Large antrochoanal polyp / JNA / NPC filling the nasopharynx.

3. Bleeding Polypus of the Septum

A benign lobular capillary haemangioma arising from the anterior part of the nasal septum (Little’s area). Presents as a soft, dark-red, smooth or ulcerated pedunculated/sessile mass causing recurrent unilateral epistaxis and nasal obstruction. Treatment: Surgical excision along with a cuff of underlying mucoperichondrium (to prevent recurrence) and cauterization of the base.

subject: ent
title: 28. EPISTAXIS
text:
1. Causes and Plexuses of Epistaxis

• Vascular Plexuses:

1. Kiesselbach’s Plexus (Little’s Area): Anteroinferior septum; anastomoses of Anterior ethmoidal, Sphenopalatine, Greater palatine, and Superior labial arteries. Site of 90% of anterior epistaxis (children/young adults).

2. Retrocolumellar Vein: Runs vertically behind the columella across the nasal floor; common site of venous bleed in young people.

3. Woodruff’s Plexus: A plexus of large thin-walled veins situated inferior to the posterior end of the inferior turbinate (posterior part of inferior meatus). Common site of posterior epistaxis in older adults.

• Causes of Epistaxis:

• Local Causes:

1. Trauma: Nose picking (epistaxis digitorum), nasal bone/maxillofacial fractures, intranasal surgery, forceful nose blowing.

2. Infections: Acute viral rhinitis, sinusitis, atrophic rhinitis, rhinitis sicca, TB/syphilis, nasal myiasis (maggots).

3. Foreign Bodies: Neglected foreign body, rhinolith.

4. Neoplasms: Bleeding polypus of septum, Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA), inverted papilloma, sinonasal/nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

5. Deviated Nasal Septum (Spur) and atmospheric changes (high altitude).

• General (Systemic) Causes:

1. Cardiovascular: Hypertension, arteriosclerosis, mitral stenosis, pregnancy.

2. Haematological / Bleeding Disorders: Haemophilia, von Willebrand disease, leukaemia, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), aplastic anaemia, Vitamin K deficiency, Scurvy, Hereditary Haemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease).

3. Hepatic & Renal: Liver cirrhosis (deficiency of Factors II, VII, IX, X), chronic renal failure (uraemic platelet dysfunction).

4. Drugs: Anticoagulants (Warfarin, Heparin), Antiplatelets (Aspirin, Clopidogrel).

5. Acute Febrile Illnesses: Dengue haemorrhagic fever, malaria, typhoid, influenza.

2. Management of Epistaxis (Step-wise Protocol)

1. First Aid & Resuscitation (First Line of Management):

• Trotter’s Method: Make the patient sit up, leaning slightly forward over a basin, breathing quietly through the mouth and spitting out any blood in the pharynx. Pinch the soft lower part of the nose firmly between the thumb and index finger for 5–10 minutes (compresses Little’s area) and apply cold compresses (ice packs) over the nasal bridge (reflex vasoconstriction).

• Haemodynamic Stabilization: Monitor vitals (Pulse, BP), secure a wide-bore IV cannula, send blood for CBC, platelet count, PT/INR, aPTT, blood grouping and cross-matching, and start IV crystalloids/blood transfusion if in hypovolaemic shock. Administer mild sedation/antihypertensives if BP is severely elevated.

2. Suction, Decongestion, and Cauterization:

• Suction out blood clots and insert cotton pledgets soaked in 4% Lignocaine + 1:100,000 Adrenaline (or Oxymetazoline) for 10 minutes.

• If a discrete anterior bleeding point is identified, cauterize it using a Silver Nitrate (75%) bead or Endoscopic Bipolar / Suction Unipolar Electrocautery (cauterize a ring around the vessel first, then the vessel itself).

3. Anterior Nasal Packing:

• Indicated if bleeding is diffuse, profuse, or the site cannot be localized.

• Technique: Pack 1 meter of 2.5 cm ribbon gauze smeared with liquid paraffin or antibiotic ointment tightly into the nasal cavity in horizontal layers (floor to roof) or vertical layers (back to front) using Tilley’s dressing forceps. Alternatively, use Merocel™ (hydroxylated polyvinyl acetate nasal tampon) or an inflatable anterior epistaxis balloon.

• Remove pack after 24–48 hours; cover with systemic antibiotics to prevent sinusitis and Toxic Shock Syndrome.

4. Posterior Nasal Packing (Techniques for Posterior Epistaxis):

• Indicated when blood continues to trickle down the posterior pharyngeal wall despite a tight anterior pack.

• Technique 1 (Conventional Gauze Postnasal Pack): A cone-shaped gauze bolster with three silk ties is prepared. A red rubber catheter is passed through the nostril, retrieved from the mouth, tied to two silk threads, and pulled back through the nose, guiding the bolster snugly into the nasopharynx with the index finger. An anterior nasal pack is placed, and the two nasal silk threads are tied over a dental roll at the columella (the 3rd oral thread is taped to the cheek for later removal).

• Technique 2 (Foley’s Catheter / Double-Balloon Epistaxis Catheter): A 12–14 Fr Foley’s catheter is passed along the floor of the nose into the nasopharynx, the bulb is inflated with 10–15 mL of normal saline, pulled forward to impact in the choana, and an anterior nasal pack is placed. Alternatively, a Brighton / Epistaxis double-balloon catheter (posterior balloon 10 mL, anterior balloon 30 mL) is used.

• Mandatory Care: Hospitalize all patients with postnasal packs, administer humidified oxygen (hypoxia occurs via nasopulmonary reflex), and give systemic antibiotics.

5. Surgical Ligation of Vessels & Embolization (For Refractory Epistaxis):

• Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation (TESPAL): Surgical treatment of choice for refractory posterior epistaxis. A mucoperiosteal flap is elevated just posterior to the maxillary ostium, the crista ethmoidalis landmark is identified, and the sphenopalatine artery is clipped/coagulated as it exits the sphenopalatine foramen.

• Anterior & Posterior Ethmoidal Artery Ligation: For high anterosuperior bleeds (above the middle turbinate; internal carotid system). Exposed in the medial orbital wall via an external ethmoid (Lynch) incision (Rule of 24-12-6 mm from anterior lacrimal crest: Anterior ethmoidal artery at 24 mm, Posterior ethmoidal artery at +12 mm, Optic nerve at +6 mm).

• Internal Maxillary Artery Ligation: Transantral (Caldwell-Luc) approach through the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus (largely superseded by TESPAL).

• External Carotid Artery Ligation: Ligated in the neck above the origin of the superior thyroid artery.

• Angiographic Embolization: Selective embolization of the internal maxillary/facial artery using Gelfoam or polyvinyl alcohol particles (Ethmoidal arteries cannot be embolized due to risk of retinal artery occlusion and blindness).

subject: ent
title: 29. TRAUMA TO FACE
text:
1. Fractures of the Nasal Bones

• Types:

1. Depressed Fracture: Due to a frontal blow. Lower thin part of nasal bones fractures; severe blow causes an "Open-book fracture" (nasal septum collapses and nasal bones splay out) or comminuted naso-ethmoid fracture.

2. Angulated (Laterally Displaced) Fracture: Due to a lateral blow. Unilateral depression of one nasal bone or displacement of the entire nasal pyramid to the opposite side.

• Clinical Features: Swelling and tenderness of the nasal bridge, periorbital ecchymosis, nasal deformity (depressed or deviated bridge), epistaxis, bony crepitus, and nasal obstruction (always rule out septal haematoma).

• Diagnosis: Primarily clinical; X-rays (Lateral view of nasal bones, Occlusal view, Waters’ view).

• Timing & Management:

• Golden Period for Closed Reduction: Either immediately (within a few hours, before oedema appears) OR after 5–7 days (once oedema subsides, before malunion occurs at 2 weeks).

• Closed Reduction: Disimpaction and realignment of nasal bones using Walsham’s forceps and straightening/repositioning of the nasal septum using Asch’s septum forceps, followed by anterior nasal packing and an external plaster-of-Paris/thermoplastic splint for 10–14 days.

2. Fractures of the Middle Third of the Face (Le Fort Fractures & Blow-Out Fracture)

A. Le Fort Classification of Maxillary Fractures

1. Le Fort I (Transverse / Guerin’s Fracture):

• Fracture Line: Runs horizontally above the apices of the upper teeth/palate, crossing the lower nasal septum, floor/wall of maxillary sinuses, and lower pterygoid plates. Creates a "floating palate".

2. Le Fort II (Pyramidal Fracture):

• Fracture Line: Passes through the root of the nose (nasofrontal suture), lacrimal bone, medial wall and floor of the orbit, infraorbital rim/foramen, anterolateral wall of the maxillary sinus, and mid-pterygoid plates.

3. Le Fort III (Craniofacial Dysjunction):

• Fracture Line: Complete separation of the facial skeleton from the cranium. Passes through the nasofrontal suture, medial orbital wall, superior orbital fissure, lateral orbital wall, frontozygomatic suture, zygomatic arch, and root of the pterygoid plates.

• Clinical Features of Le Fort Fractures: Elongation and flattening of the midface ("Dish-face deformity"), malocclusion of teeth with anterior open bite, mobility of the upper jaw on grasping the incisors, bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ("raccoon eyes"), infraorbital anaesthesia (Le Fort II), and CSF rhinorrhoea (cribriform plate injury in Le Fort II and III).

• Management: Secure airway (intubation/tracheostomy), control haemorrhage, and perform Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF) using titanium miniplates and intermaxillary fixation (IMF) with arch bars.

B. Orbital Blow-Out Fracture

• Mechanism: Purely isolated fracture of the floor (and/or medial wall) of the orbit caused by a blunt object larger than the orbital rim (e.g., tennis/cricket ball, fist) striking the globe, transmitting sudden hydraulic pressure that blows out the thin orbital floor into the maxillary antrum while the orbital rim remains intact.

• Clinical Features:

1. Ecchymosis of eyelids and subconjunctival haemorrhage.

2. Enophthalmos and inferior displacement of the eyeball (hypoglobus).

3. Diplopia on upward and downward gaze due to entrapment of the inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles in the fracture line (confirmed by a positive Forced Duction Test).

4. Infraorbital anaesthesia (cheek and upper lip numbness).

• Diagnosis: Waters’ view X-ray or Coronal CT Scan of Orbit shows a classic "Hanging Tear-Drop Sign" (herniated periorbital fat and muscle hanging from the roof of the maxillary sinus) and haemotympanum/haemosinus.

• Treatment: Surgical exploration (via subciliary/transconjunctival approach) if there is persistent diplopia with positive forced duction test or enophthalmos >2 mm; release of entrapped muscle and reconstruction of the orbital floor using titanium mesh, Silastic sheet, or autogenous bone/cartilage graft.

3. Oroantral Fistula

• Definition & Aetiology: Pathological epithelialized communication between the oral cavity and maxillary sinus. Most common cause: Dental extraction of upper second premolar or first/second molar teeth (whose roots project into the floor of the antrum). Other causes: Unhealed Caldwell-Luc incision, carcinoma maxilla, osteomyelitis/syphilis, trauma.

• Clinical Features: Regurgitation of fluids from the mouth into the nose, unilateral foul-smelling purulent nasal discharge (chronic maxillary sinusitis), and inability to blow out cheeks/wind instruments or suck through a straw (due to air leak). Confirmed by passing a blunt probe from the alveolar socket into the antrum.

• Management:

• Acute/Fresh Fistula (<24–48 hours, small): Primary mobilization and suturing of mucoperiosteal gum margins + systemic antibiotics and avoidance of nose blowing.

• Chronic/Established Fistula: First treat maxillary sinusitis (antibiotics + FESS/antral lavage), excise the epithelialized fistulous tract, remove any retained tooth root, and close the defect using a Buccal Advancement Flap (Rehrmann’s flap), Buccal Fat Pad graft, or Palatal Rotational Flap (based on the greater palatine artery).

subject: ent
title: 30. PARANASAL SINUSES AND SINUSITIS
text:
1. Ostiomeatal Complex (OMC)

• Definition: The final common drainage and ventilation pathway of the anterior group of paranasal sinuses (Frontal, Maxillary, and Anterior Ethmoidal sinuses) located in the middle meatus.

• Anatomical Components:

1. Maxillary Sinus Ostium

2. Ethmoidal Infundibulum

3. Uncinate Process

4. Hiatus Semilunaris

5. Bulla Ethmoidalis

6. Frontal Recess

7. Middle Turbinate and Middle Meatus

• Clinical Importance (Messerklinger’s Concept): Even minor mucosal oedema or anatomical variations (Concha bullosa, Paradoxical middle turbinate, Haller cell, Deviated nasal septum, Everted uncinate process, Large agger nasi cell) in the narrow clefts of the OMC cause mucosal contact, paralyzing cilia and blocking ostia. This sets up a vicious cycle of hypoxia, retention of secretions, and secondary bacterial infection in the large dependent sinuses (maxillary and frontal). Clearing the OMC via FESS reverses disease in the larger sinuses without stripping their mucosa.

Acute and Chronic Rhinosinusitis (CRS)

A. Acute Maxillary Sinusitis

• Aetiology: Secondary bacterial invasion following acute viral rhinitis (Streptococcus pneumoniae [30%], Haemophilus influenzae [20%], Moraxella catarrhalis [12%]); Dental infections (periapical abscess of upper premolars/molars—polymicrobial/anaerobic); swimming/diving.

• Clinical Features: Fever, malaise, facial pain/pressure over the upper jaw/cheek radiating to upper teeth or supraorbital region (aggravated by stooping/coughing), tenderness over the canine fossa, mucopurulent nasal/postnasal discharge, and pus in the middle meatus on anterior rhinoscopy/endoscopy. (Note: Acute frontal sinusitis causes characteristic "Office headache"—starts on waking, peaks at midday, and subsides by evening, with tenderness on pressing the floor of the frontal sinus above the medial canthus).

• Investigations: DNE (pus in middle meatus), Waters’ view X-ray (haziness/air-fluid level), CT PNS (only if complications are suspected).

• Treatment: Medical: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (for 10–14 days), topical decongestant drops (Xylometazoline for 5 days), steam inhalation (with menthol/Tr. Benzoin Co.), analgesics, and saline sprays.

B. Chronic Rhinosinusitis (CRS)

• Definition: Inflammation of the nose and paranasal sinuses lasting ≥ 12 consecutive weeks. Divided into CRS without Nasal Polyps (CRSsNP) and CRS with Nasal Polyps (CRSwNP).

• Aetiopathogenesis (Vicious Cycle): Ostial obstruction → stagnation of secretions & impaired mucociliary clearance → local hypoxia and drop in pH → ciliary paralysis and epithelial damage → bacterial colonization (S. aureus, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, anaerobes) & Biofilm formation (protective polysaccharide matrix resistant to antibiotics) → mucosal thickening and polyp formation → further ostial block.

• Diagnostic Criteria (Requires ≥ 2 symptoms + ≥ 1 objective sign for ≥ 12 weeks):

• Major Symptoms: (1) Nasal obstruction/congestion, (2) Anterior or posterior mucopurulent nasal discharge, (3) Facial pain/pressure/fullness, (4) Hyposmia or anosmia.

• Objective Signs: Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy (oedema/mucopus/polyps in the middle meatus) AND/OR NCCT Paranasal Sinuses (mucosal thickening/opacification of OMC and sinuses).

• Management:

• Maximal Medical Therapy: Culture-directed broad-spectrum antibiotics or long-term low-dose macrolides (anti-inflammatory), Intranasal Corticosteroid sprays, high-volume isotonic saline nasal irrigations (disrupts biofilms), antihistamines/Montelukast, and short-course oral steroids (in CRSwNP).

• Surgical Management: Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) for medically refractory cases (Principles, steps, and complications are detailed in Section 50: Operative Surgery).

3. Fungal Sinusitis

1. Non-Invasive Fungal Sinusitis:

• Fungal Ball (Mycetoma): Extramucosal collection of tangled fungal hyphae (Aspergillus) in a single sinus (usually maxillary sinus) in an immunocompetent host. CT shows a hyperdense calcified/metallic-density mass without bone invasion. Treatment: Endoscopic surgical removal and wide antrostomy (no antifungals needed).

• Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS): IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to dematiaceous fungi (Bipolaris, Curvularia, Alternaria) or Aspergillus in atopic immunocompetent young adults.

• Bent and Kuhn Criteria: (1) Type I hypersensitivity, (2) Nasal polyposis, (3) Characteristic CT findings ("Double-density sign"—central hyperdense allergic mucin surrounded by hypodense oedematous mucosa, with pressure expansion/remodelling of sinus walls), (4) Eosinophilic "Allergic Mucin" (thick peanut-butter-like mucin containing eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals) without tissue invasion, and (5) Positive fungal stain (Gomori Methenamine Silver).

• Treatment: FESS (complete clearance of polyps and allergic mucin + wide sinus marsupialization) + Pre- and Postoperative Systemic and Topical Corticosteroids.

2. Invasive Fungal Sinusitis:

• Acute Fulminant Invasive Fungal Sinusitis (Rhinocerebral Mucormycosis / Phycomycosis):

• Rapidly fatal opportunistic infection caused by Mucor, Rhizopus, or Aspergillus in uncontrolled diabetics (diabetic ketoacidosis), post-COVID-19 steroid recipients, or immunocompromised patients (leukaemia, transplant, AIDS).

• Pathogenesis: Fungus has a high affinity for internal elastic lamina of arteries (angioinvasion), causing thrombosis and ischaemic coagulative necrosis.

• Clinical Features: Fever, facial/orbital pain, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, blindness, cranial nerve palsies, and a pathognomonic black necrotic eschar on the middle/inferior turbinate, septum, or hard palate.

• Diagnosis: KOH mount and biopsy showing broad, aseptate, ribbon-like hyphae branching at right angles (90^circ) in Mucor (or narrow, septate hyphae branching at acute 45^circ angles in Aspergillus); Contrast MRI of brain/orbit/PNS.

• Treatment (Medical & Surgical Emergency): (1) Strict control of diabetes/ketoacidosis and reversal of immunosuppression, (2) Aggressive radical endoscopic/open surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue until bleeding healthy tissue is reached, and (3) Systemic IV Liposomal Amphotericin-B (or Posaconazole/Isavuconazole).

• Chronic Invasive / Granulomatous Fungal Sinusitis: Slow tissue invasion by Aspergillus flavus with non-caseating giant-cell granulomas and proptosis; treated with surgical debridement + Voriconazole/Itraconazole.

4. Complications of Sinusitis

1. Local Complications:

• Mucocele / Mucopyocele: Encapsulated, expansile mucus-filled sac caused by chronic ostial obstruction. Most common in the Frontal sinus (followed by ethmoid, maxillary, sphenoid). Frontal mucocele presents as a cystic, non-tender swelling in the superomedial quadrant of the orbit (90%), displacing the eyeball forwards, downwards, and laterally with diplopia and egg-shell crackling on palpation. X-ray/CT shows loss of the scalloped outline of the frontal sinus. Treatment: Endoscopic marsupialization (Draf II/III) or external frontoethmoidectomy (Howarth’s operation).

• Osteomyelitis:

• Maxilla: Common in infants/children (infection of dental sac).

• Frontal Bone: Common in adults. Subperiosteal abscess over the anterior table of the frontal bone produces a soft, doughy, fluctuant swelling on the forehead called Pott’s Puffy Tumour (often associated with an underlying extradural abscess). Treatment: High-dose IV antibiotics, surgical drainage, and debridement of sequestra.

2. Orbital Complications (Most commonly from Ethmoid Sinusitis via thin Lamina Papyracea):

• Chandler’s Classification:

• Stage I: Preseptal cellulitis (inflammatory oedema of eyelids anterior to orbital septum; normal vision and extraocular movements).

• Stage II: Orbital cellulitis (diffuse oedema of orbital contents with proptosis, chemosis, and pain on eye movement).

• Stage III: Subperiosteal abscess (pus between lamina papyracea and periorbita; eyeball displaced downwards and laterally).

• Stage IV: Orbital abscess (pus within the orbit; severe proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and visual loss).

• Stage V: Cavernous sinus thrombosis (bilateral involvement, high picket-fence fever, CN III, IV, VI, V_1 palsies, papilloedema).

• Other Syndromes: Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome (deep orbital pain + paralysis of CN III, IV, VI, and V_1) and Orbital Apex Syndrome (Superior orbital fissure syndrome + Optic nerve [CN II] blindness).

3. Intracranial Complications: Meningitis, Extradural abscess, Subdural empyema, Brain abscess (frontal lobe), and Cavernous / Lateral Sinus Thrombophlebitis (Note: Clinical signs of Lateral Sinus Thrombophlebitis include Picket-fence fever with rigors, Griesinger’s sign [pitting oedema over posterior mastoid due to mastoid emissary vein thrombosis], Tobey-Ayer test [no rise in CSF pressure on compressing internal jugular vein on thrombosed side], Crowe-Beck test [engorgement of retinal/supraorbital veins on compressing healthy IJV], and Empty Delta sign on CECT/MR venography).

subject: ent
title: 31. ORAL CAVITY AND SALIVARY GLANDS
text:
1. Premalignant Conditions / Lesions of the Oral Cavity

• Premalignant Lesions (morphologically altered tissue in which cancer is more likely to occur): Leukoplakia, Erythroplakia, Palatal keratosis in reverse smokers.

• Premalignant Conditions (generalized state associated with significantly increased risk of cancer): Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSMF), Erosive Lichen Planus, Plummer-Vinson Syndrome, Syphilitic glossitis, Discoid lupus erythematosus.

A. Leukoplakia vs. Erythroplakia

• Leukoplakia: A clinical white patch or plaque on the oral mucosa that cannot be scraped off and cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease.

• Aetiology (6 S’s): Smoking, Spirits (alcohol), Spices, Sharp jagged tooth, Sepsis, Syphilis, and tobacco/betel quid chewing.

• Common Sites: Buccal mucosa (most common in India at the site of tobacco quid), oral commissures, lateral border of tongue, floor of mouth.

• Clinical Types: Homogeneous, Nodular (speckled), and Erosive (erythroleukoplakia—highest malignant risk). Malignant transformation rate: ~5% (1–17.5%).

• Management: Cessation of tobacco/alcohol, antioxidants (Vitamin A, Beta-carotene, Lycopene), incisional biopsy to rule out dysplasia/carcinoma, and surgical excision or CO_2 laser ablation.

• Erythroplakia: A fiery red velvety patch on the oral mucosa (due to epithelial atrophy and lack of keratin). Has a 17-fold higher malignant potential than leukoplakia (>50–90% show severe dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, or invasive carcinoma on biopsy). Treated by wide surgical/laser excision.

Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSMF)

• Definition: A chronic, insidious, premalignant condition of the oral cavity and pharynx characterized by juxta-epithelial inflammatory reaction and progressive fibroelastic transformation of the lamina propria, leading to mucosal rigidity and progressive trismus.

• Aetiopathogenesis:

• Areca Nut (Betel nut / Supari / Gutkha): Primary causative agent. Contains alkaloids (Arecoline, arecaidine) which stimulate fibroblasts to proliferate and synthesize collagen, while tannins cross-link collagen fibres, making them resistant to degradation by collagenase.

• Cell-Mediated Immune Response: Activated T-lymphocytes (high CD4^+:CD8^+ ratio) and macrophages release fibrogenic cytokines (TGF-β), which upregulate collagen synthesis and downregulate collagenase.

• Other Factors: Chillies (capsaicin hypersensitivity), tobacco, alcohol, and iron/vitamin B-complex deficiency.

• Malignant Potential: 3–7.6% transform into squamous cell carcinoma.

• Clinical Features:

• Symptoms: Burning sensation in the mouth and intolerance to spicy food, recurrent vesicular eruptions, dryness of mouth, progressive difficulty in opening the mouth (trismus), and difficulty protruding the tongue.

• Signs: Blanched, marble-like white appearance of the soft palate, faucial pillars, and buccal mucosa with loss of suppleness; palpable vertical fibrous bands in the buccal mucosa and faucial pillars; shrunken fibrotic uvula; and severe trismus.

• Management:

1. Preventive & Nutritional: Strict cessation of areca nut, pan masala, tobacco, and spicy food; correction of iron/vitamin deficiencies; antioxidants (Lycopene, Vitamin A, E, Zinc).

2. Medical: Submucosal intralesional injections of Dexamethasone (4 mg / 1 mL) + Hyaluronidase (1500 IU in 1 mL) mixed with lignocaine, injected biweekly into the fibrotic bands for 8–10 weeks + Jaw-opening physiotherapy exercises.

3. Surgical (For severe trismus where interincisal distance is <15–20 mm): Surgical release/excision of fibrous bands (with coronoidectomy/temporalis myotomy if needed) and reconstruction of the raw defect using a Buccal Fat Pad graft, Nasolabial flap, or radial forearm free flap (simple split-skin grafting causes high recurrence due to contracture).

3. Eagle’s Syndrome (Styalgia) and Frey’s Syndrome

• Eagle’s Syndrome (Styalgia):

• Etiopathogenesis: Symptomatic elongation of the styloid process (>30 mm; normal is 20–25 mm) OR calcification of the stylohyoid ligament. After tonsillectomy, scar tissue traps the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), vagus, or carotid plexus against the elongated styloid process.

• Clinical Features: Dull, aching pain in the tonsillar fossa and upper neck radiating to the ipsilateral ear, aggravated by swallowing and turning the head (Classic type—post-tonsillectomy; Carotid artery type—pain along carotid distribution on turning head).

• Diagnosis: Transoral digital palpation of the tonsillar fossa reproduces the exact pain and feels a bony projection; X-ray Towne’s / Lateral view of skull or 3D-CT Styloid.

• Treatment: Medical (Carbamazepine, Gabapentin, local steroid/lignocaine injection). Surgical: Styloidectomy (shortening the styloid process via a transoral trans-tonsillar approach after tonsillectomy or an external transcervical approach).

• Frey’s Syndrome (Gustatory Sweating / Auriculotemporal Syndrome):

• Pathogenesis: Complication appearing several months after parotidectomy or parotid trauma. Postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion (travelling in the auriculotemporal nerve, originally destined for the parotid gland) undergo aberrant regeneration and innervate the sweat glands and cutaneous blood vessels of the overlying skin.

• Clinical Features: Flushing and sweating of the preauricular/parotid skin during mastication. Confirmed by Minor’s Starch-Iodine Test (iodine painted on the cheek and dusted with dry starch turns dark blue on chewing a lemon).

• Treatment: Reassurance; Intradermal Botulinum Toxin-A injection (treatment of choice); Tympanic Neurectomy (sectioning Jacobson’s nerve on the promontory); or interposing a temporalis fascia/SCM flap or dermal graft under the skin flap.

4. Papillae of Tongue & Taste Bud

• Papillae of Tongue:

1. Vallate (Circumvallate) Papillae: 8–12 large papillae arranged in a V-shaped row just anterior to the sulcus terminalis; rich in taste buds.2. Fungiform Papillae: Rounded, reddish elevations located mainly at the tip and lateral margins of the tongue; contain taste buds.

3. Filiform Papillae: Conical, most numerous papillae covering the anterior two-thirds of the dorsum; keratinized and devoid of taste buds (provide friction for food manipulation; hypertrophied in Hairy tongue and atrophied in Bald tongue of iron deficiency).

4. Foliate Papillae: Vertical mucosal folds on the posterolateral border of the tongue; contain taste buds.

• Structure of a Taste Bud: Barrel-shaped neuroepithelial end-organ (50–70 µm) embedded in the stratified squamous epithelium. Consists of: (1) Neuroepithelial (gustatory) receptor cells with apical microvilli (taste hairs) projecting into a taste pore, (2) Supporting (sustentacular) cells, and (3) Basal (stem) cells (replace receptor cells every 10 days). Innervated by Chorda tympani (CN VII) in the anterior 2/3, Glossopharyngeal (CN IX) in the posterior 1/3 and vallate papillae, and Internal laryngeal nerve (CN X) in the vallecula and epiglottis.

5. Ranula, Sialolithiasis, and Pleomorphic Adenoma

• Ranula and Plunging Ranula:

• Ranula: A bluish, translucent, fluctuant extravasation mucocele (pseudocyst) in the floor of the mouth on one side of the frenulum, pushing the tongue upwards (resembles a frog's belly). Arises from ductal obstruction/trauma of the sublingual salivary gland.

• Plunging Ranula: A ranula that herniates through a dehiscence in the mylohyoid muscle (or behind its posterior border) into the submandibular space of the neck, presenting as a soft, transilluminant neck swelling with or without an intraoral component.

• Treatment: Complete surgical excision of the cyst along with the ipsilateral sublingual salivary gland (to prevent recurrence), or marsupialization if very large.

• Sialolithiasis (Salivary Calculi):

• Calcium phosphate and carbonate stones formed on an organic matrix of mucin/cellular debris. 80–90% occur in the submandibular gland (Wharton’s duct) (because its secretion is viscous/mucus-rich, rich in calcium, and drains against gravity through a long tortuous duct with a narrow orifice); 10–20% occur in the parotid gland.

• Clinical Features: Recurrent, painful meal-time swelling of the gland (salivary colic); stone is palpable bimanually in the floor of the mouth.

• Investigations: Intraoral occlusal radiograph (80% of submandibular stones are radio-opaque), Ultrasound, Sialography (contraindicated in acute infection), or Sialoendoscopy.

• Treatment: Stones in the anterior duct are removed intraorally by marsupializing/incising the duct over the stone (laying a stay suture behind the stone to prevent posterior slippage) or via interventional sialoendoscopy; stones at the hilum or intraglandular parenchyma require excision of the submandibular gland.

• Pleomorphic Adenoma (Benign Mixed Tumour):

• Most common benign tumour of major and minor salivary glands (80% occur in the parotid gland, usually the tail of the superficial lobe; palate is the commonest minor salivary gland site).

• Pathology: Called "mixed" because it contains both epithelial/myoepithelial cells and mesenchymal stroma (mucoid, myxoid, chondroid). Although encapsulated, it sends microscopic pseudopods through the capsule into surrounding normal gland tissue; simple enucleation leaves pseudopods behind, causing high recurrence.

• Clinical Features: Slow-growing, painless, firm, lobulated swelling in the parotid region (fills the retromandibular groove and lifts the ear lobule) with normal facial nerve function. (Sudden rapid growth, pain, skin fixity, and facial nerve palsy indicate malignant transformation into Carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma).

• Diagnosis: FNAC and Ultrasound/MRI.

• Treatment: Superficial Parotidectomy (or total conservative parotidectomy if in the deep lobe) with careful identification and preservation of the facial nerve.

6. Carcinoma of Maxilla (Maxillary Sinus)

(Detailed TNM staging, Ohngren’s & Lederman’s classifications, clinical spread, and management are fully covered in Section 50 under Maxillectomy and Chapter 40).

subject: ent
title: 32. ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF PHARYNX
text:
1. Waldeyer’s Ring

• Definition: An interrupted circular ring of subepithelial mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) strategically aggregated at the upper portals of the aerodigestive tract.

• Constituents of Waldeyer’s Ring:

1. Nasopharyngeal Tonsil (Adenoids): Single midline mass at the junction of the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx.

2. Palatine (Faucial) Tonsils: Paired ovoid masses in the lateral wall of the oropharynx between the anterior and posterior pillars.

3. Lingual Tonsils: Paired nodular masses at the base (posterior 1/3rd) of the tongue, posterior to the circumvallate papillae.

4. Tubal Tonsils (of Gerlach): Paired collections of lymphoid tissue in the fossa of Rosenmüller and around the pharyngeal opening of the Eustachian tube (torus tubarius).

5. Lateral Pharyngeal Bands: Vertical lymphoid ridges descending behind the posterior tonsillar pillars (palatopharyngeal arches).

6. Posterior Pharyngeal Wall Nodules: Scattered subepithelial lymphoid follicles on the posterior pharyngeal wall.

• Characteristics & Functions:

• Lacks afferent lymphatics; antigens enter directly through specialized surface M-cells and crypts.

• Local Immunity: B-lymphocytes in germinal centres differentiate into plasma cells producing secretory IgA, IgM, and IgG; T-lymphocytes in parafollicular zones mediate cellular immunity.

• Immune Surveillance: Alerts the systemic immune system against inhaled and ingested pathogens; maximally active between 4 and 10 years of age, regressing after puberty.

2. Divisions of Hypopharynx, Pyriform Sinus, Killian’s Dehiscence, and Pharyngeal Pouch

• Subsites of Hypopharynx (Laryngopharynx) (Extends from the plane of the hyoid bone above to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage [C3 to C6] below):

1. Pyriform Sinus (Fossa) (most common site of hypopharyngeal carcinoma—60%).

2. Postcricoid Region (30%; associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome in females).

3. Posterior Pharyngeal Wall (10%).

• Pyriform Sinus (Fossa):

• Paired梨-shaped recess lying on either side of the laryngeal inlet, forming the lateral food channels.

• Boundaries: Superiorly: Pharyngoepiglottic fold; Laterally: Thyrohyoid membrane and lamina of thyroid cartilage; Medially: Aryepiglottic fold and posterolateral surfaces of arytenoid and cricoid cartilages; Apex (Inferiorly): Level of the cricopharyngeus (upper oesophageal sphincter).

• Clinical Importance: The internal laryngeal nerve runs submucosally in its lateral wall (site for local anaesthetic block [Krause’s fossa]; causes referred otalgia in pyriform carcinoma; common site for foreign body impaction; rich lymphatic drainage through thyrohyoid membrane to Level II/III nodes).

• Killian’s Dehiscence ("Gateway of Tears"):

• A potential triangular weak anatomical area in the posterior wall of the hypopharynx between the two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle:

• Superiorly: Oblique fibres of the thyropharyngeus (propulsive).

• Inferiorly: Transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus (sphincteric).

• Clinical Importance: (1) Site of herniation of pharyngeal mucosa forming a Pharyngeal Pouch (Zenker’s Diverticulum), and (2) Commonest site of iatrogenic perforation during rigid oesophagoscopy (hence called "Gateway of Tears").

• Pharyngeal Pouch (Zenker’s Diverticulum):

• Pathogenesis: A pulsion diverticulum (false diverticulum containing only mucosa and submucosa) where hypopharyngeal mucosa herniates posteriorly through Killian’s dehiscence due to neuromuscular incoordination (spasm or failure of relaxation of the cricopharyngeal sphincter during pharyngeal contraction). Starts in the midline and turns to the left in the neck.

• Clinical Features (Usually elderly males >60 years):

1. Progressive dysphagia (appears after a few swallows once the pouch fills and compresses the oesophagus).

2. Regurgitation of undigested food eaten hours/days earlier (especially at night on lying down), causing nocturnal coughing fits and aspiration pneumonia.

3. Gurgling noise in the neck on swallowing and a compressible left neck swelling (Boyce’s sign).

4. Halitosis, weight loss, and rare development of carcinoma within the pouch.

• Diagnosis: Barium Swallow (anterior-posterior and lateral views delineate the pouch; rigid oesophagoscopy is hazardous as the scope enters the wide mouth of the pouch and perforates its fundus).

• Management:

1. External Cervical Excision of the Pouch + Cricopharyngeal Myotomy (for large pouches in fit patients).

2. Dohlman’s Endoscopic Procedure / Endoscopic Stapling or CO_2 Laser Diverticulotomy: Endoscopic division of the common party wall (including the cricopharyngeus muscle) between the pouch and the oesophagus using a double-bladed Weerda diverticuloscope (preferred in elderly/high-risk patients).

subject: ent
title: 33. ADENOIDS
text:
1. Adenoids and Adenoid Facies

• Anatomy: Nasopharyngeal tonsil located at the junction of the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx. Composed of vertical ridges of lymphoid tissue separated by clefts; lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar, stratified squamous, and transitional epithelium. Unlike palatine tonsils, adenoids have NO crypts and NO capsule. Present at birth, enlarge physiologically up to 6 years, atrophy at puberty, and disappear by 20 years.

• Clinical Features of Adenoid Hypertrophy:

1. Nasal Symptoms: Bilateral nasal obstruction → chronic mouth breathing, difficulty feeding in infants, chronic wet bubbly mucopurulent rhinorrhoea, recurrent rhinosinusitis, and rhinolalia clausa (denasal toneless voice).

2. Aural Symptoms (blocking the Eustachian tube orifice/torus tubarius): Retracted tympanic membrane, fluctuating conductive hearing loss, Otitis Media with Effusion (Glue ear), and recurrent Acute Otitis Media.

3. General Symptoms:

• Adenoid Facies: Characteristic facial appearance resulting from chronic nasal obstruction and prolonged mouth breathing in a growing child:

1. Elongated, dull, expressionless face with an open mouth.

2. Pinched-in nostrils (due to disuse atrophy of alae nasi).

3. Hitched-up short upper lip.

4. Prominent, crowded, protruding upper incisors.

5. High-arched hard palate (loss of moulding action of the tongue against the palate).

6. Hypoplastic maxilla (loss of pneumatization).

• Obstructive Sleep Apnoea (OSA) (most common cause of paediatric OSA), nocturnal enuresis, Aprosexia (lack of concentration/mental dullness due to hypoxia and disturbed sleep), and Pulmonary hypertension / Cor pulmonale in severe cases.

• Diagnosis: Posterior rhinoscopy / Flexible nasopharyngoscopy, and X-ray Soft Tissue Nasopharynx (Lateral view) (shows soft tissue shadow hanging from posterosuperior wall narrowing the nasopharyngeal airway).

• Treatment:

• Conservative: Intranasal corticosteroid sprays (Mometasone/Fluticasone), antihistamines, decongestants, and breathing exercises for mild cases.

• Surgical: Adenoidectomy (curetment with St. Clair Thomson’s guarded adenoid curette, endoscopic microdebrider, or coblation; combined with myringotomy and grommet insertion if OME is present). (Contraindications and complications are detailed in Section 50: Operative Surgery).

subject: ent
title: 34. TUMOURS OF NASOPHARYNX
text:
1. Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)

• Clinical Vignette Diagnosis: Adolescent male (10–20 years) presenting with recurrent, spontaneous, profuse, painless epistaxis and progressive unilateral/bilateral nasal obstruction with a smooth, reddish-pink lobulated mass in the nasal cavity/nasopharynx → Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA).

• Aetiopathogenesis & Pathology:

• Most common benign tumour of the nasopharynx, occurring exclusively in adolescent males (10–20 years); it is testosterone-dependent (arises from a hormone-sensitive hamartomatous vascular nidus).

• Site of Origin: Posterolateral wall of the nasal cavity at the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen (junction of the sphenoidal process of the palatine bone with the horizontal ala of the vomer and root of the pterygoid process).

• Histopathology: Benign, unencapsulated, locally invasive fibrovascular tumour composed of endothelium-lined vascular spaces lacking a complete muscular or elastic coat embedded in a dense collagenous fibrous stroma. Because the vessels lack a contractile muscle layer, they cannot vasoconstrict, leading to torrential, life-threatening bleeding and non-responsiveness to topical adrenaline.

• Routes of Spread:

1. Medially/Anteriorly: Fills nasopharynx and nasal cavity, pushing the septum to the opposite side; invades ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary sinuses.

2. Laterally: Through the sphenopalatine foramen into the pterygopalatine fossa (pushing the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus forwards) → through the pterygomaxillary fissure into the infratemporal fossa and cheek.

3. Superiorly (Orbit): Through the inferior orbital fissure into the orbit → causes proptosis and "Frog-face deformity"; and through the superior orbital fissure.

4. Intracranially: Into the Middle Cranial Fossa (via erosion of greater wing of sphenoid/foramen lacerum, lying lateral to the ICA, or via the sphenoid sinus, lying medial to the ICA and cavernous sinus) and Anterior Cranial Fossa.

• Clinical Features:

1. Profuse, recurrent, spontaneous, unprovoked epistaxis (hallmark symptom) leading to severe anaemia.

2. Progressive nasal obstruction, mucopurulent discharge, and rhinolalia clausa (denasal speech).

3. Conductive hearing loss and Otitis Media with Effusion (due to Eustachian tube blockage).

4. Signs: Smooth or lobulated, pinkish-purple, firm, compressible mass in the posterior nasal cavity and nasopharynx. (Warning: Never perform digital palpation or outpatient biopsy, as it triggers torrential, fatal haemorrhage).

5. Late Signs (due to extension): Broadening of the nasal bridge, proptosis ("Frog-face deformity"), swelling of the cheek and infratemporal fossa, palatal bulge, and cranial nerve palsies (CN II, III, IV, V, VI).

• Investigations & Radiological Signs:

1. Contrast-Enhanced CT Scan (CECT) of Nose, PNS, and Skull Base (Investigation of Choice):

• Shows an intensely enhancing soft-tissue mass centred at the sphenopalatine foramen with bony remodelling/erosion.

• Holman-Miller Sign (Antral Sign): Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus due to tumour expansion in the pterygopalatine fossa (pathognomonic of JNA).

• Hondousa Sign: Widening of the gap between the ramus of the mandible and the maxillary body (indicating infratemporal fossa extension).

2. Contrast MRI: Evaluates soft-tissue intracranial (dural/cavernous sinus) and orbital extensions.

3. Four-Vessel Carotid Angiography / Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): Shows intense "tumour blush" and identifies the feeding vessels—primarily the Internal Maxillary Artery and ascending pharyngeal artery (from External Carotid Artery), and any feeders from the Internal Carotid Artery in large intracranial tumours. Allows preoperative transcatheter embolization (24–48 hours prior to surgery) using Gelfoam or polyvinyl alcohol particles, which drastically reduces intraoperative blood loss.

• Management:

• Immediate Emergency Intervention: Resuscitation, IV fluids, blood grouping/cross-matching and blood transfusion, and anterior/posterior nasal packing to tamponade acute bleeding.

• Surgical Excision (Treatment of Choice) (performed 24–48 hours after preoperative embolization, with 2–4 units of cross-matched blood ready):

• Approaches based on tumour stage/extent:

1. Endoscopic Transnasal Resection: Treatment of choice for tumours limited to the nose, nasopharynx, ethmoid/sphenoid sinuses, and pterygopalatine fossa (Fisch Stage I & II).

2. Transpalatal Approach (Wilson’s) or Transpalatal + Sublabial (Sardana’s Approach): For nasopharyngeal and lateral extensions.

3. Lateral Rhinotomy / Midfacial Degloving with Medial Maxillectomy or Le Fort I Transmaxillary Approach.

4. Maxillary Swing (Facial Translocation / Wei’s Approach) or Fisch Infratemporal Fossa Approach: For extensive infratemporal fossa and cheek extensions.

5. Combined Craniofacial Resection: For intradural intracranial extensions.

• Radiotherapy (30–35 Gy in 15–18 fractions / Stereotactic Radiotherapy): Reserved for unresectable intracranial extensions (cavernous sinus invasion or ICA blood supply) or recurrent inoperable tumours.

• Hormonal Therapy: Flutamide (androgen receptor blocker) preoperatively for 6 weeks to shrink tumour volume.

2. Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC) and Trotter’s Triad

• Aetiopathogenesis:

1. Genetic: High susceptibility in Southern Chinese (Cantonese), Taiwanese, and Mongoloid populations (including Northeast India); associated with HLA-A2 and HLA-Bsin2.

2. Viral: Strong association with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) (IgA antibodies to Viral Capsid Antigen [VCA] and Early Antigen [EA] are used as tumour markers for screening and prognosis).

3. Environmental/Dietary: Consumption of salted preserved fish (volatile nitrosamines) from childhood, Vitamin C deficiency, and indoor smoke from burning incense/wood (polycyclic hydrocarbons).

• Pathology:

• Most Common Site of Origin: Fossa of Rosenmüller (Pharyngeal recess) in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx.

• WHO Histopathological Classification:

• Type I (25%): Keratinizing Squamous Cell Carcinoma (radioresistant, no EBV association).

• Type II (12%): Non-keratinizing Differentiated Carcinoma.

• Type III (63%): Non-keratinizing Undifferentiated Carcinoma (Lymphoepithelioma) (strong EBV association, highly radiosensitive).

• Clinical Features:

1. Cervical Lymphadenopathy (Most common presenting feature: 60–90%): Painless enlargement of upper deep jugular (Level II) and posterior triangle/spinal accessory (Level V) lymph nodes; bilateral in 50%. (Node of Rouviere—highest lateral retropharyngeal node is the first echelon node).

2. Otologic: Unilateral Otitis Media with Effusion (OME) / Serous Otitis Media, conductive deafness, and tinnitus due to Eustachian tube obstruction (Clinical Dictum: Unilateral serous otitis media in an adult mandates nasopharyngeal endoscopy to rule out NPC).

3. Nasal: Epistaxis (blood-stained postnasal discharge), unilateral nasal obstruction, and denasal voice.

4. Ophthalmoneurologic (Cranial Nerve Palsies):

• Direct upward spread through the foramen lacerum into the cavernous sinus involves CN VI (Abducens nerve—earliest cranial nerve paralysed, causing lateral rectus palsy and diplopia), followed by CN III, IV, and V (corneal anaesthesia and facial pain).

• Posterolateral spread into the parapharyngeal/jugular foramen space involves CN IX, X, XI (Jugular Foramen / Vernet’s Syndrome), CN XII, and the cervical sympathetic chain (Horner’s Syndrome).

5. Trotter’s Triad (Sinus of Morgagni Syndrome): Seen when NPC invades laterally through the sinus of Morgagni:

• (1) Conductive deafness (Eustachian tube obstruction).

• (2) Ipsilateral immobility of the soft palate (invasion of levator veli palatini / CN X).

• (3) Ipsilateral temporoparietal / mandibular neuralgia (invasion of mandibular nerve V_3 at foramen ovale).

• Investigations: Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy and Biopsy; CECT and Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of nasopharynx, skull base, and neck; Pure Tone Audiometry & Tympanometry; EBV serology (IgA-VCA, IgA-EA).

• Management:

• Radiotherapy is the Mainstay of Treatment (nasopharynx is surgically inaccessible and Type II/III tumours are highly radiosensitive):

• Stage I & II: Definitive External Beam Radiotherapy (IMRT) (66–70 Gy to primary tumour and bilateral neck nodes).

• Stage III & IV: Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) using weekly Cisplatin + IMRT (70 Gy).

• Residual / Recurrent Disease: Radical Neck Dissection for persistent neck nodes; Intracavitary Brachytherapy, Stereotactic Radiotherapy, or Endoscopic/Maxillary-swing Salvage Nasopharyngectomy for local recurrence.

3. Thornwaldt’s Disease (Pharyngeal Bursitis)

Infection or cystic dilatation of the nasopharyngeal bursa (Pouch of Luschka)—a median epithelial-lined recess in the posterior wall of the nasopharynx within the adenoid mass, representing the embryonic attachment of the notochord to the pharyngeal endoderm. Clinical Features: Persistent foul-smelling postnasal drip with crusting, dull occipital headache, nasal obstruction, and a smooth, midline, fluctuant cystic swelling on the posterosuperior nasopharyngeal wall. Treatment: Antibiotics + Endoscopic marsupialization and excision of the anterior cyst wall.

subject: ent
title: 35 & 36. ACUTE AND CHRONIC PHARYNGITIS & TONSILLITIS
text:
1. Anatomy of Palatine Tonsil, Tonsillar Bed, and Blood Supply

• Boundaries of Tonsillar Fossa: Anteriorly: Palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar); Posteriorly: Palatopharyngeal arch (posterior pillar); Apex: Soft palate; Base: Dorsal surface of posterior 1/3rd of tongue.

• Surfaces & Crypts: Medial surface is covered by non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium dipping into 12–15 crypts (largest is crypta magna / intratonsillar cleft near the upper pole, representing the ventral part of the 2nd pharyngeal pouch). Lateral surface is covered by a fibrous capsule separated from the tonsillar bed by loose areolar tissue (containing the paratonsillar vein of Denis Browne).

• Relations of the Bed of the Tonsil (From medial to lateral):

1. Loose areolar peritonsillar space (containing paratonsillar vein).

2. Pharyngobasilar fascia.

3. Superior constrictor muscle and Styloglossus muscle.

4. Buccopharyngeal fascia.

5. Structures immediately lateral to the superior constrictor (in the parapharyngeal space): Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), Styloid process (if elongated), Facial artery (looping close to the lower pole), Internal carotid artery (2.5 cm posterolateral), submandibular salivary gland, posterior belly of digastric, medial pterygoid muscle, and angle of the mandible.

• Arterial Blood Supply of the Tonsil (5 Arteries—All from External Carotid System):

1. Tonsillar branch of the Facial artery (Main arterial supply; pierces superior constrictor at the lower pole).

2. Ascending palatine artery (branch of facial artery).

3. Ascending pharyngeal artery (branch of external carotid artery).

4. Dorsal lingual branches of the lingual artery.

5. Descending palatine (Lesser palatine) artery (branch of maxillary artery; supplies upper pole).

2. Acute Tonsillitis and Differential Diagnosis of Membrane Over Tonsil

• Aetiology of Acute Tonsillitis: Most commonly Group A β-haemolytic *Streptococcus* (*S. pyogenes*), Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, or Haemophilus influenzae (often secondary to viral URI in school-going children).

• Clinical Types: (1) Acute Catarrhal/Superficial (viral), (2) Acute Follicular (crypts filled with yellow purulent spots), (3) Acute Parenchymatous (uniformly enlarged, red tonsils almost meeting in midline), and (4) Acute Membranous (exudate from crypts coalesces into a whitish non-adherent membrane on the medial surface).

• Clinical Features: Severe sore throat, odynophagia, high fever (38^circ–40^circC) with chills, referred ipsilateral otalgia (via CN IX), foetid breath, congested/swollen tonsils and pillars, and enlarged, tender jugulodigastric (tonsillar) lymph nodes.

• Treatment: Bed rest, warm saline gargles, analgesics (Paracetamol), and Systemic Antibiotics for 7–10 days—Drug of Choice: Penicillin / Amoxicillin (40–50 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses, or Adult 500 mg TDS) or Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (625 mg TDS) (Erythromycin/Azithromycin in penicillin-allergic patients).

• Complications:

• Local/Suppurative: Chronic tonsillitis, Peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy), Parapharyngeal abscess, Retropharyngeal abscess, Suppurative cervical lymphadenitis, Acute otitis media.

• Systemic/Non-suppurative: Acute Rheumatic Fever, Post-streptococcal Acute Glomerulonephritis (PSAGN), Subacute bacterial endocarditis.

Differential Diagnosis of a White Patch / Membrane Over the Tonsil

1. Acute Membranous Tonsillitis: Pyogenic (Streptococcus); abrupt onset with high fever; whitish-yellow membrane is strictly confined to the medial surface of the tonsil, is easily wiped off with a swab, and leaves no bleeding surface.

2. Faucial Diphtheria: Caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae; insidious onset, low-grade fever (100^circ–101^circF) but disproportionate severe toxaemia and tachycardia; dirty-grey tenacious pseudomembrane that extends beyond the tonsil onto the pillars, soft palate, and uvula, is firmly adherent, and leaves a raw bleeding surface on removal; associated with "Bull-neck" cervical lymphadenopathy. Confirmed by Albert’s stain (metachromatic granules) and culture on Loeffler’s serum slope. Treated urgently with IV Diphtheria Antitoxin (20,000–100,000 units) + Benzylpenicillin/Erythromycin.

3. Vincent’s Angina (Trench Mouth): Insidious onset with mild fever and fetor oris; caused by a symbiotic infection of a fusiform bacillus (*Fusobacterium necrophorum*) and a spirochaete (*Borrelia vincentii*). Greyish necrotic membrane (usually unilateral) over the tonsil and interdental gingival papillae that is easily removed, revealing a deep, ragged ulcer.

4. Infectious Mononucleosis (Glandular Fever): Caused by Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) in young adults; bilateral marked tonsillar enlargement covered with a greyish-white membrane, petechiae at the hard-soft palate junction, generalized lymphadenopathy (especially posterior triangle nodes), and splenomegaly. Ampicillin causes a generalized maculopapular rash. Confirmed by atypical lymphocytes (>10%) on peripheral smear and a positive Paul-Bunnell / Monospot test (heterophile antibodies).

5. Candidiasis (Oral Thrush): Creamy-white curdy plaques in immunocompromised/debilitated patients or infants; easily scraped off leaving erythematous mucosa.

6. Agranulocytosis & Acute Leukaemia: Necrotic ulceromembranous lesions over tonsils and oral mucosa in a severely toxic/anaemic patient; diagnosed by CBC, peripheral smear (blast cells or severe neutropenia), and bone marrow biopsy.

7. Traumatic Ulcer / Post-Tonsillectomy Slough: White fibrinous healing slough appearing 24 hours after trauma or surgery.

8. Aphthous Ulcer & Malignancy of Tonsil (ulcerated SCC or Lymphoma).

9. Keratosis Pharyngis: Benign hyperkeratinization of crypt epithelium presenting as horny, yellowish-white, conical excrescences on the tonsils and pharyngeal wall. They are firmly adherent, cannot be wiped off, and have no surrounding inflammation or constitutional symptoms (differentiating it from acute follicular tonsillitis). Requires no active treatment (reassurance).

Causes of Unilateral Tonsillar Enlargement

1. Neoplastic: Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma (most common in children/young adults), Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Tonsil (adults), Minor salivary gland tumour.

2. Infective: Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy) (pushes tonsil medially), Intratonsillar abscess, Tonsillolith (calculus in crypt), Vincent’s angina, Tuberculosis/Actinomycosis of tonsil.

3. Extratonsillar (Apparent Enlargement / Medial Displacement): Parapharyngeal space tumour (deep lobe parotid pleomorphic adenoma, schwannoma, carotid body tumour), Parapharyngeal abscess, or Internal carotid artery aneurysm.

3. Chronic Tonsillitis

• Types: (1) Chronic Follicular (crypts full of yellowish cheesy plugs), (2) Chronic Parenchymatous (marked lymphoid hyperplasia causing OSA, dysphagia, and muffled speech), and (3) Chronic Fibroid (small, fibrotic, infected tonsils).

• Cardinal Signs of Chronic Tonsillitis:

1. Persistent flushing (congestion) of the anterior tonsillar pillars compared to the rest of the pharyngeal mucosa.

2. Expression of frank fluid pus or cheesy material from the tonsillar crypts on pressing the anterior pillar with a tongue depressor (Irwin Moore’s sign).

3. Enlargement of the jugulodigastric (tonsillar) lymph nodes (non-tender between attacks; enlarged and tender during acute exacerbations).

• Treatment: Tonsillectomy (Indications, contraindications, techniques, and complications are detailed in Section 50: Operative Surgery).

subject: ent
title: 37. HEAD AND NECK SPACE INFECTIONS
text:
1. Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)

• Definition & Aetiology: Collection of pus in the peritonsillar space (potential space between the fibrous capsule of the tonsil medially and the superior constrictor muscle laterally). Usually occurs in adults as a complication of acute tonsillitis when crypta magna gets obstructed and forms an intratonsillar abscess that bursts through the capsule. Bacteriology: Polymicrobial—Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A β-haemolytic), Staphylococcus aureus, and anaerobes (Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus).

• Clinical Features:

• General: High fever (up to 104^circF), chills, rigors, malaise, and dehydration.

• Local Symptoms (Unilateral):

1. Severe unilateral throat pain and marked odynophagia (unable to swallow even saliva, which dribbles from the angle of the mouth).

2. "Hot-potato voice" (muffled, thick speech due to palatal oedema).

3. Ipsilateral referred earache (via CN IX).

4. Trismus (due to spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle lying just lateral to the superior constrictor).

5. Halitosis and torticollis (neck tilted to the side of the abscess).

• Examination Signs:

1. Marked congestion and asymmetric bulging of the soft palate and anterior pillar above the upper pole of the tonsil.

2. Tonsil is pushed downwards and medially (often buried in oedematous folds).

3. Uvula is swollen, oedematous, and pushed across the midline to the opposite side.

4. Enlarged, tender ipsilateral jugulodigastric lymph nodes.

• Treatment:

1. Medical (For early peritonsillitis): Hospitalization, IV fluids, high-dose IV antibiotics covering aerobes and anaerobes (Ceftriaxone/Co-amoxiclav + Metronidazole or Clindamycin), analgesics, and warm saline/hydrogen peroxide mouthwashes.

2. Incision and Drainage (For frank abscess):

• Done under topical anaesthesia/sedation in the sitting position.

• Site of Incision: At the point of maximum bulge above the upper pole of the tonsil, OR just lateral to the junction of a vertical line drawn along the anterior pillar and a horizontal line drawn through the base of the uvula.

• Using a guarded St. Clair Thomson’s peritonsillar knife (or a No. 11 blade taped with micropore leaving only the distal 0.5 cm exposed), a small stab incision is made through the mucosa, and a closed sinus forceps (or Quinsy forceps) is inserted and opened to evacuate pus. Re-opened the next day if pus re-accumulates.

3. Interval Tonsillectomy: Performed 4–6 weeks after resolution of the abscess. ("Hot" / Abscess tonsillectomy during the acute phase carries risks of bleeding and aspiration).

• Complications: Parapharyngeal abscess, Laryngeal oedema (stridor), Internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis (Lemierre’s syndrome), Carotid artery erosion/blowout, Aspiration pneumonia/lung abscess (if spontaneous rupture occurs during sleep), and Septicaemia.

2. Retropharyngeal Space and Retropharyngeal Abscess

• Clinical Vignette Diagnosis: 60-year-old diabetic patient presenting with severe throat pain, odynophagia, dysphagia, and fever 7 days after a chicken bone stuck in the throat → Acute Retropharyngeal Abscess.

• Surgical Anatomy of Retropharyngeal & Prevertebral Spaces:

1. Retropharyngeal Space (Space of Gillette): Lies behind the pharynx and oesophagus between the buccopharyngeal fascia anteriorly and the alar/prevertebral fascia posteriorly. Extends from the base of the skull to the bifurcation of the trachea (T4) in the superior mediastinum.
