Divided into two lateral compartments (Spaces of Gillette) by a midline fibrous raphe; each contains retropharyngeal lymph nodes (Nodes of Rouviere) which atrophy by 3–4 years of age. (Note: The Danger Space lies between the alar fascia and prevertebral fascia, extending from the skull base to the diaphragm).

2. Prevertebral Space: Lies between the prevertebral fascia anteriorly and the cervical vertebral bodies/muscles posteriorly; extends from the skull base to the coccyx.

Comparison of Acute vs. Chronic Retropharyngeal Abscess

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-003]]

• Complications of Acute Retropharyngeal Abscess: Spontaneous rupture causing fatal aspiration pneumonia/asphyxia,  laryngeal oedema, spread to the parapharyngeal space, and descending necrotizing mediastinitis.

3. Ludwig’s Angina (Submandibular Space Infection)

• Clinical Vignette Diagnosis: 40-year-old diabetic female with fever, swelling of the floor of the mouth, trismus, and a brawny woody-hard swelling in the submandibular and submental neck 1 week after lower molar root canal treatment → Ludwig’s Angina.

• Surgical Anatomy: Rapidly spreading, bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular space, which is divided by the mylohyoid muscle into:

1. Sublingual compartment (above mylohyoid, below oral mucosa).

2. Submaxillary and submental compartment (below mylohyoid, above deep cervical fascia).

(The two compartments communicate freely around the posterior free border of the mylohyoid muscle).

• Aetiology:

1. Dental Infections (80%): Periapical abscess or extraction of lower second and third molar teeth (whose roots extend below the mylohyoid line, directly infecting the submaxillary space; premolar roots lie above the mylohyoid line).

2. Submandibular sialadenitis, penetrating injuries of the floor of the mouth, and mandibular fractures.

3. Bacteriology: Mixed aerobic (α-haemolytic Streptococci, Staphylococci) and anaerobic (Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus) organisms.

• Clinical Features:

• Severe odynophagia, dysphagia, muffled voice, drooling of saliva, marked trismus, and high fever/toxaemia.

• Intraoral: Floor of the mouth is oedematous, indurated, and elevated ("Double-tongue appearance"); the tongue is progressively pushed upwards and backwards against the palate, threatening acute upper airway obstruction.

• External Neck: Bilateral, brawny, woody-hard, tender, non-fluctuant swelling in the submental and submandibular regions ("Bull-neck") without suppuration initially.

• Investigations: CBC, Blood sugar, Blood culture, and CECT of Neck (evaluates airway compromise, gas formation, and any localized pus collection).

• Management:

1. Immediate Airway Management (Top Priority): Hospitalization in ICU; if stridor or impending airway obstruction is present, perform an awake fibreoptic nasotracheal intubation or Emergency Tracheostomy under local anaesthesia.

2. High-Dose IV Antibiotics: Covering aerobes and anaerobes (IV Ceftriaxone / Piperacillin-Tazobactam + Metronidazole or Clindamycin) + IV fluids and glycaemic control.

3. Surgical Decompression (Incision and Drainage): Indicated if tension/airway compromise increases or no improvement occurs within 24–48 hours. A transverse submandibular collar incision extending from one angle of the mandible to the other (2 cm below the mandible) is made, dividing the deep cervical fascia and mylohyoid muscle vertically in the midline to decompress both submaxillary and sublingual spaces (usually yields serosanguinous fluid rather than frank pus). Extraction of the offending carious molar tooth.

• Complications: Acute asphyxia (tongue fallback + laryngeal oedema), spread to parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal spaces, mediastinitis, septicaemia, and aspiration pneumonia.

subject: ent
title: 38. SNORING AND SLEEP APNOEA
text:
1. Obstructive Sleep Apnoea Syndrome (OSAS)

• Definitions:

• Apnoea: Complete cessation of airflow at the nose and mouth lasting ≥ 10 seconds during sleep.

• Hypopnoea: Reduction in airflow by ≥ 50% for ≥ 10 seconds associated with a ≥ 4% drop in oxygen saturation (SpO_2) or an EEG arousal.

• Apnoea-Hypopnoea Index (AHI) / Respiratory Disturbance Index (RDI): Average number of apnoea plus hypopnoea episodes per hour of sleep. Normal: <5/hr; Mild OSA: 5–14/hr; Moderate OSA: 15–29/hr; Severe OSA: ≥ 30/hr.

• Aetiology:

• In Children: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy (Most common cause), craniofacial anomalies (Pierre-Robin sequence, Down syndrome, Treacher-Collins), choanal stenosis.

• In Adults: Obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m^2), thick short neck (collar size >42 cm in males, >37.5 cm in females), male gender, alcohol/sedative use, hypothyroidism, and upper airway anatomical narrowing:

• Level I (Nose/Nasopharynx): DNS, nasal polyps, inferior turbinate hypertrophy.

• Level II (Velopharynx/Oropharynx): Elongated thick soft palate and uvula, tonsillar hypertrophy, redundant pharyngeal folds.

• Level III (Hypopharynx/Tongue base): Macroglossia, lingual tonsil hypertrophy, retrognathia/micrognathia, omega-shaped epiglottis.

• Pathophysiology & Consequences: Pharyngeal dilator muscle relaxation during REM sleep → upper airway collapse → hypoxia (↓ pO_2), hypercapnia (uparrow pCO_2), and acidosis → systemic vasoconstriction (Systemic hypertension) and pulmonary vasoconstriction (Pulmonary hypertension, Cor pulmonale, Right heart failure), polycythaemia, cardiac arrhythmias, and repeated EEG micro-arousals causing sleep fragmentation.

• Clinical Features:

• Nocturnal: Loud disruptive snoring, witnessed apnoeic spells followed by loud gasping/choking, restless sleep, nocturnal enuresis (in children), gastro-oesophageal reflux.

• Daytime: Excessive daytime sleepiness (quantified by Epworth Sleepiness Scale >10/24), morning headaches, chronic fatigue, poor memory/concentration, irritability, decreased libido, and increased risk of motor vehicle accidents.

• Investigations:

1. Complete ENT Evaluation & Müller’s Manoeuvre: Flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy performed while the patient makes a maximal inspiratory effort against a closed nose and mouth; identifies the site and degree of collapse at the retropalatal (velum) and retroglossal (tongue base) levels. Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy (DISE) under propofol sedation is the dynamic gold standard.

2. Overnight Polysomnography (PSG) (Gold Standard Investigation): Simultaneously records EEG (sleep stages), EOG (eye movements), Submental EMG (muscle tone), ECG, Nasal/Oral airflow (thermistor), Thoracoabdominal respiratory effort, Pulse oximetry (SpO_2), and body position.

3. Cephalometric Radiographs / CT / MRI and thyroid profile.

• Management:

• In Children: Adenotonsillectomy is the definitive treatment of choice (curative in >85–90%).

• In Adults:

1. Medical / Non-Surgical:

• Lifestyle Modification: Weight reduction, avoidance of alcohol/sedatives/smoking before bedtime, and positional therapy (sleeping in lateral position—sewing a tennis ball to the back of pyjamas).

• Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP): Non-surgical gold standard for moderate-to-severe OSA; delivers positive pressure (5–20 cm H_2O) via a nasal mask, acting as a pneumatic splint to prevent pharyngeal collapse. (BiPAP or Auto-CPAP if CPAP is not tolerated).

• Oral Appliances: Mandibular Advancement Device (MAD) or Tongue-Retaining Device (TRD).

2. Surgical Management (For CPAP failure/intolerance or correctable anatomical obstruction):

• Nasal Surgery: Septoplasty, turbinoplasty, polypectomy (improves CPAP compliance).

• Palatal Surgery: Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) (excision of tonsils, uvula, and posterior rim of soft palate), Laser-Assisted Uvulopalatoplasty (LAUP), or Coblation/Radiofrequency palatal stiffening.

• Tongue Base / Skeletal Surgery: Coblation/Laser lingual tonsillectomy and midline glossectomy, Genioglossus advancement with mandibular osteotomy, Hyoid myotomy and suspension, or Maxillomandibular Advancement Osteotomy (MMA).

• Tracheostomy: Ultimate surgical gold standard (bypasses entire upper airway obstruction) in life-threatening severe OSA with cor pulmonale.

subject: ent
title: 39 & 54. NECK MASSES AND THYROID
text:
Classification / Differential Diagnosis of Neck Swellings

• Midline Neck Swellings:

1. Congenital/Developmental: Thyroglossal duct cyst (most common), Sublingual/Submental dermoid cyst, Thymic cyst.

2. Inflammatory/Lymph Nodal: Submental lymphadenitis, Prelaryngeal (Delphian) and Pretracheal lymph nodes, Ludwig’s angina.

3. Thyroid: Goitre of thyroid isthmus, Pyramidal lobe nodule, Thyroid carcinoma.

4. Miscellaneous: Lipoma, Sebaceous cyst, Subhyoid bursitis, Laryngocele (combined).

• Lateral Neck Swellings:

1. Submandibular Triangle: Submandibular lymphadenitis/metastasis, Submandibular sialadenitis/calculus/tumours, Plunging ranula.

2. Carotid Triangle: Branchial cleft cyst, Carotid body tumour (Chemodectoma), Carotid artery aneurysm, Jugulodigastric / Deep cervical lymphadenopathy (Reactive, Tuberculous, Metastatic carcinoma, Lymphoma), Sternomastoid tumour of infancy, External laryngocele, Schwannoma of vagus/sympathetic chain.

3. Posterior Triangle: Cystic hygroma (Cavernous lymphangioma), Spinal accessory/Supraclavicular lymph nodes (Virchow’s node), Subclavian aneurysm, Cervical rib, Lipoma.

2. Thyroglossal Duct Cyst and Lingual Thyroid

• Thyroglossal Duct Cyst:

• Embryology: The thyroid gland develops from a median endodermal diverticulum at the foramen caecum (junction of anterior 2/3rd and posterior 1/3rd of the tongue). The thyroglossal duct descends in the midline through the tongue musculature, passes anterior, through, or posterior to the body of the hyoid bone, and reaches the lower neck to form the thyroid lobes. Normally, the duct obliterates by the 8th–10th week of gestation; persistence of an epithelial remnant forms a thyroglossal duct cyst anywhere along its path (Subhyoid [most common], suprahyoid, intralingual, or over the thyroid/cricoid cartilage).

• Clinical Features: Painless, smooth, rounded (2–4 cm), cystic midline neck swelling (usually in children/young adults). Pathognomonic Signs:

1. Moves upwards on swallowing (attached to hyoid bone).

2. Moves upwards on protrusion of the tongue (attached via thyroglossal tract to the foramen caecum).

(If infected or incised, it forms a thyroglossal fistula with a hood of skin superiorly—never congenital).

• Investigations:

1. Ultrasound of the Neck: Confirms cystic nature and mandatory verification of the presence of a normal orthotopic thyroid gland (since the cyst may rarely contain the patient's only functioning thyroid tissue).

2. Thyroid Function Tests (TSH, T_3, T_4) and FNAC (rules out papillary carcinoma arising in the cyst [<1%]).

3. Radionuclide Thyroid Scan (^99mTc or ^123I): Done if the normal thyroid gland is not seen on USG or if hypothyroidism is present.

• Management (Sistrunk’s Operation): Complete surgical excision of the cyst, the entire thyroglossal tract, the central part (body) of the hyoid bone, and a core of suprahyoid tongue base muscle up to the foramen caecum. (Simple excision without removing the body of the hyoid bone results in a high recurrence rate).

• Lingual Thyroid:

• Embryology: Failure of the thyroid anlage to descend from the foramen caecum, resulting in an ectopic thyroid mass at the base of the tongue (in 70% of cases, it is the ONLY functioning thyroid tissue in the body).

• Clinical Features: More common in females (presents at puberty/pregnancy due to increased TSH demand). Causes dysphagia, muffled voice ("hot-potato voice"), stridor/dyspnoea, or haemoptysis. Indirect laryngoscopy shows a smooth, reddish-purple, vascular, midline mass at the base of the tongue posterior to the circumvallate papillae.

• Investigations: Thyroid Scan (^99mTc / ^123I) (confirms uptake at tongue base and absence of cervical thyroid), TSH/Thyroid profile (often hypothyroid), and CT/MRI (Biopsy is contraindicated due to torrential bleeding).

• Treatment: (1) Suppressive Therapy with L-Thyroxine (suppresses TSH and shrinks the mass in mild cases); (2) Surgical Excision (via transoral laser/coblation/robotic or transhyoid pharyngotomy) or Radioiodine (^131I) ablation if causing severe airway obstruction/dysphagia, followed by lifelong thyroxine replacement.

3. Branchial Cyst & Carotid Body Tumour

• Branchial Cleft Cyst: Arises from remnants of the second branchial cleft/cervical sinus of His. Presents in the 2nd–3rd decade as a smooth, fluctuant, non-transilluminant cystic swelling in the upper neck along the anterior border of the upper 1/3rd of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (If associated with a Second Arch Branchial Fistula, the external opening is at the junction of the lower 1/3rd and upper 2/3rd of the anterior border of the SCM; the tract ascends deep to the platysma, passes between the external and internal carotid arteries, superficial to the hypoglossal and glossopharyngeal nerves, and opens internally into the tonsillar fossa). Treatment: Complete surgical excision of the cyst (and tract via step-ladder incisions).

• Carotid Body Tumour (Chemodectoma / Paraganglioma): Arises from non-chromaffin paraganglionic chemoreceptor cells at the carotid bifurcation. Slow-growing, painless, firm, pulsatile swelling at the level of the hyoid bone with a carotid bruit. Fontaine’s Sign: The mass is freely mobile from side to side (horizontally), but NOT vertically. Investigations: CECT / Gadolinium MRI ("Salt and pepper appearance"), MR Angiography / DSA showing pathognomonic splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries ("Lyre’s Sign"), and 24-hour urinary VMA/metanephrines (Biopsy/FNAC is strictly contraindicated). Treatment: Preoperative embolization followed by subadventitial surgical excision (or Radiotherapy in elderly/unfit patients).

subject: ent
title: 40. ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF LARYNX
text:
1. Laryngeal Cartilages, Membranes, and Cavities

• Laryngeal Cartilages (9 Cartilages: 3 Unpaired, 3 Paired):

• Unpaired Cartilages (3):

1. Thyroid Cartilage: Largest cartilage (Hyaline cartilage); two alae meet anteriorly at an angle of 90^circ in males (Adam's apple) and 120^circ in females. Develops from 4th and 6th branchial arches.

2. Cricoid Cartilage: Hyaline cartilage; the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway (signet-ring shaped with a narrow anterior arch and broad posterior lamina). Develops from the 6th arch.

3. Epiglottis: Leaf-like yellow elastic fibrocartilage forming the anterior wall of the laryngeal inlet; attached to the thyroid angle by the petiole (thyroepiglottic ligament) and to the hyoid bone by the hyoepiglottic ligament. Develops from the hypobranchial eminence (3rd and 4th arches).

• Paired Cartilages (3 pairs = 6):

1. Arytenoid Cartilages: Pyramidal hyaline cartilages (except the vocal process and apex, which are elastic cartilage) articulating with the cricoid lamina; has a vocal process anteriorly (attaches vocal ligament) and a muscular process laterally (attaches intrinsic muscles).

2. Corniculate Cartilages (of Santorini): Elastic fibrocartilage articulating with the apices of the arytenoids.

3. Cuneiform Cartilages (of Wrisberg): Rod-shaped elastic fibrocartilage embedded in the aryepiglottic folds anterior to the corniculate cartilages.

• (Clinical Note: Hyaline cartilages [Thyroid, Cricoid, body of Arytenoid] undergo ossification/calcification starting at age 20–25 years and can mimic a foreign body on X-ray; Elastic fibrocartilages [Epiglottis, Corniculate, Cuneiform, apex/vocal process of Arytenoid] never calcify).

• Cricothyroid Membrane & Its Surgical Importance:

• Extrinsic/intrinsic fibroelastic membrane connecting the upper border of the cricoid arch to the lower border of the thyroid cartilage; its central thickened part forms the cricothyroid ligament and its lateral parts extend upwards to form the conus elasticus (cricovocal membrane), whose free upper border is the vocal ligament.

• Surgical Importance:

1. Site for Emergency Cricothyrotomy (Laryngotomy / Mini-tracheostomy) and Transtracheal Jet Ventilation in acute upper airway obstruction (since most laryngeal foreign bodies/lesions impact at or above the vocal cords, and the membrane is superficial and avascular).

2. Route for percutaneous EMG-guided Botulinum toxin injection into the thyroarytenoid muscle in spasmodic dysphonia.

3. Pathway for extralaryngeal spread of subglottic and anterior commissure laryngeal carcinomas to the prelaryngeal (Delphian) lymph node.

• Cavity and Spaces of the Larynx:

• Ventricle of the Larynx (Sinus of Morgagni): Deep elliptical recess between the false vocal cords (vestibular folds) above and the true vocal cords below. From its anterior part arises a blind diverticulum lined by mucus glands called the Saccule of the larynx (which lubricates the vocal cords—"oil-can of the larynx"; abnormal air-filled dilatation of the saccule forms a Laryngocele).

• Rima Glottidis (Glottis): Elongated anteroposterior slit between the true vocal cords anteriorly and the vocal processes/bases of the arytenoid cartilages posteriorly (narrowest part of the adult larynx; ~24 mm in males, ~16 mm in females). Divided into anterior 2/3rd (intermembranous / phonatory glottis) and posterior 1/3rd (intercartilaginous / respiratory glottis).

• Reinke’s Space: Potential subepithelial space representing the superficial layer of the lamina propria of the true vocal cord, bounded superiorly and inferiorly by the arcuate lines (junction of squamous and respiratory epithelium), anteriorly by the anterior commissure (Broyles’ ligament), and posteriorly by the vocal process of the arytenoid. It is rich in loose areolar tissue and devoid of lymphatics (hence early glottic T1 cancer does not metastasize to lymph nodes; fluid accumulation here causes Reinke’s oedema).

2. Differences Between Infant and Adult Larynx & Functions of Larynx

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-004]]

• Functions of the Larynx:

1. Protection of Lower Airways (Phylogenetically oldest & most vital function): Achieved by (a) Three-tier sphincteric closure during swallowing (laryngeal inlet/aryepiglottic folds, false vocal cords, and true vocal cords), (b) Reflex cessation of respiration (mediated via CN IX), and (c) Cough reflex ("Watch-dog of the lungs").

2. Respiration: Regulates airflow; vocal cords abduct during inspiration and adduct slightly during expiration.

3. Phonation: Aerodynamic-myoelastic voice production (adducted vocal cords are set into vibration by subglottic expiratory air pressure, releasing puffs of air that generate the fundamental laryngeal tone).

4. Fixation of the Chest: Closure of the glottis fixes the thoracic cage, providing a fulcrum for pectoral/abdominal muscles during heavy lifting, climbing, coughing, defaecation, micturition, and childbirth.

• Laryngeal Crepitus (Boccca’s Sign): A normal grating sensation felt when the larynx (thyroid cartilage) is grasped between the thumb and fingers and moved from side to side over the prevertebral fascia and cervical spine. Absence of laryngeal crepitus indicates a space-occupying lesion behind the larynx, classically Postcricoid Carcinoma or retropharyngeal abscess/oedema.

subject: ent
title: 41. INFLAMMATIONS OF LARYNX
text:
1. Acute Epiglottitis vs. Acute Laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup)

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-005]]

2. Tuberculosis of the Larynx

• Aetiology & Pathology: Almost always secondary to open cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis via bronchogenic spread (infected sputum settles in the posterior larynx) or haematogenous/lymphatic spread. Affects males in the middle age group.

• Sites Affected (Posterior Larynx Predominates): (1) Interarytenoid region (most common), (2) Ventricular bands (false cords), (3) True vocal cords, and (4) Epiglottis.

• Clinical Features:

• Symptoms: Weakness of voice (phonasthenia) progressing to hoarseness, severe excruciating pain in the throat radiating to the ears, marked odynophagia (painful swallowing), cough with expectoration, haemoptysis, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature.

• Cardinal Laryngeal Signs:

1. Unilateral congestion of the vocal cord (especially posterior part) with impaired adduction (earliest sign).

2. Mamillated / heaped-up swelling or granulations in the interarytenoid region.

3. "Mouse-nibbled" appearance of the vocal cords (multiple superficial ragged ulcerations along the free margins).

4. "Turban Epiglottis" (marked pseudo-oedema and cellular infiltration of the epiglottis).

5. Swollen arytenoids (pear-shaped) and aryepiglottic folds against a background of marked pallor of the surrounding pharyngeal mucosa.

• Diagnosis: Sputum for AFB and CBNAAT (GeneXpert), Chest X-ray, and Direct Laryngoscopy & Biopsy (mandatory to rule out co-existing or mimicking laryngeal carcinoma).

• Treatment: Standard Antitubercular Therapy (ATT) (2HRZE + 4HRE), strict voice rest, and analgesics/superior laryngeal nerve block for severe odynophagia.

subject: ent
title: 42. CONGENITAL LESIONS OF LARYNX AND STRIDOR
text:
1. Stridor: Definition, Classification, and Causes

• Definition: Stridor is an abnormal, high-pitched, musical respiratory sound produced by turbulent airflow through a narrowed or partially obstructed larynx or extrathoracic/intrathoracic tracheobronchial tree. (Differentiation: Stertor is a low-pitched, guttural snoring/snorting sound originating from partial obstruction in the nasopharynx or oropharynx, e.g., adenotonsillar hypertrophy or tongue fallback).

• Classification of Stridor (By Phase of Respiration & Site of Obstruction):

1. Inspiratory Stridor: Indicates obstruction at the Supraglottic larynx or Pharynx (e.g., Laryngomalacia, Acute epiglottitis, Retropharyngeal abscess).

2. Biphasic Stridor (Both Inspiratory & Expiratory): Indicates obstruction at the Glottis, Subglottis, or Cervical Trachea (e.g., Laryngeal web, Bilateral vocal cord paralysis, Subglottic stenosis/haemangioma, Acute laryngotracheobronchitis, Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis).

3. Expiratory Stridor (Wheeze): Indicates obstruction in the Intrathoracic Trachea or Bronchi (e.g., Bronchial foreign body, Vascular ring).

• Causes of Stridor:

• In Infants and Children (Mnemonic: CONGENITAL / ACQUIRED):

1. Congenital: Laryngomalacia (most common congenital cause), Congenital vocal cord paralysis (2nd most common), Congenital subglottic stenosis, Laryngeal web, Subglottic haemangioma, Laryngeal cyst/laryngocele, Vascular rings (double aortic arch, anomalous innominate artery), Bilateral choanal atresia, Pierre-Robin sequence.

2. Inflammatory: Acute laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup—most common acute cause), Acute epiglottitis, Laryngeal diphtheria, Acute retropharyngeal abscess.

3. Traumatic: Foreign body aspiration (sudden onset stridor in a playing child), Post-intubation subglottic oedema/stenosis, Thermal/corrosive burns.

4. Neoplastic: Juvenile recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.

5. Miscellaneous: Laryngismus stridulus (hypocalcaemic tetany/rickets).

• In Adults (e.g., 50–65-year-old smoker with hoarseness and stridor):

1. Neoplastic: Carcinoma of the Larynx (Glottic/Subglottic/Transglottic—most common in adult smokers), Carcinoma of the hypopharynx/thyroid/trachea, Large laryngeal polyp/papilloma.

2. Neurogenic: Bilateral abductor vocal cord paralysis (post-thyroidectomy, malignancy).

3. Inflammatory: Ludwig’s angina, Parapharyngeal/Retropharyngeal abscess, Adult acute epiglottitis, Tuberculous/Syphilitic laryngitis, Angioneurotic oedema.

4. Traumatic: Laryngotracheal trauma/stenosis, Foreign body (bolus obstruction).

• Evaluation & Management of Stridor:

• History: Age of onset (at birth → web/vocal cord palsy; 2 weeks → laryngomalacia; 2–3 months → subglottic haemangioma), mode of onset (sudden choking → foreign body), relation to position and feeding, quality of cry/voice.

• Investigations: Pulse oximetry, Flexible Fibreoptic Laryngoscopy (awake, dynamic evaluation), X-ray soft tissue neck (AP & Lateral) and Chest X-ray (inspiratory & expiratory views), CT/MRI Neck and Chest, and Direct Laryngoscopy & Rigid Bronchoscopy under GA.

• Management: Humidified oxygen, nebulized adrenaline and IV steroids, Emergency Airway Securement (Tracheostomy—immediate surgical management of choice for a 65-year-old male with proliferative laryngeal carcinoma presenting in stridor; or endotracheal intubation/cricothyrotomy), followed by definitive treatment of the underlying cause.

2. Laryngomalacia, Congenital Subglottic Stenosis, and Laryngeal Web

• Laryngomalacia (Congenital Laryngeal Stridor):

• Most common congenital anomaly of the larynx (60–75%) and the commonest cause of stridor in infancy.

• Pathogenesis: Excessive flaccidity and neuromuscular immaturity of the supraglottic laryngeal cartilages, which get sucked inwards during inspiration.

• Clinical Features: Intermittent, low-pitched, inspiratory stridor appearing within the first 2 weeks of life. Stridor worsens on crying, feeding, or lying supine, and improves/disappears when the infant is placed in the prone position. The child's cry is completely normal, and cyanosis is rare. Self-limiting; spontaneously resolves by 18–24 months of age.

• Diagnosis (Flexible Fibreoptic Laryngoscopy in an awake infant):

1. Elongated epiglottis curled longitudinally upon itself ("Omega-shaped epiglottis" [Omega]).

2. Floppy, tall, foreshortened aryepiglottic folds sucked into the glottis on inspiration.

3. Prominent, redundant mucosa over the arytenoids prolapsing anteriorly.

• Treatment: 90% require only conservative management (reassurance, upright feeding, anti-reflux therapy). In severe cases (failure to thrive, cyanotic spells, cor pulmonale—10%), Endoscopic Supraglottoplasty (Aryepiglottoplasty) using CO_2 laser or cold microscissors is performed.

• Congenital Subglottic Stenosis: Narrowing of the subglottic lumen (diameter <4.0 mm in a full-term neonate or <3.0 mm in a premature neonate) due to a thickened/elliptical cricoid cartilage or submucosal fibrosis. Presents with recurrent croup-like biphasic stridor with a normal cry. Mild cases (Cotton-Myer Grade I & II) are managed conservatively or with endoscopic balloon dilatation; severe cases (Grade III & IV) require tracheostomy followed by Laryngotracheoplasty (Anterior/Posterior cricoid split with costal cartilage graft) or Cricotracheal resection.

• Laryngeal Web: Persistence of an epithelial/fibrous web across the anterior part of the glottis with a concave posterior free margin (75% glottic) due to incomplete recanalization of the embryonic larynx. Presents at birth with a weak/absent cry (aphonia) and biphasic stridor. Treatment: Thin webs are incised endoscopically with a CO_2 laser; thick webs require excision via laryngofissure and placement of a McNaught tantalum/Silastic keel between the thyroid alae for 4–6 weeks to prevent reformation of anterior commissure adhesions.

subject: ent
title: 43. LARYNGEAL PARALYSIS
text:
1. Nerve Supply of Larynx and Theories of Vocal Cord Position

• Nerve Supply of Larynx (Branches of Vagus Nerve [CN X]):

• Motor:

• Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve (RLN) supplies ALL intrinsic muscles of the larynx EXCEPT the cricothyroid muscle (Note: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the ONLY abductor of the vocal cords; Lateral cricoarytenoid, Thyroarytenoid, and Interarytenoid are adductors; Interarytenoid receives bilateral innervation).

• External Laryngeal Nerve (branch of Superior Laryngeal Nerve) supplies the Cricothyroid muscle (tensor and adductor of the vocal cord).

• Sensory:

• Above the vocal cords: Internal Laryngeal Nerve (branch of Superior Laryngeal Nerve, piercing the thyrohyoid membrane).

• Below the vocal cords: Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve.

• Positions of the Vocal Cord from the Midline:

• Median: 0 mm (Midline—normal phonation / RLN palsy).

• Paramedian: 1.5 mm (Strong whisper / RLN palsy).

• Intermediate (Cadaveric): 3.5 mm (Neutral position—combined RLN + SLN palsy).

• Gentle Abduction: 7.0 mm (Quiet respiration).

• Full Abduction: 9.5 mm (Deep inspiration).

• Theories Explaining Median/Paramedian Position in RLN Palsy:

1. Semon’s Law: In all progressive organic lesions of the motor nerves of the larynx, the abductor fibres (which are phylogenetically newer and metabolically more vulnerable) are paralysed earlier and recover later than the adductor fibres; hence the vocal cord is pulled into the median/paramedian position by the unopposed adductors.

2. Wagner and Grossman Theory (Currently Accepted): In pure recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis, all intrinsic muscles are paralysed, but the cricothyroid muscle (supplied by the intact superior laryngeal nerve) remains functional and keeps the vocal cord adducted and tense in the paramedian position. In high vagal (combined) lesions, the cricothyroid is also paralysed, so the cord falls laterally into the cadaveric (intermediate) position.

2. Causes of Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve (RLN) Paralysis

• Why Left RLN Palsy is More Common than Right (2:1): The left RLN arises from the vagus in the thorax, hooks around the arch of the aorta distal to the ligamentum arteriosum, and ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove, giving it a much longer intrathoracic and cervical course than the right RLN (which hooks around the first part of the right subclavian artery in the root of the neck).

• Causes of Left vs. Right RLN Palsy:

• Cervical Causes (Common to Left, Right, and Bilateral):

1. Thyroid Surgery (most common iatrogenic cause) and Malignant Thyroid Tumours.

2. Carcinoma of the Cervical Oesophagus or Hypopharynx.

3. Metastatic Cervical Lymphadenopathy.

4. Penetrating or blunt neck trauma and cervical spine surgery.

• Intrathoracic / Mediastinal Causes (Specific to Left RLN):

1. Bronchogenic Carcinoma (Left upper lobe)—most common neoplastic cause.

2. Carcinoma of the Thoracic Oesophagus.

3. Mediastinal Lymphadenopathy (metastatic, lymphoma, tuberculosis).

4. Aneurysm of the Arch of Aorta.

5. Ortner’s Syndrome (Cardiovocal Syndrome): Compression of the left RLN by an enlarged left atrium (mitral stenosis) or dilated pulmonary artery.

6. Intrathoracic / Cardiothoracic surgery (PDA ligation, pneumonectomy).

• Causes Specific to Right RLN: Aneurysm of the right subclavian artery, Carcinoma of the apex of the right lung (Pancoast tumour), and Tuberculosis of the right apical/cervical pleura.

• Idiopathic / Viral Neuritis (~20–30%).

3. Clinical Features and Management of Vocal Cord Paralysis

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-006]]

(Note: Unilateral Superior Laryngeal Nerve Palsy causes paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle and ipsilateral supraglottic anaesthesia; features include loss of high-pitched singing voice, vocal fatigue, wavy slack cord, and askew position of the glottis with the posterior commissure pointing towards the paralysed side).

subject: ent
title: 44. BENIGN LARYNGEAL TUMOURS AND LESIONS
text:
1. Non-Neoplastic Benign Lesions of the Larynx

1. Vocal Nodules (Singer’s or Screamer’s Nodes):

• Aetiopathogenesis: Caused by chronic vocal abuse or misuse (speaking at unnatural low pitches or shouting at high intensities in teachers, singers, hawkers, and talkative children). Maximum amplitude of cord vibration and mechanical shearing trauma occurs at the junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds of the free edge of the true vocal cords (midpoint of the membranous cord). Trauma causes subepithelial oedema and haemorrhage in Reinke’s space (early soft reddish nodules), which later undergoes hyalinization, fibrosis, and overlying epithelial hyperplasia (late hard whitish nodules).

• Clinical Features: Hoarseness, vocal fatigue, breathiness, and neck pain on prolonged talking. Indirect/rigid laryngoscopy shows bilateral, symmetrical, pinpoint to pea-sized nodules strictly at the junction of the anterior 1/3rd and posterior 2/3rd of the vocal cords.

• Treatment:

• Early/Soft Nodules & All Children: Voice rest and Intensive Speech Therapy (vocal hygiene and re-education—curative in most cases).

• Large, Fibrotic, Long-standing Nodules in Adults: Microlaryngeal surgical excision (using cold microinstruments or CO_2 laser, preserving the underlying vocal ligament) followed by mandatory postoperative speech therapy to prevent recurrence.

2. Vocal Cord Polyp:

• Aetiology: Caused by sudden vocal trauma (single episode of shouting) combined with smoking, allergy, or reflux, leading to submucosal capillary rupture, haemorrhage, and oedema in Reinke’s space. Commonly affects men aged 30–50 years.

• Clinical Features: Hoarseness, diplophonia (double voice), and intermittent choking/stridor if large and pedunculated. Laryngoscopy shows a unilateral, solitary, soft, smooth, sessile or pedunculated reddish/translucent mass arising from the junction of the anterior 1/3rd and posterior 2/3rd of the vocal cord.

• Treatment: Microlaryngeal excision (microflap technique or CO_2 laser) + cessation of smoking and speech therapy.

3. Reinke’s Oedema (Bilateral Diffuse Polyposis):

• Aetiology: Bilateral symmetrical collection of gelatinous fluid in the subepithelial Reinke’s space along the entire length of the membranous vocal cords. Caused by heavy chronic cigarette smoking, vocal abuse, hypothyroidism (myxoedema), and Laryngopharyngeal Reflux (LPR).

• Clinical Features: Middle-aged men and women presenting with a low-pitched, rough, gruff masculine voice (often using false cords for phonation). Laryngoscopy shows bilateral, diffuse, pale/translucent, fusiform "baggy" swellings of the membranous vocal cords.

• Treatment: Cessation of smoking, antireflux/thyroid therapy, speech therapy, and Microlaryngeal Surgery (Microflap technique): making a longitudinal incision on the superior surface of the cord, sucking out the gelatinous fluid, trimming redundant mucosa while preserving the medial free vibrating edge, and redraping the flap (done in stages or avoiding the anterior commissure to prevent glottic web formation).

4. Laryngocele:

• Definition & Aetiology: An abnormal air-filled cystic dilatation of the laryngeal saccule communicating with the laryngeal lumen. Caused by chronically raised transglottic intralaryngeal air pressure in trumpet players, glass-blowers, weight-lifters, or chronic coughers. (Warning: In an adult, a laryngocele may be secondary to an occult carcinoma of the laryngeal ventricle obstructing the saccule neck).

• Classification (3 Types):

1. Internal Laryngocele: Confined entirely within the larynx (medial to the thyroid cartilage); presents as a smooth submucosal swelling of the false cord and aryepiglottic fold.

2. External Laryngocele: Distended saccule herniates through the thyrohyoid membrane (at the point where the superior laryngeal nerve and vessels pierce it) and presents as a compressible neck swelling.

3. Combined (Mixed) Laryngocele: Has both internal and external components connected by an isthmus across the thyrohyoid membrane.

• Clinical Features: Hoarseness, cough, airway obstruction, and a soft, reducible swelling in the lateral neck at the level of the thyrohyoid membrane that expands on coughing or Valsalva manoeuvre and empties on compression with a gurgling sound (Bryce’s Sign).

• Investigations: Indirect/flexible laryngoscopy, X-ray soft tissue neck (AP & Lateral views during Valsalva), and CT Scan of Neck.

• Treatment: Surgical excision via an external lateral cervical approach (transthyrohyoid) for external/combined laryngoceles, or endoscopic CO_2 laser marsupialization for purely internal laryngoceles. Always perform direct laryngoscopy to rule out ventricular carcinoma.

5. Sulcus Vocalis: A longitudinal groove or invagination along the medial free vibrating edge of the true vocal cord where the epithelium is tethered directly to the deep vocal ligament (obliterating Reinke’s space), congenital or post-inflammatory. Causes a high-pitched, breathy, hoarse voice and incomplete glottic closure (spindle-shaped gap on stroboscopy). Treated by voice therapy, microsurgical excision of the sulcus, or fat/collagen/fascia augmentation into Reinke’s space.

2. Juvenile Laryngeal Papillomatosis (Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis - RRP)

• Aetiopathogenesis: Most common benign neoplasm of the larynx in children (3–5 years). Caused by Human Papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11 (double-stranded DNA virus), transmitted vertically from a mother with maternal vaginal condyloma acuminata during vaginal delivery. Viral DNA resides latently in the basal cells of normal-looking respiratory mucosa, accounting for relentless recurrence.

• Clinical Features:

• Triad: Progressive hoarseness / aphonia, croupy cough, and biphasic stridor / respiratory distress.

• Signs: Multiple, pinkish-white, friable, warty/mulberry-like clusters of papillomas involving the true and false vocal cords, anterior commissure, epiglottis, and subglottis (may seed distally into the trachea and bronchi, especially if tracheostomy is performed).

• Management:

1. Endoscopic Surgical Debulking (Mainstay): Repeated Microlaryngoscopic ablation using a CO_2 Laser, KTP Laser, or Powered Laryngeal Microdebrider, carefully preserving the vocal ligament and anterior commissure (to prevent glottic webbing and stenosis). Avoid tracheostomy unless life-threatening, as it promotes distal tracheobronchial seeding.

2. Adjuvant Medical Therapy (for aggressive/frequently recurring disease): Intralesional Cidofovir or Bevacizumab (Avastin), systemic Interferon alfa-2a, Indole-3-carbinol, and Quadrivalent/Nonavalent HPV Vaccination (Gardasil). (Radiotherapy is strictly contraindicated as it induces malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma).

subject: ent
title: 45. CARCINOMA LARYNX
text:
1. Clinical Vignette, Aetiology, Classification, and Clinical Features

• Clinical Vignette Diagnosis: 55-year-old male smoker and alcoholic presenting with hoarseness for 3 months followed by stridor → Carcinoma of the Larynx (Glottic / Transglottic Carcinoma).

• Aetiology & Premalignant Conditions:

• Risk Factors: Cigarette/Bidi Smoking (benzopyrene) and Alcohol (synergistic 15-fold increased risk), Laryngopharyngeal reflux, HPV, occupational exposure (asbestos, mustard gas, wood dust, petroleum), and prior neck irradiation.

• Premalignant Conditions of Larynx: Laryngeal Leukoplakia / Keratosis, Erythroplakia, Chronic hyperplastic laryngitis, and Adult/irradiated laryngeal papilloma.

• Histopathology: 90–95% are Squamous Cell Carcinomas (Glottic lesions are usually well-differentiated; Supraglottic lesions are often poorly differentiated/anaplastic).

Comparison of Supraglottic, Glottic, and Subglottic Carcinoma

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-007]]

• Causes of Vocal Cord Fixation (T3 Stage): (1) Infiltration of the thyroarytenoid (vocalis) muscle, (2) Invasion of the paraglottic space, (3) Invasion of the cricoarytenoid joint, or (4) Involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

2. TNM Staging of Glottic Carcinoma (AJCC)

• T_1: Tumour limited to vocal cord(s) (may involve anterior/posterior commissure) with normal vocal cord mobility (T_1a: one cord; T_1b: both cords).

• T_2: Tumour extends to supraglottis and/or subglottis, AND/OR with impaired vocal cord mobility.

• T_3: Tumour limited to the larynx with vocal cord fixation, AND/OR invades the paraglottic space or pre-epiglottic space, and/or inner cortex of thyroid cartilage.

• T_4a: Moderately advanced; tumour invades through the outer cortex of the thyroid cartilage and/or invades extralaryngeal tissues (trachea, strap muscles, thyroid gland, oesophagus).

• T_4b: Very advanced; invades prevertebral space, encases carotid artery, or invades mediastinal structures.

3. Investigations and Management

• Investigations:

1. Indirect Laryngoscopy & Flexible/Rigid Video-Laryngoscopy (with Stroboscopy): Evaluates site, morphology (exophytic vs. ulcerative), hidden areas, and vocal cord mobility.

2. Neck Examination: Palpation for laryngeal widening, tenderness (perichondritis), loss of laryngeal crepitus, and cervical lymph nodes.

3. CECT Scan of Neck & Chest (1–2 mm cuts): Evaluates pre-epiglottic and paraglottic space invasion, thyroid/cricoid cartilage destruction, subglottic extension, and nodal staging.

4. Direct Laryngoscopy & Microlaryngoscopy under GA with Biopsy: Examines hidden areas (infrahyoid epiglottis, anterior commissure, laryngeal ventricle, subglottis, and apex of pyriform sinus) and obtains tissue for histopathological diagnosis (Supravital staining with Toluidine Blue highlights carcinoma in situ).

• Treatment Options by Stage:

1. Immediate Airway Securement (If presenting in Stridor): Emergency Tracheostomy (high tracheostomy is permissible if total laryngectomy is planned).

2. Early Stage (T_1 and T_2, N_0 — Voice/Organ-Preserving Modalities, >85–90% cure):

• Definitive External Beam Radiotherapy (66–70 Gy; preserves normal voice quality), OR

• Transoral Endoscopic CO_2 Laser Microsurgery (TLM) (for T_1 mobile cordal lesions), OR

• Conservation Open Partial Laryngectomy: Laryngofissure with Cordectomy, Vertical Partial (Frontolateral) Laryngectomy (for anterior commissure/impaired mobility), or Supraglottic Horizontal Partial Laryngectomy (for T_1/T_2 supraglottic tumours with mobile cords and good pulmonary function).

3. Advanced Stage (T_3 and T_4 or N^+ Disease):

• Organ-Preservation Protocol (For T_3 lesions without extensive cartilage destruction): Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) (Cisplatin + 70 Gy RT), reserving total laryngectomy for salvage.

• Total Laryngectomy + Neck Dissection + Postoperative Radiotherapy: Treatment of choice for all T_4a lesions (cartilage invasion/extralaryngeal spread), T_3 lesions with poor laryngeal function/stridor, transglottic/subglottic cancers, and radiation failures (Salvage Laryngectomy).

• Vocal Rehabilitation After Total Laryngectomy:

1. Tracheo-Oesophageal Speech (Gold Standard): Creation of a tracheo-oesophageal puncture (primary or secondary) and insertion of a one-way silicone Voice Prosthesis (Blom-Singer or Provox valve); occluding the stoma shunts pulmonary air into the pharyngo-oesophageal segment to produce fluent speech.

2. Oesophageal Speech: Swallowing air into the upper oesophagus and eructating it to vibrate the pharyngo-oesophageal segment (speaks 6–10 words/breath; hands-free).

3. Artificial Larynx (Electrolarynx): Battery-operated vibrating device held against the neck skin.

subject: ent
title: 46. VOICE AND SPEECH DISORDERS
text:
• Rhinolalia Clausa (Hyponasality): Lack of nasal resonance for nasal consonants (M, N, NG sound like B, D, G) due to blockage of the nasal cavity or nasopharynx. Causes: Common cold, allergic rhinitis, nasal polyposis, DNS, adenoid hypertrophy, choanal atresia, nasopharyngeal angiofibroma/carcinoma.

• Rhinolalia Aperta (Hypernasality): Excessive nasal resonance for non-nasal oral consonants due to velopharyngeal insufficiency (failure of the soft palate to seal off the nasopharynx from the oropharynx) or an abnormal communication. Causes: Cleft palate, submucous cleft palate, congenitally short palate, palatal paralysis (diphtheria, bulbar palsy, post-CVA), post-adenoidectomy, oronasal fistula.

• Puberphonia (Mutational Falsetto Voice): Persistence of a high-pitched childhood voice in adolescent/adult males whose physical and laryngeal development is otherwise normal; psychological in origin (emotional immaturity/maternal over-fixation).

• Diagnosis & Treatment: Gutzmann’s Pressure Test: Pressing the thyroid prominence backwards and downwards relaxes the overstretched vocal cords and immediately produces a normal low-pitched masculine voice. Treated by Speech Therapy using Gutzmann’s manoeuvre and Isshiki Type III Thyroplasty (relaxation/shortening thyroplasty) in refractory cases.

• Functional (Hysterical) Aphonia: Sudden loss of voice in emotionally labile young females; patient communicates in a whisper. Laryngoscopy shows vocal cords in the abducted position that fail to adduct on phonation, but adduct normally on coughing (sound of cough is normal and loud). Treated by reassurance, speech therapy, and psychotherapy.

• Dysphonia Plica Ventricularis (Ventricular Dysphonia): Phonation produced by the false vocal cords (ventricular folds) usurping the function of the true cords, resulting in a rough, low-pitched, unpleasant voice. May be secondary (compensatory to true cord paralysis, fixation, or excision) or functional/psychogenic (due to hyperkinetic vocal strain). Treated by voice therapy.

subject: ent
title: 47. FOREIGN BODIES OF AIR PASSAGES
text:
• Aetiology & Site of Lodgement:

• Most common in children <4 years of age; Peanut / Groundnut is the most common vegetable foreign body.

• Right Main Bronchus is the most common site of bronchial lodgement because it is (1) wider, (2) more vertical (more in line with the tracheal lumen, at a 25^circ angle vs. 45^circ on the left), and (3) the carina is situated slightly to the left of the midline.

• Vegetal Bronchitis: Vegetable foreign bodies (peanuts, seeds, beans) contain free fatty acids that trigger a violent chemical mucosal inflammation (vegetal bronchitis) and absorb water to swell up rapidly, converting partial obstruction into total obstruction.

• Clinical Features (Three Clinical Stages):

1. First Stage (Initial Period of Impact): Sudden violent paroxysms of choking, gagging, coughing, wheezing, and cyanosis while eating or playing.

2. Second Stage (Symptomless Interval): Mucosa adapts and cough reflexes fatigue; lasts hours to weeks (often leads to delayed/missed diagnosis).

3. Third Stage (Stage of Complications / Site-Specific Symptoms):

• Laryngeal Foreign Body: Large FB causes complete obstruction, aphonia, cyanosis, and sudden death ("Cafe coronary"). Partially obstructing FB causes hoarseness, croupy cough, aphonia, odynophagia, dyspnoea, and biphasic/inspiratory stridor.

• Tracheal Foreign Body: Sharp FB causes cough and haemoptysis. A loose tracheal FB moving up and down between the carina and subglottis produces a pathognomonic Triad: (1) Asthmatoid wheeze (heard best at the patient's open mouth), (2) Audible slap (heard as the FB strikes the subglottis during cough/expiration), and (3) Palpatory thud (felt by a finger placed over the cricoid/trachea).

• Bronchial Foreign Body: Classic clinical Triad: (1) Persistent cough, (2) Wheezing, and (3) Unilateral diminished or absent air entry on chest auscultation.

• Four Mechanisms of Bronchial Obstruction & Sequelae:

1. Partial (Bypass-valve) Obstruction: Air passes both in and out → causes wheeze only.

2. One-Way Check-Valve (Ball-valve) Obstruction: Bronchus dilates during inspiration allowing air in, and narrows during expiration trapping air distally → causes Obstructive Emphysema (hyperinflated lung, mediastinal shift to opposite side, and risk of pneumothorax).

3. Complete (Stop-valve) Obstruction: Air can neither enter nor exit; distal air is absorbed → causes Obstructive Atelectasis (Collapse) (mediastinal shift to same side).

4. Drowned Lung, Pneumonitis, Bronchiectasis, and Lung Abscess (late complications).

• Investigations:

• X-ray Neck (AP & Lateral) and Chest X-ray (Inspiratory & Expiratory PA and Lateral views): Identifies radio-opaque FBs (Note: A flat coin in the trachea lies in the sagittal plane—seen edge-on in AP view and flat in lateral view, aligned with the vocal cords). For radiolucent vegetable FBs, expiratory chest X-ray or fluoroscopy shows air-trapping (obstructive emphysema) or atelectasis. Virtual Bronchoscopy (Spiral CT) if diagnosis is doubtful.

• Management:

1. Immediate First Aid for Complete Laryngeal Choking:

• In Adults and Children >1 year: Heimlich Manoeuvre (Abdominal Thrusts)—stand behind the patient, wrap arms around the upper abdomen, place a clenched fist in the epigastrium below the xiphisternum, and give rapid upward and backward thrusts to force residual pulmonary air out and expel the foreign body.

• In Infants <1 year: 5 Back Blows (with infant prone and head-down over the forearm) alternating with 5 Chest Thrusts (Never perform blind finger sweeps or abdominal thrusts in infants due to risk of liver rupture).

• If Heimlich manoeuvre fails: Emergency Cricothyrotomy / Needle Cricothyroidotomy or Tracheostomy.

2. Definitive Management: Removal via Rigid Ventilating Bronchoscopy under General Anaesthesia using optical peanut/alligator forceps (Dormia basket or Fogarty balloon catheter for smooth spherical objects).

subject: ent
title: 48. LARYNGOTRACHEAL TRAUMA
text:
• Aetiology: Blunt neck trauma (automobile dashboard/steering wheel injury, clothesline injury, strangulation, karate blow) or Penetrating trauma (knife, gunshot). Ossified cartilages in adults (>40 years) fracture easily; paediatric cartilages are resilient.

• Pathology: Supraglottic/subglottic haematoma and mucosal oedema, mucosal tears (causing subcutaneous surgical emphysema), dislocation of cricoarytenoid or cricothyroid joints (causing RLN injury), fractures of the hyoid bone, thyroid cartilage (vertical/transverse), or cricoid cartilage, and laryngotracheal separation (avulsion of trachea from cricoid with retracting distal stump and bilateral RLN palsy).

• Clinical Features:

• Symptoms: Stridor/respiratory distress, hoarseness or aphonia, haemoptysis, odynophagia, and neck pain.

• Signs (Beck’s Triad of Laryngeal Fracture): (1) Subcutaneous surgical emphysema (crepitus in neck), (2) Loss of normal thyroid prominence (flattening of anterior neck contour), and (3) Palpable fracture displacement or bony/cartilaginous crepitus.

• Investigations: Flexible Fibreoptic Laryngoscopy (assesses airway, vocal cord mobility, haematoma, exposed cartilage), High-Resolution CT Scan of Larynx/Neck with 3D Reconstruction (investigation of choice), X-ray cervical spine (to rule out C-spine fracture), and Gastrografin swallow (to rule out oesophageal tear).

• Management:

1. Airway Securement: Awake Tracheostomy under local anaesthesia is the safest method in moderate-to-severe laryngeal trauma (blind endotracheal intubation is hazardous as it can create false passages or precipitate complete laryngotracheal separation).

2. Conservative Management (For minor trauma with intact mucosa, no displaced fractures, and stable airway): Hospitalization, voice rest, humidified oxygen, head-end elevation, IV Corticosteroids (reduces oedema), IV Antibiotics (prevents perichondritis), and anti-reflux therapy.

3. Open Surgical Exploration & Repair (Ideally within 24 hours to 3–5 days): Indicated for displaced cartilage fractures, exposed cartilage, large mucosal lacerations, vocal cord avulsion/immobility, or laryngotracheal separation. Performed via a transverse neck incision (or laryngofissure): mucosal tears are sutured with absorbable sutures, anterior commissure is reconstituted, displaced thyroid/cricoid fractures are reduced and fixed with titanium miniplates or wires, and an internal laryngeal stent (Montgomery laryngeal stent or Silastic keel) is placed for 2–6 weeks to prevent laryngeal stenosis.

subject: ent
title: 49. OESOPHAGUS AND DYSPHAGIA
text:
1. Anatomical Constrictions of Oesophagus & Physiology of Deglutition (Swallowing)

• Anatomical Constrictions of the Oesophagus (Distances from Upper Incisor Teeth in Adults):

1. First Constriction (Pharyngo-oesophageal junction / Cricopharyngeal sphincter): At the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (C6 vertebra) — 15 cm from upper incisors (Narrowest part of the entire GI tract apart from the appendix; commonest site of foreign body impaction and iatrogenic perforation).

2. Second Constriction (Aortic arch crossing): At T4 vertebra — 22.5–25 cm from upper incisors.

3. Third Constriction (Left main bronchus crossing): At T5 vertebra — 25–27.5 cm from upper incisors.

4. Fourth Constriction (Diaphragmatic hiatus / Lower oesophageal sphincter): At T10 vertebra — 40 cm from upper incisors.

Physiology of Deglutition (Three Phases)

1. Oral (Buccal) Phase (Voluntary): Food is masticated, lubricated with saliva, formed into a bolus on the dorsum of the tongue, and propelled posteriorly into the oropharynx by upward and backward elevation of the tongue against the hard palate.

2. Pharyngeal Phase (Involuntary Reflex—mediated via CN IX and X to the swallowing centre in the medulla): Once the bolus touches the faucial pillars/posterior pharyngeal wall, four coordinated events occur simultaneously:

• Closure of Nasopharynx: Soft palate elevates against Passavant’s ridge on the posterior pharyngeal wall (prevents nasal regurgitation).

• Closure of Oropharyngeal Isthmus: Tongue presses against palate and palatoglossal arches contract (prevents oral reflux).

• Protection/Closure of Larynx: Temporary apnoea, elevation of the larynx under the base of the tongue, retroflexion of the epiglottis, and three-tier sphincteric closure (aryepiglottic folds, false cords, and true vocal cords).

• Pharyngeal Propulsion & Upper Oesophageal Sphincter (UOS) Relaxation: Sequential peristaltic contraction of pharyngeal constrictors coincides with reflex relaxation of the cricopharyngeal sphincter, propelling the bolus into the oesophagus.

3. Oesophageal Phase (Involuntary): Cricopharyngeal sphincter closes; primary and secondary peristaltic waves propel the bolus down the oesophagus while the Lower Oesophageal Sphincter (LOS) relaxes ahead of the wave to allow entry into the stomach.

2. Causes, Investigations, and Management of Dysphagia

• Classification of Causes of Dysphagia:

1. Pre-oesophageal Causes (Oral and Pharyngeal Phases):

• Oral: Ulcerative stomatitis, Ludwig’s angina, carcinoma/paralysis of tongue, cleft palate, trismus, severe xerostomia.

• Pharyngeal: Acute tonsillitis, Quinsy, Retropharyngeal/Parapharyngeal abscess, Carcinoma of tonsil/base of tongue/pyriform sinus, Pharyngeal pouch (Zenker’s), Bulbar/pseudobulbar palsy, Myasthenia gravis.

2. Oesophageal Causes:

• In the Lumen: Foreign body, Benign stricture, Plummer-Vinson web, Schatzki’s ring.

• In the Wall:

• Organic: Carcinoma of the oesophagus, Acute/Reflux oesophagitis, Corrosive/ Benign strictures, Leiomyoma.

• Motility Disorders: Hypomotility (Achalasia cardia, Scleroderma) or Hypermotility (Diffuse oesophageal spasm, Nutcracker oesophagus, Cricopharyngeal spasm).

• Outside the Wall (Extrinsic Compression): Retrosternal/malignant goitre, Mediastinal lymphadenopathy/tumours, Cervical osteophytes (Forestier’s disease), Enlarged left atrium, Aortic aneurysm, Dysphagia Lusoria (compression of the oesophagus by an aberrant right subclavian artery arising from the left side of the aortic arch and passing behind the oesophagus).

• Diagnostic Clues & Investigations:

• History: Sudden onset (→ foreign body); Progressive dysphagia first to solids and then to liquids with weight loss (→ malignancy or stricture); Intermittent dysphagia more to liquids than solids (→ motility disorder / achalasia cardia); Feeling of a lump in the throat between meals that disappears on eating food without true dysphagia (→ Globus Pharyngeus [Globus Hystericus], often linked to LPR or anxiety).

• Investigations:

1. Complete oral, pharyngeal, indirect laryngoscopic, and neck examination + CBC and iron profile.

2. X-ray Soft Tissue Neck (Lateral view) & Chest X-ray.

3. Barium Swallow (Oesophagogram):

• Carcinoma oesophagus: Irregular mucosal filling defect with overhanging edges ("Apple-core" / "Rat-tail" appearance) without massive proximal dilatation.

• Achalasia cardia: Massively dilated, tortuous oesophagus (megaoesophagus) with a smooth, symmetrical conical narrowing at the lower end ("Bird-beak" / "Pencil-tip" appearance).

• Diffuse oesophageal spasm: "Corkscrew" or "Rosary-bead" oesophagus.

• Dysphagia lusoria: Oblique indentation on posterior oesophagus ("Bayonet sign").

4. Flexible Fibreoptic / Rigid Oesophagoscopy and Biopsy: Mandatory for direct visualization and tissue diagnosis.

5. Oesophageal Manometry (gold standard for motility disorders) and 24-hour Ambulatory pH Monitoring (gold standard for GERD).

3. Specific Oesophageal Disorders

• Plummer-Vinson Syndrome (Paterson-Brown-Kelly Syndrome):

• Components (Classic Pentad): (1) Chronic Iron-Deficiency (Hypochromic Microcytic) Anaemia, (2) Dysphagia due to a postcricoid oesophageal web (subepithelial fibrosis/atrophy at the cricopharyngeal junction), (3) Atrophic glossitis (bald, smooth red tongue), (4) Angular cheilitis / stomatitis, and (5) Koilonychia (spoon-shaped brittle nails). Associated with achlorhydria and splenomegaly.

• Clinical Importance: Predominantly affects middle-aged females (>40 years). It is a premalignant condition—10% develop Postcricoid Squamous Cell Carcinoma (or carcinoma of the oral cavity/oesophagus).

• Diagnosis: CBC & peripheral smear, low serum iron and ferritin, Barium swallow (shows a thin anterior shelf-like web in the postcricoid region on lateral view), and Oesophagoscopy.

• Treatment: (1) Oral/Parenteral Iron and Vitamin B-complex supplementation (corrects anaemia and often resolves early webs), (2) Endoscopic dilatation (bougienage) of the postcricoid web, and (3) Lifelong endoscopic surveillance for postcricoid malignancy.

• Achalasia Cardia: Degeneration of Auerbach’s myenteric plexus in the lower oesophagus causing (1) aperistalsis in the body of the oesophagus and (2) high resting pressure with failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS). Causes dysphagia (more to liquids than solids), nocturnal regurgitation, and weight loss; Bird-beak sign on barium swallow. Treatment: Laparoscopic Modified Heller’s Cardiomyotomy (with Dor/Toupet partial fundoplication), Pneumatic balloon dilatation, or Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM).

• Gastro-Oesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD), Laryngopharyngeal Reflux (LPR), and Barrett’s Oesophagus:

• GERD & LPR: Incompetence/transient relaxation of the LOS allows gastric acid and pepsin to reflux into the oesophagus (causing heartburn, regurgitation, oesophagitis, and peptic stricture) and up to the posterior larynx (LPR—causes chronic throat clearing, globus pharyngeus, hoarseness, posterior laryngitis/interarytenoid pachydermia, contact ulcers/granulomas on vocal processes, subglottic stenosis, and paroxysmal laryngospasm).

• Barrett’s Oesophagus: A premalignant condition caused by chronic GERD in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal oesophagus is replaced by specialized intestinal-type columnar metaplasia with goblet cells (30–40 times increased risk of Oesophageal Adenocarcinoma).

• Treatment of GERD/LPR: Lifestyle modifications (elevating head of bed by 6 inches, avoiding meals 3 hours before sleep, avoiding caffeine/alcohol/spicy/fatty foods, weight loss), Proton Pump Inhibitors (Omeprazole 20 mg / Pantoprazole 40 mg BD 30 mins before meals for 8–12 weeks), prokinetics (Domperidone/Itopride), and Laparoscopic Nissen’s 360^circ Fundoplication for refractory cases.

• Benign Strictures of Oesophagus: Caused by corrosive (alkali/acid) burns (most common in children/suicidal adults), reflux peptic oesophagitis, impacted foreign bodies, or post-surgical anastomosis. Presents with progressive dysphagia (solids → liquids). Diagnosed by barium swallow and oesophagoscopy. Treatment: Serial Prograde Endoscopic Dilatation (using Savary-Gilliard bougies over a guidewire or CRE balloon dilators), Gastrostomy with retrograde dilatation (Tucker’s bougies), or Surgical Oesophageal Replacement / Bypass (gastric pull-up or colonic interposition) for refractory long-segment strictures.
