title: 50 & 53. OPERATIVE SURGERY AND INSTRUMENTS
text:
1. Tympanoplasty and Myringoplasty

• Definitions:

• Tympanoplasty: An operation performed to (1) eradicate disease from the middle ear and (2) reconstruct the hearing mechanism, with or without tympanic membrane grafting and with or without mastoidectomy.

• Myringoplasty: An operation in which the reconstructive procedure is strictly limited to the repair of a perforation of the pars tensa of the tympanic membrane (assuming the ossicular chain is intact and mobile and the middle ear is disease-free).

• Wullstein’s Classification of Tympanoplasty (5 Types):

• Type I (Myringoplasty): Perforation of tympanic membrane with a normal, intact, and mobile ossicular chain. Graft is placed on the malleus/annulus.

• Type II: Perforation of tympanic membrane with erosion of the malleus. Graft is placed onto the incus or remnant of malleus.

• Type III (Myringostapediopexy / Columella Tympanoplasty): Malleus and incus are absent/necrosed, but stapes superstructure is intact and mobile. Graft is placed directly on the stapes head.

• Type IV (Cavum Minor / Round Window Baffle): Malleus, incus, and stapes superstructure are absent, but the stapes footplate is mobile. Footplate is left exposed to the exterior to receive sound waves directly, while a graft is placed between the oval and round windows to create an air-pocket (cavum minor) connecting the Eustachian tube to the round window (providing acoustic phase protection).

• Type V (Fenestration Operation): Stapes footplate is fixed (as in otosclerosis/tympanosclerosis), but the round window is functional. A new window (fenestra) is created in the horizontal semicircular canal and covered with a graft.

• Myringoplasty:

• Graft Materials: Temporalis fascia (most common autograft—low metabolic rate, similar thickness to TM), Tragal perichondrium, Tragal/conchal cartilage, vein, or periosteum.

• Techniques:

1. Underlay Technique (Most common): Margins of perforation are freshened (rimmed), tympanomeatal flap is elevated, middle ear is packed with antibiotic-soaked Gelfoam, and the fascia graft is placed medial to the tympanic membrane remnant/annulus and medial to the handle of malleus. (Advantage: No risk of burying squamous epithelium or blunting the anterior sulcus; Complication: Graft medialization or adhesion to promontory).

2. Overlay Technique: Outer squamous epithelial layer of the tympanic membrane remnant is completely stripped off, and the graft is placed lateral to the fibrous layer/annulus and tucked under the handle of malleus. (Complications: Blunting of the anterior tympanomeatal angle, Lateralization of the graft away from the malleus handle causing conductive deafness, and Epithelial pearls).

2. Mastoidectomy: Cortical, Radical, and Modified Radical

A. Cortical Mastoidectomy (Simple / Complete Mastoidectomy / Schwartz Operation)

• Definition: Complete exenteration of all accessible mastoid air cells converting them into a single cavity communicating with the mastoid antrum, while preserving the posterior bony meatal wall intact and not disturbing the middle ear structures.

• Indications: (1) Acute coalescent mastoiditis, (2) Incompletely resolved acute otitis media with reservoir sign, (3) Masked (latent) mastoiditis, (4) Initial surgical approach for Endolymphatic sac surgery, Facial nerve decompression, Cochlear implantation, and Posterior tympanotomy (Combined approach tympanoplasty).

• Surgical Steps:

1. Incision: Curved postaural (Wilde’s) incision 1 cm behind the retroauricular sulcus (more horizontal in infants <2 years to avoid the superficial facial nerve at the undeveloped mastoid tip).

2. Exposure: Elevate periosteum to expose the mastoid cortex, MacEwen’s (suprameatal) triangle, spine of Henle, and zygomatic root; apply Mollison’s self-retaining haemostatic mastoid retractor.

3. Cortical Drilling & Exposure of Antrum: Using a cutting burr under continuous irrigation, drill in the MacEwen’s triangle (bounded superiorly by temporal line/supramastoid crest, anteroinferiorly by posterosuperior bony meatal wall, and posteriorly by a vertical tangent to the external canal) to enter the mastoid antrum (12–15 mm deep in adults; remove Korner’s septum if present). Identify the dome of the lateral semicircular canal and short process of incus in the aditus.

4. Exenteration of Air Cells: Exenterate all accessible air cells (zygomatic, tegmen, sinodural angle, perisinus, retrofacial, and mastoid tip cells exposing digastric ridge), delineating the tegmen antri (superiorly), sigmoid sinus plate (posteriorly), and intact posterior bony canal wall (anteriorly) (Trautmann’s triangle lies bounded by the bony labyrinth anteriorly, sigmoid sinus posteriorly, and superior petrosal sinus/dura superiorly).

5. Closure: Irrigate cavity, bevel bony edges, place a postaural drain if infected, and close in layers.

• Complications of Mastoidectomy:

1. Facial Nerve Injury (mostcommonly at the second genu or vertical mastoid segment).

2. Dislocation of the Incus (causing conductive hearing loss) or drilling on the ossicular chain (causing sensorineural hearing loss).

3. Injury to the Horizontal Semicircular Canal (labyrinthine fistula → severe vertigo, nystagmus, and dead ear).

4. Injury to the Sigmoid Venous Sinus (profuse venous bleeding).

5. Injury to the Middle Cranial Fossa Dura (Tegmen plate) → CSF leak, meningitis, or brain hernia.

6. Perichondritis of pinna and wound infection.

• Named Instruments Used in Mastoidectomy: Mollison’s self-retaining mastoid retractor, Jansen’s mastoid retractor, Lempert’s endaural retractor, Farabeuf’s periosteal elevator, Lempert’s curette (scoop), MacEwen’s cell seeker and curette.

B. Radical vs. Modified Radical Mastoidectomy (Canal Wall Down Procedures)

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-008]]

3. Informed Consent / Counselling for Ear & Laryngeal Surgeries

A valid informed consent must include: (1) Patient identification & Diagnosis, (2) Name and nature of the proposed procedure (in patient's native language), (3) Expected benefits and realistic outcomes, (4) Alternative treatment options (e.g., hearing aid vs. surgery), (5) Specific material risks and complications, and (6) Dated signatures of the patient, witness, and doctor.

1. Counselling / Informed Consent for Stapedectomy:

• Indication & Procedure: Surgical removal of part/whole of the fixed stapes footplate in Otosclerosis and replacement with a Teflon/titanium piston under local/general anaesthesia.

• Expected Benefit & Alternative: 90% chance of closure of air-bone gap and hearing improvement; Hearing aid is a safe non-surgical alternative (surgery is purely elective).

• Specific Risks to Document: (1) 1–2% risk of permanent worsening of hearing or total sensorineural deafness ("Dead Ear"), (2) Temporary postoperative dizziness/vertigo and vomiting (or late perilymph fistula), (3) Alteration or loss of taste on the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue (metallic taste due to stretching/division of the chorda tympani nerve), (4) Rare risk of Facial Nerve Paralysis (<1%) (due to dehiscent/overhanging facial nerve), (5) Tympanic membrane perforation, and (6) Displacement/necrosis of prosthesis requiring revision surgery.

2. Counselling / Informed Consent for Radical / Modified Radical Mastoidectomy:

• Indication & Primary Aim: Unsafe atticoantral CSOM (cholesteatoma). Primary aim is to make the ear safe and dry (preventing life-threatening brain abscess/meningitis); hearing preservation/improvement is secondary (in Radical mastoidectomy, severe conductive hearing loss of 50–60 dB will result).

• Specific Risks to Document: (1) Facial nerve palsy (asymmetry of face, inability to close eye), (2) Vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss / Dead ear (labyrinthine fistula), (3) Alteration of taste (chorda tympani injury), (4) Wide external ear opening (Meatoplasty) and a permanent mastoid cavity requiring lifelong periodic doctor visits (every 6–12 months) for wax/debris cleaning and lifelong water precautions (no swimming), (5) Persistent/discharging cavity (10–25%), and (6) Injury to dura/sigmoid sinus or perichondritis of pinna.

3. Informed Consent for Direct Laryngoscopy (and Biopsy) under General Anaesthesia:

• Indication & Procedure: Passing a rigid metallic tube through the mouth under GA to inspect hidden areas of the larynx/hypopharynx and take a biopsy of a suspected growth (or excise a benign lesion).

• Specific Risks to Document: (1) Injury to lips, gums, and tongue (laceration/bruising), (2) Chipping, loosening, or avulsion of upper incisor teeth (especially carious/crowned teeth), (3) Postoperative hoarseness or change in voice, (4) Bleeding from the biopsy site, (5) Postoperative laryngeal oedema or laryngospasm causing stridor and the potential need for an Emergency Tracheostomy, and (6) Neck pain or general anaesthetic risks in a 65-year-old patient.

Septoplasty vs. Submucous Resection (SMR)

• Incisions Used in Septal Surgery:

1. Killian’s Incision: Curvilinear incision made 2–3 mm posterior to the mucocutaneous junction in the nasal mucosa (used in SMR and posterior septal deviations; cannot access the caudal septal border).

2. Freer’s Hemitransfixion Incision: Vertical incision made right at the caudal border of the septal cartilage on one side (used in Septoplasty, giving full access to caudal dislocations and the entire septum).

3. Complete Transfixion Incision: Through-and-through incision at the caudal septal border (used in septorhinoplasty).

Differences Between SMR and Septoplasty

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-009]]

• Complications of Septoplasty / SMR: (1) Reactionary/Secondary Epistaxis, (2) Septal Haematoma and Septal Abscess, (3) Septal Perforation (due to bilateral opposing mucosal tears), (4) Supratip Depression / Saddle Nose Deformity (excessive removal of dorsal cartilage strut), (5) Columellar Retraction and Drooping of Nasal Tip (loss of caudal strut), (6) Flapping of Nasal Septum (in SMR), (7) Nasal Synechiae, (8) CSF Rhinorrhoea (avulsion of perpendicular plate of ethmoid at cribriform plate), and (9) Toxic Shock Syndrome.

5. Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS)

• Principles of FESS (Messerklinger):

1. Most chronic sinus infections are rhinogenic—infection spreads from the nose to the sinuses, and the Ostiomeatal Complex (OMC) in the middle meatus is the key area of pathogenesis.

2. Mucociliary clearance of the sinuses is genetically directed towards the natural ostium (e.g., maxillary sinus cilia always beat towards the natural ostium in the infundibulum, even if an inferior meatal antrostomy is made).

3. Clearing obstruction at the OMC and frontal recess restores ventilation and normal mucociliary drainage, allowing reversibly diseased mucosa in the larger dependent sinuses (maxillary and frontal) to heal spontaneously without radical mucosal stripping.

• Basic Steps of FESS (Anterior-to-Posterior / Stammberger’s Technique):

1. Decongestion and endoscopic submucosal infiltration with 1% Lignocaine + 1:100,000 Adrenaline.

2. Medialization of the middle turbinate.

3. Uncinectomy (Infundibulectomy): Incision and removal of the uncinate process to expose the ethmoidal infundibulum.

4. Middle Meatal Antrostomy (MMA): Identification of the natural maxillary ostium and widening it (joining any accessory ostium to prevent recirculation phenomenon).

5. Anterior Ethmoidectomy (Bullectomy): Opening and removing the bulla ethmoidalis (staying medial to the lamina papyracea and inferior to the skull base/anterior ethmoidal artery).

6. Penetration of the Ground (Basal) Lamella & Posterior Ethmoidectomy (if posterior ethmoids are diseased).

7. Sphenoidotomy and Frontal Recess Clearance (Draf I/II) (if indicated).

• Complications of FESS:

• Major Complications:

• Orbital: Injury to Lamina Papyracea → Orbital fat herniation, Retrobulbar Orbital Haematoma (caused by injury to the anterior ethmoidal artery, which retracts into the orbit causing rapid proptosis, rock-hard globe, and blindness due to optic nerve ischaemia—requires emergency lateral canthotomy/cantholysis and endoscopic orbital decompression), Diplopia (injury to medial rectus/superior oblique), and Direct Optic Nerve Injury / Blindness (in the posterior ethmoid/Onodi cell or sphenoid sinus).

• Intracranial: CSF Rhinorrhoea (injury to lateral lamella of cribriform plate or fovea ethmoidalis), Meningitis, Pneumocephalus, Brain abscess, and Intracranial haemorrhage.

• Vascular: Torrential Haemorrhage from injury to the Internal Carotid Artery (in the lateral wall of the sphenoid sinus) or Sphenopalatine/Anterior ethmoidal artery.

• Nasolacrimal: Injury to the Nasolacrimal Duct (anterior to natural maxillary ostium) → Epiphora.

• Minor Complications: Periorbital ecchymosis, Subcutaneous surgical emphysema of eyelids (on blowing nose), Nasal synechiae/adhesions (lateralization of middle turbinate), Stenosis of middle meatal or frontal ostium, Dental/infraorbital numbness, and Postoperative epistaxis.

6. Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy

• Absolute Contraindications for Tonsillectomy: (1) Haemoglobin <10 g/dL, (2) Acute upper respiratory tract infection or acute tonsillitis (wait 3–4 weeks), (3) Children <3 years of age (small blood volume), (4) Overt or Submucous Cleft Palate (causes hypernasality/velopharyngeal insufficiency), (5) Uncorrected Bleeding Disorders (Haemophilia, leukaemia, ITP, aplastic anaemia), (6) During a Polio epidemic (risk of bulbar poliomyelitis), and (7) Uncontrolled systemic diseases (hypertension, diabetes).

• Complications of Tonsillectomy:

• Immediate: Primary Haemorrhage (at surgery), Reactionary Haemorrhage (within 24 hours), Injury to pillars/uvula/soft palate/teeth, Aspiration of blood, Laryngeal spasm/oedema, and Surgical emphysema.

• Delayed: Secondary Haemorrhage (5th–10th postoperative day), Infection (parapharyngeal abscess, otitis media), Pulmonary complications (atelectasis, lung abscess), Scarring of soft palate, Tonsillar remnants, and Compensatory hypertrophy of lingual tonsils.

• Management of Post-Tonsillectomy Haemorrhage:

1. Reactionary Haemorrhage (Occurs within the first 24 hours, usually first 4–6 hours):

• Causes: Slippage of ligature, failure to ligate a vessel that was in spasm or masked by hypotensive anaesthesia/adrenaline, or presence of a blood clot in the tonsillar fossa (prevents contraction of the superior constrictor muscle around piercing vessels).

• Clinical Signs of Concealed Bleeding in a Child: Frequent swallowing reflex, rising pulse rate (tachycardia), progressive pallor, restlessness, hypotension, and vomiting of dark coffee-ground altered blood.

• Management:

• Secure IV access, send blood for grouping, cross-matching, and Hb, and start IV fluids/blood transfusion.

• Step 1 (Clot Removal & Pressure): Inspect pharynx, remove the blood clot from the tonsillar fossa with forceps/suction, and apply a gauze swab soaked in 1:1,000 adrenaline or hydrogen peroxide with firm pressure for 5–10 minutes.

• Step 2 (Return to OT—"Second Anaesthetic"): If bleeding persists, shift immediately to the OT under general anaesthesia, identify the bleeding vessel, and ligate with silk or coagulate with bipolar diathermy (if diffuse, suture the anterior and posterior pillars together over a haemostatic bolster).

2. Secondary Haemorrhage (Occurs between the 5th and 10th postoperative day):

• Cause: Secondary bacterial infection of the tonsillar fossa causing premature separation of the fibrinous slough and necrosis of vessel walls.

• Management: Hospitalization, IV fluids/blood transfusion, removal of clots, hydrogen peroxide gargles, parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics (Co-amoxiclav/Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole), tranexamic acid, and electrocoagulation/pillar suturing under GA if bleeding is profuse.

• Complications of Adenoidectomy: (1) Reactionary/Primary Haemorrhage (managed by postnasal pack), (2) Injury to Eustachian tube orifice (causing tubal stenosis and OME), (3) Velopharyngeal Insufficiency (Rhinolalia aperta) and nasal regurgitation (especially in undiagnosed submucous cleft palate—identified preoperatively by a bifid uvula, zona pellucida, and a notch in the posterior hard palate), (4) Grisel’s Syndrome (Non-traumatic atlanto-axial subluxation presenting with severe neck pain and torticollis due to paraspinal muscle spasm and decalcification of the transverse ligament of the atlas following infection/electrocautery over the prevertebral fascia—take precautions in Down syndrome patients who have congenital atlanto-axial instability), (5) Nasopharyngeal stenosis, and (6) Recurrence of adenoids.

7. Tracheostomy

• Functions of Tracheostomy:

1. Provides an alternative pathway for breathing, bypassing any upper airway obstruction above the stoma.

2. Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing anatomical dead space by 30–50% (normal dead space is ~150 mL) and decreasing airflow resistance.

3. Protects the lower airways (using a cuffed tube) against aspiration of pharyngeal secretions (coma, bulbar palsy) or blood (maxillofacial trauma, pharyngeal surgery).

4. Permits easy tracheobronchial toilet (suctioning) of retained secretions in patients unable to cough.

5. Permits prolonged Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation (IPPV) beyond 72 hours.

6. Route to administer general anaesthesia when oral/nasal intubation is impossible (severe trismus, large laryngeal tumours).

• Indications for Tracheostomy (3 Categories):

1. Upper Respiratory Tract Obstruction: Acute infections (epiglottitis, croup, diphtheria, Ludwig’s angina, retropharyngeal abscess), Trauma (laryngotracheal fractures, maxillofacial fractures, burns), Neoplasms (carcinoma larynx/hypopharynx/thyroid), Foreign body larynx, Bilateral abductor vocal cord paralysis, Congenital anomalies (laryngeal web, bilateral choanal atresia).

2. Retained Tracheobronchial Secretions: Coma (head injury, CVA, drug overdose), Respiratory muscle paralysis (poliomyelitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis, high cervical cord injury), Spasm of respiratory muscles (tetanus, eclampsia), Painful cough (flail chest).

3. Respiratory Insufficiency: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (emphysema, chronic bronchitis, severe bronchiectasis) requiring assisted ventilation.

• Types of Tracheostomy:

• By Timing: Emergency, Elective (Tranquil) (Therapeutic or Prophylactic), and Permanent.

• By Anatomical Level (in relation to the thyroid isthmus, which lies against the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings):

• High Tracheostomy: Above the isthmus (1st ring)—avoided because it causes perichondritis of the cricoid cartilage and subglottic stenosis (only indicated in carcinoma larynx prior to total laryngectomy).

• Mid Tracheostomy (Preferred): Through the 2nd and 3rd (or 3rd and 4th) tracheal rings after retracting or dividing the thyroid isthmus.

• Low Tracheostomy: Below the isthmus (trachea is deep, close to innominate vessels and pleura).

• Other Types: Percutaneous Dilatational Tracheostomy (bedside ICU procedure using Seldinger guidewire and serial dilators under bronchoscopic guidance) and Mini-Tracheostomy (Cricothyrotomy) (emergency opening through the cricothyroid membrane).

• Boundaries of the Tracheostomy Triangle (Jackson’s Safety Triangle):

• Superiorly (Base): Lower border of the cricoid cartilage.

• Inferiorly (Apex): Suprasternal notch.

• Laterally (on either side): Anterior borders of the sternocleidomastoid muscles (and carotid sheaths).

• Surgical Steps of Tracheostomy:

1. Position: Supine with a sandbag under the shoulders to extend the neck and bring the trachea anteriorly.

2. Anaesthesia: Local infiltration with 1–2% Lignocaine + Adrenaline (or GA with endotracheal tube in place, especially in children).

3. Incision: Vertical midline incision (from lower border of cricoid to 1 cm above sternal notch—used in emergencies for rapid bloodless access) OR Transverse collar incision (5 cm long, two finger-breadths above the sternal notch—used in elective cases for a better cosmetic scar).

4. Dissection: Separate strap muscles vertically in the midline raphe and retract laterally; displace anterior jugular veins.

5. Thyroid Isthmus: Retract upwards with a blunt hook, or divide between haemostats and transfix-ligate.

6. Opening Trachea: Inject 0.5 mL of 4% lignocaine intratracheally (suppresses cough reflex), fix the cricoid with a sharp tracheal hook, make a vertical incision across the 2nd and 3rd (or 3rd and 4th) tracheal rings, and excise a small circular window of anterior tracheal wall in adults (In infants/children, make only a simple vertical slit with stay sutures on either side; never excise tracheal cartilage in children and never cut the 1st tracheal ring).

7. Insertion & Fixation: Insert an appropriately sized tracheostomy tube using tracheal dilators, inflate the cuff, secure neck tapes with a reef knot in flexed neck position, and loosely approximate skin edges (never suture skin tightly around the tube, as air leak causes severe subcutaneous surgical emphysema and pneumomediastinum).

• Postoperative Care: Constant nursing supervision (paper and pencil/bell for communication, as patient is aphonic), humidification of inspired air (nebulizer/wet gauze), aseptic periodic suctioning (apply suction only while withdrawing the catheter), inner tube cleaning every 4–6 hours, periodic cuff deflation (every 2 hours for 5 mins to prevent tracheal pressure necrosis; cuff pressure <25 cm H_2O), and Decannulation (by progressive corking/downsizing of the tube for 24 hours).

• Complications of Tracheostomy:

1. Immediate (Intraoperative): (a) Haemorrhage (anterior jugular veins, thyroid isthmus, thyroidea ima), (b) Apnoea (due to sudden washing out of hypercapnic CO_2 respiratory drive—treated by giving Carbogen [5% CO_2 + 95% O_2] or assisted ventilation), (c) Pneumothorax / Pneumomediastinum (injury to apical pleura, especially in children), (d) Injury to recurrent laryngeal nerves, (e) Injury to the posterior tracheal wall and oesophagus (tracheo-oesophageal fistula), and (f) Aspiration of blood.

2. Intermediate (First few hours to days): (a) Reactionary/secondary bleeding, (b) Accidental displacement or blockage of tube (by thick mucus crusts), (c) Subcutaneous surgical emphysema, (d) Tracheitis and crusting, (e) Atelectasis/lung abscess, and (f) Local wound infection.

3. Late (Prolonged tube use): (a) Torrential fatal haemorrhage from erosion of the Innominate (Brachiocephalic) Artery, (b) Subglottic / Tracheal stenosis, (c) Tracheo-oesophageal fistula (pressure necrosis from overinflated cuff), (d) Tracheomalacia, (e) Difficult decannulation in children (due to peristomal granulations, anterior tracheal wall buckling, or psychological dependence), and (f) Persistent tracheocutaneous fistula or keloid scar.

• Types of Tracheostomy Tubes:

1. Metallic Tubes (Non-cuffed, Double-lumen—Silver/German silver alloy):

• Fuller’s Bivalve Metallic Tube: Consists of a split (bivalved) outer tube (whose two blades are pinched together for easy insertion without an obturator) and a longer inner tube with a dorsal fenestration (speaking hole) and two handles. (Disadvantage: Sharp edges of the split outer blades can pinch tracheal mucosa and cause granulations/stenosis).

• Jackson’s Metallic Tube: Consists of three parts: a solid (non-split) outer tube with a rotating lock on the shield, a closely fitting inner tube, and a pilot obturator for smooth, atraumatic insertion.

2. Non-Metallic Tubes (PVC, Silicone, Silastic—Thermolabile/Atraumatic):

• Portex Cuffed PVC Tube: Single-lumen tube with a low-pressure, high-volume inflatable cuff and pilot balloon. When inflated, it prevents aspiration of pharyngeal secretions/blood and allows positive-pressure mechanical ventilation.

• Fenestrated Tubes, Suction-aid Cuffed Tubes (with subglottic suction port above the cuff), Adjustable-flange Long Tubes (for obese necks or low tracheal stenosis), and Speaking Valves (Passy-Muir valve).

8. Rigid Oesophagoscopy and Bronchoscopy (Complications)

• Complications of Rigid Oesophagoscopy:

1. Perforation of the Oesophagus (Most serious complication): Most commonly occurs just above the cricopharyngeal sphincter at Killian’s dehiscence ("Gateway of Tears"), at the site of an impacted sharp foreign body/stricture, or at the lower end near the cardia. Presents with severe interscapular/neck pain, surgical emphysema in the neck, abrupt high fever, tachycardia, and crunching sound over the heart (Hamman’s sign) → leads to fatal acute mediastinitis, pneumothorax, or empyema.

2. Injury to lips, tongue, and avulsion of upper incisor teeth.

3. Laceration of pharyngeal mucosa or dislocation/injury of arytenoids.

4. Tracheal compression by the scope in infants causing cyanosis.

• Indications, Contraindications, and Complications of Rigid Bronchoscopy:

• Indications: Diagnostic (unexplained haemoptysis, chronic cough/wheeze >4 weeks, lobar atelectasis/obstructive emphysema, vocal cord palsy, bronchoalveolar lavage/biopsy) and Therapeutic (Removal of tracheobronchial foreign bodies [Gold Standard], suctioning of thick mucus plugs/atelectasis, laser/stent management of airway tumours).

• Contraindications: Unstable cervical spine fracture/atlanto-axial dislocation, severe trismus/ankylosis of TMJ (use flexible bronchoscope), aortic aneurysm, and severe uncorrected hypoxia/coagulopathy.

• Complications: Injury to teeth/lips, Laryngospasm and Bronchospasm, Postoperative subglottic laryngeal oedema (if scope is oversized or procedure exceeds 20 minutes in children), Haemorrhage from biopsy site, Pneumothorax / Mediastinal emphysema (bronchial perforation), and Hypoxia / Cardiac arrest.

9. Caldwell-Luc Operation and Maxillectomy

• Caldwell-Luc Operation (Anterior Antrostomy): Opening the maxillary antrum through the canine fossa via a sublabial incision (from lateral incisor to 2nd molar), removing irreversible antral pathology, and creating a counter-opening (nasoantral window) in the inferior meatus.

• Current Indications: (1) Removal of large foreign bodies, displaced tooth roots, or large odontogenic cysts/tumours, (2) Excision of antrochoanal polyp recurrence/fungal ball inaccessible by FESS, (3) Pterygopalatine fossa approach (internal maxillary artery ligation, Vidian neurectomy), (4) Transantral orbital decompression, and (5) Repair of blow-out orbital floor fractures.

• Contraindication: Children <17 years (damages unerupted secondary dentition).

• Complications: Infraorbital nerve anaesthesia/paraesthesia (numbness of cheek and upper lip), numbness/devitalization of upper canine and premolar teeth (injury to anterior/middle superior alveolar nerves), Sublabial oroantral fistula, facial swelling, and nasolacrimal duct injury.

• Carcinoma of Maxilla (Maxillary Sinus) and Maxillectomy:

• Classifications of Maxillary Sinus Carcinoma:

1. Ohngren’s Line: Imaginary plane extending from the medial canthus of the eye to the angle of the mandible. Divided into Infrastructural (anteroinferior) growths (present early, easily resectable, good prognosis) and Suprastructural (posterosuperior) growths (invade orbit, ethmoids, pterygopalatine fossa, and skull base early; poor prognosis).

2. Lederman’s Classification: Uses two horizontal lines of Sebileau passing through the floors of the orbits and the floors of the antra, dividing the region into: Suprastructure (ethmoid, sphenoid, frontal sinuses, and olfactory area), Mesostructure (maxillary sinus and respiratory nasal cavity), and Infrastructure (alveolar process and hard palate).

• Clinical Features of Spread: Medial spread (nasal obstruction, epistaxis), Anterior spread (swelling of cheek), Inferior spread (loosening of upper molar/premolar teeth, ill-fitting dentures, palatal bulge/ulcer), Superior spread (proptosis, upward globe displacement, diplopia, infraorbital anaesthesia), and Posterior spread (into pterygopalatine/infratemporal fossa causing severe trismus).

• Types of Maxillectomy:

1. Medial Maxillectomy (via Lateral Rhinotomy or Midfacial Degloving): Resection of lateral nasal wall, ethmoids, and medial wall of maxilla (for Inverted Papilloma).

2. Partial (Infrastructure) Maxillectomy: For hard palate/alveolar tumours.

3. Total Maxillectomy (via Weber-Fergusson incision): Complete resection of the maxilla (preserving the eye if periorbita is uninvolved) + obturator prosthesis rehabilitation.

4. Total Maxillectomy with Orbital Exenteration (if tumour breaches the periorbita into orbital fat) + Postoperative Radiotherapy / Chemoradiotherapy.

title: 51. RECENT ADVANCES
text:
1. LASERS in ENT

• Definition: LASER is an acronym for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Laser light is monochromatic (single wavelength), coherent (all waves in phase), and collimated (parallel non-divergent beam).

• Types of Lasers Used in ENT & Their Clinical Uses:

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-010]]

• Safety Precautions in Laser Surgery:

1. Eye Protection: Patient’s eyes are covered with double-layered wet saline gauze pads; all OT personnel must wear wavelength-specific protective goggles (Clear glass/plastic spectacles for CO_2; Amber/orange glasses for Argon/KTP; Blue-green glasses for Nd:YAG).

2. Skin/Tissue Protection: Cover exposed face and tissues around the target with wet saline-soaked towels.

3. Endotracheal Tube & Anaesthetic Precautions: Use laser-resistant metallic/silicone endotracheal tubes (or wrap red rubber tubes with reflective metallic aluminium/copper tape); inflate the cuff with methylene-blue-coloured normal saline (not air—acts as a heat sink and signals cuff puncture immediately); keep FiO_2 < 30–40% and avoid Nitrous Oxide (N_2O) (use air + oxygen + volatile agent).

4. Smoke Evacuation: Continuous dual suction to evacuate laser plume (contains viable HPV viral DNA particles).

5. Protocol for Endotracheal Tube Airway Fire: (1) Immediately stop ventilation and disconnect the oxygen circuit, (2) Douse the fire by pouring normal saline into the throat, (3) Immediately extubate/remove the burning endotracheal tube, (4) Re-intubate / mask-ventilate the patient, (5) Perform rigid/flexible bronchoscopy to assess thermal injury and remove charred debris, and (6) Administer IV corticosteroids, antibiotics, and humidified oxygen in ICU.

2. ENT Manifestations of HIV / AIDS

• Otologic: Kaposi’s sarcoma of pinna/canal, Severe seborrhoeic dermatitis, Necrotizing (Malignant) Otitis Externa (Pseudomonas/Aspergillus), Recurrent Acute Otitis Media, Serous Otitis Media (OME) (secondary to nasopharyngeal lymphoid hyperplasia or Kaposi’s sarcoma), Herpes Zoster Oticus (Ramsay-Hunt Syndrome), and Sensorineural Hearing Loss (HIV auditory neuropathy, CMV/cryptococcal meningitis, ototoxic drugs).

• Nasal & Paranasal Sinuses: Recurrent/chronic bacterial rhinosinusitis, Acute Fulminant Invasive Fungal Sinusitis (*Aspergillus / Mucormycosis*), Giant nasal herpetic ulcers, Epistaxis (ITP), and Sinonasal Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma (B-cell) or Kaposi’s sarcoma.

• Oral Cavity & Pharynx (Most Common & Earliest Manifestations):

1. Oral & Oesophageal Candidiasis (Thrush): Most common opportunistic infection (indicates declining CD4^+ count <400/μL).

2. Oral Hairy Leukoplakia (OHL): Vertically corrugated, non-scrapable white patch on the lateral border of the tongue caused by Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV); pathognomonic predictor of progression to AIDS.

3. Kaposi’s Sarcoma: Violaceous/purplish nodules or plaques, most commonly on the hard and soft palate and gingiva (caused by HHV-8).

4. Recurrent Giant Aphthous Ulcers, Severe necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis/periodontitis, Adenotonsillar hypertrophy, and Extranodal Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma.

• Neck & Salivary Glands: Persistent Generalized Lymphadenopathy (PGL), Tuberculous/fungal cervical lymphadenitis, Xerostomia, and Bilateral Benign Lymphoepithelial Cysts of the Parotid Glands (characteristic cystic parotid enlargement in HIV).

3. Brachytherapy and Coronavirus (COVID-19) in ENT

• Brachytherapy: Form of radiotherapy where a sealed radioactive source (Iridium-192 [^192Ir] wires/seeds, Caesium-137 [^137Cs], or Gold-198 [^198Au] grains) is placed directly inside (Interstitial implant, e.g., Early T_1/T_2 Carcinoma of the Lip, Anterior 2/3rd of Tongue, Floor of Mouth, or Buccal Mucosa) or adjacent to the tumour (Intracavitary, e.g., Recurrent/Residual Carcinoma of the Nasopharynx). Delivers a very high localized radiation dose to the tumour with a rapid inverse-square law dose fall-off, sparing surrounding normal structures (mandible, salivary glands).

• Coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2 / COVID-19) and ENT:

1. Pathogenesis & Tropism: SARS-CoV-2 binds via its spike protein to ACE-2 and TMPRSS2 receptors, which are expressed in highest density on the ciliated respiratory epithelium of the nasal cavity/nasopharynx and the sustentacular (supporting) cells of the olfactory neuroepithelium (hence nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal swabs have the highest viral load).

2. Key ENT Manifestations: Sudden-onset Anosmia / Hyposmia and Ageusia / Dysgeusia (often the sole presenting symptom without nasal obstruction/rhinorrhoea), Sore throat, Acute viral rhinosinusitis, Parotitis, Sudden sensorineural hearing loss / vestibular neuritis, and Post-COVID-19 Acute Invasive Rhinocerebral Mucormycosis (triggered by virus-induced immune dysregulation, hyperferritinaemia, uncontrolled diabetes, and systemic corticosteroid therapy).

3. Aerosol-Generating Procedures (AGPs) in ENT: Diagnostic nasal endoscopy, flexible laryngoscopy, epistaxis management, tracheostomy, FESS, mastoid drilling, and bronchoscopy generate high-risk viral aerosols, mandating N95/FFP3 respirators, eye protection, and full PPE.

title: 52. CLINICAL METHODS IN ENT
text:
1. Structures Seen on Posterior Rhinoscopy and Indirect Laryngoscopy

• Structures Seen on Posterior Rhinoscopy:

1. Median Plane: Posterior free border of the nasal septum (vomer) and Uvula/upper surface of soft palate inferiorly.

2. Anterior Wall (Through both Choanae): Posterior ends of Superior, Middle, and Inferior Turbinates and the Superior, Middle, and Inferior Meatuses.

3. Lateral Wall: Pharyngeal opening of the Eustachian tube, Torus tubarius (tubal elevation), Fossa of Rosenmüller (pharyngeal recess above and behind the torus), and Salpingopharyngeal fold.

4. Roof and Posterior Wall: Nasopharyngeal tonsil (Adenoids).

• Structures Seen on Indirect Laryngoscopy (IDL):

1. Oropharynx: Base (posterior 1/3rd) of tongue, circumvallate papillae, lingual tonsils, right and left valleculae, median glossoepiglottic fold, and lateral glossoepiglottic (pharyngoepiglottic) folds.

2. Larynx: Epiglottis (free margin, lingual and laryngeal surfaces, tubercle), aryepiglottic folds, arytenoid mounds, cuneiform and corniculate tubercles, interarytenoid region (posterior commissure), ventricular bands (false vocal cords), true vocal cords, anterior commissure, subglottis, and upper tracheal rings.

3. Hypopharynx (Laryngopharynx): Right and left pyriform sinuses (fossae), postcricoid region (anterior wall), and posterior pharyngeal wall.

(Note: In the laryngeal mirror, anterior structures appear at the top of the mirror and posterior structures at the bottom, while right and left remain unchanged—anteroposterior inversion).

2. Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy (DNE), Waters’ View X-Ray, and Neck Lymph Node Levels

• Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy (DNE): Performed under topical anaesthesia + decongestant (4% Lignocaine + Oxymetazoline packs) using a 0^circ or 30^circ 4 mm (or 2.7 mm paediatric) rigid Hopkins rod-lens endoscope in Three Passes:

• First Pass (Along the floor of the nose to the nasopharynx): Examines the nasal septum, inferior turbinate, inferior meatus (Hasner’s valve of nasolacrimal duct), choana, Eustachian tube orifice, torus tubarius, fossa of Rosenmüller, and posterior nasopharyngeal wall.

• Second Pass (Medial to the middle turbinate, directed posterosuperiorly): Examines the posterior part of the middle turbinate, superior turbinate, superior meatus (openings of posterior ethmoidal cells), and sphenoethmoidal recess (ostium of the sphenoid sinus).

• Third Pass (Into the middle meatus): Examines the Ostiomeatal Complex—uncinate process, hiatus semilunaris, bulla ethmoidalis, accessory/natural maxillary ostium, and frontal recess.

• Waters’ View (Occipitomental View / Nose-Chin Position):

• Positioning: Patient’s nose and chin touch the X-ray cassette with the orbitomeatal line at an angle of 37^circ to the film (projected with an open mouth to visualize the sphenoid sinus through the open mouth). This angle projects the dense petrous pyramids below the floors of the maxillary sinuses.

• Structures Best Visualized: Maxillary sinuses (best view), Frontal sinuses, Sphenoid sinus (through open mouth), Nasal bones, Frontal process of maxilla, Zygoma, Zygomatic arch, and Infraorbital rim/floor of orbit (Tripod and blow-out fractures). (Note: Caldwell View [Occipitofrontal / Nose-Forehead position, 15^circ–20^circ caudal tilt] is the best plain X-ray view for the Frontal and Ethmoid sinuses).

• Levels of Cervical Lymph Nodes (Memorial Sloan-Kettering Classification):

• Level I: Submental (Level IA) (in submental triangle between anterior bellies of digastric and hyoid) and Submandibular (Level IB) (in digastric triangle).

• Level II (Upper Jugular Group): Along upper 1/3rd of IJV, from skull base to lower border of hyoid bone (or carotid bifurcation); subdivided by spinal accessory nerve into IIA (anterior) and IIB (posterior).

• Level III (Middle Jugular Group): Along middle 1/3rd of IJV, from lower border of hyoid bone to lower border of cricoid cartilage (or omohyoid crossing).

• Level IV (Lower Jugular Group): Along lower 1/3rd of IJV, from lower border of cricoid cartilage to clavicle (includes Virchow’s node).

• Level V (Posterior Triangle Group): Between posterior border of SCM, anterior border of trapezius, and clavicle; subdivided by inferior belly of omohyoid into VA (Spinal accessory nodes above) and VB (Transverse cervical / Supraclavicular nodes below). (Note: Ho’s Supraclavicular Triangle is bounded by the medial end of clavicle, lateral end of clavicle, and point where neck meets shoulder; nodal metastasis here in NPC is staged as N_3b).

• Level VI (Anterior / Central Visceral Compartment): Between the two common carotid arteries, from hyoid bone above to suprasternal notch below (includes Prelaryngeal [Delphian], Pretracheal, and Paratracheal [recurrent laryngeal nerve] nodes).

• Level VII: Superior Mediastinal lymph nodes (below suprasternal notch to innominate artery).

3. Nuggets: Ventilation Tube, Lermoyez Syndrome, CHARGE Syndrome, and Lignocaine

• Ventilation Tube (Grommet / Tympanostomy Tube): Collar-button-shaped tube (made of Teflon, Silicone, Titanium, or Fluoroplastic; e.g., Shepard, Armstrong, Shah, or Goode T-tube for long-term use) inserted through a radial myringotomy incision in the anteroinferior or anterosuperior quadrant of the tympanic membrane to provide long-term middle ear ventilation and pressure equalization in Chronic Otitis Media with Effusion (Glue Ear), recurrent acute otitis media, or atelectatic ear. Spontaneously extrudes in 6–12 months. Complications: Otorrhoea, blockage, premature extrusion, tympanosclerosis (hyaline plaques—most common), residual perforation, and cholesteatoma.

• Lermoyez Syndrome ("Ménière’s Disease in Reverse"): A rare variant of Ménière’s disease where the sequence of symptoms is reversed—first there is progressive deterioration of sensorineural hearing and worsening tinnitus, followed suddenly by an attack of acute vertigo, immediately after which the hearing improves dramatically ("the vertigo that makes you hear").

• CHARGE Syndrome: Congenital autosomal dominant disorder (CHD7 gene mutation) consisting of: Coloboma of the eye, Heart defects, Atresia of the choanae, Retarded growth and development, Genital hypoplasia, and Ear anomalies/deafness.

• Lignocaine (Xylocaine) in ENT: Amide-type local anaesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels.

• Concentrations & Routes: 4% topical solution (for surface anaesthesia of nasal cavity, pharynx, and larynx; 10% spray delivering 10 mg/puff); 1% or 2% solution with 1:100,000 or 1:200,000 Adrenaline (for infiltration anaesthesia and vasoconstriction in ear/septal/FESS surgery); 2% Viscous (for painful oral/pharyngeal ulcers).

• Maximum Safe Dose: Plain Lignocaine: 3–4.5 mg/kg (max 300 mg in adults); Lignocaine with Adrenaline: 7 mg/kg (max 500 mg in adults). (Toxicity causes circumoral numbness, tinnitus, muscle twitching, generalized convulsions, and cardiovascular collapse; treated with oxygenation, IV Midazolam, and 20% Intralipid emulsion).

title: FINAL ADDENDUM: REMAINING HIGH-YIELD SHORT ANSWERS (RGU / TU)
text:
1. Inverted Papilloma (Ringertz Tumour / Schneiderian Papilloma)

• Definition & Aetiology: A benign, locally aggressive neoplasm arising from the non-olfactory ectodermal respiratory mucosa (Schneiderian membrane) of the nose and paranasal sinuses. Associated with Human Papillomavirus (HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18).

• Pathology: So-named because the hyperplastic squamous/transitional epithelium inverts (invaginates downwards) into the underlying stroma rather than growing exophytically, with an intact basement membrane.

• Site of Origin: Lateral wall of the nose (most commonly in the middle meatus / fontanelle area), secondarily invading the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses.

• Three Classic Clinical Characteristics:

1. Always Unilateral (predominantly affects males aged 40–70 years).

2. High propensity for local bone destruction and recurrence after simple removal.

3. Associated with Squamous Cell Carcinoma in 10–15% of cases (synchronous or metachronous).

• Clinical Features: Unilateral nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis, blood-stained nasal discharge; examination reveals a unilateral, pale-pink, fleshy, lobulated polypoidal mass that bleeds on touch (may be hidden behind simple inflammatory sentinel polyps).

• Investigations: CECT & Contrast MRI of PNS (CT shows unilateral mass with focal hyperostosis/cone-shaped bone thickening at the exact site of tumour attachment; MRI shows a pathognomonic "Convoluted Cerebriform Pattern" on T2/post-contrast T1 images) + Biopsy.

• Treatment: Wide Surgical Excision via Endoscopic Medial Maxillectomy (or Open Lateral Rhinotomy / Midfacial Degloving with Medial Maxillectomy) with drilling of the underlying bone at the attachment site. (Radiotherapy is contraindicated in benign inverted papilloma as it induces malignant transformation).

2. Parapharyngeal Space: Anatomy and Surgical Approaches

• Anatomy: Inverted pyramid-shaped potential fascial space lateral to the pharynx:

• Base (Superiorly): Base of the skull (petrous temporal and sphenoid bones).

• Apex (Inferiorly): Greater cornu of the hyoid bone.

• Medial Wall: Buccopharyngeal fascia covering the superior constrictor muscle (tonsillar bed).

• Lateral Wall: Ramus of mandible, medial pterygoid muscle, and deep lobe of the parotid gland.

• Posterior Wall: Prevertebral fascia and cervical vertebrae.

• Compartments (Divided by the Styloid Process and Styloid Muscles/Fascia):

1. Prestyloid (Anterior) Compartment: Contains fat, loose areolar tissue, internal maxillary artery, inferior alveolar/lingual/auriculotemporal nerves, and the deep lobe of the parotid gland. (Abscess here causes Triad: [1] Medial displacement of the tonsil and tonsillar pillars, [2] Marked trismus due to medial pterygoid spasm, and [3] External swelling behind the angle of the mandible).

2. Poststyloid (Posterior / Neurovascular) Compartment: Contains the Internal Carotid Artery, Internal Jugular Vein, Cranial Nerves IX, X, XI, and XII, Cervical Sympathetic Chain, and deep cervical/parapharyngeal lymph nodes. (Abscess/tumour here causes bulge of the lateral pharyngeal wall behind the posterior pillar, parotid swelling, and lower cranial nerve palsies/Horner's syndrome without significant trismus).

• Surgical Approaches to Parapharyngeal Space:

1. For Parapharyngeal Abscess: External Transcervical Approach via a horizontal collar incision 2–3 cm below the angle of the mandible, dissecting bluntly along the medial surface of the medial pterygoid muscle towards the styloid process (Never drain intraorally due to risk of injuring the great vessels).

2. For Parapharyngeal Tumours (Salivary 50% [deep lobe pleomorphic adenoma], Neurogenic 30% [schwannoma], Paragangliomas 20%): Transcervical, Transcervical-Transparotid (for deep lobe parotid dumbbell tumours), or Transcervical-Transmandibular (Mandibulotomy) approach.

3. Fibrous Dysplasia of Maxilla (Craniofacial Fibrous Dysplasia)

• Pathology: Benign, self-limiting fibro-osseous disorder of unknown aetiology (activating mutation of GNAS1 gene) where normal cancellous bone is replaced by proliferating fibrous connective tissue and immature woven bone trabeculae lacking osteoblastic rimming.

• Types: Monostotic (70–80%) (involves a single bone—Maxilla is the most common craniofacial bone affected, followed by mandible, frontal, and ethmoid), Polyostotic (20%), and McCune-Albright Syndrome (Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + Café-au-lait skin spots + Precocious puberty).

• Clinical Features: Starts in childhood/adolescence (10–20 years) and arrests after puberty. Presents with painless, slow, progressive, unilateral asymmetrical swelling of the cheek/maxilla, obliteration of the gingivobuccal sulcus, malocclusion/crowding of teeth, nasal obstruction, and upward displacement of the globe.

• Diagnosis: CT Scan (Bone Window) shows a classic "Ground-glass" or "Orange-peel" radio-opaque appearance expanding the maxilla and obliterating the maxillary sinus lumen without a discrete capsule; Biopsy shows "Chinese-letter pattern" of woven bone trabeculae.

• Treatment: Defer surgery until skeletal maturity/puberty; conservative surgical contouring (bone shaving/paring) via a sublabial degloving approach for cosmetic deformity or compressive symptoms. (Radiotherapy is strictly contraindicated as it induces osteosarcoma transformation).

Myringotomy (Operative Steps & Indications)

• Definition: Surgical incision of the tympanic membrane to drain middle ear fluid/pus or insert a ventilation tube (grommet).

• Indications:

1. Acute Suppurative Otitis Media (ASOM): (a) Severe excruciating otalgia with a tense bulging drum, (b) Incomplete resolution despite antibiotics (persistent conductive deafness/opaque drum), (c) Complications of ASOM (facial nerve palsy, labyrinthitis, meningitis), and (d) Recurrent ASOM.

2. Otitis Media with Effusion (OME / Serous or Mucoid "Glue Ear") persisting >3 months with bilateral hearing loss >25–30 dB.

3. Otitic Barotrauma (Aero-otitis media) and Atelectatic Tympanic Membrane (Grade II/III retraction pockets).

• Types of Incisions & Technique:

• Performed under an operating microscope using a sickle knife or Spear-head myringotome:

1. In Acute Suppurative Otitis Media: A curvilinear (circumferential) incision is made in the posteroinferior quadrant of the pars tensa (where the drum bulges maximally and is away from the ossicles).

2. In Otitis Media with Effusion (for Grommet insertion): A small radial incision (parallel to radial collagen fibres to prevent fibre transection and permanent perforation) is made in the anteroinferior or anterosuperior quadrant; thick glue is aspirated (sometimes using a second counter-incision on the "beer-can principle"), and the grommet is flanged into place.

• (Warning: Never incise the posterosuperior quadrant, as it damages the incudostapedial joint, stapes, and chorda tympani nerve).

5. Acute Parotitis & Scarlet Fever

• Acute Suppurative Parotitis: Acute bacterial infection of the parotid gland, most commonly caused by *Staphylococcus aureus via retrograde ascent through Stensen’s duct in elderly, postoperative, dehydrated, or debilitated patients with xerostomia. Presents with sudden severe pain (worse on jaw movement), high fever, tender brawny parotid swelling lifting the ear lobule, and purulent discharge exuding from a red, pouting Stensen’s duct orifice (opposite the upper 2nd molar) on gentle massage of the gland. Treatment: IV hydration, oral hygiene, sialogogues (lemon drops), IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (Cloxacillin/Co-amoxiclav/Vancomycin), and Surgical Incision and Drainage (Blair’s preauricular incision) raising a skin flap and opening loculi with a blunt haemostat parallel to the branches of the facial nerve* if an abscess forms.

• Scarlet Fever: Acute infection caused by erythrogenic-toxin-producing Group A β-haemolytic *Streptococcus* (*S. pyogenes*). Characterized by: (1) Acute exudative tonsillitis/pharyngitis, (2) Punctate erythematous blanching "sandpaper" skin rash with circumoral pallor and linear petechiae in skin folds (Pastia’s lines), and (3) "Strawberry Tongue" (initially a white-coated tongue with prominent red fungiform papillae ["White strawberry tongue"], which desquamates by day 4–5 to leave a beefy-red shiny tongue with prominent papillae ["Red strawberry / Raspberry tongue"]). Treated with Penicillin V / Amoxicillin for 10 days.

— END OF COMPREHENSIVE EXAM NOTES —

subject: ent
title: I. REMAINING NOSE & PARANASAL SINUS TOPICS
text:
1. Congenital Swellings of the Nose: Nasal Dermoid, Glioma, and Meningoencephalocele

• Clinical Importance: Any midline or intranasal polypoidal swelling in an infant or young child must be evaluated radiologically (CT and MRI) before biopsy or avulsion to avoid opening the subarachnoid space (causing CSF rhinorrhoea and fatal meningitis).

• Nasal Dermoid Cyst:

• Types: (1) Simple subcutaneous dermoid (anterior to nasal bones) or (2) Dermoid with an external midline pit/sinus on the nasal dorsum with a tuft of hair protruding from the punctum (Pathognomonic).

• Intracranial Connection: The sinus tract may pass deep to the nasal bones, through the foramen caecum or cribriform plate, and attach to the dura.

• Treatment: Complete surgical excision (combined neurosurgical-rhinologic approach if intracranial extension exists).

Differentiation Between Nasal Glioma and Intranasal Meningoencephalocele

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-011]]

2.Nasolacrimal System & Endoscopic Dacryocystorhinostomy (Endo-DCR)

• Anatomy: Tears from the upper and lower puncta → canaliculi → common canaliculus → Lacrimal sac (lies in the lacrimal fossa formed by the lacrimal bone and frontal process of maxilla, just anterior to the attachment of the middle turbinate) → Nasolacrimal duct → opens into the anterior part of the inferior meatus, guarded by Hasner’s valve.

• Indication for Endo-DCR: Chronic dacryocystitis / Epiphora due to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct distal to the medial common canaliculus (confirmed by lacrimal syringing—regurgitation of mucopurulent fluid from the opposite punctum).

• Surgical Steps of Endoscopic DCR:

1. Decongestion and infiltration of the lateral nasal wall just anterior to the axilla of the middle turbinate.

2. Elevation and excision of a 1 × 1.5 cm mucoperiosteal flap anterior to the uncinate process over the maxillary line (frontal process of maxilla).

3. Removal of the thick bone of the frontal process of maxilla (using Kerrison punch or diamond DCR burr) and thin lacrimal bone to expose the entire medial wall of the lacrimal sac.

4. Tenting the medial wall of the sac with a Bowman’s lacrimal probe passed through the inferior canaliculus, incising the sac vertically with a sickle knife, and marsupializing its anterior and posterior flaps widely into the nasal cavity (stented with a bicanalicular Crawford silicone tube for 6 weeks if needed).

• Advantages over External DCR: No external facial scar, preserves the orbicularis oculi lacrimal pump mechanism (medial canthal tendon is not disrupted), can be done in acute dacryocystitis/lacrimal abscess, and allows simultaneous correction of intranasal pathology (DNS, polyps).

3. Vidian Neurectomy (Section of Nerve of Pterygoid Canal)

• Anatomy of Vidian Nerve: Formed at the foramen lacerum by the union of:

1. Greater Superficial Petrosal Nerve (preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the superior salivatory nucleus via CN VII → relays in the sphenopalatine ganglion to supply nasal and lacrimal glands).

2. Deep Petrosal Nerve (postganglionic sympathetic vasoconstrictor fibres from the internal carotid plexus).

• It runs through the pterygoid (Vidian) canal in the floor of the sphenoid sinus to reach the sphenopalatine ganglion in the pterygopalatine fossa.

• Indication: Intractable, profuse watery rhinorrhoea in severe Vasomotor Rhinitis or Allergic Rhinitis unresponsive to medical therapy (ipratropium/steroids).

• Surgical Approaches: Transnasal Endoscopic Approach (current standard—exposing the Vidian canal medial and inferior to the sphenopalatine foramen), Transantral (Caldwell-Luc) approach, or Trans-septal approach.

• Complication: Dry eye (Xerophthalmia / Loss of reflex lacrimation) due to interruption of secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland (requires artificial tear drops).

4. Non-Healing Midline Granuloma (Extranodal NK/T-Cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type)

• Terminology: Formerly called Stewart’s granuloma, Polymorphic reticulosis, or Lethal midline granuloma; now proven by immunohistochemistry to be an Extranodal Angiocentric NK/T-Cell Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma strongly associated with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV).

Differentiation Between Wegener’s Granulomatosis and NK/T-Cell Lymphoma (Midline Granuloma)

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-012]]

5. Malignant Tumours of the Nasal Cavity & Paranasal Sinuses

1. Esthesioneuroblastoma (Olfactory Neuroblastoma):

• Malignant neuroectodermal tumour arising from the olfactory neuroepithelium in the upper one-third of the nasal cavity (cribriform plate, superior turbinate, upper septum).

• Bimodal age distribution: Peaks at 10–20 years and 50–60 years.

• Clinical Features: Unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis; presents as a cherry-red, polypoidal, friable vascular mass in the roof of the nasal cavity (biopsy causes brisk bleeding). Invades the cribriform plate (anterior cranial fossa) and orbit (proptosis, diplopia).

• Kadish Staging: Stage A: Confined to nasal cavity; Stage B: Confined to nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses; Stage C: Extends beyond nasal cavity and sinuses (orbit, skull base, intracranial, or nodal/distant metastasis).

• Histopathology: Lobules of small round blue cells with neurofibrillary stroma and Homer-Wright pseudorosettes / Flexner-Wintersteiner true rosettes; positive for Synaptophysin, Chromogranin, Neuron-Specific Enolase (NSE), and S-100.

• Treatment: Craniofacial Resection (CFR) (or Endoscopic Anterior Skull Base Resection) followed by Postoperative Radiotherapy (± Cisplatin/Etoposide chemotherapy).

2. Adenocarcinoma of Ethmoid Sinus: Strongly associated with occupational exposure to hardwood dust in furniture and cabinet makers (and leather workers). Arises in the ethmoid labyrinth and upper nasal cavity; treated by Craniofacial Resection + Postoperative Radiotherapy.

3. Sinonasal Malignant Melanoma: Arises from neural crest melanocytes in the respiratory mucosa (anterior nasal septum is the commonest site, followed by inferior/middle turbinates). Presents at 50–70 years as a slaty-grey or bluish-black polypoidal mass (or non-pigmented amelanotic melanoma) with epistaxis. Confirmed by HMB-45, Melan-A, and S-100 immunostaining. Treated by Wide Surgical Excision + Postoperative RT.

subject: ent
title: II. REMAINING ORAL CAVITY & SALIVARY GLAND TOPICS
text:
1. Ulcers of the Oral Cavity & Behçet’s Syndrome

• Recurrent Aphthous Stomatitis (RAS):

• Etiology: Autoimmune T-cell mediated mucosal destruction, nutritional deficiencies (Vitamin B_12, Folic acid, Iron), emotional stress, hormonal changes, food allergies, or GI diseases (Coeliac/Crohn’s disease).

• Site Peculiarity: Strictly involves non-keratinized movable oral mucosa (inner lips, buccal mucosa, lateral/ventral tongue, floor of mouth, soft palate) and spares keratinized attached mucosa (hard palate and gingiva—unlike Herpes simplex ulcers, which involve the hard palate and gingiva and are preceded by vesicles and fever).

• Clinical Types:

1. Minor Aphthous Ulcers (Mikulicz’s aphthae—80%): Multiple, small (2–10 mm), painful oval ulcers with a yellowish necrotic floor surrounded by an erythematous halo; heal spontaneously in 7–14 days without scarring.

2. Major Aphthous Ulcers (Sutton’s disease—10%): Large (2–4 cm), deep, crateriform painful ulcers lasting 3–6 weeks that heal with scarring.

3. Herpetiform Ulcers (10%): Crops of 10–100 tiny pinpoint (1–2 mm) ulcers that coalesce.

• Treatment: Topical corticosteroid paste (Triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% in Orabase), topical anaesthetic gel (2% Lignocaine viscous or Choline salicylate before meals), Tetracycline mouthwash (250 mg dissolved in 50 mL water—swish and swallow QID), Chlorhexidine gluconate mouthwash, and correction of Vitamin B_12/folate/iron deficiency.

• Behçet’s Syndrome (Oculo-Oro-Genital Syndrome): Chronic multisystem vasculitis (associated with HLA-B51) characterized by a Classic Triad:

1. Recurrent Oral Aphthous-like Ulcers (punched-out edges).

2. Recurrent Genital Ulcerations (scrotum, penis, vulva).

3. Ocular Lesions (Relapsing iridocyclitis / uveitis with hypopyon, retinal vasculitis).

• (Positive Pathergy Test: Pustule formation 24–48 hours after a sterile needle prick to the forearm).

2. Carcinoma of the Oral Cavity (Tongue & Buccal Mucosa)

• Carcinoma of Anterior Two-Thirds (Oral) Tongue:

• Site of Predilection: Middle third of the lateral border of the tongue (most common site) and ventral surface; tip and dorsum are rare.

• Gross Types: (1) Ulcerative / Ulcero-infiltrative (most common—indurated non-healing ulcer with raised everted edges and necrotic floor), (2) Exophytic / Papillary, (3) Submucosal nodule / Fissure.

• Spread:

• Local: Deep extrinsic tongue muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus → causes ankyloglossia [fixation/deviation of tongue] and T4a stage), floor of mouth, and mandible.

• Lymphatic: Rich lymphatics with frequent bilateral cross-drainage. Tip → Submental (Level IA) and Jugulo-omohyoid (Level III) nodes; Lateral border → Ipsilateral Submandibular (Level IB) and Jugulodigastric (Level II) nodes.

• Clinical Features: Painless lump/ulcer initially; later local pain, referred ipsilateral otalgia (via Lingual nerve →Mandibular nerve [V_3] → Auriculotemporal nerve), excessive salivation, blood-stained saliva, foetor oris, slurred speech, difficulty protruding tongue, and enlarged hard cervical lymph nodes.

• Treatment:

• Stage I (T_1 ≤ 2 cm, N_0): Transoral Wide Local Excision (with 1 cm healthy margin) OR Interstitial Brachytherapy.

• Stage II (T_2 >2 to 4 cm, N_0): Wide Excision / Partial Glossectomy + Elective Supraomohyoid Neck Dissection (Levels I–III) (since occult nodal metastasis rate exceeds 30–40% if Depth of Invasion [DOI] >4 mm).

• Stage III & IV (T_3/T_4 or N^+): Combined Modality Therapy—Hemiglossectomy / Total Glossectomy + Marginal or Segmental Mandibulectomy (if bone invaded) + Radical/Modified Radical Neck Dissection ("Commando Operation") with Radial Forearm Free Flap or Pectoralis Major Myocutaneous (PMMC) Flap reconstruction, followed by Postoperative Radiotherapy / Chemoradiotherapy.

• Carcinoma of Buccal Mucosa:

• Most common site of oral cancer in India due to keeping the tobacco-lime-betel quid ("Khaini / Pan") in the lower gingivobuccal sulcus ("Indian Oral Cancer").

• Verrucous Carcinoma (Ackerman’s Tumour): A distinct low-grade variant of well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma seen in elderly tobacco chewers, most commonly on the buccal mucosa and gingiva. Presents as a slow-growing, white, velvety/warty exophytic cauliflower-like mass that invades locally by "pushing margins" but rarely metastasizes to lymph nodes. Treatment is Wide Surgical Excision (Radiotherapy is avoided as it may induce anaplastic transformation).

3. Salivary Gland Tumours (Benign & Malignant) and Sjogren’s Syndrome

• Rule of Salivary Gland Neoplasms: Larger the salivary gland, higher the proportion of benign tumours; smaller the salivary gland, higher the proportion of malignant tumours (Parotid: 80% benign, 20% malignant; Submandibular: 50% benign, 50% malignant; Sublingual & Minor salivary glands: 20% benign, 80% malignant).

• Warthin’s Tumour (Papillary Cystadenoma Lymphomatosum / Adenolymphoma):

• Second most common benign parotid tumour (5–10%). Exclusively involves the tail of the parotid gland in older male smokers (50–70 years; M:F = 5:1); bilateral in 10% and multicentric.

• Soft-to-cystic encapsulated mass containing brownish mucoid fluid; histologically composed of double-layered eosinophilic oncocytic epithelium forming papillary projections supported by a dense lymphoid stroma with germinal centres.

• Shows a "Hot Spot" on Technetium-99m (^99mTc) Pertechnetate Scan (because oncocytes concentrate technetium but cannot excrete it). Treated by Superficial Parotidectomy.

• Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma:

• Most common malignant tumour of the parotid gland and most common salivary malignancy in children.

• Composed of mucin-producing cells, epidermoid (squamous) cells, and intermediate cells. Graded into Low-grade (predominantly mucinous/cystic; 90% 5-year survival; treated by superficial/total parotidectomy preserving facial nerve) and High-grade (predominantly solid epidermoid cells; aggressive; 30% 5-year survival; treated by radical parotidectomy with facial nerve sacrifice and cable grafting + neck dissection + postoperative RT).

• Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma (Cylindroma):

• Most common malignant tumour of the submandibular, sublingual, and minor salivary glands (especially hard palate).

• Slow-growing but relentless infiltrative tumour with two hallmark biological behaviours:

1. Marked propensity for Perineural Invasion (spreads along nerve sheaths for centimetres beyond visible tumour margins, causing severe deep pain and facial nerve paralysis; requires wide skip-margin resection).

2. Late Haematogenous Distant Metastases to the lungs ("cannon-ball" metastases), brain, and bone (10–20 years after initial treatment).

• Histologically shows a classic "Swiss-cheese" (cribriform), tubular, or solid pattern. Treated by Radical Surgical Resection + Postoperative Radiotherapy (or Fast Neutron Beam Therapy).

• Sjogren’s Syndrome (Sicca Syndrome):

• Autoimmune exocrinopathy (90% in middle-aged females) with lymphocytic infiltration and acinar destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands:

• Primary Sjogren’s Syndrome: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (Xerophthalmia) + Xerostomia + Bilateral diffuse parotid enlargement (Benign lymphoepithelial lesion).

• Secondary Sjogren’s Syndrome: Above triad PLUS an autoimmune connective tissue disorder (most commonly Rheumatoid Arthritis, SLE, or Scleroderma).

• Diagnosis: Schirmer’s test (<5 mm wetting in 5 mins), Positive Anti-Ro (SS-A) and Anti-La (SS-B) autoantibodies, Rheumatoid Factor, and Lower Labial Minor Salivary Gland Biopsy (gold standard—shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis). Carries a 40-fold increased risk of developing Parotid B-cell Non-Hodgkin’s (MALT) Lymphoma.

title: III. REMAINING PHARYNGEAL, OESOPHAGEAL & NECK TOPICS
text:
1. Tumours of the Oropharynx & Hypopharynx

• Carcinoma of the Base (Posterior 1/3rd) of Tongue:

• Remains asymptomatic (silent) for a long time; often presents as an occult primary with bilateral jugulodigastric (Level II) cervical lymph node metastasis (70%).

• Late symptoms: Sore throat, lump in throat, referred ipsilateral otalgia (via CN IX), "Hot-potato" voice, dysphagia, and fixation of tongue on infiltrating deep muscles.

• Palpation under anaesthesia is mandatory, as these tumours infiltrate deeply submucosally and are much larger than they appear on mirror inspection.Strongly associated with HPV-16 in younger non-smokers (p16-positive tumours have a much better prognosis).

• Carcinoma of the Pyriform Sinus vs. Postcricoid Carcinoma:

[[TABLE:ent-tbl-013]]

2. Corrosive Burns of the Oesophagus

• Pathology:

• Alkalies (Caustic soda/NaOH, Lye, Drain cleaners, Button batteries): Cause liquefaction necrosis, saponifying fats and penetrating deeply through all muscle layers of the oesophagus into the mediastinum (causing severe strictures and perforation).

• Acids (Sulphuric, Hydrochloric, Nitric, Bathroom cleaners): Cause coagulative necrosis, forming a superficial eschar that limits deeper penetration in the oesophagus (though they cause severe pyloric spasm and antral damage in the stomach).

• Three Pathological Stages: (1) Stage of Acute Necrosis (first 1–4 days), (2) Stage of Ulceration and Granulation (slough separates at 5–14 days—wall is weakest between days 5 and 15; endoscopy/bougienage is contraindicated during this window), and (3) Stage of Cicatrization / Stricture Formation (begins at 2–3 weeks and progresses over months).

• Management Protocol:

1. Immediate Resuscitation: Hospitalize, treat shock and acid-base imbalance with IV fluids, relieve pain with parenteral narcotic analgesics, and perform Tracheostomy if laryngeal oedema/stridor is present. (Strictly avoid emetics and blind gastric lavage, as re-exposure of the oesophagus to the corrosive causes perforation).

2. Nasogastric Tube Insertion: Passed gently (preferably under endoscopic guidance) to maintain a lumen for feeding and act as a stent against complete stricture obliteration.

3. Medical Therapy: Parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics (for 3–6 weeks), Systemic Corticosteroids (started within 48 hours to inhibit fibroblastic stricture formation in second-degree burns, unless perforation is suspected), and IV Proton Pump Inhibitors.

4. Early Diagnostic Oesophagoscopy (within 12–48 hours): Performed gently to grade mucosal injury (Zargar’s classification); never advance the scope past the first severe circumferential burn.

5. Follow-up & Stricture Management: Serial barium swallows at 2–3-week intervals; established strictures are treated by prograde/retrograde endoscopic dilatation or colonic/gastric bypass.

3. Cystic Hygroma (Cavernous Lymphangioma)

• Embryology & Site: Congenital malformation of the lymphatic system arising from sequestration or failure of the embryonic jugular lymph sac to communicate with the internal jugular venous system. Most commonly located in the Posterior Triangle of the neck (supraclavicular region) (may extend into the anterior triangle, floor of mouth, tongue, axilla, or superior mediastinum).

• Clinical Features: 90% present before 2 years of age (often at birth, causing obstructed labour). Presents as a large, soft, doughy, multilocular, cystic, compressible, non-tender swelling that is brilliantly transilluminant (Pathognomonic). Rapidly enlarges during upper respiratory infections or intracystic haemorrhage, causing stridor, respiratory distress, and dysphagia.

• Treatment: Complete surgical excision preserving vital neurovascular structures (facial, vagus, spinal accessory, phrenic, and hypoglossal nerves, and carotid sheath), or Intralesional sclerotherapy with OK-432 (Picibanil) or Bleomycin.

subject: ent
title: IV. QUICK-FIRE INSTRUMENT & RADIOLOGY SPOTTERS
text:
1. Thudicum’s vs. Vienna Nasal Speculum: Used for Anterior Rhinoscopy. Thudicum’s speculum is held suspended on the index finger of the left hand and compressed between the middle and ring fingers; introduced closed and withdrawn partially open to avoid plucking nasal vibrissae.

2. St. Clair Thomson’s Long-Bladed Nasal Speculum & Killian’s Self-Retaining Long-Bladed Nasal Speculum: Used in SMR and Septoplasty; inserted between the two elevated mucoperichondrial flaps to visualize and resect the cartilaginous/bony septum without tearing the flaps.

3. Ballenger’s Swivel Knife: Used in SMR to excise the quadrilateral septal cartilage in one piece; its U-shaped blade swivels 360^circ to follow the direction of the cut (anteroposteriorly, downwards, and anteriorly).

4. Luc’s Forceps: Fenestrated grasping forceps used in SMR/Septoplasty (to remove septal bone/cartilage), Caldwell-Luc operation (to strip diseased antral mucosa), Nasal polypectomy, and punch biopsies.

5. Walsham’s Forceps & Asch’s Septum Forceps: Used for closed reduction of fractured nasal bones and septum. Walsham’s forceps has one unpadded blade (inserted inside the nostril) and one broader rubber-guarded blade (placed externally over the skin) to disimpact and elevate the lateral nasal bone wall. Asch’s forceps has two symmetrical angled blades inserted along the nasal floor on either side of the nasal septum to disimpact and straighten the fractured septum and vomer.

6. Lichtwitz Trocar and Cannula: Straight sharp trocar inside a cannula with a side-ring handle; used for Proof Puncture (Antral Lavage) through the inferior meatus (1.5–2 cm behind the anterior end of the inferior turbinate, directed towards the ipsilateral pinna).

7. Boyle-Davis Mouth Gag & Draffin’s Bipods: Used in Tonsillectomy, Adenoidectomy, Palatopharyngoplasty (UPPP), Cleft palate repair, and Transpalatal excision of JNA. Consists of a Boyle’s frame and interchangeable Davis slotted tongue blades (which accommodate the endotracheal tube in the central slot). Suspended at the desired angle of neck extension using Draffin’s bipods anchored in Magauran’s plate.

8. Denis Browne’s Tonsil Holding Forceps: Box-jointed forceps with fenestrated spoon-shaped jaws (upper jaw is smaller and fits inside the lower jaw when closed, grasping the tonsil firmly without tearing it) used to pull the tonsil medially during dissection tonsillectomy.

9. Waugh’s Long Toothed Dissection Forceps: Used to hold the mucosa of the anterior pillar while making the initial tonsillectomy incision and to grasp bleeders for cauterization.

10. Tonsil Dissector and Anterior Pillar Retractor: Double-ended instrument: the blunt flat end dissects the tonsil capsule from the loose areolar peritonsillar space, and the C-shaped curved end retracts the anterior pillar to inspect the tonsillar bed for bleeding points.

11. Eve’s Tonsil Snare: Used at the end of tonsillectomy dissection; its wire loop (25 SWG wire) is threaded over the tonsil onto its lower pole pedicle and closed, crushing and cutting the pedicle (releasing tissue thromboplastin to seal the tonsillar branch of the facial artery and minimize bleeding).

12. Negus Curved Artery Forceps & Negus Knot Tier: Usedtogether to ligate deep bleeding vessels in the tonsillar fossa; the sharply curved tip of the Negus forceps replaces the straight haemostat, allowing the silk ligature pushed by the Negus knot tier to slip smoothly off the tip around the vessel.

13. St. Clair Thomson’s Guarded Adenoid Curette: Used for Adenoidectomy; held like a dagger and swept downwards in the midline from the posterior border of the vomer along the nasopharyngeal vault. The cage/guard with sharp teeth catches the shaved adenoid mass and prevents it from falling into the pharynx/larynx.
