subject: medicine
title: 1. Arterial Pulse, Collapsing Pulse & Irregularly Irregular Pulse [KU 25, 15, RGU, TU]
text:
CHAPTER 13: CARDIOLOGY (Davidson Ch. 16)

SECTION 13.1 — FUNCTIONAL ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY

1. Arterial Pulse, Collapsing Pulse & Irregularly Irregular Pulse [KU 25, 15, RGU, TU]

•  Definition & Physiology: The arterial pulse is the pressure wave generated by left ventricular (LV) systole propagating along the arterial tree. Its character is determined by stroke volume and arterial compliance.

•  Assessment: Rate and rhythm are assessed at the radial artery; character and volume are best assessed at a large central artery (carotid or brachial).

•  Abnormalities of Character and Volume:

•  Normal Pulse: Smooth upstroke, dome-shaped summit, and gradual downstroke with a dicrotic notch.

•  Slow-rising, Weak, and Delayed Pulse (Pulsus parvus et tardus): Caused by severe aortic stenosis (impeded ventricular emptying).

•  Collapsing / Large Volume / Bounding Pulse (Water-hammer pulse):

•  Features: Rapid upstroke, high amplitude, precipitous downstroke (collapsing quality accentuated by raising the patient's arm above the level of the heart), and a wide pulse pressure.

•  Causes:

1.  Pathological: Severe aortic regurgitation, Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA), large arteriovenous fistula, Paget’s disease of bone, ruptured sinus of Valsalva.

2.  Hyperdynamic states: Severe anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, sepsis/fever, pregnancy, wet beri-beri.

•  Jerky Pulse: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) — rapid initial percussion wave followed by dynamic mid-systolic outflow obstruction.

•  Pulsus Bisferiens (double peak in systole): Combined aortic stenosis and regurgitation, or HOCM.

•  Pulsus Paradoxus: Exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic BP (>10 mmHg). Causes: Cardiac tamponade, severe acute asthma/COPD, constrictive pericarditis.

•  Pulsus Alternans: Alternating strong and weak beats with a regular rhythm; signifies severe LV systolic failure.

•  Causes of Irregularly Irregular Pulse:

1.  Atrial fibrillation (most common — irregular in both time and volume; associated with a pulse deficit >10/min between apical rate and radial pulse).

2.  Atrial flutter with variable AV block.

3.  Multifocal atrial tachycardia (seen in severe COPD).

4.  Frequent multifocal ventricular or atrial ectopics (extrasystoles).

subject: medicine
title: 2. Conduction System of the Heart [KU 25, 22]
text:
2. Conduction System of the Heart [KU 25, 22]

•  Pathway of Electrical Activation:

Conduction system of the heart: pathway of electrical activation from the sinoatrial node to the Purkinje fibres.

•  Key Anatomical & Physiological Points:

•  SA Node: Pacemaker of the heart; supplied by the Right Coronary Artery (RCA) in 60% and Left Circumflex (LCX) in 40%.

•  Annulus Fibrosus: Fibrous skeleton electrically insulating atria from ventricles except at the AV node.

•  AV Node: Supplied by the RCA in 90% of individuals (hence inferior MI causes transient AV block).

•  His–Purkinje System: Conducts very rapidly, allowing near-simultaneous depolarisation of the entire ventricular myocardium (septum depolarises first from left to right).

subject: medicine
title: 3. Mitral Valve Apparatus [KU 24, 23]
text:
3. Mitral Valve Apparatus [KU 24, 23]

•  Components of the Mitral Valve Complex: Functional competence of the mitral valve depends on the coordinated action of 6 anatomical structures:

1.  Left Atrial Wall: Enlargement pulls the posterior leaflet away from coaptation.

2.  Mitral Annulus: Fibromuscular ring forming part of the cardiac skeleton; dilates in heart failure ("functional MR").

3.  Mitral Valve Leaflets:

•  Anterior (septal/aortic) leaflet: Larger, semicircular, continuous with the aortic root.

•  Posterior (mural) leaflet: Smaller, crescentic, divided into three scallops (P1, P2, P3); attached to 2/3rds of the annulus.

4.  Commissures: Anterolateral and posteromedial junctions where leaflets meet.

5.  Chordae Tendineae: Fibrous strings connecting valve leaflets (primary, secondary, and tertiary chordae) to the papillary muscles, preventing prolapse into the LA during systole.

6.  Papillary Muscles & Left Ventricular Myocardium:

•  Anterolateral papillary muscle: Dual blood supply (LAD and LCX).

•  Posteromedial papillary muscle: Single blood supply (PDA, usually from RCA) — hence much more prone to ischaemic rupture in inferior MI.

subject: medicine
title: 4. Apex Beat [KU 24]
text:
4. Apex Beat [KU 24]

•  Definition: The lowest and outermost point of definite cardiac impulse palpable on the chest wall, caused by the forward rotation and impact of the left ventricle against the anterior chest wall during early isovolumetric contraction.

•  Normal Site: 5th left intercostal space, 1 cm medial to the mid-clavicular line (or ~9 cm from the midline).

•  Abnormalities of the Apex Beat:

•  Thrusting / Hyperdynamic (Volume Overload): Displaced laterally and downwards, diffuse, forceful but non-sustained. Causes: Mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation, VSD.

•  Heaving (Pressure Overload): Forceful, sustained, localised (undisplaced until late heart failure). Causes: Aortic stenosis, systemic hypertension, HOCM.

•  Tapping: Palpable first heart sound (S1). Cause: Mitral stenosis.

•  Double Impulse: Palpable S4 (atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle) + systolic impulse. Cause: HOCM.

•  Dyskinetic: Displaced, uncoordinated bulge. Cause: Anterior LV aneurysm (post-MI).

•  Impalpable: Obesity, emphysema/COPD (hyperinflated chest), pericardial effusion, dextrocardia, shock.

subject: medicine
title: 5. Anatomy of Coronary Circulation [KU 21]
text:
5. Anatomy of Coronary Circulation [KU 21]

•  Origin: Arise from the left and right aortic sinuses of Valsalva just superior to the aortic valve. Coronary blood flow occurs predominantly during diastole.

•  1. Left Main Coronary Artery (LMCA): Runs for <2.5 cm and bifurcates into:

•  Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery: Runs in the anterior interventricular groove to the apex.

•  Branches: Septal perforators and Diagonal branches.

•  Territory: Anterior wall of LV, apex, and anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum.

•  Left Circumflex (LCX) Artery: Runs posteriorly in the left atrioventricular groove.

•  Branches: Obtuse marginal (OM) branches.

•  Territory: Lateral, posterior, and inferior walls of LV; supplies SA node in 40% and AV node in 10%.

•  2. Right Coronary Artery (RCA): Runs in the right atrioventricular groove.

•  Branches: Sinoatrial nodal branch (60%), Right ventricular marginal branch, AV nodal branch (90%), and Posterior Descending Artery (PDA) in 90% of people ("Right dominant circulation"; in the remaining 10%, PDA arises from LCX — "Left dominant").

•  Territory: Right atrium, Right ventricle, inferoposterior wall of LV, posterior one-third of the interventricular septum.

•  3. Venous Drainage: Coronary veins run alongside arteries, draining into the Coronary Sinus in the posterior AV groove, which empties into the right atrium.

subject: medicine
title: 6. Electrocardiogram (ECG) [KU 24]
text:
SECTION 13.2 — INVESTIGATIONS IN CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE

6. Electrocardiogram (ECG) [KU 24]

•  Principle: Records electrical depolarisation and repolarisation of the myocardium via 10 skin electrodes (4 limb, 6 chest) generating 12 leads:

•  Bipolar Limb Leads: I, II, III.

•  Augmented Unipolar Limb Leads: aVR, aVL, aVF.

•  Unipolar Precordial (Chest) Leads: V1–V2 (RV), V3–V4 (Septum/Apex), V5–V6 (LV).

•  Standard Calibration: Paper speed = 25 mm/sec (1 small square = 0.04 s; 1 large square = 0.20 s); Voltage sensitivity = 10 mm/mV. Heart rate = 300 ÷ number of large squares between R waves.

•  Components, Normal Values & Clinical Abnormalities (Systematic Reading):

1.  P Wave: Atrial depolarisation (Normal duration <0.12 s, amplitude <2.5 mm).

•  Absent: Atrial fibrillation, sinoatrial block, junctional rhythm.

•  Tall peaked (P pulmonale): Right atrial enlargement (cor pulmonale).

•  Broad, notched/bifid (P mitrale): Left atrial enlargement (mitral stenosis).

2.  PR Interval: Onset of P wave to onset of QRS (Normal: 0.12–0.20 s).

•  Prolonged (>0.20 s): First-degree AV block.

•  Shortened (<0.12 s): Pre-excitation syndromes (Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome with delta wave).

3.  QRS Complex: Ventricular depolarisation (Normal duration <0.12 s; Cardiac axis -30° to +90°).

•  Broad (≥ 0.12 s): Bundle branch block (RBBB: 'M' pattern/rSR' in V1; LBBB: 'M' pattern in V5–V6), ventricular tachycardia, ventricular pacing.

•  High Voltage (S in V1 + R in V5/V6 > 35 mm): Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH).

•  Pathological Q Waves (>1 small square wide and >25% of R wave depth): Full-thickness (transmural) myocardial infarction.

4.  ST Segment: Isoelectric period of ventricular contraction.

•  ST Elevation: Acute STEMI (convex upwards, territorial), acute pericarditis (widespread, concave upwards/saddle-shaped), Prinzmetal’s vasospastic angina, LV aneurysm (persistent).

•  ST Depression: Subendocardial ischaemia/NSTEMI, digoxin effect ("reverse tick").

5.  T Wave: Ventricular repolarisation.

•  Tall tented: Hyperkalaemia, hyperacute MI.

•  Inverted: Myocardial ischaemia, ventricular hypertrophy ("strain" pattern), bundle branch block, pulmonary embolism (S1Q3T3).

6.  QT Interval: Total duration of ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation (Normal QTc: <0.44 s in males, <0.46 s in females).

•  Prolonged: Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, congenital Long QT syndromes, drugs (amiodarone, sotalol, macrolides, tricyclics) — predisposes to Torsades de pointes.

title: 7. Cardiac Biomarkers: Cardiac Enzymes, Troponins & Brain Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) [KU 19, 18, 17, TU]
text:
7. Cardiac Biomarkers: Cardiac Enzymes, Troponins & Brain Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) [KU 19, 18, 17, TU]

A. Cardiac Troponins (cTnI and cTnT) & Cardiac Enzymes

•  Pathophysiology: Troponin I (cTnI) and Troponin T (cTnT) are structural regulatory proteins of the cardiac sarcomere (actin–myosin complex) released into the blood upon myocyte necrosis. High-sensitivity troponin (hs-cTn) assays are the gold standard for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction (AMI).

•  Kinetics of Cardiac Biomarkers Post-MI:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-001]]

•  Non-ACS Causes of Elevated Cardiac Troponin (Myocardial Injury):

•  Cardiac: Acute heart failure/pulmonary oedema, myocarditis, tachyarrhythmias, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, aortic dissection, LVH.

•  Non-cardiac: Acute pulmonary embolism (RV strain), septic shock, chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance).

B. Brain (B-type) Natriuretic Peptide (BNP & NT-proBNP)

•  Physiology: Secreted by ventricular cardiomyocytes in response to wall stretch and volume/pressure overload as a 108-amino-acid prohormone, cleaved into active BNP (32 amino acids) and inactive NT-proBNP (76 amino acids; longer half-life, more stable for laboratory assay).

•  Physiological Actions: Promotes natriuresis and diuresis, causes vasodilation, and inhibits the sympathetic nervous system and RAAS (broken down by neprilysin).

•  Clinical Applications:

1.  Diagnosis of Heart Failure: High negative predictive value — normal levels virtually rule out heart failure in an acutely breathless patient (distinguishes cardiac dyspnoea from COPD).

2.  Prognostication: Levels correlate directly with NYHA functional class, severity of LV systolic dysfunction, and mortality risk.

3.  Monitoring Therapy: Serial levels help guide heart failure treatment.

title: 8. Peripheral / Pedal Oedema: Differential Diagnosis & Evaluation [KU 25, 18, RGU]
text:
SECTION 13.3 — SYMPTOMS AND SIGNS IN CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE

8. Peripheral / Pedal Oedema: Differential Diagnosis & Evaluation [KU 25, 18, RGU]

•  Pathophysiology: Accumulation of excess interstitial fluid due to increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, decreased plasma oncotic pressure, increased capillary permeability, or lymphatic obstruction.

•  Differential Diagnosis of Peripheral Oedema:

1.  Increased Hydrostatic Pressure (Bilateral):

•  Right or biventricular heart failure, cor pulmonale, constrictive pericarditis.

•  Renal sodium and water retention (AKI, CKD, acute nephritic syndrome).

•  Venous insufficiency / varicose veins, inferior vena cava obstruction, pregnancy.

2.  Reduced Plasma Oncotic Pressure (Hypoalbuminaemia <30 g/L — Bilateral, generalised):

•  Nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria >3.5 g/day).

•  Chronic liver disease / Cirrhosis (impaired hepatic albumin synthesis).

•  Severe malnutrition (kwashiorkor) or protein-losing enteropathy / malabsorption.

3.  Increased Capillary Permeability / Drugs:

•  Calcium channel blockers: Amlodipine, nifedipine (pre-capillary arteriolar dilatation).

•  Sodium-retaining drugs: NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, fludrocortisone, pioglitazone.

•  Sepsis, angioedema.

4.  Unilateral Pedal Oedema: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT), cellulitis, chronic lymphatic obstruction (filariasis, malignancy, radiation).

5.  Non-pitting Lower Limb Oedema: Lymphoedema, hypothyroidism (myxoedema), pretibial myxoedema (Graves’ disease).

•  Clinical & Diagnostic Evaluation:

•  History: Onset, diurnal variation (worse in evening in cardiac/venous; facial puffiness in morning in renal), orthopnoea/PND (cardiac), frothy urine (nephrotic), jaundice/alcohol (hepatic), drug history (amlodipine).

•  Examination: Check pitting vs non-pitting, upper level of oedema, JVP (elevated in cardiac/renal fluid overload; normal/low in nephrotic/cirrhosis), basal lung crepitations, ascites, and hepatomegaly.

•  Investigations: Urine dipstick & spot PCR (proteinuria), RFT & electrolytes, LFT & serum albumin, ECG, Chest X-ray, NT-proBNP, Echocardiogram, and Lower limb venous Doppler (if unilateral).

subject: medicine
title: 9. Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP): Waveforms, Significance, Cannon Waves & Hepatojugular Reflux [KU 24, 23, 15, RGU]
text:
9. Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP): Waveforms, Significance, Cannon Waves & Hepatojugular Reflux [KU 24, 23, 15, RGU]

•  Principle: The internal jugular vein (IJV) is in direct, valveless continuity with the superior vena cava and right atrium (RA). Examined with the patient reclining at 45°; normal vertical height is ≤ 3 cm above the sternal angle (adding 5 cm gives RA pressure ≤ 8 cmH2O).

•  Normal JVP Waveform & Significance:

Normal jugular venous pulse waveform: a, c and v waves with x and y descents.

•  a wave: Right atrial contraction (just precedes S1 and carotid pulse).

•  c wave: Closure and upward bulging of the tricuspid valve during early isovolumetric RV contraction.

•  x descent: Atrial relaxation and downward pulling of the tricuspid annulus during RV systole.

•  v wave: Passive venous filling of the right atrium against a closed tricuspid valve during late ventricular systole.

•  y descent: Rapid passive emptying of the RA into the RV after the tricuspid valve opens in early diastole.

•  Abnormalities of JVP & Clinical Significance:

•  Elevated JVP: Right ventricular failure, biventricular heart failure, fluid overload, pericardial effusion/tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, SVC obstruction (non-pulsatile).

•  Kussmaul’s Sign: Paradoxical rise in JVP during inspiration. Causes: Constrictive pericarditis, right ventricular infarction, restrictive cardiomyopathy.

•  Prominent / Giant a waves: Forceful atrial contraction against resistance — Tricuspid stenosis, severe pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary stenosis.

•  Absent a waves: Atrial fibrillation.

•  Cannon a waves: Giant surges seen when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve (AV dissociation).

•  Regular cannon waves: Junctional rhythm, AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT).

•  Irregular cannon waves: Complete (third-degree) heart block, ventricular tachycardia (pathognomonic sign of AV dissociation).

•  Giant v waves (cv fusion wave replacing x descent):Tricuspid regurgitation (associated with pulsatile liver).

•  Rapid, deep y descent (Friedreich’s sign): Constrictive pericarditis, severe tricuspid regurgitation.

•  Slow y descent: Tricuspid stenosis, right atrial myxoma.

•  Hepatojugular (Abdominojugular) Reflux:

•  Method: Apply firm, sustained pressure over the periumbilical abdomen for 10–15 seconds while observing the JVP with the patient breathing normally.

•  Normal response: Transient rise in JVP (<3 cm) that falls back within 3–4 cardiac cycles.

•  Positive test: Sustained rise in JVP of >3–4 cm throughout compression, followed by an abrupt drop of ≥ 4 cm on release.

•  Significance: Unmasks incipient/latent right ventricular failure, RV infarction, tricuspid regurgitation, or constrictive pericarditis, and helps distinguish the venous pulse from the carotid arterial pulse.

title: 10. Heart Murmurs & Dynamic Auscultation [KU 24, 21, RGU]
text:
10. Heart Murmurs & Dynamic Auscultation [KU 24, 21, RGU]

•  Causes of Mid-Diastolic Murmur (MDM): Low-pitched, best heard with the bell of the stethoscope:

1.  Structural Valve Stenosis: Mitral stenosis (at apex, preceded by opening snap, pre-systolic accentuation), Tricuspid stenosis (lower left sternal edge, increases on inspiration).

2.  Functional Stenosis:Austin Flint murmur in severe aortic regurgitation (regurgitant jet impinges on the anterior mitral leaflet, partially closing it).

3.  Acute Valvulitis:Carey Coombs murmur in acute rheumatic fever (oedema of mitral cusps).

4.  Atrial Tumour: Left atrial myxoma (obstructing mitral orifice, associated with "tumour plop").

5.  Increased Diastolic Flow Across Non-stenosed Valve: Severe mitral regurgitation, large VSD, PDA (mitral flow murmur); large ASD (tricuspid flow murmur).

•  Continuous Murmur:

•  Definition: Begins in systole and continues without interruption through the second heart sound (S2) into all or part of diastole due to continuous blood flow from a high-pressure to a low-pressure chamber/vessel throughout the cardiac cycle. (Note: Must be distinguished from a "to-and-fro" murmur like AS+AR, which stops briefly at S2).

•  Causes:

1.  Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA): Gibson’s "machinery" murmur at the left 2nd intercostal space/infraclavicular area.

2.  Ruptured Sinus of Valsalva aneurysm into the right atrium or right ventricle.

3.  Coronary arteriovenous fistula or systemic/pulmonary AV fistula.

4.  Venous hum (benign, heard in children at base of neck; obliterated by jugular compression) or Mammary souffle (pregnancy).

•  Dynamic Auscultation in Cardiac Diseases:

•  1. Respiration:

•  Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart → accentuates Right-sided murmurs (TR, PS, TS — Carvallo’s sign).

•  Expiration increases blood flow to the left heart → accentuates Left-sided murmurs (MR, AS, AR, MS).

•  2. Valsalva Manoeuvre (Forced expiration against a closed glottis) & Standing:

•  Decreases venous return and LV end-diastolic volume → decreases intensity of almost all murmurs (especially AS), EXCEPT:

•  HOCM: Murmur becomes louder (smaller LV cavity worsens dynamic outflow tract obstruction).

•  Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP): Click moves earlier in systole and murmur becomes longer/louder.

•  3. Squatting / Passive Leg Raising:

•  Increases venous return and systemic afterload → increases AS, MR, AR murmurs; decreases HOCM murmur and delays MVP click.

•  4. Isometric Handgrip:

•  Increases systemic vascular resistance (afterload) → increases AR, MR, and VSD murmurs; decreases AS and HOCM murmurs.

title: 11. Other Cardiovascular Signs & Presentations [KU 24, 22, 19, TU]
text:
11. Other Cardiovascular Signs & Presentations [KU 24, 22, 19, TU]

•  Cyanosis: Bluish discoloration of skin and mucous membranes when absolute concentration of deoxygenated haemoglobin in capillary blood exceeds 5 g/dL (oxygen saturation usually <85–90%).

•  Central Cyanosis (warm extremities; affects tongue and lips):

•  Cardiac Causes (Right-to-left shunts): Tetralogy of Fallot, Eisenmenger’s syndrome (large VSD, PDA, ASD with reversal of shunt), Transposition of the great arteries, Tricuspid atresia, Ebstein’s anomaly.

•  Pulmonary Causes: Severe COPD, acute severe asthma, massive pneumonia, pulmonary fibrosis, acute pulmonary embolism, pulmonary AV fistula.

•  Abnormal Haemoglobin: Methaemoglobinaemia, sulphaemoglobinaemia.

•  Peripheral Cyanosis (cold extremities; tongue spared): Low cardiac output (cardiogenic shock, heart failure), cold exposure, Raynaud’s phenomenon, peripheral arterial occlusion.

•  Ortner’s Syndrome (Cardiovocal Syndrome): Hoarseness of voice and "bovine" cough caused by compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve between the enlarged pulmonary artery and a massively dilated left atrium (classically in severe mitral stenosis).

•  Cardiothoracic Ratio (CTR):

•  Definition: Ratio of the maximal horizontal width of the heart shadow to the maximal internal transverse diameter of the thoracic cage on a standard erect PA chest X-ray in full inspiration.

•  Normal value:≤ 0.5 (50%).

•  Causes of Cardiomegaly (CTR >0.5): LV or RV chamber dilatation (heart failure, valvular regurgitation, dilated cardiomyopathy), pericardial effusion (globular heart), apparent cardiomegaly (AP view, poor inspiration, pectus excavatum).

•  Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR):

•  Diagnosis of Cardiac Arrest: Unconscious, unresponsive, and absent central (carotid) pulse with absent or agonal breathing.

•  Basic Life Support (BLS): Call for help/defibrillator → High-quality chest compressions (depth 5–6 cm, rate 100–120/min, allow complete recoil, minimise interruptions) at a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio.

•  Advanced Life Support (ALS):

•  Shockable Rhythms (VF / Pulseless VT): Immediate biphasic defibrillation (150–200 J) → resume CPR for 2 mins → Adrenaline 1 mg IV and Amiodarone 300 mg IV after the 3rd shock.

•  Non-Shockable Rhythms (Asystole / Pulseless Electrical Activity): Immediate Adrenaline 1 mg IV (repeat every 3–5 mins) + continuous CPR.

•  Correct Reversible Causes (4 Hs & 4 Ts): Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo-/hyperkalaemia (metabolic), Hypothermia; Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Toxins, Thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary).

•  Syncope: Transient loss of consciousness and postural tone due to global cerebral hypoperfusion, characterised by rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery.

•  Three Principal Mechanisms:

1.  Reflex / Neurally Mediated Syncope: Vasovagal faint, carotid sinus hypersensitivity, situational syncope (cough, micturition).

2.  Orthostatic Hypotension: Hypovolaemia, autonomic neuropathy (diabetes, Parkinson’s), drugs (antihypertensives, vasodilators).

3.  Cardiac Syncope:Arrhythmias (Stokes–Adams attacks in complete heart block, sick sinus syndrome, VT) or Structural Outflow Obstruction (severe aortic stenosis, HOCM, massive pulmonary embolism, atrial myxoma).

•  Differential Diagnosis: Epileptic seizure (aura, tongue bite, prolonged post-ictal confusion), hypoglycaemia, TIA/vertebrobasilar insufficiency, psychogenic pseudosyncope.

title: 12. Major Classes of Cardiovascular Drugs [KU 21, 20, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 13.4 — CARDIOVASCULAR DRUGS

12. Major Classes of Cardiovascular Drugs [KU 21, 20, 15, TU, RGU]

A. Beta-Blockers (Class II Antiarrhythmics)

•  Classification & Examples:

•  Cardioselective (β1-selective): Bisoprolol (1.25–10 mg OD), Metoprolol (25–100 mg BD), Atenolol (25–100 mg OD), Nebivolol.

•  Non-selective (β1 + β2): Propranolol, Nadolol, Sotalol (also Class III).

•  Combined α1 + β-blockers: Carvedilol (3.125–25 mg BD), Labetalol (200–2400 mg/day).

•  Indications:

1.  Cardiovascular: Angina pectoris, Acute myocardial infarction (reduces infarct size and mortality), Chronic stable heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (Bisoprolol, Carvedilol, Metoprolol — reduces mortality by 33%), Tachyarrhythmias (rate control in AF/flutter, SVT, VT prophylaxis, Long QT syndrome), Aortic dissection, HOCM, Marfan syndrome, Hypertension (if compelling indication present).

2.  Non-cardiac: Thyrotoxicosis (propranolol), Portal hypertension/variceal prophylaxis (propranolol/carvedilol), Migraine prophylaxis, Essential tremor, Anxiety.

•  Contraindications: Bronchial asthma, Acute decompensated heart failure / pulmonary oedema, Second- or third-degree AV block, Severe sinus bradycardia (<50/min), Cardiogenic shock, Severe peripheral arterial disease / Raynaud’s phenomenon, Cocaine toxicity or Phaeochromocytoma (without prior α-blockade).

B. ACE Inhibitors & Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs)

•  Examples & Doses:

•  ACE Inhibitors: Ramipril (1.25–10 mg OD), Enalapril (2.5–20 mg BD), Lisinopril (2.5–40 mg OD), Perindopril.

•  ARBs: Losartan (25–100 mg OD), Telmisartan (20–80 mg OD), Valsartan (40–160 mg BD), Candesartan (4–32 mg OD).

•  Mechanism: ACE inhibitors block conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II and inhibit bradykinin degradation; ARBs selectively block the AT1 receptor (hence no bradykinin accumulation and no dry cough). Both cause efferent glomerular arteriolar dilatation, reduce preload/afterload, and inhibit aldosterone-mediated cardiac/renal remodelling.

•  Indications: Hypertension (first-line in <55 yrs or with diabetes), Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, Post-MI ventricular dysfunction, Diabetic nephropathy and proteinuric CKD, Scleroderma renal crisis.

•  Contraindications:

1.  Pregnancy and breastfeeding (teratogenic — oligohydramnios, fetal renal dysplasia).

2.  Bilateral renal artery stenosis (or unilateral stenosis in a solitary kidney — precipitates acute renal failure).

3.  Hyperkalaemia (K+ > 5.5 mmol/L).

4.  History of angioedema (with ACE inhibitors).

C. Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs)

•  Examples & Doses:

•  Dihydropyridines (Vascular selective):Amlodipine (2.5–10 mg OD), Nifedipine (30–90 mg SR OD), Nicardipine (20–40 mg TDS).

•  Non-dihydropyridines (Rate-limiting / Myocardial selective):Verapamil (40–120 mg TDS or 240 mg SR OD), Diltiazem (60–120 mg TDS or 200–400 mg SR OD).

•  Uses: Hypertension (first-line in >55 yrs), Chronic stable angina, Prinzmetal’s vasospastic angina, SVT and rate control in AF (Verapamil, Diltiazem), Raynaud’s phenomenon (Nifedipine).

•  Side Effects: Pedal oedema, flushing, headache (dihydropyridines); bradycardia, AV block, constipation, negative inotropy/worsening heart failure (verapamil/diltiazem — never combine with β-blockers).

D. HMG-CoA Reductase Inhibitors (Statins)

•  Examples: Atorvastatin (10–80 mg OD), Rosuvastatin (5–40 mg OD), Simvastatin (20–40 mg nocte).

•  Mechanism: Competitively inhibit hepatic 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis → depletes intracellular cholesterol → upregulates hepatic LDL receptors → lowers LDL-C by up to 60%, reduces triglycerides by up to 40%, increases HDL-C by 10%, and exerts pleiotropic effects (plaque stabilisation, anti-inflammatory, improved endothelial function).

•  Indications: Secondary prevention in all patients with established ASCVD (ACS, stable angina, stroke, PAD); Primary prevention in diabetes (>40 yrs), familial hypercholesterolaemia, CKD, and 10-year CVD risk ≥ 10%.

•  Adverse Effects: Myalgia, myositis, rhabdomyolysis (monitor CK if symptomatic; risk increased with fibrates, macrolides, ciclosporin), asymptomatic elevation of hepatic transaminases (ALT >3× ULN warrants cessation), slight increase in new-onset type 2 diabetes; contraindicated in pregnancy.

E. Antihypertensives Safe in Pregnancy & Parenteral Antihypertensives

•  Four Antihypertensives Safe in Pregnancy:

1.  Labetalol (oral or IV — first-line).

2.  Nifedipine (modified-release oral).

3.  Alpha-methyldopa (oral).

4.  Hydralazine (oral or parenteral).

•  Parenteral Antihypertensive Drugs (for Hypertensive Emergencies):

1.  IV Labetalol (2 mg/min infusion up to 200 mg).

2.  IV Sodium Nitroprusside (0.3–1.0 µg/kg/min).

3.  IV Glyceryl Trinitrate (GTN) (10–200 µg/min — drug of choice in ACS/acute pulmonary oedema).

4.  IV/IM Hydralazine or IV Nicardipine / Esmolol.

(Note: Classification of Antiarrhythmic Drugs is covered in detail under Question 14).

subject: medicine
title: 13. Heart Failure (Chronic & Acute Pulmonary Oedema) [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 17, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 13.5 — HEART FAILURE

13. Heart Failure (Chronic & Acute Pulmonary Oedema) [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 17, 16, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignettes: 60M with CAD; 45M with raised JVP, S3, basal creps & hepatomegaly; 55M smoker with sudden pink frothy sputum & LV S3; 65F/56M with progressive dyspnoea & pedal oedema)

1. Definition & Classification

•  Definition: A clinical syndrome that develops when the heart cannot maintain an adequate cardiac output to meet the metabolic demands of the tissues, or can do so only at the expense of an elevated ventricular filling pressure.

•  Classification:

•  By Anatomical Side:

1.  Left Heart Failure (LVF): Reduction in LV output and increase in LA and pulmonary venous pressure → pulmonary congestion/oedema.

2.  Right Heart Failure (RVF): Reduction in RV output and increase in RA and systemic venous pressure → raised JVP, congestive hepatomegaly, peripheral pitting oedema (Cor pulmonale when secondary to chronic lung disease).

3.  Biventricular (Congestive) Heart Failure (CCF): Both ventricles affected (either primary global pathology like dilated cardiomyopathy/IHD, or RV failure secondary to chronic LV failure).

•  By Ejection Fraction: HFrEF (EF ≤ 40% — systolic dysfunction) vs HFpEF (EF ≥ 50% — diastolic dysfunction/stiff ventricle).

•  By Output: Low-output HF vs High-output HF.

•  By Time Course: Acute HF (e.g., post-MI) vs Chronic HF (compensated vs acute-on-chronic decompensation).

2. Aetiology & Mechanisms of Heart Failure (Davidson Box 16.12)

1.  Reduced Ventricular Contractility (Myocardial Disease): Coronary artery disease / Myocardial infarction (segmental akinesia/dyskinesia), Myocarditis, Dilated cardiomyopathy (alcohol, idiopathic, post-partum, doxorubicin).

2.  Ventricular Outflow Obstruction (Pressure Overload):

•  Left: Systemic hypertension, Aortic stenosis, HOCM.

•  Right: Pulmonary hypertension, Pulmonary valve stenosis.

3.  Ventricular Inflow Obstruction: Mitral stenosis, Tricuspid stenosis, Endomyocardial fibrosis.

4.  Ventricular Volume Overload:

•  Left: Mitral regurgitation, Aortic regurgitation, VSD, PDA.

•  Right: Atrial septal defect, Tricuspid regurgitation.

5.  Diastolic Dysfunction (Impaired Filling): Left ventricular hypertrophy/fibrosis, Restrictive cardiomyopathy (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis), Constrictive pericarditis, Cardiac tamponade.

6.  Arrhythmias: Atrial fibrillation (loss of atrial kick + rapid rate), Tachycardiomyopathy, Complete heart block.

7.  High-Output States: Severe anaemia, Thyrotoxicosis, Wet beri-beri (thiamine deficiency), Paget’s disease, Large AV fistula.

•  Factors Precipitating Acute Decompensation of Chronic Stable Heart Failure:

•  Acute myocardial ischaemia or infarction.

•  Onset of arrhythmias (especially Atrial Fibrillation).

•  Non-adherence or inappropriate reduction of heart failure medications/dietary salt excess.

•  Intercurrent infection (e.g., pneumonia, UTI).

•  Pulmonary embolism.

•  Administration of negative inotropes (β-blockers, verapamil) or fluid-retaining drugs (NSAIDs, steroids).

•  Development of high-output states (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy) or IV fluid overload.

3. Pathophysiology & Compensatory Mechanisms

•  Starling’s Law: Initially, increased preload (end-diastolic volume) stretches sarcomeres to maintain stroke volume. In heart failure, the Starling curve shifts downwards and to the right; overstretching leads to declining performance and pulmonary/systemic congestion.

•  Neurohumoral Activation (Vicious Circle of Heart Failure):

1.  Sympathetic Nervous System (SNS) Activation: Increases heart rate and contractility initially, but chronically causes arteriolar vasoconstriction (increased afterload), myocyte apoptosis, myocardial fibrosis, and fatal arrhythmias.

2.  Renin–Angiotensin–Aldosterone System (RAAS) Activation: Renal hypoperfusion stimulates renin → Angiotensin II (potent vasoconstrictor → increases afterload) and Aldosterone (causes renal sodium and water retention → increases preload/oedema, potassium wasting, and myocardial fibrosis).

3.  Vasopressin (ADH) & Endothelin-1 Release: Causes further vasoconstriction and free water retention (hyponatraemia).

4.  Counter-regulatory Natriuretic Peptides (ANP & BNP): Released by stretched atria and ventricles to promote natriuresis and vasodilation, but are overwhelmed in advanced HF (degraded by neprilysin).

5.  Ventricular Remodelling: Hypertrophy of non-infarcted myocardium with thinning, dilatation, and functional mitral/tricuspid regurgitation.

4. Clinical Features

•  Symptoms:

•  Left-sided: Exertional dyspnoea, Orthopnoea, Paroxysmal Nocturnal Dyspnoea (PND), nocturnal cough with pink frothy sputum (in acute pulmonary oedema), wheeze ("cardiac asthma").

•  Right-sided: Bilateral ankle/sacral swelling, abdominal distension (ascites), right upper quadrant ache (hepatic congestion).

•  Low Cardiac Output / Systemic: Fatigue, poor effort tolerance, anorexia, weight loss ("cardiac cachexia"), oliguria, nocturia, confusion.

•  NYHA Functional Classification of Dyspnoea:

•  Class I: No limitation during ordinary physical activity.

•  Class II: Slight limitation during ordinary activity (comfortable at rest).

•  Class III: Marked limitation of normal activities (less than ordinary activity causes symptoms; comfortable at rest).

•  Class IV: Unable to undertake any physical activity without symptoms; symptoms present even at rest.

•  Physical Signs:

•  General: Tachypnoea, sinus tachycardia, cold/clammy/cyanosed peripheries, narrow pulse pressure, pulsus alternans.

•  Neck:Elevated JVP (with prominent a and v waves, and positive hepatojugular reflux).

•  Precordium: Displaced apex beat (cardiomegaly), Third heart sound (S3 gallop rhythm), pansystolic murmur of functional MR or TR.

•  Lungs: Bilateral fine basal end-inspiratory crepitations (extending throughout lung fields in acute pulmonary oedema), expiratory wheeze, stony dullness of pleural effusions.

•  Abdomen & Limbs:Tender, smooth, pulsatile hepatomegaly, ascites, bilateral pitting pedal or sacral oedema.

5. Investigations

1.  Chest X-Ray (Erect PA):

•  Alveolar oedema (bilateral perihilar "bat’s wing" hazy opacification).

•  B — Kerley B lines (horizontal interstitial septal lines in the costophrenic angles due to dilated lymphatics).

•  Cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio >0.5).

•  Distended upper lobe pulmonary veins (upper lobe blood diversion).

•  Effusions (bilateral or right-sided pleural effusions, interlobar fissure fluid).

2.  12-Lead ECG: Assesses for acute/prior MI (pathological Q waves, ST–T changes), LVH, LBBB (indicates dyssynchrony), or arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation).

3.  Cardiac Biomarkers:

•  Serum NT-proBNP / BNP: Markedly elevated (confirms diagnosis and predicts prognosis).

•  Serum Troponin I/T: To rule out acute coronary syndrome as the precipitant.

4.  Transthoracic Echocardiography (2D + Doppler) — Pivotal Investigation:

•  Quantifies LV ejection fraction (LVEF), chamber dimensions, regional wall motion abnormalities (CAD), valvular lesions (AS, MS, MR, AR), pulmonary artery systolic pressure, and pericardial disease.

5.  Blood Tests: U&Es (renal impairment, hypokalaemia from diuretics, hyperkalaemia from RAAS blockers, dilutional hyponatraemia), FBC (anaemia), TFTs (thyrotoxicosis/hypothyroidism), LFTs (congestive hepatopathy), Fasting glucose/HbA1c and Lipid profile.

6. Management

##### A. Emergency Management of Acute Left Ventricular Failure / Acute Pulmonary Oedema [KU 25, 24, 22, 17, TU]

•  Immediate Resuscitation:

1.  Posture: Sit the patient upright with legs dependent (reduces venous return/preload).

2.  High-Flow Oxygen: Administer 60–100% O2 via face mask to maintain SpO2 94–98%.

3.  Non-Invasive Ventilation:Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) at 5–10 mmHg via tight-fitting mask (reduces preload, decreases work of breathing, and forces fluid out of alveoli).

4.  Intravenous Loop Diuretic:Furosemide 50–100 mg IV stat (followed by infusion 5–10 mg/hr) — produces rapid venodilation (within 15 mins, reducing preload) followed by potent diuresis.

5.  Intravenous Vasodilators (if SBP >110 mmHg):IV Glyceryl Trinitrate (GTN) infusion 10–200 µg/min (or sublingual GTN initially), titrated every 10 mins (reduces both preload and afterload).

6.  Intravenous Opiates (use sparingly only in severe agitation/distress): Morphine 2.5–5 mg IV slowly with metoclopramide 10 mg IV (reduces sympathetic drive and venodilates, but risk of respiratory depression).

7.  Inotropes & Mechanical Support (if hypotensive / Cardiogenic Shock, SBP <90 mmHg):

•  Dobutamine infusion (2.5–10 µg/kg/min) to augment contractility.

•  Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) counterpulsation and urgent coronary revascularisation (if ACS-induced).

8.  Treat Precipitating Cause: Urgent DC cardioversion for rapid AF/VT, primary PCI for STEMI.

##### B. Management of Chronic Heart Failure [KU 24, 21, 16, RGU]

•  1. General & Non-Pharmacological Measures:

•  Patient education, daily weight monitoring, salt restriction (<2–3 g/day), fluid restriction (1.5 L/day in severe HF/hyponatraemia), smoking cessation, alcohol abstinence, regular moderate aerobic exercise (cardiac rehabilitation), and Influenza, COVID-19, and Pneumococcal vaccinations.

•  2. Pharmacological Therapy (The Four Pillars of Disease-Modifying Therapy in HFrEF + Diuretics):

•  Symptomatic Relief (Fluid Overload):

•  Loop Diuretics: Furosemide (40–160 mg/day) or Torasemide/Bumetanide. In resistant oedema, combine with a thiazide (Bendroflumethiazide/Metolazone) for sequential nephron blockade.

•  Pillar 1 — RAAS / Neprilysin Inhibition (Reduces Afterload, Preload & Remodelling):

•  ARNI (Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibitor):Sacubitril–Valsartan (start 24/26 mg BD, target 97/103 mg BD) — prevents breakdown of endogenous ANP/BNP while blocking AT1 receptors; superior mortality benefit over ACE inhibitors alone.

•  ACE Inhibitors: Enalapril (target 10 mg BD), Ramipril (target 10 mg OD), or Lisinopril (reduces mortality by ~20%).

•  ARBs: Losartan, Valsartan, or Candesartan (if ACEi intolerant due to cough).

•  Pillar 2 — Beta-Blockers (Counteract Sympathetic Toxicity & Sudden Death):

•  Bisoprolol (start 1.25 mg OD → target 10 mg OD), Carvedilol (start 3.125 mg BD → target 25 mg BD), or Metoprolol succinate (start low and titrate slowly over 12 weeks once euvolaemic; reduces mortality by 33%).

•  Pillar 3 — Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists (MRAs):

•  Spironolactone or Eplerenone (25–50 mg OD) — blocks aldosterone-induced myocardial fibrosis and potassium loss; significantly reduces mortality in severe HF and post-MI HF (monitor K+).

•  Pillar 4 — SGLT2 Inhibitors:

•  Dapagliflozin (10 mg OD) or Empagliflozin (10 mg OD) — promotes osmotic diuresis/natriuresis and improves myocardial energetics; reduces HF hospitalisation and cardiovascular mortality irrespective of diabetes status (in both HFrEF and HFpEF).

•  Adjunctive Pharmacotherapy:

•  Ivabradine (If channel blocker, 2.5–7.5 mg BD): Reduces SA nodal rate; indicated in patients in sinus rhythm with HR >75/min despite maximal β-blocker (or β-blocker intolerance).

•  Hydralazine + Isosorbide Dinitrate: Combined arterial and venous vasodilators; used when ACEi/ARBs are contraindicated (e.g., severe renal failure/hyperkalaemia).

•  Digoxin (0.0625–0.25 mg OD): For ventricular rate control in coexisting AF, or to reduce hospitalisations in NYHA Class III–IV (no mortality benefit).

•  3. Device & Surgical Therapies:

•  Cardiac Resynchronisation Therapy (CRT-P / CRT-D — Biventricular Pacing): Paces RV and LV (via coronary sinus lead) simultaneously; indicated in NYHA II–IV, LVEF ≤ 35%, sinus rhythm with LBBB (QRS ≥ 130–150 ms) — improves symptoms and survival.

•  Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator (ICD): Primary prevention of sudden arrhythmic death in LVEF ≤ 35% despite optimal medical therapy, or secondary prevention in survivors of VT/VF arrest.

•  Coronary Revascularisation (CABG / PCI): For "hibernating" viable myocardium.

•  Ventricular Assist Devices (LVAD) & Cardiac Transplantation: For refractory end-stage HF in young patients.

7. Complications of Heart Failure

•  Renal impairment (cardiorenal syndrome), Electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia, dilutional hyponatraemia), Congestive hepatopathy / cardiac cirrhosis, Thromboembolism (DVT, pulmonary embolism, systemic stroke), Atrial fibrillation, and Malignant ventricular arrhythmias (VT/VF) causing sudden cardiac death (50% of deaths).

title: 14. Digoxin & High-Altitude Pulmonary Oedema [KU 24, 20]
text:
14. Digoxin & High-Altitude Pulmonary Oedema [KU 24, 20]

•  Digoxin — Uses & Toxicity:

•  Mechanism: Cardiac glycoside (from Digitalis lanata) that inhibits sarcolemmal Na+/K+-ATPase → increases intracellular Na+ and Ca2+ (positive inotropic effect) and enhances vagal tone at the AV node (slows AV conduction and prolongs refractory period).

•  Clinical Uses:

1.  Ventricular rate control in Atrial Fibrillation and Atrial Flutter (especially with coexisting heart failure or sedentary elderly patients).

2.  Severe chronic Heart Failure (NYHA Class III–IV) in sinus rhythm to reduce hospital admissions.

•  Predisposing Factors for Toxicity: Renal impairment (renally excreted), hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypothyroidism, old age, drugs (amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine).

•  Features of Digoxin Toxicity:

•  Extracardiac: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, and Xanthopsia (yellow-green halos around visual objects).

•  Cardiac (Arrhythmias): Sinus bradycardia, AV nodal block, Ventricular bigeminy / multifocal ectopics, Atrial tachycardia with variable (2:1) AV block (classic), Bidirectional VT, Ventricular fibrillation. (Note: Down-sloping "reverse tick" ST depression is the "digoxin effect" and does not indicate toxicity).

•  Management of Toxicity: Stop digoxin, correct hypokalaemia, atropine/temporary pacing for bradyarrhythmias, lidocaine for ventricular arrhythmias, and Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digibind) in life-threatening toxicity.

•  High-Altitude Pulmonary Oedema (HAPE):

•  Pathogenesis: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema occurring in unacclimatised individuals ascending rapidly above 2500–3000 metres. Hypobaric hypoxia causes uneven, exaggerated hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction → severe pulmonary arterial hypertension → capillary stress failure and leakage of high-protein fluid into alveoli (with normal LA pressure/PCWP).

•  Clinical Features: Onset 2–4 days after ascent; dry cough progressing to dyspnoea at rest, pink frothy sputum, cyanosis, tachycardia, low-grade fever, and diffuse lung crepitations.

•  Management:Immediate descent (at least 500–1000 m), high-flow oxygen, portable hyperbaric chamber (Gamow bag), and pulmonary vasodilators (Nifedipine 20 mg SR BD/TDS or Sildenafil/Tadalafil). (Diuretics are NOT indicated).

title: 15. Classification of Antiarrhythmic Drugs (Vaughan Williams) [KU 21, 18, 17]
text:
SECTION 13.6 — CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIAS

15. Classification of Antiarrhythmic Drugs (Vaughan Williams) [KU 21, 18, 17]

•  Class I — Sodium (Na+) Channel Blockers (Membrane-stabilising agents):

•  Class Ia (Block Na+ channel + prolong action potential): Quinidine, Disopyramide, Procainamide. (Uses: AF/VT; Side effects: anticholinergic effects, QT prolongation/Torsades).

•  Class Ib (Block Na+ channel + shorten action potential; act selectively on ischaemic/depolarised ventricular tissue): Lidocaine (IV bolus 50–100 mg), Mexiletine. (Uses: Acute ischaemic VT/VF; Side effects: CNS toxicity — tremor, convulsions).

•  Class Ic (Potent Na+ channel block with no effect on action potential duration): Flecainide, Propafenone. (Uses: Pharmacological cardioversion of recent-onset AF ["pill-in-the-pocket"], WPW syndrome; Contraindicated in structural/ischaemic heart disease due to pro-arrhythmic mortality risk).

•  Class II — Beta-Adrenoceptor Antagonists (β-Blockers):

•  Examples: Bisoprolol, Metoprolol, Atenolol, Propranolol, Esmolol.

•  Action: Suppress SA nodal automaticity, slow AV nodal conduction, and prevent catecholamine-induced arrhythmias (SVT, AF rate control, post-MI VT prophylaxis, Long QT syndrome).

•  Class III — Potassium (K+) Channel Blockers (Prolong Action Potential & Refractory Period):

•  Examples:Amiodarone, Dronedarone, Sotalol (also Class II).

•  Amiodarone [KU 18]:

•  Pharmacology: Possesses Class I, II, III, and IV actions; minimal negative inotropy (safe in severe LV dysfunction); extremely long tissue half-life (25–110 days).

•  Uses: Rhythm control in AF/flutter, life-threatening or refractory VT and cardiac arrest (shock-refractory VF/pVT).

•  Dose: IV 300 mg over 20–60 mins, then 900 mg over 24 hrs via central line; Oral 200 mg TDS for 1 wk → 200 mg BD for 1 wk → 100–200 mg OD maintenance.

•  Adverse Effects: Corneal microdeposits (universal, reversible), Photosensitivity and slate-grey skin discoloration, Thyroid dysfunction (Type I & II thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism), Pulmonary fibrosis/alveolitis, Hepatotoxicity, Peripheral neuropathy, QT prolongation (low risk of Torsades), and Drug interactions (inhibits metabolism of Warfarin and Digoxin — halve their doses).

•  Class IV — Slow Calcium (Ca2+) Channel Blockers:

•  Examples:Verapamil, Diltiazem.

•  Action: Slow conduction and prolong refractoriness in SA and AV nodes. Used for termination/prophylaxis of SVT and rate control in AF.

•  Unclassified Antiarrhythmic Agents:

•  Adenosine (A1 receptor agonist — transient complete AV block to terminate SVT).

•  Digoxin (enhances vagal tone at AV node — AF rate control).

•  Atropine (muscarinic antagonist — sinus bradycardia/AV block).

•  Ivabradine (If channel blocker in SA node).

•  Magnesium Sulphate (drug of choice for Torsades de pointes).

subject: medicine
title: 16. Atrial Fibrillation (AF) [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 18, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
16. Atrial Fibrillation (AF) [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 18, 16, TU, RGU]

•  Definition & Classification: The most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia, characterised by uncoordinated, rapid atrial activation (350–600/min) with loss of mechanical atrial contraction and an irregular ventricular response.

•  Paroxysmal AF: Self-terminating within 7 days (usually <48 hrs).

•  Persistent AF: Lasts >7 days or requires electrical/pharmacological cardioversion.

•  Permanent AF: Accepted by patient and physician; rhythm control no longer pursued.

•  Pathogenesis: Initiated by rapid ectopic firing arising from muscular sleeves in the pulmonary veins and sustained by multiple interacting re-entry wavelets within structurally remodelled/fibrosed atria.

•  Causes of Atrial Fibrillation ([KU 25] — Mnemonic: PIRATES):

1.  Valvular Heart Disease: Especially Rheumatic Mitral Stenosis and mitral regurgitation.

2.  Hypertension and Coronary Artery Disease (including acute MI).

3.  Heart Failure & Cardiomyopathies (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive).

4.  Endocrine / Metabolic:Thyrotoxicosis (may be occult in elderly), Obesity, Diabetes mellitus, Electrolyte disturbances.

5.  Respiratory Disease: Pneumonia, Pulmonary embolism, COPD, Obstructive sleep apnoea.

6.  Toxins: Acute or chronic Alcohol excess ("Holiday heart syndrome"), Caffeine.

7.  Other: Sinoatrial disease ("tachy-brady syndrome"), Atrial septal defect, Pericarditis, Post-cardiothoracic surgery, Idiopathic ("Lone AF").

•  Clinical Features:

•  Symptoms: Palpitations, breathlessness, fatigue, chest pain (rate-related ischaemia), dizziness/syncope, or acute decompensation of heart failure (due to loss of atrial kick and shortened diastolic filling time). May be asymptomatic and present with an embolic stroke.

•  Signs:

1.  Irregularly irregular pulse (varying in both timing and volume).

2.  Apex–radial pulse deficit >10 beats/min (weak LV contractions fail to open the aortic valve).

3.  Absent a waves on JVP.

4.  Variable intensity of the first heart sound (S1) and absence of fourth heart sound (S4) or pre-systolic accentuation in mitral stenosis.

•  Investigations:

•  12-Lead ECG ([KU 24]):

1.  Absent P waves, replaced by chaotic, fine or coarse baseline fibrillation (f) waves (350–600/min, best seen in V1).

2.  Irregularly irregular (completely random) R–R intervals with narrow QRS complexes (unless pre-existing bundle branch block or WPW accessory pathway).

•  24-hour Holter / Ambulatory ECG: If paroxysmal AF suspected.

•  Transthoracic Echocardiogram: To assess LA size, mitral valve disease, and LV systolic function (Transoesophageal echo [TOE] to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus prior to cardioversion).

•  Blood Tests:Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4), U&Es (K+, Mg2+), FBC, Coagulation profile.

•  Management of Atrial Fibrillation ([KU 18, 16]):

•  1. Acute / Emergency Management:

•  Haemodynamically unstable (SBP <90 mmHg, acute pulmonary oedema, ongoing ischaemia): Immediate Synchronised DC Cardioversion (120–150 J biphasic) under sedation/anaesthesia + IV heparin.

•  Stable, onset <24–48 hours: Pharmacological cardioversion with IV Flecainide (2 mg/kg over 30 mins, max 150 mg — only if no structural/ischaemic heart disease) or IV Amiodarone (if structural heart disease present), OR DC cardioversion.

•  Onset >48 hours (or unknown duration): Do NOT cardiovert immediately due to risk of thromboembolism. Either anticoagulate for a minimum of 3 weeks prior to cardioversion (and continue for at least 4 weeks post-cardioversion), or perform TOE to rule out LA appendage thrombus before cardioversion.

•  2. Long-Term Strategy — Rate Control vs Rhythm Control:

•  Rate Control Strategy (First-line for Permanent AF & Elderly [KU 18]):

•  First-line:Beta-blockers (Bisoprolol 2.5–10 mg OD, Metoprolol) OR Rate-limiting Calcium Channel Blockers (Verapamil 40–120 mg TDS, Diltiazem 200–400 mg OD — avoid CCBs in HFrEF).

•  Second-line / Add-on:Digoxin (0.0625–0.25 mg OD — controls resting rate but poor control during exercise; useful in heart failure).

•  Refractory cases:"Pace and Ablate" — permanent pacemaker implantation followed by catheter ablation of the AV node.

•  Rhythm Control Strategy (Preferred in young, symptomatic, paroxysmal/recent-onset AF, or reversible cause):

•  Pharmacological maintenance of sinus rhythm: β-blockers, Flecainide or Propafenone (if normal heart), Sotalol, Dronedarone, or Amiodarone (most effective, used if LV dysfunction present).

•  Catheter Ablation:Pulmonary Vein Isolation (PVI) using radiofrequency, cryoablation, or pulsed-field ablation (electroporation) — 75% success in paroxysmal AF; improves survival in HFrEF.

•  3. Stroke Prevention (Thromboembolism Prophylaxis):

•  Valvular AF (Moderate-to-severe Mitral Stenosis or Mechanical Prosthetic Valve): Mandatory lifelong Warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0 for MS; DOACs are contraindicated).

•  Non-Valvular AF: Assess stroke risk using the CHA2DS2-VA Score (Davidson 25e update):

•  Congestive heart failure / LV dysfunction = 1

•  Hypertension = 1

•  Age ≥ 75 years = 2

•  Diabetes mellitus = 1

•  Stroke / TIA / systemic thromboembolism history = 2

•  Vascular disease (prior MI, PAD, aortic plaque) = 1

•  Age 65–74 years = 1

•  (Interpretation: Score 0 = No anticoagulation; Score 1 = Consider oral anticoagulation; Score ≥ 2 = Oral anticoagulation strongly recommended. Assess bleeding risk using HAS-BLED score).

•  Choice of Oral Anticoagulant:Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) — Apixaban (5 mg BD), Rivaroxaban (20 mg OD), Edoxaban (60 mg OD), or Dabigatran (150 mg BD) are preferred over Warfarin (INR 2.0–3.0) due to lower intracranial bleeding risk and no need for INR monitoring. (Aspirin monotherapy is ineffective and obsolete).
