title: 17. Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT) [KU 24, 17, RGU]
text:
17. Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT) [KU 24, 17, RGU]

•  Definition & Types: Regular narrow-complex tachycardias (QRS <0.12 s, rate 140–240/min) originating above or involving the AV node:

1.  AV Nodal Re-entrant Tachycardia (AVNRT — most common): Micro-re-entry circuit within the AV node involving a "slow" pathway (antegrade) and a "fast" pathway (retrograde).

2.  AV Re-entrant Tachycardia (AVRT — e.g., Wolff–Parkinson–White [WPW] Syndrome): Macro-re-entry circuit using the AV node antegradely and an accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) retrogradely (orthodromic AVRT — narrow QRS). In sinus rhythm, WPW shows a short PR interval (<0.12 s) and a slurred upstroke of the QRS (Delta wave).

3.  Focal Atrial Tachycardia.

•  Clinical Features: Abrupt onset and termination of rapid, regular, forceful palpitations, dizziness, chest discomfort, dyspnoea, and polyuria (due to atrial stretch releasing ANP).

•  ECG Findings: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia (140–240/min); P waves are either buried within the QRS complex or appear as a pseudo-r' wave in V1.

•  Management ([KU 17]):

•  1. Acute Termination:

•  Haemodynamically Unstable (hypotension, pulmonary oedema): Immediate Synchronised DC Cardioversion.

•  Haemodynamically Stable:

1.  Vagal Manoeuvres:Carotid sinus massage (after excluding carotid bruit) or Modified Valsalva manoeuvre (increases vagal tone and transiently blocks the AV node).

2.  Intravenous Adenosine (Drug of Choice):6 mg rapid IV bolus into a large-bore cannula followed by rapid saline flush; if unsuccessful after 1–2 mins, give 12 mg IV, and a further 12–18 mg IV if needed. (Side effects: transient facial flushing, chest tightness, bronchospasm — contraindicated in asthma; potentiated by dipyridamole, antagonised by theophylline).

3.  Alternatives (if Adenosine contraindicated/fails):IV Verapamil (5–10 mg over 2 mins) or IV Beta-blocker (Metoprolol 5 mg / Esmolol). (Note: Avoid verapamil and digoxin in WPW with pre-excited AF as they accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway, precipitating VF).

•  2. Long-Term Prevention:

•  Catheter Ablation (Treatment of Choice): Radiofrequency ablation of the slow AV nodal pathway (in AVNRT) or accessory pathway (in WPW) — curative in >95%.

•  Pharmacological Prophylaxis: Oral β-blockers, Verapamil/Diltiazem, or Flecainide/Propafenone.

subject: medicine
title: 18. Ventricular Tachycardia (VT) & Torsades de Pointes [KU 25, 23, TU]
text:
18. Ventricular Tachycardia (VT) & Torsades de Pointes [KU 25, 23, TU]

•  Definition: Three or more consecutive ventricular beats at a rate >100–120/min with broad QRS complexes (≥ 0.12 s). Sustained VT lasts >30 seconds or causes haemodynamic collapse.

•  Aetiology:

•  Ischaemic Heart Disease (most common): Acute MI (triggered activity/automaticity) or scar-mediated re-entry from prior MI.

•  Cardiomyopathies: Dilated, Hypertrophic (HOCM), Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC).

•  Channelopathies / Normal Heart VT: Long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) VT.

•  Metabolic / Drugs: Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, digoxin toxicity.

•  ECG Features Favouring VT over SVT with Aberrancy:

1.  AV dissociation (P waves marching independently of QRS — pathognomonic).

2.  Capture beats (occasional normal narrow QRS) and Fusion beats (hybrid QRS complex — pathognomonic).

3.  Very broad QRS complexes (>140 ms in RBBB pattern or >160 ms in LBBB pattern).

4.  Positive or negative concordance across all chest leads (V1–V6) and extreme axis deviation ("northwest axis").

5.  History of prior myocardial infarction.

•  Management of Ventricular Tachycardia ([KU 23]):

•  1. Acute Management:

•  Pulseless VT: Treat as cardiac arrest — Unsynchronised Defibrillation (150–200 J) + CPR.

•  Haemodynamically Unstable VT (SBP <90 mmHg, chest pain, heart failure): Immediate Synchronised DC Cardioversion under sedation.

•  Haemodynamically Stable Monomorphic VT:

•  IV Amiodarone: 300 mg (5 mg/kg) over 20–60 mins, followed by 900 mg infusion over 24 hrs.

•  IV Lidocaine: 50–100 mg bolus, followed by infusion (alternative if amiodarone unavailable, though may depress LV function).

•  Correct hypokalaemia (K+ > 4.5 mmol/L), hypomagnesaemia, hypoxia, and acidosis. If drugs fail, perform elective DC cardioversion.

•  2. Long-Term Prevention:

•  Beta-blockers + Amiodarone (Class Ic drugs are contraindicated in post-MI/structural heart disease).

•  Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator (ICD): Indicated in all survivors of VT with haemodynamic compromise or LVEF ≤ 35%.

•  Catheter Ablation: Curative in idiopathic RVOT/fascicular VT; adjunctive in scar-related VT.

•  Torsades de Pointes ("Twisting of the Points") [TU]:

•  Definition: Polymorphic VT occurring in the setting of prolonged QT interval, where QRS complexes twist progressively around the isoelectric baseline; may degenerate into VF.

•  Causes: Congenital Long QT syndromes (LQT1–3), Electrolyte depletion (↓ K+, ↓ Mg2+, ↓ Ca2+), Bradycardia, and QT-prolonging drugs (Class Ia/III antiarrhythmics [sotalol, quinidine], macrolides, fluoroquinolones, tricyclics, antipsychotics, hydroxychloroquine).

•  Management:

1.  IV Magnesium Sulphate (First-line treatment of choice):8 mmol (2 g) IV over 10–15 mins, followed by infusion of 72 mmol over 24 hrs (effective even if serum Mg2+ is normal).

2.  Stop all QT-prolonging drugs and correct hypokalaemia.

3.  Temporary transvenous overdrive pacing (at 90–110/min) or IV Isoprenaline infusion (increases heart rate, which shortens the QT interval; avoid isoprenaline in congenital Long QT syndrome, where β-blockers and ICD are used).

subject: medicine
title: 19. Bradycardia, Sick Sinus Syndrome, Complete Heart Block, Stokes–Adams Syndrome & Pacemakers [KU 22, 21, 20, RGU]
text:
19. Bradycardia, Sick Sinus Syndrome, Complete Heart Block, Stokes–Adams Syndrome & Pacemakers [KU 22, 21, 20, RGU]

A. Sinus Bradycardia & Sick Sinus Syndrome

•  Causes of Sinus Bradycardia (<60/min) [KU 22, 20]:

•  Physiological: Athletes, during sleep (high vagal tone).

•  Pathological (Extrinsic):Inferior wall MI, Hypothyroidism, Hypothermia, Obstructive jaundice, Raised intracranial pressure (Cushing’s reflex), Drugs (β-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, amiodarone, organophosphates).

•  Intrinsic:Sinoatrial disease (Sick Sinus Syndrome).

•  Sick Sinus Syndrome (Sinoatrial Disease) [KU 22]:

•  Pathogenesis: Idiopathic degenerative fibrosis or ischaemia of the SA node, common in the elderly.

•  ECG / Holter Manifestations: Persistent sinus bradycardia, sinoatrial block, sinus arrest with prolonged pauses, junctional escape rhythms, and alternating paroxysms of atrial fibrillation/flutter/SVT followed by long sinus pauses upon termination ("Tachy-brady syndrome").

•  Management:Dual-chamber Permanent Pacemaker (DDD) for symptomatic bradycardia/pauses, combined with rate-controlling drugs or catheter ablation if tachy-brady syndrome is present.

B. Complete (Third-Degree) Heart Block & Stokes–Adams Syndrome [KU 21, 20, RGU]

•  Definition: Complete failure of AV conduction in which no atrial impulses reach the ventricles; the atria and ventricles beat independently (AV dissociation), and life is sustained by a slow junctional (40–50/min, narrow QRS) or ventricular (25–35/min, broad QRS) escape rhythm.

•  Causes:

•  Congenital: Maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies (neonatal lupus).

•  Acquired: Idiopathic fibrosis of the His–Purkinje system (Lev’s/Lenègre’s disease — most common in elderly), Acute MI (inferior MI → transient AV nodal block; extensive anterior MI → infranodal block with grave prognosis), Calcific aortic stenosis, Infective endocarditis (aortic root abscess), Sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, Chagas disease, Cardiac surgery/TAVI, Drugs (digoxin, β-blockers, verapamil).

•  Clinical Features:

•  Stokes–Adams Syndrome [KU 20]: Recurrent episodes of sudden, unheralded syncope caused by transient ventricular asystole (or Torsades) in patients with complete or Mobitz Type II AV block. The patient collapses pale and pulseless (a brief anoxic seizure may occur if asystole is prolonged), followed by a characteristic facial flush upon resumption of cardiac contraction and rapid recovery of consciousness without post-ictal confusion.

•  Examination Findings: Slow regular pulse (25–45/min) that does not accelerate with exercise, wide pulse pressure (high stroke volume), irregular cannon a waves in the JVP, and variable intensity of the first heart sound (S1).

•  ECG Findings: P waves (rate ~80/min) and QRS complexes (rate ~30–40/min) are regular but completely dissociated with constantly changing PR relationships.

•  Treatment of Choice ([KU 21]):

•  Emergency / Acute:IV Atropine (0.6 mg boluses up to 3 mg — effective if block is at AV node, e.g., inferior MI) or IV Isoprenaline infusion (2 mg in 500 mL 5% dextrose at 10–60 mL/hr) + Temporary Transvenous (or Transcutaneous) Pacing.

•  Definitive Treatment of Choice:Permanent Dual-Chamber Pacemaker (DDD) — indicated in all patients with acquired complete heart block or Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block, even if asymptomatic, as it prevents sudden death and improves survival.

C. Pacemakers in Heart Disease [RGU]

•  Indications for Permanent Pacing:

1.  Complete (3rd-degree) AV block and Mobitz Type II 2nd-degree AV block (regardless of symptoms).

2.  Symptomatic Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) block or persistent AV block post-MI.

3.  Symptomatic Sick Sinus Syndrome (sinus arrest/pauses, tachy-brady syndrome).

4.  Trifascicular or alternating bundle branch block with syncope.

5.  Carotid sinus hypersensitivity or malignant cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope.

6.  Cardiac Resynchronisation Therapy (CRT-P/D): Biventricular pacing in HFrEF (EF ≤ 35%) with LBBB.

•  Generic Pacemaker Code: 1st letter = Chamber paced (A, V, D); 2nd letter = Chamber sensed (A, V, D); 3rd letter = Response to sensing (I = inhibited, T = triggered, D = dual); 4th letter = R (rate-responsive).

•  Complications:Early: Pneumothorax, haemothorax, cardiac perforation/tamponade, pocket haematoma, lead displacement. Late: Pocket/lead infection (endocarditis), lead fracture, Pacemaker syndrome (hypotension and dizziness in VVI pacing due to loss of AV synchrony and retrograde V–A conduction).

subject: medicine
title: 20. Stable Angina, Prinzmetal’s Angina & Treadmill Test [KU 23, 22, 16]
text:
SECTION 13.7 — CORONARY ARTERY DISEASES

20. Stable Angina, Prinzmetal’s Angina & Treadmill Test [KU 23, 22, 16]

•  Stable Angina Pectoris [KU 16]:

•  Definition & Pathophysiology: Transient myocardial ischaemia due to an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand, typically caused by a fixed atherosclerotic coronary stenosis reducing luminal cross-sectional area by ≥ 70%.

•  Three Cardinal Clinical Features:

1.  Constricting/heavy central retrosternal chest discomfort, radiating to the left arm, neck, or jaw (Levine’s clenched fist sign).

2.  Precipitated reproducibly by physical exertion (or cold weather, heavy meal, emotional stress).

3.  Relieved promptly by rest or sublingual GTN within 5 minutes.

•  Investigations: Resting 12-lead ECG (often normal; may show prior MI or T-wave flattening), CT Coronary Angiography (first-line diagnostic test of choice), Exercise ECG (TMT), Stress Echocardiography / Myocardial Perfusion Scan, and Invasive Coronary Angiography.

•  Management:

•  Secondary Prevention (Improves Prognosis): Smoking cessation, Aspirin 75 mg OD (or Clopidogrel 75 mg OD), High-intensity Statin (Atorvastatin 80 mg OD), ACE inhibitor (if diabetes, hypertension, or LV dysfunction).

•  Anti-anginal Drug Therapy (Symptom Relief):

•  Immediate relief: Sublingual GTN spray (400 µg) or tablet.

•  First-line prophylaxis:Beta-blocker (Bisoprolol 5–10 mg OD) OR Calcium channel blocker (Amlodipine 5–10 mg OD; or Verapamil/Diltiazem if β-blocker contraindicated).

•  Second-line add-on: Long-acting oral nitrate (Isosorbide mononitrate — ensure 8-hr nitrate-free interval to prevent tolerance), Nicorandil (K+ channel activator, 10–30 mg BD), Ivabradine (If blocker, 5–7.5 mg BD), or Ranolazine (late inward Na+ current inhibitor, 375–750 mg BD).

•  Coronary Revascularisation:PCI with drug-eluting stents (for 1- or 2-vessel disease with refractory symptoms) or CABG (using Left Internal Mammary Artery [LIMA] to LAD + saphenous vein grafts — improves survival in Left Main Stem stenosis, 3-vessel disease, or 2-vessel disease involving proximal LAD, especially with LV dysfunction or diabetes).

•  Prinzmetal’s (Vasospastic / Variant) Angina [KU 22]:

•  Pathophysiology: Transient, focal coronary artery vasospasm (often occurring in angiographically normal coronary arteries or near a minor plaque), causing transmural myocardial ischaemia.

•  Clinical Features: Unprovoked episodes of angina occurring at rest, classically in the early hours of the morning, associated with transient ST-segment elevation on the ECG during pain.

•  Treatment:Calcium channel blockers (Nifedipine, Diltiazem) and Long-acting nitrates + smoking cessation. (Beta-blockers are contraindicated as unopposed α-adrenergic vasoconstriction worsens coronary spasm).

•  Treadmill Test (TMT / Exercise ECG) — Indications & High-Risk Findings [KU 23]:

•  Procedure: 12-lead ECG and BP recorded while exercising on a motorized treadmill using the Bruce Protocol.

•  Indications:

1.  To objectively assess symptoms and exercise tolerance in stable angina.

2.  Risk stratification and prognosis in known CAD.

3.  To evaluate efficacy of medical therapy or coronary revascularisation.

4.  To diagnose and evaluate exercise-induced arrhythmias.

•  Positive Test Criteria:Planar (horizontal) or down-sloping ST-segment depression ≥ 1 mm (80 ms after J-point), ST elevation, reproduction of typical angina, or fall in BP.

•  High-Risk Findings: Ischaemia at low workload (Stage 1 or 2 of Bruce protocol), fall in systolic BP during exercise, widespread/marked (>2 mm) or prolonged ST depression (>5 mins into recovery), or exercise-induced VT.

•  Contraindications: Acute MI (<2 days), unstable angina, severe symptomatic aortic stenosis, decompensated heart failure, acute myocarditis/pericarditis, aortic dissection.

subject: medicine
title: 21. Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS): Unstable Angina, NSTEMI & STEMI [KU 25, 24, 22, 20, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
21. Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS): Unstable Angina, NSTEMI & STEMI [KU 25, 24, 22, 20, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignettes: 45M/65M/50M smoker with severe retrosternal chest pain radiating to jaw/left arm & profuse sweating; Evaluation of sudden-onset chest pain)

1. Definition & Classification of Acute Coronary Syndrome

•  ACS encompasses a spectrum of acute myocardial ischaemic states resulting from abrupt reduction in coronary blood flow:

1.  ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI): Complete thrombotic occlusion of a major epicardial coronary artery causing transmural myocardial necrosis → persistent ST elevation (or new LBBB) on ECG + elevated cardiac troponin.

2.  Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI): Partial occlusion of a major vessel or complete occlusion of a minor vessel causing subendocardial necrosis → ST depression / T-wave inversion on ECG + elevated cardiac troponin.

3.  Unstable Angina (UA) [KU 17]: New-onset severe angina, rapidly worsening (crescendo) angina, or angina at rest with ischaemic ECG changes, but NO elevation of cardiac troponin (no myocyte necrosis).

•  Universal Classification of Myocardial Infarction (Types 1–5):

•  Type 1 MI: Spontaneous MI due to atherosclerotic plaque rupture/erosion with intraluminal thrombus.

•  Type 2 MI: Secondary to oxygen supply–demand imbalance without atherothrombosis (e.g., severe anaemia, sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, hypotension).

•  Type 3 MI: Sudden cardiac death with ischaemic symptoms/ECG changes before biomarkers can be drawn.

•  Type 4 MI: Associated with PCI (4a = procedural, 4b = stent thrombosis, 4c = restenosis).

•  Type 5 MI: Associated with CABG surgery.

2. Risk Factors & Aetiopathogenesis [KU 25, 24, 15]

•  Risk Factors for CAD / AMI:

•  Non-modifiable: Increasing age, Male sex (and post-menopausal females), Family history of premature CAD (<50 yrs in male, <55 yrs in female first-degree relative).

•  Modifiable:Cigarette smoking (most important modifiable factor), Hypertension, Hypercholesterolaemia (↑ LDL, ↑ Lp(a), ↓ HDL), Diabetes mellitus, Central obesity / Metabolic syndrome, Physical inactivity, Social deprivation.

•  Aetiopathogenesis:

1.  Endothelial Dysfunction & Plaque Formation: LDL particles enter the subendothelial intima, undergo oxidation, and are phagocytosed by macrophages to form foam cells (fatty streak) → vascular smooth muscle migration forms a fibrous cap over a lipid-rich necrotic core (fibroatheroma).

2.  Plaque Vulnerability & Rupture: Activated macrophages at the shoulder regions of an eccentric plaque secrete matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α, IFN-γ) that degrade collagen and thin the fibrous cap → mechanical shear stress (e.g., BP surge) causes plaque fissuring, erosion, or rupture.

3.  Atherothrombosis & Vasospasm: Exposure of subendothelial collagen and tissue factor triggers platelet adhesion (via vWF and GP Ib), activation, and aggregation (via GP IIb/IIIa receptors), alongside coagulation cascade activation (fibrin mesh) and local coronary vasospasm (thromboxane A2, serotonin).

4.  Irreversible Myocyte Necrosis: Starts in the subendocardium within 20–30 minutes of total occlusion and spreads as a wavefront towards the epicardium over 6–12 hours (hence early reperfusion salvages jeopardised myocardium).

3. Clinical Features & Differential Diagnosis

•  Symptoms:

•  Prolonged (>20–30 mins), severe, crushing/constricting central retrosternal chest pain occurring at rest, radiating to the left (or both) arms, neck, jaw, back, or epigastrium, not relieved by rest or GTN.

•  Associated autonomic symptoms: Profuse sweating (diaphoresis), nausea, vomiting, extreme anxiety (angor animi — fear of impending death), breathlessness, or syncope.

•  Silent / Painless MI: Common in older patients, patients with diabetes mellitus (autonomic neuropathy), and post-operative patients (presents with acute dyspnoea/LVF, delirium, syncope, or unexplained hypotension).

•  Physical Signs:

•  Sympathetic activation: Pallor, cold clammy skin, sinus tachycardia, mild hypertension.

•  Vagal activation (characteristic of Inferior MI): Sinus bradycardia, hypotension, vomiting.

•  Signs of LV dysfunction: Quiet S1, S3 or S4 gallop, diffuse apex, basal lung crepitations (Killip Class: Class I = no crepitations; Class II = crepitations <50% lung fields; Class III = frank pulmonary oedema; Class IV = cardiogenic shock), raised JVP (especially in Right Ventricular MI), and low-grade fever.

•  Differential Diagnosis of Acute Severe Chest Pain ([KU 25, 24, 18]):

1.  Acute Coronary Syndrome (STEMI / NSTEMI / UA).

2.  Acute Aortic Dissection (abrupt tearing interscapular pain, pulse/BP asymmetry, early diastolic murmur of AR).

3.  Acute Pulmonary Embolism (pleuritic pain, sudden dyspnoea, haemoptysis, hypoxia, DVT signs).

4.  Acute Pericarditis (sharp pleuritic pain relieved by sitting forward, pericardial friction rub).

5.  Tension Pneumothorax (unilateral hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal shift).

6.  Oesophageal Rupture (Boerhaave’s syndrome) or severe gastro-oesophageal reflux/spasm.

4. Investigations [KU 25, 24, 20, RGU]

1.  12-Lead ECG (Mandatory within 10 minutes of arrival):

•  STEMI Criteria: ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in two contiguous limb leads OR ≥ 2 mm in two contiguous chest leads, OR new-onset LBBB.

•  Serial Evolution of ECG Changes in STEMI:

•  Minutes: Hyperacute tall peaked T waves → Convex ST-segment elevation ("current of injury").

•  Hours to Days: Diminution of R wave height, development of pathological Q waves, resolution of ST elevation, and deep symmetrical T-wave inversion.

•  Weeks/Months: T waves normalise; Q waves persist permanently (old infarct scar).

•  Localisation of Infarct Territory on ECG:

•  Anteroseptal (V1–V4): LAD artery.

•  Anterolateral (I, aVL, V4–V6): LAD / Diagonal / LCX.

•  Inferior (II, III, aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I, aVL): RCA (85%) or LCX. (Always record right-sided leads V3R, V4R in inferior MI to detect RV infarction).

•  Posterior: Reciprocal tall R waves and ST depression in V1–V3 (ST elevation in V7–V9).

•  NSTEMI / UA ECG: Planar or down-sloping ST depression (≥ 1 mm) and/or deep T-wave inversion without Q waves.

•  ECG of Acute Inferior Wall MI ([KU 25, 20]):

ECG of acute inferior wall myocardial infarction: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in leads I and aVL.

1.  Cardiac Biomarkers: Serial High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin I or T (hs-cTn) at 0 and 2–3 hours (rise and/or fall with at least one value >99th percentile confirms MI; normal in Unstable Angina).

2.  Routine Blood Tests: FBC (leucocytosis), U&Es, Blood glucose & HbA1c, Fasting lipid profile (within 24 hrs of admission), CRP/ESR.

3.  Chest X-Ray: To detect pulmonary oedema or cardiomegaly (and exclude pneumothorax/mediastinal widening).

4.  Echocardiography: Assesses LVEF, regional wall motion abnormalities, and mechanical complications (MR, VSD, mural thrombus, pericardial effusion).

5.  Risk Stratification (in NSTEMI/UA): Calculate the GRACE Score (Age, HR, SBP, Creatinine, Killip class, Cardiac arrest, ST deviation, Elevated troponin) to predict in-hospital mortality and guide timing of invasive angiography.

5. Management of Acute Coronary Syndrome [KU 25, 24, 22, 20, 18]

##### A. Immediate Emergency Management (First 12–24 Hours)

1.  Hospitalisation & Monitoring: Admit to Coronary Care Unit (CCU), continuous ECG telemetry (defibrillator at bedside), IV access.

2.  Oxygen Therapy: Give O2only if hypoxic (SpO2 < 90–94%) or in pulmonary oedema.

3.  Analgesia:IV Morphine 5–10 mg (or Diamorphine 2.5–5 mg) + IV Metoclopramide 10 mg (antiemetic), titrated until pain-free (reduces sympathetic drive, preload, and arrhythmia risk).

4.  Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT) — Loading Dose:

•  Aspirin 300 mg orally (chewed/crushed) immediately (reduces mortality by 25%).

•  Plus a P2Y12 Receptor Antagonist:

•  Ticagrelor 180 mg stat (followed by 90 mg BD), OR

•  Prasugrel 60 mg stat (followed by 10 mg OD — preferred if proceeding to PCI; contraindicated in prior stroke/TIA or age ≥ 75 yrs), OR

•  Clopidogrel 300–600 mg stat (followed by 75 mg OD — used if thrombolysis is given or high bleeding risk).

5.  Anti-ischaemic Therapy:

•  Sublingual or IV GTN for ongoing chest pain or LVF (strictly avoid nitrates in RV infarction or hypotension).

•  Early Beta-Blocker: Oral or IV Metoprolol (5–15 mg IV over 5 mins, then 50 mg BD orally) — reduces pain, infarct size, and VF risk (avoid if pulmonary oedema, HR <65/min, SBP <105 mmHg, or AV block).

6.  Reperfusion Strategy (Depends on STEMI vs NSTEMI/UA):

•  In STEMI (presenting within 12 hours of symptom onset):

•  1. Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (Primary PCI — Treatment of Choice): Immediate coronary angiography with thrombo-aspiration, balloon angioplasty, and drug-eluting stent deployment if achievable within 120 minutes of diagnosis (restores patency in >95%, preserves LV function, and halves re-infarction and mortality). Adjunctive GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors (Tirofiban, Abciximab) may be used if high thrombus burden.

•  2. Thrombolytic (Fibrinolytic) Therapy [TU]: Indicated if Primary PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes. Greatest benefit when given within the first 2 hours ("Golden Hour").

•  Agents:Tenecteplase (TNK-tPA) (weight-adjusted single IV bolus), Reteplase (rPA) (double IV bolus), Alteplase (tPA), or Streptokinase (1.5 million units IV over 60 mins).

•  Contraindications to Thrombolysis: Any prior haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic stroke within 6 months, CNS neoplasm/AVM, recent major trauma/surgery (<1 month), active internal bleeding/peptic ulcer, aortic dissection, severe uncontrolled hypertension (>180/110 mmHg), pregnancy.

•  Post-thrombolysis: Administer Fondaparinux (2.5 mg SC OD) or Enoxaparin (1 mg/kg SC BD) and transfer for routine early angiography/PCI within 24 hours (or Rescue PCI immediately if reperfusion fails, i.e., <50% ST resolution at 60–90 mins).

•  In NSTEMI / Unstable Angina (Thrombolysis is CONTRAINDICATED):

•  Anticoagulation:Fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC OD (best safety/efficacy profile) or Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC BD) for up to 8 days or until revascularisation.

•  Risk-Stratified Coronary Angiography: Perform inpatient coronary angiography + PCI/CABG within 24–72 hours if GRACE score >140 (intermediate-to-high risk), elevated troponin, or dynamic ST changes; immediate angiography (<2 hrs) if haemodynamic instability or refractory angina.

##### B. Late Management & Secondary Prevention (Preventing Recurrence) [KU 24, 20, 18]

1.  Lifestyle Modification & Cardiac Rehabilitation:

•  Smoking cessation (halves 5-year mortality), Mediterranean-style diet (rich in fruit, vegetables, oily fish; low saturated fat), weight control, graded aerobic exercise, and strict control of diabetes (SGLT2 inhibitors / GLP-1 agonists) and hypertension.

2.  Long-Term Secondary Prevention Pharmacotherapy (Mnemonic — DABS-M):

•  Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT):Aspirin 75 mg OD lifelong + P2Y12 inhibitor (Ticagrelor 90 mg BD, Prasugrel 10 mg OD, or Clopidogrel 75 mg OD) for 12 months.

•  ACE Inhibitor (or ARB):Ramipril (2.5–10 mg OD) or Enalapril — prevents adverse ventricular remodelling, heart failure, and recurrent MI.

•  Beta-Blocker:Bisoprolol (2.5–10 mg OD) or Metoprolol — reduces long-term mortality by 25% (especially in LV systolic dysfunction).

•  High-Intensity Statin:Atorvastatin 80 mg OD lifelong irrespective of baseline cholesterol (target LDL-C <1.4–2.0 mmol/L; add Ezetimibe/PCSK9i if needed).

•  Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonist (MRA):Eplerenone or Spironolactone (25–50 mg OD) — indicated if LVEF ≤ 35–40% with clinical heart failure or diabetes.

3.  Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator (ICD): If LVEF remains ≤ 30–35% at least 40 days post-MI.

6. Complications of Myocardial Infarction [KU 25, 24, 16, TU, RGU]

1.  Arrhythmias (Most common cause of early death):

•  Ventricular Fibrillation (VF): Major cause of pre-hospital sudden death; early VF (<48 hrs) responds to prompt defibrillation with good long-term prognosis.

•  Ventricular Tachycardia (VT), Accelerated Idioventricular Rhythm (reperfusion arrhythmia — benign), Atrial Fibrillation.

•  Bradyarrhythmias & AV Block: Sinus bradycardia and transient AV nodal block in Inferior MI (responds to atropine); Mobitz II or Complete Heart Block in Anterior MI (indicates extensive septal damage; requires temporary/permanent pacing).

2.  Haemodynamic Complications:

•  Acute Left Ventricular Failure / Pulmonary Oedema and Cardiogenic Shock (if >40% LV myocardium infarcted).

•  Right Ventricular Infarction: Triad of hypotension, elevated JVP, and clear lung fields (treated with IV fluid loading; avoid nitrates/diuretics).

3.  Mechanical Complications (Typically occur 2–7 days post-MI due to coagulative necrosis) [TU]:

•  Papillary Muscle Rupture: Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture (inferior MI) → acute severe mitral regurgitation, harsh apical pansystolic murmur, and flash pulmonary oedema.

•  Interventricular Septal Rupture (VSD): Sudden haemodynamic collapse with a loud harsh pansystolic murmur and thrill at the left sternal border + step-up in O2 saturation in RV.

•  Left Ventricular Free Wall Rupture: Causes acute haemopericardium, cardiac tamponade, pulseless electrical activity (PEA), and sudden death.

•  Left Ventricular Aneurysm (Late): Dyskinetic apical bulge, persistent ST elevation on ECG, heart failure, VT, and mural thrombus.

4.  Pericardial Complications:

•  Acute Post-Infarct Pericarditis (days 2–3).

•  Dressler’s Syndrome [KU 18]: Autoimmune pericarditis occurring 2–10 weeks post-MI, characterised by fever, pleuritic chest pain, pericardial/pleural effusions, and raised ESR (treated with high-dose aspirin, colchicine, or steroids).

5.  Thromboembolic Complications: LV mural thrombus → systemic arterial embolism (stroke, acute limb ischaemia); DVT and pulmonary embolism.

title: 22. Marfan Syndrome & Coarctation of the Aorta [KU 23, 21, RGU, TU]
text:
SECTION 13.8 — DISEASE OF AORTA

22. Marfan Syndrome & Coarctation of the Aorta [KU 23, 21, RGU, TU]

A. Marfan Syndrome [KU 23, 21]

•  Genetics & Pathogenesis: Autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder (prevalence 1 in 5000) caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene (chromosome 15) encoding fibrillin-1, leading to defective microfibril formation, loss of extracellular matrix integrity, and excessive TGF-β signalling.

•  Clinical Features:

1.  Skeletal System: Tall stature with arm span > height and reduced upper-to-lower segment ratio, Arachnodactyly (long, slender spider-like fingers — positive Walker–Murdoch wrist sign and Steinberg thumb sign), High-arched palate with crowded teeth, Pectus excavatum or carinatum, Kyphoscoliosis, Pes planus (flat feet), and Joint hypermobility.

2.  Cardiovascular System (Major cause of mortality): Cystic medial necrosis of the aorta → Ascending aortic root dilatation and aneurysm, Aortic dissection (Type A), Aortic regurgitation, and Mitral valve prolapse with mitral regurgitation.

3.  Ocular System:Ectopia lentis (upward and outward lens dislocation), severe myopia, retinal detachment.

4.  Respiratory & Other: Spontaneous apical pneumothorax (apical blebs), striae atrophicae, dural ectasia, inguinal hernias.

•  Diagnosis & Management:

•  Diagnosis: Clinical (Ghent criteria), Slit-lamp eye exam, Serial Echocardiography / CT angiography (to monitor aortic root diameter), and FBN1 genetic testing.

•  Management: Avoid strenuous isometric exercise/contact sports; Beta-blockers (Propranolol/Atenolol) and ARBs (Losartan — inhibits TGF-β) to slow aortic root dilatation; Elective prophylactic aortic root replacement (Bentall or valve-sparing David procedure) when aortic root diameter exceeds 4.5–5.0 cm.

B. Coarctation of the Aorta [TU]

•  Pathophysiology: Congenital narrowing of the aorta at the aortic isthmus just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery (at the site of insertion of the ductus arteriosus). Twice as common in males; strongly associated with Turner syndrome (45,X), Bicuspid aortic valve (>50%), and Circle of Willis "berry" aneurysms.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Upper body hypertension (headache, epistaxis) with normal or low BP in the lower limbs (leg claudication/weakness).

•  Radio-femoral delay and weak femoral pulses.

•  Palpable collateral vessels around the scapulae and intercostal spaces (Suzman’s sign).

•  Mid-systolic murmur heard loudest posteriorly over the interscapular area, plus an ejection click/murmur of a bicuspid aortic valve.

•  Investigations:

•  Chest X-Ray:"Figure of 3" sign (indentation of the aorta with pre- and post-stenotic dilatation) and Inferior rib notching (Roesler’s sign) of the 3rd to 8th ribs due to dilated intercostal collaterals.

•  ECG & Echo: Left ventricular hypertrophy; Doppler echo shows high-velocity jet in descending aorta.

•  CT / MR Angiography: Definitive investigation of choice.

•  Complications & Management:

•  Complications: LV failure, Intracranial haemorrhage (ruptured berry aneurysm), Aortic dissection/rupture, Infective endarteritis.

•  Management: Surgical resection with end-to-end anastomosis, or percutaneous balloon angioplasty with stenting.

title: 23. Systemic Hypertension: Classification, Secondary Causes, Target-Organ Damage & Hypertensive Emergencies [KU 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 13.9 — HYPERTENSION

23. Systemic Hypertension: Classification, Secondary Causes, Target-Organ Damage & Hypertensive Emergencies [KU 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignettes: 65M with angina, MI & BP 180/100; 32M with headache, BP 220/130 & papilloedema)

1. Definition & Classification of Blood Pressure (British Hypertension Society / ISH)

•  Clinic BP Threshold for Diagnosis: ≥ 140/90 mmHg (confirmed by Ambulatory BP Monitoring [ABPM] daytime average ≥ 135/85 mmHg).

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-002]]

2. Causes of Secondary Hypertension (5–10% of cases; suspect if age <40 yrs or resistant HTN) [KU 22, 19]

1.  Renal Disease (Most common secondary cause [KU 16, RGU]):

•  Renal Parenchymal Disease: Acute/chronic glomerulonephritis, Diabetic nephropathy, Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), Chronic pyelonephritis/reflux nephropathy.

•  Renovascular Hypertension:Renal artery stenosis (Atherosclerosis in elderly [ostial]; Fibromuscular dysplasia in young females [string-of-beads appearance]). Suspect if asymmetric kidneys, abdominal bruit, recurrent flash pulmonary oedema, or >30% rise in creatinine after starting ACEi/ARB.

2.  Endocrine Causes [KU 19]:

•  Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s syndrome / Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia): Hypertension + hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis + high Aldosterone:Renin Ratio (ARR).

•  Phaeochromocytoma / Paraganglioma: Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, pallor + elevated 24-hr urinary/plasma metanephrines.

•  Cushing’s Syndrome: Centripetal obesity, striae, proximal myopathy + positive overnight dexamethasone suppression test.

•  Acromegaly, Primary Hyperparathyroidism, Hypothyroidism, and Thyrotoxicosis.

•  Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (11β-hydroxylase or 17α-hydroxylase deficiency) & Liddle’s syndrome.

3.  Vascular:Coarctation of the aorta (radio-femoral delay).

4.  Drugs & Toxins: Alcohol excess, Oral contraceptive pill (oestrogen), NSAIDs, Glucocorticoids, Ciclosporin/Tacrolimus, Erythropoietin, Sympathomimetics/Cocaine, Liquorice.

5.  Other:Obstructive sleep apnoea, Pre-eclampsia / Pregnancy-induced hypertension.

3. Target-Organ Damage (Complications) & Assessment [KU 23, TU, RGU]

1.  Heart: Left ventricular hypertrophy (heaving apex, S4; assessed by ECG and Echo), Heart failure (HFpEF and HFrEF), Coronary artery disease / Myocardial infarction, Atrial fibrillation.

2.  Brain: Ischaemic stroke, Intracerebral haemorrhage (Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms), Transient ischaemic attack (TIA), Vascular dementia, Hypertensive encephalopathy.

3.  Retina — Keith–Wagener–Barker Grading of Hypertensive Retinopathy:

•  Grade 1: Arteriolar narrowing, tortuosity, and increased light reflex ("Silver wiring").

•  Grade 2: Grade 1 + Focal constriction of veins at arteriovenous crossings ("AV nipping").

•  Grade 3: Grade 2 + Retinal ischaemia (Flame-shaped or blot haemorrhages and "Cotton-wool" exudates).

•  Grade 4: Grade 3 + Papilloedema (swelling of the optic disc — hallmark of malignant hypertension).

4.  Kidneys: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis (benign hyaline arteriolosclerosis or malignant fibrinoid necrosis) → Albuminuria / Proteinuria and Chronic Kidney Disease (assessed by Urine ACR and serum creatinine/eGFR).

5.  Blood Vessels: Aortic aneurysm, Aortic dissection, Peripheral arterial disease.

4. Stepwise Management of Systemic Hypertension (NICE / ISH Guidelines)

•  Lifestyle Modifications: Weight reduction (BMI 20–25), Dietary salt restriction (<6 g/day), DASH / Mediterranean diet, Moderation of alcohol, Regular aerobic exercise (30 mins 5×/wk), Smoking cessation.

•  Pharmacological Stepwise Algorithm (Target BP <140/90 mmHg; <130/80 mmHg in diabetes/CKD):

•  Step 1:

•  Age <55 years (or Diabetes of any age):A — ACE inhibitor (Ramipril) or ARB (Losartan/Telmisartan).

•  Age ≥ 55 years or Black African/Caribbean descent:C — Calcium Channel Blocker (Amlodipine).

•  Step 2:A + C (ACEi/ARB + CCB).

•  Step 3:A + C + D (Add a Thiazide-like diuretic, e.g., Indapamide or Chlortalidone).

•  Step 4 (Resistant Hypertension):A + C + D + Low-dose Spironolactone (25 mg OD, if K+ ≤ 4.5 mmol/L) or an α-blocker (Doxazosin) / β-blocker (Bisoprolol).

5. Hypertensive Emergencies & Accelerated (Malignant) Hypertension [KU 24, 20, TU, RGU]

•  Definitions:

•  Hypertensive Emergency (Accelerated / Malignant Hypertension): Severe elevation of BP (typically ≥ 180/120 mmHg) accompanied by acute, life-threatening target-organ damage:

1.  Grade 3 or 4 Hypertensive Retinopathy (retinal haemorrhages, exudates, or papilloedema).

2.  Hypertensive Encephalopathy (severe headache, visual loss, confusion, seizures, coma).

3.  Acute Coronary Syndrome / Myocardial Infarction(as in the 65M vignette) or Acute Left Ventricular Failure / Pulmonary Oedema.

4.  Acute Aortic Dissection.

5.  Acute Kidney Injury / Microangiopathic Haemolytic Anaemia (MAHA).

6.  Eclampsia / Severe Pre-eclampsia.

•  Hypertensive Urgency: Severe BP elevation (≥ 180/120 mmHg) without acute target-organ damage (treated with oral antihypertensives over 24–48 hrs).

•  Pathology of Malignant Hypertension:Fibrinoid necrosis of small arteries and arterioles with onion-skin intimal proliferation and intravascular thrombosis (MAHA). Untreated 1-year mortality is >90%.

•  Management of Hypertensive Emergency / Accelerated Hypertension:

•  Crucial Principle:Avoid precipitous lowering of BP! Cerebral autoregulation is reset to a higher level in chronic hypertension; dropping BP too rapidly causes watershed cerebral infarction, occipital blindness, myocardial ischaemia, or acute renal failure.

•  Target: Controlled reduction of Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) by 20–25% over the first 1–2 hours, then gradually to ~150/90–100 mmHg over 24–48 hours. (Exception: In Acute Aortic Dissection, lower SBP rapidly to <120 mmHg and HR <60/min within 20 minutes).

•  Drug Treatment (in HDU/ICU):

•  In uncomplicated accelerated hypertension with retinal changes alone, bed rest and oral therapy (Amlodipine or Atenolol/Labetalol) is often safest.

•  Parenteral Therapy (if encephalopathy, LVF, ACS, or dissection):

1.  IV Labetalol: 2 mg/min infusion (max 200 mg) — ideal for encephalopathy, eclampsia, and aortic dissection.

2.  IV Glyceryl Trinitrate (GTN): 10–200 µg/min — ideal for ACS/MI and acute pulmonary oedema.

3.  IV Sodium Nitroprusside: 0.3–1.0 µg/kg/min (light-sensitive; risk of cyanide toxicity).

4.  IV Nicardipine or IV Hydralazine (in pregnancy).

•  (Avoid loop diuretics initially unless pulmonary oedema is present, as pressure natriuresis causes intravascular volume depletion, which further activates RAAS).

title: 24. Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) [KU 24, 18, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 13.10 — DISEASE OF THE HEART VALVES

24. Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) [KU 24, 18, 15, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignette: 18M with fever, right knee arthritis, chest pain, relative tachycardia, apical pansystolic murmur & prolonged PR interval)

•  Definition & Aetiopathogenesis: An acute, multisystem, immune-mediated inflammatory disease occurring 2–3 weeks after pharyngeal infection with Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) in children and young adults (5–15 years).

•  Molecular Mimicry: Antibodies and T-cells directed against streptococcal M-protein and N-acetylglucosamine cross-react with human cardiac myosin, sarcolemmal proteins, valvular endothelium, synovial tissue, and basal ganglia neurons (Aschoff bodies are pathognomonic granulomas in the myocardium).

•  Clinical Features & Revised Jones Criteria ([KU 24, 18]):

•  Major Manifestations (Mnemonic: JONES):

1.  Carditis (Pancarditis — 50–60%):

•  Endocarditis: Valvulitis affecting mitral (>90%) and aortic valves → apical pansystolic murmur of mitral regurgitation, soft mid-diastolic Carey Coombs murmur, or early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation.

•  Myocarditis:Disproportionate sinus tachycardia (sleeping pulse >100/min), cardiomegaly, S3 gallop, heart failure.

•  Pericarditis: Chest pain, pericardial friction rub, effusion.

2.  Migratory Polyarthritis (75%): Acute, painful, asymmetric, fleeting inflammation of large joints (knees, ankles, elbows, wrists) that responds dramatically to salicylates within 24–48 hrs without residual deformity. (In high-risk/endemic populations, aseptic monoarthritis or polyarthralgia is accepted as a major criterion in the 2015 Revised Jones Criteria).

3.  Sydenham’s Chorea (St Vitus’ Dance — up to 30%): Late neurological manifestation (3–6 months post-infection); purposeless, involuntary choreiform movements of hands/face, emotional lability, hypotonia, "milkmaid’s grip", and "jack-in-the-box" tongue.

4.  Erythema Marginatum (<5%): Evanescent pink macules with serpiginous red borders and pale centres on the trunk and proximal limbs (sparing the face).

5.  Subcutaneous Nodules (5–7%): Small (0.5–2 cm), firm, painless nodules over extensor bony surfaces (olecranon, occiput, tendons); strongly associated with severe carditis.

•  Minor Manifestations:

1.  Fever (≥ 38.5°C; ≥ 38.0°C in high-risk populations).

2.  Arthralgia (monoarthralgia in high-risk populations; cannot be counted if arthritis is used as a major criterion).

3.  Elevated Acute Phase Reactants: ESR ≥ 60 mm/hr (≥ 30 in high-risk) or CRP ≥ 3.0 mg/dL + Leucocytosis.

4.  Prolonged PR Interval (First-degree AV block) on ECG(cannot be counted if carditis is used as a major criterion).

5.  Previous history of rheumatic fever or rheumatic heart disease.

•  Plus Essential Criterion — Supporting Evidence of Preceding Group A Streptococcal Infection:

•  Elevated or rising Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titre (>200 IU in adults, >300 IU in children) or Anti-DNase B titre.

•  Positive throat swab culture or rapid streptococcal antigen test.

•  Diagnostic Requirement:2 Major OR 1 Major + 2 Minor criteria + Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (Isolated chorea or indolent carditis is sufficient without streptococcal evidence).

•  Management of Acute Rheumatic Fever:

1.  Bed Rest: Until symptoms, temperature, WBC, and ESR/CRP normalise.

2.  Eradication of Residual Streptococcal Infection: Single dose of Inj. Benzathine Benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units IM OR Oral Phenoxymethylpenicillin (Penicillin V) 250–500 mg QDS for 10 days (Erythromycin/Azithromycin if penicillin-allergic).

3.  Anti-inflammatory Therapy:

•  Arthritis without severe carditis:High-dose Aspirin 60–100 mg/kg/day in 4–6 divided doses (dramatic relief within 24 hrs; continue until ESR normalises, then taper).

•  Carditis with heart failure or severe arthritis:Oral Prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day in divided doses until ESR normalises, then taper gradually over 2–4 weeks.

4.  Management of Complications:

•  Heart failure: Diuretics, ACE inhibitors, digoxin; urgent valve repair/replacement if refractory acute valve rupture.

•  Chorea: Diazepam, Haloperidol, or Sodium Valproate.

5.  Secondary Prophylaxis ([TU]): To prevent recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis and progressive rheumatic valve damage:

•  Inj. Benzathine Benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units IM every 3–4 weeks (most effective) OR Oral Penicillin V 250 mg BD (or Sulfadiazine / Erythromycin 250 mg BD if allergic).

•  Duration: Continue until age 21 or for 5 years after the last attack (if no carditis); until age 21 or for 10 years (if mild carditis without residual valve disease); or until age 40 or lifelong (if established chronic rheumatic valvular disease).

subject: medicine
title: 25. Mitral Stenosis (MS) [KU 24, 20, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
25. Mitral Stenosis (MS) [KU 24, 20, 16, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignettes: 38M / 18M with exertional dyspnoea, PND, palpitations, irregularly irregular pulse with pulse deficit >10, loud S1, opening snap & mid-diastolic murmur)

•  Complete Diagnosis of Vignette:Chronic Rheumatic Heart Disease with Severe Mitral Stenosis, complicated by Atrial Fibrillation and Left Heart Failure.

•  Aetiology: Almost always chronic rheumatic heart disease (>95%; 2/3rds female; commissural fusion, leaflet thickening/calcification, and chordal shortening producing a "fish-mouth" or "buttonhole" orifice). Rare causes: congenital MS, Lutembacher’s syndrome (ASD + MS), severe senile annular calcification.

•  Pathophysiology:

•  Normal mitral valve area (MVA) is 4–6 cm2. Symptoms begin when MVA <2.0 cm2; Critical/Severe MS is <1.0 cm2.

•  Narrowed mitral orifice impedes diastolic LV filling → elevated Left Atrial (LA) pressure → LA hypertrophy and dilatation → Atrial Fibrillation (loss of atrial contraction + tachycardia shortens diastole, precipitating acute pulmonary oedema).

•  Chronic elevation of LA pressure causes passive pulmonary venous congestion → reactive pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction and obliterative intimal hyperplasia → Pulmonary Hypertension → RV hypertrophy, RV dilatation, functional tricuspid regurgitation, and right heart failure.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Symptoms: Progressive exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, palpitations (AF), fatigue (low cardiac output), haemoptysis (rupture of bronchial veins ["pulmonary apoplexy"], pink frothy sputum, or pulmonary infarction), hoarseness (Ortner’s syndrome), dysphagia (LA compressing oesophagus), or systemic thromboembolism (stroke).

•  Physical Signs ([TU, RGU]):

1.  General:Mitral facies (malar flush with pinched, cyanotic cheeks due to low cardiac output and vasoconstriction).

2.  Pulse: Small-volume pulse; irregularly irregular (if in AF).

3.  JVP: Prominent a wave (in pulmonary hypertension with sinus rhythm); absent a wave in AF; giant v wave if functional TR develops.

4.  Palpation: Undisplaced tapping apex beat (palpable loud S1), diastolic thrill at apex (in left lateral position), left parasternal heave (RVH), and palpable P2 in left 2nd ICS (pulmonary hypertension).

5.  Auscultatory Signs of Mitral Stenosis ([TU, RGU]):

•  Loud, snapping first heart sound (S1) (leaflets held wide open at end-diastole by high LA pressure and slammed shut; becomes soft if valve is heavily calcified/immobile).

•  Loud P2 (in pulmonary hypertension).

•  Opening Snap (OS): High-pitched early diastolic sound heard just medial to the apex (diaphragm). The A2–OS interval is inversely proportional to severity (shorter interval = higher LA pressure = more severe MS).

•  Low-pitched, rough, rumbling Mid-Diastolic Murmur (MDM): Best heard at the apex with the bell of the stethoscope, patient in the left lateral decubitus position in held expiration after exercise; duration of the murmur correlates with severity; shows pre-systolic accentuation in sinus rhythm (lost in AF).

•  Signs of Pulmonary Hypertension:Graham Steell murmur (early diastolic decrescendo murmur of functional pulmonary regurgitation at left upper sternal edge) and pansystolic murmur of functional TR at lower left sternal edge.

•  Investigations:

•  Chest X-Ray Findings in Mitral Stenosis ([KU 24]):

1.  Straightening of the left heart border (due to enlargement of the left atrial appendage and main pulmonary artery).

2.  Double right heart border (shadow of enlarged LA behind RA).

3.  Splaying/widening of the carinal angle (>90°) with upward elevation of the left main bronchus.

4.  Upper lobe pulmonary venous diversion, Kerley B lines, pulmonary haemosiderosis, and mitral valve calcification.

•  ECG:P mitrale (broad, bifid P wave in lead II) or Atrial Fibrillation; Right axis deviation and tall R wave in V1 (RVH).

•  Echocardiography (Gold Standard): "Hockey-stick" doming of anterior mitral leaflet, restricted orifice area on planimetry (<1.0 cm2 = severe), mean trans-mitral diastolic gradient (>10 mmHg = severe), LA size, pulmonary artery pressure, and TOE to exclude LA appendage thrombus.

•  Complications: Atrial fibrillation, Systemic thromboembolism (embolic stroke, acute limb/mesenteric ischaemia), Acute pulmonary oedema, Pulmonary hypertension and Right heart failure, Haemoptysis, Ortner’s syndrome, Infective endocarditis (rare in isolated MS).

•  Management:

•  1. Medical Management:

•  Rate Control (Crucial to prolong diastolic filling time):Beta-blockers, Verapamil/Diltiazem, or Digoxin.

•  Diuretics: Loop diuretics (Furosemide) to relieve pulmonary and systemic congestion.

•  Anticoagulation: Lifelong Warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0) is mandatory in all MS patients with AF, prior thromboembolism, or dense LA spontaneous echo contrast/thrombus (DOACs are NOT approved for moderate/severe MS).

•  Secondary Rheumatic Fever Prophylaxis: Benzathine penicillin or oral Penicillin V.

•  2. Interventional & Surgical Management (Indicated in symptomatic moderate-to-severe MS or asymptomatic severe MS with pulmonary hypertension >50 mmHg / new-onset AF):

•  Percutaneous Balloon Mitral Valvuloplasty (PBMV — Treatment of Choice): A balloon catheter is passed via the femoral vein and across the interatrial septum (trans-septal puncture) to dilate the fused commissures.

•  Criteria: Symptomatic severe MS, mobile, non-calcified valve leaflets, no (or trivial) mitral regurgitation, and no left atrial thrombus on TOE.

•  Surgical Mitral Valvotomy (Closed or Open): If PBMV is unavailable.

•  Mitral Valve Replacement (MVR): Indicated when the valve is heavily calcified/rigid, or associated with moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation or persistent LA thrombus.

subject: medicine
title: 26. Mitral Regurgitation (MR) & Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP) [KU 18, TU, RGU]
text:
26. Mitral Regurgitation (MR) & Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP) [KU 18, TU, RGU]

•  Aetiology of Mitral Regurgitation:

•  Primary (Organic — leaflet/chordal pathology):Mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous degeneration), Rheumatic heart disease, Infective endocarditis, Acute MI with papillary muscle rupture.

•  Secondary (Functional — LV dilatation/remodelling): Ischaemic cardiomyopathy, Dilated cardiomyopathy, Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (SAM).

•  Cardiovascular Examination Findings in Chronic MR ([RGU]):

•  Pulse: Regular or irregularly irregular (AF); sharp/brisk upstroke.

•  Apex Beat:Displaced laterally and downwards, thrusting/hyperdynamic (volume overload), often with a systolic thrill.

•  Parasternal Heave: Due to systolic expansion of the enlarged LA anteriorly or secondary RVH.

•  Auscultation:

1.  Soft or absent first heart sound (S1) (incomplete leaflet coaptation).

2.  Wide splitting of S2 (early A2 due to shortened LV ejection time) with loud P2 if pulmonary hypertension is present.

3.  Loud third heart sound (S3) (rapid early diastolic filling of LV) + short mid-diastolic flow murmur in severe MR.

4.  High-pitched, blowing Apical Pansystolic Murmur radiating to the left axilla and left infrascapular area (anterior leaflet prolapse jet radiates to axilla/back; posterior leaflet prolapse jet radiates to base/sternum).

•  Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP / Barlow’s Syndrome / Floppy Mitral Valve) [TU]:

•  Pathology: Myxomatous degeneration of mitral leaflets and chordae; associated with Marfan and Ehlers–Danlos syndromes.

•  Clinical Features: More common in young women; often asymptomatic or presents with atypical chest pain and benign palpitations.

•  Auscultation:Mid-systolic click (tensing of elongated chordae) followed by a late systolic murmur. Squatting delays the click and shortens the murmur; standing/Valsalva moves the click earlier and lengthens the murmur.

•  Complications: Chordal rupture causing severe acute MR, infective endocarditis, arrhythmias.

•  Management of Mitral Regurgitation ([KU 18]):

•  Medical Management:Diuretics (furosemide) for pulmonary congestion, Vasodilators (ACE inhibitors/ARBs) to reduce afterload and regurgitant fraction (especially in acute MR, hypertension, or functional HFrEF), Rate control + Anticoagulation for AF, and GDMT + CRT for functional MR.

•  Surgical / Interventional Management (Indicated in symptomatic severe MR, or asymptomatic severe MR with LVEF ≤ 60% or LV end-systolic dimension ≥ 40–45 mm, new AF, or pulmonary hypertension):

•  Surgical Mitral Valve Repair (Annuloplasty ring + chordal reconstruction): Treatment of choice over replacement as it preserves subvalvular apparatus and LV function without needing lifelong anticoagulation.

•  Mitral Valve Replacement (MVR) or Percutaneous Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair (TEER / MitraClip) in high surgical risk patients.

subject: medicine
title: 27. Aortic Stenosis (AS) & Aortic Regurgitation (AR) [KU 17, RGU]
text:
27. Aortic Stenosis (AS) & Aortic Regurgitation (AR) [KU 17, RGU]

A. Aortic Stenosis [KU 17, RGU]

•  Causes of Aortic Stenosis ([KU 17]):

1.  Infants/Children: Congenital valvular, subvalvular, or supravalvular aortic stenosis (Williams syndrome).

2.  Young/Middle-aged Adults (40–60 yrs):Calcification and fibrosis of a congenitally Bicuspid Aortic Valve; Chronic Rheumatic Heart Disease (almost always accompanied by mitral valve disease).

3.  Older Adults (>65 yrs):Senile calcific degenerative aortic stenosis (most common cause in developed countries).

•  Clinical Features ([RGU]):

•  Classic Symptomatic Triad of Severe Aortic Stenosis ([RGU] — Mnemonic: SAD):

1.  Syncope (Exertional): Fixed cardiac output fails to rise despite exercise-induced peripheral vasodilation (mean survival 3 years).

2.  Angina (Exertional): Increased O2 demand of hypertrophied LV + subendocardial compression (mean survival 5 years).

3.  Dyspnoea / Heart Failure: Diastolic and eventually systolic LV failure (mean survival <2 years).

•  Physical Signs:

•  Pulse:Slow-rising, low-volume, delayed pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and narrow pulse pressure.

•  Precordium: Undisplaced, sustained, heaving apex beat; systolic thrill in the aortic area (2nd right ICS), suprasternal notch, and carotids.

•  Auscultation:Soft or absent A2 (with reversed/paradoxical splitting of S2), audible S4, ejection click (in young patients with mobile bicuspid valve), and a harsh, crescendo–decrescendo (diamond-shaped) Ejection Systolic Murmur at the 2nd right ICS radiating to the carotid arteries (and high-pitched musical component radiating to the apex — Gallavardin phenomenon).

•  Investigations & Management:

•  Echo: Calcified restricted cusps; Severe AS defined by Peak velocity ≥ 4.0 m/s, Mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg, and Valve area <1.0 cm2.

•  Management:Prompt Aortic Valve Replacement (Surgical AVR or Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation [TAVI]) is mandatory once symptoms develop or if LVEF <50%.

B. Peripheral & Central Signs of Chronic Severe Aortic Regurgitation [RGU]

•  Causes:Valvular: Rheumatic heart disease, Infective endocarditis, Bicuspid aortic valve. Aortic Root Dilatation: Marfan syndrome, Syphilitic aortitis, Ankylosing spondylitis, Aortic dissection, Hypertension.

•  Central Signs:

•  Displaced, hyperdynamic, thrusting apex beat + audible S3.

•  High-pitched, blowing, decrescendo Early Diastolic Murmur along the left sternal edge (3rd–4th ICS), best heard with the diaphragm, patient leaning forward in held expiration.

•  Ejection systolic flow murmur at aortic area ("to-and-fro" murmur) and Austin Flint mid-diastolic murmur at apex.

•  Peripheral Signs (Due to High Stroke Volume & Wide Pulse Pressure):

1.  Collapsing (Water-hammer) pulse & Corrigan’s sign (visible vigorous carotid pulsations in the neck).

2.  De Musset’s sign: Head nodding synchronous with each heartbeat.

3.  Quincke’s sign: Capillary pulsations visible in the nail beds on light compression.

4.  Müller’s sign: Systolic pulsations of the uvula.

5.  Landolfi’s sign: Alternating constriction and dilatation of the pupils.

6.  Traube’s sign: "Pistol-shot" booming systolic and diastolic sounds heard over the femoral arteries.

7.  Duroziez’s sign: Systolic and diastolic ("to-and-fro") murmur heard over the femoral artery when compressed with the stethoscope bell.

8.  Hill’s sign: Popliteal cuff systolic BP exceeds brachial cuff systolic BP by >20 mmHg (>60 mmHg in severe AR).

9.  Rosenbach’s sign (pulsatile liver) & Gerhardt’s sign (pulsatile spleen).

subject: medicine
title: 28. Infective Endocarditis (IE) [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, 17, TU, RGU]
text:
28. Infective Endocarditis (IE) [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, 17, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignettes: 20–25M with childhood valvular disease, fever >2–4 weeks, pallor, clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes, splenomegaly & apical pansystolic murmur)

1. Definition & Pathophysiology

•  Definition: Microbial infection of the endothelial surface of the heart (most commonly heart valves, septal defects, or prosthetic material), characterised pathologically by vegetations (friable masses of platelets, fibrin, microorganisms, and inflammatory cells).

•  Pathophysiology:

1.  Endothelial Injury: High-velocity turbulent blood jet across a congenital or acquired lesion (e.g., MR, AR, VSD, PDA, prosthetic valve) damages the endothelium (Note: Low-pressure lesions like secundum ASD have minimal risk).

2.  Non-Bacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis (NBTE): Platelets and fibrin deposit on exposed subendothelial collagen to form a sterile vegetation.

3.  Transient Bacteraemia & Adherence: Microorganisms entering the bloodstream (from dental procedures, skin sepsis, IV drug use, or GI/GU tracts) adhere to the sterile vegetation via adhesins.

4.  Proliferation & Sequelae: Organisms proliferate within the avascular fibrin–platelet mesh protected from host phagocytes → local tissue destruction (cusp perforation, chordal rupture, aortic root abscess), systemic septic embolisation, and circulating immune complex deposition (glomerulonephritis, vasculitic skin lesions).

2. Aetiology & Microbiology (Davidson Box 16.94)

1.  Staphylococci (Most common overall cause):

•  Staphylococcus aureus: Leading cause of acute IE (can invade normal valves) and right-sided tricuspid IE in IV drug users (causes florid vegetations, rapid valve destruction, and septic pulmonary emboli).

•  Coagulase-negative Staphylococci (S. epidermidis): Leading cause of early prosthetic valve endocarditis (<1 year post-surgery). (S. lugdunensis causes destructive native valve IE).

2.  Streptococci:

•  Oral (Viridans) Streptococci (S. mitis, S. sanguinis, S. mutans): Commensals of oral cavity; classic cause of subacute native valve IE.

•  Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis): Associated with colonic carcinoma / polyps (mandatory colonoscopy).

3.  Enterococci (E. faecalis, E. faecium): Enter from GI or genitourinary tract in older men.

4.  HACEK Group Organisms ([KU 20] — Fastidious, slow-growing Gram-negative bacilli from the oropharynx):

•  H — Haemophilus (Aggregatibacter) aphrophilus

•  A — Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans

•  C — Cardiobacterium hominis

•  E — Eikenella corrodens

•  K — Kingella kingae

5.  Culture-Negative Endocarditis Causes:

•  Prior antibiotic therapy (most common), Coxiella burnetii (Q fever — farm animal contact), Bartonella spp., Brucella spp., Fungi (Candida, Aspergillus — large vegetations in immunocompromised/IVDU), Chlamydia, Legionella, and Non-infective (Marantic / Libman–Sacks endocarditis in SLE or malignancy).

3. Clinical Features ([KU 24, TU])

•  1. Systemic Features of Infection: Persistent fever, night sweats, rigors, malaise, anorexia, weight loss, normochromic normocytic anaemia, and splenomegaly (30–40%, in subacute IE).

•  2. Cardiac Manifestations:

•  New or changing regurgitant heart murmur (85–90%).

•  Acute heart failure / Pulmonary oedema (due to cusp perforation or chordal rupture).

•  Conduction blocks (prolonged PR / complete AV block): Signifies extension of infection into the septum (aortic root abscess).

•  3. Embolic Phenomena (Left-sided → systemic; Right-sided → pulmonary):

•  Cerebral emboli (embolic stroke, mycotic aneurysm, brain abscess), splenic/renal/mesenteric infarction, acute coronary embolism, acute limb ischaemia, Janeway lesions (painless erythematous/haemorrhagic macules on palms and soles), and Splinter haemorrhages (linear subungual streaks).

•  4. Immune Complex / Vasculitic Phenomena:

•  Osler’s nodes: Painful, tender, violaceous subcutaneous nodules on the pulp of fingertips and toes.

•  Roth’s spots: Boat-shaped retinal haemorrhages with pale centres on fundoscopy.

•  Petechial haemorrhages on conjunctivae, palate, and skin.

•  Digital clubbing (in long-standing subacute IE >6 weeks).

•  Immune-complex glomerulonephritis: Microscopic haematuria (60–70%), red cell casts, proteinuria, AKI.

4. Diagnosis & Investigations — Modified Duke Criteria [KU 24, TU, RGU]

•  Modified Duke Criteria:

•  Major Criteria (2):

1.  Positive Blood Cultures:

•  Typical IE microorganism (Viridans streptococci, S. gallolyticus, HACEK, S. aureus, or community-acquired Enterococci) from 2 separate blood cultures, OR

•  Persistently positive blood cultures (≥ 2 positive cultures drawn >12 hours apart, or all of 3 / majority of ≥ 4 cultures drawn ≥ 1 hour apart), OR

•  Single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetii (or phase I IgG titre >1:800).

2.  Evidence of Endocardial Involvement:

•  Positive Echocardiogram: Oscillating intracardiac mass (vegetation), myocardial abscess, or new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve, OR

•  New valvular regurgitation (worsening/changing of pre-existing murmur is not sufficient).

•  Minor Criteria (5):

1.  Predisposing heart condition or intravenous drug use.

2.  Fever ≥ 38.0°C.

3.  Vascular phenomena: Major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhage, conjunctival haemorrhages, Janeway lesions.

4.  Immunological phenomena: Glomerulonephritis, Osler’s nodes, Roth’s spots, Rheumatoid factor.

5.  Microbiological evidence: Positive blood culture not meeting major criteria, or serological evidence of active infection.

•  Definite IE:2 Major OR 1 Major + 3 Minor

•  Definite IE:2 Major OR 1 Major + 3 Minor OR 5 Minor criteria.

•  Possible IE:1 Major + 1 Minor OR 3 Minor criteria.

•  Key Diagnostic Investigations:

1.  Blood Cultures (Pivotal): Collect 3 to 6 sets (aerobic & anaerobic) from different peripheral venepuncture sites at ≥ 30-minute intervals before starting antibiotics (do not wait for fever spikes; never draw from indwelling lines).

2.  Echocardiography:

•  Transthoracic Echo (TTE): First-line (sensitivity ~65%; detects vegetations >2–4 mm and valve damage).

•  Transoesophageal Echo (TOE): Sensitivity >90% (detects vegetations 1–1.5 mm); mandatory if TTE is negative with high clinical suspicion, in prosthetic valve IE, or to detect aortic root/paravalvular abscess.

3.  Other Tests: FBC (normocytic normochromic anaemia, leucocytosis), CRP & ESR (elevated; serial CRP monitors treatment response), Urine microscopy (microscopic haematuria, red cell casts, proteinuria), Serial 12-lead ECG (prolongation of PR interval or new AV block = aortic root abscess), Chest X-ray (cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema, or multiple cavitating septic emboli in right-sided IE).

5. Management & Prevention of Infective Endocarditis [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 19, 17]

•  1. General Measures: Multidisciplinary management (cardiologist, microbiologist, cardiothoracic surgeon); remove any source of infection (extract abscessed teeth, remove infected central lines/devices).

•  2. Antimicrobial Therapy (Bactericidal, Parenteral, Prolonged — 4 weeks for native valves, 6 weeks for prosthetic valves):

•  Empirical Therapy (started after blood cultures drawn):

•  Subacute Native Valve:IV Amoxicillin (2 g 6 times daily) + Gentamicin (1 mg/kg BD) or Ceftriaxone.

•  Acute Native Valve / Sepsis:IV Flucloxacillin (2 g 4–6 times daily) + Gentamicin (or Vancomycin if penicillin-allergic/MRSA risk).

•  Prosthetic Valve IE:IV Vancomycin (1 g BD) + IV Gentamicin (1 mg/kg BD) + Oral Rifampicin (300–600 mg BD).

•  Targeted Therapy (by Organism & MIC — Davidson Box 16.96):

•  Fully Penicillin-Sensitive Streptococci (MIC ≤ 0.125 mg/L):IV Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 4-hourly for 4 weeks (or a 2-week short course of Benzylpenicillin + Gentamicin if uncomplicated native valve IE with vegetation <5 mm).

•  Enterococci:IV Amoxicillin (2 g 4-hourly) or Vancomycin + IV Gentamicin for 4–6 weeks.

•  Methicillin-Sensitive Staphylococci (MSSA):IV Flucloxacillin 2 g 4–6-hourly for 4 weeks (add Rifampicin + Gentamicin for 6 weeks if prosthetic valve).

•  Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococci (MRSA):IV Vancomycin + Oral Rifampicin for 4–6 weeks.

•  HACEK organisms:IV Ceftriaxone 2 g OD for 4–6 weeks.

•  3. Indications for Cardiac Surgery (Debridement + Valve Repair/Replacement — required in ~50%):

1.  Refractory Heart Failure or cardiogenic shock due to acute severe aortic or mitral regurgitation/valve obstruction.

2.  Uncontrolled / Persistent Infection: Paravalvular abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, heart block, or persistent fever/bacteraemia despite 7–10 days of appropriate antibiotics, or fungal / prosthetic valve IE.

3.  Prevention of Systemic Embolism: Large left-sided vegetations (>10 mm with ≥ 1 embolic episode, or >15 mm isolated mobile vegetation).

•  4. Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis [KU 23, 22]:

•  Indications (High-Risk Cardiac Lesions Only):

1.  Prosthetic heart valves (surgical or transcatheter/TAVI) or prosthetic material used for valve repair.

2.  Previous episode of infective endocarditis.

3.  Congenital heart disease: Unrepaired cyanotic CHD, or CHD repaired with prosthetic material/devices (for the first 6 months post-procedure, or lifelong if residual shunt/valvular regurgitation persists).

•  Procedures Requiring Prophylaxis: Invasive oro-dental procedures involving manipulation of gingival tissue, periapical region of teeth, or perforation of oral mucosa (+ good daily oral hygiene).

•  Regimen (30–60 mins before procedure):Oral Amoxicillin 2 g (or 3 g) single dose (or Clindamycin 600 mg / Azithromycin 500 mg if penicillin-allergic).

subject: medicine
title: 29. Congenital Heart Diseases: ASD, VSD, Tetralogy of Fallot & Eisenmenger’s Syndrome [KU 25, 22, 18, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 13.11 — CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE

29. Congenital Heart Diseases: ASD, VSD, Tetralogy of Fallot & Eisenmenger’s Syndrome [KU 25, 22, 18, 15, TU, RGU]

A. Classification of Congenital Heart Disease [KU 22, RGU]

•  Acyanotic Congenital Heart Diseases:

•  With Left-to-Right Shunt (Increased Pulmonary Blood Flow):Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD — 30%, most common), Atrial Septal Defect (ASD — 10%), Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA — 10%), Atrioventricular septal defect.

•  Obstructive Lesions (Without Shunt): Pulmonary stenosis (7%), Coarctation of the aorta (7%), Congenital aortic stenosis (6%).

•  Cyanotic Congenital Heart Diseases ([KU 22, RGU] — Mnemonic: 5 Ts + E):

1.  Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) — Most common cyanotic CHD in children after infancy.

2.  Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) — Most common cyanotic CHD presenting in the newborn period.

3.  Tricuspid Atresia (with hypoplastic RV).

4.  Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC).

5.  Truncus Arteriosus & Pulmonary Atresia.

6.  Ebstein’s Anomaly (apical displacement of dysplastic tricuspid valve into RV ("atrialised RV"), associated with maternal lithium exposure, severe TR, WPW accessory pathways, and RA-to-LA shunt via ASD).

7.  Eisenmenger’s Syndrome (late shunt reversal in large VSD, PDA, or ASD).

B. Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) [TU]

•  Types:

1.  Ostium Secundum ASD (80%): Defect in the fossa ovalis mid-septum.

2.  Ostium Primum ASD (15%): Defect in the lower AV septum; associated with a cleft anterior mitral leaflet (MR) and Down syndrome.

3.  Sinus Venosus ASD (5%): High in septum near SVC entry; associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage.

•  Pathophysiology & Clinical Features: Left-to-right shunt from LA → RA → RV volume overload and pulmonary plethora. Usually asymptomatic in childhood; presents in adulthood with exertional dyspnoea, atrial fibrillation/flutter, or right heart failure.

•  Classical Examination Findings:

•  Left parasternal heave (RV dilatation).

•  Wide, FIXED splitting of the second heart sound (S2) — wide due to delayed RV emptying/RBBB; fixed because the defect equalises LA and RA pressures throughout inspiration and expiration.

•  Ejection systolic flow murmur at the pulmonary area (left 2nd ICS) + mid-diastolic tricuspid flow murmur at lower left sternal edge (in large shunts).

•  Investigations & Management:

•  ECG:Incomplete RBBB (rSR' in V1) + Right axis deviation (in Ostium Secundum) OR Left axis deviation (in Ostium Primum).

•  CXR: Enlarged RA, RV, and pulmonary artery trunk with pulmonary plethora.

•  Echo (TTE/TOE): Diagnostic.

•  Management:Percutaneous transcatheter closure (using an Amplatzer septal occluder device for secundum ASD) or surgical patch closure if pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio (Qp:Qs) is ≥ 1.5:1 (contraindicated once Eisenmenger’s syndrome develops).

C. Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) [RGU]

•  Anatomy: 80% are perimembranous; 20% are muscular.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Small VSD (Maladie de Roger): Asymptomatic; produces a very loud, harsh pansystolic murmur with a palpable thrill at the lower left sternal edge (3rd–4th ICS). Often closes spontaneously in childhood.

•  Large VSD: Presents at 4–6 weeks of life (as fetal pulmonary vascular resistance falls) with heart failure (tachypnoea, feeding difficulty, failure to thrive, hepatomegaly), biventricular hypertrophy, loud P2, pansystolic murmur, and apical mid-diastolic mitral flow murmur.

•  Management: Small VSDs require only observation and good dental hygiene; large VSDs with heart failure or pulmonary hypertension (Qp:Qs ≥ 1.5:1) require diuretics/ACE inhibitors followed by surgical patch closure (or percutaneous device closure) before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease develops.

D. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) [KU 15]

•  Four Anatomical Components of Fallot’s Tetralogy:

1.  Right Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction (Pulmonary Stenosis): Usually subvalvular (infundibular muscular spasm) ± valvular/supravalvular.

2.  Large, Non-restrictive Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) (perimembranous).

3.  Overriding of the Aorta over the interventricular septum (receives blood from both RV and LV).

4.  Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH) (concentric, secondary to systemic RV pressures).

(Note: Addition of an ASD = Pentalogy of Fallot).

•  Pathophysiology & Clinical Features:

•  Severity of cyanosis is determined by the severity of the RV outflow tract obstruction, which shunts deoxygenated RV blood right-to-left across the VSD into the overriding aorta.

•  Cyanotic ("Tet") Spells: Paroxysms of worsening central cyanosis, tachypnoea, and syncope triggered by crying, feeding, or exertion (sympathetic surge causes dynamic infundibular spasm → acute increase in right-to-left shunting).

•  Squatting after exertion (Fallot’s sign): Children characteristically squat to relieve dyspnoea — kinking the femoral arteries increases systemic vascular resistance (afterload), which reduces the right-to-left shunt and forces more blood into the lungs.

•  Examination: Central cyanosis, grade 3–4 digital clubbing, stunting of growth, polycythaemia, left parasternal heave, single S2 (soft/absent P2), and a loud harsh ejection systolic murmur at the pulmonary area (derived from the pulmonary stenosis, not the VSD; during a cyanotic spell, the murmur becomes shorter/disappears).

•  Investigations & Management:

•  CXR:"Boot-shaped heart" (Coeur en sabot) due to uplifted RV apex and concave main pulmonary artery bay, with oligemic lung fields.

•  ECG: Right axis deviation and marked RVH. Echo: Diagnostic.

•  Management:

•  Cyanotic Spell: Knee-chest position, high-flow O2, IV morphine, IV fluids, IV Propranolol (relaxes infundibular spasm), and IV Phenylephrine (increases SVR).

•  Surgical:Definitive Total Surgical Correction (patch closure of VSD + resection/widening of infundibular stenosis) in infancy. Palliative modified Blalock–Taussig shunt (subclavian-to-pulmonary artery Gore-Tex graft) if pulmonary arteries are severely hypoplastic.

E. Eisenmenger’s Syndrome [KU 25, 18, TU]

•  Definition & Pathogenesis: The development of severe, irreversible pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) in a patient with a congenital left-to-right cardiac shunt (large VSD, PDA, or ASD), leading to reversal of the shunt (right-to-left) and central cyanosis.

•  Pathology (Plexogenic Pulmonary Arteriopathy): Persistent high pulmonary blood flow and pressure cause endothelial shear injury → medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, necrotising arteritis, and plexiform lesions with obliteration of distal pulmonary arterioles → pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) exceeds systemic vascular resistance (SVR).

•  Clinical Features ([KU 18, TU]):

•  Symptoms: Progressive exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, chest pain (RV angina), exertional syncope, haemoptysis (rupture of dilated bronchial arteries or pulmonary infarction), and features of hyperviscosity from secondary polycythaemia (headache, visual disturbances, dizziness).

•  Physical Signs:

1.  Central Cyanosis and Digital Clubbing: Generalized in VSD and ASD; Differential Cyanosis and Clubbing (toes cyanosed and clubbed, fingers pink and unclubbed) is pathognomonic of PDA with Eisenmenger’s syndrome (shunt enters aorta distal to left subclavian artery).

2.  JVP: Prominent a waves (and giant v waves if functional TR develops).

3.  Precordium: Left parasternal heave, palpable P2, loud booming P2, pulmonary ejection click, disappearance of the original shunt murmur (VSD/PDA murmur disappears as pressures equalise), Graham Steell early diastolic murmur (PR), and pansystolic murmur of TR.

•  Complications: Right heart failure, Paradoxical embolism & Cerebral abscess (venous clots/bacteria bypass pulmonary filter), Haemoptysis, Secondary polycythaemia & gout, Sudden arrhythmic death, and  >50% maternal mortality in pregnancy.

•  Investigations:CXR: Dilated central pulmonary arteries with peripheral "pruning" of lung fields; ECG: Severe RVH and P pulmonale; Echo: Bidirectional/right-to-left shunt and severe PAH.

•  Management:

•  Surgical closure of the defect is strictly CONTRAINDICATED (the defect acts as a "pop-off" relief valve for the failing RV).

•  General: Strictly avoid pregnancy, vasodilators, dehydration, high altitude, and general anaesthesia. Venesection only if symptomatic hyperviscosity with haematocrit >65%.

•  Medical: Pulmonary vasodilators (Bosentan / Macitentan [endothelin antagonists], Sildenafil / Tadalafil [PDE-5 inhibitors], Prostacyclin analogues), diuretics for RV failure.

•  Definitive:Combined Heart–Lung Transplantation (or Bilateral Lung Transplant with surgical shunt repair).
