title: 30. Cardiomyopathies (Dilated, Hypertrophic, Restrictive, Post-partum, Takotsubo) & Myocarditis [KU 24, 21, 17, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 13.12 — DISEASE OF MYOCARDIUM

30. Cardiomyopathies (Dilated, Hypertrophic, Restrictive, Post-partum, Takotsubo) & Myocarditis [KU 24, 21, 17, TU, RGU]

A. Classification & Overview of Cardiomyopathies [TU, RGU]

•  Definition: Primary diseases of the heart muscle not secondary to ischaemic, hypertensive, valvular, or congenital heart disease.

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-003]]

(Other Specific Types:Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy [ARVC]: Autosomal dominant desmosomal mutation [Plakophilin-2] → fibro-fatty replacement of RV myocardium → epsilon wave & T-inversion in V1–V3, VT, and sudden death. Takotsubo ["Broken Heart"] Cardiomyopathy: Acute catecholamine-mediated apical ballooning of LV triggered by severe emotional/physical stress in post-menopausal women, mimicking anterior STEMI with normal coronaries; reversible within weeks).

B. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM / HOCM) [KU 21, 17]

•  Pathophysiology: Autosomal dominant sarcomeric gene mutation → marked Asymmetric Septal Hypertrophy (ASH), myocardial fibre disarray, and fibrosis. High velocity of blood across the narrowed LV outflow tract draws the anterior mitral valve leaflet towards the septum via the Venturi/drag effect (Systolic Anterior Motion — SAM), causing dynamic LVOT obstruction and mitral regurgitation, alongside a stiff, non-compliant LV (diastolic dysfunction) and subendocardial ischaemia.

•  Clinical Features ([KU 17]):

•  Symptoms:Exertional angina, Exertional dyspnoea, Exertional syncope/pre-syncope, Palpitations, and Sudden Cardiac Death (most common cause of sudden death in young competitive athletes).

•  Physical Signs:

1.  Jerky arterial pulse (rapid initial upstroke followed by sudden mid-systolic collapse as dynamic obstruction develops).

2.  Prominent a wave in JVP (reduced RV compliance).

3.  Double apical impulse (palpable pre-systolic S4 + sustained systolic heave).

4.  Audible S4 (in sinus rhythm).

5.  Harsh late-peaking Ejection Systolic Murmur at the lower left sternal border (does NOT radiate to carotids):

•  Increases in intensity with manoeuvres that decrease LV cavity size (Standing up, Valsalva manoeuvre, inotropes, nitrates, diuretics).

•  Decreases in intensity with manoeuvres that increase LV volume/afterload (Squatting, Passive leg raising, Isometric handgrip).

6.  Apical pansystolic murmur of mitral regurgitation (secondary to SAM).

•  Investigations:

•  ECG: LVH, deep "dagger-like" septal Q waves in inferolateral leads, bizarre giant T-wave inversions (especially in Apical HCM [Yamaguchi syndrome]).

•  Echocardiogram (Diagnostic): Asymmetric septal hypertrophy (≥ 15 mm; septal-to-posterior wall ratio >1.3:1), SAM of mitral valve, dynamic LVOT gradient.

•  Cardiac MRI: Quantifies late gadolinium enhancement (fibrosis burden) and 24-hr Holter screens for non-sustained VT.

•  Risk Factors for Sudden Cardiac Death in HCM (Indications for ICD):

1.  Prior cardiac arrest or sustained VT.

2.  Family history of premature sudden death (<40 yrs) from HCM.

3.  Unexplained recurrent syncope.

4.  Massive LV wall thickness (≥ 30 mm).

5.  Non-sustained VT on Holter monitoring.

6.  Abnormal (flat or hypotensive) BP response to exercise, or extensive fibrosis (>15%) on Cardiac MRI.

•  Management:

•  General: Avoid strenuous competitive sports and dehydration; genetic counselling and cascade screening of 1st-degree relatives.

•  Medical:Beta-blockers (first-line — slow heart rate, prolong diastole, reduce contractility and LVOT gradient), Verapamil (if β-blocker intolerant), Disopyramide (negative inotrope added for refractory obstruction), and Mavacamten (novel selective cardiac myosin ATPase inhibitor). (Strictly avoid Digoxin, Nitrates, Diuretics, and Dihydropyridine CCBs as they worsen LVOT obstruction).

•  Invasive Septal Reduction Therapy (for refractory symptoms with gradient ≥ 50 mmHg):Surgical Septal Myectomy (Morrow procedure) or Percutaneous Alcohol Septal Ablation (infusion of absolute alcohol into the 1st septal perforator branch of LAD to induce controlled basal septal infarction).

•  ICD Implantation: For patients with high-risk features for sudden death.

C. Post-Partum (Peripartum) Cardiomyopathy (PPCM) [KU 24]

•  Definition: An idiopathic form of dilated cardiomyopathy presenting with heart failure secondary to LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF < 45%) towards the end of pregnancy (last month) or within the first 5 months post-partum, in the absence of any pre-existing cardiac disease.

•  Risk Factors & Pathogenesis: Multiparity, advanced maternal age (>30 yrs), multifetal (twin) pregnancy, pre-eclampsia/hypertension, African ancestry; mediated by angiogenic imbalance (cleavage of prolactin into an anti-angiogenic 16-kDa fragment that damages cardiomyocytes).

•  Clinical Features: Dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, cough, pedal oedema, tachycardia, raised JVP, displaced apex, S3 gallop, and high risk of intracardiac mural thrombus and systemic/pulmonary thromboembolism.

•  Management:

•  During Pregnancy: Loop diuretics, β-blockers (metoprolol/bisoprolol), Hydralazine + Nitrates, and LMWH anticoagulation (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, MRAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors are teratogenic and CONTRAINDICATED before delivery).

•  Post-Partum: Standard 4-pillar HFrEF therapy (ACEi/ARB, β-blocker, Spironolactone, SGLT2i), Anticoagulation (if LVEF <35%), and Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist to block prolactin secretion in severe cases).

•  Prognosis: ~50% recover normal LV function within 6 months; subsequent pregnancy carries a high risk of relapse and mortality if LVEF has not normalised.

D. Myocarditis [TU]

•  Causes of Myocarditis:

1.  Viral Infections (Most common):Coxsackie B virus, Adenovirus, Influenza A & B, SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), HIV, Parvovirus B19, Dengue.

2.  Bacterial:Corynebacterium diphtheriae (toxin), Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease — causes AV block), Mycoplasma, Streptococci.

3.  Protozoal & Parasitic:Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease), Toxoplasma gondii.

4.  Drugs & Toxins: Alcohol, Anthracyclines (Doxorubicin), Cocaine, Clozapine, Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors (Nivolumab, Ipilimumab), mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccines (rare, in young males), Hypersensitivity (penicillins, sulphonamides).

5.  Autoimmune / Inflammatory: SLE, Sarcoidosis, Giant-cell myocarditis, Acute rheumatic fever.

•  Clinical Features & Management: Follows a viral prodrome; ranges from asymptomatic ECG changes or pleuritic/ischaemic chest pain to fulminant heart failure/cardiogenic shock, AV blocks, or sudden arrhythmic death. Diagnosed by elevated Troponin I/T, Echo, and Cardiac MRI (Lake Louise criteria — subepicardial/mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement). Treatment is supportive (heart failure therapy, arrhythmia control, strict avoidance of strenuous physical exercise for 3–6 months).

title: 31. Acute Pericarditis, Pericardial Effusion, Cardiac Tamponade & Constrictive Pericarditis [KU 23, 20, 18, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 13.13 — DISEASE OF PERICARDIUM

31. Acute Pericarditis, Pericardial Effusion, Cardiac Tamponade & Constrictive Pericarditis [KU 23, 20, 18, TU, RGU]

A. Acute Pericarditis [KU 23, TU]

•  Causes of Acute Pericarditis & Pericardial Effusion ([KU 23]):

1.  Infectious:Viral (Coxsackie B, echovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, HIV — most common, often termed "idiopathic"), Bacterial (Tuberculosis [commonest in India], S. pneumoniae, S. aureus [purulent]), Fungal.

2.  Post-Myocardial Infarction: Early fibrinous pericarditis (1–3 days post-MI) or Late autoimmune Dressler’s syndrome (2–10 weeks post-MI).

3.  Metabolic:Uraemia (advanced renal failure — indication for urgent dialysis), Myxoedema (hypothyroidism).

4.  Autoimmune / Connective Tissue Disease: SLE, Rheumatoid arthritis, Acute rheumatic fever, Systemic sclerosis.

5.  Neoplastic (typically haemorrhagic effusion): Metastatic carcinoma of lung or breast, lymphoma, mesothelioma.

6.  Trauma / Iatrogenic: Post-cardiac surgery (post-pericardiotomy syndrome), pacemaker/PCI perforation, mediastinal radiotherapy, drugs (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid).

•  Clinical Features:

•  Sharp, central retrosternal pleuritic chest pain: Radiates to the neck and trapezius ridge (phrenic nerve supply); aggravated by inspiration, coughing, swallowing, and lying supine, and relieved by sitting upright and leaning forward.

•  Pericardial Friction Rub (Pathognomonic): High-pitched, superficial, leathery/scratching "to-and-fro" sound (up to 3 components: atrial systole, ventricular systole, early ventricular diastole), best heard with the diaphragm at the lower left sternal edge with the patient leaning forward in held expiration.

•  Investigations:

•  12-Lead ECG:Widespread concave-upwards ("saddle-shaped") ST-segment elevation (across both anterior and inferior leads) with PR-segment depression (most specific early sign); later diffuse T-wave inversion (without pathological Q waves).

•  Bloods (raised CRP, ESR, WBC; mild troponin elevation if myopericarditis) and Echocardiogram (normal or shows effusion).

•  Management: Treat underlying cause; High-dose Aspirin (600 mg 4–6 times daily) or NSAIDs (Ibuprofen 600 mg TDS / Indometacin 50 mg TDS) with PPI cover + Colchicine (0.5 mg BD for 3 months — halves recurrence rate). (Avoid glucocorticoids in viral/idiopathic pericarditis as they increase relapse rates; steroids ARE indicated as an adjunct to ATT in tuberculous pericarditis to prevent constriction).

B. Pericardial Effusion & Cardiac Tamponade [KU 23, 20, TU, RGU]

•  Pericardial Effusion ([RGU]): Accumulation of >50 mL fluid in the pericardial sac (serous, fibrinous, purulent, or haemorrhagic [TB, malignancy]).

•  Clinical Signs of Large Effusion: Quiet/muffled heart sounds, impalpable apex beat (or apex palpable medial to the left border of cardiac dullness), increased area of cardiac dullness, and Ewart’s sign (patch of dullness, bronchial breathing, and aegophony beneath the angle of the left scapula due to compression of the left lower lobe by the distended pericardial sac).

•  Chest X-Ray ([RGU]): Symmetrical, globular ("water-bottle" or "money-bag") enlargement of the cardiac silhouette (requires >250 mL fluid) with clear lung fields.

•  ECG:Low-voltage QRS complexes and Electrical Alternans (beat-to-beat alternation in QRS axis and amplitude caused by the heart swinging within the fluid-filled sac).

•  Cardiac Tamponade ([KU 23, 20, TU]):

•  Definition & Pathophysiology: Life-threatening acute heart failure caused by compression of the heart chambers by a tense pericardial effusion, which raises intrapericardial pressure above ventricular filling pressures → impairs diastolic filling of RV and LV → precipitous drop in stroke volume and cardiac output. During inspiration, increased RV filling shifts the interventricular septum to the left (ventricular interdependence), further compromising LV filling and causing pulsus paradoxus.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Beck’s Triad:

1.  Systemic Hypotension (with narrow pulse pressure and tachycardia).

2.  Grossly Elevated JVP (with prominent systolic x descent and absent y descent).

3.  Soft, muffled, or distant heart sounds.

•  Pulsus Paradoxus: Exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic BP of >10 mmHg (radial pulse may disappear on inspiration).

•  Dyspnoea with clear lung fields, oliguria, restlessness, and collapse/PEA arrest.

•  Investigations:Urgent Bedside Echocardiogram (Pivotal): Demonstrates circumferential pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium and right ventricle, dilated non-collapsible IVC, and exaggerated respiratory variation (>25%) in mitral/tricuspid inflow velocities.

•  Emergency Management:

1.  Urgent Percutaneous Pericardiocentesis under echocardiographic guidance (via subxiphoid or apical approach, leaving a pigtail drain in situ).

2.  IV fluid resuscitation to maintain preload (strictly avoid diuretics and vasodilators).

3.  Surgical Pericardiotomy (pericardial window) if tamponade is due to ventricular free-wall rupture, aortic dissection, trauma, or recurrent malignant effusion.

C. Chronic Constrictive Pericarditis [KU 18]

•  Aetiology & Pathology: Progressive fibrous thickening, scarring, and calcification of the pericardium that encases the heart in a rigid, non-compliant shell, severely restricting mid-to-late diastolic ventricular filling. Causes:Tuberculosis (most common in developing countries), post-cardiac surgery, mediastinal irradiation, purulent or viral pericarditis, rheumatoid arthritis.

•  Clinical Features ([KU 18] — Right-sided venous congestion predominates; lungs are clear):

1.  Fatigue, wasting, and dyspnoea (without orthopnoea/PND).

2.  Rapid, low-volume pulse; Atrial Fibrillation in 30%.

3.  Grossly elevated JVP with a steep, rapid x and y descent ("W" or "M" sign / Friedreich’s sign).

4.  Kussmaul’s Sign: Paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration (rigid pericardium cannot accommodate inspiratory venous return).

5.  Loud, high-pitched early diastolic "Pericardial Knock" (heard just after S2 due to abrupt cessation of rapid early diastolic ventricular filling as the heart hits the rigid shell).

6.  Massive ascites (ascites praecox — disproportionate to pedal oedema), marked tender hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and peripheral oedema (often misdiagnosed as liver cirrhosis).

7.  Pulsus paradoxus (in ~1/3rd of cases).

•  Investigations & Management:

•  CXR (Lateral view) & CT/MRI Thorax:Heavy pericardial calcification (50%) and pericardial thickening (>4 mm) with normal-sized heart.

•  Echo & Cardiac Catheterisation: Septal bounce, equalisation of diastolic pressures in all 4 chambers, and "dip-and-plateau" (square-root sign) on ventricular pressure trace.

•  Management: Loop diuretics and Spironolactone for fluid overload + Antituberculous therapy (if TB); definitive treatment is Surgical Pericardiectomy (decortication).

title: 32. Bronchopulmonary Segments & Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs) [KU 22, 19, 21, TU]
text:
CHAPTER 14: RESPIRATORY MEDICINE (Davidson Ch. 17)

SECTION 14.1 & 14.2 — FUNCTIONAL ANATOMY & INVESTIGATIONS

32. Bronchopulmonary Segments & Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs) [KU 22, 19, 21, TU]

A. Bronchopulmonary Segments [KU 19]

•  Definition: Anatomically and functionally independent pyramidal subdivisions of a lung lobe (base at pleura, apex at hilum), each aerated by its own tertiary (segmental) bronchus, supplied by its own segmental branch of the pulmonary and bronchial arteries, and surrounded by a connective tissue septum (allowing surgical segmentectomy without damaging adjacent segments).

•  Segmental Anatomy (10 Right, 8–9 Left):

•  Right Lung (10 Segments):

•  Right Upper Lobe (3): Apical, Posterior, Anterior.

•  Right Middle Lobe (2): Lateral, Medial.

•  Right Lower Lobe (5): Apical (Superior — commonest site of aspiration pneumonia in supine patients), Medial basal, Anterior basal, Lateral basal, Posterior basal.

•  Left Lung (8–9 Segments):

•  Left Upper Lobe (4): Apicoposterior (1+2), Anterior (3), Superior Lingular (4), Inferior Lingular (5).

•  Left Lower Lobe (4–5): Apical (Superior), Anteromedial basal, Lateral basal, Posterior basal.

B. Pulmonary Function Tests (Spirometry, Lung Volumes & Diffusion Capacity) [KU 22, 21, TU]

•  1. Dynamic Spirometry & Reversibility:

•  Measures Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (FEV1), Forced Vital Capacity (FVC), and the FEV1/FVC ratio (Normal ≥ 0.70 or >70%).

•  Obstructive Ventilatory Defect (FEV1/FVC < 0.70, FEV1 ↓↓): Seen in Asthma, COPD, Bronchiectasis.

•  Bronchodilator Reversibility Testing: Repeat spirometry 15–20 mins after inhaling 400 µg Salbutamol. An increase in FEV1 (or FVC) of ≥ 12% AND ≥ 200 mL indicates significant reversibility (>15% and >400 mL strongly favours Asthma over COPD).

•  Restrictive Ventilatory Defect (FEV1/FVC normal or increased ≥ 0.70, FVC ↓↓, FEV1 ↓): Seen in Interstitial Lung Disease (pulmonary fibrosis), Kyphoscoliosis, Neuromuscular weakness, Pleural effusion/thickening.

•  Flow–Volume Loops: Differentiates intrathoracic small airway obstruction ("scooped-out" concave expiratory limb in COPD/asthma) from large upper airway/tracheal obstruction (flattened plateau on inspiratory and/or expiratory limb).

•  2. Static Lung Volumes (Measured by Helium Dilution or Body Plethysmography):

•  Total Lung Capacity (TLC) and Residual Volume (RV):Increased (hyperinflation/air-trapping) in COPD/Emphysema; Decreased (<80% predicted) in Interstitial Lung Disease.

•  3. Carbon Monoxide Transfer Factor (TLCO / DLCO) & Transfer Coefficient (KCO):

•  Measures gas exchange across the alveolar–capillary membrane using a single breath of 0.3% CO.

•  Decreased TLCO:Emphysema (alveolar wall destruction — distinguishes emphysema from chronic bronchitis and asthma), Interstitial Lung Disease / Pulmonary Fibrosis, Pulmonary vascular disease, Severe anaemia.

•  Increased TLCO:Asthma, Alveolar haemorrhage (Goodpasture’s), Polycythaemia.

•  Summary of PFT Abnormalities in Interstitial Lung Disease ([KU 21]):

1.  Restrictive spirometry: Disproportionately reduced FVC, reduced FEV1, and normal or elevated FEV1/FVC ratio (>0.70–0.80).

2.  Reduced static lung volumes: ↓ TLC, ↓ FRC, and ↓ RV.

3.  Markedly reduced gas transfer: ↓↓ TLCO (DLCO) and ↓ KCO.

4.  Arterial blood gases & Exercise testing: Resting or exercise-induced arterial oxygen desaturation (↓ PaO2) with hypocapnia (↓ PaCO2 — Type I respiratory failure).

subject: medicine
title: 33. Digital Clubbing & Hypertrophic Pulmonary Osteoarthropathy (HPOA) [KU 25, 24, 21, 17, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 14.3 — SYMPTOMS AND SIGNS IN RESPIRATORY DISEASES

33. Digital Clubbing & Hypertrophic Pulmonary Osteoarthropathy (HPOA) [KU 25, 24, 21, 17, 15, TU, RGU]

A. Digital Clubbing [KU 25, 24, 21, 17]

•  Definition & Pathogenesis: Painless, symmetrical bulbous enlargement of the soft tissues of the terminal phalanges of the fingers and toes, with increased longitudinal and transverse curvature of the nails. Thought to be mediated by megakaryocytes and platelet clumps bypassing the pulmonary capillary bed (or released from lung pathology) and impacting in digital capillaries, where they release Platelet-Derived Growth Factor (PDGF) and VEGF, inducing fibrovascular proliferation.

•  Clinical Grading / Stages of Clubbing:

•  Grade 1: Softening and fluctuation of the nail bed (increased ballotability on palpation).

•  Grade 2: Obliteration of the normal lovibond (hyponychial) angle (>180°, normally ~ 160°) with loss of Schamroth’s window (absence of the diamond-shaped gap when dorsal surfaces of opposite terminal phalanges are apposed).

•  Grade 3: Increased longitudinal and lateral convexity of the nail ("Parrot-beak" appearance).

•  Grade 4: Swelling of the entire distal digit ("Drumstick" fingers).

•  (Often considered Grade 5: Hypertrophic Pulmonary Osteoarthropathy).

•  Causes of Digital Clubbing (Davidson Box 17.8):

•  1. Respiratory / Thoracic Causes (~80% of cases) [KU 25, 24]:

•  Malignancy:Bronchogenic carcinoma (especially Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer — squamous & adenocarcinoma), Pleural mesothelioma, Pleural fibroma.

•  Chronic Suppurative Lung Disease:Bronchiectasis, Lung abscess, Empyema thoracis, Cystic fibrosis.

•  Interstitial Lung Disease:Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF), Asbestosis.

•  Infections: Chronic cavitary / fibrotic Pulmonary Tuberculosis (late sequela). (Note: Uncomplicated COPD, asthma, and acute pneumonia do NOT cause clubbing).

•  2. Cardiovascular Causes:

•  Cyanotic Congenital Heart Diseases (Tetralogy of Fallot, Eisenmenger’s syndrome, TGA).

•  Subacute Infective Endocarditis.

•  Atrial myxoma, Axillary/brachial arteriovenous aneurysm or dialysis fistula (unilateral clubbing).

•  3. Gastrointestinal & Hepatic Causes:

•  Liver cirrhosis (especially Primary Biliary Cholangitis).

•  Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn’s disease, Ulcerative colitis).

•  Coeliac disease, GI lymphoma.

•  4. Endocrine & Miscellaneous:

•  Thyrotoxicosis (Graves’ disease — Thyroid acropachy).

•  Congenital / Familial (Idiopathic — 5–10%) / Primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (Pachydermoperiostosis).

B. Hypertrophic Pulmonary Osteoarthropathy (HPOA) [KU 15]

•  Definition: A paraneoplastic syndrome characterised by the triad of:

1.  Digital clubbing.

2.  Painful, symmetrical periostitis (subperiosteal new bone formation) of the distal ends of long bones (distal tibia, fibula, radius, and ulna), causing severe burning shin/wrist pain and local tenderness.

3.  Symmetrical polyarthropathy of adjacent ankles, knees, and wrists (often with pitting oedema over the anterior shins).

•  Causes: Most commonly Bronchogenic carcinoma (especially Adenocarcinoma and Squamous cell carcinoma; rare in small-cell carcinoma) and Pleural mesothelioma.

•  Investigation & Treatment: X-rays of distal tibia/radius show parallel subperiosteal new bone formation ("tramline" periosteal reaction); isotope bone scan shows increased cortical uptake. Resolves rapidly upon resection of the primary lung tumour; symptomatic relief with NSAIDs or bisphosphonates.

subject: medicine
title: 34. Acute Breathlessness & Massive Haemoptysis [KU 24, 15, RGU]
text:
34. Acute Breathlessness & Massive Haemoptysis [KU 24, 15, RGU]

A. Respiratory Causes & Evaluation of Sudden-Onset Dyspnoea [KU 24]

•  Respiratory Causes of Sudden-Onset Dyspnoea (Minutes to Hours):

1.  Spontaneous Pneumothorax (especially Tension Pneumothorax).

2.  Acute Pulmonary Thromboembolism.

3.  Acute Severe Asthma or Acute Exacerbation of COPD.

4.  Foreign Body Inhalation / Acute Laryngeal Obstruction (Anaphylaxis/Angioedema).

5.  Lobar Collapse (mucus plug) or Acute Pneumonia / ARDS.

(Non-respiratory causes: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema/MI, Cardiac tamponade, Metabolic acidosis [DKA], Psychogenic hyperventilation).

•  Evaluation: Rapid ABCDE assessment → Check SpO2, RR, HR, BP, JVP, tracheal position (shifted away in tension pneumothorax; towards in collapse), percussion (hyper-resonant in pneumothorax; stony dull in effusion), and auscultation (stridor = upper airway; polyphonic wheeze = asthma/COPD; fine basal creps = pulmonary oedema; bronchial breathing = pneumonia; normal chest with severe hypoxia = Pulmonary Embolism). Confirm with ABG, Urgent Portable CXR, 12-lead ECG, D-dimer/CTPA, and Troponin/NT-proBNP.

B. Massive Haemoptysis [KU 15, RGU]

•  Definition: Expectoration of >100–150 mL of blood in a single episode or >500–600 mL over 24 hours, OR any volume of bleeding that causes airway obstruction/asphyxiation or haemodynamic instability. (90% of massive haemoptysis originates from the high-pressure systemic bronchial artery circulation).

•  Major Causes (Davidson Box 17.9):

1.  Bronchiectasis (hypertrophied tortuous bronchial arteries).

2.  Pulmonary Tuberculosis (active cavitary disease or rupture of a Rasmussen’s aneurysm in an old TB cavity).

3.  Intracavitary Aspergilloma (Mycetoma) or Lung Abscess.

4.  Bronchogenic Carcinoma.

5.  Pulmonary Infarction / Embolism, Mitral Stenosis, and Alveolar Haemorrhage Syndromes (Goodpasture’s disease, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis).

•  Emergency Management of Massive Haemoptysis:

1.  Airway Protection & Positioning (First Priority — patients die of asphyxiation, not exsanguination):

•  Nurse the patient upright, or in the lateral decubitus position with the bleeding lung DEPENDENT (downwards) (if the side of bleeding is known) to prevent blood spilling into and flooding the healthy lung.

•  Give high-flow oxygen, suction the airway, and if bleeding is torrential, perform selective endotracheal intubation of the unaffected main bronchus or insert a double-lumen endotracheal tube (Carlen’s tube).

2.  Haemodynamic Resuscitation & Medical Haemostasis:

•  Two large-bore IV cannulae, fluid resuscitation, cross-match blood, FBC, coagulation screen.

•  Reverse any anticoagulants/coagulopathy (FFP, Vitamin K, Prothrombin complex, Platelets).

•  Administer IV Tranexamic Acid (500 mg–1 g TDS — antifibrinolytic) and IV Terlipressin (vasopressin agonist).

3.  Localisation & Definitive Intervention:

•  Bronchial Artery Arteriography and Embolisation (BAE — Treatment of Choice): Interventional radiology cannulation and embolisation of the bleeding bronchial artery (>85% immediate success).

•  Rigid Bronchoscopy (under GA): Allows superior suctioning, airway control, iced-saline/adrenaline lavage, balloon tamponade, or laser/electrocautery of central tumours.

•  CT Thorax / CTPA: Once stabilised, to identify the underlying cause.

•  Emergency Surgical Lobectomy: Last resort if BAE fails and bleeding is localised.

subject: medicine
title: 35. Bronchial Asthma: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, Stepwise Therapy & Acute Severe Asthma [KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 19, 18, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 14.4A — ASTHMA

35. Bronchial Asthma: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, Stepwise Therapy & Acute Severe Asthma [KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 19, 18, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignettes: 20M on two-wheeler in dusty atmosphere with sneezing, dyspnoea & bilateral polyphonic wheeze; 45M with winter wheezing exacerbation)

1. Definition & Pathophysiology

•  Definition: A chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterised by airway hyper-responsiveness (AHR) and variable, reversible airflow obstruction, leading to recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing, particularly at night and in the early morning.

•  Aetiopathogenesis:

•  Gene–Environment Interaction: Strong association with atopy (elevated IgE, personal/family history of allergic rhinitis, eczema) and environmental triggers (house dust mite [Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus], pollens, animal dander, Aspergillus spores, viral URTIs, cold air, exercise, air pollution, tobacco smoke, and drugs like β-blockers and Aspirin/NSAIDs [Samter’s triad: asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin sensitivity]).

•  Type 2 (Eosinophilic) Airway Inflammation: Inhaled allergens cross-link IgE on mast cells (Early Phase Reaction within 15–30 mins: release of histamine, leukotrienes LTC4/D4, and prostaglandin D2 causing acute bronchospasm and mucosal oedema) → Th2 lymphocytes secrete IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 (Late Phase Reaction at 4–12 hrs: recruitment of eosinophils and neutrophils, mucus hypersecretion with Curschmann spirals and Charcot–Leyden crystals).

•  Airway Remodelling (in chronic severe asthma): Subepithelial basement membrane fibrosis, smooth muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia, goblet cell metaplasia, and angiogenesis → fixed airway narrowing.

2. Clinical Features & Diagnosis (Davidson Box 17.19)

•  Clinical Features: Episodic wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness, and dry cough with diurnal variation (worse at night/early morning — "morning dipping"). Examination during an attack reveals tachypnoea, hyperinflated chest, prolonged expiration, and widespread bilateral polyphonic expiratory wheezes (rhonchi); examination may be completely normal between attacks. Look for nasal polyps, allergic rhinitis, and flexural eczema.

•  Diagnostic Investigations:

1.  Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO): Elevated (>50 ppb in adults, >35 ppb in children) — marker of eosinophilic airway inflammation and predicts steroid responsiveness.

2.  Spirometry with Bronchodilator Reversibility: Obstructive defect (FEV1/FVC < 0.70) with an increase in FEV1 of ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL (>15% and >400 mL gives high diagnostic confidence) 20 mins after inhaled salbutamol.

3.  Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) Diary Monitoring: Demonstrates >20% diurnal variation on ≥ 3 days/week for 2 weeks (early morning dip).

4.  Bronchial Challenge Testing (if spirometry is normal): Methacholine, histamine (PC20 < 8 mg/mL), mannitol, or Exercise test (≥ 15% fall in FEV1 after 6 mins of strenuous exercise).

5.  Allergy & Blood Tests: Peripheral blood eosinophilia (>0.3–0.4 × 109/L), elevated total and allergen-specific serum IgE, skin-prick testing.

6.  Chest X-Ray: Usually normal (or hyperinflated); done to exclude pneumothorax, pneumonia, or Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA) (fleeting infiltrates/mucus plugging).

3. Classes of Drugs & Stepwise Management of Chronic Asthma (GINA Guidelines) [KU 24, 18, 16, TU]

•  Main Classes of Anti-Asthma Drugs ([KU 24]):

1.  Bronchodilators (Relievers & Controllers):

•  β2-Adrenoceptor Agonists:Short-acting (SABA): Salbutamol, Terbutaline. Long-acting (LABA):Formoterol (rapid onset + long duration), Salmeterol, Vilanterol.

•  Antimuscarinics (Anticholinergics):Short-acting (SAMA): Ipratropium bromide. Long-acting (LAMA):Tiotropium [RGU] (18 µg DPI or 5 µg Respimat OD; side effects: dry mouth, urinary retention in BPH, glaucoma), Glycopyrronium.

•  Methylxanthines: Theophylline, Aminophylline (narrow therapeutic index; inhibits PDE and antagonises adenosine).

2.  Anti-inflammatory Agents (Controllers / Preventers):

•  Inhaled Corticosteroids (ICS): Beclometasone, Budesonide, Fluticasone, Ciclesonide (side effects: oral candidiasis, hoarseness — prevented by using a spacer and rinsing mouth).

•  Systemic Corticosteroids: Oral Prednisolone, IV Hydrocortisone.

•  Leukotriene Receptor Antagonists (LTRAs):Montelukast (10 mg nocte), Zafirlukast (especially useful in exercise-induced and aspirin-sensitive asthma).

•  Mast Cell Stabilisers: Sodium cromoglicate, Nedocromil.

3.  Targeted Biological Therapies (for Severe Type 2 Asthma — Step 5):

•  Omalizumab (Anti-IgE mAb).

•  Mepolizumab, Reslizumab (Anti-IL-5 mAb) & Benralizumab (Anti-IL-5 receptor mAb).

•  Dupilumab (Anti-IL-4/IL-13 receptor mAb).

•  Tezepelumab (Anti-TSLP [thymic stromal lymphopoietin] mAb).

•  Step-Care Therapy in Adults (GINA Track 1 — Preferred MART [Maintenance and Reliever Therapy] Regimen using ICS–Formoterol) [KU 16, TU]:

•  (SABA monotherapy is no longer recommended because it does not treat underlying airway inflammation and increases risk of severe exacerbations/death).

•  Steps 1–2 (Mild Asthma):As-needed only low-dose ICS–Formoterol (e.g., Budesonide/Formoterol 200/6 µg taken whenever needed for symptom relief). (Alternative Track 2: Step 1 = Take ICS whenever SABA is taken; Step 2 = Low-dose maintenance ICS + as-needed SABA).

•  Step 3:Low-dose maintenance ICS–Formoterol (1 puff BD) + as-needed low-dose ICS–Formoterol as reliever (or Low-dose ICS–LABA + LTRA).

•  Step 4:Medium-dose maintenance ICS–Formoterol (2 puffs BD) + as-needed low-dose ICS–Formoterol as reliever.

•  Step 5 (Severe Uncontrolled Asthma):Add-on LAMA (Tiotropium), switch to high-dose ICS–Formoterol, add Azithromycin (3×/wk), and refer for Phenotyping & Biological Therapy (Omalizumab, Mepolizumab, Benralizumab, Dupilumab, Tezepelumab); low-dose oral Prednisolone only as a last resort.

•  Patient Education & Prevention of Further Episodes ([KU 18]):

•  Avoid known triggers (wear a dust mask/helmet visor when riding a two-wheeler in dusty traffic, avoid smoking/NSAIDs/β-blockers, control house dust mites).

•  Check Metered-Dose Inhaler (MDI) technique (and use a spacer device) at every visit.

•  Provide a Written Personalised Asthma Action Plan based on symptoms and personal best PEF (when to start a 5-day rescue course of Prednisolone 40–50 mg OD if PEF falls <75% of best).

4. Acute Severe Asthma (Status Asthmaticus) [KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 19, 15, TU, RGU]

•  Immediate Clinical Assessment of Severity (Davidson Box 17.23):

1.  Acute Severe Asthma:

•  PEF 33–50% of predicted (or best) (<200 L/min).

•  Inability to complete sentences in one breath.

•  Respiratory rate ≥ 25 breaths/min.

•  Heart rate ≥ 110 beats/min.

2.  Life-Threatening Asthma (Any one feature):

•  PEF <33% of predicted (or best) (<100 L/min).

•  SpO2 < 92% or PaO2 < 8 kPa (60 mmHg).

•  Normal or raised PaCO2 (≥ 4.6–6.0 kPa [35–45 mmHg]) — critical warning sign of impending respiratory muscle exhaustion!

•  Silent chest, Cyanosis, or Feeble respiratory effort.

•  Bradycardia, dysrhythmia, or Hypotension.

•  Exhaustion, confusion, delirium, or coma.

3.  Near-Fatal Asthma: Raised PaCO2 and/or requiring mechanical ventilation with raised inflation pressures.

•  Emergency Management of Acute Severe Asthma (Step-by-Step Protocol):

1.  High-Flow Controlled Oxygen: Administer high-concentration O2 (40–60% via mask) immediately to maintain SpO2 94–98% (do not withhold oxygen even if PaCO2 is elevated).

2.  High-Dose Inhaled Short-Acting β2-Agonists (First-Line Bronchodilator):

•  Salbutamol 5 mg (or Terbutaline 10 mg) via an oxygen-driven nebuliser, repeated every 15–20 minutes (or continuous nebulised salbutamol 5–10 mg/hr in severe/refractory cases).

3.  Add Nebulised Anticholinergic (Ipratropium Bromide):

•  Nebulised Ipratropium bromide 500 µg every 4–6 hours added to salbutamol in all acute severe or life-threatening attacks (produces synergistic bronchodilation).

4.  Early Systemic Corticosteroids (Mandatory in ALL cases):

•  Oral Prednisolone 40–50 mg OD for at least 5 days OR IV Hydrocortisone 100–200 mg stat (then 100 mg 6-hourly IV if vomiting or unable to swallow).

5.  Intravenous Magnesium Sulphate (if life-threatening features or poor response at 1 hour):

•  IV MgSO4 1.2–2.0 g infused over 20 minutes (relaxes bronchial smooth muscle by blocking calcium channels).

6.  Intravenous Aminophylline (in refractory cases under ICU supervision):

•  Loading dose 5 mg/kg IV over 20 mins (omit loading dose if already on oral theophylline), followed by infusion of 0.5–1.0 mg/kg/hr with ECG and serum level monitoring.

7.  IV Fluids & Electrolyte Correction: Correct dehydration and monitor serum potassium closely (high-dose β2-agonists and steroids drive K+ into cells, causing hypokalaemia). (Routine antibiotics are NOT indicated unless bacterial pneumonia is present; sedatives are strictly contraindicated).

8.  Monitoring & Indications for Endotracheal Intubation / Mechanical Ventilation ([TU, RGU]):

•  Repeat PEF at 15–30 mins and ABG within 1 hour if initially hypoxic or normocapnic.

•  Intubate and Ventilate (IPPV) if: Coma, respiratory arrest, progressive exhaustion/drowsiness, or deteriorating arterial blood gases despite optimal therapy (PaO2 < 8 kPa and falling, PaCO2 > 6 kPa and rising, or falling arterial pH).

subject: medicine
title: 36. COPD, Cor Pulmonale, Respiratory Failure & Long-Term Oxygen Therapy [KU 24, 22, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 14.4B — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE (COPD)

36. COPD, Cor Pulmonale, Respiratory Failure & Long-Term Oxygen Therapy [KU 24, 22, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignettes: 45M with 3-month winter productive cough, cyanosis, barrel chest, liver dullness pushed down to 8th ICS & polyphonic rhonchi; 52M chronic smoker with COPD presenting with leg oedema, raised JVP, RV S3 & tender hepatomegaly)

1. Definitions & Risk Factors

•  COPD: A preventable and treatable disease characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and persistent airflow limitation (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70) due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases.

•  Chronic Bronchitis (Clinical definition): Cough productive of sputum on most days for at least 3 consecutive months in each of 2 consecutive years (hypertrophy of submucosal mucus glands [↑ Reid index] and goblet cell hyperplasia).

•  Emphysema (Pathological definition): Abnormal, permanent enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis (Centriacinar in upper lobes of smokers; Panacinar in lower lobes in α1-antitrypsin deficiency; Paraseptal near pleura causing bullae/pneumothorax).

•  Risk Factors (Davidson Box 17.25):

•  Environmental:Cigarette smoking (accounts for 95% in developed countries; >10–20 pack-years), Indoor biomass fuel smoke (wood/dung cooking in poorly ventilated homes — major cause in rural women in India), Occupational dusts (coal, silica, cadmium), Childhood respiratory infections/low birth weight.

•  Host:Severe α1-antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency (PiZZ genotype — unopposed neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar elastin; suspect in young smokers <45 yrs with basal panacinar emphysema and liver disease).

2. Pathophysiology & Cor Pulmonale

•  Chronic protease–antiprotease and oxidant–antioxidant imbalance → small airway inflammation/fibrosis + loss of alveolar elastic recoil (loss of radial traction) → premature dynamic airway collapse during expiration → air-trapping and dynamic hyperinflation (flattens the diaphragm, placing it at a severe mechanical disadvantage).

•  Pathogenesis of Cor Pulmonale (52M Vignette): Destruction of the pulmonary capillary bed + chronic alveolar hypoxia-induced pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling → Pulmonary Hypertension → Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH) and Right Heart Failure (Cor Pulmonale), combined with hypercapnia-mediated renal sodium and water retention → raised JVP, RV S3, tender hepatomegaly, and pedal oedema.

3. Clinical Features

•  Symptoms: Chronic "smoker’s cough" with mucoid/purulent sputum, progressive exertional breathlessness (graded by mMRC Dyspnoea Scale 0–4), wheeze, weight loss/muscle wasting (cachexia), and morning headaches (hypercapnia).

•  Physical Signs:

•  Inspection:Pursed-lip breathing (generates intrinsic PEEP to prevent airway collapse), tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoids, scalenes), supraclavicular/intercostal indrawing, hyperinflated "barrel-shaped" chest (increased AP diameter), Hoover’s sign (paradoxical inward movement of lower costal margins on inspiration due to a low, flat diaphragm).

•  Palpation:Reduced cricosternal distance (<3 fingers), tracheal tug, reduced symmetrical chest expansion, impalpable apex beat.

•  Percussion: Generalized hyper-resonance with loss of superficial cardiac dullness and downward displacement of upper border of liver dullness (to 7th–8th right ICS).

•  Auscultation: Quiet/diminished vesicular breath sounds with prolonged expiratory phase, bilateral polyphonic expiratory wheezes (rhonchi), and coarse early inspiratory crackles (that clear or change on coughing); heart sounds loudest in the epigastrium.

•  Systemic Signs: Central cyanosis, flapping tremor (asterixis) and bounding pulse (due to CO2 retention), and signs of Cor Pulmonale (elevated JVP with giant v waves, left parasternal heave, loud P2, RV S3, tender hepatomegaly, bilateral pitting pedal oedema). (Note: Clubbing is NEVER a feature of uncomplicated COPD — if present, suspect coexisting bronchogenic carcinoma or bronchiectasis).

•  Classical Phenotypes:"Pink Puffers" (Emphysema-predominant: thin, cachectic, severe dyspnoea, hyperinflated, maintain normal PaCO2 and PaO2 until late) vs "Blue Bloaters" (Chronic bronchitis-predominant: obese, productive cough, early hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, secondary polycythaemia, and cor pulmonale/oedema).

4. Investigations, GOLD Criteria & BODE Index [KU 24, 15, TU]

1.  Spirometry & GOLD Classification of Airflow Limitation Severity ([KU 24]):

•  Diagnostic Criterion: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70.

•  GOLD Grading (based on post-bronchodilator FEV1% predicted):

•  GOLD 1 (Mild): FEV1 ≥ 80% predicted.

•  GOLD 2 (Moderate): 50% ≤ FEV1 ≤ 79% predicted.

•  GOLD 3 (Severe): 30% ≤ FEV1 ≤ 49% predicted.

•  GOLD 4 (Very Severe): FEV1 < 30% predicted.

•  (Combined GOLD Assessment also incorporates symptom burden [mMRC ≥ 2 or CAT score ≥ 10] and exacerbation history [≥ 2 moderate or ≥ 1 hospitalised exacerbation/year] into Groups A, B, and E).

2.  Chest X-Ray Findings in Emphysema ([KU 15, TU]):

•  Hypertranslucent (dark) lung fields with >10 posterior ribs (or >6 anterior ribs) visible above the diaphragm.

•  Low, flat hemidiaphragms.

•  Long, narrow "tubular" heart shadow (unless cor pulmonale develops).

•  Enlarged central pulmonary arteries with peripheral vascular pruning (attenuation) and bullae.

•  Increased retrosternal airspace on lateral view.

3.  Other Investigations:

•  HRCT Thorax: Detects centrilobular/panacinar emphysema and bullae.

•  Lung Volumes & Diffusion: ↑ TLC, ↑ RV, ↑ RV/TLC ratio; ↓↓ TLCO (in emphysema).

•  Arterial Blood Gases: Type I or Type II respiratory failure (with compensatory raised HCO3- in chronic hypercapnia).

•  FBC (secondary polycythaemia), Serum α1-antitrypsin level, ECG & Echocardiogram (P pulmonale, RVH, pulmonary artery pressure in cor pulmonale).

4.  BODE Index (Prognostic Composite Score in COPD — 0 to 10 points) [TU]:

•  B — Body Mass Index (≤ 21 kg/m2 = 1 point).

•  O — Airflow Obstruction (FEV1% predicted: ≥ 65=0; 50–64=1; 36–49=2; ≤ 35=3).

•  D — Dyspnoea (mMRC scale: 0–1=0; 2=1; 3=2; 4=3).

•  E — Exercise capacity (6-Minute Walk Distance: ≥ 350 m=0; 250–349 m=1; 150–249 m=2; ≤ 149 m=3).

•  (Score 7–10 carries an 80% 4-year mortality).

5. Management of Stable COPD & Acute Exacerbations (AECOPD)

•  A. Management of Stable COPD:

1.  Smoking Cessation (Varenicline, Bupropion, NRT): The only intervention proven to slow the accelerated rate of FEV1 decline and alter natural history (along with LTOT).

2.  Pulmonary Rehabilitation: 6–12 weeks of supervised exercise training, nutritional support, and breathing techniques — improves exercise capacity and quality of life.

3.  Vaccinations: Annual Influenza and COVID-19, Pneumococcal (PCV20 / PPSV23), and RSV vaccines.

4.  Inhaled Bronchodilator & Anti-inflammatory Therapy:

•  Mild occasional symptoms: Short-acting bronchodilator (SABA [Salbutamol] or SAMA [Ipratropium]) as reliever.

•  Persistent Dyspnoea / Frequent Exacerbations (Cornerstone of Therapy):Combined Long-Acting Bronchodilators (LABA + LAMA) in a single inhaler (e.g., Indacaterol/Glycopyrronium, Umeclidinium/Vilanterol, or Formoterol + Tiotropium).

•  Triple Therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS, e.g., Fluticasone/Umeclidinium/Vilanterol): Indicated in patients with frequent exacerbations AND blood eosinophils ≥ 300 cells/µL (or asthma–COPD overlap).

5.  Oral Adjunctive Therapies:Roflumilast (PDE-4 inhibitor, 500 µg OD) in severe chronic bronchitis with frequent exacerbations; Prophylactic Azithromycin (250–500 mg 3×/week); Mucolytics (Carbocisteine / N-acetylcysteine); Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα mAb) for eosinophilic COPD; Diuretics (Furosemide) for cor pulmonale oedema.

6.  Long-Term Oxygen Therapy (LTOT) [RGU, TU]:

•  Proven to improve survival when administered via nasal cannulae from a home oxygen concentrator for at least 15 hours/day (ideally >20 hours/day) to achieve PaO2 ≥ 8 kPa (60 mmHg) in non-smoking, clinically stable COPD patients (assessed on 2 occasions 3 weeks apart):

•  Criterion 1: Resting PaO2 < 7.3 kPa (55 mmHg) on room air, OR

•  Criterion 2: Resting PaO2 7.3–8.0 kPa (55–60 mmHg) PLUS evidence of Pulmonary Hypertension, Cor Pulmonale (peripheral oedema), or Secondary Polycythaemia (Haematocrit >55%).

7.  Surgical / Bronchoscopic Interventions: Bullectomy, Lung Volume Reduction Surgery (LVRS) or bronchoscopic endobronchial one-way valves (for heterogeneous upper-lobe emphysema), and Lung Transplantation.

•  B. Management of Acute Exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) & Type II Respiratory Failure [KU 24, 22]:

•  Types of Respiratory Failure ([KU 24, 22]):

•  Type I (Hypoxaemic) Respiratory Failure:PaO2 < 8.0 kPa (60 mmHg) with normal or low PaCO2 (≤ 6.0 kPa [45 mmHg]) due to V/Q mismatch or shunt. Causes: Pneumonia, acute asthma, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary oedema, ARDS, pulmonary fibrosis, pneumothorax.

•  Type II (Hypercapnic / Ventilatory) Respiratory Failure ([KU 22]):PaO2 < 8.0 kPa (60 mmHg) with elevated PaCO2 (>6.0 kPa [45 mmHg]) due to alveolar hypoventilation. Causes:COPD, life-threatening asthma, opiate/sedative overdose, brainstem stroke, Guillain–Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis, motor neuron disease, severe kyphoscoliosis, obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

•  Treatment of AECOPD & Acute-on-Chronic Type II Respiratory Failure:

1.  Controlled Oxygen Therapy ([RGU, TU]): Deliver 24% or 28% oxygen via a fixed-performance Venturi mask (or 1–2 L/min nasal prongs) strictly targeting SpO2 88–92%. (Giving uncontrolled high-flow oxygen to chronic CO2 retainers abolishes their hypoxic ventilatory drive and worsens V/Q mismatch via release of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction [Haldane effect], precipitating lethal hypercapnic coma/CO2 narcosis).

2.  Nebulised Bronchodilators (driven by compressed air, not oxygen):Salbutamol 2.5–5 mg + Ipratropium bromide 500 µg every 4–6 hours.

3.  Systemic Corticosteroids:Oral Prednisolone 30 mg OD for 5 days (or IV Hydrocortisone).

4.  Antibiotics (if increased sputum purulence/volume or consolidation): Amoxicillin, Doxycycline, Co-amoxiclav, or Clarithromycin for 5 days.

5.  Non-Invasive Ventilation (BiPAP — NIV):Treatment of choice for persistent respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35 and PaCO2 > 6.5 kPa [49 mmHg]) despite 1 hour of optimal medical therapy and controlled oxygen — halves mortality and need for intubation.

6.  Invasive Mechanical Ventilation: If NIV fails, pH <7.25 with coma, or respiratory arrest.

subject: medicine
title: 37. Bronchiectasis [KU 23, 22, 20, 19, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 14.4C — BRONCHIECTASIS

37. Bronchiectasis [KU 23, 22, 20, 19, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignettes: 25M / 52M with past pulmonary TB, chronic copious foul-smelling purulent sputum that increases with postural change, halitosis, haemoptysis, clubbing & coarse leathery crepitations)

1. Definition & Pathogenesis

•  Definition: Abnormal, permanent, irreversible dilatation of one or more bronchi with destruction of the elastic and muscular components of the bronchial wall.

•  Pathogenesis (Cole’s "Vicious Cycle" Hypothesis): An initial infectious or obstructive insult damages mucociliary clearance → stasis of thick mucus in airways → chronic bacterial colonisation (H. influenzae, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus) → persistent intense neutrophilic inflammation releasing proteolytic enzymes (neutrophil elastase, MMPs) → destruction of bronchial wall cartilage/elastin, transmural scarring, dilated bronchiectatic cavities (cylindrical, varicose, or cystic/saccular), and hypertrophy of tortuous bronchial arteries (predisposing to massive haemoptysis).

2. Aetiology (Davidson Box 17.31)

1.  Post-Infectious (Most Common):

•  Post-Tuberculous Bronchiectasis (most common cause in India; classically affects the upper lobes / infraclavicular area due to fibrous traction or bronchial stenosis by tuberculous lymph nodes).

•  Severe childhood infections (Whooping cough [Bordetella pertussis], Measles, Adenovirus).

•  Necrotising bacterial pneumonia (S. aureus, Klebsiella) or Lung abscess.

2.  Congenital / Hereditary Defects of Mucociliary Clearance:

•  Cystic Fibrosis (autosomal recessive CFTR gene mutation on chromosome 7).

•  Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (Immotile Cilia Syndrome): Dynein arm defect; Kartagener’s syndrome = Triad of Bronchiectasis + Chronic sinusitis + Situs inversus (dextrocardia).

•  Young’s Syndrome (obstructive azoospermia + sinopulmonary infections) and Yellow Nail Syndrome.

3.  Immunodeficiency States: Primary hypogammaglobulinaemia (Common Variable Immunodeficiency [CVID], X-linked agammaglobulinaemia), HIV.

4.  Allergic & Autoimmune:Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA — central/proximal bronchiectasis), Rheumatoid arthritis, Ulcerative colitis.

5.  Localised Bronchial Obstruction (affecting a single lobe): Inhaled foreign body (right lung), endobronchial tumour/carcinoid, or extrinsic compression by enlarged hilar lymph nodes (Brock’s middle lobe syndrome).

3. Clinical Features [KU 23, 22, 20]

•  Symptoms:

•  Chronic daily persistent cough with copious, foul-smelling (fetid), purulent sputum that is posturally dependent (worse in the mornings and increases on lying on the side opposite to the affected lung).

•  Haemoptysis (50–70%): Ranges from blood-streaked sputum during infective exacerbations to life-threatening massive haemoptysis from eroded bronchial arteries.

•  Halitosis (foul breath), recurrent febrile chest infections, pleuritic chest pain, exertional dyspnoea, weight loss, and fatigue.

•  Physical Signs:

•  General:Digital clubbing (classic feature), halitosis, fever, cachexia, and central cyanosis / cor pulmonale (in advanced bilateral disease).

•  Chest Examination:Coarse, leathery inspiratory and expiratory crepitations (crackles) over the affected lobes (most commonly basal/infrascapular, or infraclavicular in post-TB bronchiectasis) that shift or lessen after vigorous coughing, accompanied by low-pitched rhonchi and bronchial breathing (over large cystic cavities/fibrosis).

4. Investigations

1.  High-Resolution CT (HRCT) of the Thorax (Gold Standard Diagnostic Investigation):

•  Bronchial internal diameter greater than the accompanying pulmonary artery branch ("Signet-ring sign").

•  Lack of normal tapering of bronchi towards the periphery ("tram-track" appearance).

•  Visualization of bronchi within 1 cm of the costal pleura.

•  Bronchial wall thickening, mucus plugging ("tree-in-bud"), and cystic/saccular spaces with air–fluid levels.

2.  Chest X-Ray: May be normal in mild disease; advanced disease shows "ring shadows" (dilated bronchi seen end-on), "tramline shadows" (thickened parallel bronchial walls), tubular shadows, and crowded lung markings.

3.  Sputum Microbiology: Gram stain, aerobic culture, and AFB/GeneXpert & NTM culture (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Aspergillus fumigatus, and Non-tuberculous mycobacteria [M. avium complex]).

4.  Aetiological Workup: Serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM for CVID), Total IgE & Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG (for ABPA), Sweat chloride test / CFTR genetics (for CF), Nasal nitric oxide & ciliary electron microscopy (for PCD), and Bronchoscopy (if localised lobar bronchiectasis to exclude foreign body or tumour).

5.  Spirometry: Obstructive ventilatory defect (FEV1/FVC < 0.70).

5. Complications & Management [KU 23, 22, 20]

•  Complications: Recurrent pneumonia, Massive haemoptysis, Lung abscess, Empyema, Metastatic brain abscess, Type II respiratory failure, Cor pulmonale, and Secondary (AA) systemic amyloidosis (causing nephrotic syndrome).

•  Management (and Prevention of Exacerbations):

1.  Airway Clearance / Postural Drainage Physiotherapy (Cornerstone of Daily Therapy):

•  Postural drainage (positioning the patient with the affected lobe uppermost for 10–15 mins twice daily) combined with the Active Cycle of Breathing Technique (ACBT), chest percussion, and oscillating positive expiratory pressure devices (Flutter valve / Acapella).

•  Inhaled hypertonic saline (6–7%) or mucolytics (Carbocisteine) before physiotherapy to aid sputum clearance; inhaled bronchodilators if airflow obstruction is present.

2.  Antibiotic Therapy:

•  Acute Exacerbations: 10–14 days of targeted higher-dose antibiotics — Amoxicillin / Co-amoxiclav (625 mg TDS) or Doxycycline; if colonised with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, use Oral Ciprofloxacin (500–750 mg BD) or IV anti-pseudomonal β-lactams (Piperacillin–Tazobactam 4.5 g QDS, Ceftazidime 2 g TDS, or Meropenem) + IV Aminoglycoside.

•  Long-term Prophylaxis (if ≥ 3 exacerbations/year):Low-dose oral Azithromycin (250–500 mg 3 times/week — anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial; exclude NTM first) or Long-term nebulised colistin/tobramycin/gentamicin for chronic P. aeruginosa colonisation.

3.  Management of Haemoptysis: Treat underlying infection, oral/IV Tranexamic acid, and Bronchial Artery Embolisation (BAE) for massive or recurrent haemoptysis.

4.  Surgical Resection (Lobectomy / Segmentectomy): Indicated only in localised unilateral bronchiectasis refractory to medical therapy or causing life-threatening recurrent haemoptysis. Bilateral lung transplantation for end-stage disease.

5.  Prevention: Childhood immunisation (measles, pertussis, BCG, H. influenzae type b), annual Influenza and Pneumococcal vaccination, and prompt treatment of TB and foreign body aspiration.

title: 38. Pneumonia (Community-Acquired, Viral/COVID & Pneumocystis) & Lung Abscess [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 18, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 14.5 — INFECTIONS OF RESPIRATORY SYSTEM (PNEUMONIA, LUNG ABSCESS & TB)

38. Pneumonia (Community-Acquired, Viral/COVID & Pneumocystis) & Lung Abscess [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 18, 16, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignettes: 45F with 7-day fever/cough, BP 86/50, SpO2 84% & right infra-axillary bronchial breathing; 50M with fever, rusty sputum, hypotension & hypoxia; 36M with right lower lobe pneumonia)

A. Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 18]

•  Definition & Classification of Pneumonia: An acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma associated with recently developed radiological consolidation.

•  By Clinical Setting:Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP), Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP) (onset ≥ 48 hours after hospital admission), Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP), Aspiration/Suppurative Pneumonia, and Pneumonia in the Immunocompromised Host.

•  By Anatomical Pattern:Lobar pneumonia (homogeneous consolidation of one or more lobes, passing through stages of congestion, red hepatisation, grey hepatisation, and resolution) vs Bronchopneumonia (patchy, multilobar peribronchial alveolar consolidation).

•  Aetiology of CAP ([KU 24, 22] — Davidson Box 17.38):

1.  Typical Bacteria:Streptococcus pneumoniae (Commonest cause — ~50%), Haemophilus influenzae (common in COPD), Staphylococcus aureus (post-influenza; causes multilobar cavitating pneumonia and pneumatoceles), Klebsiella pneumoniae (alcoholics/diabetics; affects upper lobes causing bulging fissures and "red-currant jelly" sputum), Moraxella catarrhalis.

2.  Atypical Bacteria:Mycoplasma pneumoniae (young adults; epidemics; extrapulmonary cold agglutinin haemolytic anaemia, erythema multiforme, Guillain–Barré, bullous myringitis), Legionella pneumophila (contaminated air-conditioning/water towers; hyponatraemia, diarrhoea, confusion, deranged LFTs), Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Chlamydophila psittaci (birds), Coxiella burnetii (Q fever).

3.  Respiratory Viruses:Influenza A & B, SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), RSV, Adenovirus, Parainfluenza, Varicella.

•  Clinical Features ([KU 24]):

•  Symptoms: Acute onset high fever, rigors, malaise, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, and cough (initially dry, then productive of mucopurulent or "rusty" sputum in pneumococcal pneumonia), or confusion/delirium in the elderly.

•  Expected Respiratory Examination Findings in Lobar Consolidation:

1.  Inspection: Tachypnoea, central cyanosis (in severe CAP), restricted chest movement on the affected side. (Herpes labialis is common in pneumococcal pneumonia).

2.  Palpation:Trachea is CENTRAL; reduced chest expansion and increased tactile vocal fremitus (TVF) over the consolidated lobe.

3.  Percussion:Woody / impaired dullness over the affected lobe.

4.  Auscultation:High-pitched tubular Bronchial Breath Sounds (harsh, equal inspiratory and expiratory length with a pause between them), fine/coarse crepitations (rales), pleural friction rub, increased vocal resonance, whispering pectoriloquy, and aegophony (bleating nasal quality of spoken voice).

•  Severity Assessment & Prognostic Features — CURB-65 Score [KU 24, 18]:

•  Assign 1 point for each of the following 5 features:

•  C — Confusion (new-onset disorientation in person, place, or time, or Abbreviated Mental Test score ≤ 8/10).

•  U — Blood Urea >7 mmol/L (>42 mg/dL).

•  R — Respiratory rate ≥ 30 breaths/min.

•  B — Low Blood pressure (Systolic <90 mmHg or Diastolic ≤ 60 mmHg).

•  65 — Age ≥ 65 years.

•  Stratification & Site of Care:

•  Score 0–1 (Low severity, mortality <1.5%): Outpatient home oral treatment.

•  Score 2 (Moderate severity, mortality ~9%): Hospital inpatient treatment.

•  Score 3–5 (Severe CAP, mortality 15–50% — as in the 45F and 50M vignettes): Urgent hospital/ICU admission.

•  Other Adverse Prognostic Indicators ([KU 18]): Multilobar involvement, severe hypoxaemia (PaO2 < 8 kPa or SpO2 < 90%), positive blood cultures (bacteraemia), WBC >20 × 109/L or leucopenia <4 × 109/L, hypoalbuminaemia, hyponatraemia, and metabolic acidosis.

•  Investigations:

•  Chest X-Ray: Homogeneous lobar or segmental opacification with an air bronchogram; identifies complications (parapneumonic effusion, cavitation). (Repeat CXR at 6 weeks to ensure resolution and exclude underlying bronchogenic carcinoma in smokers/>50 yrs).

•  Pulse Oximetry & ABG: Assesses Type I or Type II respiratory failure and lactate/acidosis.

•  Microbiology (in Moderate-to-Severe CAP): Sputum Gram stain and culture, Blood cultures (2 sets before antibiotics), Urine for Pneumococcal and Legionella antigen, and Throat/nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral NAAT/PCR (Influenza, SARS-CoV-2, Mycoplasma).

•  Blood Tests: FBC, U&Es, LFTs, CRP, Serum Procalcitonin (distinguishes bacterial from viral infection).

•  Complications of Pneumonia ([KU 25, 22, 21] — Davidson Box 17.43):

1.  Parapneumonic pleural effusion (common, >40%) and Empyema thoracis.

2.  Suppurative pneumonia / Lung abscess and Pneumatoceles / Pneumothorax (especially S. aureus).

3.  Lobar collapse (due to retained viscid sputum).

4.  Acute Respiratory Failure (Type I or II) and ARDS.

5.  Septic shock, AKI, and Multi-organ failure.

6.  Bacteraemic / Metastatic spread: Meningitis, endocarditis, septic arthritis, pericarditis, myocarditis.

7.  Cardiac arrhythmias (Atrial fibrillation) and Venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE).

•  Management of Community-Acquired Pneumonia ([KU 25, 24]):

1.  Oxygen & Ventilatory Support: High-flow oxygen to maintain SpO2 94–98% (88–92% if pre-existing hypercapnic COPD); CPAP or Intubation and Mechanical Ventilation in ICU if refractory hypoxaemia, progressive hypercapnia, or shock.

2.  Fluid Resuscitation & Haemodynamic Support: IV crystalloids for dehydration/hypotension; IV Noradrenaline if septic shock persists (as in the 45F and 50M vignettes with BP <90/60).

3.  Empirical Antibiotic Therapy (Start immediately within 1 hour in severe CAP — Davidson Box 17.42):

•  Low Severity (CURB-65 = 0–1):Oral Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days (or Doxycycline 200 mg stat then 100 mg OD / Clarithromycin 500 mg BD if penicillin-allergic).

•  Moderate Severity (CURB-65 = 2):Oral/IV Amoxicillin 500 mg–1 g TDS PLUS Clarithromycin 500 mg BD (to cover both typical and atypical pathogens; or Doxycycline / Levofloxacin 500 mg OD if penicillin-allergic).

•  Severe CAP (CURB-65 = 3–5):IV Co-amoxiclav 1.2 g TDS (or IV Ceftriaxone 1–2 g OD / Cefuroxime 1.5 g TDS) PLUS IV Clarithromycin 500 mg BD (or IV Levofloxacin 500 mg BD if Legionella suspected; add Vancomycin/Linezolid if MRSA suspected).

4.  Supportive Care: Analgesia (Paracetamol/NSAIDs) for pleuritic pain, DVT prophylaxis (LMWH), chest physiotherapy if sputum retention.

B. Lung Abscess & Suppurative Pneumonia [KU 25, RGU]

•  Definition: A localised, cavitating collection of pus within the lung parenchyma accompanied bynecrotic destruction of lung tissue.

•  Aetiopathology ([KU 25]):

1.  Aspiration of Infected Oropharyngeal / Gastric Material (Most Common Cause):

•  Risk factors: Reduced consciousness (alcoholism, drug overdose, general anaesthesia, stroke, seizures), dysphagia/bulbar palsy, achalasia, and poor dental hygiene / periodontal sepsis.

•  Anatomical site: Gravitates to dependent segments — Apical (superior) segment of the right lower lobe or posterior segment of the right upper lobe in supine patients.

•  Microbiology: Polymicrobial oral anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, Prevotella melaninogenica, Fusobacterium necrophorum, Peptostreptococcus) mixed with aerobic bacteria.

2.  Primary Necrotising Bacterial Pneumonia:Staphylococcus aureus (including Panton–Valentine Leukocidin [PVL]-producing MRSA), Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Actinomyces israelii, and Burkholderia pseudomallei (melioidosis).

3.  Bronchial Obstruction (Post-obstructive abscess): Bronchogenic carcinoma, carcinoid tumour, or inhaled foreign body.

4.  Haematogenous (Septic) Emboli: Right-sided tricuspid infective endocarditis in IV drug users (S. aureus), or Lemierre’s syndrome (oropharyngeal infection with Fusobacterium necrophorum causing septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein and metastatic cavitating lung abscesses).

5.  Secondary Infection of Pre-existing Cavities: Cavitating lung infarct, tuberculous cavity, hydatid cyst, or fungal cavity.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Symptoms: Insidious or acute onset of high remittent ("swinging") fever, rigors, night sweats, profound malaise, rapid weight loss, pleuritic chest pain, and cough. Sudden expectoration of copious amounts of foul-smelling (fetid), purulent, often blood-stained sputum occurs when the abscess ruptures into a bronchus.

•  Physical Signs: Toxic/ill appearance, rapidly developing digital clubbing (can appear within 10–14 days), anaemia, halitosis, dullness to percussion, bronchial (or cavernous/amphoric) breathing, coarse crepitations, and a pleural friction rub.

•  Investigations:

1.  Chest X-Ray: Homogeneous consolidation initially, evolving into a thick-walled radiolucent cavity containing a horizontal air–fluid level.

2.  CT Thorax: Defines exact segmental location, wall thickness, excludes an underlying obstructing endobronchial tumour, and differentiates a lung abscess (spherical, thick irregular wall, acute angle with chest wall, destroys adjacent lung) from a loculated empyema (lenticular, smooth wall, obtuse angle with chest wall, compresses lung).

3.  Sputum & Blood Microbiology: Gram stain, aerobic/anaerobic cultures, AFB/GeneXpert (to exclude TB), fungal culture.

4.  Flexible Bronchoscopy: Essential in smokers/older patients or atypical locations to exclude bronchogenic carcinoma or remove a foreign body, and to obtain BAL for microbiology.

•  Complications:Empyema thoracis, Bronchopleural fistula / Pyopneumothorax, Massive haemoptysis, Metastatic brain abscess, Sepsis/ARDS, Residual localised bronchiectasis, and Secondary AA amyloidosis (if chronic).

•  Treatment:

1.  Prolonged Antibiotic Therapy (4–6 weeks):

•  Aspiration / Anaerobic Lung Abscess:IV Co-amoxiclav 1.2 g TDS (or IV Ceftriaxone 2 g OD + IV Metronidazole 500 mg TDS), or Clindamycin (600 mg TDS IV/PO), stepping down to oral therapy once afebrile until radiographic resolution.

•  Specific Pathogens: Add Flucloxacillin (for MSSA) or Vancomycin / Linezolid (for MRSA / PVL-S. aureus); prolonged high-dose Penicillin for Actinomycosis (6–12 months).

2.  Postural Drainage & Chest Physiotherapy: Crucial to drain pus from the cavity (avoid if massive haemoptysis).

3.  Percutaneous CT-Guided Catheter Drainage or Surgical Resection (Lobectomy): Reserved for large abscesses (>6 cm) that fail to respond to 2–3 weeks of medical therapy, or complicated by massive haemoptysis or obstructing neoplasm.

C. Viral (COVID-19) Pneumonia & Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (PCP) [KU 16, TU]

•  COVID-19 Pneumonia [TU]:

•  Aetiopathogenesis: Caused by SARS-CoV-2 (single-stranded RNA betacoronavirus) binding to ACE2 receptors on type II alveolar pneumocytes and vascular endothelial cells → direct viral cytopathic injury followed in severe cases (days 7–10) by a dysregulated hyperinflammatory "cytokine storm" (IL-6, IL-1, TNF-α), diffuse alveolar damage (hyaline membranes), and pulmonary microvascular immunothrombosis.

•  Clinical Features: Fever, dry cough, fatigue, myalgia, anosmia/ageusia, progressing to dyspnoea and "happy (silent) hypoxia" (SpO2 < 90% with minimal distress initially), tachypnoea, and ARDS.

•  Investigations: Nasopharyngeal RT-PCR / Rapid antigen test; lymphopenia, raised CRP, Ferritin, LDH, and D-dimer; HRCT Thorax shows bilateral peripheral and basal ground-glass opacities (GGO) and crazy-paving/consolidation.

•  Complications:ARDS, Pulmonary thromboembolism, Myocarditis/arrhythmias, Acute kidney injury, Secondary bacterial/fungal infections (COVID-associated mucormycosis and invasive aspergillosis).

•  Management: Controlled oxygen, awake prone positioning, CPAP / High-flow nasal oxygen (or invasive lung-protective ventilation in ARDS), Dexamethasone 6 mg OD for 10 days (in all patients requiring oxygen — reduces mortality), Tocilizumab / Sarilumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) or Baricitinib (JAK inhibitor) in rapidly worsening hypoxia with high CRP, Remdesivir (antiviral in early hypoxia), and LMWH thromboprophylaxis.

•  Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (PCP) [KU 16, TU]:

•  Aetiology: Opportunistic fungal infection occurring in profound cell-mediated immunodeficiency (HIV with CD4 count <200 cells/µL, solid organ/stem cell transplant, high-dose steroids/chemotherapy).

•  Clinical Features: Subacute onset (over weeks) of progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, and fever, with a paucity of chest signs on auscultation but marked exercise-induced oxygen desaturation.

•  Investigations: CXR/HRCT shows bilateral symmetrical perihilar "bat-wing" ground-glass interstitial infiltrates (sparing the lung apices and periphery; pleural effusions are rare, pneumothorax may occur); Elevated serum β-1,3-D-glucan and LDH; confirmed by Induced sputum or Bronchoalveolar Lavage (BAL) stained with Gomori methenamine silver (GMS), Giemsa, immunofluorescence, or PCR.

•  Treatment:High-dose Co-trimoxazole (Trimethoprim–Sulfamethoxazole 120 mg/kg/day in 3–4 divided doses IV/PO for 21 days) (Alternatives: Clindamycin + Primaquine, or IV Pentamidine) PLUS Adjuvant Prednisolone (40 mg BD for 5 days → 40 mg OD for 5 days → 20 mg OD for 11 days) if PaO2 < 9.3 kPa (70 mmHg) or A–a gradient >4.7 kPa.

•  Prophylaxis for PCP ([KU 16]): Indicated in all HIV patients with CD4 count <200 cells/µL, oral candidiasis, or after an episode of PCP (secondary prophylaxis) until CD4 >200 cells/µL for >3 months on ART. Regimen:Oral Co-trimoxazole 960 mg (1 DS tablet) OD (or 480 mg OD / 960 mg 3×/wk; Alternatives: Dapsone 100 mg OD, Atovaquone, or monthly nebulised Pentamidine).
