title: 39. Tuberculosis: Pulmonary, Extrapulmonary (Adrenal/Pleural/Miliary), Diagnostics, Treatment & MDR/XDR-TB [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 19, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 14.5B — TUBERCULOSIS (PULMONARY, PLEURAL, MILIARY & DRUG-RESISTANT TB)

39. Tuberculosis: Pulmonary, Extrapulmonary (Adrenal/Pleural/Miliary), Diagnostics, Treatment & MDR/XDR-TB [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 19, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignette: 50M with 2-month fever, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, productive cough, haemoptysis, right apical crackles, palmar/plantar hyperpigmentation & BP 80/50 mmHg)

•  Complete Diagnosis of the 50M Clinical Vignette ([KU 21]):Post-Primary (Reactivation) Right Upper Lobe Cavitary Pulmonary Tuberculosis complicated by Disseminated Tuberculous Adrenalitis causing Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison’s Disease).

1. Pathogenesis & Clinical Presentations of Tuberculosis

•  Aetiopathogenesis: Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, transmitted via inhalation of aerosolised droplet nuclei. Alveolar macrophages phagocytose bacilli and transform into epithelioid cells and Langhans multinucleate giant cells, forming a caseating granuloma surrounded by T-lymphocytes.

•  Primary TB: Peripheral subpleural Ghon focus + enlarged hilar lymph nodes = Primary (Ranke) Complex. Usually heals with calcification (latent TB) or progresses in children/immunocompromised to pleural effusion or miliary/meningeal TB.

•  Post-Primary (Adult Reactivation) Pulmonary TB: Reactivation of dormant bacilli in the high-oxygen environment of the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes (or apical segment of lower lobes).

•  Clinical Features of Pulmonary TB:

•  Systemic: Insidious fever (evening rise), drenching night sweats, anorexia, profound weight loss, malaise.

•  Pulmonary:Chronic cough (>2–3 weeks) — initially dry, then mucopurulent, haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea.

•  Signs: Apical flattening/volume loss, tracheal deviation towards the fibrotic apex, dullness, and post-tussive apical crackles / bronchial breathing.

•  External / Hypersensitivity Markers of TB ([TU]):Erythema nodosum, Phlyctenular conjunctivitis, Scrofula (matted cervical lymphadenitis with collar-stud abscess/sinus), Lupus vulgaris, and Poncet’s disease (reactive aseptic polyarthritis).

•  Pleural Tuberculosis ([KU 24]):

•  Pathogenesis: Results from rupture of a subpleural caseous focus into the pleural space, triggering a delayed (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction to mycobacterial proteins (or direct tuberculous empyema).

•  Clinical Features: Fever, night sweats, weight loss, unilateral pleuritic chest pain followed by progressive dyspnoea and stony-dull percussion with absent breath sounds.

•  Diagnostic Investigations:

•  Ultrasound-guided Pleural Fluid Aspiration: Straw/amber-coloured Exudate (by Light’s criteria: Protein >30 g/L, fluid:serum protein >0.5, LDH >0.6), predominantly lymphocytic (>80%), low glucose, and markedly elevated Pleural Fluid Adenosine Deaminase (ADA >40 IU/L) and Interferon-γ.

•  Microbiology & Biopsy: Pleural fluid AFB smear (<10%) and culture (25%) have low sensitivity; Closed (Abrams) or Thoracoscopic Pleural Biopsy is the gold standard (demonstrates caseating granulomas on histology and positive MTB culture/GeneXpert in ~80%).

•  Treatment: Standard 6-month anti-tubercular therapy (2HRZE / 4HR) + therapeutic thoracentesis if breathless (short course of oral prednisolone accelerates fluid resorption in severe symptoms).

•  Miliary Tuberculosis ([KU 21, TU]):

•  Definition & Pathogenesis: Acute or subacute haematogenous dissemination of M. tuberculosis throughout the lungs and reticuloendothelial organs (liver, spleen, bone marrow, meninges, adrenals).

•  Clinical Presentation:

•  Classical Miliary TB: 2–3 weeks of high fever, night sweats, anorexia, marked weight loss, dry cough, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, choroidal tubercles on fundoscopy (pathognomonic yellowish retinal lesions), and tuberculous meningitis (headache, neck stiffness — in 25%). Chest auscultation is often normal early on, later showing fine widespread crackles.

•  Cryptic Miliary TB (in the elderly): Presents as pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO), progressive wasting, and pancytopenia / leukaemoid reaction, often with a normal initial CXR and negative tuberculin skin test (anergy).

•  Diagnosis of Miliary TB ([KU 21]):

1.  Chest X-Ray & HRCT Thorax: Uniform, discrete 1–2 mm ("millet-seed") micronodular opacities distributed evenly throughout all lung fields (HRCT is much more sensitive than CXR early in the disease).

2.  Fundoscopy: Choroidal tubercles.

3.  Microbiology & Tissue Biopsy: Sputum/BAL for AFB, MGIT culture, and GeneXpert MTB/RIF; Bone marrow aspiration/trephine biopsy and Liver biopsy (high yield for caseating granulomas and culture); Lumbar puncture if any meningeal symptoms.

•  Management: Immediate 6-month standard ATT (2HRZE / 4HR; extended to 12 months with adjuvant Dexamethasone/Prednisolone if CNS/meningeal involvement is present).

2. Diagnosis & Newer Diagnostic Methods in Tuberculosis [KU 22, 21]

1.  Sputum Microscopy (2 spot/early-morning samples):

•  LED Fluorescent Microscopy with Auramine–Rhodamine stain (faster and 10% more sensitive than conventional Ziehl–Neelsen acid-fast stain).

2.  Newer Rapid Molecular / Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAATs — WHO Recommended First-Line Diagnostic Test) [KU 22]:

•  Xpert MTB/RIF & Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (CBNAAT) and Truenat MTB-RIF: Automated cartridge-based real-time PCR assays that simultaneously detect M. tuberculosis DNA AND rpoB gene mutations conferring Rifampicin resistance within 2 hours (high sensitivity even in smear-negative and extrapulmonary specimens).

•  Line Probe Assays (LPA):

•  First-line LPA (GenoType MTBDRplus): Detects resistance to Rifampicin (rpoB) and Isoniazid (katG and inhA).

•  Second-line LPA (GenoType MTBDRsl): Detects resistance to Fluoroquinolones (gyrA/gyrB) and Second-line injectables (rrs).

•  Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS): Gold standard for comprehensive drug susceptibility profiling.

3.  Automated Liquid Culture Systems:

•  BACTEC MGIT-960 (Mycobacteria Growth Indicator Tube): Detects mycobacterial growth by fluorescence within 1–2 weeks (compared to 4–8 weeks on solid Löwenstein–Jensen [LJ] media) and enables phenotypic Drug Susceptibility Testing (DST).

4.  Urine Lateral Flow Lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) Assay: Point-of-care urinary antigen test used in severely immunocompromised HIV patients (CD4 <100–200 cells/µL).

5.  Immunological Tests for Latent TB Infection (LTBI):

•  Interferon-Gamma Release Assays (IGRAs — QuantiFERON-TB Gold & T-SPOT.TB): Measure T-cell release of IFN-γ in response to MTB-specific antigens (ESAT-6 and CFP-10); unlike the Mantoux Tuberculin Skin Test (TST), IGRAs do not give false-positive results from prior BCG vaccination or most non-tuberculous mycobacteria.

6.  (In the 50M Vignette with hypotension, palmar pigmentation, and hyponatraemia/hyperkalaemia: Perform an ACTH [Synacthen] stimulation test, baseline 8 am plasma cortisol & ACTH, and CT Adrenals [which shows bilateral adrenal enlargement/calcification]).

3. Complications of Pulmonary Tuberculosis [KU 21, TU]

•  Pulmonary Complications:Post-TB Bronchiectasis, Massive haemoptysis (Rasmussen’s aneurysm), Intracavitary Aspergilloma / Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis, Spontaneous pneumothorax / Bronchopleural fistula, Tuberculous empyema, Fibrothorax / Destroyed lung, Scar carcinoma, and Cor pulmonale / Type II respiratory failure.

•  Non-Pulmonary / Extrapulmonary Complications ([TU]):

•  Tuberculous laryngitis and Ileocaecal/anorectal enteritis (from swallowing heavily infected sputum).

•  Adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease) (as in the 50M vignette).

•  CNS TB (meningitis, tuberculoma), Pott’s spine (thoracolumbar spondylodiscitis with cold psoas abscess and paraplegia), Constrictive pericarditis, Genitourinary TB (sterile pyuria, "thimble bladder", epididymo-orchitis, Fallopian tube infertility), Poncet’s polyarthritis, and Secondary (AA) systemic amyloidosis.

4. Anti-Tubercular Treatment (ATT): First-Line Regimens, Pharmacology & Toxicity [KU 24, 23, 21, 19, 16, 15]

•  Standard Regimen for Drug-Susceptible TB (WHO / National TB Elimination Programme [NTEP — formerly RNTCP Category I] [KU 19]):

•  Intensive Phase (2 Months): Daily fixed-dose combination of 4 drugs — HRZE (Isoniazid [H] + Rifampicin [R] + Pyrazinamide [Z] + Ethambutol [E]).

•  Continuation Phase (4 Months): Daily HR (WHO) or HRE (India NTEP, due to higher background isoniazid resistance).

•  (Total duration = 6 months; extended to 9–12 months in CNS/meningeal and Spinal/Bone TB. Daily weight-band Fixed-Dose Combination [FDC] tablets with Directly Observed Therapy [DOT / Video-DOT] are standard).

•  First-Line Anti-Tubercular Drugs — Mechanism, Doses, Uses & Side Effects [KU 24, 23, 21, 16, 15]:

1.  Isoniazid (INH — Isonicotinic Acid Hydrazide, 5 mg/kg/day, max 300 mg) [KU 21]:

•  Mechanism: Prodrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (katG); inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (InhA enzyme) in the mycobacterial cell wall. Potent early bactericidal activity against rapidly dividing extracellular and intracellular bacilli.

•  Uses: First-line treatment of all forms of active TB (penetrates CSF well) and LTBI chemoprophylaxis (6H or 3HR).

•  Adverse Effects:

•  Peripheral Neuropathy (glove-and-stocking sensory neuropathy due to competitive inhibition of pyridoxine [Vitamin B6] metabolism — prevented by co-prescribing Pyridoxine 10–20 mg/day, especially in pregnancy, diabetes, alcoholics, HIV, malnutrition, and CKD).

•  Hepatotoxicity (idiosyncratic hepatitis; more common in older age, alcoholics, and slow acetylators).

•  Drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus (lupoid reactions), optic neuritis, seizures/psychosis, pellagra, and sideroblastic anaemia.

2.  Rifampicin (10 mg/kg/day, max 600 mg) [KU 15]:

•  Mechanism: Binds to the β-subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB), inhibiting RNA transcription. Unique sterilising activity against semi-dormant persister bacilli, making 6-month short-course therapy possible.

•  Clinical Uses of Rifampicin ([KU 15]):

1.  Cornerstone of Tuberculosis (active and latent) and Non-tuberculous mycobacterial (M. kansasii, MAC) treatment.

2.  Leprosy (Multidrug therapy — monthly dose).

3.  Prosthetic valve / MRSA Infective Endocarditis and prosthetic joint infections (biofilm penetration).

4.  Chemoprophylaxis of Meningococcal (Neisseria meningitidis) and Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis contacts.

5.  Brucellosis (combined with Doxycycline) and Legionnaires' disease.

•  Adverse Effects:

•  Hepatotoxicity (cholestatic or hepatocellular) and transient asymptomatic hyperbilirubinaemia.

•  Harmless orange-red discoloration of urine, tears, sweat, and soft contact lenses.

•  "Flu-like" syndrome, Thrombocytopenic purpura, haemolytic anaemia, and acute interstitial nephritis.

•  Potent Cytochrome P450 Inducer: Accelerates hepatic metabolism and reduces efficacy of oral contraceptive pills (advise barrier/alternative contraception), Warfarin, Corticosteroids (can precipitate Addisonian crisis in patients with subclinical adrenal TB — crucial in the 50M vignette: always start Hydrocortisone before or alongside Rifampicin!), Oral sulfonylureas, and HIV protease/integrase inhibitors.

3.  Pyrazinamide (25 mg/kg/day):

•  Mechanism: Converted by pyrazinamidase (pncA) to pyrazinoic acid; sterilises dormant intracellular bacilli within the acidic environment of macrophage phagolysosomes.

•  Adverse Effects:Hepatotoxicity (most hepatotoxic first-line drug), Hyperuricaemia and Acute Gout (inhibits renal tubular urate secretion), arthralgia, gastrointestinal intolerance, photosensitivity rash.

4.  Ethambutol (15 mg/kg/day):

•  Mechanism: Bacteriostatic; inhibits arabinosyl transferase (embB), blocking arabinogalactan cell wall synthesis.

•  Adverse Effects:Dose-dependent Retrobulbar Optic Neuritis — presents with loss of red–green colour vision and reduced visual acuity (check Snellen chart and Ishihara colour plates at baseline; stop immediately if visual symptoms occur; reduce dose in renal failure).

5.  (Streptomycin [15 mg/kg IM] — no longer a routine first-line drug: causes vestibulocochlear [8th cranial nerve] ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; contraindicated in pregnancy).

5. Multidrug-Resistant (MDR) & Extensively Drug-Resistant (XDR) Tuberculosis [KU 25, 24, 22, 19, TU, RGU]

•  Definitions (Updated WHO 2021–2024 Definitions in Davidson 25e, p. 563):

•  Rifampicin-Resistant TB (RR-TB): Resistance to Rifampicin detected by genotypic (GeneXpert) or phenotypic methods, with or without resistance to other drugs.

•  Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR-TB): Resistance to at least BOTH Isoniazid and Rifampicin.

•  Pre-Extensively Drug-Resistant TB (Pre-XDR-TB): MDR/RR-TB that is also resistant to any Fluoroquinolone (Levofloxacin or Moxifloxacin).

•  Extensively Drug-Resistant TB (XDR-TB) [KU 22]: MDR/RR-TB that is resistant to any Fluoroquinolone AND at least one additional Group A drug (Bedaquiline or Linezolid).

•  Factors Contributing to Emergence of Drug-Resistant TB: Previous incomplete/irregular TB treatment, poor patient adherence, lack of DOT supervision, inappropriate drug regimens/dosages, poor-quality drugs or stock-outs, and direct transmission of MDR strains.

•  Second-Line Drugs Used in MDR/XDR Tuberculosis (WHO Grouping) [KU 24, 19, TU]:

•  Group A (Core All-Oral Drugs — Include all three):

1.  Bedaquiline (Bdq): Diarylquinoline that inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase (monitor ECG for QTc prolongation and LFTs).

2.  Fluoroquinolones:Levofloxacin (Lfx) or Moxifloxacin (Mfx) (DNA gyrase inhibitors).

3.  Linezolid (Lzd): Oxazolidinone protein synthesis inhibitor (monitor for bone marrow suppression and optic/peripheral neuropathy).

•  Group B (Add one or both in longer regimens):

1.  Clofazimine (Cfz): Riminophenazine dye (causes reddish-brown skin pigmentation).

2.  Cycloserine (Cs) or Terizidone: Cell wall inhibitor (causes CNS toxicity/psychosis — give with pyridoxine).

•  Group C & Newer Nitroimidazoles (Used in BPaLM or when Group A/B drugs cannot be used):

1.  Pretomanid (Pa) and Delamanid (Dlm) (novel nitroimidazoles inhibiting mycolic acid synthesis).

2.  Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, Imipenem–Cilastatin / Meropenem (with clavulanate), Amikacin (or Streptomycin), Ethionamide / Prothionamide, and p-Aminosalicylic acid (PAS).

•  Current WHO Recommended Treatment Regimen for MDR/RR-TB (Davidson 25e, p. 563):

•  6-Month All-Oral BPaLM Regimen (Treatment of Choice):Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid (600 mg OD) + Moxifloxacin (800 mg OD) for 6 months (or BPaL without moxifloxacin for 6–9 months in Pre-XDR-TB with fluoroquinolone resistance).

•  (Alternative 9-month all-oral regimen or 18-month individualised longer regimen using Group A + Group B drugs if ineligible for BPaLM).

title: 40. Bronchogenic Carcinoma, Pancoast Tumour & Paraneoplastic Syndromes [KU 24, 21, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 14.6 — TUMOURS OF THE BRONCHUS AND LUNG

40. Bronchogenic Carcinoma, Pancoast Tumour & Paraneoplastic Syndromes [KU 24, 21, 15, TU, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignettes: 60M chronic smoker with 4-month cough, haemoptysis, cachexia, right upper-limb pain & right ptosis; 45M chronic smoker with right chest pain, streaky haemoptysis, engorged neck veins & wasting of small muscles of right hand)

•  Complete Diagnosis of the Clinical Vignettes:Right Apical Bronchogenic Carcinoma (Superior Sulcus / Pancoast Tumour) with invasion of the Lower Brachial Plexus (C8–T1), Cervical Sympathetic Chain (Horner’s Syndrome), and Superior Vena Cava Obstruction.

1. Risk Factors & Histological Classification

•  Risk Factors:Cigarette smoking (responsible for >85% of cases; risk proportional to pack-years and tar content), Passive smoking, Radon gas exposure, Occupational carcinogens (Asbestos [synergistic 50-fold risk with smoking], arsenic, chromium, nickel, beryllium, silica, diesel exhaust, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons), and Pulmonary fibrosis.

•  Histological Types:

•  Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC — ~85%):

1.  Adenocarcinoma (35–40%): Most common type overall and most common in non-smokers and women; usually peripheral; associated with EGFR, ALK, and ROS1 driver mutations.

2.  Squamous Cell Carcinoma (25–30%): Strongly smoking-related; usually central/endobronchial; most common type to cavitate and cause PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia.

3.  Large-Cell Carcinoma (10–15%): Poorly differentiated, peripheral.

•  Small-Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC — ~15%) [TU]: Arises from neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells; central/hilar location; highly aggressive with early widespread haematogenous and mediastinal metastases; strongly associated with SIADH, Ectopic ACTH syndrome, and Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome; inoperable at presentation (treated with Cisplatin + Etoposide chemotherapy + thoracic/prophylactic cranial irradiation).

2. Clinical Features (Local, Invasive, Metastatic & Non-Metastatic) [KU 24, 21, TU, RGU]

•  1. Local Endobronchial Symptoms:

•  Persistent cough (or change in character of a chronic smoker’s cough — most common early symptom).

•  Haemoptysis (streaky blood-staining; rarely massive erosion of a pulmonary vessel).

•  Bronchial Obstruction: Unilateral fixed monophonic wheeze, lobar or whole-lung collapse (mediastinal shift towards affected side, dullness, absent breath sounds), or recurrent/non-resolving post-obstructive pneumonia or lung abscess.

•  Breathlessness (due to collapse, large pleural effusion, or lymphangitis carcinomatosa).

•  2. Local Intrathoracic Invasion / Mediastinal Spread:

•  Pleura & Chest Wall: Pleuritic chest pain, haemorrhagic malignant pleural effusion, osteolytic rib destruction, intercostal nerve pain.

•  Pancoast Syndrome (Superior Pulmonary Sulcus Tumour — Apical Lung Cancer) [KU 24, 21, TU]:

•  Apical lung tumour (usually NSCLC) invading the thoracic inlet structures:

1.  Lower Brachial Plexus (C8, T1, T2 nerve roots): Severe, unrelenting pain radiating down the medial (ulnar) aspect of the shoulder and forearm, with weakness and wasting of the intrinsic small muscles of the hand and numbness in the C8/T1 dermatomes.

2.  Cervical Sympathetic Chain (Stellate Ganglion) — Ipsilateral Horner’s Syndrome:

•  Partial Ptosis (drooping of upper eyelid — paralysis of Müller’s muscle).

•  Miosis (constricted pupil with preserved light reflex).

•  Anhidrosis (loss of sweating on the ipsilateral side of the face).

•  Apparent Enophthalmos.

3.  Erosion of 1st and 2nd Ribs or upper thoracic vertebrae (spinal cord compression).

•  (Differential Diagnosis of Apical Mass: Apical pulmonary TB, Mesothelioma, Lymphoma, Metastasis, Thoracic outlet syndrome).

•  Superior Vena Cava Obstruction (SVCO): Facial and neck plethora/swelling, conjunctival chemosis, headache, non-pulsatile distended neck veins, dilated collateral veins on anterior chest wall, and positive Pemberton’s sign (facial congestion and stridor on raising both arms above the head).

•  Left Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Palsy: Paralysis of left vocal cord → hoarseness of voice and "bovine" cough.

•  Phrenic Nerve Palsy: Unilateral elevated hemidiaphragm with paradoxical upward movement on sniffing.

•  Oesophagus & Pericardium: Progressive dysphagia; haemorrhagic pericardial effusion / tamponade or atrial fibrillation.

•  3. Distant Metastatic Spread:

•  Cervical/supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Virchow’s/scalene node), Brain (focal deficits, seizures, headache), Bone (pathological fractures, spinal cord compression), Liver (jaundice, tender hepatomegaly), and Adrenal glands.

•  4. Non-Metastatic Extrapulmonary (Paraneoplastic) Manifestations of Lung Cancer ([TU, RGU] — Davidson Box 17.65):

•  Endocrine:

1.  SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion): Euvolaemic hyponatraemia (Small-cell lung cancer).

2.  Ectopic ACTH Syndrome: Rapid-onset Cushing’s syndrome with severe hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, weight loss, and hyperpigmentation (Small-cell lung cancer and Bronchial carcinoid).

3.  Humoral Hypercalcaemia of Malignancy: Secretion of Parathyroid Hormone-related Peptide (PTHrP) (Squamous cell carcinoma).

4.  Gynaecomastia: Secretion of β-hCG (Large-cell carcinoma).

5.  Carcinoid Syndrome: Flushing, diarrhoea, wheeze (Bronchial neuroendocrine carcinoid).

•  Neurological (Autoantibodies such as Anti-Hu / Anti-VGCC — mostly Small-cell lung cancer):

•  Lambert–Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS): Autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels → proximal limb weakness and autonomic dysfunction that improves after repeated muscle contraction.

•  Subacute cerebellar degeneration, Peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy, Limbic encephalitis, Retinopathy.

•  Skeletal & Cutaneous:

•  Digital Clubbing and Hypertrophic Pulmonary Osteoarthropathy (HPOA) (Adenocarcinoma & Squamous cell).

•  Dermatomyositis / Polymyositis and Acanthosis nigricans.

•  Haematological, Vascular & Renal:

•  Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau’s sign), Marantic endocarditis, Membranous nephropathy (nephrotic syndrome).

3. Investigations & Staging [KU 24, 21]

1.  Imaging:

•  Chest X-Ray: Spiculated peripheral mass, cavitating lesion, unilateral hilar enlargement, apical mass with rib destruction (Pancoast), lobar collapse, or pleural effusion.

•  Contrast-Enhanced CT Thorax and Upper Abdomen: Defines primary tumour size, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and liver/adrenal metastases.

•  Whole-Body 18F-FDG PET-CT Scan: Accurately stages mediastinal lymph nodes and occult distant metastases prior to radical surgery/radiotherapy; MRI Brain and MRI Thoracic Inlet (best for assessing brachial plexus/spinal invasion in Pancoast tumour).

2.  Tissue Biopsy & Molecular Profiling (Mandatory for Histological & Genetic Diagnosis):

•  Central Tumours:Flexible Fibreoptic Bronchoscopy with direct biopsy, brushings, and washings.

•  Peripheral Tumours (including Pancoast tumour):CT-guided Percutaneous Transthoracic Needle Biopsy.

•  Mediastinal / Supraclavicular Nodes:Endobronchial Ultrasound-guided Transbronchial Needle Aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) or US-guided FNA of supraclavicular node.

•  Molecular Testing (in NSCLC/Adenocarcinoma): Test biopsy tissue for EGFR mutations, ALK rearrangements, ROS1, BRAF, and PD-L1 expression.

3.  Physiological Fitness Assessment: Spirometry (FEV1) and TLCO, plus cardiopulmonary exercise testing before lung resection.

4. Management

•  1. Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC):

•  Stage I & II (Localised):Curative Surgical Resection (Lobectomy or Pneumonectomy) ± adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy. If medically inoperable, Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy (SBRT / SABR) or radical radiotherapy.

•  Stage III / Pancoast Tumour: Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy followed by surgical resection (in resectable Pancoast tumours) or consolidation immunotherapy (Durvalumab).

•  Stage IV (Metastatic NSCLC):

•  Targetable Driver Mutation Present: Oral Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs) — e.g., Osimertinib / Erlotinib / Afatinib for EGFR-mutant tumours; Alectinib / Crizotinib for ALK-positive tumours.

•  No Driver Mutation:Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors (Pembrolizumab / Nivolumab — anti-PD-1) alone (if PD-L1 ≥ 50%) or combined with Platinum-doublet chemotherapy (Cisplatin/Carboplatin + Pemetrexed or Paclitaxel).

•  2. Small-Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC):

•  Combination Chemotherapy (Cisplatin/Carboplatin + Etoposide) + Thoracic radiotherapy (in limited-stage disease) + Prophylactic Cranial Irradiation (PCI) in responders.

•  3. Palliative Measures:

•  SVCO: Immediate high-dose Dexamethasone (16 mg/day), Endovascular SVC stenting, and urgent radiotherapy (for NSCLC) or chemotherapy (for SCLC).

•  Palliative Radiotherapy: For haemoptysis, bone metastasis pain, brachial plexus pain, or brain metastases.

•  Endobronchial Laser / Stenting: For main airway obstruction/stridor.

•  Indwelling Pleural Catheter or Talc Pleurodesis: For recurrent malignant pleural effusion.

title: 41. Pneumoconiosis, Silicosis & Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis [KU 22, 20, 19]
text:
SECTION 14.8 — OCCUPATIONAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL LUNG DISEASE

41. Pneumoconiosis, Silicosis & Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis [KU 22, 20, 19]

A. Causes of Pneumoconiosis [KU 22]

•  Definition: Permanent alteration of lung structure due to the inhalation of inorganic mineral dusts and the tissue reactions of the lung to its presence, excluding bronchitis and emphysema.

•  Classification & Causes (Davidson Box 17.81):

1.  Fibrogenic Dusts:

•  Crystalline Silica (Quartz):Silicosis (stone cutting, quarrying, sandblasting, mining, pottery, foundry work).

•  Coal Dust:Coal Worker’s Pneumoconiosis (CWP) — Simple CWP or Progressive Massive Fibrosis (PMF); Caplan’s syndrome = CWP/silicosis + seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis + cavitating pulmonary rheumatoid nodules.

•  Asbestos Fibres (Chrysotile [white], Crocidolite [blue], Amosite [brown]): Asbestosis (lower lobe fibrosis), Benign calcified pleural plaques, Diffuse pleural thickening, Benign pleural effusion, Bronchogenic carcinoma, and Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma.

•  Beryllium:Berylliosis (aerospace/electronics/nuclear industries — causes a chronic non-caseating granulomatous lung disease indistinguishable from sarcoidosis).

2.  Inert (Non-Fibrogenic) Radiodense Dusts (Cause benign nodular CXR shadowing without fibrosis or PFT impairment):

•  Iron Oxide:Siderosis (arc welders).

•  Tin Oxide:Stannosis (tin smelting).

•  Barium Sulphate:Baritosis.

B. Silicosis [KU 19]

•  Aetiopathogenesis: Inhalation of respirable crystalline silica (quartz) particles (<5 µm) in stone quarry workers, sandblasters, miners, tunnel drillers, and pottery workers. Alveolar macrophages engulf silica particles, which are toxic to phagolysosomes → macrophage death, release of fibrogenic cytokines (TGF-β, TNF-α, IL-1) and free radicals → formation of concentric hyalinised collagenous silicotic nodules (birefringent silica particles visible under polarised light).

•  Clinical Forms:

1.  Chronic Simple Silicosis: Appears after 10–20 years of exposure; asymptomatic or mild cough/dyspnoea; CXR/HRCT shows multiple discrete 3–5 mm upper-zone nodular opacities and characteristic "egg-shell" calcification of hilar lymph nodes.

2.  Complicated Silicosis / Progressive Massive Fibrosis (PMF): Coalescence of nodules into large (>1 cm) conglomerate fibrotic masses in the upper lobes with cavitation, restrictive/mixed PFT defect, progressive dyspnoea, respiratory failure, and cor pulmonale.

3.  Accelerated Silicosis: Develops after 5–10 years of heavy exposure.

4.  Acute Silicoproteinosis: Follows intense short-term exposure to fine silica dust (e.g., sandblasting in confined spaces) → alveoli fill with PAS-positive lipoproteinaceous material (similar to pulmonary alveolar proteinosis), causing rapidly fatal respiratory failure.

•  Complications: Greatly increased susceptibility to Pulmonary Tuberculosis ("Silicotuberculosis" — silica impairs macrophage killing of MTB), Non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection, Lung cancer (silica is a Group 1 carcinogen), COPD, Caplan’s syndrome, and autoimmune connective tissue diseases (Systemic sclerosis — Erasmus syndrome).

•  Management: Immediate removal from further silica dust exposure, smoking cessation, screening and treatment for latent/active TB, supportive therapy (bronchodilators, oxygen, vaccination), Nintedanib for progressive pulmonary fibrosis, and lung transplantation in end-stage disease.

C. Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis) — Management [KU 20]

•  Overview: An immunologically mediated (Type III immune-complex and Type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity) diffuse parenchymal lung disease affecting the alveoli and terminal bronchioles, caused by repeated inhalation of organic dusts/antigens:

•  Farmer’s Lung: Spores of thermophilic actinomycetes (Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula) in mouldy hay.

•  Bird Fancier’s Lung: Avian serum proteins in pigeon/budgerigar droppings and feathers.

•  Malt Worker’s Lung:Aspergillus clavatus.

•  Clinical & Diagnostic Features:

•  Acute HP: Presents 4–8 hours after heavy antigen exposure with fever, chills, malaise, dry cough, dyspnoea, and bibasal end-inspiratory crackles/squeaks.

•  Chronic HP: Insidious progressive dyspnoea and upper/mid-zone pulmonary fibrosis.

•  Investigations: Restrictive PFTs with ↓ TLCO; Positive serum precipitating IgG antibodies (precipitins) to the offending antigen; HRCT Thorax shows patchy ground-glass opacities, centrilobular nodules, and "mosaic attenuation" (air-trapping on expiration) or upper-zone traction bronchiectasis; BAL shows marked CD8+ T-cell lymphocytosis.

•  Management of Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis ([KU 20]):

1.  Complete Avoidance of Antigen Exposure (Cornerstone of Management): Remove the patient from the offending environment (rehouse pet birds, change occupational role) or, if unavoidable, reduce antigen load (dry hay before storage) and use powered air-purifying respirators / high-efficiency dust masks.

2.  Corticosteroid Therapy (in Acute or Subacute Symptomatic Disease):Oral Prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day (30–40 mg/day) until clinical, physiological, and radiological resolution occurs, followed by a slow taper over several months down to 10 mg/day and eventual cessation.

3.  Steroid-Sparing Immunosuppressants (in Chronic Relapsing HP):Mycophenolate mofetil or Azathioprine.

4.  Antifibrotic Therapy (in Progressive Fibrotic HP):Nintedanib (150 mg BD) slows FVC decline.

5.  Supportive Care: High-flow oxygen in acute hypoxaemic episodes, LTOT and pulmonary rehabilitation in chronic fibrosis, and referral for Lung Transplantation in end-stage respiratory failure.

title: 42. Acute Pulmonary Embolism (PE) & Pulmonary Hypertension [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 20, TU]
text:
SECTION 14.9, 14.10 & 14.11 — PULMONARY VASCULAR, UPPER AIRWAY & PLEURAL DISEASES

42. Acute Pulmonary Embolism (PE) & Pulmonary Hypertension [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 20, TU]

(Covers Clinical Vignette: Elderly male developing painful right lower limb swelling after a long-haul flight, presenting with sudden-onset breathlessness)

A. Acute Pulmonary Embolism (PE) [KU 25, 22, TU]

•  Aetiology & Risk Factors (Virchow’s Triad: Venous stasis, Endothelial injury, Hypercoagulability):

•  >90% arise from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the proximal lower limb/pelvic veins.

•  Risk Factors ([KU 22, TU]):

1.  Immobility / Venous Stasis:Prolonged air/road travel (>4 hours — "Economy-class syndrome"), prolonged bed rest, hospitalisation, stroke/spinal cord injury, congestive heart failure.

2.  Surgery & Trauma:Major orthopaedic surgery (hip/knee replacement), pelvic/abdominal surgery, lower limb fractures (within 3 months).

3.  Malignancy: Active visceral or haematological cancer (especially pancreatic, lung, GI, brain) and chemotherapy.

4.  Hormonal / Reproductive:Pregnancy and puerperium, Combined oral contraceptive pill, Hormone replacement therapy (HRT), Tamoxifen.

5.  Inherited & Acquired Thrombophilias:Factor V Leiden mutation, Prothrombin G20210A mutation, Antithrombin III / Protein C / Protein S deficiency, Antiphospholipid syndrome, Nephrotic syndrome.

•  Clinical Features (Classified by Haemodynamic Severity — Davidson Box 17.84):

1.  Acute Massive (High-Risk) PE: Obstruction of >50% of pulmonary arterial bed (e.g., saddle embolus) → acute RV pressure overload and failure → syncope/collapse, central crushing chest pain, severe dyspnoea, central cyanosis, hypotension/cardiogenic shock (SBP <90 mmHg), raised JVP, RV S3 gallop, loud P2, and oliguria.

2.  Acute Small/Medium (Submassive / Low-Risk) PE: Occlusion of segmental pulmonary artery causing pulmonary infarction → acute pleuritic chest pain, sudden dyspnoea, haemoptysis, tachypnoea, tachycardia, low-grade fever, localised pleural rub, and a small haemorrhagic pleural effusion (+ unilateral calf swelling/tenderness of DVT).

3.  Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH): Progressive exertional dyspnoea and right heart failure.

•  Investigations & Diagnostic Algorithm:

1.  Clinical Probability Assessment (Two-Level Wells Score for PE):

•  Clinical signs of DVT (3.0), PE is #1 diagnosis or equally likely (3.0), HR >100/min (1.5), Immobilisation ≥ 3 days or surgery in past 4 weeks (1.5), Previous DVT/PE (1.5), Haemoptysis (1.0), Malignancy (1.0).

•  Score >4 = PE Likely → proceed directly to CTPA (start interim anticoagulation if delayed).

•  Score ≤ 4 = PE Unlikely → perform quantitative Plasma D-dimer (if negative, safely excludes PE; if positive, proceed to CTPA).

2.  CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA — First-Line Gold Standard Diagnostic Test): Directly visualises intraluminal filling defects (e.g., saddle or lobar/segmental thrombus) and RV enlargement. (If CTPA is contraindicated due to severe renal failure or contrast allergy, perform a V/Q [Ventilation–Perfusion] scan or Proximal Leg Vein Compression Doppler Ultrasound).

3.  12-Lead ECG: Most common finding is sinus tachycardia and anterior (V1–V4) T-wave inversion; larger emboli show the classic S1Q3T3 pattern (deep S in I, Q wave and inverted T in III), right axis deviation, or new incomplete/complete RBBB.

4.  Arterial Blood Gases:Hypoxaemia (↓ PaO2) with hypocapnia (↓ PaCO2) and respiratory alkalosis (wide A–a gradient); metabolic acidosis in massive PE.

5.  Chest X-Ray: Often normal in acute massive PE (excludes pneumothorax/pneumonia); may show focal oligemia (Westermark’s sign), enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla’s sign), peripheral wedge-shaped opacity above the diaphragm (Hampton’s hump), linear atelectasis, elevated hemidiaphragm, or small bloody pleural effusion.

6.  Bedside Echocardiography & Biomarkers (Risk Stratification): RV dilatation/hypokinesia (McConnell’s sign) and elevated Serum Troponin I/T and NT-proBNP identify intermediate-high/high-risk PE.

•  Management of Acute Pulmonary Embolism:

1.  General Supportive Care: High-flow oxygen to correct hypoxaemia; cautious IV fluid bolus (500 mL) and vasopressors (Noradrenaline/Dobutamine) for hypotension; opiates for severe pleuritic pain.

2.  Anticoagulation (Mainstay of Therapy for All Patients):

•  Immediate Parenteral:Subcutaneous Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH) (e.g., Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD or 1.5 mg/kg OD) or Fondaparinux (or IV Unfractionated Heparin if eGFR <30 mL/min or considering thrombolysis).

•  Oral Anticoagulation:Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs — First-line):Apixaban (10 mg BD for 7 days, then 5 mg BD) or Rivaroxaban (15 mg BD for 21 days, then 20 mg OD) — can be started directly without LMWH lead-in; OR Edoxaban / Dabigatran (after 5 days of LMWH); OR Warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0, bridged with LMWH for ≥ 5 days).

•  Duration of Anticoagulation:3 months for provoked PE (e.g., surgery/flight); indefinite/lifelong for unprovoked PE or persistent risk factors (active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome).

3.  Systemic Thrombolytic Therapy (Indicated in Acute Massive PE with Haemodynamic Instability / Shock, SBP <90 mmHg):

•  IV Alteplase (rt-PA) 100 mg over 2 hours (or 50 mg bolus in imminent cardiac arrest), or Streptokinase / Tenecteplase.

•  Surgical or Catheter-Directed Pulmonary Embolectomy: If thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails.

4.  Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) Filter: Inserted only if there is an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation (active major bleeding) or recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation.

B. Pulmonary Hypertension (PH) [KU 24, 23, 20, TU]

•  Definition: Mean Pulmonary Artery Pressure (mPAP) ≥ 25 mmHg at rest (recently updated to >20 mmHg with PVR >2 Wood units) measured by right heart catheterisation.

•  Clinical Classification of Pulmonary Hypertension (WHO 5 Groups — Davidson Box 17.86) [TU]:

•  Group 1 — Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH): Idiopathic (IPAH — young females), Heritable (BMPR2 gene mutation), Drug-induced (anorexigens/fenfluramine, dasatinib), Connective tissue disease (Systemic sclerosis / CREST syndrome, SLE), HIV, Portal hypertension (portopulmonary), Congenital heart disease (shunts/Eisenmenger’s), Schistosomiasis, Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease.

•  Group 2 — PH due to Left Heart Disease (Most common overall): LV systolic/diastolic failure, Mitral stenosis/regurgitation, Aortic valve disease.

•  Group 3 — PH due to Lung Diseases and/or Hypoxia: COPD, Interstitial lung disease, Obstructive sleep apnoea, High altitude.

•  Group 4 — Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH): Unresolved organised pulmonary emboli.

•  Group 5 — Multifactorial / Unclear Mechanisms: Sarcoidosis, haematological/myeloproliferative disorders.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Symptoms: Insidious exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, anginal chest pain (RV ischaemia), exertional syncope, haemoptysis, hoarseness (Ortner’s syndrome).

•  Signs:Prominent a wave in JVP (and giant v wave of functional TR), left parasternal heave (RVH), palpable and loud booming P2, right ventricular S4 and S3, pulmonary ejection click, Graham Steell early diastolic murmur (PR), pansystolic murmur of TR, pulsatile hepatomegaly, ascites, and pedal oedema.

•  Investigations: CXR (enlarged central pulmonary arteries with peripheral pruning), ECG (RVH and P pulmonale), Doppler Echocardiography (estimates pulmonary artery systolic pressure from tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity: PASP = 4v2 + RAP), V/Q scan (to exclude CTEPH), HRCT thorax, Autoimmune screen (anti-centromere/SCL-70), and Right Heart Catheterisation with Acute Vasoreactivity Testing (gold standard).

•  Management:

•  General: Diuretics for RV failure, Long-term oxygen therapy (maintain PaO2 > 8 kPa), Oral anticoagulation (mandatory in CTEPH and IPAH), Digoxin, strict avoidance of pregnancy (>30–50% mortality).

•  Targeted Pulmonary Vasodilator Therapy (for Group 1 PAH):

1.  High-dose Calcium Channel Blockers (Nifedipine, Amlodipine — only in the 10% with a positive acute vasodilator test).

2.  Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) Inhibitors:Sildenafil (20 mg TDS) or Tadalafil (40 mg OD); or Guanylate cyclase stimulator (Riociguat — also drug of choice for inoperable CTEPH).

3.  Endothelin Receptor Antagonists:Bosentan, Ambrisentan, or Macitentan.

4.  Prostacyclin Analogues / Receptor Agonists:IV Epoprostenol, Nebulised Iloprost, Treprostinil, or oral Selexipag.

•  Surgical:Pulmonary Thromboendarterectomy (curative in CTEPH), Balloon atrial septostomy (bridge), and Double-Lung or Heart–Lung Transplantation.

title: 43. Obstructive Sleep Apnoea/Hypopnoea Syndrome (OSAHS) [KU 24, 18, TU]
text:
43. Obstructive Sleep Apnoea/Hypopnoea Syndrome (OSAHS) [KU 24, 18, TU]

•  Definition & Pathogenesis: Recurrent partial (hypopnoea) or complete (apnoea, lasting ≥ 10 seconds) collapse and obstruction of the upper pharyngeal airway (at the level of the soft palate and tongue base) during sleep, due to loss of tone in pharyngeal dilator muscles (genioglossus, palatoglossus). Each apnoea causes progressive hypoxia and hypercapnia → vigorous inspiratory effort against the occluded pharynx → brief cortical micro-arousal that restores muscle tone and opens the airway with a loud snort, resulting in severe sleep fragmentation and nocturnal sympathetic surges.

•  Risk Factors:Obesity (70% — parapharyngeal fat pads; neck circumference >43 cm), Male sex (2:1), Retrognathia/micrognathia, Nasal obstruction/tonsillar hypertrophy, Acromegaly, Hypothyroidism, Alcohol and sedatives before bed.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Nocturnal:Loud, habitual snoring in all positions, witnessed apnoeas by bed partner, nocturnal choking/gasping awakenings, restless sleep, and nocturia.

•  Daytime:Excessive daytime somnolence (falling asleep in monotonous situations; 3- to 9-fold increased risk of road traffic accidents), unrefreshing sleep, early morning headaches, poor concentration/cognitive impairment, irritability, depression, and systemic hypertension, atrial fibrillation, insulin resistance, and pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale (especially when combined with COPD — "Overlap syndrome").

•  Diagnosis of Obstructive Sleep Apnoea ([KU 24, 18]):

1.  Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) Questionnaire: Quantifies daytime propensity to doze across 8 situations (maximum score 24; normal <10; score >10–11 is abnormal, severe OSA averages 16).

2.  Overnight Polysomnography (PSG — Gold Standard) or Home Respiratory Polygraphy / Overnight Pulse Oximetry:

•  Records nasal airflow, thoracoabdominal respiratory effort (present in obstructive apnoea; absent in central apnoea), SpO2 (repetitive "saw-tooth" oxygen desaturations), snoring, ECG, and EEG.

•  Apnoea–Hypopnoea Index (AHI): Number of apnoeas (≥ 10 s pause) + hypopnoeas (≥ 10 s 50% airflow reduction with ≥ 4% SpO2 drop) per hour of sleep:

•  Mild OSAHS: AHI 5–14 / hour.

•  Moderate OSAHS: AHI 15–29 / hour.

•  Severe OSAHS: AHI ≥ 30 / hour.

3.  Exclude Endocrine Causes: Check Thyroid function tests (TSH) and IGF-1 (if acromegalic features).

•  Management:

1.  Lifestyle & General Measures:Weight loss (diet, GLP-1 agonists/tirzepatide, or bariatric surgery), avoid alcohol and sedatives/hypnotics in the evening, sleep in lateral position, and advise not to drive until daytime sleepiness is controlled (notify driving licensing authority).

2.  Nocturnal Nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP — Gold Standard Treatment of Choice): Delivers air at 5–15 cmH2O via a tight-fitting nasal mask to act as a pneumatic splint holding the pharynx open throughout the respiratory cycle — dramatically abolishes apnoeas, daytime somnolence, and lowers BP.

3.  Mandibular Advancement Device (Oral Splint): Holds the lower jaw and tongue forward; effective in mild-to-moderate OSA or CPAP intolerance.

title: 44. Pleural Effusion, Light’s Criteria, Chylothorax & Empyema [KU 23, 22, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
44. Pleural Effusion, Light’s Criteria, Chylothorax & Empyema [KU 23, 22, 15, TU, RGU]

A. Pleural Effusion: Aetiology, Clinical Assessment & Light’s Criteria [KU 23, 22, TU, RGU]

•  Aetiology:

•  Transudative Effusions (↑ hydrostatic pressure or ↓ oncotic pressure; often bilateral):

1.  Congestive Cardiac Failure (LVF) (most common transudate).

2.  Hepatic Cirrhosis (hepatic hydrothorax).

3.  Nephrotic Syndrome / severe hypoalbuminaemia (malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy).

4.  Peritoneal Dialysis, Hypothyroidism (Myxoedema), Constrictive Pericarditis, Meigs’ Syndrome (benign ovarian fibroma + ascites + right pleural effusion).

•  Exudative Effusions ([KU 22, TU, RGU] — ↑ capillary permeability or impaired lymphatic drainage; often unilateral):

1.  Infections:Bacterial Pneumonia (Parapneumonic effusion & Empyema), Tuberculosis (commonest cause of lymphocytic exudate in young adults in India).

2.  Malignancy:Bronchogenic carcinoma, Metastatic breast/ovarian/GI cancer, Lymphoma, Malignant Mesothelioma.

3.  Pulmonary Infarction / Thromboembolism.

4.  Autoimmune / Connective Tissue Diseases:Rheumatoid arthritis (very low glucose <1.6 mmol/L, high LDH, cholesterol crystals in chronic effusion), Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).

5.  Subdiaphragmatic / GI Disorders:Acute pancreatitis or pancreatic pseudocyst (↑↑ pleural fluid amylase, left-sided), Subphrenic abscess, Oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave’s — low pH, salivary amylase).

6.  Drug-Induced Pleural Effusion ([TU]):Amiodarone, Methotrexate, Nitrofurantoin, Bromocriptine, Phenytoin/Hydralazine/Isoniazid (drug-induced lupus), Dasatinib.

•  Clinical Signs of Pleural Effusion ([RGU]):

•  Inspection & Palpation: Tachypnoea, decreased chest wall movement on affected side, trachea and apex beat shifted to the CONTRALATERAL side (in large effusions >1 L; if trachea is central or pulled towards the effusion, suspect underlying bronchial obstruction/atelectasis by lung cancer or trapped lung by mesothelioma), and absent tactile vocal fremitus.

•  Percussion:"Stony dullness" over the fluid, rising towards the axilla (Ellis’s S-shaped curve).

•  Auscultation:Markedly diminished or absent breath sounds and absent vocal resonance over the effusion, with a zone of bronchial breathing and aegophony just at the upper border of the effusion (due to compressed lung).

•  Investigations & Light’s Criteria ([KU 23, 22]):

1.  Chest X-Ray & Thoracic Ultrasound: CXR shows blunting of costophrenic angle (>200 mL fluid required on PA view) and a homogeneous dense opacity with a concave upward meniscus ascending to the axilla. Bedside Ultrasound is more sensitive, detects septations/loculations, and guides safe aspiration.

2.  Diagnostic Pleural Aspiration (Thoracentesis) — Light’s Criteria ([KU 23, 22]):

•  When pleural fluid protein is between 25 and 35 g/L (or in all sampled effusions), an effusion is classified as an EXUDATE if it meets ONE OR MORE of the following 3 Light’s Criteria:

1.  (Pleural fluid protein)/(Serum protein) > 0.5

2.  (Pleural fluid LDH)/(Serum LDH) > 0.6

3.  Pleural fluid LDH > (2)/(3) (67%) of the upper limit of normal serum LDH

•  Serum–Pleural Fluid Albumin Gradient (SPAG) [KU 22]:

•  In patients with congestive heart failure or cirrhosis receiving diuretic therapy, water is reabsorbed from the pleural space, concentrating the protein and causing Light’s criteria to falsely misclassify ~25% of transudates as exudates.

•  Calculation: SPAG = Serum Albumin - Pleural Fluid Albumin.

•  Interpretation: If SPAG > 1.2 g/dL (12 g/L), the effusion is a true TRANSUDATE despite meeting Light’s criteria (alternatively, a Serum–Fluid Total Protein gradient >3.1 g/dL or elevated pleural fluid NT-proBNP confirms a cardiac transudate).

3.  Further Pleural Fluid Analysis ([RGU]):

•  Appearance: Straw-coloured (transudate, TB), Purulent/turbid (empyema), Milky (chylothorax, pseudochylothorax), Haemorrhagic / Blood-stained ([RGU] — Malignancy, Pulmonary infarction, Trauma, Benign asbestos effusion, Mesothelioma; if pleural fluid haematocrit >50% of peripheral blood haematocrit = true Haemothorax).

•  Cytology & Differential Cell Count:Neutrophils predominate in parapneumonic effusion, PE, and acute pancreatitis; Lymphocytes predominate in TB, Malignancy, and Lymphoma; Malignant cell clumps on cytology (positive in ~60% of malignant effusions).

•  Biochemistry & Microbiology:pH <7.2 and Glucose <3.3 mmol/L (60 mg/dL) indicate complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema (necessitating chest tube drainage), rheumatoid effusion, advanced malignancy, or oesophageal rupture; ADA >40 IU/L & GeneXpert/culture for TB; Amylase for pancreatitis; Triglycerides & Chylomicrons for chylothorax.

4.  CT Thorax with Pleural-Phase Contrast & Pleural Biopsy: CT-guided biopsy or Medical Thoracoscopy (gold standard, >95% diagnostic sensitivity for malignancy and TB).

•  Management of Unilateral / Malignant / Recurrent Pleural Effusion ([TU]):

•  Treat the underlying cause (diuretics for LVF, antibiotics + intercostal drainage for empyema, ATT for TB).

•  Therapeutic Thoracentesis: Remove no more than 1.5 L at a single sitting to prevent re-expansion pulmonary oedema.

•  Recurrent Malignant Pleural Effusion: Drain the pleural cavity completely via an intercostal tube and perform Chemical Pleurodesis by instilling sterile graded Talc slurry (4–5 g) (or Doxycycline/Bleomycin) into the pleural space to obliterate it; OR insert a Tunnelled Indwelling Pleural Catheter (IPC) for outpatient domiciliary drainage (especially if "trapped lung" prevents lung re-expansion).

B. Chylothorax & Milky Pleural Fluid [KU 15, TU]

•  Two Causes of Milky White Pleural Fluid ([TU]):

1.  True Chylothorax (lymphatic chyle leak from thoracic duct).

2.  Pseudochylothorax (Chyliform effusion) (cholesterol crystal accumulation in a long-standing chronic encysted effusion, classically rheumatoid pleuritis or chronic tuberculous effusion) or Empyema (supernatant clears on centrifugation in empyema, whereas chylothorax and pseudochylothorax remain turbid).

•  Chylothorax [KU 15]:

•  Definition: Accumulation of lymphatic fluid (chyle) in the pleural space due to disruption or obstruction of the thoracic duct. (Anatomical note: The thoracic duct crosses from right to left at the T5 vertebra; hence damage below T5 causes a right-sided chylothorax, and damage above T5 causes a left-sided chylothorax).

•  Causes:

1.  Trauma / Iatrogenic (50%): Thoracic surgery (oesophagectomy, cardiovascular surgery), central venous catheterisation, penetrating chest trauma.

2.  Neoplastic Obstruction (most common non-traumatic cause):Mediastinal Lymphoma, metastatic bronchogenic carcinoma.

3.  Miscellaneous:Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) (in young women), Filariasis, Tuberculosis, Yellow nail syndrome, Subclavian vein thrombosis.

•  Diagnosis: Milky-white, odourless exudative fluid that does not clear on centrifugation; Pleural fluid Triglycerides >110 mg/dL (1.24 mmol/L), Presence of Chylomicrons on lipoprotein electrophoresis (gold standard), and Cholesterol <200 mg/dL (in Pseudochylothorax, Cholesterol is >200 mg/dL with cholesterol crystals and Triglycerides <50 mg/dL).

•  Management: Intercostal tube drainage (avoid prolonged drainage as it causes profound malnutrition and T-lymphocyte immunodeficiency), Low-fat diet supplemented with Medium-Chain Triglycerides (MCT) (absorbed directly into the portal vein, bypassing the thoracic duct) or Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN), Octreotide (reduces splanchnic lymph flow), treatment of underlying lymphoma, and Thoracic Duct Embolisation or Surgical Ligation + pleurodesis if persistent.

title: 45. Pneumothorax, Tension Pneumothorax & Intercostal Drainage [KU 25, 24, 23, 20, RGU]
text:
45. Pneumothorax, Tension Pneumothorax & Intercostal Drainage [KU 25, 24, 23, 20, RGU]

(Covers Clinical Vignette: 36M with sudden-onset breathlessness, cough, cyanosis, hypotension, left-sided hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds & tracheal deviation to the right)

•  Complete Diagnosis of Vignette:Left-Sided Tension Pneumothorax.

1. Classification & Aetiopathology of Pneumothorax [KU 25, 24, RGU]

•  Definition: Presence of air in the pleural space between the visceral and parietal pleura.

•  Aetiological Classification (Davidson Box 17.92):

1.  Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax (PSP): Occurs in young (15–30 yrs), tall, thin males without overt underlying lung disease due to rupture of small apical subpleural blebs (smoking increases risk 20-fold).

2.  Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax (SSP): Occurs in patients >50 years with pre-existing lung disease (carries much higher mortality):

•  COPD (rupture of emphysematous bullae — most common), Acute severe asthma.

•  Pulmonary Tuberculosis, Necrotising pneumonia (S. aureus pneumatoceles), Lung abscess, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

•  Cystic Fibrosis, Bronchiectasis, Lung cancer, Marfan/Ehlers–Danlos syndromes, Interstitial lung diseases (IPF, Sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, Lymphangioleiomyomatosis), Catamenial pneumothorax (thoracic endometriosis).

3.  Traumatic Pneumothorax: Penetrating or blunt chest injury (rib fractures) or Iatrogenic (subclavian/IJV central line insertion, pleural aspiration/biopsy, CT-guided lung biopsy, transbronchial biopsy, positive-pressure mechanical ventilation barotrauma).

•  Pathophysiological Types (Davidson Fig. 17.71):

1.  Closed Pneumothorax: Pleural tear seals off as the lung deflates; mean intrapleural pressure remains negative; air resorbs spontaneously.

2.  Open Pneumothorax (Bronchopleural Fistula): Persistent fistulous communication between bronchus and pleural space; intrapleural pressure equals atmospheric pressure (0 cmH2O); predisposes to pyopneumothorax/empyema.

3.  Tension (Valvular) Pneumothorax [KU 25, 23, 20]: The pleural breach acts as a one-way ball-valve — air enters the pleural space during inspiration (or coughing) but cannot escape during expiration → intrapleural pressure progressively rises well above atmospheric pressure (positive) → complete collapse of the ipsilateral lung + mediastinal shift to the opposite side → compression of the contralateral lung and kinking/compression of the venae cavae and right atrium, severely impairing venous return and causing obstructive cardiogenic shock and rapid death.

2. Clinical Features & Investigations [KU 25, 24, 23]

•  Symptoms: Sudden-onset unilateral sharp pleuritic chest pain and acute breathlessness.

•  Physical Signs of Simple vs Tension Pneumothorax:

•  Inspection & Palpation: Tachypnoea, asymmetrical reduced movement of affected hemithorax, absent tactile vocal fremitus.

•  Percussion:Hyper-resonant (tympanitic) percussion note over the affected hemithorax.

•  Auscultation:Markedly diminished or absent breath sounds and absent vocal resonance on the affected side (+ Hamman’s crunch if pneumomediastinum).

•  Additional Signs Specific to Tension Pneumothorax ([KU 25, 23]):

1.  Rapidly worsening respiratory distress and central cyanosis.

2.  Marked sinus tachycardia and systemic hypotension (obstructive shock).

3.  Grossly elevated JVP (impaired venous return).

4.  Deviation of the trachea and cardiac apex beat AWAY from the affected side (to the contralateral side).

•  Investigations:

•  (Crucial Exam Point: Tension pneumothorax is a CLINICAL diagnosis — NEVER delay emergency needle decompression to obtain a chest X-ray!)

•  Erect PA Chest X-Ray (for non-tension pneumothorax): Shows a sharply defined convex visceral pleural line with complete absence of lung markings (hypertranslucency) peripheral to it. (Size is measured at the level of the hilum from the lung edge to the chest wall: <2 cm = small; ≥ 2 cm = large).

•  CT Thorax: Used in complex cases to differentiate a large emphysematous bulla (concave inner margin) from a loculated pneumothorax (convex lung edge).

3. Management of Pneumothorax & Intercostal Tube Drainage [KU 25, 24, 23, 20, RGU]

•  1. Emergency Management of Tension Pneumothorax ([KU 25, 23, 20]):

1.  Immediate Needle Decompression (Thoracocentesis): Insert a large-bore (14G or 16G) intravenous cannula into the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line (just above the upper border of the 3rd rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle) on the affected side (or 5th ICS anterior axillary line). A hiss of escaping air confirms the diagnosis and converts the tension pneumothorax into a simple open pneumothorax, restoring venous return and BP.

2.  High-Flow Oxygen (10–15 L/min): Corrects hypoxia and accelerates pleural air resorption 4-fold (by washing out nitrogen from capillary blood and increasing the partial pressure gradient for nitrogen diffusion out of the pleural cavity).

3.  Follow Immediately with Formal Intercostal Chest Drain Insertion connected to an underwater-seal drainage bottle (leave the decompression cannula in place until bubbling is confirmed in the underwater-seal bottle).

•  2. Management of Spontaneous Pneumothorax ([KU 24, RGU] — BTS Guidelines, Davidson Fig. 17.72):

•  Asymptomatic Primary or Secondary Pneumothorax (of any size): Conservative observation (+ high-flow oxygen if admitted with SSP).

•  Symptomatic Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax (PSP, age <50 yrs, no underlying lung disease):

•  First-line:Percutaneous Needle Aspiration (16G cannula in 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line with a 50 mL syringe and three-way tap, aspirating up to a maximum of 2.5 L of air) OR an Ambulatory Heimlich one-way valve device.

•  If needle aspiration fails (>2.5 L aspirated or lung fails to re-expand), insert a small-bore (8–14 Fr) Seldinger Intercostal Chest Drain.

•  Symptomatic Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax (SSP, age >50 yrs with smoking history or underlying lung disease) or High-Risk Features (Hypoxia, Bilateral, Haemopneumothorax):

•  Admit to hospital, give controlled oxygen, and proceed directly to Intercostal Chest Drain Insertion (as needle aspiration has a high failure rate in SSP).

•  3. Intercostal Chest Tube Drainage (ICD) — Technique & Care [KU 23]:

•  Site — The "Triangle of Safety" (Davidson Fig. 17.73):

•  Anterior border: Lateral edge of Pectoralis major.

•  Posterior border: Lateral edge of Latissimus dorsi.

•  Inferior border (base): Horizontal line at the level of the 5th intercostal space (nipple level).

•  Apex: Base of the axilla.

•  Management of Chest Drain:

•  Connect to an underwater-seal bottle (kept below the level of the patient's chest; fluid column swings with respiration and bubbles when air escapes).

•  NEVER clamp a bubbling chest drain (risk of precipitating fatal tension pneumothorax).

•  Removal: Remove the drain the morning after the lung has fully re-expanded on CXR AND bubbling has completely ceased for 24 hours.

•  Persistent Air Leak (Bronchopleural Fistula): If bubbling continues after 48 hours (in SSP) or 3–5 days (in PSP), apply low-pressure thoracic suction (-10 to -20 cmH2O) and refer for Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) (stapling/resection of apical blebs/bullae + surgical pleurodesis by pleural abrasion, pleurectomy, or talc poudrage).

•  4. Discharge Advice & Prevention of Recurrence (Recurrence rate ~25–30% at 1 year):

•  Strictly advise Smoking Cessation (reduces recurrence risk 4-fold).

•  Air Travel: Strictly contraindicated if a closed pneumothorax is present (trapped gas expands by 25–30% at cabin altitude); delay flying until at least 7 days after CXR confirms complete resolution.

•  Underwater Scuba Diving:Permanently contraindicated lifelong unless bilateral surgical pleurectomy has been performed.

•  Indications for Definitive VATS Pleurodesis: Second ipsilateral pneumothorax, first contralateral pneumothorax, synchronous bilateral pneumothorax, persistent air leak (>3–5 days), or high-risk professions (airline pilots, divers).

title: 46. Renal Biopsy, Routine Urine Examination & Asymptomatic Urinary Abnormalities [KU 20, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
CHAPTER 15: NEPHROLOGY AND UROLOGY (Davidson Ch. 18)

SECTION 15.1 & 15.2 — INVESTIGATIONS & PRESENTING PROBLEMS IN RENAL DISEASE

46. Renal Biopsy, Routine Urine Examination & Asymptomatic Urinary Abnormalities [KU 20, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

A. Renal Biopsy — Indications, Contraindications & Complications [KU 18]

•  Procedure: Percutaneous ultrasound-guided needle biopsy of the lower pole of a native kidney (or upper pole of a transplanted kidney in the iliac fossa) under local anaesthesia. Tissue is examined by Light Microscopy, Immunofluorescence, and Electron Microscopy.

•  Indications (Davidson Box 18.5):

1.  Unexplained Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) or Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN) where pre-renal and post-renal causes have been excluded.

2.  Nephrotic Syndrome or Glomerular Proteinuria (Spot PCR >100 mg/mmol or >1 g/24 hrs) in Adults.

3.  Nephrotic Syndrome in Children that has atypical features or is steroid-resistant (fails to respond to 4–6 weeks of prednisolone).

4.  Acute Nephritic Syndrome (unless typical self-limiting childhood post-streptococcal GN).

5.  Renal Involvement in Systemic Diseases (e.g., SLE [to classify Lupus Nephritis Class I–VI and guide immunosuppression], ANCA vasculitis, Goodpasture’s, Myeloma/Amyloidosis).

6.  Unexplained Renal Allograft (Transplant) Dysfunction (to distinguish acute cellular/antibody rejection from calcineurin inhibitor toxicity or BK virus nephropathy).

7.  Unexplained Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) with normal-sized kidneys.

•  Contraindications:

1.  Uncorrected bleeding diathesis / coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia (stop antiplatelets/anticoagulants 5–7 days prior).

2.  Uncontrolled severe hypertension (≥ 160/100 mmHg — markedly increases bleeding risk).

3.  Bilateral small, shrunken echogenic kidneys (<60% predicted size / <8–9 cm — high bleeding risk and only shows end-stage fibrosis).

4.  Solitary native kidney (relative contraindication; transplanted kidneys are biopsied).

5.  Multiple bilateral cysts (ADPKD), hydronephrosis, or active acute pyelonephritis / perinephric abscess.

•  Complications: Microscopic/visible haematuria (common, resolves in 24–48 hrs), Clot colic and ureteric obstruction, Perinephric haematoma, Massive retroperitoneal haemorrhage (requiring angiographic coil embolisation or nephrectomy in <0.5%), and Intrarenal arteriovenous fistula.

B. Routine Urine Examination, Proteinuria, Microalbuminuria, Bence Jones Proteinuria & Sterile Pyuria [KU 20, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

•  1. Routine Urine Examination (Physical, Chemical Dipstick & Microscopy) [RGU, TU]:

•  Physical: Volume, colour (smoky/cola-coloured = glomerular haematuria; red = lower tract bleed, haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, rifampicin, beetroot), specific gravity (1.003–1.030).

•  Chemical Dipstick: pH (4.5–8.0), Protein (detects albumin >300 mg/L; does NOT detect Bence Jones light chains), Blood, Glucose, Ketones, Nitrites (Gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae converting urinary nitrates), and Leucocyte esterase (neutrophils).

•  Urine Microscopy of Centrifuged Sediment:

•  Cells:Dysmorphic RBCs (acanthocytes) = glomerular bleeding; Isomorphic RBCs = urological bleeding; WBCs (>5/HPF = pyuria); Eosinophils (acute interstitial nephritis).

•  Urinary Casts (Formed on a Tamm–Horsfall mucoprotein matrix in distal tubules):

•  Hyaline casts: Normal urine, fever, exercise, diuretics.

•  Red Blood Cell (RBC) casts: Pathognomonic of Glomerulonephritis / Acute Nephritic Syndrome.

•  White Blood Cell (WBC) casts:Acute pyelonephritis or Acute interstitial nephritis.

•  Muddy-brown coarse granular / epithelial cell casts:Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN).

•  Fatty casts & "Maltese cross" oval fat bodies:Nephrotic Syndrome.

•  Broad waxy casts:Advanced Chronic Kidney Disease (dilated atrophic tubules).

•  Crystals: Envelope-shaped = Calcium oxalate; Coffin-lid = Struvite (infection); Rhomboid/rosette = Uric acid; Hexagonal = Cystinuria.

•  2. Asymptomatic Urinary Abnormalities (Proteinuria & Microscopic Haematuria) [KU 20, 18, 16, TU]:

•  Causes of Proteinuria ([KU 16]):

1.  Transient / Functional (Benign): Fever, strenuous exercise, heart failure, UTI, Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria (absent on first-morning void).

2.  Glomerular Proteinuria (Increased permeability of GBM/podocytes — predominantly albumin; often >1–3.5 g/day): Minimal change disease, FSGS, Membranous nephropathy, IgA nephropathy, Diabetic nephropathy, Lupus nephritis, Amyloidosis.

3.  Tubular Proteinuria (Impaired proximal tubular reabsorption of low-molecular-weight proteins like β2-microglobulin; always <1.5–2 g/day): Acute/chronic tubulo-interstitial nephritis, Fanconi syndrome, heavy metal toxicity.

4.  Overflow Proteinuria:Multiple Myeloma (Bence Jones proteinuria [RGU] — monoclonal free κ or λ immunoglobulin light chains [25 kDa] overproduced by malignant plasma cells, freely filtered at the glomerulus, exceeding tubular reabsorptive capacity; causes a "protein gap" where urinary spot PCR is markedly elevated while dipstick/ACR is negative; detected by urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation).

•  Microalbuminuria (Moderately Increased Albuminuria) [TU]:

•  Definition: Urinary albumin excretion of 30–300 mg/24 hours (Spot Albumin:Creatinine Ratio [ACR] of 2.5–30 mg/mmol in males or 3.5–30 mg/mmol in females [30–300 mg/g]), which is below the detection threshold of standard urine dipsticks.

•  Significance: Earliest clinical marker of Diabetic Nephropathy and generalized endothelial dysfunction/cardiovascular risk; indication to initiate ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy (and SGLT2 inhibitor).

•  Causes of Haematuria ([KU 18, TU]):

•  Glomerular (Non-visible or cola-coloured, painless, with dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, proteinuria, and hypertension):IgA nephropathy (most common), Post-infectious GN, Alport syndrome, Thin basement membrane disease, Lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis, Goodpasture’s disease.

•  Non-Glomerular / Urological (Isomorphic RBCs, no casts/proteinuria; visible haematuria mandates CT Urogram + Cystoscopy to rule out malignancy):Renal cell carcinoma, Transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma of bladder/ureter, Prostate cancer, Urolithiasis (renal/ureteric stones), Urinary tract infection / Schistosomiasis / Renal TB, Benign prostatic enlargement, Polycystic kidney disease, Trauma, Anticoagulants/bleeding disorders.

•  3. Causes of Sterile Pyuria (Pus cells/WBCs in urine with negative routine aerobic bacterial culture) [TU]:

1.  Partially treated bacterial UTI (recent antibiotic use — most common).

2.  Renal / Genitourinary Tuberculosis (classic — send 3 early-morning urine samples for AFB, MGIT culture, and GeneXpert).

3.  Fastidious atypical organisms:Chlamydia trachomatis, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma, Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

4.  Tubulo-interstitial Nephritis (drug-induced: NSAIDs, PPIs, penicillins) and Renal papillary necrosis (analgesic nephropathy, diabetes, sickle-cell disease).

5.  Urolithiasis (renal/bladder calculi), Bladder tumour, Indwelling catheter, Polycystic kidney disease, or Kawasaki disease.

•  4. Causes of Polyuria (Urine volume >3 Litres/24 hours) [KU 17, 15]:

1.  Solute / Osmotic Diuresis (Urine osmolality >300 mOsm/kg):Uncontrolled Diabetes Mellitus (glycosuria), SGLT2 inhibitors, Mannitol, High-protein enteral feeding/urea diuresis, Hypercalcaemic/hypokalaemic tubular injury, Diuretic phase of recovering ATN or post-obstructive diuresis.

2.  Water Diuresis (Hypotonic urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg):

•  Primary Polydipsia (psychogenic excess fluid intake — low plasma osmolality/sodium).

•  Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (Cranial Diabetes Insipidus): Pituitary surgery, trauma, craniopharyngioma, sarcoidosis.

•  Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus):Lithium toxicity, Hypercalcaemia, Hypokalaemia, Chronic interstitial nephritis, Congenital AVPR2 / AQP2 mutations.

subject: medicine
title: 47. Acute Nephritic Syndrome & Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) [KU 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, 17, 16, 15, RGU]
text:
SECTION 15.2A & 15.3 — NEPHRITIC SYNDROME & GLOMERULAR DISEASES

47. Acute Nephritic Syndrome & Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) [KU 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, 17, 16, 15, RGU]

•  (Covers Clinical Vignettes: 15M / 16M / 19F with recent skin/throat infection, periorbital facial puffiness, pedal oedema, oliguria, smoky/cola-coloured haematuria & BP 150–160/100 mmHg)

1. Definition & Pathophysiology of Acute Nephritic Syndrome [KU 23, 16]

•  Definition: A clinical syndrome of acute glomerular inflammation characterised by the pentad of:

1.  Haematuria (visible smoky/cola-coloured or microscopic, with dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts).

2.  Oliguria (<400 mL/day) and Acute Kidney Injury (Azotaemia — ↑ urea and creatinine).

3.  Systemic Hypertension (due to avid renal sodium and water retention).

4.  Oedema (classically early morning periorbital facial puffiness spreading to ankles/generalised fluid overload).

5.  Mild-to-moderate Proteinuria (usually sub-nephrotic, <3.5 g/24 hrs).

•  Pathophysiology: Immune-complex deposition or in situ antibody binding in the glomerulus activates the complement cascade → recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages + proliferation of endocapillary/mesangial cells → narrowing of glomerular capillary lumina (↓ GFR → oliguria, azotaemia, and avid distal tubular Na+ and water retention → expanded intravascular volume, hypertension, and oedema) + focal breaks in the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) allowing RBCs and protein to leak into Bowman’s space.

2. Causes & Differential Diagnosis of Acute Nephritic Syndrome [KU 20, 19]

1.  Post-Infectious / Infection-Related Glomerulonephritis (Low Serum C3):

•  Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) (most common in children/adolescents).

•  Non-streptococcal infections: Subacute Infective Endocarditis, Staphylococcal sepsis, Shunt nephritis, Hepatitis B & C, HIV, Malaria.

2.  Primary Glomerular Diseases:

•  IgA Nephropathy (Berger’s Disease):Key differential diagnosis in young adults! Differentiated from PSGN by synpharyngitic haematuria (occurs within 1–2 days of an URTI rather than 1–3 weeks later) and normal serum C3 levels.

•  Mesangiocapillary Glomerulonephritis (MCGN / MPGN): Persistent hypocomplementaemia (low C3 for >8 weeks).

3.  Multisystem / Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN):

•  Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (Lupus Nephritis Class III/IV): Positive ANA, anti-dsDNA, low C3 and C4.

•  IgA Vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein Purpura): Palpable purpura on buttocks/legs + arthralgia + abdominal pain + nephritis.

•  ANCA-Associated Small-Vessel Vasculitis: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (c-ANCA/PR3) and Microscopic polyangiitis (p-ANCA/MPO).

•  Anti-GBM Disease (Goodpasture’s Disease): Pulmonary haemorrhage + crescentic GN.

4.  Genetic:Alport Syndrome (haematuria + sensorineural deafness + lenticonus).

3. Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) [KU 22, 20, 17, 15]

•  Aetiopathogenesis: An immune-complex-mediated acute diffuse endocapillary proliferative glomerulonephritis occurring after infection with nephritogenic strains of Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus (S. pyogenes — M types 1, 2, 4, 12, 49), with a characteristic latent period of:

•  1–2 weeks (10 days) after Streptococcal Pharyngitis (tonsillitis), OR

•  3–6 weeks after Streptococcal Skin Infection (Impetigo / Pyoderma)(as in the 16M vignette).

•  Renal Pathology:

•  Light Microscopy:Diffuse global endocapillary hypercellularity (proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells) with heavy infiltration by neutrophils ("exudative GN").

•  Immunofluorescence:"Starry-sky" / "lumpy-bumpy" granular deposits of IgG and C3 along the capillary walls and mesangium.

•  Electron Microscopy: Characteristic large subepithelial electron-dense "humps".

•  Investigations & Evaluation for Alternative Diagnoses ([KU 24, 22, 20]):

1.  Urinalysis & Microscopy ([KU 24, RGU]): Smoky/brown urine; dipstick positive for blood (+++) and protein (+ to ++); microscopy shows dysmorphic RBCs (acanthocytes), Red Blood Cell (RBC) casts, granular casts, and polymorphs. Spot urine PCR usually <100–200 mg/mmol.

2.  Renal Function & Electrolytes: Elevated blood urea and serum creatinine, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, and dilutional hyponatraemia.

3.  Complement Levels (Crucial):Markedly decreased Serum C3 (and CH50) with normal C4 (activation of alternative complement pathway). C3 normalises within 6–8 weeks in PSGN (if C3 remains low beyond 8 weeks, suspect MCGN, Lupus nephritis, or infective endocarditis).

4.  Evidence of Preceding Streptococcal Infection:

•  Elevated ASO (Antistreptolysin O) titre (positive in 95% after pharyngitis, but often low/false-negative after skin infection because skin lipids inhibit streptolysin O).

•  Elevated Anti-DNase B and Anti-hyaluronidase titres (test of choice after skin impetigo).

•  Throat or skin lesion swab culture.

5.  Autoimmune Screen (to exclude alternative diagnoses):ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA (PR3/MPO), Anti-GBM antibodies, and Hepatitis B/C/HIV serology.

6.  Renal Ultrasound & Renal Biopsy: Ultrasound shows normal or slightly enlarged echogenic kidneys. Renal biopsy is NOT routinely required in typical childhood PSGN, but is indicated if there is anuria/rapidly progressive renal failure (RPGN), nephrotic-range proteinuria, normal initial C3, or failure of C3 and renal function to recover within 6–8 weeks.

•  Emergency Complications of Acute Glomerulonephritis / PSGN ([KU 22, 19, 15]):

1.  Hypertensive Encephalopathy: Severe headache, vomiting, visual disturbance, confusion, and generalised tonic–clonic seizures due to acute severe hypertension.

2.  Acute Left Ventricular Failure and Pulmonary Oedema (due to acute salt and water overload).

3.  Severe Hyperkalaemia (causing fatal cardiac arrhythmias) and Severe Metabolic Acidosis.

4.  Acute Oliguric/Anuric Renal Failure and Crescentic RPGN (<1% in children; higher in adults).

5.  Uraemic Encephalopathy / Pericarditis.

•  Management of Acute Glomerulonephritis / PSGN ([KU 22, 20, 19, 17]):

•  (Disease is self-limiting in >95% of children and most adults; treatment is supportive targeting fluid overload, hypertension, and electrolytes).

1.  Salt and Fluid Restriction: Restrict dietary sodium (<1–2 g/day) and restrict daily fluid intake to previous day’s urine output + 500 mL (insensible losses); monitor daily weight, BP, and input–output chart.

2.  Diuretic Therapy (First-line for Oedema, Pulmonary Congestion & Hypertension):IV or Oral Loop Diuretic (Furosemide 1–2 mg/kg or 40–120 mg/day) to induce natriuresis and restore euvolaemia.

3.  Antihypertensive Therapy:Calcium Channel Blockers (Nifedipine, Amlodipine) or vasodilators (Hydralazine); in hypertensive encephalopathy, administer IV Labetalol or IV Sodium Nitroprusside + IV Lorazepam/Phenytoin for seizures. (Use ACE inhibitors with caution in the acute oliguric phase due to risk of worsening GFR and hyperkalaemia).

4.  Management of Hyperkalaemia & Acidosis: Restrict dietary potassium, give IV Calcium gluconate (if ECG changes), Insulin–dextrose infusion, potassium binders (Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate / Calcium resonium), and oral/IV Sodium bicarbonate.

5.  Antibiotic Therapy: A 10-day course of Oral Phenoxymethylpenicillin (Penicillin V) or Amoxicillin (or single IM Benzathine Penicillin / Oral Erythromycin) to eradicate any residual nephritogenic streptococci and prevent spread to contacts.

6.  Dialysis (Haemodialysis / Peritoneal Dialysis): Indicated for refractory pulmonary oedema, refractory hyperkalaemia (K+ > 6.5 mmol/L), severe metabolic acidosis, or uraemic encephalopathy/pericarditis. (Immunosuppressive steroids are NOT indicated in uncomplicated PSGN, but pulses of IV Methylprednisolone are used if biopsy shows >50% crescents/RPGN).
