title: 48. Specific Glomerular Diseases: IgA Nephropathy, RPGN, Goodpasture’s, Alport’s & Deposition Diseases [KU 23, TU, RGU]
text:
48. Specific Glomerular Diseases: IgA Nephropathy, RPGN, Goodpasture’s, Alport’s & Deposition Diseases [KU 23, TU, RGU]

A. IgA Nephropathy (Berger’s Disease) [KU 23, TU]

•  Epidemiology & Pathogenesis: The most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide (especially in Asia). Caused by mucosal synthesis of galactose-deficient polymeric IgA1, which triggers autoantibodies → circulating immune complexes deposit in the glomerular mesangium, activating the alternative/lectin complement pathway. (Systemic variant with purpuric rash, arthralgia, and abdominal pain = IgA Vasculitis / Henoch–Schönlein Purpura).

•  Clinical Presentations:

1.  Recurrent Episodic Visible (Macroscopic) Haematuria in children/young adults, classically occurring within 24–72 hours of a viral upper respiratory tract infection ("synpharyngitic haematuria").

2.  Asymptomatic Persistent Microscopic Haematuria ± sub-nephrotic proteinuria and hypertension (most common presentation in older adults).

3.  Progressive CKD (20–30% progress to ESRD over 20 years) or rarely Nephrotic syndrome / Crescentic RPGN.

•  Diagnosis: Polyclonal rise in serum IgA (in 50%), Normal serum C3 and C4; Renal Biopsy shows mesangial cell proliferation and matrix expansion on light microscopy (graded by the Oxford MEST-C score: Mesangial hypercellularity, Endocapillary hypercellularity, Segmental sclerosis, Tubular atrophy/interstitial fibrosis, Crescents) and diffuse dominant mesangial IgA (+ C3) deposition on immunofluorescence.

•  Management:

1.  Optimise BP (<120–130/80 mmHg) & Reduce Proteinuria: Maximum tolerated dose of ACE inhibitor (Ramipril) or ARB (Losartan) PLUS an SGLT2 Inhibitor (Dapagliflozin / Empagliflozin) + Sparsentan (dual endothelin–angiotensin receptor antagonist).

2.  Immunosuppression (if persistent proteinuria >1 g/day despite 3–6 months of supportive care):Targeted-release ileal Budesonide (Nefecon) (suppresses mucosal Peyer’s patch IgA production with fewer systemic side effects) or a 6-month course of systemic corticosteroids.

B. Rapidly Progressive (Crescentic) Glomerulonephritis (RPGN) & Goodpasture’s Disease [TU]

•  Definition: A clinical syndrome of rapid loss of renal function (50% decline in GFR) over days to weeks accompanied by nephritic urinary sediment (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts), proteinuria, and oliguria. The pathological hallmark on renal biopsy is extensive extracapillary Crescent Formation in >50% of glomeruli (proliferation of parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating macrophages + fibrin in Bowman’s space compressing the glomerular tuft, triggered by rupture of the GBM).

•  Immunopathological Classification of RPGN (3 Types):

1.  Type I — Anti-GBM Antibody Disease (Goodpasture’s Disease) (~15%) [TU]:

•  Pathogenesis: Autoantibodies (IgG) directed against the non-collagenous (NC1) domain of the α3 chain of Type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes (strongly associated with HLA-DR15 [DR2]; pulmonary haemorrhage is triggered by cigarette smoking, hydrocarbons, or viral infection).

•  Clinical Features: Bimodal age (young men 20–30 yrs present with Goodpasture’s syndrome = Pulmonary haemorrhage [haemoptysis, dyspnoea, alveolar infiltrates, ↑ KCO] + Crescentic RPGN; older patients 60–70 yrs present with isolated renal-limited anti-GBM disease).

•  Diagnosis: Positive Serum Anti-GBM antibodies + Renal biopsy showing crescentic GN with smooth, ribbon-like LINEAR IgG deposition along the GBM on immunofluorescence.

•  Management: Urgent Plasma Exchange (Plasmapheresis) daily for 2 weeks (to remove circulating anti-GBM antibodies) + High-dose Corticosteroids (IV Methylprednisolone then oral Prednisolone) + Oral Cyclophosphamide (to stop new antibody synthesis).

2.  Type II — Immune-Complex Mediated RPGN (~25%):

•  Causes:Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (Class IV), Post-streptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy / Henoch–Schönlein purpura, Cryoglobulinaemia.

•  Immunofluorescence:"Lumpy-bumpy" GRANULAR immune deposits.

3.  Type III — Pauci-Immune RPGN (~60% — Most common in adults):

•  Causes:ANCA-Associated Small-Vessel Vasculitides — Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA — c-ANCA / anti-PR3), Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA — p-ANCA / anti-MPO), and Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA).

•  Immunofluorescence:Negative or scanty ("pauci-immune") immunoglobulin staining; light microscopy shows focal segmental necrotising glomerulonephritis with crescents.

•  Management:High-dose IV Methylprednisolone + IV Cyclophosphamide or Rituximab (± Plasma exchange or Avacopan [C5a receptor inhibitor]).

C. Alport’s Syndrome & Glomerular Deposition Diseases [TU, RGU]

•  Alport’s Syndrome [TU, RGU]:

•  Genetics: Hereditary basement membrane disorder caused by mutations in the COL4A5 gene (X-linked recessive — 85%) or COL4A3 / COL4A4 genes (autosomal recessive/dominant), resulting in defective assembly of the α3α4α5Type IV collagen network in the glomerulus, cochlea, and eye.

•  Clinical Triad:

1.  Progressive Hereditary Nephritis: Persistent microscopic/episodic visible haematuria from childhood → progressive proteinuria, hypertension, and End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) by age 15–30 years in affected males.

2.  Bilateral High-Frequency Sensorineural Deafness.

3.  Ocular Abnormalities:Anterior lenticonus (conical protrusion of the lens capsule — pathognomonic "oil-droplet" reflex), dot-and-fleck retinopathy.

•  Diagnosis:Electron Microscopy of Renal Biopsy shows splitting, lamination, and alternating thinning and thickening of the GBM (" Basket-weave" appearance); genetic testing.

•  Management:ACE inhibitors and SGLT2 inhibitors to delay ESRD; Renal Transplantation (note: 3–5% of transplanted patients develop de novoanti-GBM disease in the allograft because the recipient's immune system recognises the normal α5(IV) collagen in the donor kidney as foreign).

•  Glomerular Deposition Diseases [TU]:

1.  Renal Amyloidosis:AL (Primary) Amyloidosis (monoclonal λ or κ light chains in myeloma/plasma cell dyscrasia) or AA (Secondary) Amyloidosis (serum amyloid A in rheumatoid arthritis, bronchiectasis, TB, Crohn’s). Presents with massive nephrotic syndrome, large kidneys, and progression to CKD; biopsy shows acellular eosinophilic deposits that stain apple-green birefringence under polarised light with Congo Red stain.

2.  Monoclonal Immunoglobulin Deposition Disease (Light-Chain Deposition Disease): Nodular glomerulosclerosis (κ light chains) in myeloma.

3.  Diabetic Nodular Glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules).

4.  Cryoglobulinaemic Glomerulonephritis & Fibrillary / Immunotactoid Glomerulopathy.

5.  Fabry’s Disease: X-linked α-galactosidase A deficiency (globotriaosylceramide lipid deposition in podocytes).

subject: medicine
title: 49. Nephrotic Syndrome [KU 24, 23, 22, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 15.2B — NEPHROTIC SYNDROME

49. Nephrotic Syndrome [KU 24, 23, 22, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

•  (Covers Clinical Vignette: 40M with generalised anasarca, decreased urine output, BP 120/80, 24-hr proteinuria 3.5 g & serum albumin 2.0 g/dL)

1. Definition ([KU 17])

•  Nephrotic Syndrome is a clinical complex defined by the classic triad (plus hyperlipidaemia and lipiduria):

1.  Heavy ("Nephrotic-Range") Proteinuria:>3.5 g/24 hours (or spot Urine Protein:Creatinine Ratio [PCR] >350 mg/mmol [>3.5 g/g] / Albumin:Creatinine Ratio [ACR] >300 mg/mmol).

2.  Hypoalbuminaemia: Serum albumin <30 g/L (<3.0 g/dL).

3.  Generalised Pitting Oedema (Anasarca).

4.  (Associated features:Hypercholesterolaemia / Hyperlipidaemia and Lipiduria).

2. Aetiology & Differential Diagnosis [KU 24, 15]

•  A. Primary Glomerular Diseases (Podocytopathies — Diagnosis by Renal Biopsy, see Davidson Box 18.15):

1.  Minimal Change Disease (MCD): Accounts for >80% of nephrotic syndrome in children and ~20–25% in adults. Secondary associations: NSAIDs, Hodgkin’s lymphoma, atopy. Light microscopy & IF: Completely normal; Electron microscopy: Diffuse effacement (fusion) of podocyte foot processes (associated with anti-nephrin antibodies). Responds dramatically to oral corticosteroids.

2.  Membranous Nephropathy (MN): Commonest primary cause in European adults (40–60 yrs). Primary (75%): Autoantibodies against podocyte M-type Phospholipase A2 Receptor (anti-PLA2R). Secondary (25%):Solid tumours (lung, colon, breast), Hepatitis B, SLE (Class V), Drugs (NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold). Biopsy: Diffuse thickening of GBM with subepithelial "spikes" on silver stain and granular IgG/C3 on IF. Rule of thirds: 1/3rd spontaneous remission, 1/3rd persistent nephrosis, 1/3rd progress to ESRD.

3.  Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS): Commonest primary cause in adults of African descent (APOL1 gene risk alleles). Primary: Circulating permeability factor; Secondary: HIV, heroin, morbid obesity, reflux nephropathy; Genetic: Nephrin (NPHS1) or Podocin (NPHS2) mutations.

4.  Mesangiocapillary Glomerulonephritis (MCGN / MPGN) & IgA Nephropathy (mixed nephrotic–nephritic).

•  B. Secondary Systemic Causes of Nephrotic Syndrome:

1.  Diabetic Nephropathy (Most common cause of nephrotic-range proteinuria overall in adults).

2.  Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (Lupus Nephritis).

3.  Amyloidosis (AL and AA) & Multiple Myeloma.

4.  Infections: Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV, Malaria (Plasmodium malariae), Syphilis, Filariasis.

5.  Drugs: NSAIDs, Gold, Penicillamine, Pamidronate, Anti-VEGF therapies (Bevacizumab).

6.  Pre-eclampsia (in pregnancy).

•  (Differential Diagnosis of Generalised Anasarca in the 40M Vignette: Nephrotic syndrome, Decompensated liver cirrhosis, Congestive cardiac failure, Severe malnutrition/protein-losing enteropathy — distinguished by JVP [normal in nephrotic/cirrhosis; raised in CCF] and 3.5 g/day proteinuria).

3. Pathophysiology & Clinical Features [KU 22, 15, TU]

•  Pathophysiology of Oedema (Two Mechanisms — see Davidson Fig. 19.4):

1.  "Underfill" Hypothesis (Classical): Massive urinary albumin loss exceeds hepatic synthetic capacity → hypoalbuminaemia (↓ plasma oncotic pressure) → fluid shifts from intravascular to interstitial space → intravascular hypovolaemia activates RAAS, sympathetic nervous system, and ADH → secondary renal sodium and water retention.

2.  "Overfill" Hypothesis (Primary Intrarenal Sodium Retention): Filtered plasminogen/proteases in the nephrotic tubular lumen directly activate epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the collecting duct, causing primary avid sodium retention and volume expansion.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Frothiness of urine (due to high protein content lowering surface tension).

•  Insidious generalised pitting oedema: Starts as early-morning periorbital puffiness, progressing to dependent bilateral lower limb oedema, scrotal/vulval oedema, ascites, and bilateral pleural effusions (anasarca) — notably without orthopnoea or raised JVP (unless renal failure coexists).

•  Xanthelasma and Muehrcke’s lines (paired white transverse bands on nail beds due to hypoalbuminaemia).

•  Blood pressure may be normal/low (in minimal change/amyloid) or elevated (in FSGS/membranous/diabetic).

4. Complications of Nephrotic Syndrome ([KU 23, 15] — Davidson Box 18.13)

1.  Venous & Arterial Thromboembolism (Hypercoagulable State):

•  Mechanism: Urinary loss of endogenous anticoagulants (Antithrombin III, Protein C, Protein S, plasminogen) + increased hepatic synthesis of Fibrinogen, Factor V, and Factor VIII + platelet hyperaggregability and haemoconcentration (exacerbated by over-diuresis).

•  Manifestations:Renal Vein Thrombosis (presents with acute loin pain, macroscopic haematuria, and sudden worsening of renal function; most common in Membranous Nephropathy), Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT), Pulmonary Embolism, and Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.

2.  Increased Susceptibility to Severe Bacterial Infections:

•  Mechanism: Urinary loss of Immunoglobulin G (IgG) and alternative complement Factor B (opsonins) + oedematous fluid acting as a culture medium.

•  Manifestations:Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP), cellulitis, pneumonia, and meningitis, characteristically caused by encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae) and Gram-negative bacilli.

3.  Hypercholesterolaemia & Accelerated Atherosclerosis:

•  Low plasma oncotic pressure stimulates non-specific hepatic synthesis of apoB-containing lipoproteins (VLDL and LDL) + reduced lipoprotein lipase activity → marked elevation of total and LDL cholesterol → premature coronary artery disease.

4.  Acute Kidney Injury (AKI): Due to intravascular hypovolaemia/over-diuresis (pre-renal), acute tubular necrosis, renal vein thrombosis, or drug-induced interstitial nephritis.

5.  Protein Malnutrition & Trace Element Deficiencies: Loss of Muscle mass, Vitamin D-binding protein (hypocalcaemia/osteomalacia), Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), and Transferrin (microcytic anaemia).

5. Investigations ([KU 15, RGU])

1.  Urine Investigations ([RGU]):

•  Urine Dipstick:3+ or 4+ Protein (± microscopic haematuria).

•  Urine Microscopy:Lipiduria — Fatty casts and "Oval fat bodies" (desquamated tubular cells containing cholesterol esters that show a characteristic "Maltese cross" appearance under polarised light).

•  Quantification of Proteinuria: Spot Urine PCR >350 mg/mmol (ACR >300 mg/mmol) or 24-hour urinary protein >3.5 g/24 hrs.

2.  Blood Tests:

•  Serum Albumin <30 g/L (<3.0 g/dL), Urea, Creatinine, and Electrolytes.

•  Fasting Lipid Profile (↑↑ Total cholesterol, ↑↑ LDL, ↑ Triglycerides).

•  Aetiological Screen (Davidson Box 18.12): Fasting blood glucose & HbA1c (diabetes), ANA, anti-dsDNA, C3 & C4 (SLE/MCGN), Serum Anti-PLA2R antibodies (70–80% sensitive and nearly 100% specific for primary Membranous Nephropathy), Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV serology, Serum Protein Electrophoresis, Serum Free Light Chains & Urine Bence Jones protein (in patients >40–50 yrs to exclude myeloma/AL amyloidosis).

3.  Renal Ultrasound & Percutaneous Renal Biopsy:

•  Ultrasound assesses renal size and Doppler excludes renal vein thrombosis.

•  Renal Biopsy (with LM, IF, and EM) is mandatory in all adults with unexplained nephrotic syndrome (unless typical diabetic nephropathy with retinopathy or strongly positive anti-PLA2R with normal eGFR).

6. Management of Nephrotic Syndrome ([KU 24, 16, 15])

•  A. General Supportive Management (Applies to All Causes):

1.  Control of Oedema & Sodium Balance:

•  Dietary Salt Restriction (<2 g sodium /  <80–100 mmol/day) and moderate fluid restriction.

•  Diuretic Therapy: High-dose oral or IV Loop Diuretic (Furosemide 40–240 mg/day). In severe/resistant oedema, add a thiazide (Metolazone 2.5–5 mg or Bendroflumethiazide) + potassium-sparing diuretic (Amiloride or Spironolactone). (Aim for gradual weight loss of 0.5–1.0 kg/day; avoid aggressive over-diuresis as it precipitates hypovolaemic AKI and thrombosis). Salt-poor 20% Human Albumin infusion + IV Furosemide is reserved only for refractory anasarca with intravascular hypovolaemia.

2.  Reduction of Proteinuria (Antiproteinuric Therapy):

•  ACE Inhibitor (Ramipril, Enalapril) or ARB (Losartan, Telmisartan) titrated to maximum tolerated dose + SGLT2 Inhibitor (Dapagliflozin) — reduces intraglomerular filtration pressure, lowers proteinuria by 30–50%, and slows CKD progression.

3.  Management of Hyperlipidaemia:High-intensity Statin (Atorvastatin 20–40 mg OD / Rosuvastatin) ± Ezetimibe.

4.  Thromboembolism Prophylaxis:Prophylactic or therapeutic anticoagulation (LMWH or Warfarin) is indicated in high-risk patients with severe hypoalbuminaemia (Serum albumin <20–25 g/L), especially in Membranous Nephropathy, or if prolonged immobilisation.

5.  Infection Prevention & Nutrition:Pneumococcal and annual Influenza vaccinations; normal protein diet (0.8–1.0 g/kg/day — high-protein diets worsen proteinuria and do not raise serum albumin).

•  B. Specific Disease-Modifying Immunosuppressive Therapy (Guided by Histology):

•  Minimal Change Disease:Oral Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (max 60–80 mg) for 4–16 weeks until remission, then taper; if frequent relapses or steroid-dependent, use Cyclophosphamide, Tacrolimus/Ciclosporin, Mycophenolate mofetil, or Rituximab.

•  Primary FSGS: High-dose Prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) or Ciclosporin / Tacrolimus (secondary/genetic FSGS is treated with RAAS + SGLT2 blockade only).

•  Idiopathic Membranous Nephropathy: Conservative antiproteinuric therapy for 6 months in mild disease (as 1/3rd remit spontaneously); in severe nephrosis or declining eGFR, give Rituximab (first-line), Tacrolimus, or the Modified Ponticelli Regimen (alternating monthly cycles of corticosteroids and oral Cyclophosphamide for 6 months).

subject: medicine
title: 50. Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) [KU 18, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 15.4 — GENETIC RENAL DISEASE

50. Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) [KU 18, 15, TU, RGU]

•  Genetics & Epidemiology: The most common inherited kidney disease (prevalence 1 in 1000; accounts for 10% of all ESRD). Inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with near-complete penetrance:

•  PKD1 gene mutation (Chromosome 16 — 85% of cases): Encodes Polycystin-1; severe phenotype with median age of ESRD at 50–55 years.

•  PKD2 gene mutation (Chromosome 4 — 15% of cases): Encodes Polycystin-2; milder phenotype with median age of ESRD at 70 years.

•  Pathogenesis: Defective polycystin complex in the primary cilia of renal tubular epithelial cells disrupts intracellular Ca2+ signalling and elevates cAMP, driving relentless tubular cell proliferation, active chloride-driven fluid secretion into cysts, and compression/fibrosis of surrounding normal nephrons.

•  Clinical Features (Renal & Extrarenal Manifestations [KU 18, 15] — Davidson Box 18.21):

•  1. Renal Manifestations:

•  Bilateral, asymmetric, Bosselated (nodular) Palpable Renal Masses (move with respiration, bimanually ballotable, resonant band of colon anteriorly).

•  Dull dragging loin/abdominal ache (due to heavy enlarged kidneys) or Acute severe loin pain / colic (due to intracystic haemorrhage, cyst rupture, cyst infection, or renal calculi [uric acid and calcium oxalate stones occur in 20%]).

•  Visible or Non-visible Haematuria (with little or no proteinuria).

•  Early-onset Systemic Hypertension (70–80% — mediated by intrarenal ischaemia and RAAS activation; often precedes decline in GFR).

•  Recurrent Urinary Tract and Cyst Infections.

•  Progressive Chronic Kidney Disease leading to ESRD (Note: Anaemia is less severe than in other causes of CKD because interstitial cysts produce erythropoietin).

•  2. Extrarenal Manifestations ([KU 15]):

1.  Polycystic Liver Disease (Hepatic Cysts — >70%): Commoner and larger in females; liver synthetic function is preserved. (Cysts also occur in the pancreas, spleen, and seminal vesicles).

2.  Intracranial "Berry" Aneurysms (~10%): Located in the Circle of Willis; rupture causes fatal subarachnoid haemorrhage (clusters in specific families).

3.  Cardiovascular Abnormalities:Mitral Valve Prolapse (25%), Aortic regurgitation, aortic root dilatation, and LVH.

4.  Gastrointestinal / Connective Tissue:Colonic diverticulosis and Abdominal wall / Inguinal hernias.

•  Diagnosis:

•  Renal Ultrasound (Screening Method of Choice — Unified Ravine/Pei Criteria in patients with a positive family history):

•  Age 15–39 years:≥ 3 unilateral or bilateral renal cysts.

•  Age 40–59 years:≥ 2 cysts in each kidney.

•  Age ≥ 60 years:≥ 4 cysts in each kidney.

•  MRI Abdomen: Quantifies Height-Adjusted Total Kidney Volume (htTKV) to predict rapid progression.

•  MR Angiography (MRA) of Brain: Screening for berry aneurysms is indicated in patients with a family history of intracranial aneurysm/subarachnoid haemorrhage or high-risk occupations (e.g., airline pilots).

•  Management:

1.  Strict Blood Pressure Control:ACE Inhibitors (Ramipril/Lisinopril) or ARBs are first-line (target <130/80 mmHg, or <110/75 mmHg in young patients at high risk of progression — HALT-PKD trial).

2.  Disease-Modifying Therapy — Tolvaptan: Oral selective Vasopressin V2-Receptor Antagonist — lowers intracellular cAMP in collecting duct cells, slowing cyst growth (TKV increase) and the rate of eGFR decline. (Causes marked aquaresis [polyuria/thirst] and requires monthly LFT monitoring for hepatotoxicity).

3.  Management of Complications:

•  Cyst Infection: Requires lipid-soluble antibiotics that penetrate cyst walls (Ciprofloxacin or Co-trimoxazole) for 2–4 weeks.

•  Cyst Haemorrhage: Bed rest, analgesia (avoid NSAIDs), high fluid intake.

•  ESRD:Renal Transplantation (pre-transplant native nephrectomy may be required if massive kidneys leave no pelvic space) or Haemodialysis.

subject: medicine
title: 51. Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) & Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) [KU 25, 23, 22, 20, 17, 15, TU]
text:
SECTION 15.6 — ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY (AKI)

51. Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) & Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) [KU 25, 23, 22, 20, 17, 15, TU]

•  (Covers Clinical Vignettes: 20F / 30M with 2 days of severe diarrhoea and vomiting, oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/hr, tachycardia 108/min & hypotension BP 90/60–70 mmHg)

•  Complete Diagnosis of the Clinical Vignettes:Pre-Renal Acute Kidney Injury (progressing to Ischaemic Acute Tubular Necrosis if prolonged) secondary to Severe Hypovolaemia from Acute Gastroenteritis.

1. Definition & KDIGO Staging of AKI

•  Definition: A sudden, potentially reversible reduction in kidney excretory function developing over hours to days.

•  KDIGO Diagnostic & Staging Criteria:

•  Diagnosis of AKI (any one):

1.  Rise in serum creatinine by ≥ 26.5 µmol/L (0.3 mg/dL) within 48 hours, OR

2.  Rise in serum creatinine to ≥ 1.5 times baseline within the prior 7 days, OR

3.  Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hour for >6 hours.

•  Staging:Stage 1: Creatinine 1.5–1.9× baseline (or ≥ 0.3 mg/dL rise) / Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6–12 hrs; Stage 2: Creatinine 2.0–2.9× baseline / Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥ 12 hrs; Stage 3: Creatinine ≥ 3.0× baseline, or creatinine ≥ 354 µmol/L (4.0 mg/dL), or initiation of RRT, or anuria for ≥ 12 hrs.

2. Classification & Causes of Acute Kidney Injury [KU 25, 22, 20, 17, TU]

•  1. Pre-Renal AKI (55–60% — Renal Hypoperfusion without Structural Parenchymal Damage) [TU]:

•  Intravascular Volume Depletion:Severe vomiting, diarrhoea (gastroenteritis/cholera), haemorrhage, burns, diabetic ketoacidosis, excessive diuretic therapy.

•  Reduced Effective Arterial Blood Volume / Pump Failure: Cardiogenic shock, acute heart failure, Sepsis / Septic shock (systemic vasodilation), Hepatorenal syndrome, Pancreatitis/peritonitis (third-spacing).

•  Impaired Renal Autoregulation (Drugs):NSAIDs (inhibit prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilation) + ACE Inhibitors / ARBs (inhibit angiotensin II–mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction), Calcineurin inhibitors (Ciclosporin/Tacrolimus).

•  2. Intrinsic Renal AKI (35–40% — Structural Damage to Glomeruli, Tubules, Interstitium, or Vessels):

•  A. Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN — 85% of intrinsic AKI) [TU]:

•  Ischaemic ATN: Prolonged or severe pre-renal hypoperfusion/shock, major surgery, sepsis.

•  Nephrotoxic ATN:

•  Exogenous Toxins/Drugs:Aminoglycosides (gentamicin), Radiographic iodinated contrast media, Cisplatin, Amphotericin B, Tenofovir, Ethylene glycol, Heavy metals, Snake bite, Russell’s viper envenomation.

•  Endogenous Pigments/Proteins:Myoglobinuria (Rhabdomyolysis from crush injury, status epilepticus, statins), Haemoglobinuria (massive intravascular haemolysis, malaria, incompatible transfusion), Myeloma light-chain cast nephropathy, Uric acid crystals (tumour lysis syndrome).

•  B. Acute Tubulo-Interstitial Nephritis (AIN): Allergic drug reaction (NSAIDs, Proton Pump Inhibitors, Penicillins, Rifampicin), Infections (Leptospirosis, Hantavirus, Pyelonephritis), Sarcoidosis.

•  C. Glomerular Disease (RPGN / Acute Nephritic Syndrome): Post-streptococcal GN, Lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis, Anti-GBM disease.

•  D. Intrarenal Vascular Disease (Thrombotic Microangiopathies):Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome (HUS), TTP, Malignant hypertension, Scleroderma renal crisis, Cholesterol atheroembolism, Renal artery/vein thrombosis.

•  3. Post-Renal (Obstructive) AKI (5–10% — Obstruction to Urine Flow):

•  Bladder Neck / Urethral (Most common):Benign Prostatic Enlargement (BPE), Prostate cancer, Urethral stricture, Blocked urinary catheter, Neurogenic bladder.

•  Ureteric (Must be bilateral or in a solitary kidney): Bilateral ureteric calculi, Retroperitoneal fibrosis, Pelvic malignancy (Carcinoma of cervix, bladder, colon), Sloughed renal papillae.

3. Pathophysiology of Pre-Renal AKI vs Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) [TU]

•  Pre-Renal Autoregulation: When renal perfusion falls, afferent arterioles dilate (via prostaglandins) and efferent arterioles constrict (via Angiotensin II) to maintain intraglomerular filtration pressure, while Aldosterone and ADH stimulate avid tubular reabsorption of sodium, urea, and water (producing scanty, concentrated urine with low urinary Na+). If renal perfusion is promptly restored, GFR normalises immediately.

•  Pathophysiology of ATN (3 Phases):

1.  Initiation & Maintenance (Oliguric) Phase (lasts 1–3 weeks): Severe ischaemia or nephrotoxins damage the metabolically active proximal convoluted tubule (S3 segment) and thick ascending limb of Loop of Henle (located in the hypoxic outer medulla) → loss of brush border, necrosis and apoptosis of tubular epithelial cells, sloughing of necrotic cells into the lumen forming obstructing Tamm–Horsfall casts, back-leak of glomerular filtrate across denuded tubular basement membranes into the interstitium, and intense tubuloglomerular feedback–mediated afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction → profound fall in GFR.

2.  Diuretic (Polyuric) Phase: As tubular cells regenerate, lumen obstruction clears and GFR returns before the immature regenerating tubular cells recover their ability to concentrate urine and reabsorb sodium/potassium → marked polyuria (3–5 L/day) with risk of dehydration, hypokalaemia, and hypomagnesaemia.

3.  Recovery Phase: Complete restoration of tubular function over weeks.

4. Investigations in AKI (Differentiating Pre-Renal AKI from ATN) [KU 23, TU]

•  Distinguishing Pre-Renal AKI from ATN on Urine & Blood Indices:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-004]]

•  Other Essential Investigations:

•  Urgent 12-Lead ECG and Venous Blood Gas / U&Es (to detect life-threatening hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis).

•  Urinalysis & Spot PCR: Haematuria + proteinuria = Glomerulonephritis/Vasculitis; Myoglobinuria (dipstick positive for blood with no RBCs on microscopy + elevated Serum Creatine Kinase [CK]) = Rhabdomyolysis.

•  FBC & Peripheral Blood Film: Eosinophilia (drug-induced AIN); Thrombocytopenia + schistocytes + high LDH (HUS/TTP).

•  Renal Ultrasound: Mandatory within 24 hours to exclude hydronephrosis (post-renal obstruction) and assess kidney size (normal size in AKI vs <9 cm shrunken kidneys in CKD).

•  Immunology & Myeloma Screen (ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, C3/C4, serum free light chains) + Renal Biopsy (if unexplained intrinsic AKI).

5. Complications & Management of AKI [KU 25, 23, 15, TU]

•  Complications of AKI ([KU 23]):

1.  Life-threatening Hyperkalaemia (ventricular fibrillation / cardiac arrest).

2.  Intractable Fluid Overload & Acute Pulmonary Oedema.

3.  Severe High-Anion-Gap Metabolic Acidosis.

4.  Uraemic Complications:Uraemic Pericarditis / Tamponade, Uraemic Encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis, myoclonus, seizures, coma), and Uraemic Bleeding Diathesis (platelet dysfunction, upper GI bleeding).

5.  Severe Infections / Sepsis (leading cause of death in AKI) and Progression to Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD).

•  Stepwise Management of Pre-Renal AKI & Established AKI ([KU 23, TU] — Davidson Box 18.27):

1.  Assess & Optimise Volume Status (Immediate Resuscitation in Pre-Renal AKI):

•  If Hypovolaemic (as in the 20F and 30M gastroenteritis vignettes): Administer rapid Intravenous Crystalloid Fluid Boluses (500 mL–1 L of Balanced Crystalloid [Hartmann’s / Ringer’s Lactate / Plasma-Lyte] or 0.9% Normal Saline over 15–60 mins), monitoring HR, BP, JVP, lung bases, and hourly urine output via a urinary catheter.

•  Once Euvolaemic (in established oliguric ATN): Strictly restrict daily fluid intake to previous 24-hour urine output + 500 mL (to cover insensible losses) to prevent iatrogenic pulmonary oedema!

•  If Fluid-Overloaded (Pulmonary Oedema): Sit upright, give high-flow O2, and administer high-dose IV Furosemide (80–200 mg); if no diuretic response in anuria, proceed to urgent Dialysis/Ultrafiltration.

2.  Treat the Underlying Cause:

•  Stop ongoing GI fluid losses; give broad-spectrum antibiotics and vasopressors (Noradrenaline) if septic shock; relieve urinary tract obstruction immediately (urethral catheterisation or percutaneous nephrostomy); give high-dose steroids if drug-induced AIN or crescentic GN.

3.  Medication Review ("Sick-Day Rules"):

•  Immediately STOP all nephrotoxic and potassium-retaining drugs:NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, Spironolactone/Amiloride, Diuretics (if hypovolaemic), Metformin, and Aminoglycosides.

•  Adjust doses of all renally excreted drugs (e.g., antibiotics, LMWH, digoxin) according to GFR.

4.  Emergency Management of Hyperkalaemia (if K+ > 6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes):

•  10 mL of 10% Calcium Gluconate IV over 5–10 mins (stabilises myocardium) → 10 units Soluble Insulin in 50 mL 50% Dextrose IV over 15–30 mins + Nebulised Salbutamol 5–10 mg (shifts K+ into cells) → Oral potassium binder (Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate / Patiromer / Calcium resonium) or Haemodialysis.

5.  Correct Severe Metabolic Acidosis:IV Sodium Bicarbonate (1.26% or 8.4%) if arterial pH < 7.1–7.2 and patient is not fluid-overloaded.

6.  Nutritional & Supportive Care: Provide adequate calories (25–30 kcal/kg/day) and protein (0.8–1.2 g/kg/day) with potassium/phosphate restriction; Proton Pump Inhibitor (Omeprazole) for stress ulcer prophylaxis; monitor electrolytes during the polyuric recovery phase.

7.  Indications for Emergency Haemodialysis / Renal Replacement Therapy in AKI ([KU 20, 16, 15] — Mnemonic: AEIOU):

•  A — Severe Acidosis (refractory metabolic acidosis with pH < 7.1 or HCO3- < 10 mmol/L).

•  E — Refractory Electrolyte derangement (Hyperkalaemia K+ > 6.5 mmol/L with ECG changes resistant to medical therapy).

•  I — Intoxications / Poisonings (Salicylates, Lithium, Methanol, Ethylene glycol).

•  O — Refractory Fluid Overload (Acute Pulmonary Oedema unresponsive to high-dose loop diuretics).

•  U — Symptomatic Uraemia (Uraemic Pericarditis, Uraemic Encephalopathy, or uraemic bleeding).

subject: medicine
title: 52. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) [KU 24, 23, 19, 18, 17, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 15.7 & 15.8 — CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE (CKD) & RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY (RRT)

52. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) [KU 24, 23, 19, 18, 17, TU, RGU]

•  (Covers Clinical Vignette: 35-year-old individual with mild pallor, BP 160/100 mmHg & raised blood urea and serum creatinine)

1. Definition & KDIGO Staging of CKD [TU]

•  Definition: Abnormalities of kidney structure (e.g., albuminuria ACR ≥ 3 mg/mmol, abnormal urinary sediment, or polycystic/scarred kidneys on imaging) OR decreased kidney function (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2), present for >3 months, with implications for health.

•  KDIGO Staging of CKD (CGA Classification: Cause, GFR Category G1–G5, and Albuminuria Category A1–A3 — Davidson Box 18.3):

•  GFR Categories:

•  Stage G1: GFR ≥ 90 mL/min/1.73 m2 (Normal or high GFR, with other markers of kidney damage).

•  Stage G2: GFR  60–89 mL/min/1.73 m2 (Mildly decreased, with other markers of kidney damage).

•  Stage G3a: GFR  45–59 mL/min/1.73 m2 (Mildly to moderately decreased).

•  Stage G3b: GFR  30–44 mL/min/1.73 m2 (Moderately to severely decreased).

•  Stage G4: GFR  15–29 mL/min/1.73 m2 (Severely decreased — prepare for RRT).

•  Stage G5:GFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2 or on Dialysis (Kidney Failure / End-Stage Renal Disease [ESRD]).

•  Albuminuria Categories (Spot Urine ACR):A1: <3 mg/mmol (<30 mg/g); A2: 3–30 mg/mmol (30–300 mg/g); A3: >30 mg/mmol (>300 mg/g).

2. Aetiology of Chronic Kidney Disease & ESRD ([KU 19, 18, 17] — Davidson Box 18.28)

1.  Diabetes Mellitus (Diabetic Nephropathy — 30–45%):Single most common cause of CKD and ESRD worldwide.

2.  Tubulo-Interstitial Diseases (20–30%): Reflux nephropathy (chronic pyelonephritis), Obstructive uropathy (BPH, stones), Drug/toxin-induced (NSAIDs, lithium, aristolochic acid, CKDu in agricultural workers).

3.  Glomerulonephritis (10–20%):IgA nephropathy (most common), FSGS, Membranous nephropathy, MCGN.

4.  Hypertension & Renovascular Disease (10–20%): Hypertensive nephrosclerosis, Bilateral atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis.

5.  Congenital & Inherited Kidney Diseases (~10%):Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), Alport syndrome, Medullary cystic kidney disease.

6.  Systemic Inflammatory / Paraprotein Diseases (5–10%):SLE (Lupus nephritis), ANCA-associated vasculitis, Multiple myeloma, Amyloidosis.

3. Clinical Features & Multisystem Complications of CKD [KU 24, 23, 17, RGU]

•  (Usually asymptomatic until Stage G4/G5 when eGFR < 15–20 mL/min/1.73 m2; nocturia and polyuria due to loss of medullary concentrating ability are often the earliest symptoms).

•  Symptoms & Physical Signs ([KU 24, RGU] — Davidson Fig. 18.23):

1.  General & Cutaneous: Fatigue, lethargy, pruritus (itching) with scratch excoriations (due to uraemic toxins and hyperphosphataemia), sallow earthy-yellow complexion (urochrome retention + anaemia), pallor, easy bruising, "Half-and-half" nails (Lindsay’s nails — brown distal arc), and "uraemic frost" (in terminal untreated uraemia).

2.  Cardiovascular (Leading Cause of Death in CKD):Systemic Hypertension (80–90% — sodium/water retention + RAAS activation), Left Ventricular Hypertrophy, Accelerated Atherosclerosis & Medial Vascular Calcification (coronary artery disease, heart failure, sudden arrhythmic death), Fluid overload (raised JVP, pulmonary and pedal oedema), and Uraemic Pericarditis (pericardial friction rub / haemorrhagic tamponade).

3.  Haematological — Anaemia of CKD ([KU 23]):

•  Type:Normochromic, normocytic anaemia (becomes prominent once eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m2).

•  Causes of Anaemia in CKD ([KU 23]):

1.  Relative deficiency of renal Erythropoietin (EPO) production by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts (primary cause).

2.  Iron deficiency: Functional iron deficiency (inflammation increases hepcidin, which blocks duodenal iron absorption and macrophage iron release) and absolute iron deficiency (occult GI bleeding, frequent blood sampling, blood loss in haemodialysis circuits).

3.  Suppression of bone marrow erythropoiesis by retained uraemic toxins and severe secondary hyperparathyroidism (marrow fibrosis).

4.  Shortened red blood cell survival (uraemic haemolysis).

5.  Folate and Vitamin B12 deficiency (anorexia, dialysate losses).

•  Coagulopathy:Uraemic platelet dysfunction (prolonged bleeding time, epistaxis, GI bleeding).

4.  Mineral & Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD / Renal Osteodystrophy):

•  Pathogenesis (Davidson Fig. 18.25): ↓ GFR causes phosphate retention (hyperphosphataemia) → stimulates osteocytes to secrete FGF-23 + damaged proximal tubules fail to convert 25(OH)D to active 1,25(OH)2D3 (Calcitriol) (1α-hydroxylase deficiency) → ↓ intestinal calcium absorption and hypocalcaemia → persistent stimulation of parathyroid glands causes Secondary Hyperparathyroidism (↑↑ PTH; if autonomous hypercalcaemia develops = Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism).

•  Bone Lesions:Osteitis fibrosa cystica (high-turnover bone disease from ↑ PTH: subperiosteal bone resorption of middle phalanges, "rugger-jersey" spine, brown tumours), Osteomalacia (defective mineralisation), Adynamic bone disease (oversuppression of PTH), and Metastatic vascular/soft-tissue calcification (Calciphylaxis).

5.  Metabolic, Fluid & Electrolyte Abnormalities:Hyperkalaemia, High-anion-gap (and normal-anion-gap) Metabolic Acidosis (Kussmaul’s deep acidotic breathing), hyperuricaemia (gout), insulin resistance (yet increased risk of hypoglycaemia due to reduced renal insulin clearance).

6.  Gastrointestinal: Anorexia, morning nausea, vomiting, hiccups, metallic taste (ammonia), peptic ulceration/angiodysplasia.

7.  Neurological:Distal symmetrical sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy, "Restless legs" syndrome, myoclonus, asterixis, and Uraemic Encephalopathy (confusion, seizures, coma).

8.  Endocrine: Amenorrhoea, infertility, erectile dysfunction, hyperprolactinaemia.

4. Investigations in CKD [KU 17]

•  Bloods: Urea, Creatinine & eGFR (to stage CKD), Electrolytes (Na+, K+, HCO3-), Corrected Calcium (↓), Phosphate (↑), Alkaline Phosphatase (↑), Parathyroid Hormone (PTH ↑↑), and 25(OH)D, FBC + Iron studies (Ferritin, Transferrin saturation), Fasting glucose/HbA1c, Lipid profile, Hepatitis B/C & HIV serology (prior to dialysis).

•  Urine: Dipstick (blood/protein) and Spot Albumin:Creatinine Ratio (ACR) or PCR.

•  Imaging:Renal Ultrasound — typically shows bilaterally small, shrunken (<9 cm), hyperechoic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation.

•  (Exam Pearl — Causes of Normal or Enlarged Kidneys in CKD:Diabetic nephropathy [early], Amyloidosis, Multiple myeloma, Polycystic kidney disease [ADPKD], HIV-associated nephropathy, and Obstructive uropathy / hydronephrosis — Mnemonic: DAMPHO).

5. Management of Chronic Kidney Disease [KU 17, TU, RGU]

1.  Treat Reversible Factors & Underlying Cause: Relieve obstruction, avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast), provide a "Sick-Day Card" (temporarily stop ACEi/ARB, diuretics, SGLT2i, and metformin during acute vomiting/diarrhoea/fever).

2.  Retard Progression of CKD (Renoprotection):

•  Strict Blood Pressure Control: Target <140/90 mmHg (or <130/80 mmHg if diabetes or ACR > 70 mg/mmol).

•  RAAS Blockade (First-line in all Proteinuric or Diabetic CKD):ACE Inhibitor (Ramipril) or ARB (Losartan/Irbesartan) — reduces efferent arteriolar tone, intraglomerular pressure, and proteinuria.

•  SGLT2 Inhibitors (Standard of Care in Both Diabetic and Non-Diabetic CKD):Dapagliflozin 10 mg OD or Empagliflozin 10 mg OD — reduces intraglomerular pressure via tubuloglomerular feedback, slows eGFR decline, and reduces heart failure and mortality.

•  Finerenone (non-steroidal MRA) and GLP-1 receptor agonists (Semaglutide) in Type 2 diabetic CKD.

3.  Management of Complications:

•  Fluid & Potassium Balance: Dietary salt restriction (<2 g/day) + Loop diuretics (Furosemide) for oedema; low-potassium diet (<70 mmol/day) + oral potassium binders (Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate / Patiromer) for chronic hyperkalaemia.

•  Metabolic Acidosis:Oral Sodium Bicarbonate (600 mg–1.2 g TDS) to maintain serum HCO3- ≥ 22 mmol/L (slows CKD progression and prevents muscle wasting/bone loss).

•  Anaemia of CKD: Replenish iron stores first (Oral or IV Iron [Ferric carboxymaltose / Iron sucrose] to maintain Ferritin >100–200 µg/L and Transferrin saturation >20%), then start Subcutaneous Recombinant Human Erythropoietin (EPO — Epoetin alfa/Darbepoetin alfa) targeting a Haemoglobin of 100–120 g/L (10–12 g/dL)(higher targets >13 g/dL increase risk of hypertension, stroke, and vascular access thrombosis).

•  CKD–Mineral & Bone Disorder:

•  Dietary phosphate restriction (reduce dairy, nuts, colas) + Oral Phosphate Binders taken with meals (Calcium acetate / Calcium carbonate, or non-calcium binders Sevelamer or Lanthanum carbonate if calcium is high).

•  Active Vitamin D Analogues:Alfacalcidol (1α-hydroxycholecalciferol, 0.25–1 µg/day) or Calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2D3) to suppress PTH and correct hypocalcaemia.

•  Calcimimetics (Cinacalcet) or Parathyroidectomy: For refractory tertiary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia.

4.  Cardiovascular Risk Reduction: Smoking cessation, regular exercise, and Statin + Ezetimibe (Atorvastatin 20 mg OD) in all CKD patients.

5.  Preparation for Renal Replacement Therapy (when eGFR < 15–20 mL/min/1.73 m2): Patient education, Hepatitis B vaccination, preservation of forearm veins (avoid venepuncture/cannulation in non-dominant arm), early creation of an Arteriovenous Fistula (AVF), and pre-emptive Renal Transplant workup (typically initiate dialysis when symptomatic at eGFR < 10 mL/min/1.73 m2).

subject: medicine
title: 53. Renal Replacement Therapy (RRT): Haemodialysis, Peritoneal Dialysis & Renal Transplantation [KU 24, 23, 21, 20, 17, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
53. Renal Replacement Therapy (RRT): Haemodialysis, Peritoneal Dialysis & Renal Transplantation [KU 24, 23, 21, 20, 17, 16, TU, RGU]

A. Haemodialysis (HD) & Haemofiltration [KU 24, 23, 20, 16, RGU]

•  Principle: Blood is pumped from the patient through a haemodialyser containing a semipermeable membrane, across which bidirectional diffusion of small solutes (urea, creatinine, K+ moving out; HCO3- moving in) occurs down a concentration gradient into counter-current dialysate fluid, while excess water is removed by applying a negative hydrostatic transmembrane pressure (ultrafiltration). (In Haemofiltration [CVVH], used for haemodynamically unstable AKI patients in ICU, water and middle-sized solutes are removed by convective solvent drag across a highly porous membrane with infusion of replacement fluid; Haemodiafiltration [HDF] combines diffusion and convection).

•  Vascular Access:

1.  Native Arteriovenous Fistula (AVF — Gold Standard for Chronic HD): Surgical anastomosis of the radial artery to the cephalic vein at the wrist (Brescia–Cimino fistula) or brachial-cephalic at the elbow, created 3–6 months in advance to allow venous arterialisation; lowest infection and thrombosis rates.

2.  Synthetic PTFE Arteriovenous Graft.

3.  Tunnelled Cuffed Central Venous Catheter (in right internal jugular vein) or temporary non-tunnelled dual-lumen catheter (in AKI).

•  Schedule: Typically 4 hours, 3 times per week (anticoagulated with heparin), targeting a Urea Reduction Ratio (URR) >65%.

•  Indications for Haemodialysis ([KU 20, 16, 15, RGU]): See AEIOU criteria in Question 51 (Refractory Acidosis pH<7.1, Refractory Hyperkalaemia >6.5 mmol/L, Intoxications [Lithium, Salicylates, Methanol, Ethylene glycol], Refractory Pulmonary Oedema, and Uraemic Pericarditis/Encephalopathy, or Symptomatic Stage G5 CKD with eGFR < 10 mL/min/1.73 m2).

•  Complications of Haemodialysis (Davidson Box 18.36):

•  Intradialytic Hypotension and muscle cramps (rapid fluid removal).

•  Dialysis Disequilibrium Syndrome: Cerebral oedema causing headache, confusion, and seizures during initial rapid urea reduction in severely uraemic patients (prevented by short, slow initial sessions).

•  Cardiac Arrhythmias (rapid potassium and acid–base shifts).

•  Vascular Access Complications: Catheter-related bloodstream sepsis (S. aureus), AVF thrombosis, stenosis, aneurysm, or high-output cardiac failure/distal hand ischaemia ("steal" syndrome).

•  Haemorrhage (from heparinisation or venous needle disconnection), Air embolism, Dialyser membrane anaphylactoid reaction, and Dialysis-related β2-microglobulin amyloidosis (carpal tunnel syndrome, arthropathy).

B. Peritoneal Dialysis (PD) [KU 24, 21, TU, RGU]

•  Principle & Types: A permanent Silastic Tenckhoff catheter is inserted into the peritoneal cavity; the patient's own peritoneal membrane acts as the semipermeable dialysis membrane. Sterile dialysate (1.5–2.5 L) containing hyperosmolar glucose (or icodextrin glucose polymer) is instilled into the abdomen: solutes diffuse down their concentration gradient and water is removed by osmotic ultrafiltration.

•  Continuous Ambulatory Peritoneal Dialysis (CAPD): 4 manual exchanges per day (dwell time 4–6 hours).

•  Automated Peritoneal Dialysis (APD): Machine-cycled exchanges overnight during sleep.

•  Advantages over HD: Home-based independence, continuous gentle fluid/solute removal (preferred in children, elderly patients with haemodynamic instability/heart failure, and those with failed vascular access), better preservation of residual renal function.

•  Complications of Peritoneal Dialysis ([KU 21, TU] — Davidson Box 18.37):

1.  PD Peritonitis (Most Important Complication): Presents with cloudy effluent drainage bag, abdominal pain, and fever. Organisms: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis), S. aureus, and Gram-negative enteric bacilli. Treatment:Intraperitoneal antibiotics (Vancomycin + Ceftazidime/Gentamicin); catheter removal if fungal or refractory.

2.  Catheter Exit-Site & Tunnel Infection.

3.  Ultrafiltration / Peritoneal Membrane Failure: Progressive loss of osmotic gradient due to rapid glucose absorption (treated by using Icodextrin for long dwells or switching to HD).

4.  Encapsulating Peritoneal Sclerosis (Sclerosing Peritonitis): Rare, life-threatening fibrotic cocooning of the bowel after years on PD, causing intestinal obstruction and malnutrition.

5.  Mechanical & Metabolic Complications: Catheter tip migration/outflow obstruction, Peritoneal leaks / Right-sided hydrothorax (pleuroperitoneal communication), Abdominal wall hernias, and Hyperglycaemia/weight gain from glucose absorption.

C. Renal Transplantation [KU 24, 17, RGU]

•  Overview & Surgical Anatomy: The treatment of choice for ESRD — restores normal renal excretory and endocrine function, offers the best quality of life and long-term survival (1-year graft survival 95%; 5-year survival ~90%), and is the most cost-effective RRT.

•  Donor Sources:Living Donor (related or unrelated; paired kidney exchange for ABO/HLA-incompatible pairs) or Deceased Donor (brain-stem death or circulatory death).

•  Surgical Placement: Placed extraperitoneally in the iliac fossa; donor renal artery and vein are anastomosed to the recipient’s external iliac artery and vein, and donor ureter is implanted into the bladder dome (native kidneys are left in situ unless infected or massive polycystic kidneys).

•  Contraindications to Renal Transplantation ([RGU]):

1.  Active or recent uncured malignancy (except non-melanoma skin cancer).

2.  Active untreated systemic infection / sepsis.

3.  Active vasculitis or anti-GBM disease (delay until quiescent for ≥ 6 months).

4.  Severe, uncorrectable ischaemic heart disease / refractory heart failure, severe peripheral arterial disease, or advanced irreversible lung/liver disease limiting life expectancy to <2 years.

5.  Positive T-cell cross-match or high-titre donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies (unless desensitised).

•  Immunosuppression Regimen (Davidson Box 18.39):

•  Induction:Basiliximab (anti-CD25 IL-2 receptor mAb) or Anti-Thymocyte Globulin (ATG) + high-dose Methylprednisolone.

•  Maintenance Triple Therapy:

1.  Calcineurin Inhibitor:Tacrolimus (or Ciclosporin — side effects: nephrotoxicity, hypertension, post-transplant diabetes [tacrolimus], gum hypertrophy/hirsutism [ciclosporin]).

2.  Antiproliferative Agent:Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF) or Azathioprine (side effects: leukopenia, GI upset).

3.  Oral Prednisolone (tapered to 5 mg OD).

•  (Alternative: mTOR inhibitor Sirolimus / Everolimus).

•  Complications of Renal Transplantation:

•  Allograft Dysfunction:Hyperacute rejection (minutes; pre-formed ABO/HLA antibodies), Acute cellular or antibody-mediated rejection (weeks to months; treated with IV Methylprednisolone, ATG, or plasma exchange/IVIG), Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, Renal artery stenosis/thrombosis, Ureteric leak/obstruction, Chronic allograft nephropathy, and Recurrence of primary glomerular disease (FSGS, MCGN, IgA).

•  Complications of Long-Term Immunosuppression:Opportunistic Infections (Cytomegalovirus [CMV], BK polyomavirus nephropathy, Pneumocystis jirovecii, TB, Fungal) and Malignancy (Squamous and basal cell skin cancers, Post-Transplant Lymphoproliferative Disorder [EBV-driven lymphoma], Kaposi’s sarcoma).

title: 54. Drug-Induced Renal Disease & Diuretics [KU 21, 19, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 15.9, 15.10, 15.11 & 15.12 — DRUGS, UTI, STONES, INCONTINENCE & ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION

54. Drug-Induced Renal Disease & Diuretics [KU 21, 19, TU, RGU]

•  Mechanisms & Examples of Nephrotoxic Drugs ([KU 21, 19] — Davidson Box 18.42):

1.  Altered Intrarenal Haemodynamics (Pre-Renal Failure):

•  NSAIDs & COX-2 inhibitors: Block prostaglandin synthesis → afferent arteriolar constriction.

•  ACE Inhibitors & ARBs: Block angiotensin II → efferent arteriolar dilation (causes acute fall in GFR in bilateral renal artery stenosis or hypovolaemia).

•  Calcineurin Inhibitors (Ciclosporin, Tacrolimus) & Radiocontrast media (intense intrarenal vasoconstriction).

2.  Direct Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN):Aminoglycosides (Gentamicin, Amikacin), Amphotericin B, Cisplatin, Radiographic iodinated contrast media (prevented by IV 0.9% saline hydration and withholding NSAIDs/metformin), Tenofovir, Paracetamol overdose.

3.  Acute Allergic Tubulo-Interstitial Nephritis (AIN):Penicillins, Cephalosporins, Sulphonamides, Rifampicin, Proton Pump Inhibitors (Omeprazole), NSAIDs, Allopurinol.

4.  Chronic Tubulo-Interstitial Nephritis & Renal Papillary Necrosis:Lithium (also causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), Analgesic abuse (NSAIDs, Phenacetin), Ciclosporin, Aristolochic acid.

5.  Drug-Induced Glomerulonephritis:Membranous nephropathy / MCD: NSAIDs, Penicillamine, Gold; ANCA-positive vasculitis: Hydralazine, Propylthiouracil; Thrombotic microangiopathy (HUS): Ciclosporin, Tacrolimus, Mitomycin C, Anti-VEGF agents, Quinine.

6.  Intratubular Crystal Obstruction (Crystal Nephropathy):IV Aciclovir, Indinavir, Methotrexate, Sulphonamides, Chemotherapy-induced Tumour Lysis Syndrome (Uric acid).

7.  Retroperitoneal Fibrosis (Post-renal obstruction): Methysergide, Cabergoline, Bromocriptine.

•  Potassium-Sparing Diuretics & Adverse Effects of Thiazides/Spironolactone ([TU, RGU]):

•  Potassium-Sparing Diuretics: Act on principal cells of the late distal tubule and cortical collecting duct:

1.  Aldosterone (Mineralocorticoid Receptor) Antagonists:Spironolactone (25–100 mg OD) and Eplerenone (25–50 mg OD). Uses: HFrEF, Cirrhotic ascites, Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s), Resistant hypertension.

2.  Direct Epithelial Sodium Channel (ENaC) Blockers:Amiloride (5–20 mg OD) and Triamterene. Uses: Co-administered with loop/thiazide diuretics, Liddle’s syndrome, Lithium-induced nephrogenic DI.

•  Adverse Effects of Spironolactone:Hyperkalaemia (especially with ACEi/ARBs or CKD), normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, hyponatraemia, and anti-androgenic effects (painful gynaecomastia, mastalgia, impotence in males; menstrual irregularities in females — not seen with selective Eplerenone).

•  Adverse Effects of Thiazide Diuretics:Hypovolaemia, Hyponatraemia, Hypokalaemia, Hypomagnesaemia, Metabolic alkalosis, Hyperuricaemia (precipitates acute Gout), Hyperglycaemia/glucose intolerance, Hyperlipidaemia, Hypocalciuria (causes mild hypercalcaemia), and Erectile dysfunction.

title: 55. Urinary Tract Infection (UTI), Urolithiasis, Incontinence & Sildenafil [KU 15, TU, RGU]
text:
55. Urinary Tract Infection (UTI), Urolithiasis, Incontinence & Sildenafil [KU 15, TU, RGU]

A. Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) [TU]

•  Causative Organisms:Escherichia coli (75% of community UTIs), Proteus mirabilis (produces urease → splits urea to ammonia → alkaline urine and struvite staghorn calculi), Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus saprophyticus (young sexually active women), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (catheter-associated/hospital-acquired).

•  Predisposing Factors: Female sex (short urethra), sexual intercourse, pregnancy, Bladder outflow obstruction (BPE, urethral stricture), Vesico-ureteric reflux, Neurogenic bladder (diabetes, MS, spinal cord injury), Indwelling urethral catheter or urolithiasis.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Lower UTI (Cystitis): Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, strangury, cloudy/malodorous urine, haematuria.

•  Upper UTI (Acute Pyelonephritis): Classic triad of high fever with rigors, loin pain, and renal angle tenderness (+ vomiting/sepsis).

•  Investigations:Urine dipstick (positive Nitrites and Leucocyte esterase), Urine microscopy (pyuria >10 WBC/µL, WBC casts in pyelonephritis, bacteriuria), Midstream Urine (MSU) Culture (significant bacteriuria = ≥ 105 CFU/mL), Blood cultures (in pyelonephritis), and Renal Ultrasound / CT (in men, children, pyelonephritis, or recurrent UTIs to rule out obstruction/stones).

•  Management (Davidson Box 18.46):

•  Uncomplicated Cystitis:Nitrofurantoin (50 mg QDS or 100 mg MR BD) or Trimethoprim (200 mg BD) for 3 days in women (7–10 days in men). (In pregnancy: Nitrofurantoin, Amoxicillin, or Cefalexin for 7 days; asymptomatic bacteriuria MUST be treated in pregnancy).

•  Acute Pyelonephritis: Oral Ciprofloxacin (500 mg BD for 7 days) or Cefalexin / Co-amoxiclav (for 14 days); if vomiting/septic, admit for IV Ceftriaxone / Cefuroxime + IV Gentamicin; urgent nephrostomy/stent if obstructed (pyonephrosis).

B. Urolithiasis (Renal & Ureteric Stones), Urinary Catheterisation, Incontinence & Sildenafil [KU 15, TU, RGU]

•  Causes & Composition of Renal/Ureteric Stones ([TU]):

•  Composition:Calcium oxalate (60%), Calcium phosphate (15%), Magnesium ammonium phosphate (Struvite — 15%, staghorn calculi associated with Proteus infection), Uric acid (10% — radiolucent on X-ray), Cystine (1%).

•  Predisposing Causes: Dehydration / low urine volume, Primary hyperparathyroidism, Idiopathic hypercalciuria, Distal (Type 1) Renal Tubular Acidosis, Enteric hyperoxaluria (Crohn’s disease / ileal resection), Gout / Myeloproliferative disorders (uric acid), Medullary sponge kidney, Polycystic kidney disease, and Cystinuria.

•  Diagnosis & Treatment: Gold standard investigation is Non-contrast Helical CT KUB. Acute ureteric colic is treated with IM/Oral Diclofenac (NSAID) or IV Paracetamol/Morphine + α-blocker (Tamsulosin). Stones <5 mm pass spontaneously; larger stones (>6 mm) require Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL), Ureteroscopy with holmium laser lithotripsy, or Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy (PCNL). (Emergency percutaneous nephrostomy or JJ stent if obstructed infected kidney).

•  Four Complications of Urinary Catheterisation ([TU]):

1.  Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI) and Gram-negative bacteraemia/urosepsis.

2.  Urethral trauma / creation of a false passage and haematuria (or paraphimosis if foreskin is not reduced).

3.  Urethral stricture formation (late complication).

4.  Bladder stones, catheter encrustation/blockage, and bladder spasms.

•  Urinary Incontinence in the Elderly — Causes & Management [RGU]:

•  Transient Causes (Mnemonic — DIAPPERS):Delirium, Infection (UTI), Atrophic urethritis/vaginitis, Pharmaceuticals (diuretics, anticholinergics, sedatives, α-blockers), Psychological (depression), Excess fluid output (hyperglycaemia, heart failure), Restricted mobility, Stool (faecal) impaction.

•  Established Types & Management:

1.  Urge Incontinence (Detrusor Overactivity — Most common in the elderly): Sudden compelling urge to void with involuntary leakage; treated with Bladder retraining, Antimuscarinic drugs (Oxybutynin, Solifenacin, Tolterodine — caution: confusion in elderly) or β3-agonist (Mirabegron), and intravesical Botulinum toxin A injection.

2.  Stress Incontinence: Leakage on coughing/sneezing due to pelvic floor weakness (childbirth) or post-prostatectomy sphincter weakness; treated with Pelvic floor (Kegel) physiotherapy, Duloxetine, or Mid-urethral tension-free vaginal tape / colposuspension.

3.  Overflow Incontinence: Chronic urinary retention with high post-void residual volume due to Benign Prostatic Enlargement (BPE) or diabetic/neurogenic atonic bladder; treated with α1-blockers (Tamsulosin) + 5α-reductase inhibitors (Finasteride), TURP, or Clean Intermittent Self-Catheterisation (CISC).

4.  Functional Incontinence: Due to dementia or immobility; treated with prompted timed voiding and containment pads.

•  Sildenafil — Mechanism, Uses & Contraindications [KU 15]:

•  Mechanism: Selective Phosphodiesterase Type 5 (PDE-5) inhibitor — prevents degradation of cGMP (generated by nitric oxide) in vascular smooth muscle cells of the corpus cavernosum and pulmonary vasculature, producing smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation.

•  Clinical Uses:

1.  Erectile Dysfunction (First-line oral therapy): 25–100 mg taken 30–60 mins before sexual activity (effective in diabetic, vascular, neuropathic, and psychogenic erectile dysfunction).

2.  Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH): 20 mg TDS (reduces pulmonary vascular resistance and improves exercise capacity).

3.  High-Altitude Pulmonary Oedema (HAPE) prophylaxis and treatment, and severe Raynaud’s phenomenon (off-label).

•  Adverse Effects & Contraindications: Headache, facial flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion, transient blue-tinted vision (PDE-6 inhibition), and rare non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Strictly CONTRAINDICATED with organic Nitrates (GTN, isosorbide mononitrate) or Nicorandil, as synergistic cGMP accumulation causes profound, potentially fatal systemic hypotension.
