title: 72. Obesity, BMI, Leptin & Total Parenteral Nutrition [KU 25, 24, 23, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 15, TU]
text:
CHAPTER 19: NUTRITIONAL FACTORS IN DISEASE (Davidson Ch. 5)

SECTION 19.1 — DISORDERS OF ALTERED ENERGY BALANCE

72. Obesity, BMI, Leptin & Total Parenteral Nutrition [KU 25, 24, 23, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 15, TU]

1. Definition, Body Mass Index (BMI) Grading & Waist Circumference [KU 25, 24, 20, 19]

•  Definition: Abnormal or excessive accumulation of body fat (adipose tissue) resulting from a chronic positive energy balance (Energy Intake > Energy Expenditure) that presents a risk to health.

•  Body Mass Index (BMI — Quetelet’s Index) [KU 24, 20, 19]:

•  Formula: BMI = Weight in kilograms (kg)/(Height in metres [m])2

•  WHO Classification of BMI in Adults (Davidson Box 5.8 & Box 5.12):

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-005]]

•  Waist Circumference & Body Fat Distribution: Central intra-abdominal (visceral) fat ("Apple-shaped" android obesity) carries a much higher risk of insulin resistance, Type 2 diabetes, and CVD than peripheral gluteofemoral subcutaneous fat ("Pear-shaped" gynoid obesity). Very high cardiometabolic risk is indicated by a waist circumference >102 cm in European men (>90 cm in South Asian men) and >88 cm in European women (>80 cm in South Asian women).

2. Aetiology of Obesity, Reversible Causes of Weight Gain & Role of Leptin [KU 25, 24, 23, 21, 17]

•  1. Environmental Factors ("Obesogenic Environment" — Davidson Box 5.7):

•  Increased Energy Intake: Large portion sizes, frequent snacking, high availability and marketing of cheap, energy-dense ultra-processed foods rich in saturated fat (9 kcal/g) and refined sugars/sweetened beverages.

•  Decreased Energy Expenditure: Sedentary occupations, motorised transport, screen time, loss of manual labour, and reduced non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT).

•  2. Reversible Medical & Drug-Induced Causes of Weight Gain ([KU 17] — Davidson Box 5.9):

•  Endocrine Diseases:

1.  Primary Hypothyroidism.

2.  Cushing’s Syndrome.

3.  Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS).

4.  Insulinoma.

5.  Hypothalamic Tumours or Injury (Craniopharyngioma, pituitary surgery/radiotherapy) & Growth Hormone Deficiency.

•  Medications Promoting Weight Gain:

1.  Antidiabetic Drugs:Insulin, Sulphonylureas, Thiazolidinediones (Pioglitazone).

2.  Glucocorticoids (Prednisolone, Dexamethasone).

3.  Atypical Antipsychotics:Olanzapine, Clozapine, Risperidone, Quetiapine.

4.  Antidepressants: Tricyclics (Amitriptyline), Mirtazapine, SSRIs.

5.  Anticonvulsants & Anti-neuropathic Drugs:Sodium Valproate, Carbamazepine, Gabapentin, Pregabalin.

6.  Beta-Blockers and Pizotifen (migraine prophylaxis).

•  3. Genetic Factors & The Role of Leptin in Obesity ([KU 24, 23] — Davidson Fig. 5.4):

•  Polygenic susceptibility accounts for 40–70% of weight variance (e.g., FTO gene); syndromic causes include Prader–Willi syndrome (chromosome 15q deletion) and Laurence–Moon–Biedl (Bardet–Biedl) syndrome.

•  Physiology of Leptin & Hypothalamic Appetite Regulation ([KU 24, 23]):

•  Leptin is a 16-kDa peptide hormone (adipokine) encoded by the LEP (ob) gene and secreted by white adipocytes in direct proportion to total body fat mass (alongside Adiponectin, while stomach-derived Ghrelin is the only orexigenic gut hormone that stimulates hunger before meals).

•  Circulating leptin crosses the blood–brain barrier and binds to Leptin Receptors (LEPR) in the Arcuate Nucleus of the Hypothalamus, where it:

1.  Stimulates anorexigenic POMC (Pro-opiomelanocortin) / CART neurons → release α-MSH, which activates Melanocortin-4 Receptors (MC4R) to induce satiety (suppress food intake) and increase sympathetic energy expenditure (BMR).

2.  Inhibits orexigenic Neuropeptide Y (NPY) / AgRP appetite-stimulating neurons.

3.  Permissively regulates GnRH secretion and reproductive fertility (low leptin in starvation/anorexia halts ovulation).

•  Leptin in Human Obesity:

•  Monogenic Obesity: Rare congenital loss-of-function mutations in the Leptin gene (LEP), Leptin receptor (LEPR), POMC, or MC4R (most common monogenic cause, 5% of severe early-onset childhood obesity) cause insatiable hyperphagia and severe early-onset obesity. Congenital leptin deficiency is dramatically cured by recombinant human leptin (Metreleptin) injections.

•  Common Polygenic Obesity ("Leptin Resistance"): Most obese individuals have markedly ELEVATED circulating serum leptin levels, but fail to suppress appetite due to central hypothalamic leptin resistance (impaired blood–brain barrier transport and SOCS3-mediated receptor signalling blockade), so exogenous leptin therapy is ineffective in common obesity.

3. Multisystem Complications of Obesity [KU 25, 18, 15, TU]

•  (Davidson Fig. 5.6 — A BMI > 35 kg/m2 reduces life expectancy by up to 7–13 years):

1.  Endocrine & Metabolic:Insulin resistance / Metabolic syndrome, Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (relative risk increased >10-fold), Dyslipidaemia (↑ TG, ↓ HDL, small dense LDL), Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), menstrual irregularities, infertility, and precocious puberty.

2.  Cardiovascular (Leading Cause of Death):Systemic Hypertension, Coronary Artery Disease / Myocardial Infarction, Heart Failure (especially HFpEF), Atrial Fibrillation, Left ventricular hypertrophy, and Venous Thromboembolism (DVT / Pulmonary embolism).

3.  Respiratory:Obstructive Sleep Apnoea/Hypopnoea Syndrome (OSAHS), Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (Pickwickian syndrome — Type II respiratory failure & cor pulmonale), Asthma, and exertional dyspnoea.

4.  Gastrointestinal & Hepatic:Metabolic Dysfunction–Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD / MASH → cirrhosis), Cholesterol Gallstones (Cholelithiasis), and Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease (GORD) / Hiatus hernia.

5.  Musculoskeletal: Weight-bearing Osteoarthritis (knees, hips), chronic low back pain, gout, flat feet, and lower-extremity fractures.

6.  Malignancy: Increased incidence of Colorectal, Endometrial, Post-menopausal Breast, Oesophageal adenocarcinoma, Renal cell, Pancreatic, and Gallbladder/Biliary tract cancers.

7.  Neurological, Renal & Psychosocial:Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumour cerebri), Stroke, Obesity-related Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) / CKD, Stress urinary incontinence, Depression, and social stigmatisation.

4. Management of Obesity [KU 25, 21, TU]

•  (Davidson Fig. 5.8 & Box 5.10 — Modest 5–10% weight loss improves cardiometabolic risk; 10–15 kg weight loss can induce remission of Type 2 diabetes and OSA):

1.  Lifestyle & Behavioural Modification (Foundation for All Patients):

•  Structured dietary support, meal planning, elimination of sugary drinks/snacks, reduction of portion sizes, and increased daily physical activity (walking/cycling 30–60 mins 5 times/week).

2.  Supervised Weight-Loss Diets:

•  Conventional Calorie-Deficit Diet: 500–600 kcal/day deficit achieves 0.5 kg/week weight loss.

•  Low-Energy / Very-Low-Energy Formula Diets (VLEDs — ≤ 800 kcal/day): Nutritionally complete liquid meal-replacement shakes for 8–12 weeks (containing 40–50 g protein to preserve muscle and 20 g fat to prevent gallstones) achieve rapid weight loss of 1.5–2.5 kg/week and remission of Type 2 diabetes (DiRECT trial).

3.  Pharmacological Therapy for Obesity ([TU] — Indicated as an adjunct to diet/exercise if BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2, or ≥ 27 kg/m2 with obesity-related comorbidities; Davidson Box 5.10):

•  1. GLP-1 Receptor Agonists & Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonists (Most Effective Medical Therapies):

•  Tirzepatide (Mounjaro — Dual GLP-1 + GIP Receptor Agonist): 10–15 mg SC once weekly — achieves ~20–25% weight loss (rivalling bariatric surgery).

•  Semaglutide (Wegovy):2.4 mg SC once weekly (or high-dose oral) — achieves ~12–15% weight loss and proven to reduce cardiovascular events and improve HFpEF.

•  Liraglutide (Saxenda):3.0 mg SC once daily — achieves ~5–8% weight loss.

•  (Main side effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, gallstones; stop if <5% weight loss after 12 weeks on maximum dose).

•  2. Gastrointestinal Lipase Inhibitor:

•  Orlistat:120 mg orally three times daily with main meals — inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases, blocking absorption of ~30% of dietary fat (~5% weight loss). Side effects: Steatorrhoea, oily spotting, faecal urgency, flatus, and malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

•  3. Centrally Acting Appetite Suppressants:

•  Naltrexone / Bupropion (Mysimba): Opioid antagonist + noradrenaline/dopamine reuptake inhibitor (~5% weight loss).

•  Phentermine / Topiramate (Qsymia): Sympathomimetic + anticonvulsant (~10% weight loss; approved in USA, not in Europe due to CV and teratogenic risks).

4.  Bariatric / Metabolic Surgery (Most Effective & Durable Treatment — Indicated if BMI ≥ 40 kg/m2, or ≥ 35 kg/m2 with significant comorbidities like Type 2 diabetes or severe OSA; considered at BMI > 30–35 kg/m2 in recent-onset Type 2 diabetes; Davidson Fig. 5.9 & Box 5.11):

•  Procedures (performed laparoscopically):

1.  Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB): Creates a small gastric pouch anastomosed to the jejunum, bypassing the stomach and duodenum (expected 2-year weight loss 20–40 kg; rapid remission of Type 2 diabetes via enhanced GLP-1/PYY incretin surge and caloric restriction).

2.  Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy: Resects ~80% of the stomach along the greater curvature, removing the ghrelin-producing gastric fundus (expected weight loss 20–30 kg).

3.  Laparoscopic Adjustable Gastric Banding: Less commonly used now due to band slippage/erosion (weight loss 19–25 kg).

•  Complications of Bariatric Surgery: Anastomotic leak, internal hernia, stomal ulcer, Early (hypovolaemic) and Late (reactive hypoglycaemic) Dumping Syndrome, gallstones, and lifelong Micronutrient Deficiencies (Iron, Vitamin B12, Folate, Vitamin D, Calcium, and Thiamine — require lifelong supplementation and delaying pregnancy for 2 years post-surgery).

subject: medicine
title: 73. Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) & Hypoproteinaemia [KU 21, 19]
text:
73. Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) & Hypoproteinaemia [KU 21, 19]

•  Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) [KU 21]:

•  Definition: Intravenous administration of a sterile, nutritionally complete emulsion of glucose, amino acids, lipid emulsion, electrolytes, vitamins, and trace elements directly into a high-flow central vein (via a tunnelled subclavian/IJV catheter or PICC line), completely bypassing the gastrointestinal tract. (Enteral nutrition is always preferred if the gut is functional and accessible).

•  Indications for TPN ([KU 21] — Intestinal Failure where GI tract is non-functional, inaccessible, or perforated):

1.  Short Bowel Syndrome (<75–100 cm residual small intestine following massive resection for mesenteric ischaemia, Crohn’s disease, or volvulus).

2.  High-output enterocutaneous fistulae or anastomotic leaks.

3.  Prolonged postoperative ileus, mechanical bowel obstruction, or chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction.

4.  Severe acute pancreatitis / critical illness with multi-organ failure where enteral tube feeding has failed or is impossible for >5–7 days.

5.  Severe radiation enteritis or severe graft-versus-host disease of the gut.

•  Complications of TPN ([KU 21] — Davidson Box 5.23):

1.  Central Venous Catheter-Related Complications:

•  Insertion:Pneumothorax, haemothorax, subclavian/carotid arterial puncture, air embolism, brachial plexus injury.

•  Infective & Thrombotic:Catheter-Related Bloodstream Sepsis (CRBSI — S. aureus, S. epidermidis, Candida), infective endocarditis, discitis, and Central Venous Thrombosis / SVC obstruction.

2.  Metabolic & Hepatobiliary Complications:

•  Refeeding Syndrome: Severe hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, and acute thiamine deficiency (Wernicke’s encephalopathy) precipitated by insulin surge upon starting carbohydrate infusion in starved patients.

•  Hyperglycaemia (or reactive hypoglycaemia on abrupt cessation) and Hypertriglyceridaemia.

•  TPN-Associated Liver Disease:Hepatic steatosis (fatty liver) from overfeeding, acalculous cholecystitis / biliary sludge, and progressive cholestasis, liver fibrosis, and cirrhosis.

•  Metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia/osteoporosis) and micronutrient deficiencies.

•  Causes of Hypoproteinaemia / Hypoalbuminaemia [KU 19]:

1.  Decreased Synthesis:Chronic liver disease / Cirrhosis, Severe Protein-Energy Malnutrition (Kwashiorkor / Marasmus), Systemic inflammation / sepsis (albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant downregulated by IL-6/TNF-α).

2.  Increased Renal Loss:Nephrotic Syndrome.

3.  Increased Gastrointestinal Loss / Malabsorption:Protein-losing enteropathy (Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, Ménétrier’s disease, intestinal lymphangiectasia), Coeliac disease, Chronic pancreatitis, Short bowel syndrome.

4.  Increased Cutaneous Loss / Redistribution:Extensive burns, exfoliative dermatitis, sepsis/capillary leak syndrome, pregnancy/fluid overload (haemodilution).

subject: medicine
title: 74. Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K): Deficiency & Clinical Features [KU 23, 22, 20, 19, 18, 16, TU]
text:
SECTION 19.2 — MICRONUTRIENTS, VITAMINS, MINERALS AND THEIR DISEASES

74. Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K): Deficiency & Clinical Features [KU 23, 22, 20, 19, 18, 16, TU]

A. Overview of Fat-Soluble Vitamins [KU 18]

•  The Four Fat-Soluble Vitamins are Vitamins A, D, E, and K.

•  Shared Characteristics: Absorbed along with dietary lipids in chylomicrons via intestinal micelles and lymphatics; malabsorbed in biliary obstruction (cholestasis), pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis), coeliac disease, and terminal ileal resection/Crohn’s disease (Davidson Box 5.34); stored in the liver and adipose tissue (hence deficiency develops slowly, except Vitamin K, and excessive intake of Vitamins A and D causes serious toxicity).

B. Vitamin A (Retinol) Deficiency [KU 23, 22, 19]

•  Sources & Physiology: Pre-formed Retinol in animal foods (liver, egg yolk, milk, fish liver oils) and provitamin β-carotene in dark green leafy vegetables (spinach) and yellow/orange fruits (carrots, mangoes, papaya). RNI: 700 µg (men), 600 µg (women).

•  Functions: (1) 11-cis-retinal combines with opsin to form rhodopsin in retinal rod photoreceptors for scotopic (dim-light) vision; (2) Retinoic acid binds nuclear receptors (RAR/RXR) to regulate normal mucus-secreting epithelial differentiation (deficiency causes squamous metaplasia and keratinisation of ocular, respiratory, and GI epithelia); (3) Essential for immunity, growth, and fetal development.

•  Clinical Features of Vitamin A Deficiency ([KU 23, 22, 19]):

•  1. Ocular Manifestations — Xerophthalmia (WHO Grading; Leading cause of preventable childhood blindness in developing countries):

•  XN — Night Blindness (Nyctalopia): Earliest symptom (impaired dark adaptation).

•  X1A — Conjunctival Xerosis: Dryness, wrinkling, and loss of lustre of the bulbar conjunctiva.

•  X1B — Bitot’s Spots (Pathognomonic — Davidson Fig. 5.13A):Foamy, cheesy, white triangular plaques of keratinised squamous debris on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva.

•  X2 — Corneal Xerosis: Dry, hazy, lustreless cornea.

•  X3A & X3B — Corneal Ulceration and Keratomalacia (Davidson Fig. 5.13B): Liquefactive necrosis and softening/perforation of the cornea (≤ 1/3 corneal surface = X3A; >1/3 = X3B) → irreversible blindness.

•  XS — Corneal Scarring & XF — Xerophthalmic Fundus.

•  2. Extraocular Manifestations:

•  Skin — Follicular Hyperkeratosis (Phrynoderma / "Toad Skin"): Dry, rough, papular hyperkeratotic plugs in hair follicles over extensor surfaces of arms and thighs.

•  Impaired Mucosal Immunity & Squamous Metaplasia of Respiratory/GI Tracts: Markedly increased morbidity and mortality from Measles, Diarrhoea, and Bronchopneumonia in children.

•  Treatment & Prevention:

•  Treatment of Xerophthalmia / Severe Measles:Oral Retinyl Palmitate 200,000 IU (60 mg retinol) on Day 1, Day 2, and Day 14 (half dose in infants 6–12 months) + topical antibiotic eye ointment.

•  Prevention: Dietary intake of dark green leafy vegetables and yellow fruits; WHO periodic mass prophylaxis (200,000 IU orally every 6 months to pre-school children). (Note: Vitamin A is teratogenic in pregnancy — avoid high-dose supplements and liver in pregnant women).

C. Vitamin D (Cholecalciferol) Deficiency [KU 20]

•  Sources & Physiology: Cutaneous synthesis of Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) from 7-dehydrocholesterol by UV-B sunlight exposure (80–90% of supply) and dietary oily fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel), egg yolk, liver, and fortified milk/cereals. Hydroxylated in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25[OH]D — best biochemical measure of body stores), and then in the kidney (by 1α-hydroxylase under PTH control) to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25[OH]2D3 / Calcitriol), which promotes intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and bone mineralisation.

•  Causes of Deficiency: Inadequate sunlight exposure (housebound elderly, institutionalized, veiled/covered clothing, high latitude >50°, dark skin pigmentation), dietary deficiency, malabsorption (coeliac disease, biliary obstruction, bariatric surgery), chronic kidney/liver disease, and enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine).

•  Clinical Features of Vitamin D Deficiency ([KU 20]):

•  1. In Children (Before Epiphyseal Closure) — Rickets:

•  Defective mineralisation of cartilaginous growth plates → Craniotabes (soft skull bones), Delayed closure of fontanelles & Frontal bossing, Enlargement of costochondral junctions ("Rachitic Rosary"), Harrison’s sulcus (horizontal groove at lower ribcage pulled in by diaphragm), Widening and cupping of wrists and ankles, Bow legs (genu varum) or Knock knees (genu valgum), hypotonia ("pot-belly"), growth retardation, and hypocalcaemic tetany/seizures.

•  2. In Adults (After Epiphyseal Closure) — Osteomalacia:

•  Defective mineralisation of newly formed osteoid matrix → Diffuse bone pain and bony tenderness (ribs, spine, pelvis, legs), Proximal Myopathy (weakness of pelvic girdle causing a characteristic "waddling gait" and difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs), Pathological fractures and Looser’s zones (Pseudofractures / Milkman’s fractures) — radiolucent ribbons at right angles to the cortex on X-ray (femoral neck, pubic rami, lateral border of scapula, ribs), skeletal deformity (triradiate pelvis, kyphosis), and features of hypocalcaemia (paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm).

•  Biochemistry & Treatment: Low serum 25(OH)D (<25 nmol/L), low or low-normal serum calcium, low serum phosphate, elevated Alkaline Phosphatase, and elevated PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism). Treated with oral Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) loading (e.g., 50,000 IU weekly for 6–8 weeks, then 800–2000 IU/day maintenance) + oral Calcium supplementation.

D. Vitamin E & Vitamin K (Vitamin K–Dependent Clotting Factors) [KU 18, 16]

•  Vitamin E (α-Tocopherol): Potent lipid-soluble antioxidant (found in sunflower/seed oils, nuts) that protects polyunsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes from free-radical peroxidation. Deficiency occurs in severe fat malabsorption, cystic fibrosis, or congenital abetalipoproteinaemia (MTTP mutation), causing spinocerebellar ataxia, areflexia, loss of proprioception/vibration sense, ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, and haemolytic anaemia.

•  Vitamin K & Vitamin K–Dependent Clotting Factors [KU 16]:

•  Sources:Vitamin K1 (Phylloquinone) in green leafy vegetables and soya oil; Vitamin K2 (Menaquinone) synthesised by colonic bacteria.

•  Biochemical Role: Essential cofactor for hepatic microsomal γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which converts glutamate residues into γ-carboxyglutamate (Gla) residues, enabling clotting factors to chelate Ca2+ and bind to platelet phospholipid membranes.

•  List of Vitamin K–Dependent Clotting & Anticoagulant Factors ([KU 16]):

1.  Procoagulant Clotting Factors:Factor II (Prothrombin), Factor VII, Factor IX, and Factor X(Mnemonic: 1972).

2.  Endogenous Anticoagulant Proteins:Protein C and Protein S (and Protein Z).

3.  Bone Matrix Gla Proteins:Osteocalcin and Matrix Gla protein.

•  Causes & Features of Deficiency:Obstructive jaundice (lack of bile salts), malabsorption, broad-spectrum antibiotics, Warfarin therapy (inhibits Vitamin K epoxide reductase [VKOR]), and Haemorrhagic Disease of the Newborn (prevented by routine IM Vitamin K at birth). Presents with easy bruising, epistaxis, haematuria, GI bleeding, and prolonged Prothrombin Time (PT / INR) (and later APTT), corrected by IV/Oral Phytomenadione (Vitamin K1) 5–10 mg.

subject: medicine
title: 75. Water-Soluble Vitamins: Thiamine (B1/Beri-Beri), Niacin (B3/Pellagra), Vitamin B12 & Vitamin C (Scurvy) [KU 25, 24, 23, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
75. Water-Soluble Vitamins: Thiamine (B1/Beri-Beri), Niacin (B3/Pellagra), Vitamin B12 & Vitamin C (Scurvy) [KU 25, 24, 23, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

A. Thiamine (Vitamin B1) Deficiency — Beri-Beri & Wernicke–Korsakoff Syndrome [KU 25, 24, 15, RGU]

•  Sources & Biochemical Role: Found in whole-grain cereals, unmilled rice, legumes, nuts, and pork. Body stores are very small (~30 mg) and depleted within 1 month on a deficient diet. Active form Thiamine Pyrophosphate (TPP) is an essential coenzyme for carbohydrate and energy metabolism:

1.  Pyruvate dehydrogenase (links glycolysis to the Krebs cycle by converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA — deficiency causes accumulation of pyruvic and lactic acid → peripheral vasodilation).

2.  α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (in the Krebs cycle — deficiency impairs neuronal ATP synthesis).

3.  Transketolase (in the hexose monophosphate shunt — RBC transketolase activation assay confirms deficiency).

•  Causes / Risk Groups:

1.  Chronic Alcohol Misuse (commonest cause in developed countries — poor diet, impaired intestinal absorption, impaired hepatic storage/phosphorylation, and increased demand to metabolise ethanol).

2.  Diets based exclusively on polished (milled) white rice in developing countries.

3.  Hyperemesis gravidarum, Post-bariatric surgery, Refeeding syndrome / starvation, Prolonged IV dextrose without vitamins, and chronic haemodialysis/furosemide therapy.

•  Clinical Features of Thiamine Deficiency ([KU 25, 24, 15, RGU]):

•  1. Wet (Cardiovascular) Beri-Beri:

•  Accumulation of pyruvate and lactate causes intense peripheral arteriolar vasodilation → High-Output Biventricular Heart Failure presenting with generalised pitting oedema, warm extremities, bounding pulse with wide pulse pressure, elevated JVP, cardiomegaly, third heart sound (S3), and pulmonary congestion/dyspnoea.

•  2. Dry (Neurological) Beri-Beri:

•  Insidious symmetrical distal sensorimotor peripheral polyneuropathy: burning/tingling paraesthesiae in toes ("burning feet"), calf muscle tenderness and cramps, loss of ankle/knee reflexes, distal sensory loss, and progressive distal muscle wasting and weakness culminating in wrist drop and foot drop.

•  3. Cerebral Beri-Beri — Wernicke–Korsakoff Syndrome (Medical Emergency):

•  Wernicke’s Encephalopathy (Acute, Reversible): Symmetric petechial haemorrhagic lesions in the mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey matter, and medial thalami, presenting with the Classic Clinical Triad:

1.  Ocular Abnormalities (Ophthalmoplegia): Horizontal and vertical nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus (6th nerve) palsies, and conjugate gaze palsies.

2.  Cerebellar Ataxia: Wide-based, unsteady gait and truncal ataxia.

3.  Global Confusion / Delirium: Disorientation, apathy, drowsiness, or stupor.

•  Korsakoff’s Psychosis (Chronic, Frequently Irreversible): Develops if Wernicke’s is untreated; characterised by profound anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories) and retrograde amnesia, accompanied by confabulation (inventing plausible stories to fill memory gaps), with relative preservation of other cognitive functions.

•  (Infantile Beri-Beri occurs in breastfed infants of thiamine-deficient mothers, presenting at 2–6 months with acute cardiac failure, aphonia [hoarse cry], and convulsions).

•  Management of Thiamine Deficiency ([RGU]):

•  Medical Emergency — Treat Immediately on Clinical Suspicion Without Waiting for Blood Tests!

•  In Suspected Wernicke’s Encephalopathy, Wet Beri-Beri, or Malnourished/Alcoholic Patients: Administer High-Dose Parenteral Thiamine (Pabrinex) 200–500 mg IV three times daily for 3–5 days, followed by Oral Thiamine 100 mg daily (+ multivitamins and magnesium, which is a cofactor for TPP).

•  Crucial Exam Rule:ALWAYS administer IV Thiamine BEFORE or WITH any intravenous glucose/dextrose infusion in alcoholic, starved, or vomiting patients — giving glucose alone consumes the last remaining reserves of thiamine and precipitates acute Wernicke’s encephalopathy, Korsakoff’s psychosis, or lactic acidosis! (Wet beri-beri resolves dramatically within 24–48 hours of IV thiamine; dry neuropathy and Korsakoff’s psychosis recover slowly or incompletely).

B. Niacin (Vitamin B3) Deficiency — Pellagra [KU 24, 23, 17, 16, 15, TU]

•  Sources & Biochemical Role:Niacin encompasses Nicotinic acid and Nicotinamide (found in meat, fish, whole-grain cereals, peanuts, legumes), and can also be synthesised endogenously in the liver from the essential amino acid Tryptophan (60 mg of tryptophan yields 1 mg of niacin; this conversion requires Vitamin B6 [pyridoxine] and riboflavin as cofactors).

•  Function: Essential component of the coenzymes NAD+ (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide) and NADP+, which act as hydrogen/electron acceptors and donors in over 200 cellular oxidation–reduction and energy-generating reactions.

•  Causes of Pellagra:

1.  Subsistence on a Maize (Corn) or Sorghum (Jowar) Staple Diet: Maize is low in tryptophan and contains niacin bound in an biologically unavailable form (niacytin — unless treated with alkali/lime water); sorghum has high leucine which interferes with tryptophan metabolism.

2.  Chronic Alcoholism, Malnutrition, and Malabsorption (Crohn’s disease, jejuno-ileal bypass).

3.  Hartnup Disease: Rare autosomal recessive defect in the neutral amino acid transporter (SLC6A19) in renal tubules and intestinal mucosa, causing malabsorption and urinary loss of tryptophan.

4.  Carcinoid Syndrome: Metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoid tumours divert up to 60% of dietary tryptophan (normally 1%) into excessive serotonin (5-HT) synthesis, depleting niacin stores.

5.  Isoniazid (INH) Therapy: Depletes pyridoxine (Vitamin B6), blocking endogenous conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

•  Clinical Features of Pellagra — "The Disease of the 4 Ds" ([KU 24, 23, 17, 16, 15, TU]):

1.  Dermatitis (Photosensitive):

•  Bilateral, symmetrical, sharply demarcated erythema resembling severe sunburn on sun-exposed areas (dorsum of hands and forearms ["gauntlet/glove of pellagra"], feet/legs, and butterfly area of face), which progresses to vesiculation, scaling, cracking, hyperkeratosis, and brownish-black hyperpigmentation (Davidson Fig. 5.14).

•  Casal’s Necklace (Pathognomonic): A broad, sharply marginated collar of photosensitive scaling, pigmented dermatitis encircling the neck and upper sternum (C3–C4 dermatomes).

2.  Diarrhoea (Gastrointestinal Mucosal Inflammation):

•  Widespread non-infective inflammation and atrophy of the entire GI tract mucosa causing anorexia, nausea, dysphagia, a raw beefy-red painful tongue (glossitis) and angular stomatitis, achlorhydria, abdominal pain, and profuse watery (occasionally blood-stained) diarrhoea.

3.  Dementia (Neuropsychiatric / Encephalopathy):

•  Early depression, apathy, insomnia, irritability, headache, and memory loss, progressing in severe deficiency to acute delirium, hallucinations, psychosis, extrapyramidal rigidity, myelopathy/peripheral neuropathy, and dementia.

4.  Death (if untreated).

•  Diagnosis & Management:

•  Diagnosis: Clinical triad in an at-risk patient; confirmed biochemically by low 24-hour urinary excretion of niacin metabolites (N-methylnicotinamide and 2-pyridone).

•  Treatment:Nicotinamide 100 mg orally (or parenterally) three times daily for 2–3 weeks (Nicotinamide is preferred over nicotinic acid because it does not cause unpleasant prostaglandin-mediated cutaneous flushing, pruritus, or hypotension).

•  Response & Supportive Care:Dramatic clinical response within 24–48 hours (confusion and diarrhoea resolve within 1–2 days; skin lesions clear over 1–2 weeks). Provide a high-protein diet rich in tryptophan (eggs, milk, meat) + B-complex vitamins (especially Pyridoxine B6, thiamine, and riboflavin) as deficiencies usually coexist.

C. Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) Deficiency: Neurological Consequences & Therapeutic Schedule [KU 25, 17, 15, TU]

•  Sources & Physiology: Found exclusively in foods of animal origin (meat, liver, fish, eggs, dairy; RNI 1.5 µg/day). Binds gastric Intrinsic Factor (IF) (secreted by parietal cells) and is absorbed in the terminal ileum via cubilin receptors. Acts as an essential cofactor for two enzymes:

1.  Methionine Synthase (converts homocysteine to methionine and demethylates 5-methyl-THF to regenerate tetrahydrofolate for DNA synthesis — deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia).

2.  Methylmalonyl-CoA Mutase (converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA — deficiency causes accumulation of methylmalonic acid [MMA] and abnormal odd-chain fatty acids, disrupting myelin synthesis in the nervous system).

•  Causes of Deficiency:Pernicious Anaemia (autoimmune gastritis with anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies — most common cause in Western adults), Strict Vegan diet, Gastrectomy / Bariatric surgery, Terminal ileal resection or Crohn’s disease, Coeliac disease, Bacterial overgrowth, Fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum), and Drugs (Metformin, prolonged Proton Pump Inhibitors, Nitrous oxide anaesthesia).

•  Neurological Consequences of Vitamin B12 Deficiency ([KU 17, TU]):

•  (Can occur even in the absence of anaemia or macrocytosis, and is worsened if folic acid is given alone without B12!):

1.  Symmetrical Peripheral Neuropathy (Earliest and Most Common Neurological Manifestation):

•  Insidious distal paraesthesiae ("pins and needles") and numbness in the feet and fingers (stocking-and-glove distribution), with loss of ankle jerks.

2.  Subacute Combined Degeneration of the Spinal Cord (SCD — Classic Syndrome):

•  Patchy, spongy demyelination and axonal degeneration affecting BOTH the Posterior (Dorsal) Columns and the Lateral (Corticospinal) Columns of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord:

•  Posterior Column Involvement:Loss of Vibration sense (128 Hz tuning fork) and Loss of Joint Position sense (Proprioception) in the lower limbs → Sensory Ataxia with a wide-based stamping gait and a positive Romberg’s sign.

•  Lateral Corticospinal Tract Involvement:Upper Motor Neuron (Pyramidal) weakness and spasticity of the lower limbs with extensor plantar responses (positive Babinski sign) and brisk knee jerks(producing the classic triad of extensor plantars + brisk knee jerks + absent ankle jerks when combined with peripheral neuropathy).

•  Lhermitte’s Sign: Electric-shock sensation radiating down the spine upon neck flexion.

3.  Cerebral & Neuropsychiatric Manifestations:

•  Cognitive decline / reversible Dementia, memory loss, depression, irritability, or frank psychosis ("Megaloblastic Madness").

4.  Optic Neuropathy: Bilateral painless centrocaecal scotoma and Optic Atrophy with visual loss, + Autonomic neuropathy (postural hypotension, bladder/bowel incontinence, impotence).

•  Treatment & Therapeutic Schedule of Vitamin B12 Deficiency ([KU 25, 15]):

•  1. Parenteral Replacement Schedule — Intramuscular Hydroxocobalamin (Treatment of Choice in Pernicious Anaemia, Malabsorption, or Neurological Involvement):

•  Without Neurological Involvement:Inj. Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg (1 mg) IM three times a week for 2 weeks (total 6 loading doses to replenish hepatic stores), followed by maintenance of 1000 µg IM every 2–3 months (lifelong if pernicious anaemia or ileal resection).

•  With Neurological Involvement (e.g., Subacute Combined Degeneration / Neuropathy):Inj. Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg (1 mg) IM on alternate days until no further neurological improvement occurs (typically for 2–3 weeks), followed by maintenance of 1000 µg IM every 2 months lifelong.

•  2. Oral Replacement Schedule:

•  Oral Cyanocobalamin (50–150 µg daily between meals for mild dietary deficiency in vegans; or high-dose 1000–2000 µg orally daily, which achieves 1% passive diffusion independent of intrinsic factor).

•  3. Critical Therapeutic Precautions:

•  NEVER administer Folic Acid alone to a patient with undiagnosed megaloblastic anaemia without first excluding or co-treating Vitamin B12 deficiency, as folate temporarily corrects the anaemia while precipitating or accelerating irreversible Subacute Combined Degeneration of the Spinal Cord!

•  Monitor for Hypokalaemia during the first 48–72 hours of treating severe megaloblastic anaemia (rapid uptake of potassium by proliferating bone marrow erythroid precursors; a brisk reticulocyte crisis peaks at Day 5–10).

D. Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid) Deficiency — Scurvy [KU 18, 16]

•  Sources & Biochemical Role: Found in citrus fruits (oranges, lemons), berries, tomatoes, green vegetables, and potatoes (RNI 40 mg/day). Easily destroyed by prolonged cooking/boiling, heat, and alkali.

•  Functions:

1.  Essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which catalyse the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in pro-collagen to hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine, required to cross-link triple-helical mature collagen (deficiency results in fragile capillaries, defective osteoid/dentine, and poor wound healing).

2.  Potent aqueous antioxidant / reducing agent that reduces ferric (Fe3+) to ferrous (Fe2+) iron in the duodenum, enhancing non-haem iron absorption.

3.  Required for normal platelet adhesiveness, carnitine synthesis, and conversion of dopamine to noradrenaline.

•  Causes & Precipitants of Scurvy (Davidson Box 5.36):

•  Dietary Deficiency (lack of fresh fruits and vegetables for >2–3 months): Socially isolated/institutionalised elderly men ("bachelor scurvy"), chronic alcoholics, food faddists,psychiatric patients, famine/refugees, and infants fed exclusively on boiled/evaporated cow’s milk (Barlow’s disease).

•  Increased Requirement:Cigarette smoking, pregnancy/lactation, trauma, burns, surgery, and drugs (glucocorticoids, aspirin, indometacin, tetracyclines).

•  Clinical Features of Scurvy ([KU 18, 16] — Davidson Fig. 5.15 & Box 5.36):

1.  Cutaneous Manifestations (Pathognomonic):

•  Perifollicular Hyperkeratotic Papules with surrounding Perifollicular Petechial Haemorrhages (especially on the calves, thighs, buttocks, and forearms).

•  "Corkscrew Hairs": Coiled, fragmented hairs trapped within hyperkeratotic follicular plugs.

•  Spontaneous ecchymoses (bruising) on the lower limbs, splinter haemorrhages, and delayed wound healing (with breakdown of old healed scars).

2.  Oral / Gingival Manifestations (in dentate patients):

•  Swollen, spongy, purplish-red, friable gums (gingivitis) that bleed easily on minor trauma, progressing to periodontal infection and loosening/loss of teeth.

3.  Musculoskeletal & Deep Haemorrhages:

•  Painful haemarthrosis (bleeding into knee/ankle joints) and intramuscular haematomas.

•  Subperiosteal haemorrhages (especially in the femur and tibia in infants, causing excruciating bone pain and "frog-leg" pseudoparalysis + scorbutic rosary at costochondral junctions).

4.  Systemic & Haematological Manifestations:

•  Anaemia (multifactorial: blood loss into tissues/GI tract + impaired iron absorption + coexisting folate deficiency, as both vitamins share fresh vegetable sources).

•  Gastrointestinal bleeding, epistaxis, haematuria, Sjögren-like sicca syndrome, malaise, lethargy, and depression.

•  Diagnosis & Management:

•  Diagnosis: Clinical picture; confirmed by low Leucocyte Ascorbic Acid concentration (best measure of tissue stores; <7 µg/108 WBCs) or low Plasma Ascorbic Acid (<11 µmol/L, reflects recent intake). Bleeding time and capillary fragility (Hess test) are abnormal, while platelet count, PT, and APTT are normal.

•  Treatment:Oral Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid) 250 mg daily (or 100 mg TDS) for 1–2 weeks rapidly saturates tissue stores (spontaneous bleeding ceases within 24 hours; gum swelling and perifollicular haemorrhages resolve within 1–2 weeks), combined with a diet rich in fresh fruits and vegetables and folic acid / iron supplementation. (Note: Mega-doses of Vitamin C >1 g/day cause diarrhoea and calcium oxalate renal stones).

Summary of Energy-Yielding Macronutrients & Vitamin Deficiencies Overview [TU]

•  Energy-Yielding Nutrients (Davidson p. 91) [TU]:

1.  Fat:9 kcal/g (37 kJ/g) — highest energy density; stored as adipose tissue triglycerides (sufficient for ≥ 40 days of starvation); WHO goal = 15–30% of total energy (saturated fat <10%, trans fat <1%). Essential fatty acids:Linoleic acid (ω-6) and α-Linolenic acid (ω-3).

2.  Protein:4 kcal/g (17 kJ/g) — structural and functional building blocks; WHO goal = 10–15% of total energy (0.8–1.2 g/kg/day). Nine Essential Amino Acids:Histidine, Isoleucine, Leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine, Threonine, Tryptophan, Valine.

3.  Carbohydrate:3.75–4 kcal/g (16 kJ/g) — stored as liver and muscle glycogen (sufficient for 12–24 hours); WHO goal = 55–75% of total energy (free added sugars <10%; dietary fibre >25 g/day).

4.  (Alcohol provides 7 kcal/g [29 kJ/g] — non-nutrient, not stored, hepatotoxic).

•  Quick-Reference Summary of Vitamin Deficiencies [TU]:

•  Vitamin A (Retinol): Night blindness, Bitot’s spots, Xerophthalmia, Keratomalacia, Follicular hyperkeratosis.

•  Vitamin D (Cholecalciferol): Rickets (children), Osteomalacia (adults), Hypocalcaemic tetany.

•  Vitamin E (Tocopherol): Spinocerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, haemolytic anaemia.

•  Vitamin K (Phylloquinone): Coagulopathy (↓ Factors II, VII, IX, X), bruising/bleeding, Haemorrhagic disease of newborn.

•  Vitamin B1 (Thiamine): Dry & Wet Beri-Beri, Wernicke’s encephalopathy, Korsakoff’s psychosis.

•  Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin): Angular stomatitis, cheilosis, magenta glossitis, nasolabial seborrhoeic dermatitis (treated with Riboflavin 10 mg OD).

•  Vitamin B3 (Niacin): Pellagra (Dermatitis [Casal’s necklace], Diarrhoea, Dementia).

•  Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine): Peripheral neuropathy (e.g., isoniazid-induced), sideroblastic anaemia, glossitis, convulsions.

•  Biotin (B7): Scaly dermatitis, alopecia, paraesthesiae (induced by raw egg white avidin or prolonged TPN).

•  Folate (B9): Megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia, glossitis, fetal neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly — prevented by 400 µg–5 mg folic acid preconception and in 1st trimester).

•  Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin): Megaloblastic anaemia, peripheral neuropathy, Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord, optic atrophy, dementia.

•  Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid): Scurvy (swollen bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, haemarthrosis, poor wound healing).

•  (Mapped to Davidson’s 25e Chapter 22, pp. 799–876)

title: 1. Upper GI Endoscopy: Indications, Contraindications, and Complications [TU, RGU - Major Gap]
text:
CHAPTER 20 — GASTROENTEROLOGY

SECTION 20.1 — INVESTIGATIONS OF GI DISEASE

1. Upper GI Endoscopy: Indications, Contraindications, and Complications [TU, RGU - Major Gap]

Procedure Overview:

•  Performed under light intravenous sedation or using local anaesthetic throat spray after the patient has fasted for at least 4 hours.

•  With the patient in the left lateral position, the entire oesophagus (excluding the pharynx), stomach, and first two parts of the duodenum are directly visualised. Transnasal endoscopy is an alternative that allows patients to speak and swallow freely.

Indications:

•  Diagnostic:

•  Dyspepsia in patients >55 years of age or with "alarm" features (weight loss, anaemia, vomiting, haematemesis/melaena, dysphagia, palpable mass).

•  Atypical chest pain, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, or unexplained weight loss.

•  Acute or chronic gastrointestinal bleeding (including iron deficiency anaemia).

•  Screening for oesophageal varices in chronic liver disease.

•  Investigation of abnormal CT scan or barium meal findings.

•  Obtaining duodenal biopsies in suspected malabsorption (e.g., confirming coeliac disease prior to starting a gluten-free diet).

•  Therapeutic:

•  Haemostasis of bleeding lesions (adrenaline injection, thermal heater probe, clips, haemospray, variceal band ligation).

•  Dilatation of benign strictures (balloon or bougie) and palliative stent insertion for malignant strictures.

•  Placement of percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) feeding tubes.

•  Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR), endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), and radiofrequency ablation (RFA) of Barrett’s oesophagus with dysplasia or early intramucosal neoplasia.

Contraindications:

•  Absolute: Severe shock; suspected visceral perforation.

•  Relative: Recent myocardial infarction, unstable angina, or cardiac arrhythmia; severe respiratory disease; atlantoaxial subluxation (e.g., in rheumatoid arthritis).

Complications:

•  Cardiorespiratory depression secondary to intravenous sedation (more common in older adults).

•  Aspiration pneumonia.

•  Visceral perforation (oesophageal, gastric, or duodenal) and post-procedural bleeding.

•  Infective endocarditis (rare).

subject: medicine
title: 2. Acute and Chronic Diarrhoea & Organisms Causing Acute Diarrhoea [KU 24, 23, 19, RGU]
text:
SECTION 20.2 — PRESENTING PROBLEMS IN GI DISEASE

2. Acute and Chronic Diarrhoea & Organisms Causing Acute Diarrhoea [KU 24, 23, 19, RGU]

Definition:

•  Diarrhoea is defined as the passage of three or more loose or liquid stools per day (or stool weight >200 g/day). Urgency of defaecation and faecal incontinence are common accompanying symptoms.

A. Acute Diarrhoea (Duration <10–14 days):

•  Aetiopathogenesis: Extremely common; predominantly caused by faecal–oral transmission of bacteria, bacterial toxins, viruses, or parasites. Diarrhoea lasting >10 days rarely has an acute bacterial/viral infective cause.

•  Causative Organisms:

•  Viruses: Norovirus, Rotavirus, Adenovirus, Astrovirus.

•  Bacteria (Toxin-mediated / Non-invasive):Vibrio cholerae, Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC—most common cause of travellers' diarrhoea), Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens (food poisoning).

•  Bacteria (Invasive / Inflammatory / Bloody diarrhoea):Campylobacter jejuni, Salmonella spp. (non-typhoidal), Shigella spp., Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC / E. coli O157:H7), Yersinia enterocolitica, Vibrio parahaemolyticus, Clostridioides difficile (antibiotic-associated).

•  Protozoa / Parasites:Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium parvum, Cystoisospora belli.

•  Non-infective Acute Causes: Drugs (antibiotics, cytotoxic agents, PPIs, NSAIDs, SSRIs, digoxin, colchicine).

B. Chronic or Relapsing Diarrhoea (Duration >4 weeks):

•  Classified anatomically and pathophysiologically into three major categories (essential differential diagnosis for a young adult presenting with 1 month of diarrhoea):

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-006]]

subject: medicine
title: 3. Causes of Massive Splenomegaly [KU 22, TU, KU 24]
text:
3. Causes of Massive Splenomegaly [KU 22, TU, KU 24]

Definition:

•  Massive splenomegaly is defined clinically as a spleen enlarged >8 cm below the left costal margin, extending across the midline or into the pelvis/right iliac fossa, or weighing >1000 g.

Causes of Massive Splenomegaly:

1.  Haematological / Neoplastic:

•  Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML).

•  Primary myelofibrosis.

•  Lymphomas (particularly splenic marginal zone lymphoma) and Hairy cell leukaemia.

•  Prolymphocytic leukaemia (PLL).

•  Beta-thalassaemia major (extramedullary haematopoiesis).

2.  Infective / Parasitic:

•  Chronic malaria (Hyperreactive Malarial Splenomegaly / Tropical Splenomegaly Syndrome).

•  Visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar).

•  Schistosomiasis (portal hypertension).

3.  Metabolic / Storage Disorders:

•  Gaucher disease and Niemann–Pick disease.

4.  Other General Causes of Mild-to-Moderate Splenomegaly (for completeness):

•  Congestive: Portal hypertension (cirrhosis, portal or splenic vein thrombosis, Budd–Chiari syndrome), chronic congestive cardiac failure.

•  Infective: Infective endocarditis, typhoid, brucellosis, miliary TB, EBV, CMV, viral hepatitis.

•  Inflammatory: Felty syndrome (RA), SLE, sarcoidosis.

•  Haematological: Hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia, acute leukaemias.

subject: medicine
title: 4. Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding (Haematemesis): Causes and Management [KU 20, 19, 15, RGU]
text:
4. Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding (Haematemesis): Causes and Management [KU 20, 19, 15, RGU]

Definitions:

•  Haematemesis: Vomiting of blood; bright red with clots when bleeding is profuse and rapid, or black ("coffee grounds") when less severe due to acid conversion of haemoglobin to haematin.

•  Melaena: Passage of black, tarry, foul-smelling stools containing altered blood (usually from the upper GI tract, occasionally the right colon).

Causes of Acute Upper GI Haemorrhage (with Relative Frequencies):

1.  Peptic ulcer disease (35%–50%): Duodenal ulcer, gastric ulcer (strongly linked to H. pylori and NSAIDs). (Most common cause).

2.  Gastric erosions / Acute gastritis (10%–20%): Secondary to NSAIDs, aspirin, or alcohol.

3.  Oesophagitis (10%): Usually associated with hiatus hernia and GORD.

4.  Oesophageal and gastric varices (2%–9%): Secondary to portal hypertension (cirrhosis, portal vein thrombosis).

5.  Mallory–Weiss tear (5%): Linear mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction following forceful retching or vomiting.

6.  Vascular malformations (5%): Angiodysplasia, Dieulafoy lesion, Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE / watermelon stomach), hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.

7.  Malignancy (2%): Carcinoma of the stomach or oesophagus, GIST.

8.  Aorto-duodenal fistula (0.2%): Following abdominal aortic aneurysm graft repair.

Stepwise Emergency Management of Non-Variceal Upper GI Bleeding:

1.  Immediate Intravenous Access & Resuscitation:

•  Insert two large-bore (14G–16G) intravenous cannulae.

•  Infuse intravenous crystalloid fluids (e.g., 500 mL bolus over <15 minutes in haemodynamically unstable patients) to restore intravascular volume and blood pressure.

•  Blood Transfusion: Adopt a restrictive transfusion strategy; transfuse packed red cells when Hb is <70 g/L (aiming for target 70–90 g/L). Use a higher threshold (<80–90 g/L) in patients with severe haemodynamic instability or acute ischaemic heart disease.

•  Oxygen: Monitor with pulse oximetry; maintain target saturation of 94%–98%.

2.  Initial Clinical Assessment & Risk Stratification:

•  Assess circulatory status (pulse, BP, capillary refill, urine output, mental state).

•  Look for stigmata of chronic liver disease (jaundice, spider naevi, ascites, splenomegaly) to identify potential variceal bleeding.

•  Identify comorbidities (cardiorespiratory, cerebrovascular, or renal disease).

•  Calculate the Modified Blatchford Score (uses blood urea, Hb, systolic BP, pulse ≥ 100/min, melaena, syncope, hepatic disease, cardiac failure) to stratify risk pre-endoscopy. A score of ≤ 2 indicates a very low risk of needing intervention.

3.  Basic Investigations:

•  Full blood count (FBC): Hb may be falsely normal initially until haemodilution occurs over 24 hours; thrombocytopenia suggests hypersplenism.

•  Urea and electrolytes: Elevated blood urea with normal creatinine indicates a major upper GI bleed (due to intestinal absorption and hepatic metabolism of luminal blood proteins).

•  Liver function tests (LFTs) & Prothrombin time (PT/INR).

•  Cross-matching: Cross-match at least 2–4 units of packed red blood cells.

4.  Management of Antithrombotic Drugs:

•  Low-dose aspirin for secondary cardiovascular prevention should be continued.

•  Temporarily withhold P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel—unless recent coronary stenting, discuss with cardiology), warfarin, and DOACs; reintroduce early once haemostasis is securely achieved. Correct severe coagulopathy with prothrombin complex concentrate or vitamin K if actively bleeding on anticoagulants.

5.  Endoscopy (Within 24 Hours):

•  Perform upper GI endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation (or immediately after resuscitation in unstable patients); yields a diagnosis in ∼ 80% of cases.

•  Endoscopic Haemostasis: High-risk ulcers (active arterial spurting, oozing, or non-bleeding visible vessel) require dual therapy: injection of dilute adrenaline (epinephrine) around the bleeding point combined with either a thermal modality (heater probe, bipolar electrocoagulation) or a mechanical modality (endoscopic through-the-scope clips).

•  Rescue Endoscopic Therapy: Inert haemostatic mineral powder (TC-325 / Haemospray) or over-the-scope clips (OTSC) for large fibrotic vessels when standard dual therapy fails.

6.  Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) Therapy:

•  Administer to patients with high-risk ulcer stigmata post-endoscopy: Omeprazole or Pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus followed by continuous infusion of 8 mg/hr for 72 hours (or intermittent high-dose IV/oral PPI).

•  Mechanism: Neutralises intragastric pH (>6), which stabilises the blood clot by preventing pepsin-induced fibrinolysis and promoting platelet aggregation.

7.  Monitoring & Rescue Interventions (Radiology / Surgery):

•  Monitor pulse, BP, SpO2, and hourly urine output closely.

•  If rebleeding occurs after a second endoscopic attempt, refer urgently for transcatheter mesenteric angiography with arterial embolisation (preferred in frail/older patients) or emergency surgery (duodenotomy and under-running of the gastroduodenal artery for duodenal ulcers; under-running, local excision, or partial gastrectomy for gastric ulcers with mandatory biopsy to exclude malignancy).

8.  Secondary Prevention:

•  Discontinue NSAIDs permanently. Test for H. pylori and administer eradication therapy (confirming clearance via urea breath test or faecal antigen test).
