title: 5. Medical Causes of Acute Abdomen [KU 16]
text:
5. Medical Causes of Acute Abdomen [KU 16]

Non-surgical ("medical") conditions that present with acute abdominal pain mimicking a surgical acute abdomen include:

1.  Metabolic & Endocrine: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), acute intermittent porphyria, Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency), hypercalcaemia, uraemia.

2.  Haematological: Sickle-cell vaso-occlusive crisis, acute haemolytic crises, hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency), Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis).

3.  Referred Thoracic / Cardiopulmonary Pain: Inferior myocardial infarction, basal pneumonia, pleurisy, pulmonary embolism, pericarditis.

4.  Infections & Inflammatory: Acute gastroenteritis, mesenteric adenitis, typhoid fever, abdominal tuberculosis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome (chlamydial perihepatitis), familial Mediterranean fever, systemic lupus erythematosus (serositis/mesenteric vasculitis), polyarteritis nodosa.

5.  Toxins & Drugs: Lead poisoning (painter’s colic), narcotic withdrawal, alcohol-induced acute gastritis/hepatitis.

6.  Neurological: Herpes zoster (pre-eruptive phase in a thoracolumbar dermatome), tabes dorsalis (gastric crises), thoracic radiculopathy, anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome.

subject: medicine
title: 6. Odynophagia [KU 19]
text:
6. Odynophagia [KU 19]

•  Definition: Pain experienced during swallowing (distinct from dysphagia, which is difficulty in swallowing, and globus, which is the sensation of a lump in the throat).

•  Causes:

•  Infective oesophagitis:Candida albicans (oral/oesophageal thrush), Herpes simplex virus (HSV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV)—particularly in immunocompromised or HIV/AIDS patients, or those on inhaled/systemic steroids or broad-spectrum antibiotics.

•  Pill-induced oesophagitis: Direct mucosal ulceration from trapped tablets such as bisphosphonates (alendronate), tetracyclines (doxycycline), NSAIDs, potassium chloride, or iron supplements.

•  Severe reflux oesophagitis: Deep peptic ulceration of the lower oesophagus.

•  Corrosive / Caustic ingestion: Acid or alkali (bleach) burns.

•  Radiation oesophagitis and Oesophageal malignancy / perforation.

subject: medicine
title: 7. Aphthous Ulcers [KU 20]
text:
SECTION 20.3 — DISORDERS OF THE MOUTH AND SALIVARY GLAND

7. Aphthous Ulcers [KU 20]

Clinical Features:

•  Superficial, painful, rounded mucosal ulcers with a yellow–grey fibrinous base surrounded by an erythematous halo; they can occur in any part of the mouth.

•  Recurrent idiopathic aphthous ulcers affect ∼ 20% of the population, particularly young women prior to menstruation.

Underlying / Secondary Causes of Oral Ulceration (Differential Diagnosis):

•  Aphthous: Idiopathic recurrent aphthous stomatitis, premenstrual.

•  Gastrointestinal diseases: Crohn’s disease, Coeliac disease, Ulcerative colitis.

•  Systemic / Rheumatological diseases: Behçet’s disease, Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Reactive arthritis.

•  Haematological / Nutritional deficiencies: Iron, folate, or vitamin B12 deficiency; neutropenia; leukaemia.

•  Infections: Viral (Herpes simplex, Coxsackie virus, HIV), fungal (candidiasis), bacterial (syphilis, tuberculosis).

•  Dermatological conditions: Lichen planus, pemphigus vulgaris, mucous membrane pemphigoid, erythema multiforme, dermatitis herpetiformis.

•  Drugs: Nicorandil, NSAIDs, methotrexate, cytotoxic chemotherapy, Stevens–Johnson syndrome.

•  Neoplasia: Squamous cell carcinoma (suspect if solitary, painless, indurated ulcer persisting >2–3 weeks), Kaposi sarcoma.

Management:

•  Correct any underlying haematinic deficiency (iron, folate, B12) or systemic disorder.

•  Symptomatic relief: Local anaesthetic or antiseptic mouthwashes (e.g., benzydamine, chlorhexidine) and choline salicylate (8.7%) gel.

•  Anti-inflammatory therapy: Topical glucocorticoids (e.g., 0.1% triamcinolone dental paste in Orabase, or betamethasone soluble tablets used as a mouthwash).

•  Severe, refractory recurrent ulcers may require short courses of oral prednisolone, colchicine, or thalidomide.

subject: medicine
title: 8. Gastro-Oesophageal Reflux Disease (GORD) [KU 20, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 20.4 — DISORDERS OF THE OESOPHAGUS

8. Gastro-Oesophageal Reflux Disease (GORD) [KU 20, TU, RGU]

Definition:

•  Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) develops when the oesophageal mucosa is exposed to gastroduodenal contents for prolonged periods, resulting in troublesome symptoms (affecting ∼ 15% of the population) and/or mucosal damage (oesophagitis).

Physiological Mechanisms Preventing Reflux & Pathophysiology of GORD:

•  Normal Anti-Reflux Mechanisms:

1.  Lower Oesophageal Sphincter (LOS): A 3–4 cm zone of tonically contracted smooth muscle at the gastro-oesophageal junction that relaxes only transiently during swallowing.

2.  Anatomical / Crural Diaphragm: The right crus of the diaphragm pinches the oesophagus at the hiatus (especially during inspiration and straining), maintaining a positive pressure gradient between the abdomen and thorax, reinforced by the acute oblique angle of His at the cardia.

3.  Oesophageal Peristaltic Clearance & Saliva: Primary and secondary peristaltic waves rapidly clear any refluxed acid back into the stomach, while swallowed alkaline saliva neutralises residual acid.

•  Pathophysiological Factors in GORD:

•  Abnormalities of the LOS: Reduced basal LOS tone or frequent inappropriate transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations (TLOSRs) outside of swallowing.

•  Hiatus hernia: Sliding hiatus hernia results in loss of the thoraco-abdominal pressure gradient across the hiatus and loss of the oblique angle between the cardia and oesophagus.

•  Delayed oesophageal clearance: Defective oesophageal peristalsis prolongs acid contact time.

•  Gastric contents & Delayed gastric emptying: Gastric acid, pepsin, and bile cause mucosal injury; delayed gastric emptying promotes reflux.

•  Increased intra-abdominal pressure: Obesity and pregnancy.

•  Dietary & environmental factors: Fat, chocolate, alcohol, coffee, tea, and smoking relax the LOS.

Clinical Features:

•  Classical Symptoms:Heartburn (retrosternal burning discomfort rising into the chest) and regurgitation (acidic or bitter fluid rising into the throat), provoked by bending, straining, heavy lifting, or lying flat after meals.

•  Waterbrash: Reflex salivation due to vagal stimulation as acid enters the lower gullet.

•  Oesophageal & Atypical Symptoms: Odynophagia, dysphagia (due tooesophagitis, dysmotility, or peptic stricture), non-cardiac chest pain (mimicking angina, due to reflux-induced oesophageal spasm), nocturnal choking, chronic cough, hoarseness ("acid laryngitis"), recurrent pneumonia, and asthma.

Complications:

1.  Reflux oesophagitis: Ranges from mild erythema to extensive circumferential ulceration.

2.  Barrett’s oesophagus (Columnar-Lined Oesophagus - CLO): Pre-malignant adaptive metaplasia in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal oesophagus is replaced by columnar mucosa containing goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia). More common in White males >50 years with central obesity and smoking. Increases the relative risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma 40- to 120-fold (absolute risk 0.1%–0.5% per year). Molecularly driven by loss of p16 followed by somatic inactivation of TP53.

3.  Iron deficiency anaemia: Due to chronic occult blood loss from erosive oesophagitis or erosions in the neck of a large hiatus hernia (Cameron lesions).

4.  Benign peptic oesophageal stricture: Fibrous stricture in the distal oesophagus presenting with progressive dysphagia for solids more than liquids.

5.  Gastric volvulus: Twisting of a massive intrathoracic para-oesophageal hiatus hernia causing acute severe chest pain, retching, and complete dysphagia.

Investigations:

•  Young patients (<55 years) with typical symptoms and no alarm features can be treated empirically without investigation.

•  Upper GI Endoscopy: Investigation of choice if age >50–55 years, if alarm features are present (dysphagia, weight loss, anaemia, vomiting), if symptoms are atypical, or if empirical therapy fails. A normal endoscopy does not exclude GORD (non-erosive reflux disease).

•  24-Hour Oesophageal pH Monitoring & Manometry: Indicated if the diagnosis is unclear or prior to anti-reflux surgery. A slim catheter with a radiotelemetry pH probe (or wireless Bravo capsule) records intraluminal pH; an oesophageal pH < 4 for >6% of the 24-hour study time is diagnostic of GORD. Combined oesophageal impedance testing detects weakly acidic or alkaline (bile/gas) reflux.

Management:

•  Lifestyle Measures: Weight loss, avoidance of dietary triggers (fatty meals, alcohol, coffee, late-night meals), smoking cessation, and raising the head of the bed for nocturnal symptoms.

•  Medical Therapy ("Step-Down" Approach):

•  Proprietary antacids and alginates provide rapid symptomatic relief.

•  Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) (e.g., Omeprazole 20–40 mg daily, Lansoprazole 30 mg daily) are the treatment of choice; they resolve symptoms and heal oesophagitis in the majority of patients. Once remission is achieved, step down to the lowest effective maintenance dose (or H2-receptor antagonists/antacids).

•  Note on Long-Term PPI Risks: Rebound acid hypersecretion on withdrawal; malabsorption of iron, vitamin B12, and magnesium; increased risk of enteric infections (C. difficile, Salmonella, Campylobacter), microscopic colitis, acute interstitial nephritis, and progression of H. pylori-associated gastric atrophy (eradicate H. pylori if PPI needed >1 year).

•  Surgical Management:Laparoscopic fundoplication is indicated for patients who fail optimal medical therapy, those unwilling to take life-long PPIs, or those with severe volume regurgitation.

•  Management of Complications:

•  Peptic strictures: Endoscopic wire-guided balloon or bougie dilatation followed by long-term full-dose PPI.

•  Barrett’s oesophagus: PPIs control symptoms (do not induce regression). Endoscopic surveillance every 3–5 years for non-dysplastic Barrett's, and every 6 months for low-grade dysplasia. High-grade dysplasia or intramucosal carcinoma is treated with endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) followed by radiofrequency ablation (RFA) (successful in 80%–90%).

subject: medicine
title: 9. Achalasia of the Oesophagus [KU 17, TU]
text:
9. Achalasia of the Oesophagus [KU 17, TU]

Pathophysiology:

•  Primary oesophageal motility disorder characterised by:

1.  A hypertonic lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) that fails to relax in response to the swallowing wave.

2.  Failure of propagated peristaltic contraction in the oesophageal body, leading to progressive dilatation of the gullet.

•  Caused by defective release of nitric oxide by inhibitory neurons in the LOS and degeneration of ganglion cells in Auerbach’s myenteric plexus (and dorsal vagal nuclei in the brainstem). Associated with autoimmune diseases. Trypanosoma cruzi infection (Chagas disease) causes a clinically indistinguishable secondary syndrome.

Clinical Features:

•  Insidious, progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset.

•  Regurgitation of undigested food and saliva, halitosis, and episodes of retrosternal chest pain (due to oesophageal spasm in early disease).

•  Weight loss (in ∼ 1/3 of patients).

•  Nocturnal coughing, wheezing, and recurrent aspiration pneumonia due to poor oesophageal emptying.

•  Predisposes to squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus in the long term.

Investigations:

•  Upper GI Endoscopy: Mandatory in all patients to exclude carcinoma of the gastric cardia, which can infiltrate the myenteric plexus and mimic achalasia radiologically and manometrically ("pseudo-achalasia").

•  Barium Swallow: Shows a dilated, aperistaltic, food-filled oesophageal body with a smooth, symmetrical, tapered narrowing at the lower oesophageal sphincter ("bird’s beak" appearance) and absence of the gastric air bubble.

•  High-Resolution Oesophageal Manometry (Gold Standard): Confirms aperistalsis in the oesophageal body and elevated resting LOS pressure with incomplete or absent LOS relaxation on swallowing.

Management:

•  Endoscopic:

•  Pneumatic Balloon Dilatation: Forceful fluoroscopically guided dilatation using a 30–35 mm balloon to disrupt the circular muscle fibres of the LOS; improves symptoms in 80%.

•  Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM): Advanced endoscopic technique where a submucosal tunnel is created in the oesophagus to dissect the circular muscle fibres of the LOS.

•  Botulinum Toxin Injection: Endoscopic injection into the LOS induces temporary clinical remission; reserved for frail/elderly patients unfit for definitive procedures as relapse is common.

•  Surgical:

•  Laparoscopic Heller’s Cardiomyotomy: Longitudinal incision of the LOS muscle fibres, combined with a partial fundoplication anti-reflux procedure (and post-op PPIs) to prevent severe post-myotomy reflux oesophagitis.

subject: medicine
title: 10. Oesophageal Strictures [KU 16]
text:
10. Oesophageal Strictures [KU 16]

Causes of Oesophageal Stricture:

•  Benign:

•  Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (peptic stricture—most common in older adults).

•  Eosinophilic oesophagitis (mucosal rings / trachealisation).

•  Webs and rings: Schatzki ring (submucosal fibrosis at the oesophago-gastric junction causing intermittent bolus obstruction) and post-cricoid web (associated with iron deficiency anaemia in Plummer–Vinson / Paterson–Kelly syndrome, which predisposes to squamous cell carcinoma).

•  Corrosive/caustic ingestion (strong acids, alkalis, bleach).

•  Drug-induced stricture (bisphosphonates, NSAIDs, potassium supplements).

•  Post-operative scarring (anastomotic stricture after oesophageal resection), post-radiotherapy, or following prolonged nasogastric intubation.

•  Malignant:

•  Intrinsic: Squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus or gastric cardia.

•  Extrinsic compression: Bronchial carcinoma or mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Clinical Presentation & Management:

•  Presents with progressive dysphagia, worse for solids than for liquids, or acute food bolus obstruction causing absolute dysphagia.

•  Diagnosis: Upper GI endoscopy with multiple biopsies to differentiate benign from malignant strictures.

•  Treatment: Benign strictures are treated with endoscopic wire-guided balloon dilatation or bouginage, combined with long-term full-dose PPI therapy and thorough chewing of food. Malignant strictures are managed with surgical resection (if localised), chemoradiotherapy, or palliative endoscopic self-expanding metallic stent (SEMS) insertion / laser ablation.

subject: medicine
title: 11. Zollinger–Ellison Syndrome [KU 21, TU, RGU]
text:
11. Zollinger–Ellison Syndrome [KU 21, TU, RGU]

Definition & Pathophysiology:

•  A rare disorder (accounting for ∼ 0.1% of duodenal ulcers; peak age 30–50 years) characterised by severe peptic ulceration and gastric acid hypersecretion caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour (gastrinoma).

•  Around 90% of gastrinomas arise in the pancreatic head or proximal duodenal wall ("gastrinoma triangle"). Approximately 50%–66% are malignant (though slow-growing).

•  Between 20% and 60% of cases occur as part of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1) (autosomal dominant MEN1 mutation causing parathyroid hyperplasia, pituitary adenomas, and pancreatic NETs), in which tumours are invariably multifocal.

•  Mechanism:Autonomous hypergastrinaemia stimulates maximal gastric acid secretion and increases parietal cell mass 3- to 6-fold. The massive acid load lowers proximal small bowel luminal pH to ≤ 2, which inactivates pancreatic lipase and precipitates bile acids, resulting in chronic diarrhoea and steatorrhoea.

Clinical Features:

•  Severe, recurrent, and often multiple peptic ulcers occurring in unusual sites (post-bulbar duodenum, jejunum, or oesophagus) that respond poorly to standard ulcer therapy.

•  High incidence of acute ulcer bleeding and perforation.

•  Chronic watery diarrhoea and steatorrhoea (present in ≥ 1/3 of patients; may be the sole presenting feature).

Investigations:

•  Fasting Serum Gastrin Levels: Grossly elevated (10- to 1000-fold) in the presence of low gastric pH (<2). (Note: PPIs must be stopped prior to testing as they cause physiological hypergastrinaemia).

•  Secretin Stimulation Test: Intravenous secretin injection normally causes no change or a slight fall in gastrin, but in Zollinger–Ellison syndrome it produces a paradoxical and dramatic increase in serum gastrin.

•  Tumour Localisation & Staging: Combined Contrast CT and Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS), supplemented by radiolabelled somatostatin receptor scintigraphy or Gallium-68 (68Ga)-DOTATATE PET-CT scanning.

•  Genetic & Biochemical Screening for MEN 1: Check serum calcium, PTH, prolactin, and MEN1 gene mutation analysis in all patients.

Management:

•  Medical: Continuous high-dose Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) therapy (e.g., Omeprazole 40–80 mg daily) to heal ulcers and alleviate diarrhoea. Somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) reduce gastrin secretion and exert an anti-tumour effect.

•  Surgical: Surgical resection is curative for localised, unifocal sporadic tumours without metastases. Overall 5-year survival is 60%–75%.

subject: medicine
title: 12. Helicobacter pylori Infection: Pathophysiology, Consequences, Diagnosis, and Eradication Therapy [KU 24, 23, 19, 18, 17, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 20.5 — DISORDERS OF STOMACH AND DUODENUM

12. Helicobacter pylori Infection: Pathophysiology, Consequences, Diagnosis, and Eradication Therapy [KU 24, 23, 19, 18, 17, 15, TU, RGU]

Pathobiology & Virulence Factors of H. pylori:

•  H. pylori is a spiral, Gram-negative, microaerophilic rod with multiple unipolar flagella that allow it to burrow beneath the gastric mucous layer to colonise gastric-type epithelium.

•  Adhesins (BabA): Bind to Lewis b antigen on gastric epithelial cells.

•  Urease enzyme: Hydrolyses luminal urea into ammonia (NH3) and CO2, creating an alkaline "ammonia cloud" that buffers surrounding gastric acid and allows survival.

•  Cytotoxin-associated gene A (CagA): Injected into host epithelial cells via a type IV secretion system; disrupts cell signalling, replication, and apoptosis (CagA+ strains carry a higher risk of ulceration and cancer).

•  Vacuolating cytotoxin A (VacA): Secreted pore-forming protein (especially the s1/m1 form) that increases epithelial permeability, induces apoptosis, and suppresses local immune cell activity.

Pathophysiological Patterns & Consequences of H. pylori Infection:

1.  Mild Pangastritis (Majority of infected individuals): Causes asymptomatic chronic gastritis with little effect on acid secretion and no clinical disease.

2.  Antral-Predominant Gastritis (∼ 10% in Western populations) → Duodenal Ulceration:

•  Antral inflammation depletes somatostatin-producing D cells, removing tonic inhibition on G cells.

•  Resultant hypergastrinaemia stimulates an intact parietal cell mass in the gastric body to hypersecrete acid (HCl).

•  The increased acid load entering the duodenum induces duodenal gastric metaplasia, which is subsequently colonised and inflamed by H. pylori, leading to duodenal ulceration (90% of duodenal ulcers are H. pylori-positive).

3.  Corpus-Predominant Pangastritis → Gastric Ulceration & Gastric Adenocarcinoma:

•  Inflammation involving both the body (corpus) and antrum leads to multifocal atrophic gastritis, loss of parietal cells, and hypochlorhydria / achlorhydria.

•  Gastric Ulcer Pathophysiology: Arises not from excess acid, but from impaired mucosal defence at the junction of body and antral mucosa (lesser curve) due to a combination of H. pylori-induced chronic inflammation, NSAIDs, and smoking (70% of gastric ulcers are H. pylori-positive).

•  Gastric Adenocarcinoma: Hypochlorhydria allows bacterial overgrowth in the stomach, converting dietary nitrates into carcinogenic nitrosamines; combined with chronic inflammation, reactive oxygen species, and ascorbic acid depletion, this drives progression from chronic atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma (H. pylori is a WHO Class I carcinogen, implicated in 70% of gastric cancers).

4.  Extranodal Marginal-Zone B-Cell Lymphoma (Gastric MALToma): Driven by chronic H. pylori-stimulated T-cell activation and lymphoid follicle formation in the stomach; early low-grade MALT lymphomas regress completely following H. pylori eradication.

5.  Extra-gastric Associations: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, and idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

Indications for H. pylori Testing:

•  Active or past history of peptic ulcer disease.

•  Low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma or previous endoscopic resection of early gastric cancer.

•  Uninvestigated dyspepsia in patients <55 years without alarm features ("test and treat" strategy).

•  Prior to commencing long-term NSAID or PPI therapy.

•  Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, or ITP.

Methods for the Diagnosis of H. pylori Infection:

•  (Note: PPIs should be stopped 2 weeks and antibiotics 4 weeks prior to testing for active infection to prevent false-negative results).

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-007]]

Management: H. pylori Eradication Regimens & PPI Dosages:

•  First-Line Triple Therapy (7 to 14 days): Extending duration to 10–14 days and using high-dose twice-daily PPI significantly improves eradication rates.

•  High-dose Proton Pump Inhibitor (BD) + Amoxicillin (1 g BD) + Clarithromycin (500 mg BD) OR Metronidazole (400 mg BD).

•  In Penicillin-Allergic Patients:PPI (BD) + Clarithromycin (500 mg BD) + Metronidazole (400 mg BD).

•  Second-Line / Quadruple Therapy (for high clarithromycin resistance or first-line failure, 10–14 days):

•  Bismuth Quadruple Therapy: PPI (BD) + Bismuth subsalicylate/subcitrate (QDS) + Metronidazole (400 mg TDS) + Tetracycline (500 mg QDS).

•  Salvage regimens may utilise levofloxacin or rifabutin alongside amoxicillin and a PPI.

•  Common Side-Effects of Eradication Therapy: Diarrhoea (30%–50%; rarely C. difficile), metallic taste (clarithromycin/metronidazole), nausea/vomiting, abdominal cramps, headache, rash, and disulfiram-like flushing/vomiting reaction with alcohol (metronidazole).

•  Standard and High Oral Dosages of Commonly Used Proton Pump Inhibitors:

•  Omeprazole: Standard: 20 mg OD | High-dose: 40 mg OD (or 20–40 mg BD).

•  Esomeprazole: Standard: 20 mg OD | High-dose: 40 mg OD (or 20–40 mg BD).

•  Lansoprazole: Standard: 30 mg OD | High-dose: 30 mg BD.

•  Pantoprazole: Standard: 40 mg OD | High-dose: 40 mg BD.

•  Rabeprazole: Standard: 20 mg OD | High-dose: 20 mg BD.

subject: medicine
title: 13. Complications of Peptic Ulcer Disease [KU 16]
text:
13. Complications of Peptic Ulcer Disease [KU 16]

1.  Haemorrhage (Most common complication):

•  Accounts for 35%–50% of all acute upper GI bleeds. Posterior duodenal ulcers erode into the gastroduodenal artery, while lesser curve gastric ulcers erode into the left gastric artery. Presents with haematemesis, melaena, or iron deficiency anaemia.

2.  Perforation:

•  More common in duodenal than gastric ulcers (usually anterior wall ulcers) and strongly linked to NSAIDs.

•  Escaping gastroduodenal contents cause chemical and bacterial peritonitis: sudden, severe epigastric pain rapidly becoming generalised, shoulder-tip pain (phrenic nerve irritation), shallow respiration, "board-like" abdominal rigidity, absent bowel sounds, and loss of liver dullness to percussion.

•  Diagnosis: Erect chest X-ray shows free gas under the diaphragm in >50% of cases (or water-soluble contrast swallow/CT).

•  Management: Resuscitation, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, nasogastric decompression, and emergency surgical repair (simple omental patch closure), followed by H. pylori eradication and NSAID avoidance.

3.  Gastric Outlet Obstruction (Pyloric Stenosis):

•  Caused by fibrotic stricture or acute inflammatory oedema from a pyloric channel or duodenal ulcer (differential diagnosis: antral gastric carcinoma).

•  Clinical Features: Nausea, abdominal distension, early satiety, and projectile vomiting of large quantities of stale, non-bilious food eaten ≥ 24 hours previously. Examination reveals weight loss, dehydration, visible gastric peristalsis (passing from left to right across the upper abdomen), and an audible succussion splash ≥ 4 hours after the last meal or drink.

•  Biochemical Abnormality:Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.

•  Management: Nasogastric tube aspiration for 7 days to decompress the stomach; aggressive IV fluid and electrolyte replacement (at least 4 L of isotonic 0.9% saline and 80 mmol potassium in the first 24 hours); intravenous PPI therapy (which resolves oedema); and endoscopic balloon dilatation or surgery (partial gastrectomy or gastroenterostomy with vagotomy) for persistent fibrotic stenosis.

4.  Penetration: Posterior penetration of a duodenal or gastric ulcer into the pancreas, liver, or biliary tree (causing severe back pain or pancreatitis).

subject: medicine
title: 14. Risk Factors for Gastric Cancer & Virchow’s Node [TU]
text:
14. Risk Factors for Gastric Cancer & Virchow’s Node [TU]

•  Major Risk Factors for Gastric Carcinoma:

1.  Helicobacter pylori infection (contributes to 70% of cases via chronic atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia).

2.  Dietary factors: Diets rich in salted, smoked, or pickled foods, nitrates/nitrites, and lacking fresh fruits, vegetables, and vitamins C and A.

3.  Cigarette smoking and alcohol excess.

4.  Autoimmune chronic gastritis (pernicious anaemia) and Ménétrier’s disease.

5.  Adenomatous gastric polyps and previous partial gastrectomy (>20 years prior).

6.  Genetic syndromes: Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (germline CDH1 / E-cadherin mutation), Lynch syndrome (HNPCC), Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP).

•  Virchow’s Node (Troisier’s Sign):

•  Metastatic enlargement of the left supraclavicular lymph node (located in the angle between the left sternocleidomastoid muscle and the clavicle).

•  It receives lymphatic drainage from the abdominal cavity via the thoracic duct, and its presence is a classic clinical sign of advanced intra-abdominal malignancy, most notably gastric carcinoma (other metastatic signs in gastric cancer include periumbilical Sister Mary Joseph nodule and bilateral ovarian Krukenberg tumours).

subject: medicine
title: 15. Probiotics, Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS), and Acute Food Poisoning [KU 22, 15, TU]
text:
15. Probiotics, Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS), and Acute Food Poisoning [KU 22, 15, TU]

A. Probiotics:

•  Definition: Live non-pathogenic microorganisms (bacteria or yeasts) that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host by restoring gut microbial homeostasis (correcting dysbiosis).

•  Common Strains:Lactobacillus species (L. rhamnosus GG, L. acidophilus), Bifidobacterium species, Streptococcus thermophilus, and the non-pathogenic yeast Saccharomyces boulardii.

•  Mechanisms of Action: Compete with enteric pathogens for mucosal binding sites and luminal nutrients; secrete bacteriocins and organic acids (lactic/butyric acid) that lower luminal pH; enhance intestinal epithelial tight-junction barrier integrity; and modulate mucosal immune responses (down-regulating pro-inflammatory cytokines).

•  Clinical Indications in Gastroenterology:

•  Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS): Taken in capsule form for several months to reduce bloating, flatulence, and diarrhoea.

•  Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhoea & Clostridioides difficile Infection: Co-administration reduces the incidence of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

•  Infectious Gastroenteritis: Shortens the duration of acute viral/bacterial diarrhoea.

•  Ulcerative Colitis & Pouchitis:E. coli Nissle 1917 or multi-strain probiotics (VSL#3) help maintain remission in mild UC and chronic pouchitis.

B. Oral Rehydration Solution (WHO Low-Osmolarity ORS):

•  Physiological Principle: Based on the intact sodium–glucose co-transporter 1 (SGLT1) in the small intestinal brush border, which actively absorbs sodium (and consequently water passively) in the presence of equimolar glucose, even during secretory toxin-mediated diarrhoea (e.g., cholera).

•  Composition (per Litre of clean water) — Total Osmolarity 245 mOsm/L:

•  Sodium chloride: 2.6 g/L (Na+ = 75 mmol/L)

•  Glucose, anhydrous: 13.5 g/L (Glucose = 75 mmol/L)

•  Potassium chloride: 1.5 g/L (K+ = 20 mmol/L)

•  Trisodium citrate, dihydrate: 2.9 g/L (Citrate = 10 mmol/L; corrects metabolic acidosis)

•  (Total Chloride = 65 mmol/L).

C. Acute Infectious Causes of Food Poisoning (by Incubation Period):

•  <6 hours (Pre-formed toxins—predominantly vomiting):Staphylococcus aureus (dairy, meats), Bacillus cereus (reheated fried rice).

•  8–16 hours (In vivo toxin production—watery diarrhoea and cramps):Clostridium perfringens (reheated meat/poultry), Bacillus cereus (diarrhoeal toxin).

•  12–72 hours (Mucosal invasion/enterotoxins—diarrhoea, fever, dysentery): Non-typhoidal Salmonella, Campylobacter jejuni, Shigella spp., E. coli (ETEC, EHEC O157), Vibrio parahaemolyticus (seafood), Listeria monocytogenes, Norovirus.

•  18–36 hours (Neuroparalytic toxin):Clostridium botulinum (improperly canned foods).

subject: medicine
title: 16. Malabsorption Syndrome: Causes, Clinical Features, and Management [TU]
text:
SECTION 20.6 — DISORDERS OF SMALL INTESTINE

16. Malabsorption Syndrome: Causes, Clinical Features, and Management [TU]

Pathophysiological Classification & Causes of Malabsorption:

1.  Intraluminal Maldigestion (Defective hydrolysis or fat solubilisation):

•  Pancreatic enzyme deficiency: Chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic carcinoma, cystic fibrosis.

•  Bile salt deficiency / inactivation: Cholestatic liver disease (PBC, PSC), terminal ileal resection or Crohn’s disease, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (bacterial deconjugation of bile salts), Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (acid inactivation of lipase and precipitation of bile salts).

2.  Mucosal Malabsorption (Reduced absorptive surface area or brush-border enzyme defect):

•  Generalised mucosal damage (Subtotal villous atrophy): Coeliac disease, tropical sprue, Whipple disease, giardiasis, intestinal lymphoma, HIV enteropathy, radiation enteritis, hypogammaglobulinaemia.

•  Specific biochemical defects: Lactase deficiency (lactose intolerance), abetalipoproteinaemia.

•  Short bowel syndrome: Extensive small bowel surgical resection.

3.  Post-Mucosal Lymphatic Obstruction (Impaired chylomicron transport):

•  Primary intestinal lymphangiectasia, secondary lymphatic obstruction (lymphoma, tuberculosis, Whipple disease, constrictive pericarditis).

Clinical Features (Consequences of Specific Deficiencies):

•  General & Gastrointestinal: Weight loss, lethargy, malaise, depression, abdominal distension, borborygmi, cramping abdominal pain, watery diarrhoea, and steatorrhoea (bulky, pale, greasy, offensive stools that float).

•  Haematological: Anaemia (microcytic from iron deficiency; macrocytic/megaloblastic from folate or vitamin B12 deficiency); koilonychia (iron); angular stomatitis and glossitis (iron, folate, B12, riboflavin, zinc); purpura and easy bruising (vitamins K and C).

•  Musculoskeletal & Neurological: Osteomalacia/rickets and proximal myopathy (calcium and vitamin D); paraesthesia and tetany (hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia); peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord (vitamin B12); muscle wasting (protein).

•  Dermatological, Ocular & Systemic: Peripheral pitting oedema (hypoalbuminaemia); night blindness and follicular hyperkeratosis (vitamin A); bleeding gums, corkscrew hairs, and poor wound healing (vitamin C, zinc, protein); acrodermatitis enteropathica (zinc); finger clubbing.

Investigations & Management:

•  Blood tests: FBC (microcytic or macrocytic anaemia), prothrombin time (prolonged in vitamin K deficiency), serum iron/ferritin, folate, vitamin B12, calcium, phosphate, magnesium, albumin, immunoglobulins, and IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies.

•  Evaluate Small Intestine: Upper GI endoscopy with distal duodenal biopsy; stool microscopy/PCR for Giardia; small bowel MRI or barium follow-through; faecal calprotectin; glucose/lactulose hydrogen breath test (for bacterial overgrowth).

•  Evaluate Pancreas & Bile Salts:Faecal elastase; abdominal US, CT, or MRCP; 75SeHCAT scan or serum 7α-hydroxycholestenone (for bile acid malabsorption).

•  Management: Treat the specific underlying disorder (e.g., strict gluten-free diet in coeliac disease; tetracycline + folate in tropical sprue; pancreatic enzyme replacement + PPI in chronic pancreatitis; colestyramine in bile acid malabsorption; rifaximin in bacterial overgrowth) alongside targeted replacement of deficient micronutrients (iron, folate, parenteral B12, calcium, fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K, and medium-chain triglycerides).

subject: medicine
title: 17. Coeliac Disease [KU 17, TU, RGU]
text:
17. Coeliac Disease [KU 17, TU, RGU]

Definition & Pathophysiology:

•  An immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of the small bowel occurring in genetically susceptible individuals, triggered by intolerance to wheat gluten (gliadin) and related prolamin proteins in rye, barley, and (to a lesser extent) oats. Prevalence is ∼ 1% in Western populations (F:M = 2:1).

•  Genetics: Strongly associated with HLA-DQ2 (>90%) and HLA-DQ8 (8% of first-degree relatives are affected; 80% concordance in monozygotic twins).

•  Immunopathogenesis: Absorbed gluten peptides are deamidated in the lamina propria by the enzyme tissue transglutaminase (tTG). Deamidated gliadin peptides bind with high affinity to HLA-DQ2/DQ8 on antigen-presenting cells and are recognised by CD4+ T cells, triggering a Th1 immune response with release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-1). This results in increased intra-epithelial lymphocytes (IELs), crypt hyperplasia, and subtotal/total villous atrophy in the proximal small bowel.

Clinical Features:

•  Infancy & Childhood: Diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, abdominal distension, failure to thrive, growth retardation, and pubertal delay after weaning onto cereals.

•  Adulthood (Peak 3rd–4th decades): Highly variable; ranges from florid malabsorption and steatorrhoea to non-specific fatigue, weight loss, dyspepsia, bloating, recurrent oral aphthous ulceration, isolated iron or folate deficiency anaemia, and premature osteoporosis/osteomalacia.

•  Important Disease Associations:

•  Dermatitis herpetiformis (intensely itchy crops of vesicles over elbows, knees, and buttocks with granular IgA deposition at the dermo-epidermal junction; responds to gluten-free diet and dapsone).

•  HLA-linked autoimmune disorders: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (2%–8%), autoimmune thyroid disease (5%), primary biliary cholangitis (3%), Sjögren’s syndrome (3%), pernicious anaemia.

•  Selective IgA deficiency (2%), Down syndrome, microscopic colitis, splenic atrophy (hyposplenism), and neurological complications (cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, epilepsy).

Investigations:

•  (Crucial Rule: The patient MUST remain on a gluten-containing diet throughout serological and biopsy testing to avoid false-negative results).

1.  Serology (Screening Test of Choice):

•  IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies: Sensitivity and specificity >95%.

•  IgA anti-endomysial antibodies (EMA): Detected by immunofluorescence (specificity ∼ 99%).

•  Total serum IgA level must be measured concurrently; if the patient has selective IgA deficiency, IgG anti-tTG or IgG EMA must be requested.

2.  Endoscopic Distal Duodenal Biopsy (Gold Standard in Adults):

•  At least four biopsies from the second part of the duodenum (plus one from the duodenal bulb) demonstrate the classic histological triad: blunting/absence of villi (subtotal villous atrophy), crypt hyperplasia, and increased intra-epithelial lymphocytes (IELs) with chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria.

3.  Haematology, Biochemistry & Bone Density:

•  FBC (microcytic or macrocytic anaemia); blood film shows features of hyposplenism (Howell–Jolly bodies, target cells, spherocytes, acanthocytes).

•  Check ferritin, folate, B12, calcium, phosphate, albumin, and 25(OH)-vitamin D.

•  DXA scan to screen for osteoporosis in patients with high fracture risk.

Management:

•  Life-long strict Gluten-Free Diet (GFD): Complete exclusion of Barley, Rye, Oats (initially, though pure uncontaminated oats can be safely reintroduced after 6–12 months in most), and Wheat (BROW). Rice, maize (corn), potatoes, and gluten-free flours are safe substitutes. Supervised by a specialist dietitian.

•  Correction of Micronutrient Deficiencies: Replace iron, folic acid, calcium, and vitamin D until mucosal healing occurs.

•  Monitoring & Refractory Coeliac Disease (RCD): Monitor symptoms, weight, and falling anti-tTG titres. If symptoms fail to improve, the commonest cause is inadvertent gluten ingestion. If adherence is strict, exclude coexisting microscopic colitis, pancreatic insufficiency, or Refractory Coeliac Disease (Type 1 has normal IELs and responds to steroids/immunosuppressants; Type 2 has clonal aberrant IEL expansion and a 50% 5-year mortality due to progression to lymphoma).

Complications:

•  Malignancy (2-fold increased risk):Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL), small bowel adenocarcinoma, and oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

•  Ulcerative jejunoileitis: Presents with fever, abdominal pain, stricture/obstruction, or perforation.

•  Metabolic bone disease: Osteoporosis and osteomalacia.

•  Hyposplenism: Predisposes to overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus vaccination is recommended).

subject: medicine
title: 18. Tropical Sprue [TU, KU 16, RGU]
text:
18. Tropical Sprue [TU, KU 16, RGU]

Definition:

•  A chronic, progressive malabsorptive disorder occurring in residents of or visitors to tropical regions, associated with structural and functional abnormalities of the small intestine resembling coeliac disease. Endemic in southern India, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the West Indies (rare in Africa).

Aetiology & Pathogenesis:

•  An infective aetiology is strongly implicated by its epidemiological pattern, occurrence in epidemics, and onset following an acute diarrhoeal illness.

•  Although no single specific pathogen has been isolated, persistent small intestinal bacterial overgrowth with enterotoxigenic coliform bacteria (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter cloacae) is frequently demonstrated.

•  Bacterial toxins cause mucosal injury, enterocyte damage, and folate depletion, resulting in partial/subtotal villous atrophy (blunted villi, crypt hyperplasia, and inflammatory infiltration of the lamina propria).Unlike coeliac disease, mucosal damage affects the entire small intestine (including the terminal ileum, leading to early vitamin B12 and bile salt malabsorption).

Clinical Features:

•  In visitors to the tropics, onset may be acute with explosive watery diarrhoea and fever; in indigenous populations, it is typically insidious and chronic.

•  Gastrointestinal: Chronic watery diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, abdominal distension, borborygmi, anorexia, and marked weight loss.

•  Nutritional Deficiencies (Chronic Phase):

•  Megaloblastic anaemia due to combined folic acid and vitamin B12 malabsorption (presenting with pallor, fatigue, atrophic glossitis, and angular stomatitis).

•  Hypoalbuminaemia causing peripheral ankle oedema.

•  Deficiencies of calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin A (night blindness, hyperkeratosis).

Investigations & Differential Diagnosis:

•  Differential Diagnosis: In visitors to the tropics, giardiasis is the most important differential; in indigenous populations, other chronic infective diarrhoeas (Strongyloides, Cryptosporidium, Cystoisospora, intestinal tuberculosis) and coeliac disease must be excluded.

•  Stool microscopy, culture, and molecular testing: Essential to exclude Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium, and helminths (negative in tropical sprue).

•  Blood tests: Megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia with low serum/red cell folate and low serum vitamin B12; hypoalbuminaemia; hypocalcaemia; negative coeliac serology (anti-tTG negative).

•  Endoscopic Jejunal / Distal Duodenal Biopsy: Shows partial/subtotal villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate (incomplete flattening; total villous atrophy is rare compared to coeliac disease).

Treatment:

•  Antibiotic Therapy (Treatment of Choice):Tetracycline 250 mg orally four times daily for 28 days (or doxycycline) eradicates coliform overgrowth and brings about long-term remission or cure.

•  Vitamin Replacement: Pharmacological doses of oral folic acid (5 mg daily) (which independently improves symptoms and jejunal villous morphology) combined with parenteral vitamin B12 (hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM) and correction of fluid, electrolyte, and other vitamin deficiencies.

subject: medicine
title: 19. Whipple’s Disease [KU 22, TU, RGU]
text:
19. Whipple’s Disease [KU 22, TU, RGU]

Definition & Pathophysiology:

•  A rare, chronic multisystem infective disorder caused by the Gram-positive intracellular actinomycete Tropheryma whipplei.

•  Predominantly affects middle-aged White men. The bacillus resides within macrophages in the small bowel lamina propria, causing Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive "foamy" macrophages to pack the mucosa, which flattens villi and obstructs lymphatic drainage, resulting in fat malabsorption and protein-losing enteropathy.

Clinical Features (Multisystem Involvement):

1.  Gastrointestinal (>70%): Weight loss (90%), chronic diarrhoea (75%), steatorrhoea, abdominal pain, protein-losing enteropathy, ascites, and hepatosplenomegaly.

2.  Musculoskeletal (65%): Migratory, non-deforming seronegative oligo-/polyarthropathy or sacroiliitis; joint symptoms often precede GI manifestations by several years.

3.  Neurological (10%–40%): Apathy, personality change, dementia, myoclonus, seizures, supranuclear ophthalmoplegia, cranial nerve palsies, meningitis, and the pathognomonic oculomasticatory myorhythmia (convergent eye oscillations with synchronous jaw contractions).

4.  Haematological & Constitutional (40%–60%): Low-grade fever, generalised hyperpigmentation, anaemia, and peripheral/mesenteric lymphadenopathy.

5.  Cardiopulmonary (10%–20%): Culture-negative endocarditis, pericarditis, myocarditis, chronic cough, pleurisy, and pulmonary infiltrates.

Diagnosis & Management:

•  Diagnosis: Endoscopic small bowel biopsy demonstrating shortened, widened villi packed with PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria, confirmed by PCR or immunohistochemistry for T. whipplei. (CSF PCR should be performed to check for CNS involvement).

•  Management: Fatal if untreated. Treat initially with intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g daily for 2 weeks) (crosses the blood–brain barrier), followed by oral co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole) for at least 1 year (alternative: doxycycline + hydroxychloroquine). Long-term follow-up is mandatory as CNS relapse occurs in up to one-third of patients.

subject: medicine
title: 20. Carcinoid Tumours & Chronic Intestinal Pseudo-Obstruction [TU, RGU]
text:
20. Carcinoid Tumours & Chronic Intestinal Pseudo-Obstruction [TU, RGU]

A. Four Clinical Features of Carcinoid Tumours (Carcinoid Syndrome):

•  (Occurs in ∼ 5%–10% of small bowel neuroendocrine tumours, only when hepatic metastases release vasoactive mediators—5-HT/serotonin, bradykinin, histamine, tachykinins, prostaglandins—directly into the systemic venous circulation, bypassing hepatic portal inactivation. Confirmed by elevated 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid [5-HIAA]):

1.  Cutaneous Flushing: Paroxysmal erythematous/violaceous flushing of the face, neck, and upper chest accompanied by telangiectasia, triggered by alcohol, cheese, coffee, or exercise.

2.  Secretory Diarrhoea & Abdominal Cramps: Recurrent, explosive watery diarrhoea and borborygmi (or mechanical small bowel obstruction from mesenteric desmoplastic fibrosis).

3.  Bronchospasm: Paroxysmal wheezing and dyspnoea.

4.  Carcinoid Heart Disease: Endocardial fibrosis affecting the right side of the heart, leading to tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis (left heart is spared due to pulmonary monoamine oxidase inactivation of serotonin). (Pellagra may also occur due to tryptophan diversion away from niacin synthesis).

B. Causes of Chronic Intestinal Pseudo-Obstruction:

•  (Presents with recurrent clinical and radiological features of small bowel obstruction—pain, vomiting, distension, dilated bowel loops with air–fluid levels, and bacterial overgrowth—in the absence of any mechanical lumen-occluding lesion):

•  Primary / Idiopathic: Familial visceral myopathies or neuropathies; congenital aganglionosis.

•  Secondary Causes:

•  Smooth muscle / Connective tissue disorders:Systemic sclerosis (most common), amyloidosis, dermatomyositis, mitochondrial myopathies (MNGIE), muscular dystrophies.

•  Neurological / Enteric nervous system disorders: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy, Parkinson’s disease, paraneoplastic visceral neuropathy (anti-Hu antibodies in small-cell lung cancer), Chagas disease.

•  Endocrine & Metabolic: Hypothyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, acute intermittent porphyria, hypokalaemia.

•  Drugs: Opiates (narcotic bowel syndrome), anticholinergics, tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines, calcium channel blockers.

subject: medicine
title: 21. Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn’s Disease [KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 20.7 & 20.8 — COLON, RECTUM & INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE (IBD)

21. Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn’s Disease [KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]

Definition:

•  Ulcerative Colitis (UC) and Crohn’s Disease (CD) are chronic, relapsing-remitting immune-mediated inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD).

•  Crucial Distinction: Ulcerative colitis is characterised by continuous mucosal inflammation restricted to the colon and rectum, whereas Crohn’s disease is characterised by patchy, transmural, granulomatous inflammation that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus.

Aetiopathogenesis & Immunology of IBD:

•  IBD develops when genetically susceptible individuals mount an dysregulated innate and adaptive mucosal immune response against commensal intestinal microbiota.

•  Genetic Factors:

•  10% of patients have a affected first-degree relative; high concordance in monozygotic twins (40%–50% in CD; 20%–25% in UC); higher prevalence in Ashkenazi Jews.

•  Shared Loci: Polymorphisms in the HLA region and genes regulating immune signalling (IL-23R and IL-10 pathways).

•  Crohn’s Disease Specific: Associated with mutations in genes regulating innate bacterial sensing and intracellular autophagy: NOD2/CARD15 (strongly linked to fibrostenosing ileal CD), ATG16L1, and IRGM.

•  Ulcerative Colitis Specific: Associated with HLA-DRB1*0103 (linked to acute severe UC) and genes governing colonic epithelial barrier function (HNF4A, LAMB1, CDH1).

•  Environmental Factors & Microbiota:

•  Smoking:Protective in Ulcerative Colitis (UC is more common in non-smokers and ex-smokers) and appendicectomy before age 20 also protects against UC. Conversely, smoking increases the risk of Crohn’s Disease 3-fold and worsens relapse rates and post-operative recurrence.

•  Microbial Dysbiosis: Reduced diversity of beneficial Firmicutes and Bacteroides (which produce anti-inflammatory short-chain fatty acids like butyrate) alongside a relative increase in Enterobacteriaceae.

•  Relapse Triggers: Intercurrent gastroenteritis, NSAIDs, antibiotics, and emotional stress.

•  Immunological Cascade: Luminal bacterial antigens cross a leaky epithelial barrier or are taken up by M cells and presented by dendritic cells to naive CD4+ T cells in the lamina propria. Dysregulated activation of Th1 and Th17 lymphocytes (mediated by IL-12 and IL-23) releases pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-1, IL-6, IL-17), while upregulated endothelial MAdCAM-1 binds leucocyte α4β7 integrin to recruit further inflammatory cells into the gut wall, perpetuating tissue destruction.

Pathology & Differences Between Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn’s Disease:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-008]]

Clinical Features:

•  Ulcerative Colitis:

•  Cardinal symptom is bloody diarrhoea with mucus.

•  Proctitis: Fresh rectal bleeding, mucus discharge, tenesmus, and urgency (sometimes with proximal constipation).

•  Left-sided or Pancolitis: Frequent bloody diarrhoea, cramping lower abdominal pain prior to defaecation, nocturnal stools.

•  Severe / Fulminant Colitis: Anorexia, malaise, weight loss, fever, tachycardia, abdominal tenderness, and signs of systemic toxicity.

•  Crohn’s Disease:

•  Major triad: Abdominal pain, chronic diarrhoea (usually non-bloody unless colonic), and weight loss.

•  Ileal CD: Right iliac fossa pain, subacute intestinal obstruction, malabsorption (vitamin B12, bile salts, fat), and a palpable right iliac fossa mass (matted loops of inflamed bowel or abscess).

•  Perianal CD: Fleshy skin tags, fissures, perianal/ischiorectal abscesses, and fistulae (present in ≥ 50%).

Truelove and Witts Criteria for Assessing Disease Severity in Ulcerative Colitis:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-009]]

•  (Note: Acute Severe Ulcerative Colitis is defined by ≥ 6 bloody stools/day PLUS at least one feature of systemic toxicity: fever ≥ 37.8°C, tachycardia ≥ 90 bpm, Hb <100 g/L, or ESR >30 mm/hr).

Complications of Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn’s Disease:

1.  Local / Intestinal Complications:

•  Acute Severe Colitis & Toxic Megacolon: Transverse colon dilates to >6 cm on plain abdominal X-ray with mucosal islands and "thumb-printing" (mucosal oedema); carries a high risk of free colonic perforation, bacterial translocation, and fatal peritonitis.

•  Massive Lower GI Haemorrhage.

•  Colorectal Cancer & Dysplasia: Risk increases with disease duration and extent (1% at 10 years, 7% at 30 years; highest in pancolitis and coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis). Requires colonoscopic chromo-endoscopy surveillance starting 8 years after symptom onset (or annually from diagnosis if PSC is present).

•  Fistulae, Abscesses & Fibrotic Strictures (Specific to Crohn’s Disease): Enterovesical (pneumaturia, recurrent UTIs), enterovaginal, enteroenteric (blind loop bacterial overgrowth), and enterocutaneous fistulae; small bowel obstruction.

2.  Extra-Intestinal Manifestations of IBD:

•  A. Related to Active Intestinal Disease (parallel bowel flares):

•  Mucocutaneous:Erythema nodosum (painful red nodules on shins), Pyoderma gangrenosum (deep necrotic ulcer with undermined violaceous edge), aphthous mouth ulcers.

•  Ocular:Conjunctivitis, Episcleritis, and Anterior Uveitis (Iritis).

•  Musculoskeletal:Type 1 Peripheral Pauciarticular Arthritis (acute, asymmetrical, non-deforming large-joint arthritis affecting <5 joints, e.g., knees/ankles).

•  Vascular / Hepatic: Venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE, portal/mesenteric vein thrombosis), fatty liver, portal pyaemia/liver abscess.

•  B. Unrelated to Intestinal Disease Activity (follow an independent course):

•  Hepatobiliary:Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) (strongly linked to UC; predisposes to cholangiocarcinoma), autoimmune hepatitis, cholesterol gallstones (bile salt depletion in ileal CD).

•  Musculoskeletal:Sacroiliitis and Ankylosing Spondylitis (HLA-B27 associated), Type 2 Polyarticular Arthritis (symmetrical small-joint arthritis), osteoporosis and osteomalacia.

•  Renal & Systemic:Renal calcium oxalate calculi (enteric hyperoxaluria in ileal CD) and secondary AA amyloidosis.

Investigations:

•  Blood Tests: FBC (anaemia from blood loss or iron/folate/B12 malabsorption; reactive thrombocytosis), serum albumin (low in severe disease), U&Es, LFTs (raised ALP in PSC), and raised ESR and CRP.

•  Stool Tests:

•  Faecal Calprotectin: Neutrophil-derived cytosolic protein; highly sensitive for detecting intestinal mucosal inflammation, differentiating IBD from IBS, and monitoring treatment response.

•  Stool Microscopy, Culture & Clostridioides difficile Toxin Assay: Mandatory at initial presentation and during every acute flare to exclude infective colitis (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli O157, Entamoeba histolytica, C. difficile).

•  Endoscopy & Biopsy:

•  Ileocolonoscopy with segmental biopsies is the gold standard for diagnosis and assessing disease extent.

•  Important Contraindication: Full colonoscopy is contraindicated in acute severe colitis due to perforation risk; perform an unprepared flexible sigmoidoscopy instead (with biopsies to exclude CMV colitis).

•  Radiology:

•  Plain Abdominal X-ray: Essential daily in acute severe colitis to detect toxic megacolon (transverse colon diameter >6 cm), mucosal islands, thumb-printing, or proximal faecal loading.

•  MR Enterography (Small Bowel MRI): Investigation of choice for staging small bowel Crohn’s disease (distinguishes active inflammatory strictures from fibrotic strictures). Pelvic MRI (or endoanal US) is gold standard for perianal Crohn’s fistulae and pelvic abscesses.

Management of Inflammatory Bowel Disease:

•  1. Drugs Used in IBD (Pharmacology Summary):

•  5-Aminosalicylates (5-ASA):Mesalazine (Asacol, Pentasa), Sulfasalazine, Olsalazine, Balsalazide (topical suppositories/enemas or oral). First-line for inducing and maintaining remission in mild-to-moderate UC (and reduces colorectal cancer risk). No role in Crohn's disease. Monitor renal function (U&Es) annually for rare interstitial nephritis.

•  Glucocorticoids:Prednisolone (oral 40 mg/day, tapered by 5 mg/week over 8 weeks), Hydrocortisone (IV 100 mg QDS), Methylprednisolone (IV 60 mg/day), Budesonide (oral 9 mg/day for ileocaecal CD; 90% first-pass hepatic metabolism minimises systemic toxicity). Used only to induce remission; never use for maintenance. Co-prescribe calcium and vitamin D.

•  Thiopurines (Immunomodulators):Azathioprine (2–2.5 mg/kg/day) and 6-Mercaptopurine (1–1.5 mg/kg/day). Induce T-cell apoptosis; used for steroid-free maintenance in UC and CD (takes 6–12 weeks to act). Check TPMT (and NUDT15) activity prior to starting to prevent severe myelosuppression. Adverse effects: pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, flu-like myalgia, non-melanoma skin cancer, and a 2–3-fold increased risk of lymphoma.

•  Methotrexate: 15–25 mg weekly (SC) with folic acid; used for maintenance in Crohn’s disease (teratogenic).

•  Calcineurin Inhibitor:Ciclosporin (IV 2 mg/kg/day); rescue therapy in steroid-refractory acute severe UC.

•  Antibiotics:Metronidazole and Ciprofloxacin; used in perianal fistulating Crohn’s disease and acute pouchitis.

•  Biologics & Targeted Small Molecules (for moderate-to-severe refractory IBD; screen for latent TB with IGRA + CXR, and HBV, HCV, HIV, VZV prior to starting):

•  Anti-TNF-α antibodies:Infliximab (IV/SC), Adalimumab (SC), Golimumab (SC, UC only), Certolizumab (SC).

•  Anti-α4β7 integrin antibody (Gut-selective):Vedolizumab (IV/SC).

•  Anti-IL-12/23 (p40) & Anti-IL-23 (p19) antibodies:Ustekinumab, Risankizumab, Mirikizumab.

•  Oral JAK Inhibitors:Tofacitinib, Upadacitinib, Filgotinib.

•  Oral S1P Receptor Modulators (UC only):Ozanimod, Etrasimod.

•  2. Management of Mild-to-Moderate Ulcerative Colitis:

•  Proctitis: Topical mesalazine suppository (1 g nightly); add oral 5-ASA or topical steroid foam if incomplete response.

•  Left-sided or Extensive UC: Combined oral mesalazine (2.4–4.8 g/day) plus topical mesalazine enema. If incomplete response after 2–4 weeks, start oral prednisolone 40 mg daily (tapered over 8 weeks). Maintain long-term remission with once-daily oral 5-ASA, escalating to thiopurines, biologics, or JAK inhibitors if steroid-dependent or relapsing.

•  3. Medical Management of Acute Severe (Fulminant) Ulcerative Colitis:

•  Admit to hospital under joint medical and surgical care; monitor stool chart, vitals, FBC, U&Es, Albumin, CRP, and daily abdominal X-ray.

•  IV fluids and electrolyte correction (especially potassium replacement, as hypokalaemia predisposes to toxic dilatation); blood transfusion if Hb <100 g/L.

•  Subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) for VTE prophylaxis (prothrombotic state).

•  Avoid opiates, anticholinergics, NSAIDs, and antidiarrhoeal agents (precipitate toxic megacolon).

•  IV Glucocorticoids: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV four times daily or Methylprednisolone 60 mg IV daily.

•  Day 3 Assessment & Medical Rescue Therapy: If no improvement by Day 3 (e.g., >8 stools/day or 3–8 stools/day with CRP >45 mg/L), administer rescue therapy with IV Infliximab (5 mg/kg) or IV Ciclosporin (2 mg/kg).

•  Emergency Colectomy: Indicated if toxic megacolon/perforation develops, or if the patient fails to respond within 5–7 days of rescue therapy.

•  4. Management of Crohn’s Disease:

•  Smoking cessation is mandatory.

•  Induction of Remission:Budesonide (9 mg/day) for mild-to-moderate ileocaecal CD; Oral Prednisolone (40 mg/day) for moderate-to-severe or colonic CD; or Exclusive Enteral Nutrition (elemental or polymeric liquid diet for 6–8 weeks—equally effective as steroids in children).

•  Maintenance of Remission: Early introduction of Azathioprine/Mercaptopurine or Methotrexate, or Biologic therapy (Combination therapy of Infliximab + Azathioprine is most effective and prevents anti-drug antibodies). 5-ASAs are not effective in CD.

•  Perianal Fistulating CD: Pelvic MRI, surgical examination under anaesthetic (EUA) with abscess drainage and non-cutting Seton suture placement, combined with Ciprofloxacin + Metronidazole, Azathioprine, and Infliximab.

•  5. Surgical Management of IBD:

•  Ulcerative Colitis (Curative): Indicated for failed medical therapy, fulminant colitis/toxic megacolon, perforation, or dysplasia/carcinoma. Procedure is subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy (in the acute setting), followed later by completion panproctocolectomy with ileal pouch–anal anastomosis (IPAA) or permanent ileostomy.

•  Crohn’s Disease (Non-curative): Surgery is reserved for complications (fibrotic strictures, fistulae, abscesses, perforation) and must be as conservative as possible (e.g., limited segmental resection or stricturoplasty) to avoid short bowel syndrome.

title: 22. Amoebic Colitis [KU 16]
text:
22. Amoebic Colitis [KU 16]

•  Aetiopathogenesis: Caused by the protozoan Entamoeba histolytica, transmitted via the faecal–oral route through ingestion of mature quadrinucleate cysts in contaminated water or food. Trophozoites emerge in the small bowel and invade the colonic mucosa (especially the caecum and ascending colon) using proteolytic enzymes, producing classic "flask-shaped" ulcers with normal intervening mucosa.

•  Clinical Features: Incubation period ranges from 2 weeks to several months. Presents with gradual onset of lower abdominal colicky pain, tenesmus, and amoebic dysentery (profuse diarrhoea containing blood and mucus). Fever is present in only a minority.

•  Complications: Fulminant necrotising colitis, toxic megacolon, colonic perforation, amoeboma (chronic granulomatous mass in the caecum/rectum mimicking carcinoma), perianal cutaneous ulceration, and amoebic liver abscess (right lobe abscess containing "anchovy sauce" pus).

•  Diagnosis:

•  Stool wet-mount microscopy (of fresh warm stool) showing motile trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis), or stool antigen detection / PCR (which differentiates pathogenic E. histolytica from non-pathogenic E. dispar).

•  Sigmoidoscopy shows discrete ulcers with yellowish exudate; biopsy/scrapings from the ulcer edge reveal trophozoites.

•  Serum anti-amoebic antibodies (ELISA) are positive in >75% of invasive colitis and >95% of liver abscesses.

•  Management:

1.  Tissue Amoebicide (to eradicate invasive trophozoites):Metronidazole 800 mg orally three times daily for 5–10 days (or Tinidazole 2 g daily for 3 days).

2.  Luminal Amoebicide (mandatory follow-on therapy to eradicate intraluminal cysts and prevent relapse):Diloxanide furoate 500 mg orally three times daily for 10 days OR Paromomycin (25–35 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses for 7 days).

title: 23. Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) [KU 25, 24, 23, 19, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 20.9 — FUNCTIONAL BOWEL DISORDERS

23. Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) [KU 25, 24, 23, 19, TU, RGU]

Definition:

•  Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a chronic functional disorder of gut–brain interaction characterised by recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered defaecation and bowel habit, in the absence of any detectable structural or biochemical abnormality of the gut. Worldwide prevalence is ∼ 11%, predominantly affecting young women (<40 years, F:M = 2:1).

Pathophysiology:

1.  Disordered Brain–Gut Axis & Visceral Hypersensitivity: Patients have a lowered pain threshold to colonic distension due to heightened visceral afferent sensitivity and altered central nervous system pain processing.

2.  Altered Serotonergic (5-HT) Signalling & Motility: Increased post-prandial release of 5-HT occurs in diarrhoea-predominant IBS (IBS-D), whereas reduced 5-HT release occurs in constipation-predominant IBS (IBS-C).

3.  Post-Infectious Low-Grade Mucosal Immune Activation: Around 10%–15% of cases develop after an episode of acute bacterial gastroenteritis (Campylobacter, Salmonella); persistent mucosal mast cell and T-lymphocyte activation releases histamine, proteases, and tryptase that sensitise enteric neurons.

4.  Luminal Factors (Dysbiosis & Diet): Alterations in the intestinal microbiota, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), and chemical food intolerances to poorly absorbed, fermentable short-chain carbohydrates (FODMAPs—Fermentable Oligo-, Di-, and Monosaccharides, And Polyols, such as lactose, fructose, fructans, and sorbitol). Colonic bacterial fermentation of FODMAPs produces gas (H2, CO2, CH4) and osmotic fluid shifts, triggering pain and bloating. Non-coeliac gluten sensitivity and bile acid malabsorption (present in up to 1/3 of IBS-D) also overlap.

5.  Biopsychosocial Factors: Anxiety, depression, somatisation, sleep disturbance, and history of childhood adversity amplify symptom perception and illness behaviour.

Clinical Features:

•  Abdominal Pain: Colicky or cramping lower abdominal pain that is related to defaecation (typically relieved, or occasionally worsened, by opening the bowels).

•  Altered Bowel Habit: Classified into four subtypes based on predominant stool form (Bristol Stool Chart):

•  IBS-C (Constipation-predominant): Infrequent passage of hard, pellety stools with straining and tenesmus/sense of incomplete evacuation.

•  IBS-D (Diarrhoea-predominant): Frequent passage of loose, low-volume stools with morning urgency, often after meals. Nocturnal diarrhoea does NOT occur.

•  IBS-M (Mixed): Alternating constipation and diarrhoea.

•  IBS-U (Unsubtyped).

•  Associated Symptoms: Abdominal bloating, visible distension (worsening through the day), passage of clear mucus per rectum (without blood), functional dyspepsia, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue, tension headache, dyspareunia, and interstitial cystitis.

•  Physical Examination: Patients are constitutionally well without weight loss; abdominal examination is normal apart from mild tenderness over the palpable sigmoid colon.

Diagnostic Criteria (Rome IV Criteria for IBS) & Alarm Features:

•  Rome IV Criteria:Recurrent abdominal pain on average at least 1 day per week in the last 3 months (with symptom onset at least 6 months prior to diagnosis), associated with two or more of the following:

1.  Related to defaecation.

2.  Associated with a change in frequency of stool.

3.  Associated with a change in form (appearance) of stool.

•  Alarm Features ("Red Flags") Requiring Urgent Colonoscopy to Exclude Organic Disease:

•  Age >50 years at new symptom onset.

•  Unintentional weight loss.

•  Nocturnal symptoms (waking from sleep with pain or diarrhoea).

•  Rectal bleeding (fresh blood or melaena) or iron deficiency anaemia.

•  Palpable abdominal/rectal mass or lymphadenopathy.

•  Family history of colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, or coeliac disease.

•  Recent progressive change in bowel habit.

Investigations:

•  IBS is a positive clinical diagnosis made using the Rome IV criteria in the absence of alarm features; avoid over-investigation.

•  Baseline Screening Tests (All Normal in IBS):

•  Full blood count (FBC) and C-reactive protein (CRP) / ESR.

•  IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies (to exclude coeliac disease).

•  Faecal calprotectin (normal <50 µ g/g; reliably excludes IBD in patients <45 years with diarrhoeal symptoms).

•  In IBS-D, consider thyroid function tests, stool ova/cysts (Giardia), 75SeHCAT scan (to exclude bile acid diarrhoea), and colonoscopy with random biopsies (to exclude microscopic colitis if refractory).

Management of Irritable Bowel Syndrome:

1.  Positive Diagnosis, Education & Reassurance:

•  Explain the gut–brain axis and visceral hypersensitivity clearly; reassure the patient that symptoms are real, benign, and not due to cancer or colitis.

2.  Dietary & Lifestyle Modifications:

•  First-line General Advice: Eat regular meals, take time to eat, ensure adequate hydration, reduce alcohol, caffeine, and fizzy drinks, limit insoluble fibre (wheat bran, which worsens bloating) in favour of soluble fibre (oats, ispaghula), and avoid sorbitol/artificial sweeteners.

•  Second-line Dietitian-Led Trials: Supervised Low-FODMAP diet (restriction for 4–6 weeks followed by structured reintroduction), lactose exclusion, or a trial of a wheat-free diet.

•  Probiotics: A trial of probiotics for at least 4–12 weeks may improve bloating and global symptoms.

3.  Targeted Pharmacological Therapy (Tailored to Predominant Symptom):

•  For Abdominal Pain & Bloating:

•  First-line Antispasmodics: Smooth muscle relaxants such as Mebeverine (135 mg TDS), Alverine, Peppermint oil capsules, or antimuscarinics (Hyoscine butylbromide 10–20 mg TDS, Dicycloverine).

•  Second-line Central Neuromodulators (Gut–Brain Modulators): Low-dose Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs)—Amitriptyline or Imipramine 10–25 mg at night (most effective for pain and IBS-D)—or SSRIs / SNRIs (Duloxetine 30–60 mg) if TCAs fail or in IBS-C.

•  For Diarrhoea-Predominant IBS (IBS-D):

•  First-line Antidiarrhoeals:Loperamide 2–8 mg daily (titrated to stool consistency, particularly before social events) or codeine phosphate.

•  Bile Acid Sequestrants:Colestyramine or Colesevelam (if bile acid malabsorption coexists).

•  Second-line Agents:Rifaximin (non-absorbable antibiotic, 550–600 mg TDS/daily for 2 weeks), Ondansetron (5-HT3 receptor antagonist), or Eluxadoline.

•  For Constipation-Predominant IBS (IBS-C):

•  First-line Laxatives: Bulk-forming soluble fibre (Ispaghula husk) or osmotic laxatives (Polyethylene glycol / Macrogol). (Avoid lactulose as bacterial fermentation worsens gas and bloating).

•  Second-line Prosecretory & Prokinetic Agents:Linaclotide (guanylate cyclase-C receptor agonist, 290 µg OD—increases luminal fluid and reduces visceral pain), Lubiprostone (chloride channel activator), or Prucalopride (selective 5-HT4 receptor agonist).

4.  Psychological Interventions (for Refractory Symptoms after 12 Months):

•  Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT), gut-directed hypnotherapy, relaxation therapy, and biofeedback.

title: 24. Acute Pancreatitis: Causes, Pathophysiology, Clinical Features, Complications, and Management [KU 24, 20, 17, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 20.10 — DISEASE OF THE PANCREAS

24. Acute Pancreatitis: Causes, Pathophysiology, Clinical Features, Complications, and Management [KU 24, 20, 17, TU, RGU]

Aetiology (Causes of Acute Pancreatitis):

•  Common Causes (90% of cases):

1.  Gallstones (40%–50%): Small calculi/microlithiasis migrating through the ampulla of Vater.

2.  Alcohol excess (25%–30%).

3.  Idiopathic (15%–30%): Often due to occult biliary microlithiasis.

4.  Post-ERCP (1%–5% of procedures).

•  Rare Causes:

•  Metabolic:Hypertriglyceridaemia (>11.3 mmol/L / >1000 mg/dL), Hypercalcaemia (primary hyperparathyroidism).

•  Drugs:Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine, Sodium valproate, Thiazide and loop diuretics, didanosine, oestrogens, GLP-1 agonists, glucocorticoids.

•  Anatomical / Mechanical:Pancreas divisum (failure of dorsal and ventral ducts to fuse, Present in 7%–10% of population), sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, periampullary/pancreatic tumours.

•  Trauma & Post-surgical: Blunt abdominal trauma, cardiopulmonary bypass, abdominal surgery.

•  Infections:Mumps, Coxsackie virus, CMV, Mycoplasma.

•  Genetic (Hereditary pancreatitis): Cationic trypsinogen (PRSS1) or SPINK1 mutations.

•  Others: Autoimmune pancreatitis (IgG4-related), scorpion sting (Tityus trinitatis), severe hypothermia, vasculitis.

Pathophysiology:

•  Triggered by ductal hypertension/obstruction, bile reflux, or direct acinar cell toxicity (alcohol, hypercalcaemia), leading to premature intracellular activation of trypsinogen to trypsin within pancreatic acinar cells, overwhelming intracellular pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitors (SPINK1) and circulating antiproteases (α1-antitrypsin, α2-macroglobulin).

•  Active trypsin activates other zymogens (phospholipase A2, elastase), resulting in autodigestion of the pancreas and peripancreatic fat necrosis, alongside activation of NFκB, massive cytokine release, and systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).

•  Around 80% of cases are mild and self-limiting (interstitial oedematous pancreatitis), while 20% develop severe necrotising pancreatitis (overall mortality 10%).

Clinical Features:

•  Sudden onset of severe, constant epigastric pain that reaches maximum intensity within 15–60 minutes, radiates straight through to the back, and is partially relieved by sitting forward.

•  Accompanied by profuse nausea, vomiting, and retching.

•  Physical Signs: Tachycardia, fever, hypovolaemic shock, and hypoxia. Epigastric tenderness is marked, but guarding and rebound tenderness are initially absent or mild (in contrast to a perforated peptic ulcer) because the pancreas is retroperitoneal. Bowel sounds are quiet or absent due to paralytic ileus.

•  Haemorrhagic Signs (in severe necrotising pancreatitis): Ecchymotic bruising in the periumbilical region (Cullen’s sign) or in the flanks (Grey Turner’s sign), resulting from retroperitoneal blood tracking along fascial planes.

Assessment of Severity (Modified Glasgow / Imrie Criteria & Other Predictors):

•  Glasgow Criteria (Measured at Admission and 48 Hours — Score ≥ 3 indicates Severe Pancreatitis):(Mnemonic: PANCREAS)

•  PaO2 < 8 kPa (60 mmHg)

•  Age > 55 years

•  Neutrophils (WBC) > 15 × 109/L

•  Calcium (corrected serum) < 2.0 mmol/L (<8 mg/dL)

•  Renal function: Blood Urea > 16 mmol/L (BUN >45 mg/dL) after rehydration

•  Enzymes: LDH > 600 U/L or ALT/AST > 200 U/L

•  Albumin < 32 g/L (<3.2 g/dL)

•  Sugar (Blood Glucose) > 10 mmol/L (>180 mg/dL)

•  Other Predictors of Severe Disease: Obesity (BMI >30 kg/m2), pleural effusion on chest X-ray, APACHE II score >8, CRP >150 mg/L at 48 hours (or peak >210 mg/L in first 4 days), and persisting organ failure >48 hours.

Complications of Acute Pancreatitis:

1.  Systemic Complications (Predominate in First Week):

•  Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) & Hypovolaemic Shock: Due to third-space fluid sequestration and cytokine-induced capillary leak.

•  Hypoxia & Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): Due to pulmonary microthrombi, surfactant destruction by phospholipase A2, and basal atelectasis/pleural effusions.

•  Acute Kidney Injury (Pre-renal / Acute Tubular Necrosis).

•  Metabolic:Hypocalcaemia (saponification/sequestration of calcium in areas of peripancreatic fat necrosis), hyperglycaemia (islet cell disruption), and hypoalbuminaemia.

•  Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC).

2.  Local Pancreatic & Gastrointestinal Complications (Predominate After First Week):

•  Acute Peripancreatic Fluid Collection & Pancreatic Pseudocyst: Disruption of pancreatic ducts leads to a collection of amylase-rich fluid and debris in the lesser sac, which matures over ≥ 4–6 weeks into a fibrous-walled pseudocyst (lacking an epithelial lining). Pseudocysts >6 cm may compress the duodenum/bile duct, become infected, or rupture.

•  Pancreatic Necrosis (Sterile or Infected) & Walled-Off Necrosis (WON): Non-viable pancreatic/peripancreatic tissue; secondary bacterial infection (gas bubbles on CT) is the leading cause of late mortality.

•  Pancreatic Abscess: Circumscribed collection of pus.

•  Pancreatic Ascites & Pleural Effusion: Due to pancreatic duct disruption leaking into the peritoneum or thorax.

•  Vascular & GI:Splenic or portal vein thrombosis (leading to left-sided portal hypertension and gastric varices), pseudoaneurysm of the splenic/gastroduodenal artery (causing massive haemorrhage), upper GI stress ulcer bleeding, duodenal obstruction, and obstructive jaundice.

Investigations:

1.  Serum Lipase and Amylase:Elevated >3× the upper limit of normal. Serum lipase is preferred over amylase as it is more specific and remains elevated longer (serum amylase is rapidly cleared by the kidneys and normalises within 24–48 hours). Note: The magnitude of amylase/lipase elevation has NO prognostic value. Persistently elevated amylase suggests pseudocyst formation.

2.  Baseline Bloods & Severity Scoring: FBC, U&Es, glucose, calcium, LFTs (markedly raised ALT >150 U/L strongly suggests a gallstone aetiology), LDH, albumin, arterial blood gases, and serial CRP.

3.  Abdominal Ultrasound: Performed within 24 hours in all patients to detect gallstones and biliary tract dilatation.

4.  Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) of the Pancreas: Performed at least 48–72 hours after onset in patients with severe pancreatitis, persistent organ failure, or clinical deterioration. Necrotic pancreas fails to enhance after IV contrast; gas within necrosis indicates infected necrosis.

Management:

•  Resuscitation & Supportive Care:

•  Admit severe cases to HDU/ICU; monitor vitals, pulse oximetry, central venous pressure, and hourly urine output (via urinary catheter).

•  Aggressive IV Fluid Resuscitation: Goal-directed crystalloid therapy (Ringer’s lactate / Hartmann’s solution is preferred over 0.9% saline).

•  Analgesia: Strong intravenous opioid analgesics (e.g., fentanyl, morphine, pethidine).

•  Oxygen & Metabolic Control: Administer supplemental oxygen (or mechanical ventilation for ARDS); treat hyperglycaemia with insulin and symptomatic hypocalcaemia with IV calcium gluconate; give subcutaneous LMWH for VTE prophylaxis.

•  Nutrition:

•  Keep nil by mouth initially ONLY if vomiting/paralytic ileus is present (insert NG tube for ileus).

•  Commence early enteral nutrition (oral, nasogastric, or nasojejunal) within 24–48 hours as soon as resuscitated. Enteral feeding preserves gut mucosal barrier integrity, reduces bacterial translocation/endotoxaemia, and decreases mortality compared to total parenteral nutrition (TPN).

•  Antibiotics:

•  Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT indicated in sterile necrosis.

•  If infected pancreatic necrosis (confirmed by CT-guided fine-needle aspiration or gas on CT) or cholangitis is present, administer IV antibiotics that penetrate necrotic pancreatic tissue (e.g., Carbapenems [meropenem/imipenem] or Quinolones + Metronidazole).

•  Interventional Management of Gallstones & Local Complications:

•  Urgent ERCP with Biliary Sphincterotomy (within 24–72 hours): Indicated ONLY in patients with gallstone pancreatitis complicated by acute cholangitis or persistent common bile duct obstruction.

•  Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Should be performed during the same hospital admission (or within 2 weeks of resolution) in mild gallstone pancreatitis to prevent fatal recurrent attacks.

•  Infected Necrosis ("Step-Up" Approach): Delay intervention for 4 weeks if possible to allow walling-off, then perform endoscopic (EUS-guided) or percutaneous catheter drainage, escalating to minimally invasive retroperitoneal pancreatic (MIRP) necrosectomy if needed.

•  Symptomatic Pseudocysts:Wait ≥ 6 weeks for the fibrous wall to mature, then drain internally into the stomach via EUS-guided endoscopic cystogastrostomy (using a lumen-apposing metal stent [LAMS]) or surgical cystogastrostomy.
