title: 25. Chronic Pancreatitis: Causes, Clinical Features, Complications, Investigations, and Management [KU 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
25. Chronic Pancreatitis: Causes, Clinical Features, Complications, Investigations, and Management [KU 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]

Definition:

•  A chronic, progressive fibro-inflammatory disease of the pancreas characterised by irreversible fibrosis, ductal stricturing/calcification, and destruction of exocrine and eventually endocrine (islets of Langerhans) pancreatic tissue.

Aetiology (Causes — Mnemonic: TIGAR-O):

1.  T — Toxic–Metabolic:Alcohol misuse (accounts for 80% of cases in Western countries), tobacco smoking (accelerates progression), hypercalcaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, chronic kidney disease.

2.  I — Idiopathic (10%–20%): Early-onset and late-onset idiopathic types; Tropical calcific pancreatitis (occurs in young non-alcoholics in southern India/Kerala, linked to SPINK1 mutations and micronutrient/antioxidant deficiencies).

3.  G — Genetic: Hereditary pancreatitis (autosomal dominant cationic trypsinogen [PRSS1] mutation), SPINK1 (serine protease inhibitor Kazal type 1) mutations, Cystic fibrosis (CFTR mutations).

4.  A — Autoimmune Pancreatitis (AIP):

•  Type 1 AIP: Part of systemic IgG4-related sclerosing disease (elevated serum IgG4, diffuse "sausage-shaped" pancreatic enlargement, biliary strictures; responds dramatically to corticosteroids).

•  Type 2 AIP: Pancreas-specific, normal IgG4, associated with ulcerative colitis.

5.  R — Recurrent and Severe Acute Pancreatitis: Post-necrotic, radiation.

6.  O — Obstructive: Pancreas divisum, sphincter of Oddi stenosis, ductal adenocarcinoma, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN). (Note: Gallstones do NOT cause chronic pancreatitis).

Clinical Features:

•  Predominantly affects middle-aged men with alcohol dependence.

•  Abdominal Pain (>80%): Epigastric pain radiating to the back, provoked by meals and relieved by leaning forward. May occur as recurrent acute exacerbations or relentless chronic pain. Examination often shows erythema ab igne (reticular hyperpigmentation over the epigastrium/back from chronic use of a hot-water bottle) and weight loss/malnutrition.

•  Exocrine Insufficiency (Steatorrhoea): Develops when >90% of exocrine acinar tissue is destroyed; presents with pale, bulky, greasy, foul-smelling floating stools and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (though clinical vitamin deficiency is less common than in coeliac disease).

•  Endocrine Insufficiency (Pancreatogenic / Type 3c Diabetes Mellitus): Occurs in 30% overall and up to 70% in chronic fibrocalcific pancreatitis; patients are prone to severe hypoglycaemia on insulin because both insulin (beta cells) and glucagon (alpha cells) are deficient.

Complications of Chronic Pancreatitis:

•  Pancreatic pseudocysts and pancreatic ascites / pleural effusion.

•  Obstructive jaundice: Due to benign fibrotic stricture of the intrapancreatic common bile duct.

•  Duodenal stenosis and peptic ulceration.

•  Splenic or portal vein thrombosis: Leading to segmental (left-sided) portal hypertension and bleeding gastric varices.

•  Secondary diabetes mellitus and pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (malnutrition, osteopenia/osteoporosis).

•  Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (4% lifetime risk; 10–20× higher in hereditary pancreatitis) and opiate addiction.

Investigations (Structural & Biochemical Evaluation of Pancreatic Function):

1.  Imaging Tests to Establish Structural Diagnosis:

•  Plain Abdominal X-ray: Shows punctate pancreatic calcifications across the L1–L2 vertebrae in 30%.

•  Abdominal Ultrasound & Contrast CT Scan: Shows pancreatic atrophy, parenchymal calcifications, intraductal calculi, main pancreatic duct dilatation, and pseudocysts.

•  MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) & Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS): Most sensitive modalities for demonstrating main pancreatic duct irregularity/strictures ("chain of lakes" appearance) and dilated side-branches, and for planning surgical/endoscopic intervention.

2.  Biochemical Tests of Exocrine & Endocrine Pancreatic Function:

•  Faecal Pancreatic Elastase-1 (Non-invasive Test of Choice): Immunoassay on a single random stool sample. Values <200 µ g/g indicate exocrine insufficiency (<100 µ g/g indicates severe insufficiency). Simple, unaffected by exogenous enzyme supplements, and has replaced 3-day faecal fat collection.

•  Direct Secretin–Cholecystokinin Stimulation Test: Duodenal intubation to collect pancreatic juice and measure bicarbonate and enzyme output after IV secretin; gold standard sensitivity for early disease, but invasive and rarely used.

•  Endocrine Function: Fasting blood glucose and HbA1c.

•  Serum IgG4: Elevated in Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis.

•  (Note: Serum amylase and lipase are usually normal in chronic pancreatitis due to acinar destruction).

Management:

1.  Lifestyle Modification:Complete abstinence from alcohol and smoking cessation are mandatory to halt disease progression and reduce pain.

2.  Pain Relief:

•  Stepwise analgesia (paracetamol, NSAIDs, tramadol), avoiding strong opiates where possible due to high addiction risk. Add neuropathic adjuvant analgesics (Pregabalin or low-dose Amitriptyline).

•  Oral pancreatic enzyme supplements + PPI reduce CCK-mediated pancreatic stimulation and may ease pain.

•  Interventional Pain Relief (for refractory pain):Endoscopic (ERCP) pancreatic sphincterotomy, stone extraction (with extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy [ESWL]), or duct stenting; EUS-guided coeliac plexus neurolysis/block; or Surgery (Lateral pancreaticojejunostomy [Puestow / Frey procedure] for a dilated main duct, partial pancreatectomy [Whipple], or total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation).

3.  Management of Exocrine Insufficiency (Malabsorption):

•  Maintain a high-calorie, normal-fat diet (restricting fat only if steatorrhoea remains uncontrolled; supplement with medium-chain triglycerides if malnourished) and replace fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and calcium.

•  Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT — e.g., Creon): Taken with every meal and snack.

•  Co-prescribe a Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) to raise duodenal pH and prevent gastric acid inactivation of the exogenous lipase.

4.  Management of Endocrine Insufficiency: Dietary control or cautious insulin therapy (warning patients of the high risk of hypoglycaemia).

title: 26. Hypersplenism and Vaccination Strategy in Splenectomy [KU 21, 19]
text:
SECTION 20.11 — DISEASE OF SPLEEN

26. Hypersplenism and Vaccination Strategy in Splenectomy [KU 21, 19]

A. Criteria to Diagnose Hypersplenism:

1.  Splenomegaly (detected clinically or by imaging).

2.  Cytopenia(s) affecting one or more peripheral blood cell lineages (anaemia, leucopenia, and/or thrombocytopenia—most commonly pancytopenia or isolated thrombocytopenia) due to splenic pooling and premature destruction.

3.  Normal or Compensatory Hypercellular Bone Marrow (increased marrow precursors of the deficient cell lines).

4.  Correction / Resolution of the Cytopenia(s) Following Splenectomy.

B. Management of Hypersplenism:

•  Treat the underlying primary cause of splenomegaly (e.g., portal hypertension, visceral leishmaniasis, malaria, lymphoma, autoimmune disease).

•  In cirrhosis/portal hypertension, splenectomy is generally avoided due to high operative bleeding risk and portal vein thrombosis; partial splenic artery embolisation or TIPSS may be considered in selected cases.

•  Splenectomy is indicated for severe symptomatic hypersplenism, massive splenomegaly causing mechanical discomfort/infarction, or refractory hereditary/autoimmune haemolytic anaemias and ITP.

C. Vaccination Strategy & Management of the Splenectomised / Hyposplenic Patient:

•  (Asplenic patients are at life-long risk of Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection [OPSI] caused by encapsulated bacteria):

1.  Vaccination Schedule:

•  Administer vaccines at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE elective splenectomy (or 2 weeks AFTER emergency splenectomy to ensure an optimal antibody response):

•  Pneumococcal vaccine (Streptococcus pneumoniae): Conjugate vaccine (PCV) followed by 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPV23), with re-immunisation every 5 years.

•  Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccine.

•  Meningococcal vaccines (Neisseria meningitidis): Conjugate MenACWY and MenB vaccines.

•  Annual Influenza vaccine and COVID-19 vaccination.

2.  Antibiotic Prophylaxis:

•  Life-long oral Phenoxymethylpenicillin (Penicillin V) 500 mg twice daily (or a macrolide such as erythromycin/clarithromycin in penicillin-allergic patients), plus a standby supply of broad-spectrum antibiotics at home.

3.  Patient Education & General Precautions:

•  Carry a Splenectomy Medical Alert Card / Bracelet at all times.

•  Seek urgent medical attention for any febrile illness (requires immediate IV antibiotics covering pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Haemophilus).

•  Prompt disinfection and antibiotic treatment (co-amoxiclav) for animal/dog bites (high risk of fatal Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis).

•  Strict antimalarial prophylaxis when travelling to endemic areas (increased risk of severe falciparum malaria) and avoidance of tick bites (Babesia infection).

•  (Mapped to Davidson’s 25e Chapter 23, pp. 877–940)

title: 1. Liver Function Tests (LFTs), GGT, ALP, INR, and Classification of Jaundice [KU 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
CHAPTER 21 — HEPATOLOGY

SECTION 21.1 & 21.2 — INVESTIGATIONS & PRESENTING PROBLEMS IN LIVER DISEASE

1. Liver Function Tests (LFTs), GGT, ALP, INR, and Classification of Jaundice [KU 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]

A. Classification of Liver Blood Biochemistry ("Liver Function Tests"):

1.  True Markers of Hepatic Synthetic & Excretory Function (Reflect Severity & Prognosis):

•  Serum Bilirubin (<20 µ mol/L / <1.2 mg/dL): Measures hepatic uptake, conjugation (via UDP-glucuronyl transferase), and biliary excretion.

•  Serum Albumin (35–50 g/L): Synthesised exclusively by hepatocytes (8–14 g/day). Because its plasma half-life is ∼ 2 weeks, albumin is normal in acute liver failure but reduced in chronic liver disease/cirrhosis (also reduced in malnutrition, sepsis, nephrotic syndrome, and protein-losing enteropathy).

•  Prothrombin Time (PT) & International Normalised Ratio (INR): The liver synthesises coagulation factors (including vitamin K–dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X). Because these factors have short half-lives (5–72 hours), PT/INR is the most sensitive, rapidly responsive marker of acute and chronic hepatocyte synthetic dysfunction.

•  Definition of INR: INR = (Patient PT / Mean Normal Control PT)ISI, where ISI is the International Sensitivity Index of the thromboplastin reagent.

•  Vitamin K Distinction: Parenteral vitamin K (10 mg IV) corrects a prolonged PT/INR within 24–48 hours if caused by cholestatic jaundice (fat-soluble vitamin K malabsorption), but fails to correct PT/INR in parenchymal liver failure.

2.  Markers of Hepatocellular Injury (Transaminases):

•  Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) & Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST): Intracellular enzymes released during hepatocyte necrosis/inflammation. ALT is more specific for the liver, whereas AST is also present in cardiac and skeletal muscle, kidneys, and red cells.

•  AST : ALT Ratio: Normally <0.8. An AST/ALT ratio > 2.0 is characteristic of alcohol-related liver disease / alcoholic hepatitis (due to pyridoxal-6-phosphate deficiency depleting ALT and mitochondrial injury releasing AST); a ratio >1.0 in non-alcoholics suggests progression to cirrhosis.

•  Massive Elevation (>1000 U/L): Seen in acute viral hepatitis, paracetamol toxicity / drug-induced liver injury, ischaemic hepatitis ("shock liver"), and autoimmune hepatitis.

3.  Markers of Cholestasis / Biliary Epithelial Injury:

•  Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP): Located on the hepatocyte canalicular membrane; synthesis increases in intra- or extrahepatic biliary obstruction and hepatic infiltration. Non-hepatic sources of ALP include bone (Paget’s disease, osteomalacia, bone metastases, fracture healing), placenta (pregnancy), and intestine.

•  Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT): Microsomal enzyme in hepatocytes and biliary epithelium.

•  Clinical Utility of GGT: (1) Confirms hepatic origin of an elevated ALP (if ALP is raised with a normal GGT and normal 5′-nucleotidase, the source is bone or placenta); (2) Isolated GGT elevation occurs with microsomal enzyme-inducing drugs (ethanol/alcohol, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, valproate, rifampicin) and in steatotic liver disease (MASLD / ArLD).

B. Types of Jaundice & Laboratory Differentiation (Pre-Hepatic, Hepatocellular, Post-Hepatic):

•  (Clinical jaundice becomes detectable in the sclerae when serum bilirubin exceeds 40 µ mol/L (∼ 2.5 mg/dL)).

title: 2. Serum–Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) [KU 22]
text:
2. Serum–Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) [KU 22]

Definition & Calculation:

•  The Serum–Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) is the single most accurate laboratory parameter for classifying the aetiology of ascites (replacing the outdated "transudate vs exudate" ascitic total protein classification, which misclassifies up to 30% of cirrhotic patients).

•  SAAG = Serum Albumin (g/L or g/dL) - Ascitic Fluid Albumin (g/L or g/dL) (Measured on samples taken on the same day).

Interpretation & Causes:

1.  High SAAG: ≥ 11 g/L (≥ 1.1 g/dL) ⟶ Indicates Portal Hypertension (96% accuracy):

•  With Low Ascitic Protein (<25 g/L):Hepatic cirrhosis (most common), alcoholic hepatitis, late Budd–Chiari syndrome.

•  With High Ascitic Protein (≥ 25 g/L):Congestive cardiac failure, constrictive pericarditis, early Budd–Chiari syndrome, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease).

2.  Low SAAG: < 11 g/L (< 1.1 g/dL) ⟶ Indicates Non-Portal Hypertensive Ascites:

•  With High Ascitic Protein (≥ 25 g/L):Peritoneal malignancy / carcinomatosis, Tuberculous peritonitis, Acute pancreatitis (ascitic amylase >1000 U/L), serositis (SLE), hypothyroidism.

•  With Low Ascitic Protein (<25 g/L):Nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy, severe malnutrition.

title: 3. Tender Hepatomegaly, Hepato-Jugular Reflux, and Fever with Jaundice [TU, RGU]
text:
3. Tender Hepatomegaly, Hepato-Jugular Reflux, and Fever with Jaundice [TU, RGU]

•  Causes of Tender Hepatomegaly (Rapid Stretching of Glisson’s Capsule):

1.  Acute Congestive: Right ventricular failure / congestive cardiac failure, acute Budd–Chiari syndrome, acute pericardial tamponade / constrictive pericarditis.

2.  Infective / Inflammatory:Acute viral hepatitis (A, B, E), Acute alcoholic hepatitis, Amoebic liver abscess, Pyogenic liver abscess, acute cholangitis.

3.  Neoplastic: Rapidly expanding hepatocellular carcinoma or necrotic hepatic metastases (especially with intratumoral haemorrhage).

•  Hepato-Jugular Reflux (Abdomino-Jugular Reflex) — Clinical Significance:

•  Technique: With the patient semi-recumbent at 45°, apply firm, sustained pressure over the periumbilical/right upper quadrant for 10–15 seconds while observing the internal jugular vein.

•  Positive Result & Significance: A sustained rise in the JVP of >3–4 cm H2O throughout compression (followed by an abrupt drop of >4 cm on release) indicates that the right ventricle cannot accommodate the increased venous return. It is a sensitive sign of right ventricular failure, tricuspid regurgitation, constrictive pericarditis, or hypervolaemia, and confirms that hepatomegaly/ascites is of cardiac (congestive) origin.

•  Four Important Causes of Fever with Jaundice:

1.  Infections: Falciparum malaria, Leptospirosis (Weil’s disease), Dengue fever, Yellow fever, Acute viral hepatitis (prodromal phase), EBV/infectious mononucleosis.

2.  Hepatobiliary Sepsis:Acute bacterial cholangitis (Charcot’s triad: fever with rigors, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice), Pyogenic or Amoebic liver abscess, Acute cholecystitis (Mirizzi syndrome).

3.  Inflammatory / Decompensated Liver Disease:Acute alcoholic hepatitis, Cirrhosis complicated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP).

4.  Haemolytic: Septic / Clostridium perfringens intravascular haemolysis, acute haemolytic crisis in G6PD deficiency or sickle-cell disease.

subject: medicine
title: 4. Cirrhosis of the Liver, Portal Hypertension, and Decompensated Complications (Ascites, Variceal Bleeding, Hepatic Encephalopathy, SBP, and Hepatorenal Syndrome) [KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 21.3, 21.5 & 21.6 — CIRRHOSIS, PORTAL HYPERTENSION & STEATOTIC LIVER DISEASE

4. Cirrhosis of the Liver, Portal Hypertension, and Decompensated Complications (Ascites, Variceal Bleeding, Hepatic Encephalopathy, SBP, and Hepatorenal Syndrome) [KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

•  (Covers all clinical vignette Essays on chronic alcoholic patients presenting with haematemesis, melaena, ascites, jaundice, and altered sensorium/hepatic encephalopathy).

Definition & Pathophysiology of Cirrhosis:

•  Definition: Cirrhosis is a diffuse histological process characterised by widespread hepatocyte necrosis, bridging hepatic fibrosis, and the conversion of normal liver architecture into structurally abnormal regenerative nodules.

•  Pathogenesis of Hepatic Fibrosis: Following chronic hepatocyte injury, Kupffer cells (resident macrophages), platelets, and damaged hepatocytes release pro-inflammatory cytokines and growth factors (TGF-β1, PDGF, and reactive oxygen species). These activate quiescent vitamin A–storing hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells) in the space of Disse, transforming them into proliferating myofibroblasts. Activated stellate cells secrete dense type I and III collagen matrix and tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMP-1 and TIMP-2, which block matrix degradation by MMPs), while also releasing endothelin-1 (ET-1), which causes sinusoidal vasoconstriction and portal hypertension.

2. Aetiology (Causes) of Cirrhosis:

•  Steatotic Liver Disease (Most common in Western countries):

•  Alcohol-related liver disease (ArLD).

•  Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD / MASH)(formerly NAFLD/NASH).

•  Chronic Viral Hepatitis (Most common worldwide): Chronic Hepatitis B (± Hepatitis D) and Chronic Hepatitis C.

•  Autoimmune & Cholestatic Diseases:Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH), Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), secondary biliary cirrhosis (chronic bile duct strictures/stones), cystic fibrosis.

•  Inherited / Genetic Metabolic Disorders:Genetic haemochromatosis (HFE C282Y), Wilson’s disease (ATP7B), α1-antitrypsin deficiency (SERPINA1 PiZZ), glycogen storage diseases, galactosaemia.

•  Vascular (Venous Outflow Obstruction):Budd–Chiari syndrome, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease), chronic right-sided heart failure / constrictive pericarditis (cardiac cirrhosis).

•  Drugs & Cryptogenic: Long-term methotrexate or amiodarone; cryptogenic cirrhosis (mostly burnt-out MASLD).

3. Clinical Features & Physical Signs of Cirrhosis:

•  Compensated Cirrhosis: May be asymptomatic or present with non-specific fatigue, weakness, anorexia, weight loss, muscle cramps, or right upper quadrant discomfort.

•  Physical Signs on Examination:

•  Cutaneous & Circulatory Stigmata of Chronic Liver Disease:Spider telangiectasia (spider naevi) in the superior vena caval distribution, palmar erythema, leuconychia (hypoalbuminaemia), clubbing (hepatopulmonary syndrome), bruising/purpura (thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy), paper-money skin, and scratch marks (pruritus).

•  Endocrine Signs (due to hyperoestrogenism and altered androgen metabolism):Gynaecomastia, loss of axillary and pubic body hair, testicular atrophy, impotence/loss of libido in men; breast atrophy and amenorrhoea in women.

•  Aetiology-Specific Signs:Dupuytren’s contracture and bilateral parotid enlargement (alcohol); xanthelasma and tendon xanthomas (PBC); slate-grey "bronzed" skin pigmentation (haemochromatosis); Kayser–Fleischer corneal rings (Wilson’s disease).

•  Signs of Portal Hypertension:Splenomegaly and dilated collateral veins on the anterior abdominal wall radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae). Liver may be enlarged and firm initially (especially in ArLD, MASLD, haemochromatosis) or shrunken, hard, and nodular in advanced cirrhosis.

•  Signs of Hepatic Decompensation:Jaundice, ascites (shifting dullness, fluid thrill), bilateral pitting pedal oedema, fetor hepaticus (sweet musty breath odour from portosystemic shunting of mercaptans), flapping tremor (asterixis) and altered sensorium (hepatic encephalopathy), and haematemesis/melaena (variceal haemorrhage).

4. Major Complications of Cirrhosis & Their Pathogenesis:

•  A. Portal Hypertension & Gastro-Oesophageal Variceal Bleeding:

•  Pathogenesis: Defined as a Hepatic Venous Pressure Gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg; clinically significant portal hypertension occurs at HVPG >10 mmHg, and variceal bleeding risk rises above 12 mmHg. Caused by two mechanisms: (1) Increased intrahepatic vascular resistance (architectural distortion by fibrous nodules + dynamic sinusoidal constriction by stellate cells due to endothelin-1 and reduced intrahepatic nitric oxide); and (2) Increased portal venous inflow due to splanchnic arteriolar vasodilatation mediated by systemic nitric oxide (NO).

•  Classification of Portal Hypertension by Site:

•  Pre-hepatic (Pre-sinusoidal): Portal vein thrombosis, splenic vein thrombosis (pancreatitis).

•  Intrahepatic:Pre-sinusoidal (schistosomiasis, congenital hepatic fibrosis, sarcoidosis); Sinusoidal (cirrhosis—accounts for >90% in adults); Post-sinusoidal (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome / veno-occlusive disease).

•  Post-hepatic (Post-sinusoidal): Budd–Chiari syndrome, right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis.

•  Portosystemic Collateral Sites & Manifestations: Distal oesophagus and proximal stomach (oesophageal and gastric varices), stomach mucosa (portal hypertensive gastropathy causing chronic iron deficiency anaemia), umbilicus (caput medusae), anorectum (rectal varices), retroperitoneum, and stomal sites; plus splenomegaly with hypersplenism (thrombocytopenia/leucopenia).

•  B. Ascites & Refractory Ascites:

•  Pathogenesis: Portal hypertension triggers splanchnic arterial vasodilatation (mediated by nitric oxide), which causes arterial underfilling and a fall in effective systemic arterial blood volume. This activates baroreceptors, stimulating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), the sympathetic nervous system, and non-osmotic arginine vasopressin (ADH) release. The resulting renal sodium and water retention, combined with portal hypertension and reduced plasma oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminaemia), drives fluid transudation from splanchnic capillaries into the peritoneal cavity, overwhelming lymphatic return.

•  C. Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP):

•  Pathogenesis & Presentation: Translocation of enteric Gram-negative bacteria (most commonly Escherichia coli or Klebsiella) across the oedematous bowel wall into low-protein ascitic fluid. Presents with fever, abdominal pain, rebound tenderness, or unexplained hepatic encephalopathy / acute kidney injury; up to 1/3 have no abdominal signs.

•  Diagnosis:Diagnostic paracentesis showing an ascitic fluid neutrophil (PMN) count >250 × 106/L (>250 cells/mm3), plus ascitic fluid inoculated directly into blood culture bottles.

•  D. Hepatic Encephalopathy (HE):

•  Aetiopathogenesis: A reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by hepatocellular failure and portosystemic venous shunting. Gut-derived nitrogenous neurotoxins produced by colonic bacteria—principally ammonia (NH3), alongside γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), mercaptans, aromatic amino acids, and false neurotransmitters (octopamine)—bypass the cirrhotic liver and cross the blood–brain barrier, causing astrocyte swelling, cerebral oedema, and GABAergic neuro-inhibition.

•  Precipitating Factors of Hepatic Encephalopathy:

1.  Gastrointestinal haemorrhage (variceal or peptic ulcer bleed—high luminal protein load).

2.  Infection (especially Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis, UTI, pneumonia).

3.  Electrolyte & Fluid Disturbances:Hypokalaemia (increases renal ammonia production), hyponatraemia, metabolic alkalosis, and dehydration (from over-diuresis, paracentesis, vomiting, or diarrhoea).

4.  Constipation (prolongs colonic bacterial ammonia production and absorption).

5.  Drugs: Sedatives, benzodiazepines, opiates/narcotics, antidepressants, alcohol intoxication.

6.  Increased Portosystemic Shunting: TIPSS insertion or portal vein thrombosis.

7.  Acute Kidney Injury / Uraemia.

•  Clinical Features & West Haven Grading of Hepatic Encephalopathy:

•  Early features: Reversal of sleep–wake cycle (daytime somnolence, nocturnal insomnia), personality change, constructional apraxia (inability to draw a 5-pointed star or complete a number connection test), fetor hepaticus, and asterixis (flapping tremor). Later features: hyper-reflexia and bilateral extensor plantar responses.

•  Grade 1: Poor concentration, mild confusion, slurred speech, slow mentation, inverted sleep rhythm.

•  Grade 2: Drowsy but easily rousable, lethargy, disorientation in time, inappropriate/aggressive behaviour, asterixis (flapping tremor).

•  Grade 3: Marked delirium, somnolent/stuporose but rousable to voice/pain, gross disorientation, asterixis.

•  Grade 4:Coma (unresponsive to voice; may or may not respond to painful stimuli).

•  E. Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS):

•  Pathophysiology: Functional renal failure occurring in advanced cirrhosis with ascites in the absence of structural/parenchymal kidney disease. Profound splanchnic arterial vasodilatation leads to extreme activation of endogenous vasoconstrictor systems (RAAS, sympathetic nervous system, vasopressin), causing intense renal cortical arterial vasoconstriction and a sharp fall in GFR.

•  Classification:

•  HRS-AKI (formerly Type 1 HRS): Rapidly progressive acute kidney injury (↑ serum creatinine ≥ 26.5 µ mol/L [0.3 mg/dL] within 48 hours or ≥ 50% from baseline), often precipitated by SBP, GI bleeding, or alcoholic hepatitis. Poor short-term prognosis.

•  HRS-NAKI (formerly Type 2 HRS): Slowly progressive renal dysfunction associated with refractory ascites.

•  Diagnostic Criteria (International Ascites Club): (1) Cirrhosis with ascites; (2) Diagnosis of AKI; (3) No response after 2 consecutive daysof diuretic withdrawal and plasma volume expansion with IV albumin (1 g/kg/day, max 100 g); (4) Absence of shock; (5) No recent nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides); (6) Absence of parenchymal kidney disease (proteinuria <500 mg/day, microhaematuria <50 RBCs/HPF, and normal renal ultrasound).

•  F. Other Complications of Cirrhosis:

•  Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) (1%–8% annual incidence).

•  Hepatopulmonary Syndrome (HPS): Intrapulmonary vascular dilatation causing a right-to-left shunt, presenting with dyspnoea, clubbing, cyanosis, and platypnoea–orthodeoxia (arterial desaturation on standing upright).

•  Portopulmonary Hypertension: Pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction and obliteration in portal hypertension.

•  Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure (ACLF): Acute decompensation of cirrhosis with multi-organ failure and high 28-day mortality, triggered by alcoholic hepatitis or bacterial sepsis.

•  Cirrhotic Cardiomyopathy, Hepatic Hydrothorax (usually right-sided), Portal Vein Thrombosis, and Osteoporosis.

5. Investigations & Prognostic Scoring in Cirrhosis:

•  Haematology & Coagulation: FBC (normocytic anaemia of chronic disease, microcytic from GI blood loss, or macrocytic from alcohol/folate deficiency; thrombocytopenia and leucopenia from hypersplenism and low thrombopoietin); prolonged PT/INR.

•  Biochemistry: LFTs (raised bilirubin, low serum albumin, variably raised ALT/AST with AST > ALT, raised ALP/GGT); U&Es (dilutional hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, raised creatinine in HRS).

•  Aetiological Chronic Liver Disease Screen: HBsAg, anti-HCV antibody, autoantibodies (ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM-1, AMA), serum immunoglobulins (↑ IgA in ArLD/MASLD, ↑ IgG in AIH, ↑ IgM in PBC), serum ferritin and transferrin saturation (haemochromatosis), serum caeruloplasmin and 24-hr urinary copper (Wilson’s disease), and α1-antitrypsin level/phenotype.

•  Imaging & Fibrosis Assessment:

•  Abdominal Ultrasound with Doppler: Coarse, nodular liver contour with caudate/left lobe hypertrophy, splenomegaly, ascites, patency and direction of portal/hepatic vein flow, and 6-monthly HCC surveillance (alongside serum alpha-fetoprotein [AFP]).

•  Non-Invasive Fibrosis Staging:Transient Elastography (FibroScan), FIB-4 score, or Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) panel.

•  Upper GI Endoscopy: Screening for oesophageal and gastric varices and portal hypertensive gastropathy.

•  Diagnostic Ascitic Paracentesis: Check ascitic cell count/differential (PMNs >250/mm3 = SBP), albumin (to calculate SAAG ≥ 11 g/L), total protein, and culture in blood culture bottles.

•  Prognostic Scoring Systems:

•  Child–Pugh Classification: Scores 1 to 3 points for each of 5 parameters (Bilirubin, Albumin, PT prolongation/INR, Ascites, Encephalopathy — BAPAE): Class A (5–6 points), Class B (7–9 points), Class C (10–15 points).

•  MELD / MELD-Na / UKELD Score: Uses serum Creatinine, Bilirubin, INR, and Sodium to predict 3-month mortality and prioritise patients for liver transplantation (UKELD ≥ 49 or MELD ≥ 15).

6. Comprehensive Management of Cirrhosis and Its Complications:

•  A. General & Nutritional Management:

•  Treat the underlying cause (complete alcohol abstinence + thiamin in ArLD; entecavir/tenofovir in HBV; direct-acting antivirals in HCV; weight loss in MASLD).

•  Nutrition: Prevent sarcopenia with a high-protein (1.2–1.5 g/kg/day), high-calorie (35 kcal/kg/day) diet and a late-evening carbohydrate snack to prevent overnight catabolism. Do NOT restrict dietary protein in hepatic encephalopathy.

•  Avoid Hepatotoxic / Precipitating Drugs: Strictly avoid NSAIDs (precipitate HRS and variceal bleeding), ACE inhibitors, sedatives/benzodiazepines, and opiates.

•  B. Management of Varices & Acute Variceal Bleeding:

•  Primary Prophylaxis (Preventing First Bleed):Non-selective β-blocker (NSBB)—Carvedilol (6.25–12.5 mg/day) is the drug of choice (more effective than propranolol at lowering portal pressure and reducing decompensation). If NSBBs are contraindicated or not tolerated, perform endoscopic variceal band ligation (EVL) for medium/large varices.

•  Emergency Management of Acute Variceal Haemorrhage:

1.  Resuscitation & Airway Protection: Two large-bore IV cannulae, crystalloid fluids, and restrictive blood transfusion (transfuse packed RBCs when Hb <70 g/L, aiming for target 70–80 g/L; over-transfusion rebounds portal pressure and worsens rebleeding). Consider elective endotracheal intubation prior to endoscopy if massive haematemesis or encephalopathic.

2.  Immediate Vasoactive Pharmacotherapy (Start BEFORE Endoscopy):Terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4–6 hours until bleeding stops, then 1 mg IV every 4–6 hours for up to 72 hours (causes splanchnic vasoconstriction, lowering portal pressure and mortality; alternative: IV Octreotide infusion).

3.  Mandatory Prophylactic Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics:IV Ceftriaxone (1 g/day) or Piperacillin–Tazobactam for 5–7 days; significantly reduces bacterial infections (SBP), early rebleeding, and mortality.

4.  Urgent Therapeutic Endoscopy (within 12 hours):

•  Oesophageal Varices:Endoscopic Variceal Band Ligation (EVL) is the treatment of first choice (stops bleeding in >90%).

•  Gastric Varices: Endoscopic intravariceal injection of cyanoacrylate tissue glue or thrombin (or EUS-guided coiling).

1.  Rescue Therapy for Uncontrolled / Refractory Bleeding:

•  Balloon Tamponade (Minnesota or Sengstaken–Blakemore tube): Temporary bridge (max 24 hours; inflate gastric balloon with 200–250 mL air and apply traction) or a removable self-expanding covered metal oesophageal stent, while arranging definitive Emergency TIPSS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Stent Shunt).

1.  Prevention of Post-Bleed Encephalopathy: Administer lactulose and/or phosphate enemas to clear luminal blood.

•  Secondary Prophylaxis (Preventing Rebleeding): Combine Carvedilol (or propranolol) PLUS repeated Endoscopic Band Ligation every 2–4 weeks until varices are obliterated. Consider early pre-emptive TIPSS within 72 hours in high-risk Child–Pugh B/C patients.

•  C. Management of Ascites & Refractory Ascites:

•  Dietary Sodium Restriction: No-added-salt diet (80–100 mmol/day Na+). Fluid restriction (1.0–1.5 L/day) is required only if severe dilutional hyponatraemia (Na+ <125 mmol/L) is present.

•  Diuretic Therapy: First-line is the aldosterone antagonist Spironolactone (100 mg/day, stepped up to 400 mg/day) (substitute amiloride or eplerenone if painful gynaecomastia occurs), combined with loop diuretic Furosemide (40 mg/day, stepped up to 160 mg/day). Aim for weight loss of ≤ 0.5 kg/day (without peripheral oedema) or ≤ 1.0 kg/day (with oedema); monitor U&Es closely.

•  Management of Refractory Ascites (diuretic-resistant or diuretic-intolerant due to hyponatraemia/AKI):

1.  Large-Volume Paracentesis (LVP): First-line treatment; drain ascites to dryness with mandatory IV Human Albumin Solution (HAS) replacement (6–8 g of albumin per litre of ascitic fluid removed, i.e., 100 mL of 20% HAS per 2–3 L drained) to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction and HRS.

2.  TIPSS Insertion: Decompresses the portal system and resolves refractory ascites (contraindicated if severe hepatic encephalopathy or poor synthetic function).

3.  Liver Transplantation: Definitive treatment (development of ascites carries a 50% 2-year mortality).

•  D. Management of Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP):

•  Immediate empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (Cefotaxime or Ceftriaxone or Piperacillin–Tazobactam) PLUS IV Albumin infusion (1.5 g/kg on Day 1 and 1.0 g/kg on Day 3), which prevents HRS and halves mortality.

•  Secondary Prophylaxis: Life-long Norfloxacin (400 mg daily) or Co-trimoxazole (960 mg daily) (also used as primary prophylaxis if ascitic protein is <15 g/L with advanced cirrhosis).

•  E. Management of Hepatic Encephalopathy:

•  Identify and treat the precipitating factor (stop diuretics/sedatives, treat infection/SBP, correct hypokalaemia, arrest GI bleeding). Protect the airway with endotracheal intubation if GCS ≤ 8 (Grade 3–4 HE).

•  Lactulose (Non-absorbable disaccharide): Titrate (15–30 mL orally 2–3 times daily) to achieve 2–3 soft stools per day. Mechanism: Osmotic catharsis clears gut toxins, and colonic bacteria ferment lactulose to lactic/acetic acid, acidifying the colonic lumen and converting absorbable NH3 into non-absorbable ammonium ions (NH4+). Use phosphate enemas in comatose patients.

•  Rifaximin (550 mg orally twice daily): Non-absorbable antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing colonic flora; added to lactulose to prevent recurrent episodes of HE.

•  Adjuncts: L-ornithine L-aspartate (LOLA). Refer for liver transplantation if persistent/recurrent.

•  F. Management of Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS-AKI):

•  Stop all diuretics, β-blockers, and nephrotoxic drugs; exclude and treat sepsis.

•  Pharmacotherapy of Choice:IV Terlipressin (1–2 mg every 4–6 hours) PLUS IV Human Albumin (1 g/kg on Day 1, then 20–40 g/day) (alternatives: IV Noradrenaline in ICU, or oral Midodrine + SC Octreotide + Albumin).

•  Renal Replacement Therapy (Haemodialysis) & Liver Transplantation for non-responders.

title: 5. Steatotic Liver Disease: Alcohol-Related Liver Disease (ArLD) and Metabolic Dysfunction–Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD / NAFLD) [KU 20, 18, TU, RGU]
text:
5. Steatotic Liver Disease: Alcohol-Related Liver Disease (ArLD) and Metabolic Dysfunction–Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD / NAFLD) [KU 20, 18, TU, RGU]

1. Spectrum & Classification of Steatotic Liver Disease:

•  Steatotic liver disease encompasses a pathological continuum:

Simple Steatosis (Fatty Liver) ⟶ Steatohepatitis ⟶ Progressive Hepatic Fibrosis ⟶ Cirrhosis & Hepatocellular Carcinoma

•  Genetic Susceptibility: Strongly influenced in both ArLD and MASLD by the I148M polymorphism in the PNPLA3 (adiponutrin) gene.

•  Updated 2023 Nomenclature:

•  MASLD (Metabolic Dysfunction–Associated Steatotic Liver Disease)(formerly NAFLD): Hepatic steatosis in the presence of ≥ 1 cardiometabolic risk factor (central obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypertriglyceridaemia, low HDL) and low alcohol intake (<20 g/day in women, <30 g/day in men). Its inflammatory form is MASH(formerly NASH).

•  Met-ALD: Cardiometabolic risk factors combined with moderate-to-heavy alcohol intake (20–50 g/day in women, 30–60 g/day in men).

•  ArLD (Alcohol-Related Liver Disease): Intake >50 g/day in women or >60 g/day in men. (1 UK unit = 8 g ethanol; safe limit <14 units/week).

2. Pathogenesis of Alcohol-Related Liver Disease (ArLD):

•  Pathway 1 — Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH) (80%): Cytosolic ADH oxidises ethanol to acetaldehyde, which mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) converts to acetate. Both steps reduce NAD+ to NADH. The high NADH/NAD+ ratio inhibits mitochondrial β-oxidation of fatty acids and upregulates SREBP-1, driving de novo fatty acid synthesis and macrovesicular steatosis.

•  Pathway 2 — Microsomal Ethanol-Oxidising System (MEOS / CYP2E1) (20%): Inducible CYP2E1 oxidises ethanol to acetaldehyde while generating reactive oxygen species (ROS), causing lipid peroxidation, glutathione depletion, and mitochondrial damage (also predisposes heavy drinkers to paracetamol hepatotoxicity).

•  Direct Acetaldehyde Toxicity & Gut–Liver Axis: Acetaldehyde forms immunogenic protein/DNA adducts. Alcohol also increases intestinal permeability, allowing translocation of gut-derived endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide / PAMPs) into the portal vein, which activates Kupffer cells via Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) to release TNF-α, IL-1, IL-8 (neutrophil chemotaxis), and TGF-β (stellate cell fibrogenesis).

3. Clinical Syndromes of Alcohol-Related Liver Disease:

•  A. Alcohol-Related Hepatic Steatosis (Fatty Liver): Present in >90% of heavy drinkers; usually asymptomatic with mild hepatomegaly, raised GGT/MCV, and a "bright" echogenic liver on ultrasound. Completely reversible within 3 months of abstinence.

•  B. Acute Alcoholic Hepatitis:

•  Clinical Presentation: Rapid-onset jaundice, fever, anorexia, tender hepatomegaly, and features of SIRS or decompensation (ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleed) following a bout of heavy drinking.

•  Histology: Ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes, Mallory–Denk hyaline bodies, polymorphonuclear neutrophil infiltration, and pericellular/"chicken-wire" perivenular fibrosis.

•  Laboratory Profile: Leucocytosis (neutrophilia), hyperbilirubinaemia, prolonged PT/INR, and only modestly elevated transaminases (<300 U/L) with a classic AST/ALT ratio > 2.0.

•  C. Alcohol-Related Cirrhosis: Develops in 10%–20% of chronic heavy drinkers; presents with florid stigmata (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, Dupuytren’s contracture, parotid swelling) and portal hypertensive decompensation. (Note: In an alcoholic patient admitted with haematemesis who develops generalised seizures and abnormal behaviour after 24–48 hours, the primary cause of seizures is acute alcohol withdrawal / delirium tremens, with differential diagnoses including hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, Wernicke encephalopathy, subdural haematoma, and hepatic encephalopathy).

4. Poor Prognostic Factors & Severity Scoring in Alcoholic Hepatitis:

•  Maddrey’s Modified Discriminant Function (mDF):

mDF = 4.6 × [Patient PT - Control PT (seconds)] + Serum Bilirubin (mg/dL)

•  An mDF ≥ 32 defines severe alcoholic hepatitis (carrying a 15%–40% 28-day mortality).

•  Glasgow Alcoholic Hepatitis Score (GAHS):

•  Scores 5 variables (Age ≥ 50, WBC ≥ 15 × 109/L, Urea ≥ 5 mmol/L, PT ratio ≥ 1.5–2.0, and Bilirubin >125–250 µ mol/L).

•  A GAHS ≥ 9 predicts a very poor prognosis (60% 28-day mortality) and identifies patients who benefit from corticosteroid therapy.

•  Lille Score (Day 7): Failure of serum bilirubin to fall after 7 days of prednisolone indicates steroid non-response and poor prognosis (stop steroids).

5. Management of ArLD & MASLD:

•  Management of ArLD & Acute Alcoholic Hepatitis:

1.  Complete, life-long abstinence from alcohol (supported by addiction services, acamprosate, or baclofen).

2.  Prevention & Treatment of Alcohol Withdrawal & Wernicke Encephalopathy: Administer parenteral Thiamin (Vitamin B1, Pabrinex IV) for 48–72 hours before giving any IV glucose, plus symptom-triggered oral benzodiazepines (e.g., chlordiazepoxide or diazepam; use short-acting lorazepam or oxazepam if severe liver failure is present to avoid oversedation).

3.  Aggressive Nutritional Support: High-calorie, high-protein enteral feeding (via fine-bore NG tube if anorexic).

4.  Corticosteroids in Severe Alcoholic Hepatitis (mDF ≥ 32 or GAHS ≥ 9): Once active sepsis and GI bleeding are excluded, give Oral Prednisolone 40 mg daily (± IV N-acetylcysteine for 5 days). Reassess bilirubin at Day 7: if bilirubin has not fallen, discontinue prednisolone to avoid fatal fungal/bacterial sepsis; if responding, continue for 28 days. (Pentoxifylline is ineffective, as shown by the STOPAH trial).

5.  Liver Transplantation: Considered in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis after a period of sustained abstinence and multidisciplinary psychosocial evaluation.

•  Assessment & Management of MASLD / NAFLD:

•  Risk Stratification: Screen at-risk patients (T2DM, obesity, metabolic syndrome) using the FIB-4 score (Age, AST, ALT, Platelets). If FIB-4 is <1.3, advanced fibrosis is excluded; if indeterminate (1.3–2.67) or high (>2.67), perform Transient Elastography (FibroScan) or the Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) blood test.

•  Lifestyle Modification (Cornerstone):Sustained weight loss of 7%–10% via a Mediterranean-style calorie-restricted diet, avoidance of fructose/sugar-sweetened drinks, regular aerobic/resistance exercise, and alcohol avoidance resolves steatohepatitis and regresses fibrosis.

•  Pharmacological & Surgical Therapy: Aggressively treat cardiometabolic risk factors (statins are safe and beneficial in MASLD; GLP-1 receptor agonists [semaglutide, liraglutide], SGLT2 inhibitors, and pioglitazone improve MASH in patients with diabetes/obesity). Resmetirom (selective thyroid hormone receptor-β agonist) is the first FDA-approved drug specifically shown to resolve MASH and improve liver fibrosis. Bariatric surgery is effective in morbid obesity.

title: 6. Viral Hepatitis (A, B, C, D, E): Clinical Features, Serology, Natural History, Management, and Fulminant Hepatitis [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 19, 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 21.4 — INFECTIONS AND THE LIVER

6. Viral Hepatitis (A, B, C, D, E): Clinical Features, Serology, Natural History, Management, and Fulminant Hepatitis [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 19, 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]

•  (Covers the clinical vignette Essay on a 40-year-old non-alcoholic female presenting with acute jaundice, dark urine, vomiting, and right hypochondrial pain = Acute Viral Hepatitis).

1. Overview of the Main Hepatitis Viruses:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-011]]

2. Clinical Features, Investigations, Treatment & Prevention of Acute Viral Hepatitis (e.g., Hepatitis A / E / Acute B):

•  Clinical Phases:

1.  Prodromal (Pre-icteric) Phase (days to 2 weeks): Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, low-grade fever, distaste for cigarettes, and dull right upper quadrant abdominal pain (due to stretching of Glisson’s capsule).

2.  Icteric Phase (3–6 weeks): Passage of dark urine (conjugated bilirubinuria) and pale stools, followed by scleral icterus (jaundice) (systemic prodromal symptoms often improve as jaundice appears). Examination reveals mild, tender hepatomegaly, with splenomegaly and cervical lymphadenopathy in 10%–20%.

3.  Convalescent Phase: Complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 3–6 weeks in the vast majority.

•  Complications of Acute Viral Hepatitis:

•  Acute / Fulminant Liver Failure (<1% overall, up to 20% in pregnant women with HEV).

•  Cholestatic hepatitis (prolonged jaundice and pruritus with high ALP, especially in HAV).

•  Relapsing hepatitis and Post-hepatitis syndrome (protracted fatigue).

•  Aplastic anaemia (rare, severe complication).

•  Progression to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HBV, HCV, HDV only; never HAV or immunocompetent HEV).

•  Extrahepatic immune-complex syndromes: Polyarteritis nodosa and membranous glomerulonephritis (HBV); mixed cryoglobulinaemia and porphyria cutanea tarda (HCV); Guillain–Barré syndrome and neuralgic amyotrophy (HEV).

•  Confirming the Diagnosis (Investigations):

•  Liver Biochemistry: Markedly elevated serum ALT and AST (500–2000+ U/L), mixed hyperbilirubinaemia, mildly raised ALP (<2× ULN), and normal albumin. Check Prothrombin Time (PT/INR) twice daily if severe, as progressive PT prolongation heralds acute liver failure.

•  Haematology: Normal or low WBC count with relative lymphocytosis.

•  Specific Viral Serology:Anti-HAV IgM (diagnostic of acute Hepatitis A; IgG indicates past infection/immunity), Anti-HEV IgM (± HEV RNA PCR), HBsAg and Anti-HBc IgM (diagnostic of acute Hepatitis B), and Anti-HCV antibodies + HCV RNA PCR.

•  Abdominal Ultrasound: Confirms smooth hepatomegaly and excludes biliary obstruction.

•  Treatment & Prevention of Acute Viral Hepatitis (HAV / HEV):

•  Supportive Management: Rest as needed, maintain hydration and nutrition, strictly avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic/sedative drugs (paracetamol, narcotics, benzodiazepines), and monitor PT/INR and sensorium for signs of acute liver failure. Antiviral therapy is not required for HAV or uncomplicated acute HBV.

•  Prevention: Improved sanitation, safe drinking water, and hand hygiene. Active immunisation with inactivated Hepatitis A vaccine (2 doses 6–12 months apart) and recombinant Hepatitis B vaccine. Passive immunisation with intramuscular human normal immunoglobulin (for close contacts of HAV within 14 days) or Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin (HBIg) (for HBV exposure).

title: 7. Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) Infection: Serology, Natural History, Prophylaxis, and Treatment [KU 25, 24, 23, 21, 17, 16, TU]
text:
7. Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) Infection: Serology, Natural History, Prophylaxis, and Treatment [KU 25, 24, 23, 21, 17, 16, TU]

1. Serological & Virological Markers of Hepatitis B:

•  HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen): Appears 1–10 weeks after exposure; main marker of active infection. Persistence for >6 months defines chronic HBV infection.

•  Anti-HBs (Antibody to HBsAg): Appears after clearance of HBsAg; confers protective immunity. Isolated Anti-HBs positivity (with negative Anti-HBc) indicates vaccine-induced immunity; Anti-HBs + Anti-HBc IgG indicates past resolved natural infection.

•  Anti-HBc (Antibody to HBcAg core):

•  Anti-HBc IgM: Marker of acute HBV infection (and the sole marker during the "window period" in fulminant HBV when HBsAg has already been cleared).

•  Anti-HBc IgG: Persists for life in anyone ever infected with HBV (both chronic and resolved).

•  HBeAg (Hepatitis B e antigen): Secreted viral protein indicating active viral replication and high infectivity.

•  Anti-HBe (Antibody to HBeAg): Indicates seroconversion to a lower replicative state (unless a pre-core / core promoter mutant is present, which cannot secrete HBeAg despite high viral replication).

•  HBV-DNA (by Quantitative PCR): Directly measures viral load in blood; essential for staging  and monitoring antiviral treatment response.

2. Natural History: The Five Phases of Chronic Hepatitis B Infection:

1.  Phase 1: HBeAg-Positive Chronic Infection (formerly "Immune-Tolerant"):

•  HBsAg+, HBeAg+, very high HBV-DNA (>107 IU/mL), normal ALT, and normal/minimal liver histology. Prolonged (10–30 years) in perinatally infected individuals; highly infectious.

2.  Phase 2: HBeAg-Positive Chronic Hepatitis (formerly "Immune-Reactive / Clearance"):

•  HBsAg+, HBeAg+, elevated HBV-DNA (104–107 IU/mL), raised ALT, and moderate-to-severe necroinflammation and fibrosis on biopsy/elastography. Sustained immune attack leads to cirrhosis if HBeAg seroconversion is delayed.

3.  Phase 3: HBeAg-Negative Chronic Infection (formerly "Inactive Carrier"):

•  HBsAg+, HBeAg-, Anti-HBe+, low or undetectable HBV-DNA (<2000 IU/mL), normal ALT, and minimal histological activity. Low risk of cirrhosis/HCC.

4.  Phase 4: HBeAg-Negative Chronic Hepatitis (Pre-Core / Core Promoter Mutant):

•  HBsAg+, HBeAg-, Anti-HBe+, moderate-to-high fluctuating HBV-DNA (>2000 IU/mL), raised/fluctuating ALT, and active necroinflammation. Driven by mutations in the pre-core/core promoter region that abolish HBeAg synthesis while maintaining viral replication; carries the highest annual rate of progression to cirrhosis (8%–10%/year) and HCC.

5.  Phase 5: HBsAg-Negative (Occult HBV) Phase:

•  HBsAg-, Anti-HBc IgG+ (± Anti-HBs+), undetectable serum HBV-DNA, normal ALT, but intrahepatic cccDNA persists in hepatocyte nuclei. Severe immunosuppression (e.g., rituximab or high-dose chemotherapy) can trigger fatal HBV reactivation, requiring prophylactic antivirals.

3. Management & Newer Drugs for Chronic Hepatitis B:

•  Indications for Antiviral Treatment: All patients in the "Hepatitis" phases (Phase 2 and Phase 4) with HBV-DNA >2000 IU/mL accompanied by raised ALT and/or significant fibrosis (Transient Elastography >7–9 kPa or biopsy ≥ F2); all patients with compensated or decompensated cirrhosis with any detectable HBV-DNA; pregnant women with high viral load (>200,000 IU/mL) in the 3rd trimester; and patients undergoing rituximab/immunosuppressive therapy.

•  First-Line Oral Direct-Acting Nucleos(t)ide Analogues (Potent, High Genetic Barrier to Resistance):

•  (Inhibit HBV polymerase reverse transcription of pre-genomic RNA to HBV-DNA; do not eradicate nuclear cccDNA, so therapy is usually long-term/indefinite):

1.  Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF, 245 mg OD) or Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF, 25 mg OD): Nucleotide analogues; virtually zero antiviral resistance. TAF has superior renal and bone safety compared to TDF.

2.  Entecavir (0.5 mg OD; 1.0 mg OD in lamivudine-experienced): Nucleoside analogue; potent viral suppression and very low resistance rate (<1% in treatment-naive).

•  (Older drugs like Lamivudine, Adefovir, and Telbivudine are no longer used first-line due to high rates of YMDD polymerase resistance mutations).

•  Pegylated Interferon-alfa (PEG-IFN-α, 180 µg SC weekly for 48 weeks): Finite duration immunomodulatory therapy; achieves ∼ 30% HBeAg seroconversion and 3%–5% HBsAg loss in selected young patients with Genotype A/B, low viral load, and high ALT, but has significant side-effects and is contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis.

•  Newer / Emerging Agents for Functional Cure (HBsAg Loss):Bepirovirsen (an antisense oligonucleotide targeting all HBV mRNAs), small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), and capsid assembly modulators. (Bulevirtide is a novel entry inhibitor targeting the NTCP receptor, approved for HBV/HDV co-infection).

4. Hepatitis B Vaccination Schedule & Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP):

•  Vaccination Schedule (Recombinant HBsAg Vaccine — Engerix-B):

•  Standard Schedule:0, 1, and 6 months intramuscularly into the deltoid (3 doses).

•  Accelerated Schedule (for PEP, travellers, or high-risk groups):0, 1, and 2 months (or Day 0, 7, and 21), with a mandatory 4th booster dose at 12 months.

•  Check Response: Measure anti-HBs titre 1–2 months after completion in healthcare workers and renal dialysis patients (protective titre >10–100 mIU/mL).

•  Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (Needlestick Injury, Mucocutaneous Exposure, Sexual Contact, or Neonates of HBsAg+ Mothers):

•  Wash wound with soap and water; test source patient for HBsAg and recipient for HBsAg and Anti-HBs.

•  Unvaccinated Recipient or Non-Responder (Anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL) Exposed to HBsAg+ Source: Administer Active–Passive Immunisation immediately (ideally within 24–48 hours, up to 7 days):

1.  Specific Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin (HBIg) (500 IU IM for adults; 200 IU IM for neonates at birth) at one anatomical site.

2.  Accelerated Recombinant Hepatitis B Vaccine (Day 0, 1 month, 2 months, 12 months) injected into the contralateral deltoid (anterolateral thigh in neonates).

•  Previously Vaccinated Known Responder (Anti-HBs >10 mIU/mL): Reassure or give a single booster dose of HBV vaccine (HBIg is not required).

title: 8. Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Infection & Newer Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs) [KU 22, TU, RGU]
text:
8. Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Infection & Newer Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs) [KU 22, TU, RGU]

Natural History & Clinical Features:

•  Acute infection is usually subclinical/asymptomatic. 70%–80% of exposed individuals develop chronic HCV infection.

•  Over 20–30 years, 20% of chronically infected patients progress to cirrhosis (accelerated by alcohol, male sex, obesity/MASLD, and HIV/HBV co-infection), with an annual HCC risk of 3%–5% once cirrhosis is established.

•  Risk Factors: Intravenous drug use (95% of new cases in the West), unscreened blood transfusions prior to 1991, contaminated medical needles, tattooing, needlestick injury (3% risk), and vertical/sexual transmission (low risk unless HIV co-infected).

Diagnosis:

1.  Screening Test:Serum Anti-HCV IgG Antibodies (by ELISA; takes 6–12 weeks to seroconvert after acute exposure and remains positive for life even after cure).

2.  Confirmatory Test for Active Infection:Quantitative Serum HCV RNA by PCR (or HCV core antigen).

3.  Fibrosis Staging & Genotype: Assess liver fibrosis non-invasively using FIB-4, APRI, or Transient Elastography (FibroScan), and determine viral genotype (1–6; Genotypes 1 and 3 are most common).

Management: Newer Direct-Acting Antiviral Agents (DAAs):

•  Goal of Therapy: Eradicate the virus in all patients with active HCV infection, defined by a Sustained Virological Response (SVR12)—undetectable serum HCV RNA 12 weeks after completing treatment. SVR12 is achieved in >95% of patients with an 8- to 12-week course of oral, interferon-free DAAs and equates to a permanent virological cure.

•  Four Classes of Direct-Acting Antivirals (by Viral Life-Cycle Target):

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-012]]

•  Standard Pan-Genotypic Single-Tablet Regimens (Effective Across All Genotypes 1–6):

•  Sofosbuvir + Velpatasvir (Epclusa): Once daily for 12 weeks (safe in decompensated cirrhosis, combined with ribavirin).

•  Glecaprevir + Pibrentasvir (Maviret): Once daily for 8 weeks in non-cirrhotic patients.

•  Sofosbuvir + Velpatasvir + Voxilaprevir (Vosevi): Salvage therapy for DAA failures (12 weeks).
