title: 9. Acute (Fulminant) Liver Failure & Drug-Induced Liver Injury [KU 19, RGU]
text:
9. Acute (Fulminant) Liver Failure & Drug-Induced Liver Injury [KU 19, RGU]

1. Acute (Fulminant) Liver Failure (ALF):

•  Definition: A rare, life-threatening syndrome characterised by a rapid, severe deterioration in liver function resulting in jaundice, coagulopathy (INR >1.5), and hepatic encephalopathy within 12 weeks of symptom onset in a patient without pre-existing chronic liver disease.

•  O’Grady Subclassification (by Interval from Jaundice to Encephalopathy):

•  Hyperacute (<7 days):Cerebral oedema is common; caused by Paracetamol overdose and Hepatitis A and E; best spontaneous survival with medical care.

•  Acute (8–28 days): Cerebral oedema is common; caused by Hepatitis B, drugs, or cryptogenic.

•  Subacute (29 days to  12 weeks): Cerebral oedema is uncommon, ascites/splenomegaly may develop; caused by idiosyncratic drug reactions, seronegative/cryptogenic hepatitis, or autoimmune hepatitis; worst spontaneous survival without transplantation.

•  Causes of Acute Liver Failure:

•  Drugs & Toxins (70%–80% in the UK/West):Paracetamol overdose (most common in the West), idiosyncratic drug reactions (anti-tuberculous drugs [isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide], halothane, NSAIDs, phenytoin, valproate, ecstasy/MDMA, herbal remedies), Amanita phalloides mushroom poisoning.

•  Viral Infections (Most common worldwide):Hepatitis A, B (± D), and E (especially in pregnancy); rarely HSV, CMV, EBV.

•  Vascular, Metabolic & Others:Acute Wilson’s disease (presents in young adults with Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia and low ALP), Acute Budd–Chiari syndrome, Ischaemic hepatitis ("shock liver"), Acute fatty liver of pregnancy / HELLP syndrome, Autoimmune hepatitis, and malignant infiltration.

•  Clinical Features & Complications:

•  Hepatic Encephalopathy (Grades 1–4) & Cerebral Oedema / Intracranial Hypertension: Unequal or dilated sluggish pupils, systemic hypertension with bradycardia (Cushing’s reflex), hyperventilation, myoclonus, seizures, decerebrate posturing, and brainstem coning.

•  Profound Coagulopathy: Prolonged PT/INR and Factor V deficiency.

•  Metabolic: Severe hypoglycaemia (loss of hepatic gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis) and lactic metabolic acidosis.

•  Renal Failure (ATN or HRS), Hypotension / Multi-organ failure, and Bacterial (80%) or Fungal (30%) Sepsis.

•  King’s College Hospital Adverse Prognostic Criteria (Indications for Emergency Liver Transplantation):

•  In Paracetamol-Induced ALF:

•  Arterial pH < 7.30 (or <7.25) at ≥ 24 hours after overdose following fluid resuscitation; OR

•  Arterial lactate >3.5 mmol/L at presentation or >3.0 mmol/L after fluid resuscitation; OR

•  All three of: Prothrombin Time >100 seconds (INR >6.5) + Serum Creatinine >300 µ mol/L (>3.4 mg/dL) + Grade 3 or 4 Encephalopathy.

•  In Non-Paracetamol ALF:

•  Prothrombin Time >100 seconds (INR >6.5) (irrespective of encephalopathy grade); OR

•  Any three of the following five variables: (1) Age <10 or >40 years; (2) Unfavourable aetiology (idiosyncratic drug reaction, seronegative hepatitis, Wilson’s disease); (3) Interval from jaundice to encephalopathy >7 days; (4) PT >50 seconds (INR >3.5); (5) Serum Bilirubin >300 µ mol/L (>17.6 mg/dL).

•  Management of Acute Liver Failure:

•  Admit to ICU; intubate and mechanically ventilate for Grade 3–4 encephalopathy.

•  Early IV N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) infusion: Mandatory in all paracetamol overdoses and also improves transplant-free survival in early non-paracetamol ALF.

•  Prevent & Treat Hypoglycaemia: Monitor blood glucose 2-hourly and infuse 10%–20% intravenous dextrose.

•  Manage Intracranial Hypertension: Nurse head-up at 30°, avoid jugular venous compression, sedate with propofol, maintain serum sodium 145–150 mmol/L with hypertonic (3%) saline or IV mannitol (0.5–1.0 g/kg) boluses.

•  Coagulopathy: Give IV Vitamin K (10 mg), but do NOT give fresh frozen plasma (FFP) unless there is active bleeding, as PT/INR is essential for monitoring prognosis and transplant listing.

•  Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungals, continuous renal replacement therapy (haemofiltration) for AKI/acidosis, high-volume therapeutic plasma exchange (PLEX), and urgent transfer for Emergency Orthotopic Liver Transplantation.

2. Drugs Causing Hepatitis / Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI):

•  Hepatocellular Necrosis (Hepatitic Pattern):Paracetamol (dose-dependent intrinsic toxicity), Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Diclofenac, Sertraline, Halothane, Methyldopa, Ketoconazole, MDMA (ecstasy).

•  Cholestatic / Mixed Hepatitis:Co-amoxiclav (most common antibiotic cause; can cause vanishing bile duct syndrome), Flucloxacillin, Chlorpromazine, Erythromycin, Oral contraceptive pill / Oestrogens and Anabolic steroids (pure canalicular cholestasis), Carbimazole, Carbamazepine, Terbinafine, Statins.

•  Steatohepatitis / Microvesicular Steatosis:Sodium valproate, Tetracyclines, Aspirin (Reye’s syndrome), Amiodarone, Tamoxifen.

•  Chronic Hepatic Fibrosis:Methotrexate.

•  Autoimmune Hepatitis-Like Injury:Nitrofurantoin, Minocycline, Methyldopa, Immune checkpoint inhibitors (nivolumab, pembrolizumab).

•  Vascular (Sinusoidal Obstruction Syndrome): Busulfan, Cyclophosphamide, Azathioprine.

subject: medicine
title: 10. Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH) and Wilson’s Disease [RGU, TU]
text:
SECTION 21.7, 21.8, 21.9 & 21.10 — AUTOIMMUNE, METABOLIC, VASCULAR, TUMOURS & BILIARY DISEASE

10. Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH) and Wilson’s Disease [RGU, TU]

A. Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH):

•  Definition & Associations: Immune-mediated necroinflammatory disease of hepatocytes, predominantly affecting women (F:M = 5:1) with a bimodal age peak (2nd and 6th decades). Associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 and other autoimmune disorders (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, Type 1 DM, coeliac disease, Sjögren’s syndrome, ulcerative colitis, vitiligo).

•  Clinical Presentation: Ranges from asymptomatic raised transaminases or insidious fatigue, anorexia, and arthralgia to an acute icteric hepatitis (25%) or fulminant liver failure. Cirrhosis is present at diagnosis in 25%.

•  Serological Classification & Investigations:

•  Markedly raised ALT and AST with polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia, specifically markedly elevated Serum IgG.

•  Type 1 AIH (80%, young/middle-aged women): Positive Antinuclear Antibodies (ANA) (homogeneous pattern) and/or Anti-Smooth Muscle Antibodies (ASMA / anti-actin) (± anti-SLA [soluble liver antigen]).

•  Type 2 AIH (children and young adults, more aggressive): Positive Anti-Liver–Kidney Microsomal type 1 (anti-LKM-1) antibodies (directed against cytochrome P450 2D6).

•  Liver Biopsy (Mandatory to confirm diagnosis): Shows interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis) with a dense portal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate (plasma cell–rich) extending across the limiting plate into the lobule, hepatocyte rosetting, and variable bridging fibrosis.

•  Management:

•  Induction of Remission:Oral Prednisolone (30–40 mg/day) (or Budesonide 9 mg/day in non-cirrhotic patients), gradually tapered as transaminases and IgG normalise.

•  Maintenance of Remission:Azathioprine (1–2 mg/kg/day) introduced once bilirubin improves, continued for at least 3 years (often life-long due to high relapse rates). Mycophenolate mofetil or Tacrolimus are second-line options.

B. Wilson’s Disease (Hepatolenticular Degeneration):

•  Genetics & Pathophysiology: Autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13 (encoding a hepatocyte P-type ATPase copper transporter). Defective ATP7B results in: (1) failure of biliary copper excretion, causing toxic copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia (lentiform nucleus), corneas, and kidneys; and (2) failure to incorporate copper into apocaeruloplasmin, resulting in low circulating caeruloplasmin levels.

•  Clinical Features (Presents between ages 5 and 45 years):

1.  Hepatic Disease (Childhood / Early Adolescence): Asymptomatic transaminitis, recurrent acute hepatitis, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or fulminant liver failure accompanied by massive Coombs-negative intravascular haemolytic anaemia (due to sudden release of free copper from necrotic hepatocytes).

2.  Neurological & Psychiatric Disease (Late Adolescence / Young Adulthood):Extrapyramidal movement disorders (asymmetrical tremor, "wing-beating" proximal tremor, parkinsonism, dystonia, choreoathetosis, dysarthria, dysphagia, drooling, "risus sardonicus" facial grimacing), cognitive decline, personality changes, depression, and psychosis.

3.  Ocular:Kayser–Fleischer (KF) Rings—greenish-brown copper deposits in Descemet’s membrane at the corneal periphery (superior pole first), best visualised by slit-lamp examination (present in 60% of hepatic cases and >95% of neurological cases); and sunflower cataracts.

4.  Renal & Skeletal: Renal Fanconi syndrome (aminoaciduria, glycosuria, proximal renal tubular acidosis), nephrolithiasis, and osteoporosis/arthropathy.

•  Investigations:

•  Low Serum Caeruloplasmin (<0.20 g/L).

•  Elevated 24-Hour Urinary Copper Excretion (>1.6 µ mol/24 hrs / >100 µ g/24 hrs; enhanced further by a D-penicillamine challenge test).

•  Elevated Free (Non-caeruloplasmin-bound) Serum Copper (though total serum copper is low).

•  Slit-lamp eye examination for Kayser–Fleischer rings.

•  Liver Biopsy with Quantitative Hepatic Copper Measurement (Gold Standard): Hepatic parenchymal copper content >250 µ g/g dry weight.

•  MRI Brain: Symmetric T2 hyperintensity in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem ("face of the giant panda" sign in the midbrain).

•  Management:

•  Copper-Chelating Agents (First-Line):D-Penicillamine (750–1500 mg/day in divided doses, co-prescribed with pyridoxine [vitamin B6] 25 mg/day; monitor urinary copper output and FBC/urine protein for side-effects like lupus-like syndrome, marrow suppression, or nephropathy) OR Trientine (better tolerated chelator).

•  Oral Zinc Salts (Zinc acetate/sulphate): Induces intestinal enterocyte metallothionein, which binds dietary copper and prevents its absorption into the portal blood; used for maintenance or in presymptomatic/pregnant patients.

•  Important Rule: Treatment must be continued for life (including during pregnancy); abrupt discontinuation precipitates fatal acute liver failure. Emergency Liver Transplantation is curative in fulminant Wilsonian liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis. Screen all siblings.

subject: medicine
title: 11. Budd–Chiari Syndrome [KU 23, TU]
text:
11. Budd–Chiari Syndrome [KU 23, TU]

Definition & Aetiology:

•  Budd–Chiari syndrome is hepatic venous outflow obstruction caused by thrombosis or occlusion at any level from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava (IVC) and right atrium.

•  Causes (Identified in >70%):

•  Haematological / Myeloproliferative Disorders (Most common):Polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia, myelofibrosis (test for JAK2 V617F mutation in all patients), and Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria (PNH).

•  Inherited & Acquired Thrombophilias: Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A, Protein C, Protein S, or Antithrombin III deficiency, Antiphospholipid syndrome, Behçet’s disease.

•  Hormonal:Pregnancy and oral contraceptive pill use.

•  Mechanical / Local: Tumour invasion/compression (hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, adrenal carcinoma) and congenital membranous webs of the IVC.

Clinical Features:

•  Classic Clinical Triad:Abdominal pain (right upper quadrant) + Tender Hepatomegaly + Gross Ascites.

•  Acute Fulminant Form: Sudden occlusion of all three major hepatic veins causes abrupt severe RUQ pain, vomiting, marked tender hepatomegaly, refractory ascites, jaundice, and acute liver failure with encephalopathy.

•  Subacute / Chronic Form: Gradual development of gross ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, and features of portal hypertension/cirrhosis.

•  Bilateral lower limb oedema and tortuous venous collaterals over the flanks and back occur if the inferior vena cava (IVC) is also obstructed.

Investigations:

•  Ascitic Fluid Analysis: High SAAG ≥ 11 g/L with a high ascitic total protein >25 g/L in early disease.

•  Doppler Ultrasonography (First-line, sensitivity >85%): Shows absent/reversed blood flow or thrombus in the hepatic veins.

•  Contrast-Enhanced CT or MRI: Shows failure of hepatic vein opacification, patchy parenchymal enhancement, and characteristic hypertrophy of the caudate lobe (Segment I is spared and hypertrophies because its emissary veins drain directly into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the occluded main hepatic veins).

•  Liver Biopsy: Shows centrilobular (Zone 3) sinusoidal congestion, haemorrhage, and hepatocyte necrosis ("nutmeg liver") progressing to centrilobular fibrosis.

•  Thrombophilia & Haematological Workup:JAK2 V617F mutation, flow cytometry for PNH (CD55/CD59), lupus anticoagulant/anticardiolipin antibodies, Factor V Leiden, Protein C/S, Antithrombin.

Management:

•  Immediate Anticoagulation (LMWH followed by life-long Warfarin or DOAC) and treatment of the underlying prothrombotic/myeloproliferative disorder.

•  Medical management of ascites (sodium restriction + diuretics).

•  Interventional Radiology: Thrombolysis, angioplasty/stenting for short focal hepatic vein strictures or IVC webs, and covered TIPSS insertion (required in 40% of patients failing medical therapy; achieves 88% 1-year and 78% 5-year survival).

•  Liver Transplantation: Indicated for fulminant liver failure or end-stage cirrhosis.

subject: medicine
title: 12. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC), Liver Transplantation, and Gallstones [KU 20, RGU, TU]
text:
12. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC), Liver Transplantation, and Gallstones [KU 20, RGU, TU]

A. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC):

•  Risk Factors: 80%–90% arise in a cirrhotic liver. Major causes: Chronic Hepatitis B (can cause HCC even without cirrhosis via viral DNA integration), Chronic Hepatitis C, Alcohol-related cirrhosis, MASLD/MASH, Genetic haemochromatosis (30% die of HCC), Aflatoxin B1 (from Aspergillus flavus contaminating stored grains/peanuts in Africa/Asia, causing TP53 mutations), and α1-antitrypsin deficiency.

•  Clinical Presentation: Unexplained acute decompensation in a patient with previously stable cirrhosis (rapidly worsening ascites, blood-stained ascitic fluid, jaundice, variceal bleed, or portal vein thrombosis); right upper quadrant pain, weight loss, fever, and an irregular, enlarging hepatic mass with an audible arterial hepatic bruit or friction rub. Detected asymptomatically via 6-monthly ultrasound + serum AFP surveillance.

•  Investigations:

•  Serum Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP): Elevated in 50%–70% of HCCs (>400 ng/mL is strongly diagnostic).

•  Multiphasic Contrast-Enhanced CT or MRI (Diagnostic Gold Standard): Demonstrates the radiological hallmark of HCC: intense arterial-phase hyper-enhancement (as HCC is supplied by the hepatic artery) followed by rapid "washout" in the portal venous/delayed phase.

•  Biopsy: Avoid percutaneous biopsy in potentially resectable/transplantable tumours due to a 2%–4% risk of needle-tract tumour seeding.

•  Management (Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer [BCLC] Staging Strategy):

1.  Very Early / Early Stage (Single tumour or ≤ 3 nodules each ≤ 3 cm, Child–Pugh A, PS 0):

•  Surgical Hepatic Resection: Treatment of choice in non-cirrhotic patients or Child–Pugh A cirrhosis without portal hypertension.

•  Orthotopic Liver Transplantation: Curative for both the tumour and underlying cirrhosis in patients meeting the Milan Criteria (single tumour ≤ 5 cm OR up to 3 tumours each ≤ 3 cm, with no macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread; UK extended criteria allow up to 5 nodules ≤ 3 cm).

•  Local Thermal Ablation (Radiofrequency Ablation [RFA] or Microwave Ablation [MWA]): Curative for small tumours ≤ 3 cm unsuitable for surgery.

2.  Intermediate Stage (Multinodular, preserved liver function, no vascular invasion):Transarterial Chemoembolisation (TACE) or Selective Internal Radiation Therapy (SIRT / Yttrium-90 microspheres).

3.  Advanced Stage (Portal vein invasion or extrahepatic metastases, Child–Pugh A/B):Systemic Therapy: First-line standard of care is combination immunotherapy with Atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) + Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) (superior survival to multikinase inhibitors Sorafenib or Lenvatinib).

4.  Terminal Stage (Child–Pugh C or PS 3–4): Best supportive/palliative care.

B. Liver Transplantation:

•  Indications:

1.  Decompensated Cirrhosis (56%): Alcohol-related liver disease (abstinent), MASLD, PSC, PBC (bilirubin >100 µ mol/L or intractable pruritus), AIH, HBV, HCV, or metabolic diseases (Wilson’s, haemochromatosis, α1-AT deficiency) with MELD >12–15, UKELD ≥ 49, or Child–Pugh C (refractory ascites, SBP, recurrent variceal bleed, chronic encephalopathy).

2.  Hepatocellular Carcinoma (17%): Within Milan/UK transplant criteria.

3.  Acute (Fulminant) Liver Failure (8%): Meeting King’s College adverse prognostic criteria.

•  Contraindications: Extrahepatic malignancy, uncontrolled extrahepatic sepsis, active alcohol or illicit substance misuse, severe cardiopulmonary disease, and AIDS.

•  Immunosuppression & Complications: Matched by ABO blood group and size (HLA matching not required). Maintained on a calcineurin inhibitor (Tacrolimus or ciclosporin) ± mycophenolate/azathioprine and tapering steroids.

•  Early complications: Primary graft non-function (1%–2%), hepatic artery thrombosis, biliary leak/stricture, acute cellular rejection (15%–25% at days 5–30; treated with IV methylprednisolone), and opportunistic infections (CMV, bacterial, fungal, Pneumocystis).

•  Late complications: Chronic ductopenic rejection, calcineurin-induced nephrotoxicity, hypertension, diabetes, skin cancer/PTLD lymphoma, and disease recurrence. 1-year survival is 94% and 5-year survival is 84%.

C. Gallstones (Cholelithiasis):

•  Types & Risk Factors:

1.  Cholesterol / Mixed Stones (80% in West): Formed in supersaturated "lithogenic" bile due to excess cholesterol secretion, bile salt deficiency, and gallbladder stasis. Risk factors ("5 Fs"): Female sex, Increasing age (Forty+), Obesity (Fat), Pregnancy/multiparity (Fertile), Rapid weight loss/bariatric surgery, total parenteral nutrition, terminal ileal Crohn’s disease/resection, and octreotide/fibrates.

2.  Black Pigment Stones: Composed of polymerised calcium bilirubinate; caused by chronic haemolysis (hereditary spherocytosis, sickle-cell disease, thalassaemia) and cirrhosis.

3.  Brown Pigment Stones: Composed of calcium bilirubinate + fatty acid soaps in bile ducts; caused by chronic biliary bacterial or parasitic infection (E. coli, Clonorchis sinensis, Ascaris) where bacterial β-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin.

•  Clinical Features & Complications:

•  80% are asymptomatic (require no treatment).

•  Biliary Colic: Sudden, severe, constant epigastric/RUQ pain radiating to the right scapula/interscapular region lasting 1–6 hours due to transient stone impaction in the cystic duct.

•  Complications:Acute and chronic calculous cholecystitis (RUQ pain >6 hrs, fever, positive Murphy’s sign), empyema or mucocele of the gallbladder, porcelain gallbladder (calcified wall—high risk of gallbladder adenocarcinoma), Mirizzi syndrome (stone impacted in the cystic duct/Hartmann’s pouch extrinsically compressing the common hepatic duct to cause obstructive jaundice), choledocholithiasis with acute ascending cholangitis (Charcot’s triad), acute gallstone pancreatitis, and gallstone ileus (cholecystoduodenal fistula with pneumobilia and mechanical small bowel obstruction by a stone >2.5 cm impacted at the terminal ileum).

•  Diagnosis & Management:

•  Investigation of choice:Transabdominal Ultrasound (>95% specific for gallbladder stones showing echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing; MRCP or EUS is preferred for common bile duct stones).

•  Management: Asymptomatic gallbladder stones are managed conservatively. Symptomatic gallbladder stones are treated with Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy (performed within 5 days of acute cholecystitis). Common bile duct stones require ERCP with biliary sphincterotomy and stone extraction regardless of symptoms.

•  (Mapped to Davidson’s 25e Chapter 25, pp. 1015–1092)

subject: medicine
title: 1. Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), Felty’s Syndrome, Rheumatoid Factor (RF), and Anti-CCP (ACPA) Antibodies [KU 25, 24, 22, 20, 19, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
CHAPTER 23 — RHEUMATOLOGY AND BONE DISEASE

SECTION 23.1 & 23.3 — INVESTIGATIONS & RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS

1. Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), Felty’s Syndrome, Rheumatoid Factor (RF), and Anti-CCP (ACPA) Antibodies [KU 25, 24, 22, 20, 19, 16, TU, RGU]

•  (Covers both clinical vignette Essays on young females presenting with chronic symmetrical pain, morning stiffness, and swelling of small and large joints with swan-neck and boutonnière deformities).

1. Definition & Epidemiology:

•  Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a chronic, symmetrical, autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis that primarily targets synovial joints and tendon sheaths, accompanied by extra-articular systemic manifestations. Prevalence is 0.8%–1.0% worldwide, affecting women three times more frequently than men (F:M = 3:1).

2. Aetiopathogenesis of Rheumatoid Arthritis:

•  Genetic Susceptibility: 50%–60% heritability. The strongest genetic association is with HLA-DRB1 alleles (HLA-DR4 and HLA-DR1) that share a conserved 5-amino-acid sequence in the peptide-binding groove known as the "Shared Epitope" (positions 11, 70–74).

•  Environmental Trigger (Citrullination):Cigarette smoking (and mucosal inflammation such as Porphyromonas gingivalis periodontitis or altered gut/lung microbiome) activates the enzyme peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD), which post-translationally converts arginine residues in host proteins (vimentin, fibrinogen, collagen) into citrulline.

•  Autoimmune Activation & Synovial Pannus Formation:

•  Citrullinated peptides bind with high affinity to the HLA-DRB1 shared epitope on antigen-presenting cells, activating CD4+ Th1 and Th17 lymphocytes and stimulating B cells/plasma cells to produce Anti-Citrullinated Peptide Antibodies (ACPA) and Rheumatoid Factor (RF).

•  Activated T cells and synovial macrophages release pro-inflammatory cytokines—principally TNF-α, Interleukin-1 (IL-1), and Interleukin-6 (IL-6).

•  These cytokines stimulate synovial fibroblast proliferation, angiogenesis, and leucocyte recruitment, transforming the normal 1–3 cell-thick synovial lining into a hyperplastic, invasive inflammatory granulation tissue called pannus.

•  Cartilage & Bone Destruction: Synovial fibroblasts secrete matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and aggrecanase (ADAMTS-5) that degrade articular cartilage, while activated T cells and stromal cells express RANKL and M-CSF, which drive osteoclast differentiation at the bare area of the joint margin, causing periarticular osteoporosis and marginal bone erosions. Systemic IL-6 stimulates hepatic production of CRP, ESR, and hepcidin (causing anaemia of chronic disease).

3. Autoantibodies in Rheumatoid Arthritis (RF vs. Anti-CCP / ACPA):

•  Rheumatoid Factor (RF):

•  An autoantibody (most commonly IgM, though IgG and IgA also exist) directed against the Fc portion of human IgG.

•  Sensitivity & Specificity: Positive in ∼ 70% of RA patients (and 100% of those with rheumatoid nodules or vasculitis), but specificity is poor (∼ 70%–80%).

•  Other Conditions Associated with a Positive RF:Sjögren’s syndrome (90%), Mixed essential cryoglobulinaemia (90%), Systemic lupus erythematosus (30%), systemic sclerosis, Primary biliary cholangitis (50%), Chronic infections (Infective endocarditis [40%], Hepatitis B and C, Tuberculosis [15%], leprosy, malaria), sarcoidosis, and up to 20% of healthy older adults >65 years.

•  Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide Antibodies (Anti-CCP / ACPA):

•  Autoantibodies directed against citrullinated filaggrin/vimentin peptides.

•  Superior Clinical Utility: Same sensitivity as RF (∼ 70%), but much higher specificity for RA (>95%–98%). Can be detected years before clinical symptom onset, and high titres strongly predict severe erosive joint damage and extra-articular manifestations.

4. Clinical Features (Articular & Extra-Articular Manifestations):

•  Articular Features:

•  Insidious onset of symmetrical pain, swelling, tenderness, and prolonged early-morning stiffness (>30–60 minutes) that improves with movement/activity.

•  Target Joints: Symmetrical involvement of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the hands (sparing the DIP joints), wrists, and metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints of the feet (forefoot pain described as "walking on marbles", with pain on lateral MCP/MTP squeeze), spreading to knees, ankles, elbows, shoulders, and the cervical spine (atlanto-axial joint).

•  Characteristic Hand, Foot & Joint Deformities in Established RA:

•  Ulnar deviation of the fingers at the MCP joints with palmar subluxation and wasting of the small interosseous muscles.

•  Swan-neck deformity:Hyperextension of the PIP joint with flexion of the DIP joint.

•  Boutonnière ("button-hole") deformity:Flexion of the PIP joint with hyperextension of the DIP joint (due to central slip extensor tendon rupture).

•  Z-deformity ("hitchhiker’s thumb"): Flexion of the first MCP joint and hyperextension of the interphalangeal joint of the thumb.

•  Dorsal subluxation of the ulnar styloid ("piano-key sign") at the distal radio-ulnar joint, which can fray and rupture the extensor tendons of the 4th and 5th fingers (dropped fingers).

•  Flexor tenosynovitis causing trigger fingers and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome.

•  Feet: Subluxation of the metatarsal heads ("cock-up" / hammer toes), hallux valgus, and hindfoot valgus/flat foot.

•  Knees:Popliteal (Baker’s) cyst, which can rupture into the calf and mimic a deep vein thrombosis.

•  Extra-Articular Manifestations of Rheumatoid Arthritis (Occur in Seropositive [RF+/ACPA+] Erosive Disease):

1.  Systemic & Musculoskeletal: Fever, fatigue, weight loss, muscle wasting, tenosynovitis, bursitis, and secondary osteoporosis.

2.  Subcutaneous Rheumatoid Nodules (20%–30%): Firm, non-tender nodules over extensor pressure surfaces (olecranon/forearm, Achilles tendon, sacrum) and lungs; histologically show central fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes.

3.  Ocular:Secondary Sjögren’s syndrome (keratoconjunctivitis sicca — dry eyes) (most common ocular feature), episcleritis (painless superficial redness), scleritis (severe ocular pain and redness; can lead to scleromalacia perforans), and peripheral ulcerative keratitis.

4.  Pulmonary:Pleural effusions (exudate with characteristically very low pleural fluid glucose, high LDH, and low complement), rheumatoid interstitial lung disease / pulmonary fibrosis (usual interstitial pneumonia pattern at lung bases), pulmonary rheumatoid nodules, Caplan’s syndrome (cavitating pulmonary rheumatoid nodules + coal-worker’s pneumoconiosis), bronchiectasis, and obliterative bronchiolitis.

5.  Cardiac & Vascular:Pericarditis (often asymptomatic; rarely constrictive), myocarditis, conduction blocks, granulomatous aortitis, accelerated coronary atherosclerosis (leading cause of premature death in RA), and Rheumatoid Vasculitis (nail-fold infarcts, cutaneous leg ulcers, digital gangrene, mononeuritis multiplex, mesenteric arteritis).

6.  Neurological:

•  Entrapment neuropathies:Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve), ulnar nerve compression at the elbow, tarsal tunnel syndrome.

•  Peripheral sensory neuropathy or mononeuritis multiplex (vasculitic).

•  Cervical Spine (Atlanto-Axial) Subluxation: Erosion of the transverse ligament of C1 by pannus widens the space between the anterior arch of the atlas (C1) and the odontoid peg (C2) to >3 mm on lateral flexion cervical X-rays; causes occipital headache, electric-shock paraesthesiae on neck flexion (Lhermitte’s sign), spastic quadriparesis (cervical cord compression), or sudden death during anaesthetic intubation.

7.  Haematological & Renal:Anaemia of chronic disease (or iron deficiency from NSAIDs), reactive thrombocytosis, eosinophilia, Secondary AA Amyloidosis (nephrotic syndrome), and Felty’s Syndrome.

•  Components of Felty’s Syndrome [KU 24]:

•  Classic Triad:

1.  Long-standing, deforming Seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis

2.  Splenomegaly

3.  Neutropenia (often with thrombocytopenia and anaemia due to hypersplenism and anti-neutrophil antibodies).

•  Associated features: Recurrent severe bacterial infections, leg ulcers, skin hyperpigmentation, lymphadenopathy, and large granular lymphocyte (T-LGL) expansion.

5. Diagnostic Criteria (2010 ACR / EULAR Classification Criteria for RA) & Investigations:

•  2010 ACR/EULAR Diagnostic Criteria (Applied to patients with clinical synovitis in ≥ 1 joint; a total score of ≥ 6 / 10 confirms Definite RA):

1.  Joint Involvement (0–5 points): 1 large joint (0); 2–10 large joints (1); 1–3 small joints (2); 4–10 small joints (3); >10 joints with at least 1 small joint (5 points).

2.  Serology (0–3 points): Negative RF and ACPA (0); Low-positive RF or ACPA (2); High-positive (>3× ULN) RF or ACPA (3 points).

3.  Acute Phase Reactants (0–1 point): Normal CRP and ESR (0); Abnormal CRP or ESR (1 point).

4.  Duration of Symptoms (0–1 point): <6 weeks (0); ≥ 6 weeks (1 point).

•  Other Investigations & Disease Activity Monitoring:

•  Bloods: FBC (normocytic anaemia of chronic disease, thrombocytosis), ESR and CRP, U&Es, LFTs (baseline prior to DMARDs), and ACPA + IgM RF.

•  Imaging:Plain X-rays of Hands and Feet (show soft-tissue swelling, juxta-articular/periarticular osteopenia, marginal bone erosions, uniform joint space narrowing, and subluxation); Musculoskeletal Ultrasound with Power Doppler or MRI (detects early subclinical synovitis and erosions); Flexion/Extension Cervical Spine X-rays prior to general anaesthesia.

•  DAS28 Score (Disease Activity Score in 28 Joints): Combines tender joint count, swollen joint count, ESR/CRP, and patient global health VAS (0–100): >5.1 = High disease activity; 3.2–5.1 = Moderate; 2.6–3.2 = Low; <2.6 = Remission.

6. Management of Rheumatoid Arthritis (Treat-to-Target Strategy):

•  1. Multidisciplinary Non-Pharmacological Care: Patient education, smoking cessation, physiotherapy (aerobic conditioning and muscle-strengthening exercises), occupational therapy (joint protection, wrist splints, home aids), podiatry (foot orthoses), and cardiovascular/osteoporosis risk management.

•  2. Early Disease-Modifying Anti-Rheumatic Drug (DMARD) Therapy (Cornerstone — Start immediately at diagnosis aiming for DAS28 <2.6):

•  Initial Induction Regimen:

•  First-Line csDMARD:Methotrexate (MTX) 15 mg weekly orally or subcutaneously, escalated to 25 mg weekly, co-prescribed with Folic Acid 5 mg weekly (taken 24 hours after MTX). (Monitor FBC, U&Es, and LFTs every 2 weeks for 6 weeks, then monthly for 3 months, then 3-monthly; warn of teratogenicity, alcohol avoidance, and rare acute MTX pneumonitis).

•  Bridging Glucocorticoids: Co-administer short-term oral Prednisolone (30 mg daily, tapered by 5 mg every 2 weeks to stop) or an intramuscular depot injection of Methylprednisolone (80–120 mg) (or intra-articular steroid injections) to rapidly control synovitis while waiting 6–12 weeks for MTX to take effect.

•  Other Classical Synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs) (Used if MTX is contraindicated or combined with MTX as "Triple Therapy" if DAS28 >2.6):

•  Sulfasalazine (SSZ): 2–3 g daily orally (safe in pregnancy; monitor FBC/LFTs).

•  Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ): 200–400 mg daily orally (≤ 5 mg/kg/day; safe in pregnancy; requires optical coherence tomography [OCT] retinal screening after 5 years).

•  Leflunomide (LEF): 10–20 mg daily orally (inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase; monitor FBC, LFTs, and BP; requires colestyramine washout before pregnancy).

•  Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs) & Targeted Synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs):

•  (Indicated when DAS28 remains >3.2–5.1 despite ≥ 2 csDMARDs including MTX; screen for latent TB [IGRA + CXR], Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV before starting; usually co-administered with MTX):

1.  TNF-α Inhibitors (First-line bDMARDs):Adalimumab, Etanercept, Infliximab, Golimumab, Certolizumab pegol (Certolizumab does not cross the placenta and is safe throughout pregnancy). Contraindicated in active sepsis, NYHA Class III/IV heart failure, and demyelinating disease/MS.

2.  B-Cell Depleting Therapy (Anti-CD20):Rituximab (1000 mg IV × 2 infusions every 6–12 months; preferred if history of lymphoma, ILD, or seropositive RA failing anti-TNF).

3.  T-Cell Co-Stimulation Blocker (CD80/86 decoy):Abatacept (CTLA4-Ig fusion protein).

4.  IL-6 Receptor Inhibitors:Tocilizumab and Sarilumab (effective as monotherapy if MTX cannot be tolerated).

5.  Oral Janus Kinase (JAK) Inhibitors (tsDMARDs):Tofacitinib (JAK1/3), Baricitinib (JAK1/2), Upadacitinib (JAK1), and Filgotinib (JAK1). (Vaccinate against herpes zoster; use with caution in patients >65 years or with high VTE/cardiovascular risk).

•  3. Surgical Management:

•  Soft-tissue decompression & tendon surgery: Carpal tunnel decompression, extensor tenosynovectomy + radial/ulnar head excision (to prevent tendon rupture).

•  Total Joint Replacement Arthroplasty (hip, knee, shoulder, elbow) or Arthrodesis (wrist, ankle/subtalar fusion) for severe secondary osteoarthritis, and cervical spine stabilisation/fusion for progressive atlanto-axial subluxation with myelopathy.

subject: medicine
title: 2. Crystal Arthropathies: Gout and Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition (CPPD) Disease [KU 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, 15, TU]
text:
SECTION 23.2 & 23.4 — CRYSTAL-INDUCED ARTHRITIS & SPONDYLOARTHRITIS

2. Crystal Arthropathies: Gout and Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition (CPPD) Disease [KU 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, 15, TU]

1. Classification of Crystal-Associated Arthritis:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-013]]

2. Gout (Aetiology, Clinical Features, Diagnosis & Management):

•  Aetiopathogenesis:

•  Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by tissue deposition of monosodium urate monohydrate (MSU) crystals from supersaturated extracellular fluids (hyperuricaemia, >360–420 µ mol/L). Phagocytosis of MSU crystals by synovial macrophages activates the NLRP3 inflammasome, cleaving pro-IL-1β into active Interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and triggering massive neutrophil influx.

•  Causes of Hyperuricaemia:

1.  Diminished Renal Uric Acid Excretion (>90% of cases): Polygenic renal tubular urate transporter variants (SLC2A9, ABCG2), Chronic kidney disease, Drugs (Thiazide and loop diuretics, Low-dose aspirin, Ciclosporin, Tacrolimus, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol, nicotinic acid), Alcohol (lactic acidosis competes for renal tubular excretion), lead nephropathy (saturnine gout), and metabolic syndrome/insulin resistance.

2.  Increased Purine Intake: Red meat, offal, shellfish/seafood, fructose-sweetened drinks, and beer (rich in guanosine).

3.  Increased Endogenous Urate Production (<10%):Myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders, tumour lysis syndrome, severe psoriasis, haemolytic anaemias, and rare X-linked Lesch–Nyhan syndrome (HPRT deficiency).

•  Clinical Features:

•  Acute Gouty Arthritis: Explosive onset (reaching peak intensity within 2–6 hours, often waking the patient in the early morning) of excruciating pain, extreme tenderness, swelling, and shiny red overlying skin. Over 50% of first attacks affect the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra); other sites include the ankle, midfoot, knee, wrist, finger joints (often in preexisting nodal OA in elderly women on diuretics), and olecranon bursa. Untreated attacks self-resolve over 5–14 days with overlying skin desquamation and pruritus.

•  Chronic Tophaceous Gout: Develops after years of uncontrolled hyperuricaemia; characterised by chronic asymmetrical polyarthritis, white chalky subcutaneous nodules (tophi) over the extensor surfaces of fingers, olecranon, Achilles tendons, and ear helix, and uric acid nephrolithiasis / chronic urate nephropathy.

•  Investigations:

•  Joint Aspiration & Compensated Polarised Light Microscopy (Gold Standard): Turbid, neutrophil-rich synovial fluid demonstrating intracellular needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent MSU crystals (with negative Gram stain and culture to exclude septic arthritis).

•  Serum Uric Acid (SUA): Usually elevated, but can be normal during an acute attack because IL-6/acute phase response promotes uricosuria (negative acute phase reactant). Check renal function, fasting glucose, and lipids.

•  X-rays (in Chronic Gout): Asymmetrical soft-tissue swelling (tophi), well-defined "punched-out" juxta-articular erosions with overhanging sclerotic margins ("rat-bite" / "Lulworth Cove" erosions), and preservation of joint space until late disease.

•  Management of Gouty Arthritis (Drugs Used to Treat Gout):

•  A. Treatment of the Acute Gout Attack:

•  (Note: Never start or alter the dose of allopurinol/febuxostat during an acute attack, as rapid urate fluctuations prolong the flare; if the patient is already on established allopurinol, continue it unchanged).

1.  Oral Colchicine (First-line):0.5 mg 2–4 times daily (inhibits microtubule polymerisation, neutrophil migration, and NLRP3 inflammasome activation; high doses cause diarrhoea and vomiting; use caution in renal impairment and the elderly).

2.  Oral NSAIDs (First-line alternative): High-dose Naproxen (500 mg BD), Indometacin (50 mg TDS), Diclofenac, or Etoricoxib (120 mg OD) with PPI cover (avoid in renal failure, peptic ulcer, heart failure, or cardiovascular disease).

3.  Corticosteroids (Preferred in elderly patients or renal/cardiac comorbidity):

•  Joint aspiration + Intra-articular glucocorticoid injection (e.g., methylprednisolone or triamcinolone) is the safest and most rapid treatment for acute monoarthritis once sepsis is excluded.

•  Oral Prednisolone (15–35 mg daily for 3–5 days) or IM Methylprednisolone (80–120 mg).

1.  Interleukin-1 Inhibitors (for refractory attacks where colchicine, NSAIDs, and steroids are contraindicated):Anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist, 100 mg SC daily) or Canakinumab (anti-IL-1β monoclonal antibody, 150 mg SC).

2.  General: Rest, elevate the limb, and apply ice packs.

•  B. Long-Term Prophylaxis — Urate-Lowering Therapy (ULT):

•  Indications for ULT: ≥ 2 acute attacks within 12 months; presence of tophi, radiographic gouty erosions, chronic kidney disease, uric acid renal stones, or prior to cancer chemotherapy.

•  Therapeutic Target: Titrate ULT to maintain Serum Uric Acid <300 µ mol/L (<5 mg/dL) (or <360 µ mol/L [<6 mg/dL] per EULAR guidelines) to dissolve crystal deposits.

•  Mandatory Flare Prophylaxis when Starting ULT:Wait 1–2 weeks after the acute attack settles, and co-prescribe low-dose Oral Colchicine (0.5 mg OD–BD) or a low-dose NSAID for the first 3–6 months of ULT to prevent mobilization flares.

•  Drugs Used for Urate-Lowering Therapy:

1.  Xanthine Oxidase Inhibitors (First-Line):

•  Allopurinol (Drug of First Choice): Start at 100 mg daily (50 mg daily in CKD or elderly) and up-titrate by 100 mg every 4 weeks until target SUA <300 µ mol/L is achieved (max 900 mg/day). (Screen for *HLA-B*5801 in Han Chinese/South Asian populations due to risk of severe Stevens–Johnson/DRESS syndrome; reduce dose of azathioprine/6-MP by 75% if co-prescribed).

•  Febuxostat (40–80 mg daily, up to 120 mg): Second-line non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor; metabolised by the liver, so no dose adjustment is needed in mild-to-moderate renal impairment.

1.  Uricosuric Agents (Second-Line — Increase Renal Tubular Urate Excretion):

•  Benzbromarone (50–200 mg daily), Probenecid, or Sulfinpyrazone. (Contraindicated in urate over-producers, nephrolithiasis, or severe renal impairment; maintain high fluid intake).

•  Losartan (angiotensin receptor blocker) and Fenofibrate have mild uricosuric properties and are useful in patients with coexisting hypertension or hyperlipidaemia.

1.  Recombinant Uricases (Convert Uric Acid to Soluble Allantoin):

•  Pegloticase (8 mg IV every 2 weeks for severe refractory tophaceous gout) and Rasburicase (IV for chemotherapy-induced tumour lysis syndrome).

•  Lifestyle Modification: Weight loss, avoid beer/spirits, fructose drinks, offal, and shellfish, and substitute thiazide diuretics with losartan or a calcium channel blocker where possible.

3. Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition (CPPD) Disease ("Pseudogout"):

•  Risk Factors:Advancing age (>65 years), pre-existing Osteoarthritis, and metabolic disorders ("4 Hs"): Hyperparathyroidism, Haemochromatosis, Hypophosphatasia, and Hypomagnesaemia (plus Wilson’s disease).

•  Clinical Presentations:

1.  Acute CPP Crystal Arthritis ("Pseudogout"): Acute hot, swollen, painful monoarthritis most commonly affecting the knee, followed by the wrist, shoulder, or ankle, often triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery, or dehydration.

2.  Chronic CPP Crystal Arthritis (Pyrophosphate Arthropathy): Symmetrical polyarthritis superimposed on OA, targeting the wrists, 2nd and 3rd MCP joints, knees, and shoulders (mimicking RA).

3.  Axial CPPD ("Crowned Dens Syndrome"): Calcification of ligaments around the C2 odontoid peg causing acute severe neck pain, stiffness, and fever in an elderly patient (mimicking meningitis or GCA).

•  Diagnosis: Synovial fluid compensated polarised light microscopy showing rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent CPP crystals; X-rays showing linear/punctate chondrocalcinosis in fibrocartilage (knee menisci, wrist triangular fibrocartilage, symphysis pubis) and hyaline articular cartilage.

•  Management: Joint aspiration and intra-articular corticosteroid injection, ice packs, colchicine (0.5–1 mg/day), NSAIDs, or short-course oral prednisolone (plus methotrexate/hydroxychloroquine in chronic polyarticular disease, and treatment of underlying hyperparathyroidism/haemochromatosis).

title: 3. Seronegative Spondyloarthritides (SpA): Axial Spondyloarthritis (Ankylosing Spondylitis), Reactive Arthritis, and Psoriatic Arthritis [KU 25, 24, 23, TU]
text:
3. Seronegative Spondyloarthritides (SpA): Axial Spondyloarthritis (Ankylosing Spondylitis), Reactive Arthritis, and Psoriatic Arthritis [KU 25, 24, 23, TU]

1. Overview & Shared Features of the Four Types of Seronegative Spondyloarthritis:

•  The Four Major Types of Seronegative Spondyloarthritis (SpA):

1.  Axial Spondyloarthritis (axSpA): Comprising Non-radiographic axial SpA (nr-axSpA) and Radiographic axial SpA (Ankylosing Spondylitis — AS).

2.  Reactive Arthritis (ReA)(formerly Reiter’s syndrome).

3.  Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA).

4.  Enteropathic Spondyloarthritis (associated with Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn’s Disease).

•  Core Pathophysiological & Clinical Features Shared Across All Spondyloarthritides:

•  Seronegative for Rheumatoid Factor (RF) and ACPA.

•  Strong genetic association with HLA-B27 (>90%–95% in AS; 50%–70% in ReA/axial PsA/enteropathic spondylitis) and driven immunologically by the IL-23 / Th17 / IL-17 and TNF-α axis.

•  Enthesitis [KU 24]: The hallmark pathological lesion of all SpAs—inflammation at the enthesis (the site of insertion of tendons, ligaments, or joint capsules into bone), such as Achilles insertional tendinitis, plantar fasciitis, patellar tendon insertion, costosternal junctions, and greater trochanters. Leads to erosions followed by reactive new bone formation (enthesophytes / calcaneal spurs and spinal syndesmophytes).

•  Sacroiliitis and Spondylitis (presenting with inflammatory back pain: onset <45 years, morning stiffness >30 mins, improves with exercise, worsens with rest, alternating buttock pain, and waking in the second half of the night).

•  Asymmetrical oligoarthritis (predominantly affecting lower limb large joints).

•  Dactylitis ("sausage digit") (combined synovitis + tenosynovitis + enthesitis of an entire finger or toe).

•  Shared extra-articular manifestations: Acute anterior uveitis (iritis), psoriasis, mucosal ulceration, inflammatory bowel disease, and aortitis / aortic regurgitation.

2. Axial Spondyloarthritis & Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS):

•  Clinical Features:

•  Presents in young adults (20–40 years, M:F = 3:1 in radiographic AS) with insidious inflammatory low back pain and morning stiffness radiating to the buttocks, plus peripheral enthesitis (plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinitis) and asymmetrical large-joint arthritis (hips, knees, shoulders).

•  Physical Signs: Loss of normal lumbar lordosis, restricted lumbar spinal mobility in all planes confirmed by a positive Modified Schober’s test (a 10 cm midline mark above the posterior superior iliac spines expands to <15 cm on maximal forward flexion), reduced chest expansion (<5 cm due to costovertebral involvement), pain on sacroiliac joint stressing, and in advanced untreated disease, a fixed thoracolumbar kyphosis ("question-mark posture").

•  Extra-Articular Manifestations of Ankylosing Spondylitis (Mnemonic: "A"s of AS):

1.  Anterior uveitis (acute unilateral painful red eye with photophobia; occurs in 25%–40%).

2.  Aortic regurgitation and aortitis, plus AV nodal conduction heart blocks (20%).

3.  Apical pulmonary fibrosis (bilateral upper-lobe fibrobullous disease, sometimes colonised by Aspergillus).

4.  Amyloidosis (secondary AA amyloidosis causing nephrotic syndrome).

5.  Achilles tendinitis / plantar fasciitis (enthesitis) and Atlanto-axial subluxation.

6.  Inflammatory bowel disease (microscopic or overt ileocolitis in up to 50%), Osteoporosis with chalk-stick spinal fractures, Cauda equina syndrome, and sterile prostatitis (80% of men).

•  Investigations:

•  MRI of Sacroiliac Joints and Spine (STIR sequences):Gold standard for early diagnosis (nr-axSpA); demonstrates subchondral bone marrow oedema (osteitis) around the sacroiliac joints and vertebral corners (Romanus lesions) years before X-ray changes appear.

•  Plain X-rays of Pelvis and Spine (in established AS): Symmetrical sacroiliitis (blurring, marginal erosions, pseudowidening, sclerosis, and eventual bony ankylosis), squaring of lumbar vertebrae, "shiny corners" (Romanus lesions), and symmetrical bridging marginal syndesmophytes (calcification of the outer annulus fibrosus) producing the classic "bamboo spine", plus ossification of the interspinous ligaments ("dagger sign").

•  Bloods:HLA-B27 positive (>90%), raised ESR/CRP (normal in 40%), normocytic anaemia.

•  Management of Axial Spondyloarthritis:

•  First-Line: Daily structured physiotherapy and spinal extension exercises, smoking cessation, and continuous or bedtime slow-release Oral NSAIDs (e.g., Naproxen, Etoricoxib).

•  (Note: Classical synthetic DMARDs like Methotrexate and Sulfasalazine are INEFFECTIVE for axial spinal disease, though Sulfasalazine may help peripheral joint synovitis).

•  Second-Line (Biologics & Targeted Synthetic DMARDs for active axial disease failing ≥ 2 NSAIDs):

1.  TNF-α Inhibitors:Adalimumab, Infliximab, Golimumab, Certolizumab, Etanercept(monoclonal anti-TNFs are preferred over etanercept if recurrent uveitis or IBD is present).

2.  IL-17 Inhibitors:Secukinumab, Ixekizumab (anti-IL-17A), Bimekizumab (anti-IL-17A/F) (avoid in active IBD).

3.  Oral JAK Inhibitors:Upadacitinib or Tofacitinib.

3. Reactive Arthritis (ReA) [KU 25, 23, TU]:

•  Definition & Triggers: An acute, sterile inflammatory spondyloarthritis occurring 1–4 weeks after a distant bacterial infection, strongly associated with HLA-B27 (60%–80%).

•  Sexually Acquired Reactive Arthritis (SARA — M:F = 15:1): Triggered by genital Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis/cervicitis.

•  Post-Dysenteric (Enteric) Reactive Arthritis (M = F): Triggered by bacterial gastroenteritis with Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter jejuni, or Yersinia enterocolitica.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Classic Triad (formerly Reiter’s Syndrome):Asymmetrical Lower-Limb Oligoarthritis + Non-Gonococcal Urethritis + Conjunctivitis(Mnemonic: "Can’t see, can’t pee, can’t climb a tree").

•  Musculoskeletal: Acute, hot, swollen asymmetrical oligoarthritis targeting the knees, ankles, and feet, often with large effusions, Achilles enthesitis / plantar fasciitis, dactylitis, and inflammatory low back pain / sacroiliitis (15%–20%).

•  Mucocutaneous & Ocular Features:

•  Circinate balanitis: Painless superficial serpiginous erosions on the glans penis.

•  Keratoderma blennorrhagica: Waxy, yellow–brown hyperkeratotic vesico-pustular plaques on the palms and soles (clinically and histologically indistinguishable from pustular psoriasis).

•  Nail dystrophy (subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, no nail pitting), painless oral ulcers, sterile conjunctivitis, and acute anterior uveitis.

•  Investigations:

•  Joint Aspiration: Mandatory to exclude septic arthritis and crystal arthropathy (yields sterile, turbid inflammatory synovial fluid).

•  Microbiology: Urine/endocervical NAAT (PCR) swab for Chlamydia trachomatis; stool culture (usually negative by the time arthritis appears, except Salmonella) and serology.

•  Bloods: Raised ESR and CRP, neutrophilia, negative RF/ACPA/ANA, positive HLA-B27.

•  Management:

•  Most acute attacks resolve spontaneously within 3–6 months (10% develop chronic/relapsing SpA).

•  Symptomatic: Rest, Oral NSAIDs, and intra-articular corticosteroid injections for severe mono-/oligoarthritis (or short-course oral prednisolone for polyarticular disease).

•  Antibiotics: Treat confirmed Chlamydia infection (in patient and sexual partners) with Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days or a single 1 g dose of Azithromycin (antibiotics do not alter the course of post-dysenteric arthritis once established).

•  Chronic / Refractory Disease (>6 months):Sulfasalazine or Methotrexate, escalating to Anti-TNF-α biologics if unresponsive. Treat acute anterior uveitis urgently with topical/systemic steroids and mydriatics.

4. Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) & Disease-Modifying Drugs [KU 24, TU]:

•  Clinical Patterns (Five Classical Moll and Wright Subtypes): Affects ∼ 20% of patients with psoriasis:

1.  Asymmetrical Inflammatory Oligoarthritis (30%–40%): Affects <5 joints, often with dactylitis ("sausage digits").

2.  Symmetrical Polyarthritis (30%–40%): Resembles RA (predominates in women), but involves DIP joints, lacks rheumatoid nodules, and is RF-negative.

3.  Distal Interphalangeal (DIP) Joint Predominant (10%): Strongly associated with psoriatic nail dystrophy (nail pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis).

4.  Psoriatic Spondylitis (10%–20%): Asymmetrical sacroiliitis and coarse, non-marginal syndesmophytes.

5.  Arthritis Mutilans (5%): Severe, osteolytic, deforming arthritis of the fingers/toes with bone resorption ("pencil-in-cup" deformity on X-ray) and "telescoping" digits (main en lorgnette).

•  (Plus prominent enthesitis).

•  Disease-Modifying Anti-Rheumatic Drugs (DMARDs) Used in Psoriatic Arthritis [KU 24]:

1.  Classical Synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs — First-line for peripheral arthritis):

•  Methotrexate (15–25 mg weekly—drug of first choice as it treats both joint and skin psoriasis).

•  Leflunomide (10–20 mg daily), Sulfasalazine (2–3 g daily), or Ciclosporin. (Avoid systemic oral glucocorticoids as withdrawal can trigger life-threatening rebound generalised pustular psoriasis).

2.  Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs — For csDMARD-refractory peripheral or active axial PsA):

•  TNF-α Inhibitors:Adalimumab, Etanercept, Infliximab, Golimumab, Certolizumab.

•  IL-17 Inhibitors (Highly effective for both skin and joint/axial disease):Secukinumab, Ixekizumab, Bimekizumab.

•  IL-12/23 (p40) & IL-23 (p19) Inhibitors:Ustekinumab, Guselkumab, Risankizumab.

3.  Targeted Synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs — Oral Small Molecules):

•  JAK Inhibitors:Tofacitinib and Upadacitinib.

•  PDE4 Inhibitor:Apremilast (30 mg BD orally).

title: 4. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Antiphospholipid Syndrome, and Drug-Induced Lupus [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 20, 18, TU]
text:
SECTION 23.5 — AUTOIMMUNE CONNECTIVE TISSUE DISORDERS

4. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Antiphospholipid Syndrome, and Drug-Induced Lupus [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 20, 18, TU]

•  (Covers all 5 clinical vignette Essays on young females presenting with fever, arthralgia, photosensitive butterfly malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, oral ulcers, alopecia, anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, ANA positivity, and recurrent 2nd/3rd trimester abortions + left hemiplegia/stroke = Systemic Lupus Erythematosus with Secondary Antiphospholipid Syndrome).

1. Definition, Epidemiology & Aetiopathogenesis of SLE:

•  Definition: A chronic, multisystem autoimmune connective tissue disease characterised by polyclonal B- and T-cell activation, production of autoantibodies directed against nuclear and cytoplasmic antigens, and immune-complex–mediated inflammation and organ damage.

•  Epidemiology: Peak onset between 20 and 30 years of age, with a 9:1 female-to-male ratio. Prevalence is higher and disease more severe in individuals of African-Caribbean, Hispanic, and Asian descent.

•  Aetiopathogenesis:

•  Genetics: High concordance in monozygotic twins (25%–50%); polygenic association with HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3, Fcγ receptors, and type I interferon pathway genes. Rare monogenic SLE is caused by homozygous deficiency of early Classical Complement components (C1q [highest risk, >90%], C4, or C2).

•  Defective Clearance of Apoptotic Cells & Environmental Triggers: Exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light, viral infections (EBV), oestrogens, or drugs induces keratinocyte/cellular apoptosis. Defective phagocytic clearance of apoptotic blebs (due to complement deficiency) exposes intracellular nuclear antigens (dsDNA, histones, ribonucleoproteins [Ro, La, Sm, RNP]) to the immune system.

•  Tissue Injury: Autoantibodies form circulating and in situ immune complexes (Type III hypersensitivity) that deposit in the glomerular basement membrane, skin dermo-epidermal junction, synovium, choroid plexus, and serosal membranes, activating complement and recruiting neutrophils to cause necrotising vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, and serositis, while autoantibodies against RBCs, WBCs, and platelets cause Type II hypersensitivity cytopenias.

2. Clinical Features of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus:

1.  Constitutional: Fever, malaise, weight loss, severe fatigue, and lymphadenopathy.

2.  Mucocutaneous (80%):

•  Acute Cutaneous Lupus — Classic "Butterfly" Malar Rash: Fixed erythematous rash over the cheeks and nasal bridge that characteristically spares the nasolabial folds (distinguishing it from dermatomyositis; differential diagnosis of butterfly facial rash includes rosacea, seborrhoeic dermatitis, erysipelas, and pellagra).

•  Photosensitivity: Maculopapular rash triggered by UV sunlight.

•  Subacute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (SCLE): Non-scarring annular or psoriasiform polycyclic plaques on sun-exposed sites (strongly associated with anti-Ro/SS-A antibodies).

•  Chronic Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE) [TU]: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with adherent keratotic scaling, follicular "carpet-tack" plugging, central dermal atrophy, dyspigmentation, and permanent scarring alopecia on the face, ears, and scalp (only 5%–10% of isolated DLE progress to systemic SLE; treated with sunblock, potent topical steroids, and hydroxychloroquine).

•  Non-scarring diffuse alopecia, oral or nasopharyngeal ulcers (often painless, on the hard palate), Raynaud’s phenomenon, livedo reticularis, periungual telangiectasia, and cutaneous vasculitis/palpable purpura.

3.  Musculoskeletal (90%):

•  Symmetrical polyarthralgia, morning stiffness, and tenosynovitis affecting small joints of the hands, wrists, and knees. Unlike RA, joint erosions are absent, though reducible ulnar deviation and swan-neck deformities may develop from ligamentous laxity (Jaccoud’s arthropathy).

•  Myalgia, inflammatory myositis, and avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head.

4.  Renal — Lupus Nephritis (30%–50%, Major Determinant of Prognosis):

•  Ranges from asymptomatic proteinuria (>0.5 g/24 hrs) and microscopic haematuria with red cell/granular casts to nephrotic syndrome, hypertension, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (classified histologically into ISN/RPS Classes I to VI, with Class IV Diffuse Proliferative Glomerulonephritis being the most severe).

5.  Cardiopulmonary (50%):

•  Serositis:Pleuritis (pleuritic chest pain, rub, pleural effusion) and Pericarditis (most common cardiac manifestation).

•  Libman–Sacks Endocarditis [KU 21]: Non-infective verrucous endocarditis characterised by sterile, warty vegetations composed of fibrin, platelets, and immune complexes deposited on both surfaces of the mitral and aortic valve leaflets; strongly associated with antiphospholipid antibodies and can cause valvular regurgitation or systemic/cerebral cardioembolism.

•  Myocarditis, markedly accelerated coronary atherosclerosis (5- to 10-fold increased risk of premature MI), shrinking lung syndrome (diaphragmatic weakness), acute lupus pneumonitis, alveolar haemorrhage, pulmonary fibrosis, and pulmonary embolism.

6.  Neuropsychiatric Lupus (CNS Lupus):

•  Headache, seizures, acute confusional state / organic psychosis, visual hallucinations, depression, ischaemic stroke / TIA (often secondary to antiphospholipid syndrome or Libman–Sacks endocarditis), chorea, transverse myelitis, aseptic meningitis, and cranial/peripheral neuropathy.

7.  Haematological:

•  Leucopenia (<4 × 109/L) and Lymphopenia (<1.0–1.5 × 109/L) (correlates with disease activity).

•  Autoimmune Thrombocytopenia (<100 × 109/L).

•  Coombs-Positive Warm Autoimmune Haemolytic Anaemia (or normocytic anaemia of chronic disease).

8.  Secondary Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS) (Occurs in 30%–40% of SLE):

•  Characterised by recurrent arterial and venous thromboses (e.g., young-onset ischaemic stroke causing hemiplegia or DVT/PE), recurrent 2nd/3rd trimester fetal losses or ≥ 3 consecutive 1st trimester miscarriages, livedo reticularis, and thrombocytopenia, in the presence of persistent Lupus Anticoagulant, Anticardiolipin antibodies, and/or Anti-β2-glycoprotein-1 antibodies.

3. Diagnostic Criteria for SLE (ACR 11 Criteria):

•  (Any 4 or more of the 11 criteria present serially or simultaneously confirm a diagnosis of SLE — Mnemonic: SOAP BRAIN MD):

1.  S — Serositis: Pleuritis or Pericarditis.

2.  O — Oral ulcers: Oral or nasopharyngeal ulceration (usually painless).

3.  A — Arthritis: Non-erosive arthritis involving ≥ 2 peripheral joints.

4.  P — Photosensitivity.

5.  B — Blood (Haematological) disorder:Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia OR Leucopenia (<4 × 109/L) OR Lymphopenia (<1.0–1.5 × 109/L) OR Thrombocytopenia (<100 × 109/L).

6.  R — Renal disorder: Persistent proteinuria >0.5 g/24 hrs (>3+ on dipstick) OR cellular casts (red cell, haemoglobin, granular, or tubular).

7.  A — Antinuclear Antibody (ANA): Positive in abnormal titre (under the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria, ANA ≥ 1:80 is the mandatory entry criterion).

8.  I — Immunological disorder: Positive Anti-dsDNA antibody, OR positive Anti-Smith (Anti-Sm) antibody, OR positive Antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, anti-β2GP1, or lupus anticoagulant).

9.  N — Neurological disorder:Seizures or Psychosis (in the absence of offending drugs or metabolic derangements).

10.  M — Malar rash: Fixed erythema over the malar eminences, sparing the nasolabial folds.

11.  D — Discoid rash: Erythematous raised patches with adherent keratotic scaling and follicular plugging.

4. Investigations, ANA Significance & Lupus Anticoagulant:

•  Antinuclear Antibodies (ANA) & Their Significance [KU 25]:

•  ANA has 95%–100% sensitivity for SLE (a negative ANA virtually excludes SLE), but low specificity (10%–40%) as it is also positive in Sjögren’s syndrome, systemic sclerosis, polymyositis/dermatomyositis, mixed connective tissue disease, rheumatoid arthritis, autoimmune hepatitis, autoimmune thyroiditis, chronic infections, and 5% of healthy individuals. ANA titres do NOT correlate with disease activity.

•  Specific Autoantibodies (ENA & dsDNA):

•  Anti-dsDNA (Double-stranded DNA) Antibodies (by ELISA or Crithidia luciliae immunofluorescence): Highly specific (95%) for SLE; rising anti-dsDNA titres and falling complement levels predict an impending disease flare (especially lupus nephritis).

•  Anti-Sm (Smith) Antibodies: Highly specific (99%) for SLE (15%–30% sensitivity; associated with renal/CNS disease).

•  Anti-Ro (SS-A) & Anti-La (SS-B) Antibodies: Associated with SCLE, photosensitivity, Sjögren’s syndrome, ANA-negative lupus, and neonatal lupus / congenital complete heart block (transplacental IgG passage in pregnancy).

•  Anti-RNP Antibodies: Positive in SLE and 100% of Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD).

•  Anti-Histone Antibodies: Positive in >80%–95% of Drug-Induced Lupus (Four classic drugs causing Drug-Induced Lupus [TU]:Hydralazine, Procainamide, Isoniazid, Minocycline [also chlorpromazine, methyldopa, quinidine, and anti-TNF-α biologics]).

•  Lupus Anticoagulant & Antiphospholipid Antibodies [KU 21]:

•  Lupus Anticoagulant: An antiphospholipid antibody that paradoxically prolongs phospholipid-dependent coagulation tests in vitro (such as the APTT and Dilute Russell Viper Venom Time [dRVVT])—failing to correct on a 50:50 plasma mix—while causing a potent prothrombotic state in vivo (arterial/venous thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss). Tested alongside IgG/IgM Anticardiolipin and

Anti-β2-Glycoprotein-1 antibodies (must be persistently positive on two occasions ≥ 12 weeks apart).

•  Complement & Acute Phase Reactants:Low serum C3 and C4 (due to immune-complex complement consumption in active SLE). ESR is elevated, whereas CRP is characteristically NORMAL in active SLE (unless there is serositis or superimposed bacterial infection).

•  Other Essential Baseline Tests: FBC, Direct Coombs test, U&Es, Urinalysis for blood/protein/casts, 24-hr urinary protein or urine protein:creatinine ratio, and Renal Biopsy (mandatory if proteinuria or active urinary sediment is present to classify lupus nephritis and guide immunosuppression).

5. Management of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus & Secondary Antiphospholipid Syndrome:

•  1. General & Preventative Measures:

•  Strict UV light avoidance and high-factor sunblock (SPF 50); smoking cessation; aggressive control of cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, dyslipidaemia); and calcium/vitamin D + bisphosphonate prophylaxis if on long-term steroids.

•  Hydroxychloroquine (200–400 mg daily, ≤ 5 mg/kg/day): Cornerstone background therapy recommended in all SLE patients (controls rash and arthralgia, reduces flare rates, reduces thrombosis, and improves long-term survival).

•  2. Mild-to-Moderate Disease (Skin, Joints, Serositis, Mild Cytopenias):

•  Analgesics/NSAIDs (avoid if renal disease), Hydroxychloroquine, low-to-moderate dose Oral Prednisolone (5–20 mg/day), and steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (Methotrexate, Azathioprine [1–2.5 mg/kg/day, safe in pregnancy], or Mycophenolate mofetil).

•  3. Severe, Organ-/Life-Threatening Disease (Proliferative Lupus Nephritis, CNS Lupus, Severe Cardiopulmonary or Haematological Disease):

•  Induction of Remission:High-dose IV Methylprednisolone pulses (500–1000 mg daily for 3 days) followed by oral Prednisolone (40–60 mg/day, tapered to 5–10 mg/day by 3 months) COMBINED WITH either IV Cyclophosphamide (15 mg/kg pulses every 2–3 weeks for 6 cycles, with MESNA to prevent haemorrhagic cystitis; warn of infertility/ovarian failure) OR Oral Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF, 2–3 g daily) (equally effective as cyclophosphamide with fewer gonadal side-effects).

•  Maintenance of Remission:Mycophenolate mofetil or Azathioprine alongside the lowest possible dose of prednisolone.

•  Biologic Therapies for Refractory SLE:Belimumab (monoclonal antibody against BAFF/BLyS [B-cell activating factor]; approved for active SLE and lupus nephritis) or Rituximab (anti-CD20 B-cell depletion).

•  4. Management of Antiphospholipid Syndrome (Recurrent Abortions & Stroke/Thrombosis):

•  Asymptomatic aPL+ SLE patients: Primary prophylaxis with Low-dose Aspirin (75 mg daily).

•  Obstetric APS (Recurrent 2nd/3rd trimester abortions): Combination of Low-dose Aspirin (75–100 mg daily) PLUS Subcutaneous Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH, e.g., Enoxaparin) throughout pregnancy and for 6 weeks post-partum.

•  Thrombotic APS (Ischaemic Stroke / Left Hemiplegia or Venous Thrombosis):Life-long oral anticoagulation with Warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0 for venous thrombosis; target INR 2.0–3.0 plus aspirin or INR 3.0–4.0 for arterial thrombosis/stroke; Warfarin is preferred over DOACs in triple-positive/arterial APS).

title: 5. Systemic Sclerosis (CREST Syndrome, GI Manifestations), Raynaud’s Phenomenon, Sjögren’s Syndrome, and Adult-Onset Still’s Disease [KU 25, 21, 20, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
5. Systemic Sclerosis (CREST Syndrome, GI Manifestations), Raynaud’s Phenomenon, Sjögren’s Syndrome, and Adult-Onset Still’s Disease [KU 25, 21, 20, 16, TU, RGU]

1. Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma) & CREST Syndrome:

•  Subtypes & Autoantibodies:

1.  Limited Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis (lcSSc, 70% — includes CREST Syndrome): Skin thickening is restricted to sites distal to the elbows and knees (plus the face and neck). Associated with Anti-Centromere Antibodies (60%, 98% specific). Major late complication is Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH).

•  Clinical Features of CREST Syndrome [KU 16, RGU]:

•  C — Calcinosis cutis: Subcutaneous deposits of basic calcium phosphate in the finger pulps and extensor surfaces, which may ulcerate and discharge chalky material.

•  R — Raynaud’s phenomenon: Universal (often precedes other features by years), complicated by digital pitting scars and ischaemic digital ulcers/gangrene.

•  E — Oesophageal dysmotility: Smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis of the lower two-thirds of the oesophagus and LOS, causing severe reflux oesophagitis, peptic strictures, and dysphagia.

•  S — Sclerodactyly: Non-pitting puffiness progressing to tight, shiny, bound-down skin over the fingers with flexion contractures, loss of skin creases, and acro-osteolysis (resorption of terminal phalangeal tufts). Facial skin tightening causes microstomia (puckered mouth with radial furrowing) and a "beaked" nose.

•  T — Telangiectasia: Mat-like dilated capillaries on the face, lips, palms, and mucous membranes.

2.  Diffuse Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis (dcSSc, 30%): Skin thickening extends proximally to the elbows and knees and involves the trunk. Associated with Anti-Topoisomerase-1 (Anti-Scl-70) antibodies (linked to Interstitial Lung Disease / Pulmonary Fibrosis) and Anti-RNA Polymerase III antibodies (linked to Scleroderma Renal Crisis—accelerated malignant hypertension with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and acute renal failure; treated urgently with ACE Inhibitors [e.g., captopril/ramipril], which are life-saving and must be continued even if creatinine rises).

•  Gastrointestinal Manifestations of Systemic Sclerosis [KU 20] (Affects >90% of patients):

1.  Mouth: Microstomia (restricted mouth opening), xerostomia (secondary Sjögren’s), and periodontal disease.

2.  Oesophagus: Hypomotility of the lower 2/3 and hypotonic LOS causing severe GORD, erosive oesophagitis, Barrett’s oesophagus, and benign peptic strictures (treated with high-dose PPIs and prokinetics).

3.  Stomach:Gastroparesis (delayed gastric emptying causing early satiety, bloating, and vomiting) and Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE / "watermelon stomach") causing chronic iron deficiency anaemia or upper GI bleeding (treated with endoscopic argon plasma coagulation).

4.  Small Intestine: Smooth muscle fibrosis causes intestinal hypomotility, chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction, wide-mouthed jejunal diverticula, and Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO) (leading to bloating, chronic diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, and vitamin B12 deficiency; treated with rotating courses of oral antibiotics such as rifaximin, metronidazole, or ciprofloxacin).

5.  Colon & Anorectum: Wide-mouthed colonic diverticula, severe slow-transit constipation, rectal prolapse, and faecal incontinence (internal anal sphincter fibrosis).

•  Management of Systemic Sclerosis Organ Complications:

•  Skin & Interstitial Lung Disease (SSc-ILD):Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) or Cyclophosphamide, antifibrotic tyrosine kinase inhibitor Nintedanib (150 mg BD), Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R), or Rituximab.

•  Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH): Endothelin-1 receptor antagonists (Ambrisentan, Bosentan, Macitentan) combined with PDE5 inhibitors (Tadalafil, Sildenafil), soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator (Riociguat), or prostacyclin analogues (Epoprostenol).

2. Raynaud’s Phenomenon / Syndrome & Its Management [KU 25, 21]:

•  Definition: Episodic, reversible vasospasm of the digital arteries in response to cold exposure or emotional stress, producing a classic triphasic colour change: (1) White (Pallor) due to digital arterial vasospasm/ischaemia → (2) Blue (Cyanosis) due to venous stasis and deoxygenated blood → (3) Red (Rubor) due to reactive hyperaemia/reperfusion (accompanied by throbbing pain and paraesthesia).

•  Classification (Primary vs. Secondary Raynaud’s):

•  Primary Raynaud’s (Raynaud’s Disease): Idiopathic; onset in young women (<25 years), symmetrical, normal nail-fold capillaroscopy, negative ANA, and never causes digital ulceration or gangrene.

•  Secondary Raynaud’s (Raynaud’s Syndrome): Onset >25–30 years or in males, asymmetrical, associated with digital pitting scars/ulcers/gangrene and abnormal nail-fold capillaroscopy (dilated, tortuous giant capillary loops with areas of capillary dropout). Causes:Connective tissue diseases (Systemic sclerosis [>95%], SLE, Mixed connective tissue disease, Dermatomyositis, Sjögren’s), Vibration white finger (hand-arm vibration tools), Drugs (β-blockers, ergotamine, bleomycin), Cryoglobulinaemia / Cold agglutinins, and thoracic outlet obstruction (cervical rib).

•  Management of Raynaud’s Phenomenon:

1.  Non-Pharmacological / Lifestyle: Avoid cold exposure, maintain high core body temperature, wear electrically heated or thermal mittens/socks, stop smoking completely (nicotine is a potent vasoconstrictor), and stop β-blockers.

2.  First-Line Pharmacotherapy: Dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers—Oral Nifedipine (modified-release 10–20 mg BD–TDS) or Amlodipine.

3.  Second-Line Vasodilators:Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) Inhibitors (Sildenafil or Tadalafil), topical glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) ointment, losartan, or fluoxetine.

4.  Severe Refractory Raynaud’s with Digital Ulceration / Critical Ischaemia:

•  Intravenous Prostacyclin (Epoprostenol or Iloprost) infusions over 3–5 days.

•  Bosentan (oral endothelin-1 receptor antagonist; licensed to prevent new digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis).

•  Antibiotics for secondary infection and digital sympathectomy if refractory.

3. Primary Sjögren’s Syndrome / Disease [TU]:

•  Definition: Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of exocrine glands (principally lacrimal and salivary glands), affecting women aged 40–50 years (F:M = 9:1; associated with HLA-B8/DR3).

•  Clinical Features:

•  Glandular ("Sicca") Features:Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry, gritty eyes, conjunctivitis, filamentary keratitis), Xerostomia (dry mouth, difficulty swallowing dry food, rampant dental caries, oral candidiasis), parotid and salivary gland enlargement, and vaginal dryness.

•  Extraglandular Features: Severe fatigue, non-erosive polyarthralgia, Raynaud’s phenomenon, cutaneous vasculitis/purpura, interstitial lung disease, interstitial nephritis with distal (Type 1) Renal Tubular Acidosis, peripheral sensory neuropathy, and a 40-fold increased risk of B-cell Non-Hodgkin’s (MALT) Lymphoma (suspect if persistent parotid swelling, lymphadenopathy, or falling complement C4).

•  Investigations: Positive Anti-Ro (SS-A, 75%) and Anti-La (SS-B, 50%) antibodies, positive ANA (80%) and RF (90%), polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia, high ESR; Schirmer’s tear test (<5 mm wetting in 5 minutes); Rose Bengal corneal staining; and labial minor salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.

•  Management: Artificial tears (hypromellose drops by day, viscous ointment at night, punctal plugs), saliva substitutes/sugar-free chewing gum, rigorous dental hygiene, oral Pilocarpine (5 mg QDS, muscarinic agonist) to stimulate residual tear and saliva flow, Hydroxychloroquine for arthralgia/fatigue, and steroids/MMF/rituximab for systemic extraglandular organ involvement.

4. Diagnosis of Adult-Onset Still’s Disease (AOSD) [KU 21]:

•  Clinical Triad: (1) Quotidian (daily) high spiking fevers (>39°C) peaking in the late afternoon/evening; (2) Evanescent salmon-pink maculopapular rash appearing on the trunk and proximal limbs during fever spikes; and (3) Polyarthralgia / Polyarthritis (knees, wrists, ankles, with carpal ankylosis). Accompanied by sore throat (pharyngitis), lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis.

•  Laboratory Hallmarks (Yamaguchi Criteria — Diagnosis of Exclusion after ruling out infection, lymphoma, and other CTDs):

•  Markedly elevated ESR and CRP with leucocytosis (≥ 10–15 × 109/L with >80% neutrophils).

•  Extreme Hyperferritinaemia (serum ferritin often >1000 to >10,000 µ g/L with low glycosylated ferritin fraction).

•  Abnormal liver transaminases.

•  Negative ANA and Negative Rheumatoid Factor (RF).

•  Complication:Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS / Secondary HLH).

•  Treatment: NSAIDs, High-dose Corticosteroids + Methotrexate, and Interleukin-1 Inhibitors (Anakinra or Canakinumab) or IL-6R inhibitor (Tocilizumab).
