title: 6. Systemic Vasculitides: EGPA (Churg–Strauss), IgA Vasculitis (HSP), Behçet’s Disease, PAN, Takayasu’s, and Kawasaki Disease [KU 25, 23, 21, 20, TU]
text:
SECTION 23.6 & 23.7 — VASCULITIS & DISEASES OF BONE

6. Systemic Vasculitides: EGPA (Churg–Strauss), IgA Vasculitis (HSP), Behçet’s Disease, PAN, Takayasu’s, and Kawasaki Disease [KU 25, 23, 21, 20, TU]

1. Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA — formerly Churg–Strauss Syndrome) [KU 25]:

•  Definition & Pathophysiology: A rare necrotising small- and medium-vessel vasculitis characterised by extravascular necrotising granulomas, striking peripheral blood and tissue eosinophilia, and late-onset severe asthma. It is one of the three ANCA-Associated Vasculitides (AAV) (alongside Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis [GPA / Wegener’s] and Microscopic Polyangiitis [MPA]); p-ANCA (anti-Myeloperoxidase [MPO] antibodies) are positive in 40%–60% of EGPA cases.

•  Clinical Features (Evolves Through Three Classic Sequential Phases):

1.  Prodromal Allergic Phase (Lasts years): Adult-onset severe, poorly controlled asthma, allergic rhinitis, recurrent sinusitis, and nasal polyposis.

2.  Eosinophilic Phase: Marked peripheral blood eosinophilia with transient migratory pulmonary infiltrates (Löffler-like eosinophilic pneumonia) and eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

3.  Systemic Vasculitic Phase (Presents with the Classic Triad of Skin Lesions + Asymmetric Mononeuritis Multiplex + Eosinophilia):

•  Neurological (70%):Mononeuritis multiplex (acute painful foot drop or wrist drop) or symmetrical polyneuropathy.

•  Cutaneous:Palpable purpura, subcutaneous nodules, livedo reticularis, and skin infarcts.

•  Cardiac (Leading cause of mortality in EGPA):Eosinophilic myocarditis / cardiomyopathy, pericarditis, heart failure, and coronary arteritis.

•  Gastrointestinal (50%): Abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and bleeding/perforation from mesenteric vasculitis.

•  Renal: Focal segmental necrotising glomerulonephritis (less frequent than in GPA/MPA, mainly in MPO-ANCA+ patients).

•  Investigations:

•  FBC:Marked peripheral blood eosinophilia (>10% or >1.0–1.5 × 109/L), normocytic anaemia.

•  Inflammatory & Immunological Markers: Raised ESR and CRP, elevated serum IgE, and positive p-ANCA (anti-MPO) in 40%–60%.

•  Imaging & Function:HRCT Chest (migratory patchy ground-glass pulmonary infiltrates, bronchial wall thickening, pleural effusions), CT sinuses, Echocardiogram / Cardiac MRI (to detect eosinophilic myocarditis), urinalysis (haematuria/proteinuria), and nerve conduction studies (axonal mononeuritis multiplex).

•  Tissue Biopsy (Skin, Sural Nerve, Lung, or Kidney): Demonstrates small-vessel necrotising vasculitis, intense eosinophilic infiltration, and extravascular eosinophilic granulomas.

•  Management of EGPA:

•  Remission Induction:High-dose Glucocorticoids (oral Prednisolone 40–60 mg/day or IV Methylprednisolone pulses, gradually tapered) COMBINED WITHIV Cyclophosphamide (or Rituximab) in patients with severe organ-/life-threatening manifestations (cardiac, renal, CNS, mesenteric, or severe mononeuritis multiplex).

•  Targeted Anti-Interleukin-5 (IL-5) Biologic Therapy & Maintenance:Mepolizumab (monoclonal antibody against IL-5, 300 mg SC 4-weekly) or Benralizumab (anti-IL-5 receptor antibody, 30 mg SC 4-weekly) specifically block eosinophil maturation and survival, and are approved as highly effective steroid-sparing maintenance therapies in EGPA (alongside azathioprine, methotrexate, or MMF).

2. IgA Vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein Purpura — HSP) [KU 23, 21, TU]:

•  Definition & Pathophysiology: A systemic small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis caused by deposition of IgA1-containing immune complexes in the walls of arterioles, capillaries, and venules of the skin, gut, synovium, and renal glomeruli. Predominantly affects children and young adults, often 1–2 weeks after an upper respiratory tract infection (e.g., β-haemolytic streptococci).

•  Classic Clinical Tetrad:

1.  Palpable Purpura (100%): Non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpuric rash distributed symmetrically over the buttocks and extensor surfaces of the lower legs (gravity-dependent).

2.  Arthralgia / Non-deforming Arthritis (75%): Transient periarticular swelling and pain affecting the knees and ankles.

3.  Gastrointestinal Involvement (50%–70%): Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, bloody diarrhoea/melaena, and ileo-ileal intussusception (in children).

4.  Renal Involvement — IgA Nephritis (40%–50%): Microscopic or macroscopic haematuria, proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (may appear up to 4 weeks after the rash; main determinant of long-term prognosis, especially in adults).

•  Diagnosis & Management:

•  Diagnosis: Platelet count and coagulation are normal. Skin or renal biopsy with direct immunofluorescence shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis / mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis with granular IgA and C3 deposition in vessel walls/mesangium.

•  Management: Usually self-limiting over 4 weeks, requiring only supportive care and simple analgesia. Monitor urinalysis and BP for 6–12 months. Corticosteroids (for severe abdominal pain or nephritis) plus immunosuppressants (cyclophosphamide, MMF, azathioprine) are used only for severe/crescentic nephritis.

3. Diagnosis of Behçet’s Syndrome / Disease [KU 20]:

•  Definition: A systemic vasculitis of unknown cause that uniquely targets both arteries and veins of all sizes (predominantly small vessels and venules), endemic along the ancient "Silk Route" (Turkey, Middle East, Mediterranean, Japan) and strongly associated with HLA-B51.

•  International Study Group Diagnostic Criteria for Behçet’s Disease:

•  Mandatory Criterion:Recurrent Oral Ulceration (minor aphthous, major aphthous, or herpetiform ulcers recurring at least 3 times in a 12-month period, which are typically deep, painful, and multiple)

•  PLUS at least TWO of the following four criteria:

1.  Recurrent Genital Ulceration: Painful, deep ulcers on the scrotum or vulva that heal with scarring (60%–80%).

2.  Eye Lesions:Anterior uveitis (with hypopyon), Posterior uveitis, cells in the vitreous on slit-lamp examination, or retinal vasculitis (major cause of blindness).

3.  Skin Lesions:Erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopustular lesions, or acneiform nodules.

4.  Positive Pathergy Test: Development of an erythematous papule or sterile pustule >2 mm at the site of a sterile oblique skin needle-prick read at 24–48 hours.

•  Other Systemic Features: Non-deforming oligoarthritis, recurrent superficial and deep venous thrombosis (including dural venous sinus thrombosis and Budd–Chiari syndrome), pulmonary artery aneurysms, and neuro-Behçet’s (brainstem meningoencephalitis, pyramidal signs).

•  Management:Topical steroids + Oral Colchicine for mucocutaneous ulcers, erythema nodosum, and arthralgia; Systemic Corticosteroids + Azathioprine, Ciclosporin, or Anti-TNF-α (Infliximab/Adalimumab) for sight-threatening uveitis, neuro-Behçet’s, or vascular disease.

4. Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN), Takayasu’s Arteritis, and Kawasaki Disease [TU]:

•  Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN):

•  Pathology & Four Causes/Associations: Necrotising medium-sized muscular artery vasculitis causing microaneurysms and focal vessel occlusion with no glomerulonephritis and negative ANCA. Associated with: (1) Chronic Hepatitis B virus infection (most important cause, 10%–30%); (2) Hepatitis C or HIV infection; (3) Hairy cell leukaemia / myelodysplasia; and (4) Idiopathic (or DADA2 adenosine deaminase-2 deficiency).

•  Clinical Features: Fever, weight loss, myalgia, mononeuritis multiplex (70%), livedo reticularis, palpable purpura, and punched-out skin ulcers, severe renin-mediated hypertension and renal infarcts (without glomerulonephritis), mesenteric arteritis (post-prandial abdominal pain/infarction), and testicular pain (orchitis).

•  Diagnosis & Treatment:Mesenteric/renal CT or conventional angiography showing multiple saccular microaneurysms ("beading") and stenoses, or sural nerve/muscle biopsy showing transmural fibrinoid necrosis. Treated with high-dose corticosteroids + cyclophosphamide (plus antivirals and plasma exchange if HBV-associated).

•  Takayasu’s Arteritis ("Pulseless Disease"):

•  Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches (and pulmonary arteries), predominantly in young Asian women (<40 years, F:M = 8:1).

•  Clinical Features: Fever, night sweats, arthralgia, upper limb claudication, loss of brachial/radial pulses ("pulseless disease"), discrepancy in BP >10 mmHg between arms, vascular bruits (carotid, subclavian, renal), renovascular hypertension, aortic regurgitation, and visual loss/stroke.

•  Diagnosis & Treatment: Elevated ESR/CRP; CT/MR Angiography or 18F-FDG PET-CT showing smooth concentric mural thickening, stenosis, and aneurysms of the aorta and arch branches. Treated with high-dose corticosteroids + Methotrexate/Azathioprine/MMF, escalating to Anti-TNF-α or Tocilizumab, plus angioplasty/bypass once inflammation is controlled.

•  Kawasaki Disease (Mucocutaneous Lymph Node Syndrome):

•  Acute febrile medium-vessel vasculitis affecting children <5 years with a predilection for the coronary arteries.

•  Diagnostic Criteria:Persistent fever for ≥ 5 days PLUS ≥ 4 of the 5 CRASH features: (1) Conjunctival injection (bilateral, non-purulent); (2) Rash (polymorphous maculopapular); (3) Adenopathy (cervical lymphadenopathy >1.5 cm); (4) Strawberry tongue, red fissured lips, and pharyngeal erythema; (5) Hands and feet changes (erythema and indurated oedema of palms/soles, followed by periungual desquamation).

•  Complications & Treatment:Coronary artery aneurysms (25% if untreated), myocardial infarction, and myocarditis. Treat urgently within 10 days with a single infusion of Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIg, 2 g/kg over 12 hrs) PLUS Oral Aspirin (reduces coronary aneurysm risk to <5%).

title: 7. Metabolic Bone Diseases: Osteomalacia and Osteoporosis [KU 18, 17, 16]
text:
7. Metabolic Bone Diseases: Osteomalacia and Osteoporosis [KU 18, 17, 16]

1. Osteomalacia & Rickets [KU 18, 17]:

•  Definition & Pathophysiology: Defective mineralisation of newly formed bone matrix (osteoid), resulting in accumulation of thick uncalcified osteoid seams and soft, mechanically weak bone. Rickets is the equivalent disorder in growing children prior to epiphyseal growth plate fusion.

•  Causes of Osteomalacia:

1.  Vitamin D Deficiency (Most common):

•  Classical: Lack of sunlight (UVB) exposure (housebound elderly, northern latitudes, dark skin, veiled clothing) combined with poor dietary intake (oily fish, fortified dairy).

•  Gastrointestinal Malabsorption:Coeliac disease, Crohn’s disease, post-gastrectomy, chronic pancreatitis, cholestatic liver disease (PBC).

•  Increased Hepatic Catabolism:Enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital).

2.  Defective 1,25(OH)2D Synthesis or Action:

•  Chronic Kidney Disease (renal osteodystrophy—loss of renal 1α-hydroxylase).

•  Vitamin D-Resistant Rickets: Type I (1α-hydroxylase CYP27B1 mutation) and Type II (Vitamin D receptor mutation).

3.  Renal Phosphate-Wasting & Mineralisation Defects:

•  Hereditary Hypophosphataemic Rickets (X-linked dominant PHEX mutation causing excess FGF23; treated with anti-FGF23 antibody Burosumab or phosphate + calcitriol).

•  Tumour-Induced (Oncogenic) Osteomalacia (mesenchymal tumour secreting FGF23), Fanconi syndrome (proximal RTA), repeated IV ferric carboxymaltose infusions, and Hypophosphatasia (ALPL mutation).

•  Clinical Features of Osteomalacia (Adults):

•  Diffuse bone pain and tenderness (ribs, pelvis, spine, legs) and general malaise.

•  Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness (myopathy) presenting with difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs and a characteristic "waddling" gait.

•  Pathological fractures and hypocalcaemic tetany/paraesthesia (in severe cases).

•  (In childhood rickets: craniotabes, frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure, costochondral "rickety rosary", Harrison’s sulcus, widened wrists, and genu varum/valgum).

•  Diagnosis & Investigations of Osteomalacia:

•  Characteristic Biochemical Profile:

•  Markedly LOW Serum 25(OH)D (<25 nmol/L / <10 ng/mL) (in vitamin D deficiency).

•  Elevated Serum Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) (↑↑).

•  Elevated Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) (↑↑, secondary hyperparathyroidism).

•  Low Serum Phosphate (↓, due to PTH-induced phosphaturia) and Low or Normal Serum Calcium (↓ / N).

•  Plain X-rays: Generalised osteopenia, biconcave "codfish" vertebrae, and pathognomonic Looser’s zones (pseudofractures)—translucent, ribbon-like cortical stress fractures at right angles to the bone cortex with sclerotic margins, classically found in the medial femoral neck, pubic rami, ribs, axillary border of the scapulae, and tibia.

•  Undemineralised Iliac Crest Bone Biopsy (Gold Standard, rarely needed): Shows markedly increased thickness and surface extent of unmineralised osteoid seams.

•  Management:

•  Treat underlying cause (e.g., gluten-free diet in coeliac disease).

•  Vitamin D Replacement (Cholecalciferol / Vitamin D3): Loading dose of 10,000–25,000 IU daily for 2–4 weeks (or 50,000 IU weekly for 6 weeks), followed by life-long maintenance of 800–1600 IU daily plus Calcium supplements (1000 mg/day). (Use Alfacalcidol or Calcitriol in chronic renal failure or Type I vitamin D-resistant rickets).

2. Osteoporosis [KU 16]:

•  Definition: A systemic skeletal disease characterised by low bone mass (bone mineral density) and micro-architectural deterioration of bone tissue, leading to enhanced bone fragility and a consequent increase in fracture risk.

•  WHO DXA Diagnostic Criteria (Based on Bone Mineral Density [BMD] T-score at Lumbar Spine or Hip compared to a young healthy adult mean):

•  Normal: T-score ≥ -1.0 SD.

•  Osteopenia: T-score between  -1.0 and  -2.5 SD.

•  Osteoporosis:T-score ≤ -2.5 SD (Severe/established osteoporosis = T-score ≤ -2.5 SD in the presence of one or more fragility fractures).

•  Risk Factors & Secondary Causes (Mnemonic: SHATTERED):

•  Fixed: Increasing age, Female sex (post-menopausal oestrogen deficiency), family history/genetics (LRP5, WNT1), previous fragility fracture.

•  Endocrine:Hypogonadism (premature menopause, male androgen deprivation), Cushing’s syndrome, Hyperthyroidism (or levothyroxine over-replacement), Hyperparathyroidism.

•  Drugs:Systemic Glucocorticoids (>7.5 mg/day prednisolone for >3 months—inhibits osteoblasts and induces osteocyte apoptosis), Aromatase inhibitors, GnRH agonists, long-term heparin, anticonvulsants, glitazones.

•  Inflammatory, GI & Other:Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, chronic liver/renal disease, multiple myeloma, low BMI (<20 kg/m2)/anorexia nervosa, cigarette smoking, alcohol excess (>3 units/day), and immobility.

•  Clinical Presentation & Investigations:

•  Asymptomatic until a low-trauma fragility fracture occurs (from standing height or less), classically affecting the distal radius (Colles’ fracture), thoracolumbar vertebrae (acute back pain, height loss, dorsal dowager’s hump kyphosis), proximal femur (hip fracture), or proximal humerus.

•  Investigations:DXA (Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry) Scan of lumbar spine and hip + FRAX 10-year fracture risk score; spine X-rays for vertebral morphometry; Routine bone biochemistry (Calcium, Phosphate, ALP, PTH, and 25(OH)D are all NORMAL in primary osteoporosis); plus FBC, ESR, U&Es, LFTs, TFTs, anti-tTG, serum/urine electrophoresis (to exclude myeloma), and testosterone in men.

•  Management of Osteoporosis:

1.  Lifestyle & Falls Prevention: Weight-bearing and resistance exercise, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, fall-risk modification, and Calcium (1000 mg/day) + Vitamin D (800 IU/day) supplementation.

2.  First-Line Antiresorptive Therapy — Bisphosphonates:

•  Mechanism: Pyrophosphate analogues that bind to bone hydroxyapatite, are internalised by resorbing osteoclasts, and induce osteoclast apoptosis.

•  Oral Regimens:Alendronic acid (70 mg once weekly) or Risedronate (35 mg once weekly)—must be taken fasting in the morning with a full glass of plain water, remaining upright for 30–45 mins before food. Continue for 5 years, then review for a "drug holiday".

•  Parenteral Regimen:Intravenous Zoledronic Acid (5 mg infusion once annually for 3 years)—used for oral intolerance, malabsorption, or post-hip fracture.

•  Adverse Effects: Oesophageal ulceration (oral), transient flu-like acute phase response (IV), hypocalcaemia, and rare osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ) and atypical subtrochanteric femoral shaft fractures.

3.  Second-Line Antiresorptive — Denosumab (60 mg SC every 6 months):

•  Human monoclonal antibody that binds and neutralises RANKL, inhibiting osteoclast formation (safe in renal impairment; do not stop abruptly without transitioning to a bisphosphonate due to rebound vertebral fractures).

4.  Anabolic (Bone-Forming) Agents (For Severe Osteoporosis / Multiple Vertebral Fractures):

•  Teriparatide (20 µ g SC daily for 24 months) or Abaloparatide: Recombinant PTH (1–34) fragment; intermittent daily administration stimulates osteoblastic new bone formation.

•  Romosozumab (210 mg SC monthly for 12 months): Monoclonal antibody that neutralises sclerostin (SOST), exerting a dual effect of stimulating bone formation and inhibiting bone resorption(contraindicated in prior MI or stroke). Must be followed by an antiresorptive agent.

5.  Hormonal Therapies:HRT (in women <60 years with premature menopause/vasomotor symptoms) or SERM Raloxifene (60 mg daily).

title: 1. Cross-Section of the Midbrain, Circle of Willis, and Crossed Hemiplegias [KU 25, 22, 19, TU]
text:
CHAPTER 64 & CHAPTER 25 — NEUROLOGY AND STROKE MEDICINE

Anatomy, Investigations & Presenting Problems

1. Cross-Section of the Midbrain, Circle of Willis, and Crossed Hemiplegias [KU 25, 22, 19, TU]

1. Cross-Section of the Midbrain & Midbrain Syndromes [KU 25]:

•  Anatomical Structures in a Transverse Cross-Section of the Midbrain (at the level of the Superior Colliculus, from Dorsal to Ventral):

1.  Tectum (Dorsal):Superior colliculi (visual reflexes/vertical gaze) and Inferior colliculi (auditory pathway, lower midbrain).

2.  Cerebral Aqueduct (of Sylvius): Surrounded by the periaqueductal grey matter; on its ventral floor lie the Oculomotor (3rd) cranial nerve nucleus and the parasympathetic Edinger–Westphal nucleus (and Trochlear [4th] nucleus at the inferior colliculus level), alongside the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF).

3.  Tegmentum (Central): Contains the Red nucleus, the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles, the reticular formation, and the ascending sensory tracts (Medial lemniscus [dorsal column fibres], Spinothalamic tract, and trigeminal lemniscus).

4.  Substantia Nigra: Pigmented dopaminergic neurons separating the tegmentum from the crus cerebri.

5.  Crus Cerebri / Basis Pedunculi (Ventral Cerebral Peduncles): Contains the descending Corticospinal (pyramidal) and Corticobulbar tracts (with emerging 3rd nerve root fibres passing ventrally through the red nucleus and cerebral peduncle to exit in the interpeduncular fossa).

•  Crossed Hemiplegia (Brainstem Syndromes) [KU 19]:

•  Definition: A lesion in the brainstem damages ipsilateral cranial nerve nuclei/fibres (producing an ipsilateral lower motor neuron cranial nerve palsy) AND damages the descending corticospinal tract BEFORE it decussates in the lower medulla (producing a contralateral spastic hemiplegia).

•  Midbrain (Weber’s Syndrome — Cerebral Peduncle Infarction):Ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy (ptosis, dilated pupil, eye "down and out") + Contralateral hemiplegia (including contralateral UMN 7th facial palsy). (Benedikt’s syndrome involves the 3rd nerve + red nucleus, causing ipsilateral 3rd palsy + contralateral cerebellar tremor/ataxia).

•  Pons (Millard–Gubler / Foville Syndrome):Ipsilateral 6th nerve palsy and Ipsilateral LMN 7th (facial) nerve palsy + Contralateral hemiplegia.

•  Medulla (Medial Medullary Syndrome):Ipsilateral 12th (hypoglossal) nerve palsy (tongue deviates to side of lesion) + Contralateral hemiplegia + Contralateral medial lemniscus (proprioceptive) loss. (Note: Lateral Medullary [Wallenberg] Syndrome due to PICA/vertebral occlusion causes ipsilateral 5th [pain/temp], 9th, 10th [dysphagia/hoarseness], ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, vertigo, and contralateral body spinothalamic pain/temperature loss—without pyramidal hemiplegia).

2. Anatomy of the Circle of Willis [KU 22, TU]:

•  An anastomotic arterial polygon at the base of the brain (in the interpeduncular subarachnoid cistern, surrounding the optic chiasm and pituitary stalk) that interconnects the anterior (internal carotid) and posterior (vertebrobasilar) cerebral circulations and links the left and right hemispheres:

•  Anterior Circulation (Paired Internal Carotid Arteries): Each internal carotid artery bifurcates into the Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) and the Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA). The two ACAs are joined across the midline by the single Anterior Communicating Artery (ACom).

•  Posterior Circulation (Vertebrobasilar System): The two Vertebral Arteries unite at the ponto-medullary junction to form the Basilar Artery, which bifurcates at the upper border of the pons into the paired Posterior Cerebral Arteries (PCAs).

•  Anastomotic Link: Each Posterior Communicating Artery (PCom) connects the ipsilateral Internal Carotid Artery (near the MCA origin) to the ipsilateral Posterior Cerebral Artery.

•  Clinical Significance: Provides collateral blood flow if a major feeding artery is occluded, and its arterial bifurcations are the commonest sites for saccular ("berry") aneurysms causing subarachnoid haemorrhage (ACom 30%, PCom 25%, MCA bifurcation 20%).

Cross-section of the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus (tectum / superior colliculi, periaqueductal grey and aqueduct, tegmentum / red nuclei, substantia nigra, crus cerebri, CN III).

A. Cross-Section of the Midbrain (Mesencephalon) & Midbrain Syndromes [KU 25]:

•  Anatomical Structures (from Dorsal to Ventral at the level of the Superior Colliculus):

1.  Cerebral Aqueduct of Sylvius: Narrow CSF channel connecting the third and fourth ventricles, surrounded by the Periaqueductal Grey Matter (PAG).

2.  Tegmentum (Central Core):

•  Oculomotor (3rd Cranial Nerve) Nucleus and the parasympathetic Edinger–Westphal Nucleus (located ventromedially in the periaqueductal grey at the level of the superior colliculus; fascicles pass anteriorly through the red nucleus to exit in the interpeduncular fossa). (At the inferior colliculus level lies the Trochlear [4th] nerve nucleus).

•  Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF): Connects the 3rd, 4th, and 6th cranial nerve nuclei to coordinate conjugate horizontal gaze.

•  Red Nucleus: Large oval motor nucleus receiving cerebellar fibres from the superior Risk factors include polygenic susceptibility (HLA-DRB1\15:01), prior Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV) infection, low Vitamin D / low childhood sunlight exposure, and cigarette smoking.

•  Pathophysiology: Autoreactive T and B lymphocytes cross the blood–brain barrier via α4β1 integrin (VLA-4), triggering perivenular inflammation, macrophage activation, and destruction of the oligodendrocyte–myelin unit in the optic nerves, periventricular white matter, brainstem, cerebellum, and cervical spinal cord. Acute symptoms reflect reversible conduction block in demyelinated axons (which improves as oedema resolves and sodium channels redistribute), whereas late progressive disability reflects irreversible axonal degeneration.

•  Classic Focal Midbrain Syndromes ("Crossed Paralyses") [KU 19]:

1.  Weber’s Syndrome (Ventral Midbrain / Cerebral Peduncle Infarction):Ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy (complete ptosis, dilated pupil, eye "down and out") + Contralateral hemiplegia (including contralateral UMN 7th facial palsy).

2.  Benedikt’s Syndrome (Midbrain Tegmentum):Ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy + Contralateral cerebellar ataxia, intention tremor, and choreoathetosis (red nucleus/superior cerebellar peduncle involvement).

1.  Parinaud’s Dorsal Midbrain Syndrome (Tectal Compression, e.g., Pinealoma) — details not recoverable from the spliced source text; see the midbrain syndromes above.

•  Component Arteries Forming the Circle of Willis:

1.  Anterior Circulation (Internal Carotid System):

•  Left and Right Internal Carotid Arteries (ICAs) (terminate by bifurcating into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries; note that the Middle Cerebral Artery [MCA] is a continuation of the ICA and is NOT a direct structural part of the ring).

•  Left and Right Anterior Cerebral Arteries (ACAs) (A1 pre-communicating segments).

•  Single Anterior Communicating Artery (ACom) (connects the left and right ACAs across the midline).

2.  Posterior Circulation (Vertebrobasilar System):

•  The two Vertebral Arteries unite at the ponto-medullary junction to form the Basilar Artery, which bifurcates at the upper border of the pons into:

•  Left and Right Posterior Cerebral Arteries (PCAs) (P1 pre-communicating segments).

•  Left and Right Posterior Communicating Arteries (PCom) (connect the Internal Carotid Arteries anteriorly to the Posterior Cerebral Arteries posteriorly).

•  Clinical Significance:

•  Collateral Perfusion: Maintains cerebral perfusion during unilateral carotid or vertebral artery stenosis/occlusion (though anatomical congenital variations/hypoplasia are common).

•  Saccular ("Berry") Aneurysms: 85% of subarachnoid haemorrhages arise from berry aneurysms at arterial bifurcations of the Circle of Willis: Anterior communicating artery (30%), Posterior communicating artery (25%), MCA bifurcation (20%).

title: 2. Lumbar Puncture, EEG, Spasticity vs. Rigidity, Babinski Sign, Flapping Tremor, Wernicke’s Aphasia, and Cerebellar Dysfunction [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 16, 15, TU]
text:
2. Lumbar Puncture, EEG, Spasticity vs. Rigidity, Babinski Sign, Flapping Tremor, Wernicke’s Aphasia, and Cerebellar Dysfunction [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 16, 15, TU]

1. Indications and Contraindications for Lumbar Puncture (LP) [KU 25, 24]:

•  Diagnostic Indications:

1.  Suspected Central Nervous System Infections: Acute bacterial, viral, tuberculous, or fungal (cryptococcal) meningitis and viral encephalitis (via cell count, protein, glucose, Gram/ZN/India ink stain, culture, and PCR).

2.  Suspected Subarachnoid Haemorrhage (SAH): Performed ≥ 12 hours after thunderclap headache onset to detect CSF xanthochromia (bilirubin by spectrophotometry) when the initial CT brain scan is negative.

3.  Neuro-inflammatory & Autoimmune Disorders:Multiple sclerosis (unpaired CSF oligoclonal bands), Guillain–Barré syndrome (albuminocytological dissociation—raised protein with normal cell count), CIDP, Neuromyelitis optica, and Autoimmune/Paraneoplastic encephalitis.

4.  Malignant (Carcinomatous / Lymphomatous) Meningitis: CSF cytology and immunophenotyping.

5.  Measurement of CSF Opening Pressure: Diagnosis of Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) (>250 mmH2O) or Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus.

•  Therapeutic Indications:

•  Relief of raised CSF pressure in Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension and Cryptococcal meningitis.

•  Intrathecal drug administration: Spinal anaesthesia, intrathecal chemotherapy (methotrexate/cytarabine in ALL/lymphoma), intrathecal baclofen (spasticity), or nusinersen (SMA).

•  Contraindications to Lumbar Puncture:

•  Raised intracranial pressure from an intracranial space-occupying lesion or obstructive hydrocephalus (papilloedema, focal neurological deficit, or GCS ≤ 12 — must perform CT/MRI brain first due to risk of fatal tentorial/tonsillar herniation ["coning"]).

•  Coagulopathy / Bleeding Diathesis: Anticoagulant therapy, severe thrombocytopenia (<50 × 109/L), or DIC (risk of spinal epidural haematoma).

•  Local skin/soft-tissue sepsis at the lumbar puncture site, or severe cardiorespiratory instability.

2. Differences Between Spasticity and Rigidity [KU 16]:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-014]]

3. Components of Babinski’s Sign, Flapping Tremor, Wernicke’s Aphasia, Brainstem Reflexes & GCS [KU 22, 16, 15, TU]:

•  Components of Babinski’s Sign (Extensor Plantar Response): Elicited by firmly stroking the lateral aspect of the sole from the heel towards the base of the toes; indicates an upper motor neuron (corticospinal tract) lesion above S1. Comprises: (1) Tonic dorsiflexion (extension) of the great toe (hallux) at the MTP joint (mediated by extensor hallucis longus); (2) Abduction (fanning) and dorsiflexion of the other four toes; and (3) Reflex triple flexion withdrawal of the ankle, knee, and hip (contraction of tensor fasciae latae, hamstrings, and tibialis anterior).

•  Four Causes of Flapping Tremor (Asterixis) [KU 15]: A negative myoclonus (brief rhythmic loss of postural tone in outstretched dorsiflexed hands every 5–10 seconds). Causes: (1) Hepatic encephalopathy (liver failure); (2) Uraemic encephalopathy (renal failure); (3) Hypercapnic respiratory failure (CO2 retention / Type II respiratory failure); (4) Drug toxicity (phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepine, barbiturates, lithium) or Focal structural brain lesions (thalamic/parietal stroke).

•  Wernicke’s Aphasia (Receptive / Sensory Aphasia) [KU 22]: Caused by a lesion in the posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke’s area) of the dominant (left) hemisphere (typically inferior division of left MCA infarction). Characterised by: (1) Impaired auditory and written language comprehension; (2) Fluent, effortless speech with normal rate and intonation, but devoid of meaning ("word salad" / jargon aphasia) containing frequent paraphasias (word/sound substitutions) and neologisms (made-up words); (3) Impaired repetition and naming; and (4) Lack of awareness of the speech deficit (often accompanied by a contralateral superior homonymous quadrantanopia).

•  Brainstem Reflexes (Tested to Assess Brainstem Function / Brainstem Death) [KU 16]: (1) Pupillary light reflex (CN II → CN III, midbrain); (2) Corneal reflex (CN V1 → CN VII, pons); (3) Oculocephalic ("doll’s eyes") and Oculovestibular (cold caloric) reflexes (CN VIII → MLF → CN III, IV, VI, pons/midbrain); (4) Pharyngeal (gag) and Cough/Tracheal reflexes (CN IX → CN X, medulla); and (5) Apnoea test (medullary respiratory centre response to PaCO2 >6.0–6.65 kPa).

•  Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) [TU] (Minimum score 3, Maximum score 15; Coma ≤ 8):

•  Eye Opening (E1–E4): Spontaneous (4), To speech (3), To pain (2), None (1).

•  Verbal Response (V1–V5): Orientated (5), Confused (4), Inappropriate words (3), Incomprehensible sounds (2), None (1).

•  Best Motor Response (M1–M6): Obeys commands (6), Localises to supraorbital pain (5), Normal flexion withdrawal to pain (4), Abnormal spastic flexion / decorticate (3), Extension to pain / decerebrate (2), None (1).

4. Disorders of Cerebellar Function: Causes & Clinical Signs [KU 24, 21, 15]:

•  Causes of Cerebellar Dysfunction:

•  Vascular: Posterior circulation cerebellar infarction or haemorrhage (PICA, AICA, SCA).

•  Inflammatory / Demyelinating:Multiple sclerosis, post-infectious cerebellitis (varicella), gluten ataxia (coeliac disease), paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (anti-Yo/PCA-1 in ovarian/breast cancer, anti-Hu in SCLC).

•  Toxic / Drug-induced:Alcohol (acute intoxication and chronic alcoholic cerebellar vermian degeneration), Antiseizure medications (Phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine), lithium, 5-fluorouracil.

•  Neoplastic / Structural: Posterior fossa tumours (medulloblastoma, haemangioblastoma, acoustic neuroma, metastases), cerebellar abscess, Chiari malformation.

•  Metabolic & Inherited:Hypothyroidism, Vitamin B1 (Wernicke) or Vitamin E deficiency, Friedreich’s ataxia, Spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs), Ataxia telangiectasia, Wilson’s disease, and sporadic CJD.

•  Clinical Signs of a Cerebellar Lesion (Ipsilateral to the Affected Cerebellar Hemisphere — Mnemonic: DANISH):

1.  D — Dysdiadochokinesis: Inability to perform rapid, regular alternating movements (e.g., pronation/supination of the hand).

2.  A — Ataxia of Gait and Posture (Vermian lesion): Broad-based, unsteady "drunken" gait, inability to walk heel-to-toe (tandem gait), and truncal titubation (tends to fall towards the side of the lesion).

3.  N — Nystagmus: Horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus with the fast phase beating towards the side of the cerebellar lesion, plus ocular dysmetria (overshoot of saccades).

4.  I — Intention Tremor & Dysmetria (Past-Pointing): Coarse 3–5 Hz tremor that is absent at rest and worsens as the limb approaches its target on finger–nose and heel–shin testing, overshooting the target (dysmetria / past-pointing) and showing rebound phenomenon.

5.  S — Scanning / Staccato Dysarthria: Slurred, explosive speech with impaired cadence where syllables are separated ("scanning speech").

6.  H — Hypotonia & Pendular Reflexes: Reduced muscle tone and pendular knee jerks (leg continues to swing back and forth like a pendulum after eliciting the patellar reflex).

A. Lumbar Puncture (LP):

•  Diagnostic Indications:

1.  Suspected Central Nervous System Infection: Acute bacterial, viral, tuberculous, or fungal/cryptococcal meningitis and viral encephalitis.

2.  Suspected Subarachnoid Haemorrhage (SAH): Performed ≥ 12 hours after headache onset to detect xanthochromia by spectrophotometry when an initial CT brain scan is negative.

•  High-Efficacy Monoclonal Antibodies (>50% relapse reduction):

•  Ocrelizumab (IV every 6 months) and Ofatumumab (monthly SC): Anti-CD20 B-cell depleting monoclonal antibodies (Ocrelizumab is also licensed for early Primary Progressive MS).

•  Natalizumab (4-weekly IV): Anti-α4β1 integrin antibody that blocks lymphocyte entry across the blood–brain barrier (carry out JC virus serology monitoring due to risk of Progressive Multifocal Leucoencephalopathy [PML]).

•  Alemtuzumab (two IV courses 12 months apart): Anti-CD52 antibody (30% develop secondary autoimmune thyroid disease).

•  Moderate-Efficacy Oral DMTs (30%–50% relapse reduction):

•  Sphingosine-1-Phosphate (S1P) Receptor Modulators:Fingolimod, Siponimod (licensed for active Secondary Progressive MS spectrophotometry when an initial CT brain scan is negative.

1.  Neuro-inflammatory & Demyelinating Disorders:

•  Multiple Sclerosis: Detection of unpaired CSF-specific oligoclonal IgG bands.

•  Guillain–Barré Syndrome (AIDP) / CIDP: Demonstrates albuminocytological dissociation (markedly elevated CSF protein with a normal white cell count).

•  Autoimmune Encephalitis (NMDAR, Lgi1 antibodies) and neurosarcoidosis.

2.  Suspected Leptomeningeal Malignancy: Carcinomatous or lymphomatous/leukaemic meningitis (CSF cytology/flow cytometry).

3.  Measurement of CSF Opening Pressure: Essential for diagnosing Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) (opening pressure >25 cm H2O).

•  Therapeutic Indications:

1.  CSF Drainage to lower intracranial pressure in Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension and Cryptococcal meningitis.

2.  Intrathecal Drug Administration: Spinal anaesthesia, intrathecal chemotherapy (methotrexate/cytarabine in ALL or high-grade lymphoma), intrathecal baclofen (for severe spasticity), and intrathecal antisense oligonucleotides (nusinersen in spinal muscular atrophy).

•  Contraindications to Immediate Lumbar Puncture (Requires CT Brain First to Exclude Mass Effect / Coning):

•  Clinical signs of raised intracranial pressure (papilloedema) or focal neurological deficits (hemiparesis, cranial nerve palsies).

•  Depressed conscious level (GCS ≤ 12) or uncontrolled/continuous seizures.

•  Severe septic shock, cardiorespiratory compromise, or a rapidly evolving meningococcal purpuric rash.

•  Coagulopathy (INR >1.4), full therapeutic anticoagulation, or severe thrombocytopenia (platelets <50 × 109/L) (risk of spinal epidural haematoma).

•  Local skin sepsis over the lumbar puncture site (L3/L4).

B. Electroencephalography (EEG):

•  Normal Rhythms:Alpha (8–13 Hz) over occipital lobes when awake with eyes closed; Beta (>13 Hz) frontally or with benzodiazepines; Theta (4–8 Hz) and Delta (<4 Hz) in deep sleep, young children, or diffuse encephalopathy/structural focal lesions.

•  Clinical Indications for EEG:

1.  Epilepsy Classification & Prognostication: Distinguishes Generalised Epilepsy Syndromes (e.g., generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges in childhood absence epilepsy; polyspike-and-wave with photoparoxysmal response in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy) from Focal Epilepsy (focal temporal/frontal sharp waves or spikes). (Note: Inter-ictal routine EEG is normal in 50% of epilepsy patients, so a normal EEG NEVER excludes epilepsy).

2.  Video-EEG Telemetry: Differentiates epileptic seizures from dissociative non-epileptic attacks and localises the epileptogenic focus prior to epilepsy surgery.

3.  Investigation of Coma, Delirium & ICU Monitoring: Essential to diagnose Non-Convulsive Status Epilepticus and to monitor burst-suppression in refractory status epilepticus.

4.  Specific Encephalopathies & Neurodegenerative Diseases:

•  Herpes Simplex Encephalitis: Periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) and temporal slow waves.

•  Hepatic / Metabolic Encephalopathy: Diffuse slowing with triphasic waves.

•  Sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob Disease (CJD): Characteristic generalised 1–2 Hz periodic sharp/triphasic slow-wave complexes.

•  Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE): Periodic high-voltage burst complexes (Radermecker complexes).

5.  Sleep Disorders: Polysomnography with multiple sleep latency testing in narcolepsy (rapid onset of REM sleep) and REM sleep behaviour disorder.

title: 3. Presenting Problems in Neurology: Spasticity vs. Rigidity, Babinski’s Sign, Flapping Tremor, Abnormal Gaits, Wernicke’s Aphasia, Glasgow Coma Scale, Brainstem Reflexes, and Raised ICP [KU 24, 22, 16, 15, TU]
text:
3. Presenting Problems in Neurology: Spasticity vs. Rigidity, Babinski’s Sign, Flapping Tremor, Abnormal Gaits, Wernicke’s Aphasia, Glasgow Coma Scale, Brainstem Reflexes, and Raised ICP [KU 24, 22, 16, 15, TU]

A. Differences Between Spasticity and Rigidity [KU 16]:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-015]]

B. Components of Babinski’s Sign (Extensor Plantar Response) [TU]:

•  Elicitation: Firmly stroke the lateral aspect of the sole of the foot from the heel upwards towards the base of the fifth metatarsal and curve medially across the metatarsal pad.

•  Normal Response (after 1 year of age): Plantar flexion of the hallux (big toe) and other toes.

•  Components of a Positive Babinski’s Sign (Pathognomonic of an Upper Motor Neuron / Pyramidal Tract Lesion):

1.  Slow, tonic dorsiflexion (extension) of the great toe (hallux) (via recruitment of extensor hallucis longus).

2.  Abduction ("fanning") and dorsiflexion of the other four toes.

3.  Triple flexion withdrawal synergy of the lower limb (simultaneous dorsiflexion of the ankle, flexion of the knee, and flexion of the hip, accompanied by contraction of the tensor fasciae latae).

C. Four Causes of Flapping Tremor (Asterixis) [KU 15]:

(Asterixis is a coarse, jerky "negative myoclonus" caused by brief 50–200 ms lapses of postural muscle tone when the arms are outstretched and wrists dorsiflexed; indicates metabolic encephalopathy or structural thalamic/parietal lesions):

1.  Hepatic Encephalopathy (decompensated cirrhosis or acute liver failure).

2.  Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure (Type II Respiratory Failure / CO2 Retention) (e.g., severe COPD exacerbation).

3.  Uraemic Encephalopathy (severe acute or chronic renal failure).

4.  Drug Toxicity & Metabolic Derangements: Anticonvulsant toxicity (phenytoin, carbamazepine, sodium valproate), sedative overdose, severe hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, or hypomagnesaemia(Note: Unilateral asterixis is caused by a focal contralateral thalamic or parietal stroke).

D. Abnormal Types of Gait [TU]:

1.  Hemiplegic / Pyramidal Circumduction Gait (Upper Motor Neuron Lesion / Stroke): Affected arm is held flexed and adducted with reduced swing; the spastic, extended leg swings outwards in a semicircular arc from the hip (circumduction) so the toes clear the ground.

2.  Spastic Paraparetic ("Scissors") Gait (Bilateral Spinal Cord Lesion / Cerebral Palsy): Both legs are stiff, extended, and adducted at the hips, crossing over in front of each other ("scissoring") and dragging as if "walking through mud".

3.  Parkinsonian / Festinant (Extrapyramidal) Gait: Stooped posture, difficulty initiating walking (ignition failure), freezing in doorways, absent arm swing, turning en bloc, and short, rapid shuffling steps that progressively accelerate (festination) to catch up with the forward centre of gravity.

4.  Cerebellar Ataxic Gait:Broad-based, unsteady, staggering gait ("as if drunk"), reeling towards the side of a unilateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion, with an inability to perform tandem (heel-to-toe) walking.

5.  Sensory Ataxic ("Stamping") Gait (Dorsal Column / Proprioceptive Loss — Vitamin B12 deficiency, Tabes dorsalis, Sensory neuropathy): Broad-based gait where the patient watches the ground and lifts the feet high before slamming/stamping them heavily onto the floor to generate proprioceptive feedback; markedly worsens in the dark or on eye closure (positive Romberg’s sign).

6.  High-Stepping ("Foot-Drop" / Neuropathic) Gait (L5 Radiculopathy, Common Peroneal Nerve Palsy, or CMT Polyneuropathy): Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion causes the patient to lift the knee excessively high so the drooping toes clear the floor, followed by an audible "slap" as the forefoot strikes the ground first.

7.  Myopathic ("Waddling") Gait (Proximal Pelvic Girdle Weakness — Muscular Dystrophy, Polymyositis, Osteomalacia): Weakness of the hip abductors (gluteus medius) causes the pelvis to drop on the unsupported side during each stride (Trendelenburg sign), producing an exaggerated side-to-side rolling trunk movement.

8.  Apraxic Gait (Marche à petits pas): Feet appear "glued/magnetised to the floor" despite normal leg power and coordination on the bed; seen in Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus and diffuse frontal lobe small-vessel cerebrovascular disease.

E. Wernicke’s Aphasia [KU 22]:

•  Anatomical Site of Lesion: Posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke’s area — Brodmann area 22) of the dominant (usually left) cerebral hemisphere, typically caused by occlusion of the inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery.

•  Clinical Characteristics (Fluent / Receptive Aphasia):

•  Speech Output:Fluent, effortless, with normal rate, rhythm, and melody (prosody), but devoid of meaning ("word salad" or jargon aphasia), containing frequent phonemic and semantic paraphasias (word substitutions) and neologisms (invented non-words).

•  Auditory & Written Comprehension:Severely impaired (cannot understand spoken or written commands).

•  Repetition, Naming, Reading & Writing:Impaired repetition, anomia, alexia, and fluent but nonsensical writing.

•  Associated Signs: Patients typically lack insight/awareness of their speech deficit; often accompanied by a contralateral (right) superior homonymous quadrantanopia (due to involvement of Meyer’s loop of the optic radiation in the temporal lobe), usually without hemiparesis.

F. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) [TU] & Brainstem Reflexes [KU 16]:

•  Glasgow Coma Scale (Range: Minimum 3/15 to Maximum 15/15; Coma is defined as GCS ≤ 8):

•  Eye Opening (E1–E4):4 = Spontaneous; 3 = To speech; 2 = To pain/pressure; 1 = None.

•  Verbal Response (V1–V5):5 = Orientated; 4 = Confused conversation; 3 = Inappropriate words; 2 = Incomprehensible sounds; 1 = None.

•  Best Motor Response (M1–M6):6 = Obeys commands; 5 = Localises to supraorbital/trapezius pain; 4 = Normal flexion withdrawal to pain; 3 = Abnormal spastic flexion (decorticate posturing); 2 = Extension to pain (decerebrate posturing); 1 = None.

•  Brainstem Reflexes (Tested in Coma Localization and Brainstem Death Testing):

1.  Pupillary Light Reflex: Afferent: Optic nerve (CN II) → Efferent: Oculomotor nerve (CN III) (Midbrain).

2.  Corneal Reflex: Afferent: Ophthalmic division of Trigeminal nerve (CN V1) → Efferent: Facial nerve (CN VII) (Pons).

3.  Oculocephalic ("Doll’s Head" Eye) Reflex & Vestibulo-Ocular (Cold Caloric) Reflex: Irrigating the external auditory canal with ice-cold water normally causes tonic conjugate deviation of the eyes towards the irrigated ear (Afferent: Vestibulocochlear nerve [CN VIII] → MLF → Efferent: CN III and CN VI; Pons to Midbrain).

4.  Gag & Cough Reflexes: Pharyngeal/tracheal stimulation (Afferent: Glossopharyngeal nerve [CN IX] → Efferent: Vagus nerve [CN X]; Medulla).

5.  Apnoea Test: Medullary respiratory centre response to hypercapnia (PaCO2 >6.0–6.5 kPa).

title: 4. Migraine, Tension-Type Headache, and Trigeminal Neuralgia [KU 25, 23, 22, 19, 18, TU, RGU]
text:
Headache Syndromes

4. Migraine, Tension-Type Headache, and Trigeminal Neuralgia [KU 25, 23, 22, 19, 18, TU, RGU]

1. Migraine (Pathophysiology, Clinical Features, Acute Treatment & Prophylaxis):

•  Epidemiology & Pathophysiology: Affects ~ 20% of women and 6% of men, usually starting before middle age.

•  Pathogenesis of the Aura: Caused by Cortical Spreading Depression (of Leão)—a wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation (excitation) followed by prolonged hyperpolarisation (inhibition) that spreads across the cerebral cortex (most commonly occipital) at 3 mm/min.

•  Pathogenesis of the Headache: Activation of the trigeminovascular system and hypothalamic networks leads to release of Calcitonin Gene–Related Peptide (CGRP), substance P, and neurokinin A, causing neurogenic inflammation, meningeal vasodilatation, and central pain sensitisation.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Prodrome (hours to days before): Yawning, mood change, irritability, neck stiffness, food cravings.

•  Migraine WITH Aura ("Classical Migraine" — 20% of patients): Reversible focal neurological symptoms evolving gradually over 5–20 minutes.

•  Tension-Type Headache:

•  The most common primary headache: bilateral, generalised, non-pulsatile ("dull, tight band around the head" or pressure at the vertex), of mild-to-moderate intensity, not aggravated by routine physical activity, and lacking vomiting or severe photophobia/phonophobia. Treated with reassurance, stress management/relaxation physiotherapy, avoidance of analgesic overuse, and low-dose amitriptyline prophylaxis if chronic.

•  Trigeminal Neuralgia (Tic Douloureux):

•  Aetiology: Paroxysmal neuropathic facial pain in patients >50 years, usually caused by neurovascular compression of the trigeminal (5th) nerve root entry zone at the pons by an aberrant arterial loop (usually the superior cerebellar artery). In patients <50 years (or if bilateral/associated with sensory loss), exclude a pontine demyelinating plaque in Multiple Sclerosis or a cerebellopontine angle tumour (acoustic neuroma, meningioma) by MRI brain.

•  Clinical Features: Excruciating, unilateral, lancinating ("electric-shock" or stabbing) pain strictly confined to the maxillary (V2) and/or mandibular (V3) divisions of the trigeminal nerve (rarely V1).

•  Attacks last from a split-second to <2 minutes, make the patient wince (tic douloureux), and are triggered by light touch on "trigger zones", washing the face, shaving, cold wind, talking, chewing, or brushing teeth. Neurological examination is completely normal in idiopathic cases.

•  Management:

•  Drug of First Choice:Carbamazepine (100 mg BD initially, gradually titrated up to 600–1200 mg/day; monitor sodium for hyponatraemia).

•  Second-Line Drugs:Oxcarbazepine, Lamotrigine, Gabapentin, Pregabalin, Baclofen, or Phenytoin.

•  Surgical Options (for medically refractory cases):Microvascular Decompression (Jannetta procedure) (posterior fossa craniotomy to separate the offending arterial loop from the trigeminal root — provides the best long-term cure), Stereotactic Gamma-Knife Radiosurgery, or percutaneous Gasserian ganglion rhizotomy (radiofrequency thermocoagulation, glycerol injection, or balloon compression).

1. Migraine:

•  Pathophysiology: Episodic neurovascular headache disorder affecting 20% of women and 6% of men (strong genetic predisposition).

•  Migraine Aura (20% of patients): Caused by the "cortical spreading depression of Leão"—a wave of neuronal/glial depolarisation followed by hyperpolarisation spreading anteriorly across the occipital/somatosensory cortex at ~ 3 mm/min.

•  Headache Phase: Hypothalamic and brainstem activation stimulates the trigeminovascular system, releasing vasoactive neuropeptides—principally Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP), substance P, and neurokinin A—which induce neurogenic meningeal inflammation, dural vasodilatation, and central pain sensitization.

•  Triggers: Stress (or relaxation after stress—"weekend migraine"), sleep deprivation or excess, hormonal fluctuations (menstruation, combined oral contraceptive pill), missed meals, and dietary triggers (cheese, chocolate, red wine).

•  Clinical Subtypes & Features:

•  Migraine Without Aura ("Common Migraine" — 80% of cases) [KU 18]:

•  Recurrent attacks of moderate-to-severe, unilateral (or bilateral), pulsating/throbbing headache lasting 4 to 72 hours.

•  Aggravated by routine physical movement (patients prefer to lie still in a quiet, dark room, in contrast to the restless agitation of cluster headache).

•  Accompanied by nausea and/or vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia.

•  Migraine With Aura ("Classical Migraine" — 20% of cases):

•  Preceded by a fully reversible focal neurological aura evolving gradually over 5–20 minutes and lasting 10–60 minutes prior to the headache:

•  Visual aura (most common): Positive shimmering, silvery zigzag lines (fortification spectra) or flashing coloured lights (teichopsia) marching across the visual field, leaving a temporary scotoma.

•  Sensory, Language, or Motor aura: Spreading unilateral tingling/numbness (cheiro-oral distribution) or transient dysphasia.

•  Management of Migraine:

•  A. Acute Attack Treatment (Taken as early as possible at headache onset):

1.  Simple Analgesics & NSAIDs:Aspirin (600–900 mg), Ibuprofen (400–800 mg), Naproxen, or Paracetamol (1 g).

2.  Prokinetic Antiemetics:Metoclopramide (10 mg) or Domperidone (10 mg)—relieve nausea and accelerate gastric emptying to enhance analgesic absorption.

3.  Specific 5-HT1B/1D Receptor Agonists ("Triptans") (for moderate-to-severe attacks):Sumatriptan (50–100 mg oral, 6 mg subcutaneous, or 10–20 mg intranasal), Rizatriptan, Zolmitriptan, or Eletriptan. (Cause cranial vasoconstriction and inhibit trigeminal neuropeptide release; contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, previous stroke/TIA, and peripheral vascular disease).

4.  Oral CGRP Receptor Antagonists ("Gepants" — e.g., Rimegepant, Atogepant): Effective acute alternative for patients in whom triptans are contraindicated or ineffective (do not cause vasoconstriction).

5.  Warning: Limit acute analgesics/triptans to <10–15 days/month to prevent Medication Overuse Headache (MOH).

•  B. Prophylaxis of Migraine [KU 22, 23]:

•  Indications: ≥ 2–4 disabling attacks per month, prolonged/severe attacks unresponsive to acute therapy, or overuse of acute medications.

•  Lifestyle & Contraceptive Advice: Regular sleep, meals, hydration, trigger avoidance. Women who have migraine WITH aura must NOT take the combined oestrogen-containing oral contraceptive pill due to a synergistically increased risk of ischaemic stroke (switch to progesterone-only contraception).

•  First-Line Oral Prophylactic Drugs (Trial for at least 8–12 weeks):

1.  Beta-Blockers (without intrinsic sympathomimetic activity):Propranolol (80–160 mg daily), Atenolol, or Metoprolol (avoid in asthma).

2.  Tricyclic Antidepressants:Amitriptyline (10–75 mg at night) (especially useful if coexisting tension-type headache or insomnia).

3.  Angiotensin Receptor Blockers / ACE Inhibitors:Candesartan (8–16 mg daily) or Lisinopril.

4.  Antiseizure Medications:Topiramate (25–50 mg BD)(highly effective, but strictly contraindicated in women of childbearing potential without a pregnancy prevention programme due to high teratogenicity; also causes paraesthesiae, weight loss, renal stones, and acute angle-closure glaucoma).

•  Targeted Second-Line Prophylaxis (for Chronic / Refractory Migraine):

1.  Subcutaneous Monoclonal Antibodies against CGRP or the CGRP Receptor (Given monthly):Erenumab, Fremanezumab, Galcanezumab (or oral Atogepant).

2.  Cranial Botulinum Toxin Type A Injections (for chronic migraine ≥ 15 headache days/month) or greater occipital nerve block.
