title: 5. Epilepsy: Classification, Aetiopathogenesis, Investigation, Antiseizure Medications, and Status Epilepticus [KU 25, 24, 22, 20, 18, 17, TU, RGU]
text:
Epilepsy

5. Epilepsy: Classification, Aetiopathogenesis, Investigation, Antiseizure Medications, and Status Epilepticus [KU 25, 24, 22, 20, 18, 17, TU, RGU]

1. Definitions & Pathophysiology of Seizures and Epilepsy:

•  Seizure: Transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal, excessive, or hypersynchronous neuronal electrical activity in the cerebral cortex.

1.  Epilepsy: A chronic brain disorder characterised by an enduring predisposition to generate unprovoked seizures (diagnosed after ≥ 2 unprovoked seizures > 24 hours apart, OR after 1 unprovoked seizure with a high recurrence risk [≥ 60%], such as a structural cortical lesion on MRI or epileptiform EEG).

•  Pathophysiology: Imbalance between excitatory glutamatergic neurotransmission (mediated by NMDA/AMPA receptors and voltage-gated Na^+ and Ca2+ channels, generating a paroxysmal depolarisation shift) and inhibitory GABAergic (γ-aminobutyric acid) neurotransmission (which promotes Cl^- influx and membrane hyperpolarisation).

•  Generalised-onset seizures originate within and rapidly engage bilaterally distributed thalamocortical networks from the outset.

2. 2017 / 2025 ILAE Classification of Seizures:

1.  Focal-Onset Seizures:

•  Subclassified by Awareness:Focal Aware Seizures(formerly "simple partial") vs. Focal Impaired-Awareness Seizures(formerly "complex partial").

•  Subclassified by Onset:

•  Non-Motor Onset:Sensory (tingling/burning from post-central gyrus; flashing lights from occipital lobe), Cognitive (déjà vu, jamais vu, speech arrest), Emotional (sudden fear), Autonomic (rising epigastric aura), or behavioural arrest.

•  Focal to Bilateral Tonic–Clonic Seizure(formerly "secondarily generalised").

2.  Generalised-Onset Seizures:

•  Motor:Generalised Tonic–Clonic (GTCS), Clonic, Tonic, Myoclonic (brief morning shock-like jerks, e.g., in Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy), Myoclonic–tonic–clonic, Atonic ("drop attacks"), and Epileptic spasms.

•  Non-Motor (Absence):Typical Absence (formerly "petit mal" — brief 5–10 sec episodes of staring and unresponsiveness with 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG in children), Atypical absence, Myoclonic absence, Eyelid myoclonia.

3.  Unknown-Onset Seizures: Motor (tonic–clonic) or Non-motor.

3. Aetiology & Trigger Factors for Seizures:

•  Causes of Focal & Generalised Seizures:

•  Genetic / Idiopathic: Genetic Generalised Epilepsies (Childhood/Juvenile Absence Epilepsy, Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy), Benign Rolandic epilepsy, Tuberous sclerosis, Neurofibromatosis.

•  Structural Brain Lesions (Dominant in Adult-Onset >25–35 years):Cerebrovascular disease (Stroke—most common cause in older adults >50 years, intracerebral haemorrhage, AVM, cavernous haemangioma), Brain tumours (primary glioma/meningioma or metastases), Head trauma / neurosurgery, and Mesial temporal (hippocampal) sclerosis (associated with prolonged childhood febrile convulsions).

•  CNS Infections:Neurocysticercosis (most common cause of adult-onset epilepsy in India/developing world), Tuberculoma, cerebral abscess, viral encephalitis (HSV), bacterial meningitis, toxoplasmosis, HIV.

•  Metabolic & Toxic Disturbances:Hypoglycaemia, Hyponatraemia, Hypocalcaemia, Hypomagnesaemia, uraemia, hepatic failure, Alcohol withdrawal, and Drugs (tramadol, penicillins/carbapenems, isoniazid, theophylline, tricyclics, clozapine, cocaine/amphetamines).

•  Autoimmune & Degenerative:Autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDAR, anti-LGI1) and Alzheimer’s disease.

•  Common Trigger Factors for Seizures [KU 18]:

1.  Missed doses / non-adherence to antiseizure medications (most common trigger in treated epilepsy).

2.  Sleep deprivation and physical/mental exhaustion.

3.  Alcohol intake (especially binge drinking and withdrawal) and recreational drugs.

4.  Flickering / Stroboscopic lights (TV, video games—in photosensitive generalised epilepsies like JME).

5.  Intercurrent febrile illness, systemic infection, metabolic derangement, or menstruation (catamenial epilepsy).

•  Complications of Seizures:

1.  Status Epilepticus (convulsive or non-convulsive) causing cerebral hypoxia, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis/AKI, and multi-organ failure.

2.  Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP): Rare fatal cardiorespiratory arrest following an unwitnessed nocturnal tonic–clonic seizure.

3.  Traumatic Injuries: Head injury/subdural haematoma, facial fractures, severe lateral tongue biting, posterior dislocation of the shoulder, vertebral compression fractures, drowning, and burns.

4.  Aspiration Pneumonia and neurogenic pulmonary oedema.

•  Features & Diagnosis: Fever, weight loss, myalgia, livedo reticularis, palpable purpura, cutaneous ulcers, mononeuritis multiplex (70%), testicular pain, abdominal angina/mesenteric ischaemia, and severe renin-mediated hypertension from multiple renal infarcts. Confirmed Psychosocial & Cognitive Impact: Driving restrictions, occupational limitations, stigma, depression, and teratogenicity from antiseizure medications.

Additional complications (from the second epilepsy draft): Rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury, and Todd’s paresis (transient post-ictal focal weakness lasting up to 24–48 hours).

Febrile Seizures [TU]: Occur in 2%–5% of children aged 6 months to 5 years triggered by a rapid rise in temperature during an extracranial viral/bacterial febrile illness (in the absence of CNS infection/meningitis).

•  Simple Febrile Seizures (80%): Generalised tonic–clonic, duration < 15 minutes, and do not recur within 24 hours; benign prognosis (risk of subsequent adult epilepsy is only 1%–2%, similar to the general population; long-term anticonvulsants are NOT required). Managed with antipyretics, tepid sponging, and parental education.

•  Complex Febrile Seizures (20%):Focal features, duration > 15 minutes, or recurrent within 24 hours; associated with a higher risk (5%–10%) of subsequent mesial temporal sclerosis and temporal lobe epilepsy. Managed acutely with tepid sponging, paracetamol, and buccal midazolam / rectal diazepam if > 5 minutes. (Note: complex febrile seizures are focal, prolonged (> 15 mins), or multiple within 24 hours, carrying a higher risk of later mesial temporal sclerosis and temporal lobe epilepsy; prolonged seizures > 5 mins are aborted with buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam).

5. Investigation of a Suspected Case of Epilepsy [KU 17]:

1.  Eyewitness Account & 12-Lead ECG: Crucial to exclude syncope (vasovagal, cardiogenic arrhythmia, long QT syndrome) and dissociative non-epileptic attacks.

2.  Metabolic & Infection Blood Screen: Blood glucose, urea and electrolytes (Na^+), calcium, magnesium, LFTs, FBC, CRP, and HIV/syphilis/cysticercosis serology if indicated.

3.  Neuroimaging (MRI Brain is the Investigation of Choice):

•  Indications:All patients with adult-onset seizures (>16 years), any seizure with focal clinical onset (e.g., right arm twitching), focal neurological deficit, focal EEG abnormality, or drug-resistant epilepsy. MRI detects subtle cortical dysplasia, low-grade gliomas, cavernomas, and mesial temporal sclerosis (CT is used in emergencies to exclude acute bleed/space-occupying lesion).

4.  Electroencephalography (EEG):

•  Used to support classification and prognosis after a clinical diagnosis of epilepsy is made (shows generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave in absence epilepsy, polyspike-and-wave in JME, or focal spikes/sharp waves over the affected lobe in focal epilepsy).

•  Important Limitation: A routine inter-ictal EEG is normal in 50% of patients with epilepsy (and can be non-specifically abnormal in 5% of healthy people), so a normal EEG never excludes epilepsy. Diagnostic yield is increased to 85% by sleep-deprived EEG, hyperventilation, photic stimulation, or prolonged video-EEG telemetry.

6. Management of Epilepsy & Antiseizure Medications (ASMs) [KU 22, 18, 17, TU]:

•  First-Aid Management During a Seizure: Move the person away from danger (fire, water, sharp furniture); cushion the head; do NOT insert anything into the mouth or restrain movements; once convulsions cease, roll into the recovery position, check airway, and call for an ambulance + administer buccal midazolam if seizures last >5 minutes.

•  Lifestyle & Driving Advice: Avoid lone swimming, shallow baths/use showers, avoid sleep deprivation and alcohol excess; inform the driving licensing authority (in the UK, must cease driving for 6 months after a first unprovoked seizure and for 1 year seizure-free in established epilepsy).

•  Choice of Antiseizure Medication (Start with a single first-line drug at low dose and titrate slowly):

•  For Focal-Onset Seizures (with or without evolution to Bilateral Tonic–Clonic):

•  First-Line:Lamotrigine (100–200 mg/day) OR Levetiracetam (500–1500 mg BD).

•  Second-Line:Carbamazepine (400–1200 mg/day), Oxcarbazepine, Zonisamide, or Lacosamide.

•  For Generalised Tonic–Clonic (GTCS) & Myoclonic Seizures:

(Covers the clinical vignette Essay on a 40-year-old male presenting with focal motor twitching of the right upper limb progressing to a generalised tonic–clonic convulsion with tongue bite and post-ictal confusion/headache = Focal-Onset Motor Seizure Evolving to Bilateral Tonic–Clonic Seizure, localising to the Contralateral [Left] Pre-Central Motor Cortex [Frontal Lobe]).

1. Definitions & Pathophysiology:

•  Seizure: Transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal, excessive, or hypersynchronous neuronal electrical activity in the brain.

•  Epilepsy: A chronic brain disorder characterised by an enduring predisposition to generate unprovoked epileptic seizures (diagnosed after ≥ 2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart, OR after a single unprovoked seizure with a high recurrence risk [≥ 60%], such as a structural cortical lesion on MRI or epileptiform EEG).

•  Pathogenesis: Imbalance between excitatory (glutamate/aspartate acting on NMDA/AMPA receptors causing Na^+ and Ca2+ influx) and inhibitory (GABA acting on GABAA receptors causing Cl^- influx) neurotransmission, resulting in a paroxysmal depolarisation shift.

•  In Focal Seizures, discharges originate in a localised unilateral cortical network (e.g., left pre-central motor strip causing right arm clonic twitching [Jacksonian march]) and may propagate via the corpus callosum/diencephalon to both hemispheres (Focal to Bilateral Tonic–Clonic Seizure).

•  In Genetic (Idiopathic) Generalised Epilepsies (GGEs), discharges originate in thalamocortical/diencephalic circuits and engage both cerebral hemispheres simultaneously from the outset.

I. Focal-Onset Seizures (originate within networks limited to one cerebral hemisphere):

•  Subclassified by awareness:Focal aware(formerly “simple partial”) vs. Focal impaired awareness(formerly “complex partial”).

•  Motor onset: Clonic (e.g., rhythmic limb jerking), tonic, myoclonic, atonic, hyperkinetic, or automatisms (lip-smacking, chewing, picking at clothes — characteristic of temporal lobe epilepsy).

•  Non-motor onset:Sensory (tingling, visual flashes [occipital], olfactory/gustatory hallucinations), Cognitive / Experiential (déjà vu, jamais vu [temporal lobe]), Emotional (sudden fear), Autonomic (rising epigastric sensation), or behavioural arrest.

•  Focal to bilateral tonic–clonic(formerly “secondarily generalised”).

II. Generalised-Onset Seizures (rapidly engage bilaterally distributed networks from onset):

•  Motor:Generalised tonic–clonic (GTCS), clonic, tonic, myoclonic (brief shock-like jerks, typical in the morning in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy [JME]), atonic (“drop attacks”), epileptic spasms.

•  Non-motor (absence):Typical absence (abrupt 5–10 second arrest of activity and staring in children, with immediate recovery and 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG), atypical absence, eyelid myoclonia.

III. Unknown-Onset Seizures.

•  Aetiology (Causes) & Trigger Factors of Seizures:

•  Causes of Focal / Structural Seizures:Cerebrovascular disease (Stroke) (commonest cause of new-onset epilepsy in adults >50 years), Brain tumours (primary gliomas/meningiomas or metastases), Head trauma / neurosurgery, Mesial temporal (hippocampal) sclerosis (associated with prolonged childhood febrile convulsions), CNS Infections (neurocysticercosis [commonest cause in developing countries], cerebral abscess, tuberculoma, toxoplasmosis, viral encephalitis), Autoimmune encephalitis (NMDAR, Lgi1), and cortical malformations/tuberous sclerosis.

•  Metabolic & Toxic Causes (Provoked Seizures):Hypoglycaemia, Hyponatraemia, Hypocalcaemia, Hypomagnesaemia, uraemia, hepatic failure, Alcohol withdrawal, and Drugs (tramadol, tricyclics, isoniazid, penicillin/carbapenems, theophylline, cocaine/amphetamines).

•  Trigger Factors for Seizures [KU 18]:

1.  Missed doses / Non-adherence to antiseizure medications

2.  Sleep deprivation and physical/mental exhaustion

3.  Alcohol excess and alcohol withdrawal

4.  Flickering / Stroboscopic lights, TV/computer screens (in photosensitive generalised epilepsies like JME)

5.  Intercurrent febrile infections and metabolic derangements

6.  Menstruation (catamenial epilepsy) and recreational drugs.

4. Investigation of a Suspected Case of Epilepsy [KU 17]:

1.  12-Lead ECG: Mandatory in all patients with blackouts to exclude cardiac arrhythmias and Long QT syndrome.

2.  Blood Tests: Blood glucose, U&Es (sodium), calcium, magnesium, LFTs, FBC, toxicology/alcohol screen, and ASM levels (if already treated).

3.  Neuroimaging (MRI Brain is the Investigation of Choice): Indicated in all patients with adult-onset seizures (>16 years), focal-onset clinical or EEG features (e.g., right arm focal motor twitching), abnormal neurological examination, or drug-resistant epilepsy, to detect tumours, stroke, cavernomas, or mesial temporal sclerosis. (Urgent CT brain is used in the acute emergency setting).

4.  Electroencephalography (EEG): Standard, sleep-deprived, or video-telemetry EEG helps classify the epilepsy syndrome (focal vs generalised spike-and-wave) and assess recurrence risk, though a normal inter-ictal EEG does not exclude epilepsy.

Differentiating epileptic seizures from syncope and dissociative non-epileptic attacks (from the eyewitness history):

•  Syncope: postural trigger, prodromal lightheadedness / sweating, brief duration (< 30 seconds), rapid recovery. Types to exclude: vasovagal syncope, cardiogenic arrhythmia, long QT syndrome.

•  Dissociative non-epileptic attacks: prolonged (> 5 minutes) asynchronous thrashing, closed eyes with resistance to opening, pelvic thrusting, crying afterwards.

•  Features strongly confirming a generalised tonic–clonic seizure: lateral tongue-biting, cyanosis, and prolonged post-ictal confusion (> 15–30 minutes) with myalgia.

5. Antiseizure Medications (ASMs): Choice, Newer Drugs, Side-Effects, and Carbamazepine Indications [KU 22, 18, 17, TU]:

•  Choice of First-Line Antiseizure Medication by Seizure Type (NICE Guidelines):

•  Focal-Onset Seizures (± Secondary Generalisation): First-line: Lamotrigine or Levetiracetam. Second-line: Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine, Lacosamide, or Zonisamide.

•  Multifocal Motor Neuropathy (MMN) with conduction block (pure motor arm weakness with anti-GM1 antibodies; mimics MND; responds to IVIg), and Paraproteinaemic neuropathy (IgM anti-MAG antibodies, POEMS syndrome).

•  Inherited:Charcot–Marie–Tooth Disease Type 1 (CMT1 — PMP22 duplication, "inverted champagne-bottle" legs and pes cavus) and Hereditary Neuropathy with Liability to Pressure Palsies (HNPP).

2. Guillain–Barré Syndrome (GBS / Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy — AIDP) [KU 23, 22, 20, 18]:

•  Pathophysiology: An acute, post-infectious, immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy. Around 65%–70% of patients have a preceding respiratory or gastrointestinal infection 1–3 weeks earlier—most commonly Campylobacter jejuni (strongly linked to the severe Acute Motor Axonal Neuropathy [AMAN] variant), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Influenza, HIV, or Zika virus.

•  Molecular Mimicry: Antibodies generated against microbial lipo-oligosaccharides cross-react with gangliosides (e.g., GM1, GD1a, GQ1b) on peripheral nerve Schwann cells or nodes of Ranvier, triggering complement activation and macrophage-mediated segmental demyelination or axonal damage.

•  Clinical Features & Diagnostic Criteria of Guillain–Barré Syndrome:

•  Core Diagnostic Features (Required for Diagnosis):

1.  Progressive, symmetrical muscle weakness of the legs and arms (often more marked proximally than distally, ascending from the lower limbs to the upper limbs over days to a maximum nadir of ≤ 4 weeks).

2.  Generalised Areflexia or Hyporeflexia (loss of deep tendon reflexes).

•  Supportive Clinical Features:

•  Distal paraesthesia (tingling/numbness) in the hands and feet and severe neuropathic back or radicular leg pain (often precedes weakness, though objective sensory loss on examination is mild).

•  Cranial NerveGeneralised Tonic–Clonic Seizures (GTCS):Sodium Valproate (most effective, but strictly avoided in women of childbearing potential due to 10% major congenital malformation rate [spina bifida] and 30%–40% neurodevelopmental delay), Lamotrigine, or Levetiracetam.

•  Absence Seizures:Ethosuximide (first choice), Sodium Valproate, or Lamotrigine.

•  Myoclonic Seizures (JME):Levetiracetam or Sodium Valproate. (Note: Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, and Gabapentin WORSEN absence and myoclonic seizures and must be avoided in GGEs).

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-016]]

•  Clinical Indications for Carbamazepine [KU 17]:

1.  Focal-onset seizures and focal-to-bilateral tonic–clonic seizures.

2.  Trigeminal neuralgia (first-line drug of choice) and glossopharyngeal neuralgia.

3.  Neuropathic pain (e.g., painful diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia) and MS-related paroxysmal dysaesthesia.

4.  Bipolar affective disorder (second-line mood stabiliser / acute mania).

Status Epilepticus: Definition and Stepwise Emergency Management [KU 25, 24, 20, RGU]:

Definition: Continuous seizure activity lasting ≥ 5 minutes (operational threshold for emergency treatment; > 30 minutes defines established status), OR ≥ 2 sequential seizures without full recovery of consciousness between attacks. It is a life-threatening medical emergency.

Stepwise Emergency Management Protocol:

•  Stage 1: Immediate Resuscitation & Stabilisation (0–5 Minutes): Secure the airway, administer 100% high-flow oxygen, apply pulse oximetry and cardiac ECG monitoring, check blood pressure and capillary blood glucose, and secure intravenous access. Send urgent bloods for U&Es, calcium, magnesium, glucose, LFTs, FBC, coagulation, arterial blood gases, toxicology screen, and antiseizure drug levels. Correct metabolic triggers immediately: if hypoglycaemic, give 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV (or 100 mL of 20% dextrose), preceded by parenteral thiamin (Pabrinex IV) if alcohol misuse or malnutrition is suspected.

•  Stage 2: First-Line Therapy — Benzodiazepines (5–20 Minutes):If IV access is available:Lorazepam 4 mg (0.1 mg/kg) slow IV bolus (preferred due to longer CNS duration of action) OR Diazepam 10 mg IV. If no IV access (pre-hospital):Buccal or intranasal midazolam 10 mg (or rectal diazepam 10 mg). If seizures continue after 10–15 minutes:repeat the benzodiazepine dose ONCE only (watch closely for respiratory depression and hypotension).

•  Stage 3: Second-Line Therapy — Intravenous Antiseizure Medication Infusion (20–40 Minutes — Established Status):(The ESETT trial demonstrated equal efficacy of the three main agents; administer ONE of the following IV infusions): (1) Intravenous levetiracetam: 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg) infused IV over 10 minutes(easy to administer, no cardiac toxicity; reduce dose if eGFR < 30 mL/min). (2) Intravenous sodium valproate: 20–40 mg/kg (max 3000 mg) infused IV over 10 minutes (40 mg/min). (3) Intravenous phenytoin: 15–20 mg/kg (max 2000 mg) infused IV at a rate of ≤ 50 mg/min (or fosphenytoin at ≤ 150 mg PE/min) under continuous ECG and BP monitoring due to the risk of severe hypotension, bradycardia, and cardiac arrhythmias. (Alternative:IV phenobarbital 10–15 mg/kg infused at ≤ 100 mg/min).

•  Stage 4: Third-Line Therapy — Refractory Status Epilepticus (> 30–60 Minutes): Transfer immediately to the intensive care unit (ICU) for endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and general anaesthesia using continuous IV infusion of propofol, midazolam, or thiopental sodium (titrated to burst-suppression on continuous EEG monitoring for 24–48 hours while maintaining regular background antiseizure medications and investigating the underlying cause with MRI brain and lumbar puncture).

subject: medicine
title: 6. Multiple Sclerosis (MS) [KU 18, 17, TU, RGU]
text:
Neuroinflammatory & Neurodegenerative Diseases

6. Multiple Sclerosis (MS) [KU 18, 17, TU, RGU]

1. Definition, Epidemiology & Aetiopathogenesis:

Definition (continued): Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated inflammatory, demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (CNS) (sparing the peripheral nervous system), characterised by focal plaques of demyelination and axonal loss disseminated in space and time.

2. Clinical Features & Disease Subtypes of Multiple Sclerosis:

•  Clinical Course Subtypes:

1.  Relapsing–Remitting cerebellar peduncle and giving rise to the rubrospinal tract.

•  Ascending Sensory Tracts (Lateral to Red Nucleus):Medial Lemniscus (dorsal column proprioception/vibration), Spinothalamic Tract (pain/temperature), and trigeminothalamic tract.

•  Reticular Formation (Ascending Reticular Activating System — ARAS).

2.  Substantia Nigra: Pigmented dopaminergic nucleus MS (RRMS, 85%–90% at onset): Discrete subacute attacks (relapses) evolving over days to weeks, followed by complete or partial recovery over weeks to months.

3.  Secondary Progressive MS (SPMS): Gradual accumulation of disability following an initial relapsing–remitting phase.

4.  Primary Progressive separating the tegmentum from the basis pedunculi (degenerates in Parkinson’s disease).

5.  Crus Cerebri / Basis Pedunculi (Ventral Cerebral Peduncles): Contains the descending Corticospinal (Pyramidal) and Corticobulbar Tracts in the middle three-fifths (with corticopontine fibres medially and laterally).

1.  Primary Progressive MS (PPMS, 10%–15%): Steady progression of disability (usually a spastic paraparesis) from onset without acute relapses.

1.  Optic Neuritis: Subacute unilateral visual loss, pain on eye movement, early loss of colour vision (red desaturation), a central scotoma, and a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (Marcus Gunn pupil). Fundoscopy is normal initially if retrobulbar, later leaving temporal pallor of the optic disc (optic atrophy).

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-017]]

•  Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO): Lesion in the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) causing failure of adduction of the ipsilateral eye on conjugate lateral gaze, with nystagmus in the contralateral abducting eye (while convergence is spared), causing horizontal diplopia.

\  [  Cr in a patient <50 years, facial numbness, vertigo, and dysarthria.

1.  Spinal Cord Syndromes (Partial Transverse Myelitis):

•  Asymmetrical spastic paraparesis (brisk reflexes, clonus, extensor plantars), dorsal column sensory loss ("tight band/hugging" sensation around the trunk or useless hand syndrome), partial Brown–Séquard syndrome, and neurogenic bladder dysfunction (urgency, frequency, urge incontinence, detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia) and erectile dysfunction.

2.  Cerebellar Syndrome: Ataxic gait, intention tremor, scanning speech, and gaze-evoked nystagmus (Charcot’s triad: nystagmus, intention tremor, scanning dysarthria).

3.  Characteristic Clinical Phenomena:

Lhermitte’s Sign (Symptom): Electric-shock-like tingling shooting down the spine and into the limbs upon flexion of the neck (indicates a demyelinating plaque in the cervical dorsal columns).

McDonald Criteria (Dissemination in Space and Time): Dissemination in space (≥ 2 of 4 typical CNS regions) and dissemination in time, shown by gadolinium-enhancing [new] and non-enhancing [old] lesions on a single MRI, OR a new T2 lesion on follow-up MRI, OR the presence of CSF-specific oligoclonal bands.

Key Investigations:

•  MRI of the Brain and Spinal Cord with Gadolinium Contrast (Most Sensitive Investigation): Demonstrates ovoid T2 / FLAIR hyperintense plaques perpendicular to the lateral ventricles (Dawson’s fingers), corpus callosum, brainstem, and short asymmetric spinal cord lesions (< 2 vertebral segments). Active plaques (< 4 weeks old) enhance with gadolinium on T1 sequences.

•  Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Examination (Lumbar Puncture): Isoelectric focusing electrophoresis demonstrates unpaired IgG oligoclonal bands (OCBs) present in the CSF but absent in matched serum in > 90% of MS patients (confirming intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis). CSF cell count is normal or mildly lymphocytic (< 50 cells/µL).

•  Visual Evoked Potentials (VEPs): Demonstrates a prolonged latency of the P100 wave (with relatively preserved amplitude), confirming subclinical optic nerve demyelination.

•  Blood Tests to Exclude MS Mimics: Vitamin B12 level, ANA / dsDNA / antiphospholipid antibodies (SLE), serum ACE (sarcoidosis), HIV and syphilis serology, and serum aquaporin-4 (AQP4) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies (to exclude neuromyelitis optica).

4. Management of Multiple Sclerosis:

•  A. Treatment of an Acute Disabling Relapse:

•  Exclude intercurrent infection (e.g., UTI causing a pseudo-relapse).

•  Administer High-Dose Methylprednisolone (500–1000 mg IV or orally daily for 3–5 days)—shortens the duration of the acute relapse (though does not alter long-term disability). Use plasma exchange for severe steroid-refractory relapses.

•  B. Disease-Modifying Therapies (DMTs) for Active Relapsing–Remitting MS (Reduce—compresses the 3rd cranial nerve), and Middle cerebral artery bifurcation (20%).

•  Small Perforating Lenticulostriate Arteries: Arise directly at right angles from the Circle of Willis and proximal MCA/PCA to supply the basal ganglia, internal capsule, and thalamus; lipohyalinosis/occlusion causes lacunar infarcts and deep intracerebral haemorrhages.

Disease-Modifying Therapies (DMTs):

•  High-Efficacy Monoclonal Antibodies (> 50% relapse reduction):Ocrelizumab (IV every 6 months) and Ofatumumab (monthly SC): Anti-CD20 B-cell depleting monoclonal antibodies (ocrelizumab is also licensed for early primary progressive MS). Natalizumab (4-weekly IV): Anti-α4β1 integrin antibody that blocks lymphocyte entry across the blood–brain barrier (carry out JC virus serology monitoring due to risk of progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy [PML]). Alemtuzumab (two IV courses 12 months apart): Anti-CD52 antibody (30% develop secondary autoimmune thyroid disease).

•  Moderate-Efficacy Oral DMTs (30%–50% relapse reduction):Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulators:Fingolimod, Siponimod (licensed for active secondary progressive MS), Ozanimod, Ponesimod — trap lymphocytes in lymph nodes (monitor for first-dose bradycardia and macular oedema). Cladribine (pulsed oral purine analogue), Dimethyl fumarate (twice-daily oral), and Teriflunomide (daily oral).

•  Platform / Lower-Efficacy Injectable DMTs (~ 30% relapse reduction; safe in pregnancy):Interferon-beta and Glatiramer acetate.

•  C. Symptomatic & Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation:

•  Spasticity: Physiotherapy, oral Baclofen, Tizanidine, gabapentin, cannabinoid spray (Sativex), focal botulinum toxin injections, or intrathecal baclofen pump.

•  Walking impairment:Fampridine (potassium channel blocker that improves walking speed).

•  Neuropathic pain / Trigeminal neuralgia:Carbamazepine, Gabapentin, Pregabalin, Amitriptyline, Duloxetine.

•  Hypertonic Neurogenic Bladder:Anticholinergics (Solifenacin, Tolterodine, Oxybutynin) or Mirabegron, combined with clean intermittent self-catheterisation if post-void residual volume is >100 mL.

•  Fatigue & Erectile Dysfunction: Graded exercise/amantadine (fatigue); Sildenafil / Tadalafil (erectile dysfunction).

title: 7. Parkinson’s Disease and Parkinsonism [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 17, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
7. Parkinson’s Disease and Parkinsonism [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 17, 16, TU, RGU]

(Covers all 3 clinical vignette Essays on older men presenting with asymmetrical resting "pill-rolling" hand tremor, slowness of movement [bradykinesia], mask-like facies, cogwheel/lead-pipe rigidity, short shuffling festinant gait, and recurrent falls).

1. Classification & Causes of Parkinsonism:

•  Parkinsonism is a clinical extrapyramidal syndrome defined by Bradykinesia plus at least one of Rigidity, Resting Tremor, or Postural Instability.

•  Causes of Parkinsonism:

1.  Idiopathic Parkinson’s Disease (PD): Accounts for >80% of all parkinsonism.

2.  Drug-Induced Parkinsonism(typically symmetrical, with less prominent rest tremor; reversible on stopping drug):

•  Dopamine D2-receptor antagonists (Antipsychotics): Haloperidol, chlorpromazine, flupentixol, risperidone, olanzapine.

•  Antiemetics:Metoclopramide, Prochlorperazine, Cinnarizine.

•  Others:Tetrabenazine, Sodium valproate, Lithium, calcium channel blockers (flunarizine).

3.  Vascular Parkinsonism: Multi-infarct small-vessel cerebrovascular disease affecting the basal ganglia/white matter; presents with symmetrical "lower-body parkinsonism" (marche à petits pas gait, early falls, urinary incontinence, pyramidal signs, and poor response to levodopa).

4.  Atypical Degenerative Parkinsonian Syndromes ("Parkinson-Plus" Syndromes) [TU](Characterised by symmetrical onset, early falls/autonomic/bulbar features, rapid progression, and poor or absent response to Levodopa):

•  Multiple System Atrophy (MSA — α-synucleinopathy): Combines parkinsonism (MSA-P) and/or cerebellar ataxia (MSA-C) with severe early autonomic failure (postural hypotension, erectile dysfunction, urinary incontinence) and pyramidal signs.

•  Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP — Tauopathy): Symmetrical axial rigidity, early backward falls, pseudobulbar palsy, frontal cognitive decline, and the hallmark vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (inability to look down or up voluntarily).

•  Corticobasal Degeneration (CBD — Tauopathy): Markedly asymmetrical akinetic-rigid syndrome with limb apraxia, myoclonus, cortical sensory loss, dementia, and the "alien limb" phenomenon.

•  Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB — α-synucleinopathy): Early dementia, fluctuating cognition, formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder, and parkinsonism (occurring before or within 1 year of motor onset).

5.  Toxins, Genetic & Metabolic Causes: Carbon monoxide, manganese, MPTP, Wilson’s disease (always exclude in anyone <50 years), Huntington’s disease (juvenile Westphal variant), and Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, and dementia).

(Note on Causes of Falls in the Elderly from Essay [KU 21, 22]: Multifactorial—Neurological [Parkinson’s disease/PSP, stroke, peripheral neuropathy, cervical myelopathy, dementia, epilepsy], Cardiovascular / Postural Hypotension [arrhythmias, aortic stenosis, vasovagal, carotid sinus hypersensitivity], Musculoskeletal [lower limb osteoarthritis, proximal myopathy/vitamin D deficiency, foot deformities], Visual impairment [cataracts, macular degeneration], Drugs / Polypharmacy [sedatives/benzodiazepines, antihypertensives, diuretics, antidepressants], and Environmental hazards).

2. Pathogenesis & Site of Lesion in Idiopathic Parkinson’s Disease:

•  Anatomical Site of Lesion: Progressive degeneration and loss of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the pars compacta of the Substantia Nigra (SNc) in the midbrain, which project via the nigrostriatal pathway to the striatum (putamen and caudate nucleus) (clinical motor symptoms emerge only after 60%–80% of nigral dopaminergic neurons are lost).

•  Pathological Hallmark: Presence of intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions containing misfolded α-synuclein and ubiquitin (Lewy bodies) in surviving nigral, brainstem, and cortical neurons.

3. Clinical Features of Parkinson’s Disease (Motor & Non-Motor):

•  Cardinal Motor Features (Almost always Unilateral / Asymmetrical at onset):

1.  Bradykinesia / Akinesia (Mandatory feature for diagnosis): Slowness in initiating and executing movements with progressive fatiguing and decrement in amplitude and speed on repetitive tasks (e.g., finger tapping). Manifests as expressionless mask-like facies (hypomimia) with reduced blink rate, soft monotonous speech (hypophonia), progressively smaller handwriting (micrographia), loss of arm swing on walking, and difficulty turning in bed or doing up buttons.

2.  Resting Tremor (70%–80%): Coarse 4–6 Hz (or 3–4 Hz) asymmetrical resting tremor, classically affecting the thumb and index finger ("pill-rolling" tremor), forearm, leg, jaw, or chin (sparing the head). Present at rest, transiently diminishes on voluntary action, re-emerges on holding a posture, and is exacerbated by mental stress or walking.

3.  Rigidity: Increased tone present equally throughout the range of passive movement in flexors and extensors ("lead-pipe" rigidity), which becomes jerky/ratchet-like when superimposed on tremor ("cogwheel" rigidity).

4.  Postural Instability & Extrapyramidal Gait: Stooped, flexed posture; hesitation/difficulty initiating walking ("start hesitation") and "freezing" (especially in narrow doorways or when turning); and a narrow-based, short-stepped, shuffling festinant gait (accelerating forward steps chasing the centre of gravity) with impaired postural righting reflexes on the pull test, leading to falls.

•  (Crucial Normal Findings: Muscle power, deep tendon reflexes, plantar responses [flexor], and sensation are normal).

•  Non-Motor Features & Complications:

•  Pre-motor / Prodromal:Anosmia/hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams), and depression/anxiety.

•  Late Non-Motor Complications:Cognitive impairment and Parkinson’s disease dementia (30%–80%), visual hallucinations and psychosis, autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension, urinary urgency/nocturia, erectile dysfunction, sialorrhoea/drooling, seborrhoea), dysphagia, and aspiration pneumonia.

4. Diagnosis & Management of Parkinson’s Disease [KU 25, 24, 16]:

•  Diagnosis: Primarily a clinical diagnosis. Structural brain imaging (MRI/CT) is normal (used only if vascular parkinsonism or NPH is suspected). If diagnostic doubt exists between PD and essential/drug-induced tremor, a 123I-Ioflupane (DaTscan) SPECT scan demonstrates reduced presynaptic dopamine transporter uptake in the putamen in PD (normal in essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism).

•  Comprehensive Management of Parkinson’s Disease:

•  A. Multidisciplinary Allied Health Rehabilitation:

•  Physiotherapy (gait re-education, cueing strategies to overcome freezing, balance, and posture exercises), Occupational Therapy (home adaptations, grab rails, dressing/eating aids), Speech and Language Therapy (Lee Silverman Voice Treatment for hypophonia and swallowing assessment), and PD Nurse Specialist support.

•  B. Pharmacological Therapy (Symptomatic Dopaminergic Replacement):

(Initiate when symptoms cause functional impairment; never stop dopaminergic drugs abruptly as this precipitates fatal neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome):

1.  Levodopa + Peripheral Dopa-Decarboxylase Inhibitor (DDI) (Most Effective & Best-Tolerated First-Line Drug):

•  Preparations: Co-careldopa (Levodopa + Carbidopa, Sinemet) or Co-beneldopa (Levodopa + Benserazide, Madopar).

•  Rationale for DDI: Carbidopa/benserazide do not cross the blood–brain barrier; they inhibit peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine in the gut and blood vessels, thereby preventing peripheral side-effects (nausea, vomiting, postural hypotension) and allowing 10× more levodopa to enter the brain.

•  Long-Term Motor Complications of Levodopa (Develop after 3–5+ years as nigral storage capacity declines):

•  "Wearing-off" (End-of-dose deterioration): Predictable return of parkinsonism before the next dose is due.

•  "On–Off" motor fluctuations: Sudden, unpredictable switches between mobile ("on") and immobile akinetic ("off") states.

•  Peak-dose Levodopa-Induced Dyskinesias: Choreiform/dystonic involuntary movements at peak plasma levodopa levels.

2.  Dopamine Receptor Agonists (Non-Ergot Derived):

•  Ropinirole (oral), Pramipexole (oral), Rotigotine (24-hr transdermal patch), and Apomorphine (subcutaneous rescue pen-injections or continuous SC pump infusion for severe "off" periods). (Ergot-derived agonists like bromocriptine/cabergoline are avoided due to cardiac valvular and retroperitoneal fibrosis).

•  Adverse Effects: Less effective than levodopa, with higher rates of nausea, postural hypotension, daytime somnolence/sleep attacks, hallucinations, and Impulse Control Disorders (ICDs — pathological gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping, binge eating) in 15% (mandatory to counsel patients and carers).

3.  Monoamine Oxidase Type B (MAO-B) Inhibitors:

•  Rasagiline (1 mg OD) or Selegiline (5–10 mg OD). Inhibit synaptic breakdown of dopamine in the striatum; used as mild initial monotherapy or as an adjunct to levodopa to smooth out wearing-off fluctuations.

4.  Catechol-O-Methyltransferase (COMT) Inhibitors:

•  Entacapone (200 mg with each levodopa dose, or combined with levodopa/carbidopa as Stalevo), Opicapone (once daily), or Tolcapone (monitor LFTs for hepatotoxicity). Inhibit peripheral methylation of levodopa, prolonging its half-life and reducing "wearing-off" time.

5.  Amantadine (100–200 mg BD):

•  Weak NMDA glutamate antagonist with mild dopaminergic activity; primarily used to treat Levodopa-induced Dyskinesias(side-effects: livedo reticularis, ankle oedema, confusion).

6.  Anticholinergics (Trihexyphenidyl [Benzhexol], Orphenadrine):

•  Rarely used; occasionally helpful for tremor in young patients, but avoided in older patients as they cause dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, glaucoma, and severe confusion/cognitive decline.

•  C. Device-Assisted & Surgical Therapies (For Advanced PD with Refractory Motor Fluctuations, Dyskinesias, or Tremor):

•  Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS): Stereotactic implantation of electrodes into the Subthalamic Nucleus (STN) or Globus Pallidus Interna (GPi) (or ventral intermediate nucleus of the thalamus for isolated tremor).

•  Continuous Subcutaneous Apomorphine Pump, Continuous Subcutaneous Foslevodopa–Foscarbidopa Infusion, or Levodopa–Carbidopa Intestinal Gel (Duodopa) via PEG-J tube.

•  D. Management of Non-Motor Complications:

•  PD Dementia: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor Rivastigmine (or donepezil).

•  Psychosis / Hallucinations: Reduce anti-parkinsonian drugs slowly; if antipsychotic is needed, use Quetiapine or Clozapine(strictly avoid haloperidol/typical antipsychotics and metoclopramide).

•  Orthostatic Hypotension: Increase salt/fluid intake, compression stockings, Fludrocortisone or Midodrine.

•  REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder:Clonazepam or melatonin at night.

title: 8. Meningitis (Bacterial/Pyogenic, Viral, Tuberculous, and Cryptococcal) [KU 25, 24, 23, 21, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
Infections of the CNS & Raised Intracranial Pressure

8. Meningitis (Bacterial/Pyogenic, Viral, Tuberculous, and Cryptococcal) [KU 25, 24, 23, 21, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

(Covers both clinical vignette Essays on young adults presenting with high fever, headache, vomiting, altered sensorium/irritability, and signs of meningeal irritation).

1. A) [KU 24]: A late physiological brainstem response to acute, severe raised intracranial pressure and impending brainstem (tonsillar) herniation/ischaemia, consisting of the triad of:

•  Systemic Arterial Hypertension (with widening pulse pressure)etiology & Clinical Features of Meningitis:

•  Causative Organisms:

•  Acute Pyogenic (Bacterial) Meningitis:

•  Neonates (<3 months): Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae), Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes.

•  Children & Young Adults:Neisseria meningitidis (Meningococcus — Serogroups A, B, C, (sympathetic surge to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure, CPP = MAP - ICP)

•  Reflex Bradycardia (baroreceptor-mediated vagal response)

•  Irregular Respiration (Cheyne–Stokes or ataxic breathing due to medullary compression).

•  Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH — Benign Intracranial Hypertension) [KU 18]:

•  Definition & Risk Factors: Raised intracranial pressure occurring in the absence of an intracranial mass lesion, hydrocephalus, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Predominantly affects young W, Y) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcus) (Haemophilus influenzae type B in unvaccinated children).

•  Older Adults (>60 years), Immunocompromised, Pregnant, or Alcoholics:Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Listeria monocytogenes (Gram-positive intracellular rod acquired from unpasteurised dairy/pâté).

•  Post-Neurosurgery / Penetrating Skull Fracture / Shunts:Staphylococcus aureus, S. epidermidis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

•  Viral Meningitis (Most common cause overall):Enteroviruses (Coxsackie, Echovirus), Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2 —, overweight/obese women of childbearing age. Secondary associations include tetracyclines, hypervitaminosis A / oral retinoids, nitrofurantoin, and steroid withdrawal.

•  Clinical Features: Chronic daily throbbing headache, transient visual obscurations on bending/standing, pulsatile tinnitus, horizontal diplopia (from false-localising 6th nerve palsy), and bilateral papilloedema (which, if untreated, leads to progressive peripheral visual field constriction and permanent blindness from secondary optic atrophy).

•  Investigations:MRI Brain + MR Ven causes recurrent Mollaret’s meningitis), Varicella zoster virus (VZV), Mumps, HIV.

•  Chronic Meningitis:Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Tuberculous meningitis) and Cryptococcus neoformans (in HIV/immunosuppression).

•  Clinical Features & Signs of Meningeal Irritation:

•  Classic Meningitis Triad:Fever + Severe Headache + Neck Stiffness (Meningism) (accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and altered sensorium/drowsiness—>90% have at least two of headache, fever, neck stiffness, and altered consciousness).

•  Physical Signs of Meningeal Irritation ([TU]):

1.  Neck Stiffness (Nuchal Rigidity): Resistance to passive flexion of the neck (chin cannot touch the chest).

2.  Kernig’s Sign: With the patient supine and the hip and knee flexed to 90°, passive extension of the knee provokes painful hamstring spasm and resistance.

3.  Brudzinski’s Neck Sign: Passive flexion of the patient’s neck causes involuntary reflex flexion of both hips and knees.

•  Organism-Specific Clues:

•  Meningococcal sepsis:Non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash (over trunk and extremities), septic shock, DIC, and adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome).

•  Pneumococcal meningitis: Associated otitis media, sinusitis, mastoiditis, basal skull fracture (CSF rhinorrhoea), pneumonia, or splenectomy/alcoholism; high rate of seizures and coma.

•  Tuberculous meningitis: Subacute prodrome over 2–8 weeks of low-grade fever, malaise, weight loss, and headache, progressing to basal cranial nerve palsies (3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th), hydrocephalus, and endarteritis obliterans causing cerebral infarction.

2. Investigations & CSF Abnormalities Across Meningitis Types:

•  Initial Blood Tests (Before Antibiotics):Blood cultures, blood EDTA PCR for meningococcus and pneumococcus, FBC, U&Es, glucose (paired with CSF glucose), clotting screen, CRP/procalcitonin, and HIV test.

•  When to Perform CT Brain BEFORE Lumbar Puncture: Do NOT delay LP for a CT scan unless the patient has a contraindication to immediate LP: (1) Focal neurological signs; (2) Papilloedema; (3) Continuous or uncontrolled seizures; (4) GCS ≤ 12; or (5) Severe immunocompromise (e.g., HIV). (ography (Mandatory first): Excludes space-occupying lesions and dural venous sinus thrombosis (shows normal or "slit-like" ventricles and empty sella). Lumbar Puncture: Confirms elevated CSF opening pressure >25 cm H2O with completely normal CSF cell count, protein, and glucose. Formal automated perimetry to monitor visual fields.

•  Management:Weight loss (10%–15% weight reduction via diet, GLP-1 agonists, or bariatric surgery is curative); Oral Acetazolamide (500–2000 mg/day, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces choroid plexus CSF production) or Topiramate; and Optic Nerve Sheath Fenestration or Ventriculo-/Lumbo-Peritoneal Shunting if vision is threatened.

•  D. Management of Cryptococcal Meningitis [KU 24]:

1.  Induction Phase (2 weeks):Intravenous Liposomal Amphotericin B (3–4 mg/kg/day) PLUS Oral Flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses) (or single high-dose 10 mg/kg Liposomal Amphotericin B + 14 days of Flucytosine and Fluconazole).

2.  Consolidation Phase (8 weeks):Oral Fluconazole (400–800 mg daily).

3.  Maintenance Phase:Oral Fluconazole (200 mg daily) until CD4 count >100–200 cells/µ L on ART (delay starting HIV antiretroviral therapy by 4–6 weeks to prevent fatal intracranial IRIS, and perform therapeutic serial lumbar punctures to control high CSF pressure).

•  E. Complications of Bacterial & Tuberculous Meningitis:

•  Neurological:Sensorineural hearing loss / deafness (cochlear damage—most common long-term sequel), communicating or obstructive hydrocephalus, cranial nerve palsies (3rd, 6th, 7th, 8th), seizures/epilepsy, cerebral infarction (endarteritis obliterans or cortical venous thrombosis), subdural effusion or empyema, cerebral oedema with brain herniation, and cognitive/intellectual impairment.

•  Systemic: Septic shock, DIC, ARDS, SIADH (hyponatraemia), and reactive/septic arthritis.

title: 9. Disorders of Cerebellar Function [KU 24, 21, 15]
text:
9. Disorders of Cerebellar Function [KU 24, 21, 15]

1. Causes of Cerebellar Dysfunction / Ataxia:

•  Vascular: Posterior circulation cerebellar infarction or haemorrhage (PICA, AICA, or SCA territory).

•  Inflammatory / Demyelinating:Multiple sclerosis, post-infectious cerebellitis (varicella zoster), Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (anti-Yo/anti-Hu antibodies in ovarian, breast, or small-cell lung cancer), Gluten ataxia (coeliac disease).

•  Toxic & Drug-Induced:Alcohol (acute intoxication and chronic alcoholic cerebellar vermis degeneration), Antiseizure medications (Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, lamotrigine), Lithium, 5-fluorouracil, heavy metals (mercury).

•  Metabolic & Nutritional:Wernicke encephalopathy (Vitamin B1 / thiamin deficiency), Vitamin E deficiency, Hypothyroidism.

•  Structural / Neoplastic: Posterior fossa tumours (medulloblastoma, haemangioblastoma, cerebellar astrocytoma, metastases, acoustic neuroma), cerebellar abscess, Arnold–Chiari malformation.

•  Inherited & Degenerative:Friedreich’s ataxia (autosomal recessive FXN trinucleotide repeat), Autosomal dominant Spinocerebellar Ataxias (SCAs), Ataxia telangiectasia, Multiple System Atrophy (MSA-C), and Sporadic CJD.

2. Clinical Features & Signs of a Cerebellar Lesion (Mnemonic: DANISH):

(Crucial Anatomical Rule: Cerebellar hemisphere pathways are doubly crossed [or uncrossed], so a unilateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion produces IPSILATERAL clinical signs, whereas midline cerebellar vermis lesions cause truncal and gait ataxia).

1.  D — Dysdiadochokinesis: Inability to perform rapid, regular alternating movements (e.g., pronIf CT is required or LP is delayed, take blood cultures and administer empirical IV antibiotics + dexamethasone immediately within the first hour).

1.  A — Ataxia (Gait, Trunk, and Limb):

•  Limb Ataxia & Dysmetria (Hemisphere): Inability to judge distance and scale of movement during finger–nose and heel–shin testing, resulting in overshooting the target ("past-pointing" / hypermetria).

3. Management & Complications of Meningitis:

•  A. Management of Acute Bacterial (Pyogenic) Meningitis [KU 25, 21, 18]:

1.  Empirical Intravenous Antibiotics (Administer within 1 hour of arrival):

•  Adults <60 years:IV Ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily OR IV Cefotaxime 2 g four times daily.

•  Adults ≥ 60 years, Immunocompromised, Pregnant, or Alcoholics (To cover Listeria monocytogenes, which is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins):IV Ceftriaxone 2 g BD PLUS IV Amoxicillin (or Ampicillin) 2 g every 4 hours (6 times daily)(if penicillin-allergic, use IV Co-trimoxazole for Listeria).

•  If Penicillin-Resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae is Suspected: Add IV Vancomycin (15–20 mg/kg BD) or Rifampicin (600 mg BD) to Ceftriaxone.

•  Definitive Duration once Pathogen is Identified:Meningococcus: 5–7 days Ceftriaxone; Pneumococcus: 10–14 days Ceftriaxone (+ Vancomycin if resistant); Haemophilus influenzae: 10 days Ceftriaxone; Listeria monocytogenes:21 days IV Amoxicillin/Ampicillin.

2.  Adjunctive Corticosteroid Therapy:

•  Administer IV Dexamethasone 10 mg four times daily for 4 days, started before or with the first dose of antibiotics (inhibits subarachnoid cytokine surge triggered by bacterial lysis, significantly reducing sensorineural hearing loss and mortality in pneumococcal meningitis; stop if meningitis is found to be meningococcal or viral: Coarse, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus with the fast phase beating TOWARDS the side of the cerebellar lesion (and ocular dysmetria/saccadic intrusion).

1.  I — Intention Tremor (Kinetic Tremor): Coarse 3–5 Hz tremor that is absent at rest but appears during voluntary movement and progressively worsens as the finger approaches the target.

2.  S — Scanning Dysarthria ("Staccato" Speech): Slurred, explosive speech with impaired timing and cadence where words are broken up into separate syllables ("like a scanning poem").

3.  H — Hypotonia & Pendular Reflexes: Reduced muscle tone on passive manipulation, rebound phenomenon (inability to check the arm when resistance is suddenly released), and pendular knee jerks (leg continues swinging 3–4 times like a pendulum after patellar tap).

title: 10. Subarachnoid Haemorrhage (SAH) [KU 24, 23, 22, TU, RGU]
text:
10. Subarachnoid Haemorrhage (SAH) [KU 24, 23, 22, TU, RGU]

(Covers all 3 clinical vignette Essays on patients presenting with a sudden-onset severe "thunderclap" headache, vomiting, photophobia, loss of consciousness/altered sensorium, and neck rigidity).

1. Definition & Aetiology (Causes and Risk Factors):

•  Definition: Spontaneous extravasation of arterial blood into the subarachnoid space (incidence ~ 6 per 100,000/year; 30% 30-day mortality).

•  Causes of Subarachnoid Haemorrhage [KU 24]:

1.  Rupture of a Saccular ("Berry") Aneurysm (85% of spontaneous cases): Located at arterial bifurcations of the Circle of Willis:

•  Anterior communicating artery (30%)

•  Posterior communicating artery (25%)

•  Middle cerebral artery bifurcation (20%)

•  Basilar/vertebrobasilar circulation (10%).

2.  Non-Aneurysmal Perimesencephalic Haemorrhage (10%): Benign venous bleed around the midbrain with normal angiography and excellent prognosis.

3.  Arteriovenous Malformations (AVMs) & Vertebral Artery Dissection (5%).

4.  Other Rare Causes: Mycotic aneurysms (infective endocarditis), cerebral amyloid angiopathy, pituitary apoplexy, bleeding diatheses/anticoagulants, and cocaine/amphetamine misuse. (Note: Globally, head trauma is the most common non-spontaneous cause of subarachnoid blood).

•  Modifiable & Non-Modifiable Risk Factors:

•  Modifiable:Hypertension, cigarette smoking, excessive alcohol intake, and sympathomimetic drugs (cocaine).

•  Non-Modifiable / Genetic: Female sex, increasing age, positive family history (≥ 2 first-degree relatives with SAH), Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), Ehlers–Danlos syndrome type IV, Marfan syndrome, and Coarctation of the aorta.

2. Clinical Features & Differential Diagnosis of Sudden Severe ("Thunderclap") Headache:

•  Differential Diagnosis of Thunderclap Headache: (1) Subarachnoid Haemorrhage (accounts for 1 in 8 cases; must be excluded in all); (2) Intracerebral or cerebellar haemorrhage; (3) Acute bacterial or viral meningitis; (4) Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; (5) Cervical (carotid or vertebral) artery dissection; (6) Pituitary apoplexy; (7) Benign primary thunderclap / coital / exertional headache or reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS).

•  Clinical Presentation of SAH:

•  Instantaneous, explosive "thunderclap" headache (reaching maximal intensity within seconds to a minute, described as "the worst).

1.  Chemoprophylaxis for Close Contacts of Meningococcal Meningitis: Single oral dose of Ciprofloxacin 500 mg (or Rifampicin 600 mg BD for 2 days).

•  B. Management of Viral Meningitis [KU 24]:

•  Benign and self-limiting; managed with supportive care (quiet room, analgesia, antiemetics, IV fluids); antibiotics can be stopped once bacterial meningitis is excluded.

•  C. Management of Tuberculous Meningitis [TU]:

•  Start immediate Anti-Tuberculous Chemotherapy for 9–12 months: headache of my life" or "like being hit on the back of the head with a bat"), often occurring during physical exertion, straining, or sexual intercourse.

•  Accompanied by vomiting, photophobia, Collapse / transient or prolonged loss of consciousness, and epileptic seizures.

•  (Warning "Sentinel" Headache: A smaller warning bleed may precede a major rupture by days or weeks).

•  Physical Signs on Examination:

•  Irritability, depressed GCS, and reactive systemic hypertension.

•  Signs of Meningeal Irritation (Meningism):Neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity), positive Kernig’s sign, and positive Brudzinski’s sign(note: neck stiffness takes several hours to develop as subarachnoid blood degrades and may be absent initially).

•  Fundoscopy:Subhyaloid ( 2 months of Intensive Phase (Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol [or Streptomycin]) followed by 7–10 months of Continuation Phase (Isoniazid + Rifampicin), co-prescribed with Pyridoxine 25–50 mg daily.

•  Mandatory Adjunctive Corticosteroids (Reduces mortality by 30%):IV/Oral Dexamethasone (0.3–0.4 mg/kg/daypre-retinal) haemorrhages (brick-red blood tracking beneath the internal limiting membrane) or vitreous haemorrhage ( initially) or Prednisolone (60 mg/day), tapered gradually over 6–8 weeksTerson’s syndrome), and papilloedema.

•  Focal Neurological Signs:

•  Ipsilateral painful 3rd cranial nerve palsy (complete ptosis + fixed dilated pupil) due to direct compression by an expanding Posterior Communicating Artery aneurysm.

•  Hemiparesis or dysphasia (if blood extends into the brain parenchyma from an MCA aneurysm, or secondary to delayed cerebral ischaemia/vasospasm).

3. Investigations (Confirming the Diagnosis):

1.  Immediate Non-Contrast CT Brain Scan (First-Line Investigation):

•  Detects hyperdense (bright white) blood in the basal cisterns, Sylvian fissures, interhemispheric fissure, and ventricles. Sensitivity is >95%–98% within the first 6–24 hours, but declines with time as blood is cleared.

2.  Lumbar Puncture for CSF Xanthochromia (Mandatory if CT Brain is Negative):

•  Perform at least 12 hours after headache onset (to allow time for red cell lysis and enzymatic conversion of haemoglobin into oxyhaemoglobin and yellow bilirubin).

•  Centrifuge the CSF immediately and examine the supernatant by spectrophotometry for Xanthochromia (yellow discoloration due to bilirubin).

•  Importance of Xanthochromia [TU]:Reliably differentiates a true Subarachnoid Haemorrhage from a "traumatic tap" (in a traumatic tap, red cell counts fall across sequential tubes and the centrifuged supernatant is crystal clear without xanthochromia). If both CT and 12-hour CSF spectrophotometry are negative, SAH is definitively ruled out.

3.  Cerebral Angiography (CTA, MRA, or Digital Subtraction Intra-Arterial Angiography [DSA]):

•  Performed urgently once SAH is confirmed to identify the anatomical location, size, and neck morphology of the ruptured aneurysm to guide coiling or clipping.

4. Complications of Subarachnoid Haemorrhage [TU]:

1.  Rebleeding (Recurrent Haemorrhage): Highest risk in the first 24–72 hours (40% in the first 4 weeks if untreated) and carries a >50%–70% mortality; prevented by urgent endovascular coiling or surgical clipping.

2.  Delayed Cerebral Ischaemia (Cerebral Arterial Vasospasm): Occurs characteristically between Days 4 and 14 post-SAH; breakdown products of blood in the basal cisterns trigger intense spasm of large cerebral arteries, causing focal neurological deficits (hemiplegia, aphasia) or deteriorating consciousness and cerebral infarction. Prevented by oral nimodipine.

3.  Acute or Chronic Obstructive / Communicating Hydrocephalus: Blood clots obstruct the fourth ventricular outlets or arachnoid villi, causing worsening drowsiness and requiring an external ventricular drain (EVD) or ventriculo-peritoneal shunt.

4.  Hyponatraemia ("Cerebral Salt Wasting" or SIADH): Common Electrolyte complication; managed carefully with fluid balance (avoid severe fluid restriction as hypovolaemia precipitates cerebral vasospasm/infarction).

5.  Epileptic Seizures, Neurogenic Pulmonary Oedema, and Takotsubo Stress Cardiomyopathy / ECG changes.

5. Management of Subarachnoid Haemorrhage:

•  Immediate Resuscitation & General Supportive Care:

•  Secure airway (intubate if GCS ≤ 8), maintain oxygenation, strict bed rest in a quiet room, strong analgesia (paracetamol/codeine/opioids), antiemetics, and laxatives to avoid straining.

•  Stop all anticoagulants/antiplatelets and reverse coagulopathy immediately.

•  Maintain euvolaemia with intravenous 0.9% normal saline (2.5–3 L/day) and control extreme hypertension (SBP <160 mmHg) prior to securing the aneurysm.

•  Prevention of Delayed Cerebral Ischaemia (Vasospasm):

•  Administer Oral Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days (dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that selectively dilates cerebral blood vessels, reduces cerebral infarction from vasospasm, and significantly improves neurological outcome and mortality).

•  Definitive Aneurysm Occlusion (Urgent Neurosurgery / Interventional Neuroradiology Referral):

1.  Endovascular Platinum Coil Embolisation ("Coiling"):Treatment of first choice where anatomically feasible (ISAT trial showed significantly lower morbidity and better 1-year disability-free survival compared to open craniotomy).

2.  Neurosurgical Craniotomy and Microsurgical Clipping of the aneurysm neck (used for wide-necked MCA aneurysms or those with large space-occupying intracerebral haematomas requiring evacuation).

title: 11. Ring-Enhancing Brain Lesions, Neurocysticercosis, Rabies, and Tetanus [KU 23, 22, 21, 20, 19, 16, RGU]
text:
11. Ring-Enhancing Brain Lesions, Neurocysticercosis, Rabies, and Tetanus [KU 23, 22, 21, 20, 19, 16, RGU]

1. Causes of Ring-Enhancing Lesions on CT / MRI Brain & Neurocysticercosis [KU 23, 20, 16, RGU]:

•  Differential Diagnosis of Ring-Enhancing Brain Lesions (Mnemonic: MAGICAL DR):

1.  M — Metastases (bronchus, breast, melanoma, renal, GI—often multiple at the grey–white matter junction).

2.  A — Abscess (Pyogenic Bacterial Cerebral Abscess) (shows restricted diffusion in the central cavity on DWI MRI).

3.  G — Glioblastoma Multiforme (high-grade WHO Grade IV astrocytoma; irregular necrotic centre crossing corpus callosum).

4.  I — Infection (Parasitic & Mycobacterial):

•  Neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium).

•  Tuberculoma (Mycobacterium tuberculosis—often shows central T2 hypointensity).

•  Cerebral Toxoplasmosis (Toxoplasma gondii—multiple basal ganglia/corticomedullary ring lesions in HIV/AIDS with CD4 <100 cells/µ L).

•  Fungal abscess (Cryptococcus, Aspergillus).

5.  D — Demyelination (Tumefactive Multiple Sclerosis): Often shows an "open-ring" enhancement facing the cortex.

6.  L — Lymphoma (Primary CNS Lymphoma in AIDS) and R — Radiation necrosis / Resolving intracerebral haematoma.

•  Treatment of Neurocysticercosis [KU 20, RGU]:

•  Caused by larval cysts of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium ingested via faecal–oral contamination; commonest cause of adult-onset focal epilepsy in endemic regions (CT/MRI shows viable cysts with an eccentric scolex ["dot-in-hole"], colloidal ring-enhancing degenerating cysts, or calcified nodules).

•  Stepwise Management:

1.  Antiseizure Medication (ASM): Start Levetiracetam, Carbamazepine, or Phenytoin first to control seizures (this is the sole therapy needed if imaging shows only calcified, dead granulomas).

2.  Exclude Ocular and Intraventricular Cysts FIRST: Perform fundoscopy / slit-lamp examination prior to antiparasitic drugs, because killing an intraocular cyst causes severe inflammatory endophthalmitis and blindness (ocular cysts are removed surgically).

3.  Start Corticosteroids BEFORE Antiparasitic Therapy: Administer Dexamethasone (0.1 mg/kg/day) or Prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) starting 1–2 days prior to cysticidal drugs and continuing throughout treatment to suppress the intense perilesional cerebral oedema and seizures triggered by dying parasites.

4.  Antiparasitic (Cysticidal) Therapy (for viable / degenerating parenchymal cysts):Albendazole (15 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 10–14 days) (combined with Praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day if >2 viable cysts).

5.  Neurosurgery: Ventriculoperitoneal shunting or endoscopic removal for intraventricular cysts causing obstructive hydrocephalus.

2. Rabies: Clinical Features & Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (Management of Third-Degree Dog Bite) [KU 22, 21, 16]:

•  Aetiology: Caused by the bullet-shaped neurotropic RNA Rabies virus (Lyssavirus, Rhabdovirus) transmitted in the saliva of infected dogs, bats, foxes, or cats via bites, scratches, or licks on mucous membranes. The virus ascends retrogradely along peripheral nerves to the CNS; incubation is typically 4–8 weeks (shorter with deep bites on the head/neck; nearly 100% fatal once clinical symptoms appear).

•  Clinical Features of Rabies:

•  Prodromal Phase (1–10 days): Fever, malaise, headache, anxiety, and neuropathic pain, itching, or paraesthesia at the site of the healed bite wound (pathognomonic early symptom).

•  Furious (Encephalitic) Rabies (80%):

•  Hydrophobia and Aerophobia: Attempts to drink water or a draught of air on the face provoke violent, painful, jerky spasms of the diaphragm, pharynx, and inspiratory muscles, producing terror of water despite intense thirst.

•  Episodes of hyperactivity, extreme agitation, hallucinations, spitting, and delirium alternating with lucid intervals.

•  Autonomic instability (hypersalivation/frothing, lacrimation, sweating, labile hypertension, arrhythmias, hyperpyrexia), cranial nerve palsies, coma, and cardiorespiratory death within 7 days.

•  Paralytic ("Dumb") Rabies (20%): Ascending flaccid paralysis mimicking Guillain–Barré syndrome, progressing to coma.

•  Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) & Management of a Category III (Third-Degree) Dog Bite:

(WHO Exposure Categories: Category I = touching/feeding animal or licks on intact skin [no PEP needed]; Category II = nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches/abrasions without bleeding [Wound care + Rabies Vaccine]; Category III [Third-Degree] = single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches with bleeding, licks on broken skin, contamination of mucous membranes with saliva, or any bat contact [Requires Wound care + Rabies Immunoglobulin + Rabies Vaccine]).

1.  Immediate Local Wound Care (Crucial first step):

•  Wash and flush the wound thoroughly under running water with soap or quaternary ammonium detergent and povidone-iodine for at least 15 minutes.

•  Debride devitalised tissue, avoid primary suturing of the wound (leave open to prevent viral entry into nerves), and administer Tetanus toxoid prophylaxis and oral Co-amoxiclav (to prevent Pasteurella and anaerobic infection).

2.  Passive Immunisation — Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) (Mandatory for all Category III bites in unimmunised individuals, given on Day 0, up to Day 7):

•  Human Rabies Immunoglobulin (HRIG): 20 IU/kg body weight (or Equine RIG 40 IU/kg).

•  Infiltrate as much of the calculated dose as anatomically possible directly into and around the depth of the bite wound(s); inject any remaining volume intramuscularly at a site distant from the vaccine injection site.

3.  Active Immunisation — Modern Cell-Culture Anti-Rabies Vaccine (Human Diploid Cell Vaccine [HDCV], Purified Chick Embryo Cell [PCEC], or Purified Vero Cell Rabies Vaccine [PVRV]):

•  Injected into the deltoid muscle (anterolateral thigh in infants; never into the gluteal region).

•  Intramuscular Regimen (Essen / 4-dose WHO schedule):1.0 mL (or 0.5 mL) IM on Days 0, 3, 7, and between Days 14 and 28 (a 5th dose on Day 28/30 is given to immunocompromised patients).

•  Updated WHO Intradermal Regimen (2-site ID, cost-saving):0.1 mL ID at 2 sites on Days 0, 3, and 7.

•  (Note: If the patient has previously completed pre- or post-exposure rabies vaccination, do NOT give RIG; give only 2 booster doses of vaccine on Days 0 and 3).

•  Indications for Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (Days 0, 7, and 21/28): Veterinarians, animal handlers, rabies laboratory workers, and travellers to remote endemic areas.

3. Tetanus: Clinical Features and Management [KU 19]:

•  Aetiopathogenesis: Caused by Clostridium tetani, an anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive rod whose spores contaminate puncture wounds, burns,injection drug sites, or the neonatal umbilical stump. In anaerobic necrotic tissue, vegetative bacilli secrete the neurotoxin tetanospasmin, which ascends retrogradely along motor axons to the spinal cord and brainstem, where it cleaves synaptobrevin (SNARE protein) and blocks the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and Glycine from Renshaw inhibitory interneurons. This causes unopposed motor and autonomic hyperactivity.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Incubation period is 2 days to several weeks (shorter incubation <7 days predicts severe disease and high mortality).

•  Trismus ("Lockjaw"): Painless tonic spasm of the masseter muscles causing inability to open the mouth—the earliest and most common presenting sign.

-pulsating, dull, "tight band-like" or pressing headache of mild-to-moderate intensity radiating from the occiput to the forehead. Not aggravated by physical activity, and NOT accompanied by vomiting or photophobia. Pericranial muscle tenderness may be present.

•  Management: Reassurance (brain imaging is not indicated and risks incidental findings), stress management/relaxation physiotherapy, avoidance of analgesic/codeine overuse, and low-dose Amitriptyline (10–50 mg at night) for chronic tension-type headache.

3. Trigeminal Neuralgia (Tic Douloureux) [KU 22, RGU]:

•  Pathophysiology: Usually occurs in patients >50 years due to neurovascular compression of the trigeminal (5th) nerve root entry zone at the pons by an aberrant loop of the superior cerebellar artery, causing focal demyelination and ephaptic transmissionRisus Sardonicus: Sustained contraction of facial frontalis and perioral muscles producing a fixed "sardonic grin" with raised eyebrows.

•  Tonic Axial Rigidity & Opisthotonus: Board-like abdominal wall rigidity and hyperextension/arching of the neck and back (opisthotonus), with dysphagia and laryngeal spasm.

•  Violent Reflex Muscle Spasms: Excruciatingly painful tonic spasms lasting seconds to minutes, triggered by minor sensory stimuli (noise, light, touch, movement), while the patient remains fully conscious; causes exhaustion, cyanosis, apnoea/asphyxia, rhabdomyolysis, and vertebral fractures.

•  Autonomic Dysfunction (Leading cause of death in ICU): Labile severe hypertension and hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmias, profuse sweating, and hyperpyrexia.

•  Management of Established Tetanus:

1.  Neutralise Unbound Circulating Toxin (Before Wound Debridement):

•  Administer Human Tetanus Immunoglobulin (HTIG) (3000–5000 IU IM/IV) (or intravenous human normal immunoglobulin [IVIg] if HTIG is unavailable).

2.  Eradicate the Source of Toxin Production:

•  Surgical Wound Debridement of all necrotic tissue.

•  Antibiotic of Choice:Intravenous Metronidazole 500 mg every 6–8 hours for 7–10 days(preferred over Penicillin G [2–4 million units IV q4–6h] because penicillin is a structural GABA antagonist that can theoretically potentiate spasms).

3.  Control Muscle Spasms & Airway Protection:

•  Nurse in a quiet, darkened ICU room, avoiding all unnecessary tactile or auditory stimuli.

•  High-Dose Intravenous Benzodiazepines (GABA agonists):IV Diazepam or Midazolam infusion.

•  If spasms continue or compromise breathing, perform early tracheostomy / endotracheal intubation, neuromuscular blockade (vecuronium/atracurium), and mechanical ventilation.

4.  Control Autonomic Instability & Supportive Care:

•  Intravenous Magnesium Sulphate infusion (blunts catecholamine release and reduces muscle spasms) and Labetalol or morphine for sympathetic storms; maintain high-calorie enteral nutrition, hydration, and VTE prophylaxis.

5.  Active Immunisation Upon Recovery: Because the minute lethal dose of tetanospasmin is insufficient to induce natural immunity, full active vaccination with Tetanus Toxoid is mandatory during convalescence.
