title: 12. Raised Intracranial Pressure (ICP), Cushing’s Reflex, and Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension [KU 24, 18, TU]
text:
12. Raised Intracranial Pressure (ICP), Cushing’s Reflex, and Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension [KU 24, 18, TU]

1. Symptoms and Signs of Increased Intracranial Tension (Raised ICP) & Cushing’s Reflex [KU 24, TU]:

•  Normal adult ICP: <10–15 mmHg (50–200 mmH2O).

Normal adult ICP: < 10–15 mmHg (50–200 mmH2O).

Clinical Features of Raised Intracranial Pressure:

•  Headache: Typically throbbing / generalised, worse in the morning on waking, and exacerbated by coughing, sneezing, straining, bending forward, or lying flat.

•  Vomiting: Often effortless / projectile in the morning without preceding nausea.

•  Papilloedema & Visual Disturbances: Bilateral swelling and hyperaemia of the optic discs with blurring of disc margins, loss of venous pulsation, retinal flame haemorrhages, enlargement of the blind spot, and transient visual obscurations on changing posture / on standing.

•  Depressed Level of Consciousness: Progressive drowsiness, stupor / obtundation, and coma.

•  False Localising Signs:Unilateral or bilateral 6th cranial nerve (abducens) palsy (causing horizontal diplopia and failure of eye abduction due to stretching of the long intracranial course of CN VI over the petrous temporal ridge) and 3rd cranial nerve palsy (fixed dilated pupil and ptosis from uncal transtentorial herniation).

•  Brain Herniation (“Coning”) Signs:Tentorial (uncal) herniation compresses the ipsilateral 3rd cranial nerve (causing a fixed, dilated pupil followed by ptosis and contralateral / ipsilateral hemiparesis); tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses the medulla, causing respiratory arrest.

•  Cushing’s Reflex (Cushing’s Triad) [KU 24]: A late physiological brainstem vasopressor reflex triggered by ischaemia of the medullary vasomotor centre during severe intracranial hypertension and impending brainstem herniation. The classic triad: (1) Systemic arterial hypertension (with a widened pulse pressure) (reflex sympathetic vasoconstriction to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure, CPP = MAP − ICP); (2) Reflex bradycardia (baroreceptor-mediated vagal slowing of the heart); (3) Irregular respiration (Cheyne–Stokes or Biot’s ataxic breathing).

Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH — “Benign Intracranial Hypertension”) [KU 18]:

•  Definition & Epidemiology: Raised intracranial pressure (> 25 cmH2O) occurring in the absence of an intracranial mass lesion, hydrocephalus, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Strongly associated with young, overweight / obese women of childbearing age. Secondary precipitants include tetracyclines (minocycline, doxycycline), hypervitaminosis A / oral retinoids (isotretinoin), withdrawal of corticosteroids, and lithium.

•  Clinical Features: Chronic throbbing morning headache (mimicking migraine or tension headache), pulsatile tinnitus (“whooshing” sound in ears), transient visual obscurations (brief greying-out of vision lasting seconds on bending or standing), and horizontal diplopia (from a false-localising 6th nerve palsy).

•  Examination:Bilateral papilloedema with an enlarged blind spot and progressive peripheral visual field constriction on perimetry (which can lead to permanent optic atrophy and blindness if untreated — hence the older term “benign” is a misnomer). No other focal neurological signs.

•  Investigations:MRI brain with MR venography (MRV): Mandatory first step to exclude a mass lesion, hydrocephalus, and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (shows normal or small “slit-like” ventricles and an empty sella). Lumbar puncture: Confirms elevated CSF opening pressure (> 250 mmH2O) with completely normal CSF cell count, protein, and glucose. Serial automated perimetry (visual fields): Essential to monitor visual function.

•  Management: (1) Weight loss (10%–15% body weight) via diet, GLP-1 agonists, or bariatric surgery, and cessation of any offending drug (tetracyclines, retinoids). (2) Medical therapy:Acetazolamide (500–2000 mg/day — carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces choroid plexus CSF production) or Topiramate (also inhibits carbonic anhydrase and promotes weight loss). (3) Surgical intervention (for progressive visual field loss threatening sight):Optic nerve sheath fenestration or ventriculoperitoneal / lumboperitoneal CSF shunting (or venous sinus stenting).

subject: medicine
title: 13. Peripheral Neuropathy, Guillain–Barré Syndrome (AIDP), Bell’s Palsy, and Horner’s Syndrome [KU 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, 18, TU]
text:
Peripheral Nerves, Neuromuscular Junction & Muscle

13. Peripheral Neuropathy, Guillain–Barré Syndrome (AIDP), Bell’s Palsy, and Horner’s Syndrome [KU 24, 23, 22, 20, 19, 18, TU]

(Covers both clinical vignette Essays on young females presenting with distal paraesthesia followed by rapidly ascending symmetrical flaccid quadriparesis, areflexia, cranial nerve involvement, and tachypnoea 2 weeks after a febrile illness = Guillain–Barré Syndrome [Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy — AIDP]).

1. Causes & Classification of Peripheral Neuropathy [KU 24, 19, TU]:

•  Classified by anatomical distribution (Mononeuropathy [e.g., carpal tunnel], Mononeuritis multiplex [vasculitis, diabetes, leprosy, sarcoidosis, HIV], or Symmetrical length-dependent "glove-and-stocking" Polyneuropathy) and by pathological mechanism on Nerve Conduction Studies:

•  A. Axonal Polyneuropathies (Reduced action potential amplitude with preserved conduction velocity — Most Common):

•  Metabolic & Endocrine:Diabetes mellitus (most common cause in the West), Chronic renal failure (uraemia), Hypothyroidism, chronic liver disease, acromegaly.

•  Nutritional Deficiencies:Vitamin B1 (Thiamin), Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine), Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin), Vitamin E, copper deficiency.

•  Toxins:Alcohol misuse, heavy metals (lead [motor wrist-drop], arsenic, thallium, mercury).

•  Drugs:Isoniazid (prevent with pyridoxine), Vincristine, Cisplatin / Oxaliplatin, Taxanes, Bortezomib, Thalidomide, Amiodarone, Metronidazole, Nitrofurantoin, Phenytoin, Dapsone, Linezolid, Antiretrovirals, recreational nitrous oxide (N2O), organophosphates.

•  Infections, Systemic & Genetic:Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae), HIV, Lyme disease, Vasculitis / Connective tissue diseases (PAN, RA, SLE, Sjögren’s), Paraneoplastic (anti-Hu sensory neuronopathy in SCLC), AL Amyloidosis, Critical illness polyneuropathy, and Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease Type 2 (CMT2).

•  B. Demyelinating Polyneuropathies (Marked slowing of nerve conduction velocity <30–35 m/s, prolonged distal latencies, conduction block, and prolonged F-waves):

•  Acute:Guillain–Barré Syndrome (AIDP) and Diphtheria.

•  Chronic Acquired:Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) (evolves over >8 weeks; treated with IVIg, steroids, or plasma exchange).

•  Multifocal Motor Neuropathy (MMN) with conduction block (pure motor arm weakness with anti-GM1 antibodies; mimics MND; responds to IVIg), and Paraproteinaemic neuropathy (IgM anti-MAG antibodies, POEMS syndrome).

•  Inherited:Charcot–Marie–Tooth Disease Type 1 (CMT1 — PMP22 duplication, "inverted champagne-bottle" legs and pes cavus) and Hereditary Neuropathy with Liability to Pressure Palsies (HNPP).

2. Guillain–Barré Syndrome (GBS / Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy — AIDP) [KU 23, 22, 20, 18]:

•  Pathophysiology: An acute, post-infectious, immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy. Around 65%–70% of patients have a preceding respiratory or gastrointestinal infection 1–3 weeks earlier—most commonly Campylobacter jejuni (strongly linked to the severe Acute Motor Axonal Neuropathy [AMAN] variant), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Influenza, HIV, or Zika virus.

•  Molecular Mimicry: Antibodies generated against microbial lipo-oligosaccharides cross-react with gangliosides (e.g., GM1, GD1a, GQ1b) on peripheral nerve Schwann cells or nodes of Ranvier, triggering complement activation and macrophage-mediated segmental demyelination or axonal damage.

•  Clinical Features & Diagnostic Criteria of Guillain–Barré Syndrome:

•  Core Diagnostic Features (Required for Diagnosis):

1.  Progressive, symmetrical muscle weakness of the legs and arms (often more marked proximally than distally, ascending from the lower limbs to the upper limbs over days to a maximum nadir of ≤ 4 weeks).

2.  Generalised Areflexia or Hyporeflexia (loss of deep tendon reflexes).

•  Supportive Clinical Features:

•  Distal paraesthesia (tingling/numbness) in the hands and feet and severe neuropathic back or radicular leg pain (often precedes weakness, though objective sensory loss on examination is mild).

Respiratory Muscle Weakness (20%–25%): Diaphragmatic and intercostal paralysis causing tachypnoea, inability to count to 20 in one breath, and Type II hypercapnic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation.

Autonomic Dysfunction (leading cause of death in ICU): Labile severe hypertension and hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmias, profuse sweating, and hyperpyrexia. (In the detailed list: labile hypertension, postural hypotension, sinus tachycardia.)

Cranial Nerve Involvement (50%):Bilateral lower motor neuron facial (7th) nerve palsy (most common), bulbar weakness (dysphagia, dysarthria, nasal regurgitation), and ophthalmoplegia / ptosis.

Red flag — spinal cord disease: Guillain–Barré syndrome typically presents without a sharp spinal sensory level and without early bladder paralysis. If a sensory level or early bladder paralysis is present, or if urinary retention is present, urgently perform a spinal MRI to exclude acute spinal cord compression or transverse myelitis.

Miller Fisher Syndrome Variant (5%): Classic triad of Ophthalmoplegia + Ataxia + Areflexia (without limb weakness), strongly associated with anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies (> 90%).

Investigations (Confirming the Diagnosis):

1.  Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Examination (Lumbar Puncture) [KU 20]:

•  Demonstrates the classic hallmark of "Albuminocytological Dissociation": Elevated CSF Protein (>0.45 g/L, often 1.0–3.0 g/L) with a NORMAL CSF White Cell Count (≤ 5 × 106/L).

•  (Note: CSF protein may be normal in the first 7–10 days of illness; a CSF white cell count >50 × 106/L suggests an alternative diagnosis or HIV seroconversion).

2.  Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS) & Electromyography (EMG):

•  In AIDP: Multifocal motor conduction slowing, prolonged distal motor latencies, conduction block, and prolonged or absent F-waves and H-reflexes (reflecting proximal nerve root demyelination, which is the earliest electrophysiological sign). In AMAN/AMSAN: reduced compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes due to axonal loss.

3.  Bedside Spirometry (Vital Capacity — Mandatory Serial Monitoring):

•  Measure Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) every 4–6 hours (DO NOT rely on pulse oximetry or arterial blood gases alone, as hypoxia/hypercapnia is a very late pre-arrest sign in neuromuscular respiratory failure).

4.  Blood & Serological Tests: U&Es (for SIADH/hyponatraemia), stool culture/Campylobacter serology, HIV test, and anti-ganglioside antibodies (anti-GM1 in AMAN; anti-GQ1b in Miller Fisher).

Immediate Hospital / HDU / ICU Admission & Respiratory/Autonomic Monitoring:

•  Monitor Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) 4-hourly and continuous ECG and BP monitoring.

•  Elective Endotracheal Intubation and Mechanical Ventilation are indicated if FVC falls below  15–20 mL/kg (<1.0–1.5 L), or if there is rapid clinical deterioration, severe bulbar dysphagia with aspiration risk, or hypercapnia.

1.  Specific Disease-Modifying Immunotherapy (Start within 2 weeks of onset in non-ambulant/severe patients):

(Both treatments are equally effective in hastening recovery and shortening ventilation time; combining them offers no extra benefit):

•  Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIg) (Preferred due to ease of administration and fewer complications):0.4 g/kg/day IV daily for 5 consecutive days (total dose 2 g/kg).

•  OR Therapeutic Plasma Exchange (Plasmapheresis):4–5 plasma exchanges (200–250 mL/kg total) over 7–10 days.

•  CRITICAL RULE:Corticosteroids (oral prednisolone or IV methylprednisolone) are INEFFECTIVE in Guillain–Barré syndrome and are NOT recommended.

1.  Prevention & Treatment of Complications:

•  Deep Vein Thrombosis / Pulmonary Embolism Prophylaxis: Mandatory subcutaneous LMWH plus pneumatic compression stockings in all immobile patients.

•  Bulbar & Nutritional Support: Nil by mouth and nasogastric tube feeding if swallowing is unsafe to prevent aspiration pneumonia.

•  Neuropathic Pain:Gabapentin, Pregabalin, Carbamazepine, or Amitriptyline.

•  Exposure Keratitis (from facial palsy): Lubricating eye drops and taping eyelids shut at night.

•  Physiotherapy & Rehabilitation to prevent joint contractures and pressure sores. (80% recover completely within 3–6 months, 15% have residual weakness, and 4% die from respiratory failure, PE, or autonomic cardiac arrest).

3. Lower Motor Neuron Facial Palsy (Bell’s Palsy), Bell’s Phenomenon, Bilateral LMN Facial Palsy, and Horner’s Syndrome [KU 24, TU]:

•  Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) Facial (7th) Nerve Palsy & Bell’s Palsy:

•  Anatomical Distinction (LMN vs. UMN 7th Palsy): The upper facial muscles (frontalis and orbicularis oculi) receive bilateral upper motor neuron cortical innervation, whereas the lower facial muscles receive contralateral UMN innervation only. Therefore, an Upper Motor Neuron lesion (e.g., internal capsule stroke) spares the forehead (eyebrow raising and eye closure are preserved), whereas a Lower Motor Neuron lesion (7th nerve nucleus in pons or facial nerve trunk) paralyses the ENTIRE ipsilateral half of the face (both upper and lower face): loss of forehead wrinkling, inability to close the eye, flattening of the nasolabial fold, drooping of the angle of the mouth, and deviation of the mouth to the healthy side on smiling.

•  Bell’s Phenomenon [KU 24, TU]: When a patient with an LMN facial nerve palsy attempts to close their eyes, the paralysed orbicularis oculi fails to close the eyelids, and the eyeball rolls upwards and outwards (a normal protective synkinetic brainstem reflex between CN VII and CN III nuclei), leaving the white sclera visible below the cornea.

•  Bell’s Palsy: Acute idiopathic unilateral LMN 7th nerve palsy within the facial canal (associated with Herpes Simplex Virus-1 reactivation; if painful vesicles are present in the external auditory canal/pinna or soft palate, it is Ramsay Hunt Syndrome caused by Varicella Zoster Virus affecting the geniculate ganglion). Preceded by retroauricular pain, with hyperacusis (nerve to stapedius paralysis), loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani), and dry eye.

•  Management of Bell’s Palsy:Oral Prednisolone (50–60 mg daily for 7–10 days) started within 72 hours of onset significantly improves complete recovery rates (80% recover within 12 weeks); combine with artificial tears by day and eye-pad taping at night to prevent corneal ulceration.

•  Four Causes of Bilateral Facial Palsy of LMN Type [TU]:

1.  Guillain–Barré Syndrome (AIDP)

2.  Sarcoidosis (Neurosarcoidosis / Heerfordt’s syndrome)

3.  Lyme Disease (Borrelia burgdorferi)

4.  Basal Meningitis (Tuberculous, malignant, or HIV seroconversion) or Leprosy(Note: Myasthenia gravis and facioscapulohumeral/myotonic dystrophy cause bilateral myopathic/neuromuscular facial weakness).

•  Horner’s Syndrome [TU]:

•  Pathophysiology: Interruption of the ipsilateral oculosympathetic pathway along its 3-neuron course: 1st-order (Central) from hypothalamus through lateral brainstem (lateral medullary syndrome, syringomyelia) to ciliospinal centre of Budge (C8–T2); 2nd-order (Pre-ganglionic) exiting T1 root over the  pulmonary apex (Pancoast apical lung tumour, cervical rib, thyroid mass) to the superior cervical ganglion; 3rd-order (Post-ganglionic) ascending along the internal carotid artery (internal carotid artery dissection, cavernous sinus lesion, cluster headache) to the orbit.

•  Classic Clinical Features (Ipsilateral):

1.  Partial Ptosis (drooping of the upper eyelid due to paralysis of sympathetic Müller’s tarsal muscle, with elevation of the lower lid—"upside-down ptosis" causing apparent enophthalmos).

2.  Miosis (Small, Constricted Pupil) (unopposed parasympathetic sphincter pupillae action; anisocoria is most marked in dim light/darkness).

3.  Ipsilateral Facial Anhidrosis (Loss of Sweating)(affects the entire half of the face in central/pre-ganglionic lesions, but is absent or restricted to a tiny patch on the forehead in post-ganglionic internal carotid lesions because sudomotor fibres to the face travel along the external carotid artery).

4.  Heterochromia iridis (lighter-coloured iris on affected side) if congenital.

title: 14. Myasthenia Gravis [KU 24, 23, 20, 17, TU, RGU]
text:
14. Myasthenia Gravis [KU 24, 23, 20, 17, TU, RGU]

1. Pathogenesis:

•  Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an acquired autoimmune disorder of the post-synaptic neuromuscular junction (NMJ).

•  In 80%–85% of generalised MG (and 50% of ocular MG), pathogenic IgG1 and IgG3 autoantibodies are directed against nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptors (AChR) on the post-synaptic motor end-plate membrane. These antibodies impair neuromuscular transmission by three mechanisms: (1) Competitive blockade of acetylcholine binding; (2) Cross-linking and accelerated endocytosis/degradation of AChRs; and (3) Complement-mediated destruction and flattening/simplification of the post-synaptic junctional folds.

•  In 5%–10% of AChR-negative patients, IgG4 autoantibodies target Muscle-Specific Kinase (MuSK) (a post-synaptic protein essential for AChR clustering; causes prominent bulbar and respiratory weakness).

•  Thymic Abnormality:15% of patients (mainly older adults) have a Thymoma, while 65%–75% of younger patients have Thymic Follicular Hyperplasia. Associated with other autoimmune diseases (thyrotoxicosis/Graves’, hypothyroidism, pernicious anaemia, RA, SLE).

2. Clinical Features (Symptoms & Signs):

•  Bimodal onset: young women (15–40 years) and older men (>50–60 years).

•  Cardinal Hallmark:Painless, fluctuating, fatigable skeletal muscle weakness that worsens with sustained or repetitive muscle use and towards the end of the day, and improves with rest.

•  Anatomical Distribution of Weakness:

1.  Extraocular & Eyelid Muscles (Initial presentation in >65%):Asymmetrical, fatigable ptosis (demonstrating Cogan’s lid twitch sign and worsening on sustained upward gaze for 30–60 seconds) and binocular diplopia (can mimic any cranial nerve palsy or internuclear ophthalmoplegia, but pupillary reflexes are always NORMAL/SPARED). In 15%, weakness remains restricted to the eyes for >2 years (Ocular Myasthenia).

2.  Facial & Masticatory Muscles: Bilateral facial weakness producing a horizontal "myasthenic snarl" on attempting to smile, jaw-drop, and fatigable chewing (worse towards the end of a meal).

3.  Bulbar Muscles:Fatigable dysarthria (speech becomes progressively nasal and slurred during prolonged counting/talking), dysphagia with nasal regurgitation of liquids, and a weak cough.

4.  Neck & Proximal Limb-Girdle Muscles: Head-drop (neck extensor weakness) and proximal shoulder-girdle weakness (inability to comb hair or hold arms abducted without resting).

5.  Respiratory Muscles (Myasthenic Crisis): Diaphragmatic and intercostal muscle weakness causing acute Type II respiratory failure requiring urgent mechanical ventilation. (Precipitated by intercurrent infection, surgery, emotional stress, pregnancy, rapid introduction of high-dose corticosteroids, or contraindicated drugs that worsen NMJ blockade such as aminoglycosides [gentamicin], fluoroquinolones [ciprofloxacin], macrolides, tetracyclines, β-blockers, magnesium, phenytoin, and neuromuscular blocking agents).

•  (Crucial Normal Findings: Deep tendon reflexes are preserved, tone is normal, there is no muscle wasting/fasciculation, and sensation is completely normal—distinguishing MG from Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome [where reflexes are absent and return after brief exercise, caused by pre-synaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channel antibodies in small-cell lung cancer] and from GBS/botulism).

3. Diagnosis (Investigations):

1.  Serological Autoantibody Testing (First-Line):

•  Anti-Acetylcholine Receptor (Anti-AChR) Antibodies: Positive in 85% of generalised MG and 50% of ocular MG (nearly 100% specific).

•  Anti-MuSK (Muscle-Specific Kinase) and Anti-LRP4 Antibodies: Tested if Anti-AChR is negative.

•  (Anti-striated muscle antibodies are associated with thymoma).

2.  Neurophysiological Testing:

•  Repetitive Nerve Stimulation (RNS) at 3 Hz: Demonstrates a characteristic decremental response (>10% fall in compound muscle action potential [CMAP] amplitude) between the 1st and 4th/5th stimuli.

•  Single-Fibre Electromyography (SFEMG) (Most Sensitive Test, >95%): Demonstrates increased "jitter" (variability in the inter-potential interval between two muscle fibres of the same motor unit) and "blocking".

3.  Bedside Clinical Tests:

•  Ice-Pack Test: Applying an ice pack over a ptotic eyelid for 2 minutes cools the NMJ, inhibits acetylcholinesterase, and transiently improves ptosis by >2 mm (safe and sensitive).

•  Intravenous Edrophonium (Tensilon) Test (Historical): Short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (2 mg IV test dose, then 8 mg IV) produces dramatic improvement in weakness within 30 seconds lasting 5 minutes (requires resuscitation facilities and IV atropine at the bedside due to risk of severe bradycardia/bronchospasm).

4.  Thoracic Imaging & Associated Autoimmune Screen:

•  CT or MRI of the Thorax/Mediastinum:Mandatory in all patients to detect a thymoma or thymic hyperplasia.

•  Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs): Exclude coexisting hyper- or hypothyroidism.

4. Management of Myasthenia Gravis (Acute, Symptomatic & Long-Term Immunological Treatment):

•  A. Symptomatic Anticholinesterase Therapy:

•  Oral Pyridostigmine (30–120 mg every 4–6 hours, up to max 360–450 mg/day): Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that prolongs the action of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft.

•  Muscarinic Side-Effects: Abdominal colic, diarrhoea, hypersalivation, sweating, and bradycardia; prevented by co-administering the oral antimuscarinic Propantheline (15 mg). (Overdosage of pyridostigmine can cause a cholinergic crisis with depolarising weakness, fasciculations, miosis, and SLUDGE symptoms).

•  B. Long-Term Immunological & Surgical Treatment [KU 17, TU]:

1.  Corticosteroids (Induce Remission in >70%–80%):

•  Oral Prednisolone.Crucial Clinical Precaution:High initial doses of corticosteroids can precipitate a severe transient exacerbation of myasthenic weakness ("steroid dip") within the first 1–2 weeks, risking respiratory failure. Therefore, start prednisolone at a low dose (10–15 mg on alternate days) and escalate gradually to 1 mg/kg (60 mg), OR admit to hospital if rapid high-dose initiation is required. Co-prescribe bisphosphonates, calcium, and vitamin D.

2.  Steroid-Sparing Oral Immunosuppressants:

•  Azathioprine (2.0–2.5 mg/kg/day): First-line steroid-sparing agent (check TPMT activity first; takes 3–12 months to reach full effect).

•  Alternatives:Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF), Ciclosporin, Tacrolimus, or Methotrexate.

3.  Targeted Biologic Therapies (for Refractory Generalised MG):

•  Rituximab (anti-CD20; particularly effective in Anti-MuSK-positive MG), Efgartigimod alfa (neonatal Fc receptor [FcRn] blocker that accelerates clearance of pathogenic IgG autoantibodies), or Eculizumab / Ravulizumab (anti-C5 complement inhibitors for AChR-positive MG).

4.  Thymectomy:

•  Mandatory in all patients with a Thymoma (regardless of age or MG severity, to prevent local mediastinal invasion).

•  Indicated in non-thymomatous, Anti-AChR-positive Generalised MG in patients aged <45–65 years (within the first 5–7 years of disease onset; proven by the MGTX trial to improve clinical outcomes, induce remission, and reduce steroid/immunosuppressant requirements). (Not indicated in pure ocular MG or Anti-MuSK MG).

•  C. Emergency Management of Acute Myasthenic Crisis (Bulbar & Respiratory Failure):

1.  Admit to ICU, monitor Forced Vital Capacity (FVC), and perform early endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation if FVC <15–20 mL/kg or bulbar aspiration occurs (temporarily withhold pyridostigmine while ventilated to reduce bronchial secretions).

2.  Treat any precipitating infection with safe antibiotics (avoid aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and macrolides).

3.  Rapid Short-Term Immunotherapy (Onset within 2–5 days, effect lasts 4–6 weeks):

•  Plasma Exchange (Plasmapheresis — 5 exchanges over 7–10 days)OR

•  Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIg — 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days, total 2 g/kg), alongside initiation/escalation of high-dose corticosteroids and long-term immunosuppression.

title: 15. Diseases of Muscle: Causes of Proximal Myopathy, Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, Myotonic Dystrophy, and Myoclonus [KU 24, 21, 18, 17, TU, RGU]
text:
15. Diseases of Muscle: Causes of Proximal Myopathy, Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, Myotonic Dystrophy, and Myoclonus [KU 24, 21, 18, 17, TU, RGU]

1. Causes of Myopathy / Proximal Muscle Weakness [KU 24, TU]:

•  Inherited Myopathies:

1.  Muscular Dystrophies:Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy (X-linked dystrophinopathies), Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies, Facioscapulohumeral (FSH) dystrophy, Oculopharyngeal dystrophy, and Myotonic dystrophy (DM1 is predominantly distal; DM2 [PROMM] is proximal).

2.  Metabolic & Mitochondrial Myopathies: Glycogen storage diseases (McArdle’s disease [myophosphorylase deficiency], Pompe’s disease [acid maltase deficiency]), lipid β-oxidation defects (Carnitine palmitoyltransferase [CPT] deficiency), and Mitochondrial cytopathies (CPEO, Kearns–Sayre, MELAS, MERRF).

3.  Muscle Channelopathies: Hypokalaemic and hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis, myotonia congenita, malignant hyperthermia.

•  Acquired Proximal Myopathies:

1.  Inflammatory Myopathies:Polymyositis, Dermatomyositis, immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, sarcoid myopathy (Note: Inclusion Body Myositis in older adults affects distal finger flexors and quadriceps).

2.  Endocrine & Metabolic Disorders:Cushing’s syndrome, Hypothyroidism, Hyperthyroidism (Thyrotoxicosis), Osteomalacia / Severe Vitamin D deficiency, Acromegaly, Hyperparathyroidism, Addison’s disease, and Hypokalaemia / Hypercalcaemia.

3.  Drug- and Toxin-Induced Myopathies:Glucocorticoids (Steroids), Statins and Fibrates, Alcohol (acute necrotising or chronic proximal myopathy), Chloroquine / Hydroxychloroquine, Colchicine, Zidovudine (AZT), Amiodarone, Ciclosporin, Cocaine/Heroin.

4.  Infective & Paraneoplastic: Viral myositis (influenza, HIV, Coxsackie), toxoplasmosis, trichinosis, and carcinomatous neuromyopathy.

2. Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) [KU 18, RGU]:

•  Genetics & Pathophysiology:X-linked recessive disorder (incidence 1 in 3500 live male births; 1/3 are spontaneous new mutations) caused by frameshift deletions or mutations in the DMD (Dystrophin) gene at locus Xp21, resulting in complete absence of the subsarcolemmal structural protein Dystrophin (which anchors the actin cytoskeleton to the sarcolemmal dystroglycan complex). Muscle fibres undergo repetitive mechanical membrane tearing, calcium influx, necrosis, and replacement by fat and fibrous tissue. (Note: Becker Muscular Dystrophy is caused by in-frame DMD deletions that produce a partially functional truncated dystrophin protein, resulting in a much milder phenotype presenting in late childhood/adulthood).

•  Clinical Features:

•  Presents in boys aged <5 years (2–4 years) with delayed motor milestones (late walking), frequent falls, inability to run or jump, and a waddling myopathic gait with lumbar hyperlordosis.

•  Gowers’ Sign: Due to severe proximal pelvic-girdle and hip-extensor weakness, the boy uses his hands to "climb up his own legs" when rising from the floor.

•  Pseudohypertrophy of the Calves (and deltoids/infraspinatus): Calves appear enlarged and rubbery-firm due to infiltration by fat and fibrous connective tissue.

•  Progressive weakness leads to wheelchair dependence by age 10–12 years, progressive kyphoscoliosis, dilated cardiomyopathy (90%), and restrictive respiratory failure (historically fatal in the 20s, now extended to the 30s–40s with non-invasive ventilation). Mild non-progressive cognitive impairment (reduced verbal IQ) is common.

•  Investigations & Management:

•  Serum Creatine Kinase (CK):Grossly elevated (20 to 100× normal, often >10,000 U/L).

•  Genetic Testing (Multiplex Ligation-Dependent Probe Amplification [MLPA] / Sequencing of DMD gene): Confirms the diagnosis without needing a muscle biopsy (if biopsy is done, immunohistochemistry shows complete absence of dystrophin).

•  Management:Oral Corticosteroids (Prednisolone or Deflazacort) preserve muscle strength, prolong independent ambulation by 2–3 years, and delay scoliosis and respiratory decline; ACE inhibitors and β-blockers for dilated cardiomyopathy; Nocturnal Non-Invasive Ventilation (NIV) for respiratory failure; physiotherapy/orthoses; exon-skipping antisense oligonucleotides (eteplirsen, golodirsen) or stop-codon readthrough (ataluren) for specific mutations; and carrier genetic counselling for female relatives.

3. Myotonic Dystrophy (Dystrophia Myotonica) [KU 17]:

•  Genetics: The most common adult-onset muscular dystrophy (prevalence 12 per 100,000). Autosomal dominant multisystem disorder:

•  Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 (DM1 — Steinert’s disease): Caused by an unstable CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the 3^\prime untranslated region of the DMPK (myotonin protein kinase) gene on chromosome 19q. Demonstrates marked genetic anticipation (the CTG repeat expands in successive generations, especially via maternal transmission, causing severe congenital myotonic dystrophy in infants).

•  Type 2 (DM2 — Proximal Myotonic Myopathy [PROMM]): CCTG tetranucleotide repeat in CNBP gene on chromosome 3; milder, proximal weakness without anticipation.

•  Clinical Features of Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 (DM1):

1.  Myotonia (Delayed Relaxation of Skeletal Muscle After Voluntary Contraction or Percussion): Inability to release a handshake or door handle (grip myotonia) and sustained dimpling of the thenar eminence or tongue when tapped with a tendon hammer (percussion myotonia); typically worsens in the cold and improves with repeated warm-up contractions.

2.  Characteristic Pattern of Muscle Wasting & Weakness (Uniquely DISTAL and Cranial first):

•  Myopathic Facies: Long, thin, expressionless "hatchet-faced" appearance due to wasting of the temporalis, masseter, and facial muscles, accompanied by bilateral ptosis.

•  Severe wasting and weakness of the Sternocleidomastoid muscles (causing difficulty lifting the head off the pillow).

•  Distal Limb Weakness (intrinsic hand muscles and ankle dorsiflexors causing bilateral foot drop), unlike all other dystrophies which are proximal.

•  Dysarthria and pharyngeal/oesophageal dysphagia (smooth and striated muscle involvement).

3.  Multisystem Non-Muscular Manifestations (Mnemonic: ABCDEFG):

•  Alopeica (frontal balding in both men and women).

•  Block: Cardiac conduction defects (First-degree heart block, bundle branch block, complete AV block, and sudden arrhythmic death) and cardiomyopathy.

•  Cataracts: Early bilateral iridescent posterior subcapsular "Christmas-tree" lens cataracts.

•  Diabetes mellitus (insulin resistance).

•  Endocrine: Testicular atrophy and infertility/hypogonadism.

•  Gut & Hypersomnolence: Gastrointestinal dysmotility, central daytime hypersomnolence, central/obstructive sleep apnoea, and mild frontal cognitive apathy.

•  Diagnosis & Management:

•  Diagnosis:DNA genetic testing for the DMPK CTG repeat expansion (gold standard); EMG shows characteristic waxing-and-waning high-frequency myotonic discharges that sound like a "dive-bomber" aircraft on the loudspeaker; serum CK is normal or mildly elevated.

•  Management:Annual 12-lead ECG / Holter monitoring (low threshold for permanent pacemaker or ICD insertion to prevent sudden cardiac death); cataract extraction; ankle–foot orthoses (splints) for foot drop; Mexiletine (or phenytoin/carbamazepine) if myotonia is functionally disabling; Modafinil for daytime hypersomnolence; avoid depolarising muscle relaxants (suxamethonium) and general anaesthetics (high risk of prolonged post-operative respiratory depression); and genetic counselling.

4. Myoclonus [KU 21]:

•  Definition: Sudden, brief (<100 ms), shock-like involuntary muscle jerks caused by either abrupt muscle contraction (positive myoclonus) or brief inhibition of ongoing postural muscle activity (negative myoclonus, e.g., asterixis / flapping tremor). May originate from the cerebral cortex, subcortical/brainstem structures, or spinal cord.

•  Causes of Myoclonus:

1.  Physiological:Hypnic jerks (at sleep onset), hiccups, physiological startle response.

2.  Epileptic Syndromes:Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME) (morning myoclonic jerks + GTCS), Progressive myoclonic epilepsies (Unverricht–Lundborg disease, Lafora body disease, MERRF mitochondrial disease).

3.  Metabolic, Toxic & Post-Anoxic Encephalopathies:Post-cardiac arrest anoxic brain injury (Lance–Adams syndrome), Hepatic failure, Uraemia (renal failure), hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypercapnia, and Drugs (opiates, tricyclics, levodopa, lithium, gabapentin, serotonin syndrome).

4.  Neurodegenerative & Prion Diseases:Sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob Disease (CJD) (startle myoclonus), Corticobasal degeneration, Alzheimer’s disease, Lewy body dementia, and Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE).

•  Treatment: Correct underlying metabolic/drug causes; Clonazepam, Sodium Valproate, Levetiracetam, or Piracetam for cortical/epileptic myoclonus.

subject: medicine
title: 16. Cerebrovascular Disease: Ischaemic Stroke, Haemorrhagic Stroke, Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA), and Cerebral Venous Thrombosis [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 18, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
Stroke Medicine & Cerebral Venous Disease

16. Cerebrovascular Disease: Ischaemic Stroke, Haemorrhagic Stroke, Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA), and Cerebral Venous Thrombosis [KU 25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 18, 16, TU, RGU]

(Covers all 5 clinical vignette Essays on patients presenting with sudden-onset right or left hemiplegia, facial palsy, aphasia, and altered sensorium, plus both clinical vignette Essays on post-partum women presenting with headache, generalised tonic–clonic seizures, and drowsiness 1 week after delivery = Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis).

1. Definitions (Stroke, TIA, RIND, and ischaemic Penumbra):

•  Stroke (Cerebrovascular Accident): A clinical syndrome characterised by sudden-onset, focal neurological deficit (or global in coma/SAH) of presumed vascular origin, lasting >24 hours or leading to death (or with neuroimaging evidence of acute infarction/haemorrhage). In Western populations, ~ 85% are Ischaemic Strokes and ~ 15% are Haemorrhagic Strokes (10% intracerebral haemorrhage, 5% subarachnoid haemorrhage).

•  Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA) [KU 25, TU, RGU]:

•  Definition: An acute, transient episode of focal neurological or retinal dysfunction (amaurosis fugax) caused by focal cerebral or retinal ischaemia without acute infarction, in which symptoms resolve completely within 24 hours (most last <15–60 minutes).

•  Clinical Significance of TIA: A TIA is a harbinger of impending major ischaemic stroke—the risk of a completed stroke is 5%–10% within the first 7 days (highest in the first 48 hours) and 15% at 1 year. Risk is stratified using the ABCD2 score (Age ≥ 60 [1], BP ≥ 140/90 [1], Clinical features: unilateral weakness [2] or speech disturbance without weakness [1], Duration ≥ 60 mins [2] or 10–59 mins [1], Diabetes [1]). Urgent dual antiplatelet therapy, statin, blood pressure control, anticoagulation for AF, or carotid endarterectomy within 1–2 weeks prevents up to 80% of early recurrent strokes.

•  RIND (Reversible Ischaemic Neurological Deficit) [TU]: An older historical term for a focal ischaemic neurological deficit lasting >24 hours that resolves completely within 7–21 days; on modern diffusion-weighted MRI, these represent small completed cerebral infarctions and are managed identically to minor ischaemic strokes.

•  The Ischaemic Penumbra [TU]:

•  When a cerebral artery is occluded, the central ischaemic core (where cerebral blood flow [CBF] falls below 10 mL/100 g/min) undergoes rapid, irreversible neuronal necrosis within minutes.

•  Surrounding this core is the ischaemic penumbra—a rim of brain tissue with critically reduced perfusion (CBF\ 10–20 mL/100 g/min, maintained by leptomeningeal collateral vessels) that is functionally silent/electrically inactive (causing clinical neurological deficits) but structurally viable and salvageable if blood flow is rapidly restored via intravenous thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy; if not reperfused within hours, the penumbra is progressively recruited into the irreversible infarct core.

2. Risk Factors, Aetiology & Causes of Stroke in the Young:

•  Non-Modifiable Risk Factors: Advancing age, male sex, ethnicity, family history, previous TIA/stroke/MI, and genetic disorders (CADASIL [NOTCH3 mutation], Sickle-cell disease, Fabry’s disease, MELAS).

•  Modifiable Risk Factors:Hypertension (single most important risk factor for both ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke), Cigarette smoking, Diabetes mellitus, Hypercholesterolaemia (high LDL), Atrial fibrillation (5× increased risk), cardiac disease (MI, heart failure, prosthetic valves, infective endocarditis), carotid artery stenosis, obesity, excess alcohol, and oestrogen-containing oral contraceptives/HRT.

•  Causes of Stroke in the Young (<45 Years) [TU] (Always consider in young vignettes like the 30-year-old female with right hemiplegia and aphasia [KU 24]):

1.  Cervical Artery Dissection (Internal Carotid or Vertebral Artery): Accounts for up to 20% of young strokes; often follows minor neck trauma/manipulation and presents with unilateral neck/head pain + ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome followed by contralateral hemisphere stroke.

2.  Cardioembolism:Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO) (paradoxical embolism from DVT), Rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation, Infective endocarditis, prosthetic heart valves, atrial myxoma, dilated cardiomyopathy.

3.  Haematological & Prothrombotic States:Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS) (check in young females with recurrent miscarriages), Sickle-cell anaemia, Polycythaemia vera / Essential thrombocythaemia (JAK2), PNH, inherited thrombophilias (Factor V Leiden, Protein C/S/AT-III deficiency—especially with PFO or Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis), pregnancy/puerperium, and oral contraceptive pill.

4.  Inflammatory & Infective Vasculopathies:Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Primary CNS vasculitis, Takayasu’s arteritis, Behçet’s disease, Meningovascular syphilis, HIV vasculopathy, tuberculous meningitis.

5.  Genetic & Metabolic Disorders:CADASIL, Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy with Lactic Acidosis and Stroke-like Episodes (MELAS), Fabry’s disease (α-galactosidase A deficiency), and Homocystinuria.

6.  Illicit Drugs & Vascular Anomalies:Cocaine and Amphetamines (vasospasm/haemorrhage), Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), cavernous haemangiomas, and Moyamoya disease.

3. Anatomical Localisation & Bamford (Oxfordshire) Clinical Classification of Ischaemic Stroke:

•  Anatomical Localisation Note for Vignettes:

•  Left Cerebral Hemisphere (Left Middle Cerebral Artery / Internal Capsule) Lesion: Produces contralateral (right) hemiplegia, right UMN facial palsy (forehead spared; angle of the mouth deviates to the healthy left side due to unopposed left facial muscles), right hemisensory loss, right homonymous hemianopia, and Aphasia (Broca’s expressive, Wernicke’s receptive, or global).

•  Left Pons (Brainstem) Lesion: Produces Crossed Hemiplegia—ipsilateral (left) LMN facial palsy (involving forehead) + contralateral (right) arm and leg hemiplegia.

•  Bamford Clinical Stroke Syndromes [Fig. 27.29]:

1.  Total Anterior Circulation Syndrome (TACS — 15%): Occlusion of proximal MCA or ICA. All three of: (1) Contralateral motor/sensory deficit of at least 2 of face, arm, and leg; (2) Homonymous hemianopia; AND (3) Higher cortical dysfunction (e.g., Aphasia or Visuospatial neglect). Worst prognosis.

2.  Partial Anterior Circulation Syndrome (PACS — 30%): Occlusion of an MCA branch or ACA (leg > arm weakness). Two of the three TACS components, OR isolated higher cortical dysfunction (isolated aphasia), OR isolated monoparesis of one limb.

3.  Lacunar Syndrome (LACS — 20%): Thrombotic occlusion of a single small deep perforating lenticulostriate artery in the internal capsule, thalamus, corona radiata, or pons due to small-vessel lipohyalinosis (hypertension/diabetes). Presents with Pure Motor Stroke, Pure Sensory Stroke, Sensorimotor Stroke, or Ataxic Hemiparesis affecting at least 2 of face, arm, and leg, in the complete absence of cortical signs (NO aphasia, NO neglect, NO hemianopia).

4.  Posterior Circulation Syndrome (POCS — 20%): Vertebrobasilar / PCA territory. Presents with ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy with contralateral motor/sensory deficit (crossed syndromes), bilateral motor/sensory deficit, disorder of conjugate eye movement, cerebellar ataxia, or isolated homonymous hemianopia (occipital cortex).

4. Investigations in Acute Stroke:

1.  Immediate Bedside Checks:Capillary Blood Glucose (to exclude hypoglycaemia, a key stroke mimic), Blood Pressure, SpO2, temperature, and NIHSS score (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale, 0–42).

2.  Immediate Brain Imaging (Non-Contrast CT Head — within <1 hour of arrival):

•  Immediately differentiates Intracerebral Haemorrhage (bright hyperdense haematoma) from Ischaemic Stroke (may be normal in the first few hours or show early signs: hyperdense MCA sign, loss of insular ribbon/grey–white differentiation, and sulcal effacement).

•  CT Angiography (CTA) + CT Perfusion (CTP) or Diffusion-Weighted MRI (DWI): CTA identifies large-vessel occlusion (ICA, M1/M2 MCA, basilar) for mechanical thrombectomy; CTP/DWI identifies the salvageable ischaemic penumbra in late presenters (>4.5–6 hours) or wake-up strokes.

3.  Vascular, Cardiac & Blood Investigations (To Identify Cause & Risk Factors):

•  Carotid Duplex Ultrasound (or CTA/MRA): Urgent screening in anterior circulation TIA/non-disabling stroke to detect symptomatic internal carotid artery stenosis (50%–99%).

•  12-Lead ECG & Prolonged (24 hr to 14 day) Ambulatory ECG Monitoring: To detect atrial fibrillation.

•  Echocardiography (transthoracic/bubble transoesophageal): If cardioembolism, PFO, or endocarditis is suspected.

•  Bloods: FBC, U&Es, clotting screen (PT/INR, APTT), fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipid profile, ESR/CRP (giant cell arteritis/vasculitis), and Young Stroke Screen (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2GP1, ANA, HIV/syphilis serology, sickle screen, homocysteine).

5. Comprehensive Management of Acute Ischaemic Stroke & Contraindications to Thrombolysis [KU 25, 24, 22, 18, 16, TU]:

•  A. Hyperacute Reperfusion Therapy (Emergency Restoration of Blood Flow to the Penumbra):

1.  Intravenous Thrombolysis with Alteplase (rtPA) or Tenecteplase:

•  Administered within 4.5 hours of symptom onset (or up to 9 hours / wake-up stroke if CT perfusion or MRI DWI-FLAIR mismatch confirms salvageable penumbra), once CT has excluded intracranial haemorrhage.

•  Alteplase Dose:0.9 mg/kg IV (maximum 90 mg), with 10% given as an IV bolus over 1 minute and the remaining 90% infused over 60 minutes (or Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single IV bolus).

•  Blood Pressure Rule for Thrombolysis: BP must be lowered to <185/110 mmHg (using IV labetalol or GTN) before administering thrombolysis and kept <180/105 mmHg for the first 24 hours. Withhold aspirin/anticoagulants for 24 hours post-thrombolysis until a 24-hour repeat CT excludes haemorrhagic transformation (~ 3%–6% risk).

2.  Contraindications to Intravenous Thrombolysis in Acute Ischaemic Stroke [KU 22]:

•  Time window >4.5 hours from symptom onset (unless advanced perfusion imaging criteria are met).

•  Any Intracranial Haemorrhage on CT scan or history of prior Intracranial Haemorrhage.

•  Severe Uncontrolled Hypertension (BP >185/110 mmHg) refractory to IV antihypertensive therapy.

•  Recent Intracranial or Spinal Surgery, Serious Head Trauma, or Prior Ischaemic Stroke within the last 3 months.

•  Active Internal Bleeding (e.g., GI or urinary tract haemorrhage within 21 days) or major surgery/trauma at a non-compressible site within 14 days.

•  Coagulopathy or Therapeutic Anticoagulation: Platelets <100 × 109/L, INR >1.7 on warfarin, therapeutic LMWH within 24 hours, or DOAC intake within 48 hours.

•  Suspected Subarachnoid Haemorrhage, Aortic Dissection, Infective Endocarditis, or Intracranial Neoplasm / AVM.

•  Severe hypoglycaemia (<2.8 mmol/L) or extreme hyperglycaemia (>22.2 mmol/L).

3.  Endovascular Mechanical Thrombectomy (Clot Retrieval):

•  Indicated for acute ischaemic stroke caused by proximal Large-Vessel Occlusion (ICA, M1/M2 MCA, or Basilar artery) on CTA within 6 hours of symptom onset (and up to 6–24 hours if CT perfusion/MRI shows a large salvageable penumbra—DAWN / DEFUSE-3 criteria), performed alongside IV thrombolysis if eligible.

•  B. Acute Medical & Supportive Stroke Unit Care:

•  Admit to a Dedicated Acute Stroke Unit (reduces mortality and long-term dependency; NNT = 20).

•  Antiplatelet Therapy (if NOT thrombolysed, or 24 hours AFTER thrombolysis):Aspirin 300 mg daily (orally, via NG tube, or rectally) for 2 weeks, then switch to long-term secondary prevention. (In minor stroke [NIHSS ≤ 3] or high-risk TIA [ABCD2 ≥ 4], give Dual Antiplatelet Therapy [DAPT] with Aspirin + Clopidogrel for 21 days, followed by Clopidogrel 75 mg monotherapy long-term).

•  Swallowing Screen (Nil by mouth until screened): Perform a bedside swallow assessment within 4 hours; if unsafe/dysphagic, insert a nasogastric tube for hydration, nutrition, and medications to prevent aspiration pneumonia (later PEG tube if dysphagia persists >2–4 weeks).

•  Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischaemic Stroke:Do NOT acutely lower blood pressure in the first 48–72 hours (as cerebral autoregulation is impaired and perfusion of the ischaemic penumbra is pressure-dependent), UNLESS: (1) the patient is a candidate for thrombolysis (BP >185/110); (2) BP is extremely high (>220/120 mmHg); or (3) there is concomitant hypertensive encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute myocardial ischaemia, or acute left ventricular failure.

•  Physiological Homeostasis & VTE Prophylaxis: Maintain normoxia (SpO2\ 94%–98%), normoglycaemia (4–11 mmol/L), normothermia (paracetamol for fever), early mobilisation after 24 hours, and intermittent pneumatic compression stockings (avoid prophylactic heparin initially if haemorrhagic transformation risk is high).

•  Surgical Decompressive Hemicraniectomy: Considered within 48 hours in patients with "malignant" Middle Cerebral Artery territory infarction causing life-threatening space-occupying cerebral oedema and midline shift, or posterior fossa decompression for cerebellar infarction causing brainstem compression/hydrocephalus.

•  C. Secondary Prevention of Ischaemic Stroke [Fig. 27.36]:

1.  Long-Term Antiplatelet Therapy (Non-Cardioembolic Stroke):Clopidogrel 75 mg daily (first-line monotherapy) or Aspirin 75 mg + modified-release Dipyridamole 200 mg BD.

2.  Oral Anticoagulation (For Atrial Fibrillation / Cardioembolic Stroke):Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs — Apixaban, Rivaroxaban, Edoxaban, or Dabigatran) or Warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0; mandatory for mechanical valves or rheumatic mitral stenosis). Started immediately after a TIA, or delayed by 3–14 days after a moderate-to-large cerebral infarct to avoid haemorrhagic transformation.

3.  Blood Pressure Lowering: Start/optimise antihypertensives (ACE inhibitor [Perindopril] + Thiazide-like diuretic [Indapamide] or Calcium channel blocker [Amlodipine]) after the acute phase, aiming for target BP <130/80 mmHg (even in previously "normotensive" patients).

4.  High-Intensity Statin Therapy:Atorvastatin 80 mg daily regardless of baseline cholesterol, aiming to reduce LDL-C by >40%–50%.

5.  Carotid Endarterectomy: Performed within 1–2 weeks of symptom onset in patients with non-disabling carotid territory TIA or stroke who have a 50%–99% (especially 70%–99%) ipsilateral Internal Carotid Artery stenosis.

6.  Lifestyle Modification: Smoking cessation, diabetic control, alcohol moderation, low-salt diet, and exercise.

6. Intracerebral Haemorrhage (Haemorrhagic Stroke): Aetiopathogenesis & Management [KU 25, TU, RGU]:

•  Aetiopathogenesis: Accounts for 10%–15% of strokes.

•  Deep Perforating Artery Rupture (Basal ganglia/putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum): Caused by chronic hypertension inducing lipohyalinosis and Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms of small lenticulostriate/pontine arteries.

•  Lobar (Cortical) Haemorrhage: Caused by Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy (CAA) in older adults (β-amyloid deposition in cortical/leptomeningeal vessels).

•  Secondary Causes:Anticoagulant therapy (warfarin, DOACs) or thrombolysis, Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) and cavernous haemangiomas (especially in young patients), saccular aneurysms, cerebral venous thrombosis, bleeding diatheses, and cocaine/amphetamine misuse.

•  Clinical Features: Abrupt onset of focal neurological deficit (contralateral hemiplegia, gaze deviation towards the lesion, sensory loss) accompanied more frequently than ischaemic stroke by severe headache, vomiting, markedly elevated blood pressure (e.g., 170/120 mmHg), and early depression of conscious level/coma. Non-contrast CT brain immediately shows a hyperdense (white) intraparenchymal haematoma (± intraventricular extension and midline shift).

•  Management of Acute Intracerebral Haemorrhage:

1.  Resuscitation (ABCDE) and admission to an Acute Stroke Unit or Neuro-ICU.

2.  Immediate Reversal of Any Anticoagulation / Coagulopathy (Critical to prevent haematoma expansion):

•  Warfarin: Stop warfarin + give 4-Factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC, 25–50 U/kg IV) + IV Vitamin K1 (5–10 mg) immediately.

•  Dabigatran:Idarucizumab (5 g IV).

•  Apixaban / Rivaroxaban:Andexanet alfa or 4-Factor PCC.

•  Unfractionated Heparin:Protamine sulphate.

•  Severe Thrombocytopenia: Platelet transfusion. (Stop all antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs).

3.  Acute Blood Pressure Lowering (INTERACT-2 / ATACH-2 Guidelines):

•  Unlike ischaemic stroke, in acute intracerebral haemorrhage presenting within 6 hours with systolic BP 150–220 mmHg, rapidly lower Systolic Blood Pressure to a target of 130–140 mmHg within 1 hour (using IV Labetalol, Nicardipine, or GTN infusion) and maintain for 7 days to limit haematoma expansion and improve functional outcome.

4.  Management of Raised Intracranial Pressure & Neurosurgical Intervention:

•  Nurse head-up at 30°; use IV mannitol or hypertonic saline for acute transtentorial herniation.

•  Urgent Neurosurgical Evacuation / External Ventricular Drain (EVD): Indicated for Cerebellar Haematomas (>3 cm) causing brainstem compression or acute obstructive hydrocephalus (life-saving), or superficial lobar haematomas causing progressive deterioration in younger patients.

5.  Long-Term Secondary Prevention: Strict blood pressure control (<130/80 mmHg) is the single most effective measure to prevent recurrent intracerebral haemorrhage (statins and routine antiplatelets are avoided unless strong ischaemic vascular indications exist).

7. Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVT) & Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis [KU 23, 21, TU]:

•  Aetiology & Risk Factors: Accounts for <1% of strokes; much more common in young women.

•  Systemic Prothrombotic States:Pregnancy and the Puerperium (Post-partum state) (most common setting in clinical vignettes), Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill, Dehydration, Inherited Thrombophilias (Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A, Protein C, Protein S, Antithrombin deficiency), Antiphospholipid Syndrome, Myeloproliferative neoplasms (JAK2 PV/ET), Behçet’s disease, SLE, and malignancy.

•  Local Cranial Sepsis:Otitis media and mastoiditis (causes transverse/sigmoid sinus thrombosis); facial skin, dental, or paranasal sinus infection (causes cavernous sinus thrombosis).

•  Clinical Presentations by Sinus Involved:

1.  Superior Sagittal Sinus & Cortical Vein Thrombosis:

•  Presents with subacute, progressive severe headache (90%), vomiting, papilloedema (from raised ICP due to impaired CSF absorption at arachnoid villi), focal or generalised tonic–clonic seizures (40%), drowsiness/altered sensorium, and focal neurological deficits (hemiparesis or bilateral/alternating leg weakness, as parasagittal motor cortices for both legs drain into the superior sagittal sinus).

2.  Transverse / Sigmoid Sinus Thrombosis: Headache, papilloedema, hemiparesis, seizures, and extension to the jugular foramen affecting Cranial Nerves IX, X, and XI.

3.  Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis & Cranial Nerves Involved [TU]:

•  Clinical Features: High fever, toxaemia, severe periorbital headache, chemosis, periorbital oedema, painful proptosis, and papilloedema/retinal venous engorgement (often becoming bilateral).

•  Cranial Nerves Involved in Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis:

•  Running through the lumen of the cavernous sinus (alongside the internal carotid artery and sympathetic plexus):Abducens Nerve (CN VI) (earliest nerve affected).

•  Running in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus (from superior to inferior):Oculomotor Nerve (CN III), Trochlear Nerve (CN IV), Ophthalmic Division of Trigeminal Nerve (CN V1), and Maxillary Division of Trigeminal Nerve (CN V2).

•  (Results in complete internal and external ophthalmoplegia with a fixed mid-position pupil [combined parasympathetic CN III and carotid sympathetic palsy] and sensory loss over the forehead/cornea [V1] and cheek [V2]).

•  Investigations (Confirming Cerebral Venous Thrombosis):

•  MRI Brain with MR Venography (MRV) OR CT Brain with CT Venography (CTV) (Diagnostic Gold Standard): Demonstrates absence of flow / filling defect within the occluded dural venous sinus ("Empty Delta Sign" on contrast CT/CTV of the superior sagittal sinus; hyperdense "Cord Sign" on non-contrast CT), often accompanied by bilateral/parasagittal venous haemorrhagic infarction that does not conform to an arterial territory.

•  Bloods: D-dimer (usually elevated), FBC, and thrombophilia / antiphospholipid screen.

•  Complications: Venous haemorrhagic infarction, status epilepticus, severe raised intracranial pressure with visual loss (optic atrophy) or brain herniation, pulmonary embolism, and death (5%–10%).

•  Management of Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis:

1.  Immediate Therapeutic Anticoagulation (First-Line Treatment of Choice): Administer therapeutic-dose Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH) or IV Unfractionated Heparin, EVEN IN THE PRESENCE OF VENOUS INTRACEREBRAL HAEMORRHAGE (as haemorrhage is caused by venous back-pressure and anticoagulation prevents thrombus propagation and improves survival). Transition to Oral Anticoagulation (Warfarin [INR 2.0–3.0] or DOAC) for 3–6 months (for transient risk factors like pregnancy/puerperium) or indefinitely (for severe thrombophilia or recurrent CVT).

2.  Control Seizures & Raised ICP: Administer Antiseizure Medications (e.g., Levetiracetam) for patients presenting with seizures; manage raised ICP with head elevation, acetazolamide, or decompressive hemicraniectomy if impending herniation.

3.  Treat Underlying Cause: High-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical sinus/mastoid drainage in septic cavernous/transverse sinus thrombosis.

title: 26.1 Hypertensive retinopathy [KU 21]
text:
CHAPTER 26: MEDICAL OPHTHALMOLOGY

26.1 Hypertensive retinopathy [KU 21]

Definition and pathophysiology

Hypertensive retinopathy is damage to the retinal vessels and retina caused by raised systemic blood pressure. The retina is the one place where arterioles can be seen directly, so the fundus reflects both acute pressure load and chronic vascular damage.

It develops in phases:

•  Vasoconstrictive phase: raised pressure causes generalised arteriolar constriction, an autoregulatory response that protects the capillary bed.

•  Sclerotic phase: sustained hypertension thickens the arteriolar wall, narrows the lumen, and produces arteriovenous crossing changes and an exaggerated light reflex.

•  Exudative phase: breakdown of the blood–retinal barrier allows haemorrhage, exudation and retinal oedema; ischaemia produces cotton-wool spots (nerve-fibre-layer infarcts).

•  Severe / malignant phase: very high pressure overwhelms autoregulation, with disc swelling and widespread retinal damage.

Most early disease is asymptomatic and found on routine fundus examination. Visual symptoms — blurring, scotoma, or sudden loss of vision — usually mean advanced disease, macular involvement, or a complication such as a vascular occlusion.

Fig. 26.1 — Hypertensive retinopathy grading schematic. Vessel narrowing and crossing changes progress to haemorrhages and exudates, and finally to disc swelling.

Clinical features

•  Arteriolar changes: generalised narrowing, focal narrowing, irregular calibre, increased light reflex.

•  Arteriovenous crossing changes (AV nicking): the vein is compressed, deflected, or appears to stop at the point where a thickened arteriole crosses it.

•  Haemorrhages: flame-shaped in the nerve-fibre layer; dot and blot haemorrhages deeper in the retina.

•  Exudates: hard exudates (lipid) and cotton-wool spots (fluffy white patches of ischaemia).

•  Retinal oedema: including macular oedema, which threatens central vision.

•  Disc swelling: blurred disc margins and a swollen optic disc in grade 4 disease; this is hypertensive disc oedema, called papilloedema when it is bilateral and due to raised pressure.

Keith–Wagener–Barker grading

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-020]]

Scheie classification — and how it differs from Keith–Wagener–Barker

Scheie gives two separate scales, whereas Keith–Wagener–Barker gives one combined grade:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-021]]

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-022]]

The key difference is that Scheie separates the acute retinopathy (narrowing, haemorrhage, exudation, disc swelling) from the chronic sclerotic change (light-reflex widening, copper and silver wiring), so a patient can be described on both scales; Keith–Wagener–Barker merges them into a single grade.

Differential diagnosis

•  Diabetic retinopathy: microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates and neovascularisation; often bilateral and related to diabetes duration and control rather than blood pressure alone.

•  Retinal vein occlusion: sectoral or widespread haemorrhages in one venous territory, often with venous dilatation.

•  Radiation or other retinopathies, and papilloedema from raised intracranial pressure: disc swelling without the hypertensive vascular changes, or with a neurological cause — history and systemic examination separate these.

Investigations

•  Accurate blood pressure measurement, including checking for hypertensive urgency or emergency and for target-organ damage (kidney, heart, brain).

•  Dilated fundus examination and, where available, fundus photography to document the grade.

•  Optical coherence tomography if macular oedema is suspected.

•  Basic work-up for secondary hypertension and end-organ damage when indicated: renal function, urine protein, lipids, glucose, ECG, and assessment of other risk factors.

Management

•  Treat the underlying hypertension — this is the main treatment, and the retinopathy largely follows blood pressure control. Grades 1–2 are managed by sustained blood pressure and risk-factor control with ophthalmology follow-up.

•  Grade 3–4 disease, disc swelling, macular oedema, or visual loss needs urgent ophthalmology and medical assessment, because it may reflect a hypertensive emergency and needs prompt, controlled blood pressure reduction and exclusion of other end-organ damage.

•  No specific per-grade blood pressure band or single numeric target for grade 4 is stated here, because grading describes retinal findings rather than a fixed pressure threshold; the rate and target of pressure reduction are set by the clinical picture and by specialist guidance for hypertensive emergencies.

•  Control co-existing diabetes and dyslipidaemia, advise smoking cessation, and review drugs that raise blood pressure.

•  Laser, intravitreal therapy, or surgery are not treatments for hypertensive retinopathy itself; they are used for its complications (for example macular oedema or a vascular occlusion) when indicated.

Complications and prognosis

•  Macular oedema and exudative maculopathy with permanent visual loss.

•  Retinal artery or vein occlusion, and retinal detachment in severe disease.

•  Optic atrophy after prolonged disc swelling.

•  Grades 3–4 carry a worse systemic prognosis, reflecting severe hypertension and a higher risk of stroke, cardiac and renal events; early grades often improve with blood pressure control, but sclerotic changes may persist.

subject: medicine
title: 26.2 Other topics in brief
text:
26.2 Other topics in brief

Diabetic retinopathy

Retinal microvascular damage from chronic hyperglycaemia: background disease (microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates), pre-proliferative disease (cotton-wool spots, venous beading, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities), proliferative disease (new vessels that bleed and scar), and diabetic macular oedema. Screening by retinal photography, tight glycaemic and blood pressure control, laser photocoagulation, intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy, and vitrectomy for selected complications are the mainstays.

Retinal artery occlusion

Sudden, painless, monocular visual loss. Central retinal artery occlusion shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula; a branch occlusion affects one sector. It is an ocular emergency: exclude embolic sources (carotid, cardiac), check for giant cell arteritis in older patients, and manage as a stroke equivalent.

Retinal vein occlusion

Sudden painless visual loss with widespread retinal haemorrhages in the affected venous territory, venous dilatation and tortuosity, and macular oedema. Central occlusion affects the whole fundus; branch occlusion is sectoral. Risk factors include hypertension, diabetes, glaucoma and hyperviscosity; macular oedema is treated with anti-VEGF therapy or steroids, and neovascular complications with laser.

Papilloedema versus papillitis

Papilloedema is bilateral disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure, typically with preserved visual acuity early, an enlarged blind spot, headache, vomiting and transient visual obscurations. Papillitis is inflammation of the optic disc (a form of optic neuritis): usually unilateral, with reduced visual acuity, impaired colour vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and pain on eye movement. The distinction rests on laterality, visual function, and the neurological picture.

Optic neuritis

Inflammation of the optic nerve, typically in young adults, often associated with multiple sclerosis. It presents with subacute unilateral visual loss, reduced colour vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and pain on eye movement. The disc may look normal (retrobulbar neuritis) or swollen (papillitis). MRI of brain and orbits, and multiple sclerosis risk assessment, guide follow-up; corticosteroids speed recovery but do not change the final visual outcome in most cases.

Age-related macular degeneration

Degeneration of the macula in older adults, causing gradual central visual loss with preserved peripheral vision. Dry disease shows drusen and retinal pigment changes and progresses slowly; wet disease shows choroidal neovascularisation with haemorrhage, exudation and rapid visual loss, and is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections. Smoking is a modifiable risk factor; high-dose antioxidant supplements are used only in selected intermediate disease.

title: 27.1 Gestational diabetes mellitus [KU 17]
text:
CHAPTER 27: MATERNAL MEDICINE

27.1 Gestational diabetes mellitus [KU 17]

The case

A 25-year-old woman, primigravida, at 28 weeks of gestation, is found to have a random blood sugar of 250 mg/dL. The questions are: the diagnostic criteria for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), its features, and the drugs used in GDM.

One important caution first: a single random value of 250 mg/dL is not, on its own, the full diagnostic test for GDM. It is well above normal and must be acted on, but the diagnosis is completed with a formal oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) and by checking whether the picture is overt diabetes in pregnancy rather than GDM (see below).

Definitions

•  Gestational diabetes mellitus: glucose intolerance first recognised during pregnancy, usually diagnosed in the second or third trimester, in a woman without previously known diabetes.

•  Diabetes in pregnancy (overt diabetes): diabetes first detected in pregnancy that meets non-pregnant diabetes thresholds; this is managed as pre-existing diabetes, not as ordinary GDM.

•  Pathophysiology: placental hormones (human placental lactogen, progesterone, cortisol, prolactin) increase insulin resistance, especially in the second half of pregnancy. The pancreatic beta cell must increase insulin secretion to compensate; when it cannot, glucose rises.

Diagnostic criteria — IADPSG / WHO 2013, one-step 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks

The one-step test uses 75 g of oral glucose, with blood glucose measured fasting, at 1 hour, and at 2 hours. GDM is diagnosed if any one value meets or exceeds its threshold:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-023]]

Only one abnormal value is needed. Screening is at 24–28 weeks in women without diabetes before or early in pregnancy; women at high risk are tested earlier, and overt diabetes is excluded at the first antenatal visit.

Fig. 27.1 — GDM screening and diagnosis: 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks, any one value at threshold, and the separate overt-diabetes cut-offs.

Overt diabetes cut-offs in pregnancy

•  Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L).

•  HbA1c ≥ 6.5%.

•  Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms of hyperglycaemia.

On these criteria, a random value of 250 mg/dL with symptoms would meet the overt-diabetes threshold, while an asymptomatic random value still requires confirmatory formal testing; the distinction matters because overt diabetes is managed as pre-existing diabetes.

DIPSI alternative (India)

The Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Group India (DIPSI) single-step procedure uses 75 g of oral glucose irrespective of the last meal, with a 2-hour plasma glucose of ≥ 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) taken as diagnostic of GDM. It is a simpler, non-fasting alternative accepted in Indian practice alongside the IADPSG / WHO 2013 criteria.

Risk factors

•  Previous GDM or a previous macrosomic baby, family history of type 2 diabetes, obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome, older maternal age, and certain ethnic backgrounds.

•  Glucocorticoid use, multiple pregnancy, and polyhydramnios in the current pregnancy.

Features — maternal

•  Often asymptomatic; commonly detected only on screening, which is why universal screening at 24–28 weeks matters.

•  Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, fatigue, recurrent urinary or vaginal infections, and blurred vision when hyperglycaemia is marked.

•  Increased risk of pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, caesarean delivery, and later type 2 diabetes.

•  Polyhydramnios, and a higher risk of urinary tract infection and wound infection.

Features — fetal and neonatal

•  Macrosomia (large-for-gestational-age baby) with shoulder dystocia and birth trauma.

•  Polyhydramnios, preterm birth, and stillbirth in poorly controlled disease.

•  Neonatal hypoglycaemia, respiratory distress, polycythaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia, and hypocalcaemia.

•  Longer-term risk of obesity and glucose intolerance in the offspring.

Management — general principles

•  Medical nutrition therapy and regular physical activity are the first step and control many cases; self-monitoring of blood glucose (fasting and postprandial) guides treatment.

•  Glycaemic targets in pregnancy are fasting plasma glucose < 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L), 1-hour postprandial < 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L), and 2-hour postprandial < 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L); the HbA1c goal is ideally < 6% if achievable without significant hypoglycaemia.

•  Fetal surveillance with growth scans, and delivery timing individualised to glycaemic control and fetal growth; postpartum, glucose is retested (usually at 6–12 weeks) because GDM predicts later type 2 diabetes, and breastfeeding and lifestyle measures are encouraged.

Drugs used in gestational diabetes mellitus

•  Insulin — first-line drug: the preferred medication for hyperglycaemia in GDM, because it does not cross the placenta in measurable amounts and has a long safety record. Basal and prandial regimens (including NPH and rapid-acting analogues) are titrated to the fasting and postprandial targets; it is started when lifestyle measures fail to reach target, typically when fasting glucose exceeds about 95 mg/dL or postprandial values exceed target.

•  Metformin — alternative, not first-line: crosses the placenta and lacks long-term safety data in the offspring. It may be used when insulin is refused or not feasible, and it is preferred over glyburide in that situation; a substantial proportion of women on metformin alone later need supplemental insulin, and it has been associated with more preterm birth in some analyses.

•  Glyburide (glibenclamide) — limited role: an oral sulfonylurea that crosses the placenta; not a first-line agent, with more neonatal hypoglycaemia and macrosomia than metformin in comparative analyses. It is used only in limited circumstances where insulin is not an option.

•  Drugs not used: other oral and non-insulin injectable glucose-lowering agents lack safety data in pregnancy and are not recommended for GDM.

subject: medicine
title: 27.2 Hypothyroidism in pregnancy [KU 17]
text:
27.2 Hypothyroidism in pregnancy [KU 17]

Causes and presentation

The commonest cause in iodine-sufficient areas is Hashimoto thyroiditis; iodine deficiency, previous thyroid surgery or radioiodine, and drugs such as amiodarone are other causes. Many women are asymptomatic or have non-specific symptoms — fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin — that overlap with normal pregnancy, so diagnosis rests on thyroid function tests.

Diagnosis

•  Overt hypothyroidism: raised trimester-specific TSH with a low free T4.

•  Subclinical hypothyroidism: raised trimester-specific TSH with a normal free T4.

•  Check thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies, because antibody status affects the decision to treat subclinical disease.

TSH targets — ATA 2017, with the conflict stated plainly

The 2017 American Thyroid Association (ATA) guideline recommends using population- and trimester-specific TSH reference ranges where available. Where such ranges are not available, the ATA default upper limit is 4.0 mIU/L. In practice, the widely quoted trimester-specific upper limits are first trimester 2.5 mIU/L, second trimester 3.0 mIU/L, and third trimester 3.0 mIU/L, and preconception TSH should be below 2.5 mIU/L. The two statements differ — 3.0 versus 4.0 mIU/L in the later trimesters — because one is a trimester-specific range and the other is the ATA fallback when no local range exists; local laboratory ranges should be followed where available.

Treatment and monitoring

•  Levothyroxine is the drug of choice. It is the same hormone the thyroid makes, and it is safe in pregnancy; antithyroid drugs have no role in hypothyroidism.

•  Women already on levothyroxine should increase the dose by about 20–30% (commonly two extra tablets per week) as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, because thyroxine requirements rise in pregnancy and most women need a higher dose.

•  For subclinical hypothyroidism, ATA 2017 advises: if TPO antibodies are positive, consider treatment when TSH is above 2.5 mIU/L and start treatment when TSH is above 4 mIU/L; if antibodies are negative, consider treatment when TSH is 4–10 mIU/L and start treatment when TSH is above 10 mIU/L. Maternal hypothyroxinaemia (low free T4 with normal TSH) alone does not indicate treatment.

•  Recheck TSH about every 4 weeks during dose titration, then at least once per trimester once stable; keep free T4 in the upper half of the reference range.

•  After delivery, return to the pre-pregnancy levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH about 6 weeks postpartum.

Complications of untreated hypothyroidism

•  Maternal: pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, placental abruption, postpartum haemorrhage, preterm delivery, and low birth weight.

•  Fetal and neonatal: impaired neurodevelopment, especially when hypothyroidism is present in early pregnancy before the fetal thyroid is functioning, and increased perinatal morbidity and mortality.

Safe — first-line choices
