title: 27.4 Other topics in brief
text:
27.4 Other topics in brief

Physiological changes in pregnancy

Cardiac output rises by about 40%, heart rate and stroke volume increase, systemic vascular resistance falls, and blood pressure falls slightly in mid-pregnancy before returning toward baseline. Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass, causing physiological anaemia of pregnancy. Glomerular filtration rate rises, creatinine and urea fall, and the diaphragm rises as the uterus enlarges, reducing functional residual capacity. Gastrointestinal motility slows, and a hypercoagulable state develops.

Cardiac disease in pregnancy

Pre-existing heart disease is the commonest indirect cause of maternal death in many settings. Risk is highest in pulmonary hypertension, severe left-sided obstructive lesions, Marfan syndrome with aortic dilatation, and a systemic right ventricle. Management is by a multidisciplinary team: continue most cardiac drugs, avoid ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and statins, plan delivery (vaginal delivery is usually preferred, with caesarean for obstetric or specific cardiac indications), and give endocarditis prophylaxis only for high-risk lesions. Peripartum cardiomyopathy presents with heart failure in late pregnancy or the early postpartum period and is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Pre-eclampsia — medicine angle

Pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks (systolic ≥ 140 mmHg or diastolic ≥ 90 mmHg on two occasions) plus proteinuria (≥ 300 mg in 24 hours, protein/creatinine ratio ≥ 0.3, or dipstick ≥ 2+) or another end-organ feature — thrombocytopenia (platelets < 100,000 per microlitre), renal impairment (creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL or doubling), liver dysfunction (transaminases twice the upper limit), pulmonary oedema, or new cerebral or visual symptoms. Proteinuria is no longer required for the diagnosis. Severe features include systolic ≥ 160 or diastolic ≥ 110 mmHg, thrombocytopenia, liver or renal dysfunction, pulmonary oedema, persistent headache or visual symptoms, and severe epigastric or right upper quadrant pain; HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a severe variant. Magnesium sulfate prevents and treats eclamptic seizures; antihypertensives used in pregnancy include labetalol, nifedipine and methyldopa. Delivery is the only definitive treatment, and timing is balanced against maternal and fetal risk.

Anaemia in pregnancy

Anaemia in pregnancy is most often iron deficiency, with folate deficiency, haemoglobinopathies (thalassaemia, sickle cell disease), chronic disease, and blood loss as other causes. It presents with fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea and palpitations, and increases the risk of low birth weight, preterm delivery and maternal morbidity. Iron and folate supplementation, investigation of the cause, and transfusion only for severe or symptomatic anaemia are the mainstays. A haemoglobin threshold of 11 g/dL in pregnancy is the commonly used World Health Organization definition of anaemia [UNVERIFIED — see report].

subject: medicine
title: 28.1 Causes of falls in elderly [KU 22, 20, 16, 15]
text:
CHAPTER 28: AGEING AND DISEASE

28.1 Causes of falls in elderly [KU 22, 20, 16, 15]

What a fall is, and why it matters

A fall is an unintentional event in which a person comes to rest on the ground or a lower level, not caused by a major intrinsic event such as a stroke or by an overwhelming external hazard. Falls are common in older adults, are often multifactorial, and are a leading cause of injury, fracture, loss of independence, and death in this age group. A single fall is a warning; recurrent falls, or a fall with injury, always deserve assessment.

Fig. 28.1 — Falls assessment: history and examination, lying and standing blood pressure, targeted tests, then treatment of each contributor.

Intrinsic causes

•  Neurological: stroke, Parkinson disease and parkinsonism, peripheral neuropathy (especially diabetic), normal pressure hydrocephalus, cervical myelopathy, dementia and delirium.

•  Cardiovascular: orthostatic hypotension, arrhythmias, sick sinus syndrome, aortic stenosis, carotid sinus hypersensitivity, and vasovagal syncope.

•  Musculoskeletal: sarcopenia and muscle weakness, osteoarthritis (especially of hip and knee), foot problems, and deconditioning after illness or bed rest.

•  Sensory: visual impairment (cataract, macular degeneration, glaucoma, uncorrected refractive error), hearing loss, and vestibular disorders.

•  Metabolic and systemic: hypoglycaemia, anaemia, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance (hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia), vitamin D deficiency, and acute illness (infection, urinary tract infection, pneumonia) presenting as a fall.

•  Psychological: depression, fear of falling (which itself causes deconditioning and more falls), and cognitive impairment.

Drug causes

•  Sedatives and hypnotics, benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, antidepressants (especially tricyclics), opioids, and alcohol.

•  Antihypertensives, diuretics and other drugs that cause postural hypotension or electrolyte disturbance.

•  Hypoglycaemic agents (insulin, sulfonylureas) causing hypoglycaemia.

•  Anticholinergic drugs causing confusion, blurred vision, urinary retention and constipation.

•  Polypharmacy itself — the more drugs, the higher the fall risk — and recent changes in dose or new drugs.

Extrinsic and environmental causes

•  Loose rugs, trailing wires, poor lighting, slippery floors, cluttered rooms, and steps without handrails.

•  Unsuitable footwear, walking aids that are the wrong height or poorly maintained, and bifocal glasses (which blur the ground on looking down).

•  Tripping outdoors on uneven pavements, and falls getting in and out of bed, bath, or transport.

Assessment

•  History: circumstances of the fall (trip, slip, collapse, blackout, dizziness, chest pain, palpitations), prodrome, witnesses, injuries, previous falls, fear of falling, and ability to get up from the floor.

•  Drug review and alcohol history; review of all prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines.

•  Examination: lying and standing blood pressure, pulse and rhythm, cardiac murmurs, neurological examination, gait and balance (including the Timed Up and Go test), vision and hearing, feet and footwear, and a home-hazard assessment.

•  Orthostatic hypotension: a fall in systolic blood pressure of ≥ 20 mmHg or in diastolic blood pressure of ≥ 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing, from a supine baseline. It is a common, treatable contributor and must be specifically looked for.

•  Targeted tests: ECG if syncope or arrhythmia is suspected, blood glucose, full blood count, electrolytes, renal function, vitamin D, and imaging only as indicated by the history and examination. A fall is not an indication for a blanket panel of tests.

•  Red flags: syncope, chest pain, focal neurology, head injury on anticoagulation, or inability to bear weight — these need urgent assessment.

Prevention and management

•  Treat each contributor: review and reduce culprit drugs, correct vision (including cataract surgery where appropriate), treat arrhythmias and postural hypotension, and manage pain and depression.

•  Strength and balance training (for example progressive resistance exercise and Tai Chi) is the most effective single intervention for recurrent fallers.

•  Home safety assessment and modification, appropriate footwear, and correctly fitted walking aids.

•  Vitamin D supplementation where deficient, bone health assessment and treatment after a fragility fracture, and hip protectors in selected high-risk patients.

•  Education, a personal alarm, and a plan for getting up or summoning help after a fall; follow-up to check that interventions have worked.

subject: medicine
title: 28.2 Causes of unsteadiness in the elderly [RGU]
text:
28.2 Causes of unsteadiness in the elderly [RGU]

Unsteadiness is not the same as a fall

A fall is an event; unsteadiness is a symptom — a feeling of imbalance, dizziness, or difficulty walking — that may or may not lead to a fall. The two lists overlap, but unsteadiness is organised here by the balance system that is failing, because that is how it is assessed at the bedside.

Vestibular causes

•  Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: brief spinning vertigo on head movement, with nystagmus on positional testing.

•  Ménière disease: episodic vertigo with tinnitus, aural fullness and fluctuating hearing loss.

•  Vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis: prolonged vertigo, often after a viral illness, with nausea and imbalance.

•  Bilateral vestibular loss (for example from aminoglycosides): oscillopsia and imbalance that worsens in the dark or on uneven ground.

Visual causes

•  Cataract, macular degeneration, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and uncorrected refractive error — all reduce the visual input that balance depends on.

•  Bifocal and multifocal glasses, which distort the lower visual field when looking down at the ground.

Proprioceptive and peripheral nerve causes

•  Diabetic and other peripheral neuropathies, vitamin B12 deficiency, and dorsal column loss (tabes dorsalis, subacute combined degeneration): sensory ataxia, worse in the dark and with eyes closed (positive Romberg sign), with a high-stepping or stamping gait.

Central causes

•  Cerebellar disease: stroke, tumour, alcohol-related degeneration, and drugs (phenytoin) — broad-based, unsteady gait with incoordination, nystagmus and dysarthria.

•  Parkinson disease and vascular parkinsonism: shuffling gait, freezing, and postural instability.

•  Normal pressure hydrocephalus: gait apraxia with dementia and urinary incontinence.

•  Stroke, multiple sclerosis, and cerebral small-vessel disease (leukoaraiosis) causing a slow, shuffling, wide-based gait.

Musculoskeletal and systemic causes

•  Muscle weakness and sarcopenia, hip and knee osteoarthritis, foot deformity and pain, and deconditioning.

•  Anaemia, hypoglycaemia, dehydration, postural hypotension, and acute illness.

•  Anxiety and depression, which alter gait and attention, and fear of falling.

Drug causes

•  Sedatives, antiepileptics (especially phenytoin), aminoglycosides (vestibular toxicity), antihypertensives causing postural drop, and alcohol.

Assessment and management

•  Take a history of the unsteadiness itself: spinning versus light-headedness versus imbalance, triggers (head movement, standing, darkness), hearing symptoms, and falls.

•  Examine gait, Romberg sign, cerebellar signs, parkinsonian features, vestibular tests (including the Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre), vision, proprioception, and lying and standing blood pressure.

•  Treat the cause: repositioning manoeuvres for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular rehabilitation, correction of vision, B12 replacement, drug review, physiotherapy for gait and balance, and walking aids where appropriate.

subject: medicine
title: 28.3 Other topics in brief
text:
28.3 Other topics in brief

Frailty

Frailty is a state of increased vulnerability to stressors, with reduced physiological reserve, so that a minor illness causes a disproportionate loss of function. The Fried phenotype counts five items — unintentional weight loss, weakness (reduced grip strength), exhaustion, slow walking speed, and low physical activity: three or more means frail, one or two means pre-frail. The Rockwood approach counts accumulated deficits, and the Clinical Frailty Scale grades from 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill); scores of 5 and above generally indicate frailty. Frailty is partly reversible with exercise, nutrition, and treatment of contributing disease.

Delirium versus dementia

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-026]]

Delirium superimposed on dementia is common and easily missed; any acute change in an older adult with dementia should be treated as delirium until proved otherwise.

Polypharmacy

Polypharmacy is usually defined as the concurrent use of five or more medicines. It increases the risk of adverse drug reactions, falls, confusion, hospital admission, and non-adherence, and much of it is driven by prescribing cascades (a drug given for the side effect of another). Regular medication review — asking whether each drug is still indicated, effective, and safe, and deprescribing where appropriate — is the main safeguard.

Pressure ulcers

Pressure ulcers are localised damage to skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, caused by pressure, shear, or a combination. Prevention is repositioning, pressure-relieving surfaces, skin care, nutrition, and continence care. Staging: Stage 1 — non-blanchable redness of intact skin; Stage 2 — partial-thickness skin loss or blister; Stage 3 — full-thickness skin loss with subcutaneous fat visible; Stage 4 — full-thickness loss with muscle, tendon, or bone exposed. Unstageable ulcers are covered by slough or eschar so depth cannot be judged, and deep tissue injury is a purple or maroon area of intact or blistered skin from damage to underlying soft tissue. Management is pressure relief, wound care, treatment of infection, nutrition, and surgical referral for deep or non-healing ulcers.

subject: medicine
title: 1. Anatomy of the Skin, Generalised Pruritus, Nail Changes in Systemic Disease, and PUVA Therapy [KU 24, 17, TU, RGU]
text:
CHAPTER 30 — DERMATOLOGY

SECTION 30.1, 30.2 & 30.3 — ANATOMY, PRESENTING PROBLEMS & PRINCIPLES OF MANAGEMENT

1. Anatomy of the Skin, Generalised Pruritus, Nail Changes in Systemic Disease, and PUVA Therapy [KU 24, 17, TU, RGU]

A. Functional Anatomy of the Skin [KU 17]:

1.  Epidermis (0.1–0.2 mm thick; stratified squamous epithelium):

•  Keratinocytes (90% of cells): Arranged in 4 layers from deep to superficial: (1) Basal layer (stratum basale)—proliferative stem cell layer containing keratins 5 and 14, attached to the basement membrane by hemi-desmosomes (BP180/type XVII collagen, BP230); (2) Prickle cell / Spinous layer (stratum spinosum)—keratinocytes containing keratins 1 and 10, joined together by desmosomes (desmoglein-1 and -3); (3) Granular layer (stratum granulosum)—contains keratohyalin granules and filaggrin (mutations cause ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic eczema); (4) Stratum corneum (horny keratin layer)—anucleate corneocytes ("bricks") embedded in a hydrophobic ceramide/lipid bilayer ("mortar") that forms the skin’s primary barrier.

•  Non-Keratinocyte Epidermal Cells (10%):Melanocytes (neural crest–derived cells in the basal layer that synthesise melanin in melanosomes and transfer it to keratinocytes for UV protection); Langerhans cells (bone marrow–derived antigen-presenting dendritic cells); and Merkel cells (mechanoreceptors for fine touch in the basal layer).

2.  Basement Membrane Zone (Dermo-Epidermal Junction): Comprises the lamina lucida (laminin), lamina densa (type IV collagen), and sublamina densa anchoring fibrils (type VII collagen).

3.  Dermis (1–4 mm thick; papillary and reticular layers): Vascular connective tissue composed of collagen types I and III, elastin, and glycosaminoglycan ground substance synthesised by fibroblasts, housing superficial and deep vascular plexuses, nerves, mast cells, macrophages, and epidermal appendages (hair follicles, androgen-sensitive sebaceous glands, thermoregulatory cholinergic eccrine sweat glands, and axillary/anogenital apocrine sweat glands).

4.  Subcutis (Hypodermis): Adipose tissue layer acting as a shock absorber and thermal insulator.

B. Generalised Pruritus (Itch): Causes & Approach [KU 17]:

•  Primary Skin Diseases Causing Generalised Pruritus (Itch WITH Rash):Scabies, Atopic and other Eczemas, Urticaria, Psoriasis, Lichen planus, Dermatitis herpetiformis, Pre-bullous pemphigoid, mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), and Xeroderma (dry skin) of old age.

•  Secondary Systemic Causes of Generalised Pruritus (Itch WITHOUT Primary Skin Rash):

1.  Hepatobiliary (Cholestatic) Disease:Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), primary sclerosing cholangitis, extrahepatic biliary obstruction, intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, hepatitis C.

2.  Renal Disease:Chronic Kidney Disease / Uraemic Pruritus.

3.  Haematological & Malignant Disease:Iron deficiency anaemia, Polycythaemia vera (intense aquagenic pruritus after warm baths/showers), Hodgkin’s lymphoma, Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloma, and visceral carcinomas.

4.  Endocrine & Metabolic Disease:Hyperthyroidism and Hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, carcinoid syndrome.

5.  Infections & Drugs:HIV infection, parasitic helminth infections, and Drugs (opiates/morphine, chloroquine, oral contraceptives, statins).

6.  Psychogenic / Neuropathic: Delusions of infestation, anxiety/depression.

•  Investigations for Pruritus Without Rash: FBC and blood film, serum ferritin, U&Es, LFTs (bilirubin, ALP, GGT), TFTs, fasting glucose, antimitochondrial antibodies, HIV serology, and chest X-ray (for mediastinal Hodgkin’s lymphoma).

•  Non-Specific Symptomatic Management: Frequent emollients, cooling topical 1%–2% menthol in aqueous cream, sedating H1-antihistamines at night (hydroxyzine, chlorphenamine), narrowband UVB phototherapy (proven in uraemic and cholestatic pruritus), colestyramine / rifampicin / naltrexone / sertraline (in cholestatic itch), or gabapentin/pregabalin.

C. Nail Changes in Systemic Disorders [RGU]:

1.  Koilonychia (Spoon-shaped concave nails):Iron deficiency anaemia (also haemochromatosis, Raynaud’s).

2.  Digital Clubbing (Loss of nail-fold angle + boggy fluctuation + drumstick swelling): Bronchogenic carcinoma, mesothelioma, suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema, cystic fibrosis), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, cyanotic congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis, inflammatory bowel disease, and cirrhosis.

3.  Leuconychia (White nails): Total/apparent leuconychia in hypoalbuminaemia / chronic liver disease / nephrotic syndrome; Terry’s nails (proximal 80% white, distal pink rim in cirrhosis/heart failure); Half-and-half (Lindsay’s) nails (proximal half white, distal half red/brown in chronic renal failure).

4.  Beau’s Lines: Transverse horizontal grooves/indentations across all nails caused by temporary arrest of nail matrix growth during a severe acute systemic illness, high fever, chemotherapy, or shock (grow out at 0.1 mm/day on fingernails).

5.  Splinter Haemorrhages: Linear longitudinal dark red/brown streaks under the nail plate; caused by trauma (distal) or infective endocarditis / systemic vasculitis / antiphospholipid syndrome (proximal).

6.  Nail-Fold Telangiectasia & Capillary Dropout:Dermatomyositis, Systemic sclerosis, and SLE.

7.  Nail Pitting & Onycholysis:Psoriasis, Alopecia areata, eczema, and Thyrotoxicosis (Plummer’s nails—onycholysis).

8.  Yellow Nail Syndrome: Slow-growing, thickened, curved yellow nails associated with lymphoedema, bronchiectasis, and pleural effusions.

D. PUVA Therapy (Photochemotherapy) [KU 17, RGU] & Causes of Subcutaneous Nodules [KU 24]:

•  PUVA (Psoralen + Ultraviolet A [320–400 nm] Photochemotherapy):

•  Mechanism of Action: The patient ingests an oral photosensitising psoralen (8-methoxypsoralen [8-MOP] or 5-MOP, 2 hours prior to irradiation) or soaks in a topical psoralen bath (Bath PUVA). Psoralens intercalate between epidermal DNA base pairs; upon subsequent exposure to long-wave UVA (320–400 nm) radiation, psoralens form covalent inter-strand DNA cross-links, inhibiting keratinocyte hyperproliferation and inducing apoptosis of skin-infiltrating T lymphocytes.

•  Indications: Moderate-to-severe Plaque Psoriasis (when narrowband UVB fails), Palmoplantar pustulosis, Plaque-stage Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma (Mycosis fungoides), Vitiligo, Severe Chronic Eczema (especially hand/foot eczema), Alopecia areata, polymorphic light eruption (desensitisation), and chronic GVHD/morphoea.

•  Adverse Effects:

•  Acute: Nausea (with oral 8-MOP), phototoxic erythema/blistering (peaks at 48–72 hours), pruritus, and corneal/lens damage (mandatory to wear UVA-blocking sunglasses for 24 hours after oral psoralen ingestion).

•  Long-Term (Cumulative >150–200 treatments): Photo-ageing, PUVA lentigines, cataracts, and a dose-dependent increased risk of Non-Melanoma Skin Cancer (especially Squamous Cell Carcinoma) and melanoma (hence ciclosporin is contraindicated after high cumulative PUVA).

•  Causes of Subcutaneous Nodules [KU 24]: (1) Rheumatoid nodules (extensor surfaces in seropositive RA); (2) Gouty tophi (urate crystals); (3) Erythema nodosum (painful septal panniculitis on shins in sarcoidosis, TB, strep, IBD); (4) Xanthomas (tendon/tuberous xanthomas in hyperlipidaemia); (5) Neurofibromas (NF1) and Lipomas; (6) Polyarteritis nodosa / Cutaneous vasculitis, Sarcoidosis, Rheumatic fever (Aschoff nodules), and Metastatic cutaneous nodules.

subject: medicine
title: 2. Scabies, Pediculosis, Superficial Fungal Infections, and Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome [KU 25, 24, 23, 21, 19, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 30.4, 30.5 & 30.6 — SKIN INFECTIONS, INFESTATIONS, ACNE, ROSACEA & ECZEMAS

2. Scabies, Pediculosis, Superficial Fungal Infections, and Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome [KU 25, 24, 23, 21, 19, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

1. Scabies [KU 25, 24, 23, 17, 16, 15, RGU]:

•  Aetiopathogenesis: A common, highly contagious skin infestation caused by the human itch mite, Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. Transmitted by prolonged direct skin-to-skin contact (household members, overcrowded living conditions, care homes, or sexual contact). The fertilized female mite excavates a tunnel (burrow) in the stratum corneum, laying 2–3 eggs daily. After 4–6 weeks (shorter upon re-infection), a delayed Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to mite antigens and faeces develops, causing intense generalised pruritus.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Cardinal Symptom:Severe generalised pruritus that is characteristically WORSE AT NIGHT and after hot baths/showers. Affecting multiple family members/close contacts simultaneously is a key diagnostic clue.

•  Pathognomonic Primary Lesion — The Scabietic Burrow: Short (5–10 mm), serpiginous, grey–white thread-like linear ridges with a tiny dark speck (the female mite) or vesicle at the advancing end.

•  Classic Anatomical Distribution ("Circle of Hebra"):Finger webs, flexor aspects of the wrists, ulnar borders of the hands, elbows, anterior axillary folds, periumbilical skin, waist, buttocks, ankles, areolae/nipples in females, and inflammatory papules/nodules on the penis and scrotum in males.

•  Important Age Exception: In adults, the head, neck, scalp, palms, and soles are spared; however, in infants and young children, the face, scalp, palms, and soles ARE characteristically involved (often with palmoplantar vesicles and pustules).

•  Secondary Lesions: Excoriations, widespread secondary eczematisation, papular urticaria, and secondary bacterial infection (impetiginisation) with Staphylococcus aureus or nephritogenic Streptococcus pyogenes (which can lead to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).

•  Crusted ("Norwegian") Scabies: Massive infestation with millions of mites causing thick, psoriasiform hyperkeratotic crusts over the hands, feet, scalp, and trunk (often with minimal itch); occurs in immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS), elderly, debilitated, or Down syndrome patients and is extremely contagious.

•  Diagnosis (Investigations):

•  Dermatoscopy: Visualises the burrow and the dark triangular anterior part of the mite ("delta-wing jet with contrail" sign).

•  Skin Scrapings & Light Microscopy (Confirmatory): Scrape a burrow with a blunt scalpel blade using mineral oil or 10% KOH and examine under a light microscope to demonstrate the adult eight-legged mite, six-legged larvae, ova (eggs), or faecal pellets (scybala).

•  Management of Scabies:

1.  Key Principles of Successful Eradication:

•  Treat the index patient AND all household members and close physical/sexual contacts SIMULTANEOUSLY, even if they are completely asymptomatic (as asymptomatic contacts may be in the 4–6 week incubation period and will otherwise cause re-infestation).

•  Apply topical scabicides to ALL skin surfaces from the chin/neck downwards to the soles of the feet, paying special attention to the finger webs, toe clefts, under the nails, umbilicus, natal cleft, and genitalia. (In infants <2 years, the elderly, and crusted scabies, also apply to the scalp, face, and ears, avoiding the eyes).

•  Repeat the treatment after 7 days (a second application 1 week later is mandatory to kill newly hatched nymphs).

2.  Pharmacological Agents:

•  First-Line Topical Scabicide:5% Permethrin Dermal Cream: Apply to cool, dry skin over the entire body, leave on for 8–12 hours overnight, and wash off; repeat 1 week later.

•  Second-Line Topical Scabicide:0.5% Malathion Aqueous Liquid: Apply to the whole body, leave on for 24 hours, wash off, and repeat after 7 days (alternatives in some regions include benzyl benzoate 25% or crotamiton [Eurax] for babies).

•  Systemic Oral Therapy — Oral Ivermectin (200 μ g/kg single dose, repeated after 7 days): Indicated for Crusted ("Norwegian") Scabies (combined with topical permethrin and keratolytics), institutional outbreaks, immunosuppressed patients, or topical treatment failure/resistance.

3.  Environmental Decontamination & Symptomatic Care:

•  Machine-wash all clothing, bed linen, and towels used in the preceding 3 days at high temperature (≥ 50^circ–60^circC) and tumble-dry hot (or seal non-washable items in a plastic bag for 72 hours).

•  Manage Post-Scabietic Itch: Warn patients that pruritus commonly persists for 2–4 weeks after successful mite eradication due to residual hypersensitivity to dead mite antigens; treat with emollients, crotamiton cream, moderate-potency topical corticosteroids, and sedating oral antihistamines at night (plus flucloxacillin if secondarily impetiginised).

2. Pediculosis (Lice Infestation) & Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome [TU]:

•  Pediculosis:

•  Pediculosis capitis (Head lice — Pediculus humanus capitis): Transmitted by head-to-head contact in children; causes scalp itch, occipital impetiginisation, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Confirmed by wet-combing live lice; empty egg cases (nits) are cemented firmly to hair shafts. Treated with topical 4% Dimeticone lotion, 1% Permethrin, or 0.5% Malathion applied twice 7 days apart, plus regular wet-combing ("bug-busting") with conditioner.

•  Pediculosis corporis (Body lice — Pediculus humanus corporis): Lives in the seams of unwashed clothing in homelessness/overcrowding (vector for epidemic typhus, trench fever, and relapsing fever); treated by laundering/destroying infested clothing at >60^circC plus topical permethrin/oral ivermectin.

•  Pthirus pubis (Pubic / "Crab" lice): Sexually transmitted infestation of pubic, axillary, and eyelash hair; treated with whole-body permethrin/malathion (and petroleum jelly Vaseline twice daily for 2 weeks to eyelashes), treating sexual partners and screening for STIs.

•  Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS / Ritter’s Disease) [TU]:

•  Blistering, exfoliative toxin-mediated disease affecting neonates and young children (<5 years) (or adults with renal failure).

•  Pathogenesis: A localised focus of Phage Group II Staphylococcus aureus infection (umbilicus, conjunctiva, nasopharynx, or skin) releases circulating exfoliative toxins A and B (ETA/ETB), which act as serine proteases that cleave Desmoglein-1 in the epidermal granular layer, causing a very superficial intra-epidermal split just beneath the stratum corneum.

•  Clinical Features: Fever, irritability, and generalised tender scarlatiniform erythema starting periorally and in the flexures (groin/axillae), rapidly progressing within 24–48 hours to flaccid blisters, positive Nikolsky’s sign, and widespread "tissue-paper" peeling of the superficial epidermis(crucially, mucous membranes are SPARED, unlike Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis).

•  Diagnosis & Treatment: Confirmed rapidly by frozen section of a superficial skin snip (showing a subcorneal/granular layer split, vs. full-thickness epidermal necrosis in TEN) and bacterial swabs from the primary focus. Treated with immediate IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (IV Flucloxacillin + Clindamycin [to halt toxin synthesis], or Vancomycin), IV fluid resuscitation, analgesia, and bland emollients. Heals completely without scarring within 10–14 days.

3. Superficial Mycoses of the Skin & Pityriasis (Tinea) Versicolor [KU 21, 19]:

•  Three Groups of Superficial Fungal Skin Infections (Superficial Mycoses):

1.  Dermatophytoses (Ringworm / Tinea) — Keratinophilic fungi of Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton genera:

•  Tinea corporis (Body): Asymmetrical, itchy, annular erythematous plaques with an active, raised, scaly/vesicular advancing border and central clearing. (Tinea incognito occurs when misapplied topical steroids suppress the annular border and promote fungal spread).

•  Tinea cruris ("Jock itch"): Well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaques in the groins and upper inner thighs (usually T. rubrum).

•  Tinea pedis ("Athlete’s foot") & Tinea manuum: Interdigital maceration/fissuring between the 4th and 5th toes (T. rubrum, T. interdigitale), moccasin-type plantar/unilateral palmar scaling ("two feet–one hand syndrome"), or vesiculobullous eruption (T. mentagrophytes).

•  Tinea capitis (Scalp ringworm in children): Patchy alopecia with scaling, broken "black dot" hairs (endothrix T. tonsurans), green fluorescence under Wood’s light (ectothrix Microsporum canis), or a boggy, pustular inflammatory swelling (Kerion).

•  Tinea unguium (Onychomycosis): Distal and lateral subungual hyperkeratosis, yellow–brown discoloration, and crumbling of the nail plate.

•  Diagnosis:10%–20% Potassium Hydroxide (KOH) wet-mount microscopy of skin scrapings (taken from the active advancing scaly edge), nail clippings, or plucked hairs demonstrating branching septate fungal hyphae, plus fungal culture on Sabouraud’s dextrose agar.

•  Treatment:Topical Terbinafine or Topical Azoles (Clotrimazole, Miconazole) for localised skin tinea; Systemic Oral Terbinafine (250 mg daily for 6–12 weeks for nails, 2–4 weeks for skin), Oral Itraconazole, or Oral Griseofulvin (used for childhood tinea capitis) are required for scalp (tinea capitis), nail (onychomycosis), or extensive skin disease.

2.  Cutaneous Candidiasis (Candida albicans):

•  Affects warm, moist intertriginous folds (intertrigo, napkin dermatitis, angular cheilitis, oral thrush, vulvovaginitis, balanitis, chronic paronychia), producing beefy-red glazed plaques surrounded by characteristic "satellite pustules/papules". Predisposed by diabetes, obesity, broad-spectrum antibiotics, steroids, and HIV. Treated with topical nystatin/imidazoles or oral fluconazole.

3.  Pityriasis (Tinea) Versicolor [KU 21]:

•  Aetiology: Superficial infection of the stratum corneum caused by overgrowth of the lipophilic commensal yeast Malassezia globosa (and M. furfur / M. sympodialis). Triggered by hot, humid climates, sweating, greasy skin, and immunosuppression.

•  Clinical Features: Multiple, well-demarcated, oval finely (branny) scaly macules and patches coalescing over the seborrhoeic areas of the upper trunk (chest, upper back, shoulders, and neck). Lesions may be hypopigmented (in tanned/dark skin, because the yeast produces azelaic acid, a dicarboxylic acid that inhibits melanocyte tyrosinase and prevents tanning) or fawn/pink-brown hyperpigmented (in pale untanned skin).

•  Diagnosis:Wood’s UV light shows yellow–green fluorescence; KOH microscopy of skin scrapings demonstrates the pathognomonic "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance (short, curved hyphal filaments mixed with clusters of round yeast spores).

•  Management:Topical Ketoconazole 2% shampoo (or Selenium sulphide 2.5% shampoo) applied to the trunk for 10 minutes daily for 1–2 weeks, or topical imidazole creams (clotrimazole, miconazole). Extensive or recalcitrant cases respond to a short course of Oral Itraconazole (200 mg/day for 7 days) or Oral Fluconazole. (Counsel the patient that hypopigmentation takes several months to resolve after the yeast is eradicated, and monthly prophylactic ketoconazole washes prevent recurrence).

subject: medicine
title: 3. Acne Vulgaris, Rosacea, and Eczemas [KU 24, 19, 18, TU, RGU]
text:
3. Acne Vulgaris, Rosacea, and Eczemas [KU 24, 19, 18, TU, RGU]

1. Acne Vulgaris [KU 24, 19, RGU]:

•  Pathogenesis (The Four Key Pathogenic Factors in the Pilosebaceous Unit):

1.  Androgen-driven increased sebum production (Seborrhoea) at puberty.

2.  Abnormal follicular hypercornification (hyperkeratinisation) and ductal occlusion, forming the primary lesion: the microcomedone / comedone.

3.  Colonisation of the occluded pilosebaceous duct by the anaerobic diphtheroid Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes), which hydrolyses sebum triglycerides into pro-inflammatory free fatty acids.

4.  Perifollicular inflammation and immune activation (via Toll-like receptor 2 and neutrophil chemotaxis), with ductal rupture into the dermis forming nodules and cysts.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Affects the face (99%), upper back (60%), and chest (15%).

•  Non-inflammatory lesions:Open comedones ("blackheads"—dilated follicles plugged with oxidised melanin/keratin) and closed comedones ("whiteheads"—flesh-coloured papules with no visible opening).

•  Inflammatory lesions: Erythematous papules, pustules, deep tender nodules, and pseudocysts, healing with atrophic "ice-pick" or boxcar scars, hyperpigmentation, or keloid scars.

•  Severe Variants:Acne conglobata (burrowing abscesses, interconnecting sinuses, and grouped polyporous comedones on the trunk, associated with hidradenitis suppurativa) and Acne fulminans (acute ulcerative truncal acne with fever, polyarthralgia, leukocytosis, and osteolytic bone lesions). (Exclude Polycystic Ovary Syndrome [PCOS] in women with acne, hirsutism, and oligomenorrhoea, and drug-induced acne from corticosteroids, lithium, phenytoin, or anabolic steroids).

•  Stepwise Treatment of Acne Vulgaris [KU 24]:

1.  Mild Acne (Comedonal or Mild Papulopustular) — Topical Therapy:

•  Topical Retinoids (First-line for comedonal acne):Adapalene (0.1% gel), Tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid), or Trifarotene—normalise follicular keratinisation and are comedolytic and anti-inflammatory (teratogenic; cause initial dryness/irritation).

•  Topical Benzoyl Peroxide (2.5%–10% gel): Potent antimicrobial against C. acnes (without inducing antibiotic resistance) and keratolytic; often combined in fixed-dose gels with Adapalene or Clindamycin.

•  Topical Antibiotics:Clindamycin (1%) or Erythromycin (2%)(must ALWAYS be combined with benzoyl peroxide or a topical retinoid, never used as monotherapy, to prevent bacterial resistance).

•  Topical Azelaic Acid (15%–20%): Anti-comedonal, antimicrobial, and reduces post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

2.  Moderate Inflammatory Acne (or Trunk Involvement) — Systemic Antibiotics + Topical Non-Antibiotic Therapy:

•  Oral Tetracyclines for 3–6 months (First-line):Lymecycline (408 mg once daily), Doxycycline (100 mg once daily) (warn of photosensitivity and oesophagitis), or Oxytetracycline (500 mg BD on an empty stomach). (Minocycline is avoided due to lupus, hepatitis, and slate-grey pigmentation; tetracyclines are contraindicated in children <12 years and pregnancy, where Oral Erythromycin or Trimethoprim is used).

•  Always combine oral antibiotics with topical Benzoyl Peroxide or Adapalene.

•  Hormonal Anti-Androgen Therapy (in Females): Combined oestrogen + cyproterone acetate oral contraceptive pill (Co-cyprindiol / Dianette) or Oral Spironolactone.

3.  Severe Nodulocystic, Scarring, or Antibiotic-Refractory Acne — Oral Isotretinoin:

•  Oral Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid, 0.5–1.0 mg/kg/day for 16–24 weeks, cumulative dose 120–150 mg/kg): The only drug that targets all four pathogenic factors of acne (shrinks sebaceous glands and reduces sebum excretion by >90%), achieving long-term cure/remission in >85%.

•  Mandatory Monitoring & Adverse Effects:

•  Extreme Teratogenicity: Mandatory Pregnancy Prevention Programme in females of childbearing potential (effective contraception for 1 month before, throughout, and for at least 1–2 months after stopping isotretinoin, with monthly negative pregnancy tests).

•  Mucocutaneous dryness (100%): Cheilitis (cracked lips), dry skin, dry eyes, epistaxis.

•  Biochemical:Hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, and elevated liver transaminases (monitor fasting lipids and LFTs at baseline and during therapy).

•  Psychiatric: Screen for and monitor depression, mood changes, suicidal ideation, and sexual dysfunction.

•  (Co-administer oral prednisolone in the first 2–4 weeks of isotretinoin in very severe acne/acne fulminans to prevent an initial explosive "isotretinoin flare", and never combine isotretinoin with tetracyclines due to the risk of idiopathic intracranial hypertension).

4.  Physical Treatments for Cysts & Scarring: Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injections into inflamed nodules/keloids; fractional CO2 laser resurfacing, chemical peels, or subcision for atrophic scars.

2. Rosacea: Clinical Features and Management [TU]:

•  Clinical Features: Chronic inflammatory dermatosis of the central convexities of the face (cheeks, nose, chin, and forehead) affecting fair-skinned middle-aged adults (F > M):

1.  Intermittent Facial Flushing triggered by sunlight, heat, hot drinks, spicy foods, and alcohol, progressing to persistent central facial erythema and telangiectasia.

2.  Inflammatory Papules and Pustules on the central face.

3.  Crucial Negative Sign (Distinction from Acne):COMPLETE ABSENCE of Comedones (blackheads/whiteheads) and normal sebum excretion.

4.  Phymatous Changes: Sebaceous gland hyperplasia and soft-tissue fibrosis of the nose (Rhinophyma—bulbous, lobulated nose, predominantly in men).

5.  Ocular Rosacea (30%–50%): Blepharitis, conjunctivitis, grittiness, episcleritis, and rosacea keratitis.

•  Management:

•  General: Avoid triggers (sunlight, alcohol, hot/spicy food), use daily SPF 50 sunscreen, and strictly avoid topical corticosteroids (which cause severe rebound steroid rosacea and perioral dermatitis).

•  Mild-to-Moderate Papulopustular Rosacea:Topical Metronidazole (0.75% gel), Topical Azelaic acid (15% gel), or Topical Ivermectin (1% cream—targets Demodex folliculorum mites).

•  Moderate-to-Severe or Ocular Rosacea:Oral Tetracyclines (Doxycycline 40 mg modified-release or 100 mg daily, or Lymecycline 408 mg daily) for 6–12 weeks (or low-dose oral isotretinoin if refractory).

•  Persistent Erythema, Telangiectasia & Rhinophyma:Topical Brimonidine (0.33% gel—α2-adrenergic vasoconstrictor for erythema), vascular pulsed-dye laser (for telangiectasia), and CO2 laser ablation or surgical shave excision (for rhinophyma).

3. Eczema (Dermatitis): Exogenous Eczema and Stepwise Management [KU 18, RGU]:

•  Classification of Eczema (Dermatitis):

•  Endogenous Eczema:Atopic eczema (associated with filaggrin gene mutations, high IgE, Th2 [IL-4/IL-13] inflammation, flexural distribution, and susceptibility to Staphylococcus aureus and Herpes simplex [eczema herpeticum]), Seborrhoeic eczema (Malassezia yeast overgrowth on scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, presternal chest), Discoid (nummular) eczema, Asteatotic eczema ("crazy-paving" dry skin on shins of the elderly), Gravitational (venous stasis) eczema, Pompholyx (vesicular palmoplantar eczema), and Lichen simplex chronicus.

•  Exogenous (Contact) Eczema [RGU]:

1.  Irritant Contact Dermatitis (80% of occupational hand eczema): Direct non-immunological cytotoxic damage to the epidermal barrier by water ("wet work"), soaps, detergents, alkalis, acids, solvents, or friction; affects anyone with sufficient exposure without prior sensitisation (atopic individuals are predisposed).

2.  Allergic Contact Dermatitis (Type IV Cell-Mediated Delayed Hypersensitivity): Requires prior sensitisation to a specific hapten/allergen (mediated by Langerhans cells and allergen-specific memory T lymphocytes); rash appears 48–72 hours after re-exposure at the site of contact and spreads secondarily.

•  Common Allergens:Nickel (jewellery, watch-straps, jean studs), Chromate (cement, leather), Paraphenylenediamine (PPD) (hair dye, black henna tattoos), Rubber chemicals (latex gloves, shoes), Colophony (sticking plasters), Fragrances / Balsam of Peru, Preservatives (Methylisothiazolinone, parabens), and topical Neomycin / Lanolin.

•  Confirmatory Investigation:Cutaneous Patch Testing (allergens applied to the upper back in Finn chambers for 48 hours and read at 48 and 96 hours).

3.  Photo-Allergic Contact Dermatitis & Chronic Actinic Dermatitis.

•  Stepwise Management of Eczema [KU 18] (Refer to Fig. 26.32):

1.  General Measures, Education & Trigger Avoidance: Identify and eliminate exogenous irritants and contact allergens; avoid soap (use emollient soap substitutes); keep fingernails short.

2.  Baseline Topical Therapy (Cornerstone for All Eczemas):

•  Frequent, Liberal Emollients: Greasy ointments (e.g., 50:50 white soft paraffin/liquid paraffin, emulsifying ointment) for dry/chronic lichenified eczema; creams/lotions for acute weeping eczema. Restores the stratum corneum barrier and reduces steroid requirements.

•  Topical Corticosteroids (Matched to Site and Severity using the Fingertip Unit guide):

•  Mild (Hydrocortisone 1%) or Moderate (Clobetasone butyrate 0.05% [Eumovate]) for the face, neck, flexures, and infants.

•  Potent (Betamethasone valerate 0.1% [Betnovate], Mometasone furoate 0.1% [Elocon]) or Very Potent (Clobetasol propionate 0.05% [Dermovate]) for thick, lichenified plaques on the trunk, limbs, palms, and soles.

•  Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors (Steroid-Sparing Agents):Tacrolimus (0.03%–0.1% ointment) or Pimecrolimus (1% cream)—inhibit T-cell activation without causing skin atrophy or striae; ideal for delicate sites (face, eyelids, and flexures).

•  Paste Bandages, Wet Wraps & Potassium Permanganate Soaks: Diluted potassium permanganate (1:10,000) soaks dry acute weeping/exudative eczema; zinc/ichthammol paste bandages and wet wraps soothe itch and prevent scratching.

3.  Treat Secondary Infections & Control Itch:

•  Bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus): Topical fusidic acid/antiseptics (mild) or Oral Flucloxacillin / Clarithromycin for 7 days.

•  Eczema Herpeticum (punched-out monomorphic vesicles/erosions from Herpes Simplex Virus): Dermatological emergency requiring immediate Systemic Aciclovir (oral or IV) and ophthalmological review if periorbital.

•  Nocturnal Itch: Short-term sedating oral H1-antihistamines (e.g., Hydroxyzine or Chlorphenamine at night).

4.  Second-Line Phototherapy:Narrowband UVB Phototherapy (or PUVA / UVA1; localized hand/foot PUVA or oral Alitretinoin for severe chronic hand eczema).

5.  Third-Line Systemic Immunosuppressants & Targeted Biologics (For Severe Refractory Atopic Eczema):

•  Conventional Systemic Immunosuppressants: Short-term Ciclosporin (rapid onset), Methotrexate, Azathioprine, or Mycophenolate mofetil.

•  Targeted Biologics (Th2 Cytokine Blockers):Dupilumab (monoclonal antibody blocking the IL-4 receptor α-subunit shared by IL-4 and IL-13) and Tralokinumab / Lebrikizumab (specific anti-IL-13 monoclonal antibodies).

•  Oral Janus Kinase (JAK) Inhibitors:Upadacitinib, Abrocitinib, and Baricitinib.

subject: medicine
title: 4. Psoriasis [KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 20, 18, 16, 15, TU]
text:
SECTION 30.7, 30.8 & 30.9 — PSORIASIS, LICHEN PLANUS, URTICARIA & DRUG ERUPTIONS

4. Psoriasis [KU 24, 23, 22, 21, 20, 18, 16, 15, TU]

(Covers the clinical vignette Essay on a 23-year-old male presenting with sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery mica-like scales over the elbows and scalp = Chronic Plaque Psoriasis).

1. Definition, Epidemiology & Aetiopathogenesis:

•  Definition: A common, chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory and hyperproliferative skin disease affecting 1.5%–3% of the population. Shows a bimodal age of onset: Type I (Early-onset, 15–30 years), which is strongly familial, severe, and associated with HLA-Cw6; and Type II (Late-onset, 50–60 years), which is sporadic and milder.

•  Pathogenesis & Exacerbating Triggers:

•  Genetics: Polygenic inheritance (70% concordance in monozygotic twins); major susceptibility locus is PSORS1 (HLA-Cw6) on chromosome 6p, alongside genes in the IL-23R, IL-12B, and NFκB pathways.

•  Immunopathogenesis: Triggered in genetically predisposed skin, dendritic cells secrete Interleukin-23 (IL-23) and IL-12, which drive the differentiation and activation of Th17 and Th1 T-lymphocytes. These T cells release IL-17A, IL-17F, IL-22, TNF-α, and IFN-γ, which stimulate keratinocyte hyperproliferation: the epidermal transit time from the basal layer to shedding from the stratum corneum is shortened from the normal 28 days down to just 4–5 days.

•  Histopathology (Refer to Fig. 26.35): (1) Parakeratosis (retention of keratinocyte nuclei in the thickened stratum corneum) and hyperkeratosis; (2) Regular clubbed elongation of the epidermal rete ridges (acanthosis) with thinning of the suprapapillary plates; (3) Munro’s microabscesses (collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum) and spongiform pustules of Kogoj; (4) Dilated, tortuous capillary loops in the dermal papillae (which bleed when scale is scraped off—Auspitz’s sign); and (5) Perivascular T-lymphocyte infiltrate in the upper dermis.

•  Precipitating / Exacerbating Factors:

1.  Cutaneous Trauma — The Köbner (Isomorphic) Phenomenon: Development of psoriatic plaques along sites of skin injury, scratches, surgical scars, or sunburn.

2.  Infections:β-haemolytic Streptococcal pharyngitis (triggers Guttate Psoriasis) and HIV infection (causes severe, refractory psoriasis).

3.  Drugs:Lithium, β-blockers, Antimalarials (chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine), NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and abrupt withdrawal of systemic or potent topical corticosteroids (which precipitates life-threatening rebound generalised pustular or erythrodermic psoriasis).

4.  Psychological stress, Cigarette smoking (strongly linked to palmoplantar pustulosis), Alcohol excess, and Obesity.

2. Clinical Types & Presentations of Psoriasis [KU 21, 20, 15, TU]:

1.  Chronic Plaque Psoriasis (Psoriasis Vulgaris — 85%–90% of cases):

•  Symmetrical, sharply demarcated, salmon-pink/erythematous plaques covered by adherent silvery-white mica-like scales. Gentle scraping of the scale produces a "candle-grease" sign and reveals pinpoint capillary bleeding points (Auspitz’s sign).

•  Predilection Sites:Extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees, lower back / sacrum, umbilicus, and scalp (60%—well-defined thick scaly plaques extending just beyond the hairline, without permanent alopecia).

2.  Guttate Psoriasis [KU 21, TU]:

•  Occurs predominantly in children, adolescents, and young adults 1–3 weeks after an acute group A β-haemolytic streptococcal throat infection.

•  Sudden, explosive eruption of numerous small (0.2–1.0 cm), raindrop-shaped ("guttate"), erythematous scaly papules and plaques scattered symmetrically over the trunk and proximal limbs. Often resolves spontaneously within 2–3 months, but responds rapidly to narrowband UVB phototherapy (and throat infection treatment); >50% later develop chronic plaque psoriasis.

3.  Flexural (Inverse) Psoriasis:

•  Affects the axillae, groins, submammary folds, umbilicus, and natal cleft. Because of moisture and friction, plaques are smooth, glazed, shiny, and beefy-red with NO surface scale (often fissured in the natal cleft; differential diagnosis is candidal intertrigo or tinea cruris).

4.  Pustular Psoriasis:

•  Localised Palmoplantar Pustulosis: Crops of sterile yellow pustules on an erythematous base on the palms and soles that dry into brown macules with scaling; strongly associated with cigarette smoking and middle-aged women.

•  Generalised Pustular Psoriasis (von Zumbusch type): Rare, acute life-threatening dermatological emergency (often triggered by abrupt withdrawal of systemic or potent topical corticosteroids; linked to IL-36RN pathway activation). Sheets of pinpoint sterile pustules erupt on fiery-red tender skin with high fever, malaise, leucocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, and hypocalcaemia.

5.  Erythrodermic Psoriasis:

•  Confluent erythema and scaling involving >90% of the body surface area (acute skin failure).

6.  Psoriatic Nail Disease [KU 20] (Occurs in 50% overall and 85% of those with psoriatic arthritis):

•  Coarse "thimble" pitting of the nail plate (due to parakeratotic foci in the proximal nail matrix).

•  Onycholysis: Distal separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, often bordered proximally by a salmon-pink/yellowish-brown "oil-drop" (salmon patch) discoloration.

•  Subungual hyperkeratosis, nail-plate crumbling/dystrophy, and splinter haemorrhages.

3. Differential Diagnosis of Plaque Psoriasis:

•  Seborrhoeic dermatitis, Discoid / Lichenified eczema, Tinea corporis (asymmetrical with central clearing; exclude by KOH scrapings), Pityriasis rosea (herald patch followed by a "fir-tree" truncal eruption of oval plaques with an inner collarette of scale [KU 18]), Lichen planus (violaceous papules with Wickham’s striae), Secondary syphilis, Bowen’s disease (solitary plaque), and Mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma).

4. Complications of Psoriasis [KU 23, TU]:

1.  Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA): Develops in sim 25% of patients (oligoarticular, symmetrical polyarticular, DIP-predominant, psoriatic spondylitis, or arthritis mutilans, with dactylitis and enthesitis).

2.  Erythrodermic Psoriasis & Generalised Pustular Psoriasis (Acute Skin Failure): Causes hypothermia or hyperpyrexia (loss of thermoregulation), dehydration and prerenal AKI (massive transepidermal water loss), high-output cardiac failure (generalised cutaneous vasodilatation), hypoalbuminaemia / peripheral oedema (protein loss from skin and protein-losing enteropathy), and secondary bacterial sepsis.

3.  Cardiometabolic Comorbidities: Strong association with Metabolic Syndrome (central obesity, Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, MASLD) and accelerated atherosclerosis (increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke).

4.  Severe Psychosocial Impact: Depression, anxiety, social stigmatisation, alcohol misuse, and impaired quality of life (measured by DLQI alongside PASI [Psoriasis Area and Severity Index]).

5. Stepwise Management of Psoriasis [KU 22, 20, 18] (Refer to Fig. 26.37):

1.  General Measures & Lifestyle: Patient education, cardiovascular risk factor modification (weight loss, smoking cessation, alcohol reduction), and liberal emollients (to soften scale and reduce fissuring).

2.  First-Line: Topical Therapies (For Localised Plaque Psoriasis):

•  Topical Vitamin D Analogues (First-Choice):Calcipotriol, Calcitriol, or Tacalcitol—inhibit keratinocyte proliferation and promote terminal differentiation (safe long-term; max 100 g/week of calcipotriol to avoid hypercalcaemia; often combined in a fixed once-daily ointment/gel/foam with Betamethasone dipropionate [e.g., Dovobet / Enstilar]).

•  Topical Corticosteroids: Mild/moderate steroids (or topical calcineurin inhibitors) for facial, flexural, and genital psoriasis; potent steroids (combined with salicylic acid or vitamin D analogue) for scalp and thick limb plaques. (Avoid prolonged unsupervised potent steroid monotherapy due to skin atrophy, tachyphylaxis, and rebound pustular psoriasis).

•  Coal Tar Preparations, Salicylic Acid (Keratolytic for thick scalp/plantar scale), and Short-Contact Dithranol (Anthralin) (stains skin/clothing brown-purple).

3.  Second-Line: Phototherapy (For Widespread Plaque or Guttate Psoriasis Unresponsive to Topicals):

•  Narrowband UVB Phototherapy (311 nm): First-choice phototherapy (2–3 times weekly for 6–8 weeks; highly effective in guttate and plaque psoriasis).

•  PUVA (Psoralen + UVA): Reserved for thick plaques failing UVB or palmoplantar pustulosis (carries cumulative squamous cell carcinoma risk).

4.  Third-Line: Conventional Systemic Non-Biologic Drugs (For Moderate-to-Severe Psoriasis [PASI ≥ 10, DLQI >10], Erythrodermic/Pustular Psoriasis, or Psoriatic Arthritis):

(Four Major Systemic Drugs [KU 22]):

1.  Methotrexate (15–25 mg once weekly PO/SC + Folic acid 5 mg weekly): Gold-standard first-line systemic agent, especially when psoriatic arthritis coexists. (Side-effects: myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity/fibrosis, pneumonitis, teratogenicity).

2.  Ciclosporin (2.5–5 mg/kg/day orally): Calcineurin inhibitor with a rapid onset of action; ideal for acute crisis induction in erythrodermic or unstable psoriasis and in women wishing to conceive (limit continuous use to <1 year due to nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and skin cancer risk).

3.  Acitretin (10–50 mg daily orally): Systemic oral retinoid (non-immunosuppressive); particularly effective in pustular psoriasis, erythrodermic psoriasis, palmoplantar hyperkeratotic psoriasis, and combined with UVB/PUVA (Re-PUVA). (Side-effects: mucocutaneous dryness, hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatotoxicity, and severe teratogenicity—women must avoid pregnancy during treatment and for 2–3 YEARS after stopping acitretin).

4.  Fumaric Acid Esters (Dimethyl fumarate) & Oral Targeted Small Molecules:Apremilast (PDE4 inhibitor, 30 mg BD) and Deucravacitinib (oral selective TYK2 inhibitor).

5.  Fourth-Line: Targeted Biologic Therapies (For Severe Psoriasis Failing Phototherapy and Conventional Systemics; Screen for Latent TB, HBV, HCV, and HIV First):

•  TNF-α Inhibitors:Adalimumab, Infliximab (rapidly effective in generalised pustular/erythrodermic psoriasis), Etanercept, Certolizumab.

•  Anti-IL-12/23 (p40) Antibody:Ustekinumab.

•  Specific Anti-IL-23 (p19) Antibodies:Guselkumab, Risankizumab, Tildrakizumab(among the most effective agents for achieving PASI-90 clearance).

•  Anti-IL-17A, Anti-IL-17A/F & Anti-IL-17 Receptor Antibodies:Secukinumab, Ixekizumab, Bimekizumab, and Brodalumab(rapid, high-level skin and joint clearance; Spesolimab [anti-IL-36R] is targeted for generalised pustular psoriasis).

subject: medicine
title: 5. Lichen Planus, Urticaria, and Drug Eruptions [KU 25, 21, 18, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
5. Lichen Planus, Urticaria, and Drug Eruptions [KU 25, 21, 18, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

1. Lichen Planus [KU 25, TU]:

•  Pathogenesis & Associations: An idiopathic, autoimmune CD8+ T-lymphocyte–mediated inflammatory disorder targeting basal keratinocytes. Associated with Hepatitis C (and Hepatitis B) virus infection, autoimmune liver diseases (primary biliary cholangitis), ulcerative colitis, alopecia areata, thymoma/myasthenia gravis, and Lichenoid Drug Eruptions (gold, antimalarials, thiazides, β-blockers, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors).

•  Clinical Features (The "6 Ps": Planar, Purple, Polygonal, Pruritic, Papules, and Plaques):

•  Cutaneous Lesions:Intensely itchy, flat-topped, shiny, violaceous (purple) polygonal papules, crossed on their surface by a characteristic fine, lacy white network of striae known as Wickham’s striae.

•  Distribution: Symmetrical involvement of the flexor aspects of the wrists and forearms, shins/ankles (where thick hypertrophic lichen planus plaques develop), and lumbar back. Exhibits the Köbner phenomenon (new linear papules appearing along scratch marks). Resolves over 12–18 months leaving prominent post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

•  Mucosal Involvement (30%–70%): Asymptomatic white, lacy, reticulate network on the buccal mucosa and tongue, or painful erosive oral/genital lichen planus (chronic erosive oral/vulval LP carries a small risk of squamous cell carcinoma).

•  Nail (10%) & Scalp Involvement: Longitudinal nail ridging/thinning (trachyonychia) and dorsal pterygium (scarring fusion of proximal nail fold to nail bed); scalp involvement (lichen planopilaris) causes permanent scarring alopecia.

•  Histopathology: Hyperkeratosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, liquefactive degeneration of the basal epidermal layer with apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte / colloid bodies), "saw-tooth" rete ridges, and a dense band-like ("lichenoid") T-lymphocyte infiltrate hugging the dermo-epidermal junction.

•  Management: Stop any offending drug and screen for Hepatitis B/C. Potent or very potent topical corticosteroids (under occlusion or intralesional triamcinolone for hypertrophic plaques; steroid mouthwashes/pastes for oral LP) + sedating antihistamines. Extensive or erosive disease is treated with short-course oral Prednisolone, narrowband UVB / PUVA, Acitretin, or immunosuppressants (ciclosporin, methotrexate, mycophenolate).

2. Urticaria [KU 21, 16, 15, TU, RGU]:

•  Definition & Pathophysiology: Characterised by transient, pruritic, erythematous oedematous weals ("hives") caused by localised upper dermal vasodilatation and increased capillary permeability (when deeper subcutaneous/submucosal tissues of the lips, eyelids, tongue, or larynx are involved, it is termed Angioedema).

•  Driven by dermal mast cell degranulation with release of histamine, prostaglandins (PGD2), leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4), and platelet-activating factor.

•  Crucial Diagnostic Rule: Individual urticarial weals are evanescent and resolve completely within <24 hours without leaving bruising(if individual weals persist >24 hours, are painful/burning rather than itchy, and leave residual purpura/bruising, the diagnosis is Urticarial Vasculitis—check complement C3/C4, ANA, and skin biopsy). Classified as Acute Urticaria (<6 weeks) or Chronic Urticaria (≥ 6 weeks).

•  Causes of Urticaria ([RGU]):

1.  Chronic Spontaneous (Idiopathic / Autoimmune) Urticaria (>50% of chronic cases): Up to 40% are caused by functional IgG autoantibodies directed against the high-affinity IgE receptor (FcεRI) or against IgE on mast cells.

2.  IgE-Mediated Allergic (Type I Hypersensitivity) Urticaria: Foods (nuts, shellfish, fish, eggs, milk, strawberries), Drugs (penicillins, cephalosporins), insect venom stings (bee/wasp), latex, aeroallergens.

3.  Direct Non-Immunological Chemical Mast-Cell Degranulators / Pseudoallergy:Aspirin and NSAIDs (inhibit COX-1, diverting arachidonic acid to leukotrienes), Opiates (morphine, codeine), radiocontrast media, vancomycin, benzoates/salicylates. (Note: ACE Inhibitors [ramipril, lisinopril] cause isolated bradykinin-mediated angioedema without urticarial weals, as does Hereditary Angioedema [C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency]).

4.  Physical / Inducible Urticarias:Symptomatic Dermographism (linear wealing on firm stroking of skin), Cholinergic urticaria (tiny itchy papules triggered by heat, exercise, and sweating), Delayed pressure urticaria, Cold urticaria, Solar urticaria, and Aquagenic urticaria.

5.  Infections & Systemic Diseases: Viral infections (commonest cause of acute urticaria in children; prodromal Hepatitis B, EBV), parasitic helminth infections, autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto’s/Graves’), and SLE.

•  Management of Urticaria:

•  Identify and avoid triggers (stop aspirin, NSAIDs, codeine, and ACE inhibitors; cooling menthol cream).

•  First-Line Pharmacotherapy:Second-generation Non-Sedating Oral H1-Antihistamines—e.g., Cetirizine (10 mg OD), Loratadine (10 mg OD), or Fexofenadine (180 mg OD).

•  Second-Line (if unresponsive after 2 weeks):Up-titrate the non-sedating H1-antihistamine up to 4× the standard licensed daily dose; may add an H2-blocker (famotidine) or leukotriene receptor antagonist (Montelukast). (Short 3–5 day rescue courses of oral Prednisolone are reserved only for severe acute flares/angioedema).

•  Third-Line Targeted Biologic Therapy (for antihistamine-refractory Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria):Omalizumab (recombinant humanised monoclonal anti-IgE antibody, 300 mg SC every 4 weeks) or Ciclosporin / narrowband UVB. (Life-threatening anaphylaxis/laryngeal angioedema requires immediate IM Adrenaline 0.5 mg [1:1000] and carriage of an adrenaline auto-injector [EpiPen]).

3. Mechanisms of Cutaneous Drug Eruptions & Fixed Drug Eruption [KU 18, 17]:

•  Mechanisms of Drug Eruptions [KU 18]:

•  A. Non-Immunological (Predictable): Direct pharmacological/toxic effects (striae with steroids, acne with lithium/EGFR inhibitors), direct chemical mast-cell degranulation (urticaria with aspirin/NSAIDs/opiates), bradykinin accumulation (angioedema with ACE inhibitors), phototoxicity (exaggerated sunburn with doxycycline, amiodarone, thiazides, phenothiazines), or drug/metabolite deposition (slate-grey pigmentation with amiodarone/minocycline).

•  B. Immunological (Unpredictable / Idiosyncratic — Gell and Coombs Types I–IV):

1.  Type I (Immediate IgE-mediated):Urticaria, angioedema, and anaphylaxis (penicillins, cephalosporins).

2.  Type II (Cytotoxic antibody-mediated): Thrombocytopenic purpura (quinine, heparin).

3.  Type III (Immune-complex mediated):Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (palpable purpura), serum sickness, erythema nodosum (sulphonamides, penicillins, allopurinol, thiazides).

4.  Type IV (Delayed T-cell mediated — appears 4–21 days after starting drug):Exanthematous / morbilliform maculopapular eruption (most common drug rash: aminopenicillins, anticonvulsants, sulphonamides, allopurinol), Lichenoid eruption, Acute Generalised Exanthematous Pustulosis (AGEP), DRESS syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), Erythema multiforme, and Stevens–Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN).

•  Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE) [KU 17]:

•  Pathogenesis: A distinctive variant of delayed Type IV hypersensitivity mediated by intra-epidermal resident memory CD8+ T cells that remain permanently localised at a specific anatomical skin site.

•  Clinical Features: Characterised by one or a few sharply demarcated, round or oval erythematous/violaceous oedematous plaques (sometimes with a central blister) that recur at the EXACT SAME ANATOMICAL SITE(S) within 30 minutes to 8 hours every time the offending drug is ingested, and heal with persistent slate-brown post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Predilection sites are the glans penis/genitalia, lips, hands, and feet.

•  Common Culprit Drugs:Tetracyclines (doxycycline), Sulphonamides (co-trimoxazole), NSAIDs (naproxen, ibuprofen, paracetamol), Penicillins, Quinine, Fluconazole, Metronidazole, and Barbiturates.

•  Management: Permanent identification and withdrawal of the culprit drug, plus potent topical corticosteroids for acute lesions.

title: 6. Blistering (Bullous) Diseases: Pemphigus Vulgaris, Bullous Pemphigoid, Erythema Multiforme, and SJS / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) [KU 24, 20, 19, 18, TU]
text:
SECTION 30.10, 30.11, 30.12 & 30.13 — BULLOUS DISEASES, PIGMENTATION, & SKIN IN SYSTEMIC DISEASE

6. Blistering (Bullous) Diseases: Pemphigus Vulgaris, Bullous Pemphigoid, Erythema Multiforme, and SJS / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) [KU 24, 20, 19, 18, TU]

1. Causes of Acquired Bullous Lesions [TU]:

1.  Immunobullous Disorders:

•  Intra-epidermal:Pemphigus vulgaris, Pemphigus foliaceus, Paraneoplastic pemphigus.

•  Subepidermal:Bullous pemphigoid, Dermatitis herpetiformis, Linear IgA bullous dermatosis, Pemphigoid gestationis, Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, Bullous SLE.

2.  Severe Cutaneous Adverse Drug / Reactive Disorders:Stevens–Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN), Bullous Erythema Multiforme, Fixed drug eruption.

3.  Infections:Bullous impetigo and Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) (S. aureus exfoliative toxin), Herpes simplex, Herpes zoster, bullous erysipelas/cellulitis, bullous tinea pedis.

4.  Metabolic, Inflammatory & Physical:Porphyria cutanea tarda and Pseudoporphyria (naproxen, furosemide), Acute severe contact/pompholyx eczema, Insect bite reactions, Bullous diabeticorum, friction/thermal burns, and severe lower limb oedema.

2. Pemphigus Vulgaris (vs. Bullous Pemphigoid) [KU 24, 20, TU]:

•  Pathogenesis of Pemphigus Vulgaris:

•  An autoimmune intra-epidermal blistering disease (onset age 40–60 years) caused by pathogenic IgG1 and IgG4 autoantibodies directed against Desmoglein-3 and Desmoglein-1 (transmembrane cadherin adhesion proteins of desmosomes that hold epidermal keratinocytes together).

•  Autoantibody binding disrupts desmosomal adhesion, causing separation of keratinocytes (acantholysis) just above the basal layer (suprabasal intra-epidermal split). (In Pemphigus foliaceus, antibodies target Desmoglein-1 only, causing a very superficial subcorneal split with scaly crusted erosions and NO mucosal involvement).

•  Clinical Features of Pemphigus Vulgaris [KU 20]:

1.  Universal Mucosal Involvement (100%):Painful, ragged oral mucosal erosions (buccal mucosa, palate, gingiva, lips) are the presenting feature in 50%–70% of patients, often preceding skin lesions by several months and causing severe odynophagia. Pharyngeal, laryngeal, conjunctival, and genital mucosae may also be eroded.

2.  Cutaneous Flaccid Blisters & Extensive Erosions: Because the split is intra-epidermal, the blister roof is thin and fragile; flaccid, thin-walled bullae arise on normal or erythematous skin (scalp, face, chest, back, flexures) and rupture easily, leaving large, raw, painful, weeping, crusted erosions that bleed easily and heal without scarring.

3.  Positive Nikolsky’s Sign: Sliding lateral finger pressure on perilesional normal-looking skin shears off and detaches the superficial epidermis (and direct vertical pressure on an intact blister causes it to extend laterally—Asboe-Hansen sign).

•  Investigations & Comparison with Bullous Pemphigoid:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-027]]

•  Management of Pemphigus Vulgaris:

•  Supportive Care: Inpatient care if extensive (similar to burns), meticulous oral hygiene, antiseptic/steroid mouthwashes, non-adherent dressings, fluid/protein balance, and prompt treatment of secondary infection.

•  First-Line Systemic Therapy:High-Dose Oral Prednisolone (1.0 mg/kg/day) (or pulsed IV methylprednisolone) COMBINED WITH Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, 1000 mg IV × 2 infusions 2 weeks apart)—Rituximab + steroids is now the gold-standard first-line regimen achieving high rates of complete remission off steroids.

•  Steroid-Sparing Immunosuppressants:Azathioprine, Mycophenolate mofetil, or Cyclophosphamide (plus IVIg or plasmapheresis in refractory cases). (Note: Bullous pemphigoid is treated with super-potent topical clobetasol propionate, oral Doxycycline 200 mg/day [anti-inflammatory], or lower-dose oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day + azathioprine).

3. Erythema Multiforme, Stevens–Johnson Syndrome (SJS), and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) [KU 19, 18, TU]:

•  A. Erythema Multiforme (EM) [KU 19, TU]:

•  Aetiology (Provoking Factors): An acute, immune-mediated mucocutaneous reaction most commonly (>70%–80%) triggered by Infections, especially Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Orf, EBV, and Hepatitis B; less commonly triggered by Drugs (sulphonamides, penicillins, carbamazepine, barbiturates, NSAIDs) or connective tissue disease/malignancy.

•  Clinical Features: Symmetrical eruption of pathognomonic "Target" ("Bull’s-eye" or "Iris") lesions predominantly on the acral extensor surfaces, palms, and soles. A typical target lesion has three concentric zones: a dusky purpuric/blistered centre, a pale oedematous middle ring, and an outer erythematous halo. EM minor spares mucosae; EM major has target lesions plus involvement of one mucosal site (lips/mouth). Self-limiting over 2–3 weeks; treated symptomatically with topical steroids, oral antihistamines, and continuous oral Aciclovir prophylaxis (400 mg BD) for recurrent HSV-associated EM.

•  B. Stevens–Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) [KU 18, TU]:

•  Definition & Pathophysiology: SJS and TEN represent a single, life-threatening, drug-induced mucocutaneous disease spectrum characterised by widespread keratinocyte apoptosis and full-thickness epidermal necrosis mediated by drug-specific cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and NK cells releasing granulysin, perforin/granzyme B, and Fas ligand (FasL).

•  Stevens–Johnson Syndrome (SJS): Epidermal detachment involving <10% of Body Surface Area (BSA).

•  SJS–TEN Overlap: Epidermal detachment involving 10%–30% of BSA.

•  Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN): Epidermal detachment involving >30% of BSA (mortality 25%–35%).

•  Major Causative Drugs (Onset typically 1–4 weeks after starting the drug):

1.  Anticonvulsants:Carbamazepine, Lamotrigine, Phenytoin, Phenobarbital.

2.  Antibiotics:Sulphonamides (Co-trimoxazole), penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones.

3.  Allopurinol (most common cause in Europe/Asia).

4.  NSAIDs (especially oxicam derivatives like piroxicam) and Nevirapine (antiretroviral).

•  Clinical Features & Diagnosis:

•  Prodrome (1–3 days): Fever, malaise, sore throat, stinging eyes, and prominent skin pain/tenderness (early warning sign).

•  Cutaneous Lesions: Dusky-red or purpuric macules and atypical flat targets starting on the trunk and face, rapidly coalescing into flaccid blisters and full-thickness sheets of necrotic epidermis that peel off like wet tissue paper (strongly positive Nikolsky’s sign), exposing raw, bleeding dermis.

•  Severe Haemorrhagic Mucosal Involvement (>90%): Painful haemorrhagic crusting and ulceration of at least two mucosal surfaces—lips/oral cavity, conjunctivae/cornea (pseudomembranous conjunctivitis, symblepharon, corneal ulceration, and permanent blindness), genitalia/urethra, and respiratory/GI tracts.

•  Histopathology (Skin Biopsy):Full-thickness epidermal necrosis with subepidermal split and sparse dermal lymphocytic infiltrate, and negative direct immunofluorescence (distinguishing TEN from SSSS [subcorneal split] and pemphigus [positive DIF]).

•  SCORTEN Prognostic Severity Score (7 Variables — 1 point each): (1) Age >40 years; (2) Heart rate >120 bpm; (3) Underlying malignancy; (4) Detached BSA >10% on Day 1; (5) Serum Urea >10 mmol/L; (6) Serum Bicarbonate <20 mmol/L; (7) Blood Glucose ≥ 14 mmol/L. (Mortality rises from 3% for score 0–1, to 35% for score 3, and 90% for score ≥ 5).

•  Management of SJS / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis:

1.  Immediate Identification and Permanent Withdrawal of the Culprit Drug.

2.  Urgent Transfer to an Intensive Care Unit (ICU) or Specialist Burns Unit (nursed in a warm environment [30^circ–32^circC] on an air-fluidised pressure-relieving bed with reverse-barrier nursing).

3.  Aggressive Fluid, Electrolyte, and Nutritional Support: Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation (guided by urine output, CVP, and Parkland-style formulas) to replace massive insensible fluid/protein losses, and early nasogastric enteral nutrition.

4.  Skin & Wound Care: Gentle handling to avoid shearing skin; leave intact blister roofs in situ as biological dressings; apply frequent bland greasy emollients (50:50 white soft paraffin/liquid paraffin) and non-adherent silicone/paraffin gauze dressings. Do not give prophylactic systemic antibiotics; monitor skin/blood cultures daily and treat proven sepsis promptly.

5.  Mandatory Urgent Ophthalmology & Urogenital Care: Daily ophthalmology review with preservative-free lubricating eye drops, topical antibiotic/steroid drops, sweeping of the fornices, or amniotic membrane transplantation to prevent synechiae and blindness; urethral catheterisation and topical steroids to prevent urethral/vaginal strictures.

6.  Immunomodulatory Therapy:Ciclosporin, Etanercept (anti-TNF-α), or IVIg/corticosteroids are used in some specialist centres, though supportive ICU/burns care remains the primary determinant of survival.

title: 7. Disorders of Pigmentation (Vitiligo, Hypopigmentation, Hyperpigmentation) [KU 22, 18, RGU]
text:
7. Disorders of Pigmentation (Vitiligo, Hypopigmentation, Hyperpigmentation) [KU 22, 18, RGU]

1. Causes of Hypopigmented / Depigmented Patches on the Skin [KU 22]:

1.  Vitiligo (complete autoimmune loss of melanocytes; chalk-white depigmented macules).

2.  Pityriasis (Tinea) Versicolor (Malassezia yeast infection; finely scaly hypopigmented macules on upper trunk).

3.  Leprosy (Hansen’s Disease — Mycobacterium leprae): Hypopigmented or erythematous anaesthetic patches with loss of sensation and thickened peripheral nerves (tuberculoid/borderline leprosy).

4.  Post-Inflammatory Hypopigmentation (following eczema, psoriasis, burns, or cryotherapy) and Pityriasis Alba (ill-defined hypopigmented, slightly scaly patches on the cheeks of children with atopic eczema).

5.  Genetic & Miscellaneous:Tuberous sclerosis (congenital ash-leaf macules, best seen under Wood’s light), Oculocutaneous albinism (tyrosinase defect), Piebaldism (white forelock), Halo naevus, Lichen sclerosus, and idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis.

2. Vitiligo & Its Management [RGU]:

•  Pathogenesis & Associations: Acquired idiopathic disorder affecting 1% of the world’s population, caused by autoimmune cell-mediated (CD8+ T cell / IFN-γ–JAK-STAT pathway) destruction of epidermal melanocytes. Positive family history in 20%–30%. Strongly associated with other organ-specific autoimmune diseases: Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, Graves’ disease), Pernicious anaemia, Addison’s disease, Type 1 diabetes mellitus, and Alopecia areata.

•  Clinical Features:

•  Non-Segmental (Generalised) Vitiligo (90%): Symmetrical, sharply demarcated, milky/chalk-white depigmented macules and patches (accentuated under Wood’s UV light) with completely normal skin surface texture (no scaling) and normal sensation (unlike leprosy).

•  Predilection Sites:Extensor bony prominences (dorsum of hands, fingers, wrists, knees, elbows, shins), periorificial areas (around the eyes, mouth, nostrils, umbilicus, and genitalia), and flexures. Exhibits the Köbner phenomenon at sites of trauma or sunburn.

•  Segmental Vitiligo (10%): Unilateral, quasi-dermatomal distribution, usually in childhood; stabilises early.

•  Prognostic Indicators:Leucotrichia (white hairs within the patch, indicating loss of the follicular melanocyte reservoir) and acral hand/foot lesions carry a poor prognosis for repigmentation, whereas facial/truncal lesions and perifollicular pigment islands carry a good prognosis.

•  Management of Vitiligo:

1.  General Measures: Screen for thyroid disease (TFTs) and pernicious anaemia; provide psychological support, SPF 50 broad-spectrum sunscreens (to prevent sunburn of amelanotic patches and reduce tanning contrast of surrounding normal skin), and cosmetic camouflage (e.g., Dermablend).

2.  First-Line Topical Therapy (for Localised Vitiligo):

•  Potent or Very Potent Topical Corticosteroids (e.g., mometasone or clobetasol propionate) applied intermittently for 1–3 months.

•  Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors:Tacrolimus (0.1% ointment) or Pimecrolimus (1% cream)—preferred on the face, eyelids, neck, and flexures to avoid steroid-induced skin atrophy.

•  Topical Janus Kinase (JAK) Inhibitor:Ruxolitinib (1.5% cream)—blocks IFN-γ–JAK1/2 signalling and induces facial/body repigmentation.

3.  Second-Line Phototherapy (Most Effective Treatment for Generalised Vitiligo):

•  Narrowband UVB Phototherapy (311 nm) (2–3× weekly for 6–12 months; stimulates migration of melanocytes from hair follicle outer root sheaths, producing perifollicular repigmentation) or 308 nm Excimer Laser for localised patches (or PUVA).

4.  Surgical & Depigmenting Options:

•  Autologous Melanocyte Surgical Grafting (split-skin, punch, or suction-blister roof grafts) for stable, treatment-resistant segmental or focal vitiligo (stable for ≥ 12 months without Köbnerisation).

•  Depigmentation of Remaining Normal Skin (using topical monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone) in patients with >80%–90% body surface involvement.

3. Causes of Hyperpigmentation (Medical & Drug-Induced) [KU 18, RGU, TU]:

1.  Endocrine & Metabolic Disorders (Skin Changes in Endocrine Disease [TU]):

•  Addison’s Disease (Primary Adrenal Insufficiency) & Nelson’s Syndrome: Excess pituitary pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), ACTH, and α-MSH stimulate melanocytes, causing generalised bronze/brown hypermelanosis accentuated on sun-exposed areas, palmar creases, knuckles, buccal mucosa, gums, and recent scars.

•  Cushing’s Syndrome (Ectopic ACTH / Pituitary-dependent): ACTH-induced hyperpigmentation, plus thin atrophic skin, easy bruising, wide purple abdominal striae, facial plethora, hirsutism, and steroid acne.

•  Pregnancy & Oral Contraceptive Pill:Melasma (Chloasma)—symmetrical blotchy brown facial pigmentation over cheeks, forehead, and upper lip, plus darkening of the linea nigra and areolae.

•  Diabetes Mellitus & Insulin Resistance:Acanthosis nigricans, Necrobiosis lipoidica (waxy yellow atrophic plaques on shins), Diabetic dermopathy (pigmented shin spots), eruptive xanthomas, and neuropathic foot ulcers.

•  Thyroid Disease:Hyperthyroidism: Warm moist skin, palmar erythema, pretibial myxoedema, diffuse hyperpigmentation, onycholysis (Plummer’s nails), diffuse alopecia. Hypothyroidism: Pale, cool, dry, puffy myxoedematous skin, yellowish carotenaemia, and loss of outer third of eyebrows (Madarosis).

2.  Systemic & Nutritional Diseases:

•  Genetic Haemochromatosis ("Bronzed Diabetes"): Leaden/slate-grey bronze pigmentation due to combined haemosiderin and melanin deposition.

•  Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) and Chronic Renal Failure (uraemic pigmentation).

•  Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (photo-exposed hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis, and blistering).

•  Vitamin B12 Deficiency (knuckle and palmar crease hyperpigmentation) and Pellagra (niacin deficiency—photosensitive Casal’s necklace).

•  Systemic Sclerosis ("salt-and-pepper" dyspigmentation) and Whipple’s disease.

3.  Drug-Induced Hyperpigmentation:Amiodarone (slate-grey on photo-exposed face), Minocycline (blue-grey on shins/scars), Antimalarials (chloroquine [blue-grey], mepacrine [yellow]), Clofazimine (red-brown), Cytotoxic chemotherapy (bleomycin ["flagellate" linear streaks], busulfan), Phenothiazines, and heavy metals (silver [argyria], arsenic ["raindrop" pigmentation]).
