title: 8. Skin Manifestations in General Medicine: Acanthosis Nigricans, Pyoderma Gangrenosum, Cutaneous Tuberculosis, Dermatomyositis, and Sarcoidosis [KU 22, 21, 20, 18, 17, TU]
text:
8. Skin Manifestations in General Medicine: Acanthosis Nigricans, Pyoderma Gangrenosum, Cutaneous Tuberculosis, Dermatomyositis, and Sarcoidosis [KU 22, 21, 20, 18, 17, TU]

1. Acanthosis Nigricans [KU 22, 21, 17]:

•  Clinical Appearance: Symmetrical, velvety, papillomatous, dark-brown to black hyperkeratotic plaques affecting body flexures—most commonly the posterior and lateral neck, axillae, groins, and inframammary folds.

•  Pathogenesis: Driven by high circulating insulin or transforming growth factor-alpha (TGF-α) activating Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 Receptors (IGF-1R) and Epidermal Growth Factor Receptors (EGFR) on epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts, stimulating papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis.

•  Underlying Causes / Associations:

1.  Benign / Insulin-Resistance Associated (Most Common):Obesity (pseudo-acanthosis nigricans—regresses with weight loss), Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Metabolic Syndrome, and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) (HAIR-AN syndrome).

2.  Endocrine Disorders:Acromegaly, Cushing’s syndrome, hypothyroidism.

3.  Malignant (Paraneoplastic) Acanthosis Nigricans: Sudden-onset, rapidly progressive, extensive, and pruritic acanthosis nigricans in a non-obese middle-aged/older adult, often involving the lips, oral mucosa, and palms ("tripe palms"). In >80%–90% of malignant cases, the underlying tumour is an intra-abdominal Adenocarcinoma, most classically Gastric Adenocarcinoma (also pancreatic, colonic, lung, or ovarian cancer).

4.  Drugs: Nicotinic acid, systemic glucocorticoids, oral contraceptives.

2. Pyoderma Gangrenosum [KU 18]:

•  Pathogenesis: An uncommon, non-infective neutrophilic dermatosis (autoinflammatory disorder). Exhibits pathergy (lesions are triggered or worsened by minor trauma or surgical debridement).

•  Clinical Features: Starts as a painful erythematous nodule or sterile pustule (most commonly on the lower legs or peristomal skin) that rapidly breaks down centrally to form a deep, necrotic ulcer with a characteristic boggy, purulent base and a ragged, undermined, violaceous (purplish-blue) overhanging border, healing with cribriform ("sieve-like") scarring.

•  Systemic Disease Associations (Present in 50%–70% of cases):

1.  Inflammatory Bowel Disease:Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn’s Disease (most common association).

2.  Inflammatory Arthritis:Rheumatoid Arthritis and seronegative spondyloarthritis.

3.  Haematological Malignancies & Dyscrasias:Acute and chronic myeloid leukaemia, myelodysplasia, multiple myeloma, and monoclonal gammopathy (IgA).

•  Management: Avoid surgical debridement (worsens ulcer via pathergy); gentle wound dressings, analgesia, potent topical/intralesional steroids for small lesions, and First-Line Systemic Immunosuppression with High-Dose Oral Prednisolone (0.5–1 mg/kg/day) OR Oral Ciclosporin (4–5 mg/kg/day) (proven equally effective in the STOP GAP trial), or Anti-TNF-α Biologics (Infliximab / Adalimumab) (especially when associated with IBD).

3. Cutaneous Manifestations of Tuberculosis [KU 20]:

(Determined by route of inoculation and host cell-mediated immunity; histology shows caseating granulomas):

1.  Lupus Vulgaris (Paucibacillary — High Immunity): Commonest chronic progressive form, usually on the head and neck; reddish-brown plaque that reveals characteristic "apple-jelly" nodules on diascopy (pressing with a glass slide) and heals with central atrophic scarring (risk of Marjolin’s squamous cell carcinoma).

2.  Scrofuloderma (Multibacillary — Contiguous Spread): Breakdown of skin overlying a tuberculous lymph node (especially cervical), bone, or joint, forming undermined ulcers and discharging sinuses.

3.  Tuberculosis Verrucosa Cutis ("Warty TB" — Direct Exogenous Inoculation in Previously Sensitised Host): Hyperkeratotic warty plaque on the hands or feet (e.g., prosector’s wart in pathologists/butchers).

4.  Tuberculous Chancre (primary inoculation ulcer in an unsensitised host) & Acute Miliary Tuberculosis of the Skin (in immunosuppressed/HIV).

5.  Tuberculids (Hypersensitivity Reactions to Haematogenous TB Antigens — Organisms Absent on Stain):

•  Erythema Induratum of Bazin: Ulcerating lobular panniculitis on the posterior calves of women.

•  Papulonecrotic Tuberculid, Lichen Scrofulosorum, and Erythema Nodosum (septal panniculitis on shins).

•  Treatment: Standard 6-month quadruple Anti-Tuberculous Chemotherapy (2HRZE / 4HR).

4. Clinical Features of Dermatomyositis & Sarcoidosis [TU]:

•  Four Classic Clinical Features of Dermatomyositis [TU]:

1.  Heliotrope Rash: Violaceous (lilac-purple) erythema and oedema of the upper eyelids and periorbital skin.

2.  Gottron’s Papules: Violaceous, flat-topped scaly papules/plaques over the dorsal knuckles (MCP, PIP, and DIP joints).

3.  Photosensitive "Shawl Sign" (posterior neck, shoulders, upper back) and "V-Sign" (anterior chest) Erythema, plus ragged cuticles with dilated, tortuous periungual nail-fold capillary loops and mechanic’s hands (hyperkeratotic fissuring on lateral fingers in anti-Jo-1 antisynthetase syndrome).

4.  Symmetrical Proximal Muscle Weakness (difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, or lifting arms overhead, with raised CK, Interstitial Lung Disease [anti-Jo-1], and a strong association with underlying occult malignancy [lung, ovarian, breast, GI] in adults >40 years).

•  Four Clinical Features of Sarcoidosis [TU]:

(Multisystem disorder characterised by non-caseating epithelioid granulomas):

1.  Pulmonary & Mediastinal (90%):Bilateral Hilar Lymphadenopathy (BHL), pulmonary infiltrates, and upper-lobe interstitial pulmonary fibrosis (Stages I–IV on CXR).

2.  Cutaneous (30%):Erythema nodosum (acute painful red nodules on shins; part of Löfgren’s syndrome = Erythema nodosum + Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + Fever + Acute ankle polyarthralgia, which has an excellent self-limiting prognosis), Lupus pernio (chronic indurated violaceous plaques on the nose, cheeks, and ears), and scar sarcoidosis (infiltration of old scars/tattoos).

3.  Ocular (25%) & Neurological (5%):Anterior and posterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, parotid enlargement (Heerfordt’s syndrome = Anterior uveitis + Parotid swelling + Facial nerve palsy + Fever), bilateral LMN 7th cranial nerve palsy, basal meningitis, and arginine vasopressin deficiency (diabetes insipidus).

4.  Metabolic, Cardiac & Systemic:Hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria (macrophage 1α-hydroxylase autonomously converts 25(OH)D to 1,25(OH)2D), elevated serum ACE level, cardiac conduction blocks/arrhythmias, and hepatosplenomegaly. (Treated with oral Prednisolone 20–40 mg/day if vital organ involvement, hypercalcaemia, or progressive lung disease is present).

subject: medicine
title: 1. Hallucinations, Delusions, Classification of Psychotropic Drugs, Antipsychotics, Antidepressants, Mood Stabilisers (Lithium), and Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) [KU 23, 22, 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
CHAPTER 31 — MEDICAL PSYCHIATRY

SECTION 31.1 & 31.2 — PRESENTING PROBLEMS & PRINCIPLES OF MANAGEMENT

1. Hallucinations, Delusions, Classification of Psychotropic Drugs, Antipsychotics, Antidepressants, Mood Stabilisers (Lithium), and Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) [KU 23, 22, 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]

A. Hallucinations and Delusions [TU, RGU]:

•  Hallucinations:

•  Definition: A sensory perception experienced in the absence of any external stimulus (perceived as originating in external objective space with the quality of a real perception; distinct from an illusion, which is a misperception of a real external stimulus, and a pseudohallucination, which is perceived inside the mind’s eye). (Note: Hypnagogic [falling asleep] and Hypnopompic [waking up] hallucinations are normal physiological phenomena, also seen in narcolepsy).

•  Modalities & Clinical Significance:

•  Auditory Hallucinations: Characteristic of Schizophrenia (third-person voices giving a running commentary or arguing about the patient, or écho de la pensée [thoughts spoken aloud]) and Severe Psychotic Depression or Mania (second-person mood-congruent voices—derogatory/guilt-inducing in depression, grandiose in mania) or Alcoholic hallucinosis.

•  Visual Hallucinations: Characteristic of Organic Brain Disorders—Delirium (e.g., Delirium Tremens [Lilliputian hallucinations]), Dementia with Lewy Bodies, drug intoxication (hallucinogens/anticholinergics), and Charles Bonnet syndrome (in visual loss).

•  Olfactory & Gustatory Hallucinations: Characteristic of Temporal Lobe Epilepsy (unpleasant smell of burning rubber).

•  Tactile / Somatic Hallucinations:Formication (sensation of insects crawling under the skin) in cocaine/amphetamine misuse and alcohol withdrawal.

•  Delusions:

•  Definition: A fixed, false belief that is firmly held with absolute conviction despite incontrovertible evidence to the contrary, and is out of keeping with the patient’s social, educational, and cultural background.

•  Types of Delusions:Persecutory / Paranoid (belief that others are conspiring to harm one—schizophrenia, delirium, dementia); Grandiose (belief of possessing special powers, wealth, or royal/divine identity—mania); Depressive / Guilt, Hypochondriacal, and Nihilistic (Cotard’s syndrome—belief that one’s organs have rotted or one is dead) (psychotic depression); Delusions of Control / Passivity and Delusional Perception (first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia); Delusions of Reference; and Morbid Jealousy (Othello syndrome) or Erotomania (de Clérambault’s syndrome).

B. Classification of Psychotropic Drugs [TU] (Refer to Box 29.17):

1.  Antipsychotic Drugs (Neuroleptics): First-generation (Phenothiazines, Butyrophenones, Thioxanthenes) and Second-generation ("Atypical" antipsychotics) → Used in Schizophrenia, Bipolar mania, Psychotic depression, Delirium.

2.  Antidepressant Drugs: SSRIs, SNRIs, Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs), Noradrenergic and Specific Serotonergic Antidepressants (NaSSAs—Mirtazapine), MAOIs, and NMDA antagonists (Esketamine) → Used in Depressive disorders, Anxiety disorders, OCD, PTSD, Neuropathic pain.

3.  Mood-Stabilising Drugs:Lithium carbonate, Anticonvulsants (Sodium valproate, Lamotrigine, Carbamazepine), and Second-generation antipsychotics (Olanzapine, Quetiapine, Risperidone, Aripiprazole) → Used in Bipolar affective disorder.

4.  Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs:Benzodiazepines (Diazepam, Lorazepam, Chlordiazepoxide), Z-drugs (Zopiclone), Pregabalin, and β-blockers (Propranolol) → Used short-term in Acute anxiety, Insomnia, Status epilepticus, and Alcohol withdrawal.

5.  Cognitive Enhancers (Anti-Dementia Drugs): Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (Donepezil, Rivastigmine, Galantamine) and NMDA receptor antagonist (Memantine) → Used in Alzheimer’s and Lewy body dementia.

6.  CNS Stimulants:Methylphenidate, Lisdexamfetamine, Modafinil → Used in ADHD and Narcolepsy.

C. Antipsychotic Drugs & Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome [KU 23, 16, RGU]:

•  Classification & Mechanism: All antipsychotics block post-synaptic Dopamine D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway (relieving positive psychotic symptoms).

•  First-Generation (Typical) Antipsychotics:Chlorpromazine (phenothiazine), Haloperidol (butyrophenone), Flupentixol decanoate (depot injection), Sulpiride. High affinity for striatal D2 receptors → high risk of Extrapyramidal Side-Effects (EPSE).

•  Second-Generation (Atypical) Antipsychotics:Risperidone, Olanzapine, Quetiapine, Aripiprazole, Amisulpride, and Clozapine (combined 5-HT2A and D2 antagonism). Lower risk of EPSE, but higher risk of metabolic syndrome (marked weight gain, insulin resistance/Type 2 diabetes, and dyslipidaemia). Clozapine is uniquely effective in treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failed ≥ 2 antipsychotics), but causes agranulocytosis/neutropenia in 1% (mandatory weekly/fortnightly FBC monitoring), myocarditis, hypersalivation, constipation, and lowered seizure threshold.

•  Adverse Effects of Antipsychotic Drugs:

1.  Dopamine D2 Blockade (Nigrostriatal & Tuberoinfundibular):

•  Acute Dystonia (torticolis, tongue protrusion, oculogyric crisis—treated with IV/IM Procyclidine).

•  Akathisia (inner motor restlessness and inability to sit still).

•  Drug-Induced Parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor).

•  Tardive Dyskinesia (late, often irreversible choreoathetoid oro-bucco-lingual chewing/lip-smacking movements after chronic use).

•  Hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, gynaecomastia, impotence).

2.  Anticholinergic, Anti-adrenergic (α1) & Antihistaminergic (H1) Blockade: Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, postural hypotension, and sedation/weight gain.

3.  Cardiac:Prolongation of the QTc interval risking torsades de pointes ventricular arrhythmias.

•  Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) [KU 23]:

•  Pathogenesis: A rare, idiosyncratic, life-threatening medical emergency (untreated mortality 20%; treated mortality 5%) caused by abrupt central dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the striatum and hypothalamus (triggered by any antipsychotic—especially high-potency typicals like haloperidol—or by abrupt withdrawal of levodopa in Parkinson’s disease).

•  Classic Clinical Tetrad (Evolves over 24–72 hours):

1.  Severe Muscular Rigidity ("Lead-pipe" rigidity)

2.  Hyperpyrexia / High Fever (>38.5^circ–40^circC)

3.  Autonomic Instability (tachycardia, labile BP, profuse diaphoresis/sweating, tachypnoea)

4.  Altered Mental State / Delirium (agitation progressing to stupor and coma).

•  Laboratory Findings:Grossly elevated Serum Creatine Kinase (CK, often >1000–100,000 U/L) due to rhabdomyolysis (risking myoglobinuric acute kidney injury), leucocytosis, metabolic acidosis, and deranged LFTs.

•  Emergency Management of NMS:

1.  STOP the offending antipsychotic drug immediately.

2.  Admit to ICU for aggressive IV crystalloid fluid resuscitation (to prevent myoglobinuric renal failure), active cooling (cooling blankets, ice packs), and ventilatory/circulatory support.

3.  Specific Pharmacotherapy:Intravenous Dantrolene sodium (direct skeletal muscle relaxant that blocks sarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine Ca2+ release) AND/OR Oral Bromocriptine (central dopamine D2 receptor agonist, 2.5–10 mg TDS). Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) help control agitation.

D. Antidepressant Drugs & Selective Serotonin Re-uptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) [KU 22, 17, TU, RGU]:

•  Classes of Antidepressants (Refer to Box 29.24):

1.  Selective Serotonin Re-uptake Inhibitors (SSRIs — First-Line):Fluoxetine, Sertraline, Citalopram, Escitalopram, Paroxetine.

•  Clinical Uses of SSRIs [KU 22, TU]: (1) Major Depressive Disorder; (2) Anxiety Disorders (Generalised anxiety disorder, Panic disorder, Social/Agoraphobia); (3) Obsessive–Compulsive Disorder (OCD); (4) Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD); and (5) Bulimia Nervosa (high-dose fluoxetine 60 mg/day).

•  Common Side-Effects of SSRIs [KU 22, TU]:Gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, anorexia, GI bleeding risk if combined with NSAIDs), Sexual dysfunction (anorgasmia, delayed ejaculation, reduced libido), Initial transient increase in anxiety/agitation/insomnia during the first 1–2 weeks, headache, hyponatraemia (SIADH, especially in the elderly), QTc prolongation (citalopram/escitalopram), discontinuation symptoms on abrupt stopping (paroxetine), and Serotonin Syndrome (neuromuscular clonus/hyper-reflexia, autonomic instability, agitation, and hyperthermia if combined with MAOIs, tramadol, or triptans).

2.  Serotonin and Noradrenaline Re-uptake Inhibitors (SNRIs):Venlafaxine (75–375 mg/day; monitor BP for hypertension) and Duloxetine (60 mg/day; also used in diabetic neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and stress urinary incontinence).

3.  Noradrenergic and Specific Serotonergic Antidepressant (NaSSA):Mirtazapine (15–45 mg at night; α2-antagonist and 5-HT2/3/H1 blocker; causes sedation and increased appetite/weight gain, useful in depressed patients with insomnia and weight loss, with minimal sexual dysfunction).

4.  Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs):Amitriptyline, Imipramine, Clomipramine, Dosulepin, Nortriptyline. Inhibit re-uptake of both 5-HT and noradrenaline. (Adverse effects: anticholinergic [dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, delirium], α1-blockade [postural hypotension], H1-blockade [sedation, weight gain], and life-threatening cardiotoxicity in overdose [sodium channel blockade causing QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmias, seizures, and coma—treated with IV sodium bicarbonate]).

5.  Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs): Irreversible (Phenelzine, Tranylcypromine) and reversible MAO-A inhibitor (Moclobemide). Require strict dietary avoidance of tyramine-rich foods (mature cheese, pickled herring, Chianti red wine, yeast extracts/Marmite) and sympathomimetic drugs to prevent a fatal hypertensive crisis ("cheese reaction").

6.  NMDA Receptor Antagonist: Intranasal Esketamine (for treatment-resistant depression).

E. Mood Stabilisers & Lithium Therapy [KU 18, TU]:

•  Mood-Stabilising Drugs [KU 18]:Lithium carbonate (gold standard first-line for prophylaxis of bipolar disorder), Sodium valproate, Lamotrigine (particularly effective in preventing bipolar depression), Carbamazepine, and second-generation antipsychotics (Olanzapine, Quetiapine, Risperidone, Aripiprazole).

•  Lithium Carbonate ([TU]):

•  Clinical Indications: (1) Long-term prophylaxis of Bipolar Affective Disorder (prevents both manic and depressive relapses and reduces suicide risk); (2) Treatment of Acute Mania; and (3) Augmentation of antidepressants in treatment-resistant unipolar depression.

•  Pharmacokinetics & Therapeutic Drug Monitoring: Excreted unchanged by the kidneys (reabsorbed in the proximal tubule alongside sodium) with a very narrow therapeutic index:

•  Therapeutic Serum Lithium Range (sampled 12 hours post-dose):0.5–1.0 mmol/L (typically 0.6–0.8 mmol/L for maintenance, up to 0.8–1.0 mmol/L in acute mania).

•  Check baseline and 6-monthly Renal Function (U&Es/eGFR), Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs), Serum Calcium, and ECG.

•  Adverse Effects & Toxicity of Lithium:

•  Therapeutic Dose Side-Effects: Fine postural tremor, polydipsia and polyuria (Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus / Arginine Vasopressin Resistance due to ADH receptor desensitisation in collecting ducts), Weight gain, Hypothyroidism and Goitre, Hyperparathyroidism (hypercalcaemia), metallic taste, T-wave flattening on ECG, exacerbation of psoriasis/acne, and Teratogenicity (Ebstein’s anomaly of the tricuspid valve in the 1st trimester).

•  Acute Lithium Toxicity (Serum Lithium >1.5 mmol/L; life-threatening >2.0 mmol/L): Precipitated by dehydration, sodium depletion, renal impairment, or interacting drugs (Thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors). Presents with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus, myoclonus, hyper-reflexia, seizures, coma, renal failure, and death. Managed by stopping lithium, aggressive IV 0.9% saline hydration, and urgent Haemodialysis if levels are >2.5–4.0 mmol/L or if severe neurological/renal toxicity is present.

F. Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT): Indications, Side-Effects & Contraindications [RGU, TU]:

•  Procedure: Electrical induction of a brief (20–60 second) generalised tonic–clonic seizure via bilateral or unilateral cranial electrodes while the patient is briefly anaesthetised (propofol/methohexital) and paralysed with a short-acting muscle relaxant (suxamethonium) with 100% oxygenation, typically given twice weekly for 6–12 sessions.

•  Clinical Indications (Uses):

1.  Severe Depressive Disorder with Immediate Life-Threatening Risk:Refusal to eat or drink causing severe dehydration/inanition, depressive stupor, or high, acute suicidal intent.

2.  Severe Psychotic Depression (delusions of guilt/nihilism and hallucinations).

3.  Treatment-Resistant Severe Depression that has failed adequate trials of antidepressant medications and psychotherapy.

4.  Severe Catatonia (malignant catatonia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome).

5.  Severe, Prolonged, or Treatment-Refractory Mania or Puerperal Psychosis (where rapid response is vital to reunite mother and baby).

•  Adverse Effects: Post-ictal headache, muscle aching, nausea, transient confusion, and memory impairment—both retrograde amnesia (for events shortly before ECT) and anterograde amnesia (reduced by using unilateral non-dominant electrode placement).

•  Contraindications: There are no absolute contraindications if ECT is life-saving, except Raised Intracranial Pressure / Space-Occupying Brain Lesion with Mass Effect (risk of brain herniation/coning during the seizure-induced ICP surge). Relative contraindications (high anaesthetic/cardiovascular risk): Recent myocardial infarction (<3 months), unstable angina, decompensated heart failure, severe aortic stenosis, recent intracerebral haemorrhage/stroke, or untreated cerebral aneurysm/phaeochromocytoma.

title: 2. Psychosis and Schizophrenia [KU 20, 19, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
SECTION 31.3 — PSYCHIATRIC DISORDERS

2. Psychosis and Schizophrenia [KU 20, 19, 16, TU, RGU]

1. Classification of Psychosis & Differences Between Psychosis and Neurosis [TU]:

•  Classification of Psychotic Disorders:

1.  Primary ("Functional") Psychoses:

•  Schizophrenia (Paranoid, Hebephrenic, Catatonic, Simple) and Persistent Delusional Disorders.

•  Affective Psychoses:Bipolar Disorder (Manic psychosis) and Severe Depressive Episode with Psychotic Symptoms.

•  Schizoaffective Disorder (prominent schizophrenic and mood symptoms simultaneously) and Puerperal (Post-partum) Psychosis.

2.  Secondary ("Organic") Psychoses:

•  Delirium (acute confusional state due to infection, metabolic disturbance, or drug/alcohol withdrawal) and Dementia (Alzheimer’s, Lewy body).

•  Substance-Induced Psychosis: Amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis, LSD, alcohol (alcoholic hallucinosis / delirium tremens).

•  Medical / Iatrogenic:Drugs (high-dose corticosteroids, levodopa, antimalarials), Temporal lobe epilepsy, Autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDAR), neurosyphilis, SLE.

•  Key Differences Between Psychosis and Neurosis [TU]:

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-028]]

2. Schizophrenia (Aetiopathogenesis, Clinical Features [Acute, Paranoid, Chronic, Catatonia] & Management) [KU 20, 19, TU, RGU]:

•  Aetiopathogenesis: Neurodevelopmental disorder (lifetime prevalence 0.5%–1%; onset typically 15–30 years):

•  Genetics: 80% heritability (50% concordance in monozygotic twins; 10% risk in offspring of one affected parent); polygenic variants plus copy number variations (e.g., 22q11.2 deletion).

•  Neurodevelopmental & Environmental Risk Factors: Obstetric/perinatal complications (hypoxia, maternal viral infection), childhood adversity, urban upbringing, migration, and heavy adolescent cannabis use (especially high-potency THC).

•  Neurochemistry & Neuroimaging:Mesolimbic dopamine (D2) hyperactivity (causes positive psychotic symptoms) alongside mesocortical dopamine hypoactivity and glutamatergic (NMDA receptor) hypofunction (causes negative and cognitive symptoms). Structural MRI shows mild lateral ventricular enlargement and 5%–10% reduction in medial temporal lobe/hippocampal volume.

•  Clinical Features of Schizophrenia:

•  A. Acute Schizophrenia ("Positive" Symptoms — Schneider’s First-Rank Symptoms; Mnemonic: ABCD):

1.  A — Auditory Hallucinations:

•  Voices speaking the patient’s thoughts aloud (écho de la pensée / Gedankenlautwerden).

•  Third-person auditory hallucinations arguing or discussing the patient among themselves.

•  Voices giving a running commentary on the patient’s actions.

2.  B — Thought Alienation (Passivity of Thought):

•  Thought Insertion: Delusional belief that alien thoughts are being put into one’s mind by an external agency.

•  Thought Withdrawal: Belief that one’s thoughts are being taken out of one’s head.

•  Thought Broadcasting: Belief that one’s private thoughts are being broadcast aloud or accessible to others.

3.  C — Passivity Phenomena (Made Feelings, Impulses, Volition, or Somatic Passivity): Delusional belief that one’s bodily sensations, emotions, or actions are being controlled/manipulated by an external force.

4.  D — Delusional Perception: A normal real perception is suddenly and bizarrely interpreted with a fully formed delusional meaning (often persecutory or grandiose).

•  (Plus Formal Thought Disorder: loosening of associations, derailment, knight’s-move thinking, neologisms, and incoherence/"word salad", with complete lack of insight).

•  B. Clinical Subtypes (Including Paranoid Schizophrenia & Catatonia):

•  Paranoid Schizophrenia [RGU]: The most common subtype; dominated by prominent persecutory/paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations, while affect, volition, speech, and catatonic symptoms are relatively preserved (later onset and better prognosis).

•  Catatonia [TU]: Psychomotor syndrome (seen in schizophrenia, severe mood disorders, or organic encephalitis) characterised by stupor/mutism, posturing and catalepsy ("waxy flexibility"—limbs remain in awkward positions placed by the examiner), negativism, rigidity, echolalia (repeating words), and echopraxia (copying movements). (Treated urgently with high-dose Lorazepam and Electroconvulsive Therapy [ECT]).

•  C. Chronic Schizophrenia ("Negative" Symptoms):

•  5 As of Negative Symptoms: (1) Affective flattening (blunted affect); (2) Avolition / Apathy (loss of drive and motivation); (3) Asociality (social withdrawal and self-neglect); (4) Alogia (poverty of speech and thought); and (5) Anhedonia, plus executive cognitive impairment.

•  Management of Schizophrenia (Biopsychosocial Approach) [KU 19, TU]:

1.  Biological (Antipsychotic Pharmacotherapy):

•  Acute Episode: Oral Second-Generation Antipsychotics (Risperidone 4–6 mg/day, Olanzapine 10–15 mg/day, Quetiapine 300–600 mg/day, Aripiprazole, or Amisulpride) or first-generation antipsychotics (Haloperidol, Chlorpromazine). Continue for at least 1–2 years after a first episode, and long-term for relapsing illness.

•  Poor Adherence: Use long-acting intramuscular depot injections (e.g., Flupentixol decanoate, Zuclopenthixol, Paliperidone, or Risperidone depot every 2–4 weeks).

•  Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia (failure of ≥ 2 antipsychotics):Clozapine (300–600 mg/day) with mandatory FBC monitoring for agranulocytosis.

•  Physical Health Monitoring: Regularly screen and treat weight gain, diabetes (HbA1c), dyslipidaemia, hypertension, and smoking.

2.  Psychological Interventions:Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Psychosis (CBTp) (helps patients cope with residual hallucinations/delusions) and Family Psychoeducation / Therapy (reduces high "expressed emotion" in the home, which significantly lowers relapse rates).

3.  Social Rehabilitation (Care Programme Approach): Multidisciplinary community mental health team (CMHT) support, supported housing, day centres, benefits advice, and sheltered/supported employment. (Prognosis: sim 1/3 recover well, 1/3 have relapsing-remitting episodes, and 1/3 develop chronic disabling negative symptoms; 10% die by suicide).

title: 3. Mood (Affective) Disorders: Major Depression, Bipolar Disorder, and Post-Partum Psychiatric Disorders [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]
text:
3. Mood (Affective) Disorders: Major Depression, Bipolar Disorder, and Post-Partum Psychiatric Disorders [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, TU, RGU]

(Covers the clinical vignette Essay on a 55-year-old man presenting with a 4-month history of insomnia, lack of interest [anhedonia], suicidal attempts, family history, and irritable, sad, withdrawn appearance = Severe Major Depressive Disorder).

1. Depressive Disorder (Aetiopathogenesis, Diagnostic Criteria, Clinical Features & Treatment):

•  Aetiopathogenesis:

•  Biological: Polygenic heritability (sim 40%); monoamine deficiency hypothesis (reduced synaptic availability of 5-hydroxytryptamine [serotonin], noradrenaline, and dopamine in limbic/prefrontal circuits); hyperactivity of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis (hypercortisolaemia failing to suppress with dexamethasone); and organic precipitants (hypothyroidism, Cushing’s, stroke, Parkinson’s, glucocorticoids).

•  Psychological: Childhood adversity/abuse, neurotic personality traits, and Beck’s Negative Cognitive Triad (negative views of the self ["I am worthless"], the world/current experience ["Everything is bleak"], and the future ["It is hopeless"]).

•  Social: Precipitating life events involving loss (bereavement, divorce, unemployment, chronic medical illness) and lack of a close confiding relationship/social isolation.

•  Clinical Features & ICD-11 / DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria for a Depressive Episode [KU 22, 21, 16]:

•  Core Symptoms (Must be present for at least 2 WEEKS; requires at least 2 core symptoms + additional symptoms totalling ≥ 5):

1.  Pervasive Depressed (Low) Mood (present most of the day, nearly every day, unreactive to circumstances).

2.  Anhedonia: Markedly diminished interest or pleasure in activities previously enjoyed.

3.  Fatigue / Anergia: Decreased energy and increased fatigability.

•  Additional Psychological Symptoms:

•  Reduced self-esteem and self-confidence.

•  Excessive, inappropriate feelings of guilt and unworthiness.

•  Bleak and pessimistic views of the future (hopelessness).

•  Recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation, or acts of self-harm.

•  Poor concentration, indecisiveness, and subjective memory impairment (can mimic dementia in the elderly—"depressive pseudodementia").

•  Biological / Somatic ("Melancholic") Symptoms:

•  Sleep disturbance: Classically early-morning wakening (2–3 hours before usual time) or initial insomnia/hypersomnia.

•  Diurnal variation of mood (mood is worst in the morning).

•  Loss of appetite and significant weight loss (>5% body weight in a month).

•  Loss of libido.

•  Psychomotor retardation (slowed speech, movement, hunched posture, downcast gaze) or psychomotor agitation.

•  Constipation and multiple medically unexplained somatic pains.

•  Classification by Severity:Mild (4–5 symptoms, mild functional distress), Moderate (6–7 symptoms, significant functional impairment), Severe without Psychotic Symptoms (8+ symptoms, marked distress, agitation/retardation, suicidal risk), and Severe WITH Psychotic Symptoms (Psychotic Depression) (accompanied by mood-congruent delusions of guilt, poverty, hypochondriasis, or nihilism [Cotard’s syndrome] and derogatory second-person auditory hallucinations).

•  Management of Depression [KU 25, 24, 20, 19, 17, TU]:

1.  Risk Assessment: Assess immediate suicide risk (see Box 29.14); admit to a psychiatric unit (using mental health legislation if necessary) if actively suicidal, psychotic, or refusing food/fluids.

2.  Mild-to-Moderate Depression:

•  Psychological Therapies (First-line for mild depression; equally effective as drugs in moderate depression):Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) (challenges Beck’s negative cognitive triad), Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT), or Problem-Solving Therapy, plus regular aerobic exercise and sleep hygiene.

•  Antidepressant Medication (First-line for moderate-to-severe depression; combined with CBT):

•  Start an SSRI (Sertraline 50–200 mg/day, Escitalopram 10–20 mg/day, Citalopram 20–40 mg/day, or Fluoxetine 20–60 mg/day; Sertraline is safest post-myocardial infarction/in medical illness).

•  If inadequate response after 4–6 weeks at an adequate dose, switch to a different SSRI or another class: SNRI (Venlafaxine or Duloxetine), Mirtazapine (especially if prominent insomnia and weight loss), or a Tricyclic Antidepressant (Amitriptyline, Imipramine)(avoid TCAs in suicidal patients due to fatal cardiotoxicity in overdose).

•  Duration: Continue antidepressant at full therapeutic dose for at least 6–12 months after recovery (and ≥ 2 years in recurrent depression) to prevent relapse, then taper slowly over 4 weeks.

3.  Treatment-Resistant, Psychotic, or Life-Threatening Severe Depression:

•  Psychotic Depression: Combine an Antidepressant + Second-Generation Antipsychotic (e.g., Olanzapine or Quetiapine), OR administer ECT.

•  Treatment-Resistant Depression:Augmentation with Lithium carbonate or a second-generation antipsychotic (quetiapine/aripiprazole), combination of SSRI/SNRI + Mirtazapine, intranasal Esketamine, or Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) (most rapidly effective treatment for severe suicidal, catatonic, or psychotic depression).

2. Bipolar Affective Disorder (Manic-Depressive Psychosis) & Acute Mania [KU 20, 17, TU, RGU]:

•  Definition: An episodic mood disorder (lifetime prevalence 1%–2%; M = F; onset in 20s; 70% heritability) characterised by recurrent episodes of elevated mood (Mania or Hypomania) interspersed with episodes of Depressive illness.

•  Bipolar I Disorder: At least one full Manic episode (≥ 7 days, severe functional impairment or psychotic features, often requiring hospitalisation) ± depressive episodes.

•  Bipolar II Disorder: Recurrent Major Depressive episodes punctuated by milder Hypomanic episodes (≥ 4 days of elevated mood and increased energy without psychotic features or severe social/occupational breakdown).

•  Clinical Features of Mania [RGU]:

•  Mood: Abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, euphoric ("infectious joviality"), or irritable mood.

•  Speech & Thought:Pressure of speech (rapid, loud, uninterruptible speech) and flight of ideas (rapidly jumping from one topic to another via rhyming/punning associations).

•  Activity & Behaviour:Markedly increased energy and over-activity, decreased need for sleep (waking after 2–3 hours feeling fully refreshed), social and sexual disinhibition/promiscuity, reckless overspending, poor judgement, and distractibility.

•  Psychotic Features (in Severe Mania):Mood-congruent grandiose delusions (believing one has special divine powers, vast wealth, or royal identity) and auditory hallucinations, with complete lack of insight.

•  Management of Bipolar Disorder [KU 17, TU]:

1.  Drugs Used in Acute Mania [KU 17]:

•  IMMEDIATELY STOP any antidepressant drugs.

•  First-Line Anti-Manic Agents:Second-Generation Antipsychotics (Olanzapine, Risperidone, Quetiapine, Aripiprazole) or Haloperidol, often combined short-term with a Benzodiazepine (Lorazepam or Diazepam) to control acute agitation and restore sleep.

•  Mood Stabiliser Addition: Add Lithium carbonate or Sodium valproate (avoid valproate in women of childbearing age). ECT is reserved for severe refractory mania.

2.  Treatment of Acute Bipolar Depression:

•  Quetiapine, Olanzapine + Fluoxetine, or Lamotrigine. (Crucial Rule: Never prescribe an antidepressant as monotherapy in bipolar depression, as it triggers a rapid "manic switch" or rapid cycling; any antidepressant must always be co-prescribed with a mood-stabilising / anti-manic agent).

3.  Long-Term Prophylaxis (Relapse Prevention):

•  Lithium Carbonate (first-line drug of choice; target serum level 0.6–0.8 mmol/L).

•  Alternatives / Adjuncts:Sodium valproate, Lamotrigine (prevents depressive relapses), Olanzapine, Quetiapine, or Carbamazepine, combined with psychoeducation (identifying early prodromal warning signs like reduced sleep), regular circadian routines, and avoidance of shift work/illicit drugs.

3. Post-Partum Psychiatric Disorders [KU 18, TU, RGU]:

title: 4. Anxiety, Obsessive–Compulsive (OCD), Stress-Related (Adjustment/PTSD), Somatoform (Bodily Distress), Dissociative, and Personality Disorders [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]
text:
4. Anxiety, Obsessive–Compulsive (OCD), Stress-Related (Adjustment/PTSD), Somatoform (Bodily Distress), Dissociative, and Personality Disorders [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, TU, RGU]

1. Classification of Anxiety Disorders & Treatment of Panic Attacks [KU 20, 19, 17, RGU]:

•  Classification of Anxiety Disorders [KU 19] (Refer to Box 29.25):

1.  Phobic Anxiety Disorders (Situational): Excessive fear of a specific object or situation leading to avoidance behaviour and anticipatory anxiety—includes Agoraphobia (fear of crowds, public transport, or leaving home), Social Phobia, and Specific Phobias (e.g., flying, needles, heights, spiders).

2.  Panic Disorder (Paroxysmal): Recurrent, unpredictable attacks of severe acute anxiety (panic attacks) not restricted to any specific trigger, accompanied by autonomic arousal (palpitations, chest pain, choking, dizziness, trembling, sweating), hyperventilation (causing respiratory alkalosis → perioral and digital paraesthesiae and carpopedal spasm), and catastrophic cognitions (fear of dying, having a heart attack, fainting, or "going mad").

3.  Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD — Persistent): Chronic, free-floating, uncontrollable worry and apprehension lasting ≥ 6 months, accompanied by muscular tension (tension headache, restlessness, tremor), autonomic over-activity (palpitations, sweating, dry mouth, epigastric discomfort), and hypervigilance (irritability, poor concentration, initial insomnia). (Exclude organic mimics: hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, hypoglycaemia, cardiac arrhythmias, caffeine excess, and alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal).

•  Management of Panic Disorder & Anxiety Disorders [RGU]:

•  Acute Panic Attack: Reassurance, slow controlled breathing (or rebreathing into a paper bag to reverse hyperventilation-induced hypocapnia/alkalosis); short-term benzodiazepine (e.g., lorazepam) only if severe acute crisis.

•  Long-Term Management:

1.  Psychological Therapy (First-line):Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) (educating the patient that somatic symptoms are harmless results of adrenaline/hyperventilation rather than a heart attack, combined with graded exposure / systematic desensitisation for phobias and relaxation training).

2.  Pharmacotherapy:SSRIs (Escitalopram, Sertraline, Paroxetine, Fluoxetine) or SNRIs (Duloxetine, Venlafaxine) are the drugs of first choice (warn of transient increased anxiety in the first 2 weeks; continue for ≥ 6–12 months). Pregabalin is an effective second-line option in GAD; Propranolol (40–80 mg) controls somatic autonomic symptoms (palpitations, tremor). (Avoid prescribing benzodiazepines for >2–3 weeks due to tolerance and dependence).

2. Obsessive–Compulsive Disorder (OCD) [KU 24, 20, 16, TU, RGU]:

•  Definition & Clinical Features (Affects men and women equally):

•  Obsessions: Recurrent, persistent, intrusive, and unwanted thoughts, images, or impulses that enter the patient’s mind despite efforts to resist them, causing marked anxiety/distress. Crucially, the patient recognises that the obsessions are a product of their own mind (insight is preserved, distinguishing obsessions from schizophrenic thought insertion). Common themes: Fear of contamination by dirt/germs, pathological doubt (e.g., having left gas/doors unlocked), fear of harming others, need for symmetry/exactness, or intrusive blasphemous/sexual thoughts.

•  Compulsions (Rituals): Repetitive, purposeful, stereotyped mental acts or physical behaviours (e.g., ritualised hand-washing causing contact dermatitis, repeated checking of locks/switches, counting, arranging) that the patient feels driven to perform in order to neutralise the obsession and temporarily relieve anxiety.

•  Treatment of Obsessive–Compulsive Disorder [KU 24]:

1.  Psychological Therapy (First-Line):Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) incorporating Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP)—the patient is guided to deliberately expose themselves to the feared stimulus/thought (e.g., touching a "contaminated" doorknob) while refraining from performing the compulsive ritual (hand-washing) until the anxiety habituates and subsides.

2.  Pharmacological Therapy:High-Dose SSRIs (e.g., Fluoxetine 60–80 mg/day, Sertraline 150–200 mg/day, Escitalopram, Paroxetine, or Fluvoxamine) OR the serotonergic Tricyclic Antidepressant Clomipramine (150–250 mg/day) (given for at least 10–12 weeks to assess full effect and continued long-term; low-dose risperidone or aripiprazole may be added as augmentation in refractory cases).

3. Stress-Related Disorders: Acute Stress Reaction, Adjustment Disorder, and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) [KU 22, 21, 20, 16, 15, TU]:

•  A. Adjustment Disorder [KU 22, 21, 20, 16, 15]:

•  Definition & Aetiology: A maladaptive emotional and behavioural reaction developing within 1 month of an identifiable psychosocial stressor or major life change (e.g., receiving a serious medical diagnosis, bereavement, divorce, job loss, or hospitalisation) that is not of catastrophic/life-threatening proportions.

•  Clinical Features: Distress and functional impairment out of proportion to expected reactions, manifesting with low mood, tearfulness, worry, anxiety, insomnia, poor concentration, anger/irritability, or alcohol misuse/deliberate self-harm, but not meeting the severity or duration threshold for Major Depressive Disorder or GAD. Pathological grief is a severe, prolonged variant following bereavement.

•  Management:Empathic listening, reassurance, practical social support, and Problem-Solving Therapy (or brief supportive psychotherapy/counselling). Antidepressants are generally NOT required (unless it evolves into major depression); a short course of a hypnotic/benzodiazepine (<1–2 weeks) may be used for acute insomnia. Resolves as the stressor is removed or adaptation occurs.

•  B. Acute Stress Reaction & Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) [TU]:

•  Acute Stress Reaction: Transient state of "daze", bewilderment, autonomic anxiety, or withdrawal occurring immediately (within hours) after a catastrophic trauma and resolving within 2–3 days.

•  Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD): Delayed or protracted response to an exceptionally threatening or catastrophic life-threatening event (combat, sexual assault, natural disaster, major accident, ICU admission), starting within weeks to 6 months of the trauma:

1.  Re-experiencing (Intrusive) Symptoms: Vivid, distressing flashbacks, intrusive memories, and recurrent nightmares of the trauma.

2.  Avoidance & Emotional Numbing: Persistent avoidance of places, people, or conversations that trigger trauma memories, detachment, and anhedonia.

3.  Hyperarousal & Hypervigilance: Exaggerated startle response, irritability/angry outbursts, insomnia, and autonomic hyper-reactivity.

•  Management of PTSD:Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (TF-CBT) and Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) are first-line; SSRIs (Sertraline, Paroxetine) or Venlafaxine are effective pharmacological treatments (note: single-session immediate psychological "debriefing" right after trauma is ineffective and may worsen outcomes).

4. Somatoform (Bodily Distress) Disorders, Dissociative (Conversion) Disorders, and Hysteria vs. Malingering [KU 18, 15, TU, RGU]:

•  A. Somatoform Disorders (ICD-11: Disorders of Bodily Distress) & Psychosomatic Disorders [KU 18, TU, RGU]:

•  Definition: A group of disorders characterised by persistent, distressing medically unexplained physical (somatic) symptoms (MUS) and excessive health-related thoughts/behaviours that are not explained by organic pathology or primary depression/anxiety, leading to repeated medical consultations.

•  Subtypes:

1.  Somatisation Disorder (Briquet’s Syndrome) [KU 18, RGU]: Severe, chronic form starting in early adulthood (F > M), characterised by multiple, recurrent, and frequently changing medically unexplained physical symptoms affecting multiple organ systems (pain, GI, neurological, cardiorespiratory, genitourinary) persisting for >2 years, resulting in numerous negative investigations and unnecessary surgeries.

2.  Somatoform Autonomic Dysfunction (cardiac neurosis, irritable bowel syndrome, psychogenic hyperventilation).

3.  Persistent Somatoform Pain Disorder & Chronic Fatigue Syndrome.

4.  Health Anxiety Disorder (Hypochondriasis): Persistent preoccupation and fear of having a serious, progressive, undiagnosed disease (e.g., cancer) based on misinterpretation of normal bodily sensations, which persists despite normal investigations and medical reassurance.

5.  Body Dysmorphic Disorder (Dysmorphophobia): Preoccupation with an imagined defect or disfigurement in physical appearance.

•  Management of Somatoform / Bodily Distress Disorders: Follow the General Management Principles in Box 29.29: (1) Take a sympathetic history and perform a focused physical examination; (2) Acknowledge that the patient’s symptoms are real (never say "it’s all in your head"); (3) Provide a positive "functional" physiological explanation linking stress/autonomic nervous system to symptoms; (4) Avoid unnecessary repeat investigations, referrals, and surgeries (manage via regular scheduled appointments with one named doctor/GP to prevent doctor-shopping and iatrogenic harm); (5) Treat comorbid depression/anxiety or chronic pain with Antidepressants (TCAs [amitriptyline], Duloxetine, or SSRIs); and (6) Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) and graded exercise.

•  B. Dissociative (Conversion) Disorder & Difference from Factitious Disorder and Malingering [KU 18, 15, TU, RGU]:

•  Dissociative (Conversion) Disorder (Functional Neurological Disorder): Partial or complete loss of normal integration between memories of the past, awareness of identity, immediate sensations, and control of bodily movements, occurring in the absence of organic neurological disease, often precipitated by psychological stress or trauma.

•  Clinical Presentations:Motor (functional paraparesis/hemiparesis with positive Hoover’s sign, functional gait disorder, aphonia), Convulsions (dissociative non-epileptic attacks / pseudoseizures), Sensory (non-anatomical anaesthesia, tunnel vision/dissociative blindness), and Cognitive (dissociative amnesia, dissociative fugue [wandering away with loss of identity], and dissociative stupor).

•  Crucial Distinction: Dissociative/Conversion Disorder ("Hysteria") vs. Factitious Disorder vs. Malingering [KU 15] (Refer to Fig. 29.4):

[[TABLE:medicine-tbl-030]]

5. Personality Disorders & Borderline Personality Disorder [KU 25, TU]:

•  Definition & Aetiology: Deeply ingrained, enduring, and inflexible patterns of cognition, affectivity, impulse control, and interpersonal relating that deviate markedly from cultural expectations, begin in adolescence/early adulthood, are pervasive across a wide range of personal and social situations, and cause significant distress or social/occupational impairment. Caused by an interaction between genetic temperament and adverse childhood experiences (emotional neglect, physical or sexual abuse).

•  Classification (Three Classical Clusters):

•  Cluster A ("Odd / Eccentric"):Paranoid (pervasive distrust and suspiciousness), Schizoid (emotional coldness, detachment, preference for solitary activities), and Schizotypal (eccentric behaviour, magical thinking).

•  Cluster B ("Dramatic, Emotional, Erratic"):

•  Emotionally Unstable / Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) [KU 25]: (See detailed features below).

•  Dissocial (Antisocial / Psychopathic) Personality Disorder: Callous disregard for the rights and feelings of others, impulsivity, aggression, deceitfulness, irresponsibility, and complete lack of remorse or guilt.

•  Histrionic (shallow labile affect, theatricality, attention-seeking) and Narcissistic (grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy).

•  Cluster C ("Anxious / Fearful"):Anankastic (Obsessive–Compulsive) (perfectionism, rigidity, preoccupation with rules/order), Anxious (Avoidant) (hypersensitivity to rejection, feelings of inadequacy), and Dependent (submissive, clinging need to be cared for).

•  Borderline Personality Disorder (Emotionally Unstable Personality Disorder) [KU 25]:

•  Aetiology: Strongly associated with childhood sexual, physical, or emotional trauma and disrupted attachment (predominantly diagnosed in young women in clinical settings).

•  Core Clinical Features:

1.  Intense, Unstable Interpersonal Relationships alternating between extremes of idealisation and devaluation ("splitting").

2.  Frantic Efforts to Avoid Real or Imagined Abandonment.

3.  Marked Affective Instability / Emotional Dysregulation (rapid mood shifts lasting hours, with inappropriate, intense anger).

4.  Chronic Feelings of Inner Emptiness and Disturbed Identity / Self-Image.

5.  Impulsivity in self-damaging areas (substance/alcohol misuse, binge eating, reckless spending/sex).

6.  Recurrent Suicidal Behaviour, Threats, or Deliberate Self-Harm (e.g., repetitive self-cutting or overdoses used to relieve overwhelming emotional tension).

7.  Transient, Stress-Related Paranoid Ideation or Severe Dissociative Symptoms.

•  Management of Borderline Personality Disorder:

•  Psychological Therapy (Cornerstone):Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) (combines individual and group skills training in mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness; proven to reduce self-harm and hospitalisation) or Mentalisation-Based Therapy (MBT).

•  Consistent, Clear Clinical Boundaries: Managed via a coordinated multidisciplinary care plan avoiding crisis-driven prolonged hospital admissions.

•  Pharmacotherapy: No drug cures BPD; medications are used only for specific comorbid disorders (e.g., SSRIs for comorbid depression) or short-term crisis management, avoiding polypharmacy and sedatives with overdose potential.

title: 5. Eating Disorders: Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa [KU 23, 18, TU, RGU]
text:
5. Eating Disorders: Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa [KU 23, 18, TU, RGU]

(Covers the clinical vignette Essay on a 20-year-old female presenting with food avoidance, purging, excessive exercise, and BMI 16.5 kg/m2 = Anorexia Nervosa).

1. Anorexia Nervosa [TU, RGU]:

•  Epidemiology & Pathogenesis: Lifetime prevalence 1%–2% in females (90% of patients are female; peak onset 15–19 years). Predisposed by genetic heritability (30%–50%), perfectionist/anankastic personality traits, and societal pressures; precipitated by dieting or life stressors.

•  Diagnostic Criteria for Anorexia Nervosa (ICD-11 / DSM-5) [Box 29.27]:

1.  Significantly Low Body Weight: Body weight maintained at least 15% below expected weight OR a Body Mass Index (BMI) ≤ 17.5–18.5 kg/m2 (in the vignette, BMI = 16.5 kg/m2).

2.  Self-Induced Weight Loss: Achieved by avoidance of "fattening" high-calorie foods, often combined with excessive exercise, self-induced vomiting, or misuse of laxatives/diuretics (Restricting subtype vs. Binge-eating/Purging subtype).

3.  Profound Body Image Distortion & Morbid Fear of Fatness: Intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted perception of body shape such that patients perceive themselves as "fat" even when severely emaciated.

4.  Widespread Endocrine Dysfunction (Hypothalamic–Pituitary–Gonadal Axis Suppression): Manifesting as secondary amenorrhoea in females (or loss of libido/impotence in males), elevated growth hormone and cortisol, and a "sick euthyroid" low-T3 state.

•  Medical Consequences & Physical Signs of Anorexia Nervosa (and Bulimia) [Box 29.26]:

•  Cutaneous & Dental: Emaciation, dry scaly skin, fine downy lanugo hair over the back, forearms, and cheeks, yellowish skin (hypercarotenaemia) on palms/soles, brittle hair/alopecia, cold blue extremities (acrocyanosis), calluses on the dorsum of the knuckles from self-induced vomiting (Russell’s sign), dental enamel erosion (perimolysis from gastric acid), and bilateral painless parotid/salivary gland enlargement.

•  Cardiovascular (Major Medical Cause of Death):Sinus bradycardia, hypotension / postural hypotension, mitral valve prolapse, myocardial atrophy, and ECG abnormalities (prolonged QTc interval, ST depression, U waves) predisposing to fatal ventricular arrhythmias (torsades de pointes).

•  Electrolyte & Metabolic:Hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis (from vomiting/diuretics), hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, elevated transaminases, and Refeeding Syndrome (see below).

•  Endocrine & Skeletal: Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (amenorrhoea), growth retardation/pubertal arrest, and severe premature Osteoporosis with vertebral/fragility fractures (due to oestrogen deficiency, hypercortisolaemia, and malnutrition).

•  Haematological & GI:Normocytic anaemia, leucopenia, and thrombocytopenia (gelatinous bone marrow transformation); delayed gastric emptying (gastroparesis), acute gastric dilatation, and severe constipation.

•  Management of Anorexia Nervosa:

1.  Setting of Care: Most patients are managed as outpatients by a specialist multidisciplinary eating disorders team. Urgent Inpatient Medical/Psychiatric Admission (using compulsory mental health legislation if necessary to save life) is indicated if: BMI <13–14 kg/m2, rapid weight loss (>1 kg/week), severe bradycardia (<40 bpm), hypotension (<80/50 mmHg), prolonged QTc, severe electrolyte derangement (K+<2.5–3.0 mmol/L, hypoglycaemia, or hypophosphataemia), or high suicide risk.

2.  Controlled Nutritional Rehabilitation & Prevention of Refeeding Syndrome:

•  Aim for steady, collaborative weight gain of 0.5–1.0 kg/week (inpatients) or 0.5 kg/week (outpatients) via oral diet or, if life-threateningly refused, nasogastric tube feeding.

•  Refeeding Syndrome Precaution: Rapid carbohydrate refeeding triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, causing fatal hypophosphataemia, cardiac failure, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, and Wernicke encephalopathy. Prevent by giving oral/parenteral Thiamin (Vitamin B1) and multivitamins BEFORE feeding, starting calories cautiously, and monitoring and replacing serum Phosphate, Potassium, Magnesium, and Calcium daily.

3.  Psychological Therapies (Mainstay of Definitive Treatment):Family-Based Therapy (Maudsley FBT) (first-line in adolescents), Eating-Disorder-Focused Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT-ED), MANTRA (Maudsley Model of Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults), and Specialist Supportive Clinical Management (SSCM). (Psychotropic drugs do not promote weight gain in AN, though SSRIs treat comorbid depression/OCD once weight is partially restored).

•  Prognosis of Anorexia Nervosa:

•  Approximately two-thirds (65%) recover by 5 years, while 20% develop a chronic, intractable illness.

•  Anorexia nervosa has the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric disorder (standardised mortality ratio 4–5×; 5%–10% long-term mortality), with 60% of deaths due to medical/cardiac complications of starvation and 40% due to suicide.

2. Bulimia Nervosa [KU 23, RGU]:

•  Diagnostic Criteria & Clinical Features [Box 29.27]:

1.  Recurrent episodes of Binge Eating (consuming large quantities of food rapidly with a subjective sense of loss of control).

2.  Recurrent Inappropriate Compensatory ("Purging") Behaviours to prevent weight gain: self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics, or enemas, fasting, or excessive exercise.

3.  Morbid preoccupation with body shape and weight (fear of fatness).

4.  Crucial Distinction from Anorexia Nervosa:Body weight is maintained within or above the NORMAL range (BMI >18.5 kg/m2) and menstruation is usually preserved.

•  Physical Signs & Complications:Russell’s sign (knuckle calluses from incisors during self-induced vomiting), acid erosion of lingual dental enamel, painless bilateral parotid gland swelling, oesophagitis / Mallory–Weiss tears, and severe hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with cardiac arrhythmias.

•  Management of Bulimia Nervosa:

•  Correct electrolyte disturbances (potassium replacement).

•  Psychological Therapy (First-Line):Bulimia-Focused Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT-BN), guided self-help, or Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT).

•  Pharmacotherapy:High-Dose Fluoxetine (SSRI) at 60 mg daily (reduces bingeing and purging frequency, independent of the presence of depression). Prognosis is much better than AN, with 70% achieving full recovery.

title: 6. Alcohol Misuse, Alcohol Dependence, Alcohol Withdrawal / Delirium Tremens, Wernicke–Korsakoff Syndrome, and Substance Misuse [KU 24, 21, 18, 17, TU, RGU]
text:
6. Alcohol Misuse, Alcohol Dependence, Alcohol Withdrawal / Delirium Tremens, Wernicke–Korsakoff Syndrome, and Substance Misuse [KU 24, 21, 18, 17, TU, RGU]

(Covers the clinical vignette Essay on a young man with high-risk alcohol behaviour who develops agitation and tremulousness on hospitalisation for a medical illness = Acute Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome / Delirium Tremens).

1. Criteria for Alcohol Dependence Syndrome (ICD-11 / Edwards & Gross Criteria) [KU 18, TU] (Refer to Box 29.30):

(Diagnosed when ≥ 3 of the following occur together over the preceding 12 months):

1.  Strong Desire or Subjective Compulsion to Drink ("Craving").

2.  Impaired Capacity to Control Drinking (in terms of onset, termination, or levels of use).

3.  Narrowing of the Drinking Repertoire (stereotyped daily drinking pattern regardless of social setting).

4.  Primacy (Salience) of Drinking Over Other Activities (neglect of alternative pleasures, work, and family obligations in favour of drinking).

5.  Physiological Tolerance: Need for markedly increased amounts of alcohol to achieve intoxication or the desired effect.

6.  Physiological Withdrawal State upon stopping or reducing alcohol, or Relief Drinking (drinking early in the morning to relieve or avoid withdrawal tremors).

7.  Persistence with Drinking Despite Clear Evidence of Harmful Physical, Psychological, or Social Consequences (and rapid reinstatement after a period of abstinence).

(Note: The physical, hepatic, gastrointestinal, neurological, and psychiatric ill effects/complications of chronic alcoholism are detailed in Box 29.31 and in Chapter 21 [Hepatology, Question 5] above).

2. Acute Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome and Delirium Tremens [KU 24, 21, 18, 17, TU, RGU]:

•  Pathophysiology: Chronic alcohol consumption enhances inhibitory GABAA receptor function and inhibits excitatory NMDA glutamate receptors; the brain compensates by down-regulating GABAA receptors and up-regulating NMDA receptors and voltage-gated calcium channels. Abrupt cessation of alcohol (e.g., upon hospital admission for a medical illness or trauma) leaves unopposed glutamatergic and noradrenergic (sympathetic) CNS hyperexcitability.

•  Clinical Timeline & Features of Alcohol Withdrawal:

1.  Uncomplicated Alcohol Withdrawal (6–12 hours after last drink): Coarse postural hand tremor ("the shakes"), anxiety, restlessness, insomnia, headache, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and autonomic hyperactivity (sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, dilated pupils).

2.  Alcoholic Hallucinosis (12–24 hours): Visual, auditory, or tactile (formication) illusions and hallucinations initially in clear consciousness.

3.  Alcohol Withdrawal Seizures ("Rum Fits" — 12–48 hours): Generalised tonic–clonic seizures (often occurring in a cluster of 1–3 seizures).

4.  Delirium Tremens (DTs — 48–72 hours after last drink, lasting 3–5 days) [KU 21, RGU, TU]:

•  Occurs in sim 5% of withdrawing patients and carries a 5%–15% mortality (from cardiovascular collapse, arrhythmias, hyperthermia, or aspiration pneumonia) if untreated.

•  Classic Clinical Triad of Delirium Tremens:

1.  Severe Delirium (Acute Confusional State): Profound disorientation in time and place, extreme agitation, fear, paranoid delusions, and vivid, terrifying Visual Hallucinations (classically of miniature people or animals/insects — "Lilliputian hallucinations").

2.  Marked Coarse Generalised Tremor.

3.  Profound Autonomic Hyper-arousal: Fever, drenching sweats, severe tachycardia, and labile hypertension.

•  Management of Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome & Delirium Tremens [KU 24, 21, 18] (Refer to Fig. 29.3):

1.  Supportive Care & Monitoring:

•  Nurse in a well-lit, quiet room with reassuring staff orientation.

•  Correct fluid depletion and electrolyte disturbances (especially hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, and hypoglycaemia).

•  Monitor withdrawal severity every 60–90 minutes using the CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, Revised) scale (score ≥ 10–13 triggers medication; score ≥ 20 indicates severe withdrawal).

2.  First-Line Pharmacotherapy — Long-Acting Benzodiazepines (Cross-Tolerant GABAA Agonists that Prevent Seizures and Delirium Tremens):

•  Administered either via a Symptom-Triggered Regimen (guided by CIWA-Ar score) OR a Fixed-Dose Reducing Regimen tapered over 5–7 days:

•  Oral Chlordiazepoxide (20–40 mg QDS on Day 1, reducing daily to zero over 5–7 days) OR Oral Diazepam (10–20 mg QDS on Day 1, or 20 mg PRN for CIWA-Ar ≥ 10–13, tapered over 5–7 days).

•  (In severe Delirium Tremens or inability to take oral medication, use IV Diazepam or IV/IM Lorazepam; in patients with decompensated liver cirrhosis, use short-acting Lorazepam or Oxazepam [metabolised by glucuronidation] to prevent prolonged sedative accumulation and hepatic encephalopathy).

3.  Mandatory Prophylaxis & Treatment of Wernicke Encephalopathy:

•  Administer High-Dose Parenteral Thiamin (Vitamin B1 — IV Pabrinex 2 pairs TDS for 48–72 hours) to all patients undergoing inpatient alcohol withdrawal, ALWAYS given BEFORE any intravenous glucose infusion (as glucose metabolism consumes residual thiamin and precipitates acute Wernicke encephalopathy), followed by oral Thiamin 100 mg TDS and multivitamins.

4.  Long-Term Relapse Prevention After Detoxification:

•  Psychosocial addiction support, CBT/motivational interviewing, and Alcoholics Anonymous (AA).

•  Acamprosate (666 mg TDS) or Naltrexone (50 mg OD): Reduce alcohol craving and relapse rates.

•  Disulfiram (Antabuse, 200 mg daily): Irreversibly inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, causing unpleasant flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, and hypotension if alcohol is consumed.

3. Wernicke–Korsakoff Syndrome [KU 24, 21, TU, RGU]:

•  Aetiopathogenesis: Caused by severe Thiamin (Vitamin B1) deficiency—most commonly due to chronic alcohol misuse (poor diet, impaired jejunal absorption, reduced hepatic storage), or rarely hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, anorexia nervosa, or prolonged TPN without vitamins. Thiamin pyrophosphate is an essential cofactor for transketolase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; deficiency causes petechial haemorrhages and neuronal necrosis in the mammillary bodies, dorsomedial nuclei of the thalamus, and periaqueductal/periventricular grey matter.

•  A. Wernicke Encephalopathy (Acute Phase — Reversible Medical Emergency) [KU 24, RGU, TU]:

•  Classic Clinical Triad of Wernicke Encephalopathy:

1.  Ocular Signs (Ophthalmoplegia & Nystagmus): Horizontal and vertical nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus (6th nerve) palsies, and conjugate gaze palsies.

2.  Cerebellar Gait Ataxia: Broad-based unsteady gait and truncal instability.

3.  Global Confusion / Delirium: Disorientation, apathy, drowsiness, and inattention.

•  (Note: All three features of the triad are present simultaneously in only 10%–30% of cases; treat empirically on the basis of any one feature in an at-risk patient).

•  Treatment:Immediate High-Dose Intravenous Thiamin (Pabrinex 2 pairs IV three times daily for 3–5 days), given before any IV dextrose. Ophthalmoplegia resolves within hours to days, but if treatment is delayed, 80% progress to irreversible Korsakoff psychosis.

•  B. Korsakoff Psychosis / Syndrome (Chronic Amnesic Syndrome — Usually Irreversible) [KU 21, TU]:

•  Core Clinical Features:

1.  Profound Impairment of Episodic / Anterograde Memory (inability to form new memories after the onset of the illness) and variable retrograde amnesia, in a patient with clear consciousness and preserved immediate working memory (normal digit span) and preserved general intelligence.

2.  Confabulation: The unconscious fabrication of detailed, plausible, but imaginary accounts of recent events to fill in gaps in memory.

3.  Apathy and lack of insight into the memory deficit.

4. Substance Misuse: Cocaine and Cannabis (Marijuana) Abuse [KU 17, TU, RGU]:

•  Clinical Features of Chronic Cocaine Abuse [TU]:

•  Mechanism: Blocks presynaptic re-uptake of dopamine, noradrenaline, and serotonin, causing intense euphoria, hyperactivity, and sympathetic vasoconstriction.

•  Clinical Complications:Nasal septum ulceration and perforation (from intranasal snorting), weight loss, insomnia, tactile hallucinations of insects crawling under the skin ("formication" / "cocaine bugs"), paranoid psychosis (indistinguishable from acute paranoid schizophrenia), severe rebound crash depression with suicidal ideation and intense psychological craving on withdrawal, and life-threatening cardiovascular and cerebrovascular complications (coronary artery vasospasm / myocardial infarction, malignant hypertension, aortic dissection, intracerebral and subarachnoid haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke, seizures, hyperpyrexia, and rhabdomyolysis).

•  Effects of Chronic Marijuana (Cannabis / Δ9-THC) Abuse [KU 17]:

1.  Acute & Chronic Psychosis / Schizophrenia: Heavy cannabis use (especially high-potency skunk in adolescence) triggers acute toxic confusional states, acute paranoid psychosis, and increases the lifetime risk of developing chronic Schizophrenia 2- to 4-fold (and precipitates relapses in established schizophrenia).

2.  "Amotivational Syndrome" & Cognitive Impairment: Apathy, passivity, loss of drive, impaired short-term memory, and educational/occupational underachievement.

3.  Anxiety, Panic Attacks, and Depressive Disorders.

4.  Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome (CHS): Paradoxical cyclical episodes of intractable nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain in chronic daily users, characteristically relieved by compulsive hot baths or showers.

5.  Respiratory Complications: Chronic bronchitis, airway inflammation, and lung/head-and-neck cancer risk (when smoked with tobacco).
