title: 7. Dementia, Normal-Pressure Hydrocephalus, and Cognitive Screening (MMSE / MoCA) [KU 23, 15, RGU, TU]
text:
7. Dementia, Normal-Pressure Hydrocephalus, and Cognitive Screening (MMSE / MoCA) [KU 23, 15, RGU, TU]

1. Dementia in the Elderly: Classification, Clinical Features, and Treatable Causes [KU 15, RGU, TU]:

•  Definition: An acquired, chronic, and usually progressive clinical syndrome of global cognitive decline (affecting memory, language, visuospatial ability, executive function, and personality) occurring in clear consciousness (distinguishing it from delirium) and severe enough to impair daily social or occupational functioning.

•  Major Neurodegenerative & Vascular Subtypes of Dementia:

1.  Alzheimer’s Disease (60%–70% — Most common) [RGU]:

•  Pathology: Macroscopic cortical and hippocampal atrophy; microscopic extracellular β-amyloid (Aβ42) neuritic plaques and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles, with loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (nucleus basalis of Meynert). Genetic risk factors: Apolipoprotein E ε 4 (APOE ε 4) allele (late-onset) and autosomal dominant APP, PSEN1, PSEN2 mutations (early-onset <65 years).

•  Clinical Features ("5 As"): Insidious, steadily progressive loss of short-term (episodic) memory (forgetting recent conversations, repeating questions, misplacing items), progressing to Aphasia (word-finding difficulty), Apraxia (dressing/constructional apraxia), Agnosia (inability to recognise familiar faces/objects), Anosognosia (lack of insight into deficits), spatial disorientation (wandering/getting lost), and behavioural/psychiatric symptoms (depression, apathy, paranoid delusions, agitation).

•  Management:Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitors (Donepezil 5–10 mg OD, Rivastigmine, or Galantamine) for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s, and the NMDA Receptor Antagonist Memantine (20 mg OD) for moderate-to-severe disease (plus emerging anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies lecanemab and donanemab), alongside carer support, cognitive stimulation, and legal planning (power of attorney).

2.  Vascular Dementia (15%–20%): Caused by multiple cortical infarcts or diffuse subcortical small-vessel disease; characterised by abrupt onset, stepwise deterioration, vascular risk factors (hypertension, AF, diabetes), focal neurological/pyramidal signs, emotional lability, and marche à petits pas gait.

3.  Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB — 10%) [TU]: Characterised by cortical α-synuclein Lewy bodies and three core clinical features: (1) Fluctuating cognition and alertness; (2) Recurrent, well-formed detailed visual hallucinations (e.g., seeing people or animals); and (3) Spontaneous Parkinsonism (plus REM sleep behaviour disorder and extreme, potentially fatal sensitivity to antipsychotic drugs; treated with Rivastigmine).

4.  Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD / Pick’s Disease): Early onset (<65 years); presents with early personality change, social disinhibition, apathy, and executive dysfunction (behavioural-variant FTD) or primary progressive aphasia, with relative preservation of memory in the early stages.

•  Potentially Treatable / Reversible Causes of Dementia ("Dementia Screen") [KU 15]:

(Account for 5%–10% of presentations and MUST be excluded in all patients via blood tests and CT/MRI brain):

1.  Vitamin Deficiencies:Vitamin B12 deficiency, Folate deficiency, and Thiamin (B1) deficiency (Wernicke–Korsakoff).

2.  Endocrine & Metabolic Disorders:Hypothyroidism (Myxoedema), hypercalcaemia/hyperparathyroidism, Cushing’s syndrome, chronic hepatic or renal failure.

3.  Structural Intracranial Lesions (Surgical):Chronic Subdural Haematoma, Normal-Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH), and Benign Frontal Meningioma / Brain Tumours.

4.  Infections & Inflammatory:Neurosyphilis (general paresis of the insane), HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder, Whipple’s disease, and Autoimmune / Limbic Encephalitis (anti-LGI1/NMDAR) or cerebral vasculitis.

5.  Psychiatric & Iatrogenic:Depressive Pseudodementia (elderly patients with severe depression mimicking dementia—typically have a short history, prominent "don’t know" answers, and recover completely with antidepressants/ECT) and Drug toxicity / Anticholinergic burden or Alcohol-related brain damage.

2. Clinical Features of Normal-Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) [KU 23]:

•  A potentially reversible form of communicating hydrocephalus in older adults in which the cerebral ventricles enlarge with intermittently elevated CSF pulse pressures (normal opening pressure on single lumbar puncture).

•  Classic Clinical Triad (Hakim–Adams Triad — Mnemonic: "Wet, Wobbly, and Wacky"):

1.  Gait Disturbance ("Wobbly" — Earliest and Most Prominent Feature):Gait apraxia ("magnetic" gait) where the feet appear stuck/glued to the floor with a broad base, short shuffling steps, and difficulty initiating walking and turning, despite normal leg power on the bed.

2.  Urinary Incontinence ("Wet"): Urinary urgency and frequency progressing to frontal-type urinary incontinence with lack of awareness of bladder fullness.

3.  Cognitive Impairment / Subcortical Dementia ("Wacky"): Psychomotor slowing, apathy, executive dysfunction, and memory impairment.

•  Diagnosis & Treatment:CT or MRI brain shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical sulcal atrophy. Treated by Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) CSF Shunting (often preceded by a high-volume diagnostic CSF tap test).

3. Cognitive Screening: Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) [KU 15, RGU] (Refer to p. 1269):

•  Mini-Mental State Examination (Folstein MMSE — Maximum Score = 30 Points):

•  1. Orientation (10 points): Time (5 points: year, season, month, date, day of week) and Place (5 points: country, county/state, town/city, hospital/building, floor/ward).

•  2. Registration (3 points): Repeat 3 named objects immediately (e.g., Apple, Table, Penny).

•  3. Attention and Calculation (5 points):Serial 7s (subtract 7 from 100 five times: 93, 86, 79, 72, 65) OR spell "WORLD" backwards (D-L-R-O-W).

•  4. Delayed Recall (3 points): Recall the 3 objects registered earlier after 5 minutes.

•  5. Language & Praxis (8 points): Naming 2 objects—watch and pencil (2 points); Repeating "No ifs, ands, or buts" (1 point); Following a 3-stage verbal command (3 points); Reading and obeying "Close your eyes" (1 point); Writing a spontaneous complete sentence (1 point).

•  6. Visuospatial Construction (1 point): Copying intersecting pentagons.

•  Scoring Interpretation:Normal ≥ 24–25/30; Mild cognitive impairment / Mild dementia 18–23/30; Moderate dementia 10–17/30; Severe dementia <10/30.

•  Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA — Maximum Score = 30 Points, Normal ≥ 26/30):

•  More sensitive than the MMSE for detecting Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and executive/visuospatial dysfunction; tests Visuospatial/Executive (alternating trail-making, copying a 3D cube, clock-drawing test [ten past eleven] — 5 pts), Naming (3 animals — 3 pts), Attention (digit span, vigilance letter A tap, serial 7s — 6 pts), Language (sentence repetition, phonemic verbal fluency — 3 pts), Abstraction (similarities — 2 pts), Delayed Recall of 5 words (5 pts), and Orientation (6 pts).

subject: gynecology
title: 1.1 Lymphatic Drainage of the Cervix and Vulva
text:
CHAPTER 1: Anatomy of Female Reproductive Tract

(Covers: Draw and label lymphatic drainage of cervix [KU25,15,RGU,TU]; Lymphatic drainage of vulva [RGU,TU]; Lymphatic drainage of uterus [RGU])

Lymphatic Drainage of the Cervix

Clinical Importance: Crucial in staging and planning radical surgery (Wertheim’s hysterectomy) or radiotherapy in carcinoma cervix.

Pathway: Lymphatics from the cervix course along the uterine veins to drain into two groups of lymph nodes:

Primary Group of Nodes:

Parametrial nodes: Small, inconsistently present in the parametrium near the crossing of the ureter and uterine artery.

Obturator nodes: Located in the obturator canal (most consistently involved).

Internal iliac (Hypogastric) nodes: Along the internal iliac vessels.

External iliac nodes: Anterior and medial groups.

Sacral nodes: Located in front of the sacral promontory and lateral to the rectum.

Secondary Group of Nodes:

Receive efferents from all primary nodes and include the Common iliac nodes and Superior lumbar (para-aortic) nodes.

(Note on Uterine Corpus Drainage: Fundus drains via ovarian lymphatics to para-aortic nodes; Cornu drains along the round ligament to superficial inguinal nodes; Rest of the body drains to external iliac nodes).

B. Lymphatic Drainage of the Vulva

Anatomical Peculiarities:

Dense dermal lymphatic plexuses freely intercommunicate across the midline (explaining bilateral and contralateral metastasis in vulval cancer).

Vulval lymphatics do not cross beyond the labiocrural fold laterally.

Drainage Pathway:

Primary Nodes (Sentinel Nodes): Superficial Inguinal Lymph Nodes (arranged in a horizontal group parallel to the inguinal ligament and a vertical group along the long saphenous vein). They drain the labia majora (anterior and posterior halves), labia minora, prepuce, fourchette, and Bartholin’s glands.

Secondary Nodes: Deep Inguinal (Femoral) Lymph Nodes (5–6 nodes lying medial to the femoral vein). The uppermost node located in the femoral canal beneath the inguinal ligament is the Node of Cloquet (or Rosenmüller). Exception: The glans clitoris drains directly into the deep inguinal and external iliac nodes.

Tertiary Nodes: External Iliac and Pelvic Nodes (receive efferents from superficial and deep inguinal nodes through the femoral canal).

subject: gynecology
title: 1.2 Perineal Body (Obstetrical Perineum / Central Point of Perineum)
text:
(Covers: Perineal body [KU25,20,TU,RGU]; Anatomy of perineal body [RGU])

Definition & Situation: It is a fibromuscular, pyramidal-shaped condensation of tissue where the pelvic floor and perineal muscles/fascia meet in the midline between the lower one-third of the posterior vaginal wall anteriorly and the anal canal posteriorly.

Measurements & Boundaries:

Measures about 4 cm × 4 cm ( inches).

Base: Covered by perineal skin extending from the fourchette to the anus.

Apex: Pointed and continuous above with the rectovaginal septum (Fascia of Denonvilliers).

Musculofascial Structures Forming the Perineal Body:

Fascia:

Superficial perineal fascia (superficial fatty layer and deep membranous Colles’ fascia).

Inferior and superior layers of the urogenital diaphragm (triangular ligament / perineal membrane).

Muscles (9 muscles converge like spokes of a wheel):

Paired superficial transverse perinei.

Paired deep transverse perinei.

Paired bulbospongiosus (bulbocavernosus).

Paired levator ani (pubococcygeus / pubovaginalis fibers) inserting at the junction of the upper two-thirds and lower one-third of the vagina.

Unpaired sphincter ani externus (superficial fibers).

Clinical / Applied Importance:

Support of Pelvic Organs: Anchors the pelvic floor; supports the lower posterior vaginal wall, which indirectly supports the anterior vaginal wall, bladder, and uterus.

Maintenance of Vaginal Axis: Keeps the normal horizontal slope of the upper vagina.

Childbirth Trauma: Vulnerable to second-, third-, and fourth-degree perineal tears during the second stage of labor; laxity leads to gaping introitus, rectocele, and pelvic organ prolapse.

Episiotomy: Deliberate surgical incision through the perineal body structures during delivery to prevent irregular lacerations.

subject: gynecology
title: 1.3 Pelvic Ureter
text:
(Covers: Draw and label Pelvic ureter [KU24,21,TU]; Course of ureter and its relations [RGU]; Common sites of injury to the ureter during surgery [KU15])

Extent & Dimensions: Extends from the crossing of the pelvic brim (sacroiliac joint) to its opening into the base of the urinary bladder (trigone). It measures about 13 cm in length and 5 mm in diameter.

Course and Anatomical Relations:

At the Pelvic Brim: Enters the pelvis in front of the bifurcation of the common iliac artery over the sacroiliac joint (behind the root of the mesentery on the right, and the apex of the mesosigmoid on the left).

Along the Lateral Pelvic Wall: Courses downwards and backwards attached to the posterior peritoneum, lying anterior to the internal iliac artery and forming the posterior boundary of the ovarian fossa.

On the Pelvic Floor (Base of Broad Ligament): At the level of the ischial spine, it turns forwards and medially on the levator ani muscle within the base of the broad ligament (parametrium).

Relation to Uterine Artery (“Water under the Bridge”): About 1.5–2 cm lateral to the supravaginal cervix (at the level of the internal os), the uterine artery crosses the ureter anteriorly and from above at right angles.

Ureteric Tunnel (Tunnel of Wertheim): Soon after being crossed by the uterine artery, it enters a fibrous tunnel within the upper part of the Mackenrodt’s (cardinal) ligament, lying 1.5–2 cm lateral to the lateral vaginal fornix.

Intravesical Part: Traverses the anterior vaginal fornix and pierces the lateral angle of the bladder wall obliquely for 2 cm to open at the base of the trigone.

Sites of Anatomical Constriction in the Pelvis:

Where it crosses the pelvic brim.

Where it is crossed by the uterine artery.

In the intravesical part.

Blood Supply: Segmental supply from the ovarian, internal iliac, uterine, vaginal, superior/inferior vesical, and middle rectal arteries. (Longitudinal anastomotic vessels run in its outer adventitial sheath).

Identification at Surgery: (i) Pale glistening tubular appearance, (ii) Longitudinal arborizing vessels on its surface, (iii) Vermicular peristalsis on gentle pinching with non-toothed forceps.

Common Sites of Ureteric Injury During Gynecological Surgery (Hysterectomy):

At the pelvic brim / infundibulopelvic ligament: While clamping the ovarian vessels (where the ureter lies immediately beneath the posterior peritoneum).

Deep in the pelvis near the uterosacral ligament: Below the level of the ischial spine.

By the side of the cervix: While clamping the uterine artery and Mackenrodt’s (cardinal) ligament.

At the lateral vaginal angle / anterior fornix: While clamping and suturing the vaginal vault angles.

During pelvic peritonization: Caught in the suture while closing the posterior leaf of the broad ligament.

Radical hysterectomy (Wertheim’s): Stripping the outer adventitial sheath off the peritoneum leads to ischemia, devitalization, and sloughing necrosis (resulting in ureterovaginal fistula 7–14 days postoperatively).

subject: gynecology
title: 1.4 Pelvic Floor (Pelvic Diaphragm) and Levator Ani Muscle
text:
(Covers: Draw and label Levator ani muscle [KU22]; Draw and label pubococcygeus muscle and label its parts [KU16]; Pelvic floor [RGU]; Pelvic Diaphragm [TU])

Definition: The pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm) is a muscular partition separating the pelvic cavity above from the anatomical perineum below. It is formed by the levator ani muscles (three paired components) together with the parietal layer of pelvic fascia covering its concave upper surface and the anal fascia covering its convex inferior surface.

Components of Levator Ani Muscle:

Pubococcygeus (most medial and functional part).

Iliococcygeus (intermediate part).

Ischiococcygeus / Coccygeus (posterolateral part).

Origin: Each levator ani arises from: (i) the posterior surface of the body of the pubic bone, (ii) the condensed fascia covering the obturator internus muscle (Arcus tendineus / White line of the pelvis), and (iii) the inner surface of the ischial spine.

Insertion & Subdivisions of Pubococcygeus:

The fibers pass backwards and medially around the midline pelvic effluents:

Pubovaginalis: The most anterior fibers pass alongside the urethra and lateral walls of the vagina to insert into the perineal body, forming a ‘U’-shaped supportive sling.

Puboanalis: Fibers run between the internal and external anal sphincters to insert into the longitudinal muscle coat of the anal canal.

Puborectalis: Forms a strong ‘U’-shaped loop (puborectal sling) that winds around the posterior aspect of the anorectal junction, maintaining the anorectal angle.

Posterior fibers (Pubococcygeus proper) & Iliococcygeus: Insert into the anococcygeal raphe (levator plate) and the tip/sides of the coccyx.

Ischiococcygeus (Coccygeus): Triangular muscle arising from the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament, inserting into the upper two pieces of the coccyx and last piece of the sacrum.

Midline Gaps (Hiatuses):

Hiatus urogenitalis (anterior): Pierced by the urethra and vagina; bridged by the urogenital diaphragm.

Hiatus rectalis (posterior): Transmits the anorectal junction.

Nerve Supply: Direct branches from S3 and S4 nerve roots on the pelvic surface, and the inferior rectal and perineal branches of the pudendal nerve (S2, S3, S4) on the perineal surface.

Functions of the Levator Ani / Pelvic Floor:

Support of Pelvic Viscera: Acts like a hammock supporting the bladder, vagina, uterus, and rectum. The levator plate forms a horizontal shelf upon which the upper vagina, cervix, and rectum rest.

Counteracts Intra-abdominal Pressure: Guards the hiatus urogenitalis during coughing, sneezing, or straining.

Sphincteric Action: Pubovaginalis assists urethral closure; puborectalis assists the external anal sphincter.

Role in Parturition: Facilitates anterior internal rotation of the fetal presenting part in the second stage of labor.

Stabilization: Steadies the perineal body and stabilizes the sacroiliac and sacrococcygeal joints.

subject: gynecology
title: 1.5 Normal Vaginal Epithelium & Structure of Vagina
text:
(Covers: Draw and label Normal vaginal epithelium [KU21]; Anatomy of the vagina [RGU])

Layers of the Vaginal Wall (From within outwards):

Mucous Coat (Epithelium): Lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium resting on a basement membrane. It is completely devoid of any secreting glands, hair follicles, or sweat/sebaceous glands.

Submucous Layer: Loose areolar connective tissue rich in elastic fibers and venous plexuses.

Muscular Layer: Smooth muscle fibers arranged in an indistinct inner circular and a stronger outer longitudinal layer.

External Fibrous Coat: Derived from the condensed endopelvic fascia; tough and highly vascular.

Histological Zones of the Stratified Squamous Epithelium (Reproductive Age):

Basal Cell Layer: Single row of small, round, basophilic cuboidal cells with large nuclei resting on the basement membrane (site of active mitosis/regeneration).

Parabasal Cell Layer: 2–3 layers of oval, basophilic cells.

Intermediate Cell Layer: Multiple layers of larger, flattened, boat-shaped (navicular) cells with vesicular nuclei; rich in glycogen (predominates under progesterone influence).

Superficial Cornified Cell Layer: Flat, large, polygonal, acidophilic (eosinophilic) cells with small pyknotic nuclei; rich in glycogen (predominates under estrogen influence).

Hormonal & Age Variations (Vaginal Defense):

Newborn (0–10 days): Thick, multilayered epithelium rich in glycogen due to maternal estrogen; Döderlein’s bacilli present; acidic pH (4–5).

Childhood (2 weeks to Prepuberty): Thin (few layers), devoid of glycogen and Döderlein’s bacilli; neutral/alkaline pH (6–8)  vulnerable to vulvovaginitis.

Reproductive Period (Puberty to Menopause): Multilayered, rich in glycogen. Döderlein’s bacilli (Gram-positive anaerobic rods) convert glycogen from exfoliated cells into lactic acid, maintaining a protective acidic pH of 4.0–5.5 (average 4.5).

Postmenopause: Atrophic, thin (parabasal dominance), glycogen and Döderlein’s bacilli absent, pH neutral/alkaline (6–7).

subject: gynecology
title: 1.6 Internal Iliac Artery and Its Branches (Including Uterine Artery)
text:
(Covers: Draw and label Internal iliac artery and its Branches [KU20]; Uterine Artery [TU])

Origin & Course: The internal iliac (hypogastric) artery is the medial terminal branch of the common iliac artery, originating in front of the sacroiliac joint at the level of the lumbosacral disc. It measures about 2 to 4 cm in length. The ureter lies anteriorly and the internal iliac vein lies posteriorly. At the upper margin of the greater sciatic foramen, it divides into an Anterior division and a Posterior division.

Branches of the Internal Iliac Artery:

Posterior Division (All Parietal — No Visceral Branches):

Iliolumbar artery

Lateral sacral artery (superior and inferior)

Superior gluteal artery (largest branch)

Anterior Division:

Visceral Branches (5):

Superior vesical artery (continuation of the proximal patent part of the obliterated umbilical artery; supplies upper bladder).

Uterine artery (main blood supply to uterus).

Vaginal artery (often arises in common with uterine artery; forms anterior and posterior vaginal azygos arteries).

Inferior vesical artery (supplies bladder base, lower ureter, and upper urethra).

Middle rectal artery (supplies rectum and lower vagina).

Parietal Branches (3):

Obturator artery

Inferior gluteal artery

Internal pudendal artery (main blood supply to external genitalia and perineum via Alcock’s canal).

Note on Uterine Artery:

Course: Runs downwards and forwards on the lateral pelvic wall, then turns medially in the base of the broad ligament (Mackenrodt’s ligament). At 1.5–2 cm lateral to the internal os, it crosses above and in front of the ureter, reaches the side of the uterus, and ascends in a tortuous/spiral manner between the leaves of the broad ligament to anastomose end-on with the tubal branch of the ovarian artery in the mesosalpinx.

Branches: (1) Ureteric branch (at the crossing), (2) Descending cervical branch, (3) Circular artery of the cervix, (4) Segmental arcuate arteries  radial arteries  short basal arteries (to basal endometrium) and coiled spiral arteries (to functional endometrium), (5) Fundal branch, (6) Twigs to round ligament, (7) Tubal branch, (8) Ovarian anastomotic branch.

subject: gynecology
title: 1.7 Fallopian Tube: Anatomy, Physiology & Surgical Application
text:
(Covers: Draw and label the parts of the fallopian tube; indicate the commonest site for ectopic pregnancy [KU19,16]; Anatomy and physiology of fallopian tube with its surgical application [KU16,RGU,TU])

Gross Anatomy: Paired, hollow muscular tubes situated in the medial three-fourths of the upper free margin of the broad ligament (mesosalpinx). Each tube measures about 10 cm (4 inches) in length.

Openings (Ostia):

Uterine opening (ostium): Communicates with the superolateral angle (cornu) of the uterine cavity; measures 1 mm in diameter.

Pelvic / Abdominal ostium: Opens into the peritoneal cavity; measures 2 mm in diameter and is surrounded by 20–25 finger-like projections called fimbriae (the longest one attached to the tubal pole of the ovary is the ovarian fimbria).

Four Anatomical Parts (From Medial to Lateral):

Intramural (Interstitial) part: Traverses the muscular wall of the uterus; measures 1.25 cm ( inch) in length and 1 mm in diameter (narrowest part).

Isthmus: Almost straight, thick-walled, cord-like segment adjacent to the uterus; measures 2.5 cm (1 inch) in length and 2.5 mm in diameter.

Ampulla: Longest, widest, thin-walled, and tortuous part; measures 5 cm (2 inches) in length. It is the site of fertilization and the commonest site for tubal ectopic pregnancy (55–70%).

Infundibulum: Trumpet-shaped lateral extremity measuring 1.25 cm ( inch) in length with a maximum diameter of 6 mm, ending in the fimbriated abdominal ostium.

Histological Structure (3 Layers):

Serous coat: Peritoneum of the broad ligament covering all sides except along the line of attachment of the mesosalpinx.

Muscular coat (Myosalpinx): Smooth muscle arranged in an outer longitudinal and inner circular layer (thickest in the isthmus, thinnest in the ampulla).

Mucous membrane (Endosalpinx): Thrown into complex longitudinal branching folds (plicae), most elaborate in the ampulla. There is no submucosa and no glands. Lined by a single layer of columnar epithelium containing three cell types: (i) Ciliated columnar cells (most numerous at the fimbriae and ampulla; beat toward the uterus), (ii) Non-ciliated secretory (goblet) cells, and (iii) Intercalary / ‘Peg’ cells.

Blood Supply, Lymphatics & Nerve Supply:

Arterial: Dual supply from the uterine artery (medial two-thirds) and ovarian artery (lateral one-third) anastomosing in the mesosalpinx.

Venous: Drains via the pampiniform plexus into the ovarian and uterine veins.

Lymphatics: Drain along ovarian vessels to the para-aortic (superior lumbar) nodes.

Nerves: Sympathetic () and parasympathetic (); the tube is highly sensitive to handling, distension, and cutting.

Physiology of the Fallopian Tube:

Ovum Pick-up: At ovulation, the fimbriae sweep over the ovarian surface and muscular contractions + ciliary currents draw the cumulus-oocyte complex into the infundibulum.

Sperm Transport & Capacitation: Tubal secretions and anti-peristaltic muscular contractions assist sperm ascent to the ampulla and promote sperm capacitation.

Site of Fertilization: Occurs in the ampulla within 12–24 hours of ovulation.

Nutrition & Transport of Zygote: Tubal fluid (rich in pyruvate, lactate, electrolytes, and glycoproteins) nourishes the cleaving embryo for 3–4 days before peristalsis and ciliary beat propel the morula into the uterine cavity (aided by progesterone-induced relaxation of the uterotubal junction).

Surgical & Clinical Applications:

Tubal Sterilization (Tubectomy / Laparoscopic Ligation): Performed at the isthmus (or isthmo-ampullary junction) because its lumen is narrow and uniform, making occlusion effective with minimal failure, and leaving maximum healthy tube length for high success (75–80%) if microsurgical tubotubal reanastomosis (reversal) is requested later.

Identification at Laparotomy: Identified by tracing from the uterine cornu laterally to the fimbriated end (distinguishing it from the round and ovarian ligaments).

Ectopic Pregnancy: Ampulla is the commonest site overall (frequently ending in tubal abortion), whereas isthmic ectopic pregnancy ruptures earliest (6–8 weeks) due to its narrow, less distensible lumen.Conservative surgery (linear salpingostomy) is done on the antimesenteric border of the ampulla.

Infertility & PID: Gonococcal/chlamydial endosalpingitis destroys cilia and causes fimbrial agglutination (hydrosalpinx), जबकि genital tuberculosis affects the ampullary submucosa (tobacco-pouch appearance) and cornual ends.

subject: gynecology
title: Chapter 1: One-Word Answers / Short Questions
text:
Q1. Ovary develops from… [KU20]

Answer: Genital (Gonadal) ridge (coelomic epithelium and underlying mesenchyme of the intermediate mesoderm), while the primordial germ cells originate from the endoderm of the yolk sac (near the hindgut) and migrate to the genital ridge.

Q2. Embryological remnants of Wolffian (Mesonephric) system in females [RGU]:

Answer: Epoophoron, Paroophoron, Gartner’s duct (and Gartner’s duct cyst in the anterolateral vaginal wall). (Note: Kobelt’s tubules are of pronephric origin; Hydatid of Morgagni is of Müllerian/paramesonephric origin).

Q3. Triradiate ligament (Mackenrodt’s / Pelvirectal / Pubocervical complex) [TU]:

Answer: The Pericervical ring condensation of endopelvic fascia radiating in three directions from the supravaginal cervix: anteriorly as the pubocervical ligament, laterally as the cardinal (Mackenrodt’s / transverse cervical) ligament, and posteriorly as the uterosacral ligament.

subject: gynecology
title: 2.1 Normal Menstrual Cycle, Phases & Physiology of Menstruation
text:
CHAPTER 2: Female Reproductive Physiology

(Covers: Physiology of menstruation [KU25,24]; Define normal menstrual cycle and discuss phases of normal menstrual cycle [KU22,TU]; Draw and label Endometrium/Endometrial phase in menstrual cycle [KU23,19]; Draw and label the various hormonal pattern in a normal menstrual cycle [KU21]; Draw and label Ovarian menstrual cycle [KU20]; Proliferative phase [TU]; Secretory phase of endometrium [KU24,RGU,TU]; Corpus luteum [RGU,TU]; Physiology of ovulation [RGU,TU]; Hypothalamo-pituitary ovarian axis [RGU])

A. Definition & Normal Parameters of Menstruation

Definition: Menstruation is the visible manifestation of cyclic, physiological uterine bleeding due to the shedding of the superficial functional layer of the endometrium, resulting from the invisible interplay of hormones along the Hypothalamo-Pituitary-Ovarian (HPO) axis in the absence of pregnancy.

Prerequisites for Normal Menstruation: (1) Normal female chromosomal complement (46,XX), (2) Coordinated HPO axis, (3) Responsive endometrium, (4) Patent anatomical outflow tract, and (5) Active support of thyroid and adrenal glands.

Normal Parameters:

Age of Menarche: 11–15 years (mean: 13 years).

Cycle Length (Interval): 21–35 days (mean: 28 days).

Duration of Flow: 4–5 days (normal range: 2–7 days).

Amount of Blood Loss: 20–80 mL (average: 35 mL; ~70% occurs in the first 2 days).

B. Hormonal Regulation (HPO Axis & Two-Cell, Two-Gonadotropin Theory)

Hypothalamus: The arcuate nucleus secretes GnRH (a decapeptide, half-life 2–4 min) in a pulsatile fashion into the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system (1 pulse/hour in the follicular phase; 1 pulse/2–3 hours in the luteal phase).

Anterior Pituitary: Pulsatile GnRH stimulates gonadotrophs to synthesize and release FSH and LH.

Two-Cell, Two-Gonadotropin Concept of Ovarian Steroidogenesis:

LH acts on Theca interna cells to convert cholesterol into androgens (androstenedione and testosterone).

These androgens diffuse across the basement membrane into Granulosa cells, where FSH induces the enzyme aromatase to convert them into estrogens (estradiol-17 and estrone).

Feedback Mechanisms:

Negative Feedback: Moderate levels of estradiol () and Inhibin B (in follicular phase) / Inhibin A & Progesterone (in luteal phase) suppress FSH and LH.

Positive Feedback: When preovulatory estradiol exceeds a critical threshold of >200 pg/mL and is sustained for 24–48 hours, it exerts a positive feedback effect on the anterior pituitary, triggering the mid-cycle LH surge (and a smaller FSH surge).

C. The Ovarian Cycle (4 Phases)

Recruitment of Cohort of Follicles (Preantral Phase):

Initial recruitment of primordial follicles takes ~85 days (spanning 3 cycles) and is gonadotropin-independent.

At the start of a cycle (luteal-follicular shift), falling steroid and inhibin levels cause a rise in FSH, which rescues a cohort of 15–20 antral follicles (2–5 mm) from apoptosis.

Selection and Maturation of the Dominant Follicle (Follicular Phase — Days 1 to 14):

By Day 5–7, one follicle with the highest FSH receptor density and an estrogen-dominant microenvironment (low androgen-to-estrogen ratio) is selected as the Dominant Follicle.

Rising estrogen suppresses FSH via negative feedback, causing the remaining non-dominant follicles to undergo atresia.

FSH induces LH receptors on the granulosa cells of the dominant follicle. By Day 14, the mature Graafian follicle reaches 18–20 mm in diameter.

Ovulation (Day 14 in a 28-day cycle):

Timing: Occurs 10–12 hours after the LH peak, 32–36 hours after the onset of the LH surge, and 24–36 hours after the estradiol peak.

Mechanism of Ovulation:

Endocrine (LH/FSH surge): The LH surge triggers resumption of Meiosis-I in the primary oocyte (forming a secondary oocyte arrested at metaphase-II and the first polar body), luteinization of granulosa cells, and local synthesis of progesterone and prostaglandins. The FSH surge (aided by preovulatory 17--OH progesterone) stimulates plasminogen activator  plasmin, which activates collagenase to digest the follicular wall.

Passive stretching: Necrobiosis of the overlying tunica albuginea forming a thin conical stigma (intrafollicular pressure remains constant at 10–15 mm Hg).

Micromuscular contraction: Prostaglandin ()-mediated contraction of smooth muscle cells in the theca externa extrudes the oocyte-cumulus complex.

Corpus Luteum Formation & Regression (Luteal Phase — Days 15 to 28):

Life Cycle (4 Stages):

Stage of Proliferation: Collapsed follicle wall convolutes; granulosa cells hypertrophy into large, pale, lipid-rich granulosa lutein cells.

Stage of Vascularization (within 24 hours): Capillaries from the theca interna invade the granulosa layer, delivering LDL-cholesterol for progesterone synthesis.

Stage of Maturation (Days 4–8 post-ovulation / Day 21–22 of cycle): Attains peak size (1–2 cm) and characteristic yellow color (due to carotene pigment). Theca interna cells form paralutein (‘K’) cells at the periphery. Secretes peak progesterone (5–15 ng/mL, peaking 8 days after LH peak), estradiol, inhibin A, and relaxin.

Stage of Regression (Luteolysis — Days 22–23 onwards): In the absence of pregnancy (no hCG rescue), the corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan of 12–14 days. Local luteolytic factors (, nitric oxide, endothelin, TNF-) and withdrawal of tonic LH cause vacuolation, hyalinization, and transformation into a white scar called the corpus albicans.

D. The Endometrial Cycle (4 Phases)

The endometrium consists of a deep basal zone (stratum basalis, 1 mm) supplied by straight basal arteries (unresponsive to hormones; regenerates the endometrium) and a superficial functional zone (stratum functionalis) supplied by coiled spiral arteries.

Stage of Regeneration (Days 2 to 5):

Begins even before menstrual flow ceases and completes 2–3 days after menses.

Surface cubical epithelium regenerates from the stumps of basal glands and stromal cells; thickness is ~2 mm.

Proliferative (Follicular) Phase (Days 5 to 14):

Driven by estradiol from the growing ovarian follicle; estrogen also induces progesterone receptors in the endometrium.

Glands: Narrow, straight, and tubular; lined by low columnar epithelium with basal nuclei and active mitoses.In late proliferative phase, pseudostratification of nuclei occurs.

Stroma & Vessels: Spindle-shaped stromal cells with active mitosis; spiral arteries grow unbranched toward the surface.

Thickness: Increases to 3–4 mm (appears as a classic triple-line pattern on transvaginal ultrasound, measuring 8–11 mm total bilayer thickness preovulatory).

Secretory (Luteal) Phase (Days 15 to 28):

Driven by progesterone (and estrogen) from the corpus luteum acting on an estrogen-primed endometrium. Progesterone halts endometrial mitosis.

Early Secretory (Days 15–18): Appearance of glycogen vacuoles between the nucleus and basement membrane, pushing the nuclei upwards—known as subnuclear vacuolation, which is the earliest histological evidence of ovulation (appearing 36–48 hours post-ovulation).

Mid-Secretory (Days 19–22): Secretions move past the nucleus into the glandular lumen (nuclei return to the base). Glands become tortuous and corkscrew-shaped with luminal eosinophilic secretion and saw-toothed margins. Stroma becomes edematous (window of implantation: Days 20–24).

Late Secretory (Days 23–28): Endometrium differentiates into three zones: (i) Superficial stratum compactum (large polyhedral decidualized stromal cells around gland necks), (ii) Middle stratum spongiosum (edematous stroma, dilated tortuous glands, intensely coiled spiral arterioles), and (iii) Deep stratum basalis. Total thickness reaches 6–8 mm.

Pre-menstrual Regression (24–48 hours before menses): Fall in estrogen and progesterone causes dehydration of stroma, intense coiling of spiral arterioles, and infiltration of polymorphonuclear leukocytes and monocytes.

Menstrual Phase (Days 1 to 4) & Mechanism of Menstrual Bleeding:

Vascular Spasm & Ischemia: Withdrawal of estrogen and progesterone stimulates local synthesis of  and endothelin-1, causing intense, prolonged vasoconstriction (spasm) of the spiral arterioles at the basal layer  stasis and tissue hypoxia/ischemia.

Enzymatic Autodigestion: Ischemia destabilizes lysosomal membranes in endometrial cells, releasing proteolytic enzymes (matrix metalloproteinases / acid hydrolases) that digest the functional zone.

Relaxation & Hemorrhage: Subsequent arteriolar relaxation allows blood to escape through damaged capillary walls, forming subepithelial hematomas that rupture and shed the necrotic functional layer.

Fibrinolysis: Menstrual blood clots initially inside the uterine cavity but is rapidly liquefied by plasmin (converted from plasminogen by endometrial plasminogen activators), so menstrual blood normally does not clot unless bleeding is brisk.

Arrest of Bleeding (Hemostasis): Achieved by: (i) prolonged vasoconstriction of decapitated basal arterioles (mediated by , thromboxane , endothelin, and PAF), (ii) myometrial contractions, (iii) local platelet plug and fibrin seal, and (iv) re-epithelialization stimulated by rising estrogen from the newly recruited follicular cohort.

subject: gynecology
title: 2.2 Structure of Mature Graafian Follicle
text:
(Covers: Draw and label Structure of mature Graafian follicle [KU24,23,22,18,RGU,TU])

Size: A fully mature preovulatory Graafian follicle measures about 18–20 mm in diameter.

Microscopic Layers (From Outside Inwards):

Theca Externa: Outer condensed layer of ovarian stroma consisting of fibrous connective tissue and smooth muscle-like (micromuscular) fibers.

Theca Interna: Highly vascular layer of vacuolated,epithelioid stromal cells containing LH receptors; synthesizes androgens.

Membrana Granulosa (Limitans / Basement Membrane): Polymerized acellular basement membrane separating the vascular theca interna from the avascular granulosa layer.

Membrana Granulosa (Granulosa Cell Layer): Stratified layer of cuboidal follicular cells containing FSH and LH receptors; avascular until ovulation; aromatizes androgens into estradiol.

Antrum (Follicular Cavity): Central cavity filled with liquor folliculi (an ultrafiltrate of plasma containing high concentrations of estradiol, FSH, LH, inhibin, Oocyte Maturation Inhibitor [OMI], Luteinization Inhibitor [LI], and plasminogen).

Discus Proligerus (Cumulus Oophorus): Mound of granulosa cells anchoring the oocyte to the follicular wall.

Corona Radiata: Innermost radially arranged granulosa cells directly surrounding the zona pellucida, communicating with the oocyte via gap junctions.

Oocyte (Primary Oocyte just prior to ovulation): Measures ~130 microns (with a 20–25 micron eccentric nucleus and large nucleolus), surrounded by the vitelline membrane, perivitelline space (into which the first polar body is extruded), and an outer acellular glycoprotein coat called the zona pellucida.

subject: gynecology
title: 2.3 Source and Functions of Estrogen
text:
(Covers: Source and functions of estrogen [KU20])

Types & Potency: The three classic natural estrogens (18-carbon steroids) in order of potency are Estradiol-17 () : Estrone () : Estriol () = 100 : 10 : 1.

Sources of Estrogen:

Granulosa cells of the developing ovarian follicles and luteinized granulosa cells of the corpus luteum (predominant source of  during reproductive life; daily production 50–300 ).

Theca interna and ovarian stromal cells (minor quantity).

Peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androgens (androstenedione  estrone) in adipose tissue, muscle, and skin (major source of estrogen in postmenopausal women).

Fetoplacental unit (Syncytiotrophoblast) during pregnancy (predominantly estriol).

Physiological Actions / Functions of Estrogen:

Secondary Sexual Characteristics: Develops feminine body contour (fat deposition on breasts, hips, and thighs), feminine voice, and epiphyseal closure of long bones. (Note: Axillary and pubic hair growth depends on adrenal androgens).

Vulva & Vagina: Causes proliferation and cornification of vaginal stratified squamous epithelium, intracellular glycogen deposition  lactic acid production by Döderlein’s bacilli  maintains acidic vaginal pH (4.0–4.5) and vaginal defense.

Cervix: Causes cervical hypertrophy; makes cervical mucus copious, clear, watery, alkaline, low in protein, and rich in electrolytes (NaCl)  increases stretchability (Spinnbarkeit >10 cm) and fern pattern to facilitate sperm penetration.

Uterus (Myometrium & Endometrium): Enlarges the uterus from infantile (cervix:body = 2:1) to adult proportions (body:cervix = 2:1); increases myometrial vascularity, contractility, and oxytocin sensitivity; causes regeneration and proliferation of the endometrium and induces progesterone receptors.

Fallopian Tubes: Increases vascularity, ciliary activity, and muscular motility.

Breasts: Stimulates proliferation of the ductal system, stromal fat deposition, and pigmentation of the areola.

Endocrine (HPO Axis): Exerts negative feedback on FSH throughout the cycle, and positive feedback on LH when sustained at >200 pg/mL for 24–48 hours (triggering the mid-cycle LH surge).

Metabolic & Systemic Actions:

Bone: Inhibits osteoclastic bone resorption, increases intestinal calcium absorption and -Vitamin D  conserves bone mass and prevents osteoporosis.

Cardiovascular & Lipids: Increases HDL (especially ), decreases LDL and total cholesterol, stimulates endothelial nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin, and acts as an antioxidant (cardioprotective).

Blood & Liver: Increases hepatic synthesis of SHBG, TBG, CBG, and clotting factors (fibrinogen, Factors II, VII, IX, X) while decreasing antithrombin III.

Fluid/Electrolytes: Causes mild sodium and water retention.

subject: gynecology
title: 3.1 Definition, Classification (PALM-COEIN) & Management of AUB
text:
CHAPTER 3: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) & Dysmenorrhoea

(Covers: Essays 1 [KU24], 2 [KU21], 3 [KU19]; SE 1 [KU25], 2 [KU22], 3 [KU19], 4–9 [RGU]; SA 1 [KU25], 2 [KU24], 4 [KU17], 6–12 [RGU/TU])

A. Definitions

Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB): Any uterine bleeding that is outside the normal parameters of volume (20–80 mL), duration (4–5 days), regularity, or frequency (21–35 days).

Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (HMB) / Menorrhagia: Cyclic menstrual bleeding at normal intervals that is excessive in amount (>80 mL) and/or duration (>7 days), or bleeding that interferes with a woman’s physical, emotional, social, and material quality of life.

Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding (DUB): A state of abnormal uterine bleeding without any clinically detectable organic, systemic, or iatrogenic cause (corresponding to non-structural AUB-O and AUB-E in the modern FIGO system).

Polymenorrhoea (Epimenorrhoea): Cyclic bleeding where the menstrual cycle interval is reduced to <21 days and remains constant at that frequency. (If accompanied by heavy/prolonged flow, it is called epimenorrhagia).

Metrorrhagia: Irregular, acyclic bleeding from the uterus of variable amount (often due to surface lesions like polyps, submucous fibroids, or malignancy).

Oligomenorrhoea: Menstrual bleeding occurring >35 days apart and remaining constant at that frequency.

B. FIGO Classification of AUB (PALM-COEIN System — 2011)

Introduced by FIGO to standardize nomenclature based on etiology, dividing causes into Structural (PALM) (diagnosable by imaging/histopathology) and Non-structural (COEIN) groups:

[[TABLE:gynecology-tbl-001]]

C. Special Pathological Entities in AUB (Short Notes)

Metropathia Hemorrhagica (Schroeder’s Disease / Cystic Glandular Hyperplasia):

Pathophysiology: Seen typically in perimenopausal women (40–50 years) or adolescents due to chronic anovulation. Persistent unopposed estrogen (from persistent ovarian follicular cysts without ovulation/corpus luteum) stimulates continuous endometrial proliferation for 6–8 weeks of amenorrhoea, followed by prolonged, heavy, painless vaginal bleeding when estrogen levels fall or the thickened endometrium outgrows its blood supply (painless because  is low in the absence of progesterone).

Pathology: Uterus is symmetrically enlarged (8–10 weeks size) due to myohyperplasia. Endometrium is thick and polypoidal. Microscopically, glands show marked disparity in size—some small, some cystically dilated—giving the classic “Swiss-cheese” appearance (Simple hyperplasia without atypia), lined by tall columnar epithelium with no secretory changes and superficial stromal necrosis.

Irregular Shedding of the Endometrium (Halban’s Disease):

Pathophysiology: Ovular menorrhagia caused by incomplete atrophy of the corpus luteum due to persistent LH secretion  persistent progesterone output  prolonged desquamation and delayed regeneration beyond Day 5.

Diagnosis: Endometrial biopsy taken on Day 5 or 6 of bleeding shows a mixture of secretory and proliferative endometrium.

Irregular Ripening of the Endometrium (Luteal Phase Defect):

Pathophysiology: Poor corpus luteum function  inadequate progesterone and estrogen support  premenstrual brownish spotting for several days before proper menstrual flow begins.

Diagnosis: Endometrial biopsy shows patchy secretory changes amidst proliferative endometrium (lag phase >2 days).

D. Clinical Approach & Investigations for a Woman with HMB / AUB (e.g., 36y, 42y, 45y, 46y Multiparous Woman)

Detailed History:

Quantify blood loss (duration >7 days, passage of big clots, number of pads soaked, interference with daily life).

Pattern: Cyclic (menorrhagia—fibroid, adenomyosis, DUB) vs. Acyclic/Intermenstrual/Postcoital (polyp, cervicitis, carcinoma cervix/endometrium).

Associated pain: Secondary congestive dysmenorrhoea suggests adenomyosis, endometriosis, or PID (as in the 36-year-old lady in [KU25]); painless bleeding suggests anovulatory AUB.

Contraceptive history (Cu-IUCD, hormones), drug history (anticoagulants), and systemic symptoms (hypothyroidism, easy bruising/epistaxis).

Physical Examination:

General & Systemic: Degree of pallor, BMI (obesity in PCOS/hyperплаsia), thyroid swelling, petechiae/bruises.

Abdominal Examination: Look for any suprapubic mass.

Pelvic Examination (Speculum & Bimanual): Inspect cervix for polyps, erosion, or growth; take Pap smear. Bimanual palpation for uterine size, symmetry, mobility, and tenderness (uniformly bulky/tender in adenomyosis; irregularly enlarged/firm in fibroid; normal size in primary DUB).

Laboratory & Special Investigations:

Blood Values: Hemoglobin & Hematocrit (to assess severity of anemia), Urine pregnancy test (-hCG) (to rule out abortion/ectopic pregnancy), Thyroid Profile (TSH, free ).

Coagulation Profile: Platelet count, BT, CT, PT/INR, aPTT, and von Willebrand factor assay (mandatory in adolescent/pubertal AUB or positive bleeding history).

Transvaginal Ultrasonography (TVS) with Color Doppler (First-line Imaging): Assesses endometrial thickness (hyperplasia if >12 mm in premenopausal or >4 mm in postmenopausal), submucous/intramural fibroids, endometrial polyps, adenomyosis (“Swiss-cheese” myometrial cysts, heterogeneous myometrium), and ovarian cysts/tumors.

Saline Infusion Sonography (SIS): Gold standard ultrasound technique to delineate intracavitary lesions (submucous fibroids vs. endometrial polyps).

Endometrial Histological Evaluation (Mandatory in women ≥40–45 years, or younger women with obesity/PCOS/unresponsive acyclic bleeding to rule out hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma):

Outpatient Endometrial Sampling (Pipelle / Sharman’s curette): First-choice OPD procedure (sensitivity >90%).

Hysteroscopy and Directed Biopsy (H & B): Gold standard to directly visualize the cavity (detects polyps and submucous fibroids missed in 10–20% of blind D&Cs) and take targeted biopsy.

Dilatation and Curettage (D&C): Reserved when hysteroscopy is unavailable or for acute heavy bleeding refractory to medical therapy.

E. Management of AUB (Medical and Surgical)

Management depends on the patient’s age, desire for future fertility, underlying etiology (PALM-COEIN), and severity of bleeding.

General Measures: Rest during heavy flow; correction of anemia with oral/parenteral iron (hematinics) or packed cell blood transfusion if Hb is severely low.

Medical Management (First-Line for Non-Structural AUB / DUB and Young Women):

Non-Hormonal Therapy (Preferred during ovulatory cycles or when fertility/non-hormonal control is desired):

Antifibrinolytics — Tranexamic Acid: Counteracts endometrial fibrinolytic system (plasminogen activator). Dose: 1 g (or 500 mg–1 g) orally 3–4 times daily for 4–5 days during menstruation. Reduces menstrual blood loss (MBL) by 50%. Particularly useful in Cu-IUCD menorrhagia.

NSAIDs (Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors) — Mefenamic Acid: Inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX) and blocks  receptors, increasing the  ratio to promote vasoconstriction. Dose: 250–500 mg orally thrice daily for 3–5 days during menses. Reduces MBL by 25–40% and simultaneously relieves dysmenorrhoea.

Hormonal Therapy:

Levonorgestrel-Releasing Intrauterine System (LNG-IUS / Mirena — First-Line Choice for Long-Term HMB): Releases 20  of levonorgestrel directly into the cavity; causes endometrial glandular atrophy and stromal decidualization. Reduces MBL by up to 90–97% (“medical hysterectomy”) and is effective for 5 years. Ideal for women aged 30–46 years who have completed their family and have a normal uterine cavity.

Oral Progestogens (Mainstay for Acute & Anovulatory DUB):

To arrest acute heavy bleeding: Norethisterone acetate 5 mg or Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) 10 mg orally thrice daily until bleeding stops (usually 3–7 days), then continued at a maintenance dose for 21 days.

Cyclic therapy for cycle regulation:

5th to 25th day regimen (21 days): MPA 10 mg or Norethisterone 5 mg daily for 3–6 cycles (suppresses HPO axis and induces endometrial atrophy; effective in both ovular and anovular DUB).

15th to 25th day regimen (Luteal phase support): MPA 10 mg or Dydrogesterone 10–20 mg daily from Day 15 to 25 (used in ovular LPD or when pregnancy is desired).

Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (COCs): Low-dose monophasic pill (Ethinyl estradiol 30  + Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg) given cyclically from Day 5 to Day 25 for 3–6 cycles. Reduces MBL by 50%, regulates cycles, and provides contraception (ideal for 20–35 year olds).

Conjugated Equine Estrogen (For Acute Life-Threatening / Pubertal Bleeding): 25 mg IV every 4–6 hours (up to 3–4 doses) rapidly re-epithelializes denuded raw endometrial surfaces and promotes platelet adhesiveness. Once bleeding stops, oral COCs or progestins are started and tapered.

Other Hormonal Agents (Short-term / Pre-surgical): Danazol (200–400 mg/day for 3 months; reduces MBL by 60%), GnRH agonists (Leuprolide/Goserelin depot for 3 months to induce medical amenorrhoea and correct severe anemia prior to surgery), Ormeloxifene (Centchroman / Sevista): SERM given 60 mg twice weekly for 12 weeks, then 60 mg once weekly for 12 weeks.

Surgical Management (Indicated when medical therapy fails/is contraindicated, family is completed, or structural pathology/atypical hyperplasia is present):

Endometrial Ablation / Resection (Conservative Surgery — Day-care alternative to hysterectomy):

Criteria: Completed family, uterine size ≤10 weeks, submucous fibroid <3 cm, and malignancy/atypical hyperplasia ruled out.

First-Generation (Hysteroscopic): Transcervical Resection of Endometrium (TCRE) using a resectoscope loop (removes basal layer + 3–4 mm superficial myometrium), Rollerball ablation, or Nd:YAG Laser ablation.

Second-Generation (Global Ablation): Uterine Thermal Balloon (87°C hot saline for 8–10 min), Microwave Endometrial Ablation (MEA), Novasure (bipolar radiofrequency mesh for 90 sec).

Outcome: 30–40% achieve amenorrhoea; 70–80% overall satisfaction.

Hysterectomy (Definitive Treatment):

Indicated in women >40 years with completed family who fail medical/conservative therapy, or have complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (which carries a 29% risk of progression to cancer), large fibroids, or severe adenomyosis. Route may be vaginal (NDVH), abdominal (TAH), or laparoscopic (TLH/LAVH).

(For Complications of Hysterectomy, see Section 20.5).

(Note: For Pubertal / Adolescent AUB in a 20-year-old girl, see Chapter 4, Section 4.2).

subject: gynecology
title: 4.1 Normal Puberty & Precocious Puberty
text:
CHAPTER 4: Puberty — Normal and Abnormal

(Covers: Define puberty. Describe all physiological changes that occur in normal puberty [RGU]; Precocious puberty [KU19,RGU])

A. Normal Puberty

Definition: Puberty is the transitional period linking childhood to adulthood during which secondary sexual characteristics develop, somatic growth accelerates, and reproductive capacity (fertility) is achieved.

Endocrinology: Loss of the extreme prepubertal sensitivity of the hypothalamic “gonadostat” to negative estrogen feedback (aided by leptin from adipose tissue)  reactivation of pulsatile GnRH secretion (initially during sleep, then throughout the day)  pulsatile FSH and LH release (Gonadarche)  ovarian estradiol synthesis. Simultaneously, adrenal androgen (DHEA, DHEA-S, androstenedione) synthesis increases from age 6–8 years (Adrenarche).

Chronological Sequence of Physical Changes (Completed between 10 and 16 years):

Beginning of Growth Spurt (stimulated by GH, IGF-1, and estrogen).

Thelarche (Breast budding): Earliest clinical sign of puberty (~9.8–10 years), stimulated by estrogen (ductal growth) and later progesterone (alveolar development). Graded by Tanner Stages I to V.

Pubarche / Adrenarche: Appearance of pubic and axillary hair (~10.5–11 years) due to adrenal androgens. Graded by Tanner Stages I to V.

Peak Growth Velocity in Height (~11.5–12 years).

Menarche: Onset of first menstruation (11–15 years, mean 13 years). Initial cycles for 1–2 years are predominantly anovulatory.

Genital Organ Changes: Uterine corpus-to-cervix ratio changes from 1:2 in childhood to 1:1 at menarche and 2:1 (or 3:1) in adulthood; vaginal epithelium becomes thick, glycogen-rich, and acidic (pH 4–5) with Döderlein’s bacilli.

B. Precocious Puberty

Definition: Appearance of any secondary sexual characteristics before the age of 8 years or onset of menstruation (menarche) before the age of 10 years.

Classification & Causes:

GnRH-Dependent / Central / True / Complete / Isosexual Precocious Puberty (80%): Premature activation of the HPO axis; pubertal changes proceed in the normal orderly sequence and cycles may be ovulatory.

Constitutional / Idiopathic (Commonest — 70%).

CNS Lesions: Craniopharyngioma, hypothalamic hamartoma, pinealoma, neurofibroma, post-meningitis/encephalitis, head trauma, hydrocephalus.

Juvenile Primary Hypothyroidism (high TRH stimulates FSH/prolactin).

GnRH-Independent / Peripheral / Precocious Pseudopuberty: Excess sex steroids (estrogen  isosexual; androgen  heterosexual) independent of pituitary gonadotropins.

Ovarian: Estrogen-secreting Granulosa cell tumor or theca cell tumor (isosexual); androgen-secreting Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (heterosexual).

McCune-Albright Syndrome: Classic triad of (i) GnRH-independent sexual precocity, (ii) polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (multiple cystic bone lesions), and (iii) café-au-lait skin spots with irregular (“coast of Maine”) borders.

Adrenal: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) or virilizing adrenal tumor (heterosexual).

Ectopic hCG-secreting tumors: Hepatoblastoma, choriocarcinoma.

Iatrogenic / Exogenous: Accidental ingestion of estrogen/oral contraceptive pills or androgen creams.

Incomplete / Partial Forms (Variants of Normal):

Premature Thelarche: Isolated breast development (2–4 years of age) without bone age advancement or other pubertal signs.

Premature Pubarche: Isolated pubic/axillary hair before age 8 without bone age advancement.

Premature Menarche: Isolated cyclic vaginal bleeding without other secondary sexual characters.

Diagnosis & Investigations:

History & Examination: Order of pubertal progression (Tanner staging), growth velocity chart, neurological examination, abdominal/rectal examination for ovarian mass, skin inspection for café-au-lait spots.

X-ray of Non-dominant Hand and Wrist (Bone Age): Advanced bone age (>2 SD above chronological age) indicates sustained sex steroid exposure (leads to premature epiphyseal fusion and short adult stature).

Hormonal Assays: Basal and GnRH-stimulated FSH and LH (pubertal/elevated in central precocity; suppressed in peripheral pseudopuberty), Estradiol, Testosterone, 17-OH Progesterone & DHEA-S (for CAH/adrenal tumor), TSH & Free , and -hCG.

Imaging: Pelvic USG (uterine size, ovarian tumor/cysts), MRI Brain / Skull X-ray (mandatory in all central precocious puberty to rule out intracranial tumors), CT Abdomen (for adrenal lesions).

Management:

Central (GnRH-Dependent) Precocious Puberty:

Drug of Choice: Long-acting GnRH Agonist therapy (e.g., Leuprolide depot 3.75 mg IM every 28 days, Goserelin 3.6 mg SC monthly, or Buserelin nasal spray 100  daily).

Action: Downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors  suppresses FSH/LH and estradiol (<10 pg/mL)  halts menstruation, regresses breast/pubic hair development, and slows bone maturation so normal adult height is achieved. Continued until the normal median age of puberty (~11 years).

Alternatives (if GnRH agonist unavailable): Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) or Cyproterone acetate (suppresses menses/breasts, but does not prevent accelerated bone maturation).

Peripheral (GnRH-Independent) Precocious Puberty: Treat the specific cause—surgical removal of ovarian/adrenal tumor, hydrocortisone for CAH, thyroxine for hypothyroidism, or aromatase inhibitors (letrozole/testolactone) in McCune-Albright syndrome.

subject: gynecology
title: 4.2 Puberty Menorrhagia (Adolescent AUB)
text:
(Covers: Define puberty menorrhagia. Enumerate the causes and discuss its management [KU24,22,19,17,RGU])

Definition: Excessive (>80 mL) and/or prolonged (>7 days) uterine bleeding occurring in adolescent girls between menarche and 19 years of age.

Etiology / Differential Diagnosis of Puberty Menorrhagia:

Anovulatory Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding (DUB — Commonest, 75–95%): Due to immaturity of the hypothalamo-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis, the positive feedback mechanism of estrogen to trigger the mid-cycle LH surge is not yet established. Follicles produce unopposed estrogen  endometrial proliferation/hyperplasia without progesterone support  asynchronous, heavy, painless breakthrough or withdrawal bleeding.

Coagulation / Hematological Disorders (5–20% — Second Most Common Cause):

Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP)

von Willebrand’s Disease (vWD)

Platelet function defects (Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia), Leukemia, Aplastic anemia.

Endocrine Dysfunction:

Hypothyroidism (or hyperthyroidism)

Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS)

Infections: Genital Tuberculosis (endometrial TB), Chlamydial/pelvic infection.

Pelvic Tumors / Local Lesions (Rare): Estrogen-producing ovarian tumor (Granulosa cell tumor), uterine polyp/fibroid, sarcoma botryoides.

Pregnancy Complications: Threatened, incomplete, or septic abortion (must always be kept in mind in sexually active teenagers).

Investigations:

Complete Hemogram: Hb%, PCV, peripheral blood smear, total and differential WBC count, and platelet count.

Coagulation Profile (Mandatory): Bleeding time (BT), Clotting time (CT), PT/INR, aPTT, and von Willebrand factor antigen/ristocetin cofactor assay.

Endocrine Profile: Serum TSH, Free , serum prolactin.

Transabdominal Pelvic Ultrasonography (TAS): To assess endometrial thickness, polycystic ovaries, ovarian tumors, or congenital anomalies.

Urine Pregnancy Test (-hCG): Whenever sexual activity is suspected.

EUA and Uterine Curettage: Rarely indicated; reserved only as a last resort when life-threatening bleeding fails to respond to intensive medical therapy (curetted material sent for histopathology and TB-PCR/AFB culture).

Management Protocol:

General & Supportive Care:

Explanation, reassurance, and psychological support to the girl and her parents.

Bed rest during heavy flow.

Correction of Anemia: Oral or parenteral iron therapy; packed red cell transfusion if Hb <7–8 g/dL or hemodynamically unstable.

Medical Therapy for Anovulatory DUB:

Mild Bleeding (Hb >10 g/dL): Reassurance, iron supplements, Tranexamic acid (500 mg–1 g TID) and/or Mefenamic acid (500 mg TID) during menses, with menstrual calendar follow-up.

Moderate Bleeding (Hb 8–10 g/dL) or Persistent Heavy Flow:

Progestogen Therapy: Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) 10 mg or Norethisterone acetate 5 mg orally thrice daily until bleeding stops (usually 3–7 days), followed by once or twice daily to complete 21 days.

Low-Dose Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (COCs): Given 1 tablet 6–8 hourly (3–4 tablets/day) until bleeding stops, then tapered over 3 weeks to 1 tablet/day.

Severe / Acute Life-Threatening Bleeding (Hb <8 g/dL or hemodynamic instability):

Hospitalization, IV fluids, blood transfusion.

IV Conjugated Equine Estrogen (Premarin) 20–40 mg IV every 6–8 hours (up to 24 hours) until bleeding is controlled, followed by oral COCs or progestins tapered over 21 days. (Add antiemetics).

Maintenance / Cycle Regulation (To prevent recurrence):

Once the acute episode is controlled, give cyclic progestogens (MPA 10 mg daily from Day 5 to Day 25 or Day 15 to Day 25) or low-dose COCs for 3 to 6 consecutive cycles, after which spontaneous ovulatory cycles usually resume as the HPO axis matures.

Specific Therapy for Secondary Causes: Thyroxine for hypothyroidism; corticosteroids/IVIG/platelets for ITP; Desmopressin (DDAVP) + tranexamic acid for vWD; antitubercular therapy for genital tuberculosis; surgical removal of ovarian tumors; or uterine evacuation in case of incomplete abortion.

subject: gynecology
title: 5.1 Primary Amenorrhoea & Cryptomenorrhoea
text:
CHAPTER 5: Amenorrhoea

(Covers: SE 2 [KU24], 3 [RGU]; SA 1 [KU24,19,18,16,15], 2 [KU23,21,15], 3 [KU23], 4 [KU18], 5, 8 [RGU]; One-word answers 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 [KU])

A. Definition & Classification of Primary Amenorrhoea

Definition: Failure of onset of menstruation (menarche):

By 14 years of age in the absence of growth or development of secondary sexual characteristics, OR

By 16 years of age regardless of the presence of normal growth and secondary sexual characteristics.

Etiological Classification of Primary Amenorrhoea (With Examples):

Outflow Tract Obstruction (Cryptomenorrhoea) / Anatomical Müllerian Defects (~20% — 2nd Commonest):

Congenital Obstructive (Cryptomenorrhoea): Imperforate hymen (commonest cause of cryptomenorrhoea), transverse vaginal septum, isolated vaginal or cervical agenesis/atresia.

Congenital Agenesis: Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome (46,XX; complete agenesis of uterus and upper vagina).

Endometrial: Congenital unresponsive endometrium (receptor defect) or tubercular uterine synechiae.

Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism (Gonadal / Primary Ovarian Failure — ~40–50% — Commonest Cause of Primary Amenorrhoea):

Chromosomal / Gonadal Dysgenesis: Turner’s syndrome (45,XO) (most common single cause), Turner mosaic (45,XO/46,XX), Pure gonadal dysgenesis (46,XX or Swyer’s syndrome 46,XY), Mixed gonadal dysgenesis (45,XO/46,XY), partial X-chromosome deletion ( or ).

Normal Karyotype (46,XX): Primary ovarian failure, Resistant ovary syndrome (Savage syndrome — FSH receptor defect), Galactosemia, -hydroxylase deficiency.

Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (Hypothalamo-Pituitary Dysfunction):

Hypothalamic: Constitutional / physiological delay of puberty, Kallmann’s syndrome (GnRH deficiency with anosmia), weight loss/anorexia nervosa, excessive athletics/stress, chronic systemic illness (malnutrition, tuberculosis).

CNS / Pituitary: Craniopharyngioma, pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma), empty sella syndrome, Laurence-Moon-Biedl or Prader-Willi syndrome.

Abnormal Chromosomal / Receptor Disorders (Male Pseudohermaphroditism):

Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS / Testicular Feminization Syndrome — 46,XY).

Thyroid & Adrenal Disorders (Heterosexual Development):

Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) (21-hydroxylase deficiency), Juvenile hypothyroidism (Cretinism), Cushing’s syndrome.

B. Cryptomenorrhoea & Imperforate Hymen

Definition: A condition in which periodic shedding of the endometrium and menstrual bleeding occur normally, but the menstrual blood fails to escape from the genital tract due to a mechanical obstruction in the outflow passage.

Etiology:

Congenital (Commonest): Imperforate hymen (failure of central canalization of the Müllerian eminence / sinovaginal bulb at the urogenital sinus), transverse vaginal septum, or atresia of the upper vagina/cervix.

Acquired (Rare): Cervical stenosis following amputation, conization, or deep electrocauterization of the cervix; secondary vaginal atresia after difficult/neglected vaginal delivery.

Pathophysiology: Pent-up dark, tarry menstrual blood first distends the vagina (Hematocolpos)  then distends the cervix and uterine cavity (Hematometra)  finally enters the fallopian tubes, where fimbrial ends close by inflammatory adhesions to form Hematosalpinx. The distended vagina pushes the bladder base upwards and stretches/elongates the urethra, causing acute retention of urine.

Clinical Features:

Patient Profile: Girl aged 14–16 years with well-developed secondary sexual characters.

Symptoms: (1) Primary amenorrhoea, (2) Periodic (monthly) cyclical lower abdominal pain (which later becomes continuous), (3) Urinary symptoms: Frequency, dysuria, or acute retention of urine (often the presenting complaint).

Signs:

Per abdomen: Tense, tender suprapubic globular swelling (persists even after bladder catheterization).

Vulval inspection: A tense, bulging, bluish membrane at the introitus between the labia minora.

Per rectum: Large, fluctuant, tender mass (hematocolpos) felt anteriorly.

Pelvic USG: Confirms hematocolpos and hematometra.

Treatment:

Cruciate incision (Hymenotomy) over the bulging membrane under anesthesia, followed by partial excision of the four triangular hymenal quadrants (not too close to the vaginal mucosa) to allow spontaneous drainage of dark tarry blood.

Precautions: Never apply suprapubic pressure and never perform internal digital examination or intrauterine instrumentation immediately, as it can force blood through the tubes (causing endometriosis) or introduce ascending infection into the raw hematometra. Keep the head-end elevated and administer prophylactic antibiotics.

(For Acquired Cervical Stenosis: Simple cervical dilatation under anesthesia to drain hematometra).*

C. Turner’s Syndrome (Gonadal Dysgenesis — 45,XO)

Etiopathogenesis: Sporadic chromosomal nondisjunction resulting in complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome (45,XO in 50%; Mosaic 45,XO/46,XX in 25%; or structural deletion of short arm  / long arm ). Rapid atresia of germ cells in utero leaves the ovaries as fibrous “streak gonads” devoid of follicles, resulting in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism ().

Clinical Features:

Primary amenorrhoea and sterility (in classic 45,XO; mosaic cases may menstruate briefly).

Short stature (height <150 cm / <60 inches) — most consistent feature (due to loss of SHOX gene on ).

Sexual infantilism: Poorly developed breasts, scanty pubic/axillary hair, infantile external and internal genitalia (uterus and vagina are present but small).

Somatic Stigmata: Webbing of the neck (pterygium colli), low posterior hairline, broad shield-like chest with widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus (increased carrying angle of elbow), short 4th metatarsal/metacarpal, high-arched palate, multiple pigmented nevi, and lymphedema of hands and feet at birth.

Associated Systemic Anomalies (Mandatory to screen):

Cardiovascular (20–30%): Coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, aortic root dilatation, hypertension.

Renal (30–40%): Horseshoe kidney, unilateral renal agenesis, duplex collecting system.

Autoimmune & Metabolic: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (hypothyroidism), diabetes mellitus, sensorineural deafness, osteoporosis.

Diagnosis & Investigations:

Karyotyping (Gold standard): 45,XO (or mosaic; if Y-chromosome material is present, there is a 20–30% risk of gonadoblastoma/dysgerminoma).

Hormone Profile: Elevated Serum FSH (>40 mIU/mL) and LH, very low Serum Estradiol (<20 pg/mL).

Pelvic USG / Laparoscopy: Hypoplastic uterus and bilateral white fibrous streak gonads.

Systemic Workup: Echocardiography, Renal USG/IVU, Thyroid profile + anti-TPO antibodies, Bone Mineral Density (DEXA), and Audiometry.

Management:

Promotion of Linear Growth: Recombinant human Growth Hormone (GH) therapy started early in childhood until bone age reaches 14 years.

Induction of Puberty & Secondary Sexual Characters (Hormone Replacement Therapy): Started around 12–13 years of age initially with unopposed low-dose Conjugated Equine Estrogen (0.3 mg daily) or Ethinyl estradiol (5–10 ) for 6–12 months to stimulate breast development, then switched to cyclic estrogen (0.625–1.25 mg D1–D25) + progestogen (Medroxyprogesterone acetate 5–10 mg D16–D25) to induce withdrawal bleeding, prevent endometrial hyperplasia, and protect against osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease.

Prophylactic Gonadectomy: Indicated if mosaicism with a Y chromosome (45,X/46,XY) is detected.

Fertility: Achieved via IVF with Donor Oocyte after hormonal preparation of the uterus.

(Note on Klinefelter’s Syndrome [KU23]: A male disorder of sexchromosome nondisjunction with karyotype 47,XXY [Barr body positive]. Features: Tall eunuchoid build, small firm testes with hyalinized seminiferous tubules, azoospermia, gynecomastia, low testosterone, and elevated FSH/LH. Rarely, sex-reversal 47,XXY phenotypic females have been reported).

(Note on Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia [CAH] [RGU]: Autosomal recessive deficiency of 21-hydroxylase [95%]  cortisol &  aldosterone  ACTH  excessive adrenal androgens. Causes female pseudohermaphroditism [46,XX] with ambiguous genitalia at birth [clitoromegaly, labial fusion, persistent urogenital sinus] and salt-wasting crisis [hyponatremia, hyperkalemia]. Normal uterus/ovaries are present internally. Diagnosis: Elevated serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (>800 ng/dL) and urinary pregnanetriol. Treatment: Hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone replacement, and surgical reduction clitoroplasty + vaginoplasty).

D. Stepwise Evaluation of a 20-Year-Old Girl with Primary Amenorrhoea

History: Growth spurt, thelarche/pubarche, cyclic abdominal pain (cryptomenorrhoea), anosmia (Kallmann’s), galactorrhea/headache, stress/weight loss/exercise, family history.

Physical Examination:

Height & BMI: Short stature (<150 cm) + somatic stigmata  Turner’s syndrome.

Tanner Staging of Breasts (Marker of endogenous estrogen) and Pubic/Axillary Hair (Marker of androgen sensitivity).

Local Genital & Rectal Examination / Pelvic USG: To check patency of introitus and presence or absence of the uterus.

Diagnostic Algorithm Based on Clinical & USG Findings:

Group I: Breasts Normal + Uterus Absent (on USG): Perform Karyotype & Serum Testosterone:

46,XX + Normal female testosterone: Müllerian Agenesis (MRKH Syndrome) (absent pubic hair is not a feature—pubic hair is normal).

46,XY + Male-range testosterone + Absent/scanty pubic & axillary hair: Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (Testicular Feminization) (see Table 27.1 in Ch. 6).

Group II: Breasts Normal + Uterus Present:

Rule out Outflow tract obstruction (imperforate hymen/transverse vaginal septum  hematocolpos/hematometra on USG).

If outflow tract is patent, evaluate as Secondary Amenorrhoea (TSH, Prolactin, Progesterone Challenge Test  PCOS, hypothalamic dysfunction, or tubercular synechiae).

Group III: Breasts Absent (Sexual Infantilism) + Uterus Present: Estimate Serum FSH and LH:

FSH & LH High (Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism — FSH >40 mIU/mL): Perform Karyotype:

45,XO (Short stature): Turner’s syndrome.

46,XX (Normal height): Pure XX gonadal dysgenesis / Premature ovarian failure / Resistant ovary syndrome.

46,XY (Normal/tall height): Swyer’s syndrome (XY pure gonadal dysgenesis  requires gonadectomy).

FSH & LH Low/Normal (Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism — FSH/LH <5 mIU/mL): Perform Cranial MRI/CT and olfaction test:

Normal MRI + Anosmia  Kallmann’s syndrome.

Normal MRI + Normal olfaction  Constitutional delay / Weight- or exercise-related hypothalamic amenorrhoea.

Abnormal MRI  Craniopharyngioma or pituitary tumor.

subject: gynecology
title: 5.2 Secondary Amenorrhoea: Causes, Investigation & Management
text:
(Covers: SE 1 [KU25], 4 [TU]; SA 4, 5, 6 [RGU/TU]; SA 6, 7 [RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1, 5, 8 [KU])

A. Definition & Causes

Definition: Absence of menstruation for 6 months or more (or for a length of time equivalent to 3 previous cycles) in a woman who previously had established normal menstruation.

Etiological Classification:

Physiological Causes (Most Common Overall): Pregnancy (commonest cause of secondary amenorrhoea in reproductive age), Lactation, and Menopause.

Uterine Causes (End-Organ):

Asherman’s Syndrome (Intrauterine Synechiae): Destruction of basal endometrium and adhesion formation following overzealous puerperal/postabortal curettage or tubercular endometritis.

Post-radiation or surgical endometrial ablation.

Ovarian Causes:

Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) (commonest pathological endocrine cause).

Premature Ovarian Failure (POF / Primary Ovarian Insufficiency): Depletion of follicles before age 40 (genetic, autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, post-chemotherapy/radiotherapy, mumps oophoritis, Savage’s resistant ovary syndrome).

Androgen-producing ovarian tumor (Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor).

Pituitary Causes:

Hyperprolactinemia / Pituitary Prolactinoma (inhibits GnRH pulsatility).

Sheehan’s Syndrome: Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary following severe postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) and obstetric shock (manifests with failure of lactation, loss of axillary/pubic hair, amenorrhoea, genital atrophy, hypothyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency).

Cushing’s disease, Acromegaly, Empty sella syndrome.

Hypothalamic Causes (Most Common Pathological Cause):

Psychogenic stress/shock, sudden weight loss / Anorexia nervosa, strenuous athletic exercise (female athlete triad), pseudocyesis, craniopharyngioma.

Thyroid & Adrenal Causes: Hypothyroidism (elevated TRH stimulates both TSH and prolactin), Late-onset CAH, Cushing’s syndrome, adrenal tumor.

Iatrogenic / Drugs & Systemic Illness: Post-pill amenorrhoea (<1% after stopping COCs), dopamine-blocking/depleting drugs (phenothiazines, metoclopramide, haloperidol, reserpine, methyldopa  raise prolactin), DMPA injections, severe malnutrition, diabetes, chronic renal failure.

B. Stepwise Investigation of a Woman with Secondary Amenorrhoea (e.g., 28-year-old with Negative Pregnancy Test [KU25])

Preliminary Step (After excluding pregnancy):

Detailed history (PPH, curettage, stress/weight change, galactorrhea, hirsutism, drugs) and physical examination (BMI, thyroid, acanthosis nigricans, breast milk expression, pelvic USG).

Baseline Serum TSH and Serum Prolactin:

Elevated TSH + Low   Hypothyroidism.

Elevated Prolactin (>20 ng/mL; if >100 ng/mL, do Cranial MRI / Coned-down view of sella turcica)  Prolactinoma or drug-induced hyperprolactinemia.

Step I: Progesterone Challenge Test (PCT):

Method: Administer Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) 10 mg orally daily for 5–10 days (or Micronized progesterone 200 mg daily for 10 days, or Inj. Progesterone in oil 75 mg IM).

Positive Test (Withdrawal bleeding occurs within 2–10 days of stopping): Proves: (1) Intact HPO axis producing adequate endogenous estradiol (>30–40 pg/mL), (2) Responsive endometrium, and (3) Patent outflow tract. Indicates chronic anovulation  check LH/FSH ratio, serum testosterone, and Pelvic USG to confirm PCOS.

Negative Test (No withdrawal bleeding): Indicates either inadequate endogenous estrogen (<30 pg/mL) (no progesterone receptors induced) OR diseased/destroyed endometrium (Asherman’s syndrome). Proceed to Step II.

Step II: Estrogen–Progesterone Challenge Test:

Method: Give Conjugated Equine Estrogen 1.25 mg (or Ethinyl estradiol 0.02 mg) daily for 25 days, adding MPA 10 mg daily from Day 16 to 25 (or 1 cycle of Combined Oral Contraceptive pill).

No Withdrawal Bleeding: Confirms local uterine/endometrial factor (Asherman’s syndrome / Tubercular endometritis)  confirm by Hysteroscopy (gold standard) or HSG (honeycomb filling defects) and endometrial TB-PCR.

Withdrawal Bleeding Occurs: Proves endometrium is responsive, so the defect is low endogenous estrogen production. Proceed to Step III.

Step III: Estimation of Serum Gonadotropins (FSH & LH):

High FSH (>40 mIU/mL) & LH (Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism): Indicates Premature Ovarian Failure (POF) or Resistant Ovary Syndrome. (If age <30 years, perform Karyotype to rule out mosaic Turner’s or Y chromosome; if <35 years, screen for autoimmune antithyroid and antinuclear antibodies).

Low or Normal FSH & LH (<5 mIU/mL) (Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism): Indicates Pituitary or Hypothalamic dysfunction (Sheehan’s syndrome, stress/weight-loss amenorrhoea, or space-occupying lesion  do MRI of Brain/Pituitary).

Step IV: GnRH Dynamic Stimulation Test: IV bolus of 100  GnRH  rise in LH/FSH suggests hypothalamic cause; absent response suggests pituitary failure (Sheehan’s).

C. Management Summary

Anovulation / PCOS: Weight reduction, cyclic progestogens/COCs (if fertility not desired), or Clomiphene citrate / Letrozole  Metformin (if fertility desired).

Hyperprolactinemia / Prolactinoma: Cabergoline (0.25–0.5 mg once or twice weekly) or Bromocriptine (2.5 mg BID/TID).

Asherman’s Syndrome: Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis (using microscissors) followed by Cu-T IUCD or Foley’s pediatric catheter balloon insertion + high-dose cyclic estrogen and progestin for 2–3 months to regenerate endometrium (plus ATT if tubercular).

Premature Ovarian Failure: Long-term HRT (Estrogen + cyclic Progestin) to prevent osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease; Donor Oocyte IVF for fertility.

Sheehan’s Syndrome: Lifelong replacement of Corticosteroids, Thyroxine, and cyclic Estrogen + Progestin (and hMG + hCG for ovulation induction).
