title: Chapter 5: One-Word Answers
text:
Causes of Asherman syndrome [KU24]: Vigorous postabortal or puerperal uterine curettage (commonest), diagnostic D&C, myomectomy, or tubercular endometritis.

Chromosomal pattern in Turner’s Syndrome [KU24]: 45,XO (or mosaic 45,XO/46,XX).

Most common cause of cryptomenorrhoea [KU21]: Imperforate hymen (or low transverse vaginal septum).

Most common cause for primary amenorrhoea [KU21]: Gonadal dysgenesis (Turner’s syndrome), followed by Müllerian agenesis (MRKH syndrome).

Secondary amenorrhoea due to formation of intrauterine synechiae is called [KU24]: Asherman’s syndrome.

Karyotype of Klinefelter’s syndrome is [KU17]: 47,XXY.

Condition where menstrual blood fails to come out of the genital tract due to obstruction in the passage is called as… [KU18]: Cryptomenorrhoea.

Most common cause of amenorrhoea [KU17]: Pregnancy (physiological).

subject: gynecology
title: 6.1 Development of Uterus, Classification of Müllerian Anomalies & MRKH Syndrome
text:
CHAPTER 6: Congenital Anomalies of the Genital Tract

(Covers: Development of uterus and classification of mullerian anomalies [KU25,17,RGU]; Bicornuate uterus [RGU]; Mayer Rokitansky Kuster Hauser syndrome [RGU])

A. Embryological Development of the Uterus and Fallopian Tubes

The female internal genital tract (fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper four-fifths of the vagina) develops from the paired Paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts, which arise at 5–6 weeks of gestation as an invagination of coelomic epithelium lateral to the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts.

Each duct has three parts: (1) Cranial vertical, (2) Middle horizontal (which crosses anteriorly over the Wolffian duct), and (3) Caudal vertical.

In the absence of SRY gene, Testosterone, and Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH), the Wolffian ducts regress (leaving vestigial remnants: epoophoron, paroophoron, Gartner’s duct), while the Müllerian ducts develop:

Fallopian Tubes: Develop from the unfused cranial vertical and middle horizontal parts; the coelomic opening becomes the fimbriated abdominal ostium.

Uterus & Cervix: Develop from the fusion of the caudal vertical parts (and adjoining horizontal parts) in the midline within the urorectal septum (begins at 7–8 weeks and completes by 12 weeks) to form the uterovaginal canal.

Resorption of Septum: The intervening midline septum between the two fused ducts resorbs cephalocaudally by the 5th month (20 weeks) of intrauterine life.

Layers: Endometrial glands and lining epithelium develop from the coelomic epithelium; myometrium and endometrial stroma condense from the surrounding mesenchyme.

(Vagina is composite: Upper four-fifths from the canalized vaginal plate of the sinovaginal bulbs/Müllerian tubercle; lower one-fifth below the hymen from the endoderm of the urogenital sinus).

B. American Fertility Society (AFS / ASRM — 1988) Classification of Müllerian Anomalies

(Incidence: 3–4% in general population; 15–20% in women with recurrent mid-trimester miscarriage).

Class I: Müllerian Agenesis or Hypoplasia (Segmental):

Vaginal, (b) Cervical, (c) Fundal, (d) Tubal, (e) Combined uterovaginal agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser [MRKH] Syndrome).

Class II: Unicornuate Uterus (10%): Failure of development of one Müllerian duct. May have a communicating, non-communicating (with functional endometrium  cryptomenorrhoea/ectopic cornual pregnancy), cavitary non-communicating, or absent rudimentary horn. (Poorest pregnancy outcome: 40% live birth).

Class III: Uterus Didelphys (8%): Complete failure of lateral fusion of the two Müllerian ducts  double uterus, double cervix, and longitudinal vaginal septum. (Best pregnancy outcome among major anomalies: 64% live birth).

Class IV: Bicornuate Uterus (26%): Incomplete fusion of the fundal portion of the two Müllerian ducts, resulting in two uterine cornua with a fundal external indentation (cleft) >1 cm and a single cervix (bicornuate unicollis) or double cervix (bicornuate bicollis).

Clinical features: Often asymptomatic; may cause menorrhagia (increased endometrial surface area), dysmenorrhoea, recurrent mid-trimester abortion, preterm labor, malpresentation (breech/transverse lie), retained placenta, or PPH.

Diagnosis: Differentiated from septate uterus by MRI, 3D-TVS, or Combined HSG + Laparoscopy (bicornuate shows an external fundal cleft >1 cm between two horns on laparoscopy, whereas septate uterus has a smooth, convex/flat external fundus).

Treatment: Strassman’s abdominal unification metroplasty (indicated only in women with recurrent pregnancy loss and no other cause).

Class V: Septate Uterus (35% — Commonest Fusion Anomaly): Normal external fusion of the Müllerian ducts, but failure of resorption of the midline septum (complete or partial/subseptate).

Clinical significance: Fibromuscular septum has poor blood supply  causes highest rate of recurrent 1st/2nd trimester miscarriage (implantation on avascular septum).

Treatment: Hysteroscopic Metroplasty (Resection of septum using resectoscope or laser) — 80–89% live birth rate post-surgery and allows subsequent vaginal delivery.

Class VI: Arcuate Uterus (18%): Minor midline fundal indentation (<1 cm) into the uterine cavity with a normal external contour (considered a normal variant).

Class VII: Diethylstilbestrol (DES)-Related Anomalies: T-shaped hypoplastic uterine cavity, cervical collar/cockscomb cervix, vaginal adenosis, and clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina.

C. Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) Syndrome vs. Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome

MRKH Syndrome: Congenital complete agenesis of the vagina and uterus (represented only by bilateral rudimentary muscular uterine knobs to failure of development of the caudal Müllerian ducts.

Key Features: Phenotypic female, 46,XX karyotype, normal ovaries (normal ovulation, normal female breast development, and normal axillary/pubic hair), presenting at 15–18 years with primary amenorrhoea and inability to consummate marriage (apareunia).

Associated Anomalies: Renal anomalies in 40% (unilateral renal agenesis, pelvic/horseshoe kidney) and skeletal anomalies in 12% (fused cervical/lumbar vertebrae, scoliosis).

Management:

Psychological counseling.

Creation of a Neovagina (just prior to marriage):

Non-surgical: Frank’s serial vaginal dilators pressed against the vaginal dimple for 6–12 months.

Surgical Vaginoplasty: Dissecting a space between the bladder and rectum and lining it with a split-thickness skin graft over a mould (McIndoe-Reed operation) or human amnion graft (Chakraborty-Konar), followed by regular mould/dilator use and early sexual intercourse to prevent restenosis.

Fertility: Achieved via IVF using her own retrieved oocytes and a gestational surrogate uterus.

(For the classic differentiation table between MRKH Syndrome and Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome [Testicular Feminization], refer to Table 27.1 on Book Page 445 / PDF Page 463—Key distinctions: MRKH is 46,XX, has normal pubic/axillary hair, ovaries, and 40% renal anomalies; AIS is 46,XY, has absent/sparse pubic & axillary hair, undescended testes [labial/inguinal/abdominal] requiring gonadectomy after puberty due to 5–10% malignancy risk, a short blind vaginal pouch, and male-range serum testosterone).

subject: gynecology
title: 7A.1 Evaluation and Management of the Infertile Couple
text:
CHAPTER 7A: Infertility & Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS)

(Covers: Essays 1, 2 [KU20]; SE 1 [KU24], 4–8 [RGU,TU]; SA 1, 4–13, 16–23, 26, 28, 30, 35–41 [KU,RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1–3, 6–9 [KU])

A. Definitions & Epidemiology

Infertility: Failure to conceive after 1 year or more of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse. (Investigation is started after 1 year, or earlier after 6 months if the female partner is ≥35 years old or has known pelvic/menstrual pathology).

Primary vs. Secondary Infertility: Primary denotes couples who have never conceived; Secondary denotes couples with a previous pregnancy (regardless of outcome) who fail to conceive subsequently.

Fecundability: Probability of achieving a pregnancy within a single menstrual cycle (~20% in normal couples). Fecundity: Probability of achieving a live birth within a single cycle.

Distribution of Causes:

Male Factor: 30–40%

Female Factor: 40–55% — subdivided into: (1) Ovulatory Dysfunction (30–40%), (2) Tubal & Peritoneal Factors (25–35%), (3) Endometriosis (1–10%), (4) Uterine & Cervical Factors (5–10%).

Combined Factors: 10%

Unexplained Infertility: 10–20% (Normal semen, confirmed ovulation, patent tubes, normal cavity).

B. Male Factor Infertility: Causes, Semen Analysis (WHO) & Management

Causes of Male Infertility:

Pre-testicular (Endocrine / Coital — 1–2%): Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Kallmann’s syndrome), hyperprolactinemia, hypothyroidism, diabetes, erectile dysfunction, retrograde ejaculation.

Testicular (Defective Spermatogenesis — 30–40%): Varicocele (raises scrotal temperature), Cryptorchidism (undescended testes), Mumps orchitis, genetic (Klinefelter’s syndrome 47,XXY, Y-chromosome microdeletions [AZF region on Yq]), Sertoli-cell-only syndrome, immotile cilia (Kartagener’s syndrome), gonadotoxins (smoking, alcohol, radiation, chemotherapy, sulfasalazine, cimetidine), antisperm antibodies.

Post-testicular (Obstructive — 10–20%): Congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (CBAVD — associated with Cystic Fibrosis [CFTR] gene mutation; semen shows low volume, acidic pH, and absent fructose), post-infective epididymal block (gonorrhoea, tuberculosis), Young’s syndrome (inspissated epididymal secretions + bronchiectasis), surgical trauma (herniorrhaphy, vasectomy), hypospadias.

Idiopathic (40–50%).

WHO Criteria for Normal Semen Parameters (WHO 2010 / 2021 Lower Reference Limits — 5th Centile): (Collected by masturbation into a clean wide-mouthed glass jar after 2–3 days [up to 7 days] of sexual abstinence, and examined within 1–2 hours).

[[TABLE:gynecology-tbl-003]]

Terminology:

Aspermia: Complete failure of emission of semen (no ejaculate).

Azoospermia: Complete absence of spermatozoa in the ejaculate.

Oligozoospermia: Sperm concentration <15 million/mL.

Asthenozoospermia: Reduced progressive sperm motility (<32%).

Teratozoospermia: Reduced normal sperm morphology (<4%).

Necrozoospermia: All spermatozoa in the ejaculate are dead/immotile.

Evaluation & Management of Azoospermia / Severe Oligozoospermia: 

Repeat Semen Analysis after 4–6 weeks (since spermatogenesis takes 74 days).

Check Seminal Fluid Fructose: If absent  congenital absence of seminal vesicles and vas deferens (CBAVD) or ejaculatory duct obstruction (confirm by Transrectal Ultrasound [TRUS]).

Hormonal Profile (Serum FSH, LH, Testosterone, Prolactin, TSH):

Low FSH, Low LH, Low Testosterone: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism  treat medically with hCG (5000 IU IM 2–3 times weekly) + hMG / rFSH (75–150 IU 3 times weekly) or pulsatile GnRH pump.

High FSH, High LH, Low Testosterone + Small Testes (<20 mL): Primary testicular failure (Klinefelter’s 47,XXY, Sertoli-cell-only syndrome; confirm by Karyotype & Y-microdeletion)  Donor Insemination (AID) or Adoption.

Normal FSH, Normal LH, Normal Testosterone + Normal Testicular Volume: Obstructive Azoospermia  confirm normal spermatogenesis by Testicular Biopsy (sent in Bouin’s fluid, NOT formalin)  treat by microsurgical vasoepididymostomy / vasovasostomy OR surgical sperm retrieval (PESA [Percutaneous Epididymal Sperm Aspiration], MESA, or TESE [Testicular Sperm Extraction]) followed by ICSI (Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection).

Mild-to-Moderate Oligoasthenospermia: Stop smoking/alcohol, treat genital infection (doxycycline for leukocytospermia), clomiphene citrate (25 mg daily for 3 months), antioxidants, and Intrauterine Insemination (IUI) with washed/swim-up sperm.

C. Diagnosis (Tests) of Ovulation

(Asked repeatedly: [KU24,23,21,20,17,16,RGU,TU])

Indirect / Presumptive Evidences of Ovulation:

Menstrual History: Regular cycles every 21–35 days, presence of primary spasmodic dysmenorrhoea, premenstrual syndrome (PMS), or mid-cycle ovulatory pain/spotting (Mittelschmerz).

Basal Body Temperature (BBT) Chart: 

Principle: Post-ovulatory progesterone (and norepinephrine) is thermogenic, acting on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center to raise basal oral temperature by 0.5°F to 1.0°F (0.2°C to 0.5°C) when serum progesterone exceeds 4–5 ng/mL.

Observation: Oral temperature recorded daily on waking (before rising from bed) shows a “Biphasic Pattern”—lower in the follicular phase, a slight dip of 0.5°F at the LH surge/ovulation, followed by a sustained rise of 0.5°–1°F throughout the luteal phase (12–14 days), falling 2 days before menstruation. (Monophasic in anovulation).

Cervical Mucus Study:

Pre-ovulatory (Estrogen dominance — D12–14): Mucus is copious, clear, watery, stretches >10 cm between two glass slides (Spinnbarkeit test positive), and dries on a slide in a palm-leaf crystal pattern due to high NaCl (Fern test positive)

Post-ovulatory (Progesterone dominance — D21–23): Mucus becomes thick, viscid, scanty, loses stretchability (loss of Spinnbarkeit), and ferning disappears completely. This shift proves ovulation.

Hormone Estimations:

Mid-Luteal Serum Progesterone (Day 21 of a 28-day cycle, or 7 days before expected menses): A value >6 ng/mL (or >10 ng/mL for adequate luteal function; >30 nmol/L) confirms ovulation (follicular phase is <1 ng/mL). Most practical and reliable blood test.

Urinary LH Surge Kit (Home Dipstick Test): Performed daily from Day 11–16; ovulation occurs within 14–26 hours (always within 48 hours) of a positive urine LH surge.

Serial Transvaginal Ultrasonography (TVS Folliculometry):

Tracks growth of the dominant follicle (grows 2 mm/day to reach 18–20 mm preovulatory).

Sonographic signs of recent ovulation: (i) Sudden collapse/disappearance of the follicle with crenated margins, (ii) Appearance of internal echoes (corpus hemorrhagicum), and (iii) Free fluid in the Pouch of Douglas.

Endometrial Biopsy (Histological Dating):

Taken on Day 21–23 by Pipelle sampler. Presence of secretory endometrium confirms ovulation (subnuclear vacuolation is the earliest histological sign at 36–48 hours post-ovulation). (Not routinely done now due to invasiveness).

Direct Evidence: Laparoscopic visualization of a recent ovulation stigma or corpus luteum on the ovary, or recovery of an ovum from the POD fluid.

Conclusive Proof: Pregnancy.

D. Tests for Tubal Patency (Tubal Factor Evaluation)

(Covers: [KU24,23,20,18,16,RGU,TU]) Performed in the proliferative phase (Day 7 to Day 10 of the cycle), at least 2 days after menstrual bleeding stops (to avoid flushing an early implanted embryo or causing endometriosis). Contraindicated in active pelvic infection (PID).

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) (First-Line Screening Test):

Method: 5–10 mL of water-soluble radio-opaque contrast (e.g., Urografin / Meglumine diatrizoate) is injected transcervically using a Leech-Wilkinson cannula or pediatric Foley catheter under fluoroscopy, and two X-ray films are taken (initial filling view and 15-min delayed spill view).

Advantages: Non-surgical OPD test; precisely identifies the exact site (cornual, isthmic, or fimbrial) and side of tubal block, hydrosalpinx, tubercular changes (lead-pipe/beaded tube, tobacco-pouch), and intrauterine cavity lesions (septate/bicornuate uterus, synechiae, submucous fibroids).

Disadvantages: Radiation exposure, cramping pain, 15–20% false-positive cornual block due to tubal spasm (prevented by antispasmodics/atropine), 1–3% risk of flaring up PID.

Laparoscopy and Dye Test (Chromopertubation) — “Gold Standard”:

Method: Under general anesthesia, a laparoscope is introduced into the peritoneal cavity while methylene blue dye is pushed transcervically into the uterus. Direct visualization of blue dye spilling from both fimbrial ends confirms tubal patency 

Advantages over HSG: Directly visualizes peritubal adhesions, pelvic endometriosis, ovarian pathology (PCOS), and tubo-ovarian relationship, and allows simultaneous operative treatment (adhesiolysis, fimbrioplasty, fulguration of endometriotic implants, ovarian drilling) in the same sitting.

Limitation: Invasive (requires anesthesia) and cannot visualize the uterine cavity unless combined with hysteroscopy. Hence, HSG and Laparoscopy are complementary.

Sonohysterosalpingography (Saline Infusion Sonography / HyCoSy):

Method: Normal saline (with air bubbles or galactose echo-contrast) is instilled into the uterine cavity via a pediatric Foley catheter and tracked by Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVS) through the tubes into the Pouch of Douglas.

Advantages: No radiation, OPD procedure, superior to HSG for detecting intrauterine polyps/submucous fibroids/synechiae, and simultaneously evaluates myometrium and ovaries.

Other Tests:

Falloposcopy (transcervical flexible microendoscope to inspect entire tubal lumen) & Salpingoscopy (laparoscopic rigid scope inserted via fimbrial ostium to inspect ampullary mucosa/plicae).

Rubin’s Insufflation Test (D & I): Historical test using /air; obsolete due to high false-negative rate (33%) and inability to localize the side/site of block.

E. WHO Classification of Ovulatory Disorders & Ovulation Induction Drugs

WHO Classification of Anovulation:

WHO Group I (Hypogonadotropic Hypoestrogenic Anovulation — 5–10%): Low FSH, Low LH, Low , normal prolactin, negative progesterone challenge test (e.g., Kallmann’s syndrome, stress/weight-loss/anorexia nervosa, Sheehan’s syndrome). Treatment: hMG (FSH + LH) or Pulsatile GnRH. (Clomiphene is ineffective as endogenous GnRH/FSH is absent).

WHO Group II (Normogonadotropic Normoestrogenic Anovulation — 75–85%): Normal FSH, normal/elevated LH, normal , positive progesterone challenge test. Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) is the classic example. Treatment: Weight loss + Letrozole or Clomiphene citrate ( Metformin / Gonadotropins / Laparoscopic ovarian drilling).

WHO Group III (Hypergonadotropic Hypoestrogenic Anovulation — 10%): High FSH (>40 mIU/mL), Low  (Premature Ovarian Failure, Gonadal dysgenesis). Treatment: IVF with Donor Oocyte + HRT.

(Hyperprolactinemic Anovulation: Elevated serum prolactin  treated with Cabergoline or Bromocriptine).*

Ovulation Induction Drugs (Mechanism, Dose, Monitoring & Side Effects):

Clomiphene Citrate (CC — Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator [SERM]):

Mechanism: Binds competitively to nuclear estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus for a prolonged period, blocking negative feedback of endogenous estrogen  increases GnRH pulse frequency  increases pituitary FSH and LH secretion  follicular recruitment and growth.

Dose: Started at 50 mg orally daily for 5 days from Day 2 to Day 6 (or D3–D7) of the cycle. If ovulation does not occur, increase stepwise by 50 mg per cycle up to a maximum of 150–200 mg/day for up to 6 cycles. Ovulation occurs 5–7 days after the last tablet (around Day 12–14).

Monitoring: Folliculometry by TVS from Day 10 onwards; when dominant follicle reaches 18–20 mm, Inj. hCG 5000–10,000 IU IM can be given to trigger ovulation, with timed intercourse over the next 24–48 hours.

Results & Discrepancy: Ovulation rate is 80%, but pregnancy rate is only 40–50% because of its peripheral anti-estrogenic effects on the endometrium (thin endometrium <7 mm) and cervical mucus (thick, hostile mucus).

Side Effects: Vasomotor hot flushes (10%), twin pregnancy (5–7%), nausea, headache, visual blurring/scotomas (indication to stop drug), and mild OHSS (<1–2%).

Letrozole (Aromatase Inhibitor — Currently First-Line Drug of Choice in PCOS):

Mechanism: Selectively and reversibly inhibits the aromatase enzyme  blocks conversion of androgens to estrogens  releases the hypothalamus/pituitary from negative estrogen feedback  increases FSH secretion. Also transiently increases intraovarian androgens, which upregulate follicular FSH receptors.

Advantages over Clomiphene: Short half-life (45 hours), no peripheral anti-estrogenic effect on endometrium or cervical mucus (thick trilaminar endometrium), promotes monofollicular ovulation (lower multiple pregnancy rate), and yields higher live birth rates in PCOS.

Dose: 2.5 mg (up to 5 mg) orally daily from Day 3 to Day 7 (5 days).

Gonadotropins (hMG [75 IU FSH + 75 IU LH], Purified Urinary FSH, or Recombinant FSH):

Indications: WHO Group I anovulation, Clomiphene/Letrozole-resistant PCOS, and Controlled Ovarian Hyperstimulation (COH) for IUI/IVF.

Regimen: Started on Day 2–5 (75–150 IU IM/SC daily for 7–10 days; low-dose step-up protocol [starting at 37.5–50 IU] is used in PCOS to prevent OHSS). Monitored strictly with serial TVS folliculometry and serum estradiol (). When 1–2 follicles reach 18 mm and  is 150–300 pg/mL per follicle (and <2500 pg/mL total), Inj. hCG 5000–10,000 IU IM is given to trigger ovulation 36 hours later.

Adjuvants: Metformin (500 mg TID in insulin-resistant PCOS), Cabergoline/Bromocriptine (in hyperprolactinemia), Thyroxine (in hypothyroidism), Dexamethasone (0.5 mg at bedtime if DHEA-S is high).

F. Intrauterine Insemination (IUI) & Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART)

Intrauterine Insemination (IUI):

Principle: Injection of 0.3–0.5 mL of washed, capacitated, motile spermatozoa (prepared by density-gradient centrifugation or swim-up technique to remove seminal prostaglandins, dead sperm, and debris; minimum post-wash motile count >1 million, ideally >10 million) directly into the uterine cavity via a soft flexible catheter at the time of ovulation (34–40 hours after hCG trigger, or 24 hours after urine LH surge), usually combined with mild ovarian stimulation (COH).

Indications: (1) Hostile cervical mucus / cervical stenosis, (2) Mild-to-moderate male factor (oligoasthenospermia, hypospadias, impotence, retrograde ejaculation), (3) Immunological infertility (antisperm antibodies), (4) Minimal/mild endometriosis, (5) Unexplained infertility. (Success rate: 15–20% per cycle; 4–6 cycles recommended).

Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART): Involves manipulation of gametes/embryos outside the body:

IVF-ET (In Vitro Fertilization and Embryo Transfer — Steptoe & Edwards, 1978):

Indications: Irreparable tubal blockage, severe endometriosis, failed ovulation induction/IUI (3–6 cycles), unexplained infertility, male factor infertility, or premature ovarian failure (with donor oocyte).

Principal Steps: (1) Pituitary Downregulation using a GnRH agonist (Long luteal protocol from Day 21 of previous cycle) or GnRH antagonist (Cetrorelix) to prevent premature LH surge  (2) Controlled Ovarian Hyperstimulation (COH) with rFSH/hMG  (3) Follicular Monitoring by TVS and serum   (4) Ovulation Trigger with hCG (5000–10,000 IU) when ≥3 follicles reach 17–18 mm  (5) Transvaginal Ultrasound-Guided Oocyte Retrieval 34–36 hours after hCG under sedation  (6) In Vitro Fertilization (incubating each oocyte with 50,000–100,000 capacitated sperm for 16–18 hours) & embryo culture  (7) Embryo Transfer (ET) of 1–2 embryos at the 6–8 cell cleavage stage (Day 3) or blastocyst stage (Day 5) into the uterine cavity  (8) Luteal Phase Support with micronized progesterone (vaginal/IM) until 10–12 weeks.

ICSI (Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection): Micromanipulation injection of a single live spermatozoon directly into the ooplasm of a mature M-II oocyte 

Indications: Severe oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (<5 million/mL), obstructive/non-obstructive azoospermia (using PESA/TESE sperm), or previous fertilization failure with conventional IVF.

Other ART Methods: GIFT (Gamete Intrafallopian Transfer — requires at least one normal patent tube), ZIFT (Zygote Intrafallopian Transfer), Cryopreservation of embryos/oocytes, Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis (PGD), and Gestational Surrogacy.

subject: gynecology
title: 7A.2 Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) & Hirsutism
text:
(Covers: Essay 2 [KU20]; SE 2 [KU20,RGU], 3 [RGU,TU]; SA 2, 3 [KU24], 15 [KU17]; also links to Ch. 28 & Ch. 33)

A. Diagnostic Criteria (Rotterdam Criteria — ASRM/ESHRE 2003)

Diagnosis of PCOS requires the presence of any 2 out of the following 3 criteria (after excluding other mimics like congenital adrenal hyperplasia, thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia, and Cushing’s syndrome):

Oligo-ovulation and/or Anovulation (manifesting as oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea).

Clinical and/or Biochemical Signs of Hyperandrogenism (Hirsutism, acne, androgenic alopecia, or elevated serum free/total testosterone).

Polycystic Ovaries on Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVS): Presence of ≥12 follicles in each ovary measuring 2–9 mm in diameter arranged peripherally (“necklace appearance” around dense echogenic stroma) and/or increased ovarian volume >10  (10 mL).

B. Etiopathogenesis of PCOS

PCOS is a multifactorial, polygenic neuroendocrine-metabolic disorder involving a self-perpetuating vicious cycle:

Hypothalamic-Pituitary Dysfunction: Increased GnRH pulse frequency preferentially stimulates pituitary LH secretion over FSH ( LH : FSH ratio > 2:1 or 3:1).

Ovarian Hyperandrogenism: Tonically elevated LH (along with Insulin and IGF-1) acts on hyperplastic ovarian theca interna and stromal cells (and dysregulated P450c17 enzyme) to overproduce androgens (androstenedione and testosterone).

Arrest of Follicular Maturation (Anovulation): Relative deficiency of FSH impairs granulosa cell aromatase activity  follicles fail to convert androgens into estradiol  androgenic follicular microenvironment arrests follicles at the 2–9 mm stage (causing multiple subcapsular follicular cysts and anovulation).

Tonic Hyperestrogenic State: Excess circulating androstenedione is peripherally aromatized in adipose tissue to estrone (), which sensitizes the pituitary to GnRH ( LH) and suppresses FSH, while causing unopposed endometrial proliferation.

Obesity & Insulin Resistance (Hyperinsulinemia — 50% of cases): Compensatory hyperinsulinemia (i) directly stimulates ovarian theca cells (via IGF-1 receptors) to secrete more androgens, (ii) suppresses hepatic synthesis of Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin (SHBG)  increases biologically active free testosterone and free estradiol, and (iii) predisposes to Metabolic Syndrome (waist >88 cm, TG ≥150 mg/dL, HDL <50 mg/dL, BP ≥130/85 mm Hg, Fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL).

C. Clinical Features & Long-Term Sequelae

Clinical Features:

Menstrual Abnormalities (70%): Oligomenorrhoea (85–90%), secondary amenorrhoea, or episodes of heavy anovulatory DUB.

Anovulatory Infertility and increased risk of early miscarriage.

Features of Hyperandrogenism (70%): Hirsutism (excess coarse terminal hair in a male-pattern distribution: upper lip, chin, sideburns, chest, linea alba, inner thighs — scored by Modified Ferriman-Gallwey score ≥8), acne, oily skin, and temporal balding. (Frank virilization like clitoromegaly/deep voice is rare and points to an ovarian/adrenal tumor).

Central (Android) Obesity (50%): BMI >25 , waist-to-hip ratio >0.85.

Acanthosis Nigricans: Velvety, gray-brown hyperpigmented thickened skin plaques on the nape of the neck, axillae, and groins (cutaneous marker of severe insulin resistance; part of the HAIR-AN syndrome).

Long-Term Health Risks / Sequelae:

Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (15%) and Gestational Diabetes.

Endometrial Hyperplasia and Endometrial Carcinoma (due to chronic unopposed estrogen).

Dyslipidemia, Hypertension, Metabolic Syndrome, and Cardiovascular Disease.

Obstructive Sleep Apnea.

D. Investigations in PCOS & Hirsutism

Ultrasound (TVS): Bilateral enlarged ovaries (>10 ) with ≥12 peripheral cysts (2–9 mm) and bright echogenic stroma; also measures endometrial thickness.

Hormonal Profile (Done on Day 2–3 of cycle):

Serum LH and FSH: Elevated LH (>10 mIU/mL), normal/low FSH, LH:FSH ratio >2:1.

Serum Total & Free Testosterone: Mild-to-moderately elevated (<150 ng/dL in PCOS; if >150–200 ng/dL with rapid-onset virilism, suspect an androgen-secreting ovarian tumor like Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor).

Serum DHEA-S: Normal or mildly elevated (if >700–800 , suspect an adrenal tumor).

Morning Serum 17-Hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP): <200 ng/dL (if >800 ng/dL, diagnoses late-onset CAH).

Serum TSH and Prolactin: To exclude hypothyroidism and hyperprolactinemia (mildly raised in 20% of PCOS).

Overnight 1 mg Dexamethasone Suppression Test: Morning cortisol <1.8  rules out Cushing’s syndrome.

Metabolic Screening: 2-hour 75 g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT), Fasting Insulin (<25  normal; Fasting Glucose : Insulin ratio <4.5 indicates insulin resistance), and Fasting Lipid Profile.

E. Management of PCOS & Hirsutism

First-Line for All Overweight Patients: Lifestyle Modification & Weight Reduction:

Calorie-restricted diet and regular aerobic exercise to achieve 5–10% weight loss (target BMI <25). Even a 5% weight reduction reduces insulin and free testosterone levels, restoring spontaneous ovulation and menses.

When Fertility IS NOT Desired (Cycle Regulation, Endometrial Protection & Hirsutism):

Menstrual Regulation & Endometrial Protection:

Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (COCs — Drug of Choice): Suppress LH ( ovarian androgen synthesis) and increase hepatic SHBG ( free testosterone), while progestin protects the endometrium from hyperplasia. Prefer COCs containing anti-androgenic or lipid-friendly 3rd/4th generation progestins: Cyproterone acetate (2 mg), Drospirenone (3 mg), or Desogestrel.

Alternatively, cyclic Medroxyprogesterone acetate (10 mg for 10–14 days every 1–2 months) to induce regular withdrawal bleeding.

Specific Treatment of Hirsutism (Takes at least 6 months due to the hair follicle growth cycle):

Combined OC Pills (first-line)  Anti-Androgens:

Cyproterone acetate: 2 mg (in Diane-35) or 25–50 mg D5–D15 (competitive androgen receptor blocker + inhibits -reductase).

Spironolactone (100–200 mg/day): Aldosterone antagonist that blocks androgen receptors in hair follicles and inhibits -reductase.

Finasteride (5 mg/day): -reductase inhibitor (blocks conversion of T to DHT).

Flutamide (250 mg/day): Pure non-steroidal androgen receptor antagonist (monitor for hepatotoxicity).

Topical Eflornithine Hydrochloride (13.9% cream): Inhibits ornithine decarboxylase in facial hair follicles.

Cosmetic / Physical Hair Removal: Laser photothermolysis, electrolysis, waxing, bleaching, or epilation.

Insulin Sensitizers: Metformin (500 mg thrice daily / 1500 mg/day) in women with impaired glucose tolerance, acanthosis nigricans, or metabolic syndrome.

When Fertility IS Desired (Anovulatory Infertility):

First-Line Ovulation Induction: Letrozole (2.5–5 mg D3–D7) or Clomiphene Citrate (50–150 mg D2–D6), combined with Metformin (500 mg TID) in insulin-resistant/obese women.

Second-Line (Clomiphene-Resistant Cases):

Low-Dose Step-Up Gonadotropin Therapy (Purified/Recombinant FSH starting at 37.5–75 IU daily with strict TVS monitoring + hCG trigger), OR

Laparoscopic Ovarian Drilling (LOD): Puncturing 4–6 sites on each ovary to a depth of 3–5 mm using monopolar needle electrocautery (30–40 W for 4 sec) or laser.

Destroys androgen-producing stroma, lowers intraovarian androgens and LH, and restores spontaneous ovulation (~80%) and sensitivity to clomiphene without the risk of OHSS or multiple pregnancy.

Third-Line: IVF-ET.

title: Chapter 7A: One-Word Answers
text:
Commonly used first-line ovulation inducing drug [KU24]: Clomiphene citrate (or Letrozole in PCOS).

Direct evidence of ovulation during diagnostic laparoscopy [KU23]: Visualization of ovulation stigma on the ovary / recent corpus luteum (or detection of ovum in POD fluid).

Expand – “ICSI” [KU19]: Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection.

Drug of choice for lactation suppression / hyperprolactinemia [KU18]: Cabergoline (or Bromocriptine).

Milk secretion in non-pregnant woman [KU17]: Galactorrhea.

Ultrasound guided technique to visualize intrauterine pathology [KU24]: Saline Infusion Sonography (SIS) / Sonohysterography.

Luteinization of Graafian follicle without rupture / release of ovum [KU16]: Luteinized Unruptured Follicle (LUF) syndrome (Trapped Ovum).

Decreased sperm count in a semen sample [KU16]: Oligozoospermia (Oligospermia) (<15 million/mL).

subject: gynecology
title: 7B.1 Endometriosis
text:
CHAPTER 7B: Endometriosis & Menopause

(Covers: SE 1 [KU21], 2 [TU], 3 [RGU]; SA 2 [KU24,23,15], 3 [KU24], 4 [KU23,16], 9–11 [RGU,TU])

A. Definition & Sites

Definition: Presence of functioning endometrial tissue (both endometrial glands and stroma) outside the uterine cavity. (When located within the myometrium, it is called adenomyosis / endometriosis interna).

Common Sites:

Abdominal / Pelvic (Most Common): Ovaries (commonest site — forming endometriomas / chocolate cysts), Pouch of Douglas (cul-de-sac), Uterosacral ligaments, pelvic peritoneum, rectovaginal septum, fallopian tubes, rectosigmoid colon, appendix, and urinary bladder/ureter.

Extra-abdominal & Remote Sites: Abdominal surgical scars (cesarean section, hysterotomy, myomectomy), episiotomy scar, umbilicus, cervix, vagina, and rarely lungs/pleura (catamenial hemoptysis/pneumothorax).

B. Theories of Etiopathogenesis

No single theory explains all cases; multiple mechanisms operate:

Retrograde Menstruation Theory (Sampson’s Theory — Most Widely Accepted for Pelvic Endometriosis): Viable endometrial fragments reflux backward through the fallopian tubes during menstruation and implant on dependent pelvic peritoneal surfaces (ovaries, POD, uterosacral ligaments), where they proliferate and bleed cyclically under ovarian estrogen influence.

Coelomic Metaplasia Theory (Meyer and Ivanoff): Chronic irritation of multipotent pelvic peritoneum (derived from embryonic coelomic epithelium) by menstrual blood or inflammatory stimuli induces metaplasia into Müllerian/endometrial tissue. (Explains ovarian, rectovaginal septum, and umbilical endometriosis).

Direct Implantation Theory: Iatrogenic mechanical transplantation of endometrial/decidual cells into surgical wounds during cesarean section, hysterotomy, myomectomy, or episiotomy  scar endometriosis.

Lymphatic Theory (Halban’s Theory): Metastasis of endometrial cells via uterine lymphatics to pelvic lymph nodes.

Vascular (Hematogenous) Theory: Dissemination via venous channels to distant sites (lungs, pleura, brain, limbs).

Genetic & Immunological Theory: 6–7 fold higher risk in first-degree relatives. Defective local peritoneal cellular immunity (impaired NK cell activity and resistance to apoptosis) fails to clear refluxed menstrual debris, while activated peritoneal macrophages secrete cytokines (IL-1, TNF-, VEGF) that promote implantation and angiogenesis.

C. Pathology & Mechanisms of Infertility

Pathology: Ectopic implants respond to cyclic ovarian hormones by proliferating and bleeding during menses. Shed blood is trapped, irritating surrounding tissues to provoke intense fibrosis, puckering, and dense pelvic adhesions (leading to a frozen pelvis), though fallopian tubes usually remain patent.

Peritoneal lesions: Classic black/bluish “powder-burn” or “match-stick” spots surrounded by stellate scarring, as well as active non-pigmented subtle lesions (red flame-like, polypoid, yellow-brown patches, or circular peritoneal windows).

Ovarian Endometrioma (Chocolate Cyst): Invagination of ovarian cortex by bleeding surface implants forms a cyst filled with thick, tarry, hemosiderin-laden dark brown fluid (“chocolate cyst”). Microscopically shows endometrial glands, stroma, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages (pseudoxanthoma cells).

Mechanisms of Infertility in Endometriosis (Present in 40–60% of cases):

Anatomical Distortion (Moderate-to-Severe Disease): Dense peritubal and periovarian adhesions distort tubo-ovarian relationship, impair fimbrial pick-up of the oocyte, and alter tubal motility.

Endocrinopathies & Ovulatory Dysfunction (Minimal-to-Mild Disease): Defective folliculogenesis, anovulation, Luteal Phase Defect (LPD), Luteinized Unruptured Follicle (LUF) syndrome (trapped ovum), premature luteolysis due to excess , and hyperprolactinemia.

Hostile Peritoneal Fluid Microenvironment: Activated peritoneal macrophages and elevated prostaglandins/cytokines cause increased sperm phagocytosis, reduced sperm motility, oocyte toxicity, and impaired fertilization/implantation.

Coital Dysfunction: Severe deep dyspareunia reduces coital frequency.

D. Clinical Features & Diagnosis

Patient Profile: Nulliparous or low-parity woman aged 30–45 years, often with a history of delayed marriage/childbearing and infertility.

Symptoms: (25% are asymptomatic; severity of pain does NOT correlate with the stage/extent of lesions—it correlates with the depth of infiltration >5 mm):

Progressive Secondary (Congestive) Dysmenorrhoea (70%): Classic “co-menstrual dysmenorrhoea”—deep-seated pelvic and lumbosacral pain starts a few days before menses, worsens progressively during menstruation, and takes several days after cessation of flow to subside.

Infertility (40–60%).

Deep Dyspareunia (20–40%): Due to stretching of infiltrated uterosacral ligaments, Pouch of Douglas, or rectovaginal septum, and a fixed retroverted uterus.

Chronic Pelvic Pain (non-cyclic lower abdominal ache/backache).

Menstrual Abnormalities (20%): Menorrhagia, polymenorrhoea, or premenstrual spotting.

Organ-Specific Perimenstrual Symptoms: Dyschezia (painful defecation) or cyclical rectal bleeding (rectosigmoid involvement); cyclical dysuria/hematuria (bladder involvement); cyclical pain and bleeding from an abdominal/episiotomy scar.

Signs (Pelvic Examination — Bimanual & Rectovaginal):

Tender nodules in the Pouch of Douglas and thickened, beaded/nodular uterosacral ligaments (best felt on rectovaginal examination).

Fixed, tender retroverted uterus.

Unilateral or bilateral tender adnexal mass with restricted mobility (chocolate cyst).

Bluish spots may be seen in the posterior vaginal fornix on speculum examination.

Investigations:

Double-Puncture Diagnostic Laparoscopy — “Gold Standard”: Directly visualizes “powder-burn” and subtle implants, ovarian endometriomas, and adhesions; allows biopsy confirmation and Revised American Fertility Society (r-AFS) Staging (scored into Stage I: Minimal [1–5], Stage II: Mild [6–15], Stage III: Moderate [16–40], and Stage IV: Severe [>40]).

Transvaginal Ultrasonography (TVS) with Color Doppler: Detects ovarian endometriomas as thick-walled cysts with diffuse, homogeneous low-level internal (“ground-glass”) echoes and pericystic vascularity.

 (TVS cannot detect superficial peritoneal implants).

MRI Pelvis: Highly accurate for deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) of the rectovaginal septum and uterosacral ligaments (hyperintense on T1, hypointense on T2).

Serum CA-125: Moderately elevated (usually 35–100 U/mL) in moderate-to-severe endometriosis; not specific for diagnosis, but useful to monitor response to therapy and detect recurrence.

E. Management of Endometriosis

Management is individualized based on age, severity of pain, desire for fertility, and r-AFS stage:

Expectant Management: In asymptomatic minimal/mild disease or patients approaching menopause  observation + NSAIDs (Mefenamic acid / Ibuprofen) for pain relief and encouragement to conceive early (pregnancy induces decidual necrosis and regression of implants).

Medical Management (Hormonal Suppression — Suppressive, NOT Curative; Indicated for Pain Relief in Minimal/Mild Disease or Residual Pain):

Principle: Induces atrophy of ectopic endometrial implants by creating a pseudopregnancy, pseudomenopause, or medical oophorectomy state for 6–9 months. (Note: Hormonal therapy does NOT improve fertility and cannot dissolve dense adhesions or endometriomas >1 cm).

Regimens:

Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (“Pseudopregnancy”): Low-dose monophasic COCs given continuously (or cyclically) for 6–9 months  induces decidualization and atrophy. Cheap and well-tolerated in young women.

Progestogens (“Pseudopregnancy”):

Oral: Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) 10 mg TID (30 mg/day), Norethisterone 10–30 mg/day, or Dienogest (2 mg daily) / Dydrogesterone (10–20 mg/day) continuously for 6–9 months.

Injectable: Depot MPA (DMPA) 150 mg IM every 3 months (avoid if pregnancy is desired soon).

Intrauterine: LNG-IUS (Mirena) — highly effective for pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, and rectovaginal endometriosis.

GnRH Agonists (“Medical Oophorectomy” — Most Potent & Rapid Relief):

Leuprolide depot (3.75 mg IM monthly), Goserelin (3.6 mg SC monthly), or Nafarelin (200  intranasally BID) for 6 months.

Downregulates pituitary  hypoestrogenic amenorrhoea ( 30–45 pg/mL). If used >6 months, combine with low-dose estrogen-progestin “Add-Back Therapy” to prevent vasomotor symptoms and trabecular bone loss (osteoporosis).

Danazol (“Pseudomenopause” — 17-ethinyl testosterone derivative):

400–800 mg orally daily in 4 divided doses for 6 months. Suppresses mid-cycle FSH/LH surge, inhibits steroidogenic enzymes, lowers SHBG, and increases free testosterone  endometrial atrophy. Limited by androgenic side effects (weight gain, acne, oily skin, hirsutism, irreversible deepening of voice).

Gestrinone: 1.25–2.5 mg orally twice weekly for 6 months (similar to danazol with fewer side effects).

Aromatase Inhibitors: Anastrozole or Letrozole (for refractory pain).

Surgical Management (Treatment of Choice for Infertility, Endometriomas >3–4 cm, Deep Infiltrating Disease, or Failed Medical Therapy):

Conservative Laparoscopic Surgery (Preserving Fertility):

Laparoscopic excision or ablation/fulguration of peritoneal endometriotic implants (using bipolar diathermy or  / KTP laser), salpingo-ovariolysis (adhesiolysis to restore normal tubo-ovarian anatomy), and LUNA (laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation) for severe midline pain.

Management of Ovarian Endometrioma (Chocolate Cyst): Small cysts (<3 cm) are aspirated, irrigated, and the inner wall is vaporized by laser/diathermy; Large endometriomas (≥3–4 cm) require Laparoscopic Ovarian Cystectomy (stripping the cyst wall capsule) to prevent recurrence and preserve normal ovarian cortex.

Fertility Post-Surgery: Highest spontaneous pregnancy rate occurs within the first 6–12 months after laparoscopic surgery (do not give post-op hormonal suppression if pregnancy is desired). If spontaneous conception fails, proceed to COH + IUI (in Stage I/II) or IVF-ET (in Stage III/IV).

Definitive Surgery (Radical): Total Abdominal Hysterectomy with Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy (TAH + BSO) + excision of all visible endometriotic nodules. Indicated in women >40 years with completed family and severe intractable symptoms.

(For Scar Endometriosis: Wide local surgical excision; hormonal therapy is ineffective).

subject: gynecology
title: 7B.2 Menopause & Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT)
text:
(Covers: SA 1 [KU25,24,19], 5 [KU21], 6–8, 12–14 [RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1, 2 [KU]; also Ch. 2 SA 20, 23)

A. Definitions & Endocrinology

Menopause: Permanent cessation of menstruation at the end of reproductive life due to loss of ovarian follicular activity. Clinically confirmed retrospectively after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhoea (average age: 50 years; range 45–55 years; genetically predetermined, accelerated by smoking).

Premature Menopause: Menopause occurring at or before 40 years of age.

Endocrine Changes: Depletion of ovarian follicles  initial fall in ovarian Inhibin B, followed by a sharp drop in Serum Estradiol ( < 20 pg/mL)  loss of negative feedback  marked elevation of Serum FSH (>40 mIU/mL; 10–20 fold rise) and LH (3-fold rise). The predominant postmenopausal estrogen is Estrone (, 30–70 pg/mL), produced by peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androgens (androstenedione) in adipose tissue.

B. Clinical Features & Organ/Metabolic Complications of Menopause

Vasomotor Symptoms (70–80%):

Hot Flushes (characteristic symptom: sudden feeling of intense heat over the upper body/face lasting 1–10 minutes, coinciding with hypothalamic GnRH/LH pulses, followed by profuse sweating and palpitations) and Night Sweats causing insomnia.

Urogenital Atrophy:

Vagina & Vulva: Thinning of vaginal epithelium (Maturation Index shifts to left: 10/85/5 or 100/0/0 parabasal dominance), loss of glycogen and Döderlein’s bacilli, alkaline pH (6.0–7.5)  atrophic (senile) vaginitis, vaginal dryness, pruritus, superficial dyspareunia, and narrow introitus.

Urinary Tract: Atrophy of trigonal and urethral epithelium + loss of periurethral vascular seal and pelvic floor muscle tone  dysuria, urgency, frequency (urethral syndrome), recurrent UTIs, genuine stress incontinence, and pelvic organ prolapse.

Osteoporosis and Bone Fractures:

Loss of estrogen’s inhibition on osteoclasts and IL-1 causes accelerated trabecular and cortical bone loss (3–5% per year initially).

WHO DEXA Scan Criteria (T-score): Osteopenia: T-score between –1.0 and –2.5 SD; Osteoporosis: T-score  –2.5 SD below young adult mean.

Leads to backache, loss of height, kyphosis (“dowager’s hump”), and fractures of the vertebral body, femoral neck (hip), and distal radius (Colles’ fracture).

Cardiovascular & Cerebrovascular Disease: Loss of estrogen causes  HDL,  LDL/total cholesterol, LDL oxidation (foam cell formation), and loss of endothelial nitric oxide  atherosclerosis, coronary heart disease (IHD), myocardial infarction, and stroke.

Psychological & Neurological Changes: Anxiety, irritability, mood swings, depression, memory loss, and increased risk of dementia / Alzheimer’s disease ( brain opioid/cholinergic activity).

Skin & Hair: Thinning and wrinkling of skin due to loss of collagen (1–2%/year — “crow’s feet” and “purse-string” wrinkles), dry hair, and mild facial hirsutism.

C. Management of Menopause & Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT / MHT)

Non-Hormonal Management & Lifestyle Modifications:

Counseling, weight-bearing regular exercise, cessation of smoking/alcohol/excess caffeine.

Calcium (1000–1500 mg/day) and Vitamin  (1500–2000 IU/day) supplementation.

For Hot Flushes (when estrogen is contraindicated): SSRI / SNRIs (Paroxetine, Venlafaxine, Fluoxetine), Gabapentin, Clonidine (alpha-adrenergic agonist), Phytoestrogens (Soy isoflavones).

For Osteoporosis: Bisphosphonates (Alendronate, Risedronate, Ibandronate, Zoledronic acid — inhibit osteoclasts; Drug of Choice), SERMs (Raloxifene 60 mg/day — estrogen agonist on bone & lipids, antagonist on breast & endometrium), or Calcitonin nasal spray (200 IU/day).

Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT):

Indications: (1) Relief of moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes), (2) Urogenital atrophy, (3) Prevention of osteoporosis in high-risk women, and (4) Mandatory in Premature Ovarian Failure (<40 years), Gonadal Dysgenesis, and Surgical/Radiation Menopause until the natural age of menopause.

Benefits: 70–80% relief of hot flushes, reversal of urogenital atrophy, 2–5% increase in BMD with 25–50% reduction in vertebral and hip fractures, and 20% reduction in colorectal cancer.

Risks of HRT (WHI Trial): (1) Endometrial hyperplasia & cancer (if unopposed estrogen is given to a woman with an intact uterus), (2) Slight increase in Breast cancer (RR 1.26 with combined E+P used >5 years), (3) Venous thromboembolism (VTE) (2-fold risk with oral estrogen; avoided by transdermal route), (4) Slight increase in Coronary heart disease (CHD) & Stroke when initiated in older women (>60 years), (5) Gallbladder disease (cholelithiasis).

Absolute Contraindications to HRT:

Undiagnosed abnormal genital tract bleeding.

Known or suspected estrogen-dependent neoplasia (Carcinoma breast or Carcinoma endometrium).

Active or past history of Venous Thromboembolism (DVT / Pulmonary embolism) or arterial stroke/MI.

Active liver disease or gallbladder disease.

Available HRT Regimens (Principle: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration [3–5 years]):

Estrogen-Only Regimen (For Hysterectomized Women ONLY): Oral Conjugated Equine Estrogen (CEE) 0.3–0.625 mg daily or Micronized -Estradiol 1–2 mg daily; OR Transdermal Estradiol Patch (50  twice weekly) / Percutaneous Estradiol Gel (1 mg daily) / Subdermal Estradiol Implant (25–50 mg every 6 months).

Combined Estrogen + Progestogen Regimen (Mandatory for Women with an Intact Uterus to protect the endometrium):

Cyclic / Sequential Regimen (for perimenopausal women): Estrogen daily (D1–D25 or continuously) + Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA 2.5–5 mg), Micronized Progesterone (100–200 mg), or Dydrogesterone (5–10 mg) for the last 12–14 days of each month (causes monthly withdrawal bleed).

Continuous Combined Regimen (for postmenopausal women): Daily low-dose Estrogen (CEE 0.3–0.625 mg) + Daily Progestin (MPA 1.5–2.5 mg or Norethisterone 0.5 mg) or LNG-IUS in utero  induces endometrial atrophy and amenorrhoea.

Tibolone (2.5 mg orally daily): Synthetic 19-nortestosterone steroid with weak estrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic activity (“gonadomimetic”). Relieves hot flushes, prevents bone loss, improves libido, and does not stimulate the endometrium (no bleeding) or breast tissue. Used in women >1 year postmenopausal.

Local Vaginal Estrogen Cream / Pessary (CEE 0.625–1.25 mg or Estriol cream): Ideal for isolated atrophic vaginitis, dyspareunia, or recurrent UTI/urgency without systemic side effects.

Monitoring Prior to & Annually During HRT: BP, weight, Clinical Breast Examination + Annual Mammography, Pelvic Examination + Pap Smear, Lipid profile, and TVS for endometrial thickness (must be <4–5 mm; any unscheduled bleeding requires endometrial biopsy).

subject: gynecology
title: Chapter 7B: One-Word Answers
text:
Hormone given for flushing in post-menopausal women [KU17]: Estrogen (Estrogen + Progestogen if uterus is intact; or Tibolone).

Drug of choice in post-menopausal woman with osteoporosis [KU16,15]: Bisphosphonates (e.g., Alendronate / Zoledronic acid) or Raloxifene (SERM).

subject: gynecology
title: 7C.1 Uterine Fibroid (Leiomyoma / Myoma)
text:
CHAPTER 7C: Benign Diseases of the Uterus (Fibroid, Adenomyosis, Polyps)

(Covers: Essays 1 [KU24], 2 [KU19], 3 [KU16], 4 [KU24], 5 [KU17]; SE 1 [KU25], 2 [KU24], 3–5 [KU15,RGU,TU]; SA 1–20 [KU,RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1–3 [KU])

A. Definition, Incidence & Etiology

Definition: Uterine leiomyoma (fibroid or myoma) is the commonest benign solid tumor of the uterus and female pelvis, composed of smooth muscle cells and a variable amount of fibrous connective tissue.

Incidence & Risk Factors: Present in at least 20% of women over 30 years of age (peak incidence: 35–45 years).

Increased Risk: Nulliparity (or low parity / long secondary infertility), Obesity, Early menarche / Hyperestrogenic state, positive family history, and Black race. (Decreased risk: Multiparity, smoking).

Histogenesis & Growth:

Monoclonal origin: Arises from somatic mutation of a single neoplastic smooth muscle cell of the myometrium (40% show chromosomal abnormalities in chromosomes 6, 7, 12, or 14; MED12 mutations).

Hormone & Growth Factor Dependency: Growth is stimulated by Estrogen, Progesterone, and local polypeptide growth factors (EGF, IGF-1, TGF-). Fibroids never occur before menarche, enlarge during pregnancy, and shrink after menopause.

Pathology: Surrounded by a false capsule (pseudocapsule) formed by compressed adjacent myometrium, separated by a loose areolar plane through which blood vessels enter the periphery of the tumor (hence the center is least vascular and prone to degeneration, while calcification occurs at the periphery). Cut surface is pinkish-white with a classic whorled appearance and bulges out due to contraction of the false capsule.

B. Anatomical & FIGO Classification of Uterine Fibroids

Traditional Anatomical Classification ([Draw and label] — Fig. 19.1):

A. Body / Corporeal Fibroids (98–99%):

Interstitial / Intramural (75% — Commonest): Located within the myometrial wall.

Subperitoneal / Subserous (15%): Pushed outward beneath the serosa; may become pedunculated, burrows between the leaves of the broad ligament (Broad ligament / Intraligamentary pseudo-fibroid), or detaches from its uterine pedicle after adhering to the omentum/mesentery to derive nutrition from it (Wandering or Parasitic fibroid).

Submucous (5% — Least common, but produces MAXIMUM symptoms): Pushed inward beneath the endometrium; distorts the cavity and may become pedunculated (Fibroid polyp) and extrude through the cervix (pseudocervical fibroid).

B. Cervical Fibroids (1–2%): Arise from the supravaginal cervix (Anterior, Posterior, Lateral, or Central — expanding the cervix on all sides with the small uterine body sitting on top like the “Lantern on the dome of St. Paul’s”) or vaginal cervix (polypoidal). Distorts pelvic anatomy and displaces the ureter.

FIGO Subclassification System for Leiomyomas (PALM-COEIN: Types 0 to 8):

Submucosal (Types 0–2):

Type 0: Pedunculated intracavitary myoma (entirely within the endometrial cavity).

Type 1: Submucosal myoma with <50% intramural extension.

Type 2: Submucosal myoma with ≥50% intramural extension.

Other / Intramural & Subserosal (Types 3–8):

Type 3: 100% intramural, but contacts the endometrium.

Type 4: 100% intramural (entirely within myometrium, no contact with endometrium or serosa).

Type 5: Subserosal myoma with ≥50% intramural extension.

Type 6: Subserosal myoma with <50% intramural extension.

Type 7: Pedunculated subserosal myoma.

Type 8: Other specific locations (e.g., Cervical, Broad ligament, Parasitic).

Hybrid Leiomyomas (Transmural): Contact both endometrium and serosa, denoted by two numbers separated by a hyphen (e.g., Type 2-5).

C. Secondary Changes & Complications of Fibroids

Degenerations:

Hyaline Degeneration (65% — Most Common): Central part loses its whorled pattern and becomes soft, homogeneous, and elastic.

Cystic Degeneration: Liquefaction of hyalinized areas after menopause, forming irregular ragged cystic spaces (mimics ovarian cyst or pregnancy).

Fatty Degeneration: Deposition of fat globules around menopause.

Calcific (Calcareous) Degeneration (10%): Precipitation of calcium carbonate/phosphate in subserous or postmenopausal fibroids  “Womb stone” (seen as popcorn calcification on X-ray).

Red Degeneration (Carneous Degeneration / Necrobiosis):

Occurrence: Occurs characteristically in a large fibroid during the second half of pregnancy (mid-trimester) or puerperium.

Pathogenesis: Rapid growth leads to aseptic venous thrombosis and congestion in the periphery, with hemolysis of RBCs releasing hemoglobin and fatty acids into the tissue.

Pathology: Cut surface looks like raw beef (dark red) with a fishy odor.

Clinical Features: Acute focal abdominal pain, vomiting, mild fever, localized tenderness over the fibroid, leukocytosis, and raised ESR (confused with acute appendicitis, torsion, or placental abruption).

Management: Strictly conservative (Surgery/myomectomy is contraindicated during pregnancy due to profuse hemorrhage!). Treat with bed rest, IV fluids/hydration, analgesics (paracetamol/NSAIDs for <48h), and sedatives; symptoms subside within 7–10 days.

Sarcomatous (Malignant) Change (Leiomyosarcoma — Rare, <0.1% to 0.2%):

Warning Signs: Rapid enlargement of a fibroid, postmenopausal growth or bleeding, recurrence of a fibroid polyp, and loss of the whorled pattern (becomes soft, yellowish, friable, and hemorrhagic on cut section).

Other Complications:

Severe anemia from persistent menorrhagia.

Torsion of a pedunculated subserous fibroid (causes acute abdomen).

Rupture of a dilated surface vein over a subserous fibroid  massive intraperitoneal hemorrhage.

Infection & Sloughing necrosis of a submucous fibroid polyp.

Inversion of the uterus (chronic traction by a fundal submucous myoma).

Pressure effects: Acute retention of urine (impacted posterior wall or anterior cervical fibroid) or hydroureteronephrosis (broad ligament or lateral cervical fibroid compressing the ureter).

Pseudo-Meigs’ syndrome and Secondary Polycythemia (due to autonomous erythropoietin production by the myoma or renal compression).

D. Clinical Features & Causes of Heavy Menstrual Bleeding / Infertility

Symptoms: (75% are asymptomatic):

Menorrhagia / Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (30% — Classic Symptom): Seen in submucous and intramural fibroids.

Causes of HMB in Fibroid ([KU25]): (i) Increased surface area of the endometrium (from normal 15  up to 200 ), (ii) Interference with normal myometrial contractility (preventing compression of spiral arterioles), (iii) Compression and congestion of subjacent endometrial venous plexuses, (iv) Associated endometrial hyperplasia due to anovulation/hyperestrinism, (v) Ulceration and necrosis of the thin endometrium overlying a submucous fibroid, and (vi) Prostanoid imbalance ( relative to ).

Metrorrhagia: Due to ulceration/infection of a submucous fibroid polyp.

Dysmenorrhoea: Congestive (due to pelvic congestion or associated adenomyosis/endometriosis in 30%) or Spasmodic (uterine contractions trying to expel a submucous polyp).

Infertility (30%): Caused by distortion/elongation of the uterine cavity, cornual tubal block, impaired endometrial vascularity/nidation over a submucous myoma, and associated anovulation/endometriosis.

Abdominal Lump & Pressure Symptoms (urinary frequency/retention, constipation).

Signs: Pallor; Per abdomen: Firm, non-tender, nodular suprapubic mass arising from the pelvis (lower pole cannot be reached), dull on percussion, mobile from side to side. Bimanual examination: Uterus is not felt separate from the mass, and movement of the abdominal mass is transmitted to the cervix (except in pedunculated subserous fibroid).

Investigations:

Hemogram (Hb%), renal function tests, coagulation profile.

Ultrasonography (TAS & TVS with Color Doppler): Confirms uterine origin, number, size, and exact FIGO location (submucous vs. intramural vs. subserosal), rules out adnexal pathology, and checks kidneys for hydronephrosis.

Saline Infusion Sonography (SIS) or Diagnostic Hysteroscopy: Best for mapping submucous fibroids (Types 0, 1, 2).

MRI Pelvis: Most accurate modality for mapping multiple myomas prior to myomectomy/UAE and for differentiating a solitary fibroid from adenomyosis.

Endometrial Biopsy / Pipelle / D&C: Mandatory in women >40 years or with irregular bleeding to rule out endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma.

Intravenous Urography (IVU): Indicated in large broad ligament or cervical fibroids to trace the course of the ureters.

E. Management of Uterine Fibroids

Expectant Management (For Asymptomatic Fibroids):

Indicated if: (i) Uterine size <12 weeks, (ii) Diagnosis is certain (ovarian mass ruled out by USG), (iii) No submucous component in an infertile woman, and (iv) No hydronephrosis. Follow up every 6 months with pelvic exam and USG.

Medical Management:

Objectives: Temporary palliation of HMB to correct anemia prior to surgery, shrink fibroid size and vascularity before myomectomy/vaginal hysterectomy, or serve as a bridge to menopause in perimenopausal women. (Medical therapy is NOT a permanent cure, as fibroids regrow within 3–6 months of stopping drugs).

Drugs Used:

To reduce bleeding only: Tranexamic acid, Mefenamic acid, COCs, Oral Progestins, or LNG-IUS (Mirena) (if uterine size <12 weeks and cavity is not distorted by a submucous fibroid).

To shrink fibroid volume AND induce amenorrhoea (Preoperative / Short-term for 3–6 months):

GnRH Agonists (Leuprolide depot 3.75 mg IM monthly or Goserelin 3.6 mg SC monthly) or GnRH Antagonists (Cetrorelix): Induce medical menopause  reduce fibroid volume by 50%, reduce uterine vascularity/operative blood loss, improve Hb%, and allow Pfannenstiel or vaginal/endoscopic approach. (Disadvantage: Hyaline degeneration blurs the pseudocapsule cleavage plane, making enucleation slightly harder during myomectomy).

Antiprogesterones — Mifepristone (RU-486): 10–25 mg (or 5 mg) orally daily for 3 months  induces amenorrhoea and shrinks fibroid volume by 40–50%.

Selective Progesterone Receptor Modulators (SPRMs) — Ulipristal Acetate (5 mg daily for 3 months; requires strict liver enzyme monitoring) or Asoprisnil.

Danazol: 200–400 mg daily for 3 months.

Surgical Management:

A. Myomectomy (Conservative Surgery — Preserving the Uterus):

Indications: Symptomatic fibroid (HMB, pain, pressure), infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss due to a cavity-distorting fibroid, or a large (>12 weeks)/growing fibroid in a young woman (e.g., 25–35 years) who wishes to preserve fertility or her uterus.

Pre-requisites prior to Myomectomy ([KU16,TU]):

Husband’s Semen Analysis (must be normal in infertility cases).

Hysteroscopy / SIS / HSG to evaluate the uterine cavity (detect submucous fibroid/polyp) and confirm tubal patency.

Endometrial Biopsy & Pap Smear to rule out endometrial/cervical malignancy in irregular bleeding.

Correction of anemia (Hb >10 g/dL) and arrangement of cross-matched blood.

Informed written consent explicitly stating that “Myomectomy will be tried, but may proceed to Hysterectomy” if uncontrollable life-threatening hemorrhage or sarcoma is encountered.

Contraindications: Infected fibroid, suspected sarcoma, postmenopausal growth, pelvic/endometrial tuberculosis, and during pregnancy or cesarean section (except pedunculated subserous).

Routes & Principles of Myomectomy:

Hysteroscopic Myomectomy: Gold standard for Submucous fibroids (Types 0, 1, and small Type 2 <3–4 cm) using a resectoscope loop.

Laparoscopic Myomectomy: For subserous and selected intramural myomas (<8–10 cm, ≤3 in number).

Abdominal Myomectomy (Open Laparotomy):

Measures to minimize intraoperative blood loss: (i) Preoperative GnRH agonist/Mifepristone, (ii) Intramyometrial injection of Vasopressin (20 units diluted in 20 mL saline), (iii) Bonney’s Myomectomy Clamp (applied at the isthmus including round ligaments to occlude uterine arteries) + sponge-holding forceps on infundibulopelvic ligaments, OR a rubber catheter tourniquet passed through avascular windows in the broad ligament at the isthmus, (iv) Single midline vertical anterior wall incision (least vascular; avoids posterior wall adhesions to bowel/adnexae; posterior myomas are removed via transcavity approach or Bonney’s hood operation.

 (v) Intracapsular enucleation inside the false capsule, and (vi) Obliteration of dead space using layered mattress sutures (tire stitch)

Complications & Outcome: Intraoperative hemorrhage, injury to intramural fallopian tube/bladder/ureter, postoperative pyrexia/adhesions, recurrence rate of 30–50%, relaparotomy in 20–25%, and pregnancy rate of 40–60% (subsequent pregnancy requires mandatory hospital delivery / elective CS if the uterine cavity was breached).

B. Hysterectomy (Definitive Surgery):

Treatment of choice in symptomatic women ≥40 years or parous women who have completed their family (as in the 35y sterilized woman [KU16], 40y [KU17], and 45y [KU19]). Total hysterectomy (TAH, NDVH if ≤12–14 weeks, or TLH/LAVH) ensures zero recurrence. Ovaries are conserved if healthy in women <45 years. (In Cervical or Broad Ligament Fibroids, prior intracapsular enucleation of the myoma is done first so the displaced ureters fall back into normal position, followed by hysterectomy).

Minimally Invasive Non-Surgical Alternatives:

Uterine Artery Embolization (UAE): Percutaneous femoral artery catheterization and injection of polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) particles or gelatin microspheres into both uterine arteries  ischemic infarction and 50–60% shrinkage of fibroids with 80–90% relief of HMB. (Complications: Post-embolization syndrome [pain, fever, nausea], premature ovarian failure [2–5%], and placental abnormalities; not recommended if future pregnancy is desired).

MRI-Guided High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (MRgFUS): Non-invasive thermal coagulative necrosis of fibroid tissue under real-time MRI thermometry.

subject: gynecology
title: 7C.2 Adenomyosis
text:
(Covers: Clinical features, evaluation and management of adenomyosis [KU25,21,20,16,RGU,TU])

Definition: Adenomyosis (endometriosis interna) is a benign condition characterized by the ingrowth of functioning endometrial glands and stroma directly into the myometrium beyond 2.5 mm (or one low-power field) beneath the endometrial-myometrial interface (EMI / Junctional Zone), surrounded by reactive myometrial hyperplasia and hypertrophy.

Etiopathogenesis: Repeated childbirths, vigorous uterine curettage, cesarean section, or hyperestrogenism disrupts the subendometrial Junctional Zone (JZ) (since the endometrium lacks a submucosa), allowing basal endometrium to invaginate into the myometrium. Coexists with pelvic endometriosis in 40% and fibroids in 30%.

Pathology (Naked Eye & Microscopic — Differentiating from Fibroid [Refer Table on Book Page 660 / PDF Page 678]):

Gross: Uterus is diffusely and symmetrically enlarged (usually asymmetrical thickening of the posterior wall), soft/boggy, and rarely exceeds 12–14 weeks pregnancy size (size of a large orange). Cut surface shows a coarse, trabeculated / whorled-free appearance with tiny dark hemorrhagic cystic spots and NO false capsule (cannot be shelled out like a fibroid).

Microscopic: Islands of endometrial glands and stroma deep within hyperplastic myometrial bundles (mostly unresponsive basal-type endometrium, though some show cyclic bleeding and hemosiderin-laden macrophages).

Clinical Features:

Patient Profile: Multiparous woman aged >35–40 years. (30% are asymptomatic).

Symptoms:

Menorrhagia (70%): Due to enlarged endometrial cavity, hypervascularity, associated endometrial hyperplasia, and inadequate myometrial contractions (distorted Junctional Zone).

Progressively Increasing Secondary Dysmenorrhoea (30–50%): Colicky/congestive pain starting before menses and continuing throughout flow (marked when myometrial invasion >80%).

Deep Dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, and subfertility.

Signs: Bimanual examination reveals a uniformly enlarged (up to 12–14 weeks), globoid, softened, and tender uterus (especially premenstrually — Halban’s sign).

Investigations / Evaluation:

Transvaginal Ultrasonography (TVS) with Color Doppler (First-line): Shows: (i) Globular, asymmetric uterine enlargement (posterior wall thicker than anterior), (ii) Heterogeneous myometrial echogenicity, (iii) Multiple small anechoic myometrial cysts (2–5 mm) giving a “Swiss-cheese” or “honeycomb” appearance, (iv) Indistinct/blurred endometrial-myometrial border (loss of subendometrial halo), and (v) Diffusely increased translesional vascularity (unlike peripheral rim vascularity of a fibroid).

MRI Pelvis (Most Specific Non-Invasive Modality): T2-weighted MRI shows thickening of the low-signal Junctional Zone (JZ) >12 mm (normal <8 mm) with high-signal myometrial foci.

Histopathology of Hysterectomy Specimen: Definitive diagnosis.

Management:

Medical / Conservative Management (For young women or perimenopausal women wishing to avoid surgery):

LNG-IUS (Mirena — First-line Medical Choice): Significantly reduces menorrhagia, dysmenorrhoea, and uterine volume for 5 years.

NSAIDs (Mefenamic acid) + Tranexamic acid during menses.

Continuous Combined Oral Contraceptives, Oral Progestins (Dienogest 2 mg/day), Danazol-loaded IUD, or GnRH agonists (for temporary 3–6 months suppression).

Surgical Management:

Total Hysterectomy (TAH / NDVH / TLH — Definitive Cure): Treatment of choice in parous women ≥40 years who have completed their family.

Conservative Adenomyomectomy / Cytoreductive Surgery: Localized excision is difficult and incomplete because there is no capsule/cleavage plane, carrying a high risk of recurrence and uterine scar rupture in future pregnancy.

subject: gynecology
title: 7C.3 Uterine Polyps (Endometrial & Fibroid Polyps)
text:
(Covers: Fibroid polyp [KU20,RGU]; Endometrial polyp [KU21])

1. Endometrial (Mucous) Polyp:

Pathogenesis & Risk Factors: Localized overgrowth of endometrial glands, stroma, and thick-walled central blood vessels covered by endometrium, projecting into the cavity on a slender pedicle. Associated with hyperestrogenism, Tamoxifen therapy, HRT, obesity, hypertension, and perimenopausal age. Malignant change is rare (0.5%, higher if >10 mm or postmenopausal).

Clinical Features: Often asymptomatic; causes intermenstrual spotting, metrorrhagia, menorrhagia, postmenopausal bleeding, or infertility/miscarriage.

Diagnosis: Saline Infusion Sonography (SIS) or TVS (echogenic intracavitary mass with a single feeding vessel pedicle on Color Doppler) and Diagnostic Hysteroscopy.

Management: Hysteroscopic Polypectomy under direct vision (superior to blind avulsion/D&C), followed by endometrial curettage and histopathological examination of the polyp.

2. Fibroid (Myomatous) Polyp:

Pathogenesis: A sessile submucous corporeal fibroid (usually from the posterior wall or fundus) is extruded into the uterine cavity by uterine contractions, acquiring a broad vascular pedicle. It may dilate the cervix and protrude into the vagina.

Pathology: Covered by endometrium; the tip often undergoes ischemic necrosis, ulceration, and secondary infection with purulent/hemorrhagic discharge.

Clinical Features: Menorrhagia, continuous intermenstrual blood-stained offensive discharge, spasmodic dysmenorrhoea (colicky labor-like pain as the uterus tries to expel it), anemia, and sensation of a mass in the vagina.

Diagnosis & Differentiation from Chronic Uterine Inversion:

On speculum/bimanual exam, a firm, dark red/sloughing globular mass is seen protruding through the dilated cervical rim.

Must be differentiated from Chronic Uterine Inversion before surgery: (i) In fibroid polyp, the uterine fundus is felt in its normal position per abdomen/rectum (cup-like depression in inversion), and (ii) Sound Test: A uterine sound can be passed alongside the pedicle into the uterine cavity for normal/increased depth (>6.5 cm) all around (in complete inversion, the sound cannot be passed).

Management:

Control infection with antibiotics and correct anemia.

Hysteroscopic Resection (for intracavitary submucous fibroid polyp) OR Vaginal Myomectomy / Polypectomy (grasping the polyp with sponge forceps, twisting/transfixing the pedicle base, or shelling it out from its capsule/morcellation if large). Send for histology.

subject: gynecology
title: Chapter 7C: One-Word Answers
text:
Expansion of UAE [KU24]: Uterine Artery Embolization.

Red degeneration of fibroid is common in [KU15]: Pregnancy (second half / mid-trimester) and puerperium.

Malignant form of fibroid uterus [KU15]: Leiomyosarcoma (arises in <0.1–0.2% of fibroids).

subject: gynecology
title: 8.1 Benign Ovarian Cysts & Tumors: Classification, Dermoid, Brenner, & Complications
text:
CHAPTER 8: Benign Diseases of Ovary and Fallopian Tube

(Covers: SA 1–12 [KU,RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1–5 [KU]; also links to Ch. 14)

A. Classification of Ovarian Enlargement (WHO Classification)

Non-Neoplastic (Functional) Ovarian Cysts:

Follicular cyst (commonest functional cyst; unilocular, thin-walled, <5–8 cm, resolves spontaneously in 3–6 months).

Corpus luteum cyst (may cause delayed menses followed by bleeding or rupture with hemoperitoneum, mimicking disturbed ectopic pregnancy).

Theca lutein cysts (bilateral, multilocular cysts caused by high hCG in Hydatidiform mole [50%], Choriocarcinoma [10%], or gonadotropin hyperstimulation; regress spontaneously after molar evacuation).

Polycystic ovaries (PCOS) and Endometriotic (Chocolate) cysts.

Neoplastic Ovarian Tumors (WHO Histogenic Classification — Table 20.1):

I. Surface Epithelial-Stromal Tumors (60–70% of all ovarian neoplasms): (Each may be Benign, Borderline [low malignant potential], or Malignant):

Serous cystadenoma (40% of all ovarian tumors; 40% bilateral; 40% malignant potential; lined by ciliated tubal-type cuboidal/columnar epithelium; papillary variety contains Psammoma bodies).

Mucinous cystadenoma (20–25% of ovarian tumors; largest benign ovarian tumor; 10% bilateral; 5–10% malignant potential; multilocular with viscid glycoprotein mucin; lined by tall non-ciliated picket-fence columnar epithelium resembling endocervix).

Endometrioid tumor (5%).

Clear cell (Mesonephroid) tumor (characterized by hobnail cells).

Brenner (Transitional cell) tumor (1–2%).

II. Germ Cell Tumors (20–25%):

Benign (97%): Mature Cystic Teratoma (Dermoid Cyst).

Monodermal: Struma ovarii (thyroid tissue  hyperthyroidism), Carcinoid tumor (5-HT).

Malignant: Dysgerminoma, Endodermal Sinus (Yolk Sac) Tumor, Immature Teratoma, Non-gestational Choriocarcinoma, Embryonal carcinoma.

III. Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors (6–10%):

Granulosa cell tumor (estrogen-producing), Thecoma, Fibroma (solid benign tumor associated with Meigs’ syndrome), Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor / Androblastoma (androgen-producing), Gynandroblastoma.

IV. Metastatic (Secondary) Tumors (5%): Krukenberg tumor.

B. Mature Cystic Teratoma (Dermoid Cyst)

Origin: Arises from a single primordial germ cell arrested after the first meiotic division (parthenogenetic development of totipotent germ cell into derivatives of all three germ layers: ectoderm [predominant], mesoderm, and endoderm).

Incidence: Constitutes 97% of all ovarian teratomas and 30–40% of all ovarian tumors in reproductive age (most common ovarian tumor in young women and in pregnancy [20–40%]). Bilateral in 15–20% of cases.

Pathology (Naked Eye & Microscopic Histology [KU21]):

Gross: Moderate size (rarely >10–15 cm), unilocular, heavy cyst with a smooth, tense, pearly-white capsule. It often floats up on its pedicle to lie anterior to the uterus in the uterovesical pouch (Küstner’s sign).

Cut Section: Filled with thick, yellow, sebaceous material mixed with matted hair (liquid at body temperature, solidifies on cooling) and sometimes clear CSF. Projecting into the cavity from one side of the wall is a solid nodular eminence called Rokitansky’s protuberance (Mamilla), where teeth, bone, and cartilage are located.

Microscopic Histology (Section must always be taken from Rokitansky’s protuberance):

Ectodermal structures (Predominant): Cyst wall is lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with underlying sebaceous glands, sweat glands, hair follicles, and neural/glial tissue (choroid plexus).

Mesodermal structures: Hyaline cartilage, bone, smooth muscle, and adipose tissue.

Endodermal structures: Respiratory (ciliated columnar) or gastrointestinal epithelium, and thyroid acini (if thyroid tissue predominates >50%, it is called Struma ovarii, which can cause thyrotoxicosis).

Complications:

Torsion of the pedicle (15–20% — Commonest complication): Due to its moderate size, heavy weight (high fat content), smooth unattached surface, and long pedicle.

Rupture (1%): Spillage of irritating sebaceous fluid causes severe chemical (granulomatous) peritonitis.

Malignant Transformation (1–2% — Rare): Usually Squamous cell carcinoma arising from the squamous lining in postmenopausal women.

Diagnosis: Clinical exam (anteriorly placed mobile cystic mass) + TVS (echogenic “dermoid plug” / Rokitansky nodule, “tip of the iceberg” acoustic shadowing, and fat-fluid level) + Plain X-ray / CT of Pelvis showing radio-opaque shadows of teeth or bone.

Treatment: Ovarian Cystectomy (laparoscopic or open) in young women to preserve healthy ovarian cortex, taking care to avoid intraoperative spillage (use an endobag and copious saline lavage). In postmenopausal women, TAH + BSO.

C. Brenner Tumor & Parovarian Cyst (Short Notes)

Brenner Tumor ([KU20,RGU]):

Accounts for 1–2% of ovarian tumors; 8–10% are bilateral, occurring mostly in women >40–50 years.

Arises from urothelial (transitional cell) metaplasia of the ovarian surface epithelium.

Gross: Solid, firm, well-circumscribed, pale yellow/white tumor (usually <2 cm, up to 10 cm) resembling a fibroma; frequently coexists with a mucinous cystadenoma in the same ovary.

Histology: Solid nests/islands of transitional-like epithelial cells (Walthard cell nests) embedded in an abundant dense fibrous stroma. The nuclei have characteristic longitudinal grooves giving a “Coffee-bean” appearance.

Clinical features: Almost always benign; occasionally secretes estrogen (causing postmenopausal bleeding/endometrial hyperplasia) or presents with Meigs’ syndrome. Treatment: Unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in young women; TAH + BSO in postmenopausal women.

Parovarian (Fimbrial / Broad Ligament) Cyst ([RGU]):

True extraperitoneal cyst arising from vestigial remnants of the Wolffian (mesonephric) duct (epoophoron/Gartner’s duct) in the mesosalpinx between the fallopian tube and ovary

Characteristics: Always benign, unilocular, thin-walled, translucent cyst filled with clear watery fluid. The ovary is separate and healthy, while the fallopian tube and ovarian fimbria are stretched and elongated over the top of the cyst.

Treatment: Surgical enucleation by making a “post-box” incision on the anterior leaf of the broad ligament parallel to the round ligament, preserving the ovary and tube, while carefully identifying the ureter at the base of the broad ligament.

D. Complications of Benign Ovarian Tumors (Focus on Torsion of Ovarian Pedicle)

(Covers: Complications of ovarian cyst [KU16,RGU])

Torsion of the Ovarian Pedicle (Axial Rotation — 10–15% — Commonest Complication):

Structures Forming the Ovarian Pedicle ([Table 20.3, Book Page 298]): (i) Laterally: Infundibulopelvic ligament (containing ovarian vessels, nerves, and lymphatics), (ii) Medially: Ovarian ligament, medial end of the fallopian tube, and mesosalpinx (utero-ovarian anastomotic vessels), and (iii) Middle: Broad ligament.

Predisposing Factors: Moderate-sized tumor (8–12 cm), heavy weight (Dermoid cyst is commonest), smooth surface without adhesions, long pedicle, and sudden movement/pregnancy/puerperium.

Hemodynamic Mechanism: Initial partial rotation occludes the thin-walled low-pressure ovarian veins while thick-walled arteries continue to pump blood into the cyst  intense venous engorgement, intracystic hemorrhage, and pulsatile arterial force aggravate the torsion until complete arterial occlusion, ischemia, gangrene, and necrosis occur.

Clinical Presentation: Sudden-onset acute severe colicky lower abdominal pain with nausea/vomiting, tachycardia, low-grade fever, and a tense, tender, cystic hypogastric mass separate from the uterus.

Diagnosis: TVS with Color Doppler (enlarged edematous ovary, “whirlpool sign” of twisted pedicle, and absent/reduced central venous and arterial Doppler flow).

Management: Urgent Laparoscopy or Laparotomy. In young women, if the ovary is viable (not gangrenous), detorsion (untwisting) + ovarian cystectomy is performed to conserve the ovary; if frankly gangrenous/necrotic or in older women, salpingo-oophorectomy (ovariotomy) is done.

Intracystic Hemorrhage (common in papillary serous cystadenoma or following torsion).

Rupture of the Cyst (traumatic or spontaneous  chemical peritonitis in dermoid, or Pseudomyxoma peritonei [jelly-belly mucinous ascites] in mucinous cystadenoma/appendiceal mucocele).

Infection (secondary to torsion or from adherent bowel/salpingitis).

Malignant Transformation (highest in serous cystadenoma [40%], 5–10% in mucinous, 1–2% in dermoid).

subject: gynecology
title: Chapter 8: One-Word Answers
text:
Theca Lutein cysts are seen in ______ [KU24]: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (Hydatidiform mole / Choriocarcinoma) and Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS).

Ovarian tumour which is solid but benign [KU24]: Fibroma of the ovary (also Thecoma and Brenner tumor).

Where is Rokitansky protuberance found [KU21]: Dermoid cyst (Mature cystic teratoma) of the ovary.
