Fibroma of ovary is associated with what syndrome / Define Meig’s syndrome [KU23,19,16,RGU]: Meigs’ Syndrome — characterized by the triad of: (1) Benign solid Ovarian Fibroma (or fibroma-like tumor), (2) Ascites, and (3) Right-sided Hydrothorax (Pleural effusion), which resolve completely after surgical removal of the ovarian tumor.

subject: gynecology
title: 9.1 Painful Swollen Labium Majus: Bartholin’s Cyst and Abscess
text:
CHAPTER 9: Benign Diseases of Vulva, Vagina and Cervix

(Covers: SE 1 [KU24]; SA 2 [KU25], 4 [KU18,16,RGU])

A. Differential Diagnosis of a Painful Swollen Right Labium Majus in a 19-Year-Old ([KU24])

Acute Bartholin’s Gland Abscess (Most Common) or Infected Bartholin’s Duct Cyst.

Vulval Hematoma (history of straddle injury, fall, or sexual trauma).

Furuncle / Folliculitis / Infected Sebaceous Cyst or Vulval Cellulitis.

Strangulated Inguinolabial Hernia or infected Hydrocele of the Canal of Nuck (located in the anterior/upper part of the labium majus).

Secondary infected Vulval Condyloma / Herpes Genitalis / Chancroid.

B. Bartholin’s Abscess & Bartholin’s Cyst

Anatomy: The paired pea-sized (0.5 cm) compound racemose Bartholin’s (greater vestibular) glands lie in the superficial perineal pouch at the 5 o’clock and 7 o’clock positions, while their 2 cm ducts open into the groove between the hymen and the posterior third of the labia minora.

Etiology & Pathogenesis:

Caused by polymicrobial ascending infection: Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Bacteroides, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, or Chlamydia trachomatis.

Acute inflammation of the gland and duct (Acute Bartholinitis) causes edema and fibrosis that blocks the narrow duct ostium  pent-up purulent exudate forms a Bartholin’s Abscess (if acute/virulent) OR pent-up clear glairy mucus forms a Bartholin’s Duct Cyst (when low-grade inflammation subsides leaving a fibrotic duct occlusion).

Clinical Features:

Bartholin’s Abscess: Severe acute throbbing local pain (inability to walk or sit), fever, and dyspareunia. On Examination: Unilateral, extremely tender, hot, red, edematous, fluctuant swelling beneath the posterior half of the labium majus, expanding medially into the posterior labium minus and pushing the introitus to the opposite side (‘S’-shaped vulval cleft). Pus may exude from the congested duct opening on gentle pressure.

Bartholin’s Cyst: Painless (unless large or secondarily infected), non-tender, fluctuant, shiny swelling in the posterolateral lower vagina/labium majus causing local discomfort and superficial dyspareunia.

Investigations:

Swab of pus/discharge from the duct ostium or aspirated pus for Gram stain (intracellular Gram-negative diplococci for N. gonorrhoeae), aerobic/anaerobic culture and sensitivity, and NAAT for Chlamydia.

Complete blood count (leukocytosis in abscess) and fasting blood sugar (in recurrent abscesses).

(In women >40 years of age, biopsy of the cyst/abscess wall is mandatory to rule out Bartholin’s gland adenocarcinoma).

Treatment:

Acute Bartholinitis (Pre-suppuration stage): Bed rest, analgesics, warm sitz baths, and broad-spectrum systemic antibiotics (e.g., Amoxicillin-clavulanate or Ceftriaxone + Doxycycline + Metronidazole).

Bartholin’s Abscess & Bartholin’s Cyst — Marsupialization (Treatment of Choice):

Principle: Simple incision and drainage has a high recurrence rate; complete excision carries heavy blood loss (from the adjacent vestibular bulb), hematoma, scarring, and loss of lubricating mucus. Marsupialization creates a permanent neo-ostium to preserve gland function.

Procedure: Under anesthesia, a vertical elliptical incision (1–1.5 cm) is made on the inner mucosal aspect of the labium minus just outside the hymenal ring (never on the outer labium majus skin). Pus/mucus is drained, loculi are broken, and saline irrigation is done. The edges of the cyst/abscess wall are everted and sutured to the edges of the vaginal/vestibular mucosa using interrupted 3-0 delayed absorbable (Vicryl) sutures, leaving a circular 1 cm opening.

Alternative: Word Catheter (a short inflatable balloon-tipped catheter inserted into the incised cavity and left in place for 4–6 weeks to allow an epithelialized fistulous tract to form).

Recurrent Bartholin’s Cyst / Abscess or Woman >40 Years: Complete Surgical Excision of the gland and duct in the quiescent (non-infected) phase.

subject: gynecology
title: 9.2 Urethral Caruncle
text:
(Covers: Urethral caruncle [KU20])

Definition: A benign, small, reddish, fleshy, pedunculated or sessile lesion arising from the posterior lip of the external urethral meatus in postmenopausal women.

Etiopathogenesis & Histology: Caused by chronic hypoestrogenic atrophy, local irritation, and chronic infection of the distal urethral mucosa. Three histological types: (1) Granulomatous (vascular granulation tissue), (2) Papillomatous (covered by transitional or stratified squamous epithelium), and (3) Angiomatous (telangiectatic blood vessels).

Clinical Features:

Symptoms: Painful micturition (scalding dysuria), frequency, postmenopausal spotting/bleeding on contact with undergarments, and superficial dyspareunia.

Signs: A small (0.5–1 cm), angry bright-red, raspberry-like pea-shaped mass projecting from the posterior margin of the external urethral meatus; it is extremely tender to touch and bleeds easily on manipulation.

Differential Diagnosis: Must be differentiated from Prolapse of the urethral mucosa (which is circumferential 360° around the meatus and painless, whereas a caruncle arises only from the posterior lip and is exquisitely tender) and Urethral Carcinoma (indurated, friable, fixed, with inguinal lymphadenopathy).

Treatment: Surgical Excision and Biopsy under anesthesia, followed by electrocauterization of the base and bladder catheterization for 48 hours + local estrogen cream to prevent recurrence.

subject: gynecology
title: 9.3 Leucorrhoea
text:
(Covers: Leucorrhoea [RGU]; also links to Ch. 33)

Definition: Strictly defined as an excessive normal vaginal discharge that: (1) causes persistent vulval moistness or brownish-yellow staining of undergarments, (2) is non-purulent and non-offensive, and (3) is non-irritant and never causes pruritus. (Microscopically shows desquamated squamous cells and lactobacilli without pus cells).

Causes:

Physiological Excess (High Estrogen States): (i) Puberty, (ii) Mid-cycle around ovulation (peak estrogen stimulates endocervical mucus) and premenstrually, (iii) Pregnancy (hyperestrinism + hyperemia), (iv) Sexual excitement (Bartholin’s gland secretion), and (v) Neonatal leucorrhoea (maternal estrogen).

Cervical Causes (Cervical Leucorrhoea — Excessive Mucus): Cervical ectopy (erosion), chronic endocervicitis, cervical mucous polyp, and ectropion.

Vaginal Causes (Vaginal Leucorrhoea — Excessive Transudation from Pelvic Congestion): Uterine prolapse, acquired retroverted uterus, chronic PID, combined oral contraceptive pill use, vaginal adenosis, and general ill-health/anemia/malnutrition.

Management:Exclude specific infections by wet mount/Gram stain and Pap smear; improve general health/nutrition and local perineal hygiene; treat local cervical lesions (cauterization/cryosurgery for persistent ectopy or polypectomy) or pelvic pathology.

(Note: Indications and Technique of Pap Smear [KU25,19,18] is covered in full under Chapter 13, Section 13.1).

subject: gynecology
title: 10.1 Acute & Chronic Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
text:
CHAPTER 10: Infections of the Genital Tract & STIs

(Covers: SE 1 [KU25], 4 [RGU]; SA 2, 3, 5 [KU24], 10 [KU20], 17 [KU15], 22, 23, 32–34, 36 [RGU,TU])

A. Definition, Microbiology & Risk Factors

Definition: PID is a spectrum of polymicrobial infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract involving the endometrium (endometritis), fallopian tubes (salpingitis), ovaries (oophoritis / tubo-ovarian abscess), myometrium, parametrium, and pelvic peritoneum (pelvic peritonitis), resulting from ascending spread of microorganisms from the lower genital tract (excluding pregnancy and perioperative infections).

Microbiology (Polymicrobial):

Primary (Sexually Transmitted) Organisms: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (30%), Chlamydia trachomatis (30–40% — most common), and Mycoplasma hominis / genitalium (10%).

Secondary (Endogenous Aerobes & Anaerobes): Escherichia coli, Gardnerella vaginalis, Group B Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and anaerobes like Bacteroides fragilis, Peptostreptococcus, and Actinomyces israelii (in IUCD users).

Risk Factors: Menstruating teenagers/young women (<25 years), multiple sexual partners, absence of barrier/COC contraception, recent IUCD insertion (first 3–4 weeks), iatrogenic intrauterine procedures (D&C, HSG, surgical abortion), and previous history of PID. (Protective factors: Barrier methods [condoms] and Combined Oral Contraceptives [thick cervical mucus + shorter menses]).

B. Clinical Features & CDC Diagnostic Criteria (e.g., 26-year-old with fever, pain, and discharge [KU25])

Symptoms: Usually appear during or immediately after menstruation (due to breakdown of genital tract defense):

Bilateral lower abdominal and pelvic pain (acute onset within 3 days in gonococcal; insidious 5–7 days in chlamydial).

Fever (>38.3°C), malaise, headache, nausea, and vomiting.

Abnormal purulent or mucopurulent vaginal discharge.

Abnormal uterine bleeding (intermenstrual spotting or menorrhagia due to endometritis) and deep dyspareunia.

Right hypochondriac pain (5–10%): Due to concomitant perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis Syndrome — “violin-string” adhesions between liver capsule and anterior abdominal wall).

Signs (Pelvic Examination Findings in PID [KU15]):

Per abdomen: Bilateral lower quadrant tenderness, guarding, and rebound tenderness.

Per speculum: Congestedurethral meatus/Bartholin’s ducts; inflamed cervix with mucopurulent endocervical discharge.

Bimanual examination: Vagina feels hot; marked cervical motion tenderness (“Chandelier sign”), uterine tenderness, and bilateral adnexal tenderness or a palpable tender adnexal thickening / tubo-ovarian mass or boggy fullness in the Pouch of Douglas (pelvic abscess).

CDC Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Acute PID:

Minimum Criteria (Any ONE present in a sexually active young woman at risk): (i) Uterine tenderness, (ii) Adnexal tenderness, or (iii) Cervical motion tenderness.

Additional Criteria (To increase specificity): (i) Oral temperature >38.3°C (101°F), (ii) Abnormal mucopurulent cervical/vaginal discharge, (iii) Abundant WBCs on saline wet mount of vaginal fluid, (iv) Elevated ESR (>15 mm/hr) or C-Reactive Protein (CRP), (v) Laboratory documentation of cervical infection with N. gonorrhoeae or C. trachomatis (by NAAT).

Definitive Criteria: (i) Histopathologic evidence of endometritis on endometrial biopsy, (ii) TVS / MRI showing thickened, fluid-filled tubes (cogwheel sign / hydrosalpinx / pyosalpinx) or tubo-ovarian complex/abscess, or (iii) Laparoscopic abnormalities consistent with PID (Gold Standard — shows tubal erythema, edema, purulent exudate from fimbriae, or pyosalpinx).

C. Differential Diagnosis & Investigations

Differential Diagnosis of Acute PID / Acute Salpingitis ([KU24,TU]): (See Table 10.3 on Book Page 131 / PDF Page 149):

Acute Appendicitis (pain starts periumbilically and shifts to McBurney’s point, anorexia/vomiting prominent, unilateral right-sided tenderness high up).

Disturbed Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy (amenorrhoea, pallor, tachycardia out of proportion to normal temperature, positive urine -hCG).

Torsion or Rupture of an Ovarian Cyst / Endometrioma.

Acute Urinary Tract Infection (Pyelonephritis) or Diverticulitis.

Investigations:

Triple Swabs (taken prior to bimanual examination from: 1. Endocervix, 2. Urethra/Bartholin’s duct, and 3. High vagina) for Gram stain, aerobic/anaerobic culture, and NAAT (PCR) for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis.

Blood & Urine: CBC (leukocytosis >10,000/), ESR, CRP, Urine pregnancy test (-hCG), Urine R/E & culture, VDRL, and HIV serology.

Transvaginal Ultrasonography (TVS): To detect hydro-/pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess, or pelvic abscess in POD.

Diagnostic Laparoscopy (if diagnosis is uncertain) or Culdocentesis (pus or peritoneal fluid WBC >30,000/mL).

D. Management of Acute PID (Outpatient, Inpatient & Surgical — CDC Guidelines)

Outpatient (Ambulatory) Management (For Mild-to-Moderate Acute PID — 14 Days Therapy):

CDC 2006 / Textbook Regimen A: Levofloxacin 500 mg PO once daily (or Ofloxacin 400 mg PO BID) for 14 days WITH Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID for 14 days.

CDC 2006 / 2021 Regimen B (Preferred): Inj. Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose (updated to 500 mg IM single dose in CDC 2021) PLUS Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 14 days PLUS Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID for 14 days.

Follow-up: Re-evaluate clinically after 48–72 hours; if no improvement, hospitalize for IV therapy.

Criteria for Inpatient Hospitalization ([KU24] — CDC):

Suspected Tubo-Ovarian Abscess (TOA) or Pelvic Abscess.

Severe clinical illness, nausea/vomiting, or high fever (>38.5°C).

Surgical emergencies (e.g., acute appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy) cannot be excluded.

Failure to respond to oral outpatient therapy within 48–72 hours or inability to tolerate oral drugs.

Pregnancy or Immunodeficiency (HIV positive).

Inpatient Parenteral Antibiotic Regimens:

Bed rest in Fowler’s position, IV fluids, analgesics, and IV antibiotics continued until 24–48 hours after clinical improvement, followed by oral therapy to complete 14 days:

Regimen A: Inj. Cefoxitin 2 g IV every 6 hours (or Cefotetan 2 g IV q12h / Ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h) PLUS Doxycycline 100 mg PO or IV every 12 hours (followed by oral Doxycycline 100 mg BID + Metronidazole 500 mg BID to complete 14 days).

Regimen B (Preferred for Tubo-Ovarian / Pelvic Abscess due to superior anaerobic coverage): Inj. Clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours PLUS Inj. Gentamicin (loading dose 2 mg/kg IV/IM, followed by maintenance 1.5 mg/kg every 8 hours).

Indications for Surgery:

Pelvic Abscess pointing into the posterior fornix: Posterior Colpotomy (drainage of pus through the posterior vaginal vault + breaking loculi with a finger).

Ruptured Tubo-ovarian Abscess or Generalized Peritonitis: Urgent laparotomy, peritoneal lavage, and drainage/excision.

Unresponsive Tubo-ovarian Abscess (failing 48–72 hours of IV antibiotics): Laparoscopic or ultrasound-guided drainage, or unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy / TAH + BSO (if family completed).

Prevention of Reinfection & Partner Management:

Contact tracing and simultaneous empirical treatment of the male sexual partner (Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM + Azithromycin 1 g PO stat or Doxycycline 100 mg BID  7 days). Abstinence until both partners are cured; promote barrier contraception (condoms).

E. Complications & Late Sequelae of PID ([KU20,RGU,TU])

Immediate Complications: Pelvic peritonitis, generalized peritonitis, pelvic abscess, tubo-ovarian abscess, septicemia, and Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis).

Late Sequelae:

Tubal Factor Infertility: Risk is 12% after 1 episode, 25% after 2 episodes, and 50% after 3 episodes (due to loss of cilia, cornual block, fimbrial occlusion, hydrosalpinx, and peritubal adhesions).

Ectopic Pregnancy: Increased 6 to 10-fold.

Chronic Pelvic Pain (20%), Congestive Dysmenorrhoea, and Deep Dyspareunia (due to pelvic adhesive disease / frozen pelvis).

Chronic Pyosalpinx / Hydrosalpinx / Tubo-ovarian mass with recurrent acute exacerbations.

subject: gynecology
title: 10.2 Vaginitis (Trichomoniasis, Candidiasis, Bacterial Vaginosis), Syndromic Management & TSS
text:
(Covers: SE 2 [KU22], 3 [RGU]; SA 1 [KU25,24], 4 [KU24], 6 [KU24,18,16,15], 7 [KU23], 8 [KU22,18], 9 [KU21], 11 [KU20,15], 12 [KU19], 13 [KU19], 14 [KU18], 15 [KU17], 16 [KU16], 18 [KU15], 19–37 [RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1–5 [KU])

A. Comparative Features & Management of Common Causes of Vaginitis

=

[[TABLE:gynecology-tbl-004]]

B. Syndromic Management of STIs / Vaginal Discharge (WHO / NACO)

(Covers: SE 2 [KU22,RGU]; SA 7 [KU23], 4 [KU24])

Principle: Initiating comprehensive treatment for all common causative pathogens of a clinical syndrome (e.g., vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain, or genital ulcer) at the patient’s very first visit using standardized clinical flowcharts, without waiting for laboratory confirmation, combined with partner treatment, health education, and condom promotion.

Advantages: (1) Immediate treatment at the first visit (suitable for primary health centers with limited lab facilities), (2) Prevents loss to follow-up, (3) Breaks the chain of STI transmission immediately, and (4) Simple, cost-effective, and scientifically validated.

NACO / WHO Syndromic Kits (Color-Coded Kits in India):

Vaginal Discharge (Cervicitis + Vaginitis):

For Vaginitis (Trichomoniasis, Candidiasis, BV — Green Kit [Kit 2]): Tab. Secnidazole 2 g PO single dose (or Metronidazole 400 mg BID  7 days) + Tab. Fluconazole 150 mg PO single dose.

If Cervicitis is suspected (Gonorrhoea + Chlamydia — Grey Kit [Kit 1]): Tab. Cefixime 400 mg PO single dose + Tab. Azithromycin 1 g PO single dose.

Lower Abdominal Pain (Acute PID — Yellow Kit [Kit 6]): Tab. Cefixime 400 mg stat + Tab. Metronidazole 400 mg BID  14 days + Cap. Doxycycline 100 mg BID  14 days.

Genital Ulcer Disease (Non-Herpetic: Syphilis + Chancroid [KU24] — White Kit [Kit 3]): Inj. Benzathine Penicillin 2.4 Million Units IM single dose (half in each buttock) + Tab. Azithromycin 1 g PO single dose (or Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat / Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID  3 days for Chancroid; if penicillin-allergic, Blue Kit [Kit 4]: Doxycycline 100 mg BID  14 days + Azithromycin 1 g stat). (For Genital Herpes [Red Kit — Kit 5]: Tab. Acyclovir 400 mg TID  7 days).

C. Other Short Notes in Chapter 10

Triple Swab Test ([KU17,TU]): Taken before bimanual pelvic examination in cases of puerperal sepsis, septic abortion, or acute PID from three sites: (1) High vagina (posterior fornix), (2) Endocervical canal, and (3) External urethral meatus (after massaging the urethra from behind forwards). Sent for Gram stain, aerobic/anaerobic culture, and antibiotic sensitivity. (Note: Do not confuse with the “Three-Swab Test” using methylene blue for VVF in Chapter 18!).

Pyometra ([KU16,TU]): Collection of pus inside the uterine cavity due to cervical canal occlusion + intrauterine infection. Causes: (1) Endometrial carcinoma or Endocervical carcinoma (most important to exclude!), (2) Senile (atrophic) endometritis, (3) Tubercular endometritis, (4) Cervical stenosis following amputation, conization, or radiotherapy, (5) Infected lochiometra. Clinical Features: Intermittent offensive purulent/blood-stained discharge P/V, suprapubic cystic tender uterine swelling; TVS shows fluid-distended cavity. Management: Step 1: Simple cervical dilatation under anesthesia to drain the pus + broad-spectrum antibiotics. Step 2: Wait 7–14 days before performing fractional curettage / endometrial biopsy (to avoid uterine perforation and generalized peritonitis) to rule out malignancy, followed by definitive hysterectomy.

Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) ([RGU,TU]): Acute, life-threatening multisystem illness caused by Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1) exotoxin of Staphylococcus aureus in menstruating women using superabsorbent vaginal tampons or barrier diaphragms for prolonged periods. Diagnostic Criteria: Sudden high fever (≥38.9°C), diffuse erythroderma (“sunburn-like” macular rash) followed by desquamation of palms and soles 1–2 weeks later, hypotension/shock, and involvement of ≥3 organ systems (GI vomiting/diarrhea, muscular myalgia, mucous membrane hyperemia, renal  BUN/creatinine, hepatic  bilirubin/transaminases, thrombocytopenia , or CNS disorientation). Treatment: Immediate removal of tampon, ICU aggressive IV fluid resuscitation + vasopressors, and -lactamase-resistant antistaphylococcal antibiotics (Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h + Cloxacillin/Nafcillin or Vancomycin) for 10–14 days.

subject: gynecology
title: Chapter 10: One-Word Answers
text:
Causative organism of strawberry vaginitis / Strawberry appearance on cervix is characteristic of [KU24,17,15]: Trichomonas vaginalis.

Culture media for candidiasis [KU19]: Sabouraud’s dextrose agar medium or Nickerson’s medium.

Clue cells are seen in / Characteristic microscopic finding in bacterial vaginosis [KU18,16]: Bacterial Vaginosis (Gardnerella vaginalis — Clue cells).

subject: gynecology
title: 11.1 Female Genital Tuberculosis (FGTB)
text:
CHAPTER 11: Tuberculosis of the Female Genital Tract

(Covers: SE 1, 2 [RGU,TU]; SA 1 [KU24], 2 [KU19], 3, 4 [RGU,TU]; One-word answer 1 [KU20])

Incidence & Etiopathogenesis: Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (human type). Incidence is ~1% of gynecology OPD patients and 5–10% of infertile women in India. It is almost always secondary to a primary focus elsewhere (Lungs 50%, lymph nodes, kidneys, bones, or GI tract).

Modes of Spread:

Hematogenous (90% — Commonest): Bacilli from the primary focus seed the highly vascular fallopian tubes during puberty, remaining dormant for 4–6 years before manifesting.

Lymphatic or Direct Contiguity (10%): From tuberculous peritonitis, mesenteric lymph nodes, or intestinal TB.

Ascending (Rare): Sexual transmission from a partner with genitourinary TB (causes vulval/cervical TB).

Organs Affected & Pathology:

Fallopian Tubes (90–100% — Commonest Site of Genital TB [KU20]): Always affected bilaterally, starting in the submucosa of the ampullary region (interstitial salpingitis). Forms tubercles, caseation, fibrosis/calcification (lead-pipe or beaded tubes), tubercular pyosalpinx, salpingitis isthmica nodosa, or everted edematous fimbriae with a patent ostium and distended ampulla giving the classic “Tobacco-pouch” appearance.

Endometrium / Uterus (50–60%): Infected secondarily from the tubes via direct luminal/lymphatic spread. Tubercles form in the basal layer and come to the surface premenstrually (shed at each menses, only to be reinfected from the basal layer/tubes). Severe caseation/ulceration destroys the endometrium, causing intrauterine adhesions / synechiae (Asherman’s syndrome) or pyometra.

Ovaries (20–30%): Perioophoritis, tubo-ovarian mass, or caseating ovarian abscess.

Cervix (5–15%): Ulcerative or bright red papillary/hypertrophic growth that bleeds on touch (mimics carcinoma cervix).

Vulva & Vagina (<1%): Indolent ulcers with undermined edges. (Pelvic peritonitis occurs in 40–50%: ‘wet’ ascitic type or ‘dry’ plastic adhesive type with a doughy feel of the abdomen).

Microscopic Pathology: Classic caseating epithelioid cell granuloma containing central caseation necrosis surrounded by epithelioid cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and Langhans multinucleated giant cells.

Clinical Features:

Age: Reproductive age (20–40 years). May be completely asymptomatic (“silent TB”).

Infertility (70–80% — Commonest Presenting Complaint): Primary or secondary, due to tubal block/loss of cilia, peritubal adhesions, endometrial destruction (Asherman’s syndrome), and anovulation.

Menstrual Abnormalities (50%): Initially menorrhagia or irregular bleeding (pelvic congestion); later oligomenorrhoea or secondary amenorrhoea (endometrial destruction/synechiae or ovarian suppression).

Chronic Pelvic Pain (20–30%), tubo-ovarian mass, postcoital bleeding (cervical TB), and constitutional symptoms (low-grade fever, weight loss, night sweats).

Investigations & Diagnosis:

Premenstrual Diagnostic Endometrial Biopsy / Curettage (Done 2–3 days before menses when tubercles reach the superficial layer): Divided into two parts:

Part A in 10% Formalin: For Histopathology (epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells).

Part B in Normal Saline (NEVER formalin!): For: (i) Ziehl-Neelsen AFB staining, (ii) Culture on Löwenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium or BACTEC (gold standard for drug sensitivity), (iii) Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (PCR / GeneXpert / CBNAAT) (most sensitive [85–95%], detects <10 bacilli), and (iv) Guinea-pig inoculation.

First-day Menstrual Blood: Collected for AFB culture and TB-PCR.

Diagnostic Laparoscopy & Hysteroscopy: Laparoscopy visualizes miliary tubercles on peritoneum/tubes, beaded/rigid tubes, tobacco-pouch hydrosalpinx, and adhesions (biopsy taken). Hysteroscopy shows pale atrophic endometrium, tubercles, and Asherman’s synechiae.

Characteristic HSG Findings in Genital Tuberculosis ([TU]): (Note: HSG is contraindicated in known active TB as it flares up infection, but often reveals occult TB during routine infertility workup) 

Bilateral cornual block.

Rigid “Lead-pipe” tubes with loss of normal tortuosity.

Beaded appearance of the tube (alternating strictures and dilatations with variable filling density).

“Tobacco-pouch” or “Golf-club” appearance of the distended ampullary end.

Salpingitis isthmica nodosa (small cornual diverticula) or fluffy tubal outlines.

Calcified shadows along the course of the tubes or ovaries.

Vascular and lymphatic intravasation of dye ([Fig. 10.6]) and a shrunken, irregular, “honeycomb” or T-shaped uterine cavity (Asherman’s syndrome).

Baseline Systemic Workup: CBC, ESR, Mantoux test, Chest X-ray, and Urine AFB culture (10% have coexisting renal TB).

Management of Genital Tuberculosis:

Medical Therapy — Antitubercular Chemotherapy (DOTS / NTEP — Mainstay of Treatment, Cures 90–95%):

Intensive Phase (2 Months — 2HRZE): Daily oral Isoniazid (H) (5 mg/kg, max 300 mg + Pyridoxine 50 mg), Rifampicin (R) (10 mg/kg, max 600 mg), Pyrazinamide (Z) (20–25 mg/kg, max 2 g), and Ethambutol (E) (15–20 mg/kg).

Continuation Phase (4 Months — 4HR / 4HRE): Daily oral Isoniazid + Rifampicin (+ Ethambutol under current NTEP India guidelines) for 4 months (total 6 months). (Monitor LFTs and vision).

Surgical Management:

Indications: Persistent/recurrent tubo-ovarian abscess, pyosalpinx, or pyometra despite full ATT, or persistent menorrhagia/pelvic pain in older women.

Precaution: Must give at least 6 weeks of full-dose ATT preoperatively and continue postoperatively to prevent miliary dissemination and bowel/bladder fistula.

Procedure: TAH + BSO in women who have completed their family. (Tuboplasty is contraindicated in tubercular tubes due to poor results and 40% risk of ectopic pregnancy; for infertility, IVF-ET is offered once the endometrium is disease-free after ATT).

subject: gynecology
title: 12.1 Postmenopausal Bleeding, Endometrial Hyperplasia & Endometrial Carcinoma
text:
CHAPTER 12: Uterine (Endometrial) Cancer & Postmenopausal Bleeding

(Covers: SE 1 [KU24], 2–4 [RGU,TU]; SA 1 [KU24,22,15], 2 [KU22], 3 [KU22], 4 [KU19], 5 [KU18], 7, 8 [RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1, 2 [KU23])

A. Postmenopausal Bleeding (PMB) ([KU24,18,RGU])

Definition: Any vaginal bleeding occurring after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhoea in a woman of menopausal age (or continued menstruation beyond 55 years of age). Dictum: “Every case of postmenopausal bleeding is considered due to genital tract malignancy (10–30% incidence) unless proved otherwise.”

Causes of Postmenopausal Bleeding:

Atrophic (Senile) Endometritis / Vaginitis (Commonest Benign Cause — 50–60%).

Exogenous Estrogen (HRT) or Tamoxifen therapy (15–20%).

Endometrial or Cervical Polyps (10%).

Endometrial Hyperplasia (5–10%).

Genital Tract Malignancies (10–30%): Endometrial carcinoma, Carcinoma cervix (equally or more common in India), Uterine sarcoma, Estrogen-producing ovarian tumor (Granulosa/Theca cell tumor), Carcinoma vagina/vulva, or Fallopian tube carcinoma.

Local / Non-Gynecological Causes: Decubitus ulcer on a prolapsed uterus, forgotten ring pessary/IUCD, Urethral caruncle, cystitis/bladder carcinoma (hematuria), or hemorrhoids/rectal carcinoma.

Stepwise Evaluation of a Woman with Postmenopausal Bleeding (e.g., 79-year-old [KU24] or 55-year-old [RGU]):

History & Examination: Confirm bleeding is vaginal (not urethral/rectal); check for Corpus Cancer Syndrome (obesity, hypertension, diabetes), tamoxifen/HRT use; speculum exam to inspect vulva, urethra (caruncle), vagina (atrophy), and cervix (growth/polyp) + Pap smear; bimanual exam for uterine size (enlarged/soft in pyometra or endometrial cancer) and adnexal mass.

Transvaginal Ultrasonography (TVS — First-Line Triage): Measure double-layer Endometrial Thickness (ET).

If ET  4 mm (thin, homogeneous): Negative predictive value for cancer is >99% (indicates atrophic endometrium).

If ET > 4 mm, heterogeneous, polypoid, or intrauterine fluid (pyometra) is present  histological sampling is mandatory.

Endometrial Histological Diagnosis (Gold Standard [KU23]):

OPD Endometrial Biopsy (Pipelle sampler / Sharman’s curette), OR

Hysteroscopy and Directed Biopsy, OR

Fractional Curettage under anesthesia (ordered steps: 1. Endocervical curettage [ECC]  2. Uterine sound  3. Dilatation of internal os  4. Curettage of fundus and walls  5. Polyp forceps exploration; specimens sent in separate labeled bottles). (If pyometra is drained on dilatation, withhold curettage for 1–2 weeks under antibiotic cover to prevent uterine perforation).

B. Classification of Endometrial Hyperplasia ([KU22,23])

Caused by prolonged unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium:

[[TABLE:gynecology-tbl-005]]

C. Endometrial Carcinoma

Etiology & Risk Factors ([KU19,TU]): Driven by chronic unopposed estrogen exposure:

Corpus Cancer Syndrome ([KU24,22,15]): The classic triad of Obesity, Hypertension, and Diabetes Mellitus associated with endometrial adenocarcinoma.

Age: 75% are postmenopausal (median age 60 years).

Nulliparity / Infertility (30%) and Early Menarche / Late Menopause (>52 years).

Chronic Anovulation (PCOS) and Functioning Estrogen-Secreting Ovarian Tumors (Granulosa/Thecoma).

Unopposed Estrogen Replacement Therapy (ERT) and Tamoxifen therapy for breast cancer.

Atypical Endometrial Hyperplasia (precursor lesion).

Genetic / Familial: Lynch II Syndrome (HNPCC — Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer) carries a 40–60% lifetime risk of endometrial cancer (and 12% risk of ovarian cancer).

Pathology:

Type I (Estrogen-dependent, 80%): Endometrioid Adenocarcinoma (or adenoacanthoma / adenosquamous); arises in hyperplastic endometrium in younger/obese women; well-differentiated (Grades G1 [<5% solid], G2 [6–50% solid], G3 [>50% solid]); good prognosis.

Type II (Non-estrogen dependent, 10–20%): Uterine Papillary Serous Carcinoma and Clear Cell Carcinoma; arises in atrophic endometrium of older thin women; aggressive, early extrauterine/lymphatic spread, poor prognosis.

FIGO Surgical Staging of Endometrial Carcinoma (2009):

Stage I: Tumor confined to the corpus uteri (Endocervical glandular involvement only is Stage I):

Stage IA: No or less than half (<50%) myometrial invasion.

Stage IB: Invasion equal to or more than half (≥50%) of the myometrium.

Stage II: Tumor invades cervical stroma, but does not extend beyond the uterus.

Stage III: Local and/or regional spread of the tumor:

Stage IIIA: Tumor invades the serosa of the corpus uteri and/or adnexae.

Stage IIIB: Vaginal and/or parametrial involvement.

Stage IIIC: Metastases to pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes:

IIIC1: Positive pelvic lymph nodes.

IIIC2: Positive para-aortic lymph nodes (with or without positive pelvic nodes).

Stage IV: Tumor invades bladder and/or bowel mucosa, and/or distant metastases:

Stage IVA: Tumor invasion of bladder and/or bowel mucosa.

Stage IVB: Distant metastases (lungs, liver, bone), including intra-abdominal metastases and/or inguinal lymph nodes. (Note: Positive peritoneal cytology is reported separately without changing the stage; Histologic Grade G1, G2, or G3 is added to each stage).

Management of Endometrial Carcinoma:

Preoperative Workup: CBC, LFT, RFT, Blood sugar, Chest X-ray, ECG, TVS, and Contrast MRI Pelvis/Abdomen (best imaging to assess depth of myometrial invasion, cervical stromal extension, and lymph nodes).

Stage I Disease — Primary Surgical Staging & Treatment (Mainstay):

Exploratory laparotomy (vertical midline incision) or Laparoscopic staging  collect peritoneal washings for cytology  systematic exploration of abdomen/diaphragm/omentum/nodes  Extrafascial Total Abdominal Hysterectomy with Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy (TAH + BSO).

Uterus is cut open in the OT; Pelvic and Para-aortic Lymphadenectomy (sampling) is performed if high-risk features are present: Myometrial invasion >50% (Stage IB), Tumor size >2 cm, Grade 3 or Type II (serous/clear cell) histology, or cervical extension.

Postoperative Adjuvant Radiotherapy:

Stage IA (G1, G2): Observation only (no radiation).

Stage IA (G3) or Stage IB (G1, G2): Vaginal Vault Brachytherapy (5000–6000 cGy) to prevent vault recurrence.

Stage IB (G3) or High-risk Stage I: External Beam Pelvic Radiotherapy (EBRT 4500–5000 cGy) + Vaginal Cuff Boost.

Stage II Disease (Cervical Stromal Invasion):

Radical Hysterectomy (Wertheim’s) + BSO + Bilateral Pelvic and Para-aortic Lymphadenectomy ( adjuvant radiotherapy), OR Preoperative external + intracavitary radiation followed 6 weeks later by TAH + BSO.

Stage III, Stage IV & Recurrent Disease:

Maximal Cytoreductive (Debulking) Surgery followed by Adjuvant Combination Chemotherapy (Carboplatin + Paclitaxel or Doxorubicin + Cisplatin [AP]) and Extended-Field Pelvic/Para-aortic Radiation.

Hormonal Therapy: High-dose Progestogens (Medroxyprogesterone acetate 150–200 mg/day PO or Megestrol acetate 160 mg/day) and Tamoxifen (10–20 mg BID) are effective in well-differentiated, estrogen/progesterone receptor-positive recurrent or metastatic tumors.

title: Chapter 12: One-Word Answers
text:
Gold standard of diagnosis of endometrial carcinoma [KU23]: Histopathological examination of endometrial tissue obtained by Fractional Curettage or Hysteroscopy and Directed Biopsy.

What is the risk of developing malignancy in complex endometrial hyperplasia [KU23]: 3% in complex hyperplasia without atypia, and 29% in complex hyperplasia with atypia.

subject: gynecology
title: 13.1 Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CIN) & Cervical Cancer Screening
text:
CHAPTER 13: Premalignant & Malignant Lesions of the Cervix

(Covers: SE 3 [TU]; SA 2 [KU24], 3 [KU22], 4 [KU24,21,18], 5 [KU17], 6 [KU16,15], 7, 10–19, 22 [RGU,TU]; Ch. 9 SA 1 [KU25], 5 [KU19,18]; One-word answers 1, 3, 4, 6 [KU])

A. Transformation Zone (TZ), HPV & Pathogenesis of CIN

Squamocolumnar Junction (SCJ) & Transformation Zone ([Draw and label] — Fig. 22.3):

Original SCJ: The embryonic junction where the stratified squamous epithelium of the ectocervix meets the tall secretory columnar epithelium of the endocervix.

During puberty and first pregnancy, high estrogen levels cause the cervix to swell and evert, exposing the endocervical columnar epithelium to the acidic vaginal pH. This acid pH triggers physiological squamous metaplasia (by metaplasia of subcolumnar reserve cells and ingrowth of ectocervical squamous epithelium) to form a new Physiologically Active SCJ closer to the external os.

Transformation Zone (TZ): The dynamic area of metaplastic squamous epithelium lying between the Original SCJ (outside) and the New Active SCJ (inside). Immature metaplastic cells in the TZ are highly vulnerable to oncogenic Human Papillomavirus (HPV)—hence >95% of CIN and cervical cancers originate in the Transformation Zone.

Role of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) ([KU16,15]):

99.7% of CIN and invasive cervical cancers are associated with sexually transmitted High-Risk Oncogenic HPV types: HPV-16 (50–60%), HPV-18 (15–20%), 31, 33, 35, 45, 52, and 58. (Low-risk types HPV-6 and 11 cause benign genital warts/condyloma acuminata and low-grade lesions).

Oncogenic Mechanism: High-risk HPV DNA integrates into the host basal cell genome and overexpresses viral oncoproteins E6 (which binds and degrades host tumor-suppressor protein p53, preventing apoptosis) and E7 (which binds and inactivates Retinoblastoma [Rb] protein, causing unchecked cell-cycle progression and genomic instability).

Pathognomonic Cytopathic Effect: Koilocytosis (large vacuolated squamous cells with a sharp perinuclear halo and enlarged, irregular, hyperchromatic, often binucleate “raisinoid” nuclei).

Grading & Correlation of Dysplasia, CIN (WHO) & Bethesda System:

CIN I (Mild Dysplasia): Undifferentiated atypical cells with loss of polarity/stratification confined to the lower one-third of the epithelial thickness (Bethesda: LSIL [Low-grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion] — also includes HPV koilocytotic changes; 60% regress spontaneously, only 1% progress to invasion).

CIN II (Moderate Dysplasia): Atypical cells occupy the lower one-half to two-thirds of the epithelium (Bethesda: HSIL; 5% progress to invasion).

CIN III (Severe Dysplasia & Carcinoma-in-Situ [CIS]): Atypical cells with frequent abnormal mitoses occupy more than two-thirds to the full thickness of the epithelium, with an intact basement membrane and no stromal invasion (Bethesda: HSIL; >20% progress to invasive carcinoma over 10–15 years).

B. Screening for Cervical Cancer (Pap Smear, LBC, HPV-DNA, VIA/VILI, Colposcopy)

Exfoliative Cytology — Papanicolaou (Pap) Smear ([KU25,19,18]):

Who & When to Screen (ACOG / FOGSI Guidelines): Screening starts at 21 years of age (regardless of age of sexual debut) up to 65–70 years (stopped at 65–70 if 3 consecutive smears are negative in the past 10 years):

Ages 21–29 years: Conventional Pap smear or Liquid-Based Cytology (LBC) every 3 years.

Ages 30–65 years: Co-testing (Pap smear + High-Risk HPV DNA test) every 5 years (preferred), OR Cytology alone every 3 years.

Prerequisites & Technique of Taking a Pap Smear ([KU25]):

Prerequisites: Patient should not be menstruating; avoid sexual intercourse, vaginal douching, tampons, or vaginal creams/pessaries for 48 hours prior. Perform speculum examination BEFORE bimanual examination without any lubricant (lubricant distorts cells).

Procedure (360° sampling of the entire Transformation Zone): Expose the cervix using a Cusco’s bivalve speculum.

Ectocervical Scrape: Insert the longer bifid projection of a wooden/plastic Ayre’s spatula into the external os and rotate it firmly through 360° to scrape the entire squamocolumnar junction 

Endocervical Sampling: Insert an endocervical cytobrush into the endocervical canal and rotate it .

Slide Preparation & Fixation: Immediately spread both samples thinly and uniformly onto a labeled glass slide and fix immediately (within <5–10 seconds, before air-drying) in 95% ethyl alcohol (or spray fixative) for 30 minutes, then stain by Papanicolaou stain in the lab.

Liquid-Based Cytology (LBC): Plastic broom-like brush is rinsed directly into a vial of liquid preservative medium  centrifuged to form a uniform monolayer smear (eliminates blood/mucus/debris, reduces unsatisfactory smears, and allows reflex HPV-DNA testing from the same vial).

HPV-DNA Testing: Detects high-risk oncogenic HPV types (16, 18, etc.) by Hybrid Capture 2 (HC2) or PCR. Used for: (i) Primary co-testing with cytology in women ≥30 years, and (ii) Triage of ASC-US cytology results.

Visual Inspection Methods (Low-Cost “Single-Visit Screen-and-Treat” for Low-Resource Settings in India):

VIA (Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid): Swabbing the cervix with 3–5% freshly prepared acetic acid and inspecting with the naked eye after 1 minute. Dysplastic/CIN epithelium turns dense, well-defined opaque Acetowhite abutting the SCJ (due to reversible coagulation of high nuclear proteins in dysplastic cells).

VILI (Visual Inspection with Lugol’s Iodine / Schiller’s Test): Applying Lugol’s iodine (5%) (or Schiller’s iodine 0.3%). Normal mature glycogen-rich squamous cells stain mahogany dark brown (iodine-positive), whereas glycogen-depleted dysplastic/CIN/malignant cells remain mustard-yellow / unstained (Schiller’s positive / iodine-negative).

Colposcopy & Directed Biopsy:

Stereoscopic binocular examination of the illuminated cervix under 6x to 40x magnification after applying normal saline, green filter (to study capillaries), 3–5% acetic acid, and Lugol’s iodine.

Indications: Abnormal Pap smear (ASC-H, LSIL, HSIL, AGC, or HPV-positive ASC-US), clinically suspicious cervix, or unexplained postcoital bleeding even with a negative smear.

Abnormal Colposcopic Findings (Reid’s / Swede Index): (1) Acetowhite epithelium, (2) Punctation (dilated capillaries seen end-on as red dots), (3) Mosaicism (capillaries forming a tile-like basket pattern around dysplastic blocks), (4) Leukoplakia (hyperkeratosis), and (5) Atypical corkscrew/comma-shaped blood vessels (hallmark of early invasive cancer). Punch biopsies are taken from the worst-affected areas along with Endocervical Curettage (ECC).

C. Management of CIN

CIN I (LSIL): 60% regress spontaneously within 1–2 years. Managed by observation and repeat cytology at 6 and 12 months (or HPV DNA test at 12 months). Treat only if it persists >2 years.

CIN II & CIN III / CIS (HSIL): Require active treatment to prevent progression to invasive cancer:

A. Local Excisional Methods (Preferred as they provide a tissue specimen to rule out occult microinvasion):

LLETZ (Large Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone) / LEEP (Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure) — Treatment of Choice for CIN II & III: Under local anesthesia, a thin stainless-steel wire loop using blended low-voltage diathermy current excises the entire TZ to a depth of 8–10 mm in a single pass.

Diagnostic / Therapeutic Cervical Conization (Cold-Knife Cone or Laser Cone): Mandatory when: (i) Colposcopy is unsatisfactory (upper limit of lesion or SCJ recedes into the endocervical canal and is not fully seen), (ii) ECC is positive for CIN II/III, (iii) Microinvasion is suspected, (iv) Cytology-colposcopy-biopsy discrepancy exists, or (v) Adenocarcinoma-in-situ (AIS / CGIN) is present.

B. Local Ablative Methods (Used ONLY when: 1. Entire lesion and TZ are completely visualized, 2. ECC is negative, and 3. Invasive cancer is excluded):

Cryotherapy: Double-freeze technique (freeze 3 min – thaw 5 min – freeze 3 min) using  or  probe at –60°C to –90°C (crystallizes intracellular water; depth 5 mm).

Cold Coagulation (100–120°C), Electrodiathermy, or  Laser Vaporization (depth 7 mm).

C. Hysterectomy: Reserved for women >40 years with completed family who have persistent/recurrent CIN III, positive cone margins, associated benign uterine pathology (fibroid/prolapse), or poor compliance with follow-up.

subject: gynecology
title: 13.2 Invasive Carcinoma of the Cervix
text:
(Covers: Essays 1 [KU25], 2 [KU24], 3 [KU24,23], 4 [KU20]; SE 1 [KU15], 2, 4 [RGU]; SA 1 [KU25], 8, 9, 21 [RGU,TU]; One-word answers 2, 5, 7, 8 [KU])

A. Epidemiology, Risk Factors & Pathology

Incidence: Most common gynecological malignancy in Indian women (accounting for ~80% of female genital cancers in developing countries). Mean age: 45–55 years.

Risk Factors ([KU25,24,23]):

Persistent infection with High-Risk Oncogenic HPV (Types 16, 18, 31, 33, 45) — primary necessary cause.

Early age at first sexual intercourse (<16–18 years) and early age at first pregnancy.

Multiple sexual partners or a high-risk male partner (promiscuous male, or one whose previous wife had cervical cancer).

Multiparity (too many and too frequent births with cervical trauma).

Low socioeconomic status and poor genital hygiene.

Cigarette smoking (nicotine/cotinine concentrates in cervical mucus and damages local Langerhans cell immunity).

Immunosuppression (HIV / AIDS — an AIDS-defining illness) and history of other STIs (Chlamydia, HSV-2).

Long-term (>5 years) Combined Oral Contraceptive pill use and lack of regular Pap smear screening.

Pathology:

Site: Ectocervix / Transformation Zone (80%) and Endocervical canal (20% — expands the cervix into a barrel-shaped cervix).

Gross Types: (1) Exophytic (cauliflower-like friable fungating mass filling the upper vagina), (2) Ulcerative (excavating necrotic ulcer with raised indurated margins), and (3) Infiltrative (hard, barrel-shaped endocervical growth).

Histological Types:

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (85–90% — Commonest): Subdivided into large-cell keratinizing (with keratin pearls), large-cell non-keratinizing, and small-cell type (poorest prognosis).

Adenocarcinoma (10–15%): Endocervical mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, adenosquamous, or adenoma malignum (minimal deviation adenocarcinoma). (HPV-18 is strongly linked to adenocarcinoma).

Rare: Neuroendocrine small-cell carcinoma, sarcoma, lymphoma.

Modes of Spread:

Direct Continuity & Contiguity (Most Common): Spreads downward to the vagina, upward to the uterine body, laterally into the parametrium, cardinal ligaments, and lateral pelvic wall (encasing and compressing the ureters  hydroureteronephrosis and uremia), anteriorly to the urinary bladder base ( vesicovaginal fistula), and posteriorly along uterosacral ligaments to the rectum ( rectovaginal fistula).

Lymphatic Spread:

Primary Nodes: Parametrial, Obturator (commonest sentinel node), Internal iliac, External iliac, and Sacral nodes (involved in <1% in IA1, 5% in IA2, 16% in Stage IB, 30% in Stage II, 45% in Stage III, and 55% in Stage IV).

Secondary Nodes: Common iliac, Para-aortic, and Inguinal nodes.

Hematogenous Spread (Late): Lungs (commonest distant site), liver, bone, and brain.

(Ovarian metastasis is very rare: 0.5% in squamous cell carcinoma vs. 1.7–5% in adenocarcinoma — hence healthy ovaries can be conserved in young women with early squamous carcinoma).

B. Clinical Features, Differential Diagnosis & Diagnosis

Symptoms:

Early Stage: Often asymptomatic; classic early symptom is postcoital bleeding (contact bleeding), intermenstrual spotting, postmenopausal bleeding, or blood-stained/watery offensive vaginal discharge.

Advanced Stage: Continuous foul-smelling serosanguinous discharge, brisk vaginal hemorrhage, deep-seated pelvic pain / unilateral sciatic leg pain (sacral nerve plexus invasion), unilateral leg edema (lymphatic/venous obstruction), hematuria/dysuria or true urinary incontinence (VVF), rectal bleeding/tenesmus or RVF, flank pain/oliguria (uremia), anemia, and cachexia.

Signs:

Speculum Exam (Must precede digital exam): Reveals a red granular lesion, indurated ulcer, or friable exophytic growth that bleeds briskly on touch/friction.

Bimanual & Rectovaginal Examination (Preferably under anesthesia): Growth feels hard, indurated, and friable. Rectal examination is mandatory to assess nodular malignant induration of the parametrium and uterosacral ligaments and whether the induration reaches the lateral pelvic wall (no cancer-free space = Stage IIIB).

Differential Diagnosis of Ulcerative/Fungating Cervical Growth ([KU25,15]):

Cervical Ectopy (Erosion) / Ectropion (soft, velvety, does not bleed on gentle touch).

Cervical Tuberculosis (ulcer with undermined edges or hypertrophic growth; confirmed by biopsy showing caseating granuloma).

Syphilitic Primary Chancre / Granuloma inguinale / Herpes ulcer.

Infected / Ulcerated Fibroid Polyp or Mucous Polyp.

Incomplete Septic Abortion or Cervical Pregnancy.

Secondary Metastatic Carcinoma (from endometrium or choriocarcinoma).

Confirmation of Diagnosis & Staging Workup:

Punch / Wedge Biopsy from the edge of the growth (or Cone biopsy in preclinical microinvasive disease) is mandatory for histological confirmation.

FIGO Permitted Staging Procedures: Clinical examination under anesthesia, Colposcopy, endocervical curettage, Hysteroscopy, Cystoscopy (to check bladder mucosal invasion), Proctosigmoidoscopy, Chest X-ray, Intravenous Urography (IVU) / Renal USG (to detect hydronephrosis or non-functioning kidney), and Skeletal X-ray. (In modern practice and FIGO 2018, Contrast MRI Pelvis [best for tumor size & parametrial invasion] and CT / PET-CT [for pelvic & para-aortic lymph nodes] are routinely used).

C. FIGO Staging of Carcinoma Cervix (2009 & 2018 Update) ([KU25,24,23])

[[TABLE:gynecology-tbl-006]]

D. Management of Carcinoma Cervix (Stage-by-Stage) & Preventive Strategies

Management of Stage I Disease ([KU25,24,23]):

Stage IA1 (Microinvasive Carcinoma — Depth ≤3 mm, No Lymphovascular Space Invasion [LVSI]; Lymph node risk <0.6%):

Young woman desiring fertility: Therapeutic Cold-Knife Conization (provided surgical cone margins are negative by 3–10 mm and regular follow-up is ensured) OR Simple Trachelectomy.

Family completed: Type I Extrafascial Simple Hysterectomy (abdominal or vaginal; no lymphadenectomy required).

Stage IA1 with LVSI OR Stage IA2 (Depth 3–5 mm; Pelvic node risk 5–10%):

Young woman desiring fertility: Radical Vaginal / Abdominal Trachelectomy (Dargent’s operation — LARVT) withLaparoscopic Pelvic Lymphadenectomy (resects cervix, upper 2 cm vagina, and medial parametrium, preserving the uterine corpus by suturing it to the vaginal vault with a permanent isthmic cerclage).

Family completed: Type II Modified Radical Hysterectomy with Bilateral Pelvic Lymphadenectomy (or Intracavitary Brachytherapy if medically unfit).

Stage IB1 and Early Stage IIA1 (Lesion ≤4 cm):

Primary Radical Surgery and Primary Radiotherapy yield identical 5-year survival rates (85–90%), but Surgery is preferred in young/fit patients because: (i) ovaries can be preserved (and transposed out of the pelvis), (ii) vagina remains pliable and functional for coitus (avoids radiation vaginal stenosis), and (iii) exact surgicopathological nodal staging is obtained.

Surgical Procedure of Choice: Type III Radical Hysterectomy (Wertheim-Meigs Operation) with Bilateral Pelvic Lymphadenectomy and Para-aortic Node Sampling 

Structures removed: Uterus, cervix, upper one-third (2–3 cm) of the vagina, entire width of the parametrium (Mackenrodt’s and uterosacral ligaments) after dissecting the ureters out of the ureteric tunnel, ligation of the uterine artery at its origin from the internal iliac artery, and bilateral pelvic lymph nodes (parametrial, obturator, internal, external, and common iliac nodes).

Postoperative Adjuvant Chemoradiation: Given if high-risk features are found on histopathology (positive pelvic lymph nodes, positive surgical margins, or parametrial invasion).

Stage IB2 and IIA2 (Bulky “Barrel-shaped” Tumor >4 cm):

Treated by: (i) Primary Cisplatin-based Concurrent Chemoradiation (preferred), OR (ii) Type III Radical Hysterectomy + Pelvic/Para-aortic Lymphadenectomy, OR (iii) Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy (3 cycles of Cisplatin + Paclitaxel) to shrink the tumor followed by Radical Hysterectomy.

Management of Locally Advanced Carcinoma Cervix (Stage IIB, IIIA, IIIB, and IVA) ([KU24,RGU]):

Surgery is CONTRAINDICATED (except palliative colostomy/nephrostomy or rarely Pelvic Exenteration [Brunschwig’s operation] for central Stage IVA or central pelvic recurrence without side-wall fixation).

Treatment of Choice: Primary Concurrent Chemoradiation (CCRT):

External Beam Pelvic Radiotherapy (EBRT / Teletherapy): 4500 to 5000 cGy (45–50 Gy) in 25 fractions over 5 weeks using a Linear Accelerator (4–8 MeV) to shrink the primary tumor, sterilize the parametrium/pelvic lymph nodes, and correct tumor hypoxia/sepsis.

Concurrent Weekly Radiosensitizing Chemotherapy: Inj. Cisplatin  IV weekly during EBRT (sensitizes hypoxic tumor cells to radiation and reduces mortality by 30–50%).

Intracavitary Brachytherapy (Manchester, Paris, or Stockholm Technique using Remote Afterloading , , or  via intrauterine tandem and vaginal colpostats/ovoids): Delivers an additional 3000–4000 cGy to Point A (2 cm superior and 2 cm lateral to external os — where the uterine artery crosses the ureter) so that Point A receives a total tumoricidal dose of 7500–8500 cGy and Point B (2 cm superior and 5 cm lateral to external os — obturator node) receives 5500–6000 cGy 

Stage IVB (Distant Metastasis): Palliative Systemic Chemotherapy (Cisplatin + Paclitaxel / Topotecan + Bevacizumab) + Palliative Radiotherapy (to control pelvic bleeding or bone pain).

Complications & Causes of Death in Carcinoma Cervix ([KU25,16,TU]):

Complications of Disease: Severe vaginal hemorrhage, pyometra, vesicovaginal fistula (VVF), rectovaginal fistula (RVF), bilateral ureteric obstruction  hydronephrosis/pyelonephritis.

Causes of Death: (1) Uremia / Renal Failure (Commonest cause of death — 50%) due to bilateral ureteric obstruction in the parametrium, (2) Hemorrhage, (3) Sepsis / Peritonitis, (4) Cachexia, and (5) Distant metastases (lungs, liver).

Preventive Strategies for Carcinoma Cervix ([KU24]):

Primary Prevention:

Prophylactic HPV Vaccination: Administered to adolescent girls aged 9–14 years (2 doses 6 months apart) or 15–26 years (3 doses: 0, 1–2, and 6 months IM in deltoid) prior to sexual debut. Available vaccines: Bivalent (Cervarix — HPV 16, 18), Quadrivalent (Gardasil / India’s indigenous Cervavac — HPV 6, 11, 16, 18), and Nonavalent (Gardasil-9). Prevents >90% of CIN II/III and cervical cancers.

Health education, delaying age of marriage/first coitus, monogamy, condom use, penile hygiene/circumcision, and smoking cessation.

Secondary Prevention: Regular Cervical Screening (Pap smear / LBC, HPV-DNA testing, or VIA/VILI) and effective ablation/excision (LLETZ/Cryotherapy) of pre-invasive CIN lesions.

subject: gynecology
title: 14.1 Ovarian Malignancy: Clinical Features, Diagnosis, Staging & Management
text:
CHAPTER 14: Malignant Diseases of the Ovary and Fallopian Tube

(Covers: Essay 1 [KU17]; SE 1 [KU23], 2–4 [RGU,TU]; SA 1–6 [KU21–15], 8–15 [RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1–6 [KU])

A. Classification of Ovarian Tumors

(For full WHO Histogenic Classification, refer to Chapter 8, Section 8.1A and Table 20.1 on Book Page 291 / PDF Page 309).

Epithelial Ovarian Cancers (85–90% of all primary ovarian malignancies): Serous cystadenocarcinoma (commonest, 40–50%; bilateral in 50%), Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma (10%), Endometrioid carcinoma (15% — associated with endometrial cancer in 20% and endometriosis in 10%), Clear cell carcinoma (hobnail cells, worst prognosis), Brenner, and Undifferentiated carcinoma.

B. Clinical Features & Differentiation Between Benign and Malignant Ovarian Tumors

Symptoms (“Silent Killer”): Early stages are notoriously asymptomatic or present with vague GI complaints (abdominal bloating, dyspepsia, flatulence, early satiety, pelvic heaviness). Advanced stages present with rapidly enlarging abdominal swelling (tumor + ascites), dull abdominal pain, anorexia, marked weight loss (cachexia), respiratory distress (due to massive ascites or right-sided pleural effusion), and bilateral leg/vulval edema. Menstrual abnormalities are absent except in hormone-producing sex-cord stromal tumors.

Differentiation Between Benign and Malignant Ovarian Tumors ([KU21,RGU] — Table 20.2):

[[TABLE:gynecology-tbl-007]]

Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI): , where  = USG score (0, 1, or 3 points based on: multilocularity, solid areas, bilaterality, ascites, metastasis) and  = Menopausal status (1 for premenopausal, 3 for postmenopausal). RMI > 250 indicates a 75% risk of malignancy and mandates referral to a gynecologic oncology center for staging laparotomy.

C. Tumor Markers in Ovarian Malignancies ([KU20,TU])

CA-125 (Cancer Antigen 125): High-molecular-weight glycoprotein expressed by coelomic epithelium derivatives. Normal level is < 35 U/mL. Elevated (>65 U/mL) in 80–85% of non-mucinous Epithelial Ovarian Cancers (especially Serous cystadenocarcinoma). (False-positive benign elevations in premenopausal women: endometriosis, adenomyosis, PID, fibroids, pregnancy, peritonitis). Uses: Triage of pelvic mass (RMI), monitoring response to chemotherapy, and early detection of recurrence. (For Mucinous ovarian cancer, CA 19-9 and CEA are used; HE4 is more specific than CA-125).

Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP): Specific marker for Endodermal Sinus (Yolk Sac) Tumor and embryonal/immature teratoma.

Beta-hCG (-hCG): Specific marker for Ovarian Choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma, and 5–10% of Dysgerminomas.

Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) & Placental Alkaline Phosphatase (PLAP): Markers for Dysgerminoma.

Inhibin (A & B) and Estradiol (): Markers for Granulosa Cell Tumor [KU24].

D. FIGO Surgical Staging of Ovarian Carcinoma

Stage I: Growth limited to the ovaries:

IA: Limited to one ovary; capsule intact; no tumor on external surface; negative washings.

IB: Limited to both ovaries; capsules intact; no tumor on external surfaces; negative washings.

IC: Tumor limited to one or both ovaries, with any of: surgical spill (IC1), capsule ruptured before surgery or tumor on ovarian surface (IC2), or malignant cells in ascites or peritoneal washings (IC3).

Stage II: Growth involving one or both ovaries with pelvic extension (below the pelvic brim):

IIA: Extension and/or implants on the uterus and/or fallopian tubes.

IIB: Extension to other pelvic intraperitoneal tissues (bladder serosa, rectosigmoid, pelvic peritoneum).

Stage III: Tumor involving one or both ovaries with cytologically or histologically confirmed spread to the peritoneum outside the pelvis and/or metastasis to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes:

IIIA: Positive retroperitoneal (pelvic/para-aortic) lymph nodes only (IIIA1) OR microscopic extrapelvic peritoneal metastasis above the pelvic brim (IIIA2).

IIIB: Macroscopic extrapelvic peritoneal metastasis  2 cm in greatest dimension ( positive retroperitoneal nodes; includes capsule of liver/spleen).

IIIC: Macroscopic extrapelvic peritoneal metastasis > 2 cm in greatest dimension ( positive retroperitoneal nodes; includes omental cake and superficial liver/spleen capsule metastasis).

Stage IV: Distant metastasis excluding peritoneal metastases:

IVA: Pleural effusion with positive malignant cytology.

IVB: Parenchymal liver or splenic metastasis, and metastases to extra-abdominal organs (lungs, brain, inguinal or supraclavicular lymph nodes).

E. Management of Epithelial Ovarian Cancer

Primary Surgery — Staging Laparotomy & Primary Cytoreductive (Debulking) Surgery (Cornerstone of Treatment):

Steps of Staging Laparotomy ([RGU]):

Liberal vertical midline incision (extending above the umbilicus) to deliver the tumor intact without rupture and allow upper abdominal access.

Aspiration of ascitic fluid for cytology (if no ascites, instill 100 mL normal saline into the pelvis, paracolic gutters, and subdiaphragmatic spaces for peritoneal washings).

Systematic visual and manual exploration in a clockwise manner: pelvis, contralateral ovary, small and large bowel mesentery, omentum, paracolic gutters, liver parenchyma, spleen, right and left hemidiaphragms (take diaphragm scrapings/biopsy), and pelvic & para-aortic lymph nodes.

Multiple peritoneal biopsies from suspicious areas (or random biopsies from POD, bladder peritoneum, and paracolic gutters in apparent Stage I).

Definitive Surgery:

In Elderly / Completed Family (e.g., 75-year-old [KU17] or 40-year-old [RGU]): Total Abdominal Hysterectomy + Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy (TAH + BSO) + Infracolic/Total Omentectomy + Pelvic and Para-aortic Lymph Node Sampling (+ Appendectomy in mucinous tumors).

Why Omentectomy is done ([KU17]): The omentum (“policeman of the abdomen”) is the commonest site of transcoelomic metastasis (70%); removing the omental cake eliminates a massive bulk of tumor and markedly reduces recurrent post-operative ascites and bowel obstruction.

In Advanced Disease (Stage III/IV): Optimal Cytoreductive (Debulking) Surgery aimed at resecting all macroscopic tumor so that residual tumor nodules are < 1 cm (ideally 0 mm / R0 microscopic), which may require bowel resection or splenectomy. Small residual volume (<1 cm) drastically improves chemosensitivity and survival.

In a Young Nulliparous Woman Wishing to Preserve Fertility ([KU17]): Fertility-Sparing Surgery (Unilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy + Comprehensive Surgical Staging: peritoneal washings, omental biopsy, node sampling) is permissible ONLY if: (1) Stage IA, Grade 1 (or Grade 2) or Borderline tumor, (2) Contralateral ovary and uterus are normal, and (3) Patient is compliant for close follow-up (CA-125 & TVS), followed by completion TAH + USO after childbearing.

Adjuvant Chemotherapy:

Not required only in Stage IA/IB, Grade 1 disease.

Required in all Stage IA/IB (Grade 2 or 3), Stage IC, and Stages II to IV:

Standard First-Line Regimen (CP): Paclitaxel ( IV over 3 hours) + Carboplatin (AUC 5–6 or  IV) given every 3 weeks for 6 cycles.

Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy (NACT) + Interval Debulking Surgery: In medically unfit Stage III/IV patients with massive ascites/pleural effusion or unresectable disease on CT, give 3 cycles of Carboplatin + Paclitaxel (after biopsy/ascitic cytology confirmation)  perform Interval Cytoreductive Surgery  give 3 more cycles of chemotherapy.

Prognostic Factors ([KU17]): (1) FIGO Stage at diagnosis (5-yr survival: Stage I: 80–90%, Stage II: 60–70%, Stage III: 20–40%, Stage IV: 5–10%), (2) Volume of residual tumor after primary debulking (<1 cm vs. >1 cm), (3) Histologic type & grade (endometrioid best; clear cell/mucinous/G3 worst), (4) Ascites & peritoneal cytology, (5) Ploidy status (diploid better than aneuploid), and (6) BRCA status (BRCA-mutated tumors respond better to platinum and PARP inhibitors like Olaparib).

subject: gynecology
title: 14.2 Germ Cell, Sex Cord-Stromal & Metastatic Ovarian Tumors (Short Notes)
text:
(Covers: Dysgerminoma [KU21,TU]; Granulosa cell tumor [KU15,TU]; Krukenberg tumor [RGU])

Dysgerminoma ([KU21,TU]):

Incidence & Origin: Most common malignant germ cell tumor (30–40%) of the ovary, arising from undifferentiated primordial germ cells (female counterpart of testicular seminoma). 75% occur in children and young women (<20–30 years); 20–30% coexist with pregnancy; 5% arise in dysgenetic gonads containing a Y chromosome (46,XY Swyer’s syndrome or 45,X/46,XY) via a gonadoblastoma.

Pathology: Usually unilateral (bilateral in 10–15% — highest bilaterality among malignant germ cell tumors). Solid, firm, rubbery, bosselated mass with a smooth capsule; cut section is fleshy, lobulated, homogeneous pink-to-tan (“brain-like”).

Microscopic Histology: Sheets or cords of large, uniform, round/polygonal cells (“monotonous pattern”) with abundant clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm and large central nuclei, separated by fibrous septa heavily infiltrated with T-lymphocytes and occasional granulomas 

Tumor Markers: Elevated Serum LDH and PLAP (and -hCG in 5% due to syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells).

Management: 75% present at Stage IA.

Young woman (Stage IA): Fertility-Sparing Surgery — Unilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy + Surgical Staging. (If karyotype shows a Y chromosome, bilateral gonadectomy is mandatory).

Beyond Stage IA or Recurrent Disease: Dysgerminoma is extremely chemosensitive and radiosensitive. Systemic Chemotherapy is the treatment of choice (as it preserves fertility, unlike radiotherapy which destroys the remaining ovary): 3–4 cycles of BEP Regimen (Bleomycin + Etoposide + Cisplatin). 5-year survival rate is >95% in Stage I and 75–85% in advanced stages.

Endodermal Sinus (Yolk Sac) Tumor ([SE 4, TU]):

Second most common malignant germ cell tumor (20%); occurs at median age 15–19 years; unilateral, rapidly growing, highly malignant solid-cystic tumor.

Pathognomonic Histology: Schiller-Duval Bodies (single central capillary blood vessel surrounded by a glomerular-like space lined by cuboidal tumor cells) and intracellular eosinophilic hyaline droplets containing Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP).

Marker: Serum AFP. Treatment: Unilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy + mandatory Adjuvant BEP Chemotherapy for all stages.

Granulosa Cell Tumor ([KU15,TU]):

Most common malignant sex cord-stromal (“functioning”) tumor (2% of all ovarian tumors); 95% unilateral; 90% adult type (postmenopausal/reproductive age), 5–10% juvenile type (prepubertal girls).

Hormone Secreted: Estrogen (and Inhibin, which serves as its specific tumor marker [KU24]).

Clinical Presentation by Age: (1) Prepubertal girls: Isosexual Precocious Pseudopuberty; (2) Reproductive age: Menorrhagia / Metropathia; (3) Postmenopausal women (50%): Postmenopausal bleeding; associated with Endometrial Hyperplasia in 50% and Endometrial Adenocarcinoma in 5–10%. Also prone to spontaneous rupture causing acute hemoperitoneum.

Pathology: Solid and cystic tumor; cut section is yellow or orange (due to lipid). Microscopic Histology: Small round/polygonal granulosa cells with pale, longitudinally grooved “Coffee-bean” nuclei arranged in microfollicular rosettes around a central eosinophilic cavity called Call-Exner Bodies (Pathognomonic) 

Management: In young women (Stage IA): Unilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy + Endometrial Curettage (to rule out endometrial cancer). In older/postmenopausal women: TAH + BSO. Advanced/recurrent cases receive BEP chemotherapy. Lifelong follow-up with serum Inhibin is required as late recurrence can occur 10–30 years later.

Krukenberg Tumor ([RGU]):

A secondary (metastatic), bilateral (80%), solid ovarian adenocarcinoma originating from a primary mucin-secreting carcinoma of the Gastrointestinal tract — Stomach (pylorus, 70% — commonest), Colon, Breast, or Gallbladder/Biliary tract, spreading primarily by retrograde lymphatics (via superior gastric and para-aortic nodes).

Gross Pathology: Bilateral, solid, reniform (kidney-shaped) masses that retain the contour of the ovary, with a smooth, bosselated, white/yellow waxy surface and NO adhesions (capsule remains intact) 

Microscopic Pathology: Cellular myxomatous ovarian stroma infiltrated by mucin-laden epithelial cells whose nuclei are pushed and flattened against one side of the cell membrane, giving the pathognomonic “Signet-ring” cell appearance.

Prognosis is poor (median survival <1 year).

Tumour marker for epithelial ovarian carcinoma [KU25,23] & Normal level [KU24]: CA-125 (and HE4); Normal level of CA-125 is < 35 U/mL.

Tumour marker for granulosa cell tumour of the ovary is [KU24]: Inhibin (Inhibin B / A) and Estradiol.

Call-Exner bodies are seen in which ovarian tumor [KU18]: Granulosa cell tumor.
