subject: gynecology
title: 15.1 Classification, Follow-up of Molar Pregnancy, Invasive Mole & Choriocarcinoma
text:
CHAPTER 15: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (GTD)

(Covers: SA 1 [KU25], 2 [KU22,15,RGU,TU], 3–5 [RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1, 2 [KU20,19]; also Ch. 14 SA 7, 13)

A. Classification of GTD & GTN

Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (GTD): Spectrum of proliferative abnormalities of placental trophoblast:

Benign Premalignant Molar Pregnancies: Complete Hydatidiform Mole (46,XX diploid androgenetic) and Partial Hydatidiform Mole (69,XXY triploid).

Malignant Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia (GTN):

Persistent / Non-metastatic GTN (confined to uterus; occurs in 15% after molar evacuation).

Invasive Mole (Chorioadenoma destruens): Hyperplastic trophoblasts retaining chorionic villous structures penetrate deep into the myometrium

;causes uterine perforation with massive hemoperitoneum or vaginal metastasis.

Choriocarcinoma: Highly malignant, necrotizing, hemorrhagic tumor composed of anaplastic sheets of cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts invading myometrium and blood vessels, with COMPLETE ABSENCE of chorionic villi. 

(Antecedent pregnancy: 50% follow Hydatidiform mole, 30% follow abortion/ectopic, and 20% follow normal term pregnancy. GTN after a non-molar pregnancy is always Choriocarcinoma or PSTT).

Placental Site Trophoblastic Tumor (PSTT) & Epithelioid Trophoblastic Tumor (ETT): Arise from intermediate trophoblast; secrete hPL (human placental lactogen) and low -hCG; chemoresistant  Hysterectomy is the treatment of choice.

Common Sites of Metastasis in GTN: Hematogenous spread to Lungs (80% — commonest, showing “Cannon-ball” or “Snow-storm” shadows on Chest X-ray), Vagina (30% — bluish-purple suburethral nodule on the lower anterior vaginal wall 

(never biopsy due to torrential bleeding!), Pelvis (20%), Liver (10%), and Brain (10% — CSF : Serum -hCG ratio > 1:60).

B. Follow-up of Hydatidiform (Vesicular) Mole After Evacuation ([KU25,22,15])

Meticulous surveillance is mandatory for all women after suction evacuation of a molar pregnancy because 15–20% develop persistent post-molar GTN (15% locally invasive, 4% metastatic):

Schedule of Follow-up Visits & Serial Quantitative Serum -hCG Monitoring:

Weekly serum -hCG estimation after evacuation until 3 consecutive weekly values are normal (<5 mIU/mL) (normally achieved within 7–9 weeks).

Thereafter, monthly serum -hCG for 6 months (in complete mole; 1 month in partial mole). (In patients treated with chemotherapy for GTN, follow up monthly for 1 year in low-risk and 2 years in high-risk disease).

At Each Visit Evaluate:

History: Irregular vaginal bleeding, persistent cough, hemoptysis, or headache.

Pelvic Examination: Check for uterine involution and regression of bilateral theca lutein cysts (regress within 2–3 months as hCG falls).

Investigations: Serial serum -hCG; Chest X-ray (at baseline, and repeated only if hCG plateaus or rises); Pelvic TVS with Doppler.

Contraceptive Advice During Follow-up:

Strict avoidance of pregnancy for at least 6 months after -hCG normalizes (for 1 year after GTN chemotherapy), because a new pregnancy produces hCG and masks trophoblastic relapse.

Methods of Choice: Barrier methods (Condoms) or Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (COCs) (safe once hCG is falling/normal). IUCDs are contraindicated until hCG is normal due to the risk of uterine perforation and bleeding.

FIGO Diagnostic Criteria for Post-Molar GTN (Indication to Start Chemotherapy):

Plateau of serum -hCG ( change) for 4 measurements over a period of 3 weeks or longer (Days 1, 7, 14, 21).

Rise of serum -hCG (>10%) for 3 consecutive weekly measurements over 2 weeks or more (Days 1, 7, 14).

Persistence of detectable serum -hCG beyond 6 months after molar evacuation.

Histological diagnosis of Choriocarcinoma or evidence of metastases.

C. FIGO Anatomic Staging & WHO Prognostic Scoring System for GTN ([RGU])

FIGO Anatomic Stages: Stage I: Confined to uterus; Stage II: Genital structures outside uterus (vagina, adnexa); Stage III: Lungs ( genital involvement); Stage IV: All other distant metastatic sites (brain, liver, GI tract, kidneys).

Modified WHO Prognostic Scoring System (Table on Book Page 364 / PDF Page 382):

Scores 0, 1, 2, or 4 are assigned to 8 parameters:

Age: <40 yrs (0) vs. ≥40 yrs (1).

Antecedent pregnancy: Mole (0), Abortion (1), Term (2).

Interval from index pregnancy to chemotherapy (months): <4 (0), 4–6 (1), 7–12 (2), ≥13 (4).

Pretreatment serum hCG (mIU/mL):  (0),  (1),  (2),  (4).

Largest tumor size (including uterus): <3 cm (0), 3–5 cm (1), ≥5 cm (2).

Site of metastases: Lung/Pelvis (0), Spleen/Kidney (1), GI tract (2), Brain/Liver (4).

Number of metastases: 0 (0), 1–4 (1), 5–8 (2), >8 (4).

Previous failed chemotherapy: None (0), Single drug (2), ≥2 drugs (4).

Risk Stratification & Treatment:

Low-Risk GTN (Total WHO Score  6; Stages I–III): 100% curable with Single-Agent Chemotherapy: Inj. Methotrexate (1–1.5 mg/kg IM on Days 1, 3, 5, 7) with Folinic Acid rescue (0.1–0.15 mg/kg IM on Days 2, 4, 6, 8) repeated every 14 days, OR Inj. Actinomycin-D ( IV daily  5 days). Continue for 2 consolidation courses after -hCG becomes normal.

High-Risk GTN (Total WHO Score  7; or Stage IV): Treated with Multi-Agent Combination Chemotherapy — EMA-CO Regimen: Day 1: Etoposide (), Methotrexate ( bolus +  12-hr infusion), Actinomycin-D (0.5 mg IV); Day 2: Etoposide, Actinomycin-D, + Folinic acid rescue; Day 8: Cyclophosphamide ( IV) + Oncovin / Vincristine ( IV). Repeat every 14 days, with 3 consolidation cycles after normal hCG (Cure rate: 70–85%; add whole-brain radiation 3000 cGy for brain metastasis).

subject: gynecology
title: Chapter 15: One-Word Answers
text:
Drug of choice in persistent trophoblastic disease (Low-risk GTN) [KU20]: Methotrexate (with folinic acid / leucovorin rescue).

Commonest tumor marker in choriocarcinoma [KU19]: Beta-human Chorionic Gonadotropin (-hCG).

subject: gynecology
title: 16.1 Supports of Uterus, Etiology, Classification (POP-Q), Clinical Features & Management of Prolapse
text:
CHAPTER 16: Pelvic Organ Prolapse (POP) & Displacements

(Covers: Essays 1 [KU25], 2 [KU24], 3 [KU24], 4 [KU18]; SE 1 [KU25,RGU], 2 [KU24], 3, 4 [RGU,TU]; SA 1–30 [KU,RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1–11 [KU])

A. Anatomical Supports of the Uterus ([Draw and label] — [KU24,23,22,19,18,17])

The uterus is normally maintained in a position of anteversion (angle between long axis of cervix and vagina = ) and anteflexion (angle between long axis of uterine body and cervix = ), with the external os at the level of the ischial spines ([Fig. 15.1]). Its supports are organized into a Three-Tier System and DeLancey’s Three Levels of Vaginal Support:

Three-Tier System of Uterine Support:

I. Upper Tier (Steadying / Positional Supports — Maintain Anteversion, NO role in preventing descent):

Endopelvic fascia covering the uterus.

Round ligaments (keep the fundus pulled anteriorly).

Broad ligaments with intervening parametrial cellular tissue (act as guy-ropes).

II. Middle Tier (Direct / Fibromuscular / Ligamentous Supports — Strongest & Cardinal Support):

Pericervical Ring: Fibromuscular collar encircling the supravaginal cervix into which the condensed endopelvic ligaments insert:

Mackenrodt’s Ligaments (Cardinal / Transverse Cervical Ligaments): Fan-shaped fibromuscular condensations of endopelvic fascia extending from the lateral pelvic wall (obturator fascia) to the supravaginal cervix and upper lateral vaginal wall (chief support preventing uterine descent).

Uterosacral Ligaments: Extend from the periosteum of S2, S3, S4 vertebrae to the posterolateral supravaginal cervix at the internal os; pull the cervix backwards and upwards, maintaining anteversion and suspending the uterus/vault over the levator plate.

Pubocervical Ligaments (Fascia / Bladder Pillars): Extend from the back of the pubic bodies to the anterolateral cervix, supporting the bladder base and anterior vaginal wall.

III. Inferior Tier (Indirect / Muscular Supports — Pelvic Floor):

Pelvic Floor Muscles (Levator Ani — Pubococcygeus, Pubovaginalis, Puborectalis) and the Levator Plate (horizontal shelf supporting the upper vagina, cervix, and rectum).

Urogenital Diaphragm (Perineal Membrane).

Perineal Body and Endopelvic fascial septa (Vesicovaginal and Rectovaginal septa).

DeLancey’s Biomechanical Levels of Uterovaginal Support (1992) ([KU18] — Table 1.1, Book Page 24):

Level I (Upper — Suspension): Uterosacral and Cardinal (Mackenrodt’s) ligament complex suspending the cervix and upper third of the vagina to the pelvic walls. (Failure causes Uterovaginal prolapse, Vault prolapse, and Enterocele).

Level II (Middle — Lateral Attachment): Pubocervical fascia (anteriorly) and Rectovaginal fascia (posteriorly) attached laterally to the Arcus Tendineus Fascia Pelvis (White Line) and levator ani fascia. (Failure causes Cystocele [central or paravaginal defect] and Rectocele).

Level III (Lower — Distal Fusion): Distal third of the vagina fused anteriorly with the urethra/urogenital diaphragm and posteriorly with the perineal body and levator ani. (Failure causes Urethrocele / Stress Urinary Incontinence and Relaxed Perineum / Deficient Perineal Body).

B. Etiology / Risk Factors of Pelvic Organ Prolapse ([KU24,23,19,18,15])

Predisposing Factors:

A. Acquired (Obstetric Trauma during Vaginal Delivery — Single Most Important Factor):

Overstretching and tearing of Mackenrodt’s and Uterosacral ligaments due to: (i) Premature bearing down before full cervical dilatation, (ii) Forceful traction with forceps/ventouse before full dilatation, (iii) Prolonged second stage of labor, (iv) Fundal pressure (Credé’s expression) to deliver the placenta, and (v) Precipitate labor.

Overstretching and breaks in the endopelvic fascia (vesicovaginal and rectovaginal septa).

Neuromuscular injury (Pudendal nerve denervation) and myopathy of the Levator Ani muscle + unrepaired or imperfectly repaired perineal body tears.

Subinvolution of supporting ligaments: Multiparity with repeated closely spaced pregnancies, malnutrition/asthenia, and early resumption of heavy physical work in the puerperium.

B. Congenital (Inborn Collagen/Connective Tissue Weakness): Responsible for Nulliparous (Congenital) Prolapse (often associated with occult spina bifida or Ehlers-Danlos/Marfan syndrome).

Aggravating Factors (Operate on already weakened supports):

Postmenopausal Estrogen Deficiency (atrophy of collagen and supporting musculofascial tissues).

Chronically Raised Intra-abdominal Pressure: Chronic cough (COPD/bronchitis), chronic constipation, obesity, heavy weight-lifting occupation, or large abdominal tumors/ascites.

Increased Weight of the Uterus (fibroid, myohyperplasia).

C. Clinical Types & Classifications of Pelvic Organ Prolapse ([KU25,24,22,21,18])

Anatomical / Compartment Classification:

Anterior Vaginal Wall Prolapse: Cystocele (laxity of upper two-thirds of anterior vaginal wall with herniation of bladder base) and Urethrocele (laxity of lower one-third with urethra; combined = Cystourethrocele).

Posterior Vaginal Wall Prolapse: Enterocele (herniation of the Pouch of Douglas containing omentum/small bowel through the upper one-third of the posterior vaginal wall), Rectocele (herniation of rectum through lax middle one-third of posterior vaginal wall/rectovaginal septum), and Relaxed Perineum (torn perineal body in lower one-third).

Middle Compartment (Uterine / Apical Prolapse): (i) Uterovaginal Prolapse (commonest: cystocele occurs first, pulling the cervix down and retroverting the uterus), (ii) Congenital / Nulliparous Prolapse (uterus herniates down with inverted upper vagina without cystocele), and (iii) Secondary Vault Prolapse (following abdominal or vaginal hysterectomy).

Traditional Clinical Degrees of Uterine Prolapse (Shaw’s Classification):

First Degree (): Uterus descends below its normal level (ischial spines), but the external os remains inside the vaginal introitus.

Second Degree (): The external os protrudes outside the vaginal introitus, while the uterine body still remains inside the vagina.

Third Degree ( / Procidentia / Complete Prolapse): The entire uterus (cervix and uterine body) descends to lie completely outside the vaginal introitus with complete eversion of the vaginal walls. (Confirmed clinically by the Thumb-Finger Palpation Test: the thumb placed anteriorly and fingers placed posteriorly above the prolapsed mass outside the introitus can be apposed directly to each other without feeling the uterine fundus between them

Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) System (ICS / AUGS / SGS — 1996) ([KU24,22,21,18]): 

Full Form: Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification.

Fixed Anatomic Reference Point ([KU21]): The Plane of the Hymenal Ring (defined as Zero [0] level). Positions above (proximal to) the hymen are recorded in negative (–) cm, and positions below (distal to) the hymen are recorded in positive (+) cm during maximal Valsalva straining.

Nine Specific Measurements (Recorded in a 3×3 Tic-Tac-Toe Grid):

Anterior wall (2 points):  (3 cm proximal to external urethral meatus; range –3 to +3 cm) and  (most dependent point of upper anterior wall).

Posterior wall (2 points):  (3 cm proximal to posterior hymen; range –3 to +3 cm) and  (most dependent point of upper posterior wall).

Apical points (2 points):  (most distal edge of cervix or post-hysterectomy vaginal cuff) and  (posterior vaginal fornix / attachment of uterosacral ligaments; omitted after hysterectomy; differentiates supravaginal cervical elongation from true uterine descent).

Three Fixed Lengths:  (Genital hiatus: urethral meatus to posterior hymen),  (Perineal body: posterior hymen to mid-anal opening), and  (Total vaginal length, measured at rest after reducing prolapse).

POP-Q Stages (0 to IV):

Stage 0: No prolapse ( are all at –3 cm;  and  are between  and  cm).

Stage I: Leading edge of prolapse is more than 1 cm above the hymenal ring (quantification value < –1 cm).

Stage II: Leading edge of prolapse extends from 1 cm above to 1 cm below the hymenal ring (value  –1 cm but  +1 cm).

Stage III: Leading edge of prolapse extends > 1 cm beyond the hymenal ring, but is less than  cm (no complete vaginal eversion).

Stage IV: Complete eversion of the total length of the lower genital tract (leading edge protrudes to  cm).

D. Morbid Changes, Clinical Features & Differential Diagnosis of Mass Per Vagina

Morbid Changes in Long-Standing Prolapse:

Vaginal Mucosa & Decubitus Ulcer ([KU24,23,19]): Exposed mucosa becomes dry, thickened, keratinized, and pigmented. A Decubitus Ulcer is a trophic ulcer occurring at the most dependent part of the prolapsed mass lying outside the introitus. Pathogenesis: Venous congestion and diminished circulation (caused by constriction of the prolapsed mass by the narrow introital ring and stretching/narrowing of the uterine vessels) + surface keratinization  cracks  friction against thighs/undergarments and secondary infection  sloughing ulceration. (Malignant change is extremely rare [<0.5%]). Management of Decubitus Ulcer: (i) Pap smear / Biopsy from the ulcer margin to exclude malignancy, (ii) Manual reduction of the prolapse, and (iii) Daily intravaginal packing with a roller gauze soaked in Glycerin and Acriflavine (glycerin is hygroscopic  reduces edema and congestion; acriflavine is antiseptic) or topical Estrogen cream (in postmenopausal women) until the ulcer heals completely prior to surgery.

Supravaginal Elongation of Cervix: Caused by downward traction of the prolapsing vaginal walls/uterine weight opposed by the upward pull of the attached Mackenrodt’s ligaments, compounded by chronic venous/lymphatic congestion.

Urinary Tract Changes ([TU]): Sharp angulation of the urethra against the pubourethral ligament during straining causes incomplete bladder emptying, residual urine, bladder wall hypertrophy/trabeculation, recurrent cystitis, and downward dragging of the ureters by the elongated Mackenrodt’s ligaments/uterine arteries through the urogenital hiatus causes bilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis (rarely uremia).

Symptoms of Prolapse ([KU25]):

Feeling of “something coming down” (mass) per vaginum (worse on standing/walking/straining, relieved on lying down).

Dragging pelvic pain and low backache (relieved by rest).

Urinary Symptoms (in Cystourethrocele): Difficulty in voiding / incomplete evacuation (patient often has to digitally push up the anterior vaginal wall/mass to complete micturition), frequency, urgency, dysuria (due to cystitis), or stress urinary incontinence.

Bowel Symptoms (in Rectocele): Difficulty in defecation / incomplete evacuation (patient has to digitally splint/press the posterior vaginal wall backward to evacuate stool).

Vaginal Discharge: Leucorrhoea, or purulent/blood-stained discharge due to a decubitus ulcer (as in the 60-year-old woman in [KU24]).

Dyspareunia.

Differential Diagnosis of a Mass Per Vagina ([KU25,24,TU,RGU]):

Uterovaginal Prolapse / Cystocele / Rectocele / Enterocele. (Note: Enterocele is differentiated from Rectocele by rectovaginal examination—in enterocele, the high posterior bulge near the cervix remains above and separate from the finger in the rectum).

Anterior Vaginal Wall Cyst (Gartner’s Duct Cyst): Differentiated from a Cystocele by: (i) Anterolateral position, (ii) Tense, shiny overlying mucosa with loss of transverse vaginal rugosities, (iii) Well-defined margins, (iv) Non-reducible and no cough impulse, and (v) A metal catheter passed per urethra cannot be felt underneath the cyst mucosa.

Congenital Elongation of the Cervix: Differentiated from Uterovaginal Prolapse by: (i) Only the infravaginal (portio vaginalis) part of the cervix is elongated and conical, (ii) Vaginal fornices remain deep and at their normal high level, and (iii) Cystocele/rectocele is absent.

Fibroid Polyp or Cervical Polyp protruding through the external os.

Chronic Inversion of the Uterus (globular shaggy mass with no external os at the leading edge, cervical rim felt high up around the neck, and absence of fundus on rectal exam).

E. Management of Pelvic Organ Prolapse

Preventive: Good intranatal care (avoid premature bearing down, prolonged 2nd stage, and difficult forceps; timely episiotomy and accurate perineal repair) and postnatal Kegel’s pelvic floor exercises.

Conservative (Non-Surgical) Management:

Indications: Asymptomatic mild prolapse (Stage I), prolapse during pregnancy/puerperium, patient medically unfit for surgery, or while awaiting surgery (for healing of decubitus ulcer).

Measures: Avoid aggravating factors (treat chronic cough, constipation, obesity), Kegel’s pelvic floor muscle exercises, local Estrogen cream in postmenopausal women, and Vaginal Ring Pessary.

Use of Ring Pessary ([KU24]): A flexible silicone/rubber ring pessary (size measured from posterior fornix to 1 cm behind symphysis pubis) is inserted into the vagina above the levator ani muscles. It stretches the urogenital hiatus and vaginal walls tautly, preventing descent (palliative, not curative). Must be removed, cleaned, and inspected every 3 months to prevent vaginitis, ulceration, incarceration, or fistula.

Surgical Management (Definitive Treatment for Symptomatic Prolapse): Choice of operation depends on age, parity, desire for reproductive and menstrual function, sexual activity, medical fitness, and compartment defects:

A. In a Postmenopausal / Perimenopausal Parous Woman (>45–60 years, Family Completed — e.g., [KU25,24,18]):

Operation of Choice: Vaginal Hysterectomy with Pelvic Floor Repair (Ward-Mayo’s Operation: VH + Anterior Colporrhaphy + Posterior Colpoperineorrhaphy + McCall Culdoplasty).

(Preoperative preparation in the 60y woman with blood-stained discharge [KU24]: First exclude cervical/endometrial malignancy by Pap smear, biopsy of decubitus ulcer edge, and endometrial biopsy/TVS, pack vagina with glycerin-acriflavine / estrogen cream to heal the decubitus ulcer, treat UTI, and optimize medical comorbidities).

(For Elderly Frail Woman >70 years Unfit for Prolonged Anesthesia & Hysterectomy AND Not Sexually Active [KU25,RGU]):

Non-surgical: Silicone Ring Pessary + local estrogen cream.

Surgical (Obliterative — under local/regional anesthesia): LeFort’s Partial Colpocleisis (denuding corresponding rectangular strips of mucosa from the anterior and posterior vaginal walls and suturing them together to close the vagina, leaving two lateral mucosal tunnels for cervical drainage; prerequisite: normal Pap smear and endometrial biopsy).

B. In a Young Parous Woman (<40 years) Wishing to Preserve Her Uterus / Menstrual Function (With Supravaginal Cervical Elongation + Cystocele/Rectocele):

Operation of Choice: Fothergill’s (Manchester) Operation ([KU24,RGU]).

Composite Steps of Fothergill’s Operation:

Preliminary Dilatation and Curettage (D & C): To measure uterocervical length, rule out endometrial pathology, and dilate the cervical canal (prevents postoperative cervical stenosis and facilitates passage of Sturmdorff sutures).

Dissection of Anterior Vaginal Wall & Mobilization of Bladder: Inverted-T incision from 1.5 cm below urethral meatus to cervicovaginal junction, extending circularly around the cervix; vesicocervical ligament is divided and bladder is pushed up.

Clamping, Cutting, and Ligation of Mackenrodt’s (Cardinal) Ligaments with descending cervical arteries on both sides above the level of planned amputation.

Amputation of the Elongated Cervix at the calculated level.

Re-covering the Posterior Lip of Amputated Cervix with the posterior vaginal mucosal flap using a Sturmdorff suture (or Bonney’s stitch) 

Plication & Fixation of Cut Mackenrodt’s Ligaments in Front of the Cervical Stump (using Fothergill’s Stitch): Shortens the cardinal ligaments, elevates the cervix, and anteverts the uterus.

Anterior Colporrhaphy: Plication of pubocervical fascia under the bladder, excision of redundant anterior vaginal mucosa, and closure.

Posterior Colpoperineorrhaphy (with Enterocele repair if present): Approximation of levator ani muscles and reconstruction of the perineal body.

Complications of Fothergill’s Operation: Hemorrhage, bladder/rectal injury; Late: Cervical stenosis (hematometra), infertility (loss of cervical mucus), cervical incompetence (recurrent mid-trimester abortion / preterm labor), and cervical dystocia in labor.

C. In a Young Married / Nulliparous Woman (e.g., 19-year-old [KU24,21,17]) Wishing to Preserve Fertility (Nulliparous / Congenital Prolapse):

Sling Operations (Cervicopexy / Hysteropexy — Preserving Uterus, Cervix, and Fertility):

Purandare’s Anterior Abdominal Cervicopexy: Two strips of anterior rectus sheath (1.5 cm wide, attached laterally) or Mersilene/Prolene mesh tape are brought extraperitoneally between the leaves of the broad ligament and stitched to the anterior surface of the uterine isthmus. (Disadvantage: Pulls isthmus anteriorly, opening up the Pouch of Douglas  predisposes to enterocele; hence must be combined with Moschowitz obliteration of POD).

Virkud’s Composite Sling Operation: Mersilene tape fixed between the posterior isthmus and anterior longitudinal ligament of S1/sacral promontory on the right + a strip of anterior rectus sheath fixed anteriorly on the left + plication of left uterosacral ligament (prevents enterocele and dextrorotation).

Khanna’s Sling Operation: Tape fixed from the posterior cervix to the anterior superior iliac spines bilaterally.

Shirodkar’s Sling Operation: Fascia lata/Mersilene tape fixed from the posterior cervix to the sacral promontory (via psoas loop on the left to avoid sigmoid colon).

D. Management of Post-Hysterectomy Vault Prolapse ([KU21,RGU]):

Vaginal Route: Right Sacrospinous Ligament Fixation (Colpopexy) (fixing the vault to the right coccygeus–sacrospinous ligament complex 2 cm medial to the ischial spine using a Miya hook) + Enterocele repair (McCall Culdoplasty) + PFR; OR Total Colpocleisis (in frail elderly women).

Abdominal / Laparoscopic Route (Gold Standard for Sexually Active Women): Abdominal or Laparoscopic Sacrocolpopexy (suspending the vaginal vault to the anterior longitudinal ligament over the sacral promontory / S1–S3 using a Y-shaped polypropylene/Mersilene mesh, retroperitonealized under the posterior peritoneum).

(Note on Chronic Inversion of the Uterus [RGU]: Turning of the uterus inside-out due to incomplete puerperal inversion or traction by a fundal submucous fibroid/sarcoma 

Treatment: Always surgical—Haultain’s abdominal operation [incising the posterior constricting cervical ring and repositing the fundus] or Spinelli’s / Küstner’s vaginal operation, or hysterectomy if family is completed).

(Note on Old Complete Perineal Tear [CPT / 3rd & 4th Degree Tear] [RGU]: Disruption of perineal body and external/internal anal sphincter complex  anorectal mucosa 

Causes incontinence of flatus and feces, loss of perineum [pinkish vaginal mucosa continuous with reddish rectal mucosa], absent anal sphincter grip, and lateral skin dimples over retracted ends of sphincter ani externus. Treatment (after 3 months): Preoperative bowel preparation  Warren’s Flap-Splitting Perineorrhaphy with Overlapping/End-to-End Anal Sphincteroplasty using 3-0 PDS for rectal mucosa and 2-0 PDS figure-of-eight sutures for external anal sphincter).

text:
Visualization of endometrial cavity is done using [KU25]: Hysteroscope (Hysteroscopy).

Expand POP-Q [KU24,22,18]: Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (latest classification of prolapse).

Ring pessary is used in [KU24]: Pelvic Organ Prolapse (Uterovaginal prolapse) and Retroversion of uterus (Hodge-Smith pessary).

Name any one surgery done in Nulliparous Prolapse / Anterior sling surgery [KU23,20]: Purandare’s Cervicopexy (Anterior Rectus Sheath Sling Operation) (also Virkud’s, Khanna’s, or Shirodkar’s sling).

Procidentia [KU22]: Third-degree () complete uterovaginal prolapse where the entire uterus (cervix and body) lies outside the vaginal introitus with complete eversion of the vagina.

Fixed reference point in the POP-Q system [KU21]: Hymenal ring (Plane of the hymen = 0 level).

Plication at bladder neck during anterior colporrhaphy for stress incontinence [KU20]: Kelly’s cystourethroplasty (Kelly’s stitch).

subject: gynecology
title: 17.1 Genuine Stress Incontinence (GSI / SUI) & Urge Incontinence
text:
CHAPTER 17: Urinary Incontinence & Retention of Urine

(Covers: SA 1 [KU24,21], 2 [KU24,19,RGU,TU], 3–6 [KU20,RGU,TU]; One-word answers 1–3 [KU])

A. Genuine Stress Incontinence (GSI / Urethral Sphincter Incompetence)

Definition (ICS): Objectively demonstrable involuntary urethral loss of urine occurring during a sudden rise in intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, sneezing, laughing) when the intravesical pressure exceeds the maximum urethral closure pressure in the COMPLETE ABSENCE of detrusor contraction.

Etiopathogenesis:

Anatomic Urethral Hypermobility (80% — Commonest): Childbirth trauma to the pubocervical fascia, pubourethral ligaments, and levator ani (plus pudendal nerve injury and postmenopausal estrogen deficiency) causes descent of the bladder neck and proximal urethra below the urogenital diaphragm. Consequently, during coughing/straining, raised intra-abdominal pressure is transmitted only to the bladder and not to the proximal urethra 

and normal hammock kinking of the urethra fails.

Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency (ISD — 20%): Weakness/fibrosis of the intrinsic urethral rhabdosphincter and submucosal vascular seal (due to previous failed incontinence surgery, pelvic radiation, neurology, or aging), defined by a Maximum Urethral Closure Pressure (MUCP)  20 cm  or Valsalva Leak-Point Pressure (VLPP) < 60 cm .

Clinical Features & Diagnostic Tests for SUI ([KU24,21]):

Symptom: Escape of small spurts of urine coinciding precisely with coughing, sneezing, or exercise, without any prior urge to void, and never occurring in sleep (Table 24.2 / 24.7).

Diagnostic Tests:

Clinical Stress Test (Bonney’s / Marshall’s Test): With a full bladder, the patient is asked to cough in lithotomy (and standing) position  instantaneous escape of a spurt of urine from the external urethral meatus coinciding with the cough confirms SUI.

Midstream Urine Routine & Culture: Mandatory first step to rule out Urinary Tract Infection (UTI).

3-Day Frequency-Volume Chart (Bladder Diary) and Post-Void Residual (PVR) Urine Measurement ([KU20]: measured by catheterization or USG within 10 min of voiding; normal residual urine is < 50 mL; >100 mL indicates voiding dysfunction/retention).

Pad Test (1-Hour Extended Pad Test): Used to objectively quantify urine loss when the clinical stress test is equivocal. The patient wears a pre-weighed sanitary pad, drinks 500 mL of water in 15 minutes, walks/climbs stairs for 30 minutes, and performs provocative exercises (coughing, bending, jumping) for 15 minutes. An increase in pad weight of > 1 g at the end of 1 hour is considered significant.

Q-Tip Test: A lubricated sterile cotton swab is introduced into the urethra up to the bladder neck; an upward deflection angle of > 30° from the horizontal on straining (Valsalva) indicates anatomic urethral hypermobility (not diagnostic of SUI by itself).

Urodynamic Studies (Indicated in mixed incontinence, voiding difficulty, neurogenic bladder, or prior to/after failed continence surgery):

Uroflowmetry: Normal peak flow rate is 15–25 mL/sec (< 10 mL/sec indicates outflow obstruction or hypotonic detrusor). In uncomplicated GSI, uroflowmetry is normal with residual urine < 50 mL.

Filling and Voiding Cystometry (Multichannel Subtracted Cystometry): True detrusor pressure () is calculated by subtracting intra-abdominal/rectal pressure () from total intravesical pressure (): .

Normal Cystometric Parameters (Table 24.3): Residual urine 0–50 mL; First sensation of filling at 150–200 mL; Maximum cystometric capacity 400–600 mL; Intravesical pressure on filling 0–15 cm ; Maximum voiding detrusor pressure < 50 cm .

In GSI: Urine leakage is seen on coughing with NO rise in true detrusor pressure () (excludes detrusor overactivity).

Urethral Pressure Profilometry (UPP) & Valsalva Leak-Point Pressure (VLPP): Demonstrates decreased functional urethral length (< 3 cm) and a drop in urethral closure pressure below intravesical pressure during stress (MUCP < 20 cm  or VLPP < 60 cm  diagnoses Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency [ISD]).

Imaging & Endoscopy (Selected Cases): Transvaginal / Perineal Endosonography or Videocystourethrography (VCU) (shows loss of posterior urethrovesical angle and funneling of the bladder neck on straining); Cystourethroscopy (normal in GSI; rules out fistula, calculus, or interstitial cystitis).

Clinical Grading of SUI:

Grade I: Incontinence occurs only on severe stress (coughing, sneezing, laughing).

Grade II: Incontinence occurs on moderate exertion (running, climbing stairs, lifting weights).

Grade III: Incontinence occurs even on minimal stress or change of posture (standing/walking).

Management of Stress Urinary Incontinence ([KU24,19,RGU,TU]):

Preventive: Avoid prolonged second stage of labor and traumatic instrumental delivery; postnatal pelvic floor exercises; weight reduction (BMI < 25); treatment of chronic cough and constipation.

Conservative (Non-Surgical) Management (First-line for mild/Grade I SUI, young women planning future pregnancy, or medically unfit patients):

Supervised Pelvic Floor Muscle Training (Kegel’s Exercises): Repetitive voluntary contraction (“drawing up”) of the levator ani and periurethral striated muscles ~100 times/day for at least 3–6 months, supplemented by weighted vaginal cones (20–100 g), biofeedback, or pudendal nerve electrical stimulation.

Vaginal Devices: Ring pessary with urethral knob or bladder-neck support prosthesis.

Medical / Pharmacotherapy:

Local Estrogen Cream (in postmenopausal women with urogenital atrophy) to improve urethral mucosal coaptation, vascular plexus, and collagen tone.

Sympathomimetic (-Adrenergic Agonists) / Tricyclics: Imipramine (10–25 mg PO BID) or Ephedrine (15–30 mg PO BID) to increase bladder-neck and urethral smooth muscle tone.

Duloxetine (SNRI — Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitor): 40 mg PO BID; increases pudendal nerve stimulation of the striated urethral rhabdosphincter.

Surgical Management (Mainstay for Moderate-to-Severe SUI or Failed Conservative Therapy):

Principles: (i) Elevate and stabilize the hypermobile bladder neck and proximal urethra within the intra-abdominal pressure zone, OR (ii) Provide a tension-free mid-urethral supportive hammock/backboard, OR (iii) Augment intrinsic sphincter coaptation.

A. Mid-Urethral Tension-Free Synthetic Sling Procedures — Current Operations of Choice ([KU21] — Grade A Recommendation; Cure rate 85–90%):

Tension-Free Vaginal Tape (TVT — Ulmsten, 1996): Under local/regional anesthesia, a 1.5 cm suburethral vaginal incision is made at the mid-urethra, and a macroporous monofilament polypropylene mesh tape is passed in a ‘U’-shaped loop beneath the mid-urethra using special trocars through the retropubic space (Space of Retzius) to exit suprapubically on either side of the midline without tension. 

Check cystoscopy is mandatory to exclude bladder perforation.

Transobturator Tape (TOT — Outside-In [Delorme, 2001] or TVT-O — Inside-Out [de Leval, 2003]): The polypropylene tape is passed beneath the mid-urethra horizontally through the obturator foramina (exiting at the groin fold at the level of the clitoris) to form a natural suburethral hammock. Advantages over TVT: Completely avoids the retropubic space, minimizing the risk of bladder, bowel, or major vessel injury; shorter operating time; no routine cystoscopy required.

B. Retropubic Bladder-Neck Colposuspension (Abdominal / Laparoscopic):

Burch Colposuspension (1961 — Traditional “Gold Standard” Open/Laparoscopic Operation; 85–90% 5-year cure rate): Through the retropubic space of Retzius, 3–4 delayed absorbable/non-absorbable sutures on each side suspend the paravaginal/paraurethral endopelvic fascia (at the level of the bladder neck) to the ipsilateral iliopectineal ligament (Cooper’s ligament)

 (Complications: Detrusor overactivity, voiding difficulty, and enterocele).

Marshall-Marchetti-Krantz (MMK, 1949) Operation: Paraurethral fascia is sutured to the periosteum of the posterior aspect of the symphysis pubis and pubic cartilage. (Rarely done now due to 3–5% risk of osteitis pubis).

C. Anterior Colporrhaphy with Kelly’s Cystourethroplasty (Kelly’s Plication Stitch, 1914): Vaginal plication of the pubocervical fascia beneath the bladder neck and proximal urethra using vertical mattress sutures ([KU20]). Simple and corrects concomitant cystocele, but has a low long-term cure rate for GSI (50–60%).

D. Procedures for Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency (ISD) / Recurrent Failed SUI:

Periurethral / Transurethral Bulking Agents: Cystoscopically guided submucosal injection of GAX-collagen, Teflon, or polyacrylamide hydrogel at the bladder neck (ideal for frail elderly women unfit for anesthesia).

Pubovaginal Bladder-Neck Sling (Aldridge rectus sheath or fascia lata sling) or Artificial Urinary Sphincter.

B. Urge Incontinence & Overactive Bladder (OAB / Detrusor Overactivity)

(Covers: Urge incontinence [RGU]; Differentiation from GSI — Table 24.2 & 24.7)

Definitions:

Urge Incontinence: Involuntary leakage of urine accompanied by or immediately preceded by a strong, sudden desire to void (urgency). It may be Sensory (local irritation from cystitis, calculus, foreign body, or estrogen deficiency with a stable detrusor) or Motor (due to Detrusor Overactivity).

Overactive Bladder (OAB) / Detrusor Overactivity (DO): Second most common cause of urinary incontinence in adult women (and most common cause in elderly women); defined urodynamically as involuntary spontaneous or provoked detrusor contractions (> 15 cm ) during the filling phase while the patient is attempting to inhibit micturition.

Etiology: Idiopathic/psychosomatic (commonest), neurogenic (detrusor hyperreflexia — multiple sclerosis, Parkinsonism, stroke, spinal injury, diabetic neuropathy), or following bladder-neck continence surgery.

Key Differentiating Features (GSI vs. OAB/Urge Incontinence):

In OAB/Urge Incontinence: Leakage is preceded by urgency, associated with frequency (> 8 voids/day) and nocturia (> 1/night), volume of urine lost is large, patient cannot reach the toilet in time, and filling cystometry shows reduced capacity (< 200 mL) with involuntary detrusor contractions (> 15 cm ). (Note: In mixed incontinence, OAB must always be treated medically BEFORE undertaking surgery for GSI).

Management of OAB / Urge Incontinence:

Behavioral & Lifestyle Modifications: Restrict fluid intake to ~1–1.5 L/day, avoid caffeine/alcohol, and Bladder Retraining (“Bladder Drill”) (scheduled voiding by the clock at progressively increasing intervals of 15–30 minutes over 6 weeks to restore cortical inhibition; first-line therapy).

Pharmacotherapy — Antimuscarinic / Anticholinergic Drugs (Mainstay): Block acetylcholine at detrusor muscarinic () receptors to inhibit involuntary contractions:

Oxybutynin chloride: 5 mg PO 2–3 times daily (or transdermal patch 3.9 mg twice weekly) — First-choice drug.

Tolterodine: 1–2 mg PO twice daily (detrusor-selective, fewer side effects).

Solifenacin (5–10 mg PO once daily) or Darifenacin / Trospium chloride / Propiverine.

Common side effects: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, drowsiness. Contraindications: Narrow-angle glaucoma, myasthenia gravis, urinary retention, and intestinal obstruction.

Other drugs: Imipramine (25–50 mg at bedtime for nocturia), Desmopressin (DDAVP) (20–40  intranasally for nocturnal enuresis), and local Estrogen cream in postmenopausal women.

Refractory Cases: Intravesical Botulinum toxin-A cystoscopic injection into the detrusor, Capsaicin / Resiniferatoxin instillation, sacral neuromodulation, or augmentation (“clam”) ileocystoplasty.

subject: gynecology
title: 17.2 Causes and Management of Acute Retention of Urine in Gynecology
text:
(Covers: Causes of acute retention of urine in gynecology [RGU,TU]; Causes of retention of urine in (a) Reproductive age, (b) Pubertal age [TU])

Definition: Sudden painful inability to void urine over 12 hours in the presence of a full, distended bladder.

Etiological Classification by Age Group & Mechanism (Table 24.8):

Pubertal / Postmenarchal Age Group:

Cryptomenorrhoea (Hematocolpos) due to imperforate hymen or low transverse vaginal septum (presenting with primary amenorrhoea and cyclic lower abdominal pain; distended vagina stretches and elongates the urethra).

Impacted ovarian tumor (e.g., dermoid/germ cell tumor), acute vulvovaginitis, or genital trauma/rape.

Reproductive Age Group (Presented by Associated Menstrual Pattern):

With Short Period of Secondary Amenorrhoea (12–16 weeks): Retroverted Gravid Uterus incarcerated in the sacral hollow (cervix is pushed upwards and forwards behind the symphysis pubis, stretching the urethra and compressing the bladder neck).

With Menorrhagia: Posterior wall or fundal Uterine Fibroid impacted in the Pouch of Douglas, or a large anterior/central Cervical Fibroid.

With Irregular Bleeding & Acute Pain: Pelvic Hematocele (chronic disturbed tubal ectopic pregnancy in POD).

With Irregular Bleeding / Discharge & Fever: Pelvic Abscess in the Pouch of Douglas or Acute Bartholin’s Abscess / Severe Herpes Genitalis (reflex external sphincter spasm).

With Normal Menstrual Cycles: Impacted Ovarian Tumor in POD or Broad Ligament Tumor.

Postoperative & Postpartum Causes (Commonest Overall in Hospital Practice):

Following anterior colporrhaphy, PFR, TVT/TOT sling, or perineorrhaphy (due to periurethral edema, tight vaginal pack, and reflex spasm of the levator ani/urethral sphincter).

Radical Hysterectomy (Wertheim’s): Autonomic denervation of the pelvic splanchnic plexus ().

Epidural/spinal anesthesia, puerperal bruised perineum/vulval hematoma.

Postmenopausal / Elderly Age Group:

Incarcerated Third-Degree Uterovaginal Prolapse (Procidentia) or large cystocele (sharp angulation of urethra).

Pyometra / Hematometra, advanced Carcinoma Cervix, Vagina, or Urethra, or urethral stricture.

Neurological, Drug-Induced & Psychogenic Causes: Multiple sclerosis, spinal cord compression, diabetic neuropathy; anticholinergics, tricyclic antidepressants, epidural opioids; hysteria/lack of privacy.

Management:

Immediate Relief: Aseptic urethral catheterization (using a sterile Foley catheter; if acute retention is prolonged/chronic, leave an indwelling Foley catheter for continuous bladder drainage for 24–48 hours or until bladder tone returns and post-void residual urine is < 50–100 mL).

Definitive Treatment of the Underlying Cause: E.g., Cruciate hymenotomy for hematocolpos; continuous catheterization + prone positioning to allow spontaneous correction of retroverted gravid uterus; myomectomy/hysterectomy for impacted fibroid; or posterior colpotomy for pelvic abscess.
