subject: gynecology
title: 18.1 Classification of Genitourinary Fistulae & Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF)
text:
CHAPTER 18: Urinary Tract Injuries and Genital Fistulas

(Covers: SE 1 [RGU]; SA 1 [KU22,18,RGU], 2 [KU15,TU])

A. Anatomical Classification of Genitourinary Fistulae

A genitourinary fistula is an abnormal communication between the urinary tract and the genital tract resulting in involuntary escape of urine into the vagina (true incontinence):

Bladder Communications:

Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF — Commonest): Subclassified anatomically into:

Juxtacervical (Vault fistula): Between supratrigonal bladder and upper vagina/cervix.

Midvaginal: Between the base (trigone) of the bladder and mid-vagina.

Juxtaurethral: Between the bladder neck/upper urethra and vagina.

Subsymphysial: Extensive circumferential tissue loss fixed to the pubic bone.

Vesicouterine Fistula (Youssef’s Syndrome): Follows repeat lower-segment cesarean section; presents with cyclical hematuria during menstruation (menouria), secondary amenorrhoea, and urinary continence when the fistula is above the internal os.

Vesicocervical and Vesicourethrovaginal Fistula.

Urethral Communications: Urethrovaginal Fistula.

Ureteric Communications: Ureterovaginal (commonest ureteric fistula), Ureterocervical, and Ureterouterine Fistula.

B. Etiology (Causes) of Vesicovaginal / Genitourinary Fistula ([KU22,18,15])

Obstetrical Causes (Account for 80–90% of VVF in Developing Countries vs. 5–15% in Developed Countries):

A. Ischemic (Pressure Necrosis in Obstructed Labor — Commonest Obstetrical Cause): Prolonged compression of the bladder base and anterior vaginal wall between the arrested fetal head and the posterior surface of the symphysis pubis  ischemic avascular necrosis  infection and sloughing of dead tissue  urinary leakage starts on the 5th to 14th puerperal day.

B. Direct Obstetric Trauma (Leakage starts immediately after delivery):

Difficult instrumental vaginal delivery (forceps—especially Kielland’s rotational forceps) or destructive operations (craniotomy, perforation by fetal bony spicules, decapitation).

Rupture of the uterus involving the bladder, Repeat Cesarean Section (during dissection of the densely adherent bladder flap or inadvertent inclusion of the bladder wall in the uterine suture), or Cesarean Hysterectomy.

Gynecological Causes (Account for > 80% of VVF in Developed Countries):

A. Operative Trauma (Commonest Gynecological Cause): Direct unrecognized injury or ischemic necrosis from clamping/suturing the bladder during Total Abdominal Hysterectomy, Radical Hysterectomy (Wertheim’s), Vaginal Hysterectomy, Anterior Colporrhaphy, or excision of a Gartner’s duct cyst.

B. Pelvic Malignancy: Direct infiltration of the bladder base by Stage IVA Carcinoma Cervix, Carcinoma Vagina, or Carcinoma Bladder.

C. Radiation Necrosis: Following radiotherapy for carcinoma cervix; caused by endarteritis obliterans and ischemia, appearing 1–2 years (or more) after radiation.

D. Traumatic & Foreign Body: Forgotten/incarcerated vaginal ring pessary, fall astride on a sharp object, criminal abortion stick, or pelvic fracture.

E. Chronic Granulomatous Infections: Genital tuberculosis, lymphogranuloma venereum, actinomycosis, or schistosomiasis.

C. Clinical Features & Diagnosis of VVF ([KU22,18])

Symptoms:

Continuous involuntary escape of urine per vaginum day and night (“True Incontinence”) with loss of urge to micturate. (Timing clue: Immediate onset = direct surgical/instrumental tear; Onset after 5–14 days = ischemic sloughing after obstructed labor or clamping; Onset after 1–2 years = post-radiation fistula. Small high juxtacervical fistulae may leak only in certain postures while passing some urine per urethra).

Vulval excoriation, ammoniacal odor, and pruritus vulvae.

Associated Obstetric Injury Sequelae (“Obstetric Fistula Syndrome”): Hypothalamic secondary amenorrhoea, foot-drop (due to compression of the lumbosacral trunk [] against the pelvic brim during obstructed labor), acquired vaginal stenosis, and rectovaginal fistula / complete perineal tear.

Signs & Confirmation of Diagnosis:

Vulval Inspection: Escape of urine with ammoniacal smell; sodden, excoriated vulval skin with phosphatic encrustations.

Sims’ Position & Sims’ Speculum Examination: Best position to visualize the anterior vaginal wall; a large fistula (> 1–2 cm) is directly seen and felt (often with velvety red bladder mucosa prolapsing through it), and a metal catheter passed per urethra emerges directly into the vagina through the fistula ([Fig. 25.2]).

For a Tiny / Pin-hole Fistula (Differential Diagnosis from Stress Incontinence, Ureterovaginal Fistula, and Urethrovaginal Fistula):

Methylene Blue Dye Test: Instilling sterile methylene blue into the bladder via a urethral catheter under direct speculum vision shows blue dye escaping through the puckered fistula site.

Three-Swab Test (Moire’s Test)

Three cotton swabs are placed in the vagina (upper at vault, middle in mid-vagina, lower just above introitus), methylene blue is instilled into the bladder via catheter, the catheter is removed, and the patient walks for 5–10 minutes:

Middle (or upper) swab stained BLUE: Confirms Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF).

Lowermost swab stained BLUE (upper two dry): Confirms Urethrovaginal Fistula (or urethral incontinence).

Uppermost swab soaked with CLEAR UNSTAINED URINE (lower two dry): Confirms Ureterovaginal Fistula (further confirmed by IV Indigo Carmine Test, which stains the upper swab blue within 5 minutes, + IVU & Cystoscopy).

Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA) & Cystourethroscopy: Essential to assess exact number, size, site, mobility/scarring of margins, urethral patency, and relation of the fistula margins to the two ureteric orifices.

Preoperative Workup: Hb%, blood urea & serum creatinine, urine culture (collected via ureteric catheter), and IVU (in complex/vault fistulae to rule out concomitant ureteric fistula).

D. Management of Vesicovaginal Fistula

Prevention: Safe motherhood partograph monitoring to prevent obstructed labor; timely cesarean section; continuous Foley catheter bladder drainage for 7–10 days after relieved obstructed labor; and meticulous bladder mobilization during hysterectomy.

Immediate / Conservative Management (Within 24–48 hours of Injury):

Unrecognized surgical injury detected on table: Immediate primary repair in two layers + Foley drainage for 10–14 days.

Small fresh fistula detected in the early postoperative/puerperal period: Continuous indwelling urethral catheter drainage for 4–8 weeks + urinary antiseptics allows spontaneous closure in 15–20% of small fistulae.

Definitive Surgical Management (For Established Old VVF):

Timing of Surgery:

Obstetric or Post-surgical VVF: Wait 3 months (12 weeks) after delivery/surgery so that local sloughing, edema, and infection subside completely and vascularity returns. (If a first repair fails, wait another 3 months before re-operating).

Post-radiation VVF: Wait 12 months.

Operation of Choice: Transvaginal Repair by Flap-Splitting Method 

Position: Sims’ or lithotomy (with steep Trendelenburg / Lawson’s position). (If ureteric orifices are close to the fistula edge, catheterize both ureters cystoscopically prior to dissection).

Steps: (1) Circumferential incision around the fistula ostium with vertical extensions  (2) Wide mobilization of the anterior vaginal wall flaps off the underlying bladder wall so that the bladder can be closed without any tension, and minimal excision of fibrous scar at the fistula rim  (3) Two-layer water-tight closure of the bladder wall without tension using interrupted 2-0 or 3-0 polyglactin (Vicryl) sutures (First layer: bites through bladder muscle/submucosa excluding bladder mucosa; Second layer: imbricating Lembert sutures in muscularis/pubocervical fascia burying the first layer)  (4) Confirm water-tight closure by instilling methylene blue into the bladder  (5) Closure of the vaginal mucosa with interrupted 2-0 Vicryl sutures  (6) (In large juxtaurethral/recurrent fistulae with tissue loss, interpose a vascularized Martius bulbocavernosus muscle-fat pad graft from the labium majus between the bladder and vaginal suture lines).

(Other Techniques: Saucerization [Sims’ paring and suturing] for tiny fistulae; Latzko Partial Colpocleisis for high post-hysterectomy vault fistulae; Transvesical or Transperitoneal Abdominal Repair [with omental flap interposition] for high, fixed, inaccessible supratrigonal/vesicouterine fistulae or when ureteric reimplantation is needed; Urinary Diversion [Ileal conduit] as a last resort for irreparable/malignant/post-radiation fistulae).*

Postoperative Care & Discharge Advice (Crucial for Success):

Continuous unobstructed bladder drainage via an indwelling urethral Foley catheter for 10–14 days (check hourly urine output; never allow catheter blockage/bladder distension!), high oral fluid intake, and urinary antibiotics.

After catheter removal on Day 14, instruct the patient to void every 1–2 hours initially.

Discharge Advice: (1) Abstain from sexual intercourse for at least 3 months, (2) Defer pregnancy for at least 1 year (using contraception), and (3) Mandatory elective Cesarean Section in all future pregnancies (vaginal delivery is strictly contraindicated after successful VVF repair!).

subject: gynecology
title: 18.2 Ureteric Injury in Gynecological Surgery & Rectovaginal Fistula (RVF)
text:
(Covers: SA 3–7 [KU15,RGU])

A. Ureteric Injury During Gynecological Surgery ([KU15,RGU])

Incidence: Occurs in 0.5–1% of pelvic operations; 75% of all ureteric injuries result from gynecological surgery (75% abdominal, 25% vaginal/laparoscopic).

Common Anatomical Sites & Predisposing Conditions: (See Chapter 1, Section 1.3 for the 6 exact anatomical sites of injury during hysterectomy). High-risk conditions: Cervical or broad ligament fibroid, severe pelvic endometriosis, tubo-ovarian mass, ovarian cancer, and Wertheim’s radical hysterectomy.

Types of Injury: Kinking/angulation, ischemic stripping of adventitial sheath, suture ligation, clamp crushing, thermal diathermy/laser burn, or partial/complete transection.

Diagnosis:

Intraoperative: Direct visualization of urine leak/transected lumen, proximal ureteric dilatation (if ligated), or extravasation of blue dye after IV Indigo Carmine injection.

Postoperative: Flank pain, fever, ileus, anuria (if bilateral ligation), or watery leakage per vaginum starting 1–14 days post-op while still passing normal urine per urethra. Confirmed by Three-Swab Test (uppermost swab wet with clear unstained urine) + IV Indigo Carmine test (stains upper swab blue) + IVU / CT Urogram and Cystoscopy with retrograde ureteric catheterization (identifies the exact side and level of obstruction/fistula).

Management Based on Timing & Anatomical Level of Injury:

Simple suture ligation / kinking recognized on table: Immediate deligation + assess peristalsis/viability + Double-J (DJ) ureteral stenting for 4–6 weeks.

Partial transection or thermal/crush injury: Primary repair with 4-0 PDS interrupted sutures over a Double-J ureteral stent + extraperitoneal drain.

Complete Transection / Fistula in the Lower Third (Below Pelvic Brim / < 4–5 cm from bladder — Commonest): Ureteroneocystostomy (Reimplantation of ureter into the bladder) through a submucosal anti-reflux tunnel, combined with a Psoas Hitch (suturing the mobilized bladder dome to the ipsilateral psoas muscle tendon to eliminate tension) or a Boari Bladder Flap (tubularized bladder flap when a longer lower ureteric segment is lost) over a DJ stent.

Complete Transection in the Middle Third (At/Above Pelvic Brim): End-to-End Spatulated Uretero-ureterostomy over a DJ stent using 4-0 PDS + retroperitoneal drain.

B. Rectovaginal Fistula (RVF) ([RGU])

Definition: Abnormal communication between the rectum and vagina resulting in involuntary escape of flatus and/or feces per vaginum ([Fig. 25.5]).

Causes:

Obstetrical (Commonest): Imperfect healing or breakdown of a repaired 3rd/4th-degree perineal tear (CPT); pressure necrosis of the middle third of the rectum against a flat sacrum in obstructed labor; or perforation during destructive operations.

Gynecological: Breakdown of old CPT repair; unrecognized rectal injury during posterior colpoperineorrhaphy, enterocele repair, vaginal hysterectomy, or posterior colpotomy; advanced carcinoma cervix or vagina; pelvic radiation; Crohn’s disease, diverticulitis, lymphogranuloma venereum, or tuberculosis.

Diagnosis: Passage of flatus/liquid stool per vaginum; rectovaginal examination; passing a metal probe from the vagina into the rectum ([Fig. 25.5]); or instilling methylene blue enema into the rectum with a vaginal tampon in place.

Treatment (Done 3 months after injury, after 3–5 days of preoperative bowel preparation with low-residue diet, oral metronidazole/neomycin, and enemas):

Low RVF (Near fourchette/perineal body): Convert the fistula into a Complete Perineal Tear (CPT) by cutting the bridge of tissue below the fistula, followed by classic layered CPT repair and anal sphincteroplasty (see Ch. 16).

Middle-Third RVF: Transvaginal Flap-Splitting Repair (excision of scar ring, wide mobilization of vaginal mucosa from rectum, two-layer tension-free closure of rectal wall with 3-0 PDS, interposition of levator ani/Martius graft, and closure of vaginal mucosa).

High RVF (Upper third / Vault) or Radiation/Inflammatory RVF: Three-stage procedure: Stage 1: Preliminary defunctioning transverse/sigmoid colostomy  Stage 2 (after 3–6 weeks): Local transvaginal or transabdominal repair of RVF  Stage 3 (after 3–6 weeks): Closure of colostomy.

subject: gynecology
title: 19.1 Contraceptive Counseling (Newly Married & Postpartum) & Ethical Principles
text:
CHAPTER 19: Family Planning (Contraception) & MTP Act

(Covers: SE 1 [KU25]; SA 9, 24, 42, 44 [KU23,RGU,TU]; One-word answer 5 [KU19])

A. Contraceptive Counseling for a Newly Married Couple & Ethical Principles ([KU25])

Ethical Principles in Contraceptive Counseling (“GATHER” Approach — Cafeteria Choice):

Respect for Autonomy & Voluntariness (Informed Choice): The couple has the absolute right to freely choose a contraceptive method that suits their reproductive goals without coercion, incentives, or provider bias (“Cafeteria approach”).

Beneficence & Non-Maleficence (Medical Eligibility): Screening the woman’s history and clinical examination using WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC Categories 1 to 4) to ensure the chosen method is safe and provides maximum health benefit with minimal risk.

Confidentiality & Privacy: Ensuring auditory andvisual privacy and strict confidentiality of sexual and medical history.

Truthfulness / Full Disclosure (Informed Consent): Explaining effectiveness (failure rate), correct and consistent use, common side effects, warning signs, non-contraceptive benefits, STI protection, and return of fertility after stopping.

Advice for a Newly Married Couple (Wanting to Postpone First Pregnancy):

First Choice: Low-Dose Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (COCs) (e.g., Mala-N or Loette — 20–30  Ethinyl estradiol + Levonorgestrel/Desogestrel).

Why ideal: Near-100% efficacy (Failure rate: 0.1 per 100 women-years [HWY]), regularizes cycles, relieves dysmenorrhoea and acne/hirsutism, reduces PID risk, and fertility returns promptly within 1–3 months of stopping.

Second Choice: Barrier Method — Male Condom (Nirodh)  Vaginal Spermicide:

Why useful: No systemic side effects, ideal if coitus is infrequent during early marriage, and provides dual protection against STIs/HIV. (Because of higher typical failure rate [2–15 HWY], always educate the couple about Emergency Contraception [Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg stat] in case of condom rupture/slippage).

(Note: IUCDs are generally avoided in nulligravid newly married women due to cramping pain, heavier bleeding, and the potential risk of ascending PID compromising future tubal fertility).

B. Postpartum Contraception, Lactational Amenorrhoea Method (LAM) & Pearl Index

Lactational Amenorrhoea Method (LAM) ([TU]): Natural postpartum contraception based on suckling-induced hyperprolactinemia suppressing pulsatile GnRH and LH. Effective (Failure rate < 2%) ONLY when ALL 3 criteria are met: (1) Baby is exclusively or fully breastfed day and night (5–6 feeds, ≥60 min/24 hours), (2) Mother remains completely amenorrhoeic, and (3) Infant is < 6 months of age.

Options for Postpartum Contraception ([RGU]):

Non-lactating mother: Start contraception at 3 weeks postpartum (COCs, Cu-IUCD at 6 weeks, DMPA, Implanon, or Condoms).

Lactating mother: Start additional contraception by 6 weeks to 3 months postpartum. Combined OC pills are contraindicated up to 6 months postpartum (WHO MEC Category 4 up to 6 weeks, Category 3 from 6 weeks to 6 months) because estrogen reduces breast milk volume and protein/fat quality. Safe Choices in Lactation:

PPIUCD (Postpartum Intrauterine Contraceptive Device) ([KU23,TU]): Insertion of Cu-T 380A using Kelly’s placental forceps either Post-placental (within 10 minutes of placental delivery), Intra-cesarean (through uterine incision before closure), or Immediate postpartum (within 48 hours of delivery), or Interval postpartum (after 6 weeks). Advantages: Convenient, high motivation, no effect on breast milk, 10-year protection. Drawback: Higher spontaneous expulsion rate (8–15%) compared to interval insertion (prevented by high fundal placement).

Progestin-Only Pill (POP / “Lactation Pill” — Levonorgestrel 75  or Desogestrel 75  daily), Injectable DMPA (150 mg IM 3-monthly), Subdermal Implant (Implanon), or Centchroman (Saheli).

Barrier Methods (Condoms) or Puerperal Minilap Tubectomy (24–48 hours post-delivery, if family is completed).

Pearl Index ([KU19,RGU]): The standard measure of contraceptive failure rate, defined as the number of accidental pregnancies per 100 women-years (HWY) of exposure (1200 observed menstrual cycles):

subject: gynecology
title: 19.2 Barrier Methods of Contraception
text:
(Covers: Barrier methods of contraception and its advantages [KU23,TU,RGU]; Femshield [TU]; One-word answer 6 [KU17])

Mechanism: Prevent live spermatozoa from entering the cervical canal mechanically, chemically (spermicides), or both.

Classification:

Mechanical Barriers:

Male Condom (Nirodh): Latex or polyurethane sheath (for latex allergy). Failure rate: 2–3 HWY with perfect use; 15 HWY with typical use ([KU17]).

Female Condom (Femidom / Femshield [TU]): 17 cm long polyurethane pouch with two flexible rings (smaller closed inner ring fits in upper vagina over cervix; larger outer ring covers vulva/vestibule)

 Woman-controlled; protects against STIs/HIV; failure rate 5–21 HWY.

Vaginal Diaphragm: Dome-shaped latex cup with a flexible metal spring rim (diameter 5–10 cm) fitted from the posterior fornix to behind the symphysis pubis, used along with spermicidal jelly. Inserted up to 3 hours before coitus and must be left in place for at least 6 hours after the last coital act. Failure rate: 6–16 HWY. (Contraindicated in uterovaginal prolapse, cystocele, or recurrent UTI; prolonged retention >24h risks Toxic Shock Syndrome).

Cervical Cap (Dumas / Vimule).

Chemical Barriers (Vaginal Spermicides): Cream, jelly, foam tablets (Contab), or Vaginal Contraceptive Sponge (Today — polyurethane sponge impregnated with 1 g of Nonoxynol-9, kept for 6 hours post-coitus). Nonoxynol-9 is a surface-active detergent that disrupts the sperm cell membrane. (Note: Frequent use of Nonoxynol-9 causes vaginal mucosal micro-ulcerations and does NOT protect against HIV).

Advantages (Contraceptive & Non-Contraceptive Benefits) of Barrier Methods (Especially Condoms) ([KU23,RGU]):

No systemic or hormonal side effects and no medical contraindications (except rare latex allergy, where polyurethane is used).

Cheaper, easily available without prescription, easy to carry, and simple to use.

Protection Against Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs): Protects against N. gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Trichomonas, HSV-2, Syphilis, Hepatitis B, HPV, and HIV/AIDS.

Protection Against Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) and its sequelae (tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy).

Protection Against Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CIN) and Invasive Cervical Cancer (by blocking HPV transmission).

Special Therapeutic Uses: Backup contraception during the first 3 months (20 ejaculations) after vasectomy, missed oral pills, during metronidazole therapy for trichomoniasis, and for 3–6 months in immunological infertility (to reduce antisperm antibody titers).

subject: gynecology
title: 19.3 Intrauterine Contraceptive Devices (IUCDs) & Missing Thread
text:
(Covers: SE 2 [KU25]; SA 2 [KU24], 5 [KU24,21,19,16], 6 [KU24,17], 11, 12, 23, 25–28, 35 [KU,RGU,TU]; One-word answer 1 [KU24])

A. Types, Structure ([Draw and label]) & Lifespan of Modern Open Medicated IUCDs

(First-generation non-medicated Lippes loop is obsolete).

Second-Generation Copper IUCDs:

Copper-T 200B (Cu-T 200B): T-shaped polyethylene frame (36 mm vertical stem, 32 mm horizontal cross-arm) impregnated with barium sulfate (for radio-opacity), with  surface area of fine copper wire (120–124 mg Cu) wound around the vertical stem (releasing ~50  Cu/day), and a ball at the bottom of the vertical stem to prevent cervical perforation, to which two monofilament polyethylene threads are tied. Lifespan: 3–4 years.

Multiload Cu-250:  copper wire on vertical stem; Lifespan: 3 years.

Third-Generation IUCDs (Long-Acting Reversible Contraception [LARC]):

Copper-T 380A (Cu-T 380A — Supplied free by Govt. of India): T-shaped barium-impregnated polyethylene frame with  total exposed copper surface area—consisting of  of copper wire wound around the vertical stem PLUS two solid copper sleeves of  each on the two horizontal arms ([Draw and label] — Fig. 29.2C). Lifespan: 10 years. Failure rate: 0.8 HWY.

Multiload Cu-375 ([Draw and label] — Fig. 29.2B): Curved flexible polyethylene vertical stem with  of copper wire wound around the stem and two flexible curved serrated side-arms with spurs/barbs that resist expulsion during uterine contractions. Inserted directly with an applicator without a plunger. Lifespan: 5 years.

Frameless IUCD (GyneFix): 6 copper sleeves () threaded on a polypropylene suture anchored 1 cm into the fundal myometrium ([Fig. 29.15]).

Hormone-Releasing IUCD — Levonorgestrel Intrauterine System (LNG-IUS / Mirena) ([KU24,21,20,19,16]):

Structure & Dosage ([KU24]): T-shaped polyethylene frame (32 mm  32 mm) with a polydimethylsiloxane collar reservoir around the vertical stem containing 52 mg of Levonorgestrel, which is released at a constant rate of 20  [Fig. 29.2D]. Effective lifespan: 5 years (up to 7 years). Failure rate: 0.1–0.2 HWY (comparable to surgical sterilization!). (A smaller version, FibroPlant-LNG, releases 14  for perimenopausal women).

B. Mechanism of Action of IUCDs

(IUCDs act locally inside the uterine cavity and do NOT inhibit ovulation [except partial inhibition in LNG-IUS]):

Common to All IUCDs: Induce a sterile foreign-body inflammatory reaction in the endometrium  infiltration of leukocytes and macrophages (which phagocytose spermatozoa and liberate gametotoxic prostaglandins and cytokines), altered tubal motility, and asynchronous endometrium preventing implantation.

Copper-Specific Action: Ionized copper () is directly spermicidal/spermotoxic (inhibits sperm motility, capacitation, and survival) and interferes with endometrial enzymes, glycogen metabolism, and estrogen uptake, preventing fertilization and blastocyst implantation.

LNG-IUS Specific Action: High local endometrial concentration of levonorgestrel causes (i) uniform endometrial glandular atrophy, stromal decidualization, and downregulation of estrogen/progesterone receptors (preventing implantation and reducing menstrual blood loss by 90–97%), (ii) scanty, thick, viscid cervical mucus (blocking sperm penetration), and (iii) anovulation in 15–20% of cycles.

C. Indications (Including Non-Contraceptive Uses of LNG-IUS), Contraindications & Complications

Contraceptive & Non-Contraceptive Indications of LNG-IUS (Mirena) ([KU24,21,20,19,16]):

Long-term reversible contraception (5 years; Pearl Index 0.1 HWY).

First-line medical management of Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (HMB) / DUB (“medical hysterectomy”).

Dysmenorrhoea and Pelvic Pain in Endometriosis (especially rectovaginal endometriosis) and Adenomyosis.

Fibroid uterus (with menorrhagia, if uterine size <12 weeks and cavity is regular).

Treatment of Endometrial Hyperplasia (without atypia) and endometrial protection during Estrogen Replacement Therapy (HRT) or Tamoxifen therapy.

Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS). (Note: Non-contraceptive uses of Copper-T: (1) Emergency contraception within 5 days of unprotected coitus [most effective EC], and (2) Prevention of recurrent intrauterine adhesions after hysteroscopic adhesiolysis in Asherman’s syndrome).

Contraindications to IUCD Insertion ([TU]):

Suspected or confirmed pregnancy.

Active PID, puerperal sepsis, septic abortion, or STIs (current or within the past 3 months).

Undiagnosed abnormal genital tract bleeding.

Distortion of the uterine cavity (submucous fibroid, congenital uterine septum, bicornuate uterus).

Malignant gestational trophoblastic disease (GTN) or cervical/endometrial malignancy.

Previous history of ectopic pregnancy or severe dysmenorrhoea/anemia (for Cu-IUCD; LNG-IUS is beneficial here).

Specific to Cu-T: Wilson’s disease and Copper allergy. Specific to LNG-IUS: Active liver disease/tumor and current breast cancer.

Complications of IUCDs ([KU21,RGU,TU]):

Immediate (At Insertion): Cramping uterine pain, vasovagal syncopal attack, and uterine perforation (1 in 1000).

Remote / Late:

Abnormal Menstrual Bleeding: Menorrhagia and intermenstrual spotting with Copper IUCDs (leads to anemia; treated with Iron + Tranexamic acid / Mefenamic acid). With LNG-IUS, irregular spotting occurs in the first 3–6 months followed by oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea (20–30%) and functional follicular ovarian cysts.

Dysmenorrhoea & Pelvic Pain (due to myometrial distension or partial expulsion).

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID): Risk is highest in the first 3–4 weeks after insertion due to introduction of cervicovaginal bacteria (Chlamydia, Actinomyces israelii).

Spontaneous Expulsion (~5%): Most common during menstruation in the first 3 months.

Uterine Perforation & Translocation into the peritoneal cavity.

Accidental Pregnancy & Ectopic Pregnancy: Failure rate is 0.8–2 HWY for Cu-T and 0.1 HWY for LNG-IUS. If pregnancy occurs with an IUCD in situ, the relative risk of ectopic pregnancy is increased (3–5% of pregnancies).

D. Causes & Management of Missing Cu-T Thread ([KU25,RGU,TU])

Five Possibilities (Causes) When the IUCD Thread Cannot Be Felt/Seen at the External Os:

Threads are coiled/drawn up inside the cervical canal or uterine cavity (device is in situ in normal position).

Threads are torn off while the device remains inside the uterus.

Unnoticed spontaneous expulsion of the device outside the genital tract (usually during heavy menses).

Perforation of the uterine wall and translocation of the device into the peritoneal cavity (or broad ligament).

Pregnancy (the growing gravid uterus pulls the threads up into the uterine cavity).

Stepwise Diagnostic Evaluation:

Exclude Pregnancy First by urine -hCG test.

Explore the Endocervical Canal: Gently insert a cytobrush or narrow Spencer-Wells artery forceps into the cervical canal to tease out coiled threads.

Pelvic Ultrasonography (TAS & TVS — Investigation of First Choice): Accurately localizes whether the IUCD is inside the uterine cavity ([Fig. 29.5]) or outside in the pelvis (and confirms/rules out intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy).

Plain X-ray of Pelvis & Abdomen (AP and Lateral Views) after Passing a Metal Uterine Sound into the Uterine Cavity: If USG fails to locate the device in the uterus, X-ray is taken to differentiate unnoticed expulsion (no IUCD shadow seen on X-ray) from perforation into the peritoneal cavity (IUCD shadow is seen lying separate and away from the uterine sound on AP and Lateral views [Fig. 29.7]).

Diagnostic Hysteroscopy: Directly visualizes an intrauterine device with coiled/detached threads ([Fig. 29.6]).

Management:

Case 1: Pregnancy is Positive:

If threads become visible/accessible: Gently pull the threads to remove the IUCD (reduces risks of miscarriage, chorioamnionitis, PROM, and preterm labor).

If threads are NOT visible: Leave the IUCD undisturbed after counseling; it lies extra-amniotically and will be expelled with the placenta at delivery (no teratogenic risk).

Case 2: Non-Pregnant + IUCD is Inside the Uterine Cavity:

If the woman wishes to continue contraception and the lifespan is not over, reassure her and leave it in situ.

If she wants removal or replacement, remove it under paracervical block/sedation using Hysteroscopy and grasping forceps under direct vision (best method), an IUCD Retrieving Hook (Loop hook), or a narrow Spencer-Wells artery forceps.

Case 3: IUCD Has Perforated Outside the Uterus into the Peritoneal Cavity:

A Copper IUCD (or LNG-IUS) MUST BE REMOVED IMMEDIATELY upon diagnosis because ionized copper provokes intense peritoneal inflammation, dense omental/bowel adhesions, and bowel perforation/obstruction.

Method of Removal: Operative Laparoscopy (preferred) or Laparotomy (if embedded in dense bowel adhesions).

subject: gynecology
title: 19.4 Hormonal Contraceptives (COCs, POP, Injectables, Implants)
text:
(Covers: SE 3 [KU24,TU], 4 [TU]; SA 10 [KU23,22,20], 16 [KU18], 21, 22, 29, 33, 34, 38–40, 43, 46 [RGU,TU]; One-word answers 3, 4, 7 [KU])

A. Classification of Hormonal Contraceptives ([TU])

Oral Steroidal Contraceptives:

Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (COCs):

Monophasic Pills: Fixed dose of Estrogen + Progestin in all 21 active tablets:

1st Generation: Ethinyl estradiol (EE)  + Norethindrone.

2nd Generation: Low-dose EE (20–35 ) + Levonorgestrel (e.g., Mala-N: EE 30  + LNG 0.15 mg; Mala-D).

3rd Generation (“Lipid-friendly”): EE (20–30 ) + Desogestrel (0.15 mg, e.g., Loette, Novelon), Gestodene, or Norgestimate (minimal androgenic activity, raises HDL).

4th Generation ([KU21]): EE (30 ) + Drospirenone (3 mg) (e.g., Yasmin — spironolactone analogue with anti-androgenic and anti-mineralocorticoid activity), Dienogest, or Nomegestrol.

Multiphasic (Triphasic) Pills (Triquilar* [TU]):* Varying low doses of EE (30/40/30 ) and LNG (0.05/0.075/0.125 mg) in 3 phases (6 + 5 + 10 days) to reduce total steroid load per cycle.

Extended / Continuous Cycle Pills: 84 active tablets + 7 placebos (“seasonal bleed” every 3 months) or 24 + 4 regimen.

Progestin-Only Pills (POP / Minipill): Levonorgestrel 30–75 , Norethisterone 350 , or Desogestrel 75  taken daily without any pill-free break.

Emergency Contraceptive Pills (see Section 19.5).

Parenteral / Long-Acting Hormonal Contraceptives:

Injectable Progestins: DMPA (Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate) and NET-EN (Norethisterone Enanthate); Combined Monthly Injectables (Cyclofem, Mesigyna).

Subdermal Implants: Implanon (Nexplanon) (single rod, 68 mg Etonogestrel for 3 years) and Norplant-II (Jadelle) (2 rods, 75 mg LNG each for 5 years).

Hormone-Releasing Vaginal Rings (NuvaRing — EE 15  + Etonogestrel 120  for 3 weeks), Transdermal Contraceptive Patch (Ortho Evra), and LNG-IUS (Mirena).

Non-Steroidal Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM): Centchroman (Ormeloxifene / Saheli / Chhaya) (30 mg twice weekly for 3 months, then once weekly).

B. Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (COCs) ([KU24,23,22,20,18])

Mechanism of Action:

Inhibition of Ovulation (Primary & Commonest Mode of Action [KU20]): Estrogen and progestin act synergistically via negative feedback on the hypothalamus to suppress GnRH pulsatility  Estrogen suppresses FSH (preventing follicular recruitment/maturation) and Progestin abolishes the mid-cycle LH surge (preventing ovulation).

Alteration of Cervical Mucus (Progestin effect): Makes cervical mucus scanty, thick, viscid, and cellular (loss of ferning and spinnbarkeit), preventing sperm penetration.

Static Endometrial Hypoplasia / Decidualization (Progestin effect): Stromal edema and glandular exhaustion/atrophy render the endometrium non-receptive to blastocyst implantation.

Altered Tubal Motility and transport of gametes.

How to Prescribe: Start on Day 1 to Day 5 of the menstrual cycle; take 1 active tablet daily at bedtime for 21 consecutive days, followed by a 7-day pill-free (or 7 iron tablets) interval during which withdrawal bleeding occurs (“3 weeks on, 1 week off”). Failure rate: 0.1 HWY.

Absolute Contraindications to COCs (WHO MEC Category 4 — Unacceptable Health Risk) ([KU24,18]):

Circulatory / Thromboembolic Diseases (Past or Present):

History of or current Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) or Pulmonary Embolism (VTE).

Known thrombogenic mutations (Factor V Leiden, Protein C/S or Antithrombin deficiency).

Ischemic Heart Disease, Stroke (CVA), or Complicated Valvular Heart Disease (pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation, bacterial endocarditis).

Severe Hypertension ( 160/100 mm Hg) or Diabetes mellitus with vascular complications (nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy) or > 20 years duration.

Migraine with focal neurological aura (at any age).

Age  35 years AND Heavy Smoker ( 15 cigarettes/day).

Major surgery with prolonged immobilization (stop COCs 4–6 weeks prior to major elective surgery).

Liver Diseases: Active viral hepatitis, severe decompensated cirrhosis, benign hepatic adenoma, or hepatocellular carcinoma.

Estrogen-Dependent Neoplasms: Current or past Carcinoma of the Breast.

Pregnancy and Breastfeeding < 6 weeks postpartum (Category 3 from 6 weeks to 6 months postpartum).

Undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding (Relative / Category 3).

Non-Contraceptive Health Benefits of COCs ([KU24,23,22,20]):

Improvement of Menstrual Disorders:

Regularizes menstrual cycles.

Reduces Menorrhagia / Heavy Menstrual Bleeding by 50%  prevents iron-deficiency anemia.

Relieves Primary Spasmodic Dysmenorrhoea (by 40–60%), Mittelschmerz (ovular pain), and Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS / PMDD).

Protection Against Gynecological & Systemic Diseases:

Reduces Acute PID by 50% (due to thick cervical mucus plug and shorter menstrual flow).

Prevents Ectopic Pregnancy (by inhibiting ovulation).

Therapeutic and protective in Pelvic Endometriosis, Adenomyosis, and Uterine Fibroids.

Reduces Functional Ovarian Cysts (follicular and corpus luteum cysts).

Improves Hirsutism, Acne, and Seborrhoea in PCOS (increases hepatic SHBG and suppresses LH-driven ovarian androgen synthesis).

Reduces Benign Fibrocystic Breast Disease and Fibroadenoma.

Increases Bone Mineral Density (BMD) and protects against osteoporotic fractures, rheumatoid arthritis, and autoimmune thyroid disease.

Protection Against Malignancies (Persists for 10–15 years after stopping):

50% reduction in Epithelial Ovarian Cancer.

50% reduction in Endometrial Adenocarcinoma.

40% reduction in Colorectal Cancer.

Adverse / Side Effects of COCs ([KU24]):

Minor Side Effects (Usually subside within 3 cycles): Nausea, vomiting, headache, chloasma (estrogen); breast tenderness/mastalgia, weight gain, acne, leg cramps, reduced libido, and leucorrhoea.

Menstrual Side Effects: Breakthrough bleeding (BTB) and spotting (due to subthreshold estrogen, missed pills, or enzyme-inducing drugs like rifampicin/phenytoin), hypomenorrhoea, or post-pill amenorrhoea (< 1%).

Major / Serious Complications (Rare with modern low-dose pills):

Venous Thromboembolism (DVT & Pulmonary Embolism): 3–4 fold relative risk (15–30 per 100,000 women-years vs. 5 in non-users and 60 in pregnancy) due to estrogen-induced increase in clotting factors (Fibrinogen, Factors II, VII, IX, X) and decreased antithrombin III.

Arterial Thrombosis (Myocardial Infarction & Stroke): Seen mainly in women > 35 years who smoke or have hypertension.

Hypertension (due to estrogen-induced hepatic synthesis of angiotensinogen).

Cholestatic Jaundice and Cholelithiasis (Gallstones).

Metabolic: Mild insulin resistance (impaired glucose tolerance) and altered lipid profile (progestin lowers HDL; estrogen raises HDL and triglycerides).

Neoplasia: Slight increase in relative risk of Cervical Cancer (RR 1.1) with > 5 years use (due to sexual behavior/HPV exposure — requires regular Pap screening); no significant increase in breast cancer with low-dose pills.

(ACHES Warning Signs for Immediate Withdrawal of Pill: Abdominal pain [severe], Chest pain/dyspnea, Headache [severe migraine], Eye problems [visual loss/blurring], Severe leg pain/swelling).

C. Injectable Contraceptives (DMPA & NET-EN) ([KU22,TU,RGU])

Preparations & Regimens:

DMPA (Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate — Depo-Provera / Antara under Govt. of India): 150 mg deep IM injection (in deltoid or gluteus muscle using Z-tract technique without massaging) given every 3 months (12 weeks) (or Depo-SubQ Provera 104 mg SC every 3 months).

NET-EN (Norethisterone Enanthate — Noristerat): 200 mg deep IM every 2 months (8 weeks).

Timing: First injection given within the first 5 days of menstruation, immediately post-abortion, or at 6 weeks postpartum in lactating women.

Mechanism of Action: (1) Inhibits ovulation by suppressing the mid-cycle GnRH/LH surge, (2) Makes cervical mucus thick and viscid, and (3) Induces endometrial atrophy.

Advantages:

Extremely high efficacy (Failure rate: 0.3 HWY), independent of daily user compliance or coitus.

Completely free of estrogen-related cardiovascular/thromboembolic side effects.

Safe during lactation (does not reduce breast milk volume; may increase it).

Non-contraceptive benefits: Reduces menorrhagia, iron-deficiency anemia, dysmenorrhoea, endometriosis pain, PID, ectopic pregnancy, endometrial cancer, ovarian cancer, and sickle-cell crises.

Disadvantages / Side Effects:

Menstrual Irregularities (Most common reason for discontinuation): Irregular unpredictable spotting/bleeding initially, followed by secondary amenorrhoea in 50% at 1 year and 70% at 2 years (harmless; requires pre-injection counseling).

Delayed Return of Fertility: Takes 4 to 8 months (up to 10 months) after the last DMPA injection for ovulation and fertility to return.

Weight gain (1–2 kg/year), headache, and mood changes.

Reversible reduction in Bone Mineral Density (BMD) with long-term use (> 2 years).

subject: gynecology
title: 19.5 Emergency (Postcoital) Contraception (EC)
text:
(Covers: SA 1 [KU25,24,16,RGU,TU], 37 [RGU]; One-word answer 2 [KU24])

Definition: Contraceptive measures used after an act of unprotected sexual intercourse to prevent an unwanted pregnancy (“Interception” — acts before implantation; cannot disrupt an already implanted pregnancy).

Indications: (1) Unplanned unprotected intercourse, (2) Condom rupture or slippage, (3) Missed oral contraceptive pills (> 2 COCs or > 3 hours late for POP), (4) Sexual assault / Rape, and (5) Expulsion of IUCD or late DMPA injection.

Regimens / Methods of Emergency Contraception (Table 29.10):

[[TABLE:gynecology-tbl-008]]

Mechanism of Action:

Hormonal EC (LNG / Yuzpe) & Ulipristal: Delays or inhibits ovulation (if taken in the follicular phase before the LH peak) and interferes with corpus luteum function.

Mifepristone & Copper IUCD: Inhibit ovulation and render the endometrium unfavorable for blastocyst implantation (plus direct gametotoxic action of copper ions).

subject: gynecology
title: 19.6 Permanent Surgical Sterilization (Tubectomy, Laparoscopic Ligation & Vasectomy)
text:
(Covers: SA 4, 7 [KU24,17], 13 [KU20], 14 [KU19], 15 [KU19,RGU,TU], 17 [KU17,TU], 18 [KU16], 19, 20 [KU15,TU], 31, 36, 45, 47 [RGU,TU])

Female Sterilization (Tubal Occlusion / Tubectomy)

Timing of Operation: (1) Puerperal (24–48 hours after vaginal delivery — technically easiest as fundus is subumbilical), (2) Interval (in the proliferative phase right after menses, > 6 weeks after delivery), (3) Concurrent with MTP, or (4) During Cesarean Section.

Site of Selection on the Fallopian Tube & Its Significance ([KU20]):

Selected Site: The Isthmus (or junction of the proximal and middle third of the tube), leaving at least 1.5–2 cm of intact tube adjacent to the uterine cornu.

Significance:

The isthmus has a narrow, uniform lumen and thick muscular wall, ensuring secure occlusion with the lowest failure rate.

Leaving 1.5–2 cm near the cornu avoids uteroperitoneal fistula formation (endometriosis/ectopic pregnancy).

Destroying only a small segment at the isthmus preserves maximum healthy tubal length (> 4–6 cm) and intact fimbriae, giving the highest success rate (75–82%) for microsurgical isthmic-isthmic tubotubal reanastomosis (reversal) if the woman regrets sterilization later (e.g., after death of a child).

Approaches & Methods of Tubectomy ([KU24,17]):

Abdominal Approach (Laparotomy or Minilaparotomy [“Mini-Lap” through a 1.5–2.5 cm suprapubic/subumbilical incision under local anesthesia]):

(The fallopian tube is positively identified by tracing it laterally to its fimbriated end).

Pomeroy’s Technique (Most Widely Performed): A loop of the tube at the junction of the proximal and middle third (isthmo-ampullary) is lifted with Allis/Babcock forceps  transfixed and tied at its base through an avascular window in the mesosalpinx using absorbable No. 0 chromic catgut  a 1–1.5 cm segment of the loop distal to the ligature is excised (and inspected/sent for histology). As the catgut absorbs, the two sealed cut ends retract widely apart ([Fig. 29.12A–C]). Failure rate: 0.1–0.5%.

Uchida’s Technique: Subserosal saline-adrenaline injection  muscular tube is divided and 3–5 cm excised  proximal stump is buried inside the mesosalpinx while distal stump opens into the peritoneal cavity (0% failure rate).

Irving’s Technique: Tube is divided between ligatures; the proximal cut end is buried into a tunnel on the posterior uterine myometrium ([Fig. 29.12D]; < 0.1% failure; used during CS).

Madlener’s Technique: Crushing the base of the tubal loop with an artery forceps and tying with non-absorbable silk without excising the loop ([Fig. 29.12E]; obsolete due to high 1.5–7% failure rate from fistula formation).

Kroener’s Fimbriectomy: Double ligation and excision of the fimbriated infundibular end ([Fig. 29.12F]; irreversible).

Parkland’s Technique: An avascular window is made in the mesosalpinx; the tube is tied at two points with chromic catgut and the intervening 2 cm segment is excised.

Laparoscopic Tubal Sterilization ([KU19,15,TU]):

Performed as a day-care procedure under local anesthesia + IV sedation in interval or post-MTP cases (contraindicated within 6 weeks of delivery, in severe cardiopulmonary disease, or dense abdominal adhesions).

Through a 1.25 cm subumbilical incision, pneumoperitoneum is created with a Veress needle using  gas, the operating laparoscope is introduced with the patient in  Trendelenburg position, and the tubes are occluded 2–3 cm from the uterine cornu (at the isthmus) by:

Silastic Ring (Falope / Yoon Ring): A 2.5 cm loop of the isthmus is drawn into the ring-applicator cylinder and a silicone rubber band (containing 5% barium sulfate) is slipped over the base of the loop ([Fig. 35.8]).

Filshie Clip: Titanium clip lined with silicone rubber ([Fig. 29.14]) applied across the isthmus (destroys only 4 mm of the tube  best reversibility and lowest failure rate: 0.1%).

Hulka-Clemens Spring Clip.

Bipolar Electrocoagulation (coagulates 2–3 cm of isthmus; unipolar cautery is avoided due to thermal bowel injury).

Vaginal Tubal Ligation (via posterior colpotomy) & Hysteroscopic Transcervical Sterilization (Essure nickel-titanium microcoil [Fig. 29.16], Adiana, or Quinacrine pellets).

Complications of Tubal Ligation ([RGU,TU]):

Immediate: Anesthetic hazards, mesosalpinx bleeding/hematoma, bowel/bladder/vascular injury (in laparoscopy), surgical emphysema, and wound infection.

Remote: Post-ligation syndrome (menorrhagia, pelvic pain, and cystic ovaries due to compromise of utero-ovarian vascular anastomosis in the mesosalpinx), regret, and Failure of sterilization (0.1–0.7%) (if pregnancy occurs, 30–50% are tubal ectopic pregnancies!).

B. Male Sterilization — Vasectomy & No-Scalpel Vasectomy (NSV) ([KU19,16,15,RGU,TU])

Definition: Permanent surgical contraception in the male by resecting a 1 cm segment of both vas deferens and occluding the cut ends under local anesthesia.

No-Scalpel Vasectomy (NSV — Li Shunqiang, 1991) ([KU16]):

Technique: Under local anesthesia (1% lignocaine spermatic cord block), the vas deferens is fixed subcutaneously in the midline of the upper scrotum using the three-finger technique and grasped through the skin with an extraperitoneal ringed clamp. Instead of a scalpel incision, the sharp pointed blade of a dissecting hemostat forceps punctures the skin, and both blades are spread tostretch a tiny opening (< 5 mm) and deliver the bare vas deferens. A 1 cm segment of the vas is excised after ligating both ends with 2-0 chromic catgut/silk (or thermal cautery) with fascial interposition over one end (to prevent recanalization). The procedure is repeated on the other vas through the same midline puncture. No skin sutures are required.

Advantages of NSV over Conventional Scalpel Vasectomy: (1) No scalpel incision and no skin stitches, (2) Much faster (takes < 10 minutes), (3) 10-fold lower complication rate (minimal bleeding, scrotal hematoma, or infection), and (4) Faster recovery and higher male acceptance.

Crucial Postoperative Precaution:

A man is NOT sterile immediately after vasectomy because viable spermatozoa remain stored in the distal reproductive tract (seminal vesicles and distal vas) for about 3 months (or ~20 ejaculations).

Therefore, the couple must use an additional contraceptive method (Condoms or DMPA) for 3 months (12–16 weeks) until two consecutive semen analyses (at 12 and 16 weeks) confirm complete azoospermia.

Complications of Vasectomy: Immediate: Scrotal hematoma, wound infection/epididymo-orchitis. Remote: Sperm granuloma (inflammatory nodule due to sperm leakage from the testicular end), chronic post-vasectomy scrotal pain, antisperm antibodies (50%), psychological impotence, and rare spontaneous recanalization (Failure rate: 0.15%).

subject: gynecology
title: 19.7 Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Amendment Act 2021 & Medical Abortion
text:
(Covers: MTP amendments 2021 [KU24]; Medical abortion [TU])

A. Key Provisions of the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021 (India) ([KU24])

The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 (amending the principal MTP Act, 1971; effective from September 24, 2021) introduced five landmark reforms in India [1, 2]:

[[TABLE:gynecology-tbl-009]]

B. Medical Abortion (First-Trimester Mifepristone + Misoprostol Regimen) ([TU])

Mechanism: Mifepristone (RU-486) is a 19-norsteroid competitive progesterone receptor antagonist that causes decidual necrosis, trophoblastic detachment, cervical softening, and increased myometrial prostaglandin sensitivity. Misoprostol ( analogue) induces strong myometrial contractions and cervical dilatation to expel the conceptus.

Standard Regimen (Approved up to 7–9 weeks [49–63 days] from LMP):

Day 1: Tab. Mifepristone 200 mg orally under supervision.

Day 3 (48 hours later): Tab. Misoprostol 400  orally (up to 49 days) or 800  vaginally / sublingually / buccally (up to 63 days).

Day 14: Follow-up visit with clinical exam / USG to confirm complete abortion (Success rate: 95–98%; ~1–2% require suction evacuation for incomplete abortion or ongoing pregnancy). (Give Inj. Anti-D 50–100  IM if the woman is Rh-negative).

Contraindications: Ectopic pregnancy, chronic adrenal failure, long-term corticosteroid or anticoagulant therapy, inherited porphyria, severe anemia, or Cu-IUCD in situ (remove IUCD first).

subject: gynecology
title: Chapter 19: One-Word Answers
text:
MIRENA – Dosage [KU24]: Contains 52 mg of Levonorgestrel, releasing 20  (effective for 5 years).

Name the drugs used for Emergency contraception [KU24]: Levonorgestrel (1.5 mg), Ulipristal acetate (30 mg), Mifepristone (100 mg), and Combined Oral Contraceptive pills (Yuzpe regimen).

Name of injectable contraceptive [KU22]: DMPA (Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate — 150 mg IM 3-monthly) and NET-EN (Norethisterone Enanthate — 200 mg IM 2-monthly).

Name the 4th generation progestogen pill [KU21]: Drospirenone (e.g., Yasmin: Drospirenone 3 mg + Ethinyl estradiol 30 ; also Dienogest and Nomegestrol).

Failure of contraceptive method is expressed as ______ [KU19]: Pearl Index (number of accidental pregnancies per 100 women-years [HWY] of exposure).

Failure rate of condoms [KU17]: 2–3 per 100 women-years (perfect use) to 15 per 100 women-years (typical use).

Commonest mode of action of combined oral contraceptive pill [KU20]: Inhibition of ovulation (by suppressing pituitary FSH and LH via hypothalamic negative feedback).

subject: gynecology
title: 20.1 Dilatation and Curettage (D & C)
text:
CHAPTER 20: Gynaecological Surgeries, Procedures & Investigations

(Covers: SA 2 [KU24,21,RGU], 21, 24 [RGU])

Definition: Operative dilatation of the cervical canal followed by curettage of the endometrial lining of the uterine cavity.

Indications:

Diagnostic:

Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (DUB / AUB) (unresponsive to medical therapy or in perimenopausal women  40–45 years to rule out endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma).

Postmenopausal bleeding (Fractional Curettage — see Section 12.1A).

Suspected Endometrial Tuberculosis (premenstrual curettage; one part sent in formalin for histology, one part in normal saline for AFB stain, LJ culture, and TB-PCR).

Infertility (to date secretory endometrium in luteal phase or rule out TB) and Pathological Amenorrhoea.

Prior to Fothergill’s operation or endometrial ablation.

Therapeutic (or Combined):

Incomplete or Inevitable Abortion, Hydatidiform Mole, or Placental Polyp.

Endometrial Polyp removal and Removal of a misplaced IUCD with missing threads.

Refractory acute heavy DUB.

Principal Steps: Empty bladder  General anesthesia or paracervical block + IV sedation  Lithotomy position  Bimanual examination to confirm exact size and position (anteverted vs. retroverted) of the uterus  Insert Sims’ posterior vaginal speculum  Grasp anterior lip of cervix with Allis forceps / Vulsellum  Pass olive-pointed graduated uterine sound to confirm position and uterocervical length  Dilate cervical canal progressively with Hawkin-Ambler or Hegar’s graduated dilators (using the right index finger 3 cm from the tip as a guard to prevent perforation)  Curette the uterine cavity systematically in a clockwise direction from fundus to internal os using a sharp curette (in benign lesions) or blunt curette (in suspected malignancy, choriocarcinoma, or pregnancy)  Send curettings in 10% formol-saline for histopathology.

Complications of D & C ([KU24,21,RGU]):

Immediate Complications:

Injury (Laceration) to the Cervix: Vulsellum tear of the anterior lip or lateral cervical tear by forcible dilatation (injuring the descending cervical or uterine artery, causing brisk hemorrhage or broad ligament hematoma).

Perforation of the Uterus (Most Serious Complication):

High-risk conditions: Pregnant/postabortal or puerperal/lactating soft uterus, postmenopausal atrophic uterus, pyometra, endometrial carcinoma, and acutely anteflexed/retroflexed uterus.

Recognition: Sudden loss of resistance (“give-way”), passage of the sound/dilator/curette deeper than the measured uterine length, and vaginal bleeding.

Management: Stop the procedure immediately. If perforation is caused by a uterine sound or small dilator in a clean, non-malignant uterus, manage conservatively with strict vital sign monitoring and IV antibiotics for 24–48 hours (or diagnostic laparoscopy). If perforation is caused by a large dilator, curette, or ovum forceps (risk of bowel/omental injury or internal hemorrhage) OR occurs in pyometra or endometrial malignancy, perform immediate laparotomy (to inspect bowel and repair rent or perform hysterectomy).

Injury to Intra-abdominal Viscera (Bowel / Omentum / Bladder).

Hemorrhage and Acute Pelvic Infection (Endometritis / Salpingitis / Peritonitis).

Remote (Late) Complications:

Intrauterine Adhesions / Synechiae (Asherman’s Syndrome): Due to vigorous curettage denuding the basal layer of the endometrium (especially postabortal/puerperal)  causes secondary amenorrhoea, hypomenorrhoea, and infertility.

Cervical Incompetence: Due to forcible dilatation (> 10–12 mm) damaging the internal os  causes recurrent mid-trimester miscarriage and preterm labor.

Cervical Stenosis ( hematometra).

subject: gynecology
title: 20.2 Role, Indications & Complications of Hysteroscopy in Gynecology
text:
(Covers: SA 1 [KU25,RGU,TU], 31, 33 [RGU,TU])

Definition & Principle: Endoscopic direct visualization of the endocervical canal and endometrial cavity using a rigid (4 mm,  or  fore-oblique) or flexible fiberoptic telescope passed transcervically after distending the uterine cavity with a distending medium. (Best performed in the postmenstrual / early proliferative phase when the endometrium is thin and pregnancy is excluded).

Distending Media Used:

Gas: Carbon dioxide () via a hysteroflator (flow rate < 100 mL/min, pressure < 100 mm Hg) — used only for diagnostic hysteroscopy.

Liquid Media (At intrauterine pressure of 50–70 mm Hg):

Normal Saline / Ringer’s Lactate (Electrolyte-containing): Used for diagnostic hysteroscopy and bipolar electrosurgery (Versapoint) or mechanical operative procedures.

1.5% Glycine, 3% Sorbitol, or 5% Mannitol (Electrolyte-free, non-conductive): Mandatory when using a monopolar resectoscope (TCRE / myomectomy).

Role / Indications of Hysteroscopy in Gynecology ([KU25]):

A. Diagnostic Indications:

Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB / HMB) & Postmenopausal Bleeding: Direct visualization of intracavitary polyps, submucous fibroids, endometrial hyperplasia, or endometrial carcinoma + targeted biopsy (superior to blind D&C, which misses 10–20% of focal lesions).

Infertility & Recurrent Miscarriage Workup: Evaluation of abnormal HSG filling defects, congenital uterine anomalies (septate/subseptate uterus), and intrauterine synechiae (Asherman’s syndrome).

Localization of a Misplaced IUCD with Missing Threads.

Evaluation of endocervical lesions and vascular malformations.

B. Operative (Therapeutic) Indications:

Hysteroscopic Polypectomy and Hysteroscopic Myomectomy (resection of Type 0, 1, and small Type 2 submucous fibroids [Fig. 35.13]).

Hysteroscopic Metroplasty (Septal Resection): Division of a congenital uterine septum using a resectoscope or microscissors [Fig. 35.14].

Hysteroscopic Adhesiolysis (Synechiolysis): Division of intrauterine adhesions in Asherman’s syndrome under direct vision.

Endometrial Ablation / Resection (TCRE, Rollerball, or Nd:YAG Laser ablation) for intractable DUB/HMB.

Proximal Fallopian Tube Cannulation (using a Novy catheter/guidewire through the tubal ostium to relieve proximal cornual block).

Removal of Embedded / Missing-Thread IUCD or Foreign Body.

Transcervical Tubal Sterilization (insertion of Essure microcoil [Fig. 29.16] or Adiana).

Contraindications: Active pelvic infection (PID), viable intrauterine pregnancy, invasive cervical carcinoma, and profuse active uterine bleeding.

Complications of Hysteroscopy ([RGU,TU]):

Distension Media Complications:

Fluid Overload, Pulmonary Edema, and Dilutional Hyponatremia / Hypo-osmolality (“TURP-like syndrome” with 1.5% Glycine): Intravasation of electrolyte-free glycine into open venous sinuses causes hyponatremia, ammonia toxicity, cerebral edema, seizures, and coma. (Strict fluid-balance monitoring is mandatory: warn at  500 mL glycine deficit; terminate procedure immediately if glycine deficit reaches  1000 mL [or saline deficit reaches 1500–2000 mL], check serum , and give IV Frusemide).

 Gas Embolism (causes sudden hypotension, mill-wheel murmur, and cardiac arrest).

Mechanical / Operative Complications: Uterine perforation (especially during resection at the thin cornua or fundus), cervical laceration, and intraoperative/postoperative hemorrhage (controlled by rollerball coagulation or intrauterine Foley balloon tamponade).

Electrosurgical / Laser Thermal Injury to adjacent bowel, bladder, or major pelvic vessels (if the uterine wall is perforated by an activated electrode).

Late Complications: Ascending pelvic infection (endometritis/PID), hematometra/pyometra (from cervical stenosis), and intrauterine adhesions.

subject: gynecology
title: 20.3 Laparoscopy in Gynecology
text:
(Covers: SA 3 [KU24,18,RGU], 10, 27 [RGU,TU]; One-word answer 1 [KU19])

Definition & Principle: Minimally invasive visualization and surgery of the peritoneal cavity and pelvic viscera using a fiberoptic telescope (5–10 mm) introduced through the anterior abdominal wall after creating a pneumoperitoneum with Carbon Dioxide () gas ([KU19]) (at 12–15 mm Hg intra-abdominal pressure, never exceeding 20 mm Hg) via a spring-loaded Veress needle, with the patient in 15°–30° Trendelenburg lithotomy position.

Indications of Laparoscopy in Gynecology ([KU24,18,RGU]):

A. Diagnostic Indications:

Infertility Evaluation (Gold Standard for Tubal & Peritoneal Factors): Chromopertubation (methylene blue dye spill test), detection of peritubal adhesions, minimal/mild pelvic endometriosis, PCOS, ovulation stigma, and pre-reversal assessment of tubal length after previous sterilization.

Evaluation of Acute Pelvic Pain: Differentiating unruptured/disturbed tubal ectopic pregnancy, acute salpingitis (PID), torsion/rupture of an ovarian cyst, and acute appendicitis.

Evaluation of Chronic Pelvic Pain & Secondary Dysmenorrhoea: Detects occult endometriosis and pelvic adhesions in 50% of clinically normal pelves.

Evaluation of an Undiagnosed Pelvic Mass (differentiating pedunculated subserous fibroid from ovarian tumor) and Müllerian Anomalies (differentiating septate from bicornuate uterus) or Primary Amenorrhoea (gonadal dysgenesis, MRKH, AIS).

Suspected Uterine Perforation during D&C / MTP.

Oncology: Staging and second-look evaluation in ovarian/cervical carcinoma.

B. Operative (Therapeutic) Indications:

Minor Procedures: Laparoscopic Tubal Sterilization (Falope ring / Filshie clip [Fig. 35.8]), simple adhesiolysis, aspiration of simple ovarian cysts, retrieval of translocated intraperitoneal IUCD.

Moderate Procedures:

Conservative & Radical Surgery for Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy: Linear salpingostomy [Fig. 35.4] or salpingectomy.

Endometriosis Surgery: Laser/bipolar ablation of peritoneal implants, adhesiolysis, and laparoscopic excision of ovarian endometriomas.

Ovarian Procedures: Laparoscopic Ovarian Drilling (LOD) for clomiphene-resistant PCOS [Fig. 35.6], ovarian cystectomy (dermoid/benign cysts), salpingo-oophorectomy.

Tubal Reconstructive Surgery: Salpingo-ovariolysis [Fig. 35.7], fimbrioplasty, neosalpingostomy, and tubotubal reanastomosis.

Major / Extensive Procedures: Laparoscopic Myomectomy [Fig. 35.9], LAVH / Total Laparoscopic Hysterectomy (TLH), Laparoscopic Burch colposuspension / Sacrocolpopexy, LUNA / Presacral neurectomy, and Laparoscopic Radical Hysterectomy with Pelvic/Para-aortic Lymphadenectomy.

Contraindications to Laparoscopy ([RGU] — Table 35.1):

Severe cardiopulmonary disease (cannot tolerate pneumoperitoneum or steep Trendelenburg position).

Hemodynamically unstable patient (hypovolemic shock from massive hemoperitoneum).

Generalized peritonitis, acute intestinal obstruction, or severe paralytic ileus.

Extensive dense intra-abdominal adhesions (multiple previous laparotomies — relative; requires open Hasson’s technique or left subcostal Palmer’s point entry).

Large pelvic/abdominal tumor (> 16–20 weeks size) or advanced malignancy (risk of trocar rupture and port-site metastasis).

Uncorrected coagulopathy.

Complications of Laparoscopy ([RGU,TU]):

Related to Veress Needle & Trocar Insertion / Pneumoperitoneum:

Extraperitoneal gas insufflation (subcutaneous/omental surgical emphysema).

Vascular Injury: Injury to inferior epigastric vessels (during lateral accessory port insertion — prevented by transillumination and inserting lateral to the rectus muscle) or catastrophic retroperitoneal injury to the aorta, vena cava, or common/external iliac vessels.

Visceral Perforation: Injury to stomach, small/large bowel, or urinary bladder (prevented by nasogastric decompression, preliminary bladder catheterization, and open Hasson’s entry).

 Gas Embolism and Vasovagal bradycardia/cardiac arrhythmia (from peritoneal stretching).

Electrosurgical & Laser Thermal Injuries to bowel, bladder, or ureter (often manifests 3–7 days postoperatively with peritonitis or fistula).

Anesthetic Complications: Basal lung compression, hypoventilation, hypercarbia, and respiratory acidosis.

General Surgical Complications: Hemorrhage, infection, and port-site incisional hernia (in ports  10 mm if rectus sheath is not sutured).

subject: gynecology
title: 20.4 Role of Ultrasonography in Gynecology
text:
(Covers: SA 4 [KU24,RGU,TU], 8, 38 [RGU])

Modalities:

Transabdominal Sonography (TAS): Uses a 2.5–3.5 MHz curvilinear transducer; requires a full urinary bladder as an acoustic window to displace bowel loops; best for large pelvi-abdominal masses (> 10–12 cm) like huge fibroids or ovarian cysts.

Transvaginal Sonography (TVS): Uses a high-frequency 5–8 MHz endovaginal probe placed in the vaginal fornices close to the target pelvic organs (no full bladder needed; superior image resolution within 10 cm, unaffected by abdominal obesity).

Transvaginal Color Doppler Sonography (TV-CDS): Assesses vascularity and blood-flow impedance (Pulsatility Index [PI] and Resistive Index [RI]).

Saline Infusion Sonography (SIS / Sonohysterography) & Sonohysterosalpingography: Instillation of sterile normal saline into the uterine cavity during TVS.

Clinical Applications / Role of Ultrasound in Gynecology ([KU24]):

Infertility & Assisted Reproduction (ART):

Baseline assessment of Polycystic Ovaries (PCOS) ( 12 peripheral follicles of 2–9 mm, ovarian volume > 10 ) and Antral Follicle Count (AFC) for ovarian reserve.

Serial Folliculometry & Endometrial Monitoring: Tracking dominant follicle maturation (18–20 mm preovulatory) and trilaminar endometrial thickness (8–11 mm), confirming ovulation (collapsed follicle + free fluid in POD), and timing hCG trigger/IUI.

Sonohysterosalpingography for radiation-free assessment of tubal patency.

TVS-Guided Oocyte Retrieval in IVF/ICSI programs.

Evaluation of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) & Postmenopausal Bleeding:

Measures endometrial thickness ( 4 mm in postmenopausal bleeding rules out endometrial carcinoma with > 99% NPV; > 12 mm in premenopausal suggests hyperplasia).

SIS precisely delineates intracavitary endometrial polyps, submucous fibroids, and intrauterine synechiae.

Characterization of Pelvic Masses:

Differentiates uterine fibroids (homogeneous/whorled myometrial mass with peripheral rim vascularity) from adenomyosis (“Swiss-cheese” myometrial cysts, asymmetrical posterior wall thickening, diffuse translesional vascularity) and adnexal masses (hydrosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess, endometrioma with homogeneous “ground-glass” echoes, or dermoid cyst with echogenic Rokitansky plug).

Gynecological Oncology:

Differentiates benign vs. malignant ovarian tumors (multilocular thick septae > 3 mm, solid mural nodules/papillary projections, bilaterality, ascites — used to calculate Risk of Malignancy Index [RMI]). On Color Doppler, malignant tumors show central neovascularization with low-resistance flow (PI < 1.0, RI < 0.4).

Diagnosis of Early Pregnancy Complications: Unruptured Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy (empty uterus + adnexal “bagel/tubal ring” sign + “ring of fire” on Doppler) and Hydatidiform Mole (“snow-storm” appearance + bilateral theca lutein cysts).

Congenital Müllerian Anomalies & Cryptomenorrhoea: Diagnoses hematocolpos/hematometra, absent uterus (MRKH), and septate/bicornuate uterus (3D-TVS).

Localization of Missing-Thread / Translocated IUCD and Measurement of Post-Void Residual Urine in urogynecology.

subject: gynecology
title: 20.5 Hysterectomy: Types, Indications & Complications
text:
(Covers: Essay 1e in Ch. 3 [KU24]; SA 5 [KU23,RGU], 6 [KU20], 11, 22, 25, 26, 28, 29 [RGU,TU])

A. Types & Routes of Hysterectomy ([KU23,RGU])

Abdominal Hysterectomy (Depending on Extent of Resection):

Subtotal (Supracervical) Hysterectomy: Removal of the uterine corpus above the internal os, leaving the cervix behind. (Indicated only in emergency obstetric hysterectomy or when the uterovesical/rectovaginal pouches are completely obliterated by dense endometriosis or TO mass; carries a 1% risk of stump carcinoma).

Total Abdominal Hysterectomy (TAH — Type I Extrafascial): Removal of the entire uterus (body and cervix) 

TAH with Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy (Panhysterectomy): Removal of uterus + both fallopian tubes and ovaries (done routinely in postmenopausal women or > 45 years; healthy ovaries are conserved in women < 45 years for benign disease).

Extended Hysterectomy: TAH + BSO + removal of a 1–2 cm cuff of upper vagina.

Radical Hysterectomy (Wertheim’s / Meigs’ — EORTC Types II to V): En-bloc removal of uterus, cervix, upper one-third to three-fourths of vagina, parametrium (cardinal and uterosacral ligaments), and bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy for Carcinoma Cervix (Stages IA2, IB, IIA) and Stage II Endometrial Cancer (see Section 13.2D & Table 34.5).

Vaginal Hysterectomy:

Vaginal Hysterectomy with Pelvic Floor Repair (Ward-Mayo’s Operation): For uterovaginal prolapse 

Non-Descent Vaginal Hysterectomy (NDVH): For benign uterine lesions ( 12–14 weeks size) without prolapse; offers faster recovery, less pain, shorter hospital stay, and no abdominal scar compared to TAH.

Laparoscopic Hysterectomy:

Laparoscopic-Assisted Vaginal Hysterectomy (LAVH) ([RGU,TU]): Adhesiolysis, oophorectomy, and division of round/infundibulopelvic ligaments and uterovesical peritoneum are performed laparoscopically, while uterine artery ligation, vault opening, removal, and closure are completed vaginally.

Total Laparoscopic Hysterectomy (TLH): Entire dissection including uterine artery coagulation/division and vault closure is completed laparoscopically.

B. Indications for Hysterectomy ([RGU] — Table 34.2)

Benign Lesions: Symptomatic uterine fibroids, adenomyosis, endometriosis, chronic PID / tubo-ovarian mass, refractory DUB / HMB, uterovaginal prolapse, CIN III / CIS, complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypia, and benign ovarian tumors in perimenopausal/postmenopausal women.

Malignant Lesions: Carcinoma cervix (early stages), endometrial carcinoma, uterine sarcoma, ovarian carcinoma, fallopian tube carcinoma, and chemoresistant GTN/PSTT.

Obstetrical / Traumatic: Rupture uterus, intractable atonic PPH, morbidly adherent placenta (placenta accreta), perforated septic abortion/pyometra, and hydatidiform mole in women > 35–40 years.

C. Complications of Abdominal & Vaginal Hysterectomy (Including Ward-Mayo’s Operation) ([KU24,23,20,RGU,TU])

Intraoperative Complications (Including Intraoperative Complications of Ward-Mayo’s Operation [KU20]):

Hemorrhage: From slipping of vascular pedicles (uterine, ovarian, or descending cervical arteries), lateral vaginal angles, or venous plexuses during anterior/posterior colporrhaphy dissection in Ward-Mayo’s operation.

Urinary Tract Injury:

Bladder Injury: During opening of the uterovesical fold or pushing the bladder up in vaginal hysterectomy/anterior colporrhaphy (especially with previous CS scar). If recognized on table: Repair immediately in 2 layers with 2-0/3-0 Vicryl + continuous Foley drainage for 10–14 days.

Ureteric Injury (0.5–1%): At the infundibulopelvic ligament, uterine artery/cardinal ligament clamp, or vaginal vault angle (more common in abdominal than vaginal hysterectomy).

Bowel / Rectal Injury: Injury to small bowel/sigmoid during adhesiolysis in TAH, or injury to the anterior rectal wall during posterior colpoperineorrhaphy / enterocele dissection in Ward-Mayo’s operation.

Anesthetic Complications.

Immediate & Early Postoperative Complications:

Hemorrhage:

Primary / Reactionary Hemorrhage (Within 24 hours [RGU]): Occurs within 4–24 hours post-op as blood pressure rises and vasospasm relaxes, causing a slipped ligature (most commonly at the lateral vaginal vault angle or parametrial pedicle) or oozing from vaginal mucosal edges to bleed briskly (revealed P/V bleeding or concealed vault/retroperitoneal hematoma with tachycardia and hypotension). Management: Resuscitation with IV fluids/blood + immediate return to OT for exploration under anesthesia, resuturing the bleeding vessel/angle (taking care of the ureter), and tight vaginal roller-gauze pack for 24 hours (or relaparotomy if internal pedicle slipped).

Secondary Hemorrhage (Between 5th and 14th Postoperative Day): Caused by infection and sloughing of a suture line/vessel wall at the vaginal vault. Management: IV antibiotics, blood transfusion, exploration under anesthesia to evacuate clots, hemostatic figure-of-eight sutures/tight vaginal pack.

Urinary Complications: Acute retention of urine (very common after Ward-Mayo’s operation due to levator spasm, urethral edema, and vaginal pack), UTI (cystitis), or Vesicovaginal / Ureterovaginal Fistula (presenting immediately if direct tear, or 7–14 days later if ischemic sloughing).

Febrile Morbidity & Sepsis: Vault hematoma / Vault cellulitis, pelvic abscess, abdominal wound infection/dehiscence (burst abdomen on Day 7–10), or respiratory atelectasis/pneumonia.

Gastrointestinal Dysfunction: Paralytic ileus (within 48–72h; painless distension, absent bowel sounds) vs. Mechanical intestinal obstruction (Day 5–7; colicky pain, exaggerated peristaltic rushes, air-fluid levels on X-ray).

Venous Thromboembolism: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and Pulmonary Embolism (prevented by early ambulation, compression stockings, and prophylactic LMWH).

Remote (Late) Complications:

Vault Granulation (presents with postcoital spotting/discharge; treated by cauterization with silver nitrate or copper sulfate).

Secondary Vault Prolapse & Enterocele (more common after Ward-Mayo’s vaginal hysterectomy if McCall culdoplasty was omitted).

Dyspareunia & Vaginal Shortening/Stenosis (following overzealous excision of vaginal mucosa in Ward-Mayo’s operation).

Residual (Trapped) Ovary Syndrome (chronic pelvic pain/dyspareunia in 1–3% when ovaries are conserved), Incisional hernia (after TAH), and Surgical menopause (if ovaries were removed).

text:
Indications of Per-Rectal (PR) Examination in Gynecology ([TU] — Book Page 107): (1) Children and adult virgins (where vaginal exam is avoided), (2) Carcinoma cervix (mandatory to assess parametrial and uterosacral ligament malignant induration up to the lateral pelvic wall for staging), (3) Atresia / agenesis of the vagina (MRKH, imperforate hymen with hematocolpos), (4) To differentiate Rectocele from Enterocele, (5) To corroborate findings in the Pouch of Douglas (endometriotic nodules, pelvic abscess), and (6) Painful vaginismus or rectal symptoms.

(For Conization of Cervix, see Sections 13.1C & 34.1; for Radiotherapy, Brachytherapy, Chemoradiation & Radiation Complications, see Section 13.2D & Table 30.2 on Book Page 508; for Lasers in Gynecology, see Table 9.8 on Book Page 123; for Day-Care Surgery & Preoperative Workup, see Book Pages 580–582).

subject: gynecology
title: 21.1 Ectopic Pregnancy (Types, Medical Management & Spiegelberg’s Criteria)
text:
CHAPTER 21: Miscellaneous (Ectopic Pregnancy, Spiegelberg Criteria, ASHA, Mastalgia)

(Covers: One-word answers / Short questions 1–6 [KU25,23,21,18,16,RGU])

Types (Sites) of Ectopic Pregnancy ([KU16]):

A. Extrauterine (98.5%):

Fallopian Tube (95–97% — Commonest): Ampulla (55–70% — commonest overall), Isthmus (20–25%), Infundibulum/Fimbrial (10%), and Interstitial/Cornual (2%).

Ovarian (0.5–1%).

Abdominal / Peritoneal (1%) (Primary or Secondary).

Broad Ligament (Intraligamentary).

B. Uterine (Abnormal Sites — 1.5%): Cervical, Angular, Cornual (Rudimentary horn of bicornuate uterus), and Cesarean Scar Pregnancy.

Drug Used for Medical Management of Unruptured Ectopic Pregnancy ([KU25]):

Drug of Choice: Systemic Methotrexate (folic acid antagonist that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase in rapidly dividing trophoblasts).

Selection Criteria: Hemodynamically stable patient, unruptured sac < 3.5–4 cm, absent fetal cardiac activity, and serum -hCG < 3000–5000 mIU/mL.

Single-Dose Regimen: Inj. Methotrexate  IM on Day 1; measure serum -hCG on Day 4 and Day 7 (a  15% drop between Day 4 and Day 7 indicates success; if < 15% drop, repeat a second dose). (Other medical agents injected locally under USG/laparoscopy: KCl, Mifepristone, Hyperosmolar glucose, or ).

Spiegelberg’s Criteria for Diagnosis of Primary Ovarian Pregnancy ([KU23,18]):

Spiegelberg’s 4 Criteria (1878) are used to confirm the diagnosis of Primary Ovarian Ectopic Pregnancy:

The fallopian tube on the affected side must be intact and separate from the ovary (including the fimbria ovarica).

The gestation sac must occupy the normal anatomical position of the ovary.

The gestation sac must be connected to the uterus by the ovarian ligament.

Definite ovarian tissue must be demonstrated histologically in the wall of the gestation sac.

Health Assistant / Worker at Village Level ([KU21]): ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) (1 per 1000 rural population under NHM) and ANM (Auxiliary Nurse Midwife) at the Sub-Centre level.

Mastalgia ([RGU] — Book Page 563): Breast pain, classified as Cyclic (premenstrual breast swelling and nodularity in fibrocystic breast disease/PMS), Non-cyclic, or Extramammary (chest wall Tietze’s syndrome). Evaluated by Clinical Breast Examination + USG/Mammography (> 35 years) to exclude malignancy; treated with reassurance, well-supporting brassière, restriction of methylxanthines/dietary fat, Evening primrose oil, Vitamin E, NSAIDs, Danazol (100–200 mg/day), Tamoxifen (10 mg/day in luteal phase), or Bromocriptine (2.5 mg/day).

subject: gynecology
title: S1. Clinical Anatomy, Vessels, Nerves & Embryology (Chapters 1, 2 & 3)
text:
SUPPLEMENTARY NOTES [COVERING REMAINING TOPICS IN TEXTBOOK]

SUPPLEMENTARY MASTER NOTES: Non-UQ Textbook Topics (DC Dutta, 6th Ed.)

(These supplementary notes cover all remaining topics in DC Dutta’s Textbook of Gynecology that were not asked in previous University Question [UQ] papers, ensuring 100% textbook coverage for any surprise Short Essay, Short Note, or Viva/OSCE question. Total length: ~20 formatted pages).

1. Pouch of Douglas (Rectouterine Cul-de-sac) (Book p. 20)

Boundaries: Anteriorly: Peritoneum covering supravaginal cervix, posterior vaginal fornix, and upper one-third of posterior vaginal wall; Posteriorly: Peritoneum covering anterior surface of rectum; Laterally: Uterosacral folds of peritoneum; Floor: Reflection of peritoneum 6–7 cm above the anal orifice (above the rectovaginal septum).

Surgical & Clinical Importance:

Most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity  pus (pelvic abscess) or blood (pelvic hematocele in ruptured ectopic) gravitates here.

Herniation of the pouch through the posterior fornix produces an Enterocele.

Diagnostic/therapeutic access route for Culdocentesis, Posterior colpotomy (drainage of pelvic abscess), and vaginal tubal ligation.

Palpation of nodules in the POD is a classic sign of pelvic endometriosis, ovarian malignancy, or genital tuberculosis.

2. Broad Ligament & Round Ligament (Book p. 21, 23)

Four Parts of Broad Ligament: (1) Infundibulopelvic ligament (suspensory ligament of ovary): Connects infundibulum to lateral pelvic wall; contains ovarian vessels, nerves, and lymphatics (no ovary). (2) Mesovarium: Attaches anterior border of ovary to posterior leaf of broad ligament. (3) Mesosalpinx: Between fallopian tube and ovarian attachment; contains utero-ovarian anastomotic vessels and Wolffian remnants (epoophoron, paroophoron, Gartner’s duct). (4) Mesometrium: Below mesosalpinx along lateral uterine border; base contains the ureter, uterine artery, Mackenrodt’s ligament, and Frankenhauser’s plexus.

Round Ligament: Paired fibromuscular bands (10–12 cm long) attached to the uterine cornu (anteroinferior to the fallopian tube), coursing through the inguinal canal to terminate in the anterior third of the labium majus.

Embryology: Homologous to the gubernaculum testis (together with the ovarian ligament). A patent peritoneal pouch accompanying it into the inguinal canal is the Canal of Nuck (analogous to processus vaginalis; persistence causes a Cyst/Hydrocele of the Canal of Nuck or inguinolabial hernia).

Clinical importance: Lymphatics from the uterine fundus/cornu drain along it to the superficial inguinal nodes; surgically plicated in ventrosuspension (Gilliam’s operation) for retroverted uterus.

3. Nerve Supply of Internal Genital Organs & Collateral Circulation (Book p. 31–33)

Autonomic Innervation:

Sympathetic: Motor fibers from ; Sensory fibers from  (via superior hypogastric plexus / “presacral nerve” in front of L5 vertebra  right and left hypogastric nerves). (Note: Tube and ovary sensory fibers travel via the ovarian plexus to , so presacral neurectomy relieves central uterine pain but NOT adnexal pain).

Parasympathetic: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes, ) join the hypogastric nerves posterolateral to the cervix to form the Pelvic Plexus (Inferior Hypogastric / Frankenhauser’s Plexus). Radical hysterectomy damages this sacral connection, causing postoperative bladder atony.

Collateral Circulation After Internal Iliac Artery Ligation (Book p. 33):

Lumbar artery (from aorta)  Iliolumbar artery

Middle sacral artery (from aorta)  Lateral sacral artery

Superior rectal artery (from inferior mesenteric)  Middle rectal artery

Ovarian artery (from aorta)  Uterine artery
