subject: gynecology
title: S2. Reproductive Endocrinology, Menstruation & Diagnostics (Chapters 7, 8, 9 & 31)
text:
1. Ovarian Reserve & Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) (Book p. 76, 528–529)

Definition: Ovarian reserve denotes the quantity and quality of the primordial follicular pool remaining in the ovaries. Age is the single strongest determinant (oocytes peak at 6–7 million at 20 weeks gestation  2 million at birth  4,00,000 at puberty  ~400 ovulate in reproductive life).

Tests for Diminished Ovarian Reserve (DOR):

Cycle Day-3 Serum FSH: > 10–15 IU/L indicates poor ovarian reserve.

Cycle Day-3 Serum Estradiol (): > 60–80 pg/mL (premature follicular recruitment).

Serum Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH): Secreted by granulosa cells of preantral and small antral follicles (<6 mm). Reflects the size of the growing follicular pool independent of the menstrual cycle day; low AMH (0.2–0.7 ng/mL) indicates poor ovarian reserve.

Antral Follicle Count (AFC) on TVS: Total number of 2–10 mm follicles in both ovaries; low count (<4–6) predicts poor IVF response.

Clomiphene Citrate Challenge Test (CCCT): Giving CC 100 mg from D5–D9; elevated FSH on D10 indicates DOR.

Basal Serum Inhibin B (<40 pg/mL) and Ovarian Volume (<3 ).

2. Luteal-Placental Shift vs. Luteal-Follicular Shift & Postponement of Menses (Book p. 89, 93, 95)

Luteal-Placental Shift: The physiological transition of progesterone production from the corpus luteum of pregnancy to the syncytiotrophoblast of the placenta, occurring between 7 and 10 weeks of gestation.

Luteal-Follicular Shift: The transition period from the demise of the corpus luteum (falling , progesterone, and inhibin A) to the selection of the dominant follicle for the next cycle, driven by the intercycle rise in FSH starting 2 days before menses.

Artificial Postponement of Menstruation: Achieved by giving Norethisterone 5 mg orally twice/thrice daily OR Combined Oral Contraceptive pills (1–2 tablets daily) started at least 3–6 days before the expected date of menses and continued until the event is over. Withdrawal bleeding occurs 48–72 hours after stopping the drug.

3. Cytohormonal Study & Maturation Index (MI) (Table 9.4, Book p. 113–114)

Site of Smear: Scraped lightly from the upper one-third of the lateral vaginal wall (most hormone-sensitive area).

Maturation Index (MI): Relative percentage of Parabasal / Intermediate / Superficial squamous cells per 100 cells counted, written from left to right:

At Birth: 0 / 95 / 5 (maternal estrogen, progesterone & corticoids).

Childhood: 80 / 20 / 0 (shift to left — absence of sex steroids).

Reproductive Preovulatory (Estrogen dominance): 0 / 40 / 60 (shift to right — discrete eosinophilic superficial cornified cells with pyknotic nuclei; clean background).

Reproductive Mid-Secretory (Progesterone dominance): 0 / 70 / 30 (Midzone shift — basophilic intermediate navicular cells with folded edges in clusters; dirty background).

Pregnancy: 0 / 95 / 5 (marked navicular cell dominance).

Postpartum / Postmenopausal (Atrophic): 100 / 0 / 0 or 10 / 85 / 5 (parabasal dominance due to estrogen lack).

4. Culdocentesis (Book p. 120)

Definition: Transvaginal needle aspiration of peritoneal fluid from the Pouch of Douglas (cul-de-sac).

Indications: (1) Suspected disturbed ectopic pregnancy / hemoperitoneum, (2) Suspected pelvic abscess.

Procedure: In lithotomy position under sedation/local anesthesia, the posterior vaginal wall is retracted with Sims’ speculum and the posterior lip of the cervix is held with a vulsellum. An 18-gauge spinal needle fitted to a syringe is inserted 1 cm below the posterior cervicovaginal junction in the midline to a depth of 2 cm and aspirated:

Unclotted blood  confirms intraperitoneal hemorrhage (disturbed ectopic).

Pus  confirms pelvic abscess (proceed to posterior colpotomy).

5. Advanced Imaging (CT, MRI, PET) & Lasers in Gynecology (Book p. 118–119, 123–124)

CT vs. MRI vs. FDG-PET Scan:

CT Scan: Best for detecting enlarged retroperitoneal (pelvic/para-aortic) lymph nodes (≥2 cm), omental cake, and hepatic/brain metastases; Helical CT is the investigation of choice for pulmonary embolism.

MRI (Non-ionizing radiofrequency + magnetic field; Contrast: Gadolinium): Superior soft-tissue resolution; Gold standard non-invasive modality for: (i) Myometrial invasion depth & cervical stromal extension in endometrial cancer, (ii) Parametrial invasion and tumor volume in cervical cancer, (iii) Differentiating post-radiation fibrosis from tumor recurrence, (iv) Differentiating adenomyosis (Junctional Zone >12 mm) from fibroids, and (v) Müllerian anomalies. Safe in pregnancy; contraindicated with cardiac pacemakers/cochlear implants.

FDG-PET Scan (¹⁸F-fluoro-2-deoxyglucose): Measures high metabolic glucose uptake of malignant cells; highest sensitivity (80%) and specificity for detecting occult lymph node metastasis and recurrent ovarian/cervical cancer.

Lasers in Gynecology:

Acronym: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.

Physical Properties: Monochromatic (same wavelength), Coherent (waves in phase), and Collimated (parallel non-divergent beam). Vaporizes intracellular water at 100°C with minimal lateral thermal spread.

Common Lasers & Penetration Depth: (1) CO₂ Laser (10.6 m; penetration 0.1 mm — used for CIN, VIN, VAIN, laser conization), (2) Nd:YAG Laser (1.06 m; penetration 0.6–4.2 mm — used for hysteroscopic endometrial ablation), (3) KTP-532 (0.532 m) & Argon Laser (0.5 m) — passed via flexible fiberoptics for laparoscopic endometriosis ablation and adhesiolysis.

Hazards: Corneal/retinal eye damage (protective wavelength-specific goggles mandatory), skin burns, fire hazard from spirit/paper drapes/inflammable gases, and viral DNA transmission in laser smoke plume (requires smoke evacuator).

6. Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) (Book p. 529–530)

Definition & Etiopathogenesis: Potentially life-threatening iatrogenic complication of ovulation induction (gonadotropins + hCG trigger), appearing 3–6 days after hCG administration. Driven by massive release of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF), cytokines, nitric oxide, and the ovarian renin-angiotensin system  increased capillary permeability  third-space fluid shift from intravascular compartment into peritoneal, pleural, and pericardial cavities  hypovolemia, hemoconcentration, oliguria, renal failure, and thromboembolism.

Risk Factors: Young age (<30 yrs), PCOS, high serum estradiol (>2500–3000 pg/mL), multiple follicles (>20; “necklace sign”), hCG luteal support, and pregnancy.

Classification of Severity:

Mild (10–20%): Abdominal bloating, mild pain; ovarian size < 8 cm.

Moderate (5–10%): Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, USG ascites; ovarian size 8–12 cm.

Severe (1–2%): Clinical tense ascites  hydrothorax, ARDS, hemoconcentration (Hematocrit > 45%, WBC > 15,000/), oliguria, liver dysfunction, anasarca; ovarian size > 12 cm.

Critical: Tense ascites/hydrothorax, Hematocrit > 55%, WBC > 25,000/, acute renal failure, ARDS, and thromboembolism.

Prevention: Low-dose step-up FSH protocol, metformin co-treatment in PCOS, GnRH antagonist protocol with GnRH agonist trigger (instead of hCG), “Coasting” (withholding gonadotropins and delaying hCG until  falls to safe levels), cryopreserving all embryos without fresh transfer, and using progesterone (never hCG) for luteal support.

Management: Hospitalization in moderate/severe cases; strict intake-output, daily weight, abdominal girth, hematocrit, electrolytes, RFT/LFT; IV normal saline + 25% Human Albumin (50 mL IV) to restore intravascular volume; USG-guided paracentesis for tense ascites causing respiratory distress; thromboprophylaxis (heparin); avoid pelvic exam and surgery (unless torsion or hemorrhage occurs, as ovaries are extremely friable).

subject: gynecology
title: S3. Specific Genital Infections, STIs & HIV (Chapters 10, 11 & 12)
text:
1. Pelvic Actinomycosis & Parametritis (Book p. 144, 173–175)

Pelvic Actinomycosis: Caused by Actinomyces israelii (Gram-positive branching filamentous anaerobe), strongly associated with prolonged IUCD use. Causes chronic endometritis, foul discharge, and indurated tubo-ovarian abscess containing classic yellow “Sulfur granules” on microscopy. Treatment: Removal of IUCD + high-dose Penicillin, Doxycycline, or Fluoroquinolones for 12 weeks.

Parametritis (Pelvic Cellulitis): Extraperitoneal inflammation of the pelvic cellular tissue following puerperal/postabortal cervical tear, hysterectomy vault cuff infection, or carcinoma cervix/radiotherapy.

Pathology & Spread: Pus tracks along blood vessels/ureter to point above the inguinal ligament (Poupart’s ligament), into the thigh, buttock, or perinephric space.

Clinical features: Spiky fever (102°F) 7–10 days post-event; unilateral tender, wood-hard indurated mass in the lateral fornix extending to the pelvic wall that pushes the uterus to the contralateral side (in chronic stage, fibrosis pulls the uterus to the ipsilateral side). Treatment: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics + extraperitoneal drainage if pointing above the inguinal ligament.

2. Ulcerative & Viral/Parasitic STIs (Book p. 150–158)

[[TABLE:gynecology-tbl-012]]

3. HIV / AIDS in Gynecology (Book p. 153–156)

Virus & Pathogenesis: Double-stranded RNA retrovirus (HIV-1 & HIV-2) containing core protein p24, envelope glycoproteins (gp120, gp41), and reverse transcriptase. Targets CD4+ T-lymphocytes  progressive cellular immunodeficiency. AIDS is defined when CD4+ T-cell count falls < 200 cells/L or opportunistic infections/malignancies (Kaposi’s sarcoma, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, invasive cervical cancer) develop.

Gynecological Manifestations of HIV: (1) Severe, recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, (2) Severe/recurrent Acute PID and Tubo-ovarian abscess, (3) Ulcerative STIs (Herpes, Syphilis, Chancroid), (4) High incidence and rapid progression of HPV infection, CIN, VIN, VAIN, and Invasive Cervical Cancer.

Laboratory Diagnosis of HIV ([TU]):

Screening Test: ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) for HIV-1/2 antibodies to gp120 (sensitivity >99.5%; becomes positive after the 3–12 week window period).

Confirmatory Test: Western Blot (Immunoblot) assay.

Early / Window-Period & Viral Load Monitoring Tests: HIV-RNA by RT-PCR (Gold Standard) and p24 Core Antigen assay.

Management (HAART & Post-Exposure Prophylaxis):

HAART (Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy): Combination of 2 NRTIs (Zidovudine, Lamivudine, Tenofovir) + 1 NNRTI (Efavirenz, Nevirapine) or 1 Protease Inhibitor (Ritonavir, Indinavir). Goal is undetectable viral load (<50 copies/mL) and CD4 restoration. Add Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis if CD4 <200/L.

Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for Needle-Stick Injury (Risk of transmission is 0.3%): Immediate washing with soap and water + 28-day course of Antiretroviral Therapy started within hours (Zidovudine 300 mg BID + Lamivudine 150 mg BID [+ Tenofovir/Dolutegravir in current NACO guidelines]).

subject: gynecology
title: S4. Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) & Retroversion of Uterus (Chapters 13 & 15)
text:
1. Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) & PMDD (Book p. 182–183)

Definition & ACOG Criteria: Psychoneuroendocrine disorder characterized by the cyclic appearance of physical, psychological, and behavioral symptoms during the luteal phase (last 7–10 days) of each ovulatory cycle, severe enough to disturb daily lifestyle, with a complete symptom-free interval during the follicular phase (relieved within 2–3 days of onset of menses) and not related to any organic lesion. Severe psychiatric/functional disruption is termed Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD).

Etiopathogenesis: Altered estrogen-to-progesterone ratio in the luteal phase + decreased central nervous system serotonin and -aminobutyric acid (GABA) activity + luteal withdrawal of endogenous opioids (-endorphins) + fluid retention (aldosterone/prolactin).

Symptom Clusters: (1) Water retention: Abdominal bloating, cyclical mastalgia, edema of extremities, weight gain; (2) Neuropsychiatric: Irritability, mood swings, anxiety, depression, tearfulness, tension, headache, increased appetite; (3) Behavioral: Fatigue, insomnia, dyspareunia. (Maintained on a prospective 2-month symptom diary for diagnosis).

Management:

Lifestyle & Non-Pharmacological: Reassurance, cognitive behavioral therapy, yoga, regular aerobic exercise, and restriction of salt, caffeine, alcohol, and refined sugar in the luteal phase.

First-Line Medical Therapy — SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors): Fluoxetine (20 mg PO daily) or Sertraline (50 mg/day) given continuously or during the luteal phase (dramatically relieves PMDD/PMS).

Other Supportive Drugs: Pyridoxine (Vitamin , 100 mg BID), Alprazolam (0.25 mg BID in luteal phase for anxiety), Spironolactone (25–100 mg/day in luteal phase for bloating), and Bromocriptine (2.5 mg/day) or Evening Primrose Oil for severe mastalgia.

Suppression of Ovarian Cycle: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills containing Drospirenone (3 mg) (antimineralocorticoid + antiandrogenic), Danazol (200 mg/day), or GnRH Agonists (Leuprolide/Goserelin for 3–6 months with add-back HRT). Bilateral oophorectomy + hysterectomy is the absolute last resort.

2. Retroversion of the Uterus (Book p. 198–201, 603)

Definition & Degrees: Backward turning of the long axis of the uterus in relation to the long axis of the birth canal (present as a normal variant in 15–20% of women). Degrees: 1st Degree: Fundus is vertical, pointing toward the sacral promontory; 2nd Degree: Fundus lies in the sacral hollow, but not below the internal os; 3rd Degree: Fundus lies below the level of the internal os.

Causes: Developmental (congenital persistence of fetal position with short anterior vaginal wall) OR Acquired: Puerperal (subinvolution and lax ligaments), Prolapse (mechanical traction), Tumor (fibroid pushing/pulling uterus), or Fixed Retroversion due to Pelvic Adhesions (Pelvic endometriosis, Chronic PID / TO mass).

Clinical Features:

Mobile Retroverted Uterus: Usually asymptomatic. May occasionally cause chronic premenstrual pelvic pain/backache (pelvic congestion syndrome), deep dyspareunia (penile thrust against retroflexed fundus or prolapsed ovaries in POD), or infertility (in 3rd degree, external os points forwards away from the posterior fornix seminal pool).

Pessary Test: Inserting a Hodge-Smith pessary for 3 months after manually anteverting the uterus; if backache/dyspareunia disappears and recurs upon pessary removal, the symptoms are proved to be due to retroversion.

Management: Asymptomatic mobile RV requires no treatment. Postpartum RV is prevented by regular bladder emptying, pelvic floor exercises, and lying prone for 30–60 min twice daily. Symptomatic cases with a positive pessary test or fixed RV (endometriosis/PID) are treated by Surgical Ventrosuspension (Modified Gilliam’s Operation)—extraperitoneal fixation of a loop of each round ligament to the anterior rectus sheath lateral to the rectus muscle 

or laparoscopic plication of round ligaments.

subject: gynecology
title: S5. Benign & Premalignant Lesions of Vulva, Vagina & Cervix (Chapters 17, 18 & 22)
text:
1. Non-Neoplastic Vulval Epithelial Disorders (Vulval Dermatoses / Dystrophies) (Book p. 259–263)

ISSVD Classification (2006): (1) Lichenoid pattern: Lichen sclerosus, Lichen planus; (2) Acanthotic pattern: Lichen simplex chronicus (Squamous cell hyperplasia), Psoriasis; (3) Spongiotic pattern: Atopic/Contact dermatitis; (4) Granulomatous: Crohn’s disease; (5) Vasculopathic: Aphthous ulcers, Behçet’s disease, Plasma cell (Zoon’s) vulvitis.

Lichen Sclerosus (formerly Kraurosis Vulvae):

Patient profile & Etiology: Affects postmenopausal women (or prepubertal girls); 40% are associated with autoimmune disorders (thyroiditis, pernicious anemia, diabetes mellitus).

Distribution: Bilateral, symmetrical “Figure-of-8” (keyhole) distribution encircling the vestibule (involving labia minora, inner labia majora, clitoris, perineum, and perianal skin), never extending into the vagina.

Clinical features: Intractable pruritus vulvae, soreness, dysuria, and superficial dyspareunia (due to introital stenosis and labial fusion). Skin looks thin, parchment-like, crinkled, and ivory-white with subepithelial hemorrhages (ecchymoses) from scratching.

Histology: Thin, atrophic epidermis with loss of rete ridges, hyperkeratosis, subepithelial acellular hyalinized collagen zone, and a deep band of lymphocytic infiltration.

Malignant Potential: 1–4% risk of progression to Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Vulva (biopsy is mandatory for non-responding or ulcerated/hyperkeratotic areas after 1% toluidine blue + 1% acetic acid Collins test).

Treatment: General vulval hygiene (cotton undergarments, avoid irritants/soaps) + Topical Ultrapotent Corticosteroid — 0.05% Clobetasol propionate ointment (applied nightly for 1 month, alternate nights for 2nd month, then twice weekly). Refractory cases: Topical Tacrolimus / Pimecrolimus (calcineurin inhibitors). (Note: Topical testosterone cream is no longer used).

Behçet’s Disease: Autoimmune vasculitis characterized by the classic triad of recurrent painful oral ulcers, genital (vulval) ulcers, and ocular anterior uveitis / iridocyclitis ( monoarticular arthritis). Treated with topical/systemic corticosteroids and immunomodulators.

Lipschutz Ulcer (Ulcus Vulvae Acutum): Acute, painful ulceration of the labia minora/introitus with fever and lymphadenopathy in young girls, associated with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV). Self-limiting; treated with antiseptics and analgesics.

2. Vulvodynia & Vulval Vestibulitis Syndrome (Book p. 264–265)

Vulvodynia (“Burning Vulva Syndrome”): Chronic (>3 months) unprovoked burning, stinging, or rawness of the vulva in the absence of any visible infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic lesion (neuropathic pain). Treatment: Vulval care, Tricyclic antidepressants (Amitriptyline 10–60 mg/day), Gabapentin, and psychosexual therapy (surgery is contraindicated).

Vulval Vestibulitis Syndrome (Provoked Vestibulodynia): Severe focal pain and hyperesthesia (allodynia) localized around the Bartholin’s duct openings and vestibule on light touch (cotton-swab test) or attempted vaginal entry (entry dyspareunia). Treated with topical local anesthetics (lidocaine gel), biofeedback, amitriptyline, or surgical vestibulectomy in refractory cases.

3. VIN, Extramammary Paget’s Disease & VAIN (Book p. 318–320)

Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia (VIN I, II, III): Pre-invasive cellular atypia of vulval epithelium with intact basement membrane; mean age 33 years; strongly linked to HPV-16, 18, 31, 33, smoking, and multicentric CIN (10–80%). Diagnosed by vulvoscopy (colposcopy after 5% acetic acid) and Keyes punch biopsy. Progression to invasive cancer is <10%. Treatment: Wide local excision (with 1 cm margin), CO₂ Laser vaporization, topical 5% Imiquimod or 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) cream, or Simple / Skinning Vulvectomy in multifocal postmenopausal cases.

Extramammary Paget’s Disease of the Vulva: Special intraepithelial neoplasia in postmenopausal women presenting with pruritus and a florid, eczematous, velvety red, weeping lesion with white islands (“cake-icing” effect) on the labia majora. Histology: Large, pale, mucopolysaccharide-rich Paget cells in the epidermis. Associated with an underlying apocrine gland adenocarcinoma in 10% and synchronous carcinomas of the breast, cervix, GI, or urinary tract in 30%. Treatment: Wide local excision / Simple vulvectomy.

Vaginal Intraepithelial Neoplasia (VAIN I, II, III): HPV-induced dysplasia usually in the upper one-third of the vagina; 70% coexist with or follow treatment of CIN. Asymptomatic; detected by vaginal vault Pap smear (in hysterectomized women) and colposcopy with Lugol’s iodine. Treatment: Topical 5-FU cream, CO₂ laser vaporization, or local surgical excision of the vaginal vault.

4. Cervical Ectopy (Erosion), Ectropion & Cervical Cysts (Book p. 267–270)

Cervical Ectopy (Erosion): Replacement of the stratified squamous epithelium of the ectocervix by the single-layered mucus-secreting tall columnar epithelium of the endocervix. (It is NOT an ulcer, as it is completely lined by epithelium).

Etiology: (1) Congenital (at birth due to maternal estrogen), (2) Acquired Hormonal (high estrogen states: pregnancy, combined oral contraceptive pill use).

Pathogenesis & Healing: Histologically may be flat, follicular, or papillary. Heals by epidermidization (downgrowth of squamous epithelium or squamous metaplasia of reserve cells). Obstruction of endocervical gland mouths during healing forms Nabothian follicles (retention cysts).

Clinical features: Excessive non-irritant mucoid discharge (cervical leucorrhoea), postcoital/contact bleeding (especially in pregnancy/pill users). On Speculum: Bright-red perioral zone with a sharp outer border; feels soft and granular (grating sensation), does not bleed on gentle touch (unlike friable carcinoma).

Management: Mandatory Pap smear first to exclude CIN/malignancy. Asymptomatic cases, pregnancy, and early puerperium (<12 weeks) require no treatment; stop COCs in pill users. Persistent symptomatic ectopy is treated by Thermal Cauterization (radial linear strokes 2 mm deep), Cryosurgery (freeze-thaw-freeze at –60°C to –90°C using ), or Laser vaporization.

subject: gynecology
title: S6. Rare Gynecological Malignancies (Chapter 23)
text:
1. Carcinoma of the Vulva (Book p. 333–337, 607–608)

Incidence & Etiology: Accounts for 3–5% of female genital cancers; occurs in postmenopausal women (median age 60 years). Two etiologic pathways: (1) HPV-independent (older women): Arises in chronic Lichen sclerosus / Squamous hyperplasia (50%), (2) HPV-dependent (younger women): Linked to HPV-16, 18, VIN, and smoking.

Pathology & Sites: Commonest site is Labium Majus (60%), followed by Clitoris (20%), labium minus, and Bartholin’s gland. 90% are Squamous Cell Carcinomas; 5% are Malignant Melanomas (2nd commonest; arises on clitoris/labia minora).

Lymphatic Spread (Crucial): Spreads sequentially: Superficial inguinal nodes (Sentinel nodes)  Deep inguinal/femoral nodes (Node of Cloquet)  External iliac / Pelvic nodes. Contralateral groin spread occurs in 25% due to rich midline lymphatic crossover. Depth of stromal invasion dictates nodal risk: < 1 mm = 0% nodal metastasis; 1–2 mm = 7.5%; 3–5 mm = 30%.

Clinical Features & Diagnosis: Long-standing pruritus vulvae followed by a vulval lump, fleshy ulcer with raised everted margins, local pain, bleeding, and palpable inguinal nodes. Confirmed by Wedge / Keyes Punch Biopsy.

FIGO Staging of Carcinoma Vulva (2009):

Stage I: Tumor confined to vulva/perineum with negative nodes:

Stage IA: Lesion ≤ 2 cm in size AND stromal invasion ≤ 1.0 mm (Microinvasive).

Stage IB: Lesion > 2 cm in size OR stromal invasion > 1.0 mm.

Stage II: Tumor of any size extending to adjacent perineal structures (lower 1/3 urethra, lower 1/3 vagina, or anus) with negative nodes.

Stage III: Tumor of any size with positive inguinofemoral lymph nodes (IIIA: 1 node ≥5 mm or 1–2 nodes <5 mm; IIIB: ≥2 nodes ≥5 mm or ≥3 nodes <5 mm; IIIC: Positive nodes with extracapsular spread).

Stage IV: Invades regional/distant structures (IVA: Upper 2/3 urethra/vagina, bladder/rectal mucosa, fixed to pelvic bone, or fixed/ulcerated inguinofemoral nodes; IVB: Distant metastasis including pelvic lymph nodes).

Management:

Stage IA (Microinvasive ≤ 1 mm invasion): Wide Local Excision (with 1 cm tumor-free margin); no lymphadenectomy required.

Stage IB & Stage II (Frank Invasion > 1 mm): Radical Vulvectomy with Bilateral Inguinofemoral Lymphadenectomy using the Triple-Incision Technique (one vulval incision + two separate groin incisions — dramatically reduces wound breakdown compared to the old en-bloc butterfly incision 

 (For strict lateral lesions >2 cm from midline, Radical Local Excision + Ipsilateral Groin Node Dissection / Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy using methylene blue and Technetium-99m can be done).

Positive Groin Nodes (Stage III): Pelvic lymphadenectomy is omitted in favor of Postoperative External Beam Radiotherapy (4500–5000 cGy) to the pelvis and groins.

Advanced / Inoperable (Stage IV): Preoperative Concurrent Chemoradiation (Cisplatin + 5-FU) followed by surgical resection.

Complications of Radical Vulvectomy: Wound infection/dehiscence (commonest), seroma/lymphocyst, chronic lower-limb lymphedema, DVT/PE, introital stenosis (dyspareunia), urinary stream misdirection, and femoral hernia.

2. Primary Carcinoma of the Vagina & Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma (Book p. 337–339)

Criteria for Primary Vaginal Cancer (1% of genital cancers): Primary growth is in the vagina, while the cervix and vulva are completely uninvolved. Commonest site: Upper one-third of the posterior vaginal wall. 90% are Squamous cell carcinomas (mean age 55 years).

Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma of the Vagina: Rare adenocarcinoma occurring in adolescent girls (14–20 years) with a history of in-utero exposure to Diethylstilbestrol (DES) taken by the mother in the first trimester (risk 1 in 1000; preceded by vaginal adenosis); involves the upper third of the anterior vaginal wall.

FIGO Staging: Stage I: Limited to vaginal wall; Stage II: Involves subvaginal tissue (paracolpos) but not pelvic wall; Stage III: Extends to pelvic wall; Stage IV: Involves bladder/rectal mucosa (IVA) or distant metastasis (IVB).

Treatment: Stage I (Upper third): Radical Hysterectomy + Upper Partial Vaginectomy + Bilateral Pelvic Lymphadenectomy; Stage I (Lower third): Radical Vulvectomy + Lower Vaginectomy + Bilateral Inguinofemoral Lymphadenectomy; Stages II–IV: External Beam Radiotherapy + Interstitial/Intracavitary Brachytherapy.

3. Stump Carcinoma & Carcinoma Cervix in Pregnancy (Book p. 353–354)

Cervical Stump Carcinoma: Carcinoma developing in the residual cervical stump after subtotal hysterectomy. Classified as True Stump Carcinoma (appears > 2 years after subtotal hysterectomy) or Coincidental / False Stump Carcinoma (appears < 2 years, meaning it was already present at initial surgery). Difficult to treat due to dense bladder/rectal/ureteric adhesions to the top of the stump and absence of the uterine cavity for tandem brachytherapy  treated by radical parametrectomy + stump trachelectomy (early stage) or EBRT + vaginal ovoid brachytherapy.

Carcinoma Cervix in Pregnancy (1 in 2500 pregnancies):

Diagnosis: Pap smear  Colposcopy  Biopsy (or diagnostic shallow coin/cone biopsy in 2nd trimester only if microinvasion must be ruled out).

Management: (1) Microinvasive (Stage IA1): Continue pregnancy to term  vaginal delivery  re-evaluate at 6 weeks postpartum. (2) Invasive Cancer in 1st & Early 2nd Trimester (<20 weeks): Treat immediately as in non-pregnant state without regard to fetus (Radical hysterectomy with fetus in situ for Stage IB/IIA, or EBRT which induces spontaneous abortion). (3) Late 2nd / 3rd Trimester: Delay treatment until fetal lung maturity  deliver by Classical Cesarean Section (never lower segment CS, to avoid cutting through tumor and hemorrhage/sepsis!) followed immediately by Radical Hysterectomy + Pelvic Lymphadenectomy or postpartum chemoradiation. (Stage-for-stage survival is identical to non-pregnant women).

4. Uterine Sarcoma & Sarcoma Botryoides (Book p. 367–369)

Uterine Sarcomas (3% of uterine malignancies):

GOG Classification: (1) Leiomyosarcoma (arises de novo from myometrium or <0.1% from a fibroid; malignancy criterion: >10 mitoses per 10 HPF with nuclear atypia and coagulative necrosis), (2) Endometrial Stromal Sarcoma (low-grade [endolymphatic stromal myosis] or high-grade), and (3) Malignant Mixed Müllerian Tumor (MMMT / Carcinosarcoma) — contains both carcinomatous and sarcomatous elements (homologous if native smooth muscle/stroma; heterologous if non-native cartilage, striated muscle, or bone; associated with prior pelvic irradiation). (Rare benign variants: Intravenous leiomyomatosis and Leiomyomatosis peritonealis disseminata).

Spread & Treatment: Spreads early via bloodstream (hematogenous) to lungs and liver. Treatment: TAH + BSO + Adjuvant Pelvic Radiotherapy (reduces local recurrence in MMMT/ESS) + Chemotherapy (Doxorubicin, Ifosfamide, Gemcitabine + Docetaxel).

Sarcoma Botryoides (Embryonal Rhabdomyosarcoma): Highly malignant heterologous mixed mesodermal tumor occurring in female infants and young girls (< 8 years of age), arising from the subepithelial cambium layer of the vagina or cervix. Presents with blood-stained vaginal discharge and pinkish, edematous, grape-like polypoid masses protruding from the introitus. Histologically shows loose myxomatous stroma with striated rhabdomyoblasts (“strap cells”). Treatment: Multimodality VAC Chemotherapy (Vincristine + Actinomycin-D + Cyclophosphamide) followed by conservative surgical resection.

5. Primary Fallopian Tube Carcinoma (Book p. 369–370)

Epidemiology & Pathology: Rarest female genital tract malignancy (< 0.5%; 90% of tubal cancers are secondary from ovary/endometrium). Associated with nulliparity, infertility, and BRCA1 / BRCA2 mutations. Mostly unilateral (80%), affecting the ampulla; histology is Papillary Serous Adenocarcinoma (90%).

Clinical Features — Latzko’s Classic Triad (Pathognomonic):

Intermittent profuse watery or amber/blood-stained vaginal discharge (Hydrops tubae profluens),

Colicky lower abdominal pain (relieved as the distended tube empties through the uterus), and

Pelvic / Adnexal mass (which shrinks on bimanual compression accompanied by a gush of watery fluid from the cervix). (Also suspected when postmenopausal bleeding or a positive adenocarcinoma Pap smear persists despite a negative fractional curettage!).

Treatment: Staging Laparotomy + TAH + BSO + Omentectomy + Pelvic/Para-aortic Lymphadenectomy, followed by Paclitaxel + Carboplatin chemotherapy (identical to epithelial ovarian cancer).

6. Sertoli-Leydig Cell Tumor (Arrhenoblastoma) & Other Rare Ovarian Tumors (Book p. 294, 301, 381, 386)

Sertoli-Leydig Cell Tumor (Androblastoma / Arrhenoblastoma): Rare (<0.5%) sex cord-stromal tumor occurring in young women (20–30 years); unilateral (90%) and solid. Secretes Testosterone (>200 ng/dL). Causes a two-stage clinical picture: (1) Defeminization (oligomenorrhoea  secondary amenorrhoea, atrophy of breasts and loss of female contour), followed by (2) Masculinization / Virilization (severe hirsutism, acne, temporal balding, clitoromegaly, and irreversible deepening/hoarseness of voice). Treatment: Unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in young women; TAH + BSO in older women.

Borderline Epithelial Ovarian Tumors (Tumors of Low Malignant Potential — 10–20%): Show epithelial stratification, papillary projections, nuclear atypia, and mitotic activity, but ABSENCE of ovarian stromal invasion. Occur in younger women and carry an excellent 5-year survival (~95–100%). Treated by Unilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy (if fertility desired) or TAH + BSO + Omentectomy (no adjuvant chemotherapy required unless invasive peritoneal implants are present).

subject: gynecology
title: S7. Urogynecology: Interstitial Cystitis, Overflow Incontinence & UTI (Chapter 24)
text:
1. Painful Bladder Syndrome (Interstitial Cystitis) & Urethral Syndrome (Book p. 408–409, 412)

Painful Bladder Syndrome (PBS) / Interstitial Cystitis: Chronic inflammatory condition of the bladder wall (due to defective urothelial glycosaminoglycan [GAG] mucus layer  “leaky urothelium”, mast cell activation, or autoimmunity) characterized by suprapubic pain related to bladder filling, severe urgency, frequency, and nocturia in the absence of UTI.

Diagnosis: Diagnosis of exclusion; Cystoscopy with hydrodistension reveals reduced bladder capacity, mucosal glomerulations (petechial hemorrhages), and classic Hunner’s ulcers.

Treatment: Avoid bladder irritants (caffeine, alcohol, citrus, spices); oral Pentosan polysulfate sodium (100 mg TID) (replenishes GAG layer), Amitriptyline, antihistamines (hydroxyzine); Intravesical instillation of Dimethyl Sulfoxide (DMSO), Heparin, or Botulinum toxin; and cystoscopic hydrodistension.

Urethral Syndrome: Symptoms of dysuria, frequency, and urgency with a negative urine culture (< CFU/mL). Caused by Chlamydia/Mycoplasma urethritis, hypoestrogenic atrophy, or urethral spasm. Treated with Doxycycline (14 days), local estrogen cream, and urethral dilatation/cryosurgery.

2. Overflow Incontinence & Urinary Tract Infections (UTI) in Females (Book p. 409–413)

Overflow Incontinence: Continuous dribbling of urine from an overdistended, hypotonic/atonic bladder (chronic retention due to diabetic neuropathy, multiple sclerosis, radical hysterectomy denervation, or bladder neck obstruction by impacted pelvic tumor/retroverted gravid uterus). Urodynamics: Low peak flow rate (<10 mL/sec), high post-void residual urine (>100–500 mL), large bladder capacity, and absent detrusor contraction. Treatment: Relieve obstruction + continuous indwelling Foley catheter drainage until bladder tone recovers (residual urine <50–100 mL).

UTI in Females: 20% of women experience UTI; commonest organism is Escherichia coli (80–90%), followed by Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus.

Why females are prone: Short urethra (4 cm), close proximity of external urethral meatus to contaminated vaginal introitus and anus, trauma of sexual intercourse (“honeymoon cystitis”), pregnancy stasis, catheterization, and postmenopausal hypoestrogenism.

Asymptomatic Bacteriuria: Presence of ≥10⁵ bacteria/mL of the same species in two consecutive clean-catch midstream urine specimens without symptoms (30% progress to acute pyelonephritis if untreated in pregnancy).

Sterile Pyuria (pus cells present, routine culture negative): Suspect Renal / Urinary Tract Tuberculosis (send 3 early-morning urine samples for AFB culture) or Chlamydia.

subject: gynecology
title: S8. Sexual Assault (Rape Victim), Genital Trauma & Foreign Bodies (Chapter 26)
text:
1. Examination and Management of a Rape Victim (Sexual Assault) (Book p. 434–436)

(Note: “Rape” is a legal definition, not a medical diagnosis; the doctor’s role is to provide compassionate medical care and meticulously document forensic evidence). 1. Forensic & Medicolegal Protocol: * Examine at the earliest after obtaining written informed consent from the victim (or guardian if minor/mentally challenged) in the presence of a female attendant/chaperone, maintaining strict confidentiality. * Documentation & Evidence Collection: Record detailed history (date, time, place, number of assailants, whether she bathed/douched/changed clothes); examine and photograph all extragenital (bruises, bite marks, scratch marks) and genital/perineal injuries (hymenal lacerations, fourchette/vaginal vault tears). * Samples to Collect & Seal for Forensic Lab (Chain of Custody): (1) All stained/torn undergarments and clothing, (2) Pubic hair combings, (3) Fingernail scrapings (for perpetrator DNA typing), (4) Vaginal, endocervical, rectal, and oral swabs/smears for: (i) Motile/non-motile spermatozoa (motile sperm seen up to 4 hours; non-motile sperm up to 72 hours), (ii) Prostatic Acid Phosphatase (positive even if assailant is vasectomized/azoospermic), and (iii) DNA profiling, and (5) Baseline blood for VDRL, HIV, and HBsAg + urine pregnancy test. 2. Medical & Surgical Management: * 1. Treat Local Injuries: Repair perineal, vaginal, or posterior vaginal vault lacerations under general anesthesia; tetanus toxoid prophylaxis. * 2. Prophylaxis Against STIs (CDC Regimen — Table 26.4): * Inj. Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose (for Gonorrhoea) PLUS * Cap. Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 7 days (or Azithromycin 1 g PO stat for Chlamydia) PLUS * Tab. Metronidazole 2 g PO single dose (or 400 mg BID  7 days for Trichomoniasis/BV) PLUS * Hepatitis B Vaccination (and HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis [PEP] for 28 days if assailant is high-risk/HIV positive). * 3. Prevention of Unwanted Pregnancy (Emergency Contraception): Administer Tab. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg PO single dose (or two 0.75 mg doses 12 hours apart) within 72 hours. * 4. Psychological Support (Rape Trauma Syndrome): Empathy, counseling, anxiolytics/antidepressants, and follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks (to repeat pregnancy test, VDRL, gonorrhoea culture, and HIV serology at 6, 12, and 24 weeks).

2. Vulval Hematoma, Coital Vault Rupture & Foreign Bodies (Book p. 434, 436–437)

Vulval Hematoma: Caused by straddle injury (fall astride a hard object) rupturing the rich venous plexus of the labia majora or vestibular bulb. Small non-expanding hematomas are treated conservatively with ice packs and analgesics; large or expanding hematomas require incision under anesthesia, evacuation of clots, ligation of bleeding vessels, and obliteration of dead space with mattress sutures.

Foreign Bodies in Vagina: In children: Beads, safety pins, small toys, or pebbles  cause persistent foul-smelling, blood-stained purulent discharge; diagnosed by rectal exam/vaginoscopy and removed under anesthesia. In adults: Forgotten menstrual tampons (risk of Toxic Shock Syndrome), condoms, or forgotten ring pessaries (cause ulceration, VVF, RVF, or vaginal carcinoma).

subject: gynecology
title: S9. Intersex / Disorders of Sex Development (DSD) (Chapter 27)
text:
Summary Classification & Management of Intersex (Book p. 439–448)

Female Pseudohermaphroditism (46,XX + Ovaries + Ambiguous/Virilized External Genitalia):

Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH — 21-hydroxylase deficiency): Commonest cause of ambiguous genitalia at birth. (Covered in Chapter 5, Section 5.1C).

Maternal androgen exposure during pregnancy (danazol, progestins, maternal luteoma or Sertoli-Leydig tumor — normal infant 17-OHP).

Male Pseudohermaphroditism (46,XY + Testes + Female/Ambiguous External Genitalia):

Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (Testicular Feminization — 46,XY): (Covered in Chapter 6, Section 6.1C & Table 27.1).

-Reductase Deficiency or defective testicular steroidogenesis.

Disorders of Gonadal Development:

Turner’s Syndrome (45,XO): (Covered in Chapter 5, Section 5.1C).

Pure Gonadal Dysgenesis: Normal stature, sexual infantilism, streak gonads, normal Mullerian uterus/tubes; karyotype is 46,XX or 46,XY (Swyer’s Syndrome). (Swyer’s syndrome requires bilateral gonadectomy due to 20–30% risk of dysgerminoma/gonadoblastoma, followed by cyclic Estrogen + Progestin HRT).

Mixed Gonadal Dysgenesis (45,XO / 46,XY): Asymmetric gonads—a testis on one side and a fibrous streak gonad on the other side, with ambiguous genitalia and unilateral Müllerian derivatives. Treated by gonadectomy + clitoroplasty + HRT.

True Hermaphroditism (Ovotesticular DSD): Rare condition where both ovarian tissue (with follicles) and testicular tissue (with seminiferous tubules) exist in the same individual (as bilateral ovotestes, or ovary on one side and testis on the other). Karyotype is 46,XX (70%), 46,XY, or mosaic. Presents with ambiguous genitalia at birth and gynecomastia + menstruation (50%) at puberty. Confirmed by gonadal biopsy; discordant gonadal tissue is excised based on gender assignment.

subject: gynecology
title: S10. Radiotherapy, Chemotherapy, Immunotherapy & Gene Therapy (Chapter 30)
text:
1. Principles of Radiotherapy in Gynecology (Book p. 505–510)

Physics & Mechanism of Action: High-energy ionizing photons (X-rays from Linear Accelerators [4–8 MeV] and Gamma rays from radioactive isotopes: ⁶⁰Co, ¹³⁷Cs, ¹⁹²Ir) interact with tissue water predominantly via the Compton Scattering Effect, ejecting fast recoil electrons that ionize water () into free hydroxyl radicals () and . These free radicals cause lethal single- and double-stranded DNA breaks (most sensitive in the M [mitotic] and G2 phases of the cell cycle).

Key Radiobiological Laws:

Inverse Square Law: Radiation dose at a point is inversely proportional to the square of the distance () from the source—this is the fundamental principle of Brachytherapy, allowing a massive tumoricidal dose to the cervix while sparing the adjacent bladder and rectum.

Oxygen Enhancement Ratio (OER): Well-oxygenated cells are 2 to 3 times more radiosensitive than hypoxic cells (oxygen “fixes” free-radical DNA damage permanently). Hence anemia must be corrected before radiotherapy, and Radiopotentiators / Hypoxic Cell Sensitizers (Cisplatin, Paclitaxel, Gemcitabine, Hydroxyurea, Metronidazole, Misonidazole) are given concurrently (Chemoradiation).

Fractionation: Dividing total External Beam Radiotherapy (EBRT) into small daily fractions (180–200 cGy/day, 5 days/week) allows normal tissues (bowel, bladder, bone marrow) to repair sublethal DNA damage between fractions while tumor cells accumulate lethal damage (4 Rs of Radiobiology: Repair of sublethal injury, Reoxygenation of hypoxic tumor core, Redistribution of cells into sensitive M/G2 phases, and Repopulation of normal tissues).

Modern Techniques: 3D-Conformal Radiotherapy (3D-CRT) and Intensity-Modulated Radiotherapy (IMRT) use computer-controlled multileaf collimators to conform high-dose beams precisely to the target tumor while sparing small bowel, rectum, and bladder.

Complications of Pelvic Radiotherapy ([RGU] — Table 30.2, Book p. 508):

Early (Acute — within days/weeks): Radiation sickness (nausea, vomiting, anorexia), acute radiation enteritis/diarrhea, radiation cystitis/dysuria, proctitis, moist desquamation of vulval/perineal skin, and bone marrow suppression (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia).

Late (6 months to 2 years — due to obliterative endarteritis and avascular fibrosis): Radiation ovarian failure (artificial menopause), vaginal fibrosis and stenosis (causing apareunia — prevented by regular use of vaginal dilators with estrogen cream), chronic radiation proctosigmoiditis (rectal bleeding, tenesmus, stricture — treated with steroid retention enemas), small bowel stricture/obstruction/malabsorption, chronic hemorrhagic cystitis (contracted thimble bladder), radiation vesicovaginal or rectovaginal fistula, and osteoporotic femoral neck fracture.

2. Cell Cycle Kinetics & Cytotoxic Chemotherapy (Book p. 511–519)

Cell Cycle Kinetics & Log-Kill Hypothesis: Proliferating cells pass through  (pre-synthetic)  S (DNA synthesis)   (pre-mitotic)  M (Mitosis), while resting cells remain in .

Small tumors have a high growth fraction and short doubling time (highly chemosensitive), whereas bulky tumors have a large  resting fraction (Gompertzian growth — explaining why surgical debulking to <1 cm makes ovarian cancer chemosensitive). Antitumor drugs kill a constant fraction (percentage) rather than a constant number of cells per dose (Log-kill hypothesis), requiring intermittent multi-cycle therapy.

Classification & Specific Toxicities of Gynecological Chemotherapeutic Agents:

Alkylating Agents & Platinum Compounds (Cell-Cycle Non-Specific — act on both cycling and  cells by cross-linking DNA):

Cyclophosphamide & Ifosfamide: Cause myelosuppression, alopecia, and hemorrhagic cystitis (due to acrolein metabolite — prevented by vigorous hydration and MESNA [2-mercaptoethane sulfonate]).

Cisplatin: Causes severe nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis — prevented by pre-hydration + mannitol diuresis), ototoxicity (high-frequency hearing loss), peripheral sensory neuropathy, and severe emesis.

Carboplatin: Less nephrotoxic/neurotoxic than cisplatin; dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia); dosed by Calvert formula using GFR (AUC 5–6).

Antimetabolites (Cell-Cycle Specific — act on S-phase):

Methotrexate: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; causes stomatitis/mucositis, hepatotoxicity, myelosuppression, and pneumonitis (rescued by Folinic acid / Leucovorin).

5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) & Gemcitabine.

Antitumor Antibiotics (Cell-Cycle Non-Specific):

Actinomycin-D: Causes myelosuppression, stomatitis, and severe local tissue necrosis on extravasation.

Doxorubicin (Adriamycin): Causes cumulative irreversible cardiotoxicity (dilated cardiomyopathy) — requires baseline ECG and ECHO ejection fraction monitoring.

Bleomycin (acts on  phase): Causes pulmonary fibrosis (monitor pulmonary function tests) and hyperpigmentation; minimal myelosuppression.

Plant Alkaloids & Taxanes (Cell-Cycle Specific):

Vinca Alkaloids (Vincristine, Vinblastine — M-phase spindle poisons): Cause peripheral and autonomic neuropathy (loss of deep tendon reflexes, foot drop, paralytic ileus/constipation).

Taxanes (Paclitaxel, Docetaxel — M-phase): Stabilize microtubule polymerization; cause hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (require premedication with dexamethasone, diphenhydramine, and -blocker), neutropenia, peripheral neuropathy, bradycardia, and total alopecia.

Etoposide (-phase topoisomerase-II inhibitor) & Topotecan (Topoisomerase-I inhibitor). (Note: Chemotherapy-induced Neutropenia [<1500/] is treated with Recombinant G-CSF [Filgrastim]; severe emesis is prevented with Ondansetron [5- antagonist] + Dexamethasone).

subject: gynecology
title: S11. Pediatric & Adolescent Gynecology (Chapter 32)
text:
High-Yield Pediatric & Premenarchal Conditions (Book p. 542–546)

Neonatal Genital Crisis (0–10 days after birth): Physiological response of the newborn to transplacental maternal estrogen (and its sudden withdrawal after birth), manifesting as: (i) Neonatal leucorrhoea (mucoid cervical discharge), (ii) Withdrawal vaginal bleeding/spotting within 10 days of birth, and (iii) Bilateral breast enlargement with milky nipple discharge (“Witch’s milk”). Treatment: Reassurance only (resolves spontaneously in 1–2 weeks).

Labial Adhesions (Adhesive Vulvitis / Synechiae Vulvae): Agglutination of the labia minora in the midline from behind forwards in girls aged 1–5 years due to hypoestrogenism + mild vulvitis denuding the thin epithelium. Presents with urinary stream deflection, post-void dribbling, or pseudoincontinence, with a characteristic thin, translucent vertical raphe in the midline obscuring the introitus 

Treatment: Topical Estrogen cream applied nightly for 2–4 weeks (or gentle digital/probe separation under topical anesthetic jelly followed by estrogen/emollient cream to prevent reagglutination).

Childhood Vulvovaginitis (5–11 years): Commonest gynecological problem in premenarchal girls.

Why premenarchal girls are vulnerable: Lack of estrogen  thin vaginal epithelium (few layers), absence of glycogen and Döderlein’s bacilli, neutral/alkaline vaginal pH (6.5–7.5), absence of labial fat pads and pubic hair, close proximity of anus, and poor perineal wiping hygiene.

Causes: Non-specific polymicrobial flora (coliforms, streptococci — commonest), Threadworm (Enterobius vermicularis) migrating from the anus at night (causes nocturnal perianal/vulval itching), foreign body in vagina, or specific pathogens (Candida, Streptococcus pyogenes, N. gonorrhoeae — always suspect sexual abuse if Gonorrhoea, Chlamydia, or Trichomonas is isolated in a child!).

Management: Perineal hygiene (wiping front-to-back, warm sitz baths, cotton underwear), Albendazole/Mebendazole for threadworm, removal of foreign body, Amoxicillin for bacterial infection, and short-term topical Estrogen cream in refractory cases to thicken the vaginal defense.

subject: gynecology
title: S12. Special Topics: Pruritus Vulvae, Residual Ovary, Breast & Psychosexual Disorders (Chapter 33)
text:
1. Pruritus Vulvae (Book p. 553–555)

Definition: Sensation of itching (not pain) confined to the vulva, leading to a repetitive “itch-scratch” cycle (worse at night due to warmth and lack of distraction).

Etiology: (1) Vaginal Discharge (80% — Commonest): Candidiasis (Moniliasis) and Trichomoniasis; (2) Vulval Infections & Infestations: Threadworm (Oxyuris vermicularis), Scabies, Pediculosis pubis, Tinea cruris, Condyloma; (3) Non-Neoplastic Vulval Dermatoses: Lichen sclerosus, Lichen simplex chronicus, Psoriasis; (4) Allergy / Contact Dermatitis: Synthetic nylon undergarments, soaps, detergents, latex condoms, spermicides; (5) Premalignant & Malignant Lesions: VIN, Paget’s disease, Carcinoma vulva; (6) Systemic Diseases: Diabetes mellitus (glycosuria + candidiasis), jaundice/liver disease, chronic renal failure, iron/folate/ deficiency, thyroid disease, and psychosomatic neurosis.

Evaluation & Management: Wet mount & KOH smear of discharge, fasting/postprandial blood sugar, CBC, LFT, stool for ova/cysts, and vulval biopsy in chronic (>1 year) dermatoses; treat specific cause + cotton undergarments + 0.05% Clobetasol ointment (for lichen sclerosus) or antihistamines/hydrocortisone cream to break the itch-scratch cycle.

2. Trapped (Residual) Ovarian Syndrome vs. Ovarian Remnant Syndrome (Book p. 559)

[[TABLE:gynecology-tbl-013]]

3. Breast in Gynecology (Book p. 561–567)

Mastalgia ([RGU]): Cyclic (premenstrual breast pain and nodularity — treated with reassurance, well-fitting brassieres, NSAIDs, evening primrose oil / Vitamin E, Danazol 100–200 mg/day, Bromocriptine 2.5 mg/day, or Tamoxifen 10 mg/day in luteal phase) vs. Non-cyclic (duct ectasia, Tietze’s costochondritis).

Fibroadenoma: Commonest benign breast tumor in young women (20–35 years); firm, freely mobile (“breast mouse”), painless, well-circumscribed mass; treated by observation or excision/enucleation.

Fibrocystic Breast Disease: Commonest benign lesion in premenopausal women (20–50 years); bilateral diffuse coarse nodularity (“bag of shot” feel) with cyclic premenstrual pain. Evaluated by USG, mammography, and FNAC.

Nipple Discharge: Milky bilateral: Galactorrhea (hyperprolactinemia, hypothyroidism, phenothiazines); Bloody / Serosanguinous single-duct: Intraductal papilloma (commonest benign cause) or Intraductal carcinoma; Greenish/multicolored sticky: Mammary duct ectasia.

Breast Cancer Screening Guidelines (ACOG) & Triple Assessment:

High-Risk Factors: BRCA1 (17q) & BRCA2 (13q) mutations, affected first-degree relative, nulliparity or first birth >35 years, early menarche, late menopause, atypical ductal/lobular hyperplasia, obesity, and combined HRT.

Screening Schedule: (1) Monthly Breast Self-Examination (BSE) starting at age 20 (done 5–7 days after menses), (2) Clinical Breast Examination (CBE) every 1–3 years (ages 20–39) and annually from age 40, and (3) Screening Mammography (craniocaudal + mediolateral oblique views) every 1–2 years from age 40, and annually from age 50 (detects clustered spiculated microcalcifications before a mass is palpable).

Triple Test for a Breast Lump: (1) Clinical Breast Examination + (2) Mammography / Breast USG + (3) Fine-Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) / Core Needle Biopsy (CNB). When all three are concordant, diagnostic accuracy exceeds 99%.

4. Psychosexual Problems: Vaginismus & Dyspareunia (Book p. 567–568, 592)

Vaginismus: Psychogenically mediated involuntary painful spasm of the pubococcygeus (levator ani), bulbocavernosus, and thigh adductor muscles whenever vaginal penetration (coitus or speculum exam) is attempted, preventing consummation of marriage (apareunia).

Types: Primary (psychosexual phobia/strict upbringing; anatomical vagina is normal on EUA) vs. Secondary (triggered by a painful local lesion: vulval vestibulitis, tender episiotomy scar, or vaginitis).

Management: Treat any local painful lesion + Psychosexual counseling of couple + Behavioral desensitization using graduated vaginal dilators (trainers) + Kegel relaxation exercises. If a rigid hymenal ring or narrow introitus is present, perform Perineoplasty (Fenton’s Operation)—making a vertical (or transverse) incision through the fourchette and superficial perineal muscles and suturing it transversely to widen the introitus.

Dyspareunia ([RGU,TU]): Painful or difficult sexual intercourse:

Superficial (Entrance) Dyspareunia: Caused by narrow introitus, tough/rigid hymen, acute vulvovaginitis, Bartholin’s gland cyst/abscess, vulval vestibulitis, urethral caruncle, lichen sclerosus, postmenopausal atrophic vaginitis, or a tender episiotomy/perineorrhaphy scar.

Deep Dyspareunia: Caused by Pelvic Endometriosis (nodules in POD/uterosacral ligaments/rectovaginal septum), Adenomyosis, Chronic PID / Tubo-ovarian mass, Fixed retroverted uterus, Prolapsed ovaries in the POD, or pelvic congestion syndrome.

1. Stem Cells in Gynecology (Book p. 625–626)

Types: Totipotent (fertilized zygote/morula up to 8-cell stage  forms embryo + placenta), Pluripotent (Embryonic stem cells from inner cell mass of blastocyst  form all 3 germ layers, carry teratoma/oncogenic risk), and Multipotent (umbilical cord blood, amniotic fluid, bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells).

Applications in Urogynecology & Regenerative Medicine: (1) Stress Urinary Incontinence: Periurethral injection of autologous muscle-derived stem/progenitor cells into the rhabdosphincter to regenerate striated sphincter muscle, (2) Bladder & Vaginal Reconstruction using cell-seeded biodegradable PGA scaffolds (e.g., in MRKH vaginal agenesis), and (3) Hybrid bio-meshes for Pelvic Organ Prolapse.

subject: ophthalmology
title: ESSAY 1 & 2: SENILE CATARACT (IMMATURE & MATURE)
text:
SECTION 1: DISEASES OF THE LENS (CATARACT)

ESSAY 1 & 2: SENILE CATARACT (IMMATURE & MATURE)

(Covers KU22, KU19, TU Essays; KU26, KU23, RGU, TU Short Essays; KU25, KU24, KU23, KU20, KU18, KU16, KU14 Short Answers)

Clinical Case Identification:

Case 1 (KU22): 70-year-old diabetic/hypertensive with painless progressive diminution of vision (CF close to face), white pupillary reflex, non-visualized fundus  Mature Senile Cataract (MSC).

Case 2 (KU19, TU): Gradual painless loss of vision (CF 2.5m), greyish-white lens with iris shadow present  Immature Senile Cataract (ISC).

1. Definition & Applied Physiology (Transparency of Lens)

Definition: Any opacity in the crystalline lens or its capsule that impairs vision.

Structure of Crystalline Lens: Transparent, biconvex structure placed in the patellar fossa; diameter 9–10 mm, thickness 3.5–5 mm, refractive index 1.39, total dioptric power ~18 D (range 16–20 D). Consists of:

Lens Capsule: Thin, transparent hyaline membrane (thickest at pre-equator 14 m, thinnest at posterior pole 3 m).

Anterior Epithelium: Single layer of cuboidal cells (no posterior epithelium).

Lens Fibres (Nucleus & Cortex): Successive zones of nucleus laid down are Embryonic (up to 3 months gestation), Fetal (3 months to birth, with anterior Y-shaped and posterior inverted Y-shaped sutures), Infantile (birth to puberty), and Adult nucleus (post-puberty).

Factors Responsible for Lens Transparency [KU26]:

Avascularity of the lens.

Tightly-packed nature of lens cells, narrow lens fibre membranes, and loss of cellular organelles.

Lens proteins (Aquaporins): Major intrinsic protein belongs to the superfamily of aquaporins (MIP26 or Aquaporin 0).

Corneal/Lens Crystallins: Water-soluble proteins preventing light scattering.

Semipermeable character of the lens capsule.

Active Pump-Leak Mechanism:  ATPase pump in the anterior epithelium and lens fibre membranes regulates electrolyte/water balance, maintaining relative dehydration ( and amino acids pumped in;  and water pumped out).

Auto-oxidation & Antioxidant Mechanisms: High concentration of reduced glutathione (GSH), superoxide dismutase, catalase, Vitamin C, and Vitamin E maintain lens proteins in a reduced state.

2. Classification of Cataract [KU24]

A. Etiological Classification:

Congenital and Developmental Cataract

Acquired Cataract: Senile (Age-related), Traumatic, Complicated, Metabolic, Electric, Radiational, Toxic (Corticosteroid, Miotics, Copper/Iron), Dermatogenic (Atopic), Osseous disease-related, and Miscellaneous Syndromes (Down’s syndrome, Dystrophica myotonica, Lowe’s syndrome, Treacher-Collins syndrome [KU18]).

B. Morphological Classification:

Capsular: Anterior capsular, Posterior capsular.

Subcapsular: Anterior subcapsular, Posterior subcapsular (PSC).

Cortical: Involves major part of cortex.

Supranuclear: Involves deeper cortex just outside nucleus.

Nuclear: Involves nucleus of crystalline lens.

Polar: Anterior polar, Posterior polar.

3. Etiopathogenesis of Senile Cataract [KU20]

Risk Factors: Advancing age (>50 years), Heredity, Ultraviolet radiations, Dietary deficiency (proteins, Vitamins C, E, riboflavin), Severe dehydrational crises, Smoking (accumulates 3-hydroxykynurenine and cyanates).

Pathogenesis of Cortical Senile Cataract: Decreased levels of total proteins, amino acids, and potassium + increased sodium  Failure of  ATPase pump  Osmotic hydration of lens  Denaturation and coagulation of soluble lens proteins into insoluble proteins.

Pathogenesis of Nuclear Senile Cataract [KU20]: Intensification of age-related nuclear sclerosis + dehydration and compaction of the nucleus  Hard cataract with increased water-insoluble proteins. Urochrome or melanin pigment deposition turns the nucleus amber, brown (cataracta brunescens), black (cataracta nigra), or red (cataracta rubra).

4. Stages of Maturation of Senile Cortical Cataract [KU25, RGU, TU]

Stage of Lamellar Separation: Demarcation of cortical fibres due to fluid separation (seen only on slit-lamp; reversible).

Stage of Incipient Cataract: Early detectable opacities with clear areas between them. Two distinct types [TU]:

Cuneiform (70%): Wedge-shaped, radial spoke-like opacities extending from periphery (lower nasal quadrant first) toward centre; visual loss is delayed; vision is worse in dim light.

Cupuliform (5%): Saucer-shaped posterior subcapsular plaque right in the axial pathway; causes early marked loss of vision, glare, and day blindness (vision worse in bright light due to miosis).

Immature Senile Cataract (ISC): Opacification progresses; lens appears greyish-white; clear cortex is still present anterior to the opacity, so iris shadow is visible. In some cases, progressive hydration causes a swollen lens (Intumescent cataract), shallowing the anterior chamber.

Mature Senile Cataract (MSC): Opacification is complete (entire cortex involved); lens becomes pearly white (“ripe cataract”); no iris shadow.

Hypermature Senile Cataract (HMSC) [RGU]:

Morgagnian HMSC: Total cortex liquefies into a milky fluid bag; small brownish nucleus sinks to the bottom, shifting with head position; calcium deposits may appear on capsule.

Sclerotic HMSC: Cortex disintegrates and water leaks out  Shrunken lens, wrinkled/thickened anterior capsule, deep anterior chamber, and iridodonesis.

5. Clinical Features

Symptoms:

Glare / Intolerance to bright light (earliest symptom, especially in posterior subcapsular cataract).

Uniocular polyopia (doubling/trebling of objects due to irregular refraction across variable refractive indices).

Coloured halos around light (due to water droplets in lens; broken into segments on Fincham’s stenopaeic-slit test [KU23, TU]).

Fixed black spots in front of eyes.

Painless, gradually progressive diminution of vision:

Central opacities (cupuliform)  Early loss of vision; patient sees better in dim light (mydriasis).

Peripheral opacities (cuneiform)  Late loss of vision; patient sees better in bright light.

Nuclear sclerosis  Progressive index myopia causing deterioration of distant vision, but temporary improvement in near vision (“Second sight”).

Signs (Comparison Table):

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-001]]

6. Differential Diagnosis

ISC vs. Nuclear Sclerosis: ISC has greyish lens, iris shadow present, black spokes on distant direct ophthalmoscopy, and no improvement with pinhole. Nuclear sclerosis has no iris shadow, no black spots on red glow, and vision improves with pinhole.

MSC vs. Leukocoria: MSC has absent 4th Purkinje image and normal B-scan ultrasound.

Other Causes of Gradual Painless Loss of Vision [KU23, RGU]: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG), Age-Related Macular Degeneration (ARMD), Diabetic Retinopathy, Progressive Pterygium, Corneal Dystrophies, Optic Atrophy, Refractive Errors, Retinitis Pigmentosa.

7. Preoperative Investigations & Workup [KU22, RGU, TU]

General Medical Evaluation: BP (hypertension), RBS/FBS/HbA1c (diabetes), ECG, respiratory evaluation (asthma/COPD), dental/urinary focus of sepsis.

Ocular Examination & Retinal/Macular Function Tests:

Visual Acuity, Perception of Light (PL) (absent PL = nil visual prognosis), and Projection of Rays (PR) in 4 quadrants.

Pupillary reactions: Check for RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil) and adequacy of mydriasis.

Macular Function Tests: Two-light discrimination test, Maddox rod test, Colour perception, Entoptic visualization, Laser interferometry (LI), Potential Acuity Meter (PAM).

Slit-Lamp Examination: Corneal endothelial status (guttata; specular microscopy if count <1500 cells/), KPs, pseudoexfoliation, iridodonesis, nuclear hardness grade.

IOP Measurement: Applanation or Schiotz tonometry.

Rule out Local Septic Focus: Lid margin (blepharitis/meibomitis), conjunctiva, and Lacrimal Syringing (mandatory to rule out chronic dacryocystitis; if blocked, perform DCR/DCT first to prevent postoperative endophthalmitis).

B-scan Ultrasonography: Mandatory in Mature/Hypermature cataract where fundus is not visible (to rule out retinal detachment, vitreous haemorrhage, or intraocular tumour).

Biometry (IOL Power Calculation) [KU, RGU, TU]:

SRK Formula (Sanders, Retzlaff, and Kraff) [RGU]:

= Power of IOL in dioptres

= Specific A-constant of the lens type (e.g., 118.4 for PCIOL)

= Axial length of eyeball in mm (measured by A-scan ultrasonography or optical biometry like IOLMaster / Lenstar)

= Average corneal keratometry reading in dioptres (measured by Keratometer).

8. Management of Cataract [KU22, KU24, KU18, RGU, TU]

A. Preoperative Preparation & Counselling:

Counselling Poor Visual Prognosis [TU]: In patients with inaccurate PR, RAPD, pre-existing corneal opacity, advanced glaucoma, or diabetic maculopathy, explain clearly that surgery removes the mechanical media block (or prevents lens-induced complications) but visual recovery will be guarded/limited; obtain written informed high-risk consent.

Medications: Topical fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin 0.5% QID for 3 days), Povidone-Iodine 5% drops in conjunctival sac (most effective against endophthalmitis), Mydriatics (Tropicamide 1% + Phenylephrine 2.5%), Topical NSAID (Flurbiprofen 0.03% or Ketorolac to maintain mydriasis and prevent CME), IOP lowering (Mannitol/Acetazolamide if needed).

B. Surgical Techniques (Extracapsular Cataract Extraction - ECCE) [KU24, RGU]:

Intracapsular Cataract Extraction (ICCE): Entire lens with intact capsule is removed; now obsolete, indicated only in markedly subluxated or dislocated lenses.

Types of ECCE:

Conventional ECCE: Large limbal incision (10–12 mm), anterior capsulotomy (can-opener), manual expression of nucleus, cortex aspiration, rigid PMMA PCIOL implantation, and closure with 3–5 interrupted 10-0 nylon sutures.

Manual Small Incision Cataract Surgery (SICS): Sutureless, self-sealing valvular sclerocorneal tunnel incision (5.5–7.5 mm; straight, frown, or chevron incision), large Continuous Curvilinear Capsulorrhexis (CCC), hydrodissection, prolapse of nucleus into AC, delivery via irrigating wire vectis/Blumenthal/fishhook technique, cortical aspiration with Simcoe cannula, and rigid PCIOL implantation in the capsular bag.

Phacoemulsification [KU18, RGU, TU]: Procedure of choice worldwide.

Surgical Steps: Clear corneal incision (2.8–3.2 mm) + side-port entry  Continuous Curvilinear Capsulorrhexis (CCC)  Hydrodissection & Hydrodelineation  Ultrasonic emulsification and aspiration of nucleus using a titanium needle vibrating at 40,000 Hz (Divide and Conquer, Stop and Chop, or Direct Phaco Chop)  Bimanual cortical irrigation-aspiration  Implantation of Foldable IOL in capsular bag via injector  Sutureless hydration closure.

Advantages of Phacoemulsification: Can be done under topical anaesthesia; minimal postoperative congestion; very small incision (3.2 mm); minimal surgically induced astigmatism (SIA); closed-chamber surgery (minimal risk of expulsive haemorrhage/vitreous prolapse); rapid visual rehabilitation.

Microincision Cataract Surgery (MICS) & FLACS: Incision <2 mm; Femtosecond Laser-Assisted Cataract Surgery (FLACS) automates corneal incisions, precise CCC, and lens fragmentation.

subject: ophthalmology
title: ESSAY 3: COMPLICATIONS OF CATARACT SURGERY & AFTER-CATARACT
text:
ESSAY 3: COMPLICATIONS OF CATARACT SURGERY & AFTER-CATARACT

(Covers KU21 Essay; KU23 Short Essay; KU24, KU23, KU17, RGU, TU Short Answers)

Clinical Case Identification:

Case (KU21): 65-year-old male, 6 months post-uneventful cataract surgery with good initial recovery, now presents with painless progressive diminution of vision  After-Cataract / Posterior Capsular Opacification (PCO).

Differential Diagnosis of Late Post-op Visual Loss: Cystoid Macular Oedema (CME), Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (PBK), Pseudophakic Retinal Detachment, Late-onset Chronic Endophthalmitis (Propionibacterium acnes), IOL Decentration/Subluxation.

1. Classification of Cataract Surgery Complications [KU23, KU24, RGU, TU]

A. Preoperative / Anaesthesia-related: Retrobulbar haemorrhage, Globe perforation, Oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia), Spontaneous lens dislocation during massage.

B. Intraoperative Complications:

Tunnel incision defects: Buttonholing (too superficial), Premature entry with iris prolapse (too deep), Scleral disinsertion.

Descemet’s membrane detachment and Iridodialysis (tear of iris root).

Capsulorrhexis run-out.

Posterior Capsular Rupture (PCR) & Zonular Dehiscence (most dreaded; leads to Vitreous Loss or Nucleus Drop into vitreous cavity).

Expulsive Choroidal Haemorrhage.

C. Early Postoperative Complications [KU23]:

Hyphaema: Blood in AC from scleral tunnel or iris root; managed conservatively with bed rest, topical steroids, and cycloplegics; paracentesis if IOP rises.

Iris Prolapse: In conventional ECCE due to insecure suturing.

Striate Keratopathy: Corneal stromal oedema with Descemet’s folds due to endothelial trauma/phaco heat; managed with 5% hypertonic NaCl drops and steroids.

Flat / Shallow Anterior Chamber: Caused by Wound leak (hypotony, Seidel’s test positive), Ciliochoroidal detachment, or Pupillary block glaucoma.

Postoperative Anterior Uveitis & Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS): Sterile violent anterior segment reaction to residual viscoelastic, chemical contaminants, or ethylene oxide gas; managed with intensive topical steroids.

Acute Bacterial Endophthalmitis: Presents within 48–72 hours with severe ocular pain, loss of vision, lid oedema, chemosis, corneal haze, hypopyon, and loss of red glow. Commonest organism: Staphylococcus epidermidis. Managed as an emergency with intravitreal Vancomycin (1 mg/0.1 ml) + Ceftazidime (2.25 mg/0.1 ml) and pars plana vitrectomy.

D. Late Postoperative Complications [KU24]:

After-Cataract (Posterior Capsular Opacification - PCO)

Cystoid Macular Oedema (CME - Irvine-Gass Syndrome): Fluid in Henle’s layer 1–3 months post-op; honeycomb macula, flower-petal appearance on FFA; prevented/treated with topical NSAIDs (Ketorolac/Nepafenac) and steroids.

Delayed Chronic Endophthalmitis: Caused by low-virulence Propionibacterium acnes trapped in the capsular bag (white capsular plaque) or Fungi.

Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (PBK): Chronic endothelial decompensation requiring Penetrating Keratoplasty or DSEK.

Retinal Detachment (RD) and Epithelial / Fibrous Downgrowth.

E. IOL-Related Complications:

UGH Syndrome: Uveitis, Glaucoma, Hyphaema (classic with rigid ACIOLs).

Malpositions of IOL: Sunset syndrome (inferior subluxation), Sunrise syndrome (superior subluxation), Lost lens syndrome (complete dislocation into vitreous), Windshield wiper syndrome (small sulcus IOL moving with head).

2. Detailed Note: After-Cataract (Posterior Capsular Opacification - PCO) [KU21, KU23, KU17, RGU, TU]

Definition: Opacity which persists or develops in the pupillary area after extracapsular lens extraction.

Etiopathogenesis:

Residual cortical matter trapped between anterior and posterior capsule remnants, surrounded by fibrin or blood.

Proliferation and migration of residual equatorial anterior lens epithelial cells onto the posterior capsule, undergoing myofibroblastic metaplasia (fibrous bands) or bladder-cell differentiation. Incidence is highest in paediatric cataracts.

Clinical Types & Features:

Symptoms: Painless progressive diminution of vision, glare, and diplopia occurring months to years after surgery.

Morphological Types:

Thin Membranous PCO: Thickened, wrinkled posterior capsule.

Dense Membranous After-Cataract: Thick organized fibrous plaque.

Soemmering’s Ring: Thick ring of cortical fibres enclosed between fused anterior and posterior capsule edges behind the iris.

Elschnig’s Pearls: Vacuolated subcapsular epithelial cells clustered like soap bubbles or fish-eggs along the posterior capsule.

Management (Two Treatment Modalities) [RGU]:

Nd:YAG Laser Posterior Capsulotomy: Treatment of choice for thin membranous PCO and Elschnig’s pearls (photodisruption creates a central opening in the visual axis).

Surgical Membranectomy / Discission: Using a cystitome, Ziegler’s knife, or vitrectomy cutter for dense membranous plaques or in uncooperative children.

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ESSAYS & SHORT ANSWERS ON LENS
text:
SHORT ESSAYS & SHORT ANSWERS ON LENS

1. Congenital & Developmental Cataract [KU17, KU24, KU21, KU14, RGU, TU]

Etiology: 1/3 Idiopathic, 1/3 Hereditary (autosomal dominant), 1/3 Maternal/Fetal factors:

Maternal: Malnutrition, TORCH infections (Rubella in 1st trimester causes pearly-white nuclear cataract + microphthalmos + salt-and-pepper retinopathy + PDA + sensorineural deafness), Drugs (steroids, thalidomide).

Fetal/Infantile: Birth anoxia, Galactosaemia, Hypocalcaemia, Lowe’s syndrome, ROP.

Clinical Types [KU21, KU24]:

Congenital Capsular & Polar Cataracts (Anterior polar: pyramidal, reduplicated; Posterior polar: onion-whorl appearance, associated with Mittendorf’s dot and high risk of posterior capsular rupture during surgery).

Zonular (Lamellar) Cataract [KU14, TU]: Most common type presenting with visual impairment (50%). Bilateral; affects a specific zone of the fetal nucleus surrounding the clear embryonic nucleus; characteristic linear spokes called “riders” project outward toward the equator. Linked to autosomal dominant inheritance or Vitamin D deficiency/hypocalcaemia.

Sutural & Axial Cataracts: Cataracta centralis pulverulenta, Floriform, Coralliform, Spear-shaped.

Generalized Cataracts: Blue-dot (Cataracta punctata caerulea), Coronary cataract (club-shaped peripheral opacities at puberty), Total Rubella cataract, Congenital membranous cataract.

Management:

Workup: Density of cataract, fixation, B-scan, TORCH titres, urine for reducing substances (galactosaemia), serum calcium.

Timing of Surgery: Unilateral dense cataract  Operate as early as possible (within first few weeks) to prevent stimulus deprivation amblyopia. Bilateral dense cataract  Operate within 6 weeks of birth.

Surgical Procedure: Anterior Capsulorrhexis + Lens Aspiration (or Lensectomy) + Primary Posterior Capsulotomy (PPC) (in children <6 years) + Anterior Vitrectomy (in children <2 years).

Paediatric Aphakia Correction: Hydrophobic acrylic foldable PCIOL implantation in children >2 years (undercorrect biometry power by 20% in <2 yrs and 10% in 2–8 yrs to account for future myopic shift). Contact lenses/aphakic spectacles + aggressive Amblyopia occlusion therapy.

2. Intraocular Lenses (IOLs) & Pseudophakia [KU25, KU24, KU23, KU16, RGU]

Types of IOLs:

Based on Fixation:

Anterior Chamber IOL (ACIOL): Angle-supported (e.g., Kelman Multiflex).

Iris-Supported IOL: Singh and Worst’s Iris-Claw lens (anterior or retro-iris fixation).

Posterior Chamber IOL (PCIOL): Placed in the capsular bag (ideal) or ciliary sulcus (Modified C-loop), or Scleral-fixated IOL (SFIOL / Glued IOL).

Based on Material: Rigid (PMMA), Foldable (Hydrophobic/Hydrophilic Acrylic, Silicone, Hydrogel, Collamer), Rollable (Ultra-thin hydrogel for MICS).

Based on Focusing Ability: Unifocal, Multifocal (refractive/diffractive), Accommodative (Crystalens).

Special Function: Toric IOL (corrects astigmatism), Aspheric IOL, Aniridia IOL.

Pseudophakia [KU24, RGU]: Condition of aphakia corrected with an IOL.

Signs: Limbal/tunnel scar, slightly deep AC, mild iridodonesis, blackish pupil with bright specular reflexes from IOL surface, all 4 Purkinje images present, IOL confirmed in bag on slit-lamp after dilatation. Refractive status may be emmetropic, consecutive myopic, or consecutive hypermetropic; requires near add (+2.5 to +3 D) due to loss of accommodation.

3. Complicated, Metabolic, & Traumatic Cataracts [KU23, KU20, KU15, RGU, TU]

Complicated Cataract [KU23, RGU, TU]: Secondary to intraocular disease (anterior uveitis is the commonest cause; others: retinitis pigmentosa, pathological myopia, retinal detachment, intraocular tumours). Starts as a posterior subcapsular cortical opacity with a characteristic “breadcrumb” appearance and “polychromatic lustre” (iridescent red, green, blue particles) on slit-lamp.

Metabolic Cataracts [RGU]:

Diabetic Cataract: True diabetic cataract in young Type 1 diabetics due to aldose reductase converting glucose to sorbitol  osmotic hydration  bilateral “snowflake” or “snowstorm” cortical opacities.

Galactosaemic Cataract: Deficiency of GPUT or galactokinase  bilateral “oil-droplet” central opacity (reversible on milk-free diet).

Wilson’s Disease: Copper deposition  “Sunflower cataract” + Kayser-Fleischer ring.

Traumatic Cataract [KU20, RGU]: Concussion injury causes imbibition of aqueous and mechanical disruption of fibres, classically producing a feathery, star-shaped “Rosette cataract” [RGU] in the posterior cortex (early or late rosette). Managed by lens aspiration/phacoemulsification with PCIOL once inflammation subsides.

4. Displacements of Lens (Ectopia Lentis & Subluxation) [KU17, RGU, TU]

Causes of Dislocated/Subluxated Lens & Ectopia Lentis [KU17, RGU, TU]:

Congenital Syndromes: Marfan’s syndrome (autosomal dominant; bilateral superotemporal subluxation + arachnodactyly + aortic aneurysm), Homocystinuria (autosomal recessive; inferonasal subluxation + mental retardation), Weill-Marchesani syndrome (microspherophakia + anterior subluxation causing pupillary block), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Traumatic: Blunt trauma, Couching.

Spontaneous/Consecutive: Hypermature cataract, Buphthalmos, High myopia, Uveitis.

Subluxation vs. Dislocation [TU]:

Subluxation: Partial zonular rupture; lens displaced sideways but remains partially in pupillary area. Signs: Uniocular diplopia, irregular/deep AC, iridodonesis, phacodonesis, golden crescent edge on slit-lamp, dark crescent edge on distant direct ophthalmoscopy. Managed with spectacles or lensectomy + SFIOL/Iris-claw IOL.

Dislocation (Luxation): Complete 360° zonular rupture. Anterior dislocation into AC (looks like an oil globule; surgical emergency due to severe phacotopic glaucoma and endothelial damage). Posterior dislocation into vitreous cavity (aphakic eye; remove via pars plana vitrectomy + lensectomy if causing uveitis or glaucoma).

5. Viscoelastics (Ophthalmic Viscosurgical Devices - OVDs) [TU]

Optically clear, biologically inert, hydrophilic biopolymers used in intraocular surgery to maintain AC depth, coat and protect corneal endothelium from phaco energy/IOL touch, and perform viscodissection.

Examples: Cohesive (1% Sodium Hyaluronate - Healon) and Dispersive (2% Hydroxypropyl Methylcellulose - HPMC, Chondroitin sulphate - Viscoat). Must be thoroughly aspirated at the end of surgery to prevent severe postoperative secondary glaucoma.

subject: ophthalmology
title: ESSAY 1 & 3: PRIMARY OPEN-ANGLE GLAUCOMA (POAG)
text:
SECTION 2: GLAUCOMA

ESSAY 1 & 3: PRIMARY OPEN-ANGLE GLAUCOMA (POAG)

(Covers KU26, KU24, KU23, KU17 Essays; RGU, TU Short Essays; KU23, KU19, KU16, KU15, RGU, TU Short Answers)

Clinical Case Identification:

Case 1 (KU26): 57-year-old female, diminution of vision for 2 years, IOP 52 mmHg, biarcuate scotoma on Humphrey visual field.

Case 2 (KU24, KU17): 50-year-old lady with frequent change of presbyopic glasses and clouding of peripheral vision  Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG).

1. Definition, Classification & Aqueous Humour Dynamics

Definition of Glaucoma: A group of disorders characterized by a chronic progressive optic neuropathy resulting in characteristic optic disc changes and specific irreversible visual field defects, associated frequently (but not invariably) with raised intraocular pressure (IOP).

Classification of Glaucoma [KU26, KU23]:

Congenital / Developmental Glaucomas: Primary Congenital Glaucoma (Newborn, Infantile, Juvenile); Developmental glaucoma with associated anomalies (Aniridia, Axenfeld-Rieger, Peter’s, Sturge-Weber, Marfan’s).

Primary Adult Glaucomas: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG), Normal Tension Glaucoma (NTG), Primary Angle-Closure Disease (PACS, PAC, PACG).

Secondary Glaucomas: Lens-induced (Phacomorphic, Phacolytic), Inflammatory (Uveitic), Neovascular (NVG), Pigmentary, Pseudoexfoliative, Steroid-induced, Traumatic (Angle-recession), Aphakic/Pseudophakic, Malignant (Ciliary block).

Circulation of Aqueous Humour & Maintenance of IOP [KU16, RGU, TU]:

Normal IOP: 10–21 mmHg (Mean  mmHg).

Production: Secreted by ciliary processes at 2.3 l/min via Ultrafiltration, Active Secretion ( ATPase & Carbonic anhydrase), and Diffusion into the posterior chamber  flows through pupil into anterior chamber.

Drainage:

Trabecular (Conventional) Outflow (70–80%): Uveal meshwork  Corneoscleral meshwork  Juxtacanalicular meshwork (main site of resistance)  Schlemm’s canal (via vacuoles/biomechanical aqueous outflow pump)  Collector channels  Episcleral veins.

Uveoscleral (Unconventional) Outflow (20–30%): Ciliary body face  Suprachoroidal space  Venous circulation of ciliary body/choroid/sclera.

Factors Maintaining IOP: Rate of aqueous formation, resistance to trabecular outflow, episcleral venous pressure (~10 mmHg), central corneal thickness, diurnal variation (morning peak; >8 mmHg fluctuation is diagnostic of glaucoma).

2. Etiopathogenesis of POAG

Risk Factors (History to Elicit) [KU24]: IOP >21 mmHg, Advancing age (5th–7th decade), Positive family history (MYOC, OPTN genes), Thin Central Corneal Thickness (<545 m), High Myopia, Diabetes mellitus, Systemic hypertension (low diastolic perfusion pressure <55 mmHg), Corticosteroid responsiveness, Smoking.

Pathogenesis of Raised IOP: Thickening and sclerosis of trabecular beams + deposition of amorphous material in juxtacanalicular space + stiffening of trabecular meshwork  Failure of aqueous outflow pump and reduced outflow facility.

Pathogenesis of Optic Neuropathy (RGC Apoptosis): Mechanical compression at lamina cribrosa + Vascular insufficiency (vasospasm/impaired autoregulation)  Blockage of retrograde axoplasmic transport of neurotrophins  Programmed cell death (Apoptosis) of Retinal Ganglion Cells (RGCs) + secondary excitotoxicity (glutamate/free radicals).

3. Clinical Features of POAG

Symptoms:

Insidious and asymptomatic (“Silent thief of sight”) until late stages.

Frequent change of presbyopic glasses and difficulty in close work (due to constant pressure on ciliary muscle causing accommodative failure).

Mild eyeache/headache, delayed dark adaptation, and peripheral scotomas noticed by observant patients.

Signs:

Anterior Segment: Normal depth AC, clear cornea; sluggish pupil or RAPD in advanced asymmetric disease.

IOP Changes: Exaggerated diurnal variation (>8 mmHg) initially; permanently raised >21 mmHg later.

Optic Nerve Head (Disc) Changes [KU26, KU23]:
