Early Changes: Vertically oval cup (>0.4), Asymmetry of cup-disc ratio (>0.2 between two eyes), Loss of ISNT rule (Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal neuroretinal rim thickness), Focal notching of neuroretinal rim, Splinter haemorrhages (Drance haemorrhage) on disc margin, Wedge-shaped RNFL defects on red-free light.

Advanced Changes: Marked excavation (C:D ratio 0.7–0.9) reaching disc margin with steep edges, Bayonetting sign (sharp angulation of vessels as they climb steep cup walls), Nasal shifting of retinal vessels, Lamellar dot sign (exposed slit-like pores of lamina cribrosa), Pulsations of retinal arterioles.

Final Stage: Glaucomatous Cavernous (Schnabel’s) Optic Atrophy (deeply excavated, pale white disc).

Visual Field Defects in POAG [KU26, KU23, KU19, KU15, RGU, TU]: (Anatomical basis: Superior and inferior arcuate nerve fibres are most sensitive to damage; papillomacular bundle is most resistant, preserving central vision till the end).

Isopter contraction: Generalized constriction.

Baring of the blind spot: Exclusion of blind spot from central 30° field.

Small wing-shaped Paracentral Scotoma: Earliest clinically significant defect, appearing in Bjerrum’s area (10°–20° from fixation).

Seidel’s Scotoma: Paracentral scotoma joins the blind spot to form a sickle-shaped defect.

Arcuate (Bjerrum’s) Scotoma: Extension of Seidel’s scotoma arching over or under fixation to reach the horizontal nasal raphe.

Ring or Double Arcuate (Biarcuate) Scotoma: Upper and lower arcuate scotomas join together.

Roenne’s Central Nasal Step: Sharp right-angled defect at the horizontal meridian due to unequal progression of two arcuate scotomas.

Tubular Vision & Temporal Island: Peripheral breakthrough leaves only a tiny central island (Tubular vision [KU17, KU15] — Other causes of tubular vision: Advanced Retinitis Pigmentosa, Post-panretinal photocoagulation, Bilateral occipital lobe infarction with macular sparing, Hysterical blindness) and a resistant temporal island before total blindness.

4. Investigations (Gonioscopy & Perimetry) [KU26, KU24]

Tonometry: Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (gold standard).

Central Corneal Thickness (CCT / Pachymetry): Thin cornea underestimates IOP; thick cornea overestimates IOP.

Gonioscopy [KU26]: Biomicroscopic examination of the anterior chamber angle using a goniolens (to overcome total internal reflection at the tear-air interface).

Types: Indirect goniolenses (Goldmann, Zeiss — give mirror image of opposite angle) and Direct goniolenses (Koeppe — used in goniotomy).

Structures Seen (Anterior to Posterior): Schwalbe’s line  Trabecular meshwork  Scleral spur  Ciliary body band  Root of iris.

Shaffer’s Grading: Grade 4 (40°, wide open, all structures seen) down to Grade 0 (0°, closed, no structures seen). In POAG, angle is wide open (Grade 3–4).

Perimetry: Humphrey Automated Perimetry (24-2 or 30-2 SITA Standard).

Optic Nerve Head & RNFL Imaging: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT), Heidelberg Retinal Tomograph (HRT).

5. Management of POAG & Antiglaucoma Medications [KU26, KU24, KU23]

A. Medical Therapy (First-line): Set a Target IOP (20–30% reduction from baseline; <18 mmHg for mild, <15 mmHg for moderate, <12 mmHg for severe damage).

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-002]]

B. Laser Therapy: Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT) (532 nm Nd:YAG targeting pigmented TM cells) or Argon Laser Trabeculoplasty (ALT).

C. Surgical Therapy (Indications: Failed maximal medical/laser therapy, non-compliance, advanced field loss):

Trabeculectomy (guarded partial-thickness fistula draining aqueous from AC to subconjunctival space, augmented with Mitomycin-C 0.02% in high-risk cases).

subject: ophthalmology
title: ESSAY 2, 4, 6, 7: PRIMARY ANGLE-CLOSURE DISEASE (PACD / ACUTE CONGESTIVE GLAUCOMA)
text:
ESSAY 2, 4, 6, 7: PRIMARY ANGLE-CLOSURE DISEASE (PACD / ACUTE CONGESTIVE GLAUCOMA)

(Covers KU25, KU23, KU22, KU21, KU17 Essays; RGU Short Essay; KU19, KU18, KU16, KU15, RGU, TU Short Answers)

Clinical Case Identification:

Case (KU22, KU21, KU17): 50-year-old emotionally labile hypermetropic female with sudden excruciating ocular pain, headache, vomiting, redness, gross visual loss, coloured halos, hazy cornea, mid-dilated vertically oval fixed pupil, high IOP, and shallow AC in both eyes  Acute Primary Angle Closure (Acute Congestive Glaucoma).

1. Etiopathogenesis & Predisposing Factors [KU22, KU16]

Anatomical Predisposing Factors: Hypermetropic small eyes (short axial length <22 mm), shallow anterior chamber, small corneal diameter, thick/anteriorly placed crystalline lens, anterior iris insertion, Plateau iris configuration.

Demographic Factors: Age 50–60 years, Females > Males (3:1), Asian/Indian ethnicity, emotionally labile personality.

Precipitating Factors: Dim illumination (watching cinema/TV in dark), emotional stress/anxiety (sympathetic mydriasis), pharmacological mydriasis (atropine/tropicamide, systemic anticholinergics/bronchodilators).

Mechanism of Primary Angle Closure [KU16]: Mid-dilated pupil increases iridolenticular apposition  Relative Pupillary Block  Aqueous trapped in posterior chamber pushes peripheral flaccid iris forward (Iris Bombe)  Appositional Angle Closure (iridotrabecular contact)  Synechial Angle Closure (Peripheral Anterior Synechiae - PAS)  Acute rise in IOP.

2. Classification & Stages of Angle-Closure Glaucoma [KU25, KU15]

(Integrates ISGEO Classification [PACS, PAC, PACG] with Traditional Clinical Stages):

Stage I: Primary Angle-Closure Suspect (PACS) / Latent Stage:

Features: Asymptomatic; “Eclipse sign” positive on penlight; Van Herick slit-lamp grade 1 (PACD  corneal thickness); Gonioscopy shows >270° iridotrabecular contact (occludable angle) with normal IOP, no PAS, and normal disc/fields.

Provocative Tests: Prone-darkroom test (rise of IOP >8 mmHg after 1 hour prone in dark room).

Management: Prophylactic Nd:YAG Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) (mandatory if fellow eye had acute attack).

Stage II: Primary Angle Closure (PAC) — Subacute & Acute: (Defining criteria: >270° iridotrabecular contact + elevated IOP and/or PAS, but normal optic disc and visual fields).

A. Subacute (Intermittent) PAC: Transient attacks of unilateral blurring of vision, coloured halos around lights, and mild browache precipitated by dark rooms/stress; resolves spontaneously on sleeping or entering bright light (physiological miosis). Treated by Laser PI.

B. Acute Primary Angle Closure (Acute Congestive Glaucoma) [KU23, KU22, KU21]:

Symptoms: Sudden onset of excruciating ocular pain radiating along the 5th nerve (frontal/temporal headache), nausea, vomiting, and prostration, rapid profound loss of vision, redness, lacrimation, and photophobia.

Signs:

Oedematous lids, marked conjunctival chemosis, and ciliary + conjunctival congestion.

Cornea is steamy, oedematous (epithelial & stromal oedema), and insensitive.

Anterior chamber is very shallow with aqueous flare/cells; fellow eye also shows a shallow AC (key diagnostic clue).

Pupil is mid-dilated, vertically oval, and fixed (non-reactive to light and accommodation due to sphincter ischaemia).

IOP is markedly elevated (40–70 mmHg) — eyeball feels stony hard on digital tonometry.

Gonioscopy (after clearing corneal oedema with glycerine) shows complete 360° angle closure (Shaffer Grade 0).

Optic disc is hyperaemic and oedematous.

Sequelae of Acute Attack: Vogt’s Triad = (1) Glaukomflecken [KU20, RGU, TU] (greyish-white anterior subcapsular necrotic lens opacities), (2) Patches of sectoral irisstromal atrophy with spiral-like iris fibres, and (3) Slightly dilated, irregular, sluggish pupil.

Stage III: Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG) / Chronic Stage:

Features: >270° iridotrabecular contact + PAS + elevated IOP + glaucomatous optic disc cupping and visual field defects (identical to POAG). Results from creeping synechial closure or post-acute attack.

Stage IV: Absolute Glaucoma [KU16, TU]:

Features: Painful, irritable, completely blind eye (PL negative); perilimbal reddish-blue flush with dilated anterior ciliary veins (Caput medusae); hazy insensitive cornea with bullous/filamentary keratopathy; very shallow AC; atrophic iris with ectropion uveae; fixed dilated pupil with greenish hue; deep glaucomatous optic atrophy; stony hard globe.

Complications: Corneal ulceration, Ciliary/Equatorial staphyloma, Atrophic bulbi.

Treatment of Absolute Glaucoma: Cyclocryotherapy or Diode Laser Cyclophotocoagulation (CPC) to destroy secretory ciliary epithelium; Retrobulbar alcohol injection (1 ml 2% xylocaine followed by 1 ml 80% alcohol) for pain relief; Enucleation if intractable pain persists.

3. Differential Diagnosis of Acute Red Eye [KU21]

Must be differentiated from Acute Iridocyclitis (small irregular pupil, KPs, normal/deep AC, normal/raised IOP) and Acute Mucopurulent Conjunctivitis (superficial congestion, mucopurulent discharge, normal vision, normal pupil/IOP), and Acute Secondary Angle-Closure Glaucomas (Phacomorphic glaucoma — fellow eye has deep AC; Neovascular glaucoma).

4. Management of Acute Primary Angle Closure [KU25, KU23, KU22, KU21, KU17]

(Ocular Emergency — Immediate hospitalization): * Step 1: Immediate Medical Therapy to Lower IOP & Relieve Pain: 1. Systemic Hyperosmotic Agent: IV Mannitol 20% (1–2 g/kg body weight infused over 30–45 minutes) or Oral Glycerol 50% (if no vomiting/diabetes). 2. Systemic Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitor: Acetazolamide 500 mg IV/PO stat, followed by 250 mg QID. 3. Make patient lie supine (allows lens to fall back slightly by gravity). 4. Topical Antiglaucoma Drops: Timolol 0.5% BD + Brimonidine 0.2% BD. 5. Topical Miotic: Pilocarpine 2% eye drops — Start ONLY 1 hour after initiating hyperosmotics/acetazolamide (when IOP falls <40 mmHg), because at high IOP the iris sphincter is ischaemic and unresponsive. Instill every 15 min for 1 hour, then QID. 6. Topical Steroid: Prednisolone acetate 1% QID to reduce inflammation and PAS formation. 7. Systemic Analgesics & Antiemetics. * Step 2: Corneal Indentation (Compressive Gonioscopy): Pressing the central cornea with a 4-mirror Zeiss goniolens forces aqueous into the angle periphery to mechanically open appositional closure. * Step 3: Definitive Surgical / Laser Treatment [KU19, TU]: 1. Nd:YAG Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) [RGU] or Surgical Peripheral Iridectomy [KU18, RGU, TU]: Performed once cornea clears and PAS involve <270° (or <50%) of the angle. Creates an alternative communication between posterior and anterior chambers, bypassing pupillary block. 2. Trabeculectomy (with Mitomycin-C): Indicated when PAS involve >270° (or >50%) of the angle, or if IOP remains uncontrolled after patent LPI and medical therapy. 3. Lens Extraction (Phacoemulsification + PCIOL): Increasingly performed to deepen the anterior chamber permanently. * Step 4: Mandatory Prophylaxis for the Fellow Eye [KU17]: * The fellow eye (usually PACS) has a 50–75% risk of developing an acute attack within 5 years. Perform prophylactic Nd:YAG Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) on the fellow eye immediately. Avoid mydriatics in the fellow eye until LPI is completed.

subject: ophthalmology
title: ESSAY 8 & SHORT ESSAY 1: LENS-INDUCED GLAUCOMAS
text:
ESSAY 8 & SHORT ESSAY 1: LENS-INDUCED GLAUCOMAS

(Covers KU24, KU14 Essay; KU24 Short Essay; KU21, KU16, RGU, TU Short Answers)

Clinical Case Identification:

Case (KU24, KU14): 70-year-old female, operated for cataract in LE 2 years ago, presents with 10 days of severe pain, redness, diminution of vision in RE, circumcorneal congestion, corneal oedema, shallow AC, intumescent cataractous lens, and high IOP  Phacomorphic Glaucoma (Lens-Induced Secondary Angle-Closure Glaucoma).

1. Classification & Mechanisms of Lens-Induced Glaucomas [KU24, KU21]

A. Secondary Angle-Closure Glaucomas:

Phacomorphic Glaucoma [RGU]: Caused by a swollen, intumescent cataractous lens (mature or immature) or traumatic lens swelling. The anteroposteriorly enlarged lens pushes the iris forward, obliterating the angle directly and causing secondary pupillary block + iris bombe.

Phacotopic Glaucoma: Caused by anterior subluxation/dislocation of lens or microspherophakia blocking the pupil/angle.

B. Secondary Open-Angle Glaucomas:

Phacolytic Glaucoma (Lens Protein Glaucoma) [KU16, RGU, TU]: Occurs in Hypermature Morgagnian cataract. Soluble high-molecular-weight lens proteins leak through an intact microscopic capsule  engulfed by macrophages  swollen protein-laden macrophages and free proteins clog the open trabecular meshwork.

Lens Particle Glaucoma: Free cortical lens matter (after ECCE or penetrating trauma) directly blocks the open trabecular meshwork.

Phacoanaphylactic (Phacoantigenic) Glaucoma: Granulomatous immune-complex uveitis against liberated lens proteins clogging the trabecular meshwork.

2. Clinical Features (Phacomorphic vs. Phacolytic)

Common Symptoms: Acute onset of severe ocular pain, headache, nausea/vomiting, redness, watering, and history of long-standing preceding painless gradual loss of vision (due to senile cataract).

Distinguishing Signs:

Phacomorphic Glaucoma: Corneal oedema, very shallow anterior chamber, mid-dilated fixed pupil, swollen intumescent pearly-white cataract, high IOP. Fellow eye has a normal deep AC and open angle (differentiates it from Acute PACG).

Phacolytic Glaucoma: Corneal oedema, deep anterior chamber containing turbid aqueous with iridescent white protein particles / calcium oxalate crystals (may settle as a pseudohypopyon), open angle on gonioscopy, and a Morgagnian hypermature cataract with a sunken brownish nucleus.

3. Management, Complications & Preoperative Advice [KU24, KU14]

Immediate Medical Management: Identical to Acute PACG EXCEPT Pilocarpine is strictly CONTRAINDICATED (miotics contract the ciliary muscle, relax zonules, shift the lens-iris diaphragm further anteriorly, and worsen phacomorphic block or inflammation).

Give IV Mannitol 20% (1–2 g/kg), Oral Acetazolamide (500 mg stat, 250 mg QID), Topical Timolol 0.5% BD + Brimonidine 0.2% BD, and Topical Prednisolone acetate 1% QID (to control inflammation).

Definitive Treatment: Cataract Extraction (SICS or Phacoemulsification) with PCIOL implantation as soon as the IOP is medically lowered and inflammation is controlled.

Complications if Untreated: Glaucomatous optic atrophy (permanent blindness), Corneal endothelial decompensation, Peripheral anterior synechiae (chronic angle closure), Absolute glaucoma.

Surgical Complications Anticipated: High vitreous pressure, Expulsive choroidal haemorrhage, Zonular dehiscence (weak zonules in hypermature cataract), Run-away capsulorrhexis (due to high intralenticular pressure in intumescent lens — prevented by staining capsule with Trypan blue and aspirating liquid cortex with a 26G needle before CCC), Posterior capsular rupture, Vitreous loss.

Preoperative Advice: Explain guarded visual prognosis (due to potential optic nerve damage from 10 days of high IOP) and higher intraoperative risk of PCR/aphakia.

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ANSWERS ON GLAUCOMA
text:
SHORT ANSWERS ON GLAUCOMA

1. Primary Congenital / Infantile Glaucoma (Buphthalmos) [KU17, KU15, KU14, RGU, TU]

Definition: Developmental glaucoma due to maldevelopment of the trabecular meshwork (Trabeculodysgenesis) from neural crest cells, manifesting at birth (Newborn glaucoma, 40%) or before age 3 years (Infantile glaucoma, 55%). Bilateral in 70%; Boys > Girls; linked to CYP1B1 gene (GLC3A).

Clinical Features:

Classic Triad of Symptoms: Epiphora (lacrimation), Photophobia, and Blepharospasm (often with eye rubbing).

Buphthalmos (“Ox-eye”): Enlargement of the globe and cornea (horizontal corneal diameter >13 mm; >16 mm has poor prognosis) because infant sclera/cornea is distensible before age 3.

Corneal Oedema & Haab’s Striae: Horizontal or concentric tears in Descemet’s membrane with double contour.

Blue Sclera (stretched thin sclera showing underlying uvea), Deep Anterior Chamber, iridodonesis, flattened/subluxated lens, axial myopia, and optic disc cupping (reversible in infants if IOP is lowered early!).

Management:

Examination under Anaesthesia (EUA): Perkins tonometry, calliper corneal diameter, gonioscopy (shows flat or concave direct iris insertion into trabeculum), ophthalmoscopy.

Treatment is Primarily Surgical:

Goniotomy: Incising abnormal trabecular tissue under direct gonioscopic view using Barkan’s knife (requires clear cornea).

Trabeculotomy ab externo: Using Harm’s trabeculotome to break the inner wall of Schlemm’s canal (useful in cloudy cornea).

Combined Trabeculotomy + Trabeculectomy with Mitomycin-C: Procedure of choice in Indian eyes.

2. Secondary Glaucomas (Neovascular & Pseudoexfoliative) [KU24, KU21, KU14, RGU]

Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) [KU14]: Intractable glaucoma caused by a fibrovascular membrane growing over the iris (Rubeosis iridis) and anterior chamber angle.

Etiology (Retinal Ischaemia / VEGF-driven): Ischaemic CRVO (“90-day glaucoma”), Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR), Ocular Ischaemic Syndrome, Eales’ disease, Central Retinal Artery Occlusion, Chronic RD.

Stages: (1) Preglaucomatous stage (Rubeosis iridis), (2) Secondary Open-Angle stage (pretrabecular fibrovascular membrane), (3) Secondary Angle-Closure stage (contracture of membrane pulls iris over trabeculum like a zipper).

Management: Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) + Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Bevacizumab) to regress new vessels; Medical IOP control (atropine + steroids + timolol; avoid pilocarpine); Glaucoma Drainage Device (Ahmed Glaucoma Valve - AGV) or Cyclophotocoagulation.

Pseudoexfoliative Glaucoma (Glaucoma Capsulare) [RGU]: Secondary open-angle glaucoma associated with Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (LOXL1 gene). Characterized by deposition of grey, dandruff-like fibrillar amyloid-like material on the pupillary ruff, anterior lens capsule (target/bull’s-eye pattern with a clear mid-peripheral zone rubbed by iris), zonules (causing zonular weakness/phacodonesis), and trabecular meshwork. Gonioscopy shows heavy pigment along Schwalbe’s line (Sampaolesi’s line). Managed like POAG.

3. Ocular Hypertension [RGU] & Causes of Shallow Anterior Chamber [KU24, TU]

Ocular Hypertension [RGU]: Consistently elevated IOP >21 mmHg in an adult with an open angle, normal optic disc, and normal visual fields. Managed by observation unless high-risk factors (IOP >30 mmHg, CCT <550 m, C:D >0.7, family history) are present, in which case topical prostaglandin/timolol is started to reduce IOP by 20%.

Causes of Shallow Anterior Chamber [KU24, TU]: (1) Primary Angle-Closure Disease, (2) High Hypermetropia, (3) Phacomorphic glaucoma (intumescent cataract), (4) Anterior subluxation of lens, (5) Postoperative wound leak (Seidel’s test positive), (6) Ciliochoroidal detachment, (7) Malignant (Ciliary Block) Glaucoma (aqueous misdirection into vitreous), (8) Perforated corneal ulcer / penetrating corneal trauma.

subject: ophthalmology
title: ESSAY 1: CENTRAL RETINAL ARTERY OCCLUSION (CRAO)
text:
SECTION 3: DISEASES OF THE RETINA

ESSAY 1: CENTRAL RETINAL ARTERY OCCLUSION (CRAO)

(Covers KU23 Essay; KU25, KU24, KU21, KU20, KU16, KU14, RGU, TU Short Answers)

Clinical Case Identification:

Case (KU23): 70-year-old hypertensive/diabetic male with sudden painless loss of vision in left eye (“curtain coming down”) and a cherry-red spot at the macula  Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).

1. Etiology

Embolism (Most Common):

Cholesterol emboli (Hollenhorst plaques): Refractile orange plaques at bifurcations, arising from carotid artery atheromas.

Calcific emboli: White plaques from cardiac valves.

Platelet-fibrin emboli: Dull white, associated with Transient Ischaemic Attacks (Amaurosis fugax).

Atherosclerosis-related thrombosis at the level of lamina cribrosa (associated with hypertension and diabetes).

Vasculitis / Obliterative Arteritis: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA - medical emergency), Polyarteritis nodosa, SLE.

Raised IOP (e.g., tight scleral buckle, retrobulbar haemorrhage) and Thrombophilic disorders (hyperhomocysteinaemia).

2. Clinical Features (Other Signs to Look For) [KU23, KU21, KU16, TU]

Symptoms: Sudden, painless, profound loss of vision occurring over seconds; may be preceded by Amaurosis fugax (fleeting curtain-like blackout).

Signs:

Visual Acuity: Reduced to counting fingers, hand movements, or PL (except in 15–20% of eyes having a congenital Cilioretinal artery from posterior ciliary circulation, which spares the papillomacular bundle and preserves central 6/6 vision with a tubular field).

Pupillary Reaction: Direct light reflex is absent; marked Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil) is present.

Fundus Picture of CRAO [KU21]:

Milky-white / Pale opaque retina at the posterior pole due to ischaemic cloudy swelling of the inner retinal ganglion cell and nerve fibre layers.

Cherry-Red Spot at the Fovea: The central foveola is extremely thin, devoid of inner retinal layers and ganglion cells, allowing the normal vascular choroid and RPE to shine through as a bright red spot in stark contrast to the surrounding milky-white oedematous retina.

Marked attenuation (thread-like narrowing) of retinal arteries.

“Cattle-trucking” (Box-carring): Segmentation of the blood column in retinal veins and arterioles.

Hollenhorst plaque may be visible on the disc or at an arterial bifurcation.

Late Atrophic Stage (after 4–6 weeks): Retinal pallor resolves, leaving a pale chalky-white disc (Ischaemic/Consecutive Optic Atrophy) and thread-like occluded vessels.

3. Differential Diagnosis

Four Causes of Sudden Painless Loss of Vision in an Elderly Patient [KU23, KU24, KU14, RGU, TU]:

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)

Ischaemic Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO)

Massive Vitreous Haemorrhage (due to PDR, BRVO, wet ARMD, or PVD with retinal tear)

Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment involving the macula

Anterior Ischaemic Optic Neuropathy (AION) or Optic Neuritis.

Causes of Cherry-Red Spot at the Macula [KU25, KU24, KU20]:

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)

Commotio Retinae (Berlin’s Oedema) following blunt ocular trauma

Tay-Sachs Disease (GM2 gangliosidosis)

Niemann-Pick Disease (Sphingomyelinase deficiency)

Gaucher’s Disease, Sandhoff’s Disease, and Sialidosis (Cherry-red spot myoclonus syndrome).

4. Plan of Management [KU23]

(Ocular Emergency — Retina suffers irreversible infarction after 90–100 minutes of complete ischaemia, but aggressive treatment must be attempted in all cases presenting within 24 hours to dislodge the embolus peripherally): 1. Immediate Ocular Massage: Intermittent firm digital massage over the closed eyelid (or with a 3-mirror contact lens) for 15 seconds, then release, to mechanically dislodge the embolus. 2. Immediate Acute Lowering of IOP (increases retinal arterial perfusion pressure): * Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: Withdraw 0.1–0.2 ml of aqueous using a 27G/30G needle at the limbus. * IV Acetazolamide 500 mg stat + IV Mannitol 20% (1 g/kg). 3. Vasodilatation: * Carbogen Inhalation (mixture of 5%  + 95% ) or Rebreathing into a paper/polythene bag to induce hypercapnic vasodilation. * Sublingual Isosorbide dinitrate. 4. Rule out Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA): Check urgent ESR and C-Reactive Protein (CRP). If GCA is suspected (scalp tenderness, jaw claudication), start immediate IV Methylprednisolone 1 g/day to prevent blindness in the fellow eye. 5. Systemic Cardiovascular Workup (Stroke Protocol): Carotid Doppler ultrasound, Echocardiography, ECG, Lipid profile, BP/Diabetes control, and oral antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin/Clopidogrel).

5. Complications of CRAO [KU23]

Permanent profound visual loss and Consecutive / Ischaemic Optic Atrophy.

Rubeosis Iridis and Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) (occurs in 2–15% of cases, typically 4–6 weeks post-occlusion; treated with PRP and intravitreal anti-VEGF).

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ESSAYS ON RETINA
text:
SHORT ESSAYS ON RETINA

1. Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) [KU19, KU17, KU14, KU15, RGU, TU]

Definition & Risk Factors: Microangiopathy of retinal precapillary arterioles, capillaries, and venules caused by chronic hyperglycaemia.

Risk Factors: Duration of diabetes (most important: >20 years  90% Type 1 and 60% Type 2 develop DR), Poor glycaemic control (), Pregnancy, Systemic Hypertension, Nephropathy, Hyperlipidaemia, Smoking, Anaemia.

Pathogenesis: Chronic hyperglycaemia  Sorbitol accumulation (aldose reductase pathway) + Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs) + Protein Kinase C activation + Oxidative stress  Loss of capillary pericytes, basement membrane thickening, and endothelial damage:

Weakened capillary wall  Microaneurysms (earliest clinical lesion).

Breakdown of inner blood-retinal barrier  Retinal oedema, Hard exudates (lipoproteins in outer plexiform layer), and Dot-and-blot haemorrhages.

Microvascular capillary closure & leukostasis  Retinal ischaemia/hypoxia  Cotton-wool spots (nerve fibre layer infarcts), Venous beading, and Intraretinal Microvascular Abnormalities (IRMAs - A-V shunts).

Hypoxia-induced upregulation of VEGF (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor)  Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) (Neovascularization of disc [NVD] and elsewhere [NVE])  Vitreous haemorrhage & Tractional Retinal Detachment.

ETDRS Classification of Diabetic Retinopathy [KU19, KU17, KU14, RGU, TU]:

I. Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR):

Mild NPDR: At least one microaneurysm present.

Moderate NPDR: Microaneurysms/intraretinal haemorrhages in 2–3 quadrants, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, or mild IRMA (less than Severe NPDR).

Severe NPDR (Follows the 4–2–1 Rule — ANY ONE of the following):

4 quadrants of severe intraretinal dot-blot haemorrhages ( per quadrant) and microaneurysms.

2 quadrants of definite venous beading.

1 quadrant of prominent IRMA.

Very Severe NPDR: ANY TWO of the 4–2–1 criteria present.

II. Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) [RGU]:

Early PDR: Neovascularization at the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE), not meeting HRC criteria.

High-Risk PDR (PDR with High-Risk Characteristics - HRCs):

NVD  to  of disc area (with or without vitreous/preretinal haemorrhage).

Any NVD  disc area with vitreous or preretinal (subhyaloid) haemorrhage.

NVE  disc area with vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage.

III. Diabetic Maculopathy (Diabetic Macular Oedema - DME):

Clinically Significant Macular Oedema (CSME): Defined by ANY ONE of:

Retinal thickening at or within 500 m of the centre of the fovea.

Hard exudates at or within 500 m of the centre of the fovea with adjacent retinal thickening.

Zone of retinal thickening  disc area, any part of which is within 1 disc diameter of the foveal centre.

Angiographic Types: Focal exudative (circinate hard exudates), Diffuse exudative (cystoid spaces), Ischaemic maculopathy (enlarged FAZ on FFA), Mixed.

OCT Classification: Non-tractional DME vs. Tractional DME (taut posterior hyaloid / vitreofoveal traction).

IV. Advanced Diabetic Eye Disease (ADED): Non-resolving vitreous haemorrhage, Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD), Rubeosis iridis, and Neovascular Glaucoma.

Management of Diabetic Retinopathy:

Screening Schedule: Type 1 DM (5 years after diagnosis, then annually); Type 2 DM (at diagnosis, then annually for no/mild NPDR, 6-monthly for moderate NPDR, 3-monthly for severe NPDR).

Strict Systemic Control: Target , BP  mmHg, Lipid control (statins/fenofibrate), treat anaemia and nephropathy.

Intravitreal Anti-VEGF Therapy (First-line for Centre-Involving DME & adjunct in PDR): Ranibizumab (0.5 mg), Bevacizumab (1.25 mg), or Aflibercept (2 mg).

Intravitreal Steroids: Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) or Triamcinolone acetonide (IVTA) in pseudophakic/recalcitrant DME.

Laser Photocoagulation (Double-frequency Nd:YAG 532 nm or Argon Green) [TU]:

Focal / Modified Grid Laser: For non-centre-involving CSME.

Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP): Mainstay for High-Risk PDR and NVI. Consists of 1200–1600 laser burns (500 m spot size, 0.1 sec duration, one burn-width apart) applied outside the temporal vascular arcades up to the equator, destroying hypoxic peripheral retina to stop VEGF production.

Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): Indicated for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage (>1–3 months), Tractional Retinal Detachment involving macula, Combined tractional-rhegmatogenous RD, and Tractional DME.

2. Hypertensive Retinopathy [KU23, KU18, KU15, RGU, TU]

Pathogenesis (Three Phases):

Vasoconstrictive Phase: Diffuse and focal arteriolar narrowing due to autoregulatory vasospasm in response to raised BP.

Sclerotic Phase: Intimal hyalinization and medial hyperplasia  Broadened arteriolar light reflex (Copper-wiring and Silver-wiring) + Arteriovenous (A-V) crossing changes (nicking) where artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath:

Salus’s sign: Deflection of vein at A-V crossing (S-shaped or right-angled).

Bonnet’s sign: Banking/dilatation of vein distal to the crossing.

Gunn’s sign: Tapering/concealment of vein on either side of the crossing.

Exudative Phase: Breakdown of blood-retinal barrier and focal arteriolar fibrinoid necrosis  Flame-shaped superficial haemorrhages, Hard exudates (Macular star due to radial lipid deposition in Henle’s layer), Cotton-wool spots, and Optic disc swelling (Malignant hypertension).

Keith-Wagener-Barker (KWB) Classification / Stages [KU23, RGU, TU]:

Grade I: Mild generalized arteriolar attenuation, particularly of small branches, with broadening of arteriolar light reflex.

Grade II: Marked generalized and focal arteriolar narrowing + A-V nipping (Salus’s sign).

Grade III: Grade II changes + Copper-wiring of arterioles, Bonnet’s and Gunn’s signs, flame-shaped haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates (Macular star).

Grade IV (Malignant Hypertensive Retinopathy) [TU]: All changes of Grade III + Silver-wiring of arterioles and Papilloedema / Optic disc oedema (hallmark of Grade IV).

Associated Hypertensive Choroidopathy: Seen in acute malignant hypertension in young patients (e.g., Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension / Pre-eclampsia):

Elschnig’s spots: Small black RPE spots surrounded by yellow halos (choroidal infarcts).

Siegrist’s streaks: Linear pigmentary streaks along choroidal arterioles.

Exudative bullous retinal detachment.

Management:

Grades I & II: Routine systemic antihypertensive control and lifestyle modification.

Grade III: Systemic antihypertensive therapy + evaluation of target organ damage (renal profile, lipid profile, ECG).

Grade IV (Hypertensive Emergency): Urgent hospitalization for controlled, stepwise reduction of blood pressure (avoid precipitous drop in BP, which can cause acute ischaemic infarction of the optic nerve head and brain). In PIH/Eclampsia, appearance of hypoxic retinopathy/exudative RD is an obstetric indication for termination of pregnancy.

3. Ischaemic Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) [KU21, KU14, RGU, TU]

Etiology:Compression of the central retinal vein by a rigid atherosclerotic central retinal artery within the common fibrous sheath just behind the lamina cribrosa  turbulent flow, endothelial damage, and thrombosis.

Risk Factors: Age >50 years, Systemic hypertension, Diabetes mellitus, Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG), Hyperviscosity syndromes (polycythaemia, multiple myeloma, leukaemia), Thrombophilia (hyperhomocysteinaemia in young adults), Periphlebitis (Sarcoidosis, Behcet’s).

Clinical Features of Ischaemic CRVO (Haemorrhagic Retinopathy) [KU21, KU14]:

Symptoms: Sudden, painless, marked loss of vision (usually ).

Signs:

Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) is markedly positive (key differentiator from Non-ischaemic CRVO).

Fundus Picture (“Splashed-Tomato” or “Blood and Thunder” Fundus) [KU14]:

Massive engorgement, dilatation, and tortuosity of all branches of the central retinal vein.

Extensive superficial flame-shaped and deep blot haemorrhages covering the entire fundus from posterior pole to periphery.

Numerous Cotton-Wool Spots (typically  to 10, indicating widespread ischaemia).

Marked Optic Disc Oedema and hyperaemia.

Severe Macular Oedema and haemorrhages.

Investigations:

FFA: Shows >10 Disc Areas of Capillary Non-Perfusion (CNP).

OCT: Quantifies severe Cystoid Macular Oedema (CME).

ERG: Reduced b-wave amplitude (decreased b:a wave ratio).

Complications: Rubeosis iridis and Neovascular Glaucoma (“90-day glaucoma” / “100-day glaucoma”) develops in 20–50% of ischaemic CRVO within 3 months; Vitreous haemorrhage; Macular scarring.

Management:

Treat underlying hypertension, diabetes, hyperhomocysteinaemia, and POAG.

Intravitreal Anti-VEGF injections (Ranibizumab / Bevacizumab / Aflibercept) or Intravitreal Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) for macular oedema.

Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP): Performed promptly if iris/angle/retinal neovascularization (NVI/NVA/NVD) develops.

4. Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) [KU24, KU23, KU19, KU17, KU15, RGU, TU]

Clinical Case Identification (RGU): 20-year-old male with slowly progressive defective vision worse in the evening (Nyctalopia) and positive family history  Retinitis Pigmentosa.

Definition & Inheritance: Hereditary diffuse retinal dystrophy primarily affecting rod photoreceptors early, followed by cone degeneration (Rod-Cone Dystrophy).

Inheritance: Sporadic (50%), Autosomal Recessive (most common inherited form, severe), Autosomal Dominant (best prognosis), X-linked Recessive (least common, most severe).

Clinical Features:

Symptoms:

Night Blindness (Nyctalopia): Earliest and cardinal symptom (appears years before fundus changes).

Progressive loss of peripheral vision (patient trips over objects in dim light), culminating in Tubular Vision (central vision preserved till late).

Signs — Classic Fundus Triad of Retinitis Pigmentosa [KU19, KU17, RGU, TU]:

Jet-black “Bone-spicule” (Bone-corpuscle) retinal pigmentary clumps arranged in a perivascular distribution, starting in the equatorial (mid-peripheral) zone and spreading anteriorly and posteriorly.

Marked Attenuation (narrowing) of retinal arterioles (becoming thread-like).

Pale, Waxy-yellow Optic Disc (ultimately leading to Consecutive Optic Atrophy). (Additional findings: RPE atrophy unmasking choroidal vessels, Cystoid Macular Oedema, Posterior subcapsular complicated cataract, Myopia, Keratoconus, POAG).

Investigations:

Perimetry: Characteristic Annular (Ring-shaped) Scotoma corresponding to equatorial degeneration, which expands to leave only a tiny central island (Tubular vision).

Electroretinography (ERG): Subnormal or extinguished (scotopic rod response affected earliest, even before clinical fundus signs appear).

Electro-oculography (EOG): Subnormal Arden ratio (<150) with absence of light peak.

Systemic Syndromes Associated with Retinitis Pigmentosa [KU15]:

Usher’s Syndrome: RP + Congenital sensorineural deafness (most common syndrome).

Laurence-Moon-Biedl (Bardet-Biedl) Syndrome: RP + Obesity + Polydactyly + Hypogonadism + Mental retardation.

Refsum’s Disease: RP + Phytanic acid accumulation + Peripheral neuropathy + Cerebellar ataxia.

Kearns-Sayre Syndrome: RP + Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia + Heart block.

Bassen-Kornzweig Syndrome (Abetalipoproteinaemia): RP + Acanthocytosis + Ataxia.

Management:

No definitive cure for typical RP (Note: Voretigene neparvovec / Luxturna gene therapy is approved for RPE65-mutation retinal dystrophy).

Supportive Measures: Correct refractive error, Oral Acetazolamide for associated CME, Cataract surgery for PSC, Vitamin A Palmitate (15,000 IU/day) to slow progression, Low Vision Aids (LVAs) (magnifying devices, night-vision scopes, CCTV), Vocational rehabilitation, and Genetic counselling (avoid consanguineous marriages).

5. Retinal Detachment (RD) [KU24, KU21, KU20, KU19, KU17, RGU, TU]

Clinical Case Identification (TU): 25-year-old male with High Myopia (-7.00 D) presenting with sudden painless loss of vision, flashes of light (photopsia), and floaters  Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment.

Definition & Classification [KU21, KU24, KU20]: Separation of the neurosensory retina (NSR) from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) by subretinal fluid (SRF). Three types:

Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD - Primary): Caused by a full-thickness retinal break (hole or tear) allowing liquefied vitreous to seep into the subretinal space.

Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD): NSR pulled away mechanically by contracting fibrovascular vitreoretinal membranes (no retinal break). Causes: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy, Retinopathy of Prematurity, Eales’ disease, Penetrating trauma, Sickle-cell retinopathy.

Exudative (Serous / Solid) Retinal Detachment [RGU]: Fluid accumulates beneath NSR without a break or traction due to choroidal tumours (Choroidal melanoma, Retinoblastoma, Choroidal haemangioma), inflammations (VKH syndrome, Posterior scleritis, Sympathetic ophthalmia), or vascular disease (Coats’ disease, Toxaemia of pregnancy / Eclampsia). Hallmark: Shifting fluid with smooth, convex bullous configuration.

Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD) [KU21, RGU, TU]:

Risk Factors: High Myopia (40% of cases), Aphakia / Pseudophakia (especially after PCR/vitreous loss), Peripheral Retinal Degenerations (Lattice degeneration [most important], Snail-track degeneration), Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD), Blunt/penetrating ocular trauma, Stickler syndrome.

Pathogenesis: Dynamic vitreoretinal traction + PVD + predisposing lattice degeneration  Retinal Break (Horse-shoe tear, operculated hole, or Retinal dialysis in trauma)  Synchytic fluid vitreous seeps through break  Separates NSR from RPE.

Clinical Features:

Prodromal Symptoms: Photopsia (flashes of light due to vitreoretinal traction) and Sudden shower of floaters (vitreous haemorrhage/pigment release).

Presenting Symptoms: Appearance of a dark curtain or veil progressing across the visual field, followed by sudden painless loss of central vision when the macula detaches.

Signs:

RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil) and Hypotony (IOP is lower by ~5 mmHg).

Shaffer’s Sign (“Tobacco dusting”): Pigment granules in the anterior vitreous.

Fundus Examination (Indirect Ophthalmoscopy with Scleral Indentation):

Detached retina looks greyish-white, opaque, raised (convex), and thrown into corrugated folds that undulate/oscillate with eye movements; retinal vessels appear dark and tortuous.

Retinal Breaks appear bright red (due to underlying choroid), most commonly located in the superotemporal quadrant (distribution ofSRF follows Lincoff’s rules).

Long-standing RD signs: Retinal thinning, intraretinal cysts, subretinal demarcation lines (“high-water marks”), and Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR).

B-scan Ultrasonography: Shows a high-spike mobile membrane attached to the optic disc and ora serrata (essential in opaque media).

Management of RRD (Surgeries for RD) [TU]: (Three Basic Principles: 1. Find and seal all retinal breaks by inducing aseptic chorioretinitis via Cryopexy or Laser Photocoagulation; 2. Drain SRF; 3. Relieve vitreoretinal traction & maintain chorioretinal apposition):

Pneumatic Retinopexy: Outpatient procedure for fresh uncomplicated superior RD with a single break in the upper 8 clock hours. Cryopexy/laser to break + intravitreal injection of an expanding gas bubble ( [Sulphur hexafluoride] or  [Perfluoropropane]) + strict head positioning for 5–7 days.

Scleral Buckling: Suturing a silicone sponge (radial) or solid silicone band (circumferential encirclage) onto the external sclera to indent the eyewall against the retinal break, combined with trans-scleral cryopexy and external SRF drainage.

Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) + Endolaser + Internal Tamponade: Performed for posterior breaks, giant retinal tears, vitreous haemorrhage, pseudophakic RD, PVR, and all Tractional RDs. Uses Perfluorocarbon liquids (PFCL) to flatten the retina, endolaser around breaks, and Silicone oil or  gas for internal tamponade.

6. Leukocoria & Retinoblastoma [KU25, KU24, KU23, KU19, KU17, KU16, RGU, TU]

Leukocoria (“Amaurotic Cat’s-Eye Reflex”) [KU25, KU23, KU17, RGU]: Abnormal yellowish-white pupillary reflex in a child.

Causes / Differential Diagnosis of Leukocoria (“Pseudogliomas”):

Retinoblastoma (most dangerous malignant tumour — must be ruled out first!)

Congenital Cataract (most common overall cause)

Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP) (Stage 5 cicatricial retrolental fibroplasia)

Persistent Hyperplastic Primary Vitreous (PHPV) (unilateral, associated with microphthalmos and elongated ciliary processes)

Coats’ Disease (unilateral exudative telangiectasia in boys aged 4–10 years)

Ocular Toxocariasis (larval granuloma / chronic endophthalmitis)

Organizing Vitreous Abscess / Endophthalmitis & Coloboma of Choroid.

Retinoblastoma [KU24, KU23, KU19, KU16, RGU, TU]:

Epidemiology & Genetics: Most common primary intraocular malignant tumour of childhood (1 in 15,000 live births; mean age at diagnosis 18 months; 90% diagnosed before 3 years).

Caused by mutation/deletion of both alleles of the tumour-suppressor RB1 gene on chromosome 13q14 (Knudson’s “Two-Hit” Hypothesis).

Heritable/Germline (40%): First mutation in all somatic cells, second in retinal cell  usually bilateral and multifocal; predisposed to Pinealoblastoma (Trilateral Retinoblastoma) and secondary Osteosarcoma.

Non-heritable/Somatic (60%): Both hits in a single retinal cell  always unilateral and unifocal.

Histopathology [KU20]: Small round blue cells with large hyperchromatic nuclei, areas of necrosis and chalky calcification, arranged in characteristic Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (true central lumen — pathognomonic), Homer-Wright rosettes (central eosinophilic fibrillary tangle), Pseudorosettes (viable tumour cells clustered around blood vessels amidst necrosis), and Fleurettes (photoreceptor differentiation).

Clinical Features (4 Stages):

Stage I: Quiescent Intraocular Stage:

Leukocoria (60%) is the commonest presenting sign.

Strabismus (20%) (second commonest — esotropia/exotropia due to macular involvement).

Fundus Growth Patterns:

Endophytic: Grows inward into vitreous cavity as a friable, chalky-white mass (“cottage-cheese” appearance due to calcification) with surface vessels and vitreous seedings.

Exophytic: Grows outward into subretinal space, causing a total exudative retinal detachment.

Diffuse Infiltrating: Flat placoid retinal thickening without a discrete mass; presents with pseudohypopyon.

Stage II: Glaucomatous / Inflammatory Stage: Painful red eye, secondary buphthalmos, neovascular glaucoma, pseudohypopyon, hyphaema, or orbital cellulitis-like presentation (due to necrotic tumour).

Stage III: Extraocular Extension: Bursts through sclera or extends along optic nerve into orbit  fungating orbital mass and proptosis.

Stage IV: Distant Metastasis: Direct intracranial spread along optic nerve to brain/CSF; haematogenous spread to bone marrow, liver, and lungs; lymphatic spread to preauricular nodes.

International Classification of Retinoblastoma (ICRB) [KU24]:

Group A (Very Low Risk): Small tumours  mm confined to retina,  mm from fovea and  mm from optic disc.

Group B (Low Risk): Tumours  mm, or macular/juxtapapillary location, or cuff of subretinal fluid  mm.

Group C (Moderate Risk): Focal subretinal or vitreous seeds  mm from tumour.

Group D (High Risk): Diffuse subretinal or vitreous seeds  mm from tumour (“greasy” or “snowball” seeds).

Group E (Very High Risk): Extensive tumour  of globe, touching lens, neovascular glaucoma, anterior chamber invasion, opaque media with haemorrhage, phthisis bulbi, or aseptic orbital cellulitis.

Investigations: Examination under Anaesthesia (EUA), B-scan Ultrasound & CT Scan (demonstrates pathognomonic intralesional calcification), MRI of Orbit & Brain (choice to assess optic nerve and pineal/CNS invasion without radiation risk in germline cases). Note: FNAB is strictly contraindicated due to risk of orbital seeding.

Management:

Chemoreduction (Systemic CVE Regimen: Carboplatin + Vincristine + Etoposide) for 6 cycles to shrink tumour, followed by Focal Consolidation Therapy:

Cryotherapy (small anterior tumours) or Laser Photocoagulation / Transpupillary Thermotherapy (TTT) (small posterior tumours) or Brachytherapy ( or  plaque).

Intra-arterial Chemotherapy (Melphalan via ophthalmic artery) and Intravitreal Melphalan for vitreous seeds.

Enucleation: Treatment of choice for Group E tumours, unilateral advanced Group D with no visual potential, or optic nerve invasion. Precaution: Excise the longest possible stump of optic nerve (12–15 mm) and avoid globe perforation.

Adjuvant Chemotherapy + External Beam Radiotherapy: If histopathology of enucleated globe shows post-laminar optic nerve invasion, massive choroidal invasion, or scleral extension.

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ANSWERS ON RETINA
text:
SHORT ANSWERS ON RETINA

1. Anatomy of Retina & Normal Fundus [KU26, KU18, RGU, TU]

Ten Microscopic Layers of Retina (From Outside Inwards) [KU26, RGU]:

Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) (outer blood-retinal barrier)

Layer of Rods and Cones (outer/inner segments of photoreceptors; 120 million rods, 6.5 million cones)

External Limiting Membrane

Outer Nuclear Layer (cell bodies of rods & cones)

Outer Plexiform Layer (Henle’s layer at macula)

Inner Nuclear Layer (bipolar, horizontal, amacrine, and Muller cells — 1st order neurons)

Inner Plexiform Layer

Ganglion Cell Layer (2nd order neurons)

Nerve Fibre Layer (Stratum opticum) (axons forming optic nerve)

Internal Limiting Membrane (Blood Supply: Outer 4 layers by Choriocapillaris; Inner 6 layers by Central Retinal Artery).

Normal Fundus & Physiological Cup [KU18, TU]:

Optic Disc: Vertically oval ( mm), pink neuroretinal rim following ISNT rule, central Physiological Cup (normal C:D ratio 0.3–0.4, shelving edges, central retinal vessels emerging from its centre).

Macula Lutea: 5.5 mm diameter, located 2 disc diameters (3.4 mm) temporal to disc margin; central avascular depression is the fovea centralis (1.5 mm) containing only cones, with a central shining pit (foveola / umbo).

Retinal Vessels: Arteriovenous calibre ratio is 2:3.

2. Enucleation vs. Evisceration [KU24, KU16, KU14, RGU, TU]

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-003]]

3. Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP) [TU]

Definition & Risk Factors: Bilateral proliferative retinopathy affecting premature infants.

Risk Factors: Low gestational age (<32 weeks), Low birth weight (<1500 g; in India, screen all babies <2000 g or <34 weeks), and unmonitored high supplemental oxygen therapy (hyperoxia downregulates VEGF, halting normal centrifugal retinal vascularization; subsequent return to room air causes severe retinal hypoxia and VEGF surge).

ICROP Classification:

Zones (centred on Optic Disc): Zone I (posterior circle with radius =  disc-fovea distance), Zone II (extends to nasal ora serrata), Zone III (residual temporal crescent).

Stages: Stage 1 (Demarcation line), Stage 2 (Elevated ridge), Stage 3 (Extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation), Stage 4 (Subtotal RD: 4A extrafoveal, 4B involving fovea), Stage 5 (Total funnel-shaped RD / retrolental fibroplasia).

Plus Disease (+): Dilatation of veins and tortuosity of arterioles at the posterior pole.

Management: Screen at 4 weeks postnatal age (or 2–3 weeks in very small infants). Laser Photocoagulation (Diode/532 nm Green Laser) to the avascular peripheral retina or Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Bevacizumab/Ranibizumab) for Type 1 Pre-threshold, Threshold, and Aggressive Posterior ROP (AP-ROP). Vitrectomy for Stage 4/5.

4. Central Serous Chorioretinopathy (CSCR), Eales’ Disease & Roth’s Spots [RGU, TU]

Central Serous Chorioretinopathy (CSCR) [RGU, TU]: Localized serous detachment of the neurosensory retina at the macula due to choroidal hyperpermeability and RPE pump defect.

Risk Factors: Young adult males (20–50 yrs), Type-A personality / emotional stress, Corticosteroid use (systemic/inhaled/topical).

Clinical Features: Sudden painless mild-to-moderate blur (6/9–6/24) improving with a hypermetropic (+ve) lens, micropsia, metamorphopsia, and central positive scotoma. Fundus shows a round, dome-shaped macular elevation with a ring reflex.

Investigations: FFA shows classic “Ink-blot” pattern (80%) or “Smoke-stack” (mushroom/umbrella) pattern (20%) of hyperfluorescent leakage; OCT confirms neurosensory detachment + PED.

Treatment: Self-limiting in 80–90% within 3 months (reassure, stop steroids). Persistent/recurrent cases (>3–6 months): Focal laser photocoagulation (extrafoveal leaks), Half-fluence Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) (subfoveal leaks), or oral Eplerenone.

Eales’ Disease [RGU]: Idiopathic obliterative peripheral retinal periphlebitis (linked to hypersensitivity to Mycobacterium tuberculosis proteins) affecting healthy young adult males (20–30 years) in India, presenting with recurrent vitreous haemorrhage.

4 Stages: (1) Stage of inflammation (peripheral venous sheathing + superficial haemorrhages), (2) Stage of ischaemia (capillary non-perfusion), (3) Stage of retinal neovascularization (NVE at junction of perfused/non-perfused retina  recurrent vitreous haemorrhage), (4) Stage of sequelae (tractional RD, NVG).

Treatment: Oral steroids (active vasculitis stage), Scatter Laser Photocoagulation (neovascular stage), and Pars Plana Vitrectomy (non-resolving vitreous haemorrhage / TRD).

Roth’s Spots [TU]: Superficial retinal haemorrhages with a pale white centre (composed of fibrin-platelet thrombi, leukaemic cells, or septic emboli). Causes: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis (SABE), Acute Leukaemia, Severe Anaemia (pernicious/aplastic), Scurvy, Candidasis, HIV retinopathy.

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ESSAY 1: AMBLYOPIA
text:
SECTION 4: NEURO-OPHTHALMOLOGY

SHORT ESSAY 1: AMBLYOPIA

(Covers KU24, KU21, RGU, TU Short Essays; KU25, KU23, TU Short Answers)

1. Definition & Pathogenesis

Definition: Unilateral or (rarely) bilateral reduction of best-corrected visual acuity caused by abnormal visual experience (form vision deprivation or abnormal binocular interaction) during the critical period of visual development (birth to 6–8 years of age), in the absence of any organic lesion of the ocular media, retina, or visual pathway.

2. Classification (Types of Amblyopia) [KU23, TU]

Strabismic Amblyopia (Most Common): Results from prolonged chronic monocular suppression of the deviating eye in children with constant unilateral squint (more common in esotropia than exotropia).

Stimulus Deprivation Amblyopia (Amblyopia ex anopsia): Caused by physical obstruction of the visual axis early in life (e.g., dense congenital/traumatic cataract, severe congenital ptosis covering pupil, central corneal opacity). Carries the worst prognosis if not treated within the first few weeks of life.

Anisometropic Amblyopia: Caused by unequal refractive error between the two eyes, producing a chronically blurred retinal image in the more ametropic eye. Occurs with as little as +1.0 to +2.0 D of anisohypermetropia (more common) or >-3.0 D of anisomyopia.

Isoametropic Amblyopia: Bilateral amblyopia due to uncorrected bilateral high refractive error (e.g., hypermetropia >+5.0 D, myopia >-8.0 D).

Meridional Amblyopia: Selective amblyopia for a specific visual meridian due to uncorrected high astigmatism (>1.5 D).

3. Clinical Characteristics (Diagnostic Features)

Reduced Visual Acuity: Difference of  Snellen lines between the two eyes; Recognition acuity (reading letters) is more impaired than resolution/grating acuity.

Crowding Phenomenon: Visual acuity is significantly better when tested with isolated single letters (optotypes) than when tested with a full line of letters on Snellen’s chart.

Neutral Density Filter Effect: When viewing through a neutral density filter, visual acuity remains unchanged or slightly improves in functional amblyopia, whereas it drops sharply in organic macular/optic nerve lesions.

Fixation Pattern: May be central (foveal) or eccentric (parafoveal/macular/peripheral on visuoscopy).

Normal Pupillary Reactions (no RAPD) and normal fundus.

4. Management of Amblyopia

(Golden Rule: Younger the child, better the prognosis; must be initiated before 7–8 years of age): 1. Eliminate Deprivation / Media Opacity: Urgent cataract surgery or ptosis correction if present.

2. Full Optical Correction: Prescribe full cycloplegic refractive correction and allow 4–8 weeks of refractive adaptation. 3. Occlusion Therapy (Gold Standard): Patching the sound (normal) eye to force the brain to use the amblyopic eye. * Age-based Full-Time Schedule: 2:1 (2 days sound eye, 1 day amblyopic eye) at age 2; 3:1 at age 3; 4:1 at age 4; up to 6:1 at age 6 (prevents occlusion amblyopia in the good eye). * PEDIG Part-Time Regimen: 2 hours/day of patching for moderate amblyopia (6/12 to 6/30) and 6 hours/day for severe amblyopia (6/36 to 6/120), combined with near visual activities (drawing, video games). 4. Penalization Therapy: Blurring the sound eye using 1% Atropine drops (pharmacological penalization) or over-plus spectacles (optical penalization) in children who refuse adhesive patches. 5. Adjunctive Therapies: Pharmacologic therapy (Levodopa-Carbidopa), Pleoptics, and Dichoptic/Computerized Vision Therapy.

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ESSAY 2: OPTIC NEURITIS & PAPILLOEDEMA
text:
SHORT ESSAY 2: OPTIC NEURITIS & PAPILLOEDEMA

(Covers KU19, RGU, TU Short Essays; KU23, KU19, KU16, KU15, RGU, TU Short Answers)

1. Optic Neuritis [KU19, RGU, TU]

Definition & Anatomical Classification: Inflammatory, infectious, or demyelinating disorder of the optic nerve.

Papillitis: Anterior optic neuritis involving the intraocular optic nerve head (disc is swollen and hyperaemic); commoner in children.

Retrobulbar Neuritis [RGU, TU]: Involvement of the optic nerve behind the eyeball; commonest in adults with Multiple Sclerosis. Classically described as a condition where “neither the patient nor the ophthalmologist sees anything” (fundus is completely normal initially).

Neuroretinitis: Combined inflammation of the optic disc and peripapillary nerve fibre layer with a macular star of hard exudates (associated with cat-scratch disease, viral infections, syphilis).

Etiology:

Demyelinating Disorders (Most Common): Multiple Sclerosis (MS) (70% of MS patients develop optic neuritis), Neuromyelitis Optica (Devic’s disease) (bilateral optic neuritis + transverse myelitis; anti-Aquaporin-4 IgG positive), Schilder’s disease [RGU].

Parainfectious: Post-viral (measles, mumps, chickenpox) or post-vaccination in children.

Infectious: Ethmoid/sphenoid sinusitis, Syphilis, Tuberculosis, Lyme disease, Herpes zoster.

Autoimmune: Sarcoidosis, SLE, Polyarteritis nodosa.

Clinical Features (Diagnostic Criteria) [TU]:

Symptoms:

Subacute, unilateral, profound loss of vision progressing over 2–5 days.

Periocular / Retrobulbar Pain exacerbated by ocular movements (especially superior/medial gaze, because the superior and medial recti originate from the annulus of Zinn where their sheaths fuse with the dural sheath of the optic nerve).

Dyschromatopsia (Impaired colour vision): Severe red desaturation (red objects look washed-out pink/orange) out of proportion to visual acuity loss.

Uhthoff’s Phenomenon: Transient worsening of vision with exercise, hot bath, or fever.

Pulfrich’s Phenomenon: Altered depth perception for moving objects (a pendulum moving in a straight plane appears to move in an ellipse).

Signs:

Markedly reduced visual acuity and contrast sensitivity.

Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil) is always present in unilateral/asymmetric cases.

Fundus Changes [RGU]: Normal in acute retrobulbar neuritis; in Papillitis, the disc is hyperaemic with blurred margins, obliterated cup, mild swelling (<2–3 D), splinter haemorrhages, and posterior vitreous cells. After 4–6 weeks, temporal or diffuse pallor sets in.

Visual Fields: Central or Centrocaecal Scotoma (most common), or altitudinal/arcuate defects.

VEP: Delayed latency (prolonged  wave) and reduced amplitude; MRI Brain & Orbits with Gadolinium (to detect periventricular white matter plaques of MS).

Management (Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial - ONTT Protocol):

Intravenous Methylprednisolone (1 g/day IV for 3 days), followed by Oral Prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day for 11 days, then 4-day taper). This accelerates visual recovery and delays conversion to clinically definite MS over 2 years.

Important Rule: Oral prednisolone alone (in standard doses) is strictly CONTRAINDICATED, as ONTT proved it is ineffective and doubles the risk of recurrence!

Immunomodulatory therapy (Interferon-) if MRI confirms MS plaques.

2. Papilloedema vs. Papillitis [KU23, KU19, KU16, KU15, RGU, TU]

Definition & Causes of Papilloedema [KU19, KU16, RGU]: Bilateral passive, non-inflammatory hydrostatic swelling of the optic nerve head secondary to raised intracranial pressure (ICP), caused by axoplasmic flow stasis at the lamina cribrosa (Hayreh’s theory).

Causes: (1) Intracranial Space-Occupying Lesions (ICSOLs) (Brain tumours — especially posterior fossa/cerebellar tumours obstructing aqueduct of Sylvius, Brain abscess, Tuberculoma, Subdural haematoma), (2) Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumour cerebri) (young obese females; tetracyclines, hypervitaminosis A, oral contraceptives), (3) Meningitis / Encephalitis, (4) Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis, (5) Subarachnoid Haemorrhage, (6) Malignant Hypertension (Grade IV).

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-004]]

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ESSAY 3: OPTIC ATROPHY & TOXIC OPTIC NEUROPATHY
text:
SHORT ESSAY 3: OPTIC ATROPHY & TOXIC OPTIC NEUROPATHY

(Covers KU24, KU20, RGU, TU Short Essays; KU25, KU18, KU16, RGU, TU Short Answers)

1. Optic Atrophy [KU25, KU24, KU20, KU16, RGU, TU]

Definition: Degeneration of optic nerve axons resulting from any pathological process damaging the anterior visual pathway (from retinal ganglion cells to the lateral geniculate body). Clinically characterized by optic disc pallor, loss of small disc vessels (Kestenbaum index reduced from normal 16:4 to <6), visual loss, and visual field defects.

Ophthalmoscopic Classification, Causes & Features [KU16, RGU]:

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-005]]

* Management: Treat the underlying cause (e.g., surgical decompression of pituitary adenoma, VP shunt/acetazolamide for IIH, steroids for arteritic AION) to salvage remaining axons; Low Vision Aids and vocational rehabilitation for established atrophy.

2. Toxic / Nutritional Optic Neuropathy (Toxic Amblyopia) [KU18, RGU, TU]

Etiology (Causes & Drugs) [KU18, RGU, TU]:

Tobacco-Alcohol Amblyopia: Cyanide in pipe tobacco + Vitamin ,  (cobalamin), and folate deficiency in chronic alcoholics.

Drugs [TU]: Ethambutol (most common drug cause — dose ; causes red-green dyschromatopsia and central/bitemporal scotomas), Isoniazid, Chloramphenicol, Linezolid, Quinine (causes acute blindness with extreme arteriolar spasm), Amiodarone, Vigabatrin.

Toxins: Methanol (Methyl alcohol) (adulterated liquor; metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to formic acid and formaldehyde  severe metabolic acidosis, ganglion cell necrosis, and acute bilateral blindness; treated with gastric lavage, IV Sodium bicarbonate, IV Ethanol or Fomepizole [competitive inhibitors of alcohol dehydrogenase], and haemodialysis), Lead, Arsenic.

Clinical Features: Bilateral, symmetrical, painless, gradually progressive loss of central vision, early dyschromatopsia, bilateral Centrocaecal Scotomas (extending from fixation to blind spot, larger for red targets than white), normal fundus initially followed by temporal pallor of the optic disc (papillomacular bundle damage).

Treatment: Immediate cessation of offending drug/tobacco/alcohol + IM Hydroxocobalamin (Vitamin ) 1000 g weekly, Thiamine (), Folate, and high-protein diet.

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ANSWERS ON NEURO-OPHTHALMOLOGY
text:
SHORT ANSWERS ON NEURO-OPHTHALMOLOGY

1. Visual Pathway & Field Defects [KU25, KU24, KU23, KU21, KU17, KU16, RGU, TU]

Anatomy of Visual Pathway:

1st Order Neurons: Bipolar cells in retina.

2nd Order Neurons: Retinal Ganglion Cells  axons form Optic Nerve (Intraocular 1 mm, Intraorbital 30 mm, Intracanalicular 6–9 mm, Intracranial 10 mm)  Optic Chiasma (Nasal retinal fibres decussate/cross; Temporal retinal fibres remain uncrossed)  Optic Tract  synapse in Lateral Geniculate Body (LGB).

3rd Order Neurons: Cell bodies in LGB  axons form Optic Radiations (Geniculocalcarine tract):

Inferior fibres (Meyer’s loop) loop anteriorly through the Temporal Lobe (carry inferior retinal fibres = superior visual field).

Superior fibres pass through the Parietal Lobe (carry superior retinal fibres = inferior visual field).

Terminate in the Primary Visual Cortex (Striate Area 17) along the calcarine sulcus of the Occipital Lobe.

Visual Field Defects at Each Level [KU24, KU16, RGU, TU]:

Optic Nerve Lesion: Ipsilateral Monocular Blindness (or central/altitudinal scotoma) + absent direct light reflex.

Proximal Optic Nerve / Anterior Chiasmal Angle (Junction of Optic Nerve & Chiasma): Junctional Scotoma (Traquair) = Ipsilateral central scotoma + Contralateral superotemporal quadrantanopia (due to involvement of inferonasal fibres looping anteriorly into Wilbrand’s knee).

Central Optic Chiasma (e.g., Pituitary Adenoma, Craniopharyngioma): Bitemporal Hemianopia (damage to crossing nasal fibres).

Lateral Optic Chiasma (e.g., Bilateral Internal Carotid Aneurysms / Distended 3rd Ventricle): Binasal Hemianopia (damage to uncrossed temporal fibres).

Optic Tract Lesion: Contralateral Incongruous Homonymous Hemianopia + Wernicke’s hemianopic pupil + Contralateral bow-tie optic atrophy.

Temporal Lobe Lesion (Meyer’s Loop): Contralateral Superior Homonymous Quadrantanopia (“Pie in the Sky”).

Parietal Lobe Lesion: Contralateral Inferior Homonymous Quadrantanopia (“Pie on the Floor”).

Total Optic Radiation Lesion: Contralateral Complete Homonymous Hemianopia.

Occipital Lobe (Visual Cortex) Infarct (Posterior Cerebral Artery Occlusion) [TU]: Contralateral Congruous Homonymous Hemianopia with Macular Sparing (macular representation at the occipital pole has dual blood supply from both Posterior and Middle Cerebral Arteries) + normal pupillary reflexes + no optic atrophy.

2. Pupillary Reflexes, Pathways & Abnormalities [KU24, KU17, KU16, KU15, RGU, TU]

Light Reflex Pathway [KU24, KU16, RGU]:

Afferent: Photoreceptors  Ganglion cells  Optic nerve  Chiasma (nasal fibres cross)  Optic tract (fibres leave before LGB via superior brachium)  Pretectal Nucleus in midbrain.

Internuncial: Each pretectal nucleus projects to BOTH ipsilateral and contralateral Edinger-Westphal nuclei (anatomical basis of the consensual light reflex).

Efferent (Parasympathetic): Edinger-Westphal nucleus  3rd Cranial Nerve (inferior division)  branch to Inferior Oblique  synapses in Ciliary Ganglion  Short Ciliary Nerves  Sphincter pupillae.

Near (Accommodation-Convergence) Reflex Pathway: Retina  Visual cortex (Area 17)  Parastriate cortex (Area 18/19)  Occipitomesencephalic tract  Periaqueductal grey / Edinger-Westphal nucleus  3rd nerve  Ciliary ganglion / Accessory ganglion  Ciliary muscle (accommodation), Sphincter pupillae (miosis), and Medial recti (convergence).

Pupillary Abnormalities:

Marcus Gunn Pupil (Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect - RAPD) [KU17, RGU, TU]: Elicited by the Swinging Flashlight Test. When light is swung from the normal eye to the diseased eye, the pupil of the diseased eye paradoxically dilates instead of staying constricted. Pathognomonic of unilateral/asymmetric optic nerve lesion (optic neuritis, optic atrophy, AION) or extensive retinal disease (CRAO, ischaemic CRVO, total RD).

Argyll Robertson Pupil (ARP) [RGU, TU]: Bilateral small, irregular pupils showing Light-Near Dissociation (Accommodation Reflex Present, Light reflex absent); dilates poorly with atropine. Caused by dorsal midbrain lesion affecting pretectal internuncial fibres (Neurosyphilis / Tabes dorsalis, Pinealoma).

Adie’s Tonic Pupil [RGU]: Unilateral large dilated pupil (80% young females) with absent/sluggish light reaction and a slow, worm-like (tonic) constriction and redilatation to near target; associated with absent knee/ankle jerks (Holmes-Adie syndrome). Caused by postganglionic parasympathetic denervation at the ciliary ganglion. Confirmatory test: Constricts with weak 0.125% Pilocarpine (denervation supersensitivity).

Horner’s Syndrome (Oculosympathetic Palsy) [KU15, RGU]: Caused by lesion of the 3-neuron sympathetic pathway (Pancoast tumour, carotid dissection, brainstem stroke).

Classic Features: Mild Ptosis (1–2 mm, Muller’s muscle paralysis), Miosis (anisocoria worse in dim light with dilation lag), Ipsilateral Facial Anhidrosis, Apparent Enophthalmos, Loss of ciliospinal reflex, and Heterochromia iridis (in congenital Horner’s).

Pharmacological Tests: Fails to dilate with 4% Cocaine (confirms Horner’s); 1% Hydroxyamphetamine dilates central/preganglionic lesions but fails to dilate postganglionic lesions; 1% Apraclonidine reverses anisocoria.

Causes of Fixed Dilated Pupil [KU23, KU15]: (1) Complete 3rd cranial nerve palsy (PCA aneurysm, uncal herniation — Hutchinson’s pupil), (2) Pharmacological mydriasis (Atropine/Tropicamide — does not constrict with 1% Pilocarpine), (3) Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma / Absolute Glaucoma, (4) Traumatic Sphincter Rupture (traumatic mydriasis).

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ESSAY 1 & 2: EXTRAOCULAR MUSCLES, SQUINT & ABDUCENS PALSY
text:
SECTION 5: OCULAR MOTILITY & STRABISMUS

SHORT ESSAY 1 & 2: EXTRAOCULAR MUSCLES, SQUINT & ABDUCENS PALSY

(Covers KU25, TU Short Essays; KU26, KU25, KU24, KU23, KU22, KU21, KU20, KU19, KU18, RGU, TU Short Answers)

1. Anatomy, Nerve Supply & Actions of Extraocular Muscles [KU25, KU20, RGU, TU]

Origin & Insertion:

The 4 Recti originate from the common tendinous ring (Annulus of Zinn) at the orbital apex and insert into the sclera at progressive distances from the limbus (Spiral of Tillaux): Medial Rectus (5.5 mm)  Inferior Rectus (6.5 mm)  Lateral Rectus (6.9 mm)  Superior Rectus (7.7 mm).

The Vertical Recti (SR, IR) make an angle of 23° with the optical axis in primary gaze (hence their pure vertical action is tested in 23° abduction, and pure torsion in adduction).

The Obliques (SO, IO) insert behind the equator in the temporal sclera and make an angle of 51° with the optical axis (hence their pure vertical action [depression for SO, elevation for IO] is tested in adduction).

Nerve Supply () & Actions Table:

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-006]]

Eyelid Muscles [TU]:

Elevators of Upper Eyelid: (1) Levator Palpebrae Superioris (LPS) — originates from lesser wing of sphenoid at orbital apex, inserts into skin (forming lid crease), anterior tarsus, and superior fornix; supplied by Superior division of 3rd Cranial Nerve (elevates lid by ~15 mm); (2) Muller’s Muscle (Superior tarsal muscle) — smooth muscle arising from undersurface of LPS, inserts on upper border of tarsus; supplied by Cervical Sympathetic nerves (elevates lid by ~2 mm); (3) Frontalis — accessory elevator in severe ptosis; supplied by 7th Cranial Nerve.

Orbicularis Oculi Muscle: Striated sphincter muscle of eyelids (orbital, preseptal, pretarsal, and lacrimal [Horner’s] parts); closes eyelids and drives the lacrimal pump; supplied by Zygomatic and Temporal branches of 7th Cranial Nerve (Facial).

2. Binocular Single Vision (BSV) & Diplopia [KU25, KU24, KU23, KU21, KU19, KU18, RGU, TU]

Definition & Worth’s Three Grades of Binocular Single Vision (Tested on Synoptophore) [KU21, RGU, TU]:

Coordinated use of both eyes to produce a single mental impression. Develops by 6 months of age and completes by 6 years.

Grade I: Simultaneous Macular Perception (SMP): Ability to perceive two dissimilar images simultaneously (e.g., seeing a bird inside a cage).

Grade II: Fusion: Ability of the brain to superimpose two similar incomplete images (each lacking a small control detail) into one complete composite image with fusional reserve.

Grade III: Stereopsis: Highest grade; ability to perceive depth (third dimension) due to slight horizontal retinal disparity.

Diplopia (Causes of Uniocular vs. Binocular Diplopia) [KU25, KU24, KU23, KU19, KU18, TU]:

Uniocular Diplopia (persists when the normal eye is closed): (1) Subluxated crystalline lens or decentred IOL, (2) Iridodialysis / Polycoria / Large peripheral iridectomy (double pupil), (3) Incipient cortical cataract (water clefts), (4) Keratoconus / Irregular corneal astigmatism.

Binocular Diplopia (disappears on closing either eye): (1) Paralytic squint (3rd, 4th, or 6th cranial nerve palsy), (2) Thyroid Eye Disease (restrictive myopathy), (3) Orbital Blow-out Fracture (muscle entrapment), (4) Myasthenia Gravis, (5) Orbital space-occupying lesions displacing globe, (6) High Anisometropia (spectacle-corrected unilateral aphakia).

Uncrossed (Homonymous) Diplopia: Seen in Esotropia (e.g., 6th nerve palsy).

Crossed (Heteronymous) Diplopia: Seen in Exotropia (e.g., 3rd nerve palsy).

3. Classification, Investigations & Differentiation of Squint [KU22, RGU, TU]

Classification of Strabismus [RGU]:

Pseudostrabismus (Apparent squint): Pseudoesotropia (prominent epicanthal folds, negative angle kappa); Pseudoexotropia (hypertelorism, positive angle kappa).

Latent Squint (Heterophoria): Esophoria, Exophoria, Hyperphoria, Cyclophoria (kept latent by fusion).

Manifest Squint (Heterotropia):

Concomitant Squint: Esotropia (Infantile, Accommodative [refractive/high AC:A], Sensory), Exotropia (Intermittent, Constant, Sensory), Hypertropia.

Incomitant Squint: Paralytic squint (neurogenic/myogenic), Restrictive squint (Duane’s syndrome, Brown’s syndrome, Thyroid myopathy, Blow-out fracture), A & V Pattern strabismus.

Differentiation: Concomitant vs. Incomitant (Paralytic) Squint [KU22, RGU, TU]:

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-007]]

Investigations in Squint (Including Hirschberg Test) [RGU]:

Visual Acuity & Cycloplegic Refraction (mandatory using 1% Atropine in children <5 years; fully corrects refractive accommodative esotropia).

Hirschberg Corneal Light Reflex Test [RGU]: Point light held at 33 cm; note position of corneal reflex in squinting eye:

At pupillary margin = 15° ( Prism Dioptres)

Midway between pupil margin and limbus = 30° ( PD)

At limbus = 45° ( PD) (Each 1 mm decentration  or  PD).

Cover-Uncover Test (detects heterophoria), Direct Cover Test (confirms heterotropia), and Alternate Cover Test (measures total deviation = phoria + tropia).

Prism Bar Cover Test (PBCT) & Krimsky Test: Quantifies deviation in Prism Dioptres (apex of prism placed toward deviation).

Sensory Tests: Worth’s Four-Dot Test, Bagolini striated glasses, Synoptophore, Titmus/TNO stereopsis test.

Special Tests for Paralytic/Incomitant Squint: Diplopia Charting (using red-green goggles; red in front of right eye), Hess / Lees Screen Test, and Forced Duction Test (FDT) (positive in restrictive squint, negative in paralytic squint).

4. Abducens Nerve (6th Cranial Nerve) Palsy [TU]

Etiopathogenesis: Supplies the Lateral Rectus muscle. Because of its long intracranial course and sharp bend over the petrous apex through Dorello’s canal, it is the most commonly affected ocular motor nerve.

Causes: (1) Microvascular ischaemia (Diabetes, Hypertension, Atherosclerosis — commonest in elderly), (2) False localizing sign of Raised Intracranial Pressure (downward herniation of brainstem stretches 6th nerve over petrous tip), (3) Head trauma / Basal skull fracture, (4) Cavernous sinus lesions / Tolosa-Hunt syndrome, (5) Pontine stroke (Millard-Gubler syndrome: ipsilateral 6th + 7th nerve palsy + contralateral hemiplegia), (6) Acoustic neuroma / Nasopharyngeal carcinoma / Gradenigo’s syndrome (petrositis).

Clinical Features:

Uncrossed (Homonymous) Horizontal Diplopia, worse for distance and in lateral gaze toward the affected side.

Convergent Squint (Esotropia) in primary gaze, with Secondary deviation > Primary deviation.

Defective Abduction of the affected eye.

Compensatory Face Turn toward the affected side to maintain binocular single vision.

Management:

Investigate & Treat Underlying Cause: Blood sugar, BP, ESR, MRI Brain & Orbits.

Conservative Wait-and-Watch (for 6 months): Microvascular palsies resolve spontaneously within 3–6 months. Relieve diplopia during recovery using Temporary Occlusion, Fresnel Prisms (base-out), or Botulinum toxin injection into the ipsilateral antagonist Medial Rectus (prevents medial rectus contracture).

Surgical Treatment (if no recovery after 6–9 months):

Partial Palsy (Paresis): Ipsilateral Medial Rectus Recession + Lateral Rectus Resection.

Complete Paralysis: Vertical Muscle Transposition (Hummelsheim or Jensen procedure) — transposing halves of Superior and Inferior Recti to the Lateral Rectus insertion.

subject: ophthalmology
title: ESSAY 1: ORBITAL CELLULITIS
text:
SECTION 6: DISEASES OF THE ORBIT

ESSAY 1: ORBITAL CELLULITIS

(Covers KU16 Essay; KU24, KU18, RGU, TU Short Answers)

Clinical Case Identification:

Case (KU16): 50-year-old female with 2 days of acute pain, redness, protrusion of eyeball (proptosis), double vision, and fever $Orbital Cellulitis.

1. Definition & Etiology [KU24, KU18]

Definition: Acute purulent infection of the soft tissues of the orbit behind the orbital septum.

Modes of Infection (Causes) [KU18]:

Extension from Neighbouring Structures (Most Common - 80%):

Paranasal Sinusitis: Ethmoidal sinusitis is the commonest cause (especially in children) because the medial orbital wall (lamina papyracea) is paper-thin with congenital bony dehiscences and valveless ethmoidal veins.

Dental abscess/caries of upper jaw (via maxillary sinus), Acute dacryocystitis, Preseptal cellulitis, Facial erysipelas/furuncle.

Exogenous Infection: Penetrating orbital trauma (especially retained wooden/vegetative intraorbital foreign body) and post-surgical (enucleation, dacryocystectomy, retinal detachment surgery).

Endogenous (Metastatic) Infection: Septicaemia, puerperal sepsis, or bacterial endocarditis.

Causative Organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Haemophilus influenzae (in children <5 years), and anaerobes.

2. Pathology

Absence of lymphatics in the orbit + tight closed bony compartment + spread via thrombophlebitis of valveless orbital veins  rapid spread, Compartment syndrome with markedly raised intraorbital pressure, and extensive ischaemic tissue necrosis.

3. Clinical Features [KU16]

Symptoms:

Acute onset of severe, throbbing ocular/orbital pain, worsened by eye movements or pressure.

Rapidly progressive swelling of eyelids and protrusion of the eyeball.

Binocular diplopia and diminution of vision (in moderate-to-severe cases).

Constitutional Symptoms: High-grade fever with chills, malaise, nausea, vomiting, and prostration.

Signs:

Eyelids: Tense, red, hot, tender, woody-hard inflammatory oedema of both lids.

Conjunctiva: Marked chemosis (often protruding through the palpebral fissure and becoming desiccated) and severe congestion.

Axial or Eccentric Proptosis: Irreducible, tender proptosis (lateral/downward displacement suggests a medial/superior subperiosteal abscess).

Restricted and Painful Ocular Movements (Ophthalmoplegia).

Pupil & Vision: Visual acuity reduced and RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil) present if complicated by compressive/ischaemic optic neuropathy or CRAO.

Fundus Examination: Retinal venous engorgement, papillitis, or optic disc oedema.

4. Differential Diagnosis of Acute Inflammatory Proptosis

Preseptal Cellulitis: Infection anterior to orbital septum — periorbital lid oedema and erythema are present, but there is NO proptosis, NO chemosis, FULL painless ocular movements, normal vision (6/6), and normal pupils.

Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis: Initially unilateral, rapidly becomes bilateral; cranial nerve palsies (6th nerve earliest, then 3rd & 4th), corneal anaesthesia (5th nerve), mastoid oedema (emissary vein back-pressure), and severe toxicity/meningism.

Panophthalmitis: Complete loss of vision (PL negative) from the onset, corneal haze, pus in anterior chamber (hypopyon) and vitreous.

5. Investigations [KU16]

Complete Haemogram: Marked neutrophilic leukocytosis and raised ESR/CRP.

Microbiological Cultures: Blood culture, nasal swab, and conjunctival swab for Gram stain, KOH mount (to rule out Orbital Mucormycosis in diabetics/ketoacidosis — look for black nasal/palatal eschar), and culture/sensitivity.

High-Resolution Contrast-Enhanced CT Scan of Orbits, Paranasal Sinuses & Brain (Gold Standard): Differentiates preseptal from postseptal cellulitis, identifies Subperiosteal Abscess (lentiform collection along lamina papyracea) or Intraorbital Abscess, detects sinusitis, and rules out intracranial complications.

B-scan Orbital Ultrasonography.

6. Complications [KU16]

Ocular Complications (Blinding): Exposure keratopathy/corneal ulceration, Optic neuritis / Ischaemic optic neuropathy, Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO), Panophthalmitis.

Orbital Complications: Subperiosteal Abscess and Intraorbital Abscess.

Intracranial Complications (Life-Threatening): Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis, Purulent Meningitis, Extradural or Cerebral Abscess.

Systemic: Septicaemia / Pyaemia.

7. Treatment [KU16]

(Medical & Surgical Emergency — Immediate Hospitalization): 1. Intensive Intravenous Empirical Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics: * 3rd-Generation Cephalosporin (Inj. Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV BD or Cefotaxime 50 mg/kg IV 6-hourly) + Anti-Staphylococcal agent (Inj. Vancomycin 1 g IV BD or Flucloxacillin / Amoxicillin-Clavulanate) + Anaerobic cover (Inj. Metronidazole 500 mg IV 8-hourly) for 7–14 days, followed by oral antibiotics. 2. Supportive Therapy: * Systemic analgesics/antipyretics (NSAIDs/Paracetamol) to control pain and fever. * Nasal decongestant drops (Oxymetazoline/Xylometazoline) to promote sinus drainage. * Topical antibiotic eye ointment (Tetracycline/Moxifloxacin) and lubricants QID to protect the exposed cornea and chemosed conjunctiva. * Frequent monitoring (every 4–6 hours) of visual acuity, pupillary reactions (RAPD), ocular motility, and proptosis. 3. Surgical Intervention: * Indications: Unresponsiveness to IV antibiotics after 48 hours, deteriorating visual acuity / appearance of RAPD, or CT evidence of a large Subperiosteal or Orbital Abscess. * Procedures: Immediate Lateral Canthotomy & Cantholysis (if tight orbit causes acute compartment syndrome), Surgical Drainage of Subperiosteal Abscess (via a 2–3 cm curved superomedial Lynch incision or endoscopic transnasal ethmoidectomy) combined with Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) to drain infected sinuses.

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ANSWERS ON ORBIT
text:
SHORT ANSWERS ON ORBIT

1. Anatomy of Orbit, Surgical Spaces & Cavernous Sinus [KU21, KU14, RGU]

Bones Forming the Medial Wall of the Orbit (Anterior to Posterior) [RGU]:

Frontal process of Maxilla

Lacrimal bone (forms lacrimal fossa with maxilla)

Orbital plate of Ethmoid (Lamina papyracea) — largest and thinnest part

Body of Sphenoid

Four Surgical Spaces of the Orbit [KU21]:

Subperiosteal (Potential) Space: Between bony orbital wall and periorbita (periosteum); site of subperiosteal abscess/haematoma.

Peripheral (Extraconal) Space: Between periorbita externally and the 4 rectus muscles with their intermuscular septa internally; tumours here produce eccentric proptosis; site of peribulbar anaesthesia.
