Central (Intraconal / Retrobulbar) Space (Muscle Cone): Bounded anteriorly by Tenon’s capsule and peripherally by the 4 recti and intermuscular septa; tumours here (e.g., cavernous haemangioma, optic nerve glioma) produce axial proptosis; site of retrobulbar anaesthesia.

Tenon’s (Episcleral) Space: Potential space between sclera and Tenon’s capsule (fascia bulbi).

Cavernous Sinus & its Connections [KU14]: Paired dural venous sinus on either side of the body of sphenoid bone, traversed by the Internal Carotid Artery and 6th Cranial Nerve (Abducens) in its lumen, and 3rd, 4th,  (Ophthalmic), and  (Maxillary) nerves in its lateral wall.

Tributaries (Incoming): Superior and Inferior Ophthalmic Veins (communicate anteriorly with facial/angular vein — “danger area of face”), Central retinal vein, Sphenoparietal sinus.

Draining Channels (Outgoing): Superior and Inferior Petrosal Sinuses (to transverse/sigmoid sinus and internal jugular vein), Pterygoid venous plexus (via emissary veins), and Intercavernous sinuses (connect left and right cavernous sinuses, explaining bilateral spread in cavernous sinus thrombosis).

2. Proptosis (Unilateral, Bilateral & Axial Causes) [KU25, KU23, KU19, KU15, RGU, TU]

Definition: Forward protrusion of the eyeball beyond the orbital margins (measured by Hertel’s or Luedde’s Exophthalmometer; normal is 10–21 mm;  mm or asymmetry  mm between two eyes is diagnostic).

Important Causes of Proptosis:

Unilateral Proptosis [KU23, KU19, RGU]:

In Children: Orbital Cellulitis (Most Common), Dermoid cyst, Capillary haemangioma, Rhabdomyosarcoma (most common primary malignant orbital tumour in children), Optic nerve glioma, Retinoblastoma with orbital extension.

In Adults: Thyroid Eye Disease (Most Common), Cavernous Haemangioma (most common benign orbital tumour in adults), Idiopathic Orbital Inflammatory Disease (Pseudotumour), Lacrimal gland tumours, Frontal/Ethmoidal Sinus Mucocele.

Bilateral Proptosis [KU23, KU15, RGU]:

In Children: Metastatic Neuroblastoma (from adrenal medulla) and Leukaemic infiltration (Chloroma / Granulocytic sarcoma), Craniosynostosis (Crouzon’s / Apert’s syndrome), Histiocytosis X (Hand-Schuller-Christian disease).

In Adults: Thyroid Eye Disease (Graves’ Ophthalmopathy — Most Common), Cavernous sinus thrombosis, Lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis.

Axial Proptosis (Intraconal Lesions) [TU]: Cavernous haemangioma, Optic nerve glioma, Optic nerve sheath meningioma, Thyroid eye disease, Orbital apex schwannoma.

Intermittent Proptosis: Orbital Varix (increases on bending head forward or Valsalva manoeuvre).

Pulsatile Proptosis: Carotid-Cavernous Fistula (proptosis + chemosis + audible bruit), Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (sphenoid wing dysplasia transmitting cerebral pulsations).

3. Thyroid-Associated Ophthalmopathy (Graves’ Ophthalmopathy) [RGU, TU]

Pathogenesis: Autoimmune T-cell-mediated disorder (90% hyperthyroid, 6% euthyroid, 4% hypothyroid; Females > Males; aggravated by smoking) where TSH-receptor autoantibodies stimulate orbital fibroblasts to secrete glycosaminoglycans (hyaluronic acid) and undergo adipogenesis  oedema, enlargement, and late fibrosis of extraocular muscles (sparing the tendons) and orbital fat.

Clinical Features:

Eyelid Signs: Dalrymple’s sign (upper lid retraction in primary gaze exposing superior sclera; commonest sign in 90%), Von Graefe’s sign (upper lid lag on downgaze), Kocher’s sign (staring/frightened look), Stellwag’s sign (infrequent blinking), Enroth’s sign (puffy lid oedema), Gifford’s sign (difficulty everting upper lid).

Soft Tissue Signs: Conjunctival injection over horizontal recti insertions, chemosis, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis.

Exophthalmos: Bilateral or asymmetric axial proptosis.

Restrictive Myopathy (Order of Muscle Involvement — Mnemonic ‘I’M SLOW’): Inferior Rectus (commonest — causes restriction of elevation and hypotropia)  Medial Rectus  Superior Rectus  Lateral Rectus; Mobius’s sign (convergence insufficiency).

Sight-Threatening Complications: Exposure Keratopathy and Compressive Dysthyroid Optic Neuropathy (DON) (crowding of enlarged rectus muscles at orbital apex).

Werner’s NOSPECS Classification: 0-No signs/symptoms; 1-Only lid signs; 2-Soft tissue involvement; 3-Proptosis; 4-Extraocular muscle involvement; 5-Corneal involvement; 6-Sight loss (optic nerve compression).

CT Scan Finding: Fusiform enlargement of extraocular muscle bellies characteristically sparing the tendons (“Coca-Cola bottle sign”).

Management:

Stop smoking + Achieve systemic euthyroidism + Lubricating tear drops, head elevation, and lid taping at night.

Active Congestive Phase (Clinical Activity Score ): High-dose IV Methylprednisolone pulses (500 mg weekly for 6 weeks, then 250 mg weekly for 6 weeks) or orbital radiotherapy / Teprotumumab.

Surgical Management (Strictly in Quiescent / Inactive Phase, in this exact sequence): Step 1: Orbital Decompression (2- or 3-wall decompression; done urgently in active phase if DON/exposure ulcer fails steroids)  Step 2: Strabismus Surgery (recession of fibrotic inferior/medial rectus on adjustable sutures)  Step 3: Eyelid Surgery (LPS/Muller’s recession for lid retraction + Blepharoplasty).

subject: ophthalmology
title: ESSAY 1: BLUNT OCULAR TRAUMA & ORBITAL BLOW-OUT FRACTURE
text:
SECTION 7: OCULAR INJURIES

ESSAY 1: BLUNT OCULAR TRAUMA & ORBITAL BLOW-OUT FRACTURE

(Covers KU20 Essay; KU23, KU22, KU18, KU15, KU14, RGU, TU Short Answers)

Clinical Case Identification:

Case (KU20): Man hit on right eye by a cricket ball, presenting with 6/6 vision, binocular diplopia, periorbital ecchymosis, and subcutaneous crepitus (surgical emphysema)  Closed-Globe Blunt Trauma with Orbital Blow-out Fracture (Floor and Medial Wall).

1. Classification of Mechanical Ocular Injuries (BETT System) [KU23, KU20]

(Birmingham Eye Trauma Terminology — “Eyewall” = Cornea + Sclera): 1. Closed-Globe Injury: No full-thickness wound of eyewall. * Contusion: Blunt trauma causing direct or contre-coup intraocular damage. * Lamellar Laceration: Partial-thickness wound of eyewall. 2. Open-Globe Injury: Full-thickness wound of eyewall. * Rupture: Full-thickness wound caused by a blunt object (inside-out mechanism at weakest points: superonasal limbus/Schlemm’s canal or just behind rectus insertions). * Laceration: Full-thickness wound caused by a sharp object (outside-in mechanism): * Penetrating injury: Single entry wound, no exit wound. * Perforating injury: Both entry and exit wounds caused by the same missile. * Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB): Retained foreign body.

2. Orbital Blow-Out Fracture (Answers to KU20 Essay & RGU Short Answer)

Mechanism: Blunt impact by a rounded object larger than the orbital rim (cricket ball, tennis ball, fist) compresses orbital contents  sudden spike in intraorbital hydraulic pressure  fractures the weakest bony walls: Posteromedial Orbital Floor (maxillary roof medial to infraorbital groove) and Medial Wall (lamina papyracea of ethmoid).

Two Probable Causes of Binocular Diplopia in this Patient [KU20]:

Mechanical Entrapment of the Inferior Rectus, Inferior Oblique, or perimuscular fascia within the orbital floor fracture defect, restricting both elevation and depression (“Double Diplopia”; Forced Duction Test is positive).

Orbital Haemorrhage / Oedema or Direct Contusion / Paresis of Extraocular Muscles or their motor nerves.

Other Clinical Signs Likely in Orbital Blow-out Fracture [KU20, RGU]:

Infraorbital Nerve Anaesthesia / Paraesthesia: Numbness of lower eyelid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, and upper gums/teeth (due to damage to infraorbital nerve in the floor canal).

Enophthalmos and Mechanical Ptosis: Sinking backward and downward of the eyeball (masked initially by oedema, becomes prominent after 10–14 days) with pseudoptosis and deepening of the superior sulcus.

Ipsilateral Epistaxis (bleeding into maxillary/ethmoidal sinus) and Subcutaneous Emphysema (crepitus) worsened by nose-blowing (air forced from ethmoid/maxillary sinus into orbit/lids).

Radiological Sign (Waters’ View X-ray & Coronal CT Scan): “Tear-Drop” or “Hanging-Drop” Sign — prolapsed orbital fat and inferior rectus hanging down from the roof of the maxillary antrum.

Management of Orbital Blow-out Fracture [KU20]:

Immediate Conservative Management:

Strictly instruct patient NOT to blow the nose (prevents worsening of orbital emphysema).

Systemic Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics (Co-amoxiclav / Cefuroxime for 7–10 days) to prevent orbital cellulitis from sinus flora.

Oral NSAIDs / Analgesics, Nasal decongestant drops, and Cold compresses (short course of oral steroids to speed resolution of oedema).

Surgical Repair (Timing: Wait 10–14 days for oedema to subside, unless trapdoor fracture in a child with oculocardiac reflex requires urgent surgery):

Indications: Persistent diplopia in primary/reading gaze with positive FDT, Enophthalmos  mm, or Large fracture ( of orbital floor) with significant tissue herniation on Coronal CT.

Procedure: Transconjunctival or subciliary anterior orbitotomy  release entrapped inferior rectus and orbital fat from maxillary sinus  reconstruct orbital floor using a Titanium mesh, Porous polyethylene (Medpor), or Silicone sheet implant.

3. Ocular Manifestations of Blunt Trauma (Anterior to Posterior) [KU23, KU22, KU20, KU18, KU15, KU14, RGU, TU]

(Also answers: Four Causes of Decreased Vision Following Blunt Trauma [KU20] — e.g., Traumatic Hyphaema, Rosette Cataract/Lens Dislocation, Vitreous Haemorrhage, Commotio Retinae/Macular Hole, Choroidal Rupture, Traumatic Optic Neuropathy):

Cornea: Epithelial abrasion, Recurrent corneal erosion, Acute corneal oedema (Descemet’s tears), Blood staining of cornea (reddish-brown stroma due to total hyphaema + raised IOP).

Anterior Chamber — Traumatic Hyphaema [KU15, RGU]:

Source: Tear of major arterial circle of iris or ciliary body face.

Complications: Secondary Re-bleed (occurs on Day 3–5 due to clot lysis — much more severe than primary bleed!), Secondary Glaucoma (Red-cell, Haemolytic, Ghost-cell, and Hemosiderotic glaucoma), and Corneal Blood Staining (if IOP  mmHg for  days).

Management: Strict bed rest with  head elevation, eye shield, Topical Prednisolone 1% (reduces iritis and re-bleeding), Topical Cycloplegic (Atropine 1% / Homatropine 2%), Tranexamic acid / Aminocaproic acid (antifibrinolytic to prevent re-bleed), Timolol 0.5% + Acetazolamide for raised IOP (avoid carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and mannitol in Sickle-cell trait!), and AC Paracentesis / Washout if total (“8-ball”) hyphaema with uncontrolled IOP persists.

Iris, Pupil & Ciliary Body:

Traumatic Miosis (initial sphincter irritation) or Traumatic Mydriasis (permanent sphincter tear).

Iridodialysis [TU]: Detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body, producing a D-shaped pupil and a peripheral biconvex dark gap at the limbus (causes uniocular diplopia and glare; large iridodialysis is repaired by McCannel trans-chamber suturing).

Angle Recession: Tear between longitudinal and circular fibres of ciliary muscle  late unilateral Angle-Recession Glaucoma.

Crystalline Lens [KU22]:

Vossius Ring [TU]: Circular ring of brown iris pigment imprinted onto the anterior lens capsule (smaller than dilated pupil) due to forceful impact of contracted pupillary ruff against lens.

Concussion (Rosette) Cataract: Star/petal-shaped feathery posterior cortical opacity.

Subluxation or Dislocation of Lens (anteriorly into AC or posteriorly into vitreous).

Vitreous: Vitreous base avulsion (pathognomonic of blunt trauma), Posterior vitreous detachment, Vitreous Haemorrhage.

Choroid: Choroidal Rupture (crescentic yellowish-white streak concentric and temporal to the optic disc; if passing through fovea, causes permanent central visual loss) and Suprachoroidal haemorrhage.

Retinal Findings in Blunt Trauma [KU23, KU14, RGU, TU]:

Commotio Retinae (Berlin’s Oedema) [KU23, RGU, TU]: Contre-coup concussion injury causing disruption of photoreceptor outer segments and RPE oedema  milky-white cloudiness at the posterior pole with a central Cherry-Red Spot at the fovea. Treatment: Usually resolves spontaneously in 2–4 weeks (oral/topical steroids may be given), or leaves permanent macular pigmentary mottling / traumatic macular hole.

Traumatic Macular Hole (full-thickness punched-out red defect at fovea).

Retinal Tears & Dialysis: Inferotemporal or Superonasal Retinal Dialysis (disinsertion of retina at ora serrata)  Traumatic Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment.

Retinal / Subhyaloid Haemorrhages and Traumatic Proliferative Retinopathy.

Optic Nerve: Indirect Traumatic Optic Neuropathy (shearing injury in optic canal  sudden visual loss + RAPD; treated with high-dose IV Methylprednisolone or optic canal decompression) or Optic nerve avulsion.

subject: ophthalmology
title: SHORT ESSAY 1 & SHORT ANSWERS: CHEMICAL INJURIES & PENETRATING TRAUMA
text:
SHORT ESSAY 1 & SHORT ANSWERS: CHEMICAL INJURIES & PENETRATING TRAUMA

(Covers KU25 Short Essay; KU26, KU23, KU19, RGU, TU Short Answers)

1. Chemical Injuries to the Eye (Alkali & Acid Burns) [KU25, KU19, RGU, TU]

Etiology & Types:

Alkali Burns (Twice as common and MUCH MORE SEVERE than Acid Burns) [RGU]:

Agents: Lime / Chuna ( — commonest in India, e.g., exploding chuna packets), Ammonia ( — most rapid penetration within seconds), Caustic Soda (), Caustic Potash (), Cement/mortar.

Mechanism of Severe Damage: Alkalies dissociate and saponify cellular membrane fatty acids, extract water (hygroscopic), and combine with stromal mucopolysaccharides/collagen to cause liquefactive necrosis. Hence, alkalies penetrate rapidly and deeply into the corneal stroma, limbal stem cells, anterior chamber, iris, ciliary body, and lens, continuing damage for days.

Acid Burns:

Agents: Sulphuric acid (battery explosions), Hydrochloric acid, Nitric acid.

Mechanism: Acids cause instantaneous coagulation and precipitation of superficial tissue proteins, forming an insoluble eschar barrier that prevents deep intraocular penetration (except Hydrofluoric acid).

Clinical Features:

Acute Stage: Severe pain, blepharospasm, lacrimation, blurred vision; conjunctival chemosis, blanching/necrosis (perilimbal conjunctival and episcleral ischaemia is the critical prognostic sign reflecting Limbal Stem Cell Destruction), corneal epithelial sloughing, stromal haze/opacification, sterile anterior uveitis, and bimodal rise in IOP (initial collagen shrinkage + late trabecular damage).

Late Complications (Stage of Sequelae): Symblepharon, Ankyloblepharon, Cicatricial Entropion & Trichiasis, Severe Mucin/Aqueous-Deficient Dry Eye, Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency (LSCD) (conjunctivalization and 360° vascularization of cornea), Pseudopterygium, Persistent corneal ulceration/perforation, Complicated cataract, and Secondary glaucoma.

Roper-Hall (Ballen) Classification / Grading of Chemical Burns [RGU]:

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-008]]

Management of Chemical Injuries [KU25, KU19, TU]:

A. Immediate Emergency First-Aid (At the Site / Casualty — DO NOT waste time taking history or testing vision!):

Immediate, Copious Irrigation: Instill topical anaesthetic drops, apply a lid speculum, and irrigate thoroughly with 2–3 Litres of Normal Saline, Ringer’s Lactate, or clean tap water for at least 30 minutes until conjunctival sac pH normalizes to 7.0–7.4 (checked with litmus paper).

Double Eversion of Upper Eyelid & Mechanical Debridement: Sweep the superior and inferior fornices with a moist cotton swab and mechanically remove all embedded solid lime () particles using forceps (0.01M EDTA can be used to chelate sticky calcium hydroxide).

B. Medical Therapy (To Promote Epithelial Healing, Prevent Stromal Melting & Control Inflammation):

Topical Corticosteroids (Prednisolone acetate 1% QID-hourly) for the first 7–10 days ONLY to suppress neutrophil infiltration and uveitis (must be tapered/stopped after 10–14 days as steroids inhibit fibroblast collagen synthesis and precipitate corneal perforation!).

Collagenase Inhibitors & Stromal Repair Agents:

Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C): 10% Sodium Ascorbate eye drops 2-hourly + Oral Vitamin C (1–2 g/day) — essential cofactor for fibroblasts to hydroxylate proline and synthesize mature corneal collagen.

Topical Sodium Citrate 10% drops — chelates extracellular , inhibiting polymorphonuclear neutrophil chemotaxis and degranulation.

Oral Tetracyclines (Doxycycline 100 mg BD) — chelates zinc at the active site of Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs), inhibiting collagenase-mediated corneal melting.

Topical Autologous Serum (20%) drops and Preservative-free Lubricants.

Topical Cycloplegic (Atropine 1% eye drops — relieves ciliary spasm and prevents synechiae) + Topical Broad-Spectrum Antibiotic (Moxifloxacin 0.5% QID) + Antiglaucoma drugs (Timolol 0.5% BD + Oral Acetazolamide).

Prevention of Symblepharon: Glass rod sweeping of fornices with lubricant ointment twice daily or Symblepharon Ring ( conformer).

C. Surgical Management:

Acute Stage: Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT) (promotes epithelialization and reduces inflammation), Tenonplasty, or Cyanoacrylate glue / Tectonic Keratoplasty for impending/actual perforation.

Late Rehabilitative Stage: Symblepharon release + Simple Limbal Epithelial Transplantation (SLET) / Conjunctival Limbal Autograft (CLAU) (to restore limbal stem cells), followed 6 months later by Penetrating Keratoplasty or Keratoprosthesis (Boston KPro / Osteo-odonto-keratoprosthesis) in Grade IV bilateral blindness.

2. Penetrating Ocular Trauma, Siderosis, Chalcosis & Sympathetic Ophthalmitis [KU26, KU23, RGU, TU]

Manifestations of Penetrating Trauma to the Eye [KU26, KU23, RGU]:

Mechanical Lesions: Full-thickness corneal or corneoscleral laceration; Flat/shallow anterior chamber with aqueous leak (Seidel’s test positive); Teardrop / Pear-shaped peaked pupil pointing toward the site of Iris prolapse or ciliary body/vitreous prolapse; Hyphaema; Rupture of lens capsule with rapid flocculent traumatic cataract; Vitreous haemorrhage; Retinal tear/detachment; Expulsive haemorrhage; or Badly mutilated globe.

Infection: Exogenous Acute Purulent Endophthalmitis or Panophthalmitis (Bacillus cereus in soil/metallic injuries, Staphylococcus, Fungi in vegetative injuries).

Retained Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB) Reactions:

Inert: Glass, plastic, gold, platinum.

Suppurative: Pure copper, zinc, nickel.

Siderosis Bulbi (Iron IOFB) [TU]: Electrolytic dissociation of  ions which bind intracellular epithelial proteins, causing: (1) Rusty-brown radial subcapsular deposits on anterior lens epithelium + total cataract, (2) Heterochromia iridis (iris turns greenish then reddish-brown), (3) Pigmentary retinal degeneration (mimicking retinitis pigmentosa with extinguished b-wave on ERG), and (4) Secondary open-angle glaucoma (trabecular sclerosis).

Chalcosis (Copper Alloy / Brass / Bronze IOFB) [TU]: Electrolytic deposition of copper ions beneath basement membranes without entering cells, causing: (1) Kayser-Fleischer Ring (golden-brown ring in peripheral Descemet’s membrane), (2) Brilliant golden-green “Sunflower Cataract”, and (3) Golden metallic plaques at the posterior pole of the retina. (Localization & Removal of IOFB: Thin-slice CT Scan of Orbit is the investigation of choice; MRI is strictly contraindicated in suspected metallic IOFB! Removed via Three-port Pars Plana Vitrectomy + intraocular forceps or rare-earth magnet).

Sympathetic Ophthalmitis (Sympathetic Ophthalmia) [KU26]:

Definition: Rare, devastating, bilateral granulomatous panuveitis occurring after a penetrating ocular injury (or rarely intraocular surgery) involving uveal tissue incarceration, especially in the “Dangerous Zone” of the eye (Ciliary body region — 2 to 5 mm behind the limbus).

Terminology & Onset: The injured eye is the “Exciting Eye” and the fellow uninjured eye is the “Sympathizing Eye”. Typically develops 4 to 8 weeks after trauma (earliest 9 days; 90% within 1 year).

Etiopathogenesis: Type IV Cell-Mediated Autoimmune Delayed Hypersensitivity Reaction against exposed uveal/retinal antigens (melanin proteins or retinal S-antigen) that gain access to conjunctival lymphatics when uvea prolapses through a scleral wound. (Does not occur if frank purulent suppuration/panophthalmitis destroys the antigens).

Pathology: Diffuse lymphocytic, epithelioid, and giant-cell infiltration of the entire uveal tract (sparing the choriocapillaris) + phagocytosis of pigment + characteristic Dalen-Fuchs’ Nodules (nodular aggregations of lymphocytes and transformed RPE/epithelioid cells lying between Bruch’s membrane and RPE).

Clinical Features:

Exciting Eye: Persistent low-grade irritable plastic iridocyclitis with ciliary congestion, tenderness, and KPs.

Sympathizing Eye:

Prodromal Stage (Earliest Signs — Must be recognized!): Photophobia, transient blurring of near vision (weakening of accommodation), mild ciliary tenderness, retrolental cells/flare, and fine KPs.

Fully-Developed Stage: Severe bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with large Mutton-fat KPs, iris nodules (Koeppe’s/Busacca’s), broad posterior synechiae, vitritis, papillitis, yellowish-white peripheral choroidal infiltrates (Dalen-Fuchs’ nodules), and exudative retinal detachment.

Prophylaxis & Treatment:

Prophylaxis: Meticulous microsurgical primary repair of penetrating wounds with abscission/reposition of uveal tissue so no uvea remains incarcerated; Early Enucleation (within 14 days of injury) of a hopeless, blind, mutilated eye.

Curative Treatment (Once Sympathetic Ophthalmitis sets in):

High-Dose Corticosteroids (Mainstay): IV Methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days) followed by Oral Prednisolone (1–1.5 mg/kg/day) tapered slowly over 6–12 months + Intensive Topical Prednisolone drops (hourly), Periocular (Sub-Tenon) Triamcinolone, and Topical Atropine 1% TDS.

Systemic Immunosuppressive Agents: Cyclosporine, Azathioprine, Methotrexate, or Mycophenolate mofetil in steroid-resistant or severe cases.

subject: ophthalmology
title: 1. AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION (ARMD)
text:
ADDITIONAL NOTES FROM TEXTBOOK

UNIT 1: RETINA (SUPPLEMENTARY PORTIONS)

1. AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION (ARMD)

1. Definition & Risk Factors

Definition: Bilateral, progressive degenerative disorder of the macula affecting individuals over 50 years of age (leading cause of irreversible blindness in developed countries in >65 years).

Risk Factors: Advancing age, Caucasian race, positive family history (Complement Factor H gene polymorphism), cigarette smoking (most important modifiable risk factor), hypertension, hypermetropia, light-coloured irides, cataract surgery, and excessive sunlight (UV) exposure.

2. Classification & Clinical Features

A. Non-Exudative (Dry / Atrophic / Geographic) ARMD (90% of cases):

Symptoms: Gradual, mild-to-moderate bilateral loss of central vision, difficulty reading small print, and mild metamorphopsia.

Signs (Three Chronological Stages):

Early ARMD: Presence of Macular Drusen (extracellular PAS-positive lipid/protein deposits between RPE basement membrane and inner collagenous layer of Bruch’s membrane; <20 small hard drusen <63 μm or medium drusen ) + focal RPE hyperpigmentation/hypopigmentation.

Intermediate ARMD:  large soft drusen (>125 μm, indistinct margins that coalesce) or >20 medium drusen + non-central RPE atrophy.

Advanced Dry ARMD (Geographic Atrophy): Sharply demarcated circular areas of complete atrophy of RPE, photoreceptors, and choriocapillaris at the fovea, exposing large ribbon-like choroidal vessels.

B. Exudative (Wet / Neovascular) ARMD (10% of cases, causes 90% of severe visual loss):

Pathogenesis: Breaks in degenerated Bruch’s membrane + local VEGF upregulation  ingrowth of fragile choroidal vessels forming a Choroidal Neovascular Membrane (CNVM) beneath the RPE (Type 1 / Occult CNVM) or beneath the neurosensory retina (Type 2 / Classic CNVM).

Symptoms: Sudden, painless, rapidly progressive profound central visual loss, marked metamorphopsia (straight lines appear wavy), and a dense central positive scotoma.

Signs:

Serous or Haemorrhagic Detachment of RPE (PED) (sharply circumscribed dome-shaped elevation).

Choroidal Neovascular Membrane (CNVM): Greyish-green or pinkish-yellow subretinal lesion with a surrounding lipid ring (hard exudates) and subretinal/intraretinal haemorrhage.

Disciform Macular Scar (End-stage): Organization of subretinal blood and fibrovascular tissue into a raised, white fibrous macular scar causing permanent legal blindness.

3. Investigations

Amsler Grid Chart: Home-monitoring and office test detecting early metamorphopsia (wavy lines) and scotomas (missing squares) in the central 20° field.

Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA):

Classic CNVM: Early well-defined “lacy cartwheel” hyperfluorescence with progressive late leakage.

Occult CNVM: Fibrovascular PED (stippled hyperfluorescence) or late leakage of undetermined source.

Indocyanine Green Angiography (ICGA): Superior to FFA for visualizing choroidal circulation, occult CNVM, and Polypoidal Choroidal Vasculopathy (PCV).

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Non-invasive gold standard; demonstrates drusen, RPE detachment, subretinal fluid (SRF), intraretinal cystoid fluid, and CNVM thickness (used to guide anti-VEGF retreatment).

4. Management

Dry (Non-Exudative) ARMD:

AREDS-2 (Age-Related Eye Disease Study) Oral Antioxidant Supplementation (delays progression from intermediate to advanced ARMD by 25%): Vitamin C (500 mg) + Vitamin E (400 IU) + Lutein (10 mg) + Zeaxanthin (2 mg) + Zinc oxide (80 mg) + Cupric oxide (2 mg) (Beta-carotene is omitted in smokers due to lung cancer risk).

Smoking cessation, Amsler grid self-monitoring, protective sunglasses, and Low Vision Aids (LVAs) for Geographic Atrophy.

Wet (Exudative) ARMD:

Intravitreal Anti-VEGF Therapy (Treatment of First Choice for all CNVMs): Monthly or treat-and-extend intravitreal injections of Ranibizumab (0.5 mg), Bevacizumab (1.25 mg), Aflibercept (2 mg — VEGF-Trap), or Brolucizumab (6 mg).

Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) with Verteporfin: IV infusion of Verteporfin () activated by non-thermal 689 nm Diode Laser to selectively thrombose subfoveal/juxtafoveal classic CNVM or PCV.

Direct Thermal Laser Photocoagulation (532 nm): Reserved only for extrafoveal CNVM (>200 μm from foveal centre).

subject: ophthalmology
title: 2. CYSTOID MACULAR OEDEMA (CME), MACULAR HOLE & SOLAR RETINOPATHY
text:
2. CYSTOID MACULAR OEDEMA (CME), MACULAR HOLE & SOLAR RETINOPATHY

1. Cystoid Macular Oedema (CME)

Definition & Pathogenesis: Accumulation of fluid in the outer plexiform layer (Henle’s layer) and inner nuclear layer around the foveola due to breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier.

Etiology (Mnemonic — DEPRIVE): Diabetic maculopathy, Epinephrine / Prostaglandin analogue (Latanoprost) drops, Pars planitis / Uveitis, Retinitis pigmentosa / Retinal vein occlusion (CRVO/BRVO), Irvine-Gass syndrome (post-cataract surgery, especially with vitreous loss), Vitreomacular traction / Epiretinal membrane, Eales’ disease.

Clinical Features & Diagnosis:

Painless disminución of central vision (6/12 to 6/60) and metamorphopsia.

Slit-Lamp Biomicroscopy (+90D): Loss of foveal reflex, macular thickening, and multiple cystoid spaces giving a “Honeycomb appearance”.

FFA: Characteristic “Flower-Petal” appearance in late phases due to dye pooling in radially arranged Henle’s fibres.

OCT: Loss of foveal contour, increased retinal thickness, and hyporeflective intraretinal cystoid spaces.

Treatment: Treat underlying cause (stop prostaglandin drops); Topical NSAIDs (Nepafenac 0.1% / Bromfenac 0.09% / Ketorolac 0.5%) + Topical/Periocular/Intravitreal Steroids (Triamcinolone or Ozurdex implant); Oral Acetazolamide (in Retinitis pigmentosa CME); Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (in vascular CME); Pars Plana Vitrectomy (if vitreous incarceration in cataract wound or vitreomacular traction).

2. Macular Hole

Etiology: Idiopathic / Senile (83%) (females aged 60–80 years; caused by tangential and anteroposterior vitreofoveal traction during perifoveal PVD), Blunt Trauma (5%), High Myopia, Chronic CME.

Gass Clinical & OCT Staging:

Stage 1 (Impending Hole): Loss of foveal depression with a central yellow spot (Stage 1A) or yellow ring (Stage 1B); OCT shows foveal pseudocyst without full-thickness defect (50% resolve spontaneously on vitreofoveal separation).

Stage 2: Small full-thickness retinal defect <400 μm in diameter (centric or eccentric).

Stage 3: Full-thickness punched-out red macular hole >400 μm surrounded by a grey cuff of subretinal fluid, with yellow-white deposits at the base (Watzke-Allen slit-beam sign positive — patient sees a break in a vertical slit beam shone over the hole), without complete PVD.

Stage 4: Large full-thickness hole (>400 μm) with complete Posterior Vitreous Detachment (Weiss ring present).

Treatment: Stage 1 is observed. Stages 2, 3, and 4 require Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) + Peeling of Internal Limiting Membrane (ILM) (stained with Brilliant Blue G dye) + Gas Tamponade ( or ) with face-down positioning for 5–7 days.

3. Solar Retinopathy (Eclipse Burn), Toxic & Hereditary Maculopathies

Solar Retinopathy (Photoretinitis): Photochemical and thermal injury to foveal RPE and outer photoreceptors from viewing a solar eclipse with naked eyes or welding arc exposure. Presents within 1–4 hours with central positive scotoma, metamorphopsia, and VA 6/12–6/60. Fundus shows a small yellow foveolar spot initially, evolving in 2 weeks into a kidney/bean-shaped lamellar reddish foveolar hole with mottled pigment halo. Vision usually recovers to 6/6–6/12 over 6 months; no specific treatment (prevention via certified solar filters).

Chloroquine / Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) Maculopathy: Dose-dependent RPE toxicity (cumulative dose >100–300 g or daily dose >5 mg/kg/day for HCQ). Causes paracentral scotoma and classic “Bull’s-Eye Maculopathy” (central foveolar pigmentation surrounded by a concentric ring of RPE depigmentation, encircled by another hyperpigmented ring) + Cornea verticillata (vortex keratopathy). Screened by 10-2 Automated Perimetry, SD-OCT (flying saucer sign), and Multifocal ERG.

Best’s Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy: Autosomal dominant (BEST1 gene on 11q12); normal ERG but severely subnormal EOG (Arden ratio <150) even in carriers. Evolves through 5 stages: (1) Pre-vitelliform, (2) Vitelliform stage (“Sunny-side-up Egg-Yolk” lesion at macula) with good vision, (3) Pseudohypopyon stage, (4) Vitelliruptive (“Scrambled-egg” appearance with drop in vision), and (5) Atrophic/Cicatrized stage.

Stargardt’s Disease (Fundus Flavimaculatus): Most common hereditary juvenile macular dystrophy (autosomal recessive, ABCA4 gene); presents in 1st–2nd decade with bilateral central visual loss. Fundus shows atrophic “beaten-bronze” or “snail-slime” macula surrounded by pisciform (fish-tail) yellowish lipofuscin flecks in the RPE. FFA Pathognomonic Sign: “Dark Choroid” (Silent Choroid) due to blockage of background choroidal fluorescence by diffuse RPE lipofuscin accumulation.

subject: ophthalmology
title: 3. BRANCH RETINAL OCCLUSIONS, VASCULAR RETINOPATHIES & PHACOMATOSES
text:
3. BRANCH RETINAL OCCLUSIONS, VASCULAR RETINOPATHIES & PHACOMATOSES

1. Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO) & Branch Retinal Artery Occlusion (BRAO)

BRVO: Three times more common than CRVO; occurs at an arteriovenous crossing where a thick-walled arteriole compresses the vein (most common site: Superotemporal quadrant [60%]). Fundus shows sectoral flame-shaped haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, retinal oedema, and dilated tortuous veins strictly confined to the drainage territory of the occluded branch, respecting the horizontal raphe.

Complications: Chronic Macular Oedema (commonest cause of persistent visual loss) and Retinal Neovascularization (NVE) leading to vitreous haemorrhage.

Management: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab / Bevacizumab) or Ozurdex implant for macular oedema; Macular Grid Laser (for persistent oedema >3 months when haemorrhages clear); Sectoral Scatter Laser Photocoagulation if NVE develops.

BRAO: Caused by cholesterol/calcific embolus at an arterial bifurcation (usually temporal). Produces sectoral milky-white retinal pallor and a permanent sectoral / altitudinal visual field defect with preserved central acuity.

2. Sickle-Cell Retinopathy, Coats’ Disease & Ocular Ischaemic Syndrome (OIS)

Proliferative Sickle-Cell Retinopathy (HbSC & HbS-Thal): Impaction of rigid sickled RBCs in peripheral retinal arterioles  Goldberg’s 5 Stages: Stage I: Peripheral arteriolar occlusion; Stage II: Peripheral arteriovenous anastomoses; Stage III: “Sea-Fan” Neovascularization at the junction of perfused and non-perfused retina (hallmark); Stage IV: Vitreous haemorrhage; Stage V: Vitreoretinal traction and Tractional / Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment. (Non-proliferative signs: “Salmon-patch” haemorrhages and “Black-sunburst” RPE plaques). Treated by feeder-vessel/scatter laser photocoagulation and PPV.

Coats’ Disease: Sporadic, non-hereditary, unilateral idiopathic retinal telangiectasia affecting young boys in the first decade of life. Characterized by aneurysmal “light-bulb” telangiectatic retinal vessels leaking massive intra- and sub-retinal yellowish-white cholesterol-rich exudates  Exudative Retinal Detachment presenting as Leukocoria or strabismus. Treated by laser photocoagulation/cryotherapy of abnormal vessels and anti-VEGF.

Ocular Ischaemic Syndrome (OIS): Chronic ocular hypoperfusion due to  ipsilateral Internal/Common Carotid Artery stenosis in elderly males (60–80 years). Presents with gradual visual loss, dull ocular/brow pain (ocular angina), amaurosis fugax, delayed dark adaptation, dilated conjunctival/episcleral vessels, corneal oedema, mild anterior chamber flare (ischaemic pseudoiritis), Rubeosis iridis (66%) with Neovascular Glaucoma, and a fundus showing dilated but NON-tortuous retinal veins, narrowed arteries, mid-peripheral dot-and-blot haemorrhages, and NVD. Confirmed by Carotid Doppler Ultrasound & MR Angiography; treated by Carotid Endarterectomy / Stenting, PRP, and anti-VEGF.

3. Phacomatoses (Neurocutaneous Syndromes)

Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) Disease (Angiomatosis Retinae): Autosomal dominant (VHL gene on 3p25). Retinal capillary haemangioblastoma fed by a pair of markedly dilated, tortuous feeder artery and draining vein  massive exudation and exudative RD. Systemic associations: Cerebellar/spinal haemangioblastoma, Renal cell carcinoma, Pheochromocytoma. Treated by laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy, or brachytherapy.

Tuberous Sclerosis (Bourneville’s Disease): Autosomal dominant. Vogt’s Classic Triad: Adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas) + Epilepsy + Mental retardation + Retinal Astrocytic Hamartomas (translucent flat lesions or calcified nodular “Mulberry-like” tumours near optic disc) + Ash-leaf skin macules + Cardiac rhabdomyoma.

Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (Von Recklinghausen’s Disease): Autosomal dominant (NF1 gene on 17q11). Ocular features: Lisch nodules of iris (melanocytic hamartomas — seen in >95% after age 16), Plexiform neurofibroma of eyelids (“bag-of-worms” feel with S-shaped ptosis), Optic nerve glioma, Congenital glaucoma, Pulsatile proptosis (absence of greater wing of sphenoid), prominent corneal nerves, and Cafe-au-lait spots.

Sturge-Weber Syndrome (Encephalotrigeminal Angiomatosis): Sporadic. Ipsilateral facial Port-wine stain (Naevus flammeus) in  distribution + Diffuse Choroidal Haemangioma (“Tomato-catsup fundus”) + Ipsilateral Congenital/Developmental Glaucoma (due to angle anomaly or raised episcleral venous pressure) + Leptomeningeal haemangioma (Jacksonian epilepsy and tram-track intracranial calcification).

4. Vitreous Disorders (PVD, Asteroid Hyalosis & Synchysis Scintillans)

Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD): Separation of posterior cortical vitreous from internal limiting membrane of retina due to age-related liquefaction (synchysis) and collapse (syneresis). Presents with acute photopsia (flashes) and floaters; biomicroscopy shows a ring-shaped opacity over the optic disc (Weiss Ring — pathognomonic). Must perform indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral indentation to rule out retinal tear (occurs in 10–15%) or vitreous haemorrhage.

Asteroid Hyalosis vs. Synchysis Scintillans:

subject: ophthalmology
title: 1. NORMAL TENSION GLAUCOMA (NTG) & SECONDARY OPEN-ANGLE GLAUCOMAS
text:
UNIT 2: GLAUCOMA (SUPPLEMENTARY PORTIONS)

1. NORMAL TENSION GLAUCOMA (NTG) & SECONDARY OPEN-ANGLE GLAUCOMAS

1. Normal Tension Glaucoma (NTG / Low Tension Glaucoma)

Definition: Variant of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma characterized by typical glaucomatous optic disc cupping and visual field defects with an open angle on gonioscopy, but an IOP consistently  on diurnal phasing.

Etiopathogenesis: Chronic vascular hypoperfusion and vasospasm of the optic nerve head + abnormally low cerebrospinal fluid pressure (high translaminar pressure gradient). Strongly associated with migraine, Raynaud’s phenomenon, nocturnal systemic hypotension (overtreated hypertension with bedtime antihypertensives), sleep apnoea, and autoimmune disorders.

Distinguishing Clinical Features (vs. High-Tension POAG):

Optic Disc: Neuroretinal rim thinning is more focal/sloping with much more frequent optic disc splinter haemorrhages (Drance haemorrhages) and peripapillary atrophy.

Visual Fields: Scotomas are deeper, steeper-walled, more localized, and closer to the central fixation point early in the disease.

Management:

Lower IOP by at least 30% from baseline (target IOP 10–12 mmHg) using Prostaglandin analogues (Latanoprost), Brimonidine (neuroprotective), or Betaxolol (improves optic nerve head blood flow).

Avoid non-selective beta-blockers at night and avoid bedtime systemic antihypertensive dosing to prevent nocturnal hypotension.

Systemic Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., Nifedipine/Nimodipine) in documented vasospastic disorders; Trabeculectomy if progressive field loss occurs.

2. Pigmentary, Steroid-Induced, Traumatic & ICE-Syndrome Glaucomas

Pigmentary Glaucoma: Secondary open-angle glaucoma occurring in young myopic males (20–40 years) with Pigment Dispersion Syndrome (PDS). Posterior bowing of the mid-peripheral iris causes mechanical rubbing of the posterior iris pigment epithelium against lens zonules (Reverse pupillary block), releasing pigment granules.

Classic Triad of Signs: (1) Krukenberg’s Spindle (vertical spindle-shaped pigment deposition on central corneal endothelium), (2) Mid-peripheral radial slit-like iris transillumination defects, and (3) Dense homogeneous dark pigment band (Grade 4) over 360° of the trabecular meshwork on gonioscopy. Managed like POAG + Laser Trabeculoplasty (responds very well to ALT/SLT) or Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (flattens concave iris).

Steroid-Induced Glaucoma: Secondary open-angle glaucoma triggered by topical (most potent: Dexamethasone, Betamethasone, Prednisolone; least potent: Loteprednol, Fluorometholone, Rimexolone), periocular, intravitreal (Triamcinolone), or systemic corticosteroids.

Armaly-Becker Population Response: 5% are High responders (IOP >31 mmHg, including 90% of POAG patients, high myopes, and diabetics), 35% Moderate responders, 60% Non-responders.

Mechanism: Steroids stabilize lysosomal membranes (inhibiting hyaluronidase)  accumulation of polymerized glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in the trabecular meshwork + suppression of endothelial phagocytosis + inhibition of prostaglandin  synthesis.

Management: Immediate discontinuation of steroid (IOP normalizes in 2–4 weeks in 98%) or switch to Loteprednol/NSAIDs + Topical Timolol/Brimonidine.

Angle-Recession (Cleavage) Glaucoma: Unilateral chronic secondary open-angle glaucoma developing months to 10–20 years after blunt ocular trauma. Gonioscopy shows irregular widening of the ciliary body band (tear between longitudinal and circular ciliary muscle fibres). Glaucoma results from collateral hyaline sclerosis and scarring of the trabecular meshwork. Treated medically or by trabeculectomy with Mitomycin-C (ALT/SLT is ineffective).

Ciliary Block Glaucoma (Malignant Glaucoma / Aqueous Misdirection Syndrome): Rare, dreaded postoperative complication typically following trabeculectomy or cataract surgery in eyes with chronic Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (short hypermetropic eyes / nanophthalmos).

Mechanism: Tips of ciliary processes rotate anteriorly and press against the lens equator (ciliolenticular block), IOL (cilio-pseudophakic block), or anterior hyaloid face (ciliovitreal block)  aqueous humour is misdirected posteriorly into the vitreous cavity, pushing the entire lens-iris diaphragm forward.

Diagnostic Features: Uniformly flat/extremely shallow central AND peripheral anterior chamber + Markedly elevated IOP + Patent iridectomy + Negative Seidel’s test (no wound leak).

Management: Miotics are strictly CONTRAINDICATED (worsen ciliolenticular block!).

Medical (50% respond in 4–5 days): Topical Atropine 1% + Phenylephrine 10% (tightens zonules and pulls lens-ciliary ring backward) + IV Mannitol 20% (shrinks vitreous volume) + Oral Acetazolamide + Topical Timolol.

Laser: Nd:YAG Laser Anterior Hyaloidotomy / Capsulotomy (disrupts anterior hyaloid face in pseudophakic/aphakic eyes).

Surgical: Pars Plana Core Vitrectomy with disruption of the anterior hyaloid face.

Iridocorneal Endothelial (ICE) Syndromes: Unilateral, non-hereditary disorder in middle-aged women (30–50 years) (linked to HSV DNA) where abnormal corneal endothelial cells (“ICE cells” on specular microscopy with beaten-bronze appearance) proliferate as a membrane across the angle and iris, contracting to cause secondary synechial angle-closure glaucoma. Three clinical variants (Mnemonic: PCC):

Progressive Iris Atrophy (marked corectopia, ectropion uveae, and full-thickness stretch/melting holes — pseudopolycoria).

Chandler’s Syndrome (commonest; corneal oedema at normal/mildly raised IOP predominates; minimal iris changes).

Cogan-Reese (Iris Naevus) Syndrome (pedunculated pigmented iris nodules).

subject: ophthalmology
title: 2. AUTOMATED PERIMETRY INTERPRETATION & RECENT GLAUCOMA SURGERIES
text:
2. AUTOMATED PERIMETRY INTERPRETATION & RECENT GLAUCOMA SURGERIES

1. Humphrey Automated Perimetry (Statpac Single-Field Printout) Interpretation

1. Reliability Indices: Field is unreliable if: Fixation Losses >20%, False Positives >33% (“trigger-happy” patient  white scotomas), or False Negatives >33% (inattentive/fatigued patient  cloverleaf field).

2. Total Deviation vs. Pattern Deviation Plots:

Total Deviation: Compares patient’s threshold sensitivity at each point to age-matched normals (reflects generalized depression, e.g., cataract/miosis, + focal defects).

Pattern Deviation: Adjusts for generalized media haze/cataract to highlight purely localized glaucomatous scotomas.

3. Global Indices:

Mean Deviation (MD): Average overall elevation or depression of patient’s field compared to age-normal (severity staging: Early MD < -6 dB; Moderate MD ; Severe MD > -12 dB).

Pattern Standard Deviation (PSD) & Corrected PSD (CPSD): Measures focal irregularity/variability between adjacent points (high in localized glaucomatous scotomas).

Visual Field Index (VFI): Expressed as a percentage from 100% (normal field) to 0% (perimetric blindness), heavily weighted toward central paracentral points; used for linear regression trend analysis of progression.

4. Glaucoma Hemifield Test (GHT): Compares 5 mirror-image nerve-fibre-bundle zones in superior vs. inferior hemifields (Reported as: Within normal limits, Borderline, Outside normal limits).

5. Anderson’s Criteria for Early Glaucomatous Visual Field Defect (Any ONE of the following):

Cluster of  contiguous non-edge points on the Pattern Deviation probability plot depressed at p < 5%, with at least 1 point depressed at p < 1% in an expected nerve fibre bundle location.

PSD or CPSD depressed at p < 5%.

Glaucoma Hemifield Test (GHT) reported as “Outside Normal Limits”.

2. Non-Penetrating, Canal-Based (MIGS) & Glaucoma Drainage Device Surgeries

Non-Penetrating Filtration Surgeries (Anterior chamber is not entered, avoiding hypotony and endophthalmitis; aqueous percolates through a thin Trabeculo-Descemet’s Membrane):

Deep Sclerectomy (excision of deep scleral/corneal lamella behind Schwalbe’s line) and Viscocanalostomy (cannulation and dilation of Schlemm’s canal with high-viscosity sodium hyaluronate).

Minimally Invasive Glaucoma Surgeries (MIGS) / Internal Filtration: Trabectome (ab-interno electrocautery ablation of TM), iStent (titanium micro-bypass stent implanted into Schlemm’s canal), Canaloplasty (360° suture tensioning of Schlemm’s canal), and Ex-PRESS Mini-Shunt (stainless-steel tube placed under a trabeculectomy scleral flap).

Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDDs / Seton Implants): Tube-plate shunts draining aqueous to an equatorial sub-Tenon reservoir:

Valved (Flow-restrictive, prevents hypotony): Ahmed Glaucoma Valve (AGV) (opens at IOP >8 mmHg), Krupin valve.

Non-Valved: Molteno implant, Baerveldt implant.

Indications: Neovascular glaucoma, Failed trabeculectomy with MMC, Uveitic glaucoma, Aphakic/Paediatric glaucoma, ICE syndrome, Post-keratoplasty glaucoma.

subject: ophthalmology
title: 1. HETEROPHORIA (LATENT SQUINT) & CLINICAL TYPES OF CONCOMITANT SQUINT
text:
UNIT 3: STRABISMUS & OCULAR MOTILITY (SUPPLEMENTARY PORTIONS)

1. HETEROPHORIA (LATENT SQUINT) & CLINICAL TYPES OF CONCOMITANT SQUINT

1. Heterophoria (Latent Strabismus)

Definition & Types: Misalignment of the visual axes kept latent by the fusional mechanism, becoming manifest only when fusion is disrupted. Types: Esophoria (inward), Exophoria (outward — commonest), Hyperphoria (vertical), Cyclophoria (torsional).

Decompensation & Symptoms: Triggered by general debility, mental stress, prolonged near work, or low fusional reserve. Produces Muscular Asthenopia (frontal headache, eyeache relieved by closing one eye, blurring/running together of letters while reading, intermittent diplopia, and difficulty judging distances of moving balls in sports).

Evaluation Tests:

Cover-Uncover Test: Occlude one eye  eye deviates under cover  remove cover and observe the direction and speed of fusional recovery movement (moves inward in exophoria, outward in esophoria).

Maddox Rod Test (for Distance at 6 m): Placed in front of right eye; converts point spotlight into a perpendicular red line, dissociating fusion. Measures horizontal and vertical phoria on a Maddox tangent scale or with prisms.

Maddox Wing Test (for Near at 33 cm): Dissociates eyes mechanically via septa; right eye sees white vertical and red horizontal arrows pointing to numbers seen by left eye, directly reading horizontal, vertical, and cyclophoria.

Near Point of Convergence (NPC) (normal: <7–8 cm on RAF rule) and Fusional Reserve on Synoptophore (Normal Positive Fusional Convergence: ; Negative Fusional Divergence: ; Vertical: ).

Treatment of Decompensated Heterophoria: (1) Full refractive correction, (2) Orthoptic Convergence Exercises (pencil push-ups, synoptophore fusional reserve exercises — mainstay for Convergence Insufficiency Exophoria), (3) Relieving Prisms in spectacles (apex toward deviation, correcting  to  of phoria, especially useful in Hyperphoria), (4) Surgery in refractory large phorias.

2. Clinical Varieties of Esotropia & Exotropia

A. Infantile (Congenital) Esotropia vs. Accommodative Esotropia:

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-010]]

B. Intermittent Exotropia: Most common exodeviation; onset at 2–5 years; manifest outward drift precipitated by bright sunlight (closure of one eye in bright light — photalgia), daydreaming, or fatigue, while remaining orthophoric with good stereopsis at near. Treated by minus-lens overcorrection, orthoptic exercises, and Bilateral Lateral Rectus Recession (for divergence excess type) or Unilateral LR Recession + MR Resection (for basic type).

subject: ophthalmology
title: 2. THIRD & FOURTH CRANIAL NERVE PALSIES, RESTRICTIVE SQUINTS & NYSTAGMUS
text:
2. THIRD & FOURTH CRANIAL NERVE PALSIES, RESTRICTIVE SQUINTS & NYSTAGMUS

1. Oculomotor (3rd) & Trochlear (4th) Cranial Nerve Palsies

Third Cranial Nerve (Oculomotor) Palsy:

Etiology: Microvascular ischaemia (Diabetes, Hypertension — Pupil-sparing because pupillomotor parasympathetic fibres travel superficially in the dorsomedial pial periphery of the nerve and are spared from vasa nervorum core infarction), Posterior Communicating Artery (PCA) Aneurysm (Pupil-involving painful 3rd nerve palsy — neurosurgical emergency!), Uncal herniation (Hutchinson’s pupil), Cavernous sinus lesions, Midbrain strokes:

Weber’s Syndrome: Fascicular 3rd nerve + Cerebral peduncle  Ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy + Contralateral hemiplegia.

Benedikt’s Syndrome: Fascicular 3rd nerve + Red nucleus  Ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy + Contralateral intention tremor/hemichorea.

Clinical Features of Complete 3rd Nerve Palsy:

Complete Ptosis (paralysis of LPS; masks diplopia until lid is lifted).

Eyeball deviated “Down and Out” (Exotropia + Hypotropia + Intorsion) due to unopposed action of Lateral Rectus (6th nerve) and Superior Oblique (4th nerve).

Limitation of Adduction, Elevation, and Depression.

Fixed, Dilated Pupil (mydriasis) + Loss of Accommodation (cycloplegia) due to internal ophthalmoplegia.

Crossed Diplopia on elevating the ptotic lid.

Fourth Cranial Nerve (Trochlear) Palsy (Superior Oblique Palsy):

Unique Anatomical Features: Only cranial nerve emerging from the dorsal aspect of brainstem, completely decussates in the superior medullary velum, and is the slenderest nerve with the longest intracranial course.

Etiology: Congenital (commonest; presents with long-standing head tilt and facial asymmetry) or Closed Head Trauma (commonest acquired cause, often bilateral), Microvascular ischaemia.

Clinical Features:

Vertical and Torsional (Excyclotorsional) Diplopia, worst on looking DOWN and IN (e.g., difficulty going down stairs or reading a book).

Ipsilateral Hypertropia that increases on adduction (due to secondary Inferior Oblique overaction) and on tilting the head to the ipsilateral shoulder.

Compensatory Ocular Torticollis: Patient adopts a Contralateral Head Tilt (tilts head to opposite shoulder) + chin depression to eliminate diplopia.

Parks-Bielschowsky Three-Step Test: Diagnostic test to isolate the paretic cyclovertical muscle (Step 1: Which eye is hypertropic in primary gaze? Step 2: Does hypertropia increase in right or left gaze? Step 3: Bielschowsky Head-Tilt Test — hypertropia increases on tilting head to the side of the paretic Superior Oblique).

Surgical Treatment: Ipsilateral Inferior Oblique Weakening (Myectomy/Recession) or Superior Oblique Tucking.

2. Restrictive Squints, A-V Patterns & Strabismus Surgery Principles

Duane’s Retraction Syndrome (DRS): Congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder (hypoplasia of 6th nerve nucleus with aberrant innervation of Lateral Rectus by branches of the 3rd cranial nerve).

Huber’s Types: Type I (Most common, 80%): Marked limitation of abduction with esotropia; Type II: Limitation of adduction with exotropia; Type III: Limitation of both abduction and adduction.

Hallmark Sign (in all types): Retraction of the globe into the orbit and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on attempted ADDUCTION (due to co-contraction of Medial and Lateral Recti), with widening of palpebral fissure on attempted abduction + “Upshoot / Downshoot” phenomenon.

Brown’s Syndrome (Superior Oblique Tendon Sheath Syndrome): Congenital or acquired mechanical restriction preventing relaxation of the Superior Oblique tendon through the trochlea  Inability to elevate the eye in ADDUCTION (mimics Inferior Oblique palsy, but Forced Duction Test is strongly positive on elevating the adducted eye!).

‘A’ and ‘V’ Pattern Strabismus: Horizontally concomitant squint with vertical incomitance (‘A’ Pattern: difference  between upgaze and downgaze; ‘V’ Pattern: difference  between upgaze and downgaze). Caused by Oblique muscle dysfunction (Inferior Oblique Overaction causes V-pattern; Superior Oblique Overaction causes A-pattern). Treated by weakening the overacting oblique muscle, or if obliques are normal, vertical transposition of horizontal rectus insertions (Mnemonic MALE: Medial recti transposed toward Apex of A/V; Lateral recti transposed toward Empty space).

Surgical Principles (Recession & Resection):

Weakening Procedures: Recession (detaching muscle and suturing it posteriorly on sclera; 1 mm MR recession corrects , max 5.5 mm; 1 mm LR recession corrects , max 8 mm), Myectomy (Inferior oblique), Marginal myotomy.

Strengthening Procedures: Resection (excising aMeasured anterior segment of tendon and suturing stump at original insertion; max MR resection 8 mm, max LR resection 10 mm), Tucking (Superior oblique), Advancement.

3. Nystagmus

Definition: Involuntary, regular, rhythmic, biphasic to-and-fro oscillatory movements of the eyes.

Pendular Nystagmus: Equal velocity in both directions.

Jerk Nystagmus: Slow drift phase in one direction followed by a corrective fast saccadic phase in the opposite direction (direction of nystagmus is named after the fast phase).

Classification (CEMAS System):

Physiological Nystagmus:

Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN): Induced by viewing a rotating striped drum (used to test objective visual acuity in infants and prove functional vision in malingerers).

End-gaze Nystagmus: Fine jerk nystagmus in extreme lateral gaze (>40°).

Caloric Vestibular Nystagmus (Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex): Irrigating ear canal with water (Mnemonic COWS: Cold water  fast phase to Opposite side; Warm water  fast phase to Same side).

Pathological Nystagmus of Infancy:

Infantile Nystagmus Syndrome (INS — Congenital Motor & Sensory Nystagmus): Onset at 2–3 months; horizontal uniplanar nystagmus that dampens on convergence and has a specific gaze position of minimum oscillation (“Null Zone”), causing the child to adopt a compensatory head turn to place the eyes in the null zone for best vision. Sensory causes: Ocular albinism, Aniridia, Leber’s congenital amaurosis, Bilateral congenital cataract, Achromatopsia, Optic nerve hypoplasia. Surgical Treatment: Kestenbaum-Anderson Operation (recess-resect of all 4 horizontal recti to shift the null zone into primary gaze, eliminating the abnormal head turn).

Fusion Maldevelopment Nystagmus Syndrome (Latent Nystagmus): Absent when both eyes are open; conjugate horizontal jerk nystagmus appears immediately when one eye is occluded (fast phase beats toward the uncovered fixing eye). Associated with Infantile Esotropia. (Vision must be tested by fogging the fellow eye with a +6.0 D lens rather than an opaque occluder).

Spasmus Nutans Syndrome: Benign triad in infants (4–14 months) of asymmetric/monocular high-frequency “shimmering” pendular nystagmus + Head nodding + Torticollis; resolves spontaneously by 3–4 years (must do MRI to rule out chiasmal optic glioma).

Acquired Pathological Nystagmus (Presents with Oscillopsia —illusory movement of environment):

Downbeat Nystagmus: Fast phase downward  Craniocervical junction lesion (Arnold-Chiari malformation, cerebellar degeneration).

Upbeat Nystagmus: Dorsal brainstem/vermis lesion (stroke, demyelination).

See-Saw Nystagmus: One eye elevates and intorts while the fellow eye depresses and extorts  Parasellar / Chiasmal mass (Craniopharyngioma).

Convergence-Retraction Nystagmus: On attempted upgaze, eyes jerk inward and retract into orbit  Dorsal Midbrain (Parinaud’s) Syndrome (Pinealoma).

Ataxic (Dissociated) Nystagmus of abducting eye  Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion in Multiple Sclerosis).
