title: 1. PRESEPTAL CELLULITIS, CAVERNOUS SINUS THROMBOSIS, MUCORMYCOSIS & PSEUDOTUMOUR
text:
UNIT 4: ORBIT (SUPPLEMENTARY PORTIONS)

1. PRESEPTAL CELLULITIS, CAVERNOUS SINUS THROMBOSIS, MUCORMYCOSIS & PSEUDOTUMOUR

1. Differential Diagnosis Table: Acute Inflammatory Orbital Swellings

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-011]]

2. Rhino-Orbital-Cerebral Mucormycosis (ROCM)

Etiology & Risk Factors: Fulminant,opportunistic angioinvasive fungal infection caused by non-septate filamentous fungi of order Mucorales (Mucor, Rhizopus).

Predisposing Conditions: Uncontrolled Diabetes Mellitus with Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), Post-COVID-19 patients treated with systemic corticosteroids, Haematological malignancies, Renal failure, Deferoxamine therapy (iron acts as a growth factor for Mucor).

Pathogenesis & Clinical Features: Inhaled spores germinate in nasal turbinates/paranasal sinuses  invade arterial walls (angioinvasion) causing thrombosis and ischaemic infarction  erodes into orbit and cavernous sinus/brain.

Signs: Facial/orbital pain, proptosis, chemosis, complete ophthalmoplegia (orbital apex syndrome), CRAO (sudden blindness), and pathognomonic black necrotic eschar on the nasal turbinates, hard palate, or eyelid skin.

Diagnosis: Direct 10% KOH mount and Calcofluor-white stain of nasal/orbital biopsy showing broad, aseptate (or pauci-septate), ribbon-like hyphae branching at right angles () + Contrast MRI of Sinuses/Orbit/Brain (“Black turbinate sign”).

Management (Multidisciplinary Emergency):

Immediate reversal of Diabetic Ketoacidosis and cessation of steroids/immunosuppressants.

Systemic Antifungal Therapy: Intravenous Liposomal Amphotericin-B () for 4–6 weeks, followed by step-down oral Posaconazole or Isavuconazole.

Aggressive Surgical Debridement: Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) debridement + Retrobulbar Amphotericin-B injection () or Orbital Exenteration in extensive necrotic non-salvageable orbital involvement.

3. Idiopathic Orbital Inflammatory Disease (IOID / Orbital Pseudotumour) & Tolosa-Hunt Syndrome

IOID (Pseudotumour): Non-infective, non-neoplastic idiopathic polymorphous lymphocytic/fibrovascular orbital inflammation in adults (40–50 years). Can affect lacrimal gland (dacryoadenitis), extraocular muscles (Orbital Myositis — CT shows enlargement of muscle belly INCLUDING its tendon, unlike Thyroid Eye Disease which spares the tendon!), sclera, or diffuse orbital fat. Presents with acute painful congestive proptosis, lid swelling, diplopia, and dramatic response to Oral Corticosteroids (Prednisolone ).

Tolosa-Hunt Syndrome: Idiopathic non-specific granulomatous inflammation of the superior orbital fissure, orbital apex, or cavernous sinus, presenting with severe boring retro-orbital pain and painful ophthalmoplegia (3rd, 4th, 6th, and  nerve palsies) that resolves dramatically within 48–72 hours of systemic corticosteroid therapy.

subject: ophthalmology
title: 2. ORBITAL TUMOURS, CRANIOFACIAL DYSOSTOSES & ORBITAL SURGERY
text:
2. ORBITAL TUMOURS, CRANIOFACIAL DYSOSTOSES & ORBITAL SURGERY

1. High-Yield Orbital Tumours Summary

Rhabdomyosarcoma: Most common primary malignant orbital tumour of childhood (mean age 7–8 years). Arises from pluripotent mesenchymal cells (not extraocular muscles!). Embryonal type (commonest, superonasal quadrant, good prognosis) vs. Alveolar type (inferior quadrant, worst prognosis). Presents as explosive, rapidly progressive proptosis mimicking orbital cellulitis (but without fever/leukocytosis). Histopathology shows cross-striations (desmin/myogenin positive). Treatment: Incisional biopsy followed by Systemic Chemotherapy (Vincristine + Actinomycin-D + Cyclophosphamide) + High-dose Radiotherapy (90% survival).

Optic Nerve Glioma (Juvenile Pilocytic Astrocytoma): Slow-growing benign astrocytic hamartoma affecting children (4–8 years, Girls > Boys); 30–50% have Neurofibromatosis Type 1. Presents with gradual painless axial proptosis + early visual loss + RAPD + optic atrophy/disc oedema. X-ray Rhese view shows uniform round enlargement of optic foramen; CT/MRI shows fusiform enlargement and kinking of the optic nerve.

Optic Nerve Sheath Meningioma: Affects middle-aged women (30–50 years). Classic Hoyt-Spencer Triad: (1) Slowly progressive painless visual loss, (2) Optic atrophy, and (3) Optociliary Shunt Vessels on the optic disc. CT/MRI shows tubular thickening with “Tram-track sign” (calcification/enhancement of sheath around a lucency of the optic nerve) on axial cuts and “Doughnut sign” on coronal cuts.

Cavernous Haemangioma: Most common benign orbital tumour in adults (females 30–50 years). Well-encapsulated intraconal lesion presenting with slowly progressive painless axial proptosis, hypermetropic shift (flattening of posterior globe), and choroidal folds. Treated by complete surgical excision via lateral orbitotomy.

Carotid-Cavernous Fistula (CCF): Abnormal communication between internal carotid artery and cavernous sinus.

Direct High-Flow CCF (80%): Post-head trauma/basal skull fracture or ruptured intracavernous aneurysm. Presents with Classic Triad of Pulsatile Proptosis + Conjunctival Chemosis + Audible Cephalic Bruit (abolished by ipsilateral carotid compression in neck), “Corkscrew” arterialized epibulbar vessels (Caput medusae), ophthalmoplegia (6th nerve earliest), and secondary glaucoma (raised episcleral venous pressure). Treated by Endovascular Balloon Embolization / Coiling.

2. Craniosynostoses (Crouzon’s & Apert’s) & Orbital Surgeries

Crouzon’s Syndrome (Craniofacial Dysostosis): Autosomal dominant (FGFR2 gene); premature closure of coronal/sagittal sutures (brachycephaly), maxillary hypoplasia, hooked parrot-beak nose, bilateral proptosis due to shallow orbits, hypertelorism, V-pattern exotropia, and compressive optic atrophy.

Apert’s Syndrome (Acrocephalosyndactyly): Tower skull (oxycephaly), shallow orbits with proptosis, antimongoloid slant, and syndactyly of fingers and toes.

Orbitotomy & Exenteration:

Anterior Orbitotomy: Transcutaneous (lid crease/subciliary) or transconjunctival approach for anterior extraconal lesions.

Lateral Orbitotomy (Kronlein’s / Stallard-Wright Operation): Temporary removal of the lateral orbital wall (zygomaticofrontal bone) to access retrobulbar intraconal tumours and lacrimal gland tumours.

Orbital Exenteration: Radical mutilating surgery removing the entire eyeball, eyelids (total) or sparing lids (subtotal), retrobulbar fat, muscles, and periorbita down to bare bone. Indications: Orbital extension of Retinoblastoma, Choroidal melanoma, Sebaceous/Basal/Squamous cell carcinoma of lids, Lacrimal gland adenoid cystic carcinoma, and fulminant Orbital Mucormycosis.

subject: ophthalmology
title: 1. EXTRAOCULAR & INTRAOCULAR FOREIGN BODIES (IOFB)
text:
UNIT 5: OCULAR TRAUMA & OPHTHALMIC EMERGENCIES (SUPPLEMENTARY PORTIONS)

1. EXTRAOCULAR & INTRAOCULAR FOREIGN BODIES (IOFB)

1. Corneal Foreign Body & Management

Clinical Features: Common in lathe/grinding workers (iron/emery particles) and agricultural workers (paddy husk). Causes acute foreign body sensation, profuse reflex lacrimation, photophobia, blepharospasm, ciliary congestion, and a rust ring (within 24 hours of iron FB).

Stepwise Removal Procedure:

Instill topical anaesthetic (0.5% Proparacaine or 4% Lignocaine) and examine on slit-lamp with fluorescein stain (perform everted upper lid examination to rule out subtarsal FB causing linear vertical corneal abrasions).

Superficial loose FB is wiped off with a sterile wet cotton-tipped applicator.

Impacted epithelial/stromal FB is lifted out under slit-lamp magnification using a sterile 26G bent hypodermic needle or Foreign body spud (approaching tangentially).

Rust ring is scraped gently with a needle or Alger brush (burr).

Instill homatropine 2% (cycloplegic to relieve ciliary spasm), moxifloxacin 0.5% ointment, and patch for 24 hours. (Never prescribe topical anaesthetic drops for home use as they inhibit epithelial healing and cause neurotrophic corneal melting!).

2. Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB) — Localization & Removal

Suspect an IOFB in any history of “hammering iron on chisel” (high-velocity metallic chip).

Signs of Occult IOFB: Self-sealed linear corneal scar, iris transillumination hole, focal sector cataract/capsular track, unexplained hyphaema/vitreous haemorrhage, hypotony, or heterochromia (siderosis).

Localization Investigations:

Thin-slice (1 mm) Helical CT Scan of Orbits (Investigation of Choice): Detects and localizes radio-opaque metallic, glass, and stone IOFBs down to 0.5 mm.

B-scan Ultrasonography & UBM: Detects radiolucent (wood/vegetative) IOFBs and associated retinal detachment/vitreous haemorrhage.

Plain X-ray Orbit with Limbal Ring (Historical): Silver ring stitched at limbus; AP view and 3 lateral views (looking straight, up, and down) determine if the radio-opaque FB moves with the globe (intraocular).

Strict Contraindication: MRI is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED if a ferromagnetic metallic IOFB is suspected, as the magnetic field causes violent movement of the FB and blinding intraocular haemorrhage!

Surgical Removal of IOFB:

IOFB in Anterior Chamber: Removed through a limbal incision (3 mm internal to limbus in the quadrant over the FB) using an external hand-held electromagnet or intraocular McPherson forceps under viscoelastic protection.

IOFB in Crystalline Lens: ECCE / Phacoemulsification with removal of the FB and PCIOL implantation.

IOFB in Vitreous or Retina: Three-Port Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV)  release vitreoretinal adhesions  grasp and extract FB using intraocular foreign body forceps or intravitreal rare-earth magnet  apply Endolaser photocoagulation around any retinal impact site + gas/silicone oil tamponade.

subject: ophthalmology
title: 2. NON-MECHANICAL INJURIES & SUMMARY OF OPHTHALMIC EMERGENCIES
text:
2. NON-MECHANICAL INJURIES & SUMMARY OF OPHTHALMIC EMERGENCIES

1. Radiational, Thermal & Electrical Injuries

Ultraviolet (UV) Radiation Injury — Photophthalmia (Arc-Welder’s Flash / Snow Blindness):

Pathogenesis: UV-B and UV-C rays (290–311 nm) absorbed by corneal epithelium  latent period of 4–6 hours  nuclear fragmentation and desquamation of superficial corneal epithelial cells (Multiple Punctate Epithelial Erosions).

Clinical Features: Wakes patient at night (4–6 hours after welding without Crookes’ protective goggles or skiing on snow) with excruciating burning pain, severe photophobia, blepharospasm, and profuse tearing. Fluorescein staining shows diffuse stippled green punctate staining in the interpalpebral zone.

Treatment: Cold compresses, Topical Cycloplegic (Homatropine 2%), Lubricating & Antibiotic eye ointment with firm patching for 24 hours (epithelium regenerates completely within 24–48 hours), and oral analgesics.

Infrared Radiation Injury: Chronic exposure in glass/iron furnace workers (800–1200 nm) causes True Exfoliation of the Anterior Lens Capsule (scroll-like peeling of outer lamella of anterior capsule) and posterior discoid “Glass-Blower’s Cataract”.

Ionizing Radiation Injury (X-rays, -rays, -rays): Causes madarosis, cicatricial conjunctivitis, severe dry eye, Radiation Cataract (equatorial cells damaged  posterior subcapsular plaque after a latent period of 6 months to 2 years), and Radiation Retinopathy (microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates, and neovascularization mimicking diabetic retinopathy).

2. Master Checklist of True Ophthalmic Emergencies (Viva / Short Answer)

Minutes-to-Hours Emergencies (Immediate Action Required within Minutes):

Chemical Burns (especially Alkali burns): Immediate copious saline irrigation for 30 min.

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO): Ocular massage + AC paracentesis + Acetazolamide.

Retrobulbar Haemorrhage / Acute Orbital Compartment Syndrome: Immediate lateral canthotomy and cantholysis.

Same-Day Urgent Emergencies (Action Required within Hours):

Acute Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma & Phacomorphic Glaucoma

Open-Globe Penetrating / Perforating Injury & Retained IOFB

Acute Postoperative Bacterial Endophthalmitis (Intravitreal Vancomycin + Ceftazidime)

Orbital Cellulitis, Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis, & Rhino-Orbital Mucormycosis

Gonococcal Hyperacute Purulent Conjunctivitis / Ophthalmia Neonatorum (can perforate intact cornea within 24–48 hours; requires systemic Ceftriaxone)

Arteritic Anterior Ischaemic Optic Neuropathy (Giant Cell Arteritis) (IV Methylprednisolone to save fellow eye)

Painful Pupil-Involving 3rd Nerve Palsy (urgent CT/MR Angiography for Posterior Communicating Artery aneurysm)

Macula-On Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment.

subject: ophthalmology
title: 1. ANTERIOR ISCHAEMIC OPTIC NEUROPATHY (AION) & LEBER’S HEREDITARY OPTIC NEUROPATHY
text:
UNIT 6 & 8: VISUAL PATHWAY & DISEASES OF OPTIC NERVE (SUPPLEMENTARY PORTIONS)

1. ANTERIOR ISCHAEMIC OPTIC NEUROPATHY (AION) & LEBER’S HEREDITARY OPTIC NEUROPATHY

1. Anterior Ischaemic Optic Neuropathy (AION): Arteritic vs. Non-Arteritic

Definition: Segmental infarction of the prelaminar/laminar optic nerve head caused by occlusion of the Short Posterior Ciliary Arteries (SPCAs).

[[TABLE:ophthalmology-tbl-012]]

2. Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON) & Congenital Disc Anomalies

Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON): Maternal mitochondrial DNA point mutation (11778, 14484, or 3460) affecting young males (15–30 years). Presents with acute/subacute, painless, severe central visual loss in one eye, followed within weeks/months by the second eye.

Classic Fundus Triad in Acute Stage: (1) Circumpapillary telangiectatic microangiopathy, (2) Swelling of peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer (pseudo-papilloedema), and (3) Complete absence of dye leakage on FFA (differentiates it from true papillitis!). Evolves into bilateral primary optic atrophy with dense centrocaecal scotomas. Treated with Idebenone (ubidecarenone analogue); avoid smoking and alcohol.

Congenital Anomalies of the Optic Disc:

Optic Disc Drusen (Hyaline Bodies): Calcified acellular laminated bodies buried in the prelaminar optic nerve head in children (commonest cause of pseudopapilloedema), emerging on the surface in teens as waxy yellowish globular bodies. Shows autofluorescence and high reflectivity on B-scan ultrasound.

Optic Nerve Hypoplasia: Small grey optic disc surrounded by a yellow-pigmented peripapillary halo (“Double-Ring Sign”). Associated with maternal diabetes/alcohol use and De Morsier’s Syndrome (Septo-optic dysplasia: Optic nerve hypoplasia + absent septum pellucidum + pituitary dwarfism).

Optic Disc Pit: Small grey/oval depression on the temporal aspect of the optic disc, complicated in 40–50% of cases by serous macular schisis/detachment.

Morning Glory Syndrome: Funnel-shaped excavated optic disc surrounded by a raised chorioretinal pigment ring with radial spoke-like vessels emerging from the rim and a central tuft of white glial tissue.

Medullated (Opaque) Nerve Fibres: Myelination of retinal nerve fibres continuing anteriorly beyond the lamina cribrosa; appears as a feathery, striated white patch contiguous with the disc margin that partially obscures underlying retinal vessels and causes an enlarged blind spot.

subject: ophthalmology
title: 2. HIGHER VISUAL DYSFUNCTIONS, CORTICAL BLINDNESS, MALINGERING & ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY
text:
2. HIGHER VISUAL DYSFUNCTIONS, CORTICAL BLINDNESS, MALINGERING & ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY

1. Cortical Blindness, Visual Agnosia, Hallucinations & Malingering

Cortical Blindness: Bilateral complete loss of vision due to bilateral occipital lobe (striate cortex) lesions (basilar/posterior cerebral artery thromboembolism, severe head trauma, hypoxic encephalopathy, pre-eclampsia).

Diagnostic Criteria: (1) Complete loss of vision in both eyes, (2) Normal pupillary light reflexes (pupillary fibres diverge to pretectal nucleus before LGB), (3) Normal fundus (no optic atrophy), (4) Loss of optokinetic nystagmus and menace blink reflex, (5) Anton’s Syndrome (patient is completely blind but adamantly denies blindness and confabulates visual descriptions — due to associated parieto-occipital damage), and (6) Riddoch Phenomenon (statokinetic dissociation — ability to perceive moving targets in a blind field).

Higher Cortical Visual Disorders:

Visual Agnosia: Inability to recognize objects by sight despite normal visual acuity, while recognizing them immediately by touch or sound (lesion in bilateral ventromedial occipitotemporal cortex; Prosopagnosia = inability to recognize familiar faces).

Alexia without Agraphia: Patient can write normally but cannot read what they just wrote (lesion of left occipital cortex + splenium of corpus callosum).

Visual Hallucinations: Unformed (Elementary) flashes/geometric shapes originate from the Occipital lobe (migraine aura); Formed (Complex) scenes/people originate from the Temporal lobe or occur in visually impaired elderly patients with intact cognition (Charles Bonnet Syndrome).

Malingering vs. Hysterical Blindness:

Malingering: Deliberate feigning of visual loss (usually unilateral) for financial compensation or medico-legal gain; patient is uncooperative and exaggerates disability.

Hysterical (Functional) Blindness: Subconscious psychogenic conversion disorder (usually bilateral in young females); patient walks around obstacles effortlessly with “belle indifference” and shows tubular or spiral visual fields on perimetry.

Objective Tests to Prove Malingering:

10-Dioptre Base-Out Prism Test: Place a  base-out prism before the “blind” eye; if the eye makes an inward saccadic movement of refixation to eliminate diplopia, binocular vision is proved.

Convex Lens Fogging Test: Place a  lens before the “blind” eye and a high  fogging lens before the good eye; if the patient reads the distant Snellen chart, they are reading with the “blind” eye.

Snellen’s Coloured Letters Test (Red-Green Goggles): Place a red filter over the good eye while viewing red and green letters; a red filter makes red letters invisible against a red background, so if the patient reads all letters (including red/green), they are seeing with the “blind” eye.

Intact Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN) and Normal Pattern-Reversal VEP.

2. Foster-Kennedy Syndrome & Electrophysiological Tests (ERG, EOG, VEP)

Foster-Kennedy Syndrome: Caused by a Frontal Lobe Tumour or Olfactory Groove / Sphenoidal Wing Meningioma.

Classic Triad: (1) Ipsilateral Primary Optic Atrophy (direct compression of ipsilateral optic nerve by tumour), (2) Contralateral Papilloedema (due to generalized raised intracranial pressure; the atrophic nerve cannot swell), and (3) Ipsilateral Anosmia.

Pseudo-Foster-Kennedy Syndrome: Most commonly caused by Sequential Non-Arteritic AION (NAION) (one eye has old ischaemic optic atrophy from a past NAION attack, and the fellow eye develops acute disc oedema from a fresh NAION attack).

Electrophysiological Tests Summary:

Electroretinography (ERG): Records mass electrical action potential of the retina evoked by a flash of light using a corneal contact lens electrode:

a-wave: Initial negative deflection arising from Photoreceptors (Rods & Cones).

b-wave: Large positive deflection generated by Muller cells & Bipolar cells (inner nuclear layer).

c-wave: Positive wave from Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE).

Clinical Utility: Extinguished/subnormal in Retinitis Pigmentosa, Leber’s congenital amaurosis, Total RD, Siderosis. Negative ERG (normal a-wave, selectively reduced b-wave) is seen in CRAO, Ischaemic CRVO, X-linked Juvenile Retinoschisis, and Congenital Stationary Night Blindness. (Note: Standard flash ERG is NORMAL in Ganglion cell / Optic nerve diseases like Glaucoma and Optic Atrophy!)

Electro-oculography (EOG): Measures the standing corneoretinal potential between cornea (+ve) and RPE (-ve) during dark and light adaptation (Arden Ratio = ; Normal ). Reflects RPE–Photoreceptor interaction; classically abnormal (<150%) in Best’s Vitelliform Dystrophy.

Visually Evoked Potential / Response (VEP / VER): Occipital EEG recording in response to flash or checkerboard pattern reversal ( wave at ~100 ms). Assesses functional integrity of the macula and entire visual pathway up to the occipital cortex; shows prolonged  latency in Optic Neuritis / Multiple Sclerosis.

subject: ophthalmology
title: 1. APHAKIA & CONGENITAL LENS ANOMALIES
text:
UNIT 7: CATARACT & LENS (SUPPLEMENTARY PORTIONS)

1. APHAKIA & CONGENITAL LENS ANOMALIES

1. Aphakia (Optics, Clinical Features & Correction)

Definition: Absence of the crystalline lens from the pupillary area (most commonly post-surgical, or due to posterior dislocation of lens into vitreous, or rare congenital aphakia).

Optical Changes in an Aphakic Eye:

High Hypermetropia (parallel rays focus ~31 mm behind cornea, i.e., 7 mm behind retina).

Total dioptric power of eye is reduced from  to  (only corneal refraction remains).

Anterior focal length increases from  to ; Posterior focal length increases from  to .

Total Loss of Accommodation (requires  near addition).

Retinal Image Magnification by ~30% when corrected with aphakic spectacles (+10 D), causing intolerable Aniseikonia and Binocular Diplopia in unilateral aphakia.

Clinical Signs of Aphakia:

Profound diminution of vision for both distance and near; Erythropsia (reddish vision) and Cyanopsia (bluish vision) due to unchecked entry of UV rays.

Limbal surgical scar + peripheral iridectomy; Deep anterior chamber; Iridodonesis (tremulousness of iris due to loss of posterior lens support); Jet-black pupil; Only 1st and 2nd Purkinje images are seen (3rd and 4th lenticular Purkinje images are absent); Retinoscopy shows high hypermetropia (+10 to +12 D); Fundus shows a small hypermetropic optic disc.

Disadvantages of Aphakic Spectacles (+10 D Thick Convex Lenses):

30% Retinal Image Magnification (precludes use in unilateral aphakia).

Roving Ring Scotoma (“Jack-in-the-Box” Phenomenon): Prismatic effect of the thick convex lens creates an optically blind ring zone between  and  of the visual field; objects suddenly jump into and out of view as the patient moves their eyes (compensated by turning the head rather than moving the eyes).

Pincushion Distortion (straight door frames appear curved inward) and Spherical/Chromatic Aberrations.

False spatial orientation (objects appear closer and larger, causing the patient to pour tea beside the cup initially).

Heavy weight and poor cosmesis (frog-eye appearance).

Four Modalities for Correction of Aphakia:

Intraocular Lens (IOL) Implantation (Best Modality — 0–1% image magnification): Secondary PCIOL (in sulcus if capsular rim is intact), Scleral-Fixated IOL (SFIOL / Glued IOL), Retro-iris Fixated Iris-Claw IOL, or Angle-supported ACIOL (Kelman Multiflex).

Contact Lenses (5–7% image magnification): Allows binocular single vision in unilateral aphakia, eliminates roving ring scotoma and aberrations.

Aphakic Spectacles: Used only in bilateral aphakia when secondary IOL is contraindicated.

Refractive Corneal Surgery: Hyperopic LASIK or Epikeratophakia.

2. Congenital Anomalies of the Crystalline Lens

Lenticonus (Anterior & Posterior): Conical axial ectasia of the lens capsule and cortex, producing a characteristic “Oil-droplet reflex” in the red fundal glow on distant direct ophthalmoscopy, “scissor-reflex” on retinoscopy, and high axial lenticular myopia:

Lenticonus Anterior: Bilateral anterior conical protrusion associated with Alport’s Syndrome (hereditary haemorrhagic nephritis + sensorineural deafness + anterior lenticonus + dot-and-fleck retinopathy).

Lenticonus Posterior: Unilateral or bilateral posterior bulge associated with Lowe’s (Oculocerebrorenal) Syndrome.

Microspherophakia: Bilateral small, spherical crystalline lens (equatorial edge and zonules are entirely visible on full pupillary dilation!). Associated with Weill-Marchesani Syndrome (short stature, brachydactyly/stubby fingers). Prone to anterior subluxation causing acute pupillary-block (inverse angle-closure) glaucoma (worsened by miotics (“Inverse Glaucoma”) and relieved by mydriatics/cycloplegics!).

Coloboma of Lens: Congenital notch-like defect at the inferior equator of the lens (6 o’clock) due to localized absence of ciliary zonules from incomplete closure of the embryonic choroidal fissure.

3. Intracapsular Cataract Extraction (ICCE) vs. Extracapsular Cataract Extraction (ECCE)

subject: ophthalmology
title: 1. RETINA: PERIPHERAL DEGENERATIONS, VITREORETINOPATHIES & BLOOD DISORDERS
text:
SUPPLEMENTARY EXAM-ORIENTED NOTES (FINAL CONTINUATION)

Final Micro-Addendum: Remaining High-Yield Topics Across the 8 Units

(This final section completes the remaining sub-topics from the textbook within your 8 specified units—specifically Peripheral & Vitreoretinal Degenerations, Haematological Retinopathies, Developmental Glaucoma Syndromes, Sensory Adaptations in Strabismus (ARC & Suppression), Supranuclear Eye Movement Systems, Orbital Apex vs. Superior Orbital Fissure Syndromes, and Direct vs. Indirect Ophthalmoscopy—bringing your combined notes to 100% completion).

1. RETINA: PERIPHERAL DEGENERATIONS, VITREORETINOPATHIES & BLOOD DISORDERS

1. Peripheral Retinal Degenerations (Predisposing to Retinal Detachment)

Lattice Degeneration (Most Important):

Prevalence: Present in 6–10% of the general population and 15–20% of myopes; accounts for ~40% of all rhegmatogenous retinal detachments.

Clinical Features: Spindle-shaped, circumferentially oriented islands located between the equator and ora serrata (most commonly superotemporal quadrant, bilateral in 50%). Characterized by retinal thinning, arborizing white sclerosed vessels in a Crisscross “lattice” network, RPE hyperplasia/clumping, overlying pocket of liquefied vitreous with firm vitreoretinal adhesions at the margins, and small atrophic round holes within the lesion or horse-shoe tears at the posterior edge.

Prophylaxis: Prophylactic Laser Photocoagulation (2–3 rows of 532 nm green laser burns surrounding the lesion) is indicated if lattice with holes is present in: (i) the fellow eye of a patient with prior RD, (ii) high myopes, or (iii) prior to cataract/refractive surgery.

Snail-Track Degeneration: Variant of lattice degeneration characterized by sharply demarcated bands of tightly packed “snow-flake” or “frost-like” glistening white dots (lipid-laden glial cells) without white arborizing lines; carries a high risk of large round retinal holes.

Senile (Acquired) Retinoschisis: Splitting of the neurosensory retina at the outer plexiform layer, usually bilateral in the inferotemporal periphery of hypermetropes >50 years. Appears as a smooth, transparent, immobile, dome-shaped elevation that does not undulate and produces an ABSOLUTE scotoma on perimetry (unlike Rhegmatogenous RD, which is corrugated, mobile, and produces a relative scotoma).

White-With-Pressure (WWP) & White-Without-Pressure (WWOP): Translucent greyish-white appearance of peripheral retina induced by scleral indentation (WWP) or present spontaneously (WWOP); associated with vitreoretinal traction.

Paving-Stone (Cobblestone) Degeneration: Benign, discrete, yellowish-white punched-out areas of chorioretinal thinning in the inferior periphery of elderly eyes (does NOT predispose to RD).

2. Hereditary Vitreoretinal Degenerations

Stickler Syndrome (Hereditary Arthro-Ophthalmopathy): Autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder (COL2A1 collagen gene); most common inherited cause of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in children.

Ocular Triad: Optically empty vitreous cavity (total liquefaction + fibrillar condensations) + High Congenital Myopia + Radial perivascular lattice degeneration (leading to giant retinal tears and bilateral RD in 30%), plus presenile cortical cataract and ectopia lentis.

Systemic Features: Pierre-Robin sequence (micrognathia, glossoptosis, cleft/high-arched palate), flattened midface, hyperextensible large joints with early osteoarthritis, and sensorineural deafness.

Wagner’s Syndrome: Autosomal dominant; optically empty vitreous, preretinal avascular membranes, perivascular pigmentary changes, and chorioretinal atrophy (low incidence of RD).

Favre-Goldmann Syndrome: Autosomal recessive; nyctalopia, central and peripheral retinoschisis, bone-spicule pigmentation mimicking RP, and optically empty vitreous.

3. Anaemic & Leukaemic Retinopathies

Anaemic Retinopathy: Consistently develops when Haemoglobin falls below  (especially when coexisting with thrombocytopenia, as in aplastic or megaloblastic anaemia).

Fundus Signs: Pale fundus background, pale arterioles, dilated tortuous veins, flame-shaped and subhyaloid haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots (anoxic nerve fibre infarcts), and Roth’s spots (haemorrhages with white fibrin-platelet centres). Reverses on correcting anaemia.

Leukaemic Retinopathy: More common in Acute Leukaemias than chronic forms.

Fundus Signs: Pale orange-yellow fundus background, dilated tortuous veins with “sausage-like” segmentation, perivascular white leukaemic sheathing, abundant Roth’s spots (white centre composed of aggregated leukaemic leukocytes), large boat-shaped subhyaloid (preretinal) haemorrhages, and optic nerve head infiltration. (Anterior segment/orbital signs: Spontaneous hyphaema, Pseudohypopyon, Heterochromia iridis, and Proptosis due to Chloroma / Granulocytic sarcoma in children).

title: 2. GLAUCOMA: DEVELOPMENTAL SYNDROMES & INFLAMMATORY HYPERTENSIVE UVEITIS
text:
2. GLAUCOMA: DEVELOPMENTAL SYNDROMES & INFLAMMATORY HYPERTENSIVE UVEITIS

1. Anterior Segment Dysgenesis (ASD) Syndromes Causing Developmental Glaucoma (50% Risk)

(Caused by defective migration/differentiation of Neural Crest Cells; autosomal dominant inheritance via PITX2* and FOXC1 genes): 1. Posterior Embryotoxon: Thickened, centrally displaced, prominent Schwalbe’s line visible on slit-lamp as an irregular white ridge 0.5–1 mm inside the limbus (seen in 10–15% of normal eyes). 2. Axenfeld’s Anomaly: Posterior embryotoxon + Attached peripheral iris strands spanning across the angle to insert into the prominent Schwalbe’s line. 3. Rieger’s Anomaly: Axenfeld’s anomaly + Iris stromal hypoplasia, Corectopia (eccentric pupil), Ectropion uveae, and full-thickness iris holes (Pseudopolycoria). 4. Rieger’s Syndrome (Axenfeld-Rieger Syndrome): Rieger’s ocular anomaly + Systemic Neural Crest Defects:  Dental anomalies: Hypodontia (reduced number of teeth), Microdontia (conical peg-shaped teeth). * Facial anomalies: Maxillary hypoplasia, flat nasal bridge, telecanthus, hypertelorism. * Other defects: Redundant periumbilical skin, hypospadias, pituitary anomalies. 5. Peter’s Anomaly: Central congenital corneal leukoma (opacity) due to localized congenital absence of Descemet’s membrane and endothelium, with iridocorneal adhesions extending from the iris collarette to the margin of the central corneal opacity (Type I) or keratolenticular adhesion/cataract (Type II).

2. Specific Hypertensive Uveitis Syndromes

Posner-Schlossman Syndrome (Glaucomatocyclitic Crisis):

Unilateral, recurrent attacks of acute marked elevation of IOP (40–60 mmHg) in young adults (HLA-Bw54), lasting a few days to 2 weeks.

Diagnostic Features: White (uninflamed) eye with mild blurred vision and coloured halos + Open angle on gonioscopy + Only a few (1–5) fine non-pigmented sentinel Stellate KPs on central endothelium + Minimal aqueous flare + Slightly dilated pupil + Complete absence of posterior synechiae.

Treatment: Self-limiting; treated during attacks with Topical Steroids + Topical Timolol 0.5% / Brimonidine / Oral Acetazolamide (Miotics and Prostaglandins are contraindicated).

Fuchs’ Heterochromic Iridocyclitis (Fuchs’ Uveitis Syndrome):

Chronic, unilateral, low-grade non-granulomatous anterior uveitis in middle-aged adults.

Classic Features: Heterochromia iridis (affected iris is hypochromic/lighter due to diffuse stromal atrophy with moth-eaten appearance) + Diffuse, fine, stellate feathery KPs scattered over the ENTIRE corneal endothelium (not just Arlt’s triangle!) + Faint aqueous flare + Complete absence of posterior synechiae + Fragile angle vessels (Amsler’s sign: filiform anterior chamber haemorrhage upon paracentesis) + Complicated posterior subcapsular cataract (70%) and Secondary Open-Angle Glaucoma (15–30%).

subject: ophthalmology
title: 3. STRABISMUS: SENSORY ADAPTATIONS, SUPRANUCLEAR CONTROL & MICROTROPIA
text:
3. STRABISMUS: SENSORY ADAPTATIONS, SUPRANUCLEAR CONTROL & MICROTROPIA

1. Sensory Adaptations to Strabismus (Suppression & ARC)

(Occurs in children <7–8 years to eliminate annoying Confusion [dissimilar objects imaged on corresponding foveae] and Binocular Diplopia [single object imaged on non-corresponding retinal points]) : 1. Cortical Suppression: Active central cortical inhibition of the visual image originating from the deviating eye only under binocular viewing conditions (disappears immediately when the fixing eye is covered; if unilateral suppression persists chronically, it becomes Strabismic Amblyopia). 2. Abnormal Retinal Correspondence (ARC): Cortical sensory adaptation in small-angle concomitant esotropia where the fovea of the normal fixing eye (O) and an extrafoveal pseudo-foveal point (E) of the squinting eye acquire a common subjective visual direction, providing a crude form of binocular single vision without diplopia. * Objective Angle of Squint: Anatomical deviation measured by prism cover test or synoptophore corneal reflexes. * Subjective Angle of Squint: Angle at which the patient superimposes two images subjectively on the synoptophore. * Angle of Anomaly = . * Harmonious ARC: Subjective angle  (Angle of anomaly  Objective angle — complete sensory adaptation). * Unharmonious ARC: Angle of anomaly is greater than  but less than Objective angle. * Clinical Tests for Suppression & Retinal Correspondence: 1. Worth’s Four-Dot Test (Red glass over Right eye, Green glass over Left eye; viewing box has 1 Red, 2 Green, 1 White light): * Sees 4 lights + No manifest squint = Normal Retinal Correspondence (NRC). * Sees 4 lights + Manifest squint present = Harmonious ARC. * Sees 2 Red lights only = Left eye Suppression. * Sees 3 Green lights only = Right eye Suppression. * Sees 5 lights (2 Red + 3 Green) = Binocular Diplopia (Uncrossed in esotropia; Crossed in exotropia). 2. Bagolini Striated Glasses Test: Plano lenses with microscopic striations at  (RE) and  (LE) convert a spotlight into two oblique lines forming an ‘X’ (cross) in NRC (no squint) or Harmonious ARC (manifest squint present), whereas one line disappears in Suppression. 3. Hering-Bielschowsky After-Image Test and 4-Prism Dioptre Base-Out Test (detects micro-suppression scotoma in Microtropia — a tiny  inconspicuous esotropia with amblyopia, anisometropia, eccentric fixation, and harmonious ARC where the cover test appears negative!).

2. Supranuclear Eye Movement Systems & Gaze Palsies

Saccadic System: Generates rapid, ballistic conjugate refixation movements () to bring an object of interest onto the fovea.

Horizontal Saccades: Initiated by Contralateral Frontal Eye Field (Brodmann Area 8)  decussates in midbrain  Ipsilateral Paramedian Pontine Reticular Formation (PPRF — Horizontal Gaze Centre)  Ipsilateral 6th Nerve Nucleus (excites ipsilateral Lateral Rectus, and via internuclear neurons crossing in the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus [MLF], excites the contralateral 3rd nerve medial rectus subnucleus).

Vertical Saccades: Controlled by the Rostral Interstitial Nucleus of the MLF (riMLF) in the midbrain pretectum (lesion in pinealoma causes Parinaud’s Dorsal Midbrain Syndrome: paralysis of upgaze + convergence-retriaction nystagmus + Collier’s lid retraction + light-near dissociation of pupils).

Smooth Pursuit System: Slow tracking movements (<40°/sec) keeping a moving target on the fovea; controlled by the Ipsilateral Parieto-Occipito-Temporal junction.

Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO): Lesion of the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) (caused by Multiple Sclerosis [bilateral in young adults] or Brainstem Lacunar Infarct [unilateral in elderly]).

Classic Triad on Conjugate Lateral Gaze to the Contralateral Side: (1) Defective Adduction of the Ipsilateral Eye (on the side of MLF lesion), (2) Ataxic (Dissociated) Horizontal Abducting Nystagmus of the Contralateral Eye, and (3) Preserved Convergence (unless the lesion is rostral involving the 3rd nerve nucleus — Anterior INO of Cogan).

One-and-a-Half Syndrome (Fisher): Combined lesion of Ipsilateral PPRF/6th nucleus + Ipsilateral MLF  Complete horizontal gaze palsy toward the ipsilateral side (“one”) + INO (loss of adduction) on looking to the contralateral side (“half”); the only remaining horizontal movement is abduction of the contralateral eye.

2. Direct vs. Indirect Ophthalmoscopy (High-Yield Darkroom Comparison)

Distant Direct Ophthalmoscopy (Performed at 20–25 cm before Direct Ophthalmoscopy):

Clinical Uses: (1) Detects media opacities as dark shadows against the red fundal glow and localizes them by parallactic displacement (opacities in front of pupillary plane [cornea] move with eye movement; opacities behind pupillary plane [posterior lens/vitreous] move against eye movement), (2) Differentiates an iris hole (transmits red glow) from an iris mole/naevus (remains black), (3) Detects edge of a subluxated lens or oil-droplet reflex in keratoconus/lenticonus, and (4) Recognizes retinal detachment or intraocular tumour (greyish/yellowish reflex).

subject: pediatrics
title: 14.1 CONGESTIVE CARDIAC FAILURE (CCF)
text:
Pediatrics — High-Yield Exam Revision Notes

(Covers: Etiopathogenesis, recognition/clinical features in infants & children, management, Digoxin/Digitalization, MCQs) [KU 23, 18, 16, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 450–453

Definition

Congestive Cardiac Failure (CCF): The inability of the heart to maintain an output, at rest or during stress, necessary for the metabolic needs of the body (systolic failure) and inability to receive blood into the ventricular cavities at low pressure during diastole (diastolic failure).

Etiopathogenesis (Causes Classified by Age)

Infants:

Congenital Heart Disease (CHD): Most common cause within the first 1–2 years.

Birth–1 week: Duct-dependent systemic circulation (hypoplastic left heart syndrome, critical aortic stenosis, severe coarctation, interrupted aortic arch), obstructed TAPVC, congenital MR/TR, neonatal Ebstein anomaly.

1–4 weeks: PDA in preterms, VSD with coarctation, truncus arteriosus, TGA with large VSD/PDA.

6–8 weeks (1–2 months): Large Left-to-Right shunts (VSD, PDA, AV canal/endocardial cushion defects) as pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) falls; ALCAPA, unobstructed TAPVC.

Myocarditis and primary myocardial disease: Dilated cardiomyopathy, storage disorders (Pompe disease).

Arrhythmias: Supraventricular tachycardia (HR >180/min), ectopic atrial tachycardia, complete heart block (severe bradycardia).

Kawasaki disease with coronary occlusion.

Pulmonary hypertension: PPHN, upper airway obstruction.

Miscellaneous/Metabolic: Severe anemia (Hb  in normal heart;  in diseased heart), hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, neonatal asphyxia, sepsis.

Older Children (>5 years):

Rheumatic fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD): Acute valvular regurgitation (MR/AR).

CHD complicated by: Anemia, infection, or infective endocarditis.

Systemic hypertension: Acute glomerulonephritis, Takayasu arteritis.

Myocarditis / Cardiomyopathy (DCM, restrictive, HCM).

Cor pulmonale / Pulmonary hypertension.

Clinical Features (Recognition in Infancy & Childhood)

Symptoms in Infants:

Feeding difficulties (‘Poor feeder’): Suck-rest-suck cycle (takes only 1–2 ounces at a time due to fatigue/dyspnea, stops to rest, gets hungry again within minutes), prolonged feeding time (>20 mins).

Excessive perspiration: Diaphoresis over the forehead and occiput (especially during feeds, due to sympathetic overactivity).

** Effort intolerance / Tachypnea:** Fast breathing while feeding; baby is more comfortable when held upright against the mother’s shoulder (infant equivalent of orthopnea).

Failure to thrive: Slow weight gain (inadequate intake + high caloric expenditure of breathing). Note: Short-term rapid weight gain can occur due to fluid retention.

Others: Irritability, persistent hoarse cry, wheezing.

Signs:

Common to Left & Right-sided failure: Cardiomegaly, resting tachycardia, S3 gallop rhythm, poor peripheral pulses, cold extremities, prolonged capillary refill, cyanosis.

Left-sided failure (Pulmonary venous congestion): Tachypnea, subcostal/intercostal retractions, persistent cough (on lying down), wheezing. (Basal rales/crepitations are usually not audible in infants).

Right-sided failure (Systemic venous congestion): Tender hepatomegaly, facial puffiness. (Neck vein/JVP assessment is unhelpful in infants due to short fat neck; pedal edema occurs very late).

Management of CCF

A four-pronged approach: 1. Reducing Cardiac Work:

 * General care: Restrict physical activity; nurse infant in an incubator/warm environment () with minimal handling. Prop up at a  incline (pools edema fluid in dependent parts, reducing lung congestion).

 * Oxygen: Humidified  () if hypoxic. (Avoid indiscriminate  in large LR shunts as it causes pulmonary vasodilation and worsens pulmonary overcirculation). 

* Treat precipitating factors: Fever, infection, and anemia (packed RBC transfusion  slowly, preceded by a single IV dose of furosemide). Mechanical ventilation if severe.

 * Vasodilators (Afterload reduction): Counteract excessive catecholamine/RAAS-mediated vasoconstriction. 

* Oral ACE Inhibitors (Captopril, Enalapril): Suppress RAAS. Start at 1/4th calculated dose to prevent first-dose hypotension; monitor serum creatinine and K⁺. (Avoid in neonates and dehydration)

. * Beta-blockers (Carvedilol , Metoprolol): Used in chronic heart failure / dilated cardiomyopathy. * Acute IV Vasodilators: Sodium nitroprusside. 

2. Improving Cardiac Performance by Reducing Preload (Diuretics):

 * First-line therapy for pulmonary/systemic congestion.

 * Furosemide:  IV or  PO.

 * Spironolactone (Potassium-sparing):  PO q12h (combined with furosemide to prevent hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia and arrhythmias)

. * Diet: Avoid salt-rich foods; ensure high caloric density feeds for catch-up growth

3. Augmenting Myocardial Contractility (Inotropes):

 * Digoxin (Oral/Parenteral): 

* Dosage (Oral Total Digitalizing Dose - TDD): Preterms/Neonates: ; Infants (1 mo–1 yr): ; 1–3 yrs: ; >3 yrs: . 

* Method of Digitalization: Give 1/2 of TDD stat, followed by 1/4th after 8 hrs and 1/4th after 16 hrs. Parenteral dose is  of oral dose.

 * Maintenance Dose: 1/4th of TDD given daily in 1–2 divided doses (e.g., ).

 * Toxicity: Arrhythmias (sinus bradycardia, AV block, ventricular bigeminy), vomiting.

 * Acute IV Inotropes & Inodilators: 

* Catecholamines: Dopamine (), Dobutamine (), Epinephrine.

 * Phosphodiesterase-3 Inhibitors (Inodilators): 

Milrinone ( loading, then ).

 * Calcium sensitizer:

 Levosimendan ().

 4. Correcting the Underlying Cause: 

* Definitive surgical or catheter-based intervention (e.g., VSD/PDA closure, ALCAPA repair, coarctation repair).

One-Word / MCQ Answers: * Drug of choice for rheumatic carditis with CCF: Corticosteroids (Prednisolone ). [KU16] * Three drugs used in CCF management: Furosemide, Enalapril (or Captopril), Digoxin (or Spironolactone/Milrinone). [RGU]

subject: pediatrics
title: 14.2 CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE (CHD)
text:
A. Classification of Congenital Heart Disease & Nadas’ Criteria

(Covers: Classification of CHD, Nadas’ criteria) [KU 20, TU, RGU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 456–460

Broad Hemodynamic Classification of CHD

Acyanotic Congenital Heart Disease:

Left-to-Right Shunts (Increased Pulmonary Blood Flow):

Pre-tricuspid shunts (RV volume overload): Atrial Septal Defect (ASD), Partial Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Drainage (PAPVD).

Post-tricuspid shunts (LV volume overload): Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD), Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA), Aortopulmonary window.

Combined pre- and post-tricuspid: Atrioventricular septal defect (AV canal defect).

Obstructive Lesions (Normal Pulmonary Blood Flow):

Right-sided: Pulmonary stenosis (valvar, infundibular, supravalvar).

Left-sided: Aortic stenosis (valvar, subvalvar, supravalvar), Coarctation of aorta, Mitral stenosis / Cor-triatriatum.

Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease:

Decreased Pulmonary Blood Flow:

With VSD (Fallot physiology / RVH): Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), DORV with PS, TGA with VSD and PS, Single ventricle with PS.

With LVH: Tricuspid atresia, Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum.

Others: Ebstein anomaly, critical PS with atrial RL shunt.

Increased Pulmonary Blood Flow:

Post-tricuspid: Transposition of Great Arteries (d-TGA), Truncus arteriosus, Single ventricle without PS.

Pre-tricuspid: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC).

Severe Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (Eisenmenger Physiology):

Reversal of shunt (RL) in VSD, PDA, or ASD due to irreversible pulmonary vascular obstructive disease (PVOD).

Nadas’ Criteria for Clinical Diagnosis of Heart Disease

Presence of 1 Major OR 2 Minor criteria is essential to indicate the presence of heart disease: 

* Major Criteria (4): 1. Systolic murmur Grade III or more in intensity (or any pansystolic murmur). 2. Any diastolic murmur. 3. Central cyanosis. 4. Congestive cardiac failure. 

* Minor Criteria (5): 1. Systolic murmur Grade I or II. 2. Abnormal second heart sound (S2). 3. Abnormal electrocardiogram (ECG). 4. Abnormal chest X-ray. 5. Abnormal blood pressure.

B. Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)

(Covers: Essay on 6-week-old with suck-rest cycle, grade III murmur in left 4th ICS; Hemodynamics, clinical features, assessment of severity, complications, and management) [KU 24, 20, 17, 16, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 466–469

Clinical Scenario Answers [KU16]

Primary Cardiac Abnormality: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD).

Associated Complication leading to presenting complaints: Congestive Cardiac Failure (CCF) secondary to large Left-to-Right shunt (manifests at 6–8 weeks as neonatal pulmonary vascular resistance regresses).

Types of VSD (Anatomical Classification)

Perimembranous VSD (): Located in the membranous septum with variable extension into adjacent inlet, trabecular, or outlet muscular septum.

Muscular (Trabecular) VSD (): Located entirely within the muscular septum (apical, mid-muscular, or multiple ‘Swiss-cheese’ defects).

Inlet (AV canal type) VSD (): Posterior and inferior to the membranous defect beneath the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve.

Outlet (Subpulmonic / Supracristal / Doubly committed) VSD (): Located in the outlet septum beneath the pulmonary and aortic valves; prone to aortic cusp prolapse and AR.

Hemodynamics of VSD

In a restrictive VSD, LV systolic pressure is much higher than RV systolic pressure throughout systole  high-velocity Left-to-Right (LV to RV) shunt occurs throughout systole, generating a pansystolic murmur (PSM) and systolic thrill.

Since the shunt occurs during systole when the RV is already contracting, the shunted blood streams directly into the pulmonary artery  increased pulmonary blood flow (pulmonary plethora).

This large volume of blood returns via pulmonary veins to the Left Atrium (LA) and Left Ventricle (LV)  causes LA and LV volume overload (dilation and hypertrophy).

Increased diastolic blood flow across a normal mitral valve produces a mid-diastolic flow rumble (delayed diastolic murmur - DDM) at the apex.

Because the LV empties via two outlets (aorta and VSD), A2 occurs early; because RV ejection into the PA is prolonged, P2 is delayed  wide, variable splitting of S2 with an accentuated P2 (if pulmonary artery pressure is elevated).

Clinical Features & Assessment of Severity

Symptoms: Small VSDs are asymptomatic. Large VSDs present at 6–10 weeks of age with CCF (tachypnea, suck-rest-suck cycle, forehead sweating), failure to thrive, and recurrent lower respiratory tract infections.

Signs & Severity Assessment:

Small VSD (Maladie de Roger): Normal heart size, loud harsh pansystolic murmur (Grade IV/VI) with thrill at lower left sternal border (LLSB), normal S2 split, normal P2, no apical mid-diastolic murmur. (Very tiny muscular VSDs may produce an early ejection-like systolic murmur as they close in late systole).

Moderate-to-Large VSD (Hyperkinetic PAH): Hyperkinetic precordium, moderate-to-marked cardiomegaly (LV apex displaced down and out), systolic thrill at LLSB, loud PSM masking S1, wide variable split S2 with loud P2, S3 gallop and apical mid-diastolic flow murmur (DDM) (indicates Qp:Qs > 2:1).

Large Unrestrictive VSD with Obstructive PAH (Eisenmenger Complex): Equal LV and RV pressures. Quiet precordium with parasternal heave (RVH), no thrill, short ejection systolic murmur (or disappearance of murmur), single loud palpable S2, early diastolic Graham-Steell murmur of PR, no apical MDM, central cyanosis and clubbing.

Investigations

ECG: Small VSD is normal. Large VSD shows LV hypertrophy (LV volume overload: tall R waves and deep Q waves with tall T waves in V5, V6) or biventricular hypertrophy (Katz-Wachtel phenomenon: equiphasic RS complexes in mid-precordial leads V2–V4). Pure RVH in Eisenmenger syndrome.

Chest X-ray: Cardiomegaly (LV contour, LA enlargement), prominent main pulmonary artery segment, and pulmonary plethora (increased end-on vessels).

Echocardiography with Color Doppler: Confirms site, size, and number of VSDs, LA/LV dilation, estimates pressure gradient across VSD (to calculate RV/PA systolic pressure), and rules out aortic cusp prolapse.

Course and Complications

Spontaneous closure: Seen in  of small muscular and perimembranous VSDs (90% close by 3 years of age). Inlet and malaligned VSDs do not close.

Congestive cardiac failure and recurrent pneumonia in infancy.

Failure to thrive / Growth retardation.

Pulmonary Vascular Obstructive Disease (Eisenmenger syndrome).

Infective Endocarditis (most common CHD complicated by IE; vegetation forms on the RV side of the defect/tricuspid valve jet lesion).

Aortic Regurgitation: Prolapse of right or non-coronary aortic cusp into a subpulmonic/perimembranous VSD.

Acquired infundibular pulmonary stenosis (Gasul phenomenon): Progressive RVOT hypertrophy converting a large VSD into a TOF-like physiology.

Management

Medical Management:

Control CCF using Furosemide (), Spironolactone, and Enalapril ().

Nutritional rehabilitation (high-calorie density feeds), prompt treatment of respiratory infections, correction of anemia, and maintenance of oral/dental hygiene.

Indications & Timing of Closure:

Infants with refractory CCF and failure to thrive: Early surgical patch closure (within the first 3–6 months).

Large VSD with PAH: Surgical closure before 6–12 months to prevent irreversible PVOD.

Older children with significant shunt (Qp:Qs > 2:1): Elective surgical or transcatheter device closure (muscular/selected perimembranous VSDs in children >8–10 kg).

Any size VSD with aortic cusp prolapse / AR: Prompt surgical closure.

Contraindication to closure: Severe irreversible obstructive PAH (PVR > 8 Wood units/m² with predominant RL shunt).

C. Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)

(Covers: Hemodynamics, murmur diagram, differential cyanosis/clubbing) [KU 21, 18, 17, RGU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 469–471

Hemodynamics of PDA

PDA is a persistent communication between the descending thoracic aorta (just distal to the left subclavian artery) and the main/left pulmonary artery.

Because aortic pressure is higher than pulmonary artery pressure throughout both systole and diastole, there is a continuous Left-to-Right shunt from the aorta to the PA  produces a continuous (‘machinery’) murmur.

Increased pulmonary blood flow returns to the LA and LV  LA and LV volume overload (dilation)  apical mid-diastolic flow murmur (DDM) across the mitral valve and delayed A2 (narrow or paradoxical splitting of S2).

Diastolic runoff of blood from the aorta into the PA lowers aortic diastolic pressure, while increased LV stroke volume ejected into the aorta raises systolic pressure  wide pulse pressure and bounding peripheral pulses (water-hammer pulse).

Differential Cyanosis and Differential Clubbing

Definition: Presence of cyanosis and clubbing in the lower limbs (toes) while the upper limbs (fingers) are pink and normal.

Mechanism: Seen in PDA with severe Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (Eisenmenger physiology) and reversal of shunt (Right-to-Left). Deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery shunts via the PDA into the descending aorta distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, supplying the lower extremities, whereas the head and upper limbs receive oxygenated blood from the aortic arch branches. (Note: Left hand may occasionally show mild cyanosis if the duct opens opposite the left subclavian artery).

D. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) & Cyanotic Spells

(Covers: Essays on 6-month-old with TOF; 1-month-old with cyanosis/spells; Components, hemodynamics, clinical features, investigations, complications, and management of hypercyanotic spells) [KU 24, 22, 21, 18, 17, 15, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 463–464, 471–474

Four Anatomical Components of TOF

Large unrestrictive Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD): Malaligned, perimembranous with outlet extension.

Right Ventricular Outflow Tract (RVOT) Obstruction (Pulmonary Stenosis): Subvalvar/infundibular (most important dynamic component), valvar, annular hypoplasia, or supravalvar/branch PA stenosis.

Overriding of the Aorta: Dextroposed aorta overriding the ventricular septum.

Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH): Concentric hypertrophy secondary to systemic RV pressures.

Hemodynamics (Pathophysiology)

Because the VSD is large and unrestrictive, RV and LV systolic pressures are equalized (at systemic levels).

The direction and magnitude of shunt across the VSD depend entirely on the ratio of RVOT obstruction (pulmonary resistance) to Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR):

Mild RVOT obstruction  minimal RL or even LR shunt (‘Pink’ or Acyanotic TOF).

Moderate-to-severe RVOT obstruction  blood takes the path of least resistance from RV into the overriding aorta (Right-to-Left shunt)  central cyanosis.

Why VSD is silent & Murmur is inversely proportional to severity: Because RV and LV systolic pressures are equal, the VSD itself produces no murmur. The ejection systolic murmur (ESM)heard at the left upper sternal border originates from blood flow across the stenotic RVOT. The more severe the PS, the less blood enters the PA (more shunts into the aorta), resulting in deeper cyanosis and a shorter, softer murmur.

Why CCF does not occur in TOF: The RV is decompressed into the aorta via the large VSD, so RV pressure never exceeds systemic LV pressure. (Exceptions where CCF can occur in TOF: severe anemia, infective endocarditis, systemic hypertension, absent pulmonary valve syndrome, or large aortopulmonary collaterals).

Clinical Features

Symptoms:

Central cyanosis (usually appears at 6–12 weeks as ductus closes and infundibular hypertrophy progresses; present from birth if pulmonary atresia/critical PS).

Exertional dyspnea and exercise intolerance.

Squatting episodes on exertion (kinks femoral arteries  increases SVR  reduces RL shunt and increases pulmonary blood flow).

Hypercyanotic / Anoxic (‘Tet’) spells (peak age: 2–6 months).

Physical Signs:

Central cyanosis and pandigital clubbing.

Normal JVP (prominent ‘a’ waves are absent because RV is decompressed).

Quiet precordium, normal-sized heart, mild parasternal impulse.

Auscultation: Normal S1, single loud S2 (composed only of A2; P2 is soft and inaudible), constant aortic ejection click (due to dilated overriding aorta), and a crescendo-decrescendo Ejection Systolic Murmur (ESM) at the left 2nd/3rd intercostal space.

Complications of TOF

Hypercyanotic (Anoxic) spells: Can lead to hypoxic seizures, stroke, or death.

Cerebrovascular accidents (Stroke / Hemiplegia): Due to cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (stimulated by polycythemia, dehydration, and iron-deficiency microcytosis which reduces RBC deformability) or paradoxical embolism.

Brain abscess: Typically seen >2 years of age as right-to-left shunting bypasses the pulmonary capillary filter.

Infective endocarditis.

Polycythemia and hyperviscosity syndrome (coagulopathy, gout).

Investigations

Complete Blood Count: Polycythemia (elevated Hb/Hct); check RBC indices/ferritin to rule out relative iron-deficiency anemia.

ECG: Right axis deviation (RAD) and Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH) — tall R in V1 with abrupt transition to rS in V2.

Chest X-ray: Normal heart size, upturned cardiac apex (RVH) with concave main pulmonary artery bay (‘Coeur en Sabot’ / Boot-shaped heart), pulmonary oligemia (dark lung fields), and a right-sided aortic arch in  of cases.

Echocardiography: Diagnostic; delineates malaligned VSD, degree/level of RVOT obstruction, size of pulmonary annulus and branch PAs (McGoon ratio/Nakata index), and coronary artery anatomy.

Cyanotic / Hypercyanotic (‘Tet’) Spells & Management

Pathogenesis of Spell: Triggered by crying, feeding, defecation, or waking up in the morning  sympathetic surge / catecholamine release  infundibular spasm + tachycardia + fall in SVR  acute drop in pulmonary blood flow and increased RL shunt  severe systemic hypoxia and metabolic acidosis  stimulates respiratory center causing hyperpnea  increases systemic venous return to RV, perpetuating a vicious cycle.

Clinical Presentation of Spell: Inconsolable crying, paroxysmal hyperpnea (deep and rapid breathing), deepening cyanosis, softening or disappearance of the RVOT ejection systolic murmur, progressing to limpness, syncope, seizures, or death.

Stepwise Emergency Management of Cyanotic Spell (Table 16.15):

Knee-Chest Position (or Squatting / holding infant over mother’s shoulder with knees tucked up): Calms the infant, kinks femoral arteries to increase SVR, and reduces venous return from lower limbs.

Humidified  Oxygen: Administer via face mask/non-rebreathing mask (if it doesn’t agitate the child).

Sedation & Pain Relief (Breaks catecholamine surge & hyperpnea):

Morphine:  SC or IV slowly, OR

Ketamine:  IV or  IM (excellent choice as it sedates AND increases SVR simultaneously).

Correct Acidosis & Hypovolemia:

Normal Saline bolus:  IV (expands RV volume and opens RVOT).

Sodium Bicarbonate:  IV (diluted 1:1) to correct metabolic acidosis (which otherwise blunts vascular responsiveness and drives hyperpnea).

Beta-Blockers (Relieves infundibular spasm and slows heart rate):

Metoprolol:  IV slowly over 5 min (may repeat q5min up to 3 doses), OR Esmolol / Propranolol IV.

Vasopressors (For refractory spells to increase SVR):

Phenylephrine (-agonist):  IV bolus followed by  infusion (or Methoxamine).

Mechanical Ventilation & Emergency Surgery: If spell still persists  sedate, paralyze, intubate, ventilate, and proceed for emergency surgical palliation (Modified Blalock-Taussig [BT] shunt — subclavian to pulmonary artery Gore-Tex graft) or RVOT/PDA stenting.

Prevention of Spells & Definitive Management:

Oral Propranolol ( q6–8h) + Oral Iron therapy (to maintain Hb ).

Definitive Intracardiac Repair (ICR): Patch closure of VSD + infundibular muscle resection ( transannular patch if annulus is hypoplastic), ideally performed electively at 4–6 months of age.

E. Coarctation of Aorta & Differential Diagnosis of Neonatal Central Cyanosis

(Covers: Pulse & BP in Coarctation, MCQ; D/D of central cyanosis in a newborn) [KU 17, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 458–459, 482–483

Pulse and Blood Pressure in Coarctation of Aorta:

Pulse: Bounding brachial/radial pulses in upper limbs with weak, absent, or delayed femoral/dorsalis pedis pulses in lower limbs (Radio-femoral delay). (MCQ Answer: Coarctation of Aorta [KU17]).

Blood Pressure: Upper limb systolic hypertension with lower limb systolic BP at least  lower than upper limbs.

Differential Diagnosis of Central Cyanosis in a Newborn / 1-Month-Old Infant:

Cardiac Causes (Cyanotic CHD - Unresponsive to Hyperoxia Test,  on ):

1st week of life: d-TGA, Obstructed TAPVC, Tricuspid atresia, Pulmonary atresia, Severe Ebstein anomaly, Hypoplastic left heart syndrome.

1–4 weeks of life: Tetralogy of Fallot (severe), Truncus arteriosus, Single ventricle, Unobstructed TAPVC.

Respiratory Causes ( on Hyperoxia Test): Respiratory distress syndrome (HMD), congenital pneumonia, meconium aspiration syndrome, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, pneumothorax, choanal atresia.

Pulmonary Vascular: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN).

CNS Depression (Hypoventilation): Birth asphyxia/HIE, intracranial hemorrhage, neonatal meningitis/sepsis.

Hematological: Congenital methemoglobinemia.

title: 14.3 RHEUMATIC FEVER AND INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS
text:
A. Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF)

(Covers: Essays on 8-yr-old & 5-yr-old with migratory polyarthritis, high ESR, pansystolic murmur; Etiopathogenesis, 2015 Revised Jones Criteria for low/high risk populations, clinical features, management, and prophylaxis) [KU 24, 23, 18, 15, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 484–489

Probable Diagnosis for Clinical Scenarios

Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) with Rheumatic Carditis (Mitral Regurgitation).

Etiopathogenesis

Agent & Host: An autoimmune disorder triggered by pharyngeal (or skin) infection with Group A -hemolytic Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) in genetically susceptible children aged 5–15 years (rare <3 yrs), facilitated by overcrowding and poverty.

Pathogenesis (Molecular Mimicry): Following a latent period of 2–3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis, humoral and cell-mediated immune responses directed against streptococcal M-protein and N-acetylglucosamine cross-react with human host tissues (myosin, tropomyosin, laminin, vimentin, and basal ganglia neurons).

Humoral antibodies damage valvular endothelium  upregulation of VCAM-1  infiltration of CD4⁺ T-cells and macrophages into the valve  granulomatous inflammation (Aschoff bodies — pathognomonic perivascular granulomas with Anitschkow ‘caterpillar’ cells). While arthritis and chorea resolve without sequelae, valvular inflammation causes permanent scarring (RHD).

Clinical Features & 2015 Revised Jones Criteria (AHA / World Heart Federation)

2015 Key Modifications: 1. Stratification of populations into Low-risk vs. Moderate/High-risk (ARF incidence  school-aged children or RHD prevalence ; India falls in the Moderate/High-risk category). 2. Inclusion of Subclinical Carditis (echocardiographic valvulitis without audible murmur) as a Major criterion in all populations. 3. Inclusion of Monoarthritis and Polyarthralgia as Major criteria, and Monoarthralgia as a Minor criterion in Moderate/High-risk populations. 4. Different cut-offs for fever and ESR in Minor criteria.

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-001]]

Diagnostic Requirement (coupled with Essential Evidence of Preceding Group A Streptococcal Infection):

Initial episode of ARF: 2 Major OR 1 Major + 2 Minor criteria.

Recurrent episode of ARF: 2 Major, OR 1 Major + 2 Minor, OR 3 Minor criteria.

(Note: Chorea and indolent carditis do not require proof of preceding streptococcal infection).

Description of Major Manifestations

Carditis (): Pancarditis occurring within the first 2 weeks.

Endocarditis (Valvulitis): Mitral valve is involved in  (apical high-pitched pansystolic murmur of MR radiating to axilla; transient mid-diastolic Carey-Coombs murmur), aortic valve in  (early diastolic decrescendo murmur of AR).

Myocarditis & Pericarditis: Resting tachycardia, muffled S1, S3 gallop, cardiomegaly, CCF, pericardial friction rub.

Arthritis (): Early manifestation; migratory/fleeting polyarthritis affecting large joints (knees, ankles, wrists, elbows), exquisitely painful, red, hot, and swollen; resolves completely within 48–72 hours of starting salicylates without any residual joint deformity.

Sydenham’s Chorea (St. Vitus Dance, ): Late neuropsychiatric manifestation (latent period 1–6 months), more common in girls. Characterized by involuntary, purposeless, quasi-purposeful, jerky movements that disappear during sleep, accompanied by emotional lability, hypotonia, milkmaid’s grip, spooning/pronator sign, darting (jack-in-the-box) tongue, and hung-up knee jerk. Self-limiting (2–6 weeks).

Subcutaneous Nodules (): Late manifestation (around 6 weeks); small (), firm, painless, mobile nodules over extensor bony prominences (olecranon, patella, occiput, spinous processes); strongly associated with severe carditis.

Erythema Marginatum (<5%): Early, evanescent, pink macules with pale centers and serpiginous borders on the trunk and proximal limbs (sparing the face); non-pruritic.

Investigations

Evidence of Preceding Streptococcal Infection (Essential Criteria):

Elevated or rising Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer (>250 Todd units in adults, >333 units in children) or Anti-DNase B.

Positive throat swab culture for Group A -hemolytic Streptococcus.

Positive rapid streptococcal carbohydrate antigen test.

Inflammatory Markers: Elevated ESR, positive CRP, leukocytosis, normocytic anemia.

ECG & Chest X-ray: Prolonged PR interval (1st-degree heart block), cardiomegaly/pulmonary congestion.

Doppler Echocardiography: Detects subclinical valvulitis, annular dilation, chordal elongation/rupture, anterior mitral leaflet prolapse, and pathological MR/AR jets.

Management of Acute Rheumatic Fever

Supportive Care & Bed Rest:

Bed rest for 2–3 weeks (prolonged only if active carditis with CCF is present).

Anti-failure measures (Furosemide, Spironolactone, Enalapril, Digoxin) if CCF is present.

Eradication of Streptococcal Infection (Primary Eradication):

Single IM injection of Benzathine Penicillin G:  (if ) or  (if ), OR

Oral Penicillin V:  QID for 10 days (or Oral Amoxicillin).

If Penicillin allergic: Azithromycin ( OD for 5 days) or Erythromycin ( for 10 days).

Anti-inflammatory (Suppressive) Therapy (Total duration: 12 weeks):

Arthritis ONLY (No Carditis): Aspirin  in 4 divided doses for 2 weeks, then  for next 4–6 weeks, and tapered off.

Carditis with CCF (or Moderate-to-Severe Carditis): Oral Prednisolone  (max ) for 2–3 weeks, then tapered gradually over the next 9 weeks (overlapping with Aspirin  during tapering to prevent rebound).

Management of Sydenham Chorea:

Quiet environment; anti-inflammatory agents are not needed.

Symptomatic control: Sodium Valproate (), Carbamazepine, Haloperidol (), or Pimozide / Diazepam.

Prevention of Rheumatic Fever (Primary & Secondary Prophylaxis):

Primary Prophylaxis: Prompt 10-day penicillin/amoxicillin treatment of acute streptococcal pharyngitis.

Secondary Prophylaxis (Prevents recurrences):

Drug of Choice: IM Benzathine Penicillin G:  (if ) or  (if ) deep IM every 3 weeks (every 2 weeks in <30 kg in high-prevalence areas).

Alternatives: Oral Penicillin V  BD; if allergic to penicillin, Oral Erythromycin  BD.

Duration of Secondary Prophylaxis (WHO Guidelines):

ARF without carditis: 5 years after last attack OR until 18 years of age (whichever is longer).

ARF with healed carditis / mild MR: 10 years after last attack OR until 25 years of age (whichever is longer).

Established RHD / Severe valve disease / Post-valve surgery: Lifelong (or at least until 40 years of age).

B. Infective Endocarditis (IE)

(Covers: Clinical features, investigations, diagnostic criteria) [KU 15] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 493–496

Etiology: Streptococcus viridans (most common in subacute native valve IE), Staphylococcus aureus (acute fulminant IE, indwelling catheters), Enterococci, Pseudomonas, HACEK group, and Candida (postoperative/NICU).

Clinical Features:

Features of Infection: Unexplained prolonged fever (>7–10 days) in a child with CHD/RHD, chills, night sweats, anorexia, weight loss, pallor.

Cardiovascular features: Appearance of a new regurgitant murmur or change in pre-existing murmur, refractory CCF, systemic/pulmonary embolization (stroke, flank pain/hematuria from renal infarct, splenic infarct).

Immunological / Vasculitic phenomena: Clubbing, splenomegaly, petechiae, Splinter hemorrhages (nail bed), Osler nodes (painful tender nodules on finger/toe pulps), Janeway lesions (painless erythematous macules on palms/soles), Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages with pale centers), microscopic hematuria (immune-complex glomerulonephritis).

Investigations & Modified Duke Diagnostic Criteria:

Major Criteria (2):

Positive Blood Cultures: Typical microorganisms from 2 separate blood cultures (Three sets of blood cultures drawn 30–60 mins apart before starting antibiotics detect 95% of cases).

Evidence of Endocardial Involvement (Echocardiography): Oscillating intracardiac mass (vegetation), myocardial abscess, new partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve, or new valvular regurgitation.

Minor Criteria (5): (1) Predisposing heart condition or IV drug use; (2) Fever ; (3) Vascular phenomena (arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, Janeway lesions); (4) Immunologic phenomena (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, Rheumatoid factor); (5) Microbiological evidence (positive blood culture not meeting major criterion).

Definite IE: 2 Major, OR 1 Major + 3 Minor, OR 5 Minor criteria.

Treatment: Prolonged bactericidal IV antibiotics for 4–6 weeks (e.g., Aqueous Penicillin G/Ceftriaxone + Gentamicin for S. viridans; Cloxacillin/Vancomycin + Gentamicin for S. aureus).

title: 14.4 MISCELLANEOUS CARDIOVASCULAR TOPICS
text:
(Covers: Fetal circulation diagram, S2 splitting, Innocent murmurs, Continuous murmur D/D, PPHN, Childhood hypertension causes) [KU 23, 20, 16, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 455–456, 459–461, 471, 501–506

1. Fetal Circulation [KU 16, 20, 23]

Pathway: Oxygenated blood () from the placenta returns via the umbilical vein  bypasses the liver via the ductus venosus to enter the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) ().

Upon entering the Right Atrium (RA), the crista dividens divides the IVC stream: one-third of this well-oxygenated blood is preferentially directed across the foramen ovale into the Left Atrium (LA)  Left Ventricle (LV)  ascending aorta () to supply the coronaries and brain.

Desaturated blood from the Superior Vena Cava (SVC) () mixes with the remaining two-thirds of IVC blood in the RA  enters the Right Ventricle (RV)  ejected into the main pulmonary artery ().

Because the fetal lungs are collapsed and have high pulmonary vascular resistance, only  enters the lungs;  shunts right-to-left across the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta () and returns to the placenta via the two umbilical arteries.

Transition at Birth: Clamping of the umbilical cord removes the low-resistance placenta (SVR rises), while lung expansion lowers PVR. LA pressure exceeds RA pressure, closing the foramen ovale functionally. Rising  and falling prostaglandins constrict the ductus arteriosus (functional closure in 10–15 hrs; anatomical closure in 10–21 days  ligamentum arteriosum), and the ductus venosus closes by day 7 ( ligamentum venosum).

2. Second Heart Sound (S2) Splitting & Innocent Murmurs

Normal S2: Single in expiration, splits in inspiration ( precedes ).

Wide & Fixed Split S2: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD), TAPVC, Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB).

Wide & Variable Split S2: Pulmonary stenosis (delayed P2), VSD and Mitral regurgitation (early A2).

Single S2: Tetralogy of Fallot (P2 inaudible), Eisenmenger VSD (A2 and P2 fused), Pulmonary atresia, Truncus arteriosus.

Paradoxical (Reversed) Split S2 (P2 precedes A2; widens in expiration): Severe aortic stenosis, LBBB, large PDA.

Innocent (Functional) Systolic Murmurs (e.g., Still’s vibratory murmur): Soft (Grade I–II/VI, never  Grade IV or associated with a thrill), short mid-systolic/ejection (never pansystolic or diastolic), musical/vibratory quality at LLSB, changes intensity with posture (decreases on standing), accompanied by a normal S2, normal pulses, and asymptomatic child.

3. Differential Diagnosis of Continuous Murmur

Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) — peaks at S2.

Venous hum (disappears on lying down or compressing internal jugular vein).

Ruptured Sinus of Valsalva aneurysm (RSOV) into right heart.

Coronary arteriovenous fistula.

Aortopulmonary window.

Major aortopulmonary collateral arteries (MAPCAs) in TOF/pulmonary atresia.

Coarctation of aorta (collateral intercostal vessels).

Peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis.

Lutembacher syndrome (ASD + Mitral stenosis). (Note: VSD with AR produces a ‘to-and-fro’ murmur that mimics a continuous murmur).

4. Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN)

Failure of normal postnatal decline in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) after birth, resulting in persistent right-to-left shunting of deoxygenated blood across the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, causing severe refractory hypoxemia.

Causes: Meconium aspiration syndrome, perinatal asphyxia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, neonatal sepsis/pneumonia, RDS.

Management: Mechanical ventilation (or High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation), correction of acidosis/hypothermia/hypoglycemia, systemic vasopressors to maintain systemic BP, and selective pulmonary vasodilators (Inhaled Nitric Oxide [iNO] 10–20 ppm, Oral/IV Sildenafil, Milrinone) or ECMO.

5. Common Causes of Childhood Hypertension

Renal Parenchymal (): Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, chronic glomerulonephritis, reflux nephropathy, hemolytic uremic syndrome, polycystic kidney disease, obstructive uropathy.

Renovascular (): Takayasu aortoarteritis, fibromuscular dysplasia, renal artery thrombosis (post-umbilical artery catheterization).

Cardiovascular: Coarctation of the aorta.

Endocrine: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (-hydroxylase deficiency), Cushing syndrome, Pheochromocytoma, Neuroblastoma, primary hyperaldosteronism.

Essential (Primary) Hypertension: Associated with adolescent obesity and metabolic syndrome.
