title: 15.1 NEPHROTIC SYNDROME
text:
(Covers: Essays on 2-yr-old, 3-yr-old, 4-yr-old, and 5-yr-old presenting with periorbital puffiness progressing to generalized edema/ascites, oliguria, heavy proteinuria, no hematuria; Definition, pathogenesis, investigations, management of first episode and relapses, complications, and discharge advice) [KU 24, 23, 21, 19, 16, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 527–533

Important Note on Essay 1 [KU24]: A 2-year-old boy with 3 days of viral URI (fever/cough) followed immediately by morning facial puffiness, abdominal distension (ascites), and reduced urine output is the classic presentation of First Episode of Idiopathic (Minimal Change) Nephrotic Syndrome triggered by a respiratory infection (PSGN is rare <3 yrs, has a 1–2 week latent period after pharyngitis, and presents with cola-colored urine and hypertension, not massive ascites). Both Nephrotic Syndrome and PSGN are covered in full below.

Definition & Diagnostic Criteria

Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by the clinical and biochemical tetrad of: 1. Heavy (Nephrotic-range) Proteinuria: Urine dipstick 3+ or 4+, OR 24-hour urine protein  (), OR early morning spot Urine Protein-to-Creatinine Ratio (UPCR) . 2. Hypoalbuminemia: Serum albumin  (recent IPNA/ISPN guidelines use ; classically ). 3. Generalized Edema: Pitting edema starting periorbitally. 4. Hypercholesterolemia: Serum cholesterol .

Etiology & Histopathology

 of childhood nephrotic syndrome is Primary (Idiopathic):

Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome (MCNS / MCD): Accounts for  of cases. Light microscopy shows normal glomeruli; Immunofluorescence is negative; Electron microscopy shows diffuse effacement (fusion) of podocyte foot processes.  are steroid-sensitive.

Significant Glomerular Lesions: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS, ), Mesangioproliferative GN, C3 glomerulopathy, Membranous nephropathy.

 Secondary: IgA vasculitis (HSP), SLE, Hepatitis B, malaria, Alport syndrome.

Pathogenesis

Pathogenesis of Proteinuria: Perturbation of T-cell-mediated immunity (Th2 polarization, altered T-regulatory/Th17 axis, and circulating permeability factors) alters the electronegative charge barrier and slit-diaphragm permselectivity of glomerular podocytes  selective massive urinary loss of albumin.

Pathogenesis of Edema (Two Hypotheses):

Underfill Hypothesis (Classical): Massive albuminuria  hypoalbuminemia  decreased plasma oncotic pressure  transudation of fluid into the interstitial space  intravascular hypovolemia  secondary activation of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) and ADH  renal retention of sodium and water.

Overfill Hypothesis: Primary intrarenal defect in the distal nephron (activation of epithelial sodium channels - ENaC by filtered plasmin/proteases)  primary sodium and water retention  expanded intravascular volume.

Pathogenesis of Hyperlipidemia: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure stimulates hepatic synthesis of lipoproteins (LDL, VLDL, cholesterol) coupled with urinary loss of lipoprotein lipase.

Clinical Features

Age & Sex: Peak onset between 2 and 6 years of age (MCNS); boys affected twice as often as girls.

Presentation: Insidious onset of periorbital puffiness, most noticeable in the morning upon waking, which subsides during the day. Over days, pitting edema progresses to the legs, feet, sacrum, scrotum/labia, and abdomen (ascites, pleural effusion / anasarca).

Urine output decreases during the edema-forming phase.

Blood pressure is typically normal in MCNS (hypertension suggests FSGS/nephritic lesions).

Essential Investigations & Expected Findings

Urinalysis & Microscopy: 3+ or 4+ proteinuria (sulfosalicylic acid / dipstick); hyaline and granular casts; microscopic hematuria is absent (or transient in ).

Spot Urine Protein-to-Creatinine Ratio (UPCR):  (or 24-hr urine protein ).

Blood Biochemistry:

Serum albumin: Low (, often ).

Serum cholesterol & triglycerides: Markedly elevated ().

Blood urea, serum creatinine, and electrolytes: Normal (urea/creatinine may be transiently elevated if hypovolemic).

Complete Blood Count: Normal Hb (or hemoconcentration if hypovolemic), thrombocytosis.

Infection Screen (Prior to Steroid Therapy): Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) and Chest X-ray (if Mantoux positive or contact history).

Additional Tests (Only if atypical features present): Serum Complement C3 (normal in MCNS), ASO titer, ANA, HBsAg.

Indications for Kidney Biopsy (Not needed at onset in typical MCNS):

At Onset: Age  or , gross or persistent microscopic hematuria, sustained hypertension, renal failure not attributable to hypovolemia, low serum C3, or features of systemic disease (SLE/HSP).

During Follow-up: Steroid Resistance (no remission after 6 weeks of daily prednisolone) or prior to/after 2–3 years of calcineurin inhibitor therapy.

Management of the First Episode (ISPN 2021 Guidelines)

Specific Corticosteroid Therapy (6 + 6 Weeks Regimen):

First 6 Weeks: Oral Prednisolone at  (or , maximum ) in 1–2 divided doses daily after meals for 6 weeks.

Next 6 Weeks: Oral Prednisolone at  (or , maximum ) as a single morning dose on alternate days for 6 weeks, and then discontinued. (Response/remission usually occurs within 10–14 days).

[

Supportive & Hospital Management:

Diet & Activity: Balanced diet with normal protein () and normal calories; no added salt during edema/steroid therapy. Normal physical activity/schooling.

Management of Edema: Mild edema resolves spontaneously with steroid-induced diuresis. If edema is severe/symptomatic, give oral Furosemide ()  Spironolactone (). (Avoid diuretics if child has diarrhea, vomiting, or signs of hypovolemia).

Refractory Anasarca / Severe Hypovolemia: Cautious IV infusion of  Salt-poor Human Albumin ( over 2–4 hours) followed by IV Furosemide () at the end of infusion.

Treat intercurrent infections promptly.

Definitions of Disease Course & Management of Relapses

Remission: Urine albumin nil or trace (or UPCR ) for 3 consecutive early morning specimens.

Relapse: Urine albumin 3+ or 4+ (or UPCR ) for 3 consecutive early morning days, having been in remission previously.

Frequent Relapses (FRNS):  relapses in first 6 months after initial response, or  relapses in any 12 months.

Steroid Dependence (SDNS): 2 consecutive relapses while on alternate-day steroids or within 14 days of its discontinuation.

Steroid Resistance (SRNS): Failure to achieve complete remission despite 6 weeks of daily Prednisolone ().

Treatment of a Relapse: Prednisolone  () daily until urine protein is nil/trace for 3 consecutive days, followed by  () on alternate days for 4 weeks.

Steroid-Sparing Agents (for FRNS/SDNS): Long-term low-dose alternate-day prednisolone (), Levamisole, Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF), Oral Cyclophosphamide (12 weeks), Calcineurin Inhibitors (Tacrolimus/Cyclosporine — also drug of choice for SRNS), or Rituximab.

Complications of Nephrotic Syndrome

Serious Infections (Most common): Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and E. coli), cellulitis, pneumonia, UTI, severe varicella. (Due to urinary loss of IgG and Factor B/properdin, defective opsonization, ascites acting as culture medium, and steroid therapy).

Hypovolemia and Acute Kidney Injury (AKI): Precipitated by diarrhea, vomiting, or aggressive diuretic use.

Thromboembolism: Renal vein thrombosis, sagittal sinus thrombosis, pulmonary embolism (due to urinary loss of antithrombin III and protein S, increased fibrinogen, hemoconcentration, and thrombocytosis).

Corticosteroid Toxicity: Cushingoid facies, stunting/growth failure, hypertension, posterior subcapsular cataract, glaucoma, osteopenia, hyperglycemia.

Advice at Discharge (Parent Education)

Explain the chronic relapsing nature of the illness, reassuring parents that  outgrow relapses by adolescence with normal kidney function.

Teach parents home urine dipstick/heat-coagulation testing on first morning urine and maintenance of a daily diary (urine protein, steroid dose, infections).

Warn never to stop corticosteroids abruptly (risk of adrenal crisis).

Immunization advice: Administer Pneumococcal (PCV/PPSV23) and Varicella vaccines once in remission and off high-dose steroids for at least 4 weeks. Avoid live vaccines while on high-dose steroids ( for  days).

Report immediately if the child develops fever, abdominal pain/vomiting (peritonitis), fast breathing, or relapse of edema.

subject: pediatrics
title: 15.2 ACUTE POST-STREPTOCOCCAL GLOMERULONEPHRITIS (PSGN) & HEMATURIA
text:
(Covers: Essay on 5-yr-old with cola-colored urine, pyoderma 3 wks back, BP 132/88; Short essay on 7-yr-old with hematuria; Glomerular causes of hematuria, Etiopathogenesis, clinical features, D/D from nephrotic syndrome, investigations, complications, and management) [KU 24, 23, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 520–526

Answers to Clinical Scenario [KU23]

Most Probable Diagnosis: Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) / Acute Nephritic Syndrome.

Most Important Differential Diagnosis: Idiopathic Nephrotic Syndrome (or other causes of acute nephritic syndrome: IgA nephropathy, C3 glomerulopathy).

Points in History & Examination Differentiating Acute Nephritic Syndrome (PSGN) from Nephrotic Syndrome:

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-002]]

Causes of Hematuria in Children

Glomerular Causes (Cola-colored urine, dysmorphic RBCs >20%, RBC casts, proteinuria ):

Acute post-infectious / post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

IgA nephropathy (Berger disease — synpharyngitic hematuria).

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura nephritis).

C3 glomerulopathy (Membranoproliferative GN).

Lupus nephritis (SLE).

Alport syndrome (hereditary nephritis with sensorineural deafness and anterior lenticonus) & Thin basement membrane disease.

Non-Glomerular Causes (Bright red urine, clots, isomorphic RBCs, dysuria/pain):

Urinary tract infection (bacterial, adenoviral hemorrhagic cystitis).

Urolithiasis (renal/vesical calculi) & Idiopathic hypercalciuria.

Trauma, coagulation disorders/thrombocytopenia, Wilms tumor, Nutcracker syndrome.

Etiopathogenesis & Pathology of PSGN

Etiology: Follows infection with nephritogenic strains of Group A -hemolytic Streptococci — Pharyngitis (serotypes 4, 12; latent period 1–2 weeks) or Impetigo/Pyoderma (serotype 49; latent period 3–6 weeks).

Pathogenesis: Immune-complex mediated glomerulonephritis. Circulating or in-situ immune complexes (against streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B [SpeB] or nephritis-associated plasmin receptor [NAPlr]) deposit in the glomeruli  activate the alternate complement pathway (consuming C3)  chemotaxis of neutrophils and mesangial/endothelial cell proliferation  narrowing of glomerular capillary lumen  reduced GFR, oliguria, and salt and water retention (hypervolemia and hypertension).

Pathology:

Light Microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular, bloodless glomeruli with diffuse endocapillary proliferation and neutrophil exudation.

Immunofluorescence: Coarse granular deposits of IgG and C3 (‘starry-sky’ / ‘lumpy-bumpy’ appearance) along capillary walls and mesangium.

Electron Microscopy: Characteristic subepithelial electron-dense ‘humps’.

Clinical Features of PSGN

Abrupt onset of gross hematuria (cola/tea-colored urine, lasts 1–2 weeks), periorbital puffiness (worsened by fluid intake), oliguria, and hypertension (resolves with diuresis in 1–2 weeks).

Atypical presentations: Hypertensive encephalopathy (seizures, altered sensorium, visual loss), acute left ventricular failure/pulmonary edema, or rapidly progressive AKI.

Investigations with Expected Findings

Urine Microscopy: Dysmorphic RBCs, Red Blood Cell (RBC) casts (pathognomonic of glomerular inflammation), polymorphonuclear leukocytes, granular casts, and 1+ to 2+ proteinuria.

Renal Function Tests & Electrolytes: Elevated blood urea and serum creatinine; hyponatremia (dilutional), hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis if oliguric.

Complement Levels: Serum C3 is significantly reduced in  of patients during the acute phase and normalizes within 8–12 weeks; C4 is normal.

Serological Evidence of Streptococcal Infection:

Elevated Anti-DNase B (most sensitive test following streptococcal pyoderma/skin infection).

Elevated ASO titer (sensitive following pharyngitis, blunted in skin infections).

Chest X-ray: Cardiomegaly and pulmonary vascular congestion (hypervolemia).

Indications for Kidney Biopsy in Acute GN (Table 17.6):

Anuria or rapidly deteriorating renal function (RPGN) requiring dialysis.

Normal C3 at onset OR persistently low C3 beyond 12 weeks (suggests C3 glomerulopathy or Lupus).

Persistence of oliguria, hypertension, or azotemia beyond 7–10 days.

Gross hematuria persisting beyond 3–4 weeks or nephrotic-range proteinuria beyond 2 weeks.

Systemic features (fever, rash, arthritis suggesting SLE/vasculitis).

Complications of PSGN

Hypertensive Encephalopathy (headache, vomiting, convulsions, coma, cortical blindness).

Acute Left Ventricular Failure (Congestive Cardiac Failure) and Pulmonary Edema (due to fluid overload and hypertension).

Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) with Dyselectrolytemia (life-threatening hyperkalemia, severe metabolic acidosis, uremia).

Progression to Crescentic Glomerulonephritis (RPGN) (<1%).

Management of PSGN

Treatment is primarily supportive and directed at complications:

 1. Fluid & Salt Restriction: * Strict intake-output charting and daily weight monitoring.

 * Restrict daily fluid intake to insensible water losses () + previous 24-hour urine output. 

* Restrict dietary sodium, potassium, and protein (if azotemic) until diuresis occurs and renal function normalizes. 

2. Diuretics (Cornerstone for Fluid Overload & Edema): 

* Furosemide:  PO (or  IV in pulmonary edema/severe hypertension) induces diuresis, relieving both edema and hypervolemia-induced hypertension. 

3. Management of Hypertension: 

* Mild-to-moderate: Salt/water restriction + Furosemide + Calcium channel blockers (Nifedipine  or Amlodipine ). (Avoid ACE inhibitors and potassium-sparing diuretics like Spironolactone due to the risk of hyperkalemia)

. * Hypertensive Emergency/Encephalopathy:

 IV Sodium Nitroprusside () or IV Labetalol () + anticonvulsants.

 4. Antibiotic Therapy:

 * A 7–10 day course of Oral Penicillin V or Amoxicillin (or a single dose of IM Benzathine Penicillin; Erythromycin if allergic) is given only if active pharyngitis or pyoderma is present (and to prevent transmission of nephritogenic strains to contacts; does not alter the natural course of GN). 

5. Management of AKI & Dialysis: 

* Treat hyperkalemia (IV calcium gluconate, nebulized salbutamol, insulin-dextrose, potassium-binding resins). 

* Dialysis (Peritoneal or Hemodialysis) if refractory pulmonary edema, persistent hyperkalemia (), severe acidosis, or uremic encephalopathy.

subject: pediatrics
title: 15.3 URINARY TRACT INFECTION (UTI) & MISCELLANEOUS RENAL TOPICS
text:
(Covers: Investigation & management of 6-mo-old male with UTI; Prerenal vs Intrinsic AKI; Primary Enuresis; K+-sparing diuretic) [KU 21, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 452, 534–541, 554–555

1. Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) in a 6-Month-Old Male Infant [RGU]

Common Causative Organisms: Escherichia coli (), Klebsiella, Proteus (predisposes to struvite stones), Enterobacter, Pseudomonas, and Enterococcus (non-E. coli organisms suggest underlying structural anomalies like VUR or posterior urethral valves).

Investigations & Diagnosis:

Urine Microscopy & Dipstick: Pyuria ( in centrifuged urine or  in uncentrifuged urine); positive Leukocyte esterase and Nitrite dipstick test.

Urine Culture & Sensitivity (Gold Standard): In a non-toilet-trained 6-month-old infant, collect urine via suprapubic aspiration (significant colony count: ) or transurethral catheterization () or clean-catch midstream (). (Never use bag specimens for culture).

Blood Tests: CBC, CRP, blood culture, and serum creatinine (to rule out urosepsis and obstructive uropathy).

Imaging Protocol for a 6-Month-Old Infant (<1 year) after First UTI (ISPN Guidelines):

All infants (<1 yr) with first UTI must undergo:

Ultrasonography (USG) of Kidneys, Ureters, and Bladder (KUB): Performed during or soon after UTI to detect hydronephrosis, bladder wall thickening, or stones.

Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU): Performed 2–4 weeks after treating UTI to detect and grade Vesicoureteric Reflux (VUR) and rule out Posterior Urethral Valves (PUV) in boys.

⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA Renal Cortical Scintigraphy: Performed 4–6 months after UTI to detect permanent renal parenchymal scarring.

Treatment of UTI in a 6-Month-Old:

Uncomplicated febrile UTI: Oral Cefixime ( in 2 divided doses) or Co-amoxiclav () for 7–10 days.

Complicated UTI (high fever , toxicity, persistent vomiting, dehydration): Hospitalize and treat with parenteral IV Ceftriaxone (), Cefotaxime, or Amikacin ( OD) for 10–14 days (switching to oral once afebrile for 48 hours).

Antibiotic Prophylaxis (Cotrimoxazole  or Nitrofurantoin  single bedtime dose) is indicated if VUR is detected.

2. Differences between Prerenal and Intrinsic Renal AKI

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-003]]

3. Primary Nocturnal Enuresis & Potassium-Sparing Diuretics

Primary Enuresis: Involuntary, complete evacuation of the bladder at an inappropriate place/time at least twice a month in a child  who has never achieved a sustained 6-month period of nighttime dryness.

Management: First-line is motivational therapy (star charts, fluid restriction in evening, voiding before sleep) and Enuresis Alarm therapy (most effective,  cure).

Pharmacotherapy: Oral Desmopressin (DDAVP) ( at bedtime), Anticholinergics (Oxybutynin  if daytime urge symptoms), or Imipramine (rarely used now due to cardiotoxicity).

Commonly used Potassium-Sparing Diuretics [KU21]: Spironolactone, Amiloride, Triamterene, Eplerenone.

subject: pediatrics
title: 19.1 ACUTE LEUKEMIA (ALL & AML)
text:
(Covers: Childhood ALL — FAB & Immunophenotypic classification, clinical features, peripheral smear/diagnosis, prognostic factors/risk stratification, principles of chemotherapy/management; Classification of AML) [RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 646–654

Epidemiology & Etiology

Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is the most common childhood malignancy ( of all childhood cancers;  of leukemias), with a peak incidence at 2–5 years of age.

Predisposing Syndromes: Down syndrome (15–20x risk), Fanconi anemia, Bloom syndrome, Ataxia-telangiectasia, Neurofibromatosis-1, Li-Fraumeni syndrome.

Classification of ALL

FAB (French-American-British) Morphological Classification (Table 21.3):

L1 (): Small, homogeneous lymphoblasts, scanty cytoplasm, regular nucleus, inconspicuous nucleoli.

L2 (): Large, heterogeneous lymphoblasts, abundant cytoplasm, clefted/indented nucleus, prominent nucleoli.

L3 (): Large, homogeneous blasts, intensely basophilic cytoplasm with prominent cytoplasmic vacuolation (Burkitt-type mature B-cell leukemia).

WHO Immunophenotypic Classification (Flow Cytometry):

B-Lineage ALL (Precursor B-cell, ): Positive for CD10 (CALLA), CD19, CD20, CD22, CD79a, and TdT.

T-Lineage ALL (): Positive for cytoplasmic CD3, CD2, CD5, CD7, and TdT (associated with older boys, high WBC count, and anterior mediastinal mass).

Mature B-cell ALL (): Surface Ig positive (sIg⁺), CD19, CD20, .

Classification of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) (FAB M0–M7, Table 21.6)

M0: Minimally differentiated AML; M1: AML without maturation; M2: AML with maturation (, Auer rods common); M3: Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APML,  PML-RARA, faggot cells, DIC, treated with All-Trans Retinoic Acid [ATRA] + Arsenic trioxide); M4: Acute myelomonocytic leukemia (, gum hypertrophy); M5: Acute monocytic leukemia; M6: Erythroleukemia; M7: Acute megakaryocytic leukemia (seen in Down syndrome <3 yrs).

Clinical Features of ALL

Bone Marrow Failure:

Anemia: Pallor, fatigue, lethargy, congestive heart failure.

Thrombocytopenia: Petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gum bleeding.

Neutropenia: Recurrent or persistent fever and opportunistic infections.

Reticuloendothelial & Extramedullary Infiltration:

Generalized painless, firm, rubbery lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly ().

Bone & Joint pain (): Limp, refusal to walk, sternal tenderness (due to leukemic infiltration of periosteum; often misdiagnosed as JIA).

Anterior Mediastinal Mass (T-ALL): Causes Superior Mediastinal Syndrome (SMS) (tracheal compression, stridor, dyspnea) and Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome (facial plethora, engorged neck veins).

Sanctuary Sites:

CNS Leukemia ( at diagnosis): Headache, vomiting, papilledema, cranial nerve palsies (III, VI, VII), seizures.

Testicular Infiltration (): Painless, firm unilateral or bilateral testicular enlargement.

Oncologic Emergencies at Presentation: Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) (hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, AKI) and Hyperleukocytosis ().

Laboratory Diagnosis & Peripheral Smear in ALL

Complete Blood Count & Peripheral Blood Smear:

Normocytic normochromic anemia and thrombocytopenia.

Total Leukocyte Count (TLC) may be high (), normal, or low (aleukemic leukemia).

Peripheral Smear: Shows lymphoblasts ( size of a small lymphocyte, high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, scant agranular basophilic cytoplasm, condensed/smudged chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and absence of Auer rods).

Bone Marrow Aspiration & Trephine Biopsy (Confirmatory): Hypercellular marrow replaced by  lymphoblasts ( blasts for AML).

Cytochemistry & Immunophenotyping: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) negative, Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) block-positive, TdT positive. Flow cytometry confirms B- or T-lineage.

Diagnostic Lumbar Puncture (CSF Cytology): Checks for CNS leukemia ( with blasts); the first dose of intrathecal methotrexate is administered during the diagnostic tap.

Metabolic Panel: Serum uric acid, K⁺, PO₄³⁻, Ca²⁺, creatinine, and LDH (to screen for TLS).

Prognostic Factors & Risk Stratification in ALL (Table 21.8)

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-004]]

Principles of Management & Chemotherapy in ALL (Box 21.4)

Total duration of therapy is 2 to 2.5 years, divided into 4 phases alongside aggressive supportive care: 

1. Supportive Care (Prior to & during Chemotherapy): 

* Prevention/Treatment of Tumor Lysis Syndrome: Hyperhydration ( IV fluids without potassium) + Allopurinol () or Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase).

 * Blood component support (irradiated, leukodepleted packed RBCs and platelets), Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii, and prompt broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for febrile neutropenia.

 2. Phase 1: Remission Induction (4–6 Weeks): 

* Goal: Eradicate  of leukemic burden and restore normal hematopoiesis ( blasts in bone marrow and negative MRD). Achieved in . 

* Drugs: 3-drug regimen for Standard Risk (Prednisolone/Dexamethasone + Vincristine + L-Asparaginase); 4-drug regimen for High Risk (adds an anthracycline — Daunorubicin/Doxorubicin). (Add Imatinib/Dasatinib if Philadelphia chromosome positive). 

3. Phase 2: CNS-Directed Prophylaxis / Preventive Therapy: 

* Goal: Eradicate subclinical leukemic blasts in the CNS sanctuary site across the blood-brain barrier. 

* Regimen: Serial Intrathecal Methotrexate (or triple intrathecal therapy: Methotrexate + Cytarabine + Hydrocortisone) + systemic High-Dose IV Methotrexate (with leucovorin rescue). Cranial irradiation is reserved only for overt CNS leukemia. 

4. Phase 3: Consolidation / Intensification (4–8 Months): 

* Goal: Eliminate residual drug-resistant clones. 

* Drugs: Cyclophosphamide, Cytarabine, 6-Mercaptopurine, High-dose Methotrexate, and Delayed Intensification (re-induction).

 5. Phase 4: Maintenance / Continuation Therapy (Up to 2–2.5 Years):

 * Goal: Prevent late marrow relapse.

 * Drugs: Daily Oral 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP) + Weekly Oral Methotrexate ( monthly Vincristine and 5-day steroid pulses).

subject: pediatrics
title: 19.2 SOLID TUMORS: NEUROBLASTOMA & WILMS TUMOR
text:
(Covers: Neuroblastoma clinical features & investigations; Wilms tumor short note) [RGU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 663–667

1. Neuroblastoma

Origin: Most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood and most common malignancy in infancy ( present ); arises from neural crest cells of the sympathetic nervous system (Adrenal medulla , retroperitoneal sympathetic ganglia , posterior mediastinum , pelvis/neck ).

Clinical Features:

Abdominal mass: Firm, irregular, nodular abdominal mass that crosses the midline, accompanied by hepatomegaly, abdominal pain, and failure to thrive.

Thoracic/Cervical: Posterior mediastinal mass, spinal cord compression (dumbbell tumor causing paraplegia), apical tumor causing Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

Metastatic Features ( at diagnosis):

Orbit: Proptosis and periorbital ecchymosis (‘Raccoon eyes’).

Bone & Bone marrow: Bone pain, limp, pancytopenia.

Stage IV-S (Infants <1 yr): Massive hepatomegaly (Pepper syndrome) and bluish subcutaneous nodules (‘blueberry muffin’ skin lesions) with favorable spontaneous regression.

Paraneoplastic Syndromes:

Catecholamine excess: Sweating, flushing, episodic hypertension.

Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) secretion (Kerner-Morrison syndrome): Secretory watery diarrhea with hypokalemia.

Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia (OMA) syndrome (‘Dancing eyes, dancing feet’): Autoimmune cerebellar/brainstem syndrome.

Investigations:

Urine Catecholamine Metabolites (Diagnostic in ): Elevated 24-hour urinary Vanillylmandelic Acid (VMA) and Homovanillic Acid (HVA).

Imaging: Abdominal USG and Contrast CT/MRI (shows calcified suprarenal mass encasing major blood vessels and crossing the midline, displacing the kidney inferolaterally without distorting the calyces).

Nuclear Scintigraphy: ¹²³I-MIBG (Metaiodobenzylguanidine) scan to detect primary tumor and skeletal metastases.

Tissue Biopsy & Bone Marrow Aspiration: Small round blue cells with Homer-Wright pseudorosettes (positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, PHOX2B).

Prognostic Genetic Markers: MYCN oncogene amplification (by FISH), 1p deletion, 17q gain, elevated serum ferritin/LDH/NSE (all indicate high risk and poor prognosis).

2. Wilms Tumor (Nephroblastoma)

Genetics & Associations: Associated with mutations in WT1 (11p13) and WT2 (11p15). Syndromic associations include WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, Retardation), Denys-Drash syndrome (mesangial sclerosis, ambiguous genitalia), Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (hemihypertrophy, macroglossia, omphalocele), and horseshoe kidney.

Clinical Features: Peak age 2–3 years. Presents as an asymptomatic, smooth, firm flank mass that does NOT cross the midline, discovered accidentally by parents while bathing the child. Associated with hematuria (), hypertension () (renin production), and abdominal pain.

Histopathology: Triphasic tumor containing blastemal, stromal, and epithelial elements. Classified into Favorable (no anaplasia) and Unfavorable histology (focal or diffuse anaplasia).

Diagnosis & Staging (NWTSG Stage I–V): USG with Doppler (checks for tumor thrombus in renal vein/IVC and contralateral kidney) and Contrast CT abdomen (‘claw sign’ of renal parenchyma; intrinsic distortion of pelvicalyceal system). Chest X-ray/CT for lung metastasis (most common site). (Preoperative biopsy is avoided in upfront surgery protocols as tumor rupture upstages the tumor to Stage III).

Management: Radical nephrectomy + Multiagent chemotherapy (Vincristine + Actinomycin-D for Stage I/II; add Doxorubicin + flank irradiation for Stage III/IV). Overall survival exceeds .

subject: pediatrics
title: 20.1 JUVENILE IDIOPATHIC ARTHRITIS (JIA)
text:
(Covers: Clinical subtypes of JIA, joint involvement characteristics, diagnosis of systemic-onset JIA, disease-modifying agents) [KU 24, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 678–681

Definition

Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) (ILAR classification) is defined as arthritis of unknown etiology in one or more joints, with onset before 16 years of age and persisting for at least 6 weeks, after excluding other known causes of arthritis.

Clinical Subtypes of JIA & Joint Involvement Characteristics (Table 22.3)

Oligoarthritis ( — Most common subtype):

Involves  during the first 6 months of disease.

Subtypes: Persistent (never exceeds 4 joints) and Extended (involves  joints after first 6 months).

Characteristics: Affects young girls (3–5 years); asymmetric involvement of large lower-limb joints (knee and ankle; hip and small joints of hands are spared).

Complication: Strongly associated with ANA positivity and chronic asymptomatic anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis) in up to , requiring regular 3–6 monthly slit-lamp examinations to prevent blindness.

Polyarthritis — Rheumatoid Factor (RF) Negative ():

Involves  in the first 6 months with negative RF.

Affects young girls; symmetric or asymmetric involvement of both large and small joints (knees, wrists, ankles, cervical spine, TMJ). Less erosive than RF-positive disease; ANA-positive cases carry uveitis risk.

Polyarthritis — Rheumatoid Factor (RF) Positive ():

Involves  in the first 6 months with  positive RF tests at least 3 months apart.

Childhood equivalent of adult rheumatoid arthritis. Affects adolescent girls; symmetric, additive, erosive, and deforming polyarthritis of small joints of hands (MCP and PIP joints, sparing DIP), wrists, and feet, associated with rheumatoid nodules.

Systemic JIA (sJIA / Still’s Disease, ):

Autoinflammatory disorder affecting boys and girls equally at any age.

Diagnostic Criteria (ILAR): Arthritis in  joint accompanied or preceded by documented quotidian (daily spiking) fever of at least 2 weeks’ duration (classic twice-daily/double quotidian peak touching baseline, child looks well between spikes), plus one or more of the following:

Evanescent, non-fixed salmon-pink maculopapular rash (appears during fever spikes).

Generalized lymphadenopathy.

Hepatomegaly and/or splenomegaly.

Serositis (pericarditis, pleuritis, peritonitis).

Lab findings: Marked neutrophilic leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, high ESR/CRP, anemia of chronic inflammation; ANA and RF are negative.

Dreaded Complication: Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS) (secondary HLH) — heralded by transition from quotidian to continuous unremitting fever, hepatosplenomegaly, bleeding, pancytopenia, paradoxical fall in ESR (due to hypofibrinogenemia), hyperferritinemia (), hypertriglyceridemia, and transaminitis. Treated with IV Methylprednisolone pulses + Cyclosporine/Anakinra.

Enthesitis-Related Arthritis (ERA):

Affects older boys (); strongly associated with HLA-B27.

Asymmetric lower-limb large joint arthritis (hip, knee, ankle), sacroiliitis, and enthesitis (tenderness at insertion of Achilles tendon or plantar fascia). Associated with acute, painful, red anterior uveitis.

Psoriatic Arthritis:

Arthritis + Psoriasis (or any 2 of: dactylitis [‘sausage digit’], nail pitting/onycholysis, or psoriasis in a first-degree relative). Characteristically involves Distal Interphalangeal (DIP) joints.

Undifferentiated Arthritis: Fits no category or  category.

Disease-Modifying Anti-Rheumatic Drugs (DMARDs) in JIA

Conventional Synthetic DMARDs:

Methotrexate (Gold Standard / First-line DMARD):  given orally or subcutaneously once a week with folic acid supplementation. Monitor LFTs and CBC.

Sulfasalazine:  PO (preferred in Enthesitis-Related Arthritis).

Leflunomide and Hydroxychloroquine (adjuncts in polyarthritis).

Biological DMARDs (Targeted Therapy):

TNF- Inhibitors (for refractory polyarticular JIA, ERA, and uveitis): Etanercept, Adalimumab (preferred if uveitis is present), Infliximab, Golimumab.

IL-6 Receptor Antagonist (for Systemic JIA and polyarthritis): Tocilizumab.

IL-1 Inhibitors (for Systemic JIA and MAS): Anakinra, Canakinumab.

T-cell Costimulation Blocker: Abatacept.

(Note: Two common rheumatological diseases in children [KU24]: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis [JIA] and IgA Vasculitis [Henoch-Schönlein Purpura] / Kawasaki Disease).

subject: pediatrics
title: 20.2 VASCULITIDES: HENOCH-SCHÖNLEIN PURPURA (IgA VASCULITIS) & KAWASAKI DISEASE
text:
(Covers: HSP clinical features, diagnostic criteria, investigations, treatment; Kawasaki disease) [KU 24, 19, 18, 16, RGU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 526, 685–688

A. IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura - HSP)

Definition: Most common small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis in children (peak age 3–10 years), characterized by IgA1-dominant immune deposits in capillaries, venules, and arterioles of skin, gut, joints, and glomeruli.

Four Cardinal Clinical Features [KU16] & EULAR/PRINTO/PRES Diagnostic Criteria: Mandatory Criterion: Non-thrombocytopenic Palpable Purpura (crops of symmetric palpable purpuric/petechial rash predominantly over gravity-dependent areas — extensor surfaces of lower limbs and buttocks), PLUS at least 1 of the following 4:

Diffuse Abdominal Pain (): Colicky periumbilical pain, vomiting, hematemesis, melena. Complications: Ileo-ileal intussusception (), bowel ischemia/perforation.

Arthritis or Arthralgia (): Transient, non-deforming oligoarthritis involving large lower-limb joints (knees and ankles).

Renal Involvement (HSP Nephritis, ): Presents within 4–6 weeks (up to 6 months) with microscopic or gross hematuria, mild proteinuria, or rarely nephritic/nephrotic syndrome or RPGN.

Histopathology (Skin or Renal Biopsy): Leukocytoclastic vasculitis or proliferative glomerulonephritis with predominant IgA deposition on immunofluorescence.

Other rare features: Acute scrotal swelling/orchitis ( of boys, mimics torsion testis), CNS vasculitis, pulmonary hemorrhage.

Investigations:

CBC & Coagulation Profile: Normal platelet count (or thrombocytosis) and normal coagulation profile (rules out ITP/coagulopathy).

Urinalysis & RFT: Screen for hematuria, RBC casts, proteinuria (UPCR), and serum creatinine; monitor urine weekly for 1 month, then monthly for 6 months.

Abdominal Ultrasound: Detects bowel wall edema/hematoma and rules out ileo-ileal intussusception (‘target/doughnut sign’).

Skin Biopsy / Kidney Biopsy: Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits; renal biopsy indicated if nephrotic-range proteinuria or declining GFR.

Management:

Supportive Care: Self-limiting in most cases within 4 weeks. Hydration, bed rest, and paracetamol/NSAIDs for joint pain (avoid NSAIDs if GI bleeding or renal involvement).

Corticosteroids: Oral Prednisolone ( for 1–2 weeks, then tapered over 2 weeks) is indicated for severe abdominal pain, GI hemorrhage, orchitis, or pulmonary/CNS involvement.

Severe HSP Nephritis (Nephrotic/Crescentic GN): Pulse IV Methylprednisolone followed by oral Prednisolone + IV Cyclophosphamide / Azathioprine / MMF + ACE inhibitors.

B. Kawasaki Disease (Mucocutaneous Lymph Node Syndrome) [KU 18, 19]

Overview: Acute febrile necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis affecting infants and young children ( are  of age), with a striking predilection for the coronary arteries (leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed nations;  develop coronary artery aneurysms if untreated).

Diagnostic Criteria (Classic KD): Fever lasting for at least 5 days PLUS at least 4 of the 5 principal clinical features:

Bilateral non-exudative (non-purulent) bulbar conjunctival injection (with limbal sparing).

Oropharyngeal mucosal changes: Red, dry, cracked lips; ‘strawberry tongue’; diffuse erythema of oral/pharyngeal mucosa.

Changes in peripheral extremities:

Acute phase: Erythema and indurated edema of hands and feet.

Subacute/Convalescent phase (2–3 weeks): Periungual desquamation (peeling of skin starting around fingernails/toenails) and Beau’s lines.

Polymorphous exanthem (rash): Maculopapular, scarlatiniform, or erythema multiforme-like rash (never vesicular or bullous), accentuated in the perineal area (early perianal desquamation).

Cervical lymphadenopathy: Usually unilateral, single node  in diameter.

Additional Clinical Clues: Extreme inconsolable irritability, erythema and induration at the BCG scar site, sterile pyuria, gallbladder hydrops, and arthritis.

Investigations:

Elevated ESR and CRP, marked neutrophilic leukocytosis, normocytic anemia.

Marked Thrombocytosis (platelet count ) peaking in the 2nd–3rd week of illness.

2D Echocardiography (Mandatory at baseline, 2 weeks, and 6–8 weeks): Evaluates coronary artery internal lumen diameters (Z-scores) for ectasia or aneurysms, myocarditis, or pericardial effusion.

Treatment:

Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) (Mainstay of therapy):  as a single IV infusion over 10–12 hours, ideally within the first 10 days of illness (reduces coronary artery aneurysm risk from  to ).

Aspirin:

Acute Febrile Phase (Anti-inflammatory dose):  (or ) in 4 divided doses until the child is afebrile for 48–72 hours.

Subacute Phase (Antiplatelet dose):  once daily for 6–8 weeks (discontinued if 6-week Echo is normal; continued long-term if coronary aneurysms persist).

IVIG-Resistant KD ( with persistent fever  after IVIG): Repeat second dose of IVIG (), Infliximab (TNF- blocker,  IV), or IV Methylprednisolone pulses.

subject: pediatrics
title: 21.1 DOWN SYNDROME (TRISOMY 21)
text:
(Covers: Short essays on genetic basis, clinical/facial features, ocular findings, system-wise complications, antenatal USG/biochemical diagnosis, and genetic counseling; Atlantoaxial instability MCQ) [KU 25, 24, 22, 21, 17, 16, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 693–696, 703

Genetic Basis (Cytogenetics)

Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal disorder (incidence 1 in 800 live births), caused by triplicate genetic material of chromosome 21q22 through three mechanisms: 

1. Free Trisomy 21 (): Karyotype 47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21. Due to meiotic non-disjunction (90% maternal meiosis I); strongly associated with advanced maternal age ().

 2. Robertsonian Translocation (): Extra long arm of chromosome 21 is translocated onto another acrocentric chromosome — Group D (chromosomes 14, 13, 15; most commonly t(14;21)) or Group G (t(21;21), t(21;22)). Independent of maternal age; parental karyotyping is mandatory as  are inherited from a balanced carrier parent.

 3. Mosaicism (): 46,XX / 47,XX,+21 due to post-zygotic mitotic non-disjunction; milder clinical phenotype.

Clinical Features (Craniofacial & Physical Features)

Head & Neck: Brachycephaly, flat occiput, microcephaly, open fontanelles, short neck with redundant skin fold at the nape.

Facial Features: Flat facial profile, depressed nasal bridge, small nose, upward and outward slanting palpebral fissures (mongoloid slant), prominent epicanthic folds, small low-set dysplastic ears, small mouth with a high-arched narrow palate and protruding furrowed tongue.

Ocular Findings [KU16]: Upward palpebral slant, epicanthic folds, Brushfield spots (speckled ring of white/grey spots on the iris periphery), congenital/developmental cataracts, strabismus (esotropia), nystagmus, refractive errors (myopia), keratoconus, and blepharitis.

Hands & Feet: Short broad hands, single transverse palmar crease (Simian crease), clinodactyly (incurving of 5th finger due to hypoplasia of middle phalanx), and wide gap between 1st and 2nd toes (‘Sandal gap’ with a deep plantar furrow).

Neurological: Marked generalized hypotonia (rag-doll floppiness at birth, improves with age), joint hyperflexibility, developmental delay, and moderate-to-severe intellectual disability (IQ 25–70).

System-Wise Complications & Comorbidities

Cardiovascular ( — Chief cause of early mortality):

Endocardial cushion defect / Atrioventricular Septal Defect (AVSD / AV canal defect) ( of CHD in Down syndrome — most specific).

Perimembranous VSD, Ostium secundum ASD, PDA, Tetralogy of Fallot.

Gastrointestinal (): Duodenal atresia (‘double-bubble’ sign on X-ray), annular pancreas, tracheoesophageal fistula, Hirschsprung disease, imperforate anus, and Celiac disease.

Endocrine: Congenital and acquired autoimmune hypothyroidism (), short stature, obesity, diabetes mellitus, infertility in males.

Hematological / Oncological:

Transient Myeloproliferative Disorder (TMD) in neonates (, GATA1 mutation).

15–20-fold increased risk of Acute Leukemia (AML-M7 predominates in ; ALL predominates in ).

Orthopedic: Atlantoaxial (Atlanto-occipital) instability / subluxation ():

Clinical Clue [KU22]: Atlantoaxial subluxation causing cervical spinal cord compression must be suspected in a child with Down syndrome presenting with recent-onset gait disturbances, frequent falls, neck pain, torticollis, hyperreflexia, or bladder/bowel incontinence. Evaluated by lateral cervical spine X-rays in flexion and extension.

ENT & Respiratory: Serous otitis media, conductive/sensorineural hearing loss (), and obstructive sleep apnea.

Diagnosis & Antenatal Screening/Diagnosis of Down Syndrome

Postnatal Diagnosis: Confirmed by Karyotyping (and FISH/QF-PCR for rapid diagnosis).

Antenatal Screening (Non-Invasive):

First Trimester Combined Screen (11 to 13+6 Weeks — Detection rate ):

Ultrasonography (USG) Markers: Increased Nuchal Translucency (NT ), absent or hypoplastic nasal bone, reversed ‘a’ wave in ductus venosus, tricuspid regurgitation.

Dual Marker Maternal Serum Screen: Decreased PAPP-A (Pregnancy-Associated Plasma Protein-A) + Increased free -hCG.

Second Trimester Maternal Serum Screen (15 to 20 Weeks):

Triple Test ( sensitivity): Low -fetoprotein (AFP) + Low unconjugated Estriol () + High -hCG.

Quadruple Test ( sensitivity): Triple test + High Inhibin-A.

Second Trimester Anomaly USG (18–20 Weeks) [TU]: Increased nuchal fold thickness (), absent/hypoplastic nasal bone, short femur and humerus, echogenic intracardiac focus, congenital heart defect (AV canal), duodenal atresia (‘double-bubble’ sign), mild ventriculomegaly, pyelectasis, and echogenic bowel.

Non-Invasive Prenatal Screening (NIPS / Cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood): Done after 10 weeks gestation;  sensitivity and specificity for Trisomy 21.

Confirmatory Invasive Antenatal Diagnosis (Offered if screen risk ):

Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS): Performed at 11–13 weeks gestation.

Amniocentesis: Performed at 16–20 weeks gestation (fetal karyotyping + FISH/QF-PCR).

Cordocentesis: Performed  weeks.

Genetic Counseling & Recurrence Risk

Counsel both parents together with empathy, explaining comorbidities, early stimulation therapy, and routine screening schedule (Echo at birth; Thyroid and Hearing/Vision annually).

Recurrence Risk in Subsequent Pregnancies:

Free Trisomy 21:  (if mother ) or age-specific maternal risk (if ).

Translocation Down Syndrome (e.g., 14;21): If de novo (parents have normal karyotype): . If mother is a balanced carrier: . If father is a balanced carrier: .

Balanced 21;21 Translocation Carrier Parent [t(21q;21q)]:  of viable offspring will have Down syndrome (parents should be advised donor gamete or adoption).

title: 21.2 TURNER SYNDROME, PATTERNS OF INHERITANCE & GENETIC COUNSELING
text:
(Covers: Turner karyotype, Inheritance patterns of G6PD, Marfan, Hunter, Hemophilia; Genetic counseling; Indications for amniocentesis) [KU 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 695–703

1. High-Yield Short Answers / One-Liners

Chromosomal Abnormality in Turner Syndrome [KU20]: Complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome — Classic karyotype 45,X (); Mosaicism 45,X/46,XX (); Isochromosome 46,X,i(Xq); or Xp deletion.

Pattern of Inheritance of G6PD Deficiency [KU20]: X-linked Recessive (gene at Xq28).

Pattern of Inheritance of Hunter Syndrome (MPS Type II) [KU16]: X-linked Recessive (Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency; all other mucopolysaccharidoses are Autosomal Recessive).

Pattern of Inheritance of Marfan Syndrome [KU17]: Autosomal Dominant (FBN1 / Fibrillin-1 gene on chromosome 15q21).

Two X-Linked Recessive Disorders [KU19]: Hemophilia A & B, Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), G6PD deficiency, Hunter syndrome, Bruton X-linked agammaglobulinemia, Color blindness.

2. X-Linked Recessive Inheritance & Genetic Counseling in Hemophilia

Characteristics of X-Linked Recessive Inheritance:

Affects hemizygous males () because males have only one X chromosome.

Transmitted through clinically unaffected heterozygous carrier females ().

No male-to-male (father-to-son) transmission occurs. All daughters of an affected male are obligate carriers, while all his sons are normal.

In each pregnancy of a carrier female () with a normal male ():  of sons are affected,  of sons are normal,  of daughters are carriers, and  of daughters are normal (overall 25% risk of an affected male child per pregnancy).

Genetic Counseling in Hemophilia:

Construct a 3-generation pedigree and perform molecular mutation analysis (F8 gene inversion of intron 22 for severe Hemophilia A, or F9 gene for Hemophilia B) in the index child.

Test the mother and female siblings for carrier status using DNA mutation testing/MLPA (note:  of cases arise from de novo mutations).

Explain the  risk of disease in male fetuses of carrier mothers and offer Prenatal Diagnosis via Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS) at 11–12 weeks (fetal sex determination + mutation analysis) or Pre-implantation Genetic Diagnosis (PGD).

3. Genetic Counseling & Indications for Amniocentesis

Definition of Genetic Counseling [KU18]: A non-directive communication process that helps individuals/families understand and adapt to the medical, psychological, and familial implications of genetic disease. It integrates: (1) Accurate diagnosis and 3-generation pedigree interpretation to estimate recurrence risk; (2) Education on inheritance, management, and support resources; and (3) Non-directive counseling regarding reproductive options (prenatal diagnosis, PGD, donor gametes, adoption).

Indications for Amniocentesis (Performed at 16–20 weeks gestation) [RGU]:

Positive maternal serum screen (Dual/Triple/Quadruple test risk ) or positive NIPS for fetal aneuploidy.

Abnormal fetal ultrasound findings (structural malformations or soft markers of aneuploidy).

Previous child with a chromosomal abnormality (e.g., Down syndrome).

Parent is a known carrier of a balanced chromosomal translocation/inversion.

Both parents are carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder (e.g., -thalassemia, SMA) or mother is a carrier of an X-linked disorder where Chorionic Villus Sampling window (11–13 weeks) was missed.

Suspected congenital intrauterine infection (PCR for CMV, Toxoplasmosis).

subject: pediatrics
title: CHAPTER 24 (Q-Bank Ch 22): INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM — 1. Quick Short Answers / One-Liners
text:
Odor of Urine in Phenylketonuria (PKU) [KU17]: Musty or mousy odor (due to phenylacetic acid). (Other classic odors: Maple syrup/burnt sugar in MSUD; Sweaty feet in Isovaleric acidemia; Cabbage-like in Tyrosinemia; Cat’s urine in Multiple carboxylase deficiency).

Causes of Hypercholesterolemia / Hyperlipidemia in a Child [KU20]:

Secondary Causes: Nephrotic syndrome, Hypothyroidism, Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (von Gierke disease), cholestatic liver disease, diabetes mellitus, Niemann-Pick disease, Wolman disease, drugs (corticosteroids, cyclosporine).

Primary Causes: Familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor defect), Familial combined hyperlipidemia.

subject: pediatrics
title: CHAPTER 24 (Q-Bank Ch 22): INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM — 2. Classical Galactosemia [TU]
text:
Enzyme Defect: Autosomal recessive deficiency of Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) (less commonly Galactokinase [causes isolated cataract] or Epimerase deficiency).

Pathogenesis: Accumulation of Galactose-1-phosphate (damages liver, kidney tubules, and brain) and Galactitol (accumulates in the lens, causing osmotic cataract).

Clinical Features:

Neonates appear normal at birth, but within days of initiating breast milk or lactose-containing formula, develop vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, poor feeding, failure to thrive, prolonged conjugated/unconjugated jaundice, hepatomegaly, ascites, and coagulopathy/acute liver failure.

Bilateral ‘oil-droplet’ cataracts.

Renal Fanconi syndrome (proximal RTA, aminoaciduria, galactosuria).

High predisposition to fulminant neonatal Escherichia coli sepsis.

Untreated survivors develop intellectual disability, cirrhosis, and premature ovarian insufficiency.

Diagnosis:

Bedside Urine Screening Test: Benedict’s / Clinitest is POSITIVE for reducing substances, while Glucose Oxidase urine dipstick is NEGATIVE (confirms non-glucose reducing sugar, i.e., galactosuria).

Confirmatory Tests: Quantitative assay showing absent/reduced RBC GALT enzyme activity, elevated RBC Galactose-1-phosphate levels (), and GALT gene sequencing.

Management: Immediate and lifelong elimination of lactose/galactose from the diet (stop breast milk and animal milk; substitute with Soy-based formula or Lactose-free formula) + empirical antibiotics for E. coli sepsis in sick neonates.

subject: pediatrics
title: CHAPTER 24 (Q-Bank Ch 22): INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM — 3. Lactose Intolerance [RGU]
text:
Types: (1) Secondary lactose intolerance (most common in infants following acute rotaviral gastroenteritis, persistent diarrhea, cow’s milk protein allergy, or celiac disease due to brush-border mucosal injury); (2) Ontogenetic (Adult-type) lactase deficiency; (3) Congenital lactase deficiency (rare AR disorder presenting from day 1 of life).

Clinical Features: Osmotic diarrhea — frothy, watery, explosive acidic stools mixed with gas, perianal excoriation/erythema, abdominal distension, borborygmi, and flatulence upon ingesting milk.

Diagnosis: Stool , positive stool reducing substances ( on Benedict’s test), and Hydrogen breath test.

Management: Continue breastfeeding; in formula-fed infants with persistent diarrhea, substitute animal milk with yoghurt/curd (fermented milk has lower lactose), cereal-milk mixtures, or low-lactose/lactose-free formula, along with oral Zinc and vitamin A supplementation.

title: CHAPTER 26 (Q-Bank Ch 23): OPHTHALMIC DISORDERS — 3. High-Yield Short Answers & MCQs
text:
Four Causes of Retinitis Pigmentosa in Children [KU17]:

Laurence-Moon-Bardet-Biedl syndrome (obesity, polydactyly, hypogonadism, renal ciliopathy, retinitis pigmentosa).

Usher syndrome (congenital sensorineural deafness + retinitis pigmentosa).

Refsum disease / Peroxisomal disorders (phytanic acid accumulation).

Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome) & Kearns-Sayre syndrome / NARP (mitochondrial cytopathy) / Senior-Løken syndrome (nephronophthisis) / Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis (Batten disease).

Three Causes of Papilledema in Children [RGU]:

Intracranial Space-Occupying Lesions: Posterior fossa brain tumors (medulloblastoma, cerebellar astrocytoma), brain abscess, tuberculoma, subdural hematoma.

CNS Infections & Hydrocephalus: Tuberculous meningitis, acute bacterial meningitis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.

Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor cerebri): Hypervitaminosis A, tetracycline/nalidixic acid/steroid withdrawal, or Malignant Hypertension.

Intrauterine infection in which Congenital Cataract is seen [KU22]: Congenital Rubella Syndrome (also CMV, Toxoplasmosis, Congenital Varicella).
