subject: pediatrics
title: Q-BANK CHAPTER 8: IMMUNIZATION AND IMMUNODEFICIENCY — 1. National Immunization Schedule (NIS) & Birth Vaccines [KU 23, RGU]
text:
Vaccines given on Day 1 of Life (At Birth) [KU23]:

BCG:  (up to 1 month age;  after 1 month) Intradermal over left upper arm (deltoid insertion) using a 26G needle. Live attenuated M. bovis (Danish 1331 strain); reconstituted with Normal Saline (discard within 4 hours).

OPV-0 (Zero dose): 2 drops Orally (within first 15 days of birth).

Hepatitis B (Birth dose):  Intramuscular (anterolateral aspect of mid-thigh) within 24 hours of birth (prevents perinatal vertical transmission).

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-005]]

subject: pediatrics
title: Q-BANK CHAPTER 8: IMMUNIZATION AND IMMUNODEFICIENCY — 2. Specific Vaccines (High-Yield KUHS Questions)
text:
A. Pentavalent Vaccine [KU 24, 23, 22, TU]

Constituents (5-in-1): Diphtheria toxoid + Whole-cell Pertussis (killed Bordetella pertussis) + Tetanus toxoid (DTwP) + Recombinant Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) + Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) capsular polysaccharide (PRP) conjugated to tetanus toxoid.

Schedule, Dose & Route: 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age (minimum 4 weeks interval; can be given up to 1 year of age);  Intramuscular in the anterolateral aspect of the mid-thigh.

Storage & Open Vial Policy: Stored at  in the ILR. It is a freeze-sensitive liquid vaccine (contains aluminum adjuvant; tested by Shake Test). Follows the Open Vial Policy (opened multi-dose vial can be used for up to 28 days if cold chain is maintained and VVM is usable).

Advantages: Reduces number of pricks from 9 to 3 in primary series, decreases operational/syringe costs, and improves Hib/HepB coverage.

B. Rotavirus Vaccine (RVV) [KU 23, 21, 16, RGU, TU]

Types: Live attenuated oral vaccines:

Rotavac (116E strain - Bharat Biotech, used in NIS): Monovalent human-bovine reassortant strain (G9P[11]); dose is 5 drops () orally.

Rotasiil (Serum Institute, used in NIS): Pentavalent human-bovine reassortant (G1, G2, G3, G4, G9); lyophilized/liquid, dose is  orally.

Private sector: Rotarix (Monovalent G1P[8], 2 doses at 6, 10 wks) and Rotateq (Pentavalent, 3 doses).

NIS Schedule & Route: 3 doses at 6, 10, and 14 weeks administered Orally into the inner cheek (can be initiated up to 1 year of age in NIS).

Adverse effect / Precaution: Rare risk of intussusception (1–2 per 100,000 infants); contraindicated in infants with previous history of intussusception or Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID).

C. Polio Vaccines in NIS (bOPV & fIPV) [KU 20, RGU, TU]

Currently used Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) [KU20]: Bivalent OPV (bOPV) containing live attenuated Sabin Poliovirus Type 1 and Type 3 (Type 2 was withdrawn globally in April 2016 during the ‘tOPV to bOPV switch’ because wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999 and Sabin type 2 caused  of cVDPV and VAPP cases).

Dose & Schedule: 2 drops orally at Birth (OPV-0), 6, 10, 14 weeks, and 16–24 months.

Advantages of OPV over IPV: Easy oral administration, low cost, induces intestinal mucosal IgA immunity (prevents wild virustransmission in community), and herd immunity via contact spread.

Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV / fIPV - Salk Vaccine):

Contains killed Poliovirus Types 1, 2, and 3 (provides essential immunity against Type 2).

NIS Schedule: Fractional IPV (fIPV) —  Intradermal over the right upper arm at 6 weeks, 14 weeks, and 9 months. (Full-dose IPV is  IM).

Advantages of IPV over OPV: Zero risk of Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) or Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV); safe in immunodeficient children.

D. Measles-Rubella (MR) / MMR Vaccine & MR Campaign [KU 23, 21, RGU]

Type & Strains: Live attenuated lyophilized vaccine containing Edmonston-Zagreb strain of Measles virus and RA 27/3 strain of Rubella virus (+ Jeryl-Lynn / Hoshino strain of Mumps in MMR).

Reconstitution & Route: Reconstituted only with manufacturer-supplied sterile water diluent kept at ; must be used within 4 hours of reconstitution (else risk of Staphylococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome). Dose:  Subcutaneous in the right upper arm.

Schedule:

NIS (MR Vaccine): MR-1 at 9–12 months (completed 9 months) and MR-2 at 16–24 months.

IAP Schedule (MMR): 3 doses at 9 months, 15 months, and 4–6 years.

MR Vaccine Campaign [KU23]: A nationwide mass vaccination catch-up campaign launched by the Government of India in 2017 targeting all children aged 9 months to <15 years with a single supplementary dose of MR vaccine (regardless of prior immunization status) in schools and outreach sessions, aiming to eliminate Measles and control Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS).

E. Pneumococcal, JE, Varicella, HPV & Cancer-Preventing Vaccines

Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV) [KU19]: Polysaccharide conjugated to CRM197 carrier protein (PCV10/Pneumosil or PCV13/Prevnar). Given under NIS as  IM (anterolateral right thigh) in a 2+1 schedule: 6 weeks, 14 weeks, and Booster at 9 months. Prevents invasive pneumococcal pneumonia, meningitis, and otitis media.

Japanese Encephalitis (JE) Vaccine [KU18]: Live attenuated SA 14-14-2 strain (or killed Jeevan/Jenvac). Given in endemic districts as  Subcutaneous (left upper arm); 2 doses: JE-1 at 9–12 months and JE-2 at 16–24 months.

Varicella Vaccine [KU15]: Live attenuated Oka strain;  SC; IAP schedule: 2 doses at 15 months and 4–6 years.

Two Vaccines which Prevent Cancer [KU21]:

Hepatitis B Vaccine (prevents Hepatocellular Carcinoma).

Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccine (prevents Cervical, vaginal, vulvar, anal, and oropharyngeal cancers).

Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccine [KU20]: Recombinant L1 virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine — Bivalent (Types 16, 18), Quadrivalent (Gardasil / Cervavac: Types 6, 11, 16, 18), or Nonavalent (Gardasil-9).

Minimum age for HPV vaccine in girls [KU20]: 9 years of age.

Schedule: 9–14 years: 2 doses ( IM at 0 and 6 months);  or immunocompromised: 3 doses (0, 1–2, and 6 months).

subject: pediatrics
title: Q-BANK CHAPTER 8: IMMUNIZATION AND IMMUNODEFICIENCY — 3. Cold Chain, VVM, Shake Test, AEFI & Counseling
text:
Vaccine Vial Monitor (VVM) [KU20]: A heat-sensitive time-temperature indicator label (containing diacetylene monomer that polymerizes and darkens on cumulative heat exposure) consisting of an inner square (heat-sensitive) inside an outer purple circle (reference ring):

Stage I: Inner square is white/much lighter than outer circle  USE vaccine.

Stage II: Inner square is slightly darker, but still lighter than outer circle  USE vaccine first.

Stage III (Discard Point): Inner square color matches the outer circle  DO NOT USE.

Stage IV: Inner square is darker than the outer circle  DO NOT USE.

Vaccine vial monitor stages: usable and unusable

Cold Chain & Peripheral Storage (PHC): System of storing and transporting vaccines at  from manufacturer to child. At the Primary Health Centre (PHC), vaccines are stored in an Ice-Lined Refrigerator (ILR) for up to 1 month (Bottom basket: OPV, MR, BCG, JE, Rotavac; Upper part: freeze-sensitive DPT, Pentavalent, TT, HepB, IPV, PCV, diluents) and ice packs are frozen in a Deep Freezer. (Reverse Cold Chain: Transporting stool samples from AFP cases at  from field to WHO lab).

Shake Test: Used to check if freeze-sensitive aluminum-adjuvant vaccines (Pentavalent, DPT, HepB, Td) have been damaged by freezing. Freeze a control vial solid, thaw it, and shake both the ‘suspect’ and ‘frozen control’ vials together. If the suspect vial sediments as fast as the frozen control vial (leaving clear supernatant within minutes), it is damaged and must be discarded.

AEFI [KU24]: Expand: Adverse Event Following Immunization. Any untoward medical occurrence which follows immunization and which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the usage of the vaccine (classified into: Vaccine product-related, Vaccine quality defect-related, Immunization error-related [e.g., TSS], Immunization anxiety-related, and Coincidental events).

Autonomy & Counseling Parents of a 1-Year-Old Unimmunized Child [KU24]:

Autonomy in Medical Practice: The ethical principle that respects the right of competent patients (or parents/surrogates in pediatrics, alongside the principle of child’s best interest) to make informed, voluntary decisions about their medical care without coercion, after being fully informed of benefits, risks, and alternatives.

Counseling Approach: Use empathetic, non-judgmental communication (CASE / APAC approach): (1) Explore the parents’ specific fears, myths, or logistical barriers causing vaccine hesitancy; (2) Explain the high risk of life-threatening preventable diseases (measles, diphtheria, pertussis, pneumonia) in an unimmunized 1-year-old; (3) Reassure about vaccine safety and minor manageable side effects (fever); (4) Formulate a Catch-up Immunization Schedule (administer BCG, Pentavalent-1, OPV-1, MR-1, and PCV-1 on the first visit at different anatomical sites, followed by 2nd and 3rd doses at 4-week intervals). (Mission Indradhanush is the GoI initiative to achieve  full immunization coverage in unimmunized/partially immunized children).

(Covers: Urticaria and Angioedema; Four common skin problems in Pediatrics) [RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 739, 750–752, 759–761, 768

subject: pediatrics
title: 1. Urticaria and Angioedema [RGU]
text:
Definition: Urticaria is a vascular reaction of the skin characterized by transient, pruritic, erythematous or pale raised wheals (due to localized upper dermal edema) that appear and disappear within 24–48 hours without leaving any residual mark. When the edema extends deeper into the deep dermis and subcutaneous/submucosal tissue, it is termed Angioedema.

Etiopathogenesis: Mediated by vasoactive chemicals (chiefly histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, and bradykinin) released from dermal mast cells and basophils, triggered by:

Immunological mechanisms: Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity (foods like egg, milk, nuts, fish; drugs like penicillins, cephalosporins; insect bites/stings; aeroallergens), autoimmune (anti-FcRI antibodies), or complement-mediated (serum sickness, C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency in hereditary angioedema).

Non-immunological mechanisms (Direct mast cell degranulation): Drugs (NSAIDs/aspirin, opioids, radiocontrast media) or physical stimuli (cold, heat, pressure, exercise/cholinergic, dermographism).

Clinical Features:

Urticaria: Sudden eruption of intensely itchy, pale-pink edematous papules/plaques (wheals) surrounded by an erythematous axon-reflex flare. Individual lesions are evanescent (). Classified as Acute () or Chronic ().

Angioedema: Non-pitting, non-itchy asymmetric swelling affecting loose tissues (eyelids, lips, tongue, genitalia, larynx). May be accompanied by anaphylaxis (bronchospasm, laryngeal stridor, hypotension).

Management:

Identify and eliminate triggers (offending drugs, foods, infections).

First-line Pharmacotherapy: Second-generation non-sedating -antihistamines (Cetirizine, Levocetirizine, Fexofenadine, Loratadine); doses may be escalated up to 4-fold in refractory cases.

Severe Acute Urticaria / Anaphylaxis: IM Adrenaline (1:1000)  + short course of oral Prednisolone ( for 3–5 days).

Chronic Refractory (Autoimmune) Urticaria: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (Montelukast), Cyclosporine, or Omalizumab (anti-IgE monoclonal antibody).

subject: pediatrics
title: 2. Four Common Skin Problems in Pediatrics [TU]
text:
Scabies:

Etiology: Infestation by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis via close skin-to-skin contact.

Clinical Features: Severe nocturnal pruritus affecting family members; pathognomonic lesion is a serpentine burrow alongside papulovesicles in finger webs, flexor wrists, axillae, periumbilical area, and genitalia. In infants, palms, soles, face, and scalp are characteristically involved.

Treatment: Topical  Permethrin cream applied overnight from neck to toe (including head/face in infants) for all family contacts simultaneously + oral antihistamines (Crotamiton  in infants ; Oral Ivermectin  in ).

Impetigo (Pyoderma):

Etiology: Superficial bacterial skin infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes.

Clinical Features: Impetigo contagiosa presents as thin-walled vesicles around the mouth and nose that rupture to form characteristic honey-colored crusts; Bullous impetigo presents in neonates/infants as flaccid bullae rupturing to leave varnish-like crusts. Complication: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Treatment: Local crust removal + Topical Mupirocin () or Fusidic acid; oral Co-amoxiclav/Cephalexin/Cloxacillin if extensive.

Atopic Dermatitis (Infantile Eczema):

Etiology: Chronic relapsing pruritic inflammatory dermatosis associated with filaggrin gene defect, skin barrier dysfunction, elevated IgE, and personal/family history of atopy.

Clinical Features: Diagnosed by Hanifin and Rajka criteria. Infantile phase (3 mo–2 yrs): Itchy erythematous weeping papulovesicles on cheeks and extensors (sparing diaper area). Childhood phase (2–12 yrs): Dry, lichenified plaques in antecubital and popliteal flexures.

Treatment: Liberal emollients/moisturizers immediately after bath, avoidance of irritants, low-to-mid potency topical corticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors (Tacrolimus/Pimecrolimus) for flares, and oral antihistamines.

Diaper (Napkin) Dermatitis:

Etiology: Primary irritant contact dermatitis from prolonged contact with urine (ammonia) and fecal enzymes under occlusive diapers, frequently superinfected by Candida albicans.

Clinical Features: Irritant diaper dermatitis shows glazed erythema over the convex surfaces of buttocks/thighs, sparing the deep flexural creases. Secondary Candidal diaper dermatitis involves the deep skin folds with beefy-red erythema, scalloped borders, and satellite pustules.

Treatment: Frequent diaper changes, air-drying, barrier creams (Zinc oxide paste), mild topical hydrocortisone, and topical Clotrimazole/Miconazole if candidal infection is present.

subject: pediatrics
title: 25.1 GENERAL GUIDELINES & PREVENTION OF POISONING
text:
(Covers: General management principles of poisoning, Prevention of poisoning in children) [RGU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 776–780, 787

General Principles of Management of Poisoning

Initial Assessment & Resuscitation (ABCDE):

Airway & Breathing: Ensure patent airway; perform rapid-sequence intubation if GCS , loss of gag reflex, respiratory depression, or severe pulmonary edema. Administer .

Circulation: Secure IV access; treat hypotension with isotonic crystalloid boluses ( NS/RL) and vasopressors. Correct arrhythmias (e.g., IV Sodium Bicarbonate for wide-QRS tricyclic antidepressant cardiotoxicity).

Disability & Supportive Care: Check blood glucose (treat hypoglycemia with   Dextrose); control seizures with IV Lorazepam/Midazolam; maintain normothermia; contact the National Poisons Information Centre (NPIC), AIIMS New Delhi (1800-116-117).

Clinical Identification (Toxidromes): Identify specific toxidromes — Cholinergic (organophosphates: DUMBBELS, miosis, bradycardia), Anticholinergic (atropine, antihistamines, TCAs: delirium, mydriasis, dry flushed skin, tachycardia, urinary retention), Opioid (coma, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression), or Sympathomimetic.

Decontamination (Removal of Unabsorbed Poison):

Ocular & Dermal Decontamination: Remove contaminated clothes; flush eyes and wash skin thoroughly with copious tepid water and soap for 15–20 minutes (crucial in organophosphates).

Gastrointestinal Decontamination (Most effective within 1 hour of ingestion):

Single-Dose Activated Charcoal ( PO/NG, max ): Adsorbs most organic toxins in its porous network. Ineffective in (Mnemonic PHAILS): Pesticides, Hydrocarbons, Acids/Alkalis/Alcohols, Iron/Heavy metals, Lithium, Solvents.

Gastric Lavage: Using a large-bore orogastric tube in left lateral position ONLY if potentially lethal ingestion within 1 hour and airway is protected. Contraindicated in: Hydrocarbons (kerosene), Corrosives (acids/alkalis), and unprotected airway.

Whole Bowel Irrigation (WBI): Instillation of Polyethylene Glycol Electrolyte Solution (PEG-ES, ) for substances not bound by charcoal (Iron, Lithium, Lead, sustained-release or enteric-coated tablets).

Note: Emesis with Syrup of Ipecac is contraindicated.

Enhancement of Excretion of Absorbed Toxin:

Multiple-Dose Activated Charcoal (MDAC,  q4–6h): Interrupts enterohepatic circulation (‘gut dialysis’) for Phenobarbitone, Carbamazepine, Theophylline, Dapsone, Quinine.

Urinary Alkalinization: IV Sodium Bicarbonate () to achieve urine  traps and excretes weak acids (Salicylates, Phenobarbitone, Isoniazid, Methotrexate).

Extracorporeal Removal (Hemodialysis): For toxins with low molecular weight, low protein binding, and small volume of distribution (Salicylates, Lithium, Methanol, Ethylene glycol, Valproate, Phenobarbitone, Theophylline).

Intravenous Lipid Emulsion: For lipophilic local anesthetic, beta-blocker, or calcium-channel blocker cardiotoxicity.

Administration of Specific Antidotes: (e.g., N-acetylcysteine for Paracetamol; Atropine + Pralidoxime for Organophosphates; Naloxone for Opioids; Flumazenil for Benzodiazepines; Methylene blue for Methemoglobinemia; Desferrioxamine for Iron).

Prevention of Poisoning in Children (Table 28.10)

Passive Strategies (Most effective): Use child-resistant packaging/caps and blister packs for medications; install automatic safety locks on medicine and kitchen cabinets.

Safe Storage Practices:

Never store kerosene, turpentine, or cleaning acids in soft-drink, mineral water, or juice bottles. Keep all chemicals in their original labeled containers.

Store all medicines, pesticides, rodenticides, and button batteries locked and out of sight and reach of children.

Parental Education: Never refer to medicine as “candy/sweet” in front of children; measure pediatric liquid medications using calibrated syringes/cups rather than household spoons; dispose of unused/expired medications promptly.

subject: pediatrics
title: 25.2 HYDROCARBON (KEROSENE) POISONING
text:
(Covers: Clinical features, radiological findings, and management of Kerosene poisoning) [KU 23, 19, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 780–781

Pathogenesis

Kerosene is an aliphatic hydrocarbon with low viscosity, low surface tension, and high volatility.

Toxicity results not from GI absorption, but from pulmonary aspiration during swallowing, gagging, or vomiting. It spreads rapidly across the respiratory mucosa, inactivating Type II pneumocytes and pulmonary surfactant, causing alveolar collapse, necrotizing chemical aspiration pneumonitis, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

Clinical Features

Respiratory System (Predominant — develops within 30 mins to 6 hours):

Immediate choking, coughing, gagging, and kerosene odor on breath.

Tachypnea, nasal flaring, subcostal/intercostal retractions, grunting, wheezing, crepitations, and cyanosis, which may progress to Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) and respiratory failure.

Central Nervous System: Restlessness, irritability, drowsiness, stupor, coma, and convulsions (secondary to hypoxia and direct systemic absorption of volatile fumes).

Gastrointestinal: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain.

Systemic: Fever () and neutrophilic leukocytosis occur in the first 24–48 hours due to sterile chemical inflammation (does not indicate bacterial infection unless persisting/recurring after 48–72 hours).

Radiological Findings (Chest X-Ray)

Radiographic abnormalities appear within 2 to 6 hours of ingestion (even before clinical signs peak) and are maximal at 24–72 hours:

Punctate, mottled, perihilar densities and patchy basal bronchopneumonic infiltrates (commonly bilateral and in right middle/lower lobes).

Basal atelectasis and compensatory basal hyperinflation/emphysema.

Pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or pneumomediastinum.

Pneumatoceles (thin-walled air cysts) during the resolution phase (1–2 weeks later).

Management

Strict Contraindications (What NOT to do):

Gastric lavage and induction of emesis are STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED (as they vastly increase the risk of pulmonary aspiration).

Activated charcoal is NOT indicated (does not bind hydrocarbons and induces vomiting).

Prophylactic antibiotics and corticosteroids are NOT routinely indicated (steroids are ineffective and increase secondary bacterial infection risk).

Decontamination: Remove kerosene-soaked clothing immediately and wash the skin with soap and water to prevent cutaneous burns and inhalation of fumes.

Observation & Disposition (Fig. 28.3):

Keep child Nil Per Oral (NPO) initially.

Observe all asymptomatic children for at least 6 hours and obtain a Chest X-ray at 6 hours post-ingestion:

If child remains asymptomatic at 6 hours AND 6-hour Chest X-ray is normal  safe to discharge home.

If child is symptomatic (tachypnea/distress/hypoxia) OR Chest X-ray is abnormal  Admit to Hospital/PICU.

Supportive Respiratory & ICU Care:

Administer humidified Oxygen to maintain .

Early CPAP / Non-Invasive Ventilation or Invasive Mechanical Ventilation with PEEP for severe respiratory distress, persistent hypoxemia, or ARDS.

Nebulized bronchodilators (-agonists) if bronchospasm/wheezing is present.

IV maintenance fluids; start antibiotics only if secondary bacterial superinfection is suspected (new fever, worsening infiltrates, or clinical deterioration after 48–72 hours).

subject: pediatrics
title: 25.3 ORGANOPHOSPHORUS (OP) POISONING
text:
(Covers: List two drugs used in OP poisoning; Pharmacotherapy and management of OP poisoning) [KU 24, RGU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 777, 780, 782

Short Answer [KU24] — Two Specific Drugs (Antidotes) used in Organophosphorus Poisoning: 1. Atropine Sulfate (Antimuscarinic agent — reverses muscarinic and CNS effects). 2. Pralidoxime (2-PAM / Pralidoxime Aldoxime Methiodide) (Cholinesterase reactivator — reverses nicotinic neuromuscular blockade).

Mechanism & Clinical Features

Organophosphates irreversibly phosphorylate and inactivate Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses, causing massive acetylcholine accumulation:

Muscarinic Crisis (Mnemonic — DUMBBELS): Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis (pinpoint pupils), Bradychardia, Bronchorrhea/Bronchospasm (pulmonary edema), Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation/Sweating.

Nicotinic Effects: Muscle fasciculations, cramps, weakness, respiratory muscle paralysis, hypertension, tachycardia.

CNS Effects: Agitation, confusion, convulsions, coma, central respiratory depression.

Late phases: Intermediate syndrome (proximal muscle and respiratory paralysis at 24–96 hrs) and Delayed polyneuropathy (1–3 weeks later).

Diagnosis: Characteristic garlic-like odor, clinical toxidrome, and  reduction in plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) or RBC acetylcholinesterase activity (severe if ).

Management & Pharmacotherapy (Box 28.1)

Resuscitation & Airway: Clear copious airway secretions by suctioning; provide  Oxygen (give  before atropine to prevent ventricular fibrillation in a hypoxic myocardium); intubate and ventilate if apneic or severe weakness (avoid Succinylcholine for intubation as it is metabolized by cholinesterase).

Decontamination: Remove all clothes, wash skin, hair, and eyes thoroughly with soap and water. Perform gastric lavage + activated charcoal ONLY if ingested within 1 hour after securing the airway.

Specific Antidote 1 — ATROPINE SULFATE (Physiological Antidote):

Action: Competitively blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic and CNS receptors (has no effect on nicotinic muscle paralysis).

Dosage & Administration: Give  IV bolus initially. If no response, repeat (or double the dose) every 5–10 minutes until signs of Complete Atropinization are achieved.

End-Point of Atropinization: Drying of bronchial secretions (clear lung fields on auscultation — MOST IMPORTANT endpoint), resolution of bradycardia (normal heart rate/tachycardia), and normal systolic blood pressure (Note: Pupil dilation/mydriasis may lag behind and is not the sole endpoint).

Maintenance Infusion: Once atropinized, start a continuous IV infusion of Atropine at  of the total cumulative loading dose per hour, tapering slowly over 3–5 days. (If atropine toxicity/delirium occurs, stop infusion for 30 mins and restart at a lower rate).

Specific Antidote 2 — PRALIDOXIME (PAM) (Biochemical Antidote):

Action: Cleaves the organophosphate-cholinesterase bond and reactivates AChE before irreversible ‘aging’ of the enzyme occurs; specifically reverses nicotinic neuromuscular weakness and fasciculations.

Dosage: Loading dose of  IV infused in normal saline over 20–30 minutes, followed by a continuous IV infusion of  (or repeated q8–12h) until atropine has not been required for 12–24 hours and the child is extubated. (Note: PAM is not required in Carbamate poisoning as carbamates bind reversibly).

Supportive Care: IV Benzodiazepines (Midazolam/Lorazepam) for seizures and atropine-induced agitation.

subject: pediatrics
title: 25.4 PARACETAMOL (ACETAMINOPHEN) POISONING
text:
(Covers: Pathogenesis, clinical stages, nomogram, and management of Paracetamol poisoning) [KU 22, 19] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 780, 783

Toxic Dose & Pathogenesis

Toxic Dose in Children: Acute single ingestion of  (or repeated supratherapeutic ingestion  for consecutive days).

Pathogenesis: Normally,  of paracetamol undergoes hepatic glucuronidation/sulfation, and  is oxidized by Cytochrome P450 (CYP2E1) into the highly reactive hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine), which is immediately detoxified by hepatic glutathione. In overdose, glucuronidation pathways saturate, generating massive NAPQI that depletes hepatic glutathione stores (); unbound NAPQI covalently binds to hepatocyte macromolecules, causing centrilobular (Zone 3) hepatic necrosis and renal tubular necrosis.

Four Clinical Stages of Paracetamol Toxicity (Table 28.8)

Stage I (0.5–24 Hours): Asymptomatic, or mild anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise, diaphoresis. LFTs are normal.

Stage II (24–48 Hours — Latent Phase): Resolution of GI symptoms (false sense of recovery); right upper quadrant pain/tenderness begins; rising serum transaminases (AST/ALT) and prothrombin time.

Stage III (72–96 Hours / 3–5 Days — Hepatic Phase): Peak hepatotoxicity (AST/ALT ), jaundice, coagulopathy (INR ), hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, fulminant hepatic failure / hepatic encephalopathy, and acute kidney injury. Death occurs in this stage.

Stage IV (4–14 Days): Complete hepatic regeneration and recovery in survivors without chronic cirrhosis.

Diagnosis & Rumack-Matthew Nomogram

Gastric Decontamination: Administer Activated Charcoal ( PO) if the patient presents within 1–4 hours of ingestion.

Rumack-Matthew Nomogram: Draw a serum paracetamol concentration at 4 hours post-ingestion (or as soon as possible between 4 and 24 hours) and plot it on the semi-logarithmic Rumack-Matthew Nomogram. If the level falls above the treatment line (connecting  at 4 hours to  at 24 hours), initiate antidote therapy. (Nomogram cannot be used for staggered/chronic ingestions).

Specific Antidote Therapy: N-Acetylcysteine (NAC)

Mechanism: NAC is a sulfhydryl donor that replenishes hepatic glutathione stores, directly binds NAPQI, enhances sulfate conjugation, and exerts antioxidant/microcirculatory benefits. Maximum efficacy if started within 8 hours of ingestion (still beneficial even  in established liver failure).

Regimens (Table 28.7):

21-Hour Intravenous NAC Protocol (Preferred): Total  in  Dextrose over 21 hours:

Loading Dose:  IV over 1 hour.

Second Infusion:  IV over 4 hours.

Third Infusion:  IV over 16 hours.

72-Hour Oral NAC Protocol:  PO loading dose, followed by  PO every 4 hours for 17 doses.

King’s College Criteria for Liver Transplantation: Arterial  after fluid resuscitation, OR all three of: Grade III/IV hepatic encephalopathy + Prothrombin time  (INR ) + Serum Creatinine .

subject: pediatrics
title: 25.5 SNAKE ENVENOMATION, SCORPION STING, LEAD POISONING & DROWNING
text:
(Covers: Snake bite clinical features, Viper features, ASV & management; Scorpion sting management; Lead poisoning investigations; Near drowning) [KU 16, 15, RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 775, 784–786

1. Snakebite: Clinical Manifestations & Management [KU16, RGU, TU]

The ‘Big Four’ Venomous Snakes of India:

Elapidae (Neurotoxic): Indian Cobra (Naja naja) and Common Krait (Bungarus caeruleus).

Viperidae (Hemotoxic / Vasculotoxic): Russell’s Viper (Daboia russelii) and Saw-Scaled Viper (Echis carinatus).

Clinical Manifestations of Snake Envenomation:

Local Features (Prominent in Viper and Cobra; Absent in Krait): Fang marks, intense local pain, rapidly progressive swelling crossing joints, blistering, ecchymosis, tissue necrosis/compartment syndrome, and tender regional lymphadenitis.

Hemotoxic / Vasculotoxic Features (Viper Envenomation [TU]):

Persistent bleeding from fang marks and venipuncture sites.

Spontaneous systemic bleeding: Gingival bleeding, epistaxis, hemoptysis, hematemesis, melena, hematuria, subconjunctival hemorrhage, skin ecchymoses, and intracranial hemorrhage (due to venom-induced consumption coagulopathy / DIC).

Nephrotoxicity (Russell’s Viper): Flank pain, intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria/myoglobinuria, oliguria, and Acute Kidney Injury (acute tubular/cortical necrosis).

Hypotension/Shock (capillary leak) and Acute Pituitary Infarction (Sheehan-like syndrome in Russell’s viper).

Neurotoxic Features (Cobra & Krait Envenomation):

Descending flaccid paralysis starting with bilateral ptosis (earliest sign), diplopia, external ophthalmoplegia (‘broken neck’ sign), dysphagia, pooling of oral secretions, nasal regurgitation, dysphonia, intercostal and diaphragmatic respiratory paralysis. (Krait bites often occur painless at night while sleeping on the floor and present with unexplained morning abdominal pain and ptosis).

Investigations:

20-Minute Whole Blood Clotting Time (20WBCT — Bedside Test for Viper Bite): Place  of freshly drawn venous blood in a clean, new, dry, glass test tube and leave undisturbed for 20 minutes, then tip once. If the blood remains liquid (unclotted), it confirms hypofibrinogenemia/hemotoxic viper envenomation.

CBC (thrombocytopenia, schistocytes), PT/INR, aPTT, RFT, urine for hemoglobinuria/myoglobinuria.

Management of Snakebite (National Snakebite Protocol):

First Aid (Mnemonic: RIGHT): Reassure the victim; Immobilize the bitten limb with a splint like a fractured limb; Get to Hospital immediately; Tell the doctor of any systemic signs (ptosis, bleeding). DO NOT apply tight arterial tourniquets, incise, suck, or apply ice/chemicals.

Supportive Care: Airway protection, intubation and mechanical ventilation for neurotoxic respiratory paralysis, IV fluids for shock, and tetanus toxoid.

Specific Antidote — Polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV) [RGU]:

Equine lyophilized/liquid polyvalent immunoglobulin neutralizing all ‘Big Four’ venoms. Dose is identical in children and adults (as snakes inject the same amount of venom).

Indications for ASV: (1) Hemostatic abnormalities (positive 20WBCT or spontaneous systemic bleeding); (2) Neurotoxic signs (ptosis, paralysis); (3) Cardiovascular abnormalities (hypotension, shock, arrhythmia); (4) AKI (oliguria, hemoglobinuria); OR (5) Severe local swelling involving  of the bitten limb within 48 hours or rapidly crossing a joint.

Dosage & Administration: Initial dose is 8–10 vials () diluted in  of isotonic saline/dextrose and infused IV over 1 hour (starting slowly for the first 15 minutes to watch for anaphylaxis; skin sensitivity testing is not recommended as reactions are non-IgE anaphylactoid).

Repeat Doses:

In Neurotoxic bites: If no improvement or worsening after 1–2 hours, repeat a second dose of 8–10 vials (maximum total 20 vials) PLUS administer Atropine ( IV) followed by Neostigmine ( IM/IV) every 30 mins for 5 doses (AN Regimen — effective in postsynaptic Cobra bites; less effective in presynaptic -bungarotoxin Krait bites).

In Hemotoxic (Viper) bites: Repeat 20WBCT every 6 hours; if blood remains unclotted at 6 hours (or active bleeding persists at 1–2 hours), repeat 5–10 vials of ASV every 6 hours until coagulation is restored (up to 30 vials).

Management of ASV Anaphylactoid Reaction: Stop ASV infusion temporarily  give IM Adrenaline (1:1000, ) + IV Hydrocortisone () + IV Chlorpheniramine ()  resume ASV slowly once stabilized.

2. Scorpion Sting Management [RGU, TU]

Pathogenesis: Indian Red Scorpion (Mesobuthus tamulus) venom opens neuronal voltage-gated sodium channels, triggering an initial transient cholinergic phase (vomiting, profuse sweating, salivation, priapism, bradycardia) followed by a sustained, lethal ‘Autonomic Storm’ of massive -adrenergic stimulation  intense systemic vasoconstriction, severe hypertension, myocardial ischemia, acute left ventricular failure, and massive pulmonary edema.

Management (Fig. 28.6):

Local Pain Relief: Infiltrate  Lidocaine (without adrenaline) locally, apply ice packs, and give oral Paracetamol/NSAIDs.

Pharmacological Antidote — PRAZOSIN (Post-synaptic -Adrenergic Blocker):

Mechanism: Reverses -mediated vasoconstriction, reduces preload and afterload, restores insulin secretion, and prevents/reverses pulmonary edema (‘pharmacological sympathy-ectomy’).

Dosage:  PO (or via NG tube) given immediately (not on empty stomach; keep child supine for 3 hours to prevent first-dose orthostatic hypotension). Repeat the same dose at 3 hours, and then every 6 hours until extremities become warm, dry, and peripheral veins are full.

Scorpion Antivenom (if available early in severe autonomic storm).

Management of Pulmonary Edema & Cardiogenic Shock: Oxygen, non-invasive/invasive mechanical ventilation, IV Furosemide, IV Dobutamine (), and IV Sodium Nitroprusside / Nitroglycerin infusion.

3. Investigations in Lead Poisoning & Management of Near Drowning

Investigations in Lead Poisoning [RGU]:

Venous Blood Lead Level (BLL — Confirmatory):  is abnormal;  requires chelation therapy;  is a medical emergency (risk of acute lead encephalopathy).

Hematology & Peripheral Smear: Microcytic hypochromic anemia (due to inhibition of -ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase) with characteristic coarse basophilic stippling of RBCs (due to inhibition of pyrimidine 5’-nucleotidase).

Elevated Free Erythrocyte Protoporphyrin (FEP / Zinc Protoporphyrin - ZPP) ().

Radiographs:

X-ray Long Bones (Knee/Wrist): Dense radio-opaque metaphyseal ‘Lead lines’ at growing ends of femur, tibia, and radius.

Abdominal X-ray: Radio-opaque lead paint chips/flecks in the gut.

Renal Function & Urinalysis: Proximal renal tubular acidosis (Fanconi syndrome: glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia).

(Chelation drugs: Oral Succimer [DMSA], D-Penicillamine, IM Dimercaprol [BAL], and IV CaNa₂EDTA).

Management of Near-Drowning Child [KU15]:

Scene Rescue & Immediate BLS: Remove victim from water (stabilizing cervical spine if diving injury suspected); initiate A-B-C sequence (unlike C-A-B in primary cardiac arrest, hypoxic drowning arrest prioritizes 2 rescue breaths followed by chest compressions and ). (Do not attempt Heimlich maneuver to drain water from lungs as it causes gastric regurgitation/aspiration).

Respiratory Support: Surfactant washout causes alveolar collapse, intrapulmonary shunting, and ARDS. Administer  via non-rebreathing mask; apply early CPAP/BiPAP or endotracheal intubation with high PEEP if  or  on .

Hemodynamic & Temperature Management: Insert NG tube to decompress swallowed water; rewarm hypothermic patients (passive/active core rewarming to ); treat shock with isotonic crystalloids and inotropes.

Neuroprotection: Prevent secondary hypoxic-ischemic brain injury by maintaining normoglycemia, normocarbia, normothermia, controlling seizures, and elevating head end by . Observe all submersion victims for at least 24 hours for delayed pulmonary edema.

subject: pediatrics
title: 26.1 SHOCK IN CHILDREN
text:
(Covers: Definition, classification of shock, pathogenesis & management of Hypovolemic shock, ABCDE assessment, Capillary Refill Time) [RGU, TU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 788–789, 794–797

1. Assessment of a Seriously Ill Child: ABCDE & Capillary Refill Time

ABCDE Primary Assessment [TU]:

A — Airway: Assess patency (Clear, Maintainable with positioning/suctioning, or Not maintainable requiring intubation).

B — Breathing: Respiratory rate, work of breathing (nasal flaring, retractions, grunting, head bobbing), auscultation (stridor, wheeze, air entry), and pulse oximetry ().

C — Circulation: Heart rate and rhythm, central vs. peripheral pulses, Capillary Refill Time (CRT), skin color and extremity temperature, Blood Pressure, and end-organ perfusion (sensorium, urine output).

D — Disability (Neurological): Level of consciousness using AVPU scale (Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive) or Pediatric Glasgow Coma Scale, pupillary size/reaction, posture, and bedside blood glucose.

E — Exposure: Expose skin to check for rashes (purpura, petechiae, urticaria), trauma, burns, and measure core temperature.

Capillary Refill Time (CRT) [RGU]:

Method: Lift the extremity slightly above heart level in a warm environment; apply firm pressure for 5 seconds with the index finger/thumb over the sternum or forehead in neonates/infants (or finger pulp in older children) to blanch the skin, release pressure, and count the seconds taken for baseline skin color to return.

Interpretation: Normal CRT is . Prolonged CRT () is an early, sensitive clinical marker of cutaneous vasoconstriction, impaired microcirculation, and compensated hypovolemic/cold septic shock (appears well before hypotension develops). Flash CRT () indicates warm vasodilatory shock.

2. Definition & Classification of Shock

Definition: A critical state of acute circulatory failure resulting in inadequate delivery of oxygen and metabolic substrates to meet the cellular metabolic demands of vital organs, leading to cellular hypoxia, anaerobic metabolism, lactic acidosis, and multiorgan dysfunction.

Classification:

Hypovolemic Shock (Most common in children — Decreased Preload): Acute gastroenteritis (diarrheal dehydration), hemorrhage/trauma, burns, diabetic ketoacidosis, third-space plasma leakage (severe dengue, nephrotic syndrome).

Distributive Shock (Decreased Afterload / Systemic Vascular Resistance): Anaphylactic shock, neurogenic shock (spinal cord injury), early warm septic shock.

Cardiogenic Shock (Decreased Myocardial Contractility): Myocarditis, dilated cardiomyopathy, duct-dependent CHD (HLHS, critical AS/coarctation), arrhythmias (SVT), scorpion envenomation.

Obstructive Shock (Mechanical Obstruction to Ventricular Outflow/Filling): Tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, massive pulmonary embolism.

Septic Shock: Combines hypovolemic, distributive, and cardiogenic components.

3. Pathogenesis & Management of Hypovolemic Shock [RGU]

Pathogenesis & Compensatory Mechanisms:

Intravascular volume loss  decreased venous return (preload)  decreased ventricular end-diastolic volume  decreased Stroke Volume.

Compensated Stage (Normotensive Shock): Baroreceptor and chemoreceptor activation triggers a sympathetic catecholamine surge, RAAS activation (Angiotensin II & Aldosterone), and ADH release. This causes:

Tachycardia (maintains Cardiac Output: ).

Selective Systemic Vasoconstriction (increases SVR to maintain normal Blood Pressure: ), shunting blood away from skin, gut, and kidneys (cold extremities, prolonged CRT , weak peripheral pulses, oliguria) to preserve cerebral and coronary perfusion.

Decompensated Stage (Hypotensive Shock): Once  of intravascular blood volume is lost, compensatory mechanisms fail  hypotension (Systolic BP ), severe lactic acidosis, obtundation/coma, anuria, and cardiorespiratory arrest.

Management of Hypovolemic Shock:

Airway & Oxygenation: Maintain patent airway; administer  high-flow Oxygen via non-rebreathing mask.

Rapid Vascular Access: Insert two large-bore peripheral IV cannulae. If IV access is not achieved within 90 seconds (or 3 attempts) in decompensated shock, immediately establish Intraosseous (IO) access in the anteromedial proximal tibia.

Fluid Resuscitation (Cornerstone of Therapy):

Choice of Fluid: Isotonic Crystalloids (Ringer Lactate, Plasmalyte, or  Normal Saline). (Never use hypotonic/dextrose fluids for boluses).

Volume & Rate: Administer a rapid bolus of  over 10–20 minutes (push-pull technique over 5–10 minutes if hypotensive).

Reassess after each bolus: Check HR, BP, CRT, pulse volume, sensorium, and lung bases (for rales/hepatomegaly indicating fluid overload). Repeat  boluses (up to  in the first hour) until perfusion normalizes.

Hemorrhagic Shock: If shock persists after  of crystalloids in trauma/bleeding, transfuse Packed Red Blood Cells (O-negative or cross-matched) at .

Ongoing Replacement & Monitoring: Once shock resolves, replace ongoing deficit and maintenance fluid requirements (e.g., WHO Plan C for severe diarrheal dehydration), correct hypoglycemia/hypocalcemia/acidosis, and monitor hourly urine output (target ).

subject: pediatrics
title: 26.2 FOREIGN BODY ASPIRATION, HEIMLICH MANEUVER & HANDWASHING
text:
(Covers: Foreign body aspiration diagnosis & management; Heimlich maneuver; Steps of handwashing) [KU 20, RGU] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 791, 799, 803–804

1. Foreign Body Aspiration & Heimlich Maneuver [KU20, RGU]

Clinical Presentation & Diagnosis:

Peak age: 6 months to 3 years (peanuts, seeds, chana, toy parts).

Acute Choking Episode: Sudden witnessed onset of violent coughing, gagging, choking, aphonia, or cyanosis while eating/playing.

Laryngotracheal FB: Inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, brassy cough, severe respiratory distress.

Bronchial FB (, more common in Right Main Bronchus): Triad of unilateral wheeze, localized decreased air entry, and persistent cough.

Radiological Findings (Inspiratory & Expiratory Chest X-rays): Most FBs are radiolucent (). Due to a ball-valve check-valve mechanism, the affected lung shows obstructive hyperinflation (air-trapping) on expiratory film with mediastinal shift to the opposite side (or atelectasis if total obstruction).

Emergency Management of Choking (Severe Airway Obstruction — Unable to cry/cough/speak or cyanotic):

In an Infant ( — Back Slaps & Chest Thrusts; Heimlich is CONTRAINDICATED due to risk of liver rupture):

Place the infant prone (face-down) straddling the rescuer’s forearm with the head lower than the trunk (supporting the jaw). Deliver 5 forceful Back Blows (Slaps) between the shoulder blades using the heel of the hand.

Turn the infant supine (head lower than trunk) and deliver 5 rapid Chest Thrusts over the lower half of the sternum (1 finger-breadth below the intermammary line, similar to CPR). Repeat cycles of 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts until the object is expelled or the infant becomes unresponsive.

In a Child ( to Adolescent — HEIMLICH MANEUVER / Subdiaphragmatic Abdominal Thrusts) [KU20]:

Principle: Sudden upward elevation of the diaphragm increases intrathoracic pressure, creating an ‘artificial cough’ that expels the impacting foreign body from the airway.

Technique: Stand or kneel behind the conscious child and wrap your arms around the child’s waist. Make a fist with one hand and place the thumb side of the fist against the child’s abdomen in the midline, slightly above the umbilicus and well below the xiphoid process. Grasp the fist with the other hand and deliver a series of 5 quick, distinct inward and upward thrusts. Repeat until the foreign body is expelled or the child becomes unconscious.

If the Child/Infant becomes Unconscious: Place supine on a flat surface  begin CPR (starting with 30 chest compressions)  before giving rescue breaths, open the mouth wide and look for the foreign body (remove with Magill forceps only if visible; never perform a blind finger sweep).

Definitive Hospital Management (for stable/bronchial FB): Rigid Bronchoscopy under general anesthesia is the gold standard for both diagnosis and removal.

2. Steps of Handwashing (WHO 6-Step Hand Hygiene Technique)

Hand hygiene is the single most effective measure to prevent Healthcare-Associated Infections (HAI). Duration: 40–60 seconds with soap and water (or 20–30 seconds with alcohol-based hand rub), following the 6 steps (Mnemonic: PALM-BACK-INTER-KNUCKLE-THUMB-TIPS): 1. Palm to Palm: Wet hands, apply soap, and rub palms together in circular motion. 2. Right Palm over Left Dorsum (and vice versa) with fingers interlaced. 3. Palm to Palm with Fingers Interlaced (cleans interdigital web spaces). 4. Backs of Fingers (Knuckles) to Opposing Palms with fingers interlocked. 5. Rotational Rubbing of Left Thumb clasped in right palm (and vice versa). 6. Rotational Rubbing of Clasped Fingertips of right hand in left palm (and vice versa), followed by rinsing and drying with a single-use towel (or extended to 7th step: wrists).

subject: pediatrics
title: 26.3 ACUTE TORSION OF TESTIS
text:
(Covers: Clinical features, investigations, and management of acute torsion testis) [KU 24, 23] Source: Standard Pediatric Surgery Curriculum (Augmented for 100% KUHS Exam Accuracy)

Definition & Pathogenesis

Testicular Torsion is a true pediatric urological emergency caused by rotation (twisting) of the testis and spermatic cord around its longitudinal axis, leading to venous congestion, arterial ischemia, and hemorrhagic infarction of the testis.

Bimodal Age Peak:

Extravaginal Torsion: Occurs perinatally/neonatally (twisting of the entire cord and tunica vaginalis prior to scrotal fixation).

Intravaginal Torsion (Most common, peak at 10–16 years): Due to high investment of the tunica vaginalis on the spermatic cord allowing the testis to hang freely like a clapper in a bell (‘Bell-Clapper Deformity’, which is bilateral).

Clinical Features

Symptoms:

Sudden, excruciating unilateral scrotal pain (often waking the child from sleep or following minor trauma/sports), radiating to the ipsilateral inguinal canal and lower abdomen.

Accompanied by nausea and vomiting (). (Note: Some boys present with isolated lower abdominal pain; hence examination of the scrotum is mandatory in every boy presenting with acute abdomen).

Absence of dysuria or urethral discharge.

Physical Signs:

Erythematous, edematous, indurated, exquisitely tender hemiscrotum.

High-riding testis with an abnormal transverse lie (due to shortening of the twisted spermatic cord).

Absent Ipsilateral Cremasteric Reflex (Most sensitive clinical sign, ): Stroking the inner thigh fails to elevate the ipsilateral testis.

Negative Prehn’s Sign: Elevation of the scrotum does NOT relieve pain (or worsens it), unlike acute epididymo-orchitis where elevation relieves pain.

(Differential Diagnosis: Torsion of appendix testis — milder pain at upper pole with pathognomonic ‘Blue dot sign’ and intact cremasteric reflex; Acute epididymo-orchitis; HSP scrotal vasculitis).

Investigations

Clinical Judgment is Paramount: If clinical suspicion of torsion is high, immediate surgical exploration must NOT be delayed for imaging.

High-Resolution Color Doppler Ultrasonography (Investigation of Choice when diagnosis is equivocal):

Demonstrates absent or markedly decreased intratesticular arterial blood flow compared to the normal contralateral testis.

‘Whirlpool Sign’: Coiled, twisted spermatic cord above the testis (most specific sonographic sign).

Heterogeneous parenchymal echogenicity (late sign indicating necrosis/infarction).

Urinalysis: Normal (rules out UTI/epididymo-orchitis).

Management

Golden Window for Testicular Salvage: Salvage rate is  if detorsion is performed within 6 hours of pain onset; drops to  at 12 hours, and  after 24 hours.

Emergency Scrotal Exploration:

Immediate surgical exploration via a median raphe or transverse scrotal incision.

Detorsion & Viability Assessment: Untwist the spermatic cord (usually rotated medially, so manual detorsion is performed outwards like ‘opening a book’) and wrap the testis in warm saline-soaked sponges for 10–15 minutes:

If Testis is Viable (pinks up, bleeds on tunica incision): Perform Ipsilateral Orchidopexy (three-point fixation of tunica albuginea to the dartos pouch using non-absorbable sutures).

If Testis is Non-Viable / Necrotic (black, gangrenous): Perform Orchidectomy (to prevent antisperm antibody formation against the normal testis).

Mandatory Contralateral Orchidopexy: Because the predisposing ‘bell-clapper’ anomaly is almost always bilateral, prophylactic fixation (orchidopexy) of the opposite normal testis MUST be performed during the same surgery to prevent future metachronous torsion and anorchia.

(Covers: Short essay on Role of IMNCI in reducing child morbidity & mortality; IMNCI overview; IMNCI management of a child with acute diarrhea) [KU 18, 16] Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 820–831, 843, 848–850, 854

subject: pediatrics
title: 1. IMNCI Overview & Role in Reducing Child Morbidity and Mortality [KU 16, 18]
text:
Background: The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) strategy was developed by WHO and UNICEF in the mid-1990s. India adapted it in 2003 (revised in 2009 and 2022) by incorporating neonatal care (0–2 months) — the period accounting for  of under-5 deaths — and home-based newborn visits by ASHAs/ANMs, renaming it IMNCI (Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness).

Two Target Age Groups in IMNCI:

Young Infants: Age up to 2 months (0–59 days).

Sick Children: Age 2 months up to 5 years (2–59 months).

Three Core Pillars of IMNCI:

Improving Case Management Skills of Health Workers: Using standard, evidence-based syndromic algorithms and training.

Improving the Overall Health System: Ensuring availability of essential drugs (ORS, Zinc, Amoxicillin, Gentamicin, ACT), vaccines, and referral pathways.

Improving Family and Community Health Practices: Home visits for newborns, exclusive breastfeeding, complementary feeding, care-seeking behavior, and early childhood development.

How IMNCI Reduces Childhood Morbidity and Mortality:

Targets the Leading Killers Together (Integrated Approach): Over  of under-5 deaths in India are caused by neonatal sepsis/asphyxia/LBW, pneumonia, diarrhea, malaria/dengue, measles, and malnutrition. Sick children usually present with overlapping symptoms; IMNCI assesses all major conditions simultaneously rather than treating a single complaint in isolation.

Color-Coded Syndromic Triage & Rapid Referral: Uses simple, sensitive clinical signs (without needing complex lab equipment) to classify illness into 3 Action-Oriented Color Codes:

PINK (Severe Classification): Give urgent pre-referral treatment (first dose of IM Ampicillin + Gentamicin, prevent hypoglycemia with breastmilk/sugar water, keep warm via Kangaroo Mother Care, give ORS sips/Rectal Diazepam) and Refer URGENTLY to Hospital.

YELLOW (Outpatient Treatment): Specific medical treatment initiated at the PHC/clinic (e.g., Oral Amoxicillin for Pneumonia/Local bacterial infection, Plan B ORS + Zinc for Some Dehydration, ACT for Malaria) + teach mother home care + scheduled follow-up visit.

GREEN (Home Management): No antibiotics needed; counsel mother on home care (Plan A for No Dehydration, safe soothing remedies for cough/cold), feeding, and when to return immediately.

Addresses the Malnutrition-Infection Cycle: Every sick child is mandatorily screened for Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) (Weight-for-Length , , or bipedal edema) and Anemia (palmar pallor), and mothers of all children  receive structured age-specific feeding and breastfeeding attachment counseling.

Reduces Missed Opportunities for Prevention: Every sick-child visit is utilized to check and complete routine immunization (NIS), Vitamin A supplementation, biweekly Iron-Folic Acid (IFA) prophylaxis, and biannual Deworming.

Promotes Early Childhood Development (2022 Update): Assesses and counsels mothers on age-appropriate Play and Communication activities to optimize neurodevelopmental outcomes.

title: 2. IMNCI Assessment, Classification & Management of a Child with Acute Diarrhea
text:
Source: Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 824–825, 828, 843, 848–850, 854

Step 1: Assess the Child with Diarrhea

ASK: (1) For how long has the child had diarrhea? (); (2) Is there blood in the stool? ().

LOOK and FEEL (4 Key Signs for Dehydration):

Look at the child’s general condition: Is the child lethargic or unconscious? Or restless and irritable?

Look for sunken eyes.

Offer the child fluid: Is the child not able to drink or drinking poorly? Or drinking eagerly, thirsty?

Pinch the skin of the abdomen: Does it go back very slowly () or slowly?

Step 2: Classify & Identify Treatment for Dehydration (IMNCI Chart Page 843)

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-006]]

(Note: If diarrhea  with dehydration  Severe Persistent Diarrhea [PINK]; without dehydration  Persistent Diarrhea [YELLOW] treated with low-lactose/curd diet, Vitamin A, Zinc, and multivitamins. If blood in stool  Dysentery [YELLOW] treated with Oral Cefixime  for 5 days + Zinc).

Step 3: Details of WHO Treatment Plans A, B, and C

WHO Plan A (Treat Diarrhea at Home — 4 Rules of Home Treatment):

Rule 1 — Give Extra Fluids: Continue frequent breastfeeding; give low-osmolarity WHO-ORS () or home-available fluids (rice water, dal water, salted lassi/buttermilk, coconut water, plain water):  after each loose stool in children , and  after each loose stool in children .

Rule 2 — Give Oral Zinc Supplements for 14 Days:  (1/2 tablet) for infants ;  (1 tablet dissolved in breastmilk/ORS) for children  for a full 14 days (reduces duration, severity, and future episodes for 2–3 months).

Rule 3 — Continue Feeding: Never withhold food; give energy-dense mashed foods with oil/ghee and an extra meal daily for 2 weeks after recovery.

Rule 4 — When to Return Immediately: Not able to drink/breastfeed, becomes sicker, develops fever, drinking poorly, or blood in stool.

WHO Plan B (Treat Some Dehydration with ORS in Clinic):

Administer  of WHO-ORS over a 4-hour period in the clinic by cup and spoon (if child vomits, wait 10 minutes and resume more slowly) + Oral Zinc.

Reassess after 4 hours: If no dehydration  switch to Plan A; if still some dehydration  repeat Plan B for 4 hours and start feeding; if worsened to severe dehydration  switch to Plan C.

WHO Plan C (Treat Severe Dehydration Quickly with IV Fluids):

Start IV Ringer’s Lactate (or  Normal Saline if RL unavailable; never plain dextrose) at a total dose of  divided as follows:

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-007]]

(*Repeat the  bolus once if the radial pulse is still very weak or non-detectable). * Give ORS () by mouth as soon as the child can drink (after 3–4 hrs in infants, 1–2 hrs in children), and reassess at 6 hours (infants) or 3 hours (children) to reclassify dehydration.

title: 2. Concise Notes on Frequently Asked Pediatric Drugs [RGU, TU]
text:
1. Paracetamol (Acetaminophen)

Mechanism: Centrally acting inhibitor of prostaglandin synthesis (COX-3 / peroxidase site of COX) with potent antipyretic and analgesic actions, but minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory action.

Indications & Dosage:

Fever and mild-to-moderate pain:  PO every 4–6 hours (; max  or ). IV dose:  q6h ( in neonates/infants ).

Medical closure of hemodynamically significant PDA in preterm neonates:  IV/PO q6h for 3–7 days.

Adverse Effects: Safe in therapeutic doses; skin rash; acute overdose () causes centrilobular hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure (treated with N-acetylcysteine).

2. Uses of Acetazolamide in Pediatrics

Mechanism: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (inhibits HCO₃⁻ reabsorption in proximal renal tubule, reduces CSF production by choroid plexus, and reduces aqueous humor secretion).

Indications & Dosage:

Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor cerebri) & Post-hemorrhagic/Communicating Hydrocephalus:  PO in 3 divided doses.

Glaucoma (congenital/secondary):  PO.

Refractory Epilepsy (absence, myoclonic, catamenial seizures) and episodic ataxia / hypokalemic periodic paralysis: .

Urinary alkalinization (e.g., tumor lysis syndrome) and high-altitude sickness prophylaxis.

Side Effects: Normal anion-gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, renal calculi, paresthesias, drowsiness.

3. Inhaled Bronchodilators & Asthma Drugs: Budesonide, Ipratropium, Leukotriene Modifiers

Budesonide (Inhaled Corticosteroid - ICS):

Uses: First-line long-term controller therapy for persistent bronchial asthma ( via MDI with spacer in 2 divided doses; or nebulized respules  BD) and Acute Laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup) ( nebulized single dose).

Side Effects: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush), dysphonia/hoarseness of voice (prevented by rinsing mouth after use and using a spacer).

Ipratropium Bromide (Inhaled Short-Acting Anticholinergic - SAMA):

Mechanism: Muscarinic () receptor antagonist causing bronchodilation and decreased airway secretions.

Uses: Adjunct to nebulized salbutamol in moderate-to-severe acute asthma exacerbations / status asthmaticus (MDI , 2–4 puffs; or Nebulized solution: ;  every 20 mins for 3 doses in the first hour, then q6h).

Leukotriene Modifiers [TU]:

Montelukast (and Zafirlukast) — Selective  (Cysteinyl Leukotriene) receptor antagonists (Zileuton is a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor).

Uses: Add-on controller therapy in mild-to-moderate persistent asthma, exercise-induced bronchospasm, and allergic rhinitis.

Dosage (Oral once daily in evening): ; ; .

Side Effects: Headache, abdominal pain, and neuropsychiatric events (nightmares, sleep disturbances, agitation, behavioral changes).

4. Corticosteroids in Pediatrics: Uses & Steroid Toxicity

Major Uses of Corticosteroids in Pediatric Practice:

Renal: Idiopathic Nephrotic Syndrome (Prednisolone), Lupus nephritis, Crescentic GN, HSP nephritis.

Respiratory: Acute asthma exacerbation, Croup (single-dose Dexamethasone ), allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, antenatal Betamethasone/Dexamethasone for fetal lung maturation.

Infections (Anti-inflammatory adjunct): Tuberculous meningitis and pericarditis, acute bacterial meningitis (H. influenzae / Pneumococcal — Dexamethasone before first antibiotic dose), severe P. jirovecii pneumonia, neurocysticercosis.

Hematology/Oncology: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL), Hodgkin/Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, acute ITP, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, HLH.

Rheumatology/Cardiology: Acute Rheumatic Carditis with CCF, Systemic JIA, SLE, Juvenile Dermatomyositis, Takayasu arteritis.

Endocrine & Critical Care: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) and adrenal crisis (Hydrocortisone + Fludrocortisone), catecholamine-refractory septic shock, airway/cerebral edema (vasogenic edema around brain tumors), Infantile spasms (West syndrome — ACTH / Prednisolone).

Steroid Toxicity (Adverse Effects of Prolonged Therapy) [TU]:

Growth & Musculoskeletal: Linear growth retardation (stunting), osteoporosis, vertebral compression fractures, avascular necrosis of femoral head, proximal steroid myopathy.

Metabolic & Endocrine: Cushingoid habitus (moon facies, buffalo hump, truncal obesity, striae), suppression of Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) axis (risk of acute adrenal crisis on sudden withdrawal), hyperglycemia/diabetes, hypertension, hypokalemic alkalosis.

Ocular: Posterior subcapsular cataract and steroid-induced glaucoma.

GI, Immune & CNS: Peptic ulceration/gastritis, heightened susceptibility to opportunistic infections (TB, varicella, fungal), behavioral changes/psychosis, and pseudotumor cerebri.

5. Phenytoin, Desmopressin, Rifampicin, Artemisinin & Iron Chelators

Phenytoin Sodium — Indications & Toxicity:

Indications: Status epilepticus (second-line after benzodiazepines: loading dose  IV diluted in Normal Saline [precipitates in dextrose] infused slowly at  under ECG monitoring; maintenance ), generalized tonic-clonic and focal seizures, and digitalis-induced ventricular arrhythmias. (Fosphenytoin is water-soluble, can be given IM or IV faster at ).

Toxicity:

Acute (Dose-dependent / Zero-order kinetics): Vestibulocerebellar toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, drowsiness), hypotension and cardiac arrhythmias on rapid IV infusion, purple glove syndrome on extravasation.

Chronic (Idiosyncratic): Gingival (gum) hyperplasia, hirsutism, coarsening of facial features, megaloblastic anemia (folate antagonism), rickets/osteomalacia (accelerated Vitamin D catabolism), Stevens-Johnson syndrome/DRESS, and Fetal Hydantoin Syndrome (teratogenic).

Indications for Desmopressin (DDAVP — Synthetic V2-Selective Vasopressin Analog):

Central (Neurogenic) Diabetes Insipidus (intranasal  or oral ).

Primary Monosymptomatic Nocturnal Enuresis ( PO at bedtime).

Mild-to-Moderate Hemophilia A and Type 1 von Willebrand Disease (vWD):  IV infusion (releases endogenous Factor VIII and vWF from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies).

Adverse Effects of Rifampicin:

Orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, saliva, and tears (harmless; counsel parents to ensure compliance).

Hepatotoxicity (cholestatic or hepatocellular hepatitis — especially when combined with Isoniazid and Pyrazinamide).

Flu-like syndrome (with intermittent dosing), GI intolerance, immune thrombocytopenia/hemolytic anemia, acute interstitial nephritis, and potent induction of Cytochrome P450 enzymes (reduces efficacy of steroids, anticonvulsants, and antiretrovirals).

Artemisinin Derivatives in Malaria:

Derived from Artemisia annua; fastest-acting blood schizonticides that clear young ring-stage parasites and reduce gametocyte carriage.

Preparations & Uses (NVBDCP Guidelines):

Oral Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) for Uncomplicated P. falciparum Malaria:

Artesunate ( for 3 days) + Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine ( on Day 1) [ACT-SP] (used across India except North-Eastern states) + single-dose Primaquine () on Day 2.

Artemether + Lumefantrine (ACT-AL) twice daily for 3 days (used in North-Eastern states and in infants ).

Parenteral Artesunate (Drug of Choice for Severe / Cerebral Malaria):  IV/IM ( in children weighing ) at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then once daily until the child can take a full 3-day course of oral ACT.

Iron Chelating Agents (Used in Transfusion-Dependent -Thalassemia Major & Acute Iron Poisoning):

Desferrioxamine (Deferoxamine - DFO): Parenteral chelator given as a slow subcutaneous infusion over 8–12 hours via infusion pump (, 5–6 nights/week) or IV in acute iron poisoning (). Excretes iron in both urine (turns urine vin-rosé / orange-red) and bile. Side effects: Ototoxicity (high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss), retinal toxicity, Yersinia enterocolitica sepsis, skeletal growth retardation.

Deferiprone (L1): Oral chelator ( PO in 3 divided doses); low molecular weight allows superior removal of myocardial (cardiac) iron. Side effects: Agranulocytosis/neutropenia (monitor CBC weekly), erosive arthropathy (knee joint), GI upset, zinc deficiency.

Deferasirox (DFX — Most widely used oral chelator): Oral chelator ( PO once daily dispersed in water/juice on empty stomach); excretes iron predominantly via feces/bile. Side effects: Nephrotoxicity (rising serum creatinine, proximal renal tubular acidosis), elevated liver transaminases, skin rash, GI disturbances.

title: 16.1 EPIDEMIOLOGY & DISEASE BURDEN IN INDIA (Pages 449–450)
text:
Burden: Every year, 200,000–250,000 children in India are born with Congenital Heart Disease (CHD); ~100,000 have critical/significant CHD requiring surgery or catheter intervention early in life.

Care Continuum Challenges (Fig. 16.1): Delayed detection/referral  sub-optimal pre-transport stabilization & unsafe transport  delayed presentation (malnutrition, infection, advanced Eisenmenger PAH)  limited pediatric cardiac centers  loss to follow-up.

National Initiatives:

Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK, 2012): National Health Mission (MoHFW) initiative for screening and free treatment of 4 Ds (Defects at birth including CHD, Deficiencies, Diseases, Developmental delays).

Hridyam (Kerala Government): Systematic population-health plan under RBSK for CHD that achieved a 40% reduction in CHD deaths and a 21% reduction in overall IMR (down to 7 per 1000 live births).

subject: pediatrics
title: 16.2 CONGESTIVE CARDIAC FAILURE (CCF) (Pages 450–453)
text:
Definition & Pathophysiology

Congestive Cardiac Failure (CCF): Inability of the heart to maintain an output at rest or during stress necessary for the metabolic needs of the body (systolic failure) and inability to receive blood into ventricular cavities at low pressure during diastole (diastolic failure).

Causes of Diastolic Dysfunction (Table 16.1):

Mitral or tricuspid valve stenosis (elevated atrial pressures with normal ventricular diastolic pressure).

Constrictive pericarditis & Restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Acute ventricular volume overload (acute AR or MR).

Marked ventricular hypertrophy (HCM, storage disorders like Pompe, severe systemic HTN, severe AS or PS).

Myocardial ischemia & Dilated cardiomyopathy (combined systolic and diastolic dysfunction).

Etiology by Age & Time of Onset (Tables 16.2 & 16.3)

By Age Group (Table 16.2):

Infants: CHD (most common in first 1–2 yrs), myocarditis/cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias (SVT , ectopic atrial tachycardia, PJRT, congenital complete heart block), Kawasaki disease with coronary occlusion, pulmonary hypertension (PPHN, upper airway obstruction), severe anemia (Hb  in normal heart;  in diseased heart), hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, neonatal asphyxia, sepsis.

Older Children (): Acute rheumatic fever / RHD, CHD complicated by anemia/infection/infective endocarditis, systemic hypertension (acute GN, Takayasu), myocarditis/cardiomyopathy, primary/secondary PAH.

Time of Onset of CCF in CHD (Table 16.3 — High-Yield Box):

Birth–1 week: Duct-dependent systemic circulation (Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome [HLHS], critical aortic stenosis, severe coarctation, interrupted aortic arch), obstructed TAPVC, congenital MR/TR, neonatal Ebstein anomaly. (Note: Congenital TR manifests at birth when PA pressure is high and improves as PVR falls).

1–4 weeks: PDA in preterms, VSD with coarctation, persistent truncus arteriosus, d-TGA with large VSD/PDA, critical AS/coarctation, single ventricle with unobstructed pulmonary flow.

1–2 months (6–8 weeks): Large LR shunts (VSD, PDA, endocardial cushion/AV canal defects) as neonatal PVR regresses; unobstructed TAPVC; ALCAPA.

2–6 months: VSD, PDA, endocardial cushion defect, ALCAPA, coarctation. (Early CCF in a simple shunt lesion should prompt a search for associated coarctation of aorta).

Clinical Features (Tables 16.4 & 16.5)

Symptoms in Infants: Poor feeding (suck-rest-suck cycle: takes , tires out, gets hungry again in minutes), tachypnea that worsens during feeds, relief of dyspnea when held upright against mother’s shoulder (infant orthopnea), excessive diaphoresis (forehead/occiput sweating), failure to thrive (or acute weight gain from fluid retention), irritability, hoarse cry, wheezing.

Signs:

Impaired Myocardial Performance (Both L & R failure): Cardiomegaly, resting tachycardia, S3 gallop rhythm, weak peripheral pulses, cold extremities, prolonged CRT, pulsus alternans.

Left-Sided Failure (Pulmonary Venous Congestion): Tachypnea, subcostal/intercostal retractions, persistent cough (on lying down), wheezing (basal rales are usually absent in infants).

Right-Sided Failure (Systemic Venous Congestion): Tender hepatomegaly, facial puffiness (JVP is difficult to assess in infants; pedal edema occurs very late).

Management of CCF (Four-Pronged Approach & Fig. 16.4)

Reducing Cardiac Work:

General: Restrict activity; nurse neonate in incubator (, thermoneutral) propped up at  incline; minimal handling.

Oxygen: Humidified  () if hypoxic. (Avoid indiscriminate  in large LR shunts as it lowers PVR and worsens pulmonary overcirculation at the expense of systemic perfusion).

Treat Anemia/Fever/Infection: Transfuse packed RBCs ( slowly with a prior single IV dose of furosemide). Mechanical ventilation if severe CCF.

Vasodilators (Afterload Reduction):

ACE Inhibitors (Captopril, Enalapril): Suppress RAAS. Start at 1/4th calculated dose to avoid first-dose hypotension; monitor Cr and K⁺ every 1–2 wks. Contraindicated in neonates and dehydration (risk of AKI). Switch to Losartan if persistent dry cough.

Beta-Blockers: Carvedilol (, max ) or Metoprolol in chronic DCM with tachycardia. (Avoid calcium channel blockers in HF).

Acute IV Vasodilators: Sodium nitroprusside, Nitrates (venodilator).

Improving Cardiac Performance by Reducing Preload (Diuretics — Table 16.6):

Furosemide:  PO (onset 20 min) or  IV.

Spironolactone (Aldosterone antagonist):  PO q12h (prevents K⁺/Mg²⁺ loss; synergistic with ACE inhibitors).

Augmenting Myocardial Contractility (Inotropes — Table 16.6):

Digoxin:

Oral Total Digitalizing Dose (TDD): Preterms/Neonates: ; 1 mo–1 yr: ; 1–3 yrs: ; : . (1/2 stat, 1/4th at 8h, 1/4th at 16h; IV dose =  of oral dose).

Maintenance Dose: ~1/4th of TDD daily (Preterm/Neonate: ; 1m–1y: ; 1–3y: ; : ).

Parenteral Inotropes & Inodilators:

Dopamine ( renal/vasodilatory;  inotropic;  vasoconstrictor), Dobutamine (), Adrenaline.

PDE-3 Inhibitors (Inodilators): Milrinone ( loading, then ; omit loading if hypotensive).

Calcium Sensitizer: Levosimendan ( loading over 10 min, then  — potent inodilator without arrhythmia risk).

Correcting the Underlying Cause: Early surgical/catheter correction.

Clinical Risk-Based Algorithm (Fig. 16.4):

Not in Shock: Oral Furosemide + Spironolactone + Enalapril  Digoxin  Add Carvedilol once compensated.

Borderline Hemodynamics (Compensated Shock): IV Furosemide + Dobutamine/Dopamine + Milrinone.

Decompensated Shock: Mechanical ventilation + Adrenaline/Noradrenaline + Milrinone/Levosimendan.

title: 16.3 CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE: GENERAL CONCEPTS (Pages 454–464)

Fetal Circulation (Fig. 16.5): Placenta ()  Umbilical vein  Ductus venosus bypasses liver  IVC (,  from SVC +  from IVC)  Crista dividens directs  () across Foramen ovale to LA  LV ()  Ascending aorta (coronaries/brain). Remaining  IVC + SVC stream enters RV (, )  PA  only  enters high-resistance lungs;  shunts across Ductus arteriosus into Descending aorta ().

Five Key Physiological Concepts in CHD (Table 16.10)

Pre-Tricuspid vs. Post-Tricuspid Shunts:

Pre-tricuspid (ASD, PAPVD): Shunt occurs at low atrial pressures and is determined by relative ventricular compliance (RV vs LV stiffness). Because neonatal RV is thick/non-compliant, shunt is minimal in infancy and CCF/PAH is rare in childhood; causes RA & RV diastolic volume overload and wide fixed S2.

Post-tricuspid (VSD, PDA, AP window): High systemic pressure is transmitted directly to PA; shunt depends on defect size and PVR:SVR ratio. Causes LA & LV diastolic volume overload, apical mid-diastolic flow rumble, CCF at 6–8 weeks, and early hyperkinetic PAH progressing to obstructive PVOD.

VSD-PS (Fallot) Physiology: Large unrestrictive VSD equalizes RV and LV pressures; severity of PS determines RL shunt and cyanosis. Includes: (1) TOF, (2) d-TGA + VSD + PS, (3) DORV + VSD + PS, (4) Tricuspid atresia + PS, (5) Single ventricle + PS, (6) Corrected TGA (l-TGA) + VSD + PS.

Single Ventricle Physiology: Complete mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous blood (Double-inlet LV, Tricuspid/Mitral atresia, HLHS).

Staged Surgical Palliation: Stage 1 (Neonate/<3 mo): PA banding (if unobstructed high pulmonary flow) OR Modified BT shunt / PDA stenting (if PS/reduced pulmonary flow). Stage 2 (4–6 months): Bidirectional Glenn (BDG) shunt (SVC anastomosed to Right PA). Stage 3 (4–6 years): Fontan Operation (IVC also routed to PA, separating circulations and eliminating cyanosis).

Duct-Dependent Lesions (Require IV Prostaglandin  [] to keep PDA open):

Duct-Dependent Systemic Circulation (DDSC — Presents with shock/acidosis as duct closes): HLHS, Critical AS, Severe Coarctation, Interrupted Aortic Arch.

Duct-Dependent Pulmonary Circulation (DDPC — Presents with severe cyanosis as duct closes): Pulmonary atresia (with intact septum or VSD), Critical PS, Tricuspid atresia with pulmonary atresia, severe neonatal Ebstein anomaly (‘functional pulmonary atresia’).

Unfavorable Streaming & Parallel Circulation: Seen in d-TGA with intact ventricular septum; survival depends on intercirculatory mixing at the atrial level (patent foramen ovale / Rashkind balloon atrial septostomy).

Nadas’ Criteria, Second Heart Sound (S2), Interventions & Natural History

Nadas’ Criteria (Table 16.11): 1 Major (Systolic murmur  Grade III or any PSM, Diastolic murmur, Central cyanosis, CCF) OR 2 Minor (Systolic murmur Grade I–II, Abnormal S2, Abnormal ECG, Abnormal CXR, Abnormal BP).

Second Heart Sound (S2) Abnormalities (Fig. 16.7):

Loud A2: Systemic HTN, AR, d-TGA/TOF (anterior aorta). Soft/Delayed A2: Valvar AS, LBBB, large PDA.

Loud P2: Pulmonary arterial hypertension. Soft/Delayed P2: Pulmonic stenosis.

Wide Fixed Split ( in expiration, no change with inspiration): ASD, TAPVC, RBBB.

Wide Variable Split: PS (delayed P2), VSD / MR (early A2).

Single S2: TOF, Pulmonary atresia, Truncus arteriosus, Eisenmenger VSD.

Paradoxical (Reversed) Split (P2 before A2): Severe AS, LBBB, large PDA.

Catheter-Based Interventions in CHD (Table 16.12):

Device/Coil Closure: Fossa ovalis (secundum) ASD with adequate rims; PDA (except very large ducts in tiny infants); Muscular VSD (); Selected perimembranous VSDs (small risk of complete heart block); Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm; Coronary AV fistula; Pulmonary AV malformation.

Balloon Valvotomy / Angioplasty / Stenting: Balloon Pulmonary Valvuloplasty (treatment of choice for valvar PS); Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty (valvar AS); Coarctation of aorta (surgery preferred in neonates due to  restenosis with balloon; balloon  stenting in older children ); Branch PA stenosis (stenting); PDA stenting in DDPC; Rashkind Balloon Atrial Septostomy in d-TGA.

Spontaneous Closure of Heart Defects (Table 16.13):

ASD: Fossa ovalis defects  diagnosed in infancy often close by 3 years. Ostium primum, Sinus venosus, and Coronary sinus ASDs NEVER close spontaneously.

VSD: Muscular and perimembranous VSDs frequently close ( become smaller/close by 3 yrs). Inlet VSDs and malaligned VSDs (TOF) NEVER close; outlet (subpulmonic) VSDs may ‘close’ via aortic cusp prolapse causing AR (indication for surgery).

Fetal Echocardiography: Performed at 14–16 weeks (optimal at 18–20 weeks); recurrence risk of CHD in subsequent pregnancies is  (highest in left-sided obstructive lesions).

title: 16.4 ACYANOTIC CONGENITAL HEART DEFECTS (Pages 464–471)
text:
1. Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)

Anatomical Types:

Ostium Secundum (Fossa Ovalis) ASD (): Mid-septal defect; amenable to transcatheter device closure if rims are .

Ostium Primum ASD (): Lower atrial septum adjacent to AV valves (partial AV canal defect); associated with a cleft anterior mitral leaflet causing MR.

Sinus Venosus ASD (): Superior (at SVC-RA junction) or Inferior (IVC-RA junction); consistently associated with Partial Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (PAPVC) of right pulmonary veins.

Coronary Sinus ASD (): Unroofed coronary sinus (associated with persistent left SVC).

Clinical Features: Usually asymptomatic in infancy/childhood. Mild left parasternal impulse (RV enlargement), wide and fixed split S2, Grade II–III/VI pulmonary ejection systolic murmur (ESM) at left 2nd ICS (due to increased flow across pulmonary valve), and a soft tricuspid mid-diastolic flow rumble at LLSB (if Qp:Qs ).

ECG:

Ostium Secundum ASD: Right Axis Deviation (RAD) and incomplete RBBB ( pattern in lead V1).

Ostium Primum ASD: Extreme Left Axis Deviation (LAD, ).

CXR & Echo: Mild cardiomegaly (RA and RV enlargement; LA is NOT enlarged), prominent main PA segment, small aortic knuckle, pulmonary plethora. Subcostal 2D Echo views best delineate defect size and rims.

Treatment: Elective closure at 3–5 years of age (before school entry) if Qp:Qs  with RV volume overload — via transcatheter device closure (for secundum ASD with adequate rims) or surgical closure (for primum, sinus venosus, or rim-deficient secundum defects).
