title: 16.5 CYANOTIC CONGENITAL HEART DISEASES (Pages 471–480)
text:
1. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) (Tables 16.14–16.15 & Fig. 16.23)

Anatomic Variations (Table 16.14): (1) TOF with Absent Pulmonary Valve (aneurysmal branch PAs compressing bronchi  severe neonatal stridor/wheezing); (2) Anomalous LAD coronary artery arising from RCA crossing the RVOT (precludes transannular ventriculotomy  requires RV-to-PA conduit); (3) Right aortic arch (); (4) MAPCAs (major aortopulmonary collaterals).

Summary of TOF & Cyanotic Spell Management (Table 16.15):

Clinical: Central cyanosis, clubbing, squatting, normal JVP, quiet precordium, single loud S2 (A2), aortic ejection click, and RVOT ESM at L 2nd/3rd ICS (inversely proportional to severity).

CXR: ‘Coeur en Sabot’ (Boot-shaped heart) with upturned apex, concave pulmonary bay, oligemic lungs, right aortic arch (). ECG: RAD + RVH (tall R in V1, rS in V2).

Cyanotic Spell Protocol: (1) Knee-chest position; (2) ; (3) Morphine ( SC) or Ketamine ( IM); (4) Normal saline bolus () + Sodium bicarbonate ( IV); (5) IV Metoprolol ( over 5 min, up to 3 doses); (6) Phenylephrine ( bolus, then ) or Methoxamine; (7) Intubation/ventilation & emergency Modified BT shunt or Intracardiac Repair (VSD patch closure + infundibular resection, preserving pulmonary valve if possible to avoid late chronic PR, RV dilation, and ventricular arrhythmias).

2. Tricuspid Atresia (Fig. 16.26)

Anatomy & Hemodynamics: Complete congenital absence of the tricuspid valve with a hypoplastic RV. Systemic venous blood in RA must cross an obligatory ASD/PFO (RL shunt) into LA  complete mixing in LA  enters large LV  reaches hypoplastic RV and PA via a muscular VSD. ( have reduced pulmonary blood flow;  have transposed great arteries with increased pulmonary flow).

Distinguishing Clinical & ECG Features (vs. TOF):

Cyanotic from birth with anoxic spells, prominent ‘a’ waves in JVP and presystolic hepatic pulsations (if ASD is restrictive), Left Ventricular type of apical impulse (unlike RV impulse in TOF), single S2.

ECG (Pathognomonic): Superior / Left Axis Deviation (LAD, around ) + Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH) and tall P waves in a cyanotic infant!

Treatment: Single ventricle staged palliation (BT shunt/PA band  Bidirectional Glenn at 4–6 mo  Fontan at 4–6 yrs).

3. Ebstein Anomaly (Figs. 16.27–16.29)

Anatomy & Hemodynamics: Congenital downward apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve into the RV cavity  divides RV into a thin-walled ‘atrialized RV’ and a small functional distal RV  severe tricuspid regurgitation + massive RA dilation + RL shunt across PFO/ASD (cyanosis). High incidence () of right-sided accessory pathways (WPW syndrome and SVT).

Clinical Features: Cyanosis (severe in neonates, mild in older children), episodic palpitations (SVT), quiet precordium, widely split S1 (‘sail sound’), widely split S2, triple or quadruple gallop rhythm (S3 + S4) with a scratchy holosystolic TR murmur and mid-diastolic rumble.

ECG: Giant ‘Himalayan’ P waves (RA enlargement), Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB) with low-voltage R wave () in V1, and WPW pre-excitation (delta waves).

CXR: Massive box-shaped / balloon-shaped cardiomegaly (huge RA) with oligemic lung fields.

Treatment: Cone repair of the tricuspid valve + plication of atrialized RV + radiofrequency ablation of accessory pathways.

4. Transposition of Great Vessels (d-TGA & l-TGA) (Figs. 16.30–16.32)

d-TGA (Complete Transposition):

Anatomy: Ventriculo-arterial discordance — Aorta arises from RV (anterior and to the right of PA) and PA arises from LV  two parallel circulations (PA  is higher than Aortic ).

Presentation:

d-TGA with Intact Ventricular Septum: Presents in the first few days of life with profound central cyanosis and acidemia, single loud S2, and no significant murmur.

d-TGA with Large VSD: Milder cyanosis but presents at 4–10 weeks with severe CCF and rapid development of Eisenmenger PVOD within 2–3 months.

CXR: ‘Egg-on-side’ (or ‘Egg-on-string’) cardiac silhouette with a narrow superior mediastinal pedicle (due to anteroposterior great vessel relationship and absent thymic shadow) and plethoric lung fields.

Management: (1) IV Prostaglandin  infusion; (2) Rashkind Balloon Atrial Septostomy (BAS) for immediate intercirculatory mixing; (3) Arterial Switch Operation (ASO / Jatene procedure) with coronary button transfer — must be performed within the first 3–4 weeks of life in d-TGA with intact septum (before LV muscle mass regresses as PVR falls; if presenting late, LV training via PA band + BT shunt or Senning atrial switch is needed) and within 2–3 months in d-TGA with VSD.

Corrected TGA (l-TGA):

Atrioventricular AND Ventriculo-arterial discordance (RA  morphologic LV  PA; LA  morphologic RV  Aorta). Circulation is physiologically corrected, but presents with the classic Triad of Associated Anomalies ( each): (1) VSD  Pulmonic stenosis, (2) Left-sided Ebstein-like malformation of the systemic tricuspid valve (causes systemic AV valve regurgitation), and (3) Spontaneous Complete Heart Block ( per year).

ECG: Reversal of septal activation — Q waves present in V4R, V1 and absent in V5, V6. CXR: Straight left upper cardiac border formed by the ascending aorta.

5. Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC) (Figs. 16.33–16.34)

Anatomy: All four pulmonary veins fail to connect to the LA and drain anomalously into the systemic venous circulation/RA, with an obligatory RL shunt across an ASD/PFO ( is identical in RA, PA, LA, and Aorta).

Four Anatomical Types: (1) Supracardiac ( — Most common): Common pulmonary venous confluence drains via a left vertical vein into the left innominate vein  SVC  RA; (2) Cardiac (): Drains into coronary sinus or RA; (3) Infracardiac (): Drains via a descending vein through the esophageal hiatus into the portal vein or ductus venosus (ALWAYS obstructed); (4) Mixed ().

Two Clinical Presentations:

Obstructed TAPVC (Surgical Emergency in 1st week of life): Severe cyanosis, tachypnea, pulmonary edema, loud P2, no murmur. CXR: Normal-sized heart with diffuse ‘ground-glass’ reticular pulmonary venous congestion (mimics hyaline membrane disease/RDS!). (Note: PGE1 is unhelpful/harmful in obstructed TAPVC; requires emergency surgical repair).

Unobstructed TAPVC: Presents at 4–10 weeks with CCF, mild cyanosis, failure to thrive, and auscultatory findings identical to a large ASD (wide fixed split S2, pulmonary ESM, tricuspid MDM) + continuous venous hum at left upper sternal border. CXR: Cardiomegaly, plethora, and characteristic ‘Snowman’ or ‘Figure-of-8’ configuration (seen after 2 years of age in supracardiac TAPVC).

title: 16.7 RHEUMATIC FEVER, RHD & INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS (Pages 484–496)
text:
1. Chronic Rheumatic Valvular Heart Disease (MR, MS, AR, TR)

Mitral Regurgitation (MR — Most common lesion in children):

Hemodynamics: Systolic regurgitant leak into LA + diastolic volume overload of LA and LV.

Signs: Hyperdynamic, displaced LV apex; soft/masked S1; wide variable split S2 (early A2); apical S3 gallop; high-pitched blowing pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla and back; short mid-diastolic flow murmur (without presystolic accentuation) in severe MR.

Juvenile Mitral Stenosis (MS):

Hemodynamics: Elevated LA pressure  pulmonary venous congestion  reactive pulmonary arterial hypertension  concentric RVH.

Signs: Malar flush, low-volume pulse, tapping apex (palpable S1), left parasternal heave, palpable P2; loud snapping S1, loud P2, high-pitched Opening Snap (OS) medial to apex (shorter A2–OS interval = more severe MS), and a low-pitched rough mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation at the apex.

Treatment: Diuretics + Beta-blockers/Digoxin (slows HR to improve diastolic filling) + Percutaneous Trans-septal Mitral Commissurotomy (PTMC / Balloon Mitral Valvotomy).

Aortic Regurgitation (AR):

Peripheral Signs of Wide Pulse Pressure: Corrigan (water-hammer) collapsing pulse, Corrigan sign (dancing carotids), de Musset sign (systolic head nodding), Quincke sign (capillary pulsations), Traube sign (pistol-shot femoral sounds), Duroziez sign (systolic murmur on proximal femoral compression, diastolic murmur on distal compression), and Hill sign (popliteal systolic BP exceeding brachial systolic BP by : Mild , Moderate , Severe ).

Auscultation: Heaving displaced LV apex; high-pitched blowing decrescendo early diastolic murmur along the left sternal border (erb’s area), best heard sitting up and leaning forward in expiration; Austin-Flint apical diastolic rumble.

2. Infective Endocarditis: Antibiotic Regimens & AHA Prophylaxis (Tables 16.18 & 16.19)

Empirical & Organism-Specific IV Therapy (Table 16.18):

Streptococcus viridans / Group A Strep: Penicillin G (or Ceftriaxone) + Aminoglycoside (Gentamicin) for 4 weeks.

Enterococcus (S. faecalis): Ampicillin (or Vancomycin) + Gentamicin for 4–6 weeks.

Staphylococcus aureus: Cloxacillin / Cefazolin (or Vancomycin if MRSA) + Gentamicin for 6 weeks.

Gram-negative (E. coli / Pseudomonas): Ceftriaxone / Meropenem + Aminoglycoside for 6 weeks.

Culture-Negative IE: Ampicillin + Gentamicin for 6 weeks.

Fungal IE (Candida): IV Amphotericin B + Early Surgical Valve Excision/Replacement, followed by  of antifungal therapy.

AHA Indications for Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis (Table 16.19 — High-Yield Box): Prophylaxis is NO LONGER recommended for routine acyanotic defects (VSD, PDA, ASD, bicuspid aortic valve, MR/MS). It is indicated ONLY for the highest-risk cardiac conditions prior to dental procedures involving gingival manipulation/periapical region/mucosal perforation or invasive respiratory tract incisions:

Prosthetic cardiac valves or prosthetic material used for cardiac valve repair.

Previous history of Infective Endocarditis.

Uncorrected cyanotic CHD, including palliative shunts and conduits (e.g., BT shunt).

Completely repaired CHD with prosthetic material/device during the first 6 months after the procedure (until endothelialization occurs).

Repaired CHD with residual defects at or adjacent to the site of a prosthetic patch or device (which inhibit endothelialization).

Cardiac transplantation recipients who develop cardiac valvulopathy.

Regimen: Single oral dose of Amoxicillin  (max ) given 30–60 minutes before the procedure (Not recommended for GI or genitourinary tract procedures).

title: 16.8 MYOCARDIAL, PERICARDIAL, COVID-19 (MIS-C), HYPERTENSION & RHYTHM DISORDERS (Pages 496–512)
text:
1. Myocardial Diseases & Correctable Causes of LV Dysfunction (Table 16.20)

Must-Exclude Correctable Causes of Dilated Cardiomyopathy / LV Dysfunction in Children (Table 16.20):

Congenital: ALCAPA (Anomalous Left Coronary Artery from Pulmonary Artery), Severe Coarctation of Aorta, Critical Aortic Stenosis.

Acquired Vascular/Inflammatory: Takayasu arteritis, Severe systemic hypertension.

Incessant Tachyarrhythmias (Tachycardiomyopathy): Ectopic atrial tachycardia (EAT), Permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia (PJRT), chronic atrial flutter.

Metabolic & Nutritional: Hypocalcemia (vitamin D deficiency/hypoparathyroidism in infants — prolonged QTc), Infantile Beri-Beri (thiamine deficiency), Primary Carnitine deficiency, Hypophosphatemia, Selenium deficiency (Keshan disease).

ALCAPA: Presents at 2–4 months with crying/sweating during feeds (angina), cardiomegaly, CCF, and MR murmur. ECG shows anterolateral myocardial infarction pattern (deep wide Q waves , ST elevation, and T-wave inversion in leads I, aVL, V5, V6). Echo shows dilated RCA and retrograde flow from LCA into PA. Treated by surgical coronary reimplantation into the aorta.

Pompe Disease (GSD Type II): Presents in early infancy with profound hypotonia, macroglossia, hepatomegaly, and massive biventricular HCM. ECG is pathognomonic: Very short PR interval () + Giant QRS voltages.

Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM): Autosomal dominant sarcomeric mutations or RASopathies (Noonan). Features: Jerky/bisferiens pulse, S4, apical/LSE ejection systolic murmur that increases in intensity on standing or Valsalva (decreases LV volume) and decreases on squatting (increases LV volume). Echo shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and Systolic Anterior Motion (SAM) of anterior mitral leaflet. Treated with Beta-blockers (Propranolol/Metoprolol) and ICD for high sudden-death risk (Digoxin, inotropes, vasodilators, and diuretics are contraindicated).

2. SARS-CoV-2 Associated MIS-C & Pericardial Diseases (Pages 500–501)

MIS-C (Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children): Post-infectious hyperinflammatory shock occurring 2–6 weeks after SARS-CoV-2 exposure. Features LV systolic dysfunction, cardiogenic/vasoplegic shock, coronary artery dilation/aneurysms, AV block, and thrombosis. Labs: High CRP, ESR, ferritin, IL-6, D-dimer, fibrinogen, BNP, and troponin. Treatment: IVIG () + IV Methylprednisolone ( or pulse )  Biologics (Anakinra, Tocilizumab, Infliximab) + Low-dose Aspirin () + Therapeutic anticoagulation (LMWH if D-dimer , severe LV dysfunction, or giant coronary aneurysm).

Acute Pericarditis & Cardiac Tamponade:

Pericarditis: Sharp precordial pain relieved by sitting up and leaning forward, triphasic pericardial friction rub, diffuse concave-upward ST elevation on ECG.

Cardiac Tamponade: Beck’s Triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised JVP), pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory drop in systolic BP ), low-voltage QRS / electrical alternans on ECG, RA and RV diastolic collapse on Echo. Treated by emergency pericardiocentesis.

Chronic Constrictive Pericarditis: Most commonly tuberculous in India. Features elevated JVP with prominent ‘y’ descent (Friedreich sign), Kussmaul sign (inspiratory rise in JVP), pulsatile hepatomegaly, ascites out of proportion to pedal edema, quiet precordium, and an early diastolic pericardial knock. Treated by surgical pericardiectomy + ATT.

3. Systemic Hypertension in Children (AAP 2017 Guidelines — Tables 16.22–16.26)

Blood Pressure Cuff Selection (Table 16.24): Bladder width must be  of mid-arm circumference (midway between acromion and olecranon) and bladder length must cover  of arm circumference (Measured in the right arm after 5–10 min rest; Korotkoff Phase I = SBP, Phase V = DBP).

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-011]]

Ambulatory BP Monitoring (ABPM): Gold standard to confirm HTN, predict target-organ damage (LVH), and identify White-Coat HTN (Clinic BP , ABPM ) and Masked HTN (Clinic BP , ABPM  — common in CKD and repaired coarctation).

Treatment Target: Reduce BP to  (or  in ). First-line oral drugs: ACE Inhibitors (Enalapril) / ARBs (Losartan) (drugs of choice in CKD, diabetes, proteinuria) or Calcium Channel Blockers (Amlodipine).

Hypertensive Emergency Management (Table 16.26): Continuous IV infusion of Nicardipine ( — preferred due to safety), Labetalol (), or Sodium Nitroprusside (; risk of cyanide toxicity). Rule of BP Reduction: Lower BP by no more than  of the planned reduction over the first 8 hours (~ in the 1st hour), and gradually normalize over the next 24–36 hours to prevent cerebral/retinal ischemia.

4. Rhythm Disorders (Tables 16.27–16.34 & Figs. 16.50, 16.55)

CHD-Specific Arrhythmias (Table 16.29):

Sick Sinus Syndrome: Sinus venosus ASD, AV canal defect, Holt-Oram, Left atrial isomerism, post-Senning/Fontan.

WPW & Narrow QRS SVT: Ebstein anomaly, Corrected TGA (l-TGA).

Complete Heart Block: Maternal Lupus (Anti-Ro/La), Corrected TGA (l-TGA), post-VSD/AVSD surgical repair.

Management of Narrow QRS Tachycardia (SVT — HR  in infants,  in children, absent P waves / beat-to-beat variability — Fig. 16.50):

Hemodynamically Stable:

Vagal Maneuvers: Apply an ice-filled plastic bag over the face for 15–20 seconds in infants (diving reflex); Valsalva maneuver (blowing into a syringe) or carotid massage in older children (Eyeball pressure is CONTRAINDICATED due to retinal detachment).

Drug of Choice — ADENOSINE:  (, range , max ) rapid IV bolus via two-syringe/three-way stopcock technique into a proximal vein, immediately flushed with  normal saline. May repeat at  (max ).

Hemodynamically Unstable (Shock/Heart Failure): Immediate Synchronized DC Cardioversion at  (after IV Midazolam sedation if possible).

Definitive Cure: Catheter Radiofrequency Ablation (RFA) in children .

Management of Wide QRS Tachycardia (Ventricular Tachycardia — Fig. 16.55):

Stable with Pulse: Trial of Adenosine (if SVT with aberrancy suspected)  IV Amiodarone ( over 20–60 min), Procainamide ( over 30–60 min), or Lidocaine ( bolus).

Unstable with Pulse: Synchronized DC Cardioversion ().

Pulseless VT / Ventricular Fibrillation: Asynchronous Defibrillation () + CPR. (Torsades de pointes is treated with IV Magnesium Sulfate ).

title: 17.1 RENAL PHYSIOLOGY, ACIDIFICATION, MATURATION & EVALUATION (Pages 513–520)
text:
Tubular Sodium Handling (Fig. 17.1): Proximal Convolution Tubule (PCT) reabsorbs  of filtered Na⁺ (via Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger NHE3 and Na⁺-glucose/amino acid/phosphate cotransporters, exiting basolaterally via Na⁺/HCO₃⁻ cotransporter NBCe1); Thick Ascending Limb of Loop of Henle (TAL) reabsorbs  (via furosemide-sensitive NKCC2 cotransporter); Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT) reabsorbs  (via thiazide-sensitive NCC cotransporter); Cortical Collecting Duct (Principal cells) reabsorbs  via aldosterone-regulated, amiloride-sensitive Epithelial Sodium Channel (ENaC) in exchange for K⁺ (via ROMK) and H⁺.

Renal Acidification (Figs. 17.2 & 17.3):

PCT: Reabsorbs  of filtered HCO₃⁻ (catalyzed by luminal brush-border Carbonic Anhydrase IV and cytosolic CA II) and synthesizes NH₄⁺ from glutamine.

Distal Tubule / Collecting Duct (-Intercalated Cells): Secretes H⁺ into lumen via apical H⁺-ATPase and H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (buffered by urinary HPO₄²⁻ [titratable acid] and  to lower urine pH to ), while reclaimed HCO₃⁻ exits basolaterally via Anion Exchanger 1 (AE1 / SLC4A1).

Maturation of Renal Function: Glomerular filtration begins at 5–9 weeks gestation (beyond 16 weeks, amniotic fluid is chiefly fetal urine). At birth, GFR is low ( in term,  in preterm), doubles by 2 weeks, and reaches adult levels () by 2 years of age. Maximum urinary concentrating ability is  in neonates vs.  in older children.

Diagnostic Evaluation:

Modified Schwartz Formula for eGFR: , where  ().

Most Accurate GFR Markers: Inulin clearance (reference standard), Plasma Iohexol clearance, Serum Cystatin C (independent of muscle mass/malnutrition), and  clearance.

Water Deprivation + DDAVP Challenge Test (Table 17.1): After fluid deprivation (until  weight loss or plasma osmolality ), administer intranasal () or IM () Desmopressin (DDAVP):

Central Diabetes Insipidus: Urine osmolality rises to .

Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus: Urine osmolality fails to rise and remains .

title: 17.2 HEMATURIA, PROTEINURIA & GLOMERULONEPHRITIS (Pages 520–527, 533–534)
text:
1. Approach to Hematuria & Alport Syndrome (Tables 17.2 & 17.3, Fig. 17.7)

Definition: Presence of  in a centrifuged fresh urine specimen ( for 10 min).

Glomerular vs. Non-Glomerular Hematuria (Table 17.3 & Fig. 17.7):

Glomerular: Brown/cola/tea-colored urine, no clots, no dysuria,  Dysmorphic RBCs (acanthocytes on phase-contrast microscopy), RBC casts, proteinuria , hypertension/edema.

Non-Glomerular: Bright red blood, clots, dysuria/flank pain,  dysmorphic RBCs, no casts, proteinuria  (e.g., Idiopathic hypercalciuria — spot urine calcium:creatinine ratio  or 24-hr urinary calcium ; UTI; stones; Nutcracker syndrome — compression of left renal vein between aorta and superior mesenteric artery causing orthostatic/exercise hematuria).

Alport Syndrome (Hereditary Nephritis):

Genetics: Mutations in Type IV Collagen -chains —  X-linked (COL4A5),  Autosomal Recessive or Dominant (COL4A3, COL4A4).

Clinical Triad: (1) Persistent microscopic hematuria with episodic gross hematuria, proteinuria, and progressive CKD/ESKD by adolescence/young adulthood; (2) Bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss; (3) Ocular anomalies (Anterior lenticonus — pathognomonic ‘oil-droplet’ reflex, macular flecks, cataract).

Electron Microscopy (Diagnostic — Fig. 17.9): Irregular thickening, thinning, splitting, and lamellation of the Glomerular Basement Membrane (‘Basket-weave’ appearance).

Treatment: ACE Inhibitors (Enalapril/Ramipril) delay progression to ESKD.

2. Quantitation & Causes of Proteinuria (Table 17.4)

Urinary Protein Excretion (Timed 24-hour or First-Morning Spot Urine Protein:Creatinine Ratio [UPCR]):

Normal:  (or ) | Spot UPCR  ( in infants ).

Mild-to-Moderate (Sub-nephrotic):  () | Spot UPCR .

Heavy (Nephrotic-range):  () | Spot UPCR  (Dipstick 3+ or 4+).

Orthostatic (Postural) Proteinuria: Benign condition in tall adolescents; proteinuria is absent in the first-morning void (UPCR ) collected immediately upon waking after overnight recumbence, but present in upright afternoon samples ().

3. Spectrum of Glomerulonephritis (PSGN, RPGN, IgAN, Lupus, C3G, TINU)

Post-Streptococcal GN (PSGN): Covered in detail in Section 15.2 above. (Key: Subepithelial ‘humps’ on EM, starry-sky IgG + C3 on IF, low C3 normalizing in 8–12 weeks; Biopsy indications in Table 17.6).

Crescentic Glomerulonephritis (Rapidly Progressive GN — RPGN):

Acute nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of GFR over days to weeks and crescents in  of glomeruli.

Three Immunopathological Types:

Type I (Anti-GBM Disease / Goodpasture): Linear IgG deposits along GBM; normal C3.

Type II (Immune-Complex Mediated — Most common in children): Granular IgG/IgA and C3 deposits (Post-infectious, Lupus nephritis, IgA vasculitis, IgA nephropathy, C3G).

Type III (Pauci-Immune): Scant/absent immune deposits on IF; ANCA-positive small-vessel vasculitis (Microscopic polyangiitis [p-ANCA/MPO], Granulomatosis with polyangiitis [c-ANCA/PR3]).

Treatment: IV Methylprednisolone pulses () + Oral Prednisolone + IV Cyclophosphamide pulses + Plasmapheresis (for anti-GBM and dialysis-dependent ANCA vasculitis) / Rituximab.

IgA Nephropathy (Berger Disease):

Presents with recurrent episodes of gross hematuria occurring within 1–2 days of an upper respiratory infection (‘synpharyngitic hematuria’), with normal serum C3. Biopsy shows mesangial proliferation with dominant mesangial IgA1 deposits (scored by MEST-C Oxford classification). Treated with ACE inhibitors; steroids/immunosuppression if nephrotic proteinuria or crescents.

Lupus Nephritis:

Occurs in  of pediatric SLE; ‘Full-house’ immunofluorescence (glomerular deposits of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C4, and C1q), low serum C3 and C4, positive ANA and anti-dsDNA.

ISN/RPS Classification: Class I (Minimal mesangial), Class II (Mesangial proliferative), Class III (Focal proliferative,  glomeruli), Class IV (Diffuse proliferative,  glomeruli — most common and severe), Class V (Membranous), Class VI (Advanced sclerosing).

Treatment: All patients receive Hydroxychloroquine. Class III/IV Induction: IV Methylprednisolone pulses + Oral Prednisolone combined with either Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF) or IV Cyclophosphamide (6 monthly pulses). Maintenance (2–3 yrs): MMF or Azathioprine + low-dose Prednisolone + ACE inhibitor.

C3 Glomerulopathy (C3G — Formerly MPGN Type II & III):

Caused by dysregulation of the alternate complement pathway, driven by C3 Nephritic Factor (C3NeF) — an autoantibody that stabilizes C3 convertase () against Factor H inactivation, causing persistently low serum C3 () with normal C4.

Light microscopy shows a membranoproliferative (MPGN) pattern with lobular accentuation and ‘tram-track’ double contour splitting of GBM on silver stain. Immunofluorescence shows isolated/dominant C3 deposits.

Two EM Subtypes: (1) Dense Deposit Disease (DDD): Ribbon-like intramembranous electron-dense deposits within the GBM; (2) C3 Glomerulonephritis (C3GN): Subendothelial, mesangial, and subepithelial deposits. Treated with ACE inhibitors + MMF + Prednisolone; high recurrence rate in renal allografts.

Tubulointerstitial Nephritis with Uveitis (TINU Syndrome): Autoimmune acute interstitial nephritis (sterile pyuria, eosinophiluria, non-oliguric AKI, tubular proteinuria) associated with bilateral anterior uveitis; responds well to systemic corticosteroids.

text:
(For First Episode & Relapse Management of SSNS, see Section 15.1 above).

1. Steroid-Sparing Agents in Frequent Relapsers / Steroid-Dependent NS (Table 17.9)

Indicated when prednisolone threshold to maintain remission is  on alternate days OR features of significant steroid toxicity appear:

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-012]]

2. Steroid-Resistant Nephrotic Syndrome (SRNS) & Congenital NS (Table 17.10)

Definition of SRNS: Lack of complete remission despite 6 weeks of daily Prednisolone ( or ).

Genetic Basis of SRNS ( of initial SRNS): Mutations in podocyte slit-diaphragm/cytoskeletal genes: NPHS1 (Nephrin), NPHS2 (Podocin — most common autosomal recessive cause in childhood), WT1, PLCE1, COL4A5, TRPC6, ACTN4, INF2.

Indications for Next-Generation Genetic Testing in SRNS: (1) Congenital NS () or infantile onset (); (2) Family history of SRNS or consanguinity; (3) Extrarenal syndromic features; (4) Non-response to calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) / prior to renal transplant. (Monogenic SRNS does NOT respond to immunosuppression and has a very low risk of post-transplant recurrence, whereas non-genetic primary FSGS recurs in  of allografts).

Management of Non-Genetic SRNS (Table 17.10):

Kidney Biopsy (usually shows FSGS or MCD).

First-Line Immunosuppression — Calcineurin Inhibitor (Tacrolimus  or Cyclosporine ) for 12–36 months (achieves complete/partial remission in ) + tapering alternate-day Prednisolone.

Mandatory Renoprotective Adjunct: ACE Inhibitor (Enalapril  or Ramipril) or ARB (Losartan) to reduce proteinuria and control hypertension + Statins for persistent hyperlipidemia.

Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome (CNS — Onset  of age):

Finnish Type CNS: Autosomal recessive NPHS1 (nephrin) mutation; history of large placenta ( of birth weight), elevated amniotic/maternal serum AFP, massive proteinuria from birth, microcystic dilation of proximal tubules on histology.

Syndromic CNS: Denys-Drash syndrome (WT1 mutation: diffuse mesangial sclerosis + 46,XY disorder of sex development + Wilms tumor), Frasier syndrome (WT1: FSGS + gonadoblastoma), Pierson syndrome (LAMB2: microcoria), and TORCH infections (congenital syphilis, CMV, toxoplasmosis).

Management: Steroids/immunosuppressants are contraindicated (except in congenital syphilis treated with Penicillin). Supportive care: High-protein/high-calorie diet, ACE inhibitors + Indomethacin (to reduce GFR and urinary protein loss), Thyroxine supplementation (due to urinary loss of thyroxine-binding globulin), anticoagulation, regular IV albumin infusions, and eventual nephrectomy + dialysis + kidney transplantation.

title: 17.4 UTI, BBD, VESICOURETERIC REFLUX (VUR) & ANTENATAL HYDRONEPHROSIS (Pages 534–538, 555–557)
text:
1. Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) & Bladder Bowel Dysfunction (BBD)

Culture Colony Count Cut-offs for Significant Bacteriuria:

Suprapubic Bladder Aspiration:  (any gram-negative bacilli growth is significant).

Transurethral Catheterization:  ().

Clean-Catch Midstream Void:  ( in symptomatic febrile infants with pyuria).

Bladder Bowel Dysfunction (BBD): Combination of lower urinary tract symptoms (urgency, holding maneuvers like Vincent’s curtsy [squatting with heel pressed into perineum], daytime incontinence, incomplete bladder emptying) and functional constipation/encopresis. BBD is the single most important modifiable risk factor for recurrent UTI and persistent VUR in toilet-trained children; managed by timed voiding, double voiding, hydration, high-fiber diet, and osmotic laxatives (Polyethylene glycol / Lactulose).

ISPN Imaging Protocol after First Febrile UTI (Fig. 17.18):

Age : USG + DMSA Scan (at 4–6 mo) + MCU (at 2–4 wks) for all infants.

Age : USG + DMSA Scan; perform MCU only if USG is abnormal (hydronephrosis/bladder wall thickening), DMSA shows cortical scarring, or non-E. coli / recurrent UTI.

Age : USG only; perform DMSA and MCU only if USG is abnormal or in Recurrent Febrile UTI.

2. Vesicoureteric Reflux (VUR) (Figs. 17.19 & 17.20)

International Reflux Study Grading of VUR on MCU (Grades I–V — Fig. 17.19):

Grade I: Reflux into a non-dilated ureter only; does not reach the renal pelvis.

Grade II: Reflux into the ureter, renal pelvis, and calyces without dilatation; normal calyceal fornices.

Grade III: Mild-to-moderate dilatation/tortuosity of the ureter and renal pelvis with minimal/mild blunting of calyceal fornices.

Grade IV: Moderate dilatation/tortuosity of ureter, pelvis, and calyces with complete obliteration of sharp angles of fornices, but papillary impressions are still maintained in most calyces.

Grade V: Gross dilatation and tortuosity of ureter, pelvis, and calyces with loss of papillary impressions (clubbed calyces) and intrarenal reflux.

Management of VUR (Fig. 17.20):

Grades I & II: Spontaneous resolution in . Antibiotic prophylaxis is given only if  of age or if recurrent febrile UTIs / BBD are present.

Grades III to V: Long-term bedtime Antibiotic Prophylaxis (Cotrimoxazole  or Nitrofurantoin ; Cephalexin  in infants ) until 2–5 years of age + aggressive management of Bladder Bowel Dysfunction (BBD).

Indications for Surgical Ureteric Reimplantation (or Endoscopic Deflux injection): Grade IV–V VUR with breakthrough febrile UTIs despite prophylaxis, non-compliance, or progressive renal scarring/declining GFR.

Reflux Nephropathy: Coarse polar renal cortical scarring with clubbing of underlying calyces; major cause of secondary hypertension, proteinuria, and CKD in children.

3. CAKUT & Postnatal Evaluation of Antenatal Hydronephrosis (Pages 555–557, Fig. 17.29)

Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney (MCDK): Most common cystic renal malformation in neonates; enlarged non-functioning kidney replaced by multiple non-communicating cysts of varying sizes without central pelvis or identifiable renal parenchyma (‘bunch of grapes’). Contralateral kidney shows compensatory hypertrophy ( have contralateral VUR or PUJ obstruction). Managed conservatively with serial 6-monthly USGs as MCDK spontaneously involutes by 5–7 years.

Posterior Urethral Valves (PUV): Most common cause of lower urinary tract obstruction (LUTO) in boys. Presents with poor urinary stream/dribbling, palpable thick-walled bladder, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, and antenatal oligohydramnios. MCU (Gold standard — Fig. 17.5b): Shows dilated and elongated posterior urethra (‘keyhole sign’), abrupt transition to narrow anterior urethra, trabeculated bladder with diverticula, and secondary VUR. Treatment: Primary endoscopic valve ablation (fulguration) (or temporary vesicostomy in tiny preterms) + long-term management of ‘valve bladder’ dysfunction.

Antenatal Hydronephrosis — Postnatal Management Algorithm (ISPN / UTD Classification — Fig. 17.29):

Timing of First Postnatal USG: Perform at Day 3–7 of life (performing in first 48 hrs underestimates dilation due to physiological neonatal oliguria), EXCEPT in suspected LUTO (PUV), bilateral severe hydronephrosis, or solitary kidney, where USG + MCU are done within 24–48 hours of birth.

Based on Renal Pelvic Anteroposterior Diameter (APD) on Postnatal USG:

Normal Postnatal USG (, UTD P0): Repeat USG at 4–6 weeks of age; if normal, discharge.

Isolated Mild Hydronephrosis (, UTD P1, no calyceal/ureteric dilation): Benign transient hydronephrosis; monitor with serial USGs every 3–6 months until resolution.

Moderate-to-Severe Hydronephrosis ( [UTD P2] or  / peripheral calyceal dilation / parenchymal thinning / ureteric dilation / abnormal bladder [UTD P3]):

Perform MCU to rule out VUR/PUV.

If no VUR (or ), perform  or  Diuretic Renogram at 4–6 weeks to assess differential renal function and drainage (PUJ obstruction).

Indications for Anderson-Hynes Pyeloplasty in PUJ Obstruction: Obstructed drainage curve with differential renal function , OR  drop in differential function on serial scans, OR symptomatic/recurrent febrile UTIs/increasing APD .

title: 17.5 AKI, HUS, CKD & KIDNEY REPLACEMENT THERAPY (Pages 538–548)
text:
1. Acute Kidney Injury (AKI): KDIGO Staging & Management (Tables 17.13–17.17)

Definition: Abrupt decline in kidney function defined by an increase in serum creatinine by  within 48 hours, OR an increase to  baseline within 7 days, OR urine output  for .

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-013]]

Medical Management of AKI Complications (Table 17.16):

Fluid Overload: Restrict fluids to insensible losses ( as  Dextrose) + urine output + extrarenal losses (child should lose  body weight daily).

Hyperkalemia (): (1) 10% Calcium Gluconate  IV over 5–10 min (stabilizes myocardial membrane); (2) Nebulized Salbutamol () + IV Glucose () with Regular Insulin () + IV Sodium Bicarbonate () (shifts K⁺ intracellularly); (3) Calcium/Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate (Kayexalate)  PO/PR (eliminates K⁺ from body); (4) Dialysis if persistent .

Indications for Dialysis (KRT) in AKI: (1) Refractory Hyperkalemia (); (2) Fluid overload  or pulmonary edema refractory to diuretics; (3) Severe Metabolic Acidosis ( or ); (4) Uremic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding); (5) Severe symptomatic dysnatremia ( or ).

Comparison of KRT Modalities (Table 17.17): Peritoneal Dialysis (PD) is preferred in neonates/small infants and hemodynamically unstable children where machines are unavailable (no vascular access or anticoagulation needed). Intermittent Hemodialysis (IHD) provides the fastest solute/potassium/toxin clearance in stable children. Continuous Kidney Replacement Therapy (CKRT: CVVH/CVVHD/CVVHDF) and Sustained Low-Efficiency Dialysis (SLED) are preferred in hemodynamically unstable, critically ill PICU patients with septic shock/MODS.

2. Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) (Pages 544–545)

Diagnostic Triad: (1) Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (, schistocytes/helmet cells  on peripheral smear, Coombs-negative [except S. pneumoniae HUS], elevated LDH, low haptoglobin); (2) Thrombocytopenia (platelets ); and (3) Acute Kidney Injury (histology: glomerular and arteriolar thrombotic microangiopathy [TMA]).

Classification & Management:

Shiga-Toxin Associated HUS (STEC-HUS / Typical D+ HUS): Follows bloody diarrhea/dysentery by Verotoxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7) or Shigella dysenteriae type 1 (in India). Managed supportively with fluid/electrolyte balance, packed RBC transfusions, and dialysis.

Atypical HUS (aHUS — Complement-Mediated): Triggered by minor URI without diarrheal prodrome; relapsing course with severe hypertension and poor renal prognosis. Caused by mutations in alternate complement genes (CFH, CFI, CFB, C3, MCP/CD46, DGKE) or Anti-Factor H (Anti-FH) Autoantibodies (Anti-FH antibody-associated HUS accounts for  of pediatric aHUS in India, affecting children 5–15 yrs).

Specific Treatment: Terminal C5 inhibitor (Eculizumab / Ravulizumab); in India where eculizumab is unavailable, early daily Therapeutic Plasma Exchanges (Plasmapheresis with FFP infusion) + Immunosuppression (IV Cyclophosphamide/Rituximab + Corticosteroids followed by MMF) for Anti-FH antibody-positive HUS.

3. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) (Tables 17.18 & 17.19)

Definition: Structural or functional kidney damage lasting , or  for . Most common cause in children: CAKUT ( — PUV, reflux nephropathy, renal hypodysplasia) followed by glomerular diseases (FSGS).

KDIGO GFR Staging (For children  — Table 17.18): G1:  (normal/high with kidney damage); G2:  (mildly decreased); G3a: ; G3b: ; G4:  (severely decreased); G5:  or on dialysis (Kidney failure / ESKD). Albuminuria Stages (UPCR): A1 (), A2 (), A3 ().

Comprehensive Management of CKD Complications:

Retarding Progression: ACE Inhibitors / ARBs + strict BP control ( percentile).

Anemia of CKD: Normocytic anemia begins at . Ensure iron repletion (Ferritin , TSAT  with oral elemental iron ), then start Recombinant Human Erythropoietin (rHuEPO  SC 2–3 times/week) or Darbepoetin to target .

CKD-Mineral Bone Disease (CKD-MBD / Renal Osteodystrophy): Driven by phosphate retention + reduced renal -hydroxylase (low )  hypocalcemia  secondary hyperparathyroidism (subperiosteal bone resorption of terminal phalanges, rachitic changes). Treatment: Dietary phosphate restriction + Oral Phosphate Binders with meals (Calcium carbonate/acetate if calcium is low/normal; Sevelamer carbonate if hypercalcemic) + correct  deficiency + Active Vitamin D (Calcitriol or Alfacalcidol ).

Growth Failure: Optimize calories + correct acidosis ( with oral sodium bicarbonate) + Recombinant Human Growth Hormone (rhGH  SC daily).

Kidney Replacement Therapy (KRT): Initiated when . Pre-emptive/Live-donor Kidney Transplantation (immunosuppression: Tacrolimus + MMF + Prednisolone) is the treatment of choice over chronic CAPD/APD or maintenance HD.

title: 17.6 TUBULAR DISORDERS, NEPHROLITHIASIS & CYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASES (Pages 548–559)
text:
1. Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) (Tables 17.21 & 17.22)

All forms of RTA present with Normal Anion Gap () Hyperchloremic Metabolic Acidosis:

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-014]]

Inherited Syndromes Associated with RTA (Table 17.21):

Distal RTA (Type 1): Sensorineural deafness (ATP6V1B1, ATP6V0A4), South-Asian ovalocytosis/hemolytic anemia (SLC4A1), Amelogenesis imperfecta (WDR72). (Type 3 Combined RTA + Osteopetrosis + Cerebral calcification = Carbonic Anhydrase II deficiency).

Fanconi Syndrome (Type 2 Proximal RTA + Glycosuria + Generalized Aminoaciduria + Phosphaturia + Tubular proteinuria):

Nephropathic Cystinosis (CTNS): Most common inherited cause of Fanconi syndrome in children; lysosomal cystine accumulation causing failure to thrive, rickets, blond hair, hypothyroidism, corneal cystine crystals on slit-lamp exam, and ESKD by 10 yrs. Treated with oral Cysteamine + Cysteamine eye drops.

Lowe (Oculocerebrorenal) Syndrome (OCRL1, X-linked): Congenital cataracts/glaucoma (buphthalmos) + hypotonia/intellectual disability + Fanconi syndrome.

Others: Tyrosinemia type 1, Galactosemia, Hereditary fructose intolerance, Wilson disease, Fanconi-Bickel syndrome (GSD XI, SLC2A2), Dent disease (CLCN5, X-linked low-MW proteinuria + hypercalciuria).

2. Bartter Syndrome vs. Gitelman Syndrome (Hypokalemic Metabolic Alkalosis) (Page 552)

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-015]]

3. Nephrolithiasis & Cystic Kidney Diseases (Pages 552–559)

Characteristic Urine Crystal Shapes (Fig. 17.27): Calcium oxalate dihydrate: Envelope-shaped; Uric acid: Diamond/rhomboid/rectangular; Struvite (Triple phosphate — Proteus UTI): Coffin-lid shaped; Cystine: Flat hexagonal crystals (positive cyanide-nitroprusside test; treated with high fluid, alkalinization to , and D-penicillamine/Tiopronin).

Primary Hyperoxaluria Type 1 (AGXT): Peroxisomal liver enzyme Alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase deficiency  recurrent calcium oxalate stones, diffuse nephrocalcinosis, systemic oxalosis, and ESKD. Treated with high-dose Pyridoxine (), RNA-interference drugs (Lumasiran [targets glycolate oxidase] or Nedosiran [targets LDHA]), or combined liver-kidney transplantation.

Cystic Kidney Diseases (Ciliopathies — Fig. 17.30):

ARPKD (PKHD1 — Fibrocystin): Presents in neonates with massively enlarged, hyperechoic (‘bright’) kidneys with radially arranged microcysts in collecting ducts, Potter sequence/pulmonary hypoplasia, systemic hypertension, and Congenital Hepatic Fibrosis / Caroli disease (portal hypertension).

ADPKD (PKD1 Chr 16 / PKD2 Chr 4 — Polycystin 1 & 2): Presents in older children/adults with bilateral large irregular macrocysts, hematuria, hypertension, liver/pancreatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse, and intracranial berry aneurysms.

Nephronophthisis (NPHP1): Most common monogenic cause of ESKD in children/adolescents. Presents with polyuria, polydipsia, anemia, growth failure, and normal-to-small kidneys with corticomedullary cysts and loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Extrarenal syndromes: Senior-Løken (retinitis pigmentosa), Joubert (cerebellar vermis aplasia — ‘molar tooth sign’), Bardet-Biedl.

HNF1B Nephropathy (17q12 deletion): Single most common cause of fetal bilateral hyperechogenic kidneys on antenatal USG; associated with Renal Cysts and Diabetes (RCAD / MODY-5), hypomagnesemia, hyperuricemia, and uterine malformations.

Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APML — AML-M3) (Pages 652–653):

Characterized by abnormal hypergranular promyelocytes with bundles of Auer rods (‘Faggot cells’),  (PML-RARA fusion gene), and life-threatening DIC / hyperfibrinolysis.

Targeted Therapy: All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA / Tretinoin) + Arsenic Trioxide (ATO) induces terminal differentiation of promyelocytes into mature neutrophils without bone marrow aplasia.

ATRA Differentiation Syndrome: Complication characterized by unexplained fever, respiratory distress/pulmonary infiltrates, weight gain, peripheral edema, pleural/pericardial effusions, and hypotension due to cytokine release (capillary leak); treated immediately with IV Dexamethasone.

Down Syndrome & Leukemia:

title: 21.3 RETINOBLASTOMA, SARCOMAS, BRAIN TUMORS, HISTIOCYTOSES & ONCOLOGIC EMERGENCIES (Pages 661–676)
text:
1. Retinoblastoma (Box 21.5 & Tables 21.17–21.18)

Genetics (Knudson’s Two-Hit Hypothesis — Box 21.5): Inactivation of both alleles of the tumor suppressor gene RB1 on chromosome 13q14:

Hereditary (): Germline RB1 mutation present in all body cells (inherited AD with  penetrance) + 2nd somatic hit in retinal cell  presents early () with bilateral, multifocal tumors, risk of pinealoblastoma (‘Trilateral Retinoblastoma’), and high risk of second malignancies (Osteosarcoma, soft tissue sarcomas, melanoma — especially if radiated).

Sporadic / Non-Hereditary (): Both hits occur somatically in a single retinal cell  presents later () with unilateral, unifocal tumor.

Clinical Features & Diagnosis: Leukocoria (white pupillary ‘cat’s-eye’ reflex — most common), strabismus (2nd most common), red painful eye with glaucoma, orbital cellulitis-like picture, or proptosis. Diagnosis: Indirect ophthalmoscopy under general anesthesia + B-scan ocular USG (intralesional calcification) + Contrast MRI of orbits and brain (Biopsy/FNAC is CONTRAINDICATED due to risk of extraocular seeding).

International Classification of Intraocular Retinoblastoma (ICRB — Groups A to E, Table 21.17) & Treatment:

Group A (Very low risk): Tumor , away from foveola and optic disc  Focal therapy alone (Laser photocoagulation, transpupillary thermotherapy, or cryotherapy).

Group B (Low risk):  or macular/juxtapapillary, no seeding  Systemic Chemoreduction (VEC: Vincristine + Etoposide + Carboplatin) + Focal consolidation.

Group C (Moderate risk): Focal subretinal/vitreous seeding  from tumor  Systemic VEC or Intra-arterial (ophthalmic artery) / Intravitreal Melphalan + Focal therapy.

Group D (High risk): Diffuse vitreous/subretinal seeding  Chemoreduction + Intra-arterial/Intravitreal chemotherapy.

Group E (Unsalvageable eye): Tumor occupying  of globe, neovascular glaucoma, anterior chamber invasion, phthisis bulbi  Primary Enucleation (taking a long  optic nerve stump).

2. Rhabdomyosarcoma, Bone Tumors & Brain Tumors (Pages 667–670)

Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS): Most common pediatric soft-tissue sarcoma (head/neck , genitourinary , extremities ). Histology: Embryonal RMS () — includes Sarcoma Botryoides (‘grape-like’ polypoid mass protruding from vagina or bladder in infants; favorable prognosis); Alveolar RMS () —  PAX3-FOXO1, extremity/trunk, poor prognosis. Treated with VAC (Vincristine, Actinomycin-D, Cyclophosphamide) + surgery/RT.

Osteogenic Sarcoma vs. Ewing Sarcoma:

Osteosarcoma: Adolescent growth spurt; affects metaphysis of long bones (distal femur, proximal tibia — around the knee); associated with hereditary Retinoblastoma (RB1) and Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53). X-ray shows osteolytic-sclerotic lesion with ‘Sunburst’ periosteal reaction and Codman’s triangle. Radio-resistant; treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (High-dose Methotrexate, Doxorubicin, Cisplatin, Ifosfamide) + limb-salvage surgery.

Ewing Sarcoma (PNET): Affects diaphysis of long bones and flat bones (pelvis, ribs, femur); systemic fever/elevated ESR mimics acute osteomyelitis. Small round blue cell tumor strongly positive for CD99 (MIC2) with pathognomonic translocation  (EWSR1-FLI1). X-ray shows permeative ‘moth-eaten’ diaphyseal lysis with multi-layered ‘Onion-skin’ periosteal reaction. Radio-sensitive; treated with multiagent chemotherapy (VDC/IE) + surgery and/or radiotherapy.

Pediatric Brain Tumors (Table 21.23): Second most common childhood cancer (; infratentorial/posterior fossa predominates in children ):

Cerebellar Pilocytic Astrocytoma (WHO Grade I): Cystic cerebellar mass with enhancing mural nodule; Rosenthal fibers; BRAF fusion;  cured by surgical excision. (Optic pathway glioma = Neurofibromatosis-1; Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma = Tuberous sclerosis).

Medulloblastoma (WHO Grade IV): Midline cerebellar vermis embryonal tumor; presents with morning headache, projectile vomiting, truncal ataxia, and obstructive hydrocephalus; Homer-Wright rosettes; drops metastases down the spinal axis. Four molecular subgroups (WNT [best prognosis], SHH [Gorlin syndrome], Group 3 [MYC amplification, worst prognosis], Group 4). Treated with surgery + craniospinal irradiation (avoided in ) + chemotherapy.

Craniopharyngioma: Suprasellar tumor from Rathke’s pouch; presents with short stature (GH deficiency), bitemporal hemianopia, diabetes insipidus, and suprasellar calcifications on CT (‘motor-oil’ cyst fluid).

Brainstem (Diffuse Intrinsic Pontine) Glioma: Presents with triad of multiple cranial nerve palsies (VI, VII) + long-tract pyramidal signs + cerebellar ataxia WITHOUT raised ICP initially; dismal prognosis.

3. Histiocytoses: LCH & HLH (Tables 21.24–21.26)

Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH — Class I Dendritic Cell Disorder):

Clonal proliferation of pathologic Langerhans cells (BRAF V600E mutation in ).

Confirmatory Diagnosis: Positivity for CD1a, Langerin (CD207), and S-100 on immunohistochemistry, and tennis-racket shaped Birbeck granules on Electron Microscopy.

Clinical Spectrum (Table 21.25): (1) Skeleton ( — Eosinophilic Granuloma): Punched-out osteolytic skull lesions with beveled edges, vertebra plana, floating teeth, chronic mastoiditis/ear discharge; (2) Skin (): Refractory cradle-cap seborrheic scaling and reddish-brown crusted papules on scalp, groin, and trunk; (3) Hand-Schüller-Christian Triad: Calvarial bone defects + Exophthalmos + Central Diabetes Insipidus (pituitary stalk thickening); (4) Multisystem Risk-Organ Disease (Letterer-Siwe — ): Involvement of Liver, Spleen, and Bone Marrow (cytopenias, sclerosing cholangitis, cystic lung disease with recurrent pneumothorax).

Treatment: Multisystem LCH is treated with Vinblastine + Prednisolone for 12 months.

Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH — Class II Macrophage Disorder) (Table 21.26):

Defective NK-cell and cytotoxic T-cell granule-mediated cytolysis (Primary/Familial: PRF1 [Perforin], UNC13D, STX11, RAB27A [Griscelli], LYST [Chediak-Higashi]; Secondary: EBV, dengue, scrub typhus, leishmaniasis, malignancy, Systemic JIA [MAS])  uncontrolled macrophage activation and cytokine storm.

HLH-2004 Diagnostic Criteria (Table 21.26 — Confirmed Molecular Diagnosis OR at least 5 of the following 8 Criteria):

Fever ().

Splenomegaly.

Cytopenias affecting  lineages: , Platelets , Absolute Neutrophil Count .

Hypertriglyceridemia (fasting triglycerides ) and/or Hypofibrinogenemia ().

Hemophagocytosis in bone marrow, spleen, or lymph nodes (without malignancy).

Low or absent NK-cell activity.

Hyperferritinemia (Serum Ferritin , often ).

Elevated soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor ).

Treatment: Dexamethasone + Etoposide  Cyclosporine (HLH-94/2004 protocol) + Allogeneic HSCT for primary HLH.

4. Oncologic Emergencies & Late Effects of Cancer Therapy (Tables 21.27–21.29)

Key Oncologic Emergencies (Table 21.27):

Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS): Massive lysis of rapidly proliferating tumors (Burkitt lymphoma, T-ALL, hyperleukocytosis) releasing intracellular ions and nucleic acids.

Cairo-Bishop Laboratory TLS ( of 4): Hyperuricemia (), Hyperkalemia (), Hyperphosphatemia ( in children), and Secondary Hypocalcemia (). Clinical TLS: Lab TLS + AKI, seizures, or cardiac arrhythmia/sudden death.

Management: Aggressive IV hydration ( potassium-free and calcium-free fluid; avoid urinary alkalinization as alkaline urine precipitates calcium phosphate!) + Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor — prevents new uric acid formation) or Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase — converts existing uric acid into soluble allantoin; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency) + Hemodialysis if refractory.

Febrile Neutropenia: Single oral/axillary temperature  () or  sustained for  with  (or  expected to fall ). Managed with urgent blood cultures + empirical anti-pseudomonal -lactam (Cefoperazone-sulbactam, Piperacillin-tazobactam, Cefepime, or Meropenem)  Vancomycin/Antifungals.

Spinal Cord Compression (Neuroblastoma, Ewing, Lymphoma): Immediate IV Dexamethasone + MRI spine + Decompressive laminectomy/RT/chemotherapy.

Signature Late Effects of Chemotherapy/Radiation in Survivors (Table 21.29):

Anthracyclines (Doxorubicin/Daunorubicin ): Dilated cardiomyopathy.

Cisplatin / Carboplatin: High-frequency sensorineural hearing loss & nephrotoxicity (renal Mg²⁺ wasting).

Cyclophosphamide / Ifosfamide: Hemorrhagic cystitis (prevented by Mesna), infertility/gonadal failure, Fanconi syndrome (Ifosfamide).

Bleomycin / Busulfan: Pulmonary fibrosis.

Vincristine: Peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy (foot drop, loss of deep tendon reflexes, paralytic ileus, SIADH).

L-Asparaginase: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis, hyperglycemia.

Epipodophyllotoxins (Etoposide) & Alkylating Agents: Secondary Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).

(For JIA Subtypes, MAS, HSP, and Kawasaki Disease, refer to Sections 20.1 and 20.2 above).

title: 22.1 APPROACH TO ARTHRITIS & SYNOVIAL FLUID ANALYSIS (Pages 677–678)
text:
Synovial Fluid Characteristics (Table 22.2):

Septic Arthritis: Turbid/purulent,  ( neutrophils), low glucose, Gram stain/culture positive.

Tuberculous Arthritis: Opaque, lymphocytic predominance, elevated protein, AFB/CBNAAT positive (Poncet disease is sterile reactive polyarthritis secondary to visceral TB).

Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA): Cloudy, polymorphonuclear predominance (), sterile culture.

Non-Inflammatory Genetic Mimics of Chronic Arthritis: Progressive Pseudorheumatoid Arthropathy of Childhood (PPAC) (WISP3 mutation — platyspondyly and interphalangeal joint enlargement without elevated ESR/CRP), CACP syndrome (PRG4 lubricin mutation — Camptodactyly-Arthropathy-Coxa vara-Pericarditis), and Mucopolysaccharidoses.

subject: pediatrics
title: 22.2 SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS (SLE), JDM & OTHER VASCULITIDES (Pages 681–688)
text:
1. 2019 EULAR / ACR Classification Criteria for SLE (Box 22.1 — High-Yield Box)

Obligatory Entry Criterion: Positive Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) at a titer of  on HEp-2 cells.

Additive Classification Requirement: At least 1 clinical criterion AND a total score of  (only the highest-weighted item within each domain is counted):

Constitutional: Fever (2).

Hematologic: Leukopenia (3), Thrombocytopenia (4), Autoimmune hemolysis (4).

Neuropsychiatric: Delirium (2), Psychosis (3), Seizures (5).

Mucocutaneous: Non-scarring alopecia (2), Oral ulcers (2), Subacute cutaneous/discoid lupus (4), Acute cutaneous lupus / Malar rash sparing nasolabial folds (6).

Serosal: Pleural or pericardial effusion (5), Acute pericarditis (6).

Musculoskeletal: Joint involvement / non-erosive arthritis (6).

Renal: Proteinuria  (4), Class II or V lupus nephritis (8), Class III or IV proliferative lupus nephritis (10).

Antiphospholipid Antibodies: Anticardiolipin, anti-, or Lupus anticoagulant (2).

Complement Proteins: Low C3 or low C4 (3); Both low C3 AND low C4 (4).

SLE-Specific Antibodies: Anti-dsDNA (correlates with disease/renal activity) OR Anti-Smith (Anti-Sm) antibody (6).

Characteristic ESR-CRP Dissociation in SLE: During acute lupus flares, ESR is markedly elevated while CRP remains normal (CRP rises in SLE only if there is superadded bacterial infection, serositis, or synovitis).

Early-Onset Monogenic Lupus (): Deficiency of early classical complement components (C1q, C4, C2) or Type I Interferonopathies.

2. Juvenile Dermatomyositis (JDM) (Pages 683–684)

Bohan and Peter Diagnostic Criteria (1975): Mandatory Criterion 1: Pathognomonic Rash — Heliotrope rash (violaceous discoloration and edema of upper eyelids) and/or Gottron papules (erythematous scaly papules over extensor surfaces of MCP and PIP knuckles), PLUS at least 3 of 4 for Definite JDM (2 of 4 for Probable JDM):

Symmetric proximal muscle weakness (neck flexors, shoulder and pelvic girdles; positive Gower sign, dysphagia/nasal intonation).

Elevated serum muscle enzymes (CK, AST, ALT, LDH, Aldolase).

Myopathic EMG triad (short, small, polyphasic motor units + fibrillations).

Muscle biopsy: Perifascicular atrophy and capillary endothelial damage (T2/STIR MRI showing muscle edema has largely replaced invasive biopsy/EMG).

Complications & Treatment: Dystrophic subcutaneous calcinosis (, associated with anti-NXP2 antibodies) and lipodystrophy. Treated with IV Methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral Prednisolone + weekly subcutaneous Methotrexate for 18–24 months + sunscreens.

3. Childhood Takayasu Arteritis, Polyarteritis Nodosa & Autoinflammatory Disorders (Boxes 22.2 & 22.3)

EULAR/PRINTO/PRES Criteria for Childhood Takayasu Arteritis (Box 22.2): Mandatory: Angiographic abnormalities (conventional, CT, or MR angiography showing stenosis/occlusion/aneurysm) of the aorta or its main branches and pulmonary arteries, PLUS at least 1 of 5: (1) Decreased/absent peripheral artery pulse(s) and/or claudication; (2) Four-limb systolic BP discrepancy ; (3) Bruits over aorta or its major branches; (4) Hypertension (renovascular); (5) Elevated acute phase reactants ( or elevated CRP). Treatment: Corticosteroids + Methotrexate/MMF/Tocilizumab + percutaneous transluminal angioplasty.

EULAR/PRINTO/PRES Criteria for Childhood Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN — Box 22.3): Mandatory: Histopathology showing necrotizing vasculitis of small/medium arteries OR angiographic microaneurysms/occlusions (not due to fibromuscular dysplasia), PLUS at least 1 of 5: (1) Skin involvement (livedo reticularis, nodules, infarcts); (2) Myalgia/muscle tenderness; (3) Systemic hypertension; (4) Peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex); (5) Renal involvement (hematuria/proteinuria/impaired GFR). (Early-onset PAN with livedo reticularis and recurrent hemorrhagic/ischemic strokes is caused by monogenic Deficiency of Adenosine Deaminase 2 [DADA2], treated with TNF- blockers).

Autoinflammatory Disorders (Periodic Fever Syndromes — Page 688): Monogenic defects of innate immunity (inflammasomes) causing recurrent fevers, rash, serositis, and high ESR/CRP without high-titer autoantibodies: Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF — MEFV/pyrin, treated with Colchicine), TRAPS, Mevalonate Kinase Deficiency (Hyper-IgD syndrome), Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndromes (CAPS — NLRP3, treated with IL-1 blockers Anakinra/Canakinumab), PFAPA syndrome (Periodic Fever, Aphthous stomatitis, Pharyngitis, Cervical Adenitis), Blau syndrome (NOD2), and SAVI (Type I interferonopathy, treated with JAK inhibitors).

(For Down Syndrome, Turner Syndrome, and Hemophilia Counseling, refer to Sections 21.1 and 21.2 above).

title: 23.1 CHROMOSOMAL DISORDERS, IMPRINTING & GENETIC TESTING (Pages 689–703)
text:
1. Trisomy 18, Trisomy 13, Klinefelter Syndrome & Genomic Imprinting (Table 23.3)

Edwards Syndrome (Trisomy 18): Prominent occiput, micrognathia, low-set malformed ears, short sternum, clenched fist with overlapping of index finger over 3rd and 5th over 4th finger, rocker-bottom feet, VSD/PDA, severe intellectual disability.

Patau Syndrome (Trisomy 13): Holoprosencephaly, microcephaly, cutis aplasia of scalp, microphthalmia/coloboma, midline cleft lip and palate, postaxial polydactyly, CHD ().

Klinefelter Syndrome (47,XXY): Tall eunuchoid stature (long legs, lower segment  upper segment), gynecomastia, small firm testes, azoospermia, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (high FSH/LH, low testosterone), mild learning/behavioral difficulties; treated with testosterone replacement from puberty.

Genomic Imprinting (Chromosome 15q11–q13):

Prader-Willi Syndrome: Loss of paternally expressed genes on 15q11–q13 (70% paternal microdeletion, 25% maternal uniparental disomy [UPD]). Presents with severe neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding in infancy, followed in childhood by insatiable hyperphagia, morbid obesity, hypogonadism, almond-shaped eyes, small hands/feet, and mild-to-moderate intellectual disability.

Angelman Syndrome (‘Happy Puppet’ Syndrome): Loss of maternally expressed UBE3A gene on 15q11–q13 (maternal microdeletion or paternal UPD). Presents with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, paroxysmal inappropriate laughter, jerky ataxic (‘puppet-like’) gait, microcephaly, and seizures.

title: 24.1 CLASSIFICATION, DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH & BIOCHEMICAL AUTOPSY (Pages 704–709)
text:
1. Three Pathophysiological Categories of IEM

Disorders of Intoxication (Small Molecules): Symptom-free interval after birth followed by acute/intermittent metabolic encephalopathy precipitated by catabolism/fasting/protein load (Aminoacidopathies, Organic Acidurias, Urea Cycle Defects, Galactosemia, Hereditary Fructose Intolerance). Treatable by dietary restriction, hemodiafiltration, and scavenging drugs.

Disorders of Energy Metabolism: Cytoplasmic (Glycogen Storage Diseases, Gluconeogenesis defects, Hyperinsulinism — severe fasting hypoglycemia) and Mitochondrial (Fatty Acid Oxidation Defects [FAODs], Pyruvate dehydrogenase/carboxylase, Respiratory Chain Defects — congenital lactic acidosis, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy).

Disorders of Complex Molecules (Cellular Organelles): Lysosomal Storage Disorders, Peroxisomal Disorders, Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation (CDG) — progressive, permanent multisystem signs (dysmorphism, organomegaly, neurodegeneration) independent of diet or intercurrent catabolism.

2. Differential Diagnosis of Acute Metabolic Encephalopathy (Table 24.2 & Fig. 24.1)

First-line emergency ‘GELAAK’ panel: Blood Glucose, Electrolytes (Anion gap), Lactate, Acid-base (Blood gas), Ammonia, and Urine Ketones:

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-020]]

Gray Matter vs. White Matter Neurodegenerative Disorders (Table 24.1):

Gray Matter (Poliodystrophy — e.g., Tay-Sachs, NCL): Early onset, microcephaly, early intractable seizures & myoclonus, early cognitive decline/dementia, retinal degeneration / Cherry-red spot, abnormal ERG, spasticity occurs late.

White Matter (Leukodystrophy — e.g., Metachromatic Leukodystrophy, Krabbe, Alexander, Canavan): Later onset, macrocephaly (in Canavan/Alexander/MLC), early spasticity, ataxia & motor regression, peripheral neuropathy (absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars in MLD/Krabbe), optic atrophy, prolonged VEP & slowed NCV, seizures/dementia occur late.

3. Biochemical Autopsy in a Dying Child with Undiagnosed IEM (Table 24.3 — High-Yield Box)

Obtain informed consent and collect samples before or within 1–2 hours of death: 1. Clinical Photographs & Full-body Infantogram / Skeletal Survey (for dysmorphism, chondrodysplasia punctata, dysostosis multiplex). 2. Blood:  Heparinized plasma frozen at  (quantitative amino acids, acylcarnitines);  EDTA blood refrigerated / extracted DNA frozen at  (Whole Exome Sequencing); Dried Blood Spots (DBS) on S&S 903 filter paper air-dried at room temperature (Tandem Mass Spectrometry [TMS]). 3. Urine (): Frozen plain at  (GC-MS for organic acids, orotic acid, succinylacetone, GAGs). 4. CSF (): Frozen immediately at  (neurotransmitters, CSF amino acids/glycine [for Non-ketotic hyperglycinemia], CSF lactate). 5. Tissue Biopsies:  Punch Skin Biopsy (for fibroblast culture — store in culture medium or glucose-saline at room temperature or ; NEVER freeze skin biopsy!) AND Needle biopsies of Liver and Muscle (snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen + one piece in glutaraldehyde for EM).

4. Emergency Management of Acute IEM & Cofactor Doses (Pages 708–709, Table 24.4)

Stop all oral/enteral protein, galactose, or fat intake; prevent endogenous catabolism by infusing  Dextrose in  Saline at  maintenance (, glucose infusion rate   IV Insulin if hyperglycemic; add Intralipids  ONLY if FAOD is ruled out). (Reintroduce  protein after 48–72 hours to prevent endogenous muscle breakdown).

Hyperammonemia Protocol:

Ammonia scavengers: IV/Oral Sodium Benzoate (, conjugates glycine to form hippurate) + Sodium Phenylbutyrate/Phenylacetate (, conjugates glutamine) + L-Arginine (; use L-Citrulline in OTC/CPS-1 deficiency; omit Arginine in Arginase deficiency).

Oral Carglumic Acid (N-carbamylglutamate): Specific therapy for N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS) deficiency and organic acidemia-induced hyperammonemia.

Dialysis (Hemodialysis / CKRT preferred over Peritoneal Dialysis; Exchange transfusion is ineffective): Initiate immediately if blood ammonia  () or if coma/no drop within 2–4 hours of medical therapy.

Empirical Megavitamin / Cofactor Trial (Table 24.4):

Biotin ( PO): Biotinidase deficiency, Holocarboxylase synthetase (Multiple carboxylase) deficiency, Propionic acidemia.

Thiamine (,  up to ): Thiamine-responsive MSUD, Leigh/PDH deficiency.

Vitamin  (Hydroxocobalamin  IM): Methylmalonic acidemia (MMA), Cobalamin C/D defects.

Riboflavin (,  PO): Glutaric aciduria type I & II (MADD), Mitochondrial defects.

Pyridoxine (, ): Pyridoxine-dependent seizures ( IV), Classical Homocystinuria.

L-Carnitine ( IV/PO): Organic acidurias, Primary carnitine deficiency.

subject: pediatrics
title: 24.2 SPECIFIC INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM (Pages 709–722)
text:
1. Aminoacidopathies & Urea Cycle Defects (Fig. 24.7)

Tyrosinemia Type 1 (Hepatorenal Tyrosinemia): Autosomal recessive Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAH) deficiency  accumulation of Succinylacetone (diagnostic in blood/urine) + cabbages-like odor + acute liver failure/cirrhosis (markedly elevated -fetoprotein , high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma) + Renal Fanconi syndrome with hypophosphatemic rickets + acute porphyria-like neuropathic crises. Treatment: Oral Nitisinone (NTBC ) (inhibits 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase) + phenylalanine/tyrosine-restricted diet.

Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD): Branched-chain -ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKAD) deficiency  elevated plasma Leucine, Isoleucine, Valine, and Alloisoleucine  burnt-sugar/maple syrup odor in cerumen/urine, neonatal encephalopathy, opisthotonus, ‘fencing’ and ‘bicycling’ movements, cerebral edema; positive Urine DNPH (Dinitrophenylhydrazine) test. Treated by leucine-free formula, thiamine trial, hemodialysis in crisis, or orthotopic liver transplantation (curative).

Alkaptonuria: Homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency  urine turns black on standing/alkalinization, bluish-black pigmentation of sclera/ear cartilage (Ochronosis), and degenerative large-joint arthritis.

Phenylketonuria (PKU): Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) deficiency (or  cofactor defect)  musty/mousy urine odor, blond hair, fair skin, eczema, microcephaly, seizures, and severe intellectual disability. Diagnosis: Plasma Phenylalanine  (; classic PKU ) with Phe:Tyr ratio , positive urine Ferric chloride test (green). Treated with lifelong phenylalanine-restricted diet + Sapropterin (, ).

Classical Homocystinuria: Cystathionine -synthase (CBS) deficiency  Marfanoid habitus, pectus, osteoporosis, downward and inward (inferomedial) ectopia lentis (vs. upward and outward in Marfan syndrome), intellectual disability, and arterial/venous thromboembolism (stroke). Diagnosis: Elevated plasma homocysteine () and elevated methionine; positive urine cyanide-nitroprusside test (magenta-red). Treated with Pyridoxine (), Folic acid, Vitamin , Oral Betaine (), and methionine-restricted diet.

Urea Cycle Defects Algorithm (Figs. 24.7a & 24.7b):

Hyperammonemia + Respiratory Alkalosis + No Ketonuria  Check Plasma Citrulline:

Citrulline Absent / Very Low: Check Urine Orotic Acid:

Urine Orotic Acid LOW/Normal: Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase-1 (CPS-1) deficiency or NAGS deficiency (AR).

Urine Orotic Acid HIGH: Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency (X-linked, most common UCD!).

Citrulline Moderately Elevated () + Argininosuccinate Present: Argininosuccinic Aciduria (ASL deficiency — associated with brittle trichorrhexis nodosa hair and hepatomegaly).

Citrulline Markedly Elevated (): Citrullinemia Type 1 (ASS1 deficiency).

Elevated Plasma Arginine: Arginase deficiency (presents with progressive spastic diplegia mimicking cerebral palsy).

2. Glycogen Storage Diseases (GSDs — Fig. 24.9a)

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-021]]

3. Lysosomal Storage Disorders: Mucopolysaccharidoses (Table 24.5) & Sphingolipidoses (Fig. 24.12)

Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS — All are Autosomal Recessive EXCEPT Hunter [MPS II] which is X-linked Recessive — Table 24.5):

Common Features: Coarse gargoyle-like facies, hepatosplenomegaly, umbilical/inguinal hernias, claw-hand joint contractures, and Dysostosis Multiplex on X-ray (J-shaped sella turcica, oar/spatula-shaped ribs, anterior inferior beaking of lumbar vertebrae L1/L2 [central beaking in Morquio MPS IV], and proximal pointing [bullet-shaped] metacarpals).

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-022]]

Sphingolipidoses & Lipid Storage Disorders (Fig. 24.12 & Table 24.6):

Gaucher Disease (-Glucosidase / Glucocerebrosidase deficiency — Most common LSD):

Type I (Non-neuronopathic — ): Massive splenomegaly  hepatomegaly, pancytopenia, bone crises, avascular necrosis, and Erlenmeyer flask deformity of distal femur; NO CNS involvement.

Type II (Acute Neuronopathic — Infantile): Bulbar palsy, stridor, opisthotonus/head retroflexion, oculomotor apraxia/squint, organomegaly; fatal by 2 years.

Type III (Chronic Neuronopathic — Juvenile): Horizontal supranuclear gaze palsy, myoclonic epilepsy, ataxia + visceral disease.

Diagnosis: Enzyme assay (-glucosidase) in leukocytes + elevated plasma Glucosylsphingosine (Lyso-GL1) and Chitotriosidase; bone marrow shows Gaucher cells (‘crumpled/wrinkled tissue paper’ cytoplasm).

Treatment (Type I & III): Enzyme Replacement Therapy (Imiglucerase, Velaglucerase alfa, Taliglucerase)  IV q2wks OR Oral Substrate Reduction Therapy (Eliglustat, Miglustat).

Niemann-Pick Disease:

Type A & B (Acid Sphingomyelinase deficiency): Type A presents in infancy with massive hepatosplenomegaly, failure to thrive, rapid neurodegeneration, and macular Cherry-Red Spot (); bone marrow shows foam cells (‘sea-blue histiocytes’). Type B has visceral hepatosplenomegaly and interstitial lung disease without CNS involvement (ERT: Olipudase alfa).

Type C (NPC1/NPC2 — Defect in intracellular cholesterol trafficking): Neonatal cholestasis, splenomegaly, ataxia, and characteristic Vertical Supranuclear Gaze Palsy (treated with Miglustat).

GM2 Gangliosidoses (Tay-Sachs vs. Sandhoff Disease):

Tay-Sachs Disease (Hexosaminidase A deficiency): Presents at 3–6 months with motor regression, hypotonia progressing to spasticity, exaggerated startle response to noise (hyperacusis), macrocephaly, Macular Cherry-Red Spot (), and ABSENCE of hepatosplenomegaly.

Sandhoff Disease (Hexosaminidase A & B deficiency): Identical to Tay-Sachs PLUS mild hepatosplenomegaly and bony changes. (Note: GM1 Gangliosidosis [-galactosidase deficiency] presents with Hurler-like coarse facies + hepatosplenomegaly + Cherry-Red Spot).

Krabbe Disease (Galactocerebrosidase deficiency): Infantile leukodystrophy with extreme irritability, tonic spasms, optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, high CSF protein, and globoid cells in brain white matter.

X-Linked Adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD — Peroxisomal ABCD1 defect): Accumulation of Very Long Chain Fatty Acids (VLCFA ) in brain white matter and adrenal cortex. Presents in boys aged 4–8 years with behavioral changes/ADHD, declining school performance, visual/auditory loss, seizures, and primary adrenal insufficiency (Addisonian hyperpigmentation). MRI Brain: Characteristic symmetric butterfly-like demyelination in bilateral parieto-occipital white matter and splenium of corpus callosum (Fig. 24.15). Treated with Allogeneic HSCT in early stage + hydrocortisone replacement.

subject: pediatrics
title: 25.1 IUIS CLASSIFICATION, CLINICAL CLUES & SPECIFIC DISORDERS (Pages 723–728)
text:
1. Diagnostic Clues & Laboratory Workup by Immune Arm (Table 25.3 & Box 25.1)

B-Cell (Humoral / Antibody) Defects: Onset after 4–6 months of age (once transplacental maternal IgG wanes); recurrent sinopulmonary infections, otitis media, meningitis, and diarrhea (Giardia lamblia) with encapsulated extracellular pyogenic bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) and enteroviruses.

X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (Bruton Disease — BTK mutation): Affects boys; absent tonsils and palpable lymph nodes; profoundly reduced IgG, IgA, and IgM with absent  B cells () on flow cytometry.

Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID): Presents in late childhood/adolescence with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, giardiasis, generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias, and lymphoma risk; low IgG and IgA/IgM with normal B-cell numbers but reduced switched memory B cells.

Selective IgA Deficiency: Most common IEI; recurrent giardiasis, celiac disease, and anaphylaxis to blood products containing IgA.

T-Cell & Combined Immunodeficiencies (SCID): Onset in early infancy (); failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, persistent oral thrush, disseminated BCGosis, and pneumonia due to Pneumocystis jirovecii, CMV, Candida, and adenovirus.

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID): Pediatric emergency! Profound lymphopenia (Absolute Lymphocyte Count  in infancy) and absent thymic shadow on CXR. Most common is X-linked SCID (IL2RG common -chain defect — ); Autosomal recessive ADA deficiency () with cupping/flaring of anterior ribs. (Screened at birth by TRECs [T-cell Receptor Excision Circles] on dried blood spots).

Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS — Xp11 WAS gene): Classic triad in boys: (1) Congenital Microthrombocytopenia (bleeding with small platelet size, MPV ), (2) Refractory Eczema, and (3) Recurrent pyogenic and opportunistic infections + high risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma. Immunoglobulins: Low IgM, Elevated IgA and IgE, normal IgG.

Ataxia-Telangiectasia (ATM gene, AR): Progressive cerebellar ataxia (by 1–2 yrs)  oculocutaneous telangiectasias (by 3–6 yrs)  sinopulmonary infections (low IgA, IgE, IgG2), elevated serum -fetoprotein (AFP), extreme radiosensitivity, and lymphoid malignancies.

Hyper-IgM Syndrome (X-linked CD40LG defect): Defective immunoglobulin class-switching  very high/normal IgM with absent IgG, IgA, and IgE, neutropenia, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia / Cryptosporidium sclerosing cholangitis.

Phagocytic & Innate Immune Defects:

Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD — X-linked CYBB [gp91phox] or AR NCF1 [p47phox]): Defective phagocyte NADPH oxidase respiratory burst  inability to kill catalase-positive bacteria and fungi (Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Salmonella, and Aspergillus), causing recurrent deep organ abscesses (liver, lung), suppurative lymphadenitis, osteomyelitis, and obstructive granulomas. Diagnosis: Negative Nitroblue Tetrazolium (NBT) test and abnormal Dihydrorhodamine-123 (DHR) flow cytometry assay (confirmatory). Treatment: Lifelong Cotrimoxazole + Itraconazole prophylaxis  IFN- and HSCT.

Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 1 (LAD-1 — ITGB2 / CD18 -integrin defect): Delayed separation of umbilical cord (), severe omphalitis, necrotic skin ulcers and periodontitis with complete absence of pus formation and marked persistent neutrophilic leukocytosis (). Confirmed by absent CD11/CD18 expression on flow cytometry.

Hyper-IgE Syndrome (Job Syndrome — AD STAT3 deficiency): Triad of recurrent ‘cold’ staphylococcal skin abscesses, recurrent pneumonia with pneumatoceles, and eczematoid rash + coarse facies, scoliosis, hyperextensible joints, retained primary teeth (two rows of teeth), eosinophilia, and  (low Th17 cells). (AR DOCK8 deficiency has severe cutaneous viral infections [molluscum, HSV, HPV] and food allergies without dental/skeletal defects).

Mendelian Susceptibility to Mycobacterial Disease (MSMD): Defects in the IL-12/IL-23–IFN- pathway (IFNGR1, IL12RB1) causing disseminated BCGosis, non-tuberculous mycobacterial, and Salmonella infections.

Complement Deficiencies: C1q, C4, C2 deficiency  early-onset SLE + encapsulated bacterial infections; C5–C9 (MAC) deficiency  recurrent Neisseria meningitidis infections; C1-Esterase Inhibitor deficiency  Hereditary Angioedema (non-pruritic angioedema without urticaria, laryngeal edema, low C4; treated with C1-INH concentrate, tranexamic acid, or danazol).

(Note: For National Immunization Schedule, Vaccines, Cold Chain, VVM, Shake Test, and AEFI, refer to the complete Q-Bank Chapter 8 section in the first half of your notes).

(For Extraocular Muscles, Visual Pathway, Retinitis Pigmentosa, and Papilledema, refer to Section 23 in Part 1).

subject: pediatrics
title: 26.1 EYE SCREENING, CONGENITAL OPACITIES, VITAMIN A, INFECTIONS & ROP (Pages 729–737)
text:
Age-Appropriate Visual Acuity Assessment:

: Fixation and following light/faces, pupillary reflexes, red reflex (Bruckner test).

 (Preverbal): Preferential looking tests (Teller Acuity Cards, Cardiff cards), Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN) drum, Pattern Visual Evoked Potential (VER), and objection to occlusion of the good eye.

 (Preschool): Kay’s Picture test, HOTV matching cards, Tumbling ‘E’, or Landolt ‘C’ chart.

: Standard Snellen Visual Acuity Chart at 6 meters.

Differential Diagnosis of Congenital Corneal Opacity (Mnemonic — STUMPED, Page 731):

S — Sclerocornea

T — Trauma (forceps birth injury causing Descemet membrane tears)

U — Ulcer (congenital keratitis: HSV, rubella)

M — Mucopolysaccharidosis (Hurler, Maroteaux-Lamy) / Mucolipidosis

P — Peters anomaly (anterior segment dysgenesis with iridocorneal/keratolenticular adhesions)

E — Endothelial dystrophy (Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy — CHED)

D — Dermoid (limbal dermoid — Goldenhar syndrome) & Descemet breaks in Primary Congenital Glaucoma (Buphthalmos).

Primary Congenital Glaucoma (Buphthalmos — CYP1B1 gene, AR):

Classic Clinical Triad: Epiphora (excessive watering) + Photophobia + Blepharospasm, accompanied by corneal haziness/edema, Haab’s striae (horizontal breaks in Descemet membrane), enlarged corneal diameter ( in infancy — ‘ox-eye’ / buphthalmos), deep anterior chamber, and optic disc cupping. Treated surgically by Goniotomy or Trabeculotomy + Trabeculectomy.

Pediatric Cataract Management: Visually significant congenital cataract must be operated early (within 6–8 weeks of birth for unilateral/bilateral total cataract) to prevent irreversible stimulus-deprivation amblyopia. Intraocular Lens (IOL) implantation is routinely performed in children  of age (under 2 yrs, aphakia is corrected with contact lenses/spectacles or secondary IOL, plus patching of the good eye in unilateral cases).

Vitamin A Deficiency (Xerophthalmia) & Keratomalacia Treatment (Page 731):

WHO Classification: XN (Night blindness), X1A (Conjunctival xerosis), X1B (Bitot’s spots), X2 (Corneal xerosis), X3A (Corneal ulceration/keratomalacia  corneal surface), X3B (Keratomalacia  corneal surface), XS (Corneal scar), XF (Xerophthalmic fundus).

Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP — Page 736):

Vasoproliferative retinal disorder of preterm infants caused by hyperoxia-induced arrest of normal retinal vascularization (Phase 1) followed by hypoxia-driven VEGF-mediated retinal neovascularization (Phase 2).

Indian Screening Guidelines (RBSK / NNF): Screen all preterm neonates born at  gestation OR birth weight  (or  with risk factors like  therapy, sepsis, RDS, blood transfusions). First screening is done at 4 weeks postnatal age (or at 2–3 weeks postnatal age in extreme preterms  or  — “30-day / 4-week rule”).

Treatment of Threshold / Type 1 Pre-threshold ROP: Laser Photocoagulation of the avascular peripheral retina or Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Bevacizumab / Ranibizumab) injection.

title: 27.1 GENODERMATOSES & NEUROCUTANEOUS SYNDROMES (Pages 741–747)
text:
1. Ichthyoses & Collodion Baby (Table 27.2)

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-023]]

Collodion Baby: Newborn encased in a taut, shiny, parchment/cellophane-like membrane causing ectropion, eclabium, and sausage digits. Complications: Hypothermia, hypernatremic dehydration, skin sepsis, pneumonia. Management: High-humidity incubator, IV fluids/electrolytes, frequent bland emollients (white soft petrolatum), artificial tears (avoid keratolytics like salicylic acid or urea in neonates due to percutaneous toxicity!).

2. Epidermolysis Bullosa (EB — Mechanobullous Disorders, Table 27.3)

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-024]]

3. Neurocutaneous Syndromes (NF1 & Tuberous Sclerosis Complex) (Pages 746–747)

Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (von Recklinghausen Disease — AD, NF1 gene on Chr 17q11.2, 100% penetrance): NIH Diagnostic Criteria (Requires  of the following 7 Criteria):

 Café-au-lait macules ( in prepubertal children;  in postpubertal individuals).

 Neurofibromas of any type OR  Plexiform neurofibroma.

Axillary or Inguinal freckling (Crowe’s sign).

Optic pathway glioma.

 Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas on slit-lamp exam).

Distinctive osseous lesion: Sphenoid wing dysplasia OR congenital tibial pseudarthrosis/dysplasia.

First-degree relative with NF1.

Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC — AD, TSC1 [Hamartin, Chr 9] & TSC2 [Tuberin, Chr 16] — Table 27.4):

Major Features (11): (1) Hypomelanotic macules (,  — ‘Ash-leaf macules’, best visualized under Wood’s lamp, earliest cutaneous sign at birth); (2) Facial angiofibromas ( — ‘adenoma sebaceum’) or fibrous cephalic (forehead) plaque; (3) Ungual/periungual fibromas ( — Koenen tumors); (4) Shagreen patch (leathery connective tissue nevus on lumbosacral back); (5) Multiple retinal nodular hamartomas; (6) Cortical dysplasias / Tubers; (7) Subependymal nodules (SEN); (8) Subependymal Giant Cell Astrocytoma (SEGA); (9) Cardiac Rhabdomyoma (earliest prenatal/neonatal lesion; regresses spontaneously); (10) Renal Angiomyolipomas (); (11) Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM).

Minor Features (6): ‘Confetti’ hypopigmented skin lesions, dental enamel pits (), intraoral gingival fibromas, retinal achromic patch, multiple renal cysts, non-renal hamartomas.

Diagnosis: Definite TSC = 2 Major OR 1 Major + 2 Minor; Possible TSC = 1 Major OR  Minor.

Treatment: Vigabatrin is the drug of choice for infantile spasms (West syndrome) in TSC; mTOR inhibitors (Everolimus / Sirolimus [Rapamycin]) shrink SEGA, renal angiomyolipomas, and facial angiofibromas.
