title: 27.2 VASCULAR BIRTHMARKS, DERMATITIS, PAPULOSQUAMOUS, BULLOUS & INFECTIOUS DERMATOSES (Pages 748–771)
text:
Infantile Hemangioma vs. Port-Wine Stain (Capillary Malformation — Table 27.7):

Infantile Hemangioma (Vascular Tumor): Appears at 1–4 weeks of life, undergoes a rapid proliferative phase for 6–9 months (bright red strawberry plaque), followed by spontaneous involution ( by 5 yrs,  by 9 yrs). First-line medical therapy for complicated/periocular/airway hemangiomas: Oral Propranolol (). (Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma causes Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon: consumptive thrombocytopenia and DIC).

Port-Wine Stain (Capillary Malformation): Present at birth, grows proportionately, persists lifelong without regression. When involving the ophthalmic () division of the trigeminal nerve, it is associated with Sturge-Weber Syndrome (ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis, ‘tram-track’ cortical calcifications, focal contralateral seizures, and ipsilateral congenital glaucoma). Treated with Pulsed-Dye Laser.

Hanifin & Rajka Criteria for Atopic Dermatitis (Table 27.8): Requires  Major Criteria (1. Pruritus; 2. Typical morphology & distribution [facial/extensor in infants, flexural lichenification in children]; 3. Chronic or chronically relapsing course; 4. Personal or family history of atopy) PLUS  Minor Criteria (xerosis, ichthyosis/palmar hyperlinearity, Dennie-Morgan infraorbital fold, pityriasis alba, keratosis pilaris, white dermographism, elevated IgE, anterior subcapsular cataract, keratoconus).

Papulosquamous & Bullous Dermatoses:

Psoriasis: Silvery scales with positive Grattage test, glistening Berkeley membrane, Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on removing scale), and Koebner phenomenon. Guttate psoriasis (‘rain-drop’ papules on trunk) in children is triggered by streptococcal pharyngitis.

Lichen Planus: 5 Ps — Pruritic, Polygonal, Purple (violaceous), Plane (flat-topped) Papules with lacy white Wickham striae and Koebner phenomenon.

Pityriasis Rosea: Triggered by HHV-6 / HHV-7; starts with a single oval scaly ‘Herald patch’ with a peripheral collarette of scale, followed 1–2 weeks later by generalized crops along skin cleavage lines in a ‘Christmas-tree’ pattern on the back; self-limiting in 6–8 weeks.

Chronic Bullous Disease of Childhood (CBDC / Linear IgA Dermatosis): Most common autoimmune blistering disease in children (); tense bullae arranged in annular clusters (‘Cluster of jewels’ or ‘String of pearls’ sign) around the perioral and perigenital/lower abdominal region; linear IgA deposits at dermoepidermal junction. Drug of choice: Oral Dapsone ().

Cutaneous Infections & Leprosy (Tables 27.18–27.22):

Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS / Ritter Disease): Caused by S. aureus phage group II epidermolytic exfoliative toxins A & B (cleave Desmoglein-1 in granular layer) from a distant focus (conjunctivitis/otitis/nasopharynx). Presents in neonates/infants with fever, diffuse tender scarlatiniform erythema, periorificial crusting, positive Nikolsky sign, and tissue-paper-like desquamation; oral/ocular mucosae are SPARED (unlike Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis [TEN] where mucosae are severely eroded and cleavage is full-thickness subepidermal!). Treated with IV Cloxacillin/Vancomycin + fluids.

Cutaneous Tuberculosis (Table 27.19): Scrofuloderma (most common in children — contiguous breakdown of skin over a tuberculous cervical lymph node forming undermined sinuses); Lupus vulgaris (annular plaque with central scarring and ‘apple-jelly’ nodules on diascopy); TB verrucosa cutis (warty inoculation plaque); Tuberculids (hypersensitivity: Lichen scrofulosorum, Erythema nodosum). Treated with standard 6-month ATT (2HRZE + 4HRE).

WHO Multidrug Therapy (MDT) for Childhood Leprosy (10–15 Years — Table 27.21):

Paucibacillary ( skin lesions, slit-skin smear negative) — Duration: 6 months (within 9 mo): Monthly supervised Rifampicin  + Clofazimine  (note: 3-drug uniform regimen / or 2-drug Rifampicin  + daily Dapsone  + Clofazimine  alternate day). (For : Rifampicin  monthly, Dapsone  daily, Clofazimine  daily &  monthly).

Multibacillary ( skin lesions) — Duration: 12 months (within 18 mo): Monthly supervised Rifampicin  + Clofazimine , plus daily unsupervised Dapsone  + Clofazimine  on alternate days (or  daily).

Tinea Capitis: Non-inflammatory (‘black-dot’ / grey patch), Kerion (painful boggy inflammatory scalp swelling with pustules and occipital lymphadenopathy due to zoophilic dermatophytes), and Favus (T. schoenleinii — cup-shaped yellow crusts called scutula). Treatment of choice: Oral Griseofulvin ( for 6–8 weeks) (or oral Terbinafine for Trichophyton) +  Ketoconazole shampoo.

(For General Poisoning Principles, Kerosene, Organophosphates, Paracetamol, Lead, Snakebite, and Scorpion Sting, see Chapter 28 in Part 1).

text:
1. Systemic Response to Blood Loss & Pediatric Trauma Score (Tables 28.1 & 28.2)

Hemorrhagic Shock Classes in Children (Table 28.1): Because of strong vascular tone, hypotension does NOT occur until  of blood volume is lost (Mild : tachycardia, cool mottled skin, normal BP; Moderate : weak central/absent peripheral pulses, narrow pulse pressure, lethargy, oliguria; Severe : hypotension, bradycardia, coma, anuria).

Pediatric Trauma Score (PTS — Table 28.2): Evaluates 6 parameters scored as  (Total score ranges from ;  requires triage to a Pediatric Trauma Center;  predicts significant mortality):

[[TABLE:pediatrics-tbl-025]]

2. Pediatric Burns: Estimation & Fluid Resuscitation (Fig. 28.1, Table 28.3 & Fig. 28.2)

Estimating Burn Surface Area (%TBSA): Adult ‘Rule of Nines’ is inaccurate in children because infants have a much larger head surface area ( at birth vs.  in adults) and smaller lower limbs. Use the Lund and Browder Chart (Table 28.3) or the Child’s Palm Rule (child’s palm including fingers = ).

Hospitalization Criteria: Any 3rd-degree burn; 2nd-degree burn ; burns involving face, hands, feet, perineum, or major joints; inhalational, electrical, or chemical burns; or suspected child abuse.

Fluid Resuscitation in Burns ( — Fig. 28.2):

Parkland Formula (Replacement Fluid for Burn Losses in first 24 hours):

Give one-half () over the first 8 hours (calculated from the time of burn injury, not time of arrival!), and the remaining half () over the next 16 hours.

PLUS Maintenance Fluid: In children , add daily Holiday-Segar maintenance fluid containing  Dextrose in  Saline concurrently. Titrate fluid rate to maintain urine output .

Caloric Requirement in Burns:

Infants: .

Children:  (with  protein).

Inhalational Poisonings in Fire: (1) Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning: Administer  Oxygen via non-rebreathing mask/ET tube (shortens elimination  of carboxyhemoglobin from 4 hours to 40 minutes); (2) Cyanide Poisoning (burning plastics): Antidote of choice is IV Hydroxocobalamin () (binds cyanide to form non-toxic cyanocobalamin excreted in urine).

3. Corrosive Ingestion & Methemoglobinemia (Pages 781–784)

Corrosive Ingestion (Acids vs. Alkalis — Fig. 28.4):

Alkalis (bleach, drain cleaners, button batteries, caustic soda) cause deep liquefaction necrosis and esophageal perforation/strictures; Acids (toilet cleaners, battery acid) cause coagulation necrosis (eschar limits deep penetration, though gastric antral/pyloric injury is common).

Management: Emesis, gastric lavage, nasogastric tube insertion, activated charcoal, and neutralizing agents are STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED. Secure airway early if stridor/hoarseness; keep NPO; perform Upper GI Endoscopy between 12 and 24 hours (avoid between 5–15 days when wall is weakest) to grade injury (Zargar Classification: Grade 0–2a  oral feeds; Grade 2b–3a  endoscopic NG tube feeds; Grade 3b circumferential necrosis  TPN/gastrostomy). Esophageal strictures are treated with serial bougie/balloon dilatation after 3–6 weeks.

Methemoglobinemia (Page 783):

Oxidation of heme iron from ferrous (Fe²⁺) to ferric (Fe³⁺) state by oxidizing drugs/toxins (Dapsone, Nitrites/Nitrates, Local anesthetics [Benzocaine/Prilocaine], Sulfonamides, Metoclopramide, Naphthalene balls, Aniline dyes).

Clinical & Lab Hallmarks: Central slate-grey cyanosis unresponsive to , ‘Saturation Gap’ (Pulse oximeter  plateaus around  despite a high/normal  on ABG!), and chocolate-brown blood that fails to turn bright red on exposure to room air (Filter paper test). Confirmed by Co-oximetry.

Specific Antidote:  Methylene Blue  () IV over 5–10 minutes (indicated if  with symptoms or  if asymptomatic). (Contraindication: G6PD Deficiency — methylene blue requires NADPH from the HMP shunt to work and will precipitate severe hemolysis in G6PD deficiency; use High-dose Ascorbic Acid or Exchange Transfusion instead!).

4. High-Yield Toxicology Clues & Antidote Table (Tables 28.6 & 28.7)

Radiopaque Substances on Abdominal X-Ray (Mnemonic — CHIPES, Table 28.6): Chloral hydrate / Calcium carbonate, Heavy metals (Lead, Mercury, Arsenic), Iron, Phenothiazines / Potassium chloride, Enteric-coated tablets, Salicylates / Sodium.

Master Antidote Pairing (Table 28.7):

Paracetamol  N-Acetylcysteine | Organophosphates  Atropine + Pralidoxime

Opioids  Naloxone ( IV) | Benzodiazepines  Flumazenil (, max )

Iron  Deferoxamine (Desferrioxamine) ( IV) | Isoniazid (INH)  Pyridoxine (, gram-for-gram)

Beta-Blockers  IV Glucagon ( bolus, then ) | Calcium Channel Blockers  IV Calcium + High-Dose Insulin-Euglycemia Therapy ( bolus +  infusion)

Tricyclic Antidepressants (Wide QRS)  IV Sodium Bicarbonate () | Digoxin  Digoxin-specific Fab fragments (Digibind)

Methanol / Ethylene Glycol  Fomepizole (or Ethanol) + Hemodialysis | Warfarin  Vitamin K1 + FFP | Heparin  Protamine Sulfate ( per  heparin).

Sequence: C – A – B (Compressions  Airway  Breathing). Check responsiveness, breathing (no breathing or only gasping), and central pulse (brachial in infants, carotid/femoral in children) simultaneously within .

2. Pediatric Cardiac Arrest Algorithm & Reversible Causes (Fig. 29.4 & Table 29.6)

Non-Shockable Rhythm (Asystole or Pulseless Electrical Activity [PEA] — Most common in children):

Immediately resume CPR + give IV/IO Epinephrine  ( of  solution) as soon as possible (within 5 minutes) and repeat every 3–5 minutes + identify and treat reversible 6 Hs & 5 Ts.

Reversible Causes of Arrest (6 Hs and 5 Ts):

6 Hs: Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion (Acidosis), Hypoglycemia, Hypo-/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia.

title: 29.2 SEPTIC SHOCK, SEDATION, HAI BUNDLES & BLOOD TRANSFUSION (Pages 794–802)
text:
1. Septic Shock Management Algorithm (Surviving Sepsis / Fig. 29.5 & Tables 29.9–29.11)

First Hour Bundle: Administer oxygen  secure IV/IO access  draw blood culture, glucose, lactate  administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour  give isotonic crystalloid boluses ( over 15–20 min, up to  in the 1st hour) while monitoring for signs of fluid overload (hepatomegaly, basal rales).

Fluid-Refractory Septic Shock (Vasoactive Drug Selection):

Cold Shock (Prolonged CRT , cold mottled extremities, weak pulses): Start IV Epinephrine infusion () as first-line inotrope.

Warm Shock (Flash CRT , bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, low DBP): Start IV Norepinephrine infusion () as first-line vasopressor.

Catecholamine-Resistant Shock: Administer Stress-dose IV Hydrocortisone ( or  bolus) + consider Milrinone (, if normotensive cold shock with high SVR) or Vasopressin / ECMO.

2. Sedation/Analgesia Scenarios & HAI Prevention Bundles (Tables 29.12–29.14)

Procedural Sedation Choices (Table 29.13):

Non-painful imaging (CT, MRI, Echo, EEG, BERA): Oral Triclofos () or Chloral hydrate () or IV Midazolam.

Painful invasive procedures (Bone marrow aspiration/biopsy, Lumbar puncture, Central line, ICD tube, Endoscopy): IV Midazolam () + IV Fentanyl () OR IV Ketamine ( IV or  IM) (dissociative anesthesia that preserves airway reflexes and increases BP/HR).

Healthcare-Associated Infection (HAI — onset  after admission up to  after discharge — Table 29.14):

VAP (Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia) Prevention Bundle: Elevate head of bed ; use cuffed endotracheal tubes with subglottic suctioning; avoid routine H2-blockers/PPIs (preserves gastric acid barrier); use sterile water in humidifiers; do not change ventilator circuits routinely unless visibly soiled; daily sedation vacation & readiness-to-extubate assessment.

CLABSI (Central Line) & CAUTI (Urinary Catheter) Bundles: Hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions with  chlorhexidine skin prep, transparent dressings, closed urinary drainage system, and prompt daily review for early removal of lines/catheters.

3. Blood Component Therapy & Transfusion Reactions (Tables 29.15–29.20)

Packed Red Blood Cell (PRBC) Transfusion Indications & Dose (Table 29.15):

 irrespective of clinical status;  with hypoxia, acidosis, dyspnea, or heart failure;  in stable PICU patients / ARDS;  in unstable septic shock / severe hypoxemia.

Dose:  of PRBCs (raises Hb by ~; infuse within 4 hours of leaving blood bank; if severe chronic anemia with , transfuse  slowly to prevent CCF).

Platelet Transfusion Thresholds (Table 29.17):

 prior to major surgery or invasive procedures (LP, liver biopsy). Dose:  (or ), infused within 20–30 minutes.

Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP — Table 29.18) vs. Cryoprecipitate:

FFP (): Contains ALL coagulation factors. Indicated for active bleeding in DIC, acute liver failure, Vitamin K deficiency/warfarin reversal, or single factor deficiency when specific concentrate is unavailable.

Cryoprecipitate (): Precipitate formed when FFP is thawed at . Rich in Factor VIII (), Fibrinogen (), von Willebrand Factor (vWF), and Factor XIII (Does NOT contain Factor IX!). Indicated in hypofibrinogenemia ( in DIC), Hemophilia A, vWD, and Factor XIII deficiency.

ABO Compatibility Rules (Table 29.16):

For Packed RBCs: O-negative is the universal RBC donor; AB is universal RBC recipient.

For FFP & Platelets: AB plasma is the universal plasma donor (contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies); O is universal plasma recipient.

title: 31.1 UN CONVENTION ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD (UN CRC), LEGISLATIONS & PROGRAMS (Pages 814–815)
text:
1. UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UN CRC, 1989 — Box 31.1)

Ratified by India in 1992; defines a child as every human being below 18 years of age and guarantees four core pillars of rights: Right to Survival, Right to Development, Right to Protection, and Right to Participation.

Key Articles of the UN CRC Applicable to Child Health (Box 31.1 — Textbook Box):

Article 2: Protection from discrimination of any kind.

Article 3: Best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration in all actions.

Article 5 & 18: Parental guidance and state assistance to parents in child-rearing.

Article 6: Inherent right to life, survival, and development.

Article 9: Right not to be separated from parents against their will.

Article 12, 14, 16, 17: Right of the child to express views freely (Article 12), freedom of expression (14), protection of privacy (16), and access to appropriate media information (17).

Article 19: Protection from all forms of physical or mental violence, injury, abuse, neglect, or maltreatment.

Article 20 & 22: Special protection for children deprived of family environment (20) and refugee children (22).

Article 23: Rights of mentally or physically disabled children to special care and dignity.

Article 24: Right to the highest attainable standard of health and access to healthcare services.

Article 27, 28, 30, 31: Right to adequate standard of living (27), Right to education (28), right to own culture/religion (30), and right to rest, leisure, and play (31).

Article 34: Protection from all forms of sexual exploitation and sexual abuse.

2. Indian Policies, Legislations & National Programs for Children

National Policies & Bodies: National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR, 2005); National Policy for Children (2013); National Plan of Action for Children (2016); National Policy for Persons with Disabilities (2006).

Landmark Child Legislations in India:

Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 (gender-neutral law protecting all children ).

Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (addresses children in conflict with law and children in need of care and protection; allows juveniles aged 16–18 years involved in heinous offences to be tried as adults after assessment by Juvenile Justice Board).

Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 (fundamental right for ages 6–14 years under Article 21A).

Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (amended 2006, 2008, 2016 — bans employment of children  and adolescents  in hazardous occupations).

Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006.

Key National Social & Protection Programs: ICDS (Integrated Child Development Services), Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS), CHILDLINE 1098 ( toll-free emergency phone outreach service for children in distress), Shishu Griha (in-country adoption homes), Ujjawala (prevention of trafficking, rescue, and rehabilitation of victims of commercial sexual exploitation), Kishori Shakti Yojana, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Mid-Day Meal (PM-POSHAN), and NHM / RBSK / IMNCI.

subject: pediatrics
title: 31.2 CHILD MALTREATMENT (ABUSE & NEGLECT), ADOPTION & FOSTER CARE (Pages 815–819)
text:
1. Types of Child Maltreatment (Table 31.1) & MoWCD Indian Data

Five Categories (Table 31.1): (1) Physical abuse (acts of commission causing actual/potential physical harm, including corporal punishment); (2) Sexual abuse (using a child for sexual gratification); (3) Emotional abuse (rejection, humiliation, terrorizing, isolation); (4) Child neglect (deprivation of health, education, nutrition, or shelter despite availability of resources — distinct from poverty; includes medical neglect like vaccine refusal and gender neglect of the girl child); (5) Child exploitation (child labor, trafficking).

Extent in India (MoWCD Study):  of children face physical abuse,  face some form of sexual abuse, and  face emotional abuse; children with disabilities are  more vulnerable.

2. Clinical Assessment & Management of Physical Abuse (Fig. 31.1)

Red Flags in History & Exam: Unexplained injury, denial of trauma, injury inconsistent with child’s developmental stage (e.g., femur fracture in a non-ambulatory infant), delay in seeking medical care, bruises on padded/protected sites (buttocks, torso, ears, neck, patterned belt/hand marks), multiple fractures in different stages of healing, posterior rib fractures, metaphyseal corner (‘bucket-handle’) fractures, or glove-and-stocking immersion scalds.

Abusive Head Trauma (Shaken Baby Syndrome): Violent shaking of an infant causing tearing of bridging veins  Classic Triad: Subdural hematoma + Bilateral multilayered Retinal hemorrhages + Diffuse encephalopathy/cerebral edema (often with no external scalp injury!).

Clinical Response Algorithm (Fig. 31.1): Medically stabilize  document history verbatim & map injuries on body diagrams  Skeletal survey X-rays (mandatory in ), CT/MRI brain, coagulation profile (to rule out bleeding disorders), and indirect ophthalmoscopy  Hospitalize if unsafe, register Medico-Legal Case (MLC), inform police / Childline 1098 / Child Welfare Committee (CWC), and arrange psychological counseling.

3. Child Sexual Abuse & The POCSO Act, 2012 (Fig. 31.2)

Definitions under POCSO Act, 2012:

Section 3: Penetrative sexual assault (Aggravated penetrative assault in Section 5 if committed by police, public servant, relative, doctor, or on a child  / disabled child).

Section 7: Non-penetrative sexual assault.

Section 11: Sexual harassment.

Section 13: Use of a child for pornographic purposes (Child Sexual Abuse Material - CSAM).

Mandatory Legal Obligations of Doctors under POCSO Act (Fig. 31.2):

Mandatory Reporting (Section 19 & 21): Every doctor/healthcare professional MUST report suspected or disclosed sexual abuse to the Special Juvenile Police Unit (SJPU), local police, or Childline 1098. Failure to report is a punishable offence (up to 6 months imprisonment and/or fine).

Free Immediate Medical Treatment (Section 27): All government AND private hospitals are legally bound to provide free first-aid and medical care without demanding police requisition or legal records first.

Child-Friendly Examination: Performed in the presence of a parent/trusted person (and by a female doctor if the victim is a girl) after informed consent; never force examination.

Comprehensive Medical Care: Treat injuries, collect forensic evidence (if presenting within  using the SAFE kit), provide Emergency Contraception (within 72 hours in post-menarchal girls), Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV (within 72 hours for 28 days), STI prophylaxis (Ceftriaxone, Azithromycin, Metronidazole), Hepatitis B & Tetanus vaccination, and trauma-focused psychological counseling.

4. Adoption & Foster Care in India (Pages 818–819)

Legal Framework for Adoption: Governed by the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act (allows citizens of all religions as well as single parents to adopt legally, conferring full biological child status) and regulated by CARA (Central Adoption Resource Authority) under the Ministry of Women and Child Development.

Adoption Procedure:

Only government-recognized Specialized Adoption Agencies (SAAs) can place children; direct private adoptions from maternity homes/hospitals are illegal.

An abandoned or surrendered child must be produced before the Child Welfare Committee (CWC), which has the sole authority to declare the child “legally free for adoption” (biological parents who surrender a child are given a 2-month reconsideration period before the child becomes legally free).

Role of Pediatrician: Screen the child prior to placement (complete physical/developmental exam, HIV, Hepatitis B [HBsAg], Hepatitis C, VDRL, vision and hearing screen; repeat window-period tests at 3 and 6 months), counsel prospective parents realistically, and discourage illegal private adoptions.

Foster Care (Model Guidelines, 2016): Temporary, non-institutional family-based care arrangement ordered by the CWC for children whose biological parents are incapacitated/imprisoned/ill, until the child can be reunited with biological parents or permanently adopted.

(For IMNCI Overview, Strategy, Color-Coding, and Diarrhea Management [Plans A, B, C], see Chapter 32 in Part 1).

title: 32.1 SALIENT 2022 IMNCI UPDATES & YOUNG INFANT (0 TO 2 MONTHS) CHARTS (Pages 820–840)
text:
1. Key Updates in the 2022 Indian IMNCI Adaptation (Pages 820–821)

Young Infants (): Streamlined signs of Possible Serious Bacterial Infection (PSBI) to 7 core signs; mandatory breastfeeding assessment; simplified diarrhea classifications; updated pre-referral management where referral is not possible (Oral Amoxicillin + IM Gentamicin for 7 days).

Children ():

Added “Convulsing now” to General Danger Signs and classified presence of any danger sign as Very Severe Disease (Pink).

Revised Pneumonia Classification (WHO 2014): Chest indrawing is now classified under YELLOW (Pneumonia) and treated on an outpatient basis with Oral Amoxicillin for 5 days! Added Pulse Oximetry ( = Pink Severe Pneumonia) and a trial of rapid-acting inhaled bronchodilator (Salbutamol 3 times, 15–20 min apart) before classifying children with wheeze + fast breathing/chest indrawing.

Revised Fever Algorithm: Added RDT for Malaria, ACT regimens, and Dengue Classification (Severe Dengue / Warning signs vs. Dengue Fever).

Revised Malnutrition Criteria: Based on Weight-for-Length (WFL) Z-scores, MUAC ( = SAM;  = MAM), and bipedal edema; separated into Complicated SAM (Pink) and Uncomplicated SAM (Yellow).

Added Care for Child Development (ECD): Mandatory assessment and counseling on Play and Communication activities alongside feeding counseling, plus updated NIS immunization, biweekly IFA, and deworming schedules.

3. IMNCI Feeding & Care for Child Development Recommendations by Age (Pages 856–861)

Age-Specific Feeding & Early Child Development (Play & Communication) Matrix:

Birth to 6 Months: Exclusive breastfeeding day and night (; wake LBW baby every 3h); no water or other fluids. Play & Communicate: Skin-to-skin contact, look into baby’s eyes and talk/smile while breastfeeding, provide colorful moving objects (rattle, ring on string) to reach for, copy baby’s sounds/gestures.

6 to 9 Months: Continue breastfeeding + start  gradually increasing to  () of thick mashed roti/rice/bread in undiluted milk, or khichri/dal/dalia/halwa with added ghee/oil and mashed vegetables/fruits, . Play & Communicate: Give clean household items (containers, metal pot and spoon) to handle, bang, and drop; respond to sounds and call child’s name.

9 to 12 Months: Continue breastfeeding + give  servings of thick energy-dense family foods  if breastfed ( if not breastfed). Play & Communicate: Hide favorite toy under a cloth (play peek-a-boo), tell names of things, teach hand gestures (“bye-bye”).

12 Months to 2 Years: Continue breastfeeding + offer food from family pot:  servings  (sit with child and help finish serving). Play & Communicate: Give things to stack up and put into/take out of containers, ask simple questions, talk about nature/pictures.

2 Years and Older: Give variety of family foods at . Play & Communicate: Help child count, name, and compare objects of different colors/shapes, chalk board, puzzles, tell stories/songs.

Master IMNCI Follow-Up Schedule (Table 32.1 — High-Yield Summary):

Return in 2 Days: Pneumonia, Dysentery, Malaria, Dengue fever, Fever (malaria unlikely, if fever persists), Measles with eye/mouth complications, Feeding problem (or Young infant with PSBI/Local infection/Jaundice/Diarrhea/Thrush).

Return in 5 Days: Acute diarrhea (if not improving), Persistent diarrhea, Acute or Chronic ear infection, Cough/cold (if not improving).

Return in 7 Days: Uncomplicated Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM).

Return in 14 Days: Anemia (and Young infant with Low weight for age).

Return in 30 Days: Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM).

title: 33.1 SIX PRINCIPLES OF RATIONAL DRUG THERAPY & MASTER FORMULARY (Pages 867–885)
text:
Six Principles of Rational Drug Prescribing (Page 867):

Genuine clinical indication for using the medication.

Use the minimum number of appropriate, familiar, and inexpensive drugs of good quality (avoid irrational fixed-dose combinations; true synergism is rare, e.g., Cotrimoxazole).

Always prescribe drugs by their generic (non-proprietary) name.

Optimum dosage, frequency, and duration to achieve desired benefit.

Prefer the oral (PO) or inhaled route over parenteral administration whenever feasible.

Anticipate, monitor, and manage adverse drug reactions (ADRs).
